SPECIAL NOTICE TO MEMBERS.

Every precaution is taken by us to ensure accuracy in these Reports, our correspondents being men on whom we can rely; should, however, any errors creep into them, upon the same being pointed out to us, we shall be most happy to give the same prominence to the correction as to the original matter. As these Reports are exclusively for the use of Members, the information contained therein must not be divulged.

NATIONAL UNION OF
Boot and Shoe Operatives.

MONTHLY REPORT.

Nearest Post Office:
34, GUILFORD STREET,
Lamb's Conduit Street, London, W.C. 1.
LONDON, W.C. 1,
Nearest Telegraph Office:
26TH JANUARY, 1920.
Red Lion Street, London, W.C. 1.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
THE STATE OF TRADE
continues good in all parts of the Kingdom, the figures recorded in the Gazette being as follows :-
At Leicester and the surrounding district employment showed little change compared with the previous month; some short time was reported owing to shortage of machinists and scarcity of material. At Northampton there was a slight decline compared with a month ago. At Norwich some overtime was reported among the women workers, but some short time was worked by the male operatives owing to the shortage of women in the closing department. At Leeds employment continued fairly good; at Stafford it was good. In Scotland generally there was little change as compared with November, and employment on the whole was good.

DISPUTES.

Disputes are still practically non-existent, and at Evam a number of the female operatives have been secured employment in the factory started by the operatives. The other members are remaining loyal.

ADVANCES.

During the month Mr. W. R. Smith, M.P., J.P., has given his Award for the County of Leicestershire so far as clickers are concerned, the following being a copy thereof:
December 22nd, 1919.
Having been appointed Umpire to determine the extent and method of adjustment of the Statement of Prices for Clickers in the County of Leicestershire, and having heard the evidence submitted by both sides, and after careful consideration of the respective claims, and with due regard to Clauses one, twelve and twenty-one of the Terms of Settlement, dated February 13th, 1919, I hereby determine that the increase upon the said Clickers' Statement shall be 85 per cent.

Belle Vue,
(Signed), WALTER R. SMITH,
Old Catton, Norwich.
Umpire.
22nd December, 1919.

MR. FRANK SHEPPARD'S AWARD.
Wigston and District Board of Arbitration for the Boot Trade.
Differences having arisen between the Manufacturers and their employees repre
sented on the Boot Trade Arbitration Board of Wigston and District in the County of
Leicestershire, and they having failed to agree, I was appointed by the Ministry of
Labour under the Industrial Courts Acts 1919, to act as Umpire to decide between
the parties concerned.
The terms of reference in the case were:
"Claim by the Workmen for the adoption of the Leicester Statements
and prices to apply on all firms in Wigston and Wigston Magna."
The hearing was fixed for January 6th, 1920, at 2.30 p.m., place of meeting,
Town Hall, City of Leicester. I therefore attended the meeting on that date, have
heard the evidence submitted to me from each side respectively, and hereby decide that
the Leicester Statements of Prices shall apply to all firms in Wigston and Wigston
Magna.
Dated, January roth, 1920.
(Signed), FRANK SHEPPARD,
ADDENDUM TO AWARD.
35, PARK STREET, BRISTOL.
The main objection urged by the Manufacturers was that prices were arranged
and agreed to in Leicester and, they "the Wigston Manufacturers never had a voice
in fixing these prices," but as soon as these prices were fixed they were imposed upon
them. I would therefore suggest that in future representations should be permitted
from Wigston and District to sit on the Leicester Board: so that the District covered
by same wages and conditions should have an equal opportunity of their point of
view being stated and discussed when any alteration is being made.
(Signed) F. SHEPPARD.
The London Board of Arbitration have completed their Clicking
Statement, the same now being in operation.
WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION ACTS.
During the month an extension of the Workmen's Compensation Acts
(War Addition) has come into operation, by which the compensation is increased
up to a maximum of 35s. per week, as and from the 1st January, 1920, and
according to the Act passed in August, 1917, it will remain in force for six
months after the "termination of the war." This point as to when the war
officially ends will undoubtedly have to be decided later. A copy of the new
Act appears on page 132.
In connection with Workmen's Compensation cases, we would once more
remind Secretaries that if it is necessary for any case to be dealt with by a
Solicitor, and payment desired from the Central Office, the consent of the
Central Office must be secured before remitting any cases to a Solicitor.
This is necessary from a financial standpoint, and also to let the General
Secretary have the full facts before legal obligations are entered into
BOOT REPAIRING BOARD.
The full Committee of the above Board has not met during the month.
A Sub-Committee has been dealing with various points which have to be finally
settled at a full meeting. Our representatives on such Board are:-Messrs.
T. F. Richards (General President), A. J. Dobbs and C. Bleakley (Council
Members), J. Buckle (Organiser), J. Osborne (Bristol No. 1 Secretary), and
W. J. Smith (Great Yarmouth Secretary).

NOMINATIONS FOR THE EDINBURGH CONFERENCE
must be taken at the February meeting nights. The Basis of Representation,
copy of which was sent to the branches more than a fortnight ago, will be
found on page 111. The suggested alterations and amendments to rules will
also be found on pps. 112-121. Owing to the position in which we find
ourselves, so far as contributions are concerned, due to the fact that the
Government is bringing in a new insurance Bill, we have not at present made
any proposals regarding any alterations either in contributions or benefits.
We propose dealing with the question as soon as possible when we know the
exact position regarding this Bill, which we feel sure the members will
recognise must make a great deal of difference to the above, especially
regarding unemployment benefit. It will also be noted that we suggest in
view of the large growth of membership of the Union, that the Council members
be increased to TWELVE. This however, really means only an extension of
two members because under new conditions which we suggest, the position of
Treasurer will be abolished, and unless therefore, an alteration was made it
would reduce the number of Council members to nine as stated in the existing
rules, with the Treasurer making ten in all. The grouping for the new
districts will appear in the February Report.
WOMEN DELEGATES.
Whilst it is not within the power of ourselves to allocate seats for women
delegates for the conference, we hope the branches will take into full con-
sideration the women membership of the Union and their claims for represen-
tation, it being important that the women members should be fully represented
so that their personal views on matters directly affecting women can be heard
at first hand from the women delegates so appointed.
ALDERMAN ALFRED HILL.
We feel sure our members will congratulate our colleague Mr. Hill, who
was appointed by a unanimous vote to the position of Alderman for the city
of Leicester. This appointment became vacant owing to the lamented death
of our late colleague, Alderman Thos. Smith, O.B.E., J.P. It seems to us very
appropriate that another boot operative should be chosen to fill the vacancy
which for so many years was so ably filled by our late comrade, and we wish
Alderman Hill good health and trust he may long be sparèd to enjoy his new
honour.

RETURNS!!!
Some Branches persistently send in their returns after the 15th, and this
month 19 Branches were late. We have several times appealed to Secretaries
to send along their returns in time, and unless it is done in future we shall
have no option but to fine the delinquents in accordance with rule.
Moreover, lateness in sending in the Monthly Returns
makes it increasingly difficult to get out the Report in
time for the Monthly Meetings.

mentary Committee of the Trade Union Congress and the Management Com-
mittee of the General Federation of Trade Unions, for funds to assist the
Austrian trade unionists in the deplorable state in which they find themselves.
owing to circumstances brought about by the war.

than by force. In this connection we would remind the members of the

"DAILY HERALD."
We propose asking for a vote of the Union at the March meeting when
voting for the delegates to conference takes place, for power to invest the sum
of ONE THOUSAND POUNDS in the Daily Herald as debenture shares. In view
of the generally agreed opinion that the times call for a paper to be run in the
interests of Labour, we feel sure we shall not appeal in vain to our members
to record their vote in favour, and allow us to invest the above-named sum
in the Herald.

INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS.
During the past few months letters have passed between ourselves and the
Secretary, H. Simon, of the German Boot Workers, as to meetings being resumed
and thereby trying to better understand the position of boot operatives gener-
ally. The German Union has also invited us to send a delegate to their Con-
ference in April of this year. After fully discussing the matter we have decided
to send Mr. J. Buckle, J.P., Union Organiser, to such Conference. We have
also decided to invite both the German and American Unions to send fraternal
delegates to our Conference at Whitsuntide. Regarding the International
Unions, this matter is to be further enquired into by Mr. Buckle when he goes
to the Conference named above. There may be some differences of opinion
about the above, we feel however that the balance of opinion is decidedly in
favour of resumption of meetings between the workers of the nations, and
thereby strive to so build up a position that will bring about such understand-
ings as to ensure that goodwill, equity and harmony will be so strong as to pre-
vent in the future any military operations one against the other.

ANNUAL RETURN PRESCRIBED BY THE REGISTRAR FOR A
REGISTERED TRADE UNION.
Having to send in a full return of Income and Expenditure for the Union
(Council and Branch combined) to the Registrar, in compliance with the different
Acts of Parliament covering Trade Unions, we shall be pleased if you will help
the Central Office by completely filling in the Form sent along, and send it
back to the General Secretary ON OR BEFORE FEBRUARY 1ST, 1920, certain.

TRADE UNION BUTTONS AND BROOCHES.
A fresh supply of buttons and brooches has recently been secured and can
be had upon application, price 6d. each, cash with order. Secretaries please
note when ordering buttons or brooches cash should ALWAYS be sent with
order.

GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
Your representatives on the Trade Board are as follows: -T. F. Richards, General
President, J. Buckle, Organiser, A. J. Dobbs and C. Bleakley, Council Members, and
J. Osborne, Bristol, Secretary.
The important feature of the month's work is the organised virulent opposition of
the boot repairing employers, whose premier officials have been stumping the country
to get up opposition to the Trade Board Statement of Prices with 334 per cent. added,
or in other words a ród. sole and heel, which comes out in actual cash to 1s. old. They
are afraid the men are going to earn a living, which has never, speaking generally, been
the case in the past. They have been successful in preventing a week's holiday with pay
being granted, and have also been successful in preventing a statement price for machinery
finishing being drawn up, and the Government official voted with them in their statements
in which they try to lead the public to believe they pay. They always quote hand finishing
prices which they never pay if they can help it, and then only in about 5 per cent. of their
output. As usual the Trade papers are opposed to the operatives, and try by influence
and innuendo to misrepresent the men's representatives, who do not look for or seek Press
patronage, but even they failed to prevent the 65s. minimum, and they would if they could
prevent the Sos. agreed to by the Committee for stitchers and the 75s. per week for Blake
sewers. These matters are very important because they have a bearing on the claims
we make upon our employers in the wholesale trade, who have not yet, in spite of the
suggestions of a minority of them, made proper provision for men who are at the beck
and call of certain firms. It is a strange corollary of human life that raw material, machi-
nery, finance has to be provided in abundance. The raw material may depreciate, the
machinery must be paid for whether it is running or not, even new machines may be
standing idle in case of breakdown, and money is never lent without a substantial charge
being made for interest alone, and yet the only commodity which is always available
without extra charge is human labour. The time is coming when Labour will have an
income first and foremost, regular and without stint; as an instance some firms pay more
holidays than the Holiday Scheme provides. We must see to it that our Unemployment
Scheme shall be for the whole trade, and not a portion of it, and we can do better for our
members than the Government can ever do with their present puny scheme. No Un-
employment scheme can be satisfactory unless such amounts are paid that will keep the
recipient from running into debt.
LEICESTER COUNTY BOARD.-The Umpire's Award has been received, and although
we asked for enough, Mr. W. R. Smith, M.P., Norwich, has given his award for Clicking,
and the difference has been lessened by 15 per cent than prevailed before, and the difference
now is from 6 per cent. to 16 per cent., or a dead II per cent. average.
We have had several meetings for Closing, Finishing and Lasting, but up to the present
the Sub-Committee's reports are not complete, but we have already agreed that the state-
ments, if not ready before, must become operative the last week in January.
WIGSTON is not included in the County Board. We refused to allow this as they are
only 3 miles from Leicester. The Board appealed to the Umpire, Alderman F. Sheppard,
and he gave Leicester statements as the controlling force for Wigston factories.
STAFFORD. As members of the Sub-Committee, with a Home Office official, we
visited Stafford on the 19th for the purpose of further studying ventilation and dust con-
ditions in boot and shoe factories. We find little to complain of with the modern, up-to-
date factories, but with the old firms much requires to be done. Our members would
be better if they would only insist on their share of ventilation, and although no one can
be expected to work in a draught, every man and every woman ought to agitate, agitate,
agitate, until the employers granted a scheme of ventilation without draughts. Further,
our women ought to have a back to the stools in the machine rooms, and a better or natural
shaped stool for those who sit all the time they are working. Comfort ought to be part
of the study of the firm, or ourselves, or both.
STONE. I had to visit Stone on this occasion owing to men being demobilised and the
firm getting disorganised. The loss in wages was more than the men were satisfied with,
and after an interview lasting six hours, we think we have made a settlement that will
be permanent. The firm had not fully realised that the 70s. was an adamant amount
not to be lessened only by permit, and we are convinced that the spirit and practice of
this company is very good indeed.
MELTON. I had a very good meeting of this Branch on the question of the work
of the County Board, and after fully explaining the work done the members expressed
themselves pleased with the prospects of an improved future. This brings me again to
the position of our Union, with its few Union Officers to do the desirable work needed.
Some of the branches, through illness and other causes, have, as yet, eleven months after
the National Agreement, no piecework statement, and a postponement of the 70s. we had
obtained.

DERBY.—It is with the deepest regret that we have to report the death
of our esteemed President, Mr. H. Murby, after a very painful and distressing
illness (consumption of lungs). It has seemed to rebound very heavy after
the loss of Mr. J. Baker, the secretary, who passed away just 12 months ago.
Mr. Murby just survived to see some efforts in Derby of his exertions, he having
worked in a quiet and reserved manner to make the Branch a success, and his
loss will be severely felt by those with whom he worked. We are pleased to
report that the membership of the Branch is still increasing, and at the present
there is only one firm in Derby who cannot claim any members of our Branch.
Another effort is being attempted to organise Melbourne where the wages are
disgraceful, and the workers seem afraid to help themselves. However, by
the help of the South Derbyshire Labour Party, we intend to once more try
our hand to get the employers to realise their workers are Englishmen. Some
of them have fought for these masters and bear wounds on their behalf, and yet
they (the masters) do not wish to recognise these comrades, but just go on
paying them the old starvation wage. In fact there are cases where they have
generously increased their wages by one shilling per week. Another firm
adopted the 48 hours scheme, but finding the hands could not earn the original
wage they graciously allowed them to work overtime to enable them to do it.
And they did it! We sometimes think the workers of Melbourne have got the
impression that if the masters have to pay more wages it will turn them bank-
rupt, and their livelihood would be gone, and yet one of the largest employers
of labour in Melbourne has accepted the Masters' Federation and Trade Board
terms. Why? Well, we suppose we must "wait and see." Trade in this
district appears fairly good.

EDINBURGH.—Our sickness during the month has been above the normal.
The repairing trade in this district has not been so quiet for a number of years
back. Members are being suspended from nearly every shop, which means
that our out-of-work benefits have increased during the month. In the last
Report we notice that the General President hinted at a scheme for the payment
of local officials. Now, in our opinion this would be all right for branches with
a large membership, but with small branches it would not be a great benefit.
In small branches the local official has to supply coal and gas in his own house,
and he can never call his home his own while acting as a branch official. But
at the same time we are pleased that the General President has taken this
matter up as this has been a sore point with secretaries of small branches for
some time back. We have got a start made with our Closing Room Quantities
Statement. Thanks to the lead given by Leicester No. 3. This will assist
branches all over the country to fix a fair value on the operations in the above
department. The following question has been asked several times since the
November Report was issued: “When did Council get the power to increase
a Political Agent's salary without consulting members of the Union?” Not
that the increase may be unnecessary under the circumstances, but the members
should have been consulted.

HALIFAX.—We have one member drawing out-of-work donation. The
members of our branch wish to draw attention to the fact that it is time we
had an organising secretary for the boot and shoe repairing if only to keep up
with the other Unions who practically only cater for that particular part of
the trade. Also we wish once again to bring it before the Council's notice,
the advisability of holding county conferences, whereby we think they would
be of great benefit to the Union, and it would be a means of bringing various
branches together, and we should be able to discuss many things which keep
cropping up in the various counties. Hoping the Council will bring this forward.

HIGHAM AND RUSHDEN.—During the month the Monthly Meeting
considered the question of Shops Committees. Rushden voted in favour,
38 for, none against. Irthlingborough voted in favour, 10 for, none against.

an amendment to Rule 165. There is a section of members who think that the
contributions should be on a higher scale, with increased benefits. Whilst
this may seem alright to the man or woman who makes no other provision,
to those who are in friendly societies, &c., there is no need. Therefore to seek
to compel all members to pay increased contributions will do more harm than
good. Let those pay who want to, by providing a new scale which allows this

[The question of "basement" factories is already under the consideration

GREAT YARMOUTH.-Trade is very good. Referring to our query
in last report of percentage to be allowed for slow workers, we believe it to be
the practice with the Shirt Makers' Trade Board to allow 7 per cent. for slow
workers. We take this to mean that some people working to a piece rate can
earn several shillings over the minimum, others on the same rate earn down
to 7 per cent. less than minimum without the employer being asked to make
up the difference. Without a proviso of this sort, and with other labour avail-
able there is the temptation for employers to dismiss slow workers rather
than make up the difference between wages earned and the Trade Board
minimum. The Council's action regarding the proposed increased minimum
was noted with approval. We hope they will be successful. The pity of it is
every increase is paid by the consumer. We cannot catch prices up on these
lines try how we may. What will be pleasing to the Council is that members
recognise the cause of high prices and are steadily following this line of thought
to its logical conclusion. We take this opportunity of thanking those who have
subscribed to the Moulders' Strike Fund. Members must not lose sight of
the fact that where Unions help each other it has far-reaching effects on em-
ployers' resistance or otherwise in meeting the Unions demands. Financial
help will prove to them quicker than any other method that it is not one Union
to be considered, but the whole movement. May we also add a word for the
need of supporting the Daily Herald. The true facts of things that matter
to us can only be learned from the Labour Press. Get the facts and reason
things out for yourselves. Journalists write to order, which are to mould
public opinion according to their instructions. You have seen in your master's
and the Government Press how to solve all Labour problems, it is produce,
produce, produce. The Government method of putting their programme into
operation is to be seen at Employment Exchanges, thousands of unemployed
waiting for the opportunity to produce. The fact is Tory and Liberal can
organise to produce war material, because they have not to study profit and
loss. (It is all loss). But they cannot organise for production of Peace
requirements. It is vested interest, profit and loss that counts with them,
and not the need of citizens.

CHANGES IN HOURS OF LABOUR.
Perhaps the most marked feature of the industrial situation in 1919 was the reduction
which was effected in weekly working hours in the principal industries. At the end of
1918 the hours usually worked in these industries ranged generally from 48 to 60 per week,
whereas by the end of 1919 the most usual range was from 44 to 48 per week. The number
of workpeople whose recognised hours of labour were reported as having been reduced,
during 1919, in the employments for which statistics of numbers affected by such changes
are available, was 6,400,000, the average reduction per head being about 6½ hours per
week. The Labour Gazette, January, 1920.

A TRIBUTE TO BRITISH TRADE.

Although our exports of footwear have steadily increased during the past few months,
the fact that boots and shoes are urgently needed in most of the world's markets, provides
an opportunity for British manufacturers such as they have never previously had in the
history of the trade. America is fully alive to the possibilities in this direction, but although
American goods obtained a footing in certain markets during the war, the merit of British
productions is still remembered, and the trade then lost may be recaptured provided it
is energetically sought. In this connection the provision of seventy million pairs of Army
boots by British producers is proving an exceedingly valuable asset to the trade during
the period of reconstruction. In no previous war were soldiers as well shod as have been
the troops of the Allies. And the fame of the British Army boot has resounded throughout
the world. Such an advertisement for British producers has a value which can hardly
be overestimated. Consequently we look for an enormous expansion in the exports of
British-made footwear during the coming year.-Extract from Leading Article in Shoe
and Leather Record, December 26th, 1919.

A MATTER OF IMPORTANCE TO LABOUR.

We note with satisfaction, not unmixed with surprise, that the City Editor of The
Times has now declared in favour of nationalising the Bank of England. Writing on
Tuesday upon the Coutts absorption, he mentioned with approval a scheme recently put
forward by Mr. J. F. Darling, formerly manager of the London Joint Stock Bank. Mr.
Darling, even before the war, sketched in outline the "conversion of the Bank of England
into a rea' ank of the British Empire." This it would automatically become if it belonged
to the nation. For ourselves, we do not see how nationalisation of the Bank of England
can be much longer delayed. The profits of the Bank are now so enormous that they have
had to be concealed by making a voluntary surrender of Excess Profit Duty at the rate
of 100 per cent. The other banks have cleverly succeeding in concealing their profits
without paying any Excess Profit Duty whatever.-Shoe and Leather Record, December
26th, 1919.

FAMINE IN AUSTRIA.
TRADE UNION APPEAL FOR IMMEDIATE ASSISTANCE.
Joint Action by the Parliamentary Committee of the Trades Union
Congress and the Management Committee of the General Federation
of Trade Unions.
The reports which have been current in the Press concerning the suffering and starva-
tion in German Austria have now been definitely authenticated by personal inquiries
conducted on behalf of the International Federation of Trade Unions. Hundreds of
thousands are suffering grievously from cold and hunger, while, to quote the words of
Edo Fimmen, the Secretary of the International Federation of Trade Unions, "thousands
must inevitably die," unless immediate help is forthcoming.
It has never been the practice of a Britisher to act maliciously towards a defeated foe.
Under the stress of actual fighting he has been noted for his care of enemy sick and wounded.
It is because we are assured of the continued existence of these human traits that we take
up the appeal which the International makes on behalf of those who are suffering in what
is, and what was, Austria. Anton Hueber, the old leader of the Austrian Trade Union
movement, stated at Amsterdam that his son had been killed in Poland and his daughter,
when her baby was born, had been so ill-nourished that she had no milk for the child.
There are hundreds of similar cases, and many thousands of little children who must
die or pass through the winter under conditions that will permanently injure them.
For us the war has ended. We desire, wherever possible, to mitigate the suffering
that follows war. We would rather also that these children should remember us with
gratitude than with hatred.
The Parliamentary Committee of the Trades Union Congress and the Management
Committee of the General Federation of Trade Unions, jointly represented as they are
in the International Federation of Trade Unions, jointly appeal for funds to enable them
to assist the Austrians to tide over the time between now and the next harvest.
This is an appeal from Labour to Labour, and we confidently look for immediate
and effective response, which will once again show that the movement is neither local,
nor national, but international.
All contributions should be addressed, in the first instance, to-
The Right Hon. C. W. BOWERMAN, P.C., M.P.,

The changes in rates of wages (including additional war wages or bonuses) reported
as having taken effect in 1919, in the trades for which statistics of the numbers of work-
people affected by such changes are compiled by the Department, resulted in an aggregate
increase of over £2,100,000 in the weekly wages of about 5,650,000 workpeople.

JOINT INDUSTRIAL (WHITLEY) COUNCIL.

The sixth meeting of the Joint Industrial (Whitley) Council met on the
27th January, 1920, at Montagu House, Whitehall, London, a report of the
proceedings appearing on pages 192-194.

We would call special attention to the following matters dealt with at the
said meeting.

agreed to:-

o: the trade that operatives and manufacturers should be well organised, and urges
that no obstacle be placed by the management of any factory in the way of any

GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
I am sorry to have to report that some employers appear to be desirous of evading
the spirit of the 1919 Agreement to the extent that they say they are not bound by the
spirit of Clause 12, which reads that the Statements must be so made or amended that
they will give the average man at least 25 per cent. above the Minimum Wage. The
letter and spirit of that sentence is without any equivocation; 70s. per week for the male
pieceworker without a permit, and 37s. od. per week for the woman over 20 years of age
who is a pieceworker, and this amount is so unpopular with our members that we are
asking for these sums to be reviewed, with the prospect of improving them owing to the
continued rise in the cost of the necessities of life, as man lives not by bread alone. Food
is not the whole of a man's troubles, be he brain or manual worker. Although many
employers are loyally carrying out our undertaking so are there those who are doing their
best to evade their undertaking. This involves the trade union official having to play the
detective, as I had to do in 1912 and found two prominent members of the other side who
had not kept their Agreement of 1909. Our present experience will cause us to tighten
the language used in future Agreements, until the time comes when such Agreements will
be enforced by Government Inspectors, and the tendency of the times is moving in that
direction. By the time these lines are in print we shall have had our meeting with the
employers, who, if rumour is correct, may advance the minimum for dayworkers, yet are
opposed to increase the remuneration for pieceworkers. If they insist upon this most
unreasonable attitude, then they will start a new policy of no piecework before we have
well got going the Payment by Result system. I do not think them so foolish. If State-
ments are delayed the employers alone are responsible for the delay. They claimed they
would be ready by April last, or ten months ago. Personally I denied they would do
anything of the kind, and doubted whether they would be complete last year. As a
matter of fact neither Northamptonshire nor Leicestershire have completed their tasks
and are not likely to for the next two months. Our future Agreements must have swifter
application.

January 22nd, 1920.-It was my painful duty to attend the funeral of my old comrade
and colleague, Ben Cooper, of the Cigarmakers' Union, on behalf of the General Federation
of Trade Unions, who for thirty-four years was the General Secretary of that body. Tom
Mann, Fred Maddison, and D. Carmichael, Secretary of the London Trades Council, of
which body Ben was treasurer, were also at the graveside.

On the 25th and 26th we held the usual Council Meetings, and considered the Half-
yearly balance sheet, which on close perusal by our members will reveal a very healthy
state of our Union, with its 97,000 members, of whom some 26,075 are financial women,
with 12,748 probationary, or in other words 45 per cent. of our membership are women.

INDUSTRIAL COUNCIL.—On the 27th the usual meeting of the Industrial Council was
held, and several important matters affecting the Trade were considered, the most import-
ant being that in future all the members of the Federation will be requested to see to it
that neither they or any member of their various staffs shall in any way show any antagon-
ism to Trade Union effort or work. We have committees working with the Home Office
for the better health conditions in the factories.

On the 28th we had the meeting of the Lasting Committee of the County Board at
Leicester.

On the 29th we held a consultation respecting the attitude to be taken towards a
firm who have resigned by request the Employers' Federation, but at present we have no
quarrels.

On the 31st we attended a conference with the Amalgainated Union of Rivetters and
Finishers, in Cartwright Gardens, London, with the object of bringing about some amal-
gamation, and we hope that having met the Executive of that body, we may make some
agreement whereby we can act together in future.

On February 3rd, at Leicester, we met as a Closing Committee and made good headway
with the Statement, the employers at the outset making two important announcements
that they were prepared to grant us the full benefit of the Umpire's Award of 85 per cent.,
and should any of the prices prove to be of less value to the girls than 50s. per week, they
would be prepared to amend them.

On February 4th we had a further meeting of the Committee and advanced the work
a further stage.

8. Waiting Time.
187
The Act of 1918 provides that a worker shall be deemed to have been employed during
the whole time during which he was present on the premises of the employer (except during
normal meal times in a room or place where no work is being done), unless the employer
can show that the worker was present for some purposes unconnected with his work or
was present without the employer's consent, express or implied, or was present only by
reason of the fact that he was resident on the premises.
A worker employed on piece work would be deemed during his waiting time to have
been employed at the general minimum time rate.
9. Time and Wages Records.
Under the Act of 1900 it was provided that on the prosecution of an employer it would
rest with the employer to show by the production of proper wages sheets or other records
of wages, or otherwise, that he had not paid, or agreed to pay, wages at less than the
minimum rate.
This provision is retained, but the Act of 1918 also makes it an offence, punishable
by a fine not exceeding £2, to fail to keep such a record of wages as is necessary to show
that the minimum rates are being paid, irrespective of whether the minimum rates are in
fact being paid.
10. Liability of Agents.
The Act of 1918 makes it possible to proceed against the agent of an employer (for
example, a manager or foreman) as well as the employer himself; and where the employer
can prove to the satisfaction of the Court that he has used diligence to enforce the execution
of the Act and that the offence was committed without his knowledge, he shall, in the
event of the conviction of the agent, be exempt from any fine, although the Court may
adjudge him due to pay any arrears of wages due to the worker on account of the under-
payment.
11. Indirect Employment.
It is provided that where the immediate employer of any worker is himself in the
employment of some other person, and the worker is employed on the premises of that
other person, that other person shall be deemed to be responsible jointly with the immedi-
ate employer for the payment of the minimum rate. Thus, for example, in the Tailoring
trade, if a machiner employed on the premises of a master tailor himself employs an under-
machiner, the master tailor is jointly responsible with the machiner for the payment of
the minimum rate to the under-machiner.
12. Learners and other special classes of Workers.
It is provided that a Trade Board may attach to the fixing of minimum rates fora
special class of workers the condition that the workers who are members of the class must
be holders of certificates to that effect issued by the Trade Board. If the special class
consists of persons who are learning the trade, the Trade Board may also attach such
conditions as they think necessary for securing the effective instruction of those persons
in the trade.
If any condition so attached is not complied with, the worker will be deemed not to
be a member of the special class; that is to say, if the conditions attached by a Trade
Board to learnership are not satisfied, the learnership rates would not be payable, and the
person employed would be entitled to the minimum rate fixed for workers other than
learners.
13. Admission of Investigating Officers and furnishing of information.
Officers are appointed by the Minister of Labour for the purpose of investigating
complaints and otherwise securing the proper observance of the Acts. They have power
to enter factories, workshops and places used for giving out work, to require the produc-
tion of wages sheets or other records which are necessary to show that the provisions
of the Acts are being complied with, and to question any person found on the premises.
Persons hindering the officers in the exercise of their powers render themselves liable
to a penalty of £5, and persons who knowingly furnish the officers with false wages sheets
or other false information or knowingly cause such to be furnished are liable on conviction
to a fine not exceeding £20, or to imprisonment for not more than three months with or
without hard labour.
OFFICE OF TRADE BOARDS,
5, CHANCERY LANE,
LONDON, W.C. 2.
November, 1919.

LEICESTER BOOT & SHOE TRADE.—BOARD OF CONCILIATION AND ARBITRATION..

Discontinuance of the War Emergency Employment of Women
in substitution for Male Labour.

DECISION OF THE BOARD.

The following resolution was adopted at a Meeting of the Board held on the 30th
day of January, 1920 :-
“That the Board instructs the Secretary to inform the Manufacturers that the engage-
ments of all women employed in Men's Departments on operations ordinarily restricted
to male labour, under the Agreement of 25th June, 1915, should be terminated by the
end of February, 1920, inasmuch as the Agreement was an emergency provision having
effect only during the continuance of the war, and that the Manufacturers are recommended
to transfer such women to departments where the work is usually performed by female
operatives.”
41, FRIAR LANE, LEICESTER,
7th February, 1920.
A. E. W. CHAMBERLIN,
Secretary.

At the suggestion of Mr. Poulton the report and the two resolutions named by Mr.
Parker were considered together.
Arising out of the report, Mr. Bleakley raised the question of the adequate and regular
inspection of factories, more especially ones in which health conditions were known to be
less perfect, and Mr. McCarthy stated that approximately 50 per cent. of the deaths in
the industry were due to Phthisis.

Phthisis in the Industry.
Mr. Poulton said that on becoming General Secretary of the National Union, he had
been so struck by the heavy mortality from Phthisis that he had made repeated representa-
tions to the Home Office, and after the presentation of figures relating to the deaths of
members of the Union for 12 years, which showed that the half yearly figures were approxi-
mately 50 per cent., had convinced the Ministry that the industry was suffering unduly.
He said that excluding the Licensed Victuallers, the Boot and Shoe Industry came second
on the list of mortality from Phthisis, and that conditions in factories compared unfavour
ably with those in Germany as regards space. On the motion of Mr. Parker, who was
seconded by Mr. Richards, the report was unanimously adopted together with the following
resolutions :-

(1) "That this Joint Industrial Council recommends that any person desiring to
start in business in a factory or workshop, shall give adequate notice to H.M. Inspector
of Factories of his intention to do so, and the address of the premises which he proposes
to occupy."
(2) " That this Joint Industrial Council recommends that the Home Secretary
should take powers to require that before any place is used as a factory or workshop,
the certificate of an Inspector of the Home Office shall first certify its fitness for the
purpose."

Merchandise Marks Act.
Mr. Poulton said that at a meeting of a certain Committee at which he had been
present on the previous day, evidence had been given which pointed to the necessity for
stronger action in ensuring that trade-marks were not tampered with.
The Council expressed full concurrence with the first part of the recommendation
of the Committee" That steps should be taken to ensure that the place of origin should
be clearly stamped so that it could not be obliterated "-but decided, while expressing
full approval of the principle of purity of material used in the manufacturing process,
to defer further consideration of the matter to a later meeting.

Unemployment Insurance Bill.
Mr. Parker drew attention to the main features of the Unemployment Insurance Bill,
and pointed out the need for considering the provision made for "contracting out" of
the scheme and the advisability of taking advantage of the provision, or as an alternative,
any amendments which they desired to put forward to the Bill as a whole.
On the motion of Mr. Hindes, seconded by Mr. Riley, it was decided that a Sub-Com-
mittee of six, three from each side, should be appointed to consider the matter.

Sickness Disablement Provident Scheme.
Mr. Riley said that the scheme which he had drawn up was based on the conviction
that the National Health Insurance Scheme did not go far enough and that it was illogical
that sick pay should be reduced after a period of six months when savings might be ex-
hausted, because a man did not recover, and further that it was difficult, in the present
circumstances, for an employer to say that a man should not come to work although he
might be a danger to the health of his fellow workers. There was need therefore for
adequate provision against poverty during sickness, and he desired to bring the necessity
before the Government by means of a resolution. On the motion of Mr. Riley
the following resolution was unanimously adopted :-
"That this Joint Industrial Council welcomes the promise of the Government,
in the coming Session of Parliament, to make provision for workers against unemploy-
ment, but would draw attention to the very inadequate provision now made under
the National Health Insurance Act for the benefit of workers who are unemployed
owing to prolonged illness, and particularly to the wholly inadequate provisions for
the treatment of persons suffering from consumption.
It urges upon the Government the immediate necessity of increasing the benefits
now payable under the Act and also an extension of the period during which full
benefits may be enjoyed.
This Council is further of the opinion that workers should be assured of suitable
maintenance benefit during the period they are medically certified as being incapaci-
tated through illness from following remunerative employment."

REPORT ON THE CONSTITUTION AND WORK OF
THE CONSUMERS' COUNCIL.

At a meeting of the Consumers' Council held at the Ministry of Food, Palace Chambers,
Westminster, on Wednesday, 19th November, 1919, it was resolved:
"That the Report on the work of the Council which had been prepared by the
Secretary and revised by the Sub-Committee be approved and circulated to the
various constituent bodies represented on the Council and the Press and in other manner
which might be thought necessary for the information of the public."
The Council further expressed their appreciation of the work of the Secretaries and the
valuable assistance rendered by them since the formation of the Council.

The Consumers' Council was formed in January, 1918. At that time the Food
situation, owing to the German submarine menace, had become very acute, and Mr. Clynes,
who had recently joined Lord Rhondda as his Parliamentary Secretary, felt the need of
enlisting the co-operation of the organised working classes and the co-operative move-
ment in the gigantic task which lay before the Ministry. Lord Rhondda readily agreed,
and suggested that the unorganised consumers should also be represented on the Council.
The following bodies were ultimately invited to send representatives :-
The Parliamentary Committee of the Co-operative Congress,
The Parliamentary Committee of the Trade Union Congress,
The War Emergency: Workers' National Committee, and
The Standing Joint Committee of Industrial Women's Organisations.
The invitation was accepted by each of those bodies and delegates appointed, as also
three delegates to represent the Unorganised Consumers.
The first meeting of the Council was presided over by Mr. Clynes, who, in explaining
the object with which they had been called together, said :-
" The Council would have access to the facts and figures on which the Ministry
based its policy. It would have no political attachment to the Government, and
would be free to give advice and record opinions without accepting responsibility for
the decisions of the Food Ministry. The Food Controller would, of course, retain
authority and responsibility for the policy of the Ministry, but the recommendations
or views of the Council would be of great value in the national interest.
" The Council could deal with problems of rationing, transport, administration,
and with all questions arising from the shortage of certain articles of food. The
interests of food producers were safeguarded by the public demand for articles of food
of every kind, and while full justice should be done to producers, and fair payment
made for their services, the Consumers' Council would be the special representative
of the interests of the public at large, and by acting within the Ministry could ascertain
for themselves the reasons why the various decisions of the Ministry were reached.
The Ministry was now an immense organisation, and had to undertake work having
the closest relation, not only to the civil population, but to millions of men who were
in the Army. In addition to the extensive machinery through which the Ministry
worked throughout the provinces, an idea of the vast extent of the work at headquarters
could be gathered from the fact that on an average 8,000 letters a day were received,
apart from sugar cards and forms. The Consumers' Council would, therefore, find
every outlet for its energies and for the advice which experienced men and women
could give in a difficult but necessary task."
Lord Rhondda, in elaborating the work which lay before the Council, said :-
" . . . as Mr. Clynes had said, he would have to take the responsibility as
Food Controller for ultimate decisions. Their relations with the Department would be
intimate and constant in character, and there would be no secrets kept back from them;
they would have access to everything, but they would realise that there were some
documents which they would not see. But the main thing to assure them of was
that there was no mystery about the department, and all possible information would be
available to them. They would give him their advice, and he would be accepting
very grave responsibility whenever they came to a unanimous decision if he rejected
their advice; but ultimately it must of necessity fall to his province and authority
to assume full responsibility for action taken. When he and Mr. Clynes took office
there was great discontent throughout the country as to prices of commodities, and
it had been decided to turn attention more particularly to prices in the first instance
rather than to supplies. Prices had been steadily advancing in all directions since
the beginning of the war. In many articles the increases had exceeded the increases
in wages, and commodities were rapidly getting beyond the reach of large sections of
the community. They had been criticised in that department for allowing theory

The trade union's leaders, while rightly actuated by the desire to get the best terms they

advantages by arbitration than by strikes. (Hear, hear.)

Policy of the Federation.
The toast was heartily drunk, and Mr. Owen Parker in responding, said during the
last 25 years the great central organisation of the industry had worked steadily with one
object in view. They had had the good fortune to meet the representatives of labour,
who had taken a broad view of the situation, but he thought it was largely due to the
leadership and well-considered policy of the Federation that it was the boast of their
industry, and their industry alone of all the industries in the country, that they could
look back on a period of more than a quarter of a century without having had a strike.

Wages Questions.
With regard to wages, Mr. Parker observed that they were now being asked to revise
the terms agreed upon, after protracted deliberations. Frankly he was not surprised
that the matter had been brought up again, and did not believe that anything would
happen to disturb the good relationships that had existed for 25 years, but while he thought
he could say that the Federation would accept the invitation of the union to meet them,
he wanted to say that the underlying policy of the agreement was payments by
results, on what was commonly called piecework rates, and they had had a
strenuous year in revising their piecework statements to bring them into line with the
national agreement. Very few statements had been worked for a sufficiently long
period to ascertain their advantage or otherwise to those who were called upon
to work them. He felt bound to protest against any idea on the part of the union
to call for a revision of statements of the result of which they, like the employers,
were entirely ignorant. (Applause.) In a few months it might be found that the
terms were such as to make a revision necessary. It was, however, necessary that they
should "wait and see." He was of opinion that the solution of labour unrest difficulties
was not entirely a question of wages. (Hear, hear.)

Organisation and Unemployment.
They must attend to the internal organisation of their factories, so that their pro-
ductive capacity might be used to the utmost. It was also necessary to see whether
they could not remove the nightmare of unemployment through short time or
sickness, and they were considering very carefully means whereby it was hoped they
would be able to make concrete proposals for industry on both sides to make itself some-
what responsible for seeing that payments were made which would avoid starvation for
those who, through no fault of their own, were left without employment. (Hear, hear.)
In conclusion, Mr. Parker said they had before them a period of the gravest possible
anxiety, but he was sure that if they were true to themselves a bright future was assured.
(Applause.)

TRADES UNION CONGRESS PARLIAMENTARY
COMMITTEE.

THE "DAILY HERALD."

TO THE OFFICIALS AND MEMBERS OF AFFILIATED SOCIETIES.
GENTLEMEN, Supplementary to the appeal made at the Special Congress in December
last on behalf of the Daily Herald, Messrs. E. Bevin (as representing the Daily Herald
Trade Union Provisional Committee), and R. Williams (representing the Directors of that
journal) recently attended before the Parliamentary Committee and requested their
endorsement of the appeal for capital which is being made to the Trade Union movement
in support of the Daily Herald, and which it is understood is now before the Executive of
every Trade Union in the country.
The deputation urged that if the paper could be printed in Manchester as well as in
London a circulation of one million copies per day would be assured within one year.
The size of the paper would be increased to ten pages, a larger revenue from advertisements
would be commanded, and the whole concern made a sound financial investment.
The deputation also stated that offers had been made by capitalist concerns to purchase
the paper, which had been refused; and that certain syndicates were contemplating
bringing out a spurious Labour paper in order to counteract the influence of the Herald.
The deputation assured the Parliamentary Committee that the Daily Herald had
command of a sum of £100,000, which would be set aside in the Bank to guarantee the
interest for five years on the £400,000 now being raised. Both the present Directors and
the Provisional Trade Union Committee gave further assurance that they were confident
The continuous
of the scheme becoming a financial success at the end of five years.
demands that were being made for the paper, and the irritation caused when it did not
arrive in the various districts as sometimes occurred under present conditions indicated
that there was a growing need for development. The aggregate circulation of the present
Sunday papers is said to reach nearly 20 millions. These papers are made much use of by
politicians opposed to the Labour movement, for they now make a practice of issuing
their statements on Saturdays so as to secure publication on Sunday, when there is no
Labour paper to counteract the influence of the capitalist Sunday press.
Any profits made from the undertakings, over and above the guaranteed interest of
Five per cent. will be used for the development of a real Labour press, able to print and
circulate all the best that Labour can produce.
The Parliamentary Committee, after hearing the deputation, decided to recommend
the Executives of the Unions to give the appeal their urgent consideration and financial
support. For further information the Parliamentary Committee refer the Unions direct
to Mr. Ernest Bevin, the Hon. Secretary of the Daily Herald Trade Union Committee,
2, Gough Square, Fleet Street, E.C. 4, who will send deputations to the Executives of any
Unions willing to receive them.
(2) EMPLOYMENT OF YOUNG PEOPLE IN DISTRIBUTIVE TRADES.
As you are aware, the Shop Assistants' Union has unceasingly struggled for over a
quarter of a century to limit the excessive hours of labour, increase the wages, and generally
improve the conditions of those employed in the distributive trades of the country. A
considerable measure of success has attended its efforts, and many of the worst phases of
employment in shop life, common 25 years ago, have been ameliorated or got rid of entirely.
By comparison with other occupations, however, the wages of those employed in the
distributive trades are, in many cases, shockingly low, while there is no normal working
week or any legal limitation to the hours of labour, except for young people under 18,
who cannot legally be employed beyond 74 hours per week. This is largely due to the fact
that the whole occupation is always being inundated with young people, often children
of even less than 14 years of age, and who, therefore, are for the most part too young to
organise. It is this fact which accounts for the slow progress made, in spite of the unceasing
efforts made by the Shop Assistants' Union, though the new Education Act, as soon as it
becomes operative, is likely to alter very considerably the position of young people entering
the distributive trades.
For the last nine or ten years serious efforts have been made to establish minimum
wage scales throughout the country, and thousands of pounds have been spent in these
efforts. During the last two or three years some measure of success has been attained.
The Union feels that until it can control the conditions of work for those who enter
employment in shop life, the improvements secured by Trade Union effort must be exceed-
ingly small for the tremendous expense and efforts made.

COUNTY MACHINISTS' PIECEWORK STATEMENT.
The following copy of a resolution was adopted at a meeting of the County
Arbitration Board held February 4th, 1920 :
"That pending the issue of the revised Machinists' Piecework Statement for the
County, the percentage advance agreed upon by the Joint Committee, namely 70
per cent., shall be paid to the female piecework operatives on the net earnings in
lieu of the War Bonus and the 20 per cent, advance as from the working week com-
mencing January 29th, 30th or 31st, being the date upon which it has been decided
that the Statement should come into operation."
In accordance with the above resolution, the operatives engaged on piecework
in the Closing Department are to receive 70 per cent. on their net earnings in place of
the War Bonus and the 20 per cent. War Wage, commencing on this week's pay day pending
the completion of the Closing Statement.

FELLOW MEMBERS,
THE STATE OF TRADE
still continues fairly good in most parts of the Kingdom, the figures issued in the Labour Gazette being as follows :-
In this trade employment during February was fairly good on the whole, but there was a considerable amount of short time, which was partly due to shortage of female labour and to difficulties in connection with the supplies of raw materials.
At Leicester employment on the whole was fair, and not quite so good as in January; a considerable amount of short time was reported. At Northampton and in the surround-ing district employment showed a slight decline; at Kettering it continued fair. At Norwich and Stafford the operatives continued well employed, and at Bristol employment was fair. In Scotland generally employment continued good.
The exports of boots and shoes in February, 1920, amounted to 78,204 dozen pairs, or 16,837 dozen pairs less than in January, 1920, and 65,284 dozen pairs less than in February, 1913.

UNEMPLOYMENT BILL.
Several meetings with the Committee of the Manufacturers' Federation
and ourselves have been held during the month, along with a representative
from the Ministry of Labour, with a view to seeing if a scheme dealing with
unemployment could not be drawn up for the industry outside the Government.
proposals. We are not in a position to report further on the matter at present,
and for the same reason we cannot state what increase, if any, to the present
contribution we shall ask for at the Whitsuntide Conference. Information,
however, will be sent out as soon as possible regarding the same.
1919 AGREEMENT REVISION.
During the past month we have held several meetings with the Executive
Committee of the Manufacturers' Federation, under the Chairmanship of
Alderman F. Sheppard, J.P., regarding the re-opening of the 1919 Agreement
with a view to increasing the minimum scale rates of pay owing to the ever-
increasing cost of living. We are not in a position to state the results at the
present time, except to say that proposals are now being considered, and
meetings arranged to go further into the matter. We hope to be able to
report fully upon the matter in the April Report.
NATIONALISATION OF MINES.
DIRECT ACTION DEFEATED BY 2,820,000.
The Special Congress was attended by about eight hundred delegates
representing 5,250,000 members, and was presided over by the Rt. Hon. J. H.
Thomas, M.P., who placed the position both for and against political action,
and shewed the dangers to the movement if a strike was decided upon. Mr.
F. Hodges, on behalf of the Miners, moved in favour of " trade union action
in the form of a general strike," and from his standpoint put up as strong a
case as possible, although he admitted from the debating standpoint the argu-
ment was against him. Very few speeches indeed were made, the evident
desire of the Congress being the issue not being mixed up with other matters-
to take the vote without numerous speeches being made. Two speakers spoke
against direct action and Mr. Hodges and Mr. Mann in favour. The result

REMEMBER THE FIFTEEΝΤΗ !
Once again we feel bound to call the serious attention of branch secretaries
to the fact that the FIFTEENTH day of each month is the latest day for
returns reaching the General Secretary. Last month many returns were late.
Branches failed to send off their returns to reach the Central Office by the
15th of the month, and this tends to upset the organisation of the work in
the General Secretary's office. We trust in future every branch secretary
will endeavour to get in his returns NOT later than the fifteenth of every month,
and before sending them see that they are properly signed. Moreover,
lateness in sending in the Monthly Returns makes it increasingly
difficult to get out the Report in time for the Monthly Meetings.

PARLIAMENTARY AGENT'S REPORT.
The end of the last Session found the Members generally somewhat wearied, and all
seemed glad of the prospect of the recess. I am afraid that for the Labour Members it
was not much of a rest, though it may have been a change. What with the campaign
for the Nationalisation of the Mines, the bye-election, and the claims of their own con-
stituencies most had a very busy time. In my own case, apart from addressing meetings,
the Royal Commission on Agriculture, and the delegation to Ireland made it almost
impossible apart from the Christmas period to spend more than a few days at home.
The delegation sent by the Parliamentary Labour Party to Ireland was a wise step.
The Irish question has always been in some respects a difficult one to study from a distance,
and an investigation on the spot, even if the time for same was limited, could only produce
good results. We were able to obtain a great deal of information, much of which was
highly discreditable to the present Government. In pre-war days it would have dismayed
all lovers of liberty and freedom, but following upon a war that was frequently stated
to be in defence of the right of small nationalities, the present condition of Ireland is such
as to cause one to wonder whether we have not drifted back rather than moved forward.
That the present conditions cannot continue with advantage to either Great Britain
or Ireland is self-evident, and one can only hope that the report of the delegation when
issued, which will be very shortly, will awaken an interest in this century old question,
which will demand a solution in a way that will end the difficulty and give to Ireland the
task and the opportunity of working out her future. The longer it is delayed the more
difficult will it become. It is a matter of extreme urgency and a big responsibility rests
upon those who refuse to view it from that standpoint. The Irish people have largely
lost confidence in the British politicians, their one remaining hope is in the British Labour
Party. Let us by establishing justice in this distressed country, prove ourselves worthy
of the trust reposed in us.
There is a general expectation that the present Session will be a critical one for the
Government, and indeed speculation is rife as to whether it will not prove to be fateful
to the Coalition. Be that as it may, if the Government survive throughout the Session,
its time will be fully occupied, for the King's speech, which is really the official declaration
of the Government legislative programme, is undoubtedly a heavy one. The debating
activities of the Labour Party during the discussion on the address showed that they are
very dissatisfied with the Government's proposals. Nationalisation of Coal Mines is
again rejected. The reference to the cost of living is a typical example of the false sense
of security and satisfaction of the Government. The people are told that" prices in these
islands are appreciably lower than elsewhere." This is certainly cold comfort to a people
who know perfectly well that profiteering in regard to the necessities of life is still rampant,
and it will require more than empty phrases on the part of the Government to remove the
present popular discontent due to abnormal prices.
The King's Speech is also remarkable for various important omissions, notably the
total absence of reference to the housing problem, which continues to exercise the minds
of the people, and to the question of the financial condition of the country.
At the last General Election, Mr. Lloyd George, forgetful of the great assistance
rendered by Labour during the war, returned to his inimitable Limehouse style and warned
the nation of the evil consequence that would follow if the "Bolsheviks" of this country
were charged with the responsibility of government. The immediate object of the Prime
Minister was to secure the defeat of Labour candidates and his misrepresentation of the
Labour policy towards Russia assisted him in achieving a large measure of success. But
how different the position is to-day! The policy of non-intervention for which Labour
alone among the political parties in our country then stood, has now been accepted by the
Prime Minister, and by Mr. Asquith, the leader of the independent Liberals. Indeed,
the Prime Minister does not hesitate to appropriate the very argument put forward during
the last Session by Mr. Clynes in his advocacy of a sane Russian policy. Mr. Clynes stated
that the best way to restore stable government in Russia was not to fight the Russian
people but to feed them.
The Prime Minister administered an unmistakeable snub to Mr. Churchill and his
ambitious schemes for carrying "liberty" to Russia at the point of the bayonet. "We
have failed to restore Russia to sanity by force, I believe we can save her by trade."
This belated admission amply justifies Labour's consistent and persistent opposition to
the blockade and to Mr. Churchill's military adventures. The Prime Minister's return to
sanity has been slow and somewhat devious. Nevertheless, Labour can congratulate
itself that it is at last within measurable distance of securing the orientation of Britain's
Russian policy on to the lines which the organised workers have been pressing for since the
signing of the Armistice.
During the past few weeks discussion on political prospects has usually brought
forward the suggestion that the Prime Minister might play for a breach with organised
Labour on the question of Nationalisation of the Mines in order that if a national stoppage

BRANCH REPORTS.
BRISTOL No. 1.-Trade has fallen off considerably with some discharges
of men. At our Branch meeting the Report of the Industrial Council held
January 27th last, gave rise to a strong discussion on the attitude taken up
by the Council on Works Committees. This Branch is of opinion that with
proper safeguards works committees can be a power for helping and not hinder-
ing the Union officials in carrying out their work. This is proved by the
working of such a committee at one of the largest firms in the district. We
therefore strongly protest against the Council's action on this important ques-
tion. We are very anxiously awaiting the result of meetings of our Council
and the Federation representatives on the minimum wage question, and trust
that the £4 asked for may be an accomplished fact.
BELFAST.-Trade remains similar to previous month, fair in the Manu-
facturing, but quiet in the Repairing. With regard to the application sent
to the Boot and Top Manufacturers, we are pleased to report that some progress
was made, the men on the 56s. minimum rate were increased up to 65s., and
the women on the 30s. minimum rate were increased to 35s. A meeting of
the Trades Board was held during the month in Belfast when the time and
piecework rates were confirmed with some slight modifications. A Sub-Com-
mittee was appointed to draw up special rates and conditions of working for
apprentices.
BURNLEY.-We are dissatisfied with our present wages and desire an
advance. We are in a considerably worse position than we were in 1914.
But to fight alone is suicidal, so we have written all secretaries in Lancashire
asking them to join us in our endeavour to better our conditions. Now,
Lancashire shopmates, rally round us, and if you will back us up we will do
the fighting. You have nothing to lose, but everything to gain.
CHESTERFIELD.-Trade very good. We agree with our General Presi-
dent in his report, that our future agreements must have swifter application.
Our members at our monthly meeting ask the Council to press the Union demand
to the fullest extent; they are now overdue, when we look round and see what
other trades are getting at the present time. Also on every hand we see the
cost of food and other necessaries of life still going up. Our members are
looking forward this time for something that will give satisfaction all round.
CHESHAM.-Trade here is slack, some of our members are being dis-
charged, others are losing time. These things with the continual increase in
the cost of living, are making our members very dissatisfied with the present
rates of pay; and if the manufacturers do not soon get a move on and meet
the increase, we might with advantage to the workers be brought under the
Trade Boards Act. Our local Labour Party have decided to contest all six
seats at the forthcoming Urban District Council election; Mr. J. Davis will be
the Boot and Shoe Operatives' candidate, taking the place of our Branch
President, who is retiring from local politics owing to ill-health.
DUNDEE. Whilst operatives in boot factories in this area are having
a plentiful supply of work, the repairer on the other hand has severely felt
the intense sluggishness of his calling, resulting in a heavy weekly bill for out-
of-work benefit. This part of the administrative machinery of a trade union
has a significance beyond its surface value. Little as the dole is, the flickering
flames of discontent are thereby lessened, enabling the country to reach more
readily the normal conditions which most people are calling loudly for to-day.
A very harmonious gathering of the members of the branch took place on
Saturday, the 21st February, in the "Stag," Hilltown, the occasion being the
presentation to Mr. John Moir of his portrait in oils, the able work of our

to us. It will gladden the hearts of a lot of our members to see the piece rates

KETTERING No. 2.--We can at last report progress with regard to the
Roughstuff Statement. Two meetings have been held, and we are hoping
that a reasonable basis to start from will be agreed upon, and that rapid pro-
gress will be made with this Statement, as the men in this department are about
tired of waiting. The position with regard to the Closing Statement is far
from satisfactory: the employers as far as our knowledge goes, have not as yet

position, but await developments. Our members were very pleased to hear
that the Council had started negotiating with regard to increasing the minimum

considerable time is being lost in the Clicking Department. Sickness is just
over normal.
KINGSWOOD AND DISTRICT.---Trade is this centre is still very quiet,
with the exception of those firms making lighter classes of footwear. Memories
of previous depressions in trade in our district are still fresh, but nothing so
dramatically sudden has been previously experienced. The outlook at the
time of writing is far from encouraging. The problems peculiar to our industry
will have to be recognised, and tackled by the responsible thinkers among
both employed and those who accept the responsibility of ownership. Our
trade has solved the problem of production, with its almost automatic power
of expansion, and in view of our present unhappy evidence of over production,
why not devote a portion of our thought and energy to a consideration of
measures of a restrictive character affecting hours of labour, control of output,
and a still more comprehensive control over the introduction of labour into
our industry. Numbers of our men, returned from the Services, triumphant
in war, find no welcome situation in civil life, and bitterly reflect, "what shall
it profit a nation, capable of winning in a tremendous war, but incapable of
organising its civil life to guarantee even a minimum standard of comfort
to its members."
LEICESTER No. 1. - Very pleased to report that we have organised
Ratby and made over 80 members, male and female, and it is hoped they will
stick together and see the benefits derived by becoming Trade Unionists.
LEEDS No. 1. - We regret to report that a falling off in the heavy and
medium work has taken place, and as a consequence our out-of-work is likely
to become much heavier, but we hope that this unfortunate change may be
only temporary. We regret to report that our sick list remains very heavy.
No doubt this is due partly to the varied changes in the weather. We are
pleased to report that by the time this report appears in print, our members
who are employed in the making and finishing of light work will be working
to the new Piece Statement, which we believe will prove satisfactory to all
employed. We are pleased to report that through the efforts of Mr. Wright,
Solicitor, we have been successful in obtaining £110 compensation for Reg. No.
35648, and also £30 for Reg. No. 101304. It is pleasing to note that the same
gave satisfaction to the two members.
LIVERPOOL.-Trade is still quiet with repairers. We have had two
members on the sick list and one on the out-of-work funds. From a financial
point of view the year that is past and gone was successful; balance, November
30th, 1918, £29 2s. 7d.; Income for the year, £248 17s. 9d.; Total, £278 os. 4d.

TRADES UNION CONGRESS PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE.

DELEGATES' REPORT OF THE ADJOURNED SPECIAL CONGRESS.

The adjourned Special Congress was held in the Central Hall, Westminster, London,
on Thursday, 11th March, 1920, commencing at to a.m., the Rt. Hon. J. H. Thomas,
M.P., chairman of the Parliamentary Committee, being in the chair. Mr. Thomas gave
a very reasoned statement pointing out the difficulties on the one hand of what would
accrue from Direct Action," and the facilities existent for bringing into being those
things which are so desired - from the workers' standpoint (on the other) if only the vote
of the workers is used in the proper way at the Ballot Box. After the statement of the
chairman the Congress agreed to back his position, the meeting without formally moving
taking the following resolution :---
"In view of the repeated refusal of the Government to Nationalise the Mines,
in accordance with the Minority Report of the Coal Industry Commission, and in
agreement with the terms of the resolution passed at the Glasgow Congress, and the
Special Congress held in December last, the Parliamentary Committee suggest the
following forms of action as a means to compel the Government to adopt the Nation-
alisation of Mines: (a) Trade Union action, in the form of a general strike."
