WELFARE WORK
AT MESSRS. SMITH & BROWN'S.

A correspondent, who is evidently a bit of a humorist, asks us to insert the following:
"The well-known firm of boot and shoe manufacturers, Messrs. Smith and Brown,
met their employees on Monday to explain to them the new welfare arrangements which
had been made. At the outset Mr. Smith first stated how very pleased he was to see
representatives of the various daily and weekly papers present, It did not always do
to keep all good things to oneself, and if this good news got into the papers many young
ladies would get to hear of it, and would be glad to know of what was being done. Mr.
Smith went on to explain the advantages which his firm hoped to bring about, as they
thought the hours which working people were working to-day, viz., 48 hours were much
too long. They, therefore, proposed commencing work in the morning at 9.30. At 10.30
there would be a half-hour break for lunch. The ladies would be supplied with either
tea, coffee or cocoa, and one-round of buttered toast. The men would be supplied with
a round of bread and cheese, with either a bottle of Bass or Guinness (here the band of the
Life Guards, which had been engaged purposely for this great day, struck up 'He's a
jolly good fellow,' and the speaker bad hard work to proceed owing to several of the workers
closing round and tapping him on the back).

Mr. Smith said that was not all the good news by all means. They considered seeing
that some of the workers lived ten minutes away from the factory, that the dinner time
had to be extended to two hours. Therefore they proposed leaving off at 12 o'clock, and
not starting again till two. When the workers returned they would be met at the gates
with trays of whatever fruit happened to be in season, as doctors all agreed that there
was nothing like fruit for the constitution, and Mr. Smith assured the workers that he was
very deeply interested in their physical welfare.

Mr. Smith then proceeded to say that no doubt the workers had noticed the sprinklers
which had been put in the roof of all the various departments, and no doubt the employees
thought that they had been put up to put out any fires which might arise. 'Oh, no,'
said he, we have something far better in view than this; and that is, whenever the atmos-
phere in the department becomes a little oppressive we shall spray through these sprinklers
20 gallons of eau-de-Cologne through the factory. (The band here struck up 'Sweet Violets.')
At 3.30 you will all retire in the roof-garden, where tea and cakes will be handed
round by smart good-looking girls (here the men broke into singing. First one commenced
with 'Come into the garden, Maud.' This appeared a bit too classical for the majority,
and all united in singing 'K-K-K-Katy, my beautiful Katy.') 'To make the time pass
pleasantly, Mr. Smith added, we are engaging a small string band to discourse sweet
music to you during tea interval. At 4 o'clock work will be resumed, and we trust that
when you get down to your various departments there will be no bunnyhugging or fox-
trotting going on, as we are anxious to close in the afternoon at 5 o'clock. Upon leaving
work for the day the girls will be supplied with a small packet of chocolate each, and the
men with either a cigar or packet of Woodbines." Mr. Smith then pointed out that
each worker would be supplied with three clean overalls per week, also the male operatives
with one suit per year and the female operatives with one new dress. Fathers of very large
families, would also receive £5 allowance per year for each child. (The band here struck
up with 'I'm a dada, I'm a dada.') Also Mr. Smith mentioned that if any one of the workers
happened to die while in their employ, a grand oak coffin, carved in Jacobean style, with
gold handles, and nicely padded eiderdown, would be provided.

Mr. Smith said there was just one more benefit he would like to mention. The firm
had decided in the interest of the health of the workers to allow a full month's holiday
during the month of August, which of course they would be paid for. (The band chipped
in here with the 'Hallelujah Chorus.')
"Now there was one favour he would like to ask, upon entering the works would
they please remember to wipe their feet on the mat. Also to make a special endeavour
to be kind and considerate to their foremen and employers. The memorable occasion was
then brought to a close by the band playing 'Rule Britannia' and 'God save Smith and
Brown' (and they will need it)."-Hinckley Times.

PLAYING FIELD FOR EMPLOYEES.
J. H. F. Willis, Ltd., Worcester, have acquired the old Worcestershire county cricket
ground, and they have presented it to their Cinderella Works employees as a recreation
ground. Mr. H. Mattock, the general manager, in handing it over, said it was the firm's
wish that the employees should manage it for and by themselves. He hoped the glorious
sporting memories of the ground would inspire them to emulation. Mr. Hardwick, on
behalf of the employees, expressed gratitude for the generosity of the firm. -Shoe Trades
Journal, February 27th, 1920.

BOOT REPAIRERS' WAGES.
Official Announcement by the Ministry of Labour.
The Ministry of Labour makes the following announcement :- --
"At a recent meeting of the Boot and Shoe Repairing Trade Board (Great Britain)
it was resolved to fix general minimum piece rates for male and female workers and general
minimum time rates and overtime rates for female workers and to vary the general minimum
time rates at present in operation for certain classes of male workers, in accordance with the
notice of proposal to fix and to vary issued by the Trade Board, on December 1, 1919.
The minimum piece rates in question are for repairing (hand-sewn and riveted work) and
for making bespoke hand-sewn, pegged and riveted work.
"The general minimum time rates fixed by the Trade Board for female workers of
21 years of age and upwards are 45s. per week of 48 hours, where such workers are employed
in a productive department on patching machines; 65s. per week of 48 hours for female
workers employed on finishing or benching work; and 2s. per hour for female workers
employed on surgical work. The Trade Board have also fixed overtime rates for female
workers and general minimum time rates for younger female workers in the trade.
"Trade Board have also resolved to fix a general minimum time rate of Is. 6d. an hour
for male workers ordinarily employed on piece work when employed on a time work basis
on work for which no general minimum piece rates are fixed; and 2s. per hour for male
workers employed on surgical work.
"The minimum rates fixed by the Trade Board will not become effective unless and
until they have been confirmed by the Minister of Labour. The Trade Board have notified
the Minister of Labour that they have fixed these rates and have suggested that they should
be made effective as from March 12, 1920.
On the receipt of an Order by the Minister of Labour confirming the rates in question,
a statutory notice setting our the particulars of the minimum rates fixed and varied by
the Trade Board will be circulated to the trade. --Shoe and Leather Record, March 5th, 1920.
S.C.W.S. BALANCE SHEET.
Year's Turnover £24,750,000.
Big Increases in Sales and Production.
The Scottish Co-operative Wholesale Society's balance sheet and statement of accounts
for the half-year ended December 27th, 1919, is now issued, and reveals continued progress.
The net sales for the half-year amount to £13,040,502 195. 1od., an increase of £2,939,006
18s. 3d. over the corresponding period of 1918, the rate of increase being 29.1 per cent.
The value of goods manufactured in the productive departments and transferred to the
distributive departments, including the direct sales of by-products from flour mills, soap
works, &c., amounted to £3,935,294 6s. Iod., an increase of £996,748 11s. 6d. over the
corresponding half-year of 1918, or 33.9 per cent.
The sales for the whole year were £24,773,381 75. 10d., an increase of £5,556,618 9s. 3d.
over the year 1918, equal to a percentage of 28.9. The total amount of these sales does
not include payments for controlled goods received from the Ministry of Food. The total
value of goods manufactured for the year 1919 at the productive departments and trans-
ferred to the distributive departments, including the direct sales of by-products from
flour mills, soap works, &c., was £7,413,135 25. 2d., an increase over 1918 of £1,769,006
Is. 6d., or 31.3 per cent.
The balance carried forward from last half-year was £21,764 10s. 2d., making the
amount available for distribution for this half-year £349,345 125. IId. After meeting
all expenses, including interest on capital, depreciation on buildings, machinery, and
plant, the directors recommend this sum for allocation as follows:-£245,017 14S. 2d.
as dividend on purchases to members and non-members at the rate of 5d. in the pound
and 2d. in the pound respectively; £27,167 145. 3d. to reserve fund; £3,755 3s. 4d.
to special fund; and ₤20,000 to be appropriated for writing down investments to current
market value; leaving a balance of £53,405 IS. 2d. to be carried forward to next half-
year's account.
During the half-year 24,598 shares were allotted to societies, of which 600 were trans-
ferred, 823 new, and 23,175 additional. The total number of shares held by societies
is now 649,995. -The Co-operative News, March 6th, 1920.

DYING VIENNA.
By EDO FIMMEN.
THE POSITION OF THE RELIEF MOVEMENT OF THE INTERNATIONAL TRADE UNIONS ON
BEHALF OF THE AUSTRIAN TRADE UNIONS, FEBRUARY 5TH, 1920.

England.
The General Federation of Trade Unions informed us that a shipment of 10,000 kilo-
grams of margarine and 1,500 cases of compressed beef, weighing about 40,000 kg., is being
sent to Holland via the Co-operative Wholesale Society at Manchester, to be distributed
amongst the working classes of Vienna. The value of this shipment is about £5,000.

Holland.
The moneys derived from the extra hours made by the Dutch trade unionists—that
is, by working on Boxing Day—are now coming in. As in various places the eight hours
overtime have not been completed as yet, and as a fairly great deal of administrative work
has still got to be done in connection with the division of the money, which has got to be
made in accordance with the wishes expressed by the members of the four different national
centres, we are not yet in a position to give details as to the total sum so far collected in
Holland.

Italy.
The Confederazione Generale del Lavoro at Milano wrote us under date of January 15th
that the moneys collected from the Italian workers for our comrades in Vienna will be
remitted to the International Federation, with the exception of a small part to be applied
for defraying the expenses for housing and maintaining a number of working-class children
from Vienna in Italy.

Spain.
The Spanish Centre "Union General de Trabajadores" wrote us on January 30th
that to its great regret it is not in a position to contribute anything—not even in a moderate
way—for alleviating the great distress of the Austrian population. This is attributed to
the difficult economic position in which the Spanish population itself is placed at this mo-
ment.
From the Centres of the other countries no reports have come to hand since our letter
of January 29th.

INDUSTRIAL COUNCILS.
ENFORCEMENT OF AGREEMENTS.
MR. JESSON asked the Minister of Labour if dissatisfaction exists in those industries-
that have established Industrial Councils when decisions and agreements arrived at are
ignored or set at defiance by those employers who are not parties to those agreements or
members of employers' associations; and whether he will consider the advisability of
making the decisions and agreements upon wages, conditions, and hours of employment
arrived at by all Industrial Councils binding upon the whole of the respective industries.
when they represent two-thirds of the workers and their employers concerned, so as to
prevent employers under-selling those who are helping to establish industrial peace ?
SIR R. HORNE: I propose to answer this question in some detail because the principle
involved is one to which public attention ought to be given. I should say, in the first place,
that while it is the fact that several Joint Industrial Councils have asked for powers to
make their agreements compulsory on the whole trade, it is far from being the case that.
this demand is universal. This division of opinion was to be expected in view of the
controversial history of this and the allied question, from which it is difficult to dissociate
it, of making awards of Courts of Arbitration compulsory. In 1913, the Industrial Council,
a body consisting of representatives of employers' associations and trade unions, under
the chairmanship of Sir George (now Lord) Askwith, reported that, subject to certain
conditions to which I need not allude, an agreement, entered into by associations of em-
ployers and workmen, representing a substantial body of those in the trade or district,
should be more applicable to the whole of the trade or district concerned. The matter
was then considered by the Trade Union Congress, at which the proposal was rejected by
a large majority. The Trade Union Congress had previously rejected the idea in 1912,
and the Labour Party adopted the same attitude in 1913. The hon. Member's proposal
was the subject of one of the recommendations of the Provisional Joint Committee of
the National Industrial Conference. I endeavoured to secure the opinion of the Trade
Union Congress in September last year, but I understand that the Parliamentary Committee
was unable to bring the matter before the main body. I made a further attempt to ascer-
tain the reception which the proposal would meet from workpeople's organisations at the
time when I was introducing the Industrial Courts Act. At that time, however, it was
rejected by the trade union organisations largely on the ground that it was proposed, and
I think justly proposed, to make compulsion two-sided, penalties for breach being provided
equally against employers and employed. Under the Trade Union Act of 1871 and the
Trade Disputes Act, 1906, not only is it impossible to enforce legally an agreement made
between employers' associations and workers' associations, but it is also impossible to
bring an action against either such association for inducing or assisting its members to
break the contract to which it has itself been a party. Contracts between employers and
workmen's associations rest, therefore, only upon the good faith of the parties to them,
and, unless the law is altered in this respect, it is difficult to see how it is possible to make
them legally binding upon persons who are not themselves parties to the agreement. The
difficulty of making compulsion apply equally to perhaps not greater than the practical
difficulties which would be involved in making agreements of joint industrial councils
compulsory on the whole trade. Not only would complicated questions of demarcation
and trade definition inevitably arise, but the question of the extent to which any given
group of employers or employed represented a large majority of the trade would require
close examination. There is the further difficulty that certain wage settlements affect
an industry, while others affect a craft extending through a number of industries. For
these reasons it is clear that the matter is not one which can be settled without a great deal
of further discussion and examination. In saying this, however, I am not averse from
giving further consideration to this matter, but unless a substantial agreement of opinion
exists among employers and workpeople I should not be prepared to introduce the necessary
legislation.
14.

THE MINIMUM PIECE RATES.
In View of Objections Received, the Ministry of Labour Postpones the Date
of Coming into Operation.
The following letter has been addressed by Mr. E. Leggett, Ministry of Labour, to
the secretary of the Boot Repairing Trade Board:
I am directed by the Minister of Labour to refer to your letter of February 23 on
the subject of the fixing by the Boot and Shoe Repairing Trade Board of Great Britain
of certain minimum rates of wages for male and female workers in the trade. I am
to state that the Minister has received preliminary notice of objections to be made
against confirmation of the rates, and, in all the circumstances of the case, he regrets
that it will not be possible for him to make an Order confirming the minimum rates
as set out in the draft notice accompanying your letter, in time to allow of March 12
being fixed as the date from which the rates shall be effective. As the Trade Board
are aware, the Act provides that a month may elapse after the fixing of a rate by the
Trade Board before the Minister's decision is given. The Shoe and Leather Record,
March 12th, 1920.

HOUSING AND HEALTH.
Boot Workers' Deputation to Dr. Addison.
Representatives of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives waited upon the
Minister of Health, Dr. Addison, yesterday afternoon with members of the Parliamentary
Committee of the Trades Union Congress, and submitted for the Minister's consideration
the resolution passed by the Congress in September last, as follows:-
"That this Congress, in view of the great shortage of dwelling houses, with its
consequent menace to the health of the people, calls upon the Government to at once
deal with this important question: (a) By making it compulsory for local authorities
to prepare and carry out immediately adequate housing schemes in their particular
areas; (b) By the Government making grants free of interest, as will enable local
authorities to erect suitable houses at a reasonable cost to the people.
"In default of any local authority not so proceeding, this Congress instructs the
Parliamentary Committee to press the Government immediately to make provision
for the proper housing of the people."
The resolution was submitted by the general president of the Union, Mr. T. F. Richards
at the Congress in September, and seconded by Mr. E. L. Poulton, J.P.
"SHOULDER HITS" ON HEALTH.
Dr. Burkitt on Criminal Apathy of Society.
HOUSING, CONSUMPTION, AND INFANTILE MORTALITY.
Dr. J. C. Burkitt, vice-chairman of the County Insurance Committee, gave an address
on "Health Matters" to the members of the Leicester and District Friendly Societies'
Council at the Foresters' Institute, last night.
Dr. Burkitt said the standard of sickness in this country was much too high. Amongst
insured persons alone there were 14,000,000 weeks lost annually in sickness, which meant
that on an average every man lost 10 days a year. Nearly 90,000 children died before
reaching their first birthday, and there were 100,000 school children in England and Wales
who suffered so badly both mentally and physically that they were unable to attend school.
Another 500,000 children were suffering from malnutrition, whilst 3,000,000 of the little
ones were afflicted with defective teeth, one of the chiefest causes of stomach derangement.
Another damnable fact was that in our large towns fully 10 per cent. of the inhabitants were
victims of venereal disease, either acquired or transmitted. These figures were a terrible
indictment, and one could not doubt that the health of the country was in a bad state.
The money spent on tuberculosis was absolutely useless, because it was not doing what
it ought to do. No child was born into the world with this dreaded disease, which was
bred in overcrowded slums. It was for them to see that the poor were not crowded together
in kennels which were not fit for human beings to live in. -The Leicester Daily Mercury,
Saturday, March 6th, 1920.

READ THIS!

I may say peace is our first purpose – a real peace, not a snarling peace, not a scowling peace, but a real peace.  A sulky angel of peace is apt to become the harbinger of a new war—not an armed peace, not an angel of peace winged with spears.

PEACE ON EARTH.

We want peace in the East and peace in the West; peace abroad and peace at home. Ten millions of slaughtered men and fifteen millions of mutilated men ought to satisfy the most bloodthirsty appetite in any land.
You can only build up on the basis of peace – and that is the first thing we have to establish.
Peace on earth and good will amongst men is not merely a great gospel, it is the soundest of political economies.

Unchecked individualism in this country is responsible for slums, sweating, prolonged hours of toil, child labour, and for starvation in periods of misfortune through ill health and unemployment ; and the legislation of the last few years especially, and even of the last fifty years, has been directed to checking the abuses that strengthened that system-
From Premier's Speech, March 18th, 1920.

THE GOLDEN FLEECE.

We do not suppose that the spinners will accept the Committee's findings without some attempt at explanation.  They will tell us that the report is an ex parte statement ; and they will justify their action as being in accordance with the business theory of "buying in the cheapest market and selling in the dearest." But no amount of excuse will suffice to allay public resentment. The fact of the excessive prosperity of the wool districts remains, and the reports of the Committee leave no room for any other conclusion than that prosperity is due to "fleecing" the public. We have read the reports with shame. We do not suggest that the dealers in wool are sinners above the rest. This is but the first crop of a Further revelations from other trades are promised us. great harvest of tares. What is to be said of business integrity under these circumstances ? And more than this, what is to be said of the commercial morality of a business community which includes so many men who are as prominent in Church and civic life as they are in the world of commerce ? The Government itself, having made colossal profits out of a necessary commodity, sells that commodity to manufacturers at a price which should permit the public to be provided with clothing at a reasonable rate. The manufacturers and merchants use their opportunity to increase their already fabulous profits at the expense of the nation. Surely it is not impossible to devise means whereby this money should be returned to the community from whom it has been taken.

TRADE DISPUTES.

The number of trade disputes beginning in February was 122. In addition 47 disputes which began before February were still in progress at the beginning of the month. The total number of workpeople directly or indirectly involved in all these disputes, new or old, was about 110,000, as compared with about 119,000 in the previous month, and about 280,000 in February, 1919. The estimated aggregate duration of all trade disputes during the month was about 450,000 days, as compared with 1,793,000 days in January, 1920, and 2,316,000 days in February, 1919. —The Labour Gazette, March, 1920.

CHANGES IN RATES OF WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR.

The changes in rates of wages reported to the Department as having been arranged to come into operation in February, with effect from that month, or from earlier dates, resulted in an increase of over £72,000 in the weekly wages of 370,000 workpeople. The principal changes affected workpeople employed in the textile dyeing, bleaching, finishing, &c., trades and iron and steel workers.  Changes in hours of labour arranged during February affected about 178,000 workpeople, whose hours were reduced by an average of three per week. —The Labour Gazette, March, 1920.

all Statements that have come into operation since the 1st January, 1920,
and the date of the present Agreement, shall be advanced by 7 per cent.
(Seven and a half per cent.).
It is agreed that to avoid the necessity for further detailed revision and
amendment to such Statements, this percentage increase shall be calculated
upon and added to the total weekly earnings of pieceworkers.
3. That this interim Agreement shall become operative the week com-
mencing 15th, 16th, 17th or 19th day of April, as the case may be, and shall be
incorporated in, and interpreted with, the National Agreement of February,
1910.

295

TRAGIC END OF MR. JOHN TAYLOR,
Secretary to Kettering No. 2 Branch.

It is with unfeigned sorrow we have to record the fact that Mr. JOHN
TAYLOR, who was Secretary to the Kettering No. 2 Branch for a long period
met with a tragic end on the 27th March, his body being found on the
railway near Isham severly mutilated. This is a sad loss to the widow
and family, and also to ourselves. For very many years Mr. Taylor had
done his part in helping forward the movement in Kettering and building
up the organisation to its present dimensions. Although of a retiring
and quiet disposition Mr. Taylor was always to be relied upon in helping
so far as he could do any movement designed to improve the lot of the
workers whether in the shoe or any other industry. To the widow and
family we tender our heartfelt regrets in the irreparable loss they have
sustained, and we can only hope that the good work done by Mr. Taylor
and the appreciation of such work by his fellows in striving to make
the world a better place to live in will be some comfort to them in this
their hour of adversity and sorrow.

REMEMBER THE FIFTEENTH !

Once again we feel bound to call the serious attention of branch secretaries
to the fact that the FIFTEENTH day of each month is the latest day for
returns reaching the General Secretary. Last month many returns were late.
Branches failed to send off their returns to reach the Central Office by the
15th of the month, and this tends to upset the organisation of the work in
the General Secretary's office. We trust in future every branch secretary
will endeavour to get in his returns NOT later than the fifteenth of every month,
and before sending them see that they are properly signed.

TRADE UNION STAMP.

This is a matter which we have stated before rests with the members to
make a success. It is in the interests of members themselves that "Stamped
Footwear" should be increasingly purchased; therefore, push the Trade
Union Stamp. Members and their families should wear only "Union Stamped
Footwear."

MONTHLY RETURNS.

We beg to call the attention of Branch Secretaries to the advisability of
keeping a copy for their own use of the Monthly Returns sent to the Central
Office. There are a number of reasons why this should be done which we need
nct particularise here; one, however, may specially be named: If the Returns
were Icst and no copy kept it would mean all the work being done over
again.

Wednesday, March 31st, 1920
Mr. W. R. Smith: To ask the Minister of Labour, whether he is aware that the National
Health Insurance Commissioners have refused sanction to the National Union of Boot
and Shoe Operatives' Approved Section to invest moneys in the Co-operative Wholesale

or corporation stock; and whether, in view of the provisions of sub-section (2) of Section

My Right Honourable Friend has asked me to reply to this question.
The general decision of the Insurance Commissioners referred to by the Honourable
Member followed the recommendations of the Investments Advisory Committee con
tained in their report of May, 1914. (Cd. paper 7498 of 1914).
In view of the present range of trustee securities I see no reason for reconsidering
that decision.

PARLIAMENTARY AGENT'S REPORT.
The policy of the Government in regard to Ireland continues to be one of repression,
and the general arrest of persons, who are imprisoned without charge or trial, has cul
minated in their release following the adoption of the hunger strike. The weakness of the
Government is shown in the fact that Mr. Bonar Law, the Leader of the House, stated
one day, that after full consideration of the case it had been decided not to interfere with
imprisonment of these men even if their detention led to their death, and the very next
day they were released, practically without condition. How can such a Government
command confidence and respect?
The position in Ireland is not made easier as a result of the shooting of policemen
that is continually taking place; this is greatly to be deplored, and in my judgment con
demned; they are but the instruments of the law, and even if the law is bad it is no justifica
tion for the shooting in cold blood men who perhaps have no liking for the work they are
called upon to do. One can only hope some way out will be found, but the policy which
forces and then gives way to the policy of direct action is not a sound one, and coming
from the statesmen
who prate about Bolshevism in their speeches against the Labour
Party, it is a lamentable manifestation of weakness and futility.
The Unemployed Insurance Bill has been before Committee, and the insurance com-
I do not think there
panies and friendly societies have succeeded in getting through an amendment enabling
them to administer the Act when passed; those of us on the Committee strongly opposed
this, as also did the Government, but the majority were against us.
has ever been a worse case of anti-Trade Union feeling than this; there was no attempt
to argue it, and though we show conclusively the only bodies who could adequately and
properly deal with the matter outside the Labour Exchanges, were the Trade Unions, it
was all in vain.
We made another effort this week to reverse the decision but failed, and then as a
protest the Labour members retired from the Committee. At the moment the impression
is that the Government will endeavour to reverse this decision on the report stage, but
it is an object lesson of the hostility towards Labour that exists, and which the further
we get away from the War will make itself manifest in the House as well as in the country.
The Representation of the People Bill introduced by the Labour Party which seeks
to extend the franchise to the basis of adult suffrage is being strenuously fought in Com-
mittee, all the resources of procedure being taken advantage of in order to defeat it. We
are continually told that by constitutional procedure through Parliament we must obtain
the changes necessary for the people, but how is that possible if the people as a whole have
no constitutional rights. It is the same old game that has been played for generations:
obtain power, and then use it to prevent anything in the way of change, for change is
fatal to vested interests; we extend education, but refuse to recognise the inevitable
eonsequence of same.
The recent debate on the cost of living was very disappointing, and it served but
to show that Mr. Asquith is not prepared to go any further than the Coalition Government
in respect of positive proposals to bring about a drastic reduction of the present abnormal
cost of living. Judged solely from the point of view of expression and delivery, the speech
was a parliamentary success, but the fact that the Prime Minister did not consider it
necessary to intervene in the debate, is sufficient proof that Mr. Asquith failed to submit
any new suggestions for the consideration of the House or the Government.
Mr. Clynes, who spoke for the Labour Party, made an excellent contribution, and
pointed out it was not sufficient to merely go on talking about increased production, there
were two other things to be considered and recognised, viz., that the increased production
of the workers would not be merely for the personal benefit of the primary owners and
controllers of wealth, and that the increased effort will not be followed by the punishment
of unemployment. While in the main appeals for increased output are directed to the
manual workers, they are receiving no more in wages than they are able to secure by their
organised efforts, and yet there are growing up great associations of commercial businesses
or trusts which are being formed artificially to raise prices to the public and thereby secure
enormous profits to themselves. A memorandum recently issued by the Board of Inland
Revenue shows that the additional profits made during the years of the War exceeded
£4,000,000,000, and that this sum was shared by the comparatively small number of 340,000
persons.
The Labour Party has again pressed the Secretary of State for War to grant a general
amnesty for those who have committed breaches of military discipline. In particular
they emphasised the special class of case of men who deserted from one unit and promptly
joined up with another. There is a substantial number of these cases, and examples have
been brought to the notice of the Party of such men who are afraid to return to their homes
because they are classed as deserters and warrants issued for their arrest.

On April 8th I was back at Stafford and held another meeting with the Branch Com
mittee. It was agreed that the Secretary and I continue our propaganda work among
employers previous to the meeting we were to have with them as a body.

CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETIES' POLITICAL WORK.

COMMANDER BELLAIRS asked the Chancellor of the Exchequer whether there are
any restrictions imposed on the use of the funds of co-operative societies for political
party purposes in connection with the immunity they enjoy from Income Tax ?
MR. BALDWIN: I would invite the attention of my hon. and gallant friend to the
provisions of Section 39 (4) of the Income Tax Act, 1918, under which a society registered
under the Industrial and Provident Societies Act, 1893, is entitled to exemption from
Income Tax under Schedules C and D, unless it sells to non-members and the number of
its shares are limited. The question of the Income Tax liability of co-operative societies
is dealt with in Section 12 of Part 5 of the Report of the Royal Commission on the Income
Tax, and if my hon. and gallant friend will refer to that Section of the Report he will
appreciate that the relief from Tax is grounded on the nature of the surpluses which arise
from the transaction of the societies, and is not connected with the manner of the dis-
tribution of those surpluses.
MAJOR MALONE: Is the hon. Gentleman aware that a large number of the members
of the co-operative societies object to their profits being used in this way, and can he say
whether the Law Officers of the Crown have been consulted as to the legality of the divi-
dends being dissipated ?
MR. BALDWIN: I have no doubt that something in connection with this matter will
come up for discussion in the course of the Financial Debate. — Parliamentary Debates,

SAD END.
KETTERING SHOE OFFICIAL'S SUICIDE ON THE LINE.
Illness and Delusions.
A pathetic story was told at the inquest, which Mr. J. T. Parker (county divisional
coroner) conducted in the waiting room of the Midland Railway Station at Isham on
Saturday afternoon, concerning the death of Mr. John Taylor, of Kettering, the well
known and esteemed trade union official whose shockingly mutilated body had been found
on the line close by.
Mr. George Wright, of Wellingborough, district controller, watched the case on behalf
of the Midland Railway Company, P.S. Jones and Parish Constable Waters, of Burton
Latimer, also being in attendance.
Harry Taylor, of 50, Broadway, Kettering, clothier's warehouseman, identified the
body as that of his father, whose full name was John James Summerley Taylor, and who
lived at the same address. Deceased was secretary to the Boot and Shoe Operatives'
Union, No. 2 Branch. His age was 57. Witness last saw him alive about 1.20 on Friday,
during the dinner-hour, when he was at home as usual. He (deceased) had an ulcerated
stomach, and that had caused him much trouble. During the past nine months, since
witness returned home from military service, he had appeared much quieter and more
depressed than he (witness) had formerly known him. The letter now produced by P.S.
Jones was in deceased's handwriting. It was dated March 26th, addressed to Mrs. Taylor,
and ran as follows:-
Dear Lizzie and all,-Cannot stand strain and worry any longer have had
nine years of it-life made unbearable. Bolshevik section up against me during the
past 12 months this after nearly 20 years' service.
Trust you and yours who have been of the best to me through life-will still
think of me and forgive me for the step I am about to take. Farewell.-JACK.
Witness-who was much overcome as the letter was read also identified the wallet
produced as belonging to his father.
The Coroner: Had he any money trouble at home?-Witness: No money trouble
at all.
No domestic quarrel at all?-No. There was no other illness in the family apart
rom his own. Witness attributed his unusual quietness and melancholy to his stomach
rouble.
George Chester, of 88, Nelson Street, Kettering, assistant secretary to the Boot and
hoe Union, said that he and deceased occupied adjoining offices in the same building.
n Friday evening a meeting was held, as usual, of the Union committee, at which deceased
nould have been present. As he did not attend, witness went to his house to enquire
bout him, and found he was not there. Witness then went to the place where deceased
ually had tea, and found that he had been there. He could, however, find no further
ace of him. Eventually he (witness) and one of the sons went to the Police Station,
d reported him as missing. The last witness saw of deceased was at 4.15, when he went
t for tea. He seemed as usual, except that for the past six months or so he had seemed
ach depressed-not himself at all. His accounts were absolutely in order. He had
the keys on his desk, and the usual amount of money was in the safe. He had been
official of the branch now for over 20 years.
The Coroner here read the above-mentioned letter, and Mr. Chester explained that new
ements (piecework, &c.) latterly coming into operation had caused the whole of the
cials an excessive amount of work and worry.
The Coroner: More since the war than during the war?-Witness: Oh, yes. During
past twelve months it had taken him (deceased) quite twice as long to do his work as
merly.
Questioned with regard to the "Bolshevik" allegation in the letter, Mr. Chester
hatically declared: "Nobody was 'up against him,' in any shape or form. I am
cive that was a delusion." Deceased had been awfully unwell-suffering from an
ated stomach-and that, witness knew, had greatly worried him.
Richard Poole, stationmaster, stated that at 6.10 that morning his attention was called
man lying on the line, close to the road bridge at the station, and in the parish of
on Latimer. The body was in three pieces, the head and one leg having been com-
-y severed from the trunk. They lay on the down fast line, and during the night a
Der of trains would have passed over the spot. Deceased had evidently been killed
train.

THE INTERNATIONAL LABOUR CONFERENCE.
WASHINGTON, D.C., December, roro.
It was our privilege, as visitors, to attend the International Labour Conference pro
vided for in the Covenant of the League of Nations.
In addition to studying the Conference, our instructions were to study and promote
the interests of the International Federation of Trade Unions.
The Conference was held in the Pan-American Buildings, Washington, D.C
opened on the 20th October. On the first day there were 32 countries represented, the
principal European exceptions being Germany, Austria, Hungary, and Russia. Owing
to representations made in London prior to the Conference Mr. G. N. Barnes specially
interviewed the Supreme Council in Paris, his object being to secure the removal of any
obstacles to the attendance in Washington of the delegates of the Central Powers.
American Embassy gave courteous and sympathetic assistance, and before the end of
September the restrictions imposed by the Treaty of Peace and the Covenant of the League
of Nations had been waived. In these circumstances it was confidently expected that the
German and Austrian representatives would be present. Unfortunately, their internal
difficulties were too great, and they were unable to make the journey.
The absence of nations which were certain to be serious competitors for the world's
business was regrettable, both from the moral and material point of view. Their presence
might have helped the healing of the world's wounds and the closing of the breaches
between the peoples. Not being present they could claim liberty to adopt, to modify,
or to reject any of the findings of the Conference in respect of wages, hours, or conditions
of Labour. That they do not regard these findings as binding may be inferred from their
attitude towards piecework, as illustrated at the International Conference of the Garment
Workers, which was recently held in Amsterdam. There they frankly argued that piece-
work offered their only means of industrial regeneration.
In fairness to these countries it must be admitted that they cannot pay the debts
incurred unless every individual within them produces very much more than is required
for his own maintenance and the maintenance of his dependents.
Much more serious than the absence of the Germans and Austrians was the official
abstention of the United States of America. Taking into consideration the object of the
Conference and the importance of the subjects to be discussed, it was more than unfortunate
that the country responsible, through its own President, for issuing the invitations to the
Conference was not officially represented. Unofficially, Secretary W. B. Wilson and Mr.
Samuel Gompers attended.
The attitude of the American people towards the Conference was reflucted by the
American Press, which, after the first day, gave only limited consideration and space to
the proceedings. Generally speaking, there was a courteous suppression of actually
hostile sentiments, but there were many who doubted the practical utility of the Con-
ference and not a few who doubted the bona-fides of those who persisted in precipitating
the Conference upon an unready community.
Not all the Americans suppressed their opinions in order to maintain the national
reputation for courtesy. Senators Sherman, Reed, and La Follette all gave utterance
to pungent criticisms. The former, speaking at New York a few days after the Conference
opened, said that the delegates had been dumped there from all parts of the world, that
they were Radicals (Reds) working for no good purpose, and they were bent on fanning
into a flame the discontent in America. If he had the power he would deport the Inter-
national Labour Conference. It was no time for such a Conference. They had enough
stormy petrels in their own country without having the Internationals to swamp them.
Americans were often kind enough to say that Senator Sherman only represented
himself. Our inquiries, however, led us to believe that, while the language used might be
typical only of Senator Sherman, the thought behind was the thought of the great mass
of the American people. They saw no advantage to the world or themselves in discussing
what they regarded as platitudes, and they feared the effect of the discussions upon the
minds and activities of those who in America are hostile to American methods and institu-
tions.
The active opposition to the Conference may be to a great extent attributed to partisan
politics, because there are men in the Republican Party who feel that to the extent they
can belittle the Peace Treaty and its machinery to that extent they can weaken the position
of the Democartic Party and that of the President.
This situation could, and ought to, have been foreseen by the British Government,
and appears to justify our conclusion that the Government, in view of the opposition of
the Senate to the Treaty of Peace and to the action of President Wilson, made a great
mistake in pushing the arrangements for the Conference and in temporarily financing it.

such cannot be large ones; for instance, Card Dressers have every man in society,
but do not number 100, but they are very important men.
Your Union was invited to take part in this Federation, but declined. Our
Federation now meets National Federated Employers on all wage questions, and con
sidering number of workers in the industry probably covers a larger proportion
workers than your own Union. My own Union at present time has nine full-time
officials. Information from A. HEADLAND, General President.
We are arriving at a position that we should link up with other societies. It is a
debatable point as to whether a great fund with no resistance is better than a great resist-
ance and no funds. We should be so well organised as to resist the opposite forces. I
know we cannot be as big as the Triple Alliance but there the miners when they struck
did not make themselves felt until they linked up with the dockers and railwaymen. If
we linked up with the Leather Federation we should be better off. We as workers should
go along this line and it would be in the right direction of one Union for the workers and
would be better for internationalism. I ask the delegates to refer this paragraph back
so that the Council can see the wisdom of linking up with these societies.
THE CHAIRMAN: What is their membership ?
MR. J. JEFFS (Northampton): The letter does not say, but it was thrown at us that

THE GENERAL SECRETARY: We are not at all, nor have we ever been, by the wildest

was moved to London, always placed at their disposal my private office at Leicester for
their meetings. We have given them practical experience and some help in their federation
business, because I know something about it. We have to bear in mind, and the point
was raised two years ago when you decided for the time being we could not alter our con-
stitution, that the rule says:
"The Union shall consist of any number of males and females working at the
boot and shoe trade, organised into branches in the United Kingdom of Great Britain
and Ireland."
No one has given notice to alter the constitution, and we have therefore no opposition,
but we have done all we could to help these people to meet with success in their efforts.
We should also bear in mind if we did carry out this amalgamation, we should have to
scrap all our agreements and start afresh, and the Council are bound to consider these
questions from the standpoint of the well-being of the whole as compared with the
federating up of a partially allied industry. They are the only reasons why we have
not gone into this federation, but we have been in a position and have shewn our fraternal
support to all sections.

MR. G. ABBOTT (Leeds): We are behind many large societies. Many unions send

the votes in the workshops. It would do away with a lot of sentiment. We know votes
have been declared null and void because of men voting in workshops. If you want to

Piecework.
MR. T. RABBITT (Wellingborough): In our district we are trying to fix up piecework

receiving less than the minimum wage. Clause 3 should be deleted.
THE CHAIRMAN: The Agreement is very intelligible to us and we have almost worn
it threadbare by giving information upon it. As I explained yesterday the resolution
was only agreed to where a man deliberately refused to earn his money, and I don't know

Parliamentary Representative's Report.
HOUSE OF COMMONS,
WESTMINSTER.
FELLOW DELEGATES, 13th May, 1920.
In presenting this, my first report to Conference, I do so with the feeling that politics to-day are of more importance than ever before to those whom we represent, and great as the task appeared before one got to close grips with the work, since that time the task that is before the Labour movement seems to be greater still. There is so much dead weight to lift, and the united effort to achieve it is not always forthcoming.
The House of Commons is called the Mother of Parliaments, it is the parent of them all, and necessarily and naturally because of its great age, much of its machinery is out of date, much of its procedure is antiquated, and does not lend itself readily for the purposes we have in view. It is slow, it is overloaded, it is in many ways cumbersome, but notwithstanding all this, it still is the constitutional expression of the public will, it is a channel through which we must seek our reforms; and not only seek them but work for and obtain them.
To many it appears to have served its purpose, and ought to give way to other methods, and I would at once admit that to a small minority like the Labour Party, it does not give much chance. It has been called a sounding board for the country, but our difficulty is we have not the medium by which to convey the sound, there is sound conveyed, but not that which is favourable to us, nor which is correct, and this brings us to the point, that a powerful and influential Press is a necessary adjunct to the Party in the House.
But with all its shortcomings, and the difficulties that exist for minorities, it is well to remember it is an excellent place for, and serves wonderfully well the interests that dominate there, and as it serves them to-day, it can be made to serve us to-morrow, and when the people realise that other political bodies no matter by what name they are known, are, on the questions that really matter up against labour every time and all the time, and when having realised this they use the franchise as a means of achieving their emancipation, then the House of Commons will be a much better and more useful institution. It largely depends upon who controls the machine as to the results obtained.
The interests represented in the House shew themselves in no unmistakable fashion whenever any attempt is made to trespass upon their preserves. It is


---
Here is the text from the image:

82

not often this takes place, but when it does, then even their pledges to Lloyd George and Bonar Law do not prevent them opposing the proposals of the Government.

As I have said it is not often this happens, but on the Transport Bill danger was scented it contained too much of the germs of co-operation, as against our good old friend competition. It also occurred on the Electricity Bill, and here at once became apparent, the impossibility of real reconstruction with the present House of Commons. To the Labour Party, these two measures while not going so far as we would wish, yet did proceed upon right lines.
A real co-ordinated system of transport is vital to this country, it must be complete, not partial, it must be nationally controlled, and then to be consistent it must belong to the nation.

This measure was most strenuously fought, every part of our system of transport that was a good paying concern was to be left to private enterprise those that shew a loss the nation could take over. The net result was the Bill was mutilated and robbed of its best features. So with regard to Elec tricity. There is no nation to whom economical central production of motive power is more important than to ourselves. Large generating stations, con- suming the vast quantities of uncommercial coal that we have, with distributing stations all over the country, could give to any industry and any house in the country cheap electric power and light, and with its cleanliness would help towards healthier conditions for the whole people. But here again it looked too much like service, and not business, and destruction was aimed at, and where the Commons failed the Lords succeeded.

The Labour Party strongly supported these measures and more than once by their support saved the Government from defeat in Committee. Our policy has been to support that which is good, amend that which is indifferent and oppose that which is bad.

The Ministry of Health Act now upon the Statute Book, should help in many ways. It was a matter of regret to the Labour Party that consistent with its passage there was no measure for the reform of the Poor Law. The Party felt that to saddle the new Ministry with the administration of the Poor Law would be a handicap. A Clause was inserted in the Bill, however, declaring that the administration of the Poor Law was only transferred pending a measure of complete reform and pledges were given by the Government to that effect.

The Party has strongly and persistently opposed compulsory MILITARY SERVICE, and the fact that it no longer exists is largely due to the efforts of Labour. The Minister for War tried to obtain in the Army Annual Bill last year one of the worst of the regulations from "Dora," which shews most conclusively that militarism is rooted firmly in their minds, and again Labour by its opposition was largely responsible for its withdrawal.

On HOUSING the Party has tried its best to obtain measures that will meet the needs of the people, but the Government by their patchy methods, and their great concern for private enterprise, coupled with the failure of the financial side of their proposals, still leave this question a matter of grave concern to the nation.

The "patriotism" of the wealthy is clearly shewn upon this question. local authorities cannot raise the money they need; great authorities like the London County Council and Birmingham Council fail to raise their loan. Why? Is it because there is no money? The capital that is being asked for by various Limited Liability Companies is being raised, some being over subscribed. How is it then we cannot get the money for housing? Because the interest offered by the companies is higher: 6 per cent. may be high for housing schemes, but when 8 per cent. is offered for cumulative preference shares, and huge

dividends are being paid upon ordinaries, then the housing of the people,

In FOREIGN AFFAIRS there is no clearing up of the dark war clouds. If
there is a break in them one day the next brings them back with greater intensity.
Russia is still the cockpit. One is entitled to ask why? Is it the conduct of
the Soviets, or is it the principle upon which they rest, that earn them the
hatred of the other nations. Militarism and capitalist domination die hard,
it will fight while there is the slightest chance, and to-day they attack Russia
because they know that if once that great nation displays to the rest of the
world, a government free from the lust of conquest, whose only desire is peace,
then the opposing forces will collapse in other countries and the day of rank
and privilege will have passed.
Our own Government is not free from responsibility in this matter-they
have supported actively the factions that seek to destroy Soviet Russia, and
after a year of wasted effort, after a wicked sacrifice of human life and treasure,
the Prime Minister told us he knew a year before it was useless and bound to
fail; and while all this goes on our troubles increase and intensify. Of what
avail is the cry for more production, when vast areas are carrying on their
policy of destruction. Nations are interdependent. How much we are needing
the goods that Russia used to send us, and how much she is wanting those
that we produce. This can be applied to ourselves, in the centres of our trade
that produces men's and youths' goods we have depression. Boots we are told,
are what the Russians need; they have the timber, we want houses; they
have dairy produce, we want it; Siberian butter is better than margarine,
and how can we hope to break the ring of prices while the products of other
nations are denied us? This question of foreign policy is most important,
and just as we must have co-operation at home so there must be between the
nations of the world.
The PEACE TREATIES do not give us great hope in that direction. I voted
against the Austrian Treaty because I believe its conditions are wrong, and
until that and the previous one with Germany is revised, there is no chance of
a settled Europe, and peaceful settlement is what is needed to-day.
It is no good saying we are better off than others. This country is still
unsettled, and while prices continue to rise, necessitating fresh agitations for
increased wages, we are but carrying the problems on to a higher plane and the
higher they go the greater the danger of a collapse that may shatter the whole
fabric of State. It is the duty of the Government to stabilise conditions as

have been audited and the Auditor's Certificate for the period appears at the end of the
analysis of accounts for your perusal. The accounts for the year ending December, 1918,
are in the hands of the Auditors, and the valuation of the Society is also proceeding. We

the 1911 Act, amounting to £790 18s. 8d. This Section is now abolished by the Amend-

appended Analysis will shew more clearly the balances relating to each particular Benefit.
The amount included under the item Sickness Benefit, includes payments to members
suffering illness as the result of war injuries, the whole of which is to be repaid to Societies

during the year under review. If our estimate proves to be correct the balance shown
at the foot of the Analysis will be increased by the amount of recoupment.

we estimate will show an approximate balance of £619 25. 8d. Should this estimation
prove correct, the balance of this account at December 31st, 1919, will stand at

gratulated on an Administration Account which will compare favourably with any other

MR. E. BROWN (Northampton No. 2) said: It seems to me there must have been
some difficulty in transfers due I suppose to the transitory period between the removal of
the office, and as there seems to be such delay can Mr. Murby give us his reason?

MR. J. W. MURBY (Insurance Manager): The question of dislocation by the removal
of the office has nothing whatever to do with it. Until the close of the war transfers were
in abeyance and since then transfers have been allowed by Act of Parliament. One
society refuses to allow the member to transfer; you don't like to lose your member.
I am however unaware of any great number of transfers outstanding. We have to deal
with the society, then the member, and it is a difficult position. Transfers can only take
place at the end of each half-year so that if you give notice now it cannot take place until
January, 1921.

MR. A. H. FOLKARD, J,P. (Norwich No. 2): Can you tell us why there is a difference

Afternoon Session.
MR. T. F. RICHARDS presided when the Conference resumed at 2 p.m., and the
General Secretary reported all the delegates in their places.
Discussion on Item 67 was resumed, and MR. W. PITTS (Northampton) suggested

MR. F. GOULD (Midsomer Norton): I am surprised that some of these delegates have

is one appeal I have to make and that is to allow the delegates to the Conference all to be
elected.
MR. J. WESCOE (Leeds): This is the first Conference I have attended for 12 years,
and the delegates who come under the rule regarding branch officers are those who have
to administer them. After the experience of the last conference I attended I thought
it was wise to stand down and let other delegates go. It was a wise decision when a majority
of the delegates altered the rule seeing the branch officers have to interpret the rule. I
say I would prefer to stand nomination every time in the ordinary way. I am not afraid
to allow my name to go forward in the ordinary way, because at least 99 per cent. of the
permanent officials would be elected. I shall be sorry if this resolution is carried.
MR. R. HARRIS (Leicester No. 2) said he could not accept the resolution, but upon the
question being put to the vote there voted for 46, against 65.

MR. C. BLEAKLEY (Council Member) seconded: We have a Branch Secretary in

MR. F. C. JEX (Norwich): If the logic of the argument used before has the same

Annual Conferences.
The Standing Orders Committee at this stage submitted the following recommendation on Rule 60, the same being agreed to:
"A National Conference of Delegates from each and every District in the Union shall meet every year for three days at the Seat of Government to deal with the general policy of the Union, the expense to be borne by the Union.
"Every third year the Conference shall meet for six days, and deal, in addition to general policy, with alterations in the constitution and rules of the Union."

runner a long way behind.

SLACKNESS OF TRADE.
MEMBERS SUSPENDED FROM WORK.
Owing to the present depression of trade, brought about by many causes, amongst them being the adverse exchanges of money and consequent restriction of purchases, members are in large numbers having to stand off from employment in many instances for a week at a time. We have fully considered the question and have decided as a temporary measure for a period of three months from this date, June 21st, 1920 when the matter will be reconsidered to allow those members who are unemployed for a whole week at a time to declare upon the Unemployment Fund-it being understood that they are entitled financially to declare upon such Fund-to meet the position of members who are thus suspended from work. It must be distinctly understood that they will call at the Branch Office each morning and sign a paper stating they are not in work of any kind, and then at the end of the week, if not having had work as stated above for a whole week, they must sign the out-of-work book for the six days before payment is made to any member. ALL HOLIDAYS EXEMPTED. No member will be allowed to declare upon the Fund during the holiday week unless previously unemployed.

KETTERING.

Arising out of the resolution which appeared in our May issue, a meeting was held at 7, Tavistock Square, London, W.C. 1, on Thursday, the 10th inst., under the chairmanship of Alderman Frank Sheppard, O.B.E., J.P. After a full day's sitting, the following resolution was proposed by Mr. Owen Parker, J.P., seconded by Mr. T. F. Richards, and carried unanimously :
"That in the opinion of this Conference the words ' until the last pay day in June' in the undertaking given by Mr. A. H. Bryan are unnecessary, since they appear to limit the provisions of Clause 2 of the 1914-1919 Agreements, and further the Kettering Boot Manufacturers' Association be asked to see this undertaking shall have full effect."

A copy of the resolution has been sent to the Kettering Association.
We have always claimed that if the workpeople put in 48 hours in the factory at the employers' request they are entitled, unless working under a permit, to be guaranteed at any rate the minimum wage applicable to their operation.

MR. W. TOWNLEY'S RESIGNATION.

We regret to have to report that Mr. W. Townley, Council member for the No. 5 District, has felt bound to resign from the Council, such resignation being due to the fact that he thought a formal ballot vote should have been taken upon the recent interim agreement. For reasons which have been already explained we did not consider it necessary for this to be done, but Mr. Townley felt unable to continue his connection with the Council, and we regret the reason for his severance.

SEVERE BLOW TO THE UNION.

DEATH OF TWO OF OUR COLLEAGUES.
We have to report with unfeigned sorrow and regret the death of
two of our colleagues from the Council during the month :-

THOMAS ORTON (Leicester).
COUNCILLOR H. SIMMONS, J.P. (Stafford).

This is unprecedented in the history of the Union that two members
of the Council lay dead at the same time. It is indeed a great blow to us,
and will be a loss to the Union that two such valued and experienced
officers should have passed away. Both of them have for many years
past carried out work of very great value both to the Union and the
community as a whole; the aim and object of both has been to as far as
possible assist the workers to a higher and better state of living. To
the relatives of both of our departed colleagues we have tendered in your
name the sincere regrets and sympathy and high appreciation of their
work, and we can only hope that the esteem with which our late colleagues
were held will be some consolation to those who are left. We were
represented at both funerals. Further references appear on pages 434-436.

BRANCH REPORTS.
BRISTOL AND KINGSWOOD No. 2. We regret having to report that
trade is bad; very few of our members are making full time, and have not felt
the advantages which the last Agreement gave them. We are glad that we
resisted the proposal of subsidised labour for the closing department. This
was brought forward a few months ago and supported by the manufacturers
and some local Union officials, and had it not been for the vigilance of a few
we should have had probably 200 girls drafted into our factories and subsidised
by the Government, but we said it had to be a unanimous acceptance for it
to be put into operation, and although we were outvoted the scheme fell through.
We want our women members to realise that, bad as their position is through
shortness of work, it might have been worse if we had not watched their interest.
The decision of Conference to raise the contributions from gd. to IS. has been
received with a deal of disappointment. Bad trade is responsible for the
pessimism that at present prevails, but we hope that things will be much
brighter in September when the increased payment becomes due. Our present
position, and we cannot think that our members won't rise to the occasion,
position has been won by years of honest endeavour to improve the operatives'
even if it means some little sacrifice
BELFAST. - We regret to report that trade has been very quiet during
the past month, we sincerely hope that it will soon brighten up again; we also
regret that our sick list is still heavy, and trust that all on the sick list will soon
be restored to health. We have tendered an application to the Masters'
Association on behalf of the Repairers for an advance of 50 per cent. on present
piece rates, and that the time rates be increased to 2s. 6d. per hour; we are
awaiting the masters' reply. In reference to the new supplementary rates for
those employed in the manufacturing end, while some of the manufacturers
have conceded the same others are waiting for the Conference between the
Irish Manufacturers' Association and representatives of our Union. We hope
the Council will arrange for the Conference at an early date. Might we suggest
that in future when the Council is making a demand for an advance of wages
or improved conditions of working to the Federated Association of Masters,
that they should at the same time notify the Irish Manufacturers' Association,
so that the plea put forward of having no representative at the Conference or
of not being advised of what was taking place until all had been settled could
not be put forward.
EDINBURGH. Our out-of-work sheet is now a clean one, but sickness

the earliest opportunity, but would like other Scottish Branches to act along
with them. The Edinburgh Branch wishes to thank the Scottish Branches
who gave financial assistance to help to entertain the delegates to Conference.
There are some of the new workers who are not earning on piece rates the
amount equivalent to the 20 per cent. on time rates, so that we are trying to get
a meeting with the employer to get the prices raised to meet the case. There
are some employers who still think that piece-workers are not entitled to this
percentage, but it is up to the employees to educate them on this point. We in
Edinburgh at time of writing are still waiting on a settlement, i.e., square stuff,
from Wages Trade Board, which we hope will be soon. The price for patching
is causing some trouble, nearly every place giving a different definition as to
what is to be paid to workmen for putting on the patch. The finishers think
that a Quantity Statement for Repairing would improve their conditions of
labour, they would certainly know at end of week that their work would have
to be paid for. We hear on every side that the A.U.C.E. are still busy organising

LIVERPOOL. Trade in this district is fairly good, but we still have members on the sick list despite the change in the weather conditions. We have been expecting trouble in the form of a strike but wiser counsels have prevailed. We note by the trade press that the General President at the Conference at Edinburgh in Whit-week is reported to have said that the financial and probationary membership is 100,443, funds £367,000. The women working in the industry were 46 per cent. of the whole membership. Referring to the strike policy, he was one of those who hoped they had finished with that. They had experience of that, and they had seen the methods by which other people got the best and good things of this life. They did not do it by striking but by the more subtle methods of manipulation which included hypnotism and mesmerism. The time had arrived when the industrial classes should have a hand in similar methods. We also note that a motion to raise the weekly contributions from ninepence to one shilling was carried. We hope the Council in adjusting the same will not forget that the Branches could do with an allowance of at least another penny per member weekly to meet local current expenses and thereby relieve the Branch Secretary of his anxiety to make ends meet.
Further, we note the recommendation that a voluntary sickness benefit scheme be adopted was agreed to by 62 votes to 42. Approved members will also note an increase in contributions and benefits in July under the National Insurance Act, 1920. Leaflets will be issued in due course, which all members ought to obtain from their Approved Society.

LONDONDERRY. - Trade is dull in the Repairing end.

MANCHESTER. - Trade very quiet, it having fallen off considerably during the month. We had Mr. McCarthy here again re the New Agreement; we visited Greggs', Libsteins', Frankenburgs', and Owens', and got advances for our members in each case. At our Monthly Meeting £3 was granted to the Widow of the late Secretary at Kettering, Mr. J. Taylor, and hope other Branches will contribute to the fund.

MIDSOMER NORTON. - Sickness for the past month has been rather heavy, and the continued trade depression has added to the gloom of the month. Nor is there at the time of writing any prospect of trade revival. Instead of becoming unemployed and depleting the funds the workpeople have nominally remained in employment and taken a share in such work as was given out on the particular firms. In view of this, we think the Council should be free, "and we have no doubt but that they are free," to assist the districts to a far greater extent than has been done by grants in aid to help the trade in this district through the most depressing period that has been known. Over a hundred pounds per week are needed to relieve cases of dire need, and care has to be taken even with this amount to ensure the scantiest minimum of existence and thus ensure some little good. The Miners have come splendidly to our aid and they naturally ask, "What does your own Union do?" Other trades and certain individuals are helping to the best of their ability, but after all, this is mere patching; the foundations of our economic life are bad, and we must all seek to learn the lessons of the present and apply our powers to the remedies we believe are necessary.

PORTSMOUTH.-The Biennial Conference has been held and gone again, and the question the ordinary member asks is how far am I affected by the decisions arrived at by the delegates. We are speaking from a Repairer's point of view, and we are wondering if repairers are likely to receive a liberal share of attention from the Executive of the Union, or are we to be allowed to run along behind the main army, and become obscure in the dust raised by that big force. We heard five or six weeks ago of District Committees being set up by the Trade Board, and we are still in the dark as to how they are to be elected. Who selected our representatives on the Trade Board? Was it Repairers or representatives of makers? Have Repairers a representative on the Executive of the Union, and how many Repairers are there in our membership? These are questions we would like answered, as locally our members are getting restless, and the A.U.C.E. is not asleep. It is now two years and eight months since this Branch was formed, and we have not had a visit from one member of the E.C. What are the experiences and opinions of other Branches who cater for Repairers? We had hopes of seeing the South strongly organised, but we are left to ourselves. A scheme was put forward by this Branch some time ago to link up the various towns south of London, but it was turned down or put in the waste paper basket. This is not biassed criticism, but just a plain statement of the temperament of our members here, and possibly other mem- bers are thinking the same. Perhaps other Branches will take this matter up and then something may be done that will make the National more attractive and so secure more members which we desire. (It must be remembered that considerable work has been done for the Repairers by the Trade Board, and our General President is Chairman of the Workmen's side of the Board.-E.L.P., Gen. Sec.)

DEATH OF COUNCILLOR H. SIMMONS, J.P., OF STAFFORD.
Thirty years' association with Boot Operatives' Union.

The placing of the Union Jack half-mast at the Guildhall on Monday conveyed the
sad news to the townspeople of Stafford of the death of Councillor Henry Simmons, J.P.,
who for the past thirty years had been officially connected with the local branch of the
National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives. His demise caused a general feeling of
regret in the borough, his wise and considered treatment of labour problems and his sound
judgment and advice in municipal matters having commended him to all classes of the
community.
The deceased, who was in his 64th year, had not enjoyed good health for some years, and
a bronchial affection was aggravated by cardiac trouble. His death was unexpected,
however, as he was out walking the previous afternoon with his eldest son, Mr. H..
usual. He passed peacefully away about 9.30 o'clock whilst in bed on Monday morning,
Simmons, of the Corporation Gas Department, and seemed in much better health than
the cause of death being heart failure.

Photo]
The late COUNCILLOR H. SIMMONS, J.P.
[Pearce, Stafford.

The late Mr. Simmons came to Stafford in 1875, the year after the birth of the National
Union of Boot Operatives in the town. He began work in one of the local boot factories,
at the time when piecework largely obtained throughout the trade, and when it was the
Simmons worked for two or three different firms in the course of his career, and gained
thorough knowledge of the trade. He was always ready to advance the legitimate claims
to as
branch of the Union in 1890 was unanimous. He continued to hold this position for 17
of the operatives for better wages and conditions, and his election as president of the local
ten years ago he took over his duties and resigned the presidentship. It was Mr. Simmons'
years, during thr secretaryship of the late Mr. Alfred Hammond, and on the latter's death
in the boot trade in Stafford, and this fact speaks volumes for the tact and discretion as
proud and justifiable boast that during his Union secretaryship no strike had taken place


---
well as sound judgment he displayed in the handling of disputes, and particularly in his
dealings with the employers, which were always of an amicable character. He was honoured
by being elected vice-chairman of the local Conciliation Arbitration Board for the shoe
trade, and served on the Local Advisory Committee in connection with the Employment
Exchange. The outstanding feature of Mr. Simmons's labours in connection with the
boot trade was the organisation of the female workers and the establishment of a minimum
wage. The valuable services which Mr. Simmons rendered to the Shoe Operatives' Union
locally were officially recognised about six years ago, when he was elected on the Executive
Council of that body in the place of Mr. Moreton, of Wolverhampton.

He had served 15 years on the Town Council the first period dating from 1808 to
1904, and the second from 1911 to the time of his death. He rendered valuable service
on several committees, and especially the Housing Committee, of which he was vice-chair-
man. He took the keenest interest in the housing question, and successfully sought re-
election on it nine years ago. The block of artizans' dwellings in Crooked Bridge-road
were erected in 1901 when he was chairman of the Housing Committee, a position now held
by Alderman Bostock. Mr. Simmons was a member of the provisional Insurance Committee
for the county, and he also served on the Military Service Tribunal for the borough, the
War Savings Association, and the Food Control Committee. In January, 1918, he was
made a magistrate for the borough on the reccommendation of the Board of Trade, the
appointment being looked upon as the reward of his long and devoted service to the trade
union movement.

The deceased leaves a widow and grown-up family of three sons (two of whom served
in the Army during the war) and two daughters.

TOWN COUNCIL TRIBUTE.

At a meeting of the Town Council on Tuesday, the Mayor (Dr. Blumer) made feeling
reference to the loss which the town and the boot trade had sustained by Councillor Simmon's
death. Elected to that Council as a representative of Labour, their late colleague never
lost sight of the fact that the interests of his party were in his keeping. He also showed
very marked interest in and the great sympathy he had always for the poorer classes; he
was also one of the pioneers of the movement which had for its object the improvement of the
housing conditions in Stafford. When he (Dr. Blumer) first brought the question of housing
forward many years ago, he looked upon Councillor Simmons as one of the props upon which
he could always rely for support in that movement. In his work on the Council the deceased
combined the double obligation he owed to his party and the ratepayers at large in a
peculiarly tactful and straightforward manner, and his sound judgment on Labour questions
were of great value on committees. Speaking of Councillor Simmons's labours on the
Military Service Tribunal, the Mayor said he always brought sound and unbiased judgment
to bear upon the cases, his intimate knowledge of factory conditions being of great value.
Dr. Blumer concluded by moving a resolution deeply regretting Councillor Simmons's
death, placing on record the Council's appreciation of his valuable services as a member
of that body, and expressing sincere sympathy with the family in their sad bereavement.

Alderman Bostock, who supported the motion, bore testimony to the great loss which
the shoe trade had sustained by the death of Councillor Simmons, who was always essentially
fair-minded, open to hear the other side, and desirous of doing justice both to those he
represented and those with whom he was negotiating.

The resolution was carried in silence, the members rising in their places.
