(Wesleyan) officiating. The mourners were Messrs. H. B. Percy and Arthur Simmons
(sons), Mr. C. Harroll, of Sidcup (son-in-law), and Mr. H. Davies (Stafford). The Mayor

LIGHT ON HIGH SODA PRICES.
Revelations before Profits Tribunal.
Revelations regarding soda prices were made at to-day's meeting of the tribunal
appointed by the Central Committee on Profiteering to hear allegations regarding whole-
sale firms. A complaint was investigated against Messrs. J. Manger & Son Limited,
of Kingsland, E.
A retail grocer declared Messrs. Manger and Son charged him IIS. for 112 lb. of soda
when the price fixed by the big manufacturers was 5s. 6d.
120 per cent. Profit.
A representative of Messrs. A. G. Collins and Brother, Cardiff, said that they had
supplied respondents with washing soda.
The chairman said that on some of the soda handled by the Cardiff firm a profit of
approximately 120 per cent. was made on the purchase price. He asked what was the
justification for such a high standard of profit in Cardiff.
Witness. We had to take a risk.
The Chairman. Then with your eyes open you went into a gamble.
Witness. Well, it was a bit of a gamble. We thought the stuff was wanted for
export.
The Chairman. The artificial forcing up of the price of soda appears to be spread
all over the country?
Witness. It is quite general.
"The Noble Army."
Witness denied a suggestion that in February the firm sold soda at a small profit
because it had not then occurred to them to " join the noble army of profiteers." (Laughter.)
The chairman said the tribunal were satisfied Messrs. J. Manger and Son had not
attempted to make an unreasonable profit, and the complaint would be dismissed.
It was clear that there was in existence a widespread gambling conspiracy on the
part of merchants and others to take advantage of the shortage of supplies in order
to force up to an outrageous height the price of all the household soda they could
lay their hands on.
The great bulk of the washing soda used in this country was made by Messrs. Brunner,
Mond and Company and the United Alkali Company, who had honourably declined to
take advantage of their position, and had maintained their normal price of £5 1os. a ton.
The Real Monopolists.
The people who were responsible for the enormous inflation of price were the specu-
lators and gamblers, who had doubtless inspired the inaccurate, misleading, and mischievous
allegations regarding monopolists and profiteering in order to cloak their own evil doings.
The evidence in this case would be referred to the Complaints Committee of the Pro-
fiteering Act Department, who had power to refer the matter to the Board of Trade, who
could initiate a prosecution. The names of other firms who had demanded prices ranging

have anything to do with the Act; such clause not having been deleted, the

"That this Congress declares its emphatic opposition to the Govern-
ment Unemployment Bill in so far as it makes provision for the adminis-
tration of unemployment benefits by Friendly Societies and others.
Further, we instruct the Trades Union Congress Parliamentary
Committee to act in accordance with the circular issued to affiliated

to have anything to do with the Act unless the objectionable clause is

This must be taken to mean not merely the administration of the Act.
but instructions will be issued to members NOT to allow any deductions from
their wages for unemployment purposes. On this matter instructions will be
issued shortly when the Parliamentary Committee of the Trade Union Congress
have agreed upon a general procedure to be adopted.

THE LABOUR PARTY CONFERENCE
has also been held since the issue of our last Report, and here again a report

AVERAGE DEATH OF BOOT OPERATIVES.
Owing to a certain statement made recently regarding the average death
of boot operatives, an examination has been made of the deaths recorded in
the January Report; excluding the males who died on active service, the
report deals with 196 deaths, which gives an average age at death of 44-63
years. Of 77 females dealt with, the average age is 45.22 years.

FIVE-WEEK MONTH.
There being five Saturdays during this month, Secretaries are asked to
make up their returns and pay for the same accordingly.

MONTHLY RETURNS.
We feel bound once again to call the serious attention of Branch Secretaries
to the fact that the FIFTEENTH day of each month is the LATEST day for
returns to reach the General Secretary. Last month many returns were late.
Branches failed to send off their returns to reach the Central Office by the
15th of the month, and this tends to upset the organisation of the work in the
General Secretary's Office. We trust in future every Branch Secretary will
endeavour to get in his returns as soon as is possible after the month (or five
weeks as the case may be) ends, and NOT to wait until the latest date for
them to reach the Office; and before sending them to see that they are in
order and properly signed.

REPORT OF THE AUDITOR.

I beg to report that I have examined the Receipts, Counterfoils
Vouchers and Bank Books, together with the various Account Books for
the Sick, Trade, Fidelity and Political Funds of the Union.
The total increase in the funds under the direct control of the Head
Office is £23,920 17s. 11d. above the funds in hand in December last, the
grand total of the Central Office funds now standing at £292.635 11s. 8d.,
as against £268,714 13s. 9d., this despite the heavy call on the Out-of-
Work Fund, which has meant an additional expenditure of £8,148 1s. 2d.
above the amount spent in the previous half-year.
I tender my thanks to the General Secretary and the Central Office
Staff for the explicit explanation given to my queries, and testify to the
careful, efficient and able manner in which the books are kept, having
regard to the great amount of detail required.
The whole of the Deeds have been examined which are shown in the
Balance Sheet, and I have to report that they are all in order and intact.
The only addition since my last audit is the Debenture Share
Certificate for your investment in the "Daily Herald."
I certify the accounts to be correct and in accordance with law.
J. B. B. ROBERTSON,
Dated 14th July, 1920.
241, Uppingham Road, Leicester.

GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.

FELLOW MEMBERS,
The most important event to my mind has been the Special Trades Union Congress at the Central Hall, Westminster, when two resolutions of great importance were carried. The first dealt with the Irish question, calling for a truce by all belligerents. a withdrawal of the troops from Ireland, and the setting up of an Irish Parliament with full Dominion powers and adequate protection for Ministers. We all supported that. The second resolution read as follows:-
" That this Congress protests against the British military domination of Ireland, and demands the withdrawal of all British troops from that country, and demands the cessation of the production of munitions of war destined to be used against Ireland and Russia.
" In case the Government refuses these demands, we recommend a general down tools policy, and call on all the trade unions here represented to carry out this policy. each according to its own constitution, by taking a ballot of its members or otherwise."
The majority of us supported that resolution.
Speaking for myself, because we had promised many of our members that they should have the right to express their opinion on the matter, and although the resolution asks for the same to be recommended, I certainly could not recommend such a course. Direct Action at the ballot box will to my mind secure the best and most speedy results and will be attained just as quickly. We, as a community, are prepared to choose the representatives of Labour in place of the representatives of other parties, whose whole being is diametrically opposed to the common ownership and control of the means of life.
MELTON MOWBRAY. On the 17th ult., I went to Melton Mowbray and met the firm of Messrs. Smith, Faire & Co., regarding the new terms of settlement and conditions of working.
SHEPSHED. On the 18th I went to Shepshed and had a good meeting of the operatives. Owing to bad trade things are not as bright as expected. Two of the firms are carrying out our national conditions of employment to the letter, whilst the other firm feel the operatives are not doing their best to assist them in bringing about successful results. I am of the opinion that in a very short time Shepshed will be in a satisfactory condition.
COUNCIL MEETING. On the 20th and 21st ult., the Monthly Council Meeting was held, when we considered the decisions of the Edinburgh Conference and preparations were made for the alteration of the rules.
LABOUR PARTY CONFERENCE. On the 22nd ult. I went to the Labour Party Conference at Scarborough, where we stayed until the 25th. Several great and important features stood out at this Conference. One was the feeling of the movement that it would be unwise to join the third International until at least all countries were in a more stable condition, and to know what methods such an International would advise the workers of the world to adopt. The subject of self-determination came up, and one delegate claimed that self-determination meant that every section of the community had a government of its own, whilst the other section would fall back on the older idea which has been universally adopted by organised workmen throughout the world that the majority rule. How far that has been successful we have only to look at our unfortunate neighbours in Ireland, and although there was a majority for the National Party as led by Mr. Redmond, Home Rule has never been granted, although clamoured for by a majority for so many, many years. The other important feature was the domination of the proletariat. Personally, I am bound to say this copying of languages from Russia may mean anything or nothing. For my own part I certainly would prefer, if there is to be any domination, that the domination be by my own class, although I prefer no domination. On the other hand it would be much better if we struggled for the Christian dictum-Love Ye One Another. Personally, my experience in the factory led me to feel pain at the domination of a dominant employer or a domineering foreman. I certainly could not subscribe to such a policy, believing as I do in the words of Wm. Morris, that "no man is good enough to be another man's master." Another important feature was the resolution of the I.L.P., which, so far as the liquor policy of the Labour Movement is concerned, has left us with Sir William Harcourt's 20 year old policy of local option. Some of us never thought that that policy was likely to become a policy of such an advanced body as the I.L.P. Not that I would complain in any sense because they have adopted for the first time in their history a liberal war-cry. On the other hand it would have been better to have stood wholly and solely by the one method of State Purchase without any trimmings. The surprise of the Conference was seeing the I.L.P. Conference carried total prohibition, that it was not introduced by them at this Conference. The only conclusion one can come to is that taking into consideration the overwhelming vote against prohibition the I.L.P. had adopted the policy of opportunism rather than lose votes at the coming election.

UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE BILL IN HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Speech by W. R. SMITH, M.P.

MR. W. R. SMITH: All of us on the Labour Benches were disappointed with the state-
ment made by the Minister in charge of the Bill in answer to the case submitted in favour
of a non-contributory scheme. His main argument seemed to be centred round the cost
that might fall either upon the employers or upon the State. I would submit to him that
if the employers or the industry were saddled with the burden he suggested, he could not
reasonably argue that it was a burden which the industry could not carry. Right hon.
Gentleman speaking from the Government Benches vary their tone when they are speaking
on public expenditure. Sometimes a few millions are most important. At other times they
do not seem to have the same significant importance. But they always have increased signi-
ficance when what is proposed is something that will contribute to the solving of a social
problem. I will make a comparison. These millions here are spoken of in very serious
The same tone was not adopted when the House asked to sanction the expenditure
terms.
of millions for scarlet uniforms. Compare the object in view in the two cases. One is a
proposal to establish a scheme of social reform that is going to help those who suffer from
the inequalities of our social and industrial system. The other had for its object the glorifi-
cation of an idea which we thought was going to be destroyed by the sacrifices of the past
few years. The serious tone adopted by Minist rs in regard to a few millions to be applied
to a scheme like this, loses any importance it might have had, when we realise that in regard
to other matters the same seriousness is not displayed. Is the expenditure which has been
mentioned the net expenditure? Are there no economies possible? Will it not mean
some economy in administration? If we can effect some economy in that direction, surely
it is a sound line of procedure, because if 'we can reduce the amount of labour of a non-
productive character, we are really helping society. There is undoubtedly in this bill an
endeavour to make the problem of unemployment, and the method of dealing with it, a
national responsibility. It is a national question. But the hon. Gentlemen who are pro-
moting this legislation have recognised, by the limitations that they themselves have estab-
lished in their Bill, that they cannot carry out this scheme in a complete national sense.
Why? Why is it that you have excepted trades?
from the operation of the Bill certain industries? It is not because those who are unem-
ployed in those industries do not need assistance, when they are unemployed. Those of us
who have experienced unemployment, can speak very feelingly on the question. We know
what it means in the home-life of the worker. The reason you have excluded them
is the difficulty of applying this principle of a contributory scheme. Why is agriculture
excepted?

MR. SMITH: Perhaps it is not in order for me to answer that question but I was under

KETTERING NO. 1.-Shopmates-Where are we? Can any of you see
a glimmer of hope-a faint luminous ray of light on which to lean? Is there
anyone with sufficient foresight, courage, strength or wisdom, who can hew
a path through the morass in which the world is now wallowing? Is there
a MAN who can and will, "with clarion call and heart aflame," arouse our
Look where you
somnolent lethargic senses, and stir once again the pulses of desire into volcanic
eruption? For such a one is surely needed, here and now.
will-politically, socially or industrially the same blank granite-like black-
ness confronts you. Internationally, the "mailed fist" is smashing and
crunching, maiming and destroying; nationally, a chain of mail is being drilled
and woven into the very fibres of our State; industrially, profit is still the
criterion of moral success; socially, the people are seething with an appallingly
aimless unrest. Surely, somehow, it is possible to calm the tempestuous
seas; to bring peace to storm-tossed Europe; to replace by honesty, morality
and nobility of purpose, in politics and industry, the shibboleths of principles
at present existing; to give to the peoples of the earth contentment and an
all-embracing joy? No, friends we are neither sullied nor ashamed; merely
temperamentally reflecting the unspoken thoughts of our members, as occasioned
by unemployment and shortness of trade. Can you wonder at our "dumps,"
our desire for the immediate Millennium, when our wives are unable to make
ends meet when the dear kiddies are going short? And are you not also
finding it so? And are you not also amazed at the thought that we only
begin to cry when our bellies are pinched, and that we relapse into stagnant,
it not time we realised that the same principles are in continuous operation
quiescent ineptitude immediately our hunger pangs are satisfied? Gad, is
whether we be hungry or gluttonously full? And if the principles are wrong
when our stomachs are empty, they must be wrong, equally so, when com-
placency atrophies and the bottom buttons are undone. Until our next,

MIDSOMER NORTON. - Trade in our district is terrible. Surely we
are in a hurry to end this desperate state of affairs which is degrading and
demoralising to men, women and children. In the old days the slave was kept
for 52 weeks in the year. In the new world so often promised by a fat business
Government, the wage slave can be turned into the street for eight weeks
or given any work which may be to the advantage of the firm to give out,

upon it for

factory control. That is the “gate to more," not necessarily more boots,

It is agreed that to avoid the necessity for further detailed revision and amendment to such Statements, this percentage increase shall be calculated upon and added to the total weekly earnings of pieceworkers.

The Conference agrees to recommend the respective organisations to ratify this Agreement, and if ratified shall be registered with the Board of Trade and the Ministry of Labour as a National Agreement.

Dated this 29th day of March, 1920.

Signed on behalf of the Manufacturers' Side of the Conference,
OWEN PARKER, President A. E. MARLOW, Vice-President.

Signed on behalf of the Operatives' Side of the Conference,
T. F. RICHARDS, Gen. President. E. L. POULTON, Gen. Secretary.

Countersigned, F. SHEPPARD, Chairman of Conference.

Here, again, we claim that very substantial advantages have been secured for the members, and that without any loss of time to the operatives (which means wages), and which is not always fully appreciated at its right value.

13. OBITUARY.

It is with deep regret we have to report the passing away of so many of our colleagues since our Leicester Conference. In fact we believe this is the heaviest list of deaths of officials ever reported to one of our conferences. It is indeed a great loss to the Union, and to the cause of labour generally that so many of our comrades, in such a short space of time, have passed to the Great Beyond. We have in your name conveyed to their relatives sincere sympathy and condolence in the loss they have severally sustained. We hope the example set by our comrades in striving to leave the world a better place than they found it will act as an additional incentive to those of us who are left to carry on the work which they had so much at heart.

HARRY BROWN, ex-Council Member and Arbitration, London Board of Arbitration.

THE LABOUR PARTY CONFERENCE.
DELEGATES' REPORT.
The Twentieth Annual Conference was held at Scarborough on June 22nd 25th, 1920,
Mr. W. H. Hutchinson being the Chairman.
The Conference was very largely attended there being not fewer than 1200 delegates.
The question of the size of the Conferences that are now taking place will in our opinion,
question of numbers it is becoming increasingly difficult to secure halls sufficiently large,
have to receive the attention of the societies in the near future, because, apart from the
and when secured the difficulty is for many of those attending hearing what is going on;
this was the case in a number of instances at Scarborough, and cannot be considered as
at all satisfactory.
The Chairman, in his opening statement, gave a résumé of the present situation as
it presented itself to him, and also called attention to points that needed dealing with
at once. Extracts from his speech appear elsewhere. The following were amongst the
more important resolutions passed at the Conference:-
Finland.
"That the Conference deplores the continuance of repressive measures by the Govern-

SCOTTISH TRADE UNION CONGRESS.
DELEGATES' REPORT.

FELLOW MEMBERS,
Summoned by the Parliamentary Committee to consider a number of public
questions of immediate interest and importance, the Scottish Trades Union Congress,
at a meeting in the Central Halls, Glasgow, on Saturday, 10th July, decided to support
a "No Rent Campaign."
In addition to urging that complete self-government to the Irish people was the only
solution to the Irish problem, and demanding the withdrawal of the Army of Occupation, a
resolution on Ireland adopted by the Congress called upon affiliated organisations to refuse
to manufacture, handle or transport munitions, or to transport troops for repression in
Ireland.
On the question of measures to reduce the Cost of Living, the Parliamentary Committee,
who urged the public control and supply of the necessaries of life, and a levy on wealth to
clear off the war debt, declined to accept a proposal for a complete stoppage of production
if deemed necessary. The Chairman said such a course would simply deplete the market
of commodities, the price of which would inevitably rise still further. To propose Direct
Action as a cure-all for every social and industrial ill was to reduce the thing to an absurdity.
They had also to bear in mind that 70 per cent. of the articles which entered into the
workingman's cost of living came from other countries, and a strike in this country would
not induce the people in those countries to sell cheaper. The resolution as proposed by
the Parliamentary Committee was adopted.
ALEC. BROWN.
M. GAMBLE.

MR. ROBERT DUNN.
Appointed Secretary of Stafford Branch of the National Union.
Mr. Robert Dunn, who is well known in trade union circles in Stafford, has been
elected secretary of the local branch of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives
vice Councillor H. Simmons, J.P. (deceased). He has been president of the branch since
1907, and, following Mr. Simmons' death, has been acting secretary.
The appointment of Mr. Dunn as branch secretary coincides with the twenty-fifth
anniversary of his service in the making department of Messrs. D. Hollin & Co. Ltd., boot
manufacturers, Stafford. His father, the late Mr. George Greenwell Dunn, went to Stafford
from London when he was nineteen years of age, and was president of the local branch of
the Amalgamated Society of Boot and Shoe Makers.
At a meeting of the Stafford Branch, on the 17th inst., Mr. D. McCarthy (Union
organiser), who presided, moved a vote of sympathy with the widow and family of the
late Councillor Simmons. The motion was carried. It was reported by Mr. J. Keogh
(auditor) that the books of the branch had been audited by the Union's Chief Clerk, and
found in perfect order.
The following were nominated for the office of president:-Messrs. J. Daly, T. Draper,
C. Gunnell, E. Housby, and J. Reynolds. A ballot was taken on the 24th inst.-The Shoe
and Leather Record, June 25th, 1920.

LEICESTER BOOT AND SHOE TRADE.
Steps to Limit Actual Unemployment.
A meeting of the Arbitration and Conciliation Board of the Trade was held yesterday.
Present: Messrs. W. A. Thompson, G. W. Hunt, J. W. Morton, J. A. Sabin, and T. W.
Smith (representing the manufacturers), Messrs. T. F. Richards, T. Adnitt, G. Parbury,
M. A. Parker, H. Cramphorn, G. Knight, A. Hill, W. H. Lowe, G. Smith and Miss M. King
(representing the operatives), and Mr. A. E. W. Chamberlin (secretary). Mr. Geo. Parbury
was elected chairman of the Board, to fill the vacancy caused by the death of Mr. Thos.
Orton.
The meeting was convened to discuss, in the present situation of the trade, the possi-
bility of the work being more equally distributed amongst the operatives, and the following
resolution was unanimously adopted :-" That with a desire to limit the amount of actual
unemployment during the present period of slackness of trade, manufacturers be advised
to work uniform short time, either departmentally or over the whole factory, in preference
to discharging or suspending operatives."-Leicester Mercury, July 23rd, 1920.

```text
RUSSIA AND POLAND.

During the month the situation between the above-named countries was
such as to make it appear that despite all denials as to this country joining
in another war, there was a great possibility of being drawn into the vortex
of war again, owing principally to the position taken up by France. The
situation became so serious that the Parliamentary Committee of the Trade
Union Congress, the Committee of the National Labour Party and the members
of the House of Commons belonging to the Labour Party had a special (joint)
meeting on the 9th inst., at the House of Commons, to review the situation,
it being felt that war must be prevented. After a long consultation it was
decided to set up a committee consisting of five representatives from each
of the three bodies named, to be called a “Council of Action," to act in the name
of the three parties upon lines which were laid down at the said meeting; the
evidence brought before such meeting being of such a character as to shew
that if there was a will to peace, then peace could be secured between Russia
```

RESOLUTION 2.
That this Conference of Trade Union and Labour representatives hails with satisfaction the Russian Government's declaration in favour of the complete independence of Poland as set forth in their Peace Terms to Poland, and realising the gravity of the international situation, pledges itself to resist any and every form of military and naval intervention against the Soviet Government of Russia.
It accordingly instructs the Council of Action to remain in being until they have secured:
(1) An absolute guarantee that the armed forces of Great Britain shall not be used in support of Poland, Baron Wrangel, or any other military or naval intrigue against the Soviet Government.
(2) The withdrawal of all British naval forces operating directly or indirectly as a blockading influence against Russia.
(3) The recognition of the Russian Soviet Government and the establishment of unrestricted trading and commercial relationships between Great Britain and Russia.
This Conference further refuses to be associated with any Alliance between Great Britain and France or any other country which commits us to any support of Wrangel and Poland, or the supply of munitions or other war material for any form of attack against Soviet Russia.
The Conference authorises the Council of Action to call for any and every form of withdrawal of Labour which circumstances may require to give effect to the foregoing policy, and calls upon every Trade Union official, Executive Committee, Local Council of Action, and the membership in general to act swiftly, loyally and courageously in order to sweep away secret bargaining and diplomacy and to assure that the foreign policy of Great Britain may be in accord with the well-known desires of the people for an end of
war and the interminable threats of war.

RESOLUTION 3.
The Council of Action is hereby authorised to take any steps that may be necessary to give effect to the decisions of this Conference and the declared policy of the Trade Union and Labour Movement.
The Conference also recommends that the Parliamentary Committee of the Trades Union Congress should raise a Special Fund to meet the financial requirements of the Council of Action, and for this purpose impose a levy equal to a halfpenny per member upon affiliated organisations as and when required.

DECLARATION OF THE RUSSIAN SOVIET GOVERNMENT ON POLISH INDEPENDENCE.
On January 28th of this year the Russian Soviet Government, while endeavouring to prevent War with Poland, made the following solemn declaration :-
"Taking into consideration the responsibility for the future of the Russian labouring masses and deeply anxious to prevent the new and countless sacrifices. sorrows and disasters that threaten both peoples, the Soviet of the People's Commissaries declares that the policy of the Russian Soviet Government with reference to Poland (being based not on temporary military or diplomatic combinations but on the basic principle of the right of every nation to decide its own destiny) recognises and will continue to recognise unreservedly and unconditionally the independence and sovereignty of the Polish Republic ; and this recognition has been made the basis of Russia's relationship with Poland from the first moment of the creation of the independent Polish State. The Soviet of People's Commissaries declares that so far as the actual interests of Poland and Russia are concerned there are no questions in dispute (either territorial, economic or any other) which cannot be solved peacefully as the result of negotiations, mutual concessions, and agreements, as is at present the case with the Esthonian Legation."
On February 2nd of this year (1920) the highest institution of the Soviet Republic, the All-Russian Central Executive Committee, over the signature of Kalinin made the


---
Here is the text from the image:

673
following declaration to the Polish people which was intended completely to dissipate
any doubts that might remain :-
"The Russian workers and peasants have recognised the independence of Poland
and they have done this, not at the last moment, not as a temporary diplomatic
combination, not under the pressure of temporary conditions. The Russian workers
hastened at the very first to recognise the independence of the Polish people, and they
recognised it unconditionally and for ever. They did this realising that the inde-
pendence of Poland is in the interests not only of your people but also of ours."
This declaration also includes the following words:
"Your enemies, who are ours, speak falsely when they tell you that the Russian
Soviet Government intends to force Communism on the Polish people with the help
of the bayonets of the Red Army. Communism is only possible in countries where
the vast majority of the working people have the will to secure it by their own initiative.
Only then is a lasting Communistic State possible, for then only can a Communistic
policy take deep root in the country. The Russian Communists are only endeavouring
to defend their own land and their own peaceful work of organisation; they have no
intention and can have no intention of establishing Communism in other countries
by force. The re-organisation of Poland in accordance with the interests of the
Polish masses must be the work of these working masses themselves."
And finally, after Mr. Pilsudski started his general advance against Russia and was
nearing Kieff, the All-Russian Central Executive Committee, after giving orders to the
Supreme Military Command to take the necessary measures for self-defence, issued, on
May 7th of this year (1920), a new Manifesto to the Polish nation in which it was stated :-
"Do not believe it when you are told that the Red Army is bringing slavery
and is going to establish Communism by force. After defeating your masters, the
Soviet Power will give the Polish Nation the right to organise itself as it chooses.
Whether you prefer to retain the present order, or whether you take over the land
and factories will be for you yourselves, Polish workers and peasants, to decide."
Copies of the above were sent out to every branch secretary of our Union
the same day the conference was held, with the decisions of the conference,
so as to enable branch officers to know the position to date. It will be seen
that the resolutions are of a very far-reaching character and such as to call
for discreet handling of a situation which is indeed one to call for the utmost
endeavours to be made to avert what might easily become a veritable disaster
for the human race. Under such circumstances it is imperative that each
one realises his duty and responsibility by doing what is possible to strengthen
the forces that are struggling to bring about peace. More than ever is it
incumbent upon all at such a time as the present to act only upon the instruc-
tions that may from time to time be issued, and thereby ensure the success
of a movement which is designed to not only avert war, but to shew to those
who may be termed the "war party" that the workers are determined that
differences between nations can be and must be settled without recourse to
arms. We felt we were acting in the interest of the membership by voting
in favour of the resolutions. These may mean even a strike and we ask the
endorsement of the membership for the action we have taken. Further
references to the conferences will be found on pages 696-700.

BRANCH BOOKS AND CONTRIBUTION CARDS.
During the period of the war we have incurred considerable liability, which
has been willingly discharged (financially), by supplying those branches who
send to the Central Office for various stationery, contribution books, letter
books, &c., at the pre-war rates. The prices have considerably increased to
us, but as most of the branches we supplied were small, we were aware what
it meant for them to struggle along and meet their financial obligations, and
the difference between the amount paid by the branch and the invoice price
was paid from central funds. In future the prices set out on the inside cover
of the Monthly Report will be deleted, and the branches ordering goods after
the end of this month will be charged at the invoice prices which the printers
charge the Central Office.

EYAM DISPUTE.

Disputes have been very few and call for no particular comment. The
dispute at EYAM (Derbyshire), was first mentioned in the March Report, 1918,
and has been continued ever since that date. The dispute arose because of
the attitude taken up by the employers refusing to recognise the Union, or in
any way to negotiate with the Union officials on behalf of their workpeople.
Attempts have been made not only by us from time to time to bring the dispute
to an end, but also by outside authorities, including the Ministry of Labour.
All these efforts, however, were unsuccessful. Practically the whole of the men
have found employment either in other centres of our trade or in other industries.
It is to the lasting credit of both the men and women at EYAM that they remained
loval and firm in their adhesion to the Union despite the position in which
from time to time they were placed, being cut off as they were from manu-
facturing centres. Mr. J. Buckle, J.P., has been in charge of the dispute right
from the commencement, and during the last few months he has started a
Closing Factory whereby work has been found at full union rates for the women
operatives. This has been so successful that the whole of them are now em-
ployed in this co-operative factory, and thus we feel we can formally state the
dispute has been brought to an end. Whilst it is true the employers still refuse
to recognise the Union they cannot view with any satisfaction from their
standpoint the course of events since March, 1918. On the other hand the work
of the Union has been not only beneficial to the shoe trade but to other trades
in that district, because the dispute itself seemed to arouse amongst the workers
in other industries the determination to improve their conditions, and as a
result very great improvements have been brought about in other industries
both in Eyam and the immediate vicinity. Mr. Buckle has devoted a great
deal of his time to secure for these women members employment, and it is one
of those unusual endings to a dispute that the members should find work by
employing themselves. We can only hope, and we have good grounds for

PARLIAMENTARY AGENT'S REPORT.
Since my last report many questions of importance to Labour have been before the
House of Commons, but none of greater importance than that of Russia and Poland.
How near this country was to being involved in another war we may know at some later
date, but no one doubts at the moment but that the policy pursued by the Government
was bound to lead this nation sooner or later into conflict, the extent or end of which
none could foretell.
The action of the Labour movement in declaring for a down tools policy in certain
events, was in every sense of the word justified: it was constitutional, because it harmonised
with the feelings of the whole people, and the Government realised that on this occasion
the war-mongers had over-reached themselves.
The speech of Mr. Lloyd George was a clever attempt to cover up the position, but the
deadly criticism that followed showed most clearly that he and his chief supporters had
pursued a policy that made peace doubtful and war almost certain.
The Labour Party had previously asked, before hostilities had really commenced
between Russia and Poland, that the League of Nations should be used to prevent this
new war, but, said Mr. Bonar Law. this is not a new war, it is a continuance of an old one,
and therefore the services of the League cannot be utilised; but now, when Russia has
beaten the Poles, the Prime Minister says the articles of the League of Nations must deter-
mine the position. It would indeed be comic were it not so tragic. But the fact that the
lives of men are placed in jeopardy in this careless, indifferent fashion surely ought to
constitute an object lesson for the people that will not be forgotten. Fortunately, Russia
has offered terms of peace that leave no excuse whatever for further war, and for the time
being the war-mongers are foiled in their object, but the country will not be safe in this
respect while men like Churchill are in office backed, as one feels they are, by financial
interests that care nothing for human life so long as dividends are high. This I know is
a strong statement to make, but let those who differ from me give any other explanation
of the situation. Here is a world torn with the results of war, with burdens that are crushing
and overwhelming, with the peoples hungering for the things that peaceful industry alone
can give, with social problems waiting solution which unless speedily dealt with threaten
to further degrade the mass of the peoples, with a yearning in the hearts of millions for a
better social order, and by a world peace alone can these things be realised, and yet, the
policy adopted by Governments is one of war, and the so-called peace settlements are but
the laying of foundations of future wars.
There is one thing, however, that stands out amidst it all, viz., Labour is the only force
that can guarantee peace, and it must be our duty to give the forces of labour greater
strength and power to enforce their will.
In regard to other matters, the Government still blunders on. The Ministry of Mines
Bill is evidence in that direction. The Coal Commission might never have been appointed,
their recommendations are ignored, as indeed they were bound to be when they proposed
to abolish private property in Mines. This is the wrong House of Commons to accept
proposals of that character, and whatever pledges may be given by the Prime Minister
or the leader of the House, if their fulfilment disturb private interests then the pledges
must go.
The Miners claim that the Bill aims at the breaking up of their Federation, by the
splitting up of the country into districts, and that the interests of the consumer will be
placed in jeopardy, and will be more than ever in the hands of the coal-owners. The
Labour Party called for the withdrawal of the Bill, but the Government had no difficulty
in securing its passage by a substantial majority.
The decision of the Government to stand by Clause 17 of the Unemployment Insur-
ance Bill as amended in Committee, which will enable Friendly Societies to administer
the benefits, is another instance of the power wielded in the House by certain interests,
The Minister of Labour is fully aware of the strong feeling of hostility to this proposal
by organised Labour, and it would not be surprising if the Government's decision was taken
against his advice. But on this question they could not control the House, powerful as
their majority is, and never have I seen prejudice shewn as on the occasion when we tried
to reverse the Committee's decision. It mattered not what arguments were used-and
never has a stronger case been put up by any body of opinion-there was no answer to it
only in the votes, which were based upon a strong anti-Trade Union feeling. It was not
that they thought we were wrong, but they were not prepared to give us a position which
might strengthen us in the future. The position at the moment is one which should cause
us to consider whether or not as members of Friendly Societies we will help to destroy our
economic position as Trade Unionists.
The Labour Party secured a substantial success in Committee on the Employment
of Women and Young Persons Bill. The clause which would have permitted employers

FELLOW MEMBERS,
During the month I have visited Stafford, Stone, Burslem and Mansfield.
Immediately before and after Bank holidays things are slack from an organising point
of view. In my last report I called attention to the conduct of the A.U.C.E. in its unfair
I made note of their
dealings with us as a Union. Here is another example of their conception of fair dealing.
When I visited Burslem in June I had a meeting of the repairers working for the Co-opera-
tive Society there. They were all members of ours except one.
complaints and saw the manager about them. He promised to lay the points in dispute
before the Committee. I was surprised when I visited Burslem on July 22nd to find that
the whole of the men, about 15, had gone over to the A.U.C.E., and this in face of the
fact that through my efforts the pieceworkers got nearly 25 per cent. increase, three men
on weekly wages were advanced 5s., and the few youths got an increase of 4s. Mr. Dunn,
of Stafford, accompanied me on this occasion. We told the men in plain English that
they did not understand the meaning of manly trade union principles or they would not
have acted as they had done. This treachery in the long run can be of no advantage to
those who for the moment seem to gain by it. There are two things that I would like to
seriously call our members' attention to. One is the banking of money with employers.
Besides being of a sneaky nature this is dangerous from a trade union point of view. Men
getting wages below the minimum have been saving in the employers' bank, and when
they have asked for the minimum they were told of how well they were doing and of what
stood to their credit. The other point is on the advantage employers are taking of the
clause dealing with the graduated scale of wages and age. I find that in some cases youths
of 20 and 21 are on piecework and only receiving the graduated scale of wages. This is an
entirely wrong interpretation of the clause. The graduated scale is not for piece rates,
but purely for weekly wages based on the young learning their trade or operations. In
the matter of saving, surely there are plenty of means to save without trusting managers
and employers with our private business. The Co-operative Societies are the right places
for working men and women to place their trust in for minding the bit they can save.
On the question of youths and girls working on piece rates while only receiving the gradu-
ated weekly wage, every branch in the Kingdom should have one policy on this question,
and that is not to allow it, or to demand the full piecework rates.
On August 9th I visited Mansfield with the view of getting the employers manufac-
turing stiffeners to pay to the Leicester Statement for this work. In no case did we come
to any terms, but we agreed to meet again in a few weeks time. Since I last visited Mans-
field there have been a good many joined the branch.

and conditions set up by the Trades Board, and the public to the new price

to show their appreciation of his valuable work by making him a presentation,

PORTSMOUTH. - We are still wondering what is to be the outcome of
all the men now unemployed, whether the Government will recognise that
these men have a right to live. Trade still continues only fair, and is it to be
wondered at, when several thousand men are not receiving any wages, and
therefore have no money to spend? There is no lack of work to be done, but
those responsible seem to be content with looking over the ruins left by the
war. We were rather surprised to know that no one who has a technical
knowledge of the boot repairing trade has been appointed to see that employers
observe the orders of the Trade Board. It seems desirable that the members
should press for the appointment of inspectors and men they know who could
well carry out the duties. Many and flagrant breaches of the orders are taking
place. The one great subject which all trade unionists are talking about is
the Congress which meets here the first week in September. We hope this will
help stir up the workers in Portsmouth and the South generally. We need
some great stimulus, as we have no great hereditary leanings towards trade
unionism. Well indeed could we once again use the words of Charles Kingsley,
in" Alton Locke," when he tries to bring home to the toilers of the South of
England the need of organisation. We are still waiting news of the formation
of the District Committees of the Trade Board. We believe these would bring
a great fillip to the efforts of the main Committees, as they cannot legislate
for districts they do not know. We have to protest at the lax way the Ministry
of Labour are carrying out the training of disabled men at Portsmouth and
Netley. We have been waiting months for tools and uppers, the men are
wasting their time, and it is a waste of public money.

REDRUTH. - The Committee looked forward to a very interesting
August meeting, seeing that the voting for the various officers of the Union
was to take place, also the Sick Scheme and the Guarantee Fund. As it was,
only fourteen members were present, and that will not look very good when
we see the result of the ballot in our next Monthly Report. It was the custom
of the branch to distribute the papers at the works, but the Committee desires
to make it known that the proper place to transact the business of the branch
is at our monthly meetings, and they wish to make an earnest appeal to the
members to try and attend, even if it means a little sacrifice. There is a
possibility of the members of the trade unions throughout the country being
called upon to make decisions of very great importance, and unless we can
get together and express our views concerning the questions which have to
be decided, we shall be unprepared - a state which we might have to pay
dearly for. To turn from our regrets, &c., we should like to say that our
members greatly appreciate the work of the Council in establishing the Holiday
Scheme. We have just resumed work after the first week's holiday in our
history, and one and all are agreed that they will do their best to see that it
has come to stay. We are pleased to say in conclusion, that we are working
full time except in one department, who resumed work two days later than
the others after the holidays, but we don't think it will continue.

PARLIAMENTARY DEBATES.
MR. L'ESTRANGE MALONE.-To ask the Food Controller if his attention has been
called to the fact that 20,000,000 pounds of sugar have passed through the Chicago customs
house from Canada during the past few days, and several million pounds more are en
route, and that Canadian sugar, which was purchased in Cuba last year and shipped to
England and then returned to Canada, is expected to be used in Chicago whether these
statements were made by Mr. William H. Clarke, collector of the port; and whether the
Ministry of Food, through the Supreme Council or other channels, will take steps to prevent
this unnecessary waste of energy in the transportation of prime necessities which are
urgently required.
SIR W. MITCHELL-THOMSON.-I was not aware of the circumstances referred to in the
question, and I regret that the information supplied by the Hon. Member does not enable
me to trace these transactions. If, however, he will supply me with more precise details
I will have them investigated.-Parliamentary Question (5346), August 4th, 1920.
MUTTON (LAMB).
MR. RATCLIFFE.-To ask the Food Controller if he will state what is the object in
diverting large supplies of last season's New Zealand lambs to the United States of America,
whether highest price realised at the Atlantic seaboard is from 162 to 181 cents. per lb.,
whilst old stocks of cut lambs are being charged here at 1s. 1d. per lb. to the retailer dis-
tributors; and will he see that in the future the best class of lambs is brought to this
country, and that the British consumer is not penalised for the benefit of the American
consumer by paying about 50 per cent. more for old stock than is paid in America for the
new stock of lambs.
SIR W. MITCHELL-THOMSON.-Some mutton and lamb has been sold for direct ship-
ment from New Zealand to the United States of America with a view to relieving the
congestion in the stores in New Zealand, saving storage charges and hastening the time
at which it will be possible for the New Zealand exporters to revert to business on normal
lines. I am unable to state the price at which this meat is sold in the United States,
but it has been sold by the Ministry at a price f.o.b. New Zealand, which gives the Imperial
Government a profit on the sale. It is obviously desirable in the interests both of the
producer in New Zealand and the taxpayer in this country that the abnormal stocks on
hand should be liquidated as rapidly as possible, and the suggestion in the latter part of
the question that the British consumer is being penalised for the benefit of the American
consumer is contrary to fact.-Parliamentary Question (5342), August 5th, 1920.
MINES (Baltic).
COLONEL WEDGWOOD asked the Prime Minister whether, in view of the present situa-
tion, he can give any information as to when the mines will be swept up in the Baltic
and freedom of trade allowed to Petrograd?
THE PRIME MINISTER.-As has already been stated in reply to a previous question
by the Hon. Member for Whitechapel, the removal of these mines is not an obligation
resting on the British Government.
LABOUR COUNCIL OF ACTION.
MR. BILLING asked the Prime Minister whether his attention had been called to the
resolutions passed at the Labour Conference on Friday last creating what is tantamount
to a Labour dictatorship, under the title of the Council of Action; whether he will state,
firstly, whether he has consulted the Law Officers of the Crown as to the carrying out of
such resolutions being contrary to constitutional law, and secondly, whether the Govern-
ment propose to permit the threatened action in any way to influence their policy; and
whether he will state that in his opinion the time has arrived definitely to declare as illegal
the organising of industrial disturbances for the purpose of achieving political ends?
THE PRIME MINISTER.-The policy of the Government in regard to Poland and Russia,
a policy which has been repeatedly communicated to the Polish Government, and which
was defined at Spa and again at Lympne, and has been fully expounded to this House,
would appear to differ in no way from that enunciated at the Labour Conference to which
the Hon. Gentleman refers. The swinging of a SLEDGE HAMMER AGAINST AN OPEN DOOR
IS MERELY MADE FOR PURPOSES OF DISPLAY. Any attempt to dictate the policy of the
Government and Parliament by industrial action strikes at the root of the democratic
constitution of this country, and will be RESISTED BY ALL THE RESOURCES AT THE GOVERN-
MENT'S COMMAND.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION ACT.
We record with pleasure that another case, this time at KINGSWOOD, has
been settled. The member, S.M., has been enabled to secure a lump sum of
£35 apart from the ordinary weekly compensation, this once again proving
the value of the member having a powerful Union behind him.

TRADE UNION CONGRESS.
Resolutions upon many questions were dealt with at the Congress, which
if carried into effect will undoubtedly prove of great benefit to the people.
A report appears on pages 746-748 from the delegates attending the Congress.
It was with pleasure we found Mr. A. E. W. O'Dell-one of the fraternal
delegates from Canada-was a member of the American Boot and Shoe Workers'
Union, he having been one of their organisers for many years past. We felt
this was a compliment to the boot and shoe industry that one of the fraternal
delegates should be a member of our own craft. Mr. O'Dell also attended
the national conference of hide and leather workers of France, held in Paris
from the 20th-24th inst., along with our General Secretary, Mr. E. L. Poulton,
J.P. We did all possible to make Mr. O'Dell's stay in this country both
enjoyable and interesting.

MORE UNION J.P.'S.
It is with great pleasure that we record the fact that Miss N. WALKER,
Clerk to the Northampton No. 2 Branch, has been elected as a lady J.P.,
taking her seat on the magisterial bench at Northampton on the 4th inst.
This is indeed a great honour to the Union.
We offer our congratulations to Mr. I. H. JOHNSON, J.P., upon his elevation
to the Magisterial bench for Northants. Mr. Johnson has been secretary to
our Daventry Branch for several years past, and we trust he will be spared
to help along the workers in that district for many years to come.

IRELAND.
During the month the General President and Mr. D. McCarthy have been
to Ireland to induce the manufacturers of that country to accept in its entirety
the 1920 National Agreement. We are pleased to record the fact that they
have agreed to pay, at least, up to the Minimum rates, and also to work to
quantity statements, and as soon as ever possible statements will be prepared
for the various boot centres in Ireland.

WATERFORD BRANCH.
We are pleased to report that we have started a Branch at WATERFORD
(Ireland), quite a goodly number of those engaged in the industry having
joined up with the Union. Already, through the activities of the General
President, decided improvements have been secured as a direct result of the
Union's influence.

THE COUNCIL

GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
TRADES CONGRESS.-The Trades Union Congress at Portsmouth this month
marks another milestone in the march of emancipation of the wage-earner, and the greatest
tribute paid to it was in the words of the Secretary (Fimmen, a Dutchman) of the Inter-
national Trade Union movement, who himself described the British Trades Union Congress
as the greatest and most important Labour body in the whole world, and the hope of the
workers of all lands. This tribute should certainly give pause and qualm of conscience
to that section of the movement who, in season and out of season, have assailed the Trade
Union movement as being played out, a thing of the past, no good, &c., &c.; and Trade
Union officials were abused until many of the critics became officials, then that ceased;
but they have all learnt the lesson that for good or ill the greatest power in the land is
the Trade Union movement, that can at any time change or improve its policy to meet
all and every necessity for the welfare of the wage-earning community.
This brings me to a most important question in the Trade Union world. The Miners
consider the Agenda before the Trades Union Congress, meet and decide to vote on
certain matters which allow of no amendment, and then speakers are chosen and no one
is allowed to speak unless chosen. They act on the rule of majority and the individual
doesn't count. The question comes to my mind that as they had 250 delegates present,
on the show of hands they vote three to our delegates' one. In future they can only have
one delegate to every 5,000 members. We ought to send our full representation, and also
continue our policy of allowing each delegate to act by using their own vote individually
if they wish it, and not force them to be dragooned by any majority no matter how
intellectual they may be.
COUNCIL OF ACTION. -The greatest move made took place on August 13th, when it
was unanimously decided that our Government was not to take part in the Polish-Russian
War, and the result annoyed the Government and the militarists of our land. We are
now confronted with another difficulty in which the Miners are demanding, and rightly so,
an increase in wages in proportion to those paid to other workers. They also demand a
reduction in the price of coal by 14s. 2d. per ton, and very properly demand that the
Government should not choose their industry for experimental purposes. I am of the
opinion that if the House of Commons had an opportunity to express their unfettered
opinion, that no profits would be allowed to be made by the Government, at least not
unless they owned the business. Should the Government mature their plans no less a
sum than £66,000,000 is likely to reach them to help to meet the taxation of the country,
but this should not be confined to one industry, and for that reason is bad in principle.

country. Now they hope to have their opportunity, as the Miners have already
handed in their notices and the men have been encouraged to look forward to a fight.

745
The world is at present in a state of ferment and unrest; the awful war through which humanity has been passing has indeed left in its train terrible problems, and it will call for the utmost we are capable of to safely steer through. On all hands the cry is for help to enable men and women and children to keep out of the morass brought about by the war: ours is a great responsibility, the obligations resting upon us are immense, and may indeed at times make one wonder where we may be forced to.

We must not, however, shirk the issue; let us ever remember the duty we owe to our common humanity, and by unity, concord and goodwill, determine that the suffering, pain and anguish of the past few years shall so nerve us for the future as to bring about such an altered and improved state as will for ever make it impossible for any repetition of such a catastrophe.

I trust your conference may result in not only the best interests of your members being served, but may have a beneficial effect upon the labour movement as a whole; that there may be in the near future such a spirit of fraternity and goodwill grow up between the various units of the human family as will give not only heart and hope to those who are now downtrodden and dispirited, but will so enhearten and inspire the forces that we striving to rid the world of all possible suffering, injustice and pain and usher in a new era, an era of peace, goodwill and justice, where poverty shall have been driven away, and the sum total of happiness be as fully as possible developed, giving to all the freest life possible and the removal of those things which are in the way and hinder humanity from attaining to those heights they are capable of reaching.

CHESHAM'S "EASTERN" ORDER.

Contract Completed and Goods Despatched by Motor Lorries.

The last consignment of what has been known at Chesham as the "Eastern" order for boots has been despatched, and according to rumour there is a larger contract to come very shortly. The order just completed came as a godsend to Chesham. When it arrived all factories, without exception, were on short time, not much more than three days per week being worked. Orders were few, and manufacturers thought the prospects black indeed-what the operatives thought may be imagined.

The contract was for boots of the British Army type, but of a lower quality. As early delivery was essential it was a case of "all hands to the pump," and overtime into the bargain.

Incidentally, the wages statement adopted at Chesham on the eve of the setting-in of short time received its first real test, and seems to have satisfied both sides the manu- facturers with regard to the quantity produced, and the men with regard to its earning possibilities.

The orders brought prosperity in another direction, for a local woodware manu- facturer had some thousands of cases to make. When packed the boots were despatched by motor lorry-the first experiment of the kind in this form of transport. It is significant as to the opinion held regarding the ultimate destination of the boots that operatives have been heard to say: "Now for civilian work once more."

Recently civilian orders have been in abeyance, and even if the rumoured contract does not mature factories may have a few weeks' respite from short time, owing to the need of catching up arrears of ordinary business. One local manufacturer, who also has a factory at Bristol, and who specialises in lighter work than it is customary to make at Chesham, is building cottages for his operatives. It is said that plans are ready for the erection of a large factory, but that they have been held up owing to the present slackness in trade.

Our Wellingborough correspondent writes: "The completion of a Russian order last week was signalised by eight dray loads of packing cases leaving one of the factories in the town for the station. A photographer met the cavalcade on the way."- Shoe and Leather Record, roth September, 1920.

In the Leicester district employment during September was bad; a large number of
operatives were working half-time or less, and some factories were closed altogether.
The position was much the same in the Northampton district: a number of factories
were closed altogether, and those that remained open were generally working less than
half the normal hours. At Kettering, and at Bristol and Kingswood, employment continued
bad. At Stafford employment was very slack, the factories being generally open for
only four days a week, and then for less than the normal hours. At Norwich (except in
the turn-shoe department, in which the operatives were fully employed) a considerable
number of workpeople were unemployed, and nearly all those who were still in employ-
ment were working only from half to three-quarter time. At Leeds also the majority
of the workpeople were on short time.

In the Rossendale district, where slippers and light shoes are manufactured, employ-
ment was fairly good.

In Scotland employment was reported as fair at Dundee, Glasgow, Kilmarnock and
Ayr, quiet at Edinburgh and slack at Maybole.

The exports of boots and shoes in September, 1920, amounted to 103,692 dozen
pairs, or 13,726 dozen pairs more than in August, 1920, but 57,943 dozen pairs less than
in September, 1913.— The Labour Gazette, October, 1920.

HONOURS FOR THE GENERAL SECRETARY.
It is with no small degree of pleasure that we have to place on record the
fact that our General Secretary, Mr. E. L. Poulton, J.P., has been unani-
mously elected Chairman to the Trades Union Congress Parliamentary
Committee for 1920-21, and consequently he will be Chairman of the
Congress next year.
This is indeed an honour to the Union, and the position has only been
held by one of our officials previously, and that as far back as 1902, when the
late Mr. W. B. Hornidge was President of the Congress.

Election of Officers.
THE CHAIRMAN explained the reason why the Joint Industrial Council's Annual
Meeting had not been held in May owing to the great number of other pressing duties to

of Workers in Factories and its desire to find a practicable scheme for making effective
provision for Unemployment in the Industry, and expressed gratitude for the effective
way with which the work of the Council has been carried out. He also appreciated the
cordial help rendered by both sides of the Council, and intimated he was retiring from the
position of Chairman with pleasant memories of his tenure of office.

MR. O. PARKER then proposed Mr. T. F. Richards be Chairman of the Council for the
ensuing year; the proposal was seconded by Mr. A. E. MARLOW. Mr. Richards, however,
preferred that Mr. Parker should continue to act as Chairman, but upon the resolution
being put to the vote, Mr. Parker declared the "ayes have it." Mr. Richards took the
Chair and thanked the Council for their support.

PRODUCTION.
A great deal of talk is being indulged in at the present time about the absolute need for increased output, and that everyone should put his best efforts forward on account of the world's need for all kinds of articles and materials. The present state of unemployment in this and other countries is a grim commentary upon the position, shewing as it does the great need for a radical alteration from the present methods in which industry is carried on, whereby the admitted needs of the peoples of the world can be supplied without throwing a great many others out of employment. It is an interesting point to notice that, with a view to keeping up prices, those who control the tea markets of the world are calling for reduced production to enable them to keep up prices. This also obtains in the rubber world, where the employers state it is necessary to reduce the output by 25 per cent.; whilst the statement a few days ago that in order to keep up the prices of cotton, which is so badly wanted by the world, it is being burned, seems to be at variance with the cry to the worker for more production. For ourselves, although we as a trade are suffering at the present time, NOT from over-production, but from under-consumption and bad distribution-as also the absolute necessity of a world peace-we believe the need of the world is for more production under proper conditions. This cry for reduced production simply to keep up prices shews what a long way we have to go before a proper state of society is brought about. We hope these things will not be lost sight of, but when the opportunity presents itself we trust the workers will shew by their votes their disapproval of such methods by putting those into positions who would, by legislative action, bring about such a reconstruction of society as will enable a just distribution of the world's supplies to take place.
TRADE UNION BUTTONS AND BROOCHES.
A fresh supply of buttons and brooches has recently been secured and can be had upon application, price 6d. each, cash with order. Secretaries, please note, when ordering buttons or brooches, cash should ALWAYS be sent with order.
MONTHLY RETURNS.
We feel bound once again to call the serious attention of Branch Secretaries to the fact that the FIFTEENTH day of each month is the LATEST day for returns to reach the General Secretary. Last month many returns were late. Branches failed to send off their returns to reach the Central Office by the 15th of the month, and this tends to upset the organisation of the work in the General Secretary's Office. We trust in future every Branch Secretary will endeavour to get in his returns as soon as is possible after the month (or five weeks as the case may be) ends, and NOT to wait until the latest date for them to reach the Office ; also before sending them to see that they are in order and properly signed.

GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
Another Outrageous Government Blunder.
I am sorry to find that owing to the present blundering, stupid and incompetent 
Government that we have at the head of affairs in the country, we are again involved in
an Industrial Crisis. The Miners I would like to have seen act on the advice of their leader,
Mr. Smillie, who went so far as to advise the reference of the trouble to an Independent
Tribunal, and no one need be surprised after the treatment the Miners received over the
Sankey Award that the men refused to have any sympathy with the Government's position.
We ourselves know that at least 5,000 men could have been found employment at
Hand-Sewn Boot and Shoe Making, had the Government been prepared to have rendered
that assistance to the men who served the Nation in the late war. We have, therefore, to
express our great sympathy with the Miners in their trouble, and fully believe that had
their demand for the 2s. been granted it would have been the best thing for the Nation as
a whole. I am still hopeful a way out of the difficulty will be found without prolongation
of the struggle that has been entered into, but whatever happens all the blame that we
can find ought to be thrown upon the Government.
Unemployment.
At the Council Meeting for the month held on the 26th and 27th of September, we
again considered the question as to whether we should become responsible for the
administering of the Unemployment Act apart from the Government Scheme, and whether
we have a scheme of our own. The General President and General Secretary, with Mr.
Buckle and Mr. Smith, M.P., were appointed to await on the Ministry of Labour to find
out how far we could do this by drawing up a scheme of our own. We also took into con-
sideration the temporary unemployment scheme, the 3 months having been concluded,
at this particulary Council Meeting, and owing to the extraordinary amount of unemploy-
ment and thereby suffering which would be entailed on our members, we have decided
to ask the members of the Union for powers to amend the Unemployment Clauses of our
Rules to read: “That any person unemployed for 12 consecutive working days shall,
upon the recommendation of the Branch Executive, be permitted to come under the rule
from the first day of becoming unemployed."
The Council recognise that we have probably doubled our membership in very recent
years, and it will require very, very serious handling to make this scheme a success owing to
the fact that trade is bad at the present moment. We ought not to be looked upon in-
dependently out of our own fund to provide this money. Already I understand an in-
timation has been sent to the Employers, but they up to the present have turned a deaf
ear to the proposal. In the circumstances they are willing to allow us, out of our own funds,
to provide for and keep our men and women standing by waiting to serve them whenever
there is a possibility of a profit being made out of their labour, which, in itself, is a fact.
We can only, therefore, hope to get this scheme of unemployment in working order at the
earliest possible date in order to release our general fund from the responsibility that is
placed upon us.
On the 28th September I attended a meeting of the Parliamentary Committee with
the General Federation of Trade Unions, to meet the Friendly Societies with the object
of trying to bring about a working arrangement whereby the Friendly Societies would not
unduly interfere with the work which some Trade Unions have been able to do so
successfully for themselves, viz., to administer unemployment benefit. Several sugges-
tions were made, one of which was: That we should permit the Friendly Societies to take
over the Benevolent side, or in other words, Sick Insurance, and let them work that, and
on the other hand they would not deign to try and take over the Unemployment side of
our work. After a lengthy discussion we advised the Chairman, Mr. J. H. Thomas, unani-
mously, to inform the Friendly Society Delegates that we could not see our way clear to
make this proposal; in fact, as the conference did not propose any working arrangements
we decided to allow each side to do its best for its own members in the future as in the past.
Trade Board.
On the 30th I attended the Trade Board meeting of the Advisory Committee, and once
more went through a great batch of permits in order to allow the unfortunate people who
are already in the Industry to be permitted to work at what the Advisory Committee
believe to be their full value. Upon this question I should like to add that we make it a
point of personal investigation with some members of the Committee as to the offer of the
employer to the particular workman, thereby doing our best to preserve a man from being
taken advantage of.
October 1st, at the Full Board Meeting, where we confirmed the previous work done,
we had an explanation from the ex-Secretary of Lord Haig, who endeavoured to explain

24TH JANUARY, 1921.

DISPUTES have been practically non-existent during the month.

NOMINATIONS for delegates to the First Annual Conference to be held in London must be taken at the February Meeting Night, and nominations sent to reach the General Secretary BEFORE the 15th prox., otherwise the same will not be accepted.

WOMEN DELEGATES.
Whilst it is not within the power of ourselves to allocate seats for women delegates for the Conference at Whitsuntide, we hope the branches will take into full consideration the women membership of the Union and their claims for representation, it being important that the women members should be fully represented so that their personal views on matters directly affecting women can be heard at first hand from the women delegates so appointed.

Nominations must also be taken for one delegate to attend the Scottish Labour Advisory Committee (Scottish branches only to nominate).

TRADE is, if anything worse, rather than better than it was last month, and the immediate prospect of any improvement does not appear to be in sight. During the month 14,662 have signed on the Out-of-Work Books, at a cost to the Union of nearly ₤18,000; these numbers are, however, not at all a full


---
reflection as to the real state of trade, there being many thousands on short
time and such short time as means in many instances only two and three days
per week, and this for a whole series of weeks. In connection with this system
of short time it is no new thing to the Shoe Trade, as members well know
We have, however, never for a moment thought, or considered that it even
approached the point of being in any way a solvent for the unemployment
problem; but simply a practical expression of sympathy of the workers to
one another to mitigate to some extent the suffering that is always existent
when bad trade prevails.
The Government, it would seem, have an idea that a general policy of
short time would act as some special charm to tide over the present period of
general slackness. It ought surely by this time to be quite clear to the Govern-
ment that what is required is a policy going down to the root of the causes.
It is indeed a satire upon the existing situation that people are begging for
the barest necessities of life on one hand, and millions of people in the aggregate
are begging for work to supply those necessities, and the raw material is at
hand to meet both situations. Yet statesmen hesitate to deal with the situation
except in the smallest possible degree, and in a way altogether unworthy of
politicians much less of statesmen. The situation is getting dangerous and
those in responsible positions ought by now to realise that men will not tolerate
the present disgraceful situation being continued. We trust therefore that
such steps will be taken by those who have the power as will relieve the
existing state of suffering, and that immediately.
We would remind the officers and members that the following instruction,
issued on the 20th December, 1920, must be rigidly adhered to :-" That the
question of Suspension Benefit should and must definitely CEASE on the
26th February, 1921, and will not be re-opened, the strain on the Funds having
already been very heavy indeed."
The figures given in the records of the Labour Gazette are:—

BOOT AND SHOE TRADE.

During December the depression in the boot and shoe trade became more acute,
and short time and unemployment increased. In many centres the Christmas holidays
were extended to a fortnight or more. The number of workpeople employed in the week
ended 18th December by those firms from whom Returns were received was about 12
per cent. less than in the corresponding week of last year, and the total wages paid by these
firms showed reductions of about 5 per cent. as compared with a month earlier, and of
nearly 24 per cent. as compared with a year earlier, notwithstanding the increases in
rates of wages granted in April last. Of 23,000 workpeople covered by Returns giving
information as to hours worked, about three-fourths worked, on average, 18 hours less
than full time in the week ended 18th December.
In the Leicester district employment continued very bad; some factories were closed,
short time was almost general, and the Christmas holidays were extended In the
Northampton district there was a further decline; large numbers of workpeople were
unemployed, nearly all the rest were on short time; the Christmas holidays were extended
in some cases to three weeks or even a month. At Kettering employment was reported
as much worse; there was much short time, and a considerable amount of unemployment.
At Bristol employment was very bad, and short time was general, while at Kingswood
there was an exceptional amount of unemployment. At Stafford most of the operatives
were working less than half-time. At Leeds short time was general, amounting to two
or three days a week in many cases At Norwich about 75 per cent. of those employed
were on short time; the Christmas holidays were extended.

At the outset Mr. Marlow read the following decision arrived at by the Scottish
Federation:-

(COPY.)
"After due consideration the Federated Associations of Boot and Shoe Manu-
facturers in Scotland have decided that they could not enter into any Scheme for
contracting out under Section 18 of the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1920, in which
the contributions to be paid were more than in the Government Scheme, and also
that in any such Scheme for contracting out of the Government Scheme there must
be joint management of the Scheme. Further, that the agreement by individual
Manufacturers to enter into any Scheme for 'contracting out' of the Government
Scheme must be optional. The Federation are also entirely opposed to the principle
of Paragraph 5 of the Suggested Special Scheme submitted by the National Union of
Boot and Shoe Operatives, which provides for an 'Under-Employment Benefit,'
and will be no party to any such Scheme"-

but intimated that if a scheme could be drawn up which would provide better benefits
than those named in the Act, the Federation would not be adverse to the same.
