SUGGESTED REVISION OF CONFERENCE AGREEMENT, 1921.
We have submitted the following as the suggested revision of the 1919
Agreement to the Manufacturers' Federation, and asked that an early meeting
of both sides should be held to consider the same :-

CLAUSE 1.- UNIFORMITY IN LABOUR PRICE OF SIMILAR CLASSES OF GOODS.-That it
is desirable that a uniform system of prices should obtain and that the general outline
or groundwork of such system should be arranged on a broad basis, so that the essential
conditions and prices can be applied or adapted to the same class of labour or material
in all areas producing similar classes of goods.

CLAUSE 2.-BASIS OF QUANTITY STATEMENTS. - Where general or shop statements
do not at present exist the Local Arbitration Boards, at the request of either side, shall
forthwith proceed upon the ratification of this Agreement to prepare Quantity Statements
for their respective districts (subject to Clause 1). All manufacturers and operatives
shall accept such statements in their entirety as a basis of payment, but the system shall
be a daywork system, and no adult operative shall be engaged at less than the minimum
wage rate, without the written permit of the Union or the Local Arbitration Board. In
cases where circumstances arise that prevent the operative from earning the minimum
or agreed wage rate owing to bad materials or special care required in the performance
of their work, such cases shall be subject to special adjustment between the employer
or his representative and the operatives or their Trade Union officials.

CLAUSE 3.-PROCEDURE RE OUTPUT. It is understood that operatives use their
trade skill and ability to the best advantage. There shall be an agreed wage for the
various operatives, such wage to be in accordance with the conditions laid down in Clauses
I and 2. The agreed wage shall only be varied when the state and condition of trade
warrant such alteration. Such agreed wage shall be fixed by the Manufacturer, Operative,
and Trade Union Official.

CLAUSE 4.-REGULATION OF CONDITIONS OF EMPLOYMENT. - Where operatives
attend at the factories on the instructions of the employers, or their representatives, work
shall be found for them for at least a whole day, except when short time is being worked,
and in that case operatives shall be informed overnight if their services will not be required
on the next working day. All operatives to be at work where practicable.

CLAUSE 5.-UNIFORMITY OF ORGANISATION.-All operatives shall be subject to the
same organisation and discipline in regard to attendance at the factories during working
hours.

CLAUSE 6.-HOURS OF LABOUR. As from March 31st, 1921, the ordinary working
week shall be a five day one of 40 hours, and meantime all statements shall be built up to
ensure the rates of wages as set forth in Clauses 7 and 8.

CLAUSE 7.-MINIMUM WAGE AND GRADUATED SCALE RATES. From the commence-
ment of the first working week on or after 31st March, 1921, the following scale of minimum
wages shall operate for male operatives employed in all Departments.
MALE OPERATIVES. Age 21, Minimum Wage 100/-.

CLAUSE 8.-MINIMUM WAGE AND GRADUATED SCALE RATES. - The national minimum
wage and graduated scale rates for female operatives shall be as follows from the commence-
ment of the first working week on or after 31st March, 1921 :-
FEMALE WORKERS.-Age 20, Minimum Wage 70/-.

CLAUSE 0. All operatives to be guaranteed a weekly wage for the 52 weeks annually ;
at not less than the Minimum Wage Rate.

CLAUSE 10. NO REDUCTION IN WAGES THROUGH NEW AGREEMENT. The wages of the
operatives who, when this Agreement comes into operation, are employed at or above the
minimum wages or graduated scale rates applicable to them by this Agreement shall not
be reduced in consequence of this Agreement. When, through special circumstances,
operations cannot be priced the wages paid to these operatives shall be the average agreed
wage rate of the adult operatives, both male and female, on the firm in question.

CLAUSE 11. NOMPILATION OF PIECE-WORK AND QUANTITY STATEMENTS BY LOCAL
ARBITRATION BOARDS. Local Boards of Arbitration will forthwith prepare new piece-
work Lr quantity statements, or revise the existing statements on a basis to ensure the
average worker earning at least 25 per cent. over the minimum wage.

All statements to be increased in proportion to the new minimum wage rates.

In the event of differences arising on a Local Arbitration Board as to the procedure
to be adopted in giving effect to this clause, either side of the Board may require the
Standing Committee of the Conference to advise upon such procedure, provided always
that the piecework or quantity rates to be finally fixed shall be determined in accordance
with the rules of such Board.

Local Boards of Arbitration operating in outlying districts accustomed to manufacture
goods of lower grades shall take this factor into consideration when estimating the pro-
ductive capacity of the average workman for the purpose of compiling piecework or
quantity statements.

CLAUSE 12. EXEMPTIONS FROM MINIMUM RATE. The minimum wage or graduated
scale rates shall not apply to clerks, engineers, mechanics, electricians, stokers, porters,
sweepers-up, lift or hoist men, caretakers and time-keepers, not engaged in actual manu-
facturing.

CLAUSE 13. PROCEDURE ON CLAIMS FOR MINIMUM RATE AND FOR PAYMENT OF LESS
THAN MINIMUM RATE. The Federation recognises the obligation upon the employers to
pay the minimum wage and graduated scale rates to all operatives to whom such rates
apply, except in cases where they hold the written permit of the Union or the Local Arbitra-
tion Board to accept less than such rates, but the obligation upon an employer to pay
such rates in cases where the operatives attain the specified ages whilst in his employ
shall be dependent in every case upon a separate application in writing being made to him
or to the manager or foreman of the department, stating the age of the applicant (of which
the employer may require reasonable proof) and the wage claimed, such application to
be made by the operative, or by the Union on his or her behalf, notwithstanding anything
contained in the Award of 10th February, 1898; and the liability of the employer to pay
the prescribed rate in the case of every lawful application shall commence at the expiration
of eight days from and including the date of the receipt by him or his manager or foreman
of the application. Should the employer decide that the operative is not qualified to earn
such rate, the employer, workman and Union representative shall endeavour to arrive
at a sum to be paid such operative. Failing any arrangements, the employer may terminate
the engagement in accordance with the contract for service, but shall pay such operative
of requisite age the prescribed rate for the last week of employment.

The procedure on claims for the minimum wage and graduated scale rates contained
in the Agreements of 26th January, 1909, and 28th July, 1909, is hereby revoked.

CLAUSE 14. GUARANTEE UNDER TERMS OF SETTLEMENT. Subject to the original
provisions of resolution 9 of the Terms of Settlement of 19th April, 1895, and the pro-
visions of the Trust Deed of 8th March, 1898, the monetary guarantee of the Federation
shall not be amenable in any case of alleged non-compliance by an Employer with agree-
ments in relation to wages, hours of labour, or conditions of employment, until after the
case has been dealt with in accordance with the procedure prescribed by rule 14 of the
Local Arbitration Board for dealing with disputes, and a decision of the Board, its Arbitra-
tors, or Umpire, has been given; but in no case shall the retrospective payment of wages
be ordered beyond the date of claim in writing sent either to the employer or to the Secretary
of the Board, whichever is earlier.

CLAUSE 15. BOY LABOUR. The restriction in the employment of boys, as provided
by the Award of 22nd August, 1892, and amended by the Agreement of 26th January,
1909 namely, one boy (under 10 years of age) to every three or fractional part of three
men (over 10 years of age) employed in the Clicking, Press, Lasting and Finishing Depart-

CLAUSE 16.--CLASSIFICATION OF FEMALE LABOUR. It is undesirable that females
should be employed amongst male operatives in the Clicking, Press, Lasting and Finishing
Departments of the trade, in which male labour is now almost exclusively employed.
The Conference therefore recommends that where females are now so employed, such
conditions shall gradually cease, and that in future no fresh female labour shall be employed
in the aforesaid departments.

CLAUSE 17-OVERTIME. No overtime shall be worked in the trade.

CLAUSE 18. UNIVERSAL APPLICATION OF NEW MINIMUM RATES. The minimum
wage and graduated scale rates fixed by this Agreement shall be simultaneously applied
to federated and non-federated manufacturers, and the Union and Federation undertakes
to bring every district up to such rates; but if at the expiration of the period for which
this Agreement has been fixed it can be shown that the Union has failed to put such rates
into general operation throughout the non-federated districts it shall be competent for
the Federation or any of its local Associations to decline to consider any further application
to increase such rates.

CLAUSE 19.-LESS FAVOURABLE TERMS BY LOCAL ARBITRATION BOARDS. In no
case shall a local Arbitration Board upon which the Federation or Union is represented,
its Arbitrators or Umpires, make any agreement or award as to wages, hours of labour,
or conditions of employment, which shall be less favourable generally to the operatives
(having regard to the local circumstances of the district) than the wages, hours and con-
ditions contained in any agreement or award made between the Federation and the Union,
or which extends beyond the period for which any such national agreement or award, or
any local agreement or award of a similar character, affecting federated manufacturers
has been fixed.

CLAUSE 20.- STRIKES AND LOCK-OUTS. - The Conference re-affirms resolution 8 of
the Terms of Settlement of 19th April, 1895, which is as follows:

No strike or lock-out shall be entered into on the part of any body of workmen,
members of the National Union, or any manufacturer represented on any Local
Board of Arbitration."

Where grievances exist they shall be investigated immediately by representatives of
the local Manufacturers' Association and of the local branch of the Union concerned,
with a view to adjustment.

Where any strike or lock-out takes place and is continued beyond the period of three
days allowed by the Agreement of 31st March, 1910, the right of the Federation or the
Union, as the case may be, to claim upon the monetary guarantee under that agreement
and the Trust Deed, may be exercised by a National Umpire appointed in accordance
with clause 9 of the Trust Deed, and on the recommendation of the Minister of Labour,
for a forfeiture either (a) by way of fine or penalty, or (b) by way of damages or com-
pensation for loss sustained, and in any case where the latter alternative is adopted the
amount of such loss shall be assessed by a committee of three representatives of the
Federation and three representatives of the Union, and in the event of their disagreement
the question shall be referred to the National Umpire.

CLAUSE 21.-STANDING COMMITTEE. -A Standing Committee of three representatives
of the Federation and three representatives of the Union, with the Chairman of the Con-
ference, shall be appointed to deal with all matters arising out of or in connection with the
Terms of Settlement of 1895, so far as they are now operative, and any other national
agreement between the Federation and the Union and this Agreement, including any dis-
putes that may arise as to the interpretation of such agreements, provided that due regard
is paid to the authoritative decisions that have already been given under these above-
named agreements.

CLAUSE 22. CONFLICT WITH LOCAL BOARDS OF ARBITRATION.--Anything in this
Agreement which is in conflict with existing local awards or agreements shall be remitted
to the parties by whom such agreements were made or to the local Boards of Arbitration.
Failing agreement by the local authority, the matter in dispute may be remitted to the
Standing Committee.

CLAUSE 23.-DURATION AND RATIFICATION OF AGREEMENT. - This Agreement shall
come into operation on the 31st March, 1921, and it shall not be competent for either side
to re-open the same till hte expiration of

REGISTERED TRADE UNION.
Having to send in a full return of Income and Expenditure for the Union
(Council and Branch combined) to the Registrar, in compliance with the different
Acts of Parliament covering Trade Unions, we shall be pleased if you will help
the Central Office by completely filling in the Form sent along, and send it
back to the General Secretary ON OR BEFORE FEBRUARY IST, 1921, certain.
FIVE-WEEK MONTH.
There being five Saturdays in this month, branch secretaries are asked to
make up their returns and pay for same accordingly.
RETURNS!!!
Some Branches persistently send in their returns after the 15th, and this
month 19 Branches were late. We have several times appealed to Secretaries
to send along their returns in time, and unless it is done in future we shall
have no option but to fine the delinquents in accordance with rule.
Moreover, lateness in sending in the Monthly Returns makes it increasingly
difficult to get out the Report in time for the Monthly Meetings.
TRADE UNION STAMP.
This is a matter which we have stated before rests with the members to
make a success. It is in the interests of members themselves that "Stamped
Footwear " should be increasingly purchased; therfeore, push the Trade Union
Stamp. Members and their families should wear only Union Stamped Footwear.
TRADE UNION BUTTONS AND BROOCHES.
A fresh supply of buttons and brooches has recently been secured and can
be had upon application, price 6d. each, cash with order. Secretaries, please
note, when ordering button. or brooches, cash should ALWAYS be sent with
order.

REPORT OF THE AUDITOR.

241. Uppingham Road, Leicester,
14th January, 1921.

To the Members of the Executive Council,
National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives.

I beg to report that I have examined at the Head Office of the
Union, the whole of the Account Books, Receipts, Vouchers, Counterfoils
and Bank Books, and certify the same to be correct and in accordance
with law.

There has been a loss on the Trade Fund during the half-year of
£21,799 15s. 10d., due without doubt to the abnormal demand for unem-
ployment benefit, £46,061 16s. 3d. being spent in this connection. The
Sick Fund has increased during the half-year by the sum of £15,677 Os. 4d.,
Political Fund £142 6s. 10d., and the Fidelity Fund 7s. 6d., and thus the
total loss on the Central Funds is reduced to £5,980 1s. 2d. The sum of
£286,655 10s. 6d. now stands to the credit of the Union at Headquarters.

I have examined the Deeds and Bonds as shewn in the Balance
Sheet, and have to report the same are in order and intact. There have
been added to the list during the half-year two Investment Bonds-the
Kettering Urban District Council and the Leicester Co-operative Print-
ing Society Limited.

To the General Secretary and his Staff I offer my thanks for their
assistance, and for the explanation given to my queries, and testify to the
careful, efficient and able manner in which the books are kept.

J. B. B. ROBERTSON,
Corporate Accountant and Public Auditor.

GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.
FELLOW MEMBERS
VOTING ON PIECEWORK U. DAYWORK.-One is really surprised in the circumstances
at the small number of members taking part in the recent vote, although there is to the
casual observer at least 17,000 votes for piccework or quantity statements or payment
by results, but with a limited output.
We make a generous estimate of the voting by assuming that there were 23,256 voters
out of the 75,616 members, and that gives us a ballot of 30.75 per cent. in these branches.

On the same reckoning the Northampton voting was 54 per cent. and in the county
45 per cent.; Leicester men's branches 18 per cent., while the Leicester women voted
1,166 for the present system and 49 for a change; Bristol and Kingswood 34 per cent.;
Leeds 19 per cent.; Norwich 31 per cent.

In spite of this, the vote must stand and be respected, although I am constantly
meeting with members who think they voted for day labour pure and simple. I am
really afraid that before a statement upon this subject can be arrived at, the members
will have to vote upon a policy for or against day labour pure and simple. I may here
say that although I think our members have a right to express their opinion for or against
this or any similar method of working, seeing they are the people who do the work, I should
deeply regret ever seeing day labour pure and simple introduced into our trade again.
I have always believed that if an employer is to buy my labour I should have a voice in
saying what price should be paid for the same. Day labour pure and simple gives no option
for the operatives to exercise that right; the result is the operative is continually worried
by the employer when no quantity statements are in existence.

I have had two votes of censure passed upon me without first of all being asked for
an explanation. The humour of the situation is this the treatment meted out to me is
the same as the Government are meting out to Ireland.

SAILORS AND SOLDIERS. On the 15th December, 1920, I attended a meeting of the
Discharged Sailors and Soldiers' Committee, when we decided not to train any more men
for our trade until occupation can be found for them.
The TRADE BOARD met on the 16th ult., to consider my request for a 50 per cent.
increase in the Trade Board prices. Such was not conceded to us, but we were enabled
to get 10s. increase on the minimum wage, making it 75s. for dayworkers, and 7% per cent.
increase on the repairing groundwork and extras, and 10 per cent. to be added to the
handsewn groundwork work only. Owing to District Boards being set up this decision
has to be reported to them before the same can be confirmed.
The COUNCIL MEETING was held on the 19th and 20th ult.
On the 21st ult. I journeyed to LEICESTER to meet the Co-operative Wholesale Society
Directors respecting the Derby factory. After a lengthy interview with them I made
arrangements to meet them at their Derby works early in January.
IRELAND.-On the 29th December a Special Meeting of the LABOUR PARTY was held
in London to consider the report of the Delegation and Commission to Ireland, and anyone
reading that report will come to the conclusion that things are very bad there, and I think
it would be well if the recommendations were given a trial. I know there are people
who cannot trust anyone, but the greatest honour of my life was when I was an M.P.
and had the opportunity of voting for Home Rule for a nation with whom we had been at
war-South Africa. The Irish may to some extent differ from the English, but I believe
they are as British as other persons in the British Empire. It is the Government them-
selves who have turned the Irish against them and I am sorry to find some Labour men
do not believe in it. I do not believe in class dictatorship; I am a democrat and I believe
in all parties in the community having a direct interest in the welfare of the nation as a
whole. At the same time I am not anxious to hand over Sinn Fein to Ulster, nor Ulster
to Sinn Fein; we must have dual parliaments for the present and I hope by comradeship
and good feeling we may be able to bring the two under one régime.
SPECIAL COUNCIL MEETINGS were held on the 4th and 5th inst. to discuss the terms
we should introduce to the employers. As I have intimated before, I think when our mem-
bers see our request there will be few suggest that the Council have not asked for enough.
On the 6th inst. I attended a special TRADE BOARD ADVISORY COMMITTEE in London,
and after five hours adopted the recommendations named above.

In the evening I went to DERBY and held a meeting of the operatives at the C.W.S.

method as to how to arrive at statements for measuring the amount of work done. Several
of the operatives thought we should not fix up statements as they were of the opinion the
Union had turned this down, but I explained that the policy of the Union was to have
piecework statements and a fixed wage to be set.
LEICESTER was visited on the following day, when I enquired into the stoppage of the

debating the question, this in spite of the fact that they did not ask permission of the
Chairman, who happened to be the secretary of one of our Leicester Branches. Occasion-
ally they do act in this manner.

There has been so little response to the many appeals made on this occasion, that one can
come to the conclusion that we are very lukewarm on this matter as on many others,
where some interest ought to be exhibited.

PARLIAMENTARY AGENT'S REPORT.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
Since my last report was written another year has come to an end, and one can
but regret that it should have finished under such conditions as to make one almost despair.
In whatever direction one turns the conditions were appalling; at home the old terror of
unemployment was again a dominating feature, thousands of our fellow workers willing
and able to work, were denied the opportunity of so doing. To those associated with
working-class life there is no need to say what this means in the homes of the people.
The situation abroad is no better, rather is it in some respects worse, for trade has
And so in a
not collapsed since the War, merely because it has never been restarted.
world where we were told the nations were hungering for the products of labour due to
scarcity following upon the War, labour is in enforced idleness, unable to produce, unable
to earn wages, and with prices still sky high the resultant misery is terrible to contemplate.

---
42
And what has Parliament done in its two years of existence to help in these matters?
Twice it has rejected a Bill brought in by the Labour Party to deal with Unemployment
Speaker after speaker from the Labour benches urged that it was not wise to wait until
the crisis was upon us before we prepared to deal with it, but that rather when trade was
fairly good we should lay our plans and be ready for whatever the future might bring.
The Government with its huge slavish majority would not heed our appeals, we might
be ever so sincere in our endeavours, but they the people of all the talents were quite
capable of meeting the situation, and so a policy of drift was followed, the only policy
that this or any other Government in the past have understood.

The refusal to do anything at home in regard to future unemployment would have
been more understandable had their foreign policy been of a different character, but it
has been one that was bound by the very nature of things to produce chaos. The so-called
Peace Treaties have not given us peace, the policy of the Entente led by France has resulted
in a kind of general paralysis in Europe, and a smouldering volcano in the Near East,
whilst our efforts in connection with Russia, moulded on the Churchill plan, have made
it impossible to restart anything in the nature of International trade.

While not desiring to be a pessimist one cannot see much hope in the immediate future,
unless steps are taken to secure exchange of goods by barter, which I do not consider
by any means impossible, or by the setting up of some form of International credits, so
that the difficulties arising out of the rates of exchange can be overcome, then some con.
siderable time must elapse before anything substantial in the way of trade can take place.
The trouble of it is the world is not run upon lines that seek to supply the people with the
things they need merely because they do need them, but rather as a means to enable
profit being made, and the lack of confidence existing in present conditions simply intensify
the difficulties of the moment.

Of course as usual it is the working class who is responsible. The high wages obtained
during the War according to many wiseacres have produced all our troubles, and the only
way out that they can suggest is to reduce them. How it can be argued that by reducing
the consuming capacity of the workers it is possible to permanently improve trade is
difficult to understand, and further, how is it possible to reduce wages with the cost of
living at its present figure?
All this constitutes a problem upon which it would be well for the workers to con-
centrate their minds, and to try and ascertain how far Parliament as at present constituted
has, or is likely to help in its solution. I am fully persuaded there is little to hope for
from this wonderful Coalition, and many of the stunts that are started by the Press are
not done with any idea of destroying it, but rather to make it more reactionary. It is
not very encouraging from a Labour point of view to find working men and women enthusing
over the return of stunt candidates, especially when one knows them at close quarters,
and I am convinced that all that kind of thing is but the old policy of distracting the minds
of the people when they shew a tendency to become, if not dangerous, then too enquiring.
It must be the purpose of us all in the New Year to press forward the claims of the
Labour movement, always believing that we stand for that which is best in the interest
of the whole of the people, and until they get some clear idea of what is wanted and make
up their minds how they intend to get it, very little in the way of real change will take
place. This is emphasised by the endeavours that are being made to secure an abandor-
ment of the supposed social programme of the Government, and the apparent readiness
of those in authority to respond to the clamour. Even in regard to houses it is being
pointed out that the figure of 500,000 as the number required was a miscalculation, and
that 150,000 will be ample for our needs; those who make these statements do not believe
them, but it is the beginning of an agitation to stop building houses as a means of economy.
It means we are back to the old state of things when material wealth counts for more
than human life, that a nation's prosperity was to be measured by accumulated wealth
rather than by the standard of the life of its people. This outlook on life must be changed.
human needs must stand first, and whether it is in regard to houses, education or any other
social question, the people must be provided with all that is necessary to develop human
life. Whatever our views of the future may be, surely one thing is certain, we shall be
more successful in our endeavours if we have a strong, healthy population to deal with.
Nothing can be done with ignorance, and a low physical standard does not produce the
courage necessary in the fight for human progress. Perhaps our opponents know this and
it may explain their hostility.

However, we must not be discouraged, but rather keep on, believing that persistent
effort will ultimately meet with success.
18th January, 1921.

WALTER R. SMITH.

The Co-operative Congress at Swansea, 1917, readily responded to this proposal by
adopting the following resolution:
“This Congress adopts the resolution passed at the Trades Union Congress,
held in Birmingham, September, 1916, and authorises the Central Board of the Co-
operative Union to appoint six representatives to meet a similar number appointed
by the Trades Union Congress Parliamentary Committee.”
As a result, six representatives from each body were duly appointed, and after a series
of meetings, a statement was agreed to which contained proposals for mutual aid and joint
action, including the formation of a National Committee to be called “The United Advisory
Council of Co-operators and Trade Unionists.”
This statement was accepted by the Trades Union Congress held at Blackpool in
September, 1917, and by the special Co-operative Conference held in London during the
following October. The most important clause included in this joint statement is that
relating to the assistance to be given to workers during trade disputes.’ This clause was
in the following terms:—
“Clause (5). The consideration of how far it is desirable and possible to ensure
the unrestricted distribution of food supplies, or the payment of benefit during im-
portant trade disputes by issuing through the various branches of the Co-operative
Movement food coupons or loans from the Co-operative Wholesale Society’s Bank
on the security of Trade Union assets.”
At first sight it appears that this clause is intended to benefit Trade Unionists only.
A careful reading of the first two lines of the clause, however, will enable co-operators to
understand its importance and its value to the Co-operative Movement. Obviously, if
the unrestricted distribution of food supplies during important trade disputes is to be
ensured through co-operative channels, arrangements must be made between the Co-opera-
tive Movement and the Trade Union Movement, as a result of which co-operative employees,
both productive and distributive, can remain at work when other workers are on strike.
The Railway Dispute.
The statement already referred to was in due course accepted and adopted by joint
conferences of Co-operators and Trade Unionists held in different parts of the country
under the auspices of the United Advisory Council of Trade Unionists and Co-operators.
Steps were afterwards taken to form local joint councils and to create machinery for joint
action. The value of these councils and the usefulness of the machinery established,
were not fully tested, however, until there arose a trade dispute of national importance
which required the attention of both the national and local advisory councils.
The railway dispute which occurred during the autumn of 1919, and which continued
during the months of September and October, was the period during which the real value
of co-operation between Trade Unionists and Co-operators was first clearly demonstrated.
Then, if not before, Co-operators and Trade Unionists became conscious of their relation-
ship and realised that the resolutions passed by their representatives in previous years
were not merely expressions of pious opinion.
The railway dispute arose chiefly because the Government, supported by the united
capitalist Press, had challenged the power of one of the largest Trade Unions in Great
Britain. At the time when that challenge was made the Government was fully equipped
for a great industrial conflict. The machinery of publicity used by the Government during
the war was almost intact. The transport facilities devised for war purposes were exactly
what Goverment departments required for use in a conflict with the National Union of
Railwaymen. Hence, when a dispute seemed probable, fleets of motor transport wagons
were rapidly mobilised, the chiefs of Government departments were called together, and
after consultation with their permanent officials, the Government were able to establish
a unity of command far superior to the inter-departmental arrangements devised by them
for the purpose of conducting war against foreign enemies.
The Government, sure of the united support of every capitalist interest, were evi-
dently quite determined to beat the railwaymen. In fact, a long strike seemed inevitable,
leading ere it ended to a general strike in all trades. Fortunately, however, their clear
understanding of the dangerous policy adopted by the Government and the prospect of
a general strike caused Co-operators and Trade Unionists to take joint action without
delay. That action will undoubtedly prove to be the first step towards a still closer
alliance between the forces of Trade Unionism and Co-operation.
Joint Action in London.
As soon as the dispute commenced, Mr. Burt Williams, secretary of the Southern
Section of the Co-operative Union, acting as secretary to the London Joint Advisory
Council of Trade Unionists and Co-operators, promptly called a special conference, which

that they will receive the support of the C.W.S. Bank when they need assistance unless their
funds are invested in accordance with the terms of the statement accepted by the Co-
operative Congress and the Trades Union Congress. If the Co-operative Movement is
to assist Trade Unionists in an industrial crisis it follows that Trade Union funds must be

At the end of 1919 the accumulated funds of the Unions affiliated to the

then, do they leave their ammunition in the hands of their enemies? There are
many reasons why it is to the advantage of Trade Unionists to invest their money in under-
takings controlled by their friends, and by investing their funds in the Co-operative Whole-
sale Society Bank they can ensure help similar to that given to the N.Ü.R. during the
railway strike.

Trade Unionists should be Co-operators.

The investment of Trade Union funds in co-operative undertakings is not, however,
the only method by which Trade Unionists can further extend Co-operative production
and distribution, and thus increase the number of workers working under guaranteed
Trade Union conditions. An increase of membership would enable the Co-operative
Movement to devleop its productive activities. If the workers then expand the market
for co-operative products, the possibilities for production on a large and economical scale,
under up-to-date systems of scientific management, would be enormously increased.

The wage-earners can create an enormous market by spending their wages in co-opera-
tive shops. As previously stated, the turnover of the Co-operative Movement in 1919
was £200,000,000. This figure, compared with the total wages bill, as represented by an
estimate based upon a war period increase of 100 per cent. (an increase rather below Board
of Trade estimates), gives the following result :-

Wage bill, 1915
Increase, 100 per cent.
Total
£830,000,000
£830,000,000
£1,660,000,000

After making due allowances for taxation, rent, insurance premiums, Trade Union
contributions, &c., it is clear that wage earners spend at least £1,000,000,000 a year with
private traders, as compared with the £200,000,000 spent by them in co-operative shops,
this despite the fact that it is through co-operative trading that the workers will secure
effective control of prices. Until the workers control prices they will never
control real wages. The Co-operative Movement offers the most immediate
and practical means for creating a really democratic system of controlling
prices. The wage-earner may, by economic necessity, be compelled to sell his labour
to the private capitalist; he is under no economic pressure which compels him to buy
his commodities from shops owned by multiple shop companies, private traders or shops
controlled by other middlemen.

Private Enterprise During the War.

The case against the system of production and distribution for private profit was
strong before the war. The rampant profiteering during the war period has made the
present system intolerable. The success of commercial groups, trusts, and combines
during the period of national suffering and sacrifice is reflected in the memorandum sub-
mitted by the Board of Inland Revenue to the Select Committee of the House of Commons
on "Increases of Wealth during the War."

The Board call attention to the estimate of Dr. Stamp (late Assistant Secretary to
the Department), a recognised expert and financial adviser to four Cabinets :-

"In the 'Economic Journal of September, 1918, Dr. J. C. Stamp published a
non-official estimate of increases of wealth. He gave the figure of £5,250,000,000 as
his estimate of the amount which should be added to the aggregate pre-war wealth
of individuals as a whole, in order to arrive at the aggregate wealth of individuals
which would be subject to, and likely to be revealed for the purposes of any general
capital levy which might be imposed at the termination of the war.

BRANCH REPORTS.
ARBROATH. -Trade in this Branch is unprecedentedly bad, and all of
our members have been treated to three weeks' holiday minus their wages.
When men and women are brought face to face with the state of affairs here
represented, it compels them to think as well as talk. Such thinking leads us
to say that if ever the bottom was knocked out of an argument, the past policy
of the Union in attempting to run an out-of-work fund on a contribution of
a half-penny for 5s. benefit, has been found lacking in forethought as well as
ordinary human sympathy. Everyone, except our half-penny financiers,
could foresee that whenever an exceptional strain was put on the fund it was
bound to snap. The result is, that when members all over the country are
urgently in need of financial assistance they cannot get it, because in past
years they did not pay a contribution sufficient to justify that expectation.
The pity is that the Council of the Union, as a whole, has always supported
that short-sighted policy, and even at the last Conference they put before the
delegates a scheme to raise the contributions by only one penny per week,
which, fortunately the Conference turned down. What we require is a
Council possessing some courage a Council that will leave off emphasising
the fallacy that by raising the contributions we will lose our members. Indeed,
the history of the Union proves quite the reverse, as every increase in the con-
tributions has been followed by an augmented membership. What the Union
requires is a fund, and a contribution, that will cover all unemployment,
whether suspension or otherwise. In bad times like the present it is not a lot
of talk that is wanted, but good Treasury notes, and the members must be
told that before these notes can be paid out they must first be paid in. The
pity is that responsible officials of the Union did not drive that point home
years ago. Meantime the poor member has to suffer, and the poorer he is
the more he has to suffer. It is unpalatable to write thus, but the foregoing,
we think, represents the facts, and the sooner the members pull the wool out
of their eyes, and view things in the light of present-day experiences, the better
it will be for all concerned. As a sequence to bad trade, and consequent
underfeeding, we have a sick list much above the normal.

SOUTHAMPTON.-Boot repairers' trade dull in sympathy with the
shipping, shipbuilding and engineering trades, from which trades there has
been a lot of discharges owing to shortness of orders, and also to cancellation
of contracts on which work had not been sufficiently advanced. We are
hoping that trade will take a spurt before long and continue on the upward
grade.

STREET. Previous reports on the state of trade in this district have
been bad but conditions have been growing gradually worse until we have
now reached a point the like of which has never before been known. After
closing down for periods of from ten days to three weeks for the Christmas
holidays our factories are only able to resume work for five or six hours a day
and only three days a week. Over 800 of our members are signing at the
Labour Exchange, and our own funds are being drawn upon to an extent
never previously experienced in Street. Although at present prospects are
very discouraging, we extend to our fellow members the best wishes for the
New Year.

WHITWICK. The Whitwick Branch wish you all a very happy and
prosperous New Year. We are sorry that we have to state at the time of
reporting that we are still on short time, making 40 hours per week, and now
as we have commenced on the new year, 1921, we are hoping that the boot
and shoe trade will soon be in a much better state, as one can see in our Monthly
Report of December that in some Branches the state of the trade is much
worse than it is in this district, and we are hoping that before long the boot
and shoe operatives all over the country will be making full time, as our trade
has had a hard time for months now. But as 1921 is but young we, the opera-
tives of the Whitwick Branch, do wish our Council and officials every success
in all their endeavours they put forth for making a much better state of things
in the boot and shoe trade, so that we may be more in line with some of the
trade unions as regards wages.

YORK. We beg to report that trade is bad in York as elsewhere. Our
members working about four days per week, with a proportionate wage; our
only hope is that trade will soon begin to brighten up, and that with some
expansion in the general trade of the country we shall share the benefit. At
our Branch meeting we discussed the question raised by our Chesterfield
comrades re District Committees, and agreed that the formation of such a
committee for the district mentioned would be a step in the right direction.
We in York have, fortunately, the South Yorkshire Statement, with its 70 per
cent. bonus, and for day workers at the Co-operative we have payment for all
holidays and six weeks' sickness per annum. If the York Co-operative can
give these conditions, and turn out work equal to its competitors, then there
is no reason why all the other Co-operative Societies should not do the same.
The sad part of the whole affair is, that working people, including trade unionists,
do not act to those whom they employ in the same manner that they expect
their employers to adopt. We shall be pleased to assist in whatever way we
can the formation of the committee. We wish to repeat our protest against
the method of distribution of Branches for the purpose of electing delegates
to National Conferences. We cannot see where any Repairing Branch is
going to be successful in getting one of its members elected.

WHY NOT CHEAPER SOAP AND MARGARINE?

The price of margarine to-day is just about the same as twelve months ago, but not
so the price of the raw materials. Ground nuts have dropped from £43 a ton to £17.
and palm kernels from £40 10s. to £25 105. Cocoa beans twelve months ago were £103
per ton, to-day they are ₤40, but cocoa and chocolate are no cheaper. Palm oil is sold
at £46 per ton instead of 190 10s., yet soap and candles have not dropped in price appreci-
ably. When is the consumer to get the benefit of these reductions? Leicester Mail,
January 6th, 1921.

RECENT BANK FAILURE.
C.W.S. Official Points the Moral for Co-operators.

ENCOURAGING STATEMENT.

M. G. Hayhurst presided over an attendance of 627 delegates, representing 131
Societies, at the London divisional meeting on Saturday.

The Chairman referred with satisfaction to the fact that the society was making great
progress. The report showed for thirteen weeks an increased receipts of 19 per cent.,
on the productive works an increase of 31 per cent. There was no business house
in the country which could show such a picture. (Applause.) “I fear no foes without,"
and Chairman added : "it is the foes within we have to watch.”

Strong Position of the Bank.

Mr. Goodwin stated that he should like to make a reference to the stability of the
Bank. I do so because a recent happening in the banking world-the failure of Farrow's
Bank-has rather brought this subject into prominence. A local bank manager recently
said to a member of a co-operative society, when talking about Farrow's failure, that the
C.W.S. Bank would be the next. (Laughter.) There have been a number of inquiries
which shows some disquietude of mind with regard to the strength of the C.W.S.
Bank. The C.W.S. Bank is a department of the society which has behind it the whole
resources of the Wholesale Society. In the first place the share capital is over £4,000,000 ;
we have a reserve fund of £3,500,000 ; and we have a depreciation fund of over £4,500,000,
making a total reserve at the back of any customer who puts money into the bank of
the Wholesale Society. (Applause.) Considering the size of the Wholesale Society, I do not think
any other bank-not excluding even the 'big five '-which has a backing
of the C.W.S.

I only want to refer to Farrow's Bank (proceeded Mr. Goodwin) beyond stating
what has been said-I believe by the Chancellor-that some estate of the real value of
what had appeared in the bank's accounts at ten times that amount, viz., £700,000.
How does that position compare with the Wholesale Society's position ? Every building
that has been put up or acquired before 1901 is standing at nothing in the society's books.
Every machine or plant or the fixtures which were bought before 1907 stands at nothing
though fully depreciated in our books by a sum amounting to nearly £400,000. I should
mention that in the society's books. In addition, while land will have appreciated very much,
like to repeat that there is no institution in this country which is in a stronger financial
position than the C.W.S., so that if you have any inquiry or any intimation that the C.W.S.
safe, it does not sound I think that you will be able to meet it very thoroughly.
I have great pleasure in stating (he continued) that the banking department is making
great progress by leaps and bounds. Trade unions are coming in as fast as we can deal with
them; and the past year has shown a most remarkable increase in that direction. I think
the relations with the trade union movement show that we are not only strong but are
able to meet all their requirements in case of need.” (Applause.)
-The Co-operative News, January 15th, 1921.

it sells. It could immediately find use for at least £20,000,000 more in the same kind of

More Worlds to Win.

ideal of trading is to sell at cost price of production and distribution. This cannot be
realised until every phase of production and distribution is in co-operative hands.
Take one example only: The Tea Department handles more tea than any other
wholesale house in the United Kingdom. The greater portion of this vast quantity-

Eighteen Million Pounds.
What Others Need.

Labour Commission's Report on Cork.
Two members of the Commission, Messrs. J. Lawson, M.P., and W. Lunn, M.P.,
were delegated to visit Cork City on Monday, December 13th, for the purpose of investigat-
ing the cause, extent, and general circumstances of the conflagration which occurred on
the previous Saturday night and during the early hours of Sunday morning.
The news of the destruction in Cork did not come as a surprise to the Commission.
During its stay in Cork the week before, the Commission could not avoid the feeling that
serious outbreak of trouble was probable. There were signs of increasing irritation,
provoked by the R.I.C. Auxiliary Division, which we were convinced at the time might
result in retaliation against the Crown Forces or in bolder or more intensified action on
the part of the Auxiliary Police.
The two members of the Commission who travelled to Cork for the special. purpose
of investigating the events of the week-end made as close an examination of the situation
as time permitted. They visited the ruined areas, and took evidence from responsible
itizens on the subject.
In view of the extended reports of the fire in the Press, it is unnecessary to specify
and describe the gutted buildings; but the newspaper accounts convey only a faint
impression of the terrible havoc wrought in the city. It would be difficult to conceive
a scene of greater desolation than that presented by the destroyed business premises in
the centre of Cork.
The whole Commission had an opportunity of seeing Cork before the latest calamity
which has befallen it. The contrast was striking and appalling. It is clear that the
incendiaries sought out the most valuable premises in the city. Large business houses
and massively fronted shops have been reduced to piles of smouldering debris, charred
woodwork, and wrenched and twisted iron girders. It was not possible even approximately
estimate the money value of the property destroyed, but business men informed the
members of the Commission that it might run into millions of pounds.
The disaster involves the unemployment of a considerable number of workers in
addition to those who will be indirectly thrown out of work as a result of the fire. The
commerce of the city has already suffered very appreciably as a result of the events of
Terent months and the incendiarism of the past week-end will strike a further blow at its
conomic activities.
Inquiries made and statements elicited enable the members of the Commission to
make the following statement, which a number of witnesses interviewed are prepared,
if given adequate guarantees for their future security, to substantiate on oath.

Delegates to the Conference.
UNEMPLOYMENT.
We are sorry we have no very strong faith in the method that has been evolved
by the Government for dealing with unemployment. A circular has been sent out,
which probably many of our readers will have received, suggesting that what work there
is should be divided out, even though it entails that no one will have a full week's work
to do. Of course, this is not a new idea, for it was put into practice some time ago in the
boot and shoe industry, and we believe it is also in operation in the cotton and other
industries. In neither, however, has it done away with unemployment.
It may provide a modicum of work for some numbers that at present have none
but it will lessen the wages of those who are at present working, and in the end will not
provide work for all those who are needing it. We recognise the force of the old saying,
Half a loaf is better than no bread," and it may be that a general and proportionate
sharing out of work might be a bridge over the awkward time until trade revives, but it
must be a very shaky bridge all the while. It may avert actual want, and so far it will
be palliative, but it will widen discontent, for it will make all the workers feel a pinch
the which they have not been accustomed, and for that very reason they will resent it all
but will operate just reversely. To run two separate shifts where one sufficed
The worst of the suggestion is it will do nothing to encourage a revival in trade,
before must necessarily be to increase costs, seeing that output will remain
the same. We had hoped the Government would have signalised the New Year with
be continued over another year, so the announcement that it would die with the end of
an announcement that E.P.D. was to be dropped. There can be no pretence that it will
the financial year would have cost nothing, and it would certainly have been some en-
couragement to manufacturers to try what better they could do than they are doing.
This, and the announcement of other retrenchments, which would mean less money out
of the public pocket, and more left in it with which to develop trade, would do more to
something that will be towards a positive cure, and not a palliation of the most
reduce unemployment than will a sharing out of the little work that is going. We need
extreme symptoms. -Shoe and Leather News, January 6th, 1921.

SOCIAL DEMOCRATIC FEDERATION.

CENTRAL OFFICE,
100, FLEET STREET, LONDON, Е.С. 4.
January 10th, 1921.

TO THE SECRETARY,
NATIONAL UNION OF BOOT AND SHOE OPERATIVES.

DEAR COMRADE,
THE EMERGENCY POWERS ACT, 1920.

During the Miners' Strike last year, the Emergency Powers Act (1920) was rushed
through Parliament, and is now on the Statute Book. It was opposed by the Parliamentary
Labour Party. Since its enactment, the emergence of many more or less important
issues aflecting the interests of the workers has tended to obscure the real nature of this
measure, and to prevent organised Labour from giving it the attention it deserves. In our
opinion, in view of the dangerous industrial position into which the Government has
allowed the country to drift, there is urgent need for the iniquitous character of this Act
being thoroughly understood, and the strongest effort being made, not only to expose
its authors, but to secure its condemnation and repeal.

On behalf of the Executive Council of the Social Democratic Federation therefore,
I beg to submit to your members the following considered opinion of the provisions of the
Act, and I shall be glad if you will inform me what steps your body has decided to take
to deal with the matter.

In addition to passing and publishing resolutions on the subject, we suggest that you
communicate your decision to your member of Parliament.

The main points to which we desire to direct your attention are :-

(1) The Executive Authority has absolute power, under Section I of the Act, to
determine whether or not a state of emergency exists, and to proclaim a state of emergenc
by Order in Council.

(2) The power of the Executive to proclaim a state of emergency, and to frame
regulations, is practically unlimited by any legal authority, or process. Section 2 (1)
gives the Home Secretary power to arrogate to himself (apart from the exclusion of power
to impose military or industrial conscription, and to make participation in a strike or
peaceful persuasion an offence) such powers as he deems necessary.

(3) The words used in the Act, to describe the purposes for which powers may be
arrogated (Section 2 (1)) are so vague and wide, as to afford no effective opportunity for
any Court to review acts done under cover of any regulations, by any Agent of the Govern-
ment.

(4) Regulations made as above, immediately operate as part of the Act (Section 2
(4)). They may be revoked, it is true, by resolution of both Houses of Parliament (Parlia-
ment having power to interpose within five days of the issue of the proclamation of a
state of emergency), but this limitation of the Home Secretary's power is vitiated by the
fact that all action taken under the regulations he has framed is valid even after the regu
lations have been revoked by Parliament.

To take by no means extreme examples, the Executive Authority may arrest and
imprison Strike leaders, and confiscate Trades Union funds, and any sentence of imprison
ment, or forfeiture of funds would continue to run, and be operative, after the repeal of
the regulations.

In addition to this, the five days' time limitation gives the Home Secretary ample
time if he cares to use it, to act unhampered by any Parliamentary criticism during the
vital period in any emergency. Besides, there is practically no hope of any regulations
of an objectionable character being revoked during a period of industrial trouble by a
resolution of both Houses of Parliament, as the Act requires.

(5) The Home Secretary and every Agent of the Government are completely protected
by the Act (Section 2 (5) ) against any legal action for compensation or redress, arising
out of the excessive or unreasonable exercise of powers under the Act. This amounts
to the withdrawal of a safeguard which in the past, to however small an extent, has pro-
tected Trades Unionists and the public against the arbitrary actions of a reactionary
Government and its officials.

If the above interpretation of the provisions of this Act is correct, we feel sure that
your organisation will realise the need for vigorous action to secure the repeal of the
measure.

Hitherto, the right and duty of the Government to protect the community by means
of such measures as are reasonably necessary to insure public peace, has been recognised.
But abuse of such power by the Government, or its Agents, was safeguarded prior to the
passing of this Act, both by Parliamentary control and the supervision of the Law Courts.
Officials were personally responsible for excesses, and the Executive Authority itself
was answerable to Parliament, which had the power to grant or refuse indemnity, on a
review of events after they had happened. That constitutional position, however, has been
swept away by the Emergency Powers Act, and in view of what may reasonably be
expected as an outcome of the present serious industrial and social position, we feel very
strongly that the general body of British workers should be well informed of their present
legal status under the new Act, and that a vigorous agitation should be set on foot for its
repeal.

The Social Democratic Federation, with its limited means, is doing all it can in the
matter. May I express the hope that your organisation also will assist.

Yours fraternally,
THOMAS KENNEY, Secretary.

WELLINGBOROUGH.—IDEAL CLOTHIERS' COMING-OF-AGE.
Fitting Celebrations of the Event.
The coming-of-age of the Ideal Clothiers Ltd., Wellingborough, was celebrated in
fitting fashion on Thursday and Friday, December 30th and 31st, by entertainments
for the employees. About 500 of the younger employees attended on the Thursday
evening, when an excellent tea was provided, followed by an entertainment to which all
the items were contributed by "Ideal" workers.
A Good Record.
Mr. L. Jessop said as a society they made their start with about fifteen employees
in all, and during the year the number increased to about fifty. Their first year's trading
amounted to £4,766, and they were as proud of that turnover as they were of what they
did last year. Their wages amounted to £503, the profit was £179, and the dividend on
the wages was £36. This year the wages were £95,304, the workers numbered 1,050,
the trade done was £614,286, the profit was £42,262, the dividend on wages £9,530, and the
capital £87,919. The total trade done during those years was £2,614,000; the total
interest was £33,051 and the total dividend on wages was £43,904. Their provident
and endowment fund stood at £14,422, and the social and educational fund at £4,487.
There was no reason why their business should not multiply in the same proportion in
the coming twenty-one years as in the past. - Co-operative News, January 8th, 1921.

SWISS SHOE AND LEATHER INDUSTRY,
Informing Official Report for 1919 Issued.
The Swiss Association of Commerce and Industry has just issued its report on Swiss
commerce and industry for the year 1919. It is an exceedingly useful publication, and
contains, besides full general information, detailed reports on the various industries.
The pages devoted to the shoe and leather trade are particularly interesting, and
present an illuminating picture of the industry under Government control. The hide
and skin merchants had to provide for the needs of the Swiss tanneries at official fixed prices.
and only those goods which could not be consumed in Switzerland were allowed to be
exported. Similarly, tanners had also to deliver leather to shoe manufacturers and
leather merchants at prices fixed by the authorities. They were allowed to export only
those goods which were not required in Switzerland. In January, 1919, the price of raw
hides and skins was reduced by about 16 per cent., and a corresponding reduction was
made in the price of leather and shoes. It is stated that business during 1919, although
satisfactory, was not brilliant when compared with the volume of trade during the war
years. Tanning materials, leather, and shoes are all exhaustively dealt with in the report.
It is interesting to note that while the importation of sole leather into Switzerland declined
in 1919, compared with 1918, the importation of upper leather during the same period was
considerably augmented. The following table shows the value of the imports in the
periods mentioned :-

MUNICIPAL BANK SCHEME, NORTHAMPTON.
Statements made at a meeting in the Liberal Club, Northampton.

Councillor Taylor, O.B.E., alluding to the proposal of a Municipal Savings Bank
said he hoped it would come some day. On occasions he thought he had the Council
with him on the point, but at others he thought they were lukewarm. Of this he was
sure, however, that the Ministry of Health was heartily in sympathy with the idea, and
he had been assured of their influence with the Treasury.

PROGRESSIVE NORTHAMPTON.
Councillor Kilby added his congratulations, and eulogised the work of Mr. Taylor, referring to his achievements with regard to the War Savings Committee, and now as chairman
of the Savings and Investment Committee. Most of the Council, he thought, though not
committed to the details, considered the proposed Municipal Bank a step in the right
direction, and of benefit to the town. They were under tremendous difficulties, for they
had no powers under existing Acts of Parliament to establish it. They had, however,
decided to approach other Municipal bodies with a view of petitioning Parliament for a
permissive measure so that with other Boroughs, Northampton might inaugurate a Mnui-
cipal bank. Their local Chancellor of the Exchequer and Town Clerk brought the matter
forward at a conference of various boroughs in London, only this week, but did not receive
a single supporter. This showed that Northampton was the most progressive Municipal
body in the Kingdom, with others lagging woefully behind.—Northampion Echo, January
28th, 1921.

FELLOW OFFICERS,

VOTING.

It has been brought to the notice of the Council
that certain Branches count their votes as soon as the ballot
is closed, but in order to prevent other centres being
influenced by the vote of one district as against another,

UNEMPLOYMENT ACT, 1920.
Instructions to Branch Officers.
CLAIMS.
As there seems to be a little misunderstanding amongst officials as to what
is, and what is not, expected of them in connection with the administration of
the 1920 Unemployment Act, the following instructions should be carried out,
because both in your own interest and those at the Head Office we want the working
of the Act to be quite clear.
First of all, the Minister of Labour was convinced that our Out-of-Work
Books were amongst the best in the country, and as a consequence he agreed
that only our own Unemployment Book should be used for both the Union and
State Benefit, rather than have one book for the Union and a State Vacant Book.
The member who is unemployed (and this does not mean suspended members
of any degree-THIS POINT SHOULD BE WELL NOTED), will report to the
Branch Officer in the usual manner, of course always assuming he is entitled to
the Union Benefit. The book will be signed in the usual manner, and the member
asked if he has lodged his Card with the Employment Exchange, and if so, the
Union's Unemployment Book will be stamped on the left-hand side with the
State Unemployment Rubber Stamp already in your possession. That ends the
business so far as the Branch Officers are concerned for at least a week. For
State purposes the week ends every Wednesday. Thus each Wednesday the
Branch Officers will fill in the form U.I.A. 75, OBTAINABLE FROM EMPLOY-
MENT EXCHANGE ONLY, and take a duplicate copy. What is required on that
particular form is for the Secretary to fill in the name of the Union at the top of
it and the name of the Branch. In Column 2 you must insert the name of your
Branch and then in Column 3 the name of the Member, whilst Column 4 will state
the days the member signed the book. This should be marked, at the top of the
columns, Thurs., Fri., Sat., Mon., Tues., Wed., and the details required will be
copied from the Out-of-Work Book. After filling in the form with an X, and
an O for the days not signed, this form will be signed at the bottom by the
Secretary in the parts 1 and 2.
These duplicate sheets will then be remitted to the EMPLOYMENT
EXCHANGE (and NOT to the Central Office), and in due course the list authoris-
ing payment, together with the names and the amount of money due to every
individual member, with a cheque for the total sum will be sent direct from the
Central Office. Thus the Central Office will take over the responsibility for pay-
ment of claims, as authorised by the Employment Exchanges. These forms will
be signed by the Members receiving benefit and returned by the Branch Secretary
to the Central Office.
It may be asked when will the money be sent along. That is an important
factor. It rests entirely with the Branch Officials as to how soon they remit
their forms to the Employment Exchange. For instance, in the Leicester
Women's case, the Claims are sent to the Leicester Exchange on Wednesday, and
after being checked are remitted to the Head Office. Cash is then remitted from
the Central Office on Friday and the Secretary is enabled to pay out on Saturday.
Another case-one of the London Branches, being on the spot, is enabled to get
their Claims through fairly soon, and they reach the Central Office on Thursday.
Cash is sent off the same day and the Secretary is here enabled to pay the Benefit
on Friday.
Another point is that the authority given to the Union clearly states that we
can only administer Benefit to THOSE MEMBERS who come under RULE 223.
A considerable amount of time has been spent on this Section of the Union's
work, and it has been the desire of all at the Central Office to try and make it as
simple as possible, and it is suggested that you will agree that now the Central
Office is taking on the responsibility of saying how many days will be allowed
and the total weekly rate of benefit, a great deal of the work has been taken off
the shoulders of Branch Officers.
February, 1921.

idly stand by and see so much suffering due to the lack of employment, when the means exist, if only the will was there to carry out the schemes. The resolutions which were unanimously passed at the conference were as follows:

Resolution I.

That this Conference accepts and endorses the Report now submitted; and reaffirms the resolution unanimously adopted by the Conference on 20th December last --
Declaring that the growing volume of unemployment is largely due to the failure of the Government to secure the resumption of trade with Russia and Central Europe;

(ii.) condemning the Government for not having taken timely action for the prevention of unemployment, as suggested by Labour;

(iii.) calling for immediate action to provide employment at wages, and where this is not done, to arrange for the provision of maintenance at not less than 40s. per week for each householder, with 25s. per week for each single man or woman, with additional allowances for dependants.

The Conference, whilst not ignoring the more fundamental causes of recurrent unemployment, now concentrates attention upon the measures necessary to meet the present emergency, and calls for

A Trade Policy:

(a) The immediate adoption of the policy of unobstructed trade with Russia;

(b) such an application of the terms of peace with ex-enemy countries as will promote the restoration of their economic life and re-establish normal commerce;

(c) concerted international arrangements for the stabilisation of the exchanges, the extension of credits, together with the promotion of commercial intercourse, and an unobstructed transport system throughout Europe;

An Expenditure Policy:

The Conference, moreover, calls upon the Government immediately to reverse its policy with regard to expenditure-

(d) By bringing promptly to an end its military adventures in Mesopotamia and elsewhere in the East;

(e) by terminating its military oppression and lawless reprisals in Ireland, which are stopping productive industry and lessening the economic resources of the country.

At the same time, the Conference demands the reversal of the policy recently inaugurated of attempting to arrest the necessary growth of much-needed services of public utility, as for example-

(a) Postponing, as far as possible, the carrying into effect of the Education Act of 1918, and discouraging all developments by the Local Education Authorities;

(b) slowing down, and in many cases actually obstructing, the building of the urgently required houses;

(c) discouraging and forbidding Local Authorities from carrying out much-needed local works of improvement.

The Conference declares that, in a period of unemployment, the policy of the Government should be one of expansion, not of contraction, of rightful and economical public expenditure; and that the necessary public works and services which must certainly be executed within each decade, ought to be, as far as possible, concentrated on the years of industrial depression, so as to avoid the waste of keeping workers in one year in idleness upon unemployment benefit, and in another year on excessive hours of labour at overtime rates.

It further declares that at the present moment there is a vast amount of necessary work waiting to be undertaken, which it would be greatly to the public advantage to put in hand at once, and which would ensure regular employment at wages for hundreds of thousands of men and women, such as-

(1) The immediate ordering by all the Government Departments and Local Authorities of the stores and necessary works which will in any case be required in the course of the next three years;

(ii.) the prohibition of all overtime (except where absolutely necessary to enable other workers to be started) in order to minimise the number of workers to be discharged;

the General Secretary's office. We trust in future every branch secretary
will endeavour to get in his returns NOT later than the fifteenth of every month,
and before sending them see that they are properly signed.

WHY CO-OPERATORS NEED MORE CAPITAL.
Why do co-operators need more capital at the present time? What special reason
is there why they should now make special efforts to increase their financial power? To
these questions answers are readily forthcoming. CO-OPERATORS NEED MORE CAPITAL,
FIRST, TO CARRY ON THEIR BUSINESS BECAUSE THE VALUE OF MONEY HAS FALLEN, AND
SECONDLY, IN ORDER THAT THEY MAY BE ABLE STILL FURTHER TO EXTEND THEIR BUSINESS.
The money invested in co-operative societies by workingmen and women forms the larger
part of the capital of the co-operative movement. This money is not kept idle in safes
or deposited in the strong-rooms of banks. It is invested in shops and buildings, in fac-
tories and warehouses, in fittings and machinery, horses and vehicles, and stocks-in-trade.
The capital is, therefore, in constant use, and it is by using it that co-operators are able
to carry on their trade and business and to reap the advantages of co-operative organisa-
tion. As a consequence of the war all of these forms of capital cost more than they formerly
did. Shops and warehouses cost more; horses and vehicles cost more; fittings and
machinery cost more; and stocks of all kinds also cost far more than they did a few years
ago. In short, CO-OPERATORS REQUIRE MORE MONEY TO CARRY ON THEIR BUSINESS SIMPLY
BECAUSE THEY FIND IT NECESSARY TO "LOCK-UP" MORE CAPITAL IN SHOPS AND BUILD-
INGS, FIXTURES AND STOCKS-IN-TRADE. Every business in the country is in exactly the
same position; every firm needs more capital. That is why private traders and manu-
facturers, great firms and businesses are raising more capital and making strenuous efforts
to persuade investors to lend them money. The Co-operative Movement needs capital
therefore, not because it is in any financial difficulty but simply because the times are such
that its business cannot be carried on if it does not control sufficient capital. Co-operative
Union News Service.

BRANCH REPORTS.
BARNSLEY. Trade is very bad here at present, most of our members
working short time, and there is no signs of trade getting any better, for at
several of the collieries around here men are being put on short time, one and
two days per week, and the glass-bottle trade, which is one of our busiest
trades around here, is also on short time, causing a great slackening in the boot
trade both in new work and also in the repairing department. We have no
one that is unemployed at present and we have also a clean sick list. We are
sorry to see from other reports that very many other districts are worse off
than we are at present; let us hope that in the next Report we shall have a
brighter state of things to look at.
BELFAST. Trade still remains in a very unsatisfactory state, many of
our members working less than half time. We regret after all the appeals
that have been made to the members to take an active and intelligent
interest in the workings of the Branch that it seems to have no effect. We
can hear of plenty of criticism of the way the business of the Branch is con-
ducted and the way in which it could be improved by some of those members.
who seldom, if ever, attend the meetings. Now, if only those members would
it would be most gladly welcomed. We would urge upon all members who
come to the meetings and give the Branch the assistance of their help,
are in arrears the absolute necessity of putting themselves in a proper position
if they desire to claim the Union benefits.
BRIGHTON. Trade is bad and large numbers out of work. We are
looking for a good time in June, when the Labour Party Conference will be
held at Brighton. Book your holidays for June-Labour Party Conference
week, when we hope to give the delegates of the N.U.B.S.O. a welcome. Don't
forget Brighton, in June.
CHESHAM. Trade here is still very bad. During the month we have
had a dispute here owing to a small firm wanting to reduce the piecework rate,
and it became necessary to stop the factory working. Mr. McCarthy took the
matter in hand, and we are pleased to report, after a visit to the firm and a
lengthy discussion, the firm agreed to pay the Green Book Rates. We beg to
thank the Stafford Branch for their donation, and we are pleased to report
the amount collected for Comrade Badminton totals £65 13s. od.
CHESTERFIELD. Trade is still very bad. The future does not look
very bright at the time of writing, but we are hoping for the best.
EDINBURGH. Trade here is very quiet; the factories have had three
weeks' holiday and still working short time. At our Monthly Meeting the
members had under discussion the proposed agreement with employers. They
think that it is some improvement on present agreement. Some doubt exists
as regards Clause 16. Members ask if this means that all female labour in
men's department is to be done away with. The Repairing Section on Piece
Rates have now been paid for the first week under Wages Trade Board-better
late than never. Glad that Wellingborough has taken up the case of married
women working in factories, as we are of opinion that when a woman marries
her husband should have enough wages to keep her comfortably at home.
Unemployment and a Special Meeting to hear the Council's case regarding
We have arranged a Labour Policy; something drastic ought to be done
to try and find work for the unemployed. We had occasion to go to the local

over the working of the Government scheme. At time of sending our report

HALESWORTH. There is a slight improvement in trade--the lasters,

Our Monthly Meeting was held last Friday and several members were present.
The members decided to nominate our President as a delegate to the Conference,

HIGHAM AND RUSHDEN. --During the month we have had the services
of our respected M.P.. Mr. W. R. Smith, who addressed eight meetings in our
Branch and the members were encouraged by his wise advice, and we believe

KETTERING No. 2.-Trade is still very pad; we have many out of
work and practically all the rest are on short time. Unfortunately, the position
at present shows no marked signs of improvement; one begins to wonder
where we shall end. A considerable number of our members have drawn their
full amount of out-of-work benefit and this number is increasing week by week.
What is to become of these members and their families with no means of
sustenance except charity? And this, forsooth, was to be a country fit for
heroes to live in! One listens with mixed feelings to some of our moderate
leaders criticising extremists' opinions, but it is becoming increasingly evident
that until we are all extremists and prepared to take extreme measures no
sound remedy will be forthcoming. One can call it direct action or any other
action, but action it must be if our members are to be allowed the right to live.
We deeply regret the death of our Burton Latimer Section President, Mr.
Will Issitt. Our organisation of 100 per cent. at Burton Latimer is in a large
measure due to his untiring efforts. His rugged nature and honesty of principle
made him greatly respected; he was ever to the fore in the fight for the uplifting
of his fellow men, and in these days we can ill afford to lose the services of this
type of man. His place at Burton will be very difficult to fill, but we are
hoping that someone, with a determination not to lose the grip of the situation,
will come forward and continue the good work done by our late friend. Our
deepest sympathy goes out to his wife and family in their sad bereavement,
but a great consolation to them should be the knowledge that for many years
he has laboured hard, and in the right direction, in doing that which is the aim
of all democratic workers, viz., to leave the world better and brighter than
they found it.
LEEDS.-Trade is exceptionally bad and the outlook at present seems
very black indeed, and as a consequence our out-of-work list is rather heavy.
We also regret to report that our sick list is also rather heavy, but we are still
hoping that a change for the better will take place before long. We would
urge upon all members to see that Statement prices are paid, and should any
employer attempt to reduce Statement prices, or want an increased output
of work without an increased remuneration, that such information should
be reported at the Branch office at once,

LONDON No. 2.-A Special Meeting was convened at Working Lads
