UNEMPLOYMENT. -A LABOUR POLICY.
MR. E. L. POULTON, J.P., Chairman.
Chairman's Address.
At the Special Labour Conference held in London on the 27th January, 1921, Mr.
Poulton said: It is to me a source of keen regret that another Special Conference has had
to be called, more especially having regard to the subject matter which is the reason for
the Conference, viz., the serious position that millions find themselves placed in owing
to lack of employment, or short time, and the prospect of the position getting worse rather
than better. I say millions, because we must always bear in mind the women and children
who are dependent upon men's wages for food, clothing and home. Moreover, when one
remembers the statements made by members of the present Government about an "AI
population," " " A land fit for heroes to live in," "Nothing too good for those who during
the war endured so much to bring victory," &c., &c., it is indeed enough to make men
feel desperate, and one need not be surprised at some of the strong things that are given
utterance to. So far from approaching to an Ar population, the present state of affairs
is rapidly tending to produce a C4 population. As to a land fit for heroes to live in, the
term is a mockery to millions, and only causes derision when it is used, seeing how entirely
absent in many lives are the elements which would give even a semblance of real meaning
to such a statement.
There is no necessity to enlarge upon the fact of the imperative need that something
must be done to assist those who are unfortunately without work with the means whereby
they and theirs can live. Too long, far too long, have we been told of the plans for meeting
the situation. The workers will not be fobbed off any longer with words and yet more
words, they call for deeds, actions, performance. It is indeed an ironic situation con
fronting one, that millions of people in this and other countries are clamouring for work
whereby wages are earned; millions are, alas, in many other cases appealing for the bare
necessities of life to keep them alive, and the materials to meet both situations are existent.
yet, owing to the absurd and out-of-date system which now obtains, both demands remain
unsatisfied. Meantime lives are sacrificed and vast suffering entailed for lack of the real
will to deal in anything like a statesman-like manner with the situation. Not many
months ago the cry went forth-loud, insistent, persistent-for more production and yet
more production. In many cases the cry was responded to; and increased production
became an accomplished fact. To-day the result is lack of employment of a vast multitude
of operatives. Yet the cry is a correct one; there is need for more production, whereby
the requirements of people in all parts of the world can be met. What, however, demands
and calls aloud for, is, drastic root remedies being applied to the system which now is in
being, and putting in its place a system which recognises that the paramount claim is,
that Humanity's needs have the first call upon the community. In my judgment, the
members of the present Government of this country are, on this vital question, guilty,
not only of grave neglect, they are also deserving of censure having regard to the lack of
foresight and the consequent suffering that has accrued to so many due to their inaction.
The portents have been plain for a long time past to those who have eyes, to see where we
were drifting to; moreover, it cannot be said that the representatives of labour have been
backward in calling attention to the growing seriousness of the situation. Time after
time both in the House of Commons, on public platforms, and through the Press, attention
steps to be taken in connection
dealt with by the various speakers, except to say that as far back as 1917 the question
with the matter. I do not propose to go into detail upon this point, because it will be
was taken up by the Labour Party and has been kept in the forefront since such date.
I want, however, to deal with the question which is being much talked about, viz., Labour
not accepting seats upon an enquiry committee, proposed to be set up by the Govern
ment, for going into the question of unemployment.

Here is the text from the image:

369
Government, who seem to act upon the method, if method it can be called, of putting off
doing anything for meeting the problem of unemployment. What is the record of the
Government in connection with unemployment questions? In February, 1919, the
industrial situation was very black and the Minister of Labour called together a repre-
sentative body of workmen and employers to talk over the situation. This body was
addressed by the Prime Minister and a most moving appeal he made to the assembly to
do something to bring to an end the crisis then existing. At a later meeting the Prime
Minister again addressed the body set up, and those who were at such meeting in room B
of the Central Hall, Westminster, will not soon forget the appeal of the Premier. The
setting up of this body was heralded forth all over the world, and statements were made
as to how the British once again had surmounted their difficulties. What, however, is
the net result? After sitting almost continuously and presenting an agreed report so
far as the major part of the report is concerned and nearly two years have passed by,
it is in the main still a report. We cannot forget the Miners' Enquiry and the largely
negative result of the same. The Consumers' Council representatives have also felt
themselves compelled to withdraw from the Food Ministry because their recommendations
were constantly ignored, and it is of interest that at a recent meeting of the Committee
for trying to find employment for ex-service disabled men, the employers-even more
than the other section-were talking of resigning because nothing was done. Again,
in relation to the Land Settlement of ex-service men, a report issued on the 15th January
shewed there were nearly 16,000 applications approved, but not provided with holdings,
despite the known desirability of increasing the number of men on the land. Then there
is the case of the way in which the question was dealt with in London just before Christmas,
which really, if it was not for the tragedy behind unemployment, was farcical, when the
Prime Minister stated that the London County Council had the matter in hand, though,
as a matter of fact the letter stating what the Government were prepared to do was not
in the possession of the London County Council until hours after the unemployed deputation
had waited upon the Prime Minister. Deputations, time and time again, have waited
upon either the Prime Minister or responsible Ministers, and always promises, promises,
promises. We are tired of promises, and using these bodies for putting off the day of
performance, and your Executive were not prepared, under such circumstances, to accept
membership of the suggested Committee. The Government know quite well what Labour
wants. Our schemes have been placed before them-both in the House of Commons
and elsewhere, and we call for them to be put into operation.
We are aware of the sinister influences at work to try and take advantage of the
present abnormal circumstances to depress the standard of life even among those in
employment: this we shall resist. We are not unmindful of the suffering upon all hands.
This we say can be dealt with if there is the will so to do without making other workers'
lives worse in the process of dealing with the unemployed. The resources of the country
are such as will, if properly applied, meet the situation.
In the many proposals we make, there is, we are convinced, not only the way out for
dealing with unemployment, but also of actually adding, in the aggregate, to the real
wealth of the country. We cannot stand idly by and see children, women and men suffer-
ing for the lack of the bare necessities of life, knowing as we do that the means really
exist for supplying those needs, if there is the determination to find the remedy. Men
and women want WORK, NOT DOLES. They demand real help, to enable them to maintain
a proper standard of life. You will be asked by resolutions to support such demands
and to create such a feeling in the country as will ensure the Government acting at once
in a manner as will bring into operation the machinery whereby the present appalling
situation may be done away with, and all who want work shall be either provided with
the same, or, failing employment, maintenance supplied-and that without any degrading
conditions being attached thereto.
It is, to me, a monstrous thing that with all the world crying out for help in the way
of Food, Clothing and Employment, Statesmen either turn a deaf ear to the cry or find
paltry excuses for delay.
Let us here to-day, at any rate, by unity and determination in our ranks, make such
a protest on the one hand against the past delay, and a demand on the other hand for
immediate and adequate dealing with a situation which already has inflicted so much
unnecessary suffering upon vast multitudes of men, women and children.

things in connection with unemployment have happened. Two especially I would call

by the totally inadequate provision they propose to embody in a further extension of the

There is no need to explain in detail the proposals of the Government; they are in my judgment totally inadequate to meet the situation. I have no doubt at all that many proposals and methods can be propounded, and the authors of such, with full faith, believe that their particular scheme is the one to adopt, which if carried out, would solve the problem. For myself, owing to the very complex state of society and the increasing interdependence of not merely one part of the country to another part, but other countries to each other, I cannot but come to the conclusion that many methods and plans must be adopted: hence I am the stronger in my belief that our policy as outlined in the pamphlet “Unemployment: a Labour Policy," contains many of the methods which ought to be pursued. There are, I feel sure, delegates here who believe that the polics known as direct action should be the policy carried out. Such a policy it might be pursued would be, by its magnitude and impressiveness, sure to influence the commun and the Government. I agree: it would do both. Would it, however, impress in such a way as to bring about what is desired, viz.: work and sustenance for those at present out of work and without the means to purchase food? I venture to say it would not. Further, if such a policy is carefully examined, it would have an effect very different from what its sponsors so ardently desire. We should by our own action stop the wheels that are already working, and in my opinion the attempt to enforce employment by such a method would, instead of finding employment, very substantially increase the number of men and women without employment, and thereby increase the difficulties of our move- ment, by adding to the suffering already existing, and failing at the same time to bring relief to the unemployed. There is a further suggestion, that as a protest against the attitude of the Government a one-day stoppage should take place as a DEMONSTRATION, and thereby shew to the whole country the feeling of the workers upon the matter. This would have at any rate the merit of self-sacrifice of those in employment, and might show that spirit of good comradeship which it is so desirable should be shewn. A third policy, and this is the only other one I intend to name, is that we should, through the Press and by meetings and the continual bombardment of the Government both as citizens and through our Labour Members in the House of Commons, keep up, and if at all possible increase the intensity of the campaign for work or maintenance. I know that such a policy has nothing to commend it from the standpoint of any startling results. I know thar it means hard humdrum work. It would be, however, in my opinion, the most effective method, and the one most likely to bring relief to our unfortunate comrades. We have also, or should bear in mind, that Labour as represented by Labour Members in the House of Commons is in a very big minority. At the present time there is an opportunity of increasing the number of Labour Members in the House. If such is done, and I HOPE IT WILL BE, it will strengthen our case as proving that the people support our policy, because it is certain that to secure success for our policy support from the people must be forthcoming. I hope therefore that however strongly we may express ourselves, and indignant we may feel against the attitude of the Government, we shall, having regard to the paramount importance of the subject and the issues at stake, back up our colleagues in the fight they are putting up, and thus shew both to the country and the Government that whilst there may be, and will be, differences in our ranks upon both policy and tactics, once a certain method has been decided upon as the method, we are quite prepared to do our part in taking it up, and supporting those of our colleagues who may be called upon to decide the best procedure for putting into practice the ideas contained in our resolutions.

I have no doubt that some amount of disappointment will be expressed at the policy that it is suggested we should carry out. It is, however, much better to face the real position, however unpleasant it is; and the fact is the Government have not, nor does there appear to be any prospect of their adopting our proposals. Under such circumstances we believe the best policy is to carry on along the lines suggested in the resolutions.

The folowing Resolutions were carried at the Adjourned Conference of the Trades
Union Congress and the Labour Party, held in the Kingsway Hall, Kingsway, London,
on Wednesday, February 23rd, 1921, at to a.m.
RESOLUTION I.
That this Conference, representative of the whole Labour Movement, is of opinion
that the Government's policy of merely extending the Unemployment Insurance Act is
amentably inadequate to meet the present situation, and bears little relation to the existing
human suffering: and emphatically reiterates its demand that comprehensive steps be
taken to restore international trade and to organise without delay national schemes of
work, and that those for whom no employment is provided should be found adequate
"The Conference concurs with the proposal of the Parliamentary Labour Party that
every possible step should be taken to press this question on the attention of the House
Commons, and to insist that the Government should take immediate action for the
benefit of the unemployed.
maintenance.
"The Conference further invites the Executive Committee of every Trade Union to
secure the affiliation of all its branches to the local Labour Parties and bring all its members
actively into political work, in order to take the earliest possible steps to promote a Labour
candidate for every constituency in which this has not yet been done.
"The Conference further declares that every opportunity should be taken to use the
Bye-Elections as a means of bringing pressure to bear on the Government by defeating
every Coalition Candidate.
"In conclusion, the Conference calls upon every wage-earning elector in East Woolwich,
Dudley. Penistone, and Kirkcaldy Boroughs to mark his or her sense of the callous refusal
of the Government to deal adequately with Unemployment by voting for the Labour
Candidates."
RESOLUTION II.
"That this National Labour Conference views with apprehension the apparently
inspired statements in the Press concerning the proposed legislation on Key Industries
and Dumping, and instructs the Executive Committee of the Labour Party and the
Parliamentary Committee of the Trades Union Congress :
(a) To consider the Government's Bill as early as possible in order to define the
attitude of the British Labour Movement towards the measure;

COUNCIL'S ADDRESS.
PIONEER BOOT WORKS.
INCREASED TURNOVER IN 1920.
The annual meeting of the Pioneer Co-operative Boot Works Ltd., was held at the
Kingsway Hall, London, on Saturday, Mr. F. J. Green, J.P., presiding.
In his annual report, Mr. James Gribble, the manager, said the new addition to the
factory was complete, and machinery had been installed with a capacity to produce 1,000
pairs of boots per week. The turnover for 1920 was £18,901 85. 9d., which was £5,369
os. 2d. in excess of the total for the previous year. This had been done on a subscribed
capital of £4,834, which was not nearly enough; to carry a proper stock of boots and raw
material at least ₤8,000 was necessary. The share capital had increased during the year
to £1,572 Ios., and in the same period £1,906 125. was paid for plant and fittings and
completion of the building.
The profit disposable was £900 7s. 6d., and in accordance with rule the management
committee decided to apportion it as follows:-To the workers, £170; customers, £204;
shareholders, £204; education fund, ₤34; provident fund, 468; reserve fund, £200;
leaving £20 7s. 6d. to carry forward to the next account.-Northampton Echo, February
21st, 1921.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION ACT.
More Claims Settled.

During the month, through the efforts of Mr. Evan Barlow, five more cases
have been settled. At Leicester No. 1, A.M. secured £175; G.P. £300, and
J.B. £100 in addition to the weekly compensation. In the Leicester No. 2
Branch E.L. obtained £200 and H.P., of Kettering, £100; thus proving once
more the usefulness of having a powerful organisation at the back of the
members.

HALF-YEARLY REPORT AND MEMBERS' NAMES APPEARING
THEREIN.
According to Rule 246, which reads as follows :-
2.46. All registered numbers shall be affixed to the names of the members who
have received sick pay, in the Half-yearly Report.
it is incumbent to name the individual amounts of money paid each
member during any half year in the Report. This method has also been
carried out in relation to Out-of-Work Pay. The recent Half-yearly Report
as a consequence of this regulation had no fewer than 243 pages taken up with
members' names and the amounts paid them. In our opinion this method,
which is very expensive indeed, is no longer necessary, and we purpose therefore
in future Half-yearly Reports to only put in the Report the aggregate amount
paid out by each Branch. We feel sure the Branches will support this proposal.
At the same time we hope every Branch will keep a detailed record of all moneys
paid out to each member upon a card system, so that the same can be immedi-
ately referred to when members claim benefit, and thereby ascertain if they
are entitled to the benefit they put in a claim for.
It must, however, be clearly understood by Branch Secretaries that the
FULL details of payments to members, whether Sick Pay or Out-of-Work Pay,
must still be sent to the Central Office (as at present) with the Monthly Returns.
REMEMBER THE FIFTEENΤΗ!
Once again we feel bound to call the serious attention of branch secretaries
to the fact that the FIFTEENTH day of each month is the latest day for
returns reaching the General Secretary. Last month many returns were late.
Branches failed to send off their returns to reach the Central Office by the
15th of the month, and this tends to upset the organisation of the work in
the General Secretary's office. We trust in future every branch secretary
will endeavour to get in his returns NOT later than the fifteenth of every month,
and before sending them see that they are properly signed.

A.U.C.E.

We have also been very busy with a decision given in our favour and against the
Amalgamated Union of Co-operative Employees, who after accepting this decision at the
1012 Congress, afterwards refused to carry the same into effect, and ultimately withdrew
from Congress in 1915, but matters have been so unsatisfactory to them that they have
formed an amalgamation with a body already members of Congress, and have applied for
affiliation, tentatively. The Parliamentary Committee have been unable to refuse the
body already affiliated, but have not committed themselves in regard to the new body.
My own view is that as the body referred to, viz., the Amalgamated Union of Co-operative
Employees, was poaching our members as late as November of last year, we shall endeavour
at the earliest opportunity to wait upon the Parliamentary Committee, and also I expect
we shall be raising the question at the Trade Union Congress meeting in Cardiff in September
with other Unions affected. It will be a sorry day for the Trade Union movement if people
can unblushingly throw to the winds the principle of first of all organising on a selfish
basis according to the particular power which public opinion can exercise over the bodies
Employees. These bodies started originally with the confidence that the general public
in authority, such as Government Employees, Municipal Workers and Co-operative
Fould stand behind them, but in every instance of late years the movement has demanded
that organisations shall not be known by the Employers' Associations or Societies, but
shall be part and parcel of all employees of one particular craft, trade or calling.
Burley Boot Co., of Leicester.
On the 25th February I had occasion to visit the firm known as the Burley Boot
C of Leicester, where notice had been given of a reduction in wages. This firm not being
feierated an investigator was asked for. I attended, saw the firm, who immediately
saw their difficulty, decided to put Lasters and Finishers on Piecework, which met with
our requirements, and put the Dayworkers back at their old rates.
Lasting Committee of the County Board.
On Tuesday, March 1st, I attended a Lasting Committee of the County Board, in
respect of several disputes, and we appointed an Umpire owing to a deadlock.
WELLINGBOROUGH.-On Wednesday I had occasion to go to Wellingborough to
investigate a question regarding Unemployment, which was found to be quite satisfactory.
Trade Board Matters.
On Monday, the 7th, I was asked by the Ministry of Labour to meet the Secretary,
Sir David Shackleton, on several important points which we had referred to the Ministry
of Labour regarding our opposition to attitudes assumed.
The first was in regard to a Foreman at a certain firm. This matter has been on
quite six months, and although there has been three Inspectors to see the man in question,
they all admit the man so changes his position that if they put him in the witness-box
they would not be responsible for what he may say, and they don't think therefore it would
be a good case to take to the Courts.
Another case is one about which I have not only written to the Ministry of Labour but
have raised the matter with the Parliamentary Committee of the Trade Union Congress,
and the Special Committee appointed by the Parliamentary Committee who look after the
interests of Trade Boards, and I have also seen the Ministry of Labour before upon this point
regarding the right of an employer to deduct a receipt stamp of 2d. from a man's wages, as to
whether this is permitted by the law or not; and although this matter has been in the hands
of the Ministry since October, there is such a difference of opinion in the minds of lawyers
in general, that if I could give personal advice and take personal responsibility I should
tell our men that wherever this deduction took place to at once stop work until the money
was given back again. In fact I hope that if anything happens anywhere that the officials
or members will immediately write to the Central Office for advice, and the point as to
whether it is legal to deduct such from a man's wages in accordance with the Act, is not
yet settled, although Mr. Bowerman has asked the question for us in Parliament, as follows:
QUESTION NO. 69.
MR. BOWERMAN: To ask the Minister of Labour if he is aware that certain employers
in the boot and shoe industry are deducting from their operatives' wages 2d. for a receipt
stamp where their earnings exceed £2, whether a deduction of this nature in connection
with the payment of wages can be held to be legal; and, if not, will the department so
inform the employers in question upon being supplied with definite information ?
ANSWER, BY SIR MONTAGU BARLOW. The question whether such action would be
legal appears to be one for the Courts to determine. A case has been brought to my
attention in which a receipt stamp has been required by an employer in the Boot Repairing
trade to which the Trade Boards Acts have been applied. The question has arisen as to
whether the payment for the stamp by the worker constitutes a deduction within the
meaning of the Acts, and the matter is at present under consideration.


---
Our third question was a protest upon Non-Unionists being on the Trade Board,
the Government having geographical notions and not representative notions, and from
that point of view their action has not given us satisfaction, and we have warned them
that although the Boards are already set for this year, another year we shall refuse to work
on the Trade Board with Non-Unionists. I should like to make it clear that this only
happens in isolated places and on the District Boards. It does not apply to the Central
Board in London.
The Ministry has also taken up the question of a firm who tried to prevent His Majesty's
Inspectors from inspecting. They say it is illegal, and cannot be permitted.
Another question was one of our members who was discharged by his employer for
accepting nominations on behalf of the Government for a seat on the District Board.
Unfortunately in this case the Inspector did not see our member's employer, and therefore
it is believed that no good purpose would be served by pressing it further.
The sixth point I had to complain of was and is that the Government in sending for
a man from Scotland to do the work which a man in London could do. and much more to
our satisfaction because he happens to have a wider experience. My only complaint
against this is that the Government asks that we shall not waste money, and this recom-
mendation will cost £7 a meeting more than the other one would have done, if our advice
had been taken in the first instance.
We have been promised by Sir David that these matters shall be treated in a very
considerate and sympathetic manner.

Union's New Demand.
On Tuesday I had an interview with the President of the Federation in regard to
the scheme for Unemployment, and he is sorry to say that so far as he is concerned it will
be impossible for any member of his side, who spends some four days per week in London
now, to give any time to the unemployment scheme this side of Easter, but he hopes to
be able to arrange a meeting afterwards. As Mr. Marlow's statements are now public
property, it will be as well for me to say here when I pressed for a meeting with their side.
said privately as he has said publicly, that his side
thing they possibly can to keep the factories going, and in some instances are not able
are so upset owing to bad trade and other causes in fact many members are doing every-
to earn the wages that are required to pay the men that the present time is most in-
opportune, and unfortunately for us, to try and press upon his members a meeting. How
far and how long he cannot say, but his view is that it will be useless to attempt or endeavour
to hold a meeting before Whitsuntide. Whether the Council will agree with that, is a
matter for further consideration.

Sewer Boots.
On the roth I had occasion to visit Wellingborough, Rushden, and Kettering, with
the object of finding out what was the method adopted in making Sewer Boots, Firemen's
Boots, Fishermen's Boots, which are very often 36 ins. high, Napoleons, and other Boots
of a similar character, in order that our friends in Yarmouth and District may not be
placed at a disadvantage. I shall endeavour at the earliest opportunity to let our
members in Yarmouth know the difference between the two. Very largely, almost
exclusively, one district does their work entirely by hand and other districts are doing
it mainly by machinery. This is the old grievance and is likely to be a grievance for some
time to come. Some people prefer the hand-sewn boot, others prefer the lower priced
article even if it happens to be the more shoddy.

Stamped Boots.
I have one other statement to make, that is, there is a movement afoot for a boot
to be placed on the market bearing a particular stamp. I don't think that anyone con-
nected with the National Union would object to such a boot if the stamp would guarantee
its purity, but at the same time it must also guarantee that it is made under Trade Union
conditions and by Trade Union labour, and I hope members of the National Union of
Boot and Shoe Operatives (who may be the only organisation in the Boot and Shoe Trade
that has a National Agreement with the Emplovers covered by a Guarantee Bond) will
insist upon their footwear bearing the Trade Union Stamp.

PARLIAMENTARY AGENT'S REPORT.
The House of Commons is once again in full working order, though perhaps viewed
from the standpoint of output it leaves much to be desired. The Government have claimed
all the time of the House up till Easter, and up to the present have been engaged chiefly
upon estimates.
There has been an amendment of the Unemployment Insurance Act whereby the
benefits are increased, to be followed later by an increased contribution. It is worth
noting that the rate of benefit now established is that which the Government refused last
year, though strongly urged to do so by the Labour Party. We shall be told of the enor-
mous number of Bills this wonderful Government has passed, but no mention will be
made of the fact that some have been necessary to correct their own failures.
The Labour Party took the fullest advantage of the various debates to press home
the policy laid down at the Special Conferences, and the passing of the 20s. benefit was
undoubtedly forced by the Party's amendment for 40s. It is however a poor amount
to face present-day needs upon, and further it would be much better had some schemes
of work been started whereby men and women could have earned wages rather than
receive benefit, and as I endeavoured to point out when speaking, to develop a foreign
policy which will permit of export trade, which at the moment is at a standstill.
It is with the greatest regret one is compelled to point out that there is little or no
prospect of anything like a general revival in trade; the productive capacity of the nation
can soon meet the demands of the home market, and with that market contracting as a
result of unemployment and under-employment, trade with other countries must be
made possible before the wheels of industry will turn again at full speed.
But the policy of this. Government and its Allies seemed to be designed to prevent
this taking place, and the debate upon the Coal Decontrol Bill shews conclusively what
effect the Peace Treaty is having in the Coal Industry. The export of Coal is practically
stopped, and the markets we used to have are being supplied with coal taken from the
Germans. The miners of Germany are working like slaves for comparatively low wages
to supply French capitalists with coal, who are using it to supply the markets that used
to receive coal from this country. What the Miners are getting out of the War at present
is intensified unemployment, and the country is being taxed to pay them out-of-work
benefit. But what matter, the man who won the war is still in charge and we must con-
tinue to trust him!
On Friday last the "German Reparation Bill" was introduced. This is an attempt
to compel Germany to pay for the War, and it aims at imposing a tax of 50 per cent. on all
German goods coming into this country. The English merchant who buys is to pay hali
the amount of his purchase to the British Government, and I suppose when sending the
remaining half to the German from whom he bought the goods he will forward a receipt
for the sum paid to the Treasury. We all know that owing to the rates of exchange,
Germany has an advantage in trading with this country, and bearing that in mind I would
like to submit the following to the consideration of our members. When once it is estab-
lished that every (I spent in buying goods from Germany means ros. paid off her debt to
us, it will I suppose be the patriotic duty of everyone to buy as much as possible from her.
All such cries as keeping out the German goods will cease. They must come here so that
we may receive the indemnity. Recently in the House of Commons I heard a member
declare that he knew of German goods being sold in this country at 6d. which could not
be produced and sold here for less than 3s. 6d. Only last week it was stated that German
gloves were being sold for 10s. 6d., which cost 25s. to be produced in England, and I may
add a strong appeal has been issued by those connected with the glove industry begging
that German goods may be kept out of this country.

Now, this is the point upon which I want some explanation. First let us bear in mind
we are taking half the selling price from the German producer. But suppose, in regard
to those articles that he can sell at 6d. as against our 3s. 6d.. he doubles the price, he will
still be selling 2s. 6d. below the British production, and in regard to the gloves, supposing
they are sold at 215. instead of IOS. 6d., they are still 4s. cheaper than our own goods.
and therefore because they are cheaper and because we shall get half the money they may
still be sold in this country. If this is so, what I want to know is, who is paying the
indemnity? A prize of 1 for the first correct answer sent in !
It is perhaps worth mentioning that Mr. Lloyd George declares that the Germans
must send their goods here or they will be faced with unemployment of an unprecedented
character in their own country. May I put another question: If Germany sending coal
to France put thousands of miners out of work both in France as well as England, what
will be the position of the workers in these other industries if Germany "must send her
goods here"? There is no prize offered for this answer, it's too simple.
accomplished that task for us is still at the head of affairs. God is in his heaven and all
But whatever else happens, let us not forget we won the war, and the man who
is well with the world.

by which we may escape from the torrent, and Labour responded practically every time.
But now when the industrial circumstance is against us, they not only do not ask for
consultation, but refuse it. I hope the worst fears of the Miners' leaders will not be realised,
but if they are, then God help us! But what I ask is what are we doing and what are we
intending to do?
During the month I took part in three of the bye-elections as well as visiting my own
constituency.
WALTER R. SMITH,
March 13th, 1921.
FOOD CONTROLLER ON FALLING PRICES.
Ministry that has Cost the Taxpayer Nothing.
"In a few weeks' time the Ministry of Food will cease to exist.
"We have every confidence that food prices will continue to fall during the spring
and summer, and that better times are in store for the much-harassed housewife."
Such was the optimistic forecast of Mr. McCurdy, the Food Controller, at the final
meeting of the Labour Food Conference in the London County Hall on Saturday.
He said that for the last six months the Ministry had been engaged in the liquidation
of the world's greatest trading corporation. The business carried on by the Food Ministry
involved a turnover of more than a thousand million pounds, and on that enormous
turnover the Ministry's net profit amounted to less than one-tenth of 1 per cent.
He claimed that successive Food Ministers had substantially achieved their purpose
as trustees of the nation. The operations of the Ministry had cost the taxpayer nothing.
Exit the Food Ministry.
In a few weeks' time, as Mr. McCurdy reminded us on Saturday, the Food Ministry
will have ceased to exist as a separate department. But we must not forget the great
part that it played in the war, and indeed for some time after the war, in steering us through
a period of economic stress. At a time when food was dangerously scarce it organised
supply, and eked it out by an exemplary system of rationing, and by fixing prices pro-
tected the consumer from exploitation. Before the Ministry was created, food
prices were rising higher in Great Britain than in any other European country;
it stands to its credit that at the end of the war prices were lower here than any-
where on the Continent.-London Chronicle, February 28th, 1921.
[There is no sort of doubt that this Department, which had a Council attached to it called
"The Consumers' Council," saved the consumers, as against the distributors, millions
of pounds. What is wanted is a Council which could continue to protect the con-
sumers.-E.L.P., Gen. Sec.]

ORGANISERS' REPORTS.

FELLOW OFFICERS AND MEMBERS,
During the month I have attended the Trade Board re the Handsewn and Repair
Work question. A meeting of the Administration Committee has also been held, at which
I was present, to deal with the question of Trainees and Permits and Apprenticeships.
At the full Board meeting a long discussion took place on the increased minimum wage,
and it was agreed to recommend an increase from 65s. minimum to 72s. minimum per week.
At this meeting the question of piecework was deferred on account of the diversity of
opinion on the amount of earnings of pieceworkers. Investigations will be made in the
various areas, and this matter will have further consideration at the next meeting.
I attended the Special Trades Union Congress re the attitude of the Trade Union
Movement on the Unemployed question. The Congress fell very flat with regard to Direct
Action, and decided that political action was the proper course to pursue.
I have also attended a Special Conference held for the purpose of forming a Constitu-
tion of various Unions represented on the Trade Board, such constitution being agreed to.
With a view to organisation I visited Sileby. I interviewed the Secretary of the
Branch, and found that, with the exception of one factory, very short time is the prevailing
order.
I have held meetings at Syston of operatives working at Eatough's, a branch of an
Earl Shilton firm, who promised to become members of the Union.
At Shepshed, I had a conversation with Mr. Johnson, the Secretary, re amalgamation
with the Sileby Branch, in view of his expressed desire to be relieved of the Secretaryship.
I found he is now out of work, against above-mentioned amalgamation, and desires to
continue as Secretary for the Branch for the time being. The firm here is on short time.
Mr. Emmett Law and myself have visited Leicester to make investigations regarding
Ald. Hill's Candidature for South Leicester. According to instructions a report has
already been forwarded to Head Office.
JOHNNIE BUCKLE.

IMPORTANCE OF HEALTH.
Foundation of Efficiency.
D. MCCARTHY.
Discussions on health as a matter affecting personal efficiency were recently held at
the "Daily Mail" Exhibition. Sir Sims Woodhead presided, and said that during the
war a number of scientific men devoted the whole of their time and energy to keeping
our great armies in a fit condition to perform their task. The same thing had now to be
done for the army of workers in mills and mines and their wives and families. Health
was the foundation of efficiency. He deprecated the pressing of the anti-waste campaign
to a point which involved false economy. If we cut down expenditure on the health,
education, and training of the people we should impair our efficiency in the future.
Sir H. Baldwin read a paper in which he said that over 90 per cent. of the population
of this country was affected by dental caries-a condition which might result in chronic
poisoning and ill-health. The serious ravages of caries and its disastrous consequences
as met with to-day were entirely preventible. It was partly a question of education ;
partly of food and feeding ; partly of method of our hygiene; and partly of a little dentistry
at the right time.
Venereal Disease.
Mr. E. B. Turner read a paper in which he described venereal disease as one of the
most prominent factors in reducing the efficiency both of the individual and the nation.
Gonorrhœa was often not taken at its true value. It was both dangerous in itself, leading
to many other illnesses, and capable of causing far-reaching mischief to others. Practically
all the people who were seen begging in the streets with the placard "Born blind" were
not born blind, but became blind because their mothers were suffering from this illness.
Speaking of syphilis, he said that one of the worst forms of madness with which the medical
profession had to deal was found in the class of cases described as " general paralysis of
the insane," which only affected those who suffered from the late stages of syphilis.
Thousands upon thousands of pounds were paid out each year as sick benefit in cases of
these and other late manifestations of syphilis, and the after-effects of gonorrhea were
responsible for very many weeks of sick pay. Speaking of the conditions which were
favourable to fighting venereal disease, he mentioned temperance-alcohol lessened a
man's power of resistance both to temptation and to disease; better housing-they could
not expect people living 12 in a room to be moral; and the provision of suitable recreation.
In the case of soldiers he had found an appeal to chivalry successful.
Tuberculosis.
Dr. Latham dealt with the prevention of tuberculosis. As a proof that the disease
is preventible he pointed out that post-mortem records showed that practically everyone
who died from other causes had evidences in his body of cured tuberculosis. The essential
thing in the prevention of the disease was the provision of healthy conditions of life; as
long as we lived in healthy conditions we retained our vitality and could defy the tubercle
bacillus. The effect of devitalising conditions had been shown by the war. The death
rate from tuberculosis doubled in Berlin between 1913 and 1918, and in Vienna to-day
50 per cent. of the children under 10 were said to be suffering from tuberculosis. He
urged the importance of beginning the treatment of tuberculosis in the really early stages
of the disease before it became infectious. Pleurisy, which in the adolescent was often
regarded as a trivial complaint, accounted for 20 per cent. of our consumptives three or
four years later. Blood-spitting and increasing lassitude with fever were also too often
disregarded. A few months' treatment at this stage would often restore the balance and
lead to health.-National Insurance Gazette, 26th February, 1921.

were allowed to cross the border and the stations were garlanded with flowers, flags,
lestoons, and some bands were playing, all this being done to excite interest in the matter
and so secure a majority for Germany.

EXTRACT FROM “VORWAERTS” OF 15th MARCH, 1921.
Return Journey of the International Trades Union Commission.
BERLIN, IOTH MARCH.-Last night, in consequence of a regrettable misunderstanding,
some members of the International Trades Union Commission returning from Upper
Silesia, were arrested at one of the railway stations here by an official of the Railway
Supervisory Service, and taken to the offices of the Chief Commissioner of Police. Here
the error was at once explained and the delegates set at liberty, being conveyed to their
hotels in cabs placed at their disposal by the officials.
We have now received further particulars regarding this unfortunate occurrence.
The Delegation, consisting of Comrades Fimmen (Holland), Jouhaux (France), Poulton
England), together with the Chief Reporter of the French Trade Union Paper" Le Peuple,"
Harmel, Wissell (Germany), and Comrades Zulawski, M.P. and Teller, M.P., Secretary
of the Polish Metal Workers' Union, had been instructed to carry out an investigation into
the present conditions prevailing in Upper Silesia, in view of the impending vote in that
country. As already announced, the delegates were refused passports at the express
command of General Le Rond. In spite of the lack of passports, however, the delegates
decided to travel as near the Frontier of Upper Silesia as possible, by going to Breslau,
and gathering there what information might be available. Yesterday afternoon they
returned from Breslau to Berlin, which city they reached about 9.30 in the evening.
Comrade Wissell who lives in the South-East got out at the Silesian Station. The
other representatives went on to the Friedrichstrasse Station. When they got out of the
train, the Polish delegate Teller found he had left his wallet in another compartment near
by.
When he had found it and was about to take possession of it, a railway supervisory
official, in uniform, declared that he must confiscate the wallet and arrest its owner. The
other Trade Union representatives, upon going up to enquire, were also placed under
arrest with him. Explanations having been given as to their identity, this intelligent
official said, "The German Michael must wake up again." The delegates were then
brought to the railway guard room at Friedrichstrasse, but although they showed their
papers they were not set at liberty, being brought by the police in motors to the office of
the Chief Commissioner of Police. Arrived there, they were taken first of all to the Criminal
Investigation Department, and Comrade Teller had to undergo an investigation lasting
lhalf an hour, during which the other delegates were sternly forbidden to speak to one
another. Finally, the Criminal Investigation Department declared it was not a case for
them, and the delegates were then taken to Police Dept. IA. There, in contrast with the
previous attitude of the officials, the delegates were treated with the greatest civility
and respect. At once the Commissioner got into communication with Comrade Wissell,
and after a few minutes, the delegates were released. The patriotic official who has acted
in this foolish manner should be held responsible for thus injuring German interests,
and diminishing the impression that had been produced by Le Rond's refusal to grant
passports to the members of the T.U. Commission. Extract from Vorwaerts, of 15th
March, 1921.

BRANCH REPORTS.
BELFAST Trade has become very much worse during the month, dis-
missals and short time being the general condition with us at present. Sickness
is much above the average. We can only hope that a change for the better
will soon come, although so far as it is possible to see the change is not in sight.
Again we would appeal to the members to take an intelligent interest in the
workings of the Branch. We would also draw the attention of all members
of being able to get the benefits when under eight weeks in arrears is most
in arrears; benefits can only be obtained by those in good standing, the margin
generous on behalf of the Union, and we do not think is conceded by any other
trade organisation, and if members fail to keep themselves right the fault
is theirs and not the officials. It would almost seem that it will be necessary
for us to take very firm action with those members who have lapsed. It is
difficult to understand why it is that some workers require to be compelled
to remain within the organisation, which has for its object their social better-
ment.
BRISTOL No. 2 AND KINGSWOOD. - We can only report that trade
is bad, worse than it was a month ago. In the Kingswood area we have
factories closing down firms of repute, who previously have always been
able to get orders, but now everything seems lifeless. At present there seems
no prospect of a lighter out-of-work bill, and the number who have drawn
their full amount and are still unemployed is increasing. A few are on relief
work, alternate weeks, but we have sufficient unemployed to build a " New
the reparation" committee
World," and we can supply a good number when the
start operations. We think they should start in Ireland; it is not far from
home, and our people could get home week-ends. We are under the impression
that there is a Reparation Department attached to the present Government
and that they really do intend to make this world a nice, quie, happy place
to live in.
CHESHAM.-Trade here is still very bad with no sign of improving.
Our Branch President and Secretary have been nominated, with two others,
by our Local Labour Party to contest four seats at the forthcoming U.D.C.
Election, and our members are being urged to turn up at the poll and use
their vote in the Labour interest. We are pleased to acknowledge further dona-
tions from Kingswood and Chesterfield Branches for Comrade Badminton.

as the making. Our sick list is heavy at the time of writing. We are still

trade being as bad as it is to-day.

rather disappointed at the new minimum wage agreed to at last Wages Trade

HALESWORTH. - We find no improvement in the trade as far as heavy

HIGHAM AND RUSHDEN.---There has been very little improvement
in trade during the month. A considerable amount of discontent has been
manifested in the district with the stoppage of Suspension Benefit; some
employers have encouraged the members (out of work temporarily) to claim
their own money regardless of rule. We have made the matter clear to most
members at meetings of suspended members at Rushden, Wollaston and
Finedon, where meetings were addressed by Branch officials. Some trouble
has arisen at one or two firms in respect to Overtime Award, which has now
been referred to National Joint Committee for settlement.

KINGSWOOD. We record the fact that never in the memory of the
oldest operative has such a period of utter stagnation been experienced in
Kingswood; the situation steadily goes from very bad to utter hopelessness.
Firms are closing down, workers discharged, and the future points to destitu-
tion in many of the homes of the operatives. The one outstanding feature is
the splendid assistance rendered by the National Union during this period
of unprecedented depression, and if gratitude be an attribute possessed by the
average member, the receipt of the out-of-work benefit will be an unforgettable
tribute to the value of Trades Unionism. " As we have sown, so shall we
reap."

LEEDS.-Trade here was never known to be as bad as it is at present,
and the outlook for the future is not so hopeful; yet we do hope that at no
distant date we shall see an improvement, which would be welcome to all.
We are pleased to report that through the efforts of Mr. W. Wright, Solicitor,
he has been successful in getting two cases of compensation settled, viz., Reg.
No. 35340 for £20, and Reg. No. 35080 for £20; this has been a very long time
in the hands of Mr. Wright, yet at the same time it was a difficult case to handle,
but satisfaction was obtained at last.

LINCOLN.-Trade is very slack in the district owing to the thousands
of men in the Engineering trades being either unemployed or on short time.
Most of the shops in the city are on short time and the same thing prevails
throughout the county.

LONDONDERRY.-Trade is very bad. In the hand-sewn and repairing
ends there is nothing doing, and as a consequence many of our members, we
are afraid, are going to have a very bad time. Our Shirt and Collar industry is
very slack, the Shipyard is practically closed down, and unless matters take
a turn for the better we are going to experience the worst time we have
had for many generations. The sympathy of the officials and members is
extended to Shopmate Wm. Donnelly, who has sustained a sad bereavement
through the death of his wife.

LIVERPOOL. With regard to trade we can only draw a gloomy picture, as we are paying out more in benefits than what we are taking in by contributions, and instead of getting better it gets worse each week. The result of ballot for Branch Secretary, as revealed by the scrutiny, is—G. Bishop, 21, W. Ellis 10, St. Helen's Section arrived too late to count, otherwise the figures would have been 33 v. 10. We shall still carry on with a " Bishop" at the helm.

MANCHESTER.-Trade is very bad, very few working full time, and it gets worse every week, especially with Repairers.
MAYBOLE.-Trade is very slack and in consequence many are thrown idle and all the rest working short time. We are now paying out the State Unemployment Benefit, which it is hoped will be better for our members as they will not have to go to a Labour Exchange, where in some cases they do not get much sympathy and guidance. We are glad to see the Conference in London decided on Political Action through the Ballot Box as against Direct Action, which is the best method of doing anything for the Labour Movement, and we are hopeful the people are at last taking an interest in their own affairs, that is, if the elections of the past weeks are any criterion of the people's views.

NEWCASTLE.-We wish to make a few remarks on the report that was published in the last Monthly Report by our branch secretary. We are very pleased to think that there are more members in the country other than those in the Newcastle Branch, who are in accordance with the attitude taken up by us. From correspondence which has come to hand we are convinced that if the repairers up and down the country will only get more into communication through branch secretaries, we shall get more attention in the future than it has been our lot to put up with in the past from our Head Officials. It is only by good organisation and keeping our members in touch with every item connected with the Union that we shall be able to keep them together, especially in view of the increasing unemployment and the tendency amongst masters to lower wages, through workers not being in the Union. A case we will mention, and hope all branch secretaries in the country will follow our example: It was brought to our notice that the big firm of Woolworth's, who have a branch in every town, are selling cut soles at Is. per pair and heels at 6d. per pair. They have a man in the window fixing, that is, benching and finishing, and charge 3s. for the job complete. Along with the President of the Masters Association, we visited this shop, and saw the work that was being done, but we could see no signs of the Trade Board notices, which should be hung up. As we could not interfere with the management of the shop, we pursued the only course that was open to us. We went to the Ministry of Labour, the Trade Board Offices, and saw the District Inspector, who took our complaint down, and promised us he would send an Inspector round the next day to see that all the conditions under the Trades Board Act were strictly carried out. As far as we can gather this man working in this shop is a stranger to the town, and if he is working under, or against Trade Union principles, we shall have to bring this matter before the public and report it to the Trades Council. This incident only occurred recently, and we have had no report from the Ministry of Labour.

NORTHAMPTON No. 1. - Trade remains very slack here. This is a
serious matter for our members as we were in hopes of considerable improve-
ment by Easter, but it seems as though we are in for a long slump, and an
extended period of unemployment. This brings us to the point as to whether
it was advisable to be rushed into administering the Unemployment Act.
Our members considered the matter at the Monthly Meeting and came to the
conclusion that it would be in the best interests of the Union to wait until
the proposed Joint Scheme came into operation.
NOTTINGHAM. We have to report the death of one of our members,
T. Percival, who served in the late War. He was badly gassed and was sent
home in 1919 and had not been able to do anything since; he had been under
treatment and died in hospital. He was buried with military honours on
February 5th in a soldier's grave. There is no change around here in trade,
many of our members only working half time.

PLYMOUTH.-Trade has been bad during the month and some of our
members find great difficulty in maintaining their Union membership. The
efforts put forth during past years to organise and build up a new social order
are now being nullified by trade depression, which is now general throughout
the trade. Short time and unemployment with all its attendant misery haunt
the footsteps of our men until their lives become something like the realisation
of Dante's Hell. The Trade papers are most depressing to read, while the
Branch Reports in our own Monthly give one a fit of the "blues.” Our
splendid organisation, built up by the hard-earned coppers and untiring efforts
of our members, is now threatened by the creeping avalanche of unemployment
and poverty. Well might our brethren cry "What must we do to be saved ?
We may point to industrial action, political action, or any other kind of action,
but we must have action that will hold us together until the storm is over
and the danger past. Our Union did well during the war by keeping our
fighting men still on the books as members, then again by the Suspension
Scheme. Is it possible to again assist our members who are genuinely waging
a war against bad trade and poverty? We believe it would be beneficial if
some method could be devised whereby the membership of anyone of proved
loyalty and sincerity could be maintained, while our industry is undoubtedly
passing through a period of abnormal depression.

PORTSMOUTH.-It would give us the greatest pleasure if we could only
report progress, but stagnation is the only word we can use to describe the
condition of things in the repairing trade at present. Very few men are working
a full week, many are working only three days, and others stood off altogether.
A very brisk competition has suddenly sprung up among the shops, and they
are cutting the prices wholesale, many dropping from 7s. Men's Soled and
Heeled to 4s. 6d. This has meant many men being stood off through inability
to pay the rates. Then the employer is up against the one-man shops, who
in many cases can cut the price and work excessive hours. Many of this class
of shop have sprung up here, and it has had a baneful effect upon the trade
in general. Most of these men got a smattering of how to put on a pair of soles
and heels in the army shoe shops. If trade was brisk the effect of these shops
would not be felt so much. Some machinery is necessary to fix a minimum
price for all repairers, which shall protect the man who is endeavouring to keep
together a business, and keep on his employees. These things are the result
of experience, and help to create hostile opinion against the operation of the
Trade Board orders. We think the visit of an inspector to Portsmouth would
be productive of some good, as complaints seem pretty prevalent of a wide
ignoring of the orders. A systematic visit would either confirm or stop such
rumours. We still hold our oldest and loyal members, but to approach men

Hughes, 9, Vant Road, Tooting, appeared to answer a summons taken out by the Ministry
of Labour for failing to pay Albert Spence, 5, Grenfell Street, Mitcham, the minimum
rate of wages applicable to a manager under an Order of the Boot Repairing Trade Board.
Mr. G. P. Low, prosecuting for the Ministry of Labour, said Spence was employed

Sequel to Case Heard at South-Western Police Court.
In the King's Bench Divisional Court, on Tuesday, before Justices Bailhache and
Shearman, Mr. Lilley, on behalf of the Ministry of Labour, moved for a rule nisi directed
to a Metropolitan magistrate calling upon him to show cause why he should not state a
special case in the following circumstances: - On February 15 information was laid against
Jolin Chas. Hughes, Vant Rd., Tooting, for not paying a minimum rate of wages under the
Trade Boards Act. Under the Act the Board of Trade had given power to promulgate
a minimum rate of wages. Under section 6 of the Trade Boards Act of 1909 it became an
offence not to pay such rate of wages, and an employer not paying them became on con-
viction liable to penalties. The amending Act, passed in 1918, empowered, in addition
to fixing the rate of wages, the fixing of the rate for managers. For the boot repairing trade
certain rates of wages were published by the order of the Ministry of Labour, which had now
become the proper authority for dealing with the matter. The information with which
their Lordships had to deal contained charges that the defendant failed to pay Albert
Alfred Spencer, who was employed by him as a manager, the regulation wages.
The defendant was the owner of a shop, and employed Spencer as his manager. He
was employed in this capacity from May 31 to September 11 last year, and there was no
other workers in the shop. His duties were to receive and execute work, take payment,
keep and render accounts, and he was in sole charge. Under the rules made by the Ministry
of Labour under the Act in part 2 of the schedule the general time rate for foremen and
managers, as defined under section 2, was 8os. for a week of 48 hours. There was also an
overtime rate of one-and-a-quarter of the ordinary rate. As defined under the Act, a
manager "shall be deemed to be a male person employed in the trade, who, whatever
the number of persons employed, is financially responsible for the management of the shop
or for dealing with customers." It was upon this point that the magistrate decided
against the Ministry.
Justice Shearman: There were no other persons employed ?
Mr. Lilley said that was so. The magistrate said he could not be a manager, dis-
missed the case, and refused to state a case.
Mir. Justice Shearman: It comes to this. If a man keeps a boot-repairing shop, and
puts a man in charge, he must pay him about £5 a week or else close the shop.
Mr. Lilley: If he leaves him in actual charge of the shop he must pay him the regu-
lation rate of wages.
Mr. Justice Shearman: Somebody employs a man to take in boots and "cobble "
them, and he cannot leave anybody there unless he pays him nearly £5 a week.
mission.
Mr. Lilley said he could not leave a man in charge as a manager. A man in charge
to mend boots might be a different thing. In this case the man received salary and com-
Mr. Justice Bailhache: The commission might bring it up to the amount.
Mr. Lilley said that was not so; the total was 68s. The Ministry were not anxious
to pursue this individual, but it had now been contended by a number of persons that a
business in charge of one man could not be a business conducted by a manager. In these
circumstances the Ministry desired the question decided under the Trade Boards Act.
The magistrate refused to state a case, saying the application was frivolous, but whatever
it might be, it was not frivolous, and it was desirable that the matter should be cleared up.
Mr. Justice Bailhache: Very well; take your order.

MR. G. ROWLERSON (Amalgamated Tailors) spoke to the following resolution :-
This Congress instructs the Parliamentary Committee to urge upon the
Government the social and economic desirability of compelling all employers
in the tailoring industry to provide adequate workshop accommodation for all
their people, and that the factory regulation be so amended that it shall be
illegal to convert any part of an occupied dwelling-house into a workshop. Further.
pending such action, lists of out-workers, at present maintained by local authorities,
shall be open to the inspection of duly authorised and responsible Trade Union
officials, in order to assist in the carrying out of wage decisions arrived at under
the Trade Boards Act.

He said: We were before you last year and many years before. There is a principle
involved in this. In your reply last year you said that owing to the far-reaching nature
of our resolution you were not prepared to pledge yourself to do away altogether with
home employment. In view of your answer we have amended the resolution, and in the
resolution before you we now ask for compulsory workshops in the tailoring trade to be
limited to the industry that is particularly affected by the evils arising from home working.
The position has been considerably intensified since the coming into being of the Trade
Boards. Owing to the Trade Boards Act the worker in the workshop has a working week
laid down of forty-eight hours, with payment at a specified rate for overtime. The employer
who desires to escape from that position closes his workshop now, and employs nothing
payment of the contribution under the Insurance Act, except under one aspect of com-
but home workers, with the result also that he escapes payment of overtime, and also the
pensation. Home-work means that the workers work long hours at a lower rate than that
agreed to by the Trade Unions and their employers. It can be proved by the employers'
books that the workers concerned can earn the minimum fixed by the Board. During
the last twelve months we have had instance after instance of employers deliberately
closing up workshops to escape the provisions of the Trade Boards Act. One case is
particularly mentioned. We have knowledge of a firm which had workshops for years
deliberately closing down, and placing a large number of men out; and this large employer
himself has been lecturing to employers' associations as to the best means of escaping
from the Trade Boards Act. We say that that in itself has accentuated the evils arising.
There is not the least doubt that the position is made much worse by this sort of thing.
and as we have amended the resolution, and now confine the application to the industry
represented by ourselves, we sincerely hope that your answer will be more favourable
than it was, so far as the principle in the resolution is concerned.

WAGES POSITION IN THE BOOT TRADE.

Economic Causes that Affect Out-Workers.
We have received several communications with regard to the statement recently
made that handsewn bootmakers employed by high-class firms in the West-end boot-
making trade had agreed to accept a reduction of 25 per cent. on making and 15 per cent.
on repair work.

Strenuous Denials.
On the one hand, several firms with first-class reputations have denied that they
are paying less wages.
This is no doubt inspired by the fact that customers are demanding a decrease of
25 per cent. in the price of boots.
At the same time we have been informed by Mr. Peter Brennan, the General Secretary
of the Amalgamated Society of Boot and Shoe Makers, and Mr. J. W. Dixon, Secretary
of the London and Provincial Union of Handsewn Boot and Shoe Makers, that no reduction
has been agreed to.

Firm's Proposal.
One firm in Dover Street had proposed to make the reduction, but it had not been
accepted.
According to Mr. Peter Brennan, the men were more likely to ask for an advance
than to accept a reduction.
The explanation of this discrepancy is that certain West End firms give out a portion
of their work to small masters.
These have in fact accepted lower rates in order to get work allotted to them.

Workmen who are employed by them have accepted lower wages,
no doubt without the knowledge or consent of either Union.
Some of these men may be non-unionists, but is is impossible to see how this may
affect the trade.
When trade is falling off the employer has been known to use the possibility of in-
creasing the output of out-workers, and their acceptance of a reduction as a means of
reducing the wages of the men directly employed by them.
That has not been successfully carried out yet, and, therefore, the reduction is a
partial and not a general one. The Star, February 24th, 1921.

WAGES IN THE BOOT AND SHOE REPAIRING TRADE.

Prosecution at Brighton.
At the Brighton Borough Bench this morning, George Blunden, 32, Sillwood Street, was summoned for failing to pay wages at not less than the minimum rate under the Trade Boards Acts, also for failing to keep the necessary records, failing to produce records, and failing to keep posted copies of notices relating to the above.
Mr. S. P. Low prosecuted for the Ministry of Labour, and Mr. F. S. Gentle represented defendant, who pleaded not guilty to the second summons and guilty to the others.
The Magistrates were Alderman Colbourne (in the chair), Mr. Clayton, Mr. Gillett. Mrs. Smith, Mr. Wallis, and Alderman Wellman.
Mr. Low withdrew the summons for failing to keep necessary records.

The Facts of the Case.
In laying the facts before the Bench, Mr. Low said the Trade Boards Acts applied mainly to trades in which the workers were not properly organised, or in which they were not localised. The Acts provided that Trade Boards should be set up consisting of an equal number of employers and workers, with certain members appointed by the Ministry of Labour. The Trade Board sat and issued notices of proposal with regard to the rates, both time and piece, which they thought were necessary for their particular trade. These notices of proposal were sent to all the known employers in the trade, and the employers were entitled to send in to the Trade Board objections to the rates. After a period of two months, the Trade Board considered the objections, and then proceeded to fix rates which they considered should be paid in the trade These rates were then sent to the Ministry of Labour for confirmation. If confirmed they became the rates legally binding in the trade and must be paid by all employers. Failure to pay them was not only a wrong to the worker, but unfair to competing employers who complied with the law. The Trade Board concerned in the present case was the Boot and Shoe Repairing Trade Board, and the Order under which they fixed their rates was dated 8th April, 1920. Defendant was a boot and shoe repairer, and he had an outworker named Paul, who was a cripple, living at 15, Carlton Hill. The work done by Paul was piecework, and the rates paid by defendant had been agreed between them some time before the Order came into operation. Early in April, 1920, shortly after the notice of fixing was issued by the Trade Board, Paul spoke to defendant about the rates. Defendant told him that the rates fixed by the Order were time rates and did not apply to him. At the end of April Paul again spoke to defend- ant, who said he would look into the matter. In May Paul sent him a copy of the piece- work rates, but in spite of this defendant did not make any alteration in the rates he paid. In June and December last year, Mr. Muir, one of the Ministry's Inspectors, called on defendant, who said he paid his workers what they earned and could not pay more. He refused to produce the records, asking what right Mr. Muir had to interfere and said he was not going to plaster his walls with notices like a little shop in a back street. "The Act," he added, "is only to give you a soft job of walking about the streets interfering with workpeople." Mr. Low stated that during the four weeks in November and December last, in respect of which defendant was summoned, Paul was underpaid to the extent of £1 6s. 4d. He asked for penalties for non-posting the notices, for failing to produce records and for underpaying, with an order for the payment of arrears due since the rates came into force.

The Defence.
For the defendant, Mr. Gentle mentioned that this was the first case of the kind in respect of the boot and shoe repairing trade in Brighton. Both Paul and defendant were 70 years of age. Defendant had to cut his prices to meet the demands of the neighbour- hood, and if he paid the rates fixed by the Board his own profit on soling and heeling a pair of boots would only be 5d. With regard to the effect on competitors of failing to com- ply with the order, defendant's nearest competitor was a man who did his own work and consequently could cut Blunden to pieces. If Paul were to go into the witness-box he would say he was satisfied, and it must not be overlooked that for the rates he was now asked to pay, defendant could employ a young man able to do much better work. Mr. Gentle explained that the failure to produce records and post notices were due to misunder- standings on defendant's part.

Magistrates' Decision.
After a lengthy consultation in private, the Chairman said the Magistrates had decided to deal with the case in a somewhat lenient manner as it was the first heard in that Court Defendant had only himself to blame. He had flouted the Order in such a way that he

UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE BILL.
Dr. Macnamara announced, in response to appeals from all parts of the House, the
consent of the Government to the raising of the Unemployment Benefit to 20s. per week
for men and ros, for women.

A Success for the Labour Party.
The Government would certainly have avoided conceding the increase if it could,
and credit is therefore due to the Labour Party for the manner in which it has hung on
to the flank of Ministers on this matter and harried them from the very opening of the
session.

The discussion actually took place on Mr. Clynes' amendment to raise the benefits
to pos, for the head of a family and 25s. for others, with 5s. for each dependent.
Mr. Clynes insisted that 18s. a week was insufficient for the maintenance of the
humblest home in Britain.

He admitted that there were some people who were tempted even by the existing
benefits to shirk jobs that they should properly accept. But the cure for that was not
a low rate of benefit, but to strengthen the regulations and administration.
A Real Economy.
The future welfare of the community depended upon the efficiency of its working
members, and that depended upon adequate housing, feeding, and clothing.
The great lesson for the Government to learn was to

Pay at the right time.
Let them do the right thing now.
-Daily Herald, February 25th, 1921.
One more clear point in favour of keeping the Labour members in the House of Commons.
-E.L.P., Gen. Sec.]

LABOUR'S BUSY DAY.
There were doings in the Labour world yesterday. The leaders of the great trade
mischievous activities of the middle-class theoretical Socialists who consider themselve
unions had a very busy day and as is usually the case when they are free from the
the heaven-sent apostles of the New Order, they considered some national question
with sound sense and with due respect to the welfare of the community as a whole. Direct
action, that pet of the ruddy-hued admirers of Leninism, has been killed stone dead.
The pleasure felt in Leicester by this excellent piece of work will be intensified by the fact
that the Lord High Executioner was Mr. E. L. Poulton, the general secretary of the National
well-balanced mind and immense abilities. Leicester predicted when the headquarters
Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives. Leicester knows and appreciates Mr. Poulton's
soon become equally familiar with Mr. Poulton's powers. At the National Conference
of the Shoe Operatives' Union were removed to London that the country generally would
at Trade Union
Dr. Poulton, in his presidential address, pulverised the case for direct action with a com
pleteness that left no room for further argument. He made it perfectly clear that a policy
of direct action to enforce legislation would inflict the greatest hardships on the very
class it was designed to benefit, and would, moreover, be bound to break down by reason
of its own unwieldiness, or develop into civil war of the most terrible kind. Mr. Clynes
and Mr. Thomas endorsed Mr. Poulton's view. After that it was inevitable that the
resolution in favour of renewed Parliamentary effort should be carried by an overwhelming
majority. This result can be accepted as the trade unions' final word on the subject
of direct action. For a long time past the "hot air merchants," as they are called, have
claimed that the great trade unions were far in advance of their leaders on this question,
and that when the time came the country would receive an unpleasant awakening. On
the contrary the direct actionists have been put to sleep by a knock-out of a very definite
kind. Interest in Labour's legislative efforts will not be lessened because constitutional
methods are to be adhered to. It will indeed be much easier to extend sympathetic
co-operation to Labour in its struggles towards a brighter and happier existence now
that it considers the health of the body politic of more importance than that of any of its
members. The Leicester Mail, February 24th, 1921.
TUBERCULOSIS IN THE BOOT TRADE.
Necessity for Greater Preventative Measures.
COUNTY INSURANCE COMMITTEE.
Mr. F. Holliday presided over a meeting of the Leicestershire Insurance Committee
yesterday.
In moving the report of the Sanatorium Benefit Sub-Committee, Mr. J. W. West
voiced his thanks to Dr. T. Robinson for his excellent report on pulmonary tuberculosis
in respect of insured persons as from 1912 to 1919.
Dr. Burkitt observed that at present they had to deal with a great number of tuber-
culosis cases, and in his opinion more should be done to stay the advance of this dreadful
disease.
People engaged in the boot and shoe industry were specially subject to the disease,
and greater measures should be taken to prevent the malady spreading in this particular
sphere. He suggested that the report be referred to the Sanatorium Benefit Sub-Committee
so that they might be able to take action in the matter.
Reference was made by the Chairman to a statement reported to have been made
by Mr. J. W. Black at a recent meeting of the County Council. to the effect that out of
281 insured persons, half of them had been cured of tuberculosis. The speaker thought
they could not accept this statement as correct. Personally, he did not think so many
cases had been cured outright. He would like to see a full-time tuberculosis officer appointed
for the county.
Mr. West thought that what Mr. Black intended to say was that half of the cases had
considerably improved, and were back again at their employment.
Dr. Robinson mentioned that from 15 to 20 persons had been cured outright. Schemes.
that meant the spending of money had been held up by the County Council, and conse-
quently a scheme they had in hand for the treatment of consumptives had also been held
in abeyance. It would take two or three years before a sanatorium could be completed.
Dr. Burkitt formally moved that the report be referred to the Sanatorium Benefit
Sub-Committee, and this course was agreed to.--Leicester Daily Mercury, March 3rd, 1921.
