LACK OF TRADE BOARD INSPECTORS!!
The Minister of Labour says "No Vacancies."
In view of the fact that much dissatisfaction exists at the lack of inspectors to enforce the rulings of the Boot Repairing Trade Board, and that in answer to a deputation on the subject the Minister regretted the staff was inadequate, but said something more than a mere technical knowledge of the trade was required, as the inspector would be expected to act as prosecutor in any cases that arose and would therefore have to be possessed of elucation and some acquaintance with legal methods, we make no apology for publishing the following correspondence between an applicant for the post of Trade Board inspector and the Ministry of Labour. We have seen the actual application and the Ministry's reply, and there is no doubt of the genuineness of either document; nor, we believe, are the qualifications of the applicant in any way open to question.
The application was as follows:
"January 24, 1921.
"Sir, I am a master man in repairing and retail boot and shoe trade, and would be glad if my application for an inspectorship under the recently constituted Trade Board could be considered by the proper authorities.
"I have been in the boot and shoe repairing trade for more than twenty years. I am 37 years of age. Before joining my father in business, I served two years in the office of Mr. Mark Attenborough, solicitor, of 35, Walbrook, E.C. I was educated at St. A
School, London, and after leaving gained an exhibition from the L.C.C. to sit for the Diploma in Literature at the University of London, under the extension scheme. After four years' study at the University I took my diploma, gaining certificates of merit at three out of the four annual examinations, besides being awarded honours for submitting an essay on Shakespearean research work. Conjointly with my study for the Diploma in Literature I obtained certificates from the University for three short courses in Biology Psychology, and Sociology.
"After my University course I attended a session at the London School of Economics and spent some months in France to perfect my knowledge of the French language. 1 served in France in the R.G.A. as a battery commandant's assistant, and after the Armistice as an instructor in French.
"My long, extensive, and practical connection with the repairing and retail boot and shoe trade, combined with my knowledge of the law, and my educational attainments should, I venture to believe, make me in most ways an ideal candidate for the post of inspector under the Boot Repairing Trade Board, and I trust that my application will receive favourable consideration.-Yours faithfully, S. W. J."
To which the Secretary to the Ministry of Labour returned the following reply:
"Ministry of Labour.
"Establishments Department,
Richmond Terrace, Whitehall, February 14, 1921.
"Sir,-With reference to your letter relative to an appointment as inspector in this Ministry, under the Trade Boards Acts (Boot Repairing), I am to say there are at present no vacancies for which you could be considered.
"I am to add that in accordance with the decision of H.M. Government, vacancies for temporary posts in Government Departments are now ordinarily being filled by discharged and demobilised sailors, soldiers and airmen, who are selected in order of merit from lists of candidates submitted by Employment Exchanges and the Appointments Department, preference being given to those disabled by war service.
"Any persons eligible under the foregoing decision will, on application being made to any Employment Exchange or office of the Appointments Department, be considered for such temporary appointments in the Government service as may be available from time to time. If a candidate is either ineligible or found to be of unsuitable qualifications for Government service, or if no appropriate Government post is vacant, every endeavour will be made to assist him in obtaining other employment, but it should be understood that whilst applications will receive every consideration, the Department is not in a position to give any guarantee of eventual employment. I am, Sir, your obedient servant,
The applicant, in forwarding the reply to a friend, writes:-"My application was made because I saw in the reports of various meetings complaints as to the want of in- spectors, and the reply of the Ministry of Labour that suitable men from the boot trade were not available. Remember, I have twenty years' experience of the trade, a knowledge of the law, and a University diploma-and am a discharged soldier. But the Ministry say in effect no inspectors are needed; yet the boot trade are crying out for them and would like some at least appointed from amongst themselves. I suppose the Ministry have the final word and that my appointment may be considered very unlikely." -The Shoe Trade Journal, February 25th, 1921.

BOOT AND SHOE TRADE.
In this trade there was a slight improvement on the whole during March, but employ-
ment was still bad, with much short time and unemployment. The improvement was
chiefly shown in the Midland district (particularly Leicester and Stafford) and in Norwich;
while other districts showed a further decline, and some (particularly Bristol and Kings-
wood) reported very severe depression.

The aggregate wage-bill of the firms making Returns showed a reduction of about
24 per cent. as compared with March of last year, in spite of the advance in rates of wages
granted last April. This reduction was due partly to a diminution of about 16 per cent.
in the number employed, and partly to a reduction in the average earnings owing to
short time.

Employment at Leicester and in the surrounding district showed some improvement
during March, and on the whole was moderate; most of the factories at Leicester closed
for only two days, as usual, at Easter. At Hinckley employment was still bad, but a
slight improvement was reported. At Northampton nearly all the factories were still
on short time. At Kettering and Wellingborough employment was reported as bad;
most of the factories in the Kettering district were closed for the whole of Easter week.

on the whole, slightly better than in February, although many firms were still very slack;

GENERAL ELECTION.
It is
Rumours are constantly heard that the Government are only waiting a
favourable moment to declare for a General Election. We urge upon all to
put their machinery in order so that whether it comes in the near future or
is delayed for some time, the workers may be found ready for the same.
of no practical value to complain after an election if it turns out contrary to
what we desire. The workers constitute the overwhelming majority of the
electorate, and should see to it that their vote is so used as will ensure those
Members being returned who will bring into existence just and equitable laws
whereby the people will be enabled to live under good conditions.
THE INDUSTRIAL OUTLOOK
is, at the time of writing, a very serious one indeed. The one outstanding
case, however, above all others is that connected with the coal industry.
In our judgment the Government are largely to blame for the situation that
has been brought about, and which threatens the whole industrial life of the
country. When one remembers the result of the Sankey Commission and
the attitude of the Government thereto, along with recent legislation for
decontrol, it does certainly have the appearance that no sort of appreciation
of the real situation had been comprehended by those in authority. Having
had experience for many years past of the advantage to the industry of setting
up a minimum rate of pay, we feel that on such a matter the miners were only

---
asking for something which is just in principle. The method of the employers
in the Mining industry in sending what amounted to an ultimatum in their
proposed new wage list could only have one result: resistance to the same,
having regard to the tremendous reductions (in many instances) the proposed
scale would mean in the weekly drawings of the miners. In our judgment
the old scale of payment should have continued until a new one agreed to jointly
was determined upon, as is done in the boot industry. It may be said that
this would result in a great loss to the owners in certain cases, seeing that
the State had withdrawn its support. Here we think the Government are
again to blame in leaving the two parties as they did. Coal is one of the
essentials in the industrial life of this country; surely therefore the question
is, is it necessary that coal which is obtainable, but expensive to raise from
the bowels of the earth, should be raised? We think the answer would be in
the affirmative. From a national standpoint the question naturally follows
are the miners who work as hard and long as other miners to work for less
because of the lack of success financially of any given mine? Here we feel
confident the answer would be "No." How then is the position to be met:
We suggest that the example which the Government set in the matter of the
Dye industry be followed a subsidy from the State in such cases. It may
be answered that this is a form of payment of wages which is pernicious; we
think not; coal is, as already stated, one of the vital things of this country,
and we cannot afford to leave coal in large quantities in the earth simply because
of the financial aspect only. Moreover, any such cases calling for a subsidy
would be proper cases for enquiry by the Government into all the causes
why the mine does not pay, and it might conceivably be that the result
of changes in the management and administration would prevent any
loss being sustained. The general situation, industrially, is one of constant
anxiety and will continue to be for some time yet. Under the circumstances
it surely is the duty of each one to, as far as possible, render assistance in getting
out of the maze in which we find ourselves and which threatens to engulf us
unless there is a statesmanlike treatment of the world-wide tragedy which
has come upon mankind as a result of the terrible war which we have just
emerged from. We urgently appeal to all our members to so work as to bring
into being that state of society which, in the words of the Labour manifesto
will make it for ever impossible for there to be any more war."

GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.

FELLOW MEMBERS,
UNEMPLOYMENT. As intimated in my last report in respect to the Unemployed
Conference held on the 23rd February, at Kingsway Hall, where our Union put before
the Conference their view of a one day's stoppage which practically met with no support,
it was a prelude to what happened last week. We predicted then that there was not the
least doubt that the Trade Union Officials and Leaders of this country would do probably
more than they ever had done to avert a stoppage. This culminated in differences
that appeared in the attitude of the Triple Alliance on Friday, the 8th of this month.
Opinions differ as to what attitude should be taken when one's organisation is out on
strike. Some think everybody should stop. If that spirit prevailed whenever there was
a strike everybody would stop every time, but as the proof of the pudding is in the eating,
the movement was put to the test and failed to respond on the date above-mentioned.
on a matter patent to everyone and helpful to all.
Now as to the Miners' position. One's whole sympathy goes out to the Miners, and
we ought to give them all the help we possibly can. They have been outrageously treated
by the sole authorities in this country for good order and in governing, that is the Govern-
ment itself. What are the motives behind the Government? I can only add two. One
is ignorance, the other is carelessness, probably I could say dishonesty too, and there
would be no trouble in proving that for the first time in history a British Government
has gone back on what appeared to be its pledged promise to a great portion of the working-
class community upon whom they were first of all depending during the late great war.
Thanks to the business foresight of Mr. Arthur Henderson, who contributed an article to
one of the Sunday papers, we find there something which has never before appeared in
favour of the Miners. In the past we were told that the Miners demanded either Nationali-
sation or a Pooling of profits. The Owners we understand wanted 17 to 20 per cent.
The Prime Minister refused. We also understood that the
Miners were willing to concede them 10 per cent. This the Prime Minister also refused
to concede, but Mr. Henderson tells us that the pool out of which poor mines were to have
wages paid to the miners equal with good mines, was to be provided by a tax per ton
on all coal, which would mean that the miner who got the biggest wage, who hewed the
greatest amount of coal, would contribute most towards the tax. This is a view which
does not appear to have come out in the discussion between the Mine Owners and the
Miners' Representatives. Speaking for myself, I believe that from whatever source the
wages might come, no one in this Kingdom has a right to expect a Miner, or for that matter
any other class of worker (but we are speaking of Miners at the present) to work unless
he gets a reasonable living wage 52 weeks in the year, and if coal must be obtained and
we have it in our midst, then we ought to be willing to subsidise the bad mine with the
most efficient machinery and organisation that can be produced, with that difference
between the wages earned and a proper wage. I am pleased to say that the head of one
of the largest Engineering firms in industry agrees with this particular view. I wish the
Miners success and hope the Prime Minister will have the common sense to deal with this
matter in a common sense manner, which has not been the case up to the present. The
Miners and Mine Owners ought to have had proper notice, and they ought to have been
advised by the Government to endeavour to bring about a settlement, without the Govern-
ment itself trying to force a wage upon men, which they have rightly refused to accept
because in many districts it is below a reasonable subsistence level.

COUNCIL MEETINGS. - On the 20th and 21st ult. we held our usual Council Meetings
and made preparations for the coming Conference, Whit Week, in the Kingsway Hall
London, where we hope to have a most successful gathering.
LONDON. - On the 15th ult. I attended a meeting of one of our firms in London who
were endeavouring to transfer from Handsewn work to that of Machine Welted, and
although for the moment the work is in a transitory stage, the men who have been accus-
tomed to work in their homes much prefer this system of what we call working indoors,
so much so that I hope we may give encouragement to indoor working and at no distant
date get the Government to discourage home employment for able-bodied persons.
STREET. - On the 16th ult. I paid a visit to Street in Somersetshire, to endeavour to
encourage a little more robustness among the members. Conditions down in Street are
very bad owing to the fact that the men are working as little as a day and a half per week.
I had a very nice meeting, very encouraging meeting, although some of the members
would have liked to have seen a larger number present. Still I should guess there were
70 to 80 present, probably 100, and I think that is very well for an ordinary branch
meeting of a small branch. However, our good friend the Secretary quite properly expects
a bit more loyalty.
I had occasion to see the management when there, because their rendering of the 85s.
minimum did not coincide with my own views, and whilst we have no complaint whatever

FELLOW MEMBERS,
ORGANISERS' REPORTS.

Herewith is my report for the month. I have visited Guiseley with a view of organising,
but once again have to report that trade is in a very bad state, and although I had con-
versations with operatives employed at the three respective factories, have been unable
to arrange for any meetings owing to the condition of the trade.
I have also visited Sileby for the purpose of organising. I met the Branch Com-
mittee with a view to discussing the position and making arrangements for getting at the
operatives. After considerable discussion it was decided to take one shop at a time when
the opportunity presents itself. Trade is very bad here and with the holiday intervening
it has interfered with our work. Messrs. Bray's has been closed down for four weeks and
Messrs. Swan & Preston's three weeks, but both firms have re-commenced operations.
I had an interview with Messrs. Moyers. This firm commenced on the County Statement
on April 9th. At a meeting of the employees I advised them to give the same a fair trial.

I have also visited Rothley and had conversations with operatives on the reason for
declining membership, and found the explanation is the very bad state of trade. The
firm of Messrs. T. G. Hunt has been closed down for two months, and Messrs. Stead &
Simpson's for the same period. Both firms have now re-commenced operations and the
workers are only too anxious to commence paying contributions to our Union again as
they recognise that a great deal has been done for them. The other firm are working
three and four days per week only.

Mr. Leader and I have visited Mountsorrel and found trade there only very moderate.
As a result of conversations with operatives we feel they will continue membership of the
Union.

Mr. Richards, Mr. Law and myself, in accordance with Council's instruction, attended
before the Leicester Labour Party Executive re Ald. Hill's South Leicester Candidature
and a permanent Election Agent for the Division. The position of the Council was put
before the above-mentioned body, and after questions were answered we were informed
that the Party's findings would be forwarded on in writing.

BRANCH REPORTS.

BARNSLEY.—Trade was very slack here, and owing to the Miners'
Strike it has become very bad,
BELFAST.—Trade continues to remain in a very unsatisfactory con-
dition; short time is being worked generally, while many of our members
are still on the unemployed list, without any prospects of being employed in
the near future; the position at the present time is most depressing.
BRISTOL AND KINGSWOOD No. 2.—Trade is still very bad with us;
our unemployed list lengthens, and at present there is very little sign of a
trade revival. The busiest places in Kingswood at present are the offices
of the N.U.B.S.O. and the Labour Exchange. We are playing an important
part in the life of the community. Everybody is wishing for a speedy settle-
ment in the coal industry, and hope when it comes it will be permanent ;
until that is achieved there cannot be any stability in any other trade, and
at the present time the great need of the people is to find work which will
enable them to live.
CHESHAM.—Trade is very bad, worse than a month ago, and members
are still being discharged. We have a large number signing the out-of-work
hook in addition to a large number of members who have drawn their full
amount of benefit. We are glad to report that our Branch President and
Secretary have been returned members of the local U.D.C.
CHESTERFIELD.—Trade is very bad, several of our members have
been given a week's notice to finish work for the firm on the 16th April. With
the Miners' lockout and the slump brings us nearly to a standstill, but we are
hoping for a speedy settlement of the lockout, and that ere long we shall
see the arrival of better things than the last few months have provided. Surely
some time we shall see people better off so that they can buy our products
and put the trade on a better basis than it is to-day. The opening of our
Foreign Trade ought soon to make an alteration for the boot trade at least.
CORK.—Trade here is a little improved, some of our members having
returned to work. It is with regret we have to report the resignation of Mr.
W. W. Cooper, Manager of the Lee Boot Company; we hope that he will
be spared long to enjoy his well-earned rest.
EDINBURGH.—The absorbing topic at present is the mining crisis.
Of course opinion differs on the case put before the public, but in our opinion
the reduction is too great according to level of cost of living. We have again
received notice to attend a District Committee meeting of Wages Trade Board
to consider minimum wages and re-adjustment of piece rates. It is nearly six
months since our claim was put forward and now we are only meeting as a
District Committee to consider these items. The local Advisory Committee
have taken up the matter of the Education Authority training adults in the
Boot Repairing Trade, but up till now they have been told to mind their own
business. Now, in the present state of the Repairing Trade, the teaching of
disabled sailors or soldiers is just putting the men into a blind alley as there is no
prospect of them receiving employment when their training has expired. Our
members are anxious about the new Agreement and when the Federation
and our Union are going to meet to discuss the proposed terms.
HIGHAM AND RUSHDEN.—We regret that during the last week the
wife of our old colleague and fellow Official (Wm. Bazeley, J.P.) passed away
after a long and painful illness ; the Monthly Meetings passed resolutions of
sympathy. Also one of the oldest and respected members, Solomon Upton,
has died. Mr. Upton was an energetic worker in the Labour cause for years,
and was a member of our Union for over 30 years; member of Branch Executive

NORWICH. It is with extreme regret that we have this month to report
the death of our late secretary, James Mason. Members of the Union will
remember that Mr. Mason retired from office February, 1920, with his health
greatly impaired. We joined with him in the hope that skilful nursing and
close medical attention would be sufficient to bring about a return to reason-
able health and opportunity for many pleasurable years of life. With much
patience and steady optimism he lived through thirteen months of pain
and suffering, to pass away suddenly on March 31st. Mr. Mason reached
the age of seventy years after a very hard and strenuous career. Active in the
shoe trade from the age of eighteen, his life was spent continuously for and on
behalf of the worker. During the thirty years of branch secretaryship he
encountered many difficulties, and with a determination that was an outstand-
ing characteristic he succeeded in building up a strong force in the shape of the
Norwich Branch. We in Norwich wished sincerely that he would have been
spared to enjoy the evening of his days, in comfort and repose, being able to
observe the working and use of the weapon he gave his life to forge. Difficult
though the present may be, we may be assured that it is immeasurably easier
for the work done by the pioneers in the days that are gone. James Mason was
of that band; his memory is left us as an inspiration to the things he believed
in. We extend our heartfelt sympathy to his widow and family.

PLYMOUTH.-Trade is still quiet, but all around we see signs of activity
and measures being taken to cope with the industrial situation. Battalions
march equipped for battle, mighty ships plough the seas and make ready to
preserve the life of the community, and we wonder what the end will be;
things look foreboding. We hope our comrades will rely on the justice of their
cause and the intelligence of our race to bring about a just and lasting settlement,
rather than enter into a trial of strength with the powers that be, for who could
doubt what the end would be.

We heartily support the Council in their proposal to exempt unemployed
members from payment of contributions, as we earnestly desire to see our
Union forces remain powerful and strong, ready to march forward when trade
revives and the opportunity arises. We hope the Council will deal liberally
with this question, and all members who have the good fortune to remain
employed support them in their efforts to preserve an organisation which will
compel respect, ready and competent at all times to maintain a standard of
life worthy of our trade and calling.

PORTSMOUTH.-Trade is showing signs of improvement, and not
before it was necessary. We cannot say there is any improvement in the interest
of our members in the affairs of the Union.

THE MINERS IN THE POLITICAL SITUATION.

By J. RAMSAY MACDONALD.

I look with some apprehension upon a new outbreak of hostilities on the coalfield.
With the demands of the miners I am in full agreement. District agreements are wrong,
Coal production is a national concern, to attach low wages to difficult work is wrong.
and the wages paid in making it up to the required total should be upon national standards.
The miners have both justice and common sense on their side.

But justice and common sense do not win battles. The time of fighting and the
conditions of fighting must be studied. The men were perfectly right to say that they
do not agree to the owners' proposal. What next?

A strike at present would only play into the hands of the masters and the scaremongers.
Capital would not suffer very much if every mine in the country were closed for a week
or two. The major markets are overstocked and this is a good time for a holiday, and the
chance for high prices and any shortage that might be felt could be put upon the miners,
who are always unpopular when they are doing anything but slaving at the coal face.
The Capitalist will be relieved of trouble, and a good text will be provided for his
next by the Prime Minister, for his next scare speech.

It will undoubtedly hamper the Labour Party at the present moment, as the last
stroke did, and will do anything but help the general labour movement, the success of which
must be a grave concern for the miners.

Important as these considerations are, there is still a bigger one to be considered.
Capital mining capitalism, from its very nature, cannot accept a national pool into which
profits are to be put and from which wages are to be paid. It must fight against that,
because it will have the support of Capitalism in general. What a strike would therefore
amount to is this: It would be an attempt to get the benefits of nationalisation by action
that would not result in nationalisation.

This seems to me to be poor fighting. Whatever may be the ostensible quarrel,
the one issue upon which the miner should fix his attention is nationalisation, for that is
the pivot round which he is moving all the time. Until he has got that he can get little
worth having. In order to get that, he must help the Labour Party and do nothing to
give a set-back to its political victories. If the miners know in their hearts that this is
the time for a big successful industrial fight, well, let them bide their time. The
persistent and watchful man gets there first.

The miners have rejected the owners' proposals, and that decision will be placed
before the owners. The owners may refuse to budge-probably will. Then there will
be no peace, no heart in work, no harmony in the coal field-only preparation for a struggle.
That will be far more disconcerting to Capitalists than a fight which they believe will end
in their victory, in broken Unions, in depleted funds, and in dispirited men. By such
actions as this, Capitalism is digging its own grave and is rousing such bitter enmity that
its system cannot last.

The miners' concern is with public opinion. They cannot win without that, because
nationalisation is an issue that that has to settle one way or another. I was very dis-
appointed with the way the nationalisation campaign was handled. Jericho walls will
not fall now by parades and blasts of trumpets. Steady persistent work must be put in
and difficult questions ought not to be dropped like hot potatoes. If it is made easy for
the great mass of uninstructed electors to believe as gospel the balderdash uttered by the
Prime Minister after that lunch, then reason and honesty will have no place in public
affairs.

The deception practised by Mr. Bonar Law, the conduct of the Government regarding
de-control, the deliberate appeal to class prejudice and interest by the Prime Minister,
and similar things, are driving the miners into a position where only considerations of how
to have their own back can move them. Unless there is a change, to talk to the miners
of honest work will be to mark one's self off as a great saint or a confounded hypocrite.

I hope the miners will address themselves to the public on the larger moral issue,
and through the Labour Party to the same public on the larger political issue, and not
obscure both by a strike that on merits would be wholly justified but as business would
be a colossal blunder. Forward (Glasgow), April 2nd, 1921.

DEATH OF MR. JAMES MASON.
The citizens of Norwich, and especially those who are connected with the shoe trade.
will regret to hear of the death of Mr. James Mason. He was at one time a member of
the City Council, and was still better known as a leader in trade unionism. Mr. Mason
was seventy years of age last January. A little more than a year ago he retired from
the Norwich secretaryship of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives, and took
over the sick secretaryship. On Wednesday night he was taken alarmingly ill, and he
died in the earlier hours of the following morning.

It is literally true to say that Mr. Mason was connected with the boot and shoe trade
throughout his life, for his father was a journeyman shoemaker before the introduction
of machinery. When 15 he went to London to learn the American peg work, but soon
returned to Norwich. Afterwards at intervals he worked at Newcastle, Leeds, Halifax,
and Manchester, whence, after more or less unsatisfactory experiences, he returned to
Norwich, and for eight years followed his trade there. Then his activities as a member
of the union made it impossible for him to find employment in his native city, and after
being out of work four months he went to Leicester, where he eventually settled down
comfortably in a factory in which his knowledge and experience in dealing with light
ladies' work secured for him warm recognition. His career as an operative came to an
end in 1890, when his position as secretary of the Norwich branch of the Union was made
a full-time office. Ml. Mason, from his early youth, was a keen supporter of the Union
and his efforts on its behalf were recognised some twelve months ago by the presentation
of a cheque for £150.

Mr. Mason had some curious experiences in the early days of his secretaryship. "S
only," he said, was my house an office, always open for the reception of members, but
members used to call me out of the factory to give them advice, and I rarely went to a
friend's house without a neighbour popping in to ask me to solve some trade problema
Eastern Evening News, 2nd April, 1921.

TRADE UNION STAMP.
TO THE EDITOR, Leicester Mail.
The idea of a Stamped Boot or Shoe as a guarantee of its wearing qualities mimized a good one, but the same will be incomplete unless the stamp also carries with the fact that it has been produced by Trade Unionists under proper conditions and in onformity with the National Agreements covering the Industry as arranged between
the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives and the Employers' Federation. Such article would strongly recommend itself with this proviso to the eight million Trade mionists and their families in this country. - Yours faithfully,
10TH MARCH, 1921.
(Signed), T. F. RICHARDS, General President.
In a letter printed elsewhere in this issue Mr. T. F. Richards discusses a point of some interest in connection with the scheme in question. A fortnight since he suggested that boots bearing the quality mark also bore the trade union stamp the support of eight million trade unionists and their families would probably be secured an idea which is
certainly worth consideration. But our counter-suggestion, that the National Union mught in return very properly instruct its members to refuse to make boots which did not comply with the specifications adopted by the Joint Committee, brings a characteristic reply from Mr. Richards, to which we direct attention. He contends that the adoption our proposal would involve securing a share in the management of boot factories to the
operatives employed. But it does nothing of the kind. If it were understood that no Tmember of the Union would perform any operation on boots containing paper or cardboard, no employer of Union labour would use such materials. The attempt to link up our sug-gestion with the question of joint management is ingenious, but there is no real connection
between the two things, as Mr. Richards must be aware. We are glad to hear that no shoddy boots are made in any of the co-operative shoe factories. That fact probably accounts in part for such success as these enterprises enjoy, for it proves that the policy of producing only sound goods is the best, no matter where or by whom it is practised.-
Shoe and Leather Record, April 8th, 1921.

HEALTH NOTES-TREATMENT OF CONSUMPTION
By T. CREW, A.F.I.
Recently, we had the important news of the Spahlinger treatment of tuberculosis, and now it is all the more pleasing to record that a distinguished medical man, Dr. Nathan Raw, M.P., has advanced certain definite views as to securing immunity from this terrible scourge. After long continued research and clinical experiment, he is convinced that there are two quite distinct forms of tuberculosis, and that it is possible to secure immunity from either disease by a vaccine prepared from the bacillus of the other. He states that human and bovine tuberculosis are separate and distinct infections, producing a different set of symptoms in the human body and that the one form confers immunity in the body from the other form. It is gratifying to know that medical science is surely attacking this great problem, which has baffled us for so many years.

The New Minister.
One regrets for various reasons the disappearance of Dr. C. Addison from the position of Minister of Health, and yet one cannot be surprised inasmuch as support accorded to him from his own profession (medical) has not been generally given. With a medical man at the head of such an important post, one would have thought that the medical fraternity would have been more united than ever to advance the cause of health in all its spheres. The appointment of Sir Alfred Mond does not suggest any greater progress than that made by the late Minister, although with his business acumen, the solution of the housing prob- lem may be greatly facilitated.

Tuberculosis.
From May Ist. the county and borough councils will deal comprehensively with the treatment of all tuberculous persons, and accordingly the grants already payable for the provision of institutional and dispensary treatment will be considerably increased, con- sequent upon the discontinuance of the contributions from the insurance committees. An important factor is that Parliament is to be asked to vote money for grants in aid of the provision of extra nourishment to those tuberculous persons under domiciliary treat- ment. Lack of funds for the provision of ancillary foods has been the chief set-back to insurance committees in the following up of suitable cases, who have received and bene- fited from institutional treatment. Nevertheless the application of extra nourishment requires the most careful administration, as only those who have experienced such can fully appreciate. Undoubtedly with the provision of full residential treatment, with the concurrent vocational training, and the wise application of after-care, there is every reason for making definite inroads into the terrible scourge of consumption. Of course, what is really needed among the community is the greater knowledge of the elementary laws of health and the understanding that it is up to the individual to play his or her part in this health problem.

Hot Water.
Do we ever realise the full virtues of hot water? Read and digest the following. Take hot water some time before breakfast, as it is a good antidote against indigestion. If you are exposed to a chill, drink plenty of hot water mixed with lemon juice and sugar added. Hot water applications will relieve the pain of a nervous headache, and also inflamed eyes. Sprains and bruises are greatly relieved by the application of hot water, which will also stop the hemorrhage of a bleeding surface. Those who suffer from insomnia can regain good sleep to a great extent after a full bath.

Range of Services.
Last week I referred to the question as to whether certain operations or other service came within the definition of range of service, and I gave instances. Decisions have now been given by referees which place the following outside the range :- Testing the eyes for errors of refraction, operation of tonsillectomy on a man aged 43 years, operation of radical cure of hernia, removal of abdominal tumour, operation for empyema, cauteri- sation of the pharynx, examination of urine for lead poisoning, operation for ischio-rectal abscess, removal of aural polypus, &c.

It is interesting to note, that where a complaint is made by one practitioner against another, involving any question of the efficiency of the medical service of insured persons, the matter is referred to the Local Medical Committee. It is possible for the latter com- mittee to make representations to the Minister of Health that the continuance on the panel of the practitioner against whom the complaint is made will be prejudicial to the efficiency of the service.—Leicester Mail, 7th April, 1921.

THE RESOLUTION.
J. RAMSAY MACDONALD.
This Conference of representatives of the Executive of the International and the
Parliamentary Parties of the countries concerned has met in consequence of the deadlock
between the Governments of the Allies and of Germany at London, and the events that
have followed.
The Conference takes note of the declaration of the German delegates that they, in
harmony with the decisions at Geneva, accept liability for all legitimate reparations.
The Socialists of the Allied countries recognise that this duty is limited by the capacity
of the German people, and should not be pushed so far as to crush the country or prevent
its economic, political, and moral reconstruction, and so condemn the working class to a
form of economic slavery.
The amount and mode of reparation should be determined by agreement between
the interested parties. Measures of coercion can never lead to a really satisfactory result.
An appeal to military force, so far from furthering the work of reparation, merely prolongs
the period of uncertainty and gives Reaction and Militarism an opportunity to strengthen
their position, to revive feelings of hatred among the peoples, and to embroil Europe
in fresh adventures. The Conference considers that the check to the London negotiations
is due to the Capitalist Powers, which, unable to prevent war, are also unable to secure
peace, and declares that only on the basis of the principles affirmed at International
Working Class Conferences can it look for a concrete solution which will re-establish a
normal situation and obliterate the material and moral traces of the war.
its ideas, ought to guide the negotiations into more fruitful channels, including arbitration
The Working Class, being more disinterested, less Jingo, and more international in
on questions of law or fact if agreement is found not to be possible, and press its decisions
upon the Governments with all its available influence.
The Conference, after having examined the concrete conditions of equitable repara
tion, has reached a unanimous agreement on the following points :-

The parties represented here pledge themselves to remove all obstacles that stand in the way of the realisation of far-reaching plans for reconstruction.
To ensure the necessary speed in the reconstruction of the devastated regions, a mixed system of delivery in kind, labour, and money should be adopted. The deliveries made by Germany should be placed to the credit of the reparation account.
With regard to the reparations in kind, it is essential to ensure, with the co-operation of the trade unions, that they will not injure the workers in either the delivering or the receiving country.

II.

The Conference notes that the German Social Democracy agrees with the principle that German payments for reparation should be increased in proportion to the growing economic prosperity of Germany.
The Conference declares its opinion that indemnities over and above those relating to the restoration of the devastated regions can be fixed so as to guarantee payments to the Allied countries, and also security to German economic life, and should be made in accordance with German prosperity. In order to do this, every effort should be made to restore international trade to its normal conditions of production and exchange. The German Government should agree that annual sums of a fixed minimum be paid bearing a proportion to the condition of the country. This sliding scale should not be created on the basis of exports only, but, like internal taxation, should take account of national wealth and income, and the Conference calls upon the working-class organisations and the Parliamentary Parties to consider how this is to be done.

III.

The Conference takes note of the disagreement between the Allied and German Governments on the subjects of (1) the value of the goods which Germany has already delivered under the provisions of the Treaty of Versailles, and (2) the amounts which Germany can pay for general reparation. It is strongly of opinion that disagreement on such things should be referred for settlement to an expert Commission appointed by the League of Nations or other authority acceptable to both sides, and requests the working-class organisations and the Parliamentary Parties of the countries concerned to press upon their Governments that business disputes on matters of fact and of legal and accepted obligations should be referred for decision to the same kind of authority as would be used when similar disputes arise between individuals. It is of the greatest importance not only that the spirit of justice should be restored in international affairs, but the forms of justice itself.
The League of Nations, to which Germany should be admitted, will not achieve its purpose, and will forfeit the hopes that the world democracy has reposed upon its development, if it fail to interest itself in the financial problems essential to the peace settlement or in those of deliveries in service and in kind in the solution of which the International Labour Bureau can play such an important part.

IV.

But the working-class does not confine its hopes for an enduring peace to the increasing activity of the League of Nations. The working-class itself, through its own organisations, should devote itself to this task.
After having established in the present meeting a unanimous agreement on the important points referred to above, the Executive Committee of the International intends to continue its investigations and negotiations until it has reached even in detail a solution of justice and of international fraternity, capable of securing the enthusiastic endorsement of all the workers.

V.

The Conference notes the declaration of the Dutch delegation that neutral countries have an interest in a speedy, peaceful, and lasting reparation agreement.
The Government and Parliament of the Netherlands have already granted credits and loans for this purpose.
If circumstances show that it is necessary to go further in this direction, the Dutch Party will gladly take the initiative in proposing a common line of action to the other neutral countries.
The delegation points cut that the intervention of the neutral countries will become more important as armaments are more and more restricted.
The Conference draws the attention of the Parliamentary groups in every country to this point.
The Conference upon Reparations which made the above declaration was composed of :

street and shop corners, getting up narrow gangways and passage ways. Here the absence
of a rear man may be more or less dangerous. The driver will very often sever his connec-
tion between the two vehicles, leaving his rear wagon unattended in the street, and pro-
weeding with his own car further along the street. That of course, leaves anything that
may happen to your imagination owing to the interference of boys and so on with the brakes
Numerous accidents can be traced to that. This uncoupling also makes it necessary for
the driver to re-couple and in the re-coupling of the permanent apparatus some little thing
runs the chance of being neglected, especially on a wet, foggy, or particularly cold night.
All this adds to the possibility of accidents. It might not appear to be much, but
my experience suggests it may be more important than it appears at first sight. I do not
like to use the word because it is hackneyed, but the psychology of the whole thing is more
important than it might appear. Commercial motor vehicles are responsible for a huge
proportion of the present street accidents. On the other hand, accidents from other
classes of road users are on the decrease, with the increasing experience of the drivers
Apparently, in the case of the ordinary passenger or private car, we are experiencing a
better time than formerly. The exception is in the commercial car, and I think it is very
largely due to this question of braking and to the overloading, upon which point, I believe
you have a Committee investigating at the present moment, and that will enlighten you
to a much greater degree than I can.

MR. G. SANDERS (United Vehicle Workers): 1 represent the 'bus workers. We re-
member how, at the beginning of the war, an Order was made, and any number of 'buses
were required in France. We used our influence with the men to allow the overcrowding
to take place. Thousands of London 'buses were taken over to France, and proved very
useful, and that had the effect of driving the 'bus passengers into the trams, and thus there
was overcrowding on the trams as well as the 'buses. The most peculiar point is that
if we take the Combine, the London General, which is the biggest concern in the country,
we find they can quite easily obviate this overcrowding if they wish to do so. They have
introduced on the London streets two new types of 'buses, the K and the S types, with
better seating accommodation, and they have taken off the streets rattling good 'buses
which could carry passengers, and sold them to the provinces, where they are now carrying
passengers. I want to say, on behalf of the union, if they have as much affection for the
welfare of the public as they make out in their pamphlets they would not have taken off
the old type 'buses until they had got more of the new type on the streets. The position,
however, is not only as I describe it in London, but in places like Bedford. I was at Bed-
ord a few weeks ago on a Saturday night. I stood at one of the termini and saw 66 grown-
up persons get off a 'bus licensed to carry 36. I got the driver and the conductor to con-
firm this, and they both agreed that that was the number. One hesitates to think what
would happen in the case of an accident with all those people in and on the vehicle. What
I have described is a common occurrence on a Saturday night at Bedford. I think, as it
is agreed that we, as a union, helped the authorities very considerably in the time of war,
that now, two years and three months after the armistice was signed, it is quite time that
overcrowding of that description was done away.

MR. POULTON : You have, Sir, I think, got the resolutions to which we shall speak
this morning. In view of their very reasonable character we hope that we shall get an
affirmative answer to each one of them. The first one is in relation to Trade Board in-
spectors. Complaint was made very strongly in more than one quarter at our last Congress
in September that, although from time to time the rates are fixed, those rates are not paid
in very many parts of the country. That is attributed to the fact that there is a lack of
inspectors to see that employers carry out the regulations laid down. We look upon this
as a very serious matter from our standpoint. It is true to say we have got regulations,
and they are supposed to be the law of the land. We find, however, as a matter of fact,
that the law is ignored, and although Ministers from time to time state that there is, at
any rate, a minimum rate of wages fixed in a particular calling or industry, as a matter
of practice there is no rate fixed because there is no one to enforce it and see that it is
carried out. We feel that this matter should be dealt with at once. Economy we know
is the great thing at the present time, but we believe that it would be the greatest possible
economy to increase the inspectors, so that those people concerned shall receive the wages
that the boards from time to time determine shall duly be paid that is at least a minimum
rate. I hope that we shall be able to secure from you such assurances that the staff will
be increased in sufficient numbers adequately to deal with these matters. Mr. Byrne will
speak to you in detail upon the point. I understand that his society has sent a number
of communications to this Department; still there is no redress. Speaking for my own
trade, although not a member of a Trade Board, my colleagues are constantly complaining
that in various parts of the country where our organisers, secretaries, and other officials
go, they find constant complaint about employers who say they know nothing whatever
about this, and "we shall not pay until somebody comes from the Government."

MR. J. TURNER (Shop Assistants) spoke in support of the following resolution :-
So
This Congress regrets the delay on the part of the Ministry of Labour in

MR. POULTON: The representative appointed for this resolution (Revision of Employment Exchange Regulations) is not here, but I propose to show the justification for bringing it by reading a very short statement made at the Congress by one of the delegates :
Should the employer wish to secure cheap labour he can apply to the Employment Exchange for a man at a wage below the district Trade Union rate, and the Exchange send a man along. There is also the anomaly that while on the one hand the Ministry of Labour sets up Trade Boards and makes their findings legal and binding on the whole of the employers in any given industry, vet, on the other hand, where there is no Trade Board, they are, through the Employment Exchanges, prepared to supply an employer with labour, no matter what the rate offered. This assists employers in playing off the unemployed against the employed, more especially during the present temporary bad period.
That statement by Mr. F. C. Langton, of the Leather Workers, may be found in the Official Report of the last Trades Union Congress, page 362. I think you will agree that upon a statement of that kind we are fully justified in bringing this matter to your notice and asking you to deal with it.
Revision of Employment Exchange Regulations.
MR. W. THORNE, M.P., next spoke in support of the following resolution :-
That this Trades Union Congress strongly protests against the continu- ance of the practice whereby workpeople are being submitted, through the Employment Exchange, to vacancies where wages are below the Trade Union rates agreed upon between the bulk of employers and the Trade Unions con- cerned, and that we call upon the Government to immediately revise the regu- lations, in order that this method shall be immediately stopped.
He said: I am extremely sorry that Mr. John Hill, the General Secretary of the Amalga- mated Union of Shipbuilding, Engineering, and Constructional Workers, is not here to put the case. It was one of the delegates of his association that moved the resolution at the Trades Union Congress. We have had this or a similar resolution at a number of our Congresses with a view to getting the matter rectified. We are not here to-day to plead that when men are on strike they should be in a position to receive unemployment benefit, but we do suggest that when men are not themselves on strike and have no quarrel at all with the employers that they should be in a position to receive unemployment benefit. The bulk of the labourers are hit harder than anybody else. When the second Amending Bill was being piloted through the Committee of the House of Commons a very old friend, Mr. John Burns, was, I believe, President of the Board of Trade. I know that the Labour Party on the Committee at that time put up a tremendously big fight. Mr. Burns was opposed to any extension in the particular direction we wished, for, he said, if unemploy- ment benefit was granted, say, to moulders' labourers or engineers' labourers, or any other labourers working for any particular craftsmen that might be out on strike, it was going to cost the State a good deal of money and be the means practically of eating up all the money that had been paid for unemployment benefit. Personally, I do not think that applies at all. As you know, that fund accumulated to the extent of some £19,000,000.

SPECIAL NOTICE TO MEMBERS.

Every precaution is taken by us to ensure accuracy in these Reports, our corres-pondents being men on whom we can rely: should, however, any errors creep into them, upon the same being pointed out to us, we shall be most happy to give the same prominence to the correction as to the original matter. As these Reports are exclusively for the use of Members, the information contained therein must not be divulged.

NATIONAL UNION OF
Boot and Shoe Operatives.

MONTHLY REPORT.

Nearest Post Office:
Lamb's Conduit St., London, W.C. 1.
Nearest Telegraph Office:
Red Lion Street, London, W.C. 1.
34, GUILFORD STREET,
LONDON, W.C. 1.
23rd MAY, 1921.

FELLOW MEMBERS,
TRADE

has improved slightly during the past month although work has been seriously curtailed owing to the Coal Dispute. The figures given in the Gazette of the Ministry of Labour are as follows:

BOOT AND SHOE TRADE.

The slight improvement noted in the previous month continued during April in certain districts, including the two principal centres of Leicester and Northampton, as also at Stafford and at Norwich; and the industry does not appear to have been so severely crippled by the effects of the coal stoppage as some other industries.

Nevertheless, the state of employment at the end of April was bad, and much below the level of April last year, even in the most favourably situated districts; while at some Centres, particularly Bristol and Kingswood, and in some of the villages of the Northampton County District, the industry was still in a state of very severe depression.

The number of workpeople in these trades whose unemployment books or out-of-work donation policies were lodged at Employment Exchanges at 29th April was 23,073. In addition, there were 17,884 claimants for benefit in respect of systematic short-time working.

COAL DISPUTE.
We have already subscribed £200 from the Central Fund to the Miners'
Fund and have received a fair amount of money from Branches in answer to
our appeal, which, together with a collection by the delegates at the Con-
ference, has enabled us to send over £520 to the Miners' Fund. In this
connection the Conference unanimously decided that we should ask the
Branches to agree to allow us to subscribe £1,000 from the Central Funds and
to put Rule 110 into operation, thereby allowing the vote to be taken at
Branch Meetings and not by ballot. We trust Branches will send the result
of their vote AT ONCE so that the money can be remitted at the earliest
possible moment. The following resolution was sent to Mr. Frank Hodges on
the instruction of the Delegates:
"This Conference of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives extends
its greetings and expresses its heartiest congratulations to the members of the
Miners' Federation of Great Britain, on the unexemplified spirit of solidarity they
have displayed throughout the present struggle.

We wish you a speedy success and assure you of our fullest individual and
collective support."

FIRST ANNUAL CONFERENCE.
The First Annual Conference is now a thing of the past. An official
report of the proceedings will be issued next month. The Conference unani-
mously endorsed the policy of the Labour Party in regard to Ireland and its
findings as follows:-
(a) That the British Army of Occupation be withdrawn.
(b) The the question of an Irish Government be relegated to an Irish Consti-
tuent Assembly elected on the basis of proportional representation by free, equal and
secret vote.
(c) That the Constitution drawn up by the Assembly be accepted provided-
(1) it affords protection to minorities; and
(2) prevents Ireland becoming a military or naval menace to Britain.
The delegates also agreed to the Labour Party's policy of War indemnities
and Reparations. The Conference showed full approval of extending our work
on the political side whilst not ignoring the industrial policy of the Union.
Upon the latter a discussion took place for more than a whole day on the

REMEMBER THE FIFTEENTH!

Once again we feel bound to call the serious attention of Branch
secretaries to the fact that the FIFTEENTH day of each month is the latest
day for returns reaching the General Secretary. Last month many returns
were late. Branches failed to send off their returns to reach the Central Office
before the 15th of the month, and this tends to upset the organisation of the
work in the General Secretary's Office. We beg to intimate that unless
returns are in before the 15th of the month, the Secretary has been instructed
to put into force the Rules governing the same.

TRADE UNION STAMP.

This is a matter which we have stated before rests with the members to
make a success. It is in the interests of members themselves that “Stamped
Footwear” should be increasingly purchased; therefore, push the Trade
Union Stamp. Members and their families should wear only “Union Stamped
Footwear.”

We remain,

£2,700 FOR MR. WILL CROOKS.

FUND TO REMAIN OPEN TILL JUNE 1st.
A sum of £2,700 has been received up to date for the Will Crooks Testimonial Fund,
and, in accordance with the wishes of Mr. and Mrs. Crooks, £2,500 of that amount has been
invested in Six per Cent. I.L.C.C. Housing Bonds.
In order to give the many friends of the popular ex-M.P. for Woolwich, who may
not yet have contributed, an opportunity of subscribing to the fund, it has been decided
to keep it open till June 1st.
Subscriptions should be sent to Mr. Arthur Henderson, at 33, Eccleston Square,
S.W. 1.
Mr. Crooks is still in Poplar Hospital, and a slight improvement is reported in his
condition. From source not stated.

GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
FIRST ANNUAL CONFERENCE. We have just concluded our first Annual Conferenc
of the members more than ever. We are still in the throes of doubt among ourselves as
gathering, which has lasted three days, and I believe has cemented the opinions and ideas
to which is the best system to adopt by our operatives in the factories, and upon ou
point we are united, that is as delegates and as representatives. There appears to be
great unanimity that statements shall be worked to, in other words, piece work with a
set wage.
have none of it, and what they are aiming for is a better distribution of the work
other words a more regulated weekly income for all concerned, if that can be brought
about. Some talk of the control of Industry; some day that may be an accomplisher
fact. At present they believe we can influence and better regulate the quantity of
work that each operative has to do. Whether we shall be successful in this matter, time
alone will show. At any rate this is a case we want the Employers to consider and
agree to.
We have had correspondence with the Employers. We are meeting them on the
24th May, with the intention of doing our very best for the membership at the present
time.
I am pleased to say that to all intents and purposes the Council of the Union have
been advised in a direction that I think will tend to the benefit of all concerned. One
greatest trouble at the present time is bad trade; unemployment and these things don't
help or encourage when improvements are contemplated. Perhaps it would not be
saying too much if I said that this is one of the best Conferences we have held so far as
the keenness of interest taken in several very debatable subjects was exhibited, and
although we have this advice from the delegates to the Conference as to the future policy
of our Union it will involve some districts making a very great change, especially those
firms who have not adopted any statements in the past. These are the factories that will
be mostly concerned and perhaps cause the greatest trouble. Still, we hope that there
will be no difficulty in getting out of this, in time.
Will our members please observe that under no circumstances must they agree to
the introduction of piece-work or quantity statements without first of all satisfying
themselves and their officers that the National Agreement which grants a 25% increase to
the piece-worker or the man on quantity statements is duly observed and, as far as
possible, guaranteed ?
LABOUR PARTY. It was my duty to fill a gap created by the Auditor of the
National Labour Party, who could not for some reason or other attend to that work, and
for four days I was engaged on this work with Mr. Robert Young, M.P. When one
takes his memory back to the time when the Labour Representation Committee was first
started, before it became the Labour Party, he feels proud of having had a hand in
starting such an organisation whose body can boast 3½ millions Trade Unionists. The
comment I want to make in this connection is that I am looking forward to the time
when the other 4½ millions Trade Unionists will belong to the Labour Party, and
although we are a great body in the Labour Party we certainly ought to be careful in the
choice of our language and ways in which we are going to approach these other Unions
to join up with us in our Political sphere. It goes without saying that we have a large
number of friends, and I would strongly recommend my Socialist friends and others when
approaching Trade Unions and Trade Unionists to endeavour to get their assistance and
support rather than indulge in constitutions; sometimes that don't help and are often
hurtful and harmful and thereby prevent the movement becoming solidified. I hope the
time is not far distant when the Labour Party will be able to claim that it has as many
members in its ranks as have the great Trade Unions themselves.
UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE. - We have held a meeting at Northampton of the
Employers on the question of Unemployment. This matter is pretty well on the road
to bring about a working agreement with a joint body formed of ourselves and the
Manufacturers, in which we fully believe our members will benefit considerably.
LONDON. On the 6th, I had occasion to meet the Metropolitan Executive of the
London Branch, the wish of the Council being to endeavour to bring about some unifica-
tion of the Branches in London. We think that much good can be done, will be done, by
this policy to prevent overlapping.
REPAIRING. On the 10th, we had our last meeting of the Profiteering Committee,
and whose duty it was to enquire into the Repairing Industry, and we have issued our
report to the Board of Trade. When that report has been accepted, I hope to be able to

---
gave our members some of the benefit or advantages that we have gained as a con-
sequence. Just to use one short statement, our investigation gave us the idea that prior
to the war the average earnings was 25 per week that was when men worked, of
course The 65 now being paid by the Trade Board for 48 hours shows an increase of
and a reduction in hours. I hope our members will please note that the Repairing
Trade Board has been no small lever to retain, to maintain, and to get the conditions
that the Wholesale Trade has brought about.
We held a special Council Meeting on the 15th, and as I said in the commencement
of this report, the rest of the time was spent at the Conference.
TRADE UNION STAMP. One other word, I wonder whether our members are
endeavouring in any particular or on any occasion to demand Trade Union Stamped
Footwear. There has been so little response to the many appeals made on this occasion
that one can come to the conclusion that we are very lukewarm on this matter as on
many others, where some interest ought to be exhibited.

SHOE TRADE PROBLEMS.
The old-time cobbler never did stick to his last; he was always ready to help set
the world in order. That is equally true of the modern shoe-hand. He holds entertaining
views on all sorts of subjects, and expresses them with refreshing candour. There is
little of the autocrat about him, too. He is quite willing to allow the other man to have
an opinion, and is ready to concede that there may be something in it. Hence meetings
or Leicester shoe operatives are usually productive of lively debate, often of a provocative
character, though in actual practice there is no body of men more conciliatory in their
industrial negotiations than those employed in our footwear factories. At the annual
meeting of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives in London yesterday the
subjects discussed ranged from a possible settlement of the Irish question to a distribution
of boots and shoes “ at wholesale prices” as a means of diminishing unemployment. We
agree with the Council of the Union that it is advisable for the operative to have "an
outlook more and more world-wide." By all means let the shoehand look towards the
stars, but he must not forget that his feet are still on the ground. The things near at hand
are apt to be neglected when men adopt telescopic lenses. A world-wide outlook is useless
if the knowledge gained is not applied to the conditions in which the spectator exists.

The shoe operative knows that what his industry needs just now more than anything
else is a revival of our export trade; he knows that in nearly all overseas markets our
manufacturers are meeting with competition keenly organised and strongly directed;
but does the operative realise that his conditions of employment are directly affected
by the selling prices of boots and shoes in overseas markets? The advocates of the limited
output can hardly be aware of it, nor can those who profess to believe that payment by
results is the cause of existing “chaos” in the industry. Nor can we imagine that an
incursion by the Union into the sphere of footwear distribution is going to help. Dis-
tribution, like manufacture itself, calls for specialised knowledge and skilful organisation.
Even if the existing means of distribution were inefficient which they are not there
still remains the greatest difficulty of all, the fact that people are extremely short of money,
their purchasing power being compulsorily limited. The salvation of the boot and shoe
trade is not to be found in the assumption of managerial and distributing duties by the
operatives' trade union, but in the recovery of the world's credit, backed by a steady
replacement of the wealth wasted during the war. It will be a painfully slow process;
of that there can be no doubt. Trade unionists can help to hasten the day of deliverance
by getting rid of the notion that they can have higher wages and shorter hours and plenty
of employment without any corresponding increase of production. The boot and shoe
industry can stand better wages than were paid in 1914, but it cannot survive smaller
production, for the lower ratio of production per worker the higher the cost, and the more
limited the demand. This is the problem the industry has to tackle, and a solution does
not present itself on the lines of the 45 a week minimum wage recently demanded by the
operatives, in face of rapidly falling wages in other industries and of prices generally.
The Leicester Mail, May 17th, 1921.

PARLIAMENTARY AGENT'S REPORT.
The Miners' lock-out is still the one topic to which all conversation seems to turn.
This is not surprising having regard to its effect upon the industries of the country, and
the general paralysis that follows in its trail. For all this the Government must be held
responsible; they were told both publicly and privately what would happen if the huge cut
in the Miners' wages were sought to be enforced. On the floor of the House they were
appealed to in terms that could not be stronger, not merely in the interests of the Miners
themselves but in the interests of the country, but all in vain; it seemed they desired to
associate with the coal owners in an attempt to smash the Miners' Federation, and which
at the moment is not meeting with success. The only thing that looks like being
smashed is the trade of the country, and the Government, like Nero, "fiddles while Rome
is burning."
But I ask our members to keep this clear in their minds, everything possible was done
by labour to prevent this trouble. Those in authority were told this big reduction in wages
would never be accepted without a struggle, which when started none could say where it
would finish nor where its effects would reach. The Government deliberately choose to
back the coal owners, though not a single one of them, when challenged by Mr. Clynes,
dare get up in the House and justify the wage offered to the men.
They had expected excess and rioting would take place and so the Reserve Force was
mobilised and a Defence Force brought into being, but up to now the only disturbance of
note is among the Reservists who want to go back to their families and their work. Their
places were to be kept open for them, but the other day I was talking to one of them who

BRANCH REPORTS.
BELFAST. - In sending our returns we have to report that there is no change in the condition of trade in so far as any improvement is concerned ; of-work expenditure. In reference to the State Unemployment Benefit we it is simply going from bad to worse, which means we have a very heavy out-
desire to enter a very strong protest against the quite too long delay there is in the claims of members being acknowledged. We are not referring to our own Head Office but to the officials in the Labour Exchange. We also regret
to report a heavy sick expenditure. We have also to record the deaths of two members: J. Wilson, of the Ballymena Section, and B. Kelly, Belfast, to whose sorrowing relatives we tender our sincere sympathy. Shopmate
Kelly's death will be a great loss to the Branch. A number of years ago he held the position of Branch Secretary ; he had also served on the Branch Committee: he was one who always took a deep and intelligent interest in
the welfare of the Branch and the interests of the members.
BRISTOL No. 2. Trade is, if anything, worse than it was a month ago. There is no demand for heavy footwear, and the position in the Kings- wood area is deplorable. Factories which closed their doors several weeks
ago are still in the same position, and the prospect of getting our members back to work is very remote. Our claims for out-of-work benefit during the
month have been very heavy and, at present, the only prospect of a lighter bill is when members have exhausted their benefit. Then the problem
becomes worse for our members as they have lost a good proportion of what they have existed upon for weeks past. Members who are working two or
make the lighter grades are in a better position, but in the best of these there three days a week are called "lucky." Fortunately the few factories which
is room for improvement. Manufacturers cry "give us markets," and the operatives, "give us work," yet we are assured that a great many people want
the boots which we are anxious to make. It seems to us that the people who want our products have not the ability to pay for them, and if their spending power is still further restricted the outlook is not cheerful. One thing we know
is that during the war the workers were able to get a living easier than they can now. We are told that the prosperity was artificial, but to us it was very
real while it lasted, and somehow we can't help thinking that if the resources of the nation were pooled there is still enough to go round and supply the
reasonable wants of us all.
CHESHAM.-Trade is still very bad here, with no sign of improvement for some time to come.
CHESTERFIELD.-Trade very bad. Most of our members are working 24 hours per week, and with the Miners still without a settlement things don't
seem very rosy at the present time.
CORK.-Trade still remains bad, the majority of our members working short time.
DESBOROUGH. We have pleasure in reporting this month that our President, Mr. W. Whymant, has been elected the new Chairman of our Urban
Council. It is an honour that he richly deserves for the many years of public service he has given. For 16 years he was Secretary of the Desborough
Branch at a time when it was not an easy thing to take a prominent part in Trade Union work, and to him, together with a few other old members, Des-
borough Trade Unionism owes a great deal, how much we shall never know. Now that the highest honour that a town can confer upon any of its citizens
has come to his lot, we congratulate him and trust that his example in public work will be followed by the young Trade Unionists who are growing up to-day.

NORWICH. Trade has continued to improve during the month, although
it appears to be quite temporary. Evidence from all quarters points to the fact

SILEBY.—Early in April Mr. J. Buckle visited Rothley and found two

the opinion when trade was better we could do some good here. However,
the coal strike has materially retarded the improvement which was manifesting
itself at Mountsorrel, Sileby and Rothley, and at Mountsorrel we had great

STAFFORD.—Trade in this centre is still improving, and we sincerely wish
that our members in other centres could report the same. Owing to the coal
dispute the manufacturers in this district have orders from the local Gas and
Electric authorities that no power can be used during the coming Whit-week.
thus throwing our members out for another unnecessary period when things
generally were turning very favourable. Will the workers, when the oppor-
tunity presents itself in the Ballot-box, remember who are responsible for this
state of things: the Government in conjunction with the mine owners, or the
miners who, in our opinion, are fighting a battle for the whole of organised
workers? The answer is simple. Our members voted £5 5s. od. as first
grant to the Daily Herald appeal on behalf of miners' wives and children.

SOUTHAMPTON.—Trade very slack. Unemployment in most trades
is a very serious consideration, and we re-echo the hope that a way will be
shortly found to settle the coal strike on terms that may be of a lasting
character, thus giving a chance to all interdependent trades to get "going
and lessening the appalling amount of unemployment.

WATERFORD.—Trade is very bad; just restarted with less hands.

REPORT
OF THE
Conference of Labour Women, Manchester.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
The Conference occupied two days, commencing April 27th, at 10.30 at
the Milton Hall, Manchester. About 600 Women Delegates from all parts
attended, representing Women Sections of local Labour Parties and other
National Organisations containing women members, which were affiliated to
the National Labour Party. Miss Margaret Bondfield was in the Chair.
After the usual welcome to Delegates from the Manchester Trades Council
and Labour Party, the business commenced. Names for Standing Orders
Committee and Tellers were submitted from the Chair for our approval. This
undemocratic action the Conference by vote disagreed with and proceeded to
nominate and elect its own Officers. Also much feeling was shown re The
Standing Joint Committee of Women's Organisations taking so large a part in
the constitution of a Labour Women's Conference, when a section of that body
was not affiliated to the National Labour Party, the feeling of the Conference
being if we are to have a Labour Women's Conference on constitutional and
democratic lines, its platform must be elected by the popular votes of the
Delegates assembled.
The greater part of the Conference time was taken up in condemnation of
the Government for its broken pledges and the deliberate delaying of reforms
long overdue, with which we entirely agreed.
Prominent among the resolutions, which numbered 67, were the Miners'
trouble. Miners' wives and daughters from all parts spoke of their conditions
of existence, of the children's often cheerless lives and surroundings in some
districts, and a strong feeling of resentment was manifested against a Govern-
ment that put the Military down in the midst of a peaceful people, all being
determined to stand by their men folk to the finish.
A resolution on Ireland demanding that this Government shall give to
Ireland whatever constitution the Irish people desire-a withdrawal of all
troops, &c. This resolution was taken up by Irish women who spoke of the
horrors perpetrated on their own kinsfolk and friends.
Unemployment and education were also discussed at some length.
Pensions for Mothers, calling upon the Government to introduce
immediately Legislation of the Washington Maternity Convention, which it
has violated, and which provided in one of its clauses 6 weeks' full mainten-
ance for nursing mothers, besides other needed reforms.
Many resolutions dealing with the removal of Sex disqualification were on
the Agenda, also Equality in Industry, equal opportunity with equal pay, and
further that Woman should be permitted to enter any occupation, Industry or
Craft, or Profession which she regards herself fitted for, and that old customs
the remuneration is the same for the work done.
