A long discussion took place on a resolution sent from several Labour Women's Sections asking that the Constitution of the National Labour Party be altered so that the four women representatives on the National Executive be nominated by Women's Sections of Local Labour Parties and elected by votes of Labour Women only. The above was a recommendation to the National Conference. It also appears in the form of a resolution on the Brighton Agenda. This recommendation we voted against, as it excludes Trade Unionists from nominating or voting for Women on the National Executive. We feel the ordinary Labour Party women in local sections are not aware that in a National sense numerically they are a very small minority against the thousands of Trades Union women affiliated to the National Labour Party. We believe, underlying the discussion on the above resolution itself according to conversation around us, the women at the Conference felt they are not being represented (only in about two instances) by women who understand the life of the working woman as it really is with all its difficulties and therefore cannot represent them.

Altogether the Conference was a struggle after knowledge and usefulness, from the old woman over 70 years of age, who could give us the history of the mines, to the girl without a vote who flashed her youthful oratory over the Conference.

The Address given by the Right Hon. Arthur Henderson, M.P., was listened to by a crowded audience of enthusiastic women such as we have never seen before, and we feel the labour cause all over the country will grow stronger and more useful and will justify more gatherings of the kind we have just had the privilege to attend.

In conclusion, we have been glad of the opportunity to attend this Conference, and we hope the members of the Union will endorse this action of the Council in sending women to a Women's Conference, and trust that in future our members will be allowed to take nominations through the Branches in the constitutional way for delegation to Conference.

Yours fraternally,

571
Just because we are so much concerned in oversea trade we are especially affected by world troubles. If there are bad harvests in Argentina we feel it. If there is depression in Russia we feel it. Conversely, world prosperity gives us trade and comfort. British export trade as a whole is a sensitive measuring instrument of the world's prosperity.

**Our Home Trade Depends on Exports.**

Some people fondly imagine that we can find in an increased home market compensa- tion for loss in the export market. That is a grave fallacy. For what is our home trade? Lanca- shire folk buy food and clothes and other goods that is home buying or home trade. But how do Lancashire people obtain the means to buy? By working upon cotton - a. foreign material and by exporting cotton goods to all parts of the world. If the foreign trade fails, Lancashire" home trade" fails with it.

So with the "home trade" of a place like Hull or Newcastle or Cardiff. It hangs upon foreign trade and shipping; declines when they decline; improves when they improve.

**Good Wages and Good Production.**

Lower wages can only help us in so far as they aid cheaper production. Cheaper and greater production we certainly must have, but wages are one factor and one only in

The curse of low wages falls not only upon the receiver, but upon the payer. The low wage industry tends to be an ill-conditioned industry, with a false economy based on sweating. The high wage industry tends to be an economic industry, because the better- aid labour is used more carefully. Where wages are low appliances are bad: where wages lish appliances are good. And a well-paid man using a good method can produce adds to the general fund of wealth the only fund from which wages or profits can be more stuff than an ill-paid man using a poor method. The higher production obtained drawn, and so the wheel comes full circle. When there is a big wage fund, there is sense in expecting a big wage from it. The results of poor production must be a poor wage, even if profit be entirely eliminated.

Too often I hear it contended that there is plenty of wealth, and that all that is needed is a better distribution. Indeed, it is not so. We have never yet in this country produced enough for a universal high standard of life. We need both a better production and a better distribution, as I endeavoured to show not only in "Riches and Poverty" in 1905, but in "The Nation's Wealth" published in 1914, and in "The Triumph of Nationalisation published in 1920.-The Labour Leader, May 20th, 1921,

**IMPORTANCE OF OVERSEAS TRADE.**

A Reuter's Trade Service message from Cape Town, dated the 13th inst., says the official Gazette announces that the importation into South Africa of boots, shoes, and slippers is now prohibited except under licence, and it is added that consignments already on the water are exempt from the prohibition. This will be unpleasant news for British boot manufacturers, having regard to the importance of the South African market. For the year 1920 the imports of boots and shoes into the Union totalled 4,091,273 pairs, the chief shipments being :-

From the United Kingdom .. 3,017,000 pairs.
the United States .. 591,000
Switzerland .. 235,000
Australia .. 233,000

The exports of boots and shoes of leather, rubber, and other materials from Great Britain to all destinations during 1920 totalled 14,601,636 pairs. It will thus be seen that South Africa took over 20 per cent. of our total shipments. The above figures, by the way, will correct the mistaken impression in some quarters that America is the chief exporter of boots and shoes to South Africa. It is British footwear that is preferred, and this explains the large shipments which have been sent by our manufacturers for several years past.

In a review of the South African shoe industry in the March-April issue of the South African Journal of Industries, reprinted in another column, it is stated that the Union's total requirements of boots are estimated at 7,000,000 pairs per annum. Factories already in operation can produce about 4,000,000 pairs, and if the building and equipment of new factories, commenced before the slump, had been completed the output would have been raised to 5,000,000 pairs per annum. Apparently the heaviness of recent imports has caused work in connection with these new factories to be stopped, so that the productive capacity of the manufacturers in the Union remains at 4,000,000 pairs. This leaves a balance of 3,000,000 pairs to be supplied from abroad. There was a surplus of imports

conditions are bad. We have spoken about that in previous deputations and we had

that something will be done in the matter.

MINISTER OF MINES
(W. C. BRIDGEMAN, ESQ., M.P.).
Wednesday, February 9th, 1921.
PRESENT: Mr. E. L. Poulton, O.B.E., Mr. H. Gosling, C.H., Right Hon. C. W. Bowerman, M.P., for the Trades Union Congress Parliamentary Committee. Mr. W. Frowen, Mr. H. Clarney, and other members of the General Federation of Firemen's Association. Mr. J. Strachan (Scotland Under-Managers).
Mr. Bridgeman (Minister of Mines) was accompanied by Mr. W. Brace (Permanent Secretary).
MR. E. L. POULTON, having introduced the deputation, said that yesterday the Home Secretary had referred them to the Mines Department. Mr. Frowen would deal with the following resolutions :-

Mineowners' Benefit Schemes.
That this Congress expresses its disapproval of any actions which seek to take away the freedom and right of citizenship from any class of workers, and that immediate steps be taken to ensure that the coalowners of Great Britain shall withdraw any scheme which prevents deputies, firemen, or examiners, or clerical and administrative staffs from enjoying the full privilege of Trade Unionists.

State Employment of Colliery Deputies.
That, in the opinion of this Congress, any legislation that has for its object an attempt to diminish the number of accidents in mines would be most likely to accomplish that object if the official who is responsible for the daily inspection of a district or mine was so placed under the protection of the Government as to enable him to make an unbiased report as to the condition of the district. We therefore instruct the Parliamentary Committee to press that the State em- ployment and payment of deputies be included in the amended Mines Bill.
And Mr. Strachan would speak to the resolution dealing with :-
Certificates of Competency (Mines).
That, in the interests of safety and efficiency, it is essential that men filling the position of the official defined in the Mines Act as superior to the fireman but inferior to the under-manager should hold at least a second-class certificate of competency under the Act, and this Congress calls upon the Government to make the necessary alteration in General Rule 47 without delay.

MR. FROWEN said that there were individuals in each colliery area who, as officials of their union, were placed at a disadvantage by reason of the mineowners' benefit schemes. The mineowner penalised the men who did not join. He did not definitely refuse them employment, although there were one or two isolated cases where that had occurred, but the men had pressure brought to bear upon them. Every precaution is taken by us to ensure accuracy in these Reports, our correspondents

FELLOW MEMBERS,
27TH JUNE, 1921.
TRADE
has improved slightly during the past month although work has been seriously
curtailed owing to the Coal Dispute. The figures given in the Gazette of the
Ministry of Labour are as follows :-

LEATHER TRADES.
In the leather trades employment showed a decline, and many workpeople were un-
employed and short time was general.

BOOT AND SHOE TRADE.
Owing to the coal dispute, and the consequent restriction of power, the slight im-
provement noted in recent months in this trade was not maintained; employment on the
whole was bad during May, and worse than a month earlier. In practically all the principal
districts there was much short time in various forms, and extensive unemployment.

The number of workpeople employed in boot, shoe and slipper making and repairing
establishments whose unemployment books or out-of-work donation policies were lodged
at Employment Exchanges at 27th May was 22,744 compared with 23,073 at 29th April
and 21,989 at 24th March. In addition, there were 17,962 claimants for benefit in respect
of systematic short-time working, compared with 17,884 at 29th April and 16,711 at 24th
March.

At Leicester, owing to the effects of the coal stoppage, employment was worse than a
month earlier, and the majority of the operatives were on short time. At Hinckley there
was a slight improvement. At Northampton and Kettering employment generally con-
tinued bad. At Higham and Rushden there was a further slight improvement, some firms
being on full time; speaking generally, however, employment was still described as bad in
this district; and in some of the neighbouring small towns of the Northampton country
district employment continued to be very bad.

At Stafford the improvement noted in several previous months continued, and only
a small amount of short time was being worked at that centre at the end of May. At
Norwich there was an improvement in some sections and a decline in others; taking the
city as a whole, a good deal of short time was still being worked.
lighter grades of boots are made.
At Bristol and Kingswood large numbers of factories were still closed down, and
Employment for those who were still working continued to be very depressed, except in a
ployment was still very bad, and a further decline was reported; there was much total un-
ment was also very bad in the Rossendale Valley.

1919 AGREEMENT.
In accordance with arrangements made we met the Executive of the
Manufacturers' Federation on May 24th, 1921, at their Offices, Tavise
Square, W.C. 1, to consider the question of the 1919 and 1920 Agreements
and the letter from the Manufacturers' Federation as to the matter standing
adjourned for at least six months.
Bearing in mind the discussion at the recent Annual Conference and the
resolution passed thereat, viz. :–
"This Conference gives full power to the Executive Council to revise
if necessary, and adjourn the time of meeting with the Manufacturers till
such time ås circumstances should appear more favourable for negotiation,
but that no reduction of present conditions be discussed till a special
conference has been held,"
the following resolution was agreed to unanimously :-
"
That this Conference of the Manufacturers' Federation Executive
and the Executive Council of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Opera-
tives having considered the question to amend the terms of the 1919
Agreement, and the revised 1920 Agreement, hereby decide to adjourn the
matter for six months. It is to be clearly understood the existing Agree-
ments will remain in full operation. Each side agrees to submit amended
terms within the six months' period."

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION ACT.
We are pleased to report that through the efforts of the Union's Solicitor
(Mr. Evan Barlow, of Leicester) two further cases of Compensation have been
settled. In one case, B., of Leicester No. 2 Branch, the sum of £200 was
secured in addition to a weekly sum of compensation and part costs; whilst
in the other case, T. of Kettering, the sum of fio was recovered.
We beg to point out, however, that lump sums are not obtainable by law,
but only by mutual consent of the operative and the Insurance Company.

TRADE BOARD.REPAIRERS WAGES.
As is well known, we through our Reports have, along with the other
workers' representatives on the Trade Board, been endeavouring to secure
an increase in the rate of pay for time workers, Circumstances have for the
time being, been of such a character as to militate against us being successful.
We put up the best possible fight, but with so many trades having to agree
to reductions, we found ourselves ultimately put in the position of having to
reconsider the situation industrially, and ascertaining that it was not possible
to secure an advance, to so act as to leave the position one wherein we could
at a future date renew our application; it was therefore ultimately agreed to
postpone the application indefinitely. We regret that our efforts were not
successful; at the same time we have been able to prevent any reductions
taking place, which should not be overlooked by anyone who might feel
inclined to indulge in adverse criticism.
CIRCULARS.
Several Circulars dealing with important matters have been sent out
during the past month; the answers asked for should be sent along to the
Central Office without delay.
CANADA.
During the month a letter has been received by the General Secretary
from the Toronto Branch of the Boot and Shoe Workers' Union of America,
stating that they have a strike in Toronto. They also state that-
"Trade conditions are very bad in Canada, with the prospect
of their becoming much worse. Many Shoemakers who have been
brought to this country from England are having a very bad time
getting along."
Having regard to these facts, we hope members will make very full enquiries
before going to Canada. We trust our comrades will be successful in their
struggle, and that a period of good trade will shortly ensue with them as
well as with ourselves.
REMEMBER THE FIFTEEΝΤΗ!
Once again we feel bound to call the serious attention of Branch secretaries
to the fact that the FIFTEENTH day of each month is the latest day for
returns reaching the General Secretary. Last month many returns were late.
Branches failed to send off their returns to reach the Central Office before the
15th of the month, and this tends to upset the organisation of the work in the
General Secretary's Office. We beg to intimate that unless returns are in
before the 15th of the month, the Secretary has been instructed to put into
force the Rules governing the same.

UNSCRUPULOUS MISREPRESENTATION BY THE PRESS.
Statements have recently appeared both in the London and provincial
newspapers which have not only been misleading but calculated to create
prejudice both against the Union and the boot operatives generally. In one
instance a case was reported that although work was offered in a certain dis
trict at trade union rates of wages, despite the large numbers out of employment
operatives refused to accept the positions. In another case it was reported
that at Northampton women were earning I per day for three days and then
declaring on the State Unemployment Fund. We at once enquirer into
these cases and in the first instance neither the local officials, the Manufacturers
Federation nor the Employment Exchange knew anything of the matter, and
the newspapers would not give us the information as to where this statement
was obtained. In Northampton the General Secretary called the attention
of our officers to the statement and a Board of Arbitration meeting was called
and after fully considering the same the following resolution was passed
"That this Joint Board, representing the Northampton Boot Manufacture
Association and the No. 2 Branch of the Boot Operatives' Union, desire to correct
the statement made at the meeting of the Northampton and District
Employment Committee in respect to the wages earned by female operatives,
and wish to correct the impression created that women are able to earn fantastic sums."
It will thus be seen how misleading certain reports in the Press are, and that
an injustice is done to the operatives generally.
FINES.
We regret to report the fact that a fine has been levied upon ARINGATE
DUBLIN, and YORK, whose returns were not in the Central Office on
the 18th inst., despite the fact that they were due BEFORE the 15th
is essential that returns should be in the Central Office prior to the 15th.
of each month to enable the work, which has considerably grown of late, to
be kept up to date.
TRADE UNION STAMP.
This is a matter which we have stated before rests with the members to
make a success. It is in the interests of members themselves that "Stamped
Footwear" should be increasingly purchased; therefore, push the Trade
Union Stamp. Members and their families should wear only “Union Stamped
Footwear."

GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
Trouble and trial is very prevalent in the industrial world owing to the great dearth
of employment in this and other countries. It would be well if the powers that be would
pull together to protect wages rather than to attack them. You cannot have good trade
with bad wages, and you cannot have peace if you make war on the sections of the com-
munity who work for you and help you to enjoy the life that is. Rumours are current of
many attempts to cut wages in certain places. Although most trade unions wish to be
law-abiding, no union worth its salt will quietly submit to this, and it is rumoured that some
employers in various trades are leaving the Emplovers' Federation in order to escape their
national agreements. It is also quite proper to remind these gentlemen who have taken
this course that each union affected will undoubtedly make note of this proceeding, and at
once take the initiative to see no departure takes place. The loyalty of the men who
belong to the great 8,000,000 trade unionists must see to it that their homes are not attacked
and reduced to pre-war conditions.

1020 AGREEMENT TO CONTINUE FOR SIX MONTHS. On the 24th May, 1921, we met the
Emplovers' Federation with the result already known, but we do hope the information
asked for several months ago, and NOT YET COMPLETE, will be sent along by those
Branches who have not complied with the request. One realises with so much unem-
ployment this task has been a difficult one, and now that matters are easier in this part
of our organisation we hope to receive the most useful data obtainable.

GENERAL FEDERATION OF TRADE UNIONS. This meeting was held on the 25th May,
when it was reported that over a quarter of a million Cotton Operatives had been notified
of a reduction.

UNEMPLOYMENT SCHEME. On the 26th May I attended a meeting between the Em-
plovers' Federation and Mr. Nathan, the expert on the Unemployment Scheme, when a
further stage was advanced.

WELLINGBOROUGH was visited on the 27th May owing to a firm outside the Federation
entering into an agreement contrary to the National Terms with their operatives. We are
still negotiating with the firm. The operatives' action has been severely criticised by
the Branch.

On Sunday, the 29th inst., we had a very fair meeting of the repairers at the Friars'
Hall, Blackfriars Bridge, London, on the need of further organisation, but I would have
preferred to have had the meeting much larger.

On Monday, the 30th, I had occasion to go to Nottingham to settle a matter between
our own members, and not with their employers, and believe that the visit will conduce to a
more harmonious spirit.

TRADE BOARD. On May 1st and 2nd I attended the Trade Board, when we discussed
at great length our claim for 72s., but after a very lengthy discussion we were advised by
the appointed members that they could concede no advance; so we have it that appointed
members have the deciding voice. We acquiesced in a postponement.

LONDON NO. 2-LONDON METRO. - On May 4th the Council advised a meeting of the
No. 2 London Branch with the object of recommending them to join up with the London
Metropolitan Branch, the reason being that after 9 years the Branch is but 156 financially
strong, and all Organisers and Council Members visiting the London Branch during the past
two years strongly recommend this course. Should the sew-round makers wish to hold
meetings sectionally we would strongly recommend the Metro. Branch to carefully con-
sider such request, as when one recalls the fact that we already have 500 members having
Hebrew names, the language difficulty, since the war, has become impotent.

BOZEAT.-May 7th included a visit to Bozeat, where probably four out of every five
in the village are unemployed, and after holding a meeting of the men and then seeing the
employers, we may be in a position after reporting to the Council to ease the situation
within the National Terms. We also attended a very interesting meeting at Finedon of
the Section there the same evening, and addressed the members on several matters.

On May 8th I went to MOUNTSORREL and held an open-air organising meeting at the
School Boot Co., and hope the same may be attended with beneficial results. On the same
day I went to SILEBY, when we met the principal of one of the largest firms who had promised
us to help in telling the men the duties to their fellow workers.
EARLS BARTON was visited on May 13th owing to a difficulty on one of the firms which
has a very good reputation for fair dealing, but shall be compelled to take the advice of
the Council on the outlook at this place.

LEICESTER. -On May 14th I visited Leicester owing to the policy of the firms sending
work to each other. Negotiations are not yet completed.

LEEDS No. 1.-Trade is considerably worse this month than last. One

LIVERPOOL.-The coal crisis is causing a lot of unemployment and
short time, more especially in the St. Helens' Section of this Branch, which
is a colliery district, and but for the fact that the majority of our present mem-
bers are Trade Unionists from principle and deny themselves certain luxuries
in their efforts to keep their contributions paid, we should soon cease to exist
as an effective Branch. We subscribed through our Central Office the sum
of ten shillings towards the Miners' Relief Fund, which is like the widow's
mite, not very much to feed hungry women and children, but is all we could
afford, as it takes us all our time to pay our way. The proposed increased
postal rates for postcards and printed matter will not improve the position.
in fact, we are of the opinion that from a business point of view it is a false
move and one that ought to be checkmated if possible. The number of Reports
we shall be able to send out by post will be very limited; members will have to
get them at the Branch Meetings or when they call to pay their contributions.
We note it has been reported in the trade press that at a recent meeting of the
Trade Board the proposed increase of wages has been postponed indefinitely,
also the guaranteed minimum time rate, which we assume refers to piece-
work.
MAYBOLE.-Trade still very slack; some of our members have drawn

Unemployment Benefit.
SIR WALTER DE FRECE asked the Minister of Labour the number of men and women,
respectively, who have exhausted their unemployment benefit in the present industrial
trouble?
THE MINISTER OF LABOUR (Dr. Macnamara): As I have already explained, the
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1921, made provision for the payment of benefit, subject
10 certain conditions, for 16 weeks in the period between 3rd March and 2nd November,
1421. Accordingly, the earliest date at which the rights to benefit under the Act can be
exhausted is 22nd June, in cases in which the conditions for the receipt of the full amount
are satisfied. There are certain exceptional cases in which applicants who are not entitled
to the full amount under the Act of 1921 have exhausted their rights. I am unable to
state the number of such cases, but relatively to the whole number they are not
numerous.
MR. HAYDAY: Those who became entitled to 48 days under the Act of November,
1920, only got a further 48 days' extension as from March or February under the 1921
Act. Surely, a large number of these must have exhausted their benefit. Is not the
percentage something like 15?
DR. MACNAMARA: Under the Act of March, 1921, the official precedent followed was
that an applicant should be able to show that he or she had been in insurable employment
for 20 weeks during 1921. That qualification is not very onerous.
MR. C. WHITE asked the Minister of Labour whether he is aware of the great delay
in payment of unemployment benefit at the employment exchange, Matlock, where many
applicants entitled to such benefit have not received any pay for 8 to 10 weeks; and
whether he will take such steps as may be necessary to facilitate the payments due, as
much suffering and privation prevails amongst the applicants ?
DR. MACNAMARA: I am having inquiry made and will inform my hon. Friend of the
result.-Parliamentary Debates, May 26th, 1921.

n respect of benefits to be £890,823, and the present value of the assets applicable
thereto to be £913,423, the balance being a surplus of £22,600.

Here is the text from the image:

627
due to the exceptional conditions which prevailed during the War. Prominent
among these sources are:
(1) the relief resulting from the decline in the birth rate and the con-
sequent fall in the number of claims for maternity benefit;
(2) the release of the Society from liability in respect of which it had
received reserve values, by deaths among male members of
military age; and
3) the high rate of interest secured on investments.

In addition, the cost of Disablement Benefit has been below the provision
made in the financial basis of the Act, and it is probable that this experience
is at least partly due to the War.

It should be noted that the sickness claims during 1913 and 1914 were con-
siderably in excess of the valuation standard and necessitated the intervention
of the Insurance Commissioners. Subsequently the experience exhibited an
improvement, doubtless in part due to the temporary influence of War conditions,
and, on balance, a small profit has accrued in respect of this benefit.

5.  Fluctuations from time to time in the sickness experience, in the rate of
mortality, and in other elements affecting the financial position of approved
societies are inevitable, and should invariably be kept in view when the distribu-
tion of surplus is being considered. The conditions under which the present
surplus has been produced, as explained above, emphasise the importance of
this point and lead to the conclusion, after proper weight is given to the pro-
visions of the Act respecting the Contingencies Fund, that £12,907 of the surplus
should be carried forward, leaving £9,693 as now available for additional benefits.
I certify, accordingly, that of the surplus disclosed by the valuation the sum of
£9,693 is disposable surplus to which the provisions of Section 37 of the Act
of 1911 apply.

6.  Having regard to the amount of the disposable surplus as certified above,
the attention of the Society is directed to the provisions of Section 37 of the Act
of 1911, and to Appendix C. to this Report.

P. N. HARVEY,

5. The other additional benefits in the list do not fall within the scope of
actuarial calculation and schemes to provide any or all of these benefits must
operate through the medium of separate funds created by transfer from the
disposable surplus. It should be observed that where such a separate fund is
set up it is entitled to its due proportion of interest as from 1st January, 1919,
and it will be supplemented by the usual State Grant so calculated that two-
ninths of the payments out of the fund will be provided by the Exchequer.

6.  In cases where the disposable surplus is sufficient for the purpose it may
be desired to provide additional benefits of more than one type. Thus, instead
of increasing the money benefits to the full extent indicated in par. (3) above,
it might be desired to increase these benefits by smaller amounts and to transfer
the part of the surplus not used in this way to a separate fund to provide other
benefits as explained in the last paragraph. For instance if the additional sick-
ness benefit were 1s. a week less than the sum named in par. (3) (with corres-
ponding reductions in the additional disablement and maternity benefits), the
amount to be transferred to the separate fund would be such proportion of the
total disposable surplus as 1s. bears to the additional sickness benefit specified
in par. (3).

NOTE.--For the "numbers" of the additional benefits mentioned in this Appendix,
reference should be made to Part II. of the Fourth Schedule to the Act of 1911.

METAL FOOTWEAR INVENTED BY A BLIND FRENCH WORKMAN.
Paris, June 3rd. A blind man employed in a factory in the Department of Vienne
claims to have invented a new material from which exceedingly durable footwear can be
made. The material used is an alloy of various metals, the secret of which has not yet
been revealed by the inventor. Shoes made with this substance weigh just under fifteen
Cunces a pair, and are, it is stated, attractive in form. It is claimed that they are as re-
sistant as iron to fire and water.-Renter.

ever and parts can be replaced.

KINGSWOOD.—We are pleased to report a little improvement in trade,
and trust that industry generally will steadily improve. We have voted the
sum of £15 to the Miners' Children, £5 Bristol Association, £5 Somerset Associa
tion, £5 to Kingswood Distress Fund. We have been unable to grant larger
amounts as we have been hit very hard in this district during the past 18
months.
LEICESTER No. 1.—During the month we made a second grant of £5
to the Miners' Fund. Trade is still very bad with our members, but now the
Miners' Strike is settled we sincerely hope there will be an early improvement.
LEICESTER No. 2.—In response to the appeal on behalf of the Miners'
Dispute Fund we made a further grant of £3.
LIVERPOOL.—Trade is still slack and we are paying out more in benefits
than we are taking in by contributions. The only thing that is bright is
the weather, which is ideal for holidays, but not for boot repairers.
MAYBOLE.—Trade is still slack, but sickness light. With the Coal
Dispute settled we are looking forward to better times. Some of our members
are getting started after six months' idleness, with the prospect of more starting
after the July holidays. We hope after the assistance that the Union has been
to its members, that everyone will be convinced of the absolute necessity for
a strong Union, and in view of what is likely to be an attempt to break our
wages, we would again urge every member to rally round the Union, as it is
their only hope of securing decent conditions.
NORWICH.—We have observed in Norwich unmistakable signs of declining
trade during the month, many of our members being discharged after a very
short period in the factory. The outlook is very little better than the worst
period last winter, although our members can find compensation in the fact
that the Government are attempting to meet their difficulties by reducing
benefit to 15s., after waiting a full week with no pay. Now that there appears
to be no opportunity of securing complete control of the National Unemploy
ment Insurance (as originally expected) we in Norwich are wondering whether
or no any useful purpose is being served in continuing a very loose, disjointed,
and partial administration of the Government's scheme. Our experience in
Norwich is not altogether a happy one. In many instances we have to meet

During the month we have seen attempts made by one or two manufacturers

PLYMOUTH. Trade is slack, and said to be by the elderly members of

months. At least we hope not to experience any reductions during the re-

continues to fall, there will be prosperous times ahead for the men engaged
in the boot trade.

SOUTHAMPTON. Trade very slack. We are anxiously waiting for a

WATERFORD. Trade still dull, but all are more hopeful of the future
now that the Miners' Dispute is favourably settled. Congratulations to all
on the splendid spirit of unity and confidence displayed at the Annual Conference,
which provided us with much useful information.
WHITWICK. We are still on short time, making 24 hours per week,
but now that the Coal Dispute is over we are looking forward to making better
time, so that the operatives may be able to get a wage which will help them
to get the necessities of life, as we all know in the boot trade that during the
last 18 months it has been undergoing a very trying time as regards the opera-
tives' side of the question. W'e as a trade union can honestly say that during
the late war we never had a general strike, and as soon as the war was over
the boot trade was very hard hit, but we are looking forward to the near future
for things to be made much better for us all, so that we can be able to earn
as much as some of the other trades in this country on less hours per week
worked, that all who get their living in the boot trade may be brought into full
work and this abominable unemployment may be a thing of the past, and with
which so many good, straight and honest men are disgusted.
YARMOUTH (GREAT). Business is very bad, and there is no prospect

continually denounced the Government for its laxity regarding houses, for its hampering
of Local Authorities, and for its hesitation and procrastination in regard to Building
Guilds, but Dr. Addison had always assured us everything possible was being done. We
could see the drifting better than he could evidently, and now it is no longer drift, but com-
plete abandonment. If I may quote a sentence from his letter, the following is instructive:

behind it. Now is the time when all of us should be making up our minds what we are

BRITISH BOOTS BARRED.
South Africa's List of Prohibited Goods.
(From our own Correspondent.)

JOHANNESBURG, JUNE 8TH, 1921
Prohibition in its worst form, in regard to the importation of boots and shoes into South Africa, has become the law, with the result that 60 per cent. of our footwear requirements from oversea will be cut out. The following list gives some idea of the drastic nature of the protection afforded local producers. It is not complete, for slight alterations may be expected.

Prohibited List.
Men's footwear in box hide, kip, splits, and common leathers. Riveted, M.S., pegged screwed, metallic fastened, or welted, costing 20s. and under.
Men's box calf boots, costing. 27s. 6d. and under.
Men's glacé kid boots, costing 25s. and under.
Men's leather slippers.
Miners' boots.
Football boots.
Children's sandals.
Youths', boys', and children's footwear, unless listed under Licensed List.
Women's footwear. All kinds costing 13s. 6d. and under. Riveted or machine ser
All welted goods costing 20s. and under.
Children's boots, shoes, and sandals, costing 6s. 9d. 7 to 10, 7s. 9d. 11 to 1.

Licensed List.
Welted footwear (men's), costing over 20s.
Pump or turn footwear.
Canvas boots and shoes.
Rubber and rope sole footwear.
Plimsols and gymnasium shoes.
Buckskin and imitation buckskin goods.
Clogs, Wellingtons and firemen's boots.
All welted footwear (women's), costing over 16s. 6d.
Machine sewn goods, costing over 13s. 6d.
White footwear 'and felt boots.

As I have stated, this list is not complete. But it means that every pair of men's boots retailed here will cost the wearer two guineas. Any footwear below that retail price will be of local manufacture. Practically all boys' and youths' goods are barred. Girls' footwear, including sandals, cannot be imported below the cost of 6s. 9d. (7 to 10 or 7s. 9d. (11 to 1). This means total prohibition. The only things we can import are clogs, Plimsols, Wellingtons, Napoleons, rope sole footwear, polo boots, and turns. They have left the home producers very little, but they expect the "old country" to buy South African skins. I mean not only calf skins but goat skins!

South Africa sends home its skins and derives a substantial revenue therefrom. If it were not for the British market the skins would not be worth the cost of flaving. But the home manufacture is not to be permitted to return the skins in the form of manufactured footwear.

The small local manufacturers cannot supply anything like the quantity of footwear required for the ever-increasing population of this huge country. They can make only rough-and-ready goods in a rough-and-ready way. It will be gathered from the Prohibited List that they realise they are not "artists" in footwear manufacturing, for they confess they are beaten when it comes to making anything in men's over 20s, and that they are right out of it in regard to pumps and turns. These terms convey to them something of craftsmanship, and they do not know how to get hold of it. In this they have my sympathy.

They also fall foul of Plimsols and gymnasium shoes, and buckskin and imitation buckskin goods. As to clogs, they simply wonder what they are, so as they cannot make them we are permitted to land them under licence.

This, of course, is how great Colonial politicians introduce a little bit of humour into their playful task of dealing a staggering blow at legitimate trading. And this, too, just at the time when we were expecting a betterment in trade conditions! We are also to have prices controlled, but this will affect local manufacturers to the same extent as oversea producers.

Strong pressure has been brought to bear on the Government by the heads of local houses, and meetings have been held, and the usual deputations appointed to interview the authorities. But all to no purpose. In the meantime, there is little hope of any relief from this one-sided piece of legislation. Still, the next few days may produce some arrangement to ease the severity of the prohibition.

ADMINISTRATIVE COMMITTEE (TRAINING) BOOT AND SHOE
TRADE BOARD.

To the Editor of the Shoe Trades Journal.
Sir. - I am directed by my committee to inform you that at their meeting Co
16th inst., under the chairmanship of W. Addington Willis, Esq., they had under consider
tion the question of curative work in boot and shoe given in hospital workshops under
control of the Ministry of Pensions. Compalints had been received from the Portsmo
Local Technical Advisory Committee in regard to such training at Netley, and according
a deputation from the Ministry of Pensions waited by request upon the Administra
Committee, and discussed both the Netley position and the general question. The dep
tion pointed out that the Netley workshops had only very recently been taken over by
Ministry, and assured the Committee that it was proposed to discontinue immediate
any occupational treatment in boot and shoe work which was being given there.

In regard to the general question, they fully appreciated the claims of the boot an
shoe trade to special consideration, in view of the large number which the trade had trained
and the danger to the trade of any entry of half-trained men through an unregulate..
channel. They desired, however, to emphasise that any training which the men receiver.
in these workshops was in no sense vocational, but purely curative, although the occupa
tional treatment must be given in an orderly manner under the instruction of a craitsman.
if the full physical and mental advantages of the treatment were to be derived. The
pointed out to the Committee that occupational treatment, although given in many other
trades, had in the boot and shoe trade special advantages for certain classes of patients.
and it was only such patients who were allotted to this work, the total number receivin、
such treatment being only some 130. They assured the Committee that, recognising the
difficulties of the trade, they would limit this form of treatment as far as possible, and under
no circumstances would sanction be given for the establishment of fresh classes. Further
the men receiving such treatment were not eligible for any grants from the Civil Liabilities
Department, nor for the grant of a kit of tools or any other form of assistance from the
Ministry to enable them to enter the trade, and by means of a notice it would be brought
prominently to their attention that this particular form of occupational treatment was
purely for curative purposes, and carried with it no promise of the continuation of their
training under the Ministry of Labour or of acceptance in the trade. The deputation
further agreed to supply the Committee from acceptance in the statistics of the number
of men receiving this form of treatment.

The Committee expressed their satisfaction with the assurances given by the deputa
tion, and the chairman tendered the thanks of the meeting to the deputation for their
attendance.-Yours faithfully,

E. D. NUTTALL,
Secretary, Administrative Committee (Training) Boot and Shoe Trade Board.
- The Shoe Trades Journal, June 24th, 1921.

PARLIAMENTARY DEBATES.
CONTRACTING OUT-UNEMPLOYMENT BILL (2), 1921.
Clause 5.-(Suspension of Power to make Special Schemes.)
"The power of the Minister under Section eighteen of the principal Act to make
special orders approving or making special schemes shall not be exercised during the
deficiency period:
Provided that this Section shall not apply in any case where notice of a proposal to
make such a special order has been published before the eighth day of June, nineteen
hundred and twenty-one."
SIR F. FLANNERY: I beg to move, at the end of the Clause, to add the words:
"Provided that this section shall not apply in any case where application has been
made to the Minister to approve a completed scheme on or before the eighth day of June,
nineteen hundred and twenty-one."
The object of this Amendment is the same as that of an Amendment moved in Com-
mittee, although the words have been slightly altered for the purpose of securing the
adhesion and consent of the Minister of Labour. When the principal Act was passed,
now nearly a year ago, a provision was made that schemes of mutual agreement between
employers and employed should be sanctioned by the Ministry. It was definitely provided
that in any particular trade, where employers and employed mutually agreed upon a
scheme for contributions and benefits in that particular trade, the sanction of the Ministry
should be given. In other words, the principle was laid down that employers and employed
should assist each other, the employer by keeping the men at work as long as possible
and the employed by not going upon unemployment benefit sooner than was absolutely
necessary. That, generally stated, is the provision of the Act which this Bill is intended
to amend. To the astonishment and consternation of everyone who wishes for good
understanding between employers and employed, there was found in this Bill the Clause
in question-Clause 5-which will destroy the results arising from the carrying out of this
provision in the original Act. It is not a straightforward attack upon the good under-
standing between employers and employed, but an attack by way of a flank movement.
There is one large interest which has escaped this attack, and that is the interest of insur-
ance employees. I hope the friendly societies will benefit by this exception. I hope the
insurance scheme, which the right hon. Gentleman has agreed to exempt from Clause 5,
is a scheme inclusive of friendly societies and all those employed by them. That will
be so much the better. I am not jealous of that in the least, but I desire other trades and
industries to have similar advantages. In Committee the hon. Member for Broxtowe
(Mr. Spencer) made this statement:
"I am interested in a scheme of the miners. The owners and workmen have been
considering the possibility of arranging a scheme of their own; but I do not know whether
they have yet made a formal application. That means that notwithstanding the fact
that the two parties have been engaged for a long time in formulating their own scheme,
of which the whole industry is in favour, they will be debarred from having a scheme
which the principal Act would have enabled them to have." - [OFFICIAL REPORT, Standing
Committee C, 21st June, 1921; col. 74.]
I cannot find words which more clearly and more adequately describes the situation in
regard to this Amendment. If during the eight months the Act has been in operation and
the still longer period during which it has been law, any trade has not formulated and
submitted a mutual scheme, that is because of want of due diligence on the part of those
concerned in the trade. If it is shown that a scheme has received the mutual approval
of employers and employed, by preparation, by agreement, and by submission to the
Ministry of Labour, then I submit such a scheme should not be extinguished and destroyed.
How is it proposed by this Clause, as it stands, that such a scheme shall be extinguished
and destroyed? If, by the 8th June, that scheme has not been advertised, then this will
be wiped away; no matter how good the scheme may be for the benefit of both sides,
no matter if the scheme is one which the Department cannot find any objection to, and
would like to see in operation, the mere fact that it has not been advertised, or published,
is going to destroy it. I hope the absurdity, the unfairness, the injustice of such a provision
will be evident, on full consideration, to my right hon. Friend the Minister of Labour.
I have made some concession, in the words I have suggested, to the difficulty my right
hon. Friend put forward in Committee. There he was asked if he would accept the Amend-
ment on the basis of a
"
special" scheme, but I have altered that to a
"
completed "
scheme, so that, if the scheme be not nebulous, be not a mere suggestion or proposal, if
it be a formulated scheme, agreed to by all concerned, a completed scheme, I submit it
ought to be accepted, and I hope it will be accepted by my right hon. Friend. Everything

"LIFE ON THE FARM," BY AN IMMIGRANT.
1. Cox
7433
Story of Strenuous Duties told at Labour Temple.
RISE EARLY AND WORK LATE.
Sixty Dollars per Month and Board for Man and Wife.
was the title of a little story told by an immigrant at the Labour
"Life on the Farm
Temple this week. The author of the story was Arthur Clegg, formerly of Manchester
England, who with his wife was sent out to Canada by the Overseas Settlement Board,
Enough the Ontario Government Labour Bureau, after getting the "once over" in Aberdeen,
Scotland, which was the nearest inspection depot from Dundee, where Clegg and his wife
had been staying. Clegg had followed the life of a British sailor for many years, and during
several years' sojourn in Australia had learned the art of farming. The object of his
visit to the Labour Temple was to get a position as a painter, he having become a knight
of the brush while enjoying his seafaring life.
722
이
31
He explained to the business agent of the Painters' and Decorators' Union that he
had been booked for Canada through the London Office of the Ontario Government Labour
Bureau. Upon the arrival of Clegg and his wife in Canada they were sent to a farm at
Craighurst, Ont., with the understanding that they would get $60 a month and board.
The duties of the couple, as previously defined, were general farm work for Clegg and cook-
ing and general housework for his wife. Mr. Clegg found his duties anything but easy,
and the stay of the couple was very brief. They left Toronto for the farm on a Friday
and were back in Toronto the following Monday. The reason for the sudden departure
from Craighurst was the imposition of more than reasonable duties. The first day's
work for Mr. Clegg started at 3.30 a.m. and would have ended between 9 and 10 p.m. if
the spirit of revolt had not overtaken the new arrival. From 3.30 to 7 a.m. Clegg fed 40
head of colts and about 14 head of working horses and milked 20 cows. Breakfast was
then provided. The rest of the morning and afternoon he was taking cans from maple
trees, and at 6 p.m. supper was the order of the day. After supper Clegg was asked to
milk the 20 cows, but after milking one cow he decided that such continuous duties were
more than he could endure, and he threw up the job. Mrs. Clegg had to rise at 4.30 a.m.
and work till 7.30 p.m.. This working day happened to be a Sunday, and the farmer
and his wife enjoyed the usual weekly church service. Clegg and his wife also complained
that they were left in the house without directions as to food, but they made their own
search and were able to satisfy their appetites.
5
5
where he was steadily employed from April to August. He afterwards worked in the
After leaving the farm Clegg obtained work in the Dunlop Tyre Company's factory,
slaughterhouse of the William Davies Company, where he contracted rheumatic fever
and had to spend some time in St. Michael's Hospital. Since he left the hospital he has
painted one house at the Island. This is the experience of one immigrant induced to come
to Canada by the alluring advertisements about "Life on the Farm "Industrial Banner,
Toronto, May 13th, 1921.

STATE UNEMPLOYMENT SECTION.

We beg to appeal to Branch Officers to immediately bank or cash cheques sent along weekly in connection with this section of our work, and so not only save trouble to themselves but also to help minimise the work at the Central Office. At the end of last month 122 cheques were outstanding on this account alone; it will be seen this greatly increases the work when balances have to be taken monthly. We feel sure that officials only need a reminder of this to help the working of the Department to run smoothly.

WAR.

Both industrially and from a military standpoint the outlook is not only unsatisfactory, it is indeed in many cases black and ominous. The wheels of industry are very slow in moving, nor does there appear to be that determination amongst statesmen which one would expect to try and meet such an unprecedented situation as now exists. We know that many statements are made

GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
Trade has altered very slightly for the better, but many firms are still unstarted.
Some have been closed for two months, others are very restless and require our frequent
attention. One would have thought that their troubles were enough without adding
abour troubles to their commercial ones; anything they can do to appease the multitude
of minds under their ægis the better for all concerned.
A visit to Wellingboro'. A meeting called of operatives was so sparsely attended
that we are determined to try again as the matter under consideration affected the
National Agreement.
On the 22nd we attended the Northampton Advisory Committee, who look after the
Educational and Organising side of the tranches. On the 24th and 25th we attended
the Council Meetings.
We have set aside the August Meeting for the preparation of our case to the
Employers in October. In the meantime we hope for the best. Short-sighted manu-
facturers are very restless; some of them think the only course is to follow in the wake
of other disturbers of the public peace. If those newspapers who advocate Political
Peace and Industrial War would bear in mind that in the ranks of Labour are many
millions of men, to my mind the best part of the nation in quantity and quality, who
have already proved their worth and can very easily do so again the circumstances being
more íavoured, and in the absence of the Sergeant-Major would be a very difficult set
to deal with once aroused. This same set of people should remember that if you
abolish the Ministry of Labour you may have to double the British Army with men
whom you may not be able to control, because to goad good men is a very dangerous
thing. I commend this to that portion of the Press who advocate the abolition of
conciliation in trade disputes.
On the 20th Sileby was visited and a firm visited to correct their view of the
National Agreement with the usual result that same should be attended to and the same
has been done.
On the 26th I went to Mansfield and found that the Firm of Royce had several men
under notice and warned the Firm that no men must be discharged whilst women were
retained in the departments usually confined to male labour, but they agreed to and
retained the men pending a further personal visit at an early date. I also learned there is
no sole cutting at Faire Bros.' Factory, but they have been making stiffenings since about
April this year. All girls get our Day Labour rates.
Rushden was visited on the 26th and a firm visited who has left the Federation
rather than pay the Holiday claims in accord with the morality of the National Holiday
scheme. We therefore approached the President, Ex-President, Secretary of the Federa-
tion and the Secretary of the Association on the matter.

BRANCH REPORTS.

BARNSLEY.—We are pleased to say that there is a chance of our members having a bit more work to do in the future owing to the settlement of the Coal Strike.
BELFAST.—We regret to report that trade still continues to remain very dull, both in the Manufacturing and Repairing. We would again appeal to our members to maintain an active and intelligent interest in the workings of the branch. We know how difficult it is to be cheerful under present conditions, but let us not get downcast, the times will surely change.
BRISTOL AND KINGSWOOD No. 2.—Trade shows a further improvement on what we reported last month, and we hope that it will continue. This applies to the heavy trade. Some factories are actually on full time after many months of very short hours. We hope that this will soon be reflected in our returns, which have not been very satisfactory to secretaries for some months past.
CHESHAM.—Trade here during the past few weeks has improved slightly, but we regret to report that some manufacturers are trying to take advantage of the men's position by offering them reduced wages to recommence work again. The position is causing the Local Officials some anxiety and is not an easy matter to deal with, having regard to the fact that some of our members have been unemployed for seven months.
EDINBURGH.—The factories in Edinburgh are still working short time and have had an extended holiday. Some shopmates who have drawn all State Unemployment are now without any income whatever and no prospect of getting work anywhere; the outlook for them is not very encouraging. Surely trade will take a turn for the better shortly. The Edinburgh Branch, if it had the funds would make an effort to organise the Boot Repairers in the Border Counties of Scotland, as they have not even heard of Wages Trade Boards in some districts. The Revised Piece Rates are now in operation, so we would advise members to see that they are paid according to schedule. The members in Edinburgh are curious to know how after the full Wages Trade Board put forward a recommendation to District Committees for a minimum of 72s. per week, then in about a month's time turned down their own decision. Surely outside pressure has been at work, as the cost of living had not fallen much during the waiting period. It would be useful if Branch Officials had at their disposal the names of the employers in their district who have been able during the boom years to pay Excess Profits Duty, as no doubt some have done. Then we would be able to meet their arguments about the trade not being able to afford better conditions to the employees.
HIGHAM AND RUSHDEN.—Trade has improved slightly during the month. The reduction in out-of-work benefit paid does not mean that the members have resumed work, as a considerable number are still out and no signs of being engaged. We regret to report that on Saturday, July 30th, the factory of Messrs. H. Jaques was totally destroyed by fire, throwing out about 80 workpeople. This is one of the best firms in our district, using the Trade Union Stamp, the Manager, Councillor J. Spencer, J.P., also being a member for a considerable number of years. We hope that the firm will secure fresh premises, as they have a considerable amount of work.
KINGSWOOD.—Trade in this centre is improving very slowly, and practically every factory was closed during August holiday week. A few firms have gone on full time, and we are hopeful that the conditions will materially improve at an early date. THE INDUSTRIAL SITUATION.
A sense of common interest could hardly be cultivated so long as one side engaged in
industry owned nothing but the labour expended in production, and the other side owned
the material and exercised full authority and control.
Employers ought not to need pushing into the path of improvement. They should
go along the path of gradual improvement by their own initiative.
Clynes suggested that, by encouraging the participation of the workers in the control
of industry, employers would get that economy, efficiency, and contentment they pro
fessed to desire.
National ownership in essential national services was an undiminished claim of
organised Labour.
"Until the electorate is ready for this fundamental change," continued Clynes, "it
is for organised Labour to direct its strength towards securing and retaining for the wage-
earners a better share of the fruits of industrial effort. So far as this share is deliberately
denied the class struggle is deepened.
"The very people who have cause to dread revolution, and appeal to others not
to provoke it are themselves the main factors tending to create in the popular mind
a disposition violently to upset social and economic conditions which rob them of
what they are justly entitled to enjoy."
Turning to the question of action by the workers, Clynes gave his opinion on the
recent coal dispute.
"It is for those who decided the course which was finally taken," he said "to answer
fort to their respective organisations. That course has been strongly criticised. It has
been criticised by some who know nothing whatever of either the facts or the psychology
of the situation and who talk loosely of what has been foolishly called Black Friday."
"There are men who think that an executive or an official can direct and move in
one direction or the other millions of workmen who entertain different points of view and
have interests not always in common. Huge masses of men are not likely to respond to
any signal which at any time a group of officials or a committee may be disposed to give
them."
"The human factors and the natural motives of individual and collective self-interest
cannot be ignored when decisions in respect to strike action have to be taken."
Clynes defended the leader of long views, who had the courage to tell men what could
not be won, rather than tell them to go on fighting anyhow, saying that in the end they
were sure to win.
The unflinching pursuit of what could be obtained, avoiding reckless clamour for what
could not be got at all, was the best sort of service from a Labour leader.
Recent industrial struggles had shown the need for using Labour's political power.
The belief that the strike weapon could accomplish anything had receded. It was now
clear that men would not engage in a risky strike for anything for which they were not
ready to vote.
"We live in a country," said Clynes, "where the people have both the right and
power to vote themselves into any social order or economic system which they prefer,
and we should put an end to the insane practice of following some new and fanciful plan
just at a moment when we were reaching a point of success for the political methods which
Labour has built up in the last generation." -MR. J. R. CLYNES, M.P., at Meeting of
General Workers.-Daily Herald, August 19th, 1921.

TRADE BOARDS.
At a meeting of the Administrative Committee of the Boot and Shoe Repairing Trade
Board (Great Britain) the following Resolutions were unanimously passed.--
(1) On the expiration of two years' working this Administrative Committee of the
Boot and Shoe Repairing Trade Board (Great Britain) desire to place on record their firm
and unanimous conviction that the operations of this Trade Board have been of great
advantage and benefit to the Industry controlled by the Board and to all those engaged
in it whether as Employers or Workers.
This Committee desire further to record their opinion, based upon their experience
of over two years that, given a real desire on the part of both Employers and Workers to
work together amicably and for the good of the Industry in which both part es are directly
and mutually interested, the Trade Board system presents most effective means for enabling
the parties to realise each other's economic difficulties, to discuss and settle their respect ve
problems with sympathy and equity, and to promote such legislation as will be for the
permanent good of the Industry as a whole, even though there may be here and there
individual temporary cases of hardship, which are inseparable from all attempts at progress
and improvement.

"DENS OF DISEASE" IN SCOTLAND.
Startling Revelations in Regard to Dwellings. Housing Halt Attacked.
Scottish housing needs were voiced in Parliament yesterday by Mr. John Robertson,
Labour member for Bothwell. He called attention to housing in Scotland and the insani-
tary conditions in mining towns and villages. According to the report of the Royal
Commission on Housing in Scotland, in 1911 about 400,000 persons resided in one-room
houses and nearly 2,000,000 in two-room houses. Houses which were condemned during
the cholera epidemic of 1840 as being unfit for human habitation were still occupied.
In one village he had visited recently there were 40 of these one-room houses, measuring
15ft. by 14ft. by 8ft., and the first he entered was occupied by 15 persons. There was no
lavatory accommodation of any kind. Living under such conditions was barbarism of
the lowest type. These insanitary houses were a monument to the complete failure of
private enterprise to provide decent housing conditions. They could only be swept out
of existence by a comprehensive system of State housing.
Mr. Wallace said Scotland's irreducible minimum requirement was 115,000 houses.
Mr. Munro, in replying, said that it must be admitted that some of the miners' dwel-
lings in Scotland were an outrage on decency and civilisation, but notwithstanding these
shocking housing conditions, the deaths from infantile mortality and tuberculosis had
steadily declined during the last 10 years. There had been no scrapping of the Govern-
ment's housing programme or refusal to revert fully to it when financial conditions became
more favourable. It would be impossible to justify to the ratepayers the indulgence on
an indefinite scheme at a time of artificial inflation in prices of both materials and labour.
Then with regard to slum areas the Government had allocated ₤200,000 per annum for the
clearance of slums in England and Scotland, and he was glad to say that the latter's share
of the money would be £30,000.

Mr. Hogge maintained that the Secretary for Scotland had wholly failed to answer
the case put forward by Mr. Robertson. The sum of £30,000 a year was altogether
inadequate to deal with slum property in Scotland.

TRADE UNION ORGANISATION. IS IT OUT OF DATE?
HOW I WOULD REVISE IT.
By the Right Hon. J. R. Clynes, M.P.

Not least among the many lessons of the recent coal stoppage was the proof it gave at the failure of trade union organisation to afford facilities to its responsible leaders to effect settlements of disputes upon their own seasoned judgment, and in accordance with known economic facts Ultimately a settlement was made which broke this tradition.
What was done affords an opportunity for the whole movement to consider upon what terms in the future leaders shall lead, and members respond to the call they receive from their leaders. The call, it should be understood, must always be dictated by a solemn regard for the men's interests.

In the early days of the trade union movement, when the organisation was newer and less complex, when employers and employees alike regarded industry as a mere personal concern, which provided profit for the one and employment for the other, it was possible and desirable for the workers' leaders to consult their followers upon every detail of policy to be pursued. The whole industrial outlook was parochial, and narrow conception of policy naturally developed. They were hard struggling days for the movement, producing cautious leaders, and false ideas regarding the real basis of industrial enterprise. There were the days when restriction of output seemed essential to ensure employment, and day rates appeared better than piece rates to maintain a fair day's pay for a fair day's work.

New Ideas.
The war, however, brought in new ideas, which have influenced all responsible leaders of industry, and would, if allowed free play, produce an attitude of mind conducive to the widest co-operation. Parochial and personal interests are giving way before the wider recognition of national and collective needs, and the true essence of industry is being acknowledged in every quarter, namely, that it exists to provide the community with the services which it requires. One may stimulate conflicting interests, and organise them for opposition of the deadliest character, but the basis of industry will remain unchanged while human needs require satisfaction.

Leading employers are realising the value of co-operation and conciliation as a means of maintaining peace with their employees, and of meeting by continuity of production and by finding markets for the things produced the extensive needs of a civilised community.

Can the same thing be said of trade union leaders? Undoubtedly it can of those who by long experience and direct contact with the leaders of employers' associations have gained an insight into the

Difficulties which Capital
has constantly to overcome in order to organise and finance industry and maintain foreign trade. Yet in time of dispute, these very leaders are precluded by the old trade union custom of plebiscite and delegate meeting from securing settlements they consider the best possible at the time!

In the case of a plebiscite the mass of men are obviously incapable of seeing all the facts of the dispute, and they consequently fail to realise the many obstacles that lie in the way of settlement along the lines of their desires. In the case of a delegate meeting. almost the same defects operate. The delegates are drawn from widely scattered areas, and are more in touch with the personal desires of the men than the full knowledge and experience of their leaders.

It is this that prevents the leaders from securing settlements, destroys their authority in the eyes of the opposition and the community, prolongs the struggle to unnecessary lengths, increases unemployment and suffering in other industries, until, finally, a settlement is arrived at, little or no better than that advised by the leaders in the first place.

This part of trade union organisation is unquestionably out of date, and unless it is revised to meet the newer conditions and ideas prevailing it will ultimately destroy trade unionism as a progressive movement. How would I revise it?

I should start by asking workmen to grant real freedom and authority to responsible leaders to secure what they believe just or expedient in the interests of the men, by giving them a real opportunity to use their knowledge of the facts in negotiating for a final settlement. Rarely would a traitor be found to misuse this power. On the contrary, men who have the real interests of their kind closely at heart would be free to lead them by progressive stages in a happier and more prosperous condition than is their lot to-day.

THE INDUSTRIAL OUTLOOK
is still very far from satisfactory, either nationally or internationally. Many
statements are being constantly made as to the need for workmen putting
their shoulder to the wheel and maintaining a maximum output; at the
same time that such statements are being made, millions of workpeople are
vainly asking for work, whereby they may be given an opportunity of
earning a wage for the labour given. The figures of the Government as
to the number unemployed do not, it is admitted, represent to the full
extent the numbers actually out of work, on account of the fact that
very many operatives have drawn their full amount of unemployment benefit
and no longer register with the Employment Exchanges. This question of
unemployment was fully discussed at the Trades Congress and the following
resolution unanimously passed relative thereto :--

" The Trades Union Congress, assembled at Cardiff, and representing
over six millions of British workers, views with grave apprehension the
increasing extent and conditions of unemployment, and reaffirms the
principle that it is the duty of the State to provide work or adequate
maintenance for every willing worker; approves the action of those Boards
of Guardians which, in the absence of proper Government assistance,
have made a serious endeavour to adequately relieve the urgent necessities
of the workless; but emphatically expresses its opinion that such a burden,
mainly due to the War, should not have been imposed on the ratepayers,
and must be removed from them.

The Congress calls upon the Government to immediately summon
Parliament and to introduce practicable schemes of work without delay,
with the necessary financial provision; and, further, to remove the gross
inequalities of rating obtaining in the London area.

The Congress is also of opinion that the Poplar Councillors, in the
stand which they believed to be the best to take, under the exceptional
circumstances, to call public attention to the distressful conditions of the
unemployed, have rendered a real national service. It pledges itself to
use all the strength at its command to secure the provision of work or
adequate maintenance for the unemployed workers throughout the country,
and instructs the new General Council, in close co-operation with the
National Executive of the Labour Party, and the Parliamentary Labour
Party, immediately to take such steps as may be necessary to secure these
objects."

We note that the Government have appointed a Committee to enquire
into the question of unemployment with a view, we presume, to ascertain
methods of dealing with the question. Meantime in various parts of the country,
owing to the desperate position in which many find themselves, there have been
disturbances. It is sincerely to be hoped that the Government will not only

Labour's Annual Parliament. The week was a very strenuous one owing to the Hall being filled by Congress during the day and turned into a Cinema at night. The week also was a very hot one outside which perhaps helped the barometer up inside. A big discussion was arrested by the withdrawal of a motion affecting the Triple Alliance, and showed itself in a much milder form later in the week. ORGANISER'S REPORT.

During the past month I have been working in London, Chesham and Manchester.
On August 23rd, 24th, 25th I visited several shops in the East End for organising purposes.
On the 25th Mr. Buckle and I addressed a good meeting of the women at Polikoff's. They
expressed themselves satisfied at the efforts we had made with the firm in negotiating for
them. It was agreed that a systematic effort be made by the women themselves to bring
in those outside the Union. On August 26th I went to Chesham to make enquiries into
conditions there. From August 20th to September 2nd I visited nearly the whole of the
shops in the Manchester area. Trade has been exceptionally bad in this district for a long
time. I went to Chesham on September 5th and remained there till the 16th. The
questions under review there are not yet settled, but will be reported on in due course.
I returned to Manchester the following week and succeeded, I believe, in creating a better
spirit of confidence among the members. Owing to the hard times mentioned there has
been a considerable falling off among the women membership. I am pleased to say that
they have responded to our appeal and have agreed in a body to pay up and rejoin according
to circumstances. On September 22nd we had a special meeting of the members. It
was the best meeting for attendance and interest taken of any in my experience held at
Manchester. There is a big orphanage and industrial school near Manchester. Through
the weakness of our organisation here in the past the shoe trade has been flooded with boy
labour from this institution Since I got to know about the conditions I have protested
to inividual manufacturers against the undue proportion of boy labour and am glad to say
that during the past twelve months there has been a decided improvement in some of the
shops. To the biggest offender at present I have now appealed again verbally and in
writing; also I wrote to the heads of this particular institution asking that, for the future
welfare of the lads themselves, careful enquiries should be made before sending any
more of them to the boot trade. A word to Branch Officers. In my experience there is
no more effective way for keeping the members together than the one of having a Shop
President wherever possible. Factory after factory where I have gone to and found some
in the Union and some outside, the excuse made by the slackers has been the absence of a
shop president.
"We were members up to the time the collector left" is the general saying.
I think that it would very largely get over the difficulty if Branch Secretaries would report
to their Executives when shop presidents ceased to bring in contributions in the ordinary
way. Efforts should be made as early as possible to replace shop presidents who have
given up their positions or who have gone to other shops.

September 24th, 1921.
D. MCCARTHY.

REPLY TO BOSSES' PLEA AGAINST WAGES.
The Daily Herald learns that the Committee on Trade Boards announced by the Minister
of Labour (Dr. Macnamara) on Monday has been constituted as follows :-

Viscount Cave (president); Lord Weir of Eastwood; Dame Adelaide Anderson, late
H.M. Chief Inspector of Factories; Dame Edith Lyttelton; James Bell, M.P., secretary
of the Oldham Weavers' Association and M.P. for the Ormskirk Division of Lancashire;
W. T. Layton, director of the National Federation of Iron and Steel Manufacturers;
Sir Arthur Pease, Bart., Darlington; E. L. Poulton, chairman of the Parliamentary Com-
mittee of the Trades Union Congress; A. Pugh, secretary of the Iron and Steel Trades
Confederation; A. MacCallum Scott, M.P. for the Bridgeton Division of Glasgow.

The secretary to the Committee is H. D. Hancock, of the Ministry of Labour.
The terms of reference laid down by Dr. Macnamara are :
To inquire into the working and effects of the Trade Boards Act, and to report
what changes, if any, are required."

NEWCASTLE. -After rather a long spell of much unemployment the
brighter for the future. There is one thing we would like to bring before the
notice of all members of our Union, that is, that there are many employers
labour who are putting their heads together and at their local Master Repairers
Association, trying to instil into the members of their association that the
Trade Board and all the Trade Board Awards in connection with our trade
are only framed to uplift and make better conditions for the workman and to
give him wages which, the employer is ever ready to state, the business cannot
pay. In our district at one of the meetings in August of the Employers'
Association, two of their high officials stated that while the Trade Board had
done a lot of good, it had also done a lot of harm, and that they were out to
smash and abolish the Trade Board. At the same meeting the member of the
National Trade Board Committee, who sits for the Northern Districts, stated
that the Association members were out for a reduction of 10 per cent. in Piece
rates. From such statements as these it is quite plain to see that the em-
ployers are hankering to get back to pre-war wages and conditions. In fact,
it has been stated to me by a member of the Masters' Association, that a lot
of propaganda work is now going on at their meetings for this end. Fellow
members, it is up to us all to instruct all members of our Union who sit on the
National Trade Board Committee, or on District Trade Board Committees,
when any proposal to reduce wages is brought forward by the employers, that
they use every weapon they can to defeat any such proposal.
