The motto of the public has been "any old thing will do," rubber soles and substitutes of every description have had a good innings, but we believe the public sooner or later will find the old maxim still true, "There is nothing like leather." We have read the resolutions passed by the Administrative Committee of the Boot and Shoe Repairing Trade Board, and at our monthly meeting a resolution was passed unanimously, fully approving the action taken by the Committee. Further, we are convinced that the Trade Board must be maintained as a permanent part of the industrial machinery under the Ministry of Labour, and if peace and plenty is to be won from the hive of industry, progress must be made along the road opened up by the pioneers of Frade Board legislation, which gives reason and equity the controlling voice in industry, instead of passion, class hatred, and vested interests.

N.B. Will the Council please publish in the Monthly Report the new General Minimum Piece Rates, fixed by the Trade Board, effective as froτο 2nd August, 1921, Schedule D (12), as this would make a handy form of refer-ence for boot repairers.

REDRUTH. There is a slight improvement in the trade, which we hope will soon warrant full time. We are pleased to know that the industry is improving generally. During the month we held our Annual Outing, and a very pleasant time was spent at Penzance.

SOUTHAMPTON. - Trade still very quiet. The unemployed are being absorbed at a very slow rate. We are hoping for the pleasure of chronicling a better story ere long.

STAFFORD. - Trade is very bad in this centre; the majority of our merr.-bers are working short time.

WATERFORD.-Trade is quiet at present.

WELLINGBOROUGH. - Trade, we are pleased to report, shows a slight improvement, but we have still a large number of members who have drawr all benefit. The wonder of it is that with all the widespread unemployment disorder is not more prevalent. If we can take this as a sign that real thinking is taking place as to the means whereby such a position cannot arise again, then it is all to the good, but if on the other hand the unemployed have been lulled to sleep by doles, then we indeed have a hard task before us to point out that the present position can be altered when the electorate decide upon such a course. Let our friends who are tired of waiting for the change remember that the Parliamentary machine has served the old parties well, and that the workers, as soon as they capture that machine, can right many of the wrongs that we now suffer from. Some of the firms are taking this trade slump as a means of trying to enforce conditions other than those laid down by the National Agreement. Members must understand that there are two parties to every agreement, and they must report every such attempt to infringe agreements to the office, to enable the matter to be taken up. Unity and organisation are needed more now than ever. Let us do all we can to make our Union a 100 per cent. membership.

YARMOUTH (GREAT). - Trade is very bad. We have a few members employed about half time, all the others have been out upwards of 18 weeks. We have not experienced anything like it for the past thirty years. It is un-doubtedly the result of the Russian Blockade; their ports were the market for our herring. The Herring Fishing collapsed last November because there was no market for them, so did our boot trade. Unemployed fishermen do not buy boots. A feeling of hopefulness is expressed by some for the fishing season now about to commence, whilst others say the markets are still stocked with last year's catch. One good sign is that the curers are laying in big stocks of curing material. The success of the Herring Fishing is of national importance;

NEW ZEALAND FEDERATED BOOT TRADE UNION.
The above Union has written as follows under date 18th July, 1921, the
letter being signed by Mr. C. A. Watts, General Secretary.
By direction of the Executive Council of the above Association I have to convey to
you the following " resolution," which has been adopted by the various Branches of our
Federation and approved by the National Executive:
"That the National Secretary be directed to communicate with the Australian
English and American Boot Trade National Federations, urging these organizations
Zealand, inquiries be made as to the state of trade in that country, and to advise
to instruct their component Branches, that before their members leave for New
their members not to accept employment in that country unless agreed to by their
Federation, and to point out that intense dissatisfaction is being caused by reason
of our New Zealand members being thrown out of work in order to make room for
workers from other countries."
In conveying the above resolution, may I say that the position in New Zealand has
been that, whilst we are working under an Award of the Arbitration Court, which fixes
the minimum rate of wage, the Court's Memorandum states "that such wage is fixed for
the lowest grade worker in the Industry," and as a matter of fact, only about one per cent.
of our members are working on the minimum rate. The object of the boot manufacturers
undoubtedly is to bring men here on the minimum rate, so that there will be a general
fall in wages, and in order to bring this into effect, the employers are urging unrestricted
immigration, and we are rapidly reaching the position of having two and three men waiting
for one job.
Under the first clause of the Award preference of employment is given to members
of our Federation, and we have had the greatest difficulty in restraining our members
from insisting on the application of this clause against fellow workers from other lands.
The Executive Council feel and know that the workers arriving here (as a rule) are good
unionists, and we will not be parties to exercising the preference clause against members
of another Union, but we have to emphasise the fact that workers who come here, when
our own are unemployed, are the cause of a feeling of bitterness and distrust in the motives
of the newly arrived.
In conversation with some of the workers (male and female) who have come here from
other lands, one is struck with the misleading statements that are made to them. I was
shown a pamphlet, stated to have been issued by the New Zealand Government, which
said that houses could be obtained in the cities of New Zealand for gs. to 125. per week,
and in the country districts the rent ranged from 6s. to 10s. per week. I wish to give this
statement an emphatic denial, as I myself am living in a five-roomed house and paying
21S. per week, and am better off than 90 per cent. of the workers. The usual rent of a
five-roomed house is from 30s. to 375. 6d. per week. This is when houses can be obtained,
and as a matter of fact, the people are living in flats and with three and four families
in a five or six-roomed house.
Whilst the Government of New Zealand state that the immigrants are being employed
and housed in this country, they do not tell the fact that in order to do this, people already
in the Dominion are being thrown out of employment and houses to enable this to be done.
As I write this letter, unemployed processions are being held in this town and the
municipal authorities are dispensing relief to the distressed families. The boot factories
of this Dominion are working only two-thirds full time, and the boot operative who comes
here thinking that he will be employed on similar work to that which he is doing in older
countries is sadly disappointed when he finds that, in 90 per cent. of the factories, he has
to make boots by the old hand method, and these boots are of the heavy type, suitable
for the farming community, being made of kip, three decked, pegged and nailed.
It is the wish of the New Zealand Boot Trade Federation that you should give publicity
to these facts, so that workers in your country should realise the position before leaving
for this Dominion, and any assistance that you may be able to give will be greatly appreciated by our members.

LORD CAVE'S COMMITTEE.
I could not admire Dr. Macnamara's disposition to run away from the Trade Boards
but, to do him justice, his first nominations to the Committee which is to "overhaul "
(his own word) the Trade Boards Act are excellent.
Mr. Poulton, Miss Anderson, and Mrs. Alfred Lyttelton are all good
friends of Labour, and Mr. MacCallum Scott is a man we would trust. The
reactionaries are not likely to get much assistance from a Committee framed
on these lines. - The Star, September 21st, 1921.

INTERNATIONAL EMIGRATION COMMISSION.
This Commission, representing 15 countries, which was constituted by the International
Labour Office as the result of a resolution passed at the International Labour Condtional
at Washington in 1919, met at Geneva from August 2nd to 11th last, under the Chairmance
ship of Lord Ullswater, ex-speaker of the House of Commons.

A large number of resolutions were passed, and these will be submitted to the Inter-
The object of the Commission was to "consider
national Labour Conference of 1922.
and report what measures can be adopted to regulate the migration of workers out of their
native country, and to protect the interests of wage earners residing in another country than
their own." The delegates from English-speaking countries were, in addition to Lord
U'llswater (who represented the British Government), Col. Obed Smith (Canadian Govern-
ment), Sir Ernest Low (Indian Government), and Mr. Gemmill (South African employers).
Workers' delegates were invited from Germany, Italy, Sweden, Australia, United States.
and Poland, but only the first three were actually present.
The Agenda contained the following points :-
(1) Emigration Agents; (2) Recruiting of bodies of Workers; (3) Deduction from Wages
in respect of Money Advanced; (4) Examination before Embarkation; (5) Hygiene on
Board Ship and in Trains; (6) Insurance during the journey; (7) Employment Exchanges;
(8) Equality of Treatment of Foreign and National Workers; (9) Documentation; (10) Co-
ordination of National Laws; (II) White Slave Traffic; (12) Other Questions.
Resolutions were passed on all the above points. It is impossible to give them here
in full, but they may be summarised as follows :-
On the first point, the Commission recommends State supervision over all persone
interested in the promotion of emigration and the punishment of persons making false
statements with a view to inducing emigration; that each government should place at
everybody's disposal free information regarding emigration; and that, so far as emigration
is concerned, every country should embody in its legislation the principle of the full responsi-
bility of principals for the acts of their employees and agents.

With regard to the second item, it is suggested that agreements be made between the
Countries concerned, on the basis that only officers or agents authorised by the Govern-
ment be allowed to recruit labour for foreign countries, that employers' and workers' organi-
ations be consulted, that the foreign workers be paid the rates of wages current in the place

PERIL OF VENEREAL DISEASE.
Sir J. Crichton-Browne on Disinfection.
On August 31st Sir James Crichton-Browne, in his presidential address at the Conference of the Sanitary Inspectors' Association at Bath, dealt at length with the question of venereal disease.
The subject, he said, was one that one would rather not refer to in a public assembly, but knowing what he did of the horrors of the disease it would be culpable prudery if he refrained, at such a meeting, from indicating what he believed was the one sure way- and that was not a clinic of coping with a grave and growing social evil.
Last year, he said, 2,023 deaths in England and Wales were due to syphilis and 2,103 to other venereal diseases. These figures however, afforded not the slightest conception of the havoc wrought by these maladies. Not less than 10 per cent. of the population of our large towns were infected with syphilis, and a much larger proportion with gonorrhea. Gonorrhea was prolific of sterility, blindness, and of rheumatic and joint affections; and syphilis was the direct cause of a vast number of cases of abortion, miscarriage, still-birth, and infant mortality, and, as a hidden assassin, was undoubtedly responsible for a large number of deaths attributed to other causes, such as aneurism, angina-pectoris, Bright's disease, and cerebral hæmorrhage. Syphilis was the sole cause of general paralysis of the insane, which killed 2,000 people in this country annually, and it was the inexorable bane of those wretched men they saw staggering about with locomotor ataxy. It was a secret poison that had until recently been allowed to circulate freely, slaying our people, undermining their manhood, and producing widespread invalidism and industrial incapacity.

A Warning Vision.
Proceeding, Sir J. Crichton-Browne said:-
It is not statistics so much as cases that touch the feelings, and if I could conjure before you the vision of a poor boy in his teens, stricken, perhaps as the result of the foolish frolic of a night, by this fell malady, terrified and undone, doomed to carry about with him for years the dread of impending calamity for himself or those who are dear to him, or if I could conduct you into the infirmary ward of one of our large asylums and show you side by side some twenty or thirty bedridden men, all in the prime of life, all men of rather a superior type, all quivering with paralysis and stuttering scraps of imbecile gibberish, mere human logs, helpless, wasted, and convulsed, waiting for death, you would I am sure, be moved to insist urgently that everything that is possible shall be done promptly to stave off this ghastly disorder.
The disease can be prevented, and if you ask why it is not prevented, the answer must be because of ignorance and negligence on the one hand and ecclesiastical prejudice and short-sighted morality on the other. Insurance Gazette, 24th September, 1921.

BRANCH REPORTS.
BARNSLEY -Trade, both manufacturing and repairing, is very slack.
Many miners and others buy their leather and repair their easy jobs at home,
but still they call themselves trade unionists so long as they pay their con-
tributions to their societies. Those who do not live amongst them have no
idea of the number who carry on this business. We know persons who work
regularly at their trade and then repair boots and shoes at home for other
people.
BURNLEY - Trade here is very bad, but we wish our members to note
that it is impossible to keep straight at the Central Office unless they pay
their contributions. We would ask them to make an effort to get straight
on the books so that we can get out of debt, as it is a very uncomfortable position
for the local officials. As far as repairers are concerned we think that there is
something that ought to be altered re out-of-work pay in this respect. A man
who is discharged either in a factory or in a repairing shop can draw out-of-
work pay, but most repairers have a regular shop. We, who are the majority
of repairers, must attend our shop every day. Many times we go for nothing,
but we are always employed. Sometimes we have for wages, after doing a
little every day, as small a sum as IOS. or less. whilst if our emplovers would
stop us we could get the benefit of both our own out-of-work and also the
state unemployment dole. There are hundreds of us who have worked more
or less every day since the State Unemployment Act came into force, who have
not earned equal to the men who have been unemployed for any given period
when men unemployed were entitled to out-of-work pay. We who have
regular shops, and we speak especially of men who work in one-man shops,
are compelled always to pay, and under no circumstances will we ever be able
to reap a benefit from it. If all contributions are the same, in the hour of need
we should have like benefits. Under present conditions we are debarred,
and it is time it was altered. For instance, ours is a repairing branch, and for
all trade has been bad for so long, notice how little out-of-work pay you have
had to pay; but the distress has been awful and been quietly borne, and can be
seen in the state of our finances at the Central Office.

PLYMOUTH.-Trade is quiet. We now have the names of Lord Cave's
Committee appointed to overhaul the Trade Boards Act, and we are pleased
to see the name of our General Secretary among them. This we look upon
as a guarantee that the workers' interest will be watched and defended, with
honesty and ability. The agitation which has been carried on against the
Trade Boards for the last two or three months has not been without its advan-
tages to the worker. We have been able to see where the opposition comes
from, and who is the real friend of the worker, and if the agitation continues
we believe the worker will be made to see the precarious position he is in,
and how necessary it is to defend himself by organisation; how his livelihood
is protected by an Act of Parliament, how Parliament can pass as many Acts
to protect his livelihood as they have to protect private property, when Parlia-
ment is composed of a majority of genuine representatives of the workers.
Te remember that the British Parliament abolished the Slave Trade in 1808,
and it took us just 100 years to get the Trade Board Act upon the Statute
Book for the abolition of sweating. Are we to scrap this Act and turn back
again into the wilderness for another 100 years? Or shall we keep our face
toward the land fit for heroes to live in ?-where the sunlight shall flood the
worker's cottage, and the abundant harvest gladden the hearts of all. This
depends upon how we use our intelligence.

Apart from export trade there is a great deal of necessary work to be done at home. The

General Council, 1921-1922.
The first General Council of the Trades Union Congress, which takes the place of the
old Parliamentary Committee, has been elected by a postal ballot of the affiliated organisa-

The Council comprises 32 members, who were elected in 18 electoral groups by the
whole Congress. The following list of members shows how the 18 electoral groups have
been combined to form six groups or sub-committees of the Council, each dealing with

"LOST NERVE: ONLY ONE WAY OUT."
A Trade Union Secretary's Suicide.
A story of nerves wrecked by worry and overwork was told at a Tottenham inques
on William David Bray, 59, branch secretary of the National Union of Boot and She-
Operatives, of Lamb Lane, Hackney, whose body was found in the River Lea.
The widow said that for some time her husband had been strange in his manner
He attempted suicide by cutting his throat last July.

A Registered Letter.
Last Thursday he had a registered letter, and seemed upset after reading it.
He went out, and said he would be back to tea. He did not return that night, and
next morning she had a letter in his hand-writing post-marked "Clapton." It read:
To the best little woman in all the world.
My darling wife, I cannot ask you to forgive me for all the trouble I have
brought you. I only hope my friends and I have some will rally round and help
you all they can. I have lost my nerve, and there is only one way out. God bless
you. Your broken-hearted husband, Bill.
Albert Mason, of Walthamstow, president of the London Metropolitan branch of the
Union, said deceased had been very strange in his manner.

Heavy Work after Fire.
His work had been very heavy, and the recent fire at Flatau's factory, Tottenham,
had thrown an extra 200 on their unemployed list, which meant more work for the secretary.
He had not been really fit for some time, and his books were muddled. A special
audit disclosed a deficit of 111, and Bray was written to.
Mr. A. M. Forbes, the coroner, said this was undoubtedly a last straw to his worries.
Verdict: Suicide whilst of unsound mind. - Star, 27th September, 1921.

GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.

FELLOW MEMBERS,

The past month has been utilised very largely in obtaining information by the
holding of Shops' Meetings and visiting Branches and Sections for the purpose of endeavor-
ing to the best of our ability to prove to the Employers' Federation in December that there
are no grounds for them to follow those trades who have been enabled to force a reduction
upon the workers, to act in a similar manner. The Executive of the Union hope to be
able, with the information at their disposal, to prove beyond a shadow of doubt that to
say the least, it is not reasonable to ask for a reduction in wages or in the earning power
of the operatives. We are applying ourselves to this particular phase of the subject,
and the places mentioned. We hope to be able, taking all things into consideration, to
stave off the attempt, signified by a good many employers, to bring an alteration on the
earning power of operatives. I do not intend at this juncture to give a resume of
request, other than that already mentioned.

CHESHAM. As the information has become public property, the Union's Execu
found it necessary to visit Chesham owing to pressure having been brought to bear by
employers upon our members in that area. We called the members together, a good
number assembled, although it would have been a pleasure for us to have seen still more
on so important an occasion. We placed the matter before them, deciding upon a course
of procedure which we intend ultimately to report to them again before coming to a definite
conclusion. It is very unfortunate in any circumstances for one section of workers in any
trade or calling to permit employers to press them to accept reductions in wages or altera-
tion in their status of living, especially when one remembers that in our industry we have
not by any manner of means obtained or demanded all we were entitled to when cost of
living was as high as 178 per cent. above pre-war, and I am sure that it will be a most
difficult task for any section of employers to prove that the boot and shoe operative to-day
when all things are considered, is receiving better remuneration than he was in 1914.
I don't believe that such a thing could be proved to any body of independent persons.

GENERAL FEDERATION OF TRADE UNIONS. - During the month I have also attended
on two different occasions, meetings of the General Federation of Trade Unions, whose
work is becoming so important that they have decided to advertise for two National
Organisers at £500 per year, with 15s. per day for out of town expenses. We feel that
this sum is not too large for work so important as we expect to be performed. The Organi-
sers, whoever they may be, will not be called upon to do such arduous work as addressing
open-air meetings, but their work will be confined largely to visiting Executives, General
Secretaries and Officers of Unions, and explain to them the benefits to be obtained by joining
up with an organisation - the largest in the United Kingdom at the present time-being
nearly two million strong, and whose accumulative funds are to act as a deterrent to any
section of employers who feel that they have to take action against any individual Trade
Union who happened to be federated. This Federation proves, as we find at our Monthly
Meetings, the numerous efforts on the part of employers to reduce wages and to get back
to old and bad conditions. Very little reflection is required to-day for any man to know
that the best he can do as an individual is to join a Trade Union, and the next best thing
is for him to see that his own Trade Union should join up with a Federation, where we hope
the smaller Trade Unions will find a haven of refuge in the General Federation of Trade
Unions, because the bigger Unions are looking after themselves by joining up with other
big Unions, leaving the smaller Unions to take "pot luck."

I am hoping that a broader spirit will yet prevail, which still exists to-day as it did
the day when the Trade Union Congress first formed the General Federation of Trade
Unions.

TRADE BOARD. -I have had occasion to also spend two days in conjunction with the
Trade Board, where we are endeavouring to put right many anomalies that existed in the
first completed statement issued by this Board. Experience has shewn us that this was
necessary and for that purpose the Advisory Committee, upon which I happen to act
with one of my colleagues, has been very active in trying to rectify the short-comings of
previous statements. Whether the opposition to Trade Boards is likely to have any
influence or not, it is not for me to say, but at the present moment there does not appear
to be any likelihood of the Trade Board being permanently injured. My own view is that
it is only the unscrupulous employers of labour who are afraid of Trade Board influence,
and I am sorry to have to say that owing to bad trade this section of the community
appear to be very numerous at the present time.

THE FRENCH FEDERATION OF GARMENT WORKERS.
By T. v. d. HEEG.

If we examine the situation of the trade union movement in the garment making
industry throughout the world, it will appear that practically all unions have emerged
from the world war stronger and more influential.

in the movement was
able to withstand the reaction which prevailed during 1920 and 1921. The news from
one country, however, is dismal. That country is France.

Some Results of Indiscriminate Striking.

During 1919 it appeared as if the trade union movement amongst the dressmakers
and tailors in the extensive garment-making industry of that great country had at last
commenced to take root. At the Congress at Lyons, in 1919, the secretary submitted
a return showing a total of 26,000 financial members, whilst the number on the books
was estimated at 40,000. A total of 26,000 financial members was not much for France,
with its extensive garment-making industry, but it held out promise for the future.

This promise has not been fulfilled. Since 1919 the French union has been steadily
on the decline, as the following figures will show :-

This backslide conveys the idea of a debacle.

The Secretary of the French Union, in his report for the period from the 1st July,
1919, to the 30th June, 1921, indicates some of the reasons which led to the great falling-
off in the number of members.

Firstly, he refers to the defeat of the workers in France on the occasion of the general
strike in May, 1920, as a consequence of which great confusion was caused in
the ranks of organised labour. He further attributes the decline to the fierce
debates on questions which have no interest for the great mass of the workers
inside the organisation itself.

actions.
The women especially were frightened by the wild revolutionary talk and
The report is written with great candour, and indicates the weak points of the French
organisation without any colouring.

The history of the French Garment Workers' Federation is like that of Trade Unionism
in France in general during recent times: Mutilated by internal dissent, the French move-
ment is like a warning light at sea for the trade unions of other countries. The Garment
Worker, October, 1921.

PARLIAMENTARY AGENT'S REPORT.
Since my last report much water has flowed under the bridges, but midst all the change that has taken place the problem of poverty arising out of unemployment remains the same, or worse.
It is perhaps worthy of mention that the Labour Party in the House have never let this question remain in abeyance. Right throughout this Parliament it has continuously and persistently raised this issue: What were the intentions of the Government? What preparations were they making to meet the conditions that were bound to evolve? What were the questions that were continually put by labour speakers to the Government, and the answer was, they had the situation in hand, and were taking steps to deal with it.
And how did they act; did they not increase the benefit payable under Unemployment Insurance? The fact that the new benefit was less in value than the pre-war rate did not seem to matter, and the hopelessness of the position did not occur to them that in developing Insurance they were doing nothing to prevent men from falling out of work. It is in this regard that their failure has been the greatest. The country has been told continually that what was needed was to get back our export trade, but what has been done in that direction? The charge that Labour bring against the Government is that their forever policy has prevented export trade rather than helped it.
But the attitude of Labour has not been confined to criticism, our policy has never been purely negative, we have put forward definite proposals, constructive in character, always urging that it is better to set idle labour to work, than to pay out benefit without return for weeks on end. Our first claim for the unemployed has been work, work, work, each of which would give the nation wealth in return, and have helped in the years ahead, useful schemes, such as building houses, schools, roads, afforestation, land reclamation, but our advice was given in vain.
We were unfit to govern, they possessed the brains, the ability, and they would fail with the situation. Neither from the point of view of national well-being, or mere commercial success can they claim any credit, in fact, so discredited is this Government that at bye-elections none can be found to carry their banner.
If Labour governs worse than the present Government, then it will be a case of God help the country.
Almost the last words spoken in the House before it rose in August were uttered by Clynes, when once again on behalf of the Party, he demanded to know what the Government intended to do in regard to unemployment. Before many days had elapsed the situation became serious and Labour demanded the calling together of Parliament to deal with the problem. The Government could not refuse. Men, hungry men, were knocking at the door, demanding justice, refusing any longer to quietly submit to suffer in silence. The Labour Mayors of London refused to allow local authorities to carry the burden which belonged to the nation, refused to permit the poverty arising from unemployment to be met by the poor themselves. Poplar Councillors had gone to prison rather than attempt the impossible of getting blood out of a stone, or in other words asking people for money where it did not exist.
And so Parliament met, but not before the Government had attempted to persuade labour to accept a share of their failures. Labour refused to contribute to a policy of delay. We had made our proposals long before, we had given ample time for consideration, we would explain them if need be, but the responsibility for action rested with them and not with us, we would render help if their proposals were sound, but we must be free to determine our action.
If ever there was a case of the mountain in labour bringing forth a mouse, surely it was in the pitiful proposals of this greatest of all Governments. Once again the poor were to help the poor, and Insurance was to be extended to dependants. Those in work were to keep those out of work. The fact that they had been doing this and had failed because the problem was too great for their Trade Union effort, counted for nothing. The further fact that industry was largely in a state of paralysis did not prevent further burdens being added. The one section of the community that continued to flourish was to be free from obligation. The great kings of finance, who during the depression were able to make their 15 per cent., plus ample amounts placed to reserve, were to contribute nothing. All those employed in that sphere, in fact all who were really able to pay, were to be exempt, while those who perhaps had only just returned to employment, and were possibly only making very short time, had to pay. The single man must pay though he could not claim any benefit.
And when it came to the benefits, they were simply staggering! The wife was to have 5s. and each dependent child Is., with a maximum of 9s. So those with large families where the need was greatest, were to have less per head. If there were six children then either the last or the first two did not need anything. What a mockery of the people

INTERNATIONAL LABOUR OFFICE. DAILY INTELLIGENCE.

Russia. Soviet Schools.
M. Amfiteatroff, the well-known Russian writer, has recently reached Helsingfors.
He has now published his experiences and impressions, of which the following is a summary.
During the Soviet regime he became a teacher in one of the model schools in Petrograd.
One of the principal schemes of the Bolsheviks on their accession to power was the
reorganisation of the schools on communistic lines with a view to lessening home and family
influence over the children and rendering them State-children, having only the interests
of the Communist State at heart.
This scheme has, however, failed for many reasons, the most important of which are
given below.

Teachers.
The quality of teaching in the schools was of a very low standard as, although the
teachers generally did their best, the majority of the old experienced ones had left the
schools and had been substituted by former members of the liberal professions, who, in
order to live, became teachers, but who had had no previous experience in that capacity.
Teachers were, perforce, more interested in obtaining the wherewithal to live than in
the education of the children: this is comprehensible when teachers were paid 700-900
roubles a month for one weekly lesson when bread cost 3,500-4,000 roubles a pound, that
is to say 4-5 hours' teaching.
Amfiteatroff was paid 3,800 roubles per month for 4 hours teaching weekly and when
he crossed the Neva by ferry, which he had to do to get to his school, the journey cost
4,000 roubles.
In order to live, teachers were therefore obliged to procure a large number of lessons
daily, and, owing to the almost complete breakdown of communications, had to walk
from one school to another, often a considerable distance, in a half-famished condition;
their teaching value was consequently very small. Furthermore, salaries were always
in arrear and in many cases never paid at all. Last August the arrears of the Commissariat
of Education amounted to 54-80 billion roubles, and with the exception of 14-15 billions
owing to the Theatrical Section, this sum consisted entirely of unpaid teachers' wages.
Rations were supposed to be issued to the teachers, but this in reality was done most
irregularly and the amount depended greatly on the goodwill and honesty of the distri-
butors.

Schools.
Besides suffering from a great lack of materials the schools were very badly heated
and the teachers and pupils had to wear hats and coats during the lessons; the sanitary
arrangements were in a deplorable condition. When Amfiteatroff left Russia, the question
of closing down a large number of schools owing to want of fuel was being considered.
Only those schools which could find their own fuel were to remain open and the pupils
from the other schools concentrated as far as possible in the heated schools. This scheme
found favour among the Bolsheviks, as they could thus cut down teaching staffs and so
save the Education Department the expense of their salaries and rations.

Social Welfare of the Pupils.
This scheme, whereby the pupils were regarded as State-workers insured by the
State and receiving salaries and which was to be the means of rendering the children
independent of their families and increasing State influence, failed chiefly owing to the
pupils' salaries not being paid for months, and when they were paid the value of the paper
money received had so depreciated as to be practically worthless. The issues of clothes,
boots, &c., which had been promised were never made and the children throughout remained
almost entirely dependent on their families.
For all these reasons the educational system of the Bolsheviks has been a failure,
and almost the only thing it has achieved is the estrangement of children from their parents.
-(Rul, 30th September to 21st October, 1921).

RELIEF ON LOAN.
The Council at their October meeting unanimously passed a resolution expressing
disapproval of the compulsatory attitude of Boards of Guardians offering "relief to be
declared on loan, and the cost thereof being recoverable by proceedings in the County
Court."
This resolution was sent to the Ministry of Health, Mr. W. R. Smith, M.P., J.P., and
the Press.

BRANCH REPORTS.

BARNSLEY. Trade here is very slack and there does not seem much
prospect of it getting better, for pits are working short time, and foundries have
very little to do, and linen trade bad. It seems a dark outlook for the winter
but we are hoping for a better change.

BELFAST. In sending our returns we have to report that trade continues
to remain very bad. We regret to report that the firm of Messrs. Rogan Bros.,
boot repairers, who had five repairing branches and who had all the bench work
done by hand, have opened a Central workshop during the month and are
having the work done by machinery, which has displaced a large number of
our members. We believe the time is opportune for the Council to formulate
a scheme for establishing boot repairing workshops in centres where there is
a reasonable population that would ensure success. We feel that in the course
of time that it would lead up to the establishing of manufacturing workshops.

BRIGHTON.-Trade being bad the employers make it their business to
blame the Trade Boards for it, but they forget that we have about 4,000 to
5,000 out of work, which only the National body can deal with. We are
strong supporters of the Trade Boards because they have raised the standard
of living of the lowest type of workers.

BRISTOL No. 2.-We can only report that trade is slowing down again
and the prospects are not bright. Our sick list is longer than usual; the sudden
change from summer to winter has been too severe a strain for many of our
members to withstand. Regret to report that a factory at Kingswood has
been gutted by fire. This was one of the few firms who were working full
time, and whose prospects were good. It will throw out of employment
about 50 operatives.

CHESHAM.-Trade here and position generally about the same as
previously.

CORK.-Trade here remains bad, the majority of our members being
suspended for an indefinite period.

EDINBURGH.-The Scottish branches held a Conference on the Wages
Trade Board Piece Rates. As there was some difference of opinion regarding
the definition of some items it was called with a view to having every district
paid the same. The Conference proved that all were not being paid alike.
However, we trust that when alterations are made in rates that a meeting
will be held to go fully into the changes. We are sorry to report that one
factory is now working only three days per week, so we are not participating
in the upper grade which several branches have intimated in last month's
Report. The new workers are anxiously awaiting the outcome of the meeting
between National Union and Employers' Federation ; let us hope that an
amicable settlement will be secured. Wishing the members the Compliments
of the Season.

HIGHAM AND RUSHDEN. -Trade in the district has improved con-
siderably although many of our members are unfortunately still unable to
get employment. A claim for a week's wages in lieu of notice from Messrs.
Curtis, Bozeat (who has closed his factory), has been secured through Messrs.
Darnell and Price. Also a case of week's wages in lieu of notice from Messrs.
Brown & Sons, Leicester, for operatives at their branch factory, Irchester,
was referred to the County Board, who decided that the claim was legitimate
and should be paid. A protest against penalising the unemployed members,
who have been out of work for more than 12 months, through no fault of their

LEICESTER WOMEN'S. -The last month finds the Leicester Women's

cerned, very previous. As a Branch we are indebted to the Council for giving

LIVERPOOL. How is trade? In the majority of cases the answer is-
Very quiet; only earned so much last week (mentioning a very low figure).
Is it any wonder members get behind with their contributions? But as we are
expected to keep our accounts straight and free from debt there is only one
course open to us, that is, conform to the rules and if members exceed the limit
of thirteen weeks to strike them off, much as we regret having to do it. Is
the one-man shop doomed in the boot repairing trade? is a query that might
well be asked at the moment, because we find that the people who have un-
limited capital, either individually or in combination, are able to equip a factory
with a full plant of machinery of an up-to-date character and are able by judi-
cious advertising, combined with price-cutting, to monopolise the trade so that
the small man is knocked out of the running or left at the post for the simple
reason that he cannot compete or make enough show for lack of capital. As
the festive season is drawing near, and this will be the last Report before Christ-
mas that will be in the hands of our members, we will close our report by
wishing all officials and members the Compliments of the Season, with a hope
that there are better times in store in the near future.
MAYBOLE. We are pleased to report trade very good and sickness
light. We have the Town Council Election past for another year; two of our
branch, the Secretary and a committeeman returned unopposed, which we think
is quite good. We had Mr. Bleakley here last week to see if we could get every-
body to work to one system, as at present some are on day wages and some
on piecework. The employers felt as it was so near the end of the year they
could not take it up just now. It is to be hoped when our Council meet the
employers on the National Agreement they will at least be able to avoid any
reduction in wages.

good, but we would very much like to see a fillip in the machine sewn trade,

a section that is still very slow although an improvement is taking place some-

PLYMOUTH. —Trade remains quiet and we can see no immediate pro-
pect of improvement, but there is one redeeming feature and just a little ray of
hope in the steady but continuous fall in the cost of living. Many of our mem-
bers earn little more than out-of-work pay, i.e., State and Union, and certainly
no more than some Boards of Guardians are paying for out-relief. But our
members, in spite of adversity, have remained loyal to the principle of Trade
Unionism and mutual help, sharing their work and abiding by the agreement.
to work short time. We see wage-cutting and proposed reductions taking place
all around, sometimes without even a consultation being allowed, while the value
of the worker sinks lower and lower like the value of the German mark. Proh-
ably there is some distant relationship between the two.

REDRUTH.-We regret having to report a further depression in trade,
which has brought about more lost time, and the outlook is gloomy. The
National Health and Unemployment Insurances and Union contributions are
a big drain on an already depleted "pay-bag," but the majority of our members
are optimistic and are looking forward to the better times which must cer-
tainly come. We take this opportunity of appealing to our members to take
a little more interest in the Branch, by attending the monthly meetings for
the purpose of discussing all matters of interest that may arise during the month.
As this will be the last published Report for the year, we tender to all "The
Compliments of the Season."

SOUTHAMPTON.-Shoe Trade very slack and, with little sign of im-
provement in the shipping, shipbuilding and engineering trades, the outlook
has not a rosy appearance.

STAFFORD. There appears to be a slight improvement in trade in this
centre, and there is great need for it; we are hoping it will continue to improve.

STREET.-With the exception of the Turnshoe departments, which are
working full time, there is very little improvement in the state of trade here.
During the month we were very greatly assisted by our Council member, Mr.
J. Manners, in the adjustment of a few local difficulties. We also had the
pleasure of a visit from Mr. W. R. Smith, M.P., who addressed a meeting of
members and a public meeting in the Crispin Hall. Although the attendance
at these meetings was not so large as we would have liked, yet Mr. Smith made
a great impression, and we are grateful for the help both he and Mr. Manners
gave our Branch.

YARMOUTH (GREAT).-Trade is very bad; the few members that are
working are not doing more than two days a week.

In recognition of the golden wedding of Mr. J. H. C. Crockett, J.P., the senior member

as citizens of their various nations. Moreover, at this morning's session I was very
much interested by the statement of my colleague Baldesi. He appealed this morning
to the non-European countries to fall into line a little more quickly with the European
countries and adopt the lead that they are giving them. Here the European countries,
strange to say-France and Great Britain propose what we as workers consider to be
a lead backwards, I hope the non-European countries, in this particular matter, will
come to the aid of the workers, and let these other countries know by their vote that
having regard to the safeguards mentioned in these particular clauses, they are going to
support to the utmost limit the workers' desire, hope and ambition of securing to every
body, so far as is possible, at least a 24-hour weekly rest.
Re Application of Convention to Night Work of Children in Devastated Regions
by the War, it was proposed to extend exemption until 1st July, 1925. I succeeded in
getting this reduced to " 31st December, 1923."
THE PRESIDENT: On an amendment handed in, 1 beg to call on Mr. Poulton.
MR. POULTON (Great Britain): Mr. President, I beg to move that in the last line of
the Recommendation, for words "1st July, 1925," there shall be substituted the words
"31st December, 1923," and I hope our friends will be able to accept the amendment
and incorporate it in the Resolution, so that we need not have a divided vote. I feel sure,
on reflection, they will see that that will give them sufficient time to enable them to deal
with the unfortunate circumstances in their respective countries. I therefore move the
amendment.
FINANCIAL AID TO WOMEN (IN AGRICULTURE) BEFORE
AND AFTER CHILD-BIRTH.
MR. POULTON (Great Britain): Mr. President, I rise to express surprise at the attitude
of Sir Daniel Hall, particularly in view of the answer of the British Government to the
Questionnaire, because the answer of the British Government to the Questionnaire was
that one of the points that they considered was that it would cost too much-not that
it was not a good measure in itself. Then they went on to say in the answer that that
thing is being carried out in Great Britain, and they recite, in a passage on Page 13 of the
blue Report D, the method by which these things are being met in Great Britain. Then
they go on to say in addition, that under the Maternity and Child Welfare Act, 1918, the
Government encourages, and aids, financial schemes of local authorities, and voluntary
agencies, for providing protection and help in the case of expectant mothers. Then they
further recite the number of things the authorities are able to do in respect of these par-
ticular matters.
In view of this, I do hope, and appeal to my colleagues, that they will not put the
British nation in a false position at this Conference, simply because there may be some
ambiguity about the word "similar." I trust, on reconsideration, and having regard to
the answers they have themselves given, and which are published to the whole world,
they will be able, on further reflection, to vote for this particular Recommendation, even
although it may have some ambiguity-and I agree to that extent with Sir Daniel Hall
in that we ought to have explicit and clarified language in these Recommendations and
Conventions. But I suggest that that is not a justification for going to the other extreme,
and saying they will vote against it.
F. L. POULTON, Gen. Sec.

INTERNATIONAL LABOUR.
The Conference at Geneva. Night Work for Children in Agriculture.
GENEVA, TUESDAY,
The International Labour Conference held a plenary session this afternoon, and for-
mally adopted the various recommendations regarding
(1) Night work for children and young persons in agriculture;
(2) Protection of women and children before and after childbirth;
(3) Living-in conditions for agricultural workers.
Speaking with regard to item one, Sir A. Deiall, British Government Delegate, said
he would abstain from voting against the practice of employing children and young persons
on night work in agriculture, as it did not exist in Great Britain.
Mr. W. Barrett, South African Government Delegate, said he was unable to accept
the recommendation regarding the protection of women and children before and after
childbirth, owing to the special conditions prevailing in South Africa.
Sir A. Deiall objected to what he described as the ambiguous wording of the recom-
mendations.

THE INTERNATIONAL CONFERENCE OF WORKING WOMEN.
DELEGATE'S REPORT.
TO THE MEMBERS OF THE COUNCIL.
GENTLEMEN,
Acting on your resolution and instruction I attended the International Conference.
of Working Women at Geneva, which held Sessions from October 17th to 25th, and closed
its proceedings after the adoption of a broad programme dealing with the social and
economic difficulties of the world of to-day. Delegates were present from Belgium, Cuba,
Czecho Slovakia, France, Great Britain, Italy, Norway, Poland, South Africa, Switzerland,
United States and China. There were also many guests from various countries. Thus
was the second meeting of the Women's International, the first meeting being held at
Washington in October, 1919.

The objects of the International Federation of Working Women (new name adopted,
are threefold: (1) to promote trade union organisation among women; (2) to develop
an international policy, giving special consideration to the needs of women and children
and to examine all projects for legislation proposed by the International Labour Conference
of the League of Nations; (3) and to promote the appointment of working women on
organisations affecting the welfare of the workers.

In order to bring about closer co-operation between the working women of Europe
the Secretariat will be located in London, England, for the next two years. The new
Executive Board is as follows:-

Mrs. Raymond Robins .. United States President.
Miss Burniaux .. Belgium Vice-President.
Mrs. Laura de Zayas Bazan .. Cuba Vice-President.
Mrs. Bozena Kubickova .. Czecho-Slovakia Vice-President.
Miss Jeanne Bouvier .. France Vice-President.
Miss Margaret Bondfield .. Great Britain Vice-President.
Signora Cabrini Casartelli .. Italy Vice-President.
Mrs. Betzy Kjelsberg .. Norway Vice-President.
Miss Sophie Dobrzanska .. Poland Vice-President.
Miss Fitzgerald .. South Africa Vice-President.
Miss Monnier .. Switzerland Vice-President.
Mrs. Maud Swartz .. United States Vice-President.
Dr. Marion Phillips .. Great Britain Secretary.
Mrs. Harrison Bell .. Great Britain Treasurer.

The Congress was opened by M. Albert Thomas, Director of the International Labour
Office, M. Oudegeest, General Secretary of the Amsterdam Trade Union Internationa
M. Jouhaux and Fimmen also addressing the Congress.

Commissions were appointed and reports were duly presented on :-
(1) The Future Constitution of the Women's International.
(2) Unemployment.
(3) Limitation of Armaments.
(4) Two Commissions on Agriculture.
(5) Anthrax.
(6) Lead Poisoning.
(7) Weekly rest day.

A lengthy report was given on the Draft Conventions adopted at Washington, and
how many countries had ratified those conventions. The British delegation was compelled
to feel humiliation at their Government deciding, on their own responsibility, not to ratify
the Washington Maternity Convention, which proposes a sufficient payment to insure
full and healthy maintenance for mother and child six weeks before and six weeks after
childbirth, apart and wholly unconnected with the Poor Law.

I was appointed on two Commissions-The Constitution and Weekly Rest Day.

The Commission for the Constitution was very interesting, and in some respects very
difficult. If all spoke one language it might have been easier, but all who have experienced
the difficulty of languages and translation will know that one word upsets the whole fabric,
although the meaning when understood is exactly what is desired by all countries.

The Weekly Rest Day we, in this country, have enjoyed since 1677. We ask for
an international law definitely fixing the rest period of one day and a half. In all cases
where this is impossible, a supplementary salary should be paid, also an equal period of rest
compensation. These conditions to apply to domestic servants and agricultural workers.

I advocated and obtained the support of Conference that 12 days' holiday with pay,
also 10 minutes' rest periods for all workers in the morning and afternoon of each full day,
concession especially is to all who never move from their work for hours at a stretch.
should be included in this Commission. From experience I know how desirable the latter

We gave the resolutions on disarmament and unemployment careful consideration,
for these two questions are in our minds closely connected, since one of the chief causes
of unemployment is the disruption of industry following a great war. Working women
do not need to be convinced of the useless waste involved in competitive armaments.
but the delegates desired to find an effective way in which to press their points of view
upon those chosen to govern them.

The disarmament resolution of the Congress was a pronouncement in favour of a policy
of total disarmament, and the Congress urged the powers convening at Washington, on
November 11th, to hold their deliberations in open session, and to take steps to bring about
total disarmament. In order to give added force to this decision, the Congress voted to
send a representative to Washington, and Miss Kate Manicom, of the Workers' Union of
Great Britain, was chosen to carry to Washington and to President Harding a message
from the working women of the world.

It was a source of pleasure for me to be able to meet Miss Steghagen, a member of the
Boot and Shoe Workers of America, who assured me their closing-room operatives earned
an average of £5 to £7 per week; other information she is posting on to me. Also Miss
Zung, of China, supplied me with information regarding the manufacture of boots and shoes
in China, which was very interesting and surprising.

Altogether the Congress was to my mind a huge success. In addition to the results
obtained, it was a great opportunity and privilege to be there. It gave new courage to
some of us who went from Great Britain feeling that everything we did was not worth
while, and seemed to give renewed faith in the new and better world that will be to-morrow.
I thank the Council for this opportunity afforded me.

Yours sincerely,
M. J. BELL-RICHARDS,
Delegate.

PARLIAMENTARY DEBATES.

BOOT AND SHOE TRADE (ADMIRALTY ORDERS).

MR. WATERSON asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Admiralty whether any
decision has been arrived at as to the advisability of anticipating future contracts for boots
and shoes for the Navy, with a view to relieving unemployment in the boot and shoe
industry; and, if so, will he state such and, if not, what is the cause of delay, and when
may a decision be expected?

COMMANDER EYRES-MONSELL: It is not possible to place orders requiring payment
in the current financial year beyond those already determined or to meet current needs,
as the money provision made by Parliament will not permit the expenditure involved.
I understand that it has not been found possible to allocate any part of the special grant
for relieving unemployment for this purpose.-(Extract from Parliamentary Debates,
Tuesday, 1st November, 1921).

MR. WATERSON asked the Secretary of State for War whether his Department has
disposed of any soiled or unsoiled Army boots during the last 12 months; if so, the amount,
and how they were disposed of, whether by private treaty or public sale; and whether any
Government Department has disposed of any stocks of boots purchased primarily for the
Army?

MR. YOUNG: I have been asked to answer this question. The Disposal Board has
sold during the past 12 months by public auction, public tender, or private treaty, approxi-
mately 1,750,000 pairs of footwear. Nearly 1,500,000 pairs were Army boots of varying
descriptions and varying degrees of serviceability, and the rest consisted of clogs, shoes,
waders, wood-soled trench boots, slippers and other miscellaneous items.-(Extract from
Parliamentary Debates, Tuesday, 8th November, 1921).

MR. WALTER SMITH,-To ask the Parliamentary Secretary to the Admiralty, if he can
state the names and addresses of the firms contracting for the supply of boots and clogs
for his department at the present time.

MR. EYRES MONSELL: No orders have been placed for boots or clogs since March
last. The names and addresses of the contractors accepted were published as usual in
the Board of Trade Labour Gazette of April last, to which I would refer the hon. Member.-
(Extract from Parliamentary Debates, 8th November, 1921).

The most important work of the week was the foundation of the new organisation
under the name of the International Federation of Working Women. The constitution
presented by commissions was adopted without amendment and with complete unanimity
save for the delegates of the Christian Trade Unions. The constitution
Unions will be excluded from membership in the future and they entered their protest
bias is trade union but the organisations of working women working for the same objects
as the Trade Union organisations are specially included as eligible for membership.
very great difficulty was found in including the specifically political organisations as the
situation in several Continental countries is now so difficult that the Trade Union reore
sentatives cannot yet attempt an organisation on that broad basis. After many meetings
words was finally agreed upon and the objects and membership of the Federation adopted
in the following terms:

OBJECT.

The object of the Federation shall be to unite organised working women in order
that they may resolve upon the means by which the standard of the life of the workers
throughout the world may best be raised.
With this purpose in view, the Federation shall :---
(a) Promote trade union organisation among women.
(b) Develop an international policy giving special consideration to the needs
of women and children, and examine closely all projects for legislation
proposed by the League of Nations, and especially by the International
Labour Conferences.
(c) Promote the appointment of women to represent organised working
women on all organisations and committees dealing with the questions
affecting the welfare of the workers.

MEMBERSHIP.

(a) The Federation shall consist of national trade union organisations, containing
women members, and affiliated to the International Federation of Trade Unions;
it shall also admit working women's organisations accepting its aims and agreeing
to work in the spirit and to follow the principles of the International Federation of
Trade Unions.
(b) Where the trade unions organisation is not affiliated with the International
Federation of Trade Unions, the Executive Board shall decide what national body
representing organised working women shall be accepted.
(c) Only one organisation shall be accepted from each country.
(d) In the case of any controversy as to eligibility, the Executive Board shall
decide, and submit that decision to the full Congress of the Federation for its approval.

The remainder of the constitution dealt with Management, the Biennial Congress,
Headquarters and Finance. It is now being printed and will be circulated as soon as

NORTHAMPTONSHIRE JOINT DISTRICT COUNCIL.
Report of the First Annual Meeting of the Northamptonshire
Joint District Council held at Northampton,
October 29th, 1921.

The president, Mr. W. Townley, Northampton No. 1, occupied the chair and repre
sentatives were present from all the districts in the County. The General President,
Mr. T. F. Richards, sent a telegram regretting that he was unable to attend, being confined
at home with an attack of influenza.

The Secretary presented the financial statement for the year, after which the following
officers were appointed :-Mr. Geo. Chester, Kettering No. 1, to be President. Mr. A.
Lyne, Northampton No. 2, to be Vice-President. Mr. S. J. B. Barnes, Desborough, to be
Secretary and Treasurer. Mr. L. Poole, Wellingborough, to be Auditor. Messrs. W
Langley, Higham and Rushden, W. A. Wyman, Wellingborough, E. Chapman, Kettering
No. 2, I. H. Johnson, Daventry, to be with the officers, the Executive Committee.

The Secretary then presented the first annual report of the District Council, as follows:
In presenting this first annual report of the work of the District Council I think it
will be interesting to preface it by giving a short account of the events that led up to its
formation.

The Council had its inception in its original form as the Northamptonshire Advisory
Committee on the 28th August, 1915. Previous to this date several joint meetings of an
informal character had been held at Wellingborough, called by Mr. S. Thompson, when he
was Council member for Northants.

The Old Advisory Committee was born as a result of the conditions brought about
by the great war, when New War Boots were being made all over the country to meet the
demands of the Allied Armies for footwear.

Under the usual method of fixing prices in each separate locality, for the different
boots, it can quite easily be understood, that with no co-ordination between the districts,
varying prices were arrived at and agreed to. This state of things was brought to an
head in the prices that were fixed by the Kettering and Northampton Boards of Arbitration
for the cutting of the Serbian Army Boots.

As a result of this anomaly, it was felt that some organisation ought to be created,
whose duty it should be to try and arrive at some uniform price and policy. A meeting
was therefore held at Wellingborough on the 28th August, 1915, when it was decided to
form a Northamptonshire Advisory Committee, the duty of this committee being to meet
when any new boot needed pricing, or when any new machines or method of production
was introduced, in order that some price might be agreed upon that should be adopted
as far as possible throughout the county.

A constitution was duly drawn up and agreed to at a meeting held at Wellingborough,
18th September, 1915, Mr. Jas. Gribble being appointed secretary and the General President,
Mr. T. F. Richards, President.

At that time, owing to the growth of the Union in the smaller places of the County,
and the desirability of linking them up in an Arbitration Board, Mr. Thos. Smith, who
had acted as umpire in many trade disputes, suggested that a Joint Board be formed for
Northants, and following a meeting in London under the chairmanship of Mr. Askwith,
it was decided that a County Board be formed for the County branches of Northampton-
shire, to deal with Civilian Statements and prices.

Later on the same problems that had manifested themselves in Northants, began to
be met in other parts of the country, and so the National Joint Standing Committee was
formed to deal with all prices relating to Government Contracts for Army work. Their
findings were issued in what was known as the Red Book of Army prices. Thus was
uniformity obtained throughout the whole of the country, in regard to this particular
class of work.

The Northamptonshire Advisory Committee, having been formed to deal with the
problems of obtaining as much uniformity as possible, its work was almost exclusively
confined to the building up of statements.

The Committee, however, having been formed for a definite purpose, and, in a way,
having almost accomplished that purpose when it had agreed to a basis for all depart-
mental statements, its influence began to wane. Being advisory in character, it possessed
the limitations of an advisory body, although there was in the idea of its formation, the
germ of a greater idea, which ultimately realised itself in the present Joint District Council.

District Councils became a part of the organisation of the Union as a result of the
passing of a resolution sent to the Edinburgh Conference of 1920 by the Kettering No. 1
and 2 branches.

Our Industrial Policy should be linked to our Educational Policy, so that there
be a coherent whole. Our National agreements should be built up to attain the
end, so that, little by little, clause by clause, we shall come to that point when we
have an agreement that will give expression to our desires.
Our Political Policy should be so framed, that it will be able to give legal sanction
to our desires as expressed in our agreements.
The problem is to devise ways and means of co-ordinating our various activities
that by a concentration of ideas, and their application to the problems that face us,
shall be in a position to advance along the road we desire to traverse.
S. J. B. BARNES,

THE BOOT AND SHOE INDUSTRY OF CANADA.
HISTORY OF THE INDUSTRY.
The early history of the boot and shoe manufacturing industry in Canada still awaits
research by the historian in the archives of the Old Régime, but a few facts of interest
relative to the beginnings of the industry have been uncovered. In 1667, the Jesuits
wrote to Old France that, as a country could not be formed entirely without the assistance
of manufactures, an industry was already in operation in the Colony making shoes and
hats, and another was contemplated for linen and leather. We are told that in the same
year, when the first census of New France was taken, showing a total population of 3.215.
there were twenty shoemakers in the colony. By 1671, one-third of all the shoes required
by the people were made out of leather manufactured locally. A tannery was established
in Quebec about 1670, and we read that in 1691 ox and moose skins were tanned in that
place. Prior to Confederation in 1867, and for several decades thereafter, the handicraft
system was general and little machinery was employed. The Census of 1871 reported
4,191 leather shoe manufacturing establishments. The majority of these, of course,
were not factories in the modern sense, but simply the establishments of small custom
shoemakers. The boot and shoe industry of Canada in 1870 gave employment to 18,719
persons, and the value of output was officially reported as $16,133,638. On this basis
it was Canada's third largest manufacturing industry. The decade 1870-80 was notable
for the introduction of the McKay sole sewing machines and various edge trimming and
finishing devices, and the period 1880-90 saw the adoption of the Goodyear sewing machinery
which revolutionised the art of shoemaking. The making of fine shoes in Canada may
indeed be said to date from about 1885-90.

INTERNATIONAL LABOUR ORGANISATION.
THIRD GENERAL CONFERENCE.
of the League of Nations opened at Geneva on the 25th October. This Geneva Conference
The third meeting of the General Conference of the International Labour Organisation
sation prescribed by Article 389 of the Treaty of Versailles. The first meeting was held
is the third of the series of annual General Conferences of the International Labour Organi
in October and November, 1919, at Washington, U.S.A., and the second at Genoa in June
The agenda of the present meeting has already been published in The
and July, 1920.
Labour Gazette, as also the list of British Delegates and their Technical Adviserse
French Government to the inclusion in the agenda of the Conference of any item con-
At the first session, on the 25th October, Viscount Burnham was elected president of
the Conference. In the following sittings the Conference discussed the objection of the
cerning agricultural labour. A resolution was passed on the 27th October, by 74 vote.
to 20, declaring the competence of the Conference to deal with matters relating to agricul.
tural labour, in the following terms :-
The Conference, considering that it has jurisdiction to deal with matters relating
to agricultural labour, and considering that the agrenda as proposed by the Governing
Body is in accord both with the decisions taken by the Washington Conference and with
the reasonable demands of the agricultural workers, decides to consider the expedienc
of retaining the question under 2, 3 and 4 of the agenda, taking each of these questions
in succession."
On the 28th October the Conference voted on the specific question whether item
of the agenda should be retained, that is: "The adaptation to agricultural labour of the
Washington decisions concerning the regulation of the hours of work." There voted 63
in favour of retention and 39 against. The requisite two-thirds majority in favour of the
item remaining on the agenda was therefore not obtained, and the question of hours of
work in agriculture was removed from the scope of the Conference. On the 31st October.
however, a resolution was carried, by 73 votes to 18, proposed by the British, Italian and
Dutch Government Delegates, in the following terms :-
"The third session of the International Labour Conference decides that the regulation
of the hours of work in agriculture be inserted in the agenda of a future session of the
Conference."
On the 29th October it was resolved to retain items 3 and 4 on the agenda by votes of go
against 17, and 93 against 13, respectively.
On the 31st October, in accordance with the procedure established at Washington
and Genoa, the Conference proceeded to set up a commission to deal with each item of
the agenda. To these commissions are referred the results of the preliminary investigations
of the International Labour Office. The appropriate commission arrives at decisions
upon each topic of the agenda, which may take the form either of draft conventions,
recommendations or resolutions, and the reports of the commissions, embodying the
texts of these decisions, are then to be discussed by the full Conference.
Eight different commissions of this kind have been set up, each consisting of an equal
number of representatives of Governments, employers and workers. Three of the com-
missions will deal with matters relating to agriculture, the first dealing with the questions
of unemployment and the protection of workers in agriculture against accidents, sickness,
invalidity and old age; the second with the protection of women and children and the
living-in conditions of agricultural workers; and the third with the question of technical
agricultural education and the guarantee to agricultural workers of the rights of association
and combination. The other commissions deal with the questions of the reform of the
constitution of the Governing Body of the International Labour Office, a weekly rest day
in industrial and commercial employment, the prohibition of the use of white lead in
painting, the disinfection of wool infected with anthrax spores, and two matters left over
from the Genoa Conference, namely, the prohibition of the employment of persons under
the age of 18 years as trimmers or stokers, and the compulsory medical examination of
all children employed on board ship.
On the 9th November the full Conference discussed a report by the Director-General
of the International Labour Office on the work of the Office since its foundation. The
Labour Gazette, November, 1921.

BOOT AND SHOE TRADE.
In this trade employment on the whole continued slack during November, with much
short time and unemployment. There was an improvement in some districts, but in others
there was a decline; on the whole, there was little change as compared with October.
The percentage of workpeople unemployed in boot, shoe and slipper making and
repairing establishments, as indicated by the unemployment books lodged at Employment
Exchanges, was 9.5 at the 2nd December, as compared with 9.7 per cent. at the
4th November. In addition, 2.4 per cent. of the workpeople were claiming benefit in
respect of systematic short-time working at the 2nd December, as compared with 2.5 per
cent. at the 4th November. According to the returns received from firms furnishing
returns, however, over 40 per cent. of the workpeople were working short time at the end
of November, to the extent of 13 hours a week on the average.

machinery is also most desirable-even spades, ploughs, sowing-machines.

the sending of these tractors might be an exceedingly wise and perhaps an
exceedingly remunerative commercial undertaking.
It would help to relieve the terrible crisis of Unemployment in the countries

which is, by ensuring production for the urgent needs of other and still more
un'ortunate people who need the goods which will be produced. This is a task
which cannot be accomplished by relief from charitable sources alone. It is
too great. The Governments must come in, and I am sure they will come in
in the end. What is the situation? Is there any lack of food in the world?

NATIONAL CONFERENCE INTERIM AGREEMENT, DECEMBER, 1921.

At a meeting of the National Joint Conference held at 7, Tavistock Square, London,
W.C. I, on Thursday, 15th December, 1921, it was agreed and determined that the clauses
regulations contained in the National Conference Agreement dated the 13th February,
319, shall remain in full force and effect, with the exception of clauses 8, 9, 10, 11 and 12
shall be substituted, and it is further agreed that these revisions in the minimum wage
of the said Agreement for which the following wage rates and piecework percentages
ad piecework percentages together with clauses 7, 8, 9 and 10, herein contained, shall
be recognised as the December, 1921, Interim Agreement.

1.  That a first reduction of 4s. per week on Daywork wages (men 23 years of age
and upwards), and 5 per cent. on Piecework earnings, shall take place on the
second pay day in January, 1922.
That a first reduction of 2s. per week on Daywork wages (women 20 years of age
and upwards), and per cent. on Piecework earnings, shall take place on the
second pay day in January, 1922.

The above reductions are conditional upon the index figure of
the cost of living not rising above 110 full points as quoted by the
Ministry of Labour in the December, 1921, issue of the "Labour
Gazette."
2.  That a second reduction of 4s. per week on Daywork wages (men 23 years of age
and upwards), and 2 ½ per cent. on Piecework earnings, shall take place on the
second pay day in June, 1922.
That a second reduction of 2s. per week on Daywork wages (women 20 years of
age and upwards), and per cent. on Piecework earnings, shall take place on the
second pay day in June, 1922.

The wage rates as fixed by Clause 2, shall remain in operation
until July 6th, 7th, or 8th, 1922.

very considerably fallen readjustments of wages will take place if such pro-
posals are endorsed. The first readjustment will take effect on the second
pay day in January, and the next one the second week in June, and no further

The membership may rest assured it is not at all a pleasant thing for us,
as representing the Union, to have to present such a report to you. We have,
however, had to bear in mind that the cost of living has come down, and also
the undisputed facts that nearly every Trade Union in the country has been
forced to face the altered circumstances brought about by such reduced costs,
and have had to readjust wages accordingly.
We are fully persuaded in our own minds that we have secured the utmost
amounts from the Employers' representatives under the various headings
that can be secured, and, as already stated, however unpleasant it may be to
have to present such a report, we feel bound to point out to the membership
that a rejection of this offer may bring about such a state of circumstances
that will not be to our advantage. We trust, therefore, that when the members
vote in JANUARY they will fully bear in mind the responsibility attaching to
their vote.
