GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.

FELLOW MEMBERS,
The month has been occupied very strenuously with the proposed alteration in
the National Agreement, the terms of which will be submitted to the delegates on December
20th at Leicester, and afterwards, we hope, submitted to the members in accordance
with our rules and regulations governing same.
Those of us who have formed the Nego-
tiating Committee cannot, neither do we wish to, dissociate ourselves with what has
been done At the same time we have done all we could to obtain what we consider as
be the best conditions obtainable, and although the full Council at the Conference obtained
a little more, still they find themselves in the position of submitting to the delegates and
then the members the best terms they have been able to get. Personally, I am sorry
the employers have decided to imitate Chesham and be determined to insist at the point
of the bayonet on a reduction in the rates. They refuse to recommend arbitration to their
members, which means they may have given us notice to withdraw from the Guarantee
Fund, and such a position must first of all be considered by our own members in conference,
and their findings referred to a ballot vote of the members, who have the power to accept
or reject our advice; and should the members make up their minds to decline them, we
should then be faced with a protracted struggle with everything favourable to the employers.
We shall have more to say than it is wise to put into print to our delegates and members,
We shall have more to say than it is wise to put into print to our delegates and members,
and strengthen our forces, and abide the time when it is most favourable to us when we
been able to secure, and take warning that if we are wise we shall double our membership
go bargaining again. On this occasion the employers had not a leg to stand on and they
had to resort to the brutal weapon of stand-and-deliver. We reminded them that the
Trade Board has a minimum of 65s., and no request has been made to alter it. Also that
the Rossendale Valley people had at present an understanding that no reduction be per-
mitted after the cost of living reached 125 per cent. as a basis. We also reminded them
of the low rates always paid to shoe workers, and that to-day they were behind many
other operatives in their hourly rate of pay, but all arguments were of no avail, they just
wielded the big stick and sat tight.

CHESHAM has been visited and every effort made to strengthen the membership
and ultimately notices were handed in, only to find that two days before their expiration
we were advised by the whole of the circumstances to withhold them for the present,
and to impose at a later date the findings of the National Conference. This we ultimately
agreed to do, and at the present time we are bound to demand that Chesham, who have
accepted the 1919 position, must toe the line by demanding 8s. per week rise for Dayworkers
and 10 per cent. rise for Pieceworkers. This should be an impetus to the whole of the
workers in that town, and this in itself should be watched by our members who think that
we are not sufficiently aggressive. Eyam, Stoney Middleton, Preston, Melbourne, Nantwich,
are still little worlds to conquer. Some day may we not add to them ?

TRADE BOARD Meetings have also been attended and the interests of our members
engaged therein. Although the employers have tabled a motion asking for a 10 per cent.
reduction on the piecework rates, we hope to minimise this by getting it lowered.
The Handsewn men belonging to the Amalgamated Union of Handsewn Men, and also
the Union known as the London and Provincial, have had a 12½ per cent. reduction imposed
upon them as early as last October, and they were compelled without a struggle to accept.
A further meeting of the Advisory Committee of the Trade Union Congress, who
assist all Trade Boards, met to choose witnesses for the Cave Committee, it being decided
that any Union has the right to choose witnesses if they think well to do so.
We have also attended a Special Conference on Unemployment at the Memorial Hall,
when, after a deputation of unemployed had addressed the Conference, an omnibus reso-
lution was carried. I am really at a loss to understand what useful purpose such Con-
ference on this occasion served, as we had dealt with the same subject with greater force
at Cardiff last September.

CO-OPERATORS AND OUR MEMBERS. - We have met the Wages Board for South Yorks.
several times, and at the last meeting they pressed for a reduction of 12½ per cent. We
took the matter to the Joint Board of Co-operators and Trade Unionists, and ultimately
agreed to 74s. per week for Dayworkers, and for the Trade Board Statement with 20 per
cent. added for Pieceworkers. This means 6½ per cent. off Pieceworkers and 6s. per week
off Dayworkers.

The GENERAL FEDERATION OF TRADE UNIONs are still making members and strength-
ening their position by degrees. Rumour has it that several big Unions who at one time
belonged to it are seriously considering their present position and comparing same to their
association with the Federation. One of the Organisers commences his duties in January.

BRANCH REPORTS.
BELFAST. We very much regret we are still unable to report any
improvement in trade. We also regret that the Belfast Master Boot Repairers'
Association has reduced the piece rates to those provided by the Trades Board.
We consider the method adopted to reduce the rates most unfair in not giving
us an opportunity of meeting them in conference to consider what the reduction
should be, nor when it should become operative. We were also very much
disappointed at the action of the Co-operative Society being the first to give
notice of a reduction in wages. The Secretary interviewed the manager and
had the reduction postponed for two weeks. We are very much disappointed
at the lack of interest which the members take in the workings of the branch.
The bad state of trade cannot but have a depressing effect upon those members,
willing to work but unable to obtain it; still that is not a sufficient reason for
any member not paying into his trade organisation which has for its object
the uplifting and improvement of its members, that he will not accept it as a
responsibility and a duty to spare two hours in the month to meet to consider
and discuss those matters that appertain to the social and industrial welfare
of the members generally.

BRISTOL AND KINGSWOOD No. 2.- We are sorry to report that trade
is very slow, and that the out-of-work and sick list is longer than for some
time past. Speculation is rife as to what changes in wages will be made as a
result of the Conference now in progress. If we take the yearly income of the
operatives as a guide, one is safe in saying that no sane impartial judge would
give a verdict for less than at present obtains. We think the industry should
offer a fair chance of a decent livelihood to those engaged in it, but recent
experience shows that it is necessary to have a private income to enable one
to maintain a decent standard of comfort. This we think is not as it should be,
as manufacturers, in spite of their losses, appear to carry on very comfortable,
and we believe that properly apportioned there is sufficient in the industry
to satisfy the needs of all. We certainly hope for the best, and we are looking
forward to 1922 to do us a better turn than 1921.

CHESHAM.-Trade here has improved since our last report, but we still
have a number of our members unemployed. We desire to thank the Council
and Organisers for the assistance rendered during the past month, and this
being our last report of the year we wish all Officers and Members a Merry
Christmas.

CHESTERFIELD.-Trade fair, though the members are working short
time. We wish all members the Compliments of the Season and hope the
New Year will be brighter for all the members than the past has been.

HALESWORTH.-Trade is not so flourishing as last month. We do not
work at all on Saturdays and the finishing department is closed on Mondays
unless there is an order or two to get off, which is very seldom.

HIGHAM AND RUSHDEN.—There is a fair trade in the District at
present. Some employers are going back on day-work. Meetings have been
held of workpeople who have been instructed to work to quantities allowed in
statements for wages paid, and not exceed same, unless paid for. Fewer
members are signing Out-of-Work Book. A very interesting event took place
at the Rushden Monthly Meeting when Mr. A. C. Allen (who had given his
services free), Tutor of Economics Class, was presented by the Branch with
Percy Wallis' latest book, "Wages and Prices." The presentation was made
by Mr. C. Bates, who paid a glowing tribute to the work done in the Economics
Class, and its advantages to the younger members of the Union. Several
members supported the President in praise of the work done.

KINGSWOOD AND DISTRICT. We are not sorry that this report is

of exceptional unemployment and its attendant evils. We extend to all
Officers and Members of the Union our compliments, wishing them individually

LIVERPOOL. - Trade is very quiet, but we do not anticipate there will

MAYBOLE. We are pleased to report sickness light and trade good.

the first for two years. We are pleased to see a settlement of the Irish question
the Compliments
dependant on Ireland for a good deal of our trade. As it is nearing

NEWCASTLE.-Trade in this district is very bad, owing to the number
of workmen on Tyneside being unemployed. Another cause is that the mining
districts round about are only working one or two days a week, and some of
the pits are not working at all. Taking everything into consideration, we are
not so baldy hit for work as some other trades. It is to be hoped that with
the advent of the New Year that things will take a turn for the better. We
notice again through the weekly trade papers that the Newcastle Employers'
Association are again raising the war cry, "Lower wages for the workmen."
Most of these employers of labour have been workmen themselves, and now
they are in business for themselves, and are able to employ one workman,
forget the time they were workers themselves, and the struggle they had for
an existence on the prices that were then paid for their labour at that time.
Surely they are not going to be the instigators of a reduction in the workers'
wages, knowing full well the conditions they had to work under when they
were workers. We are sorry for these employers, whom we used to call
brothers, that they have so soon been smitten with what we generally term
"swelled head," and think they are of some importance, and a big bug in the
trade. Each and everyone of us have our own opinion of these so-called
"gaffers." Wishing all our fellow members a Merry Christmas and a Prosperous
New Year.

PLYMOUTH. We wish all members the Compliments of the Season,
and sincerely hope that 1922 will bring new life and vigour to our trade, and
prosperity to our members. Probably the year of 1921 will stand as the
darkest in the history of our trade, for it has been a year of distress and great
anxiety, intensified by the high cost of living and trade depression. If the
real wages of the workers during 1921 could be published in a simple and
comprehensible form we believe we should hear no more about the high wages
said to be earned by the workers, certainly not in our trade. We believe that
the trade barometer has now registered the lowest mark of trade depression,
and we look forward to the New Year with fresh hope and courage, with the
Irish war ending, the Washington Conference showing signs of success, the
enormous burden of armaments lifted from the backs of the workers, it now
remains for the statesmen to free the main arteries of trade from the strangle-
hold of debt, and transfer a little more purchasing power from those who have
to those who have not. Will they do it? If not the New Year may arrive

A SPECIAL EMERGENCY CONFERENCE
On Unemployment and the International Situation, the Russian Famine and the Peace Treaty
was held in the Memorial Hall, Farringdon Street, London, E.C. on Thursday, December 8th, 1021, the Union being represented by Mr. and Mrs. Richards, and the Parliamentary Candidates of the Union also attended.

Resolutions as follows were passed:
"That this Conference of the united industrial and political Labour Movement reiterates the claims that the Trades Union Congress and the Labour Party Conference have made from time to time that Unemployment should be a national charge and concern, and emphasises at this crisis the fact that our present industrial misfortunes are largely owing to the international policy which our Government has been pursuing, particularly as regards Russia and Central Europe, and that a reversal of that policy is necessary in the interests of the wage earners of this country.

Unemployment and the Russian Famine.
"The Conference pledges its support to the Russian Workers and extends to them its sympathy in their terrible distress arising primarily out of food shortage which, however, is not only a failure of nature but a consequence of a policy of blockade and refusal to trade, and therefore calls upon the Government--
(1) To assist in a substantial way the distress for which it must accept some considerable responsibility, and so enable this country to range itself alongside the humanitarian efforts now being made to save life and relieve the suffering;
(2) To take steps at once to re-open trade, particularly for the export of articles required for immediate use in Russia, which might be made in this country, as part of a policy to relieve our own unemployed and restart industry."

Unemployment and the Economic Clauses of the Peace Treaty.
"The Conference emphatically condemns the foreign policy of the Government since the Armistice as being largely responsible for the present industrial condition of the country. and draws attention specifically to the following, which have had a direct and disastrous effect upon British Employment:
(1) The destruction of Central European trade and markets in pursuit of a policy of punishing by poverty the workers of the late enemy countries;
(2) The scheme of reparation imposed on Germany, which has clearly damaged British production and imports, as in the case of the deliveries of coal and ready-made shipping;
(3) The trade policy which has kept the mark and the coinage of Central Europe in such a fluctuating condition that international trade is almost impossible;
(4) The clauses in the Versailles and other Treaties relating to territorial distributions which have prevented peace and have kept Europe economically unsettled.

The Conference, therefore, calls upon the Government:
(1) To take immediate action with a view to the stabilisation of the exchanges
(a) by the removal of all the artificial political impediments to international trade that now exist, and
(b) by promoting normal conditions of production on the Continent of Europe by a system of credits or an international loan;
(2) To take steps at once in conjunction with our former Allies to revise the territorial and economic clauses in the Treaty of Versailles that are necessitating an armed occupation of the greater part of Central Europe;
(3) To come to an immediate arrangement with the Allies for a revision of the indemnity obligations which, whilst providing for reparation of actual destruction done in Northern France and Belgium, will frankly recognise that any general payments made by enormous exports of goods only injure the industry of the receiving nation and are indeed borne by its wage earners in the shape of low wages and unemployment, and will therefore abandon such payments;
(4) To promote an arrangement among all the nations associated in the war for the cancellation of their mutual indebtedness created by and during the state of war.

The Conference finally declares that until such a change in policy has taken place, British industry cannot be healthy and British Labour will continue to be threatened with Unemployment and wage reductions, and it holds the Government, which declines to pursue this change, responsible for the serious industrial condition of the country."

STANDING ORDERS OF THE CONFERENCE.
RULE 80.
ANNUAL MEETINGS.
Annual Meetings of the Conference shall be held on Whit Monday
and subsequent days.
TIME OF CONFERENCE MEETING.
RULE 81. On the first day of Conference the Delegates shall assemble at a
place provided for the purpose, at TEN O'CLOCK A.M. PROMPT, and
shall proceed to the election of Door Keeper and Two Tellers, and
shall also consider the President's Address and Council's Report:
after which the Conference shall adjourn at 12.30 p.m. and re-assemble
at 2 p.m., and proceed with the business of the Conference and adjourn
at 5 p.m. On Tuesday and each succeeding day, the time of meeting
shall be 9.30 a.m., adjourn at 12.30 p.m., re-assemble at 2 p.m., and
adjourn for the day at 5 p.m.
DELEGATES' QUALIFICATION.
RULE 82. The Conference shall consist of Delegates who have been clecter!
in accordance with General Rules 71 and 77:-
"Delegates shall be elected in accordance with the number of Financial
Members returned in the December Report previous to the date on which
the Conference is to be held. All Permanent Officials shall attend the
Conferences by virtue of their office, over and above the maximum of
representation. The basis of representation for delegates shall be one
delegate for every 1,000 financial members, with a minimum representa
tion of not less than fifty delegates (one-third to form a quorum)."
"The latest date for sending in amendments and additions to Rules, or
Standing Orders of Conference, shall be January 15th, in the year in
which the Conference is due to be held, and they shall be published in
the January Monthly Report. Nominations for delegates shall be taken
on the February Monthly Meeting Night, and voting for same on the
March Monthly Meeting Night."
The Council to attend by virtue of their office.
PRESIDENT OF CONFERENCE.
RULE 83.-The President of the Union, by virtue of his office, takes the chair
at all Conferences.
STANDING ORDERS COMMITTEE.
RULE 84.- A committee of five persons shall be elected from the Delegates
of the Conference, whose duty it shall be to examine the Delegates'
Credentials, and report thereon. They shall also be at the service of the
Conference to consider any questions or matters that may be relegated
to it with a view to reporting thereon during the sitting of Con-
ference. For such extra services they shall receive additional pay,
to the amount of 10s. each.

FIRST ANNUAL CONFERENCE.
London, Whitsuntide, 1921.

The following resolutions have been received for consideration at Conference at Whitsuntide.

UNION POLICY.

KILMARNOCK.-" The Kilmarnock Branch of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives call upon the Executive Council to take all necessary steps to secure the proper election of delegates to the World Congress of Labour Unions to be held in Moscow on May 1st, 1921, pledged to support a revolutionary policy aiming at the world-wide dictatorship of the Proletariat, and to affiliate this organisation to the Red International Council of Labour Unions."

KILMARNOCK.-"To sever all connections of this organisation from the Amsterdam Federation of Trade Unions, and to take all necessary steps to obtain the withdrawal of the Trade Union Congress from that organisation."

LEICESTER NO. 1. -" The Leicester Branch believing that the system of working in operation during 1920, in which payment by result with a guaranteed minimum was the best policy, hereby claims that the Union should take a vote on the following alternative, each member to have one vote only :-

Ist-Are you in favour of payment by results governed by the piece- work or quantity statements without limit?

2nd-Are you in favour of set weekly wages governed by the piece- work or quantity statements limited to the weekly wage?

3rd--Or do you prefer daywork pure and simple without statements?"

NORWICH." That the policy of the Union be directed to securing a system of weekly fixed wages guaranteed for every full working week."

NORTHAMPTON NO. 2.-" That this Conference is of the opinion that the piecework or supplementary wage system of working is contrary to the best interests of the operatives, and therefore instructs the National Council to frame the future policy of this Union on the basis of day- work system in conjunction with Quantity Statements."

LEICESTER WOMEN'S BRANCH to move.-"That the policy and method of working in this Union be piecework or payment by result with a guaranteed weekly wage and no restriction of output or limitation of earnings, with the exception of what has been the custom for many years in the trade, the sharing of work in slack times."

LEICESTER WOMEN'S BRANCH to move. -"That providing the same wages and price per operation be paid all departments in the boot and shoe trade shall be open for women to work in."

LEICESTER NO. I BRANCH to move. - "That we ask the Conference to give further powers to local officials to deal with non-federated firms regarding the different Awards given by the Union and Employers' Federation from time to time."

On the occasion of the third reading of the Government of Ireland Bill in the House
of Commons on November 11, the Rt. Hon. William Adamson, M.P., Chairman of the
Parliamentary Labour Party, made an important new pronouncement on Labour's
Irish policy, which was in strict harmony with the Scarborough resolution and removed
any doubts that may have existed regarding the interpretation of that resolution.
Briefly the policy outlined by Mr. Adamson was as follows:
(a) That the British Army of Occupation be withdrawn.
(b) That the question of Irish Government be relegated to an Irish Con-
stituent Assembly elected on the basis of proportional representation by free
equal and secret vote.
(c) That the Constitution drawn up by the Assembly be accepted provided
(1) it affords protection to minorities; and
(2) prevents Ireland becoming a military or naval menace to Britain.
We believe that along the lines contained in the said proposals the way
out of the present disgraceful and humiliating position may be found; and
we hope that our members will all do their part to bring about the change
which is so necessary in the interests of all concerned.

EUROPE.-The second question is the International position, which ought
to give pause to all who have the well-being of the people at heart. Upon all
hands we find suffering, pain, want, and lack of employment, men, women
and children dying for the lack of the necessaries of life; yet upon the other
hand raw materials and food are available if only proper methods were adopted
to so alter and adjust the machinery by which people are governed as to bring
into existence the necessary understanding between nations whereby the
wheels of commerce would once more resume their normal operations. It is
indeed heartrending to find millions of people clamouring for the barest neces-
saries of life; millions unemployed, and yet the food raw materials are existent
to meet both situations. We are sometimes told that Labour " is not fit to
govern;" this we suppose is on account of lack of business aptitude, states-
manlike outlook and general lack of training in the art of statecraft. If the
assertion is true, where is the "fitness to govern" being shewn by politicians
and statesmen of this and other countries? Upon all hands the cry goes up for
help and deliverance from the terrible state to which people have been brought ;
not by workmen being in power, but by those parties who through the centuries
have considered it their special function to assert authority over the masses,
and the present appalling situation is one of the results of such "fitness."
It is for us to have an outlook more and more world-wide; to insist upon the
machinery of Governments being so arranged that not only unemployment
will be equally dealt with but also the many other vital questions which are
pressing upon one for solution; the solution we desire can, and will only be
accomplished by unity and goodwill amongst one another. Let it therefore
be our aim whilst having many methods and plans to always have in view
the object, viz.: The emancipation of mankind from all those trammels
which hinder and hamper the people in their struggles for a just and equitable
state of society to obtain.

INDUSTRIAL COUNCIL.
During the year the Industrial Council has had before it on several occasions
the question of improved workshops, from a number of points of view, such as
better lighting, more space, better provision for cloak rooms and lavatories.
The Home Office has a number of recommendations now under consideration,
which are the result of unanimous decisions arrived at at meetings of the
Industrial Council, and we are expecting that in the near future it may be
possible to report that progress has been made in this connection.
It is essential that workshops, wherein a great part of life is lived, should
be of the best possible description, and we anticipate that you will fully support
us in our endeavours to raise the standard yet higher and higher as to the
requirements that must be carried out by any employer so far as the factory
or workshop is concerned.

Our Union is quite 25 years old in the policy of indoor working. Some branches make all their members work indoors. As late as 1008 the Hebrews of London all went indoors by arrangement with the Union. In Kingswood a lot of our members work at home, and when I was down there the question was raised as to why benefit was not forthcoming. Taking into consideration the status of the worker, if there is State money to be distributed everyone should have a fair share.

We had to have an appeal from the people who were suffering. That came and went to the Ministry of Labour and pointed out the position to them, and they stated their trouble was to find out whether an outworker was employed for one or more firms. They had as much trouble with the outworker as they did the charwoman under the Health Insurance Acts, and they asked us to satisfy ourselves that there was a contract of service, and if we could prove any workers have a contract of service with one employer we were advised such a case would go before the Referee, who is the final arbitrator to say whether the operative was entitled to benefit or not. I know my colleague has been down to one of the larger districts and scoured the area to see if he could get a definition of the individual. Some, we understand, have several employers. But we want a person who gives all his service to one employer. Some of our men have to take out lasts, and I have known where closers have taken out machines, and where they only worked for one firm. What we have to find out is, is there a contract of service ? We should not say there is a contract of service when we give a man an order for a suit of clothes. He would not admit he was your employee. It would simply be an order in the usual way. On the other hand we say if you can connect the outdoor worker as being wholly and solely in the employ of one firm, we told the Ministry of Labour we would take the responsibility of the investigation and see if such a person was in the employ of one firm or not, and we want cases to submit to the Ministry. Owing to other pressing matters I have not had time to take this matter further, although I would have preferred to have visited Kingswood again and got the cases so that we could have the whole of the details. The Act says outworkers are excluded, so as stated before we must find out if there is any contract of service; so you will appreciate our difficulty.

MR. A. J. RANDALL (Kingswood): Would it be accepted as a contract of service if an employer is responsible for Health Insurance contributions?

THE CHAIRMAN: I cannot say; if you will give us cases we will place them before the Minister of Labour.

THE GENERAL SECRETARY : With the exception of one district in a modified degree we have had no serious complaints except at Kingswood. I am rather surprised to hear Mr. Randall say certain people are charging local officials and the local labour parties because of alleged remissness in the House of Commons, because as a matter of fact I venture to say no one here knew we should have such a slump, and I would like to ask Mr. Randall if these men are paying contributions to the Fund?

MR. RANDALL: No.

THE GENERAL SECRETARY: Then they are not paying unemployment contributions because they are outworkers. The Department say you cannot have benefit because they are not paying contributions. As a matter of fact one of the kindred associations-the Amalgamated Root and Shoe Union-have made it one of their strong points that their were not within the four corners of any Unemployment Insurance Act because their members were never dismissed, and had work when there was any about. They may never work for a full week at a stretch, but they had work when any was about. You can see the difficulty we have. With Mr. Bates I went to eight of the nine sections in Higham and Rushden district and, generally speaking, men and women were receiving the money because they had or were working for one firm only, and although they may work at home they were controlled by the firm the same as if they were in the factory. The Ministry of Labour say some people have two or three firms. We have no feeling in the matter, and as Chairman of the Parliamentary Committee of the Trades Union Congress I can say such Committee have not received any complaints asking for an amendment of the Act, and I venture to suggest neither have the Labour Party, because we have joint meetings, and Mr. Henderson has never brought it before us. I think it very unfair to our Parliamentary colleagues that they should be blamed for something which even the workers themselves thought should not be done.

MR. A. J. RANDALL (Kingswood): We have some employers who are prepared to accommodate the members. If the employer is prepared to accept the responsibility can the operative get the benefit?

The problem of unemployment has been forced forward upon every occasion, and it is worth emphasis that amongst all parties of the State, Labour alone is the one that is never left the subject of unemployment-even during the war and when Labour is passed of having no policy we ask that you look to the records and see no month was allowed to go by without an attempt made to press forward this question of unemployment and so alter the position of the people. Labour is the only party that has a constructive Perhaps I may be allowed to emphasise one or two questions in order to shew the great importance of the people seeking to get control of the House of Commons. There one County Council where labour controls, i.e., the Durham County Council. The owners have formed an association and they have 34 members on the Council. They have freed education up to the secondary schools; the whole of the education in the lementary and secondary schools is free-unless the Board of Education have intervened and prevented it. It is open to the children of every parent. They are seeking to construct new schools; put up colleges and so prevent the well-to-do children having the monopoly in any positions. They introduced into the House of Commons a Bill known as the Durham Transport Bill. It sought to set up a tram and 'bus service, linking up the different parts of the county-quite a legitimate Bill for anyone to submit. It was dis- cussed in the House of Commons, and one of the arguments was that the miners did not nay rates for the houses in which they lived. When the voting took place, members of the Coalition party stood at the entrance to the lobby-it was the night Frank Hodges addressed the members upstairs-and members were pushed into the "No" lobby with the request to vote against Labour and vote against Bolshevism.
Now as to Foreign affairs. We have passed a Reparations Bill seeking to impose
a tax of 50 per cent. on all German goods coming into this country and so help pay the
debts this country has to bear. Last week the question was asked as to how much money had been collected, and the answer was £9,000 in three or four months. If you work it out you will find how long it will take to pay off the millions of debt this country has to face. The German manufacturers are quoting prices for their goods and saying to the English buyers, This is plus 50 per cent. If that is the way it will be done it will mean the
BRITISH PEOPLE PAY THE GERMAN DEBT.

You take your figure of 100-and put 50 per cent. on, it makes 150. Put on the traders' profit which is 33 per cent., it means instead of paying 50 per cent. you will pay 50 per cent. plus 334 per cent. once the goods come into this country. There is no more important question to us, and the sooner we get out of our minds the ideas of economics and false ideas between nation and nation, the better it will be for us all. It is not a matter of sympathy for our late enemies, but one of practical economics. You cannot pay debts unless it is in manufactured goods. If we are to receive manufactured goods, where is the possibility of our own people selling or making any? These goods will be received at the expense of depressing your own trade, and the second position will be worse than the first. I don't put this forward as the last word on the subject, but I ask you to reflect upon it, and the position of the country is due to the fact that the capitalists have not done as they should have done. In the times following a period of war the capitalists' views from the standpoint of the people have failed to function, and you have men hungering because of the lack of employment. There you have a complete failure of the system to operate in the interests of the people, and I ask for a full consideration of these questions to enable us to come to conclusions which I hope in the end will be for the betterment of our own people.
In conclusion 1 extend to each and every delegate an invitation for questions, which I will do my best to answer. (Applause.)

National Insurance (Health) Acts, 1911-1918
REPORT ON THE VALUATION
OF THE
ASSETS AND LIABILITIES OF THE NATIONAL UNION OF
BOOT AND SHOE OPERATIVES' APPROVED SOCIETY, No. 281,
as at 31st December, 1918.

1. In accordance with the provisions of Section 36 of the National Insurance
Act, 1911, a valuation has been made of the assets and liabilities of the above
Society, arising under Part I. of the Act, as existing at the 31st December, 1918.
The Society is approved for England, Scotland, Ireland and Wales, and the in-
formation required for the purpose of the valuation has been prepared in the
Insurance Departments concerned from returns compiled by the Society and
passed by the Government Auditors.

2. The number of members included in the valuation is 30,549, of whom
24,406 are men and 6,143 women. Of the latter, 4,519 are spinsters or widows.
1,599 employed married women, and 25 married women who have left employ-
ment and are entitled only to the limited benefits provided under Section 22
of the Act of 1918. The changes in membership which have occurred in the
period between 15th July, 1912, and 31st December, 1918, are summarised in
Appendix A, page 6.

3. The receipts and payments of the Benefit Fund during the period above
named are summarised in Appendix B, page 7, from which it will be seen that the
receipts amounted to £365,046 18s. 10d. and the payments to £154,806 1s. 7d., the
balance of £210,240 17s. 3d. representing the amount of the Fund on 31st Decem-
ber, 1918. In addition to the Benefit Fund, there stood to the credit of the Society
on 31st December, 1918, the Contingencies Fund of £12,537 0s. 9d., and the
balance of the Administration Account £4,493 18s. 10d. Assets amounting to
£228,361 18s. 6d., representing the total of these credits, namely, £227,271
16s. 10d., together with provision for certain miscellaneous liabilities amounting
to £1,090 1s. 8d., are shown in detail in the Balance Sheet contained in Form
205/A.G.D., a copy of which accompanies this Report.

4. The basis of the valuation is prescribed, under Section 36 (2) of the Act of
1911, by the National Health Insurance (Valuation) Regulations, 1919. Under
these Regulations the values of the future benefits and contributions are ascer-
tained, in effect, on the basis adopted in the calculation of the reserve values
credited to approved societies under Section 55 of the Act of 1911. The future
interest earnings on the accumulated funds (including reserve values) are thus
assumed at the rate of 3 per cent. per annum, and the future rates of mortality,
sickness, and claims for maternity benefit among the members are estimated in

Here is the text from the image:

46
due to the exceptional conditions which prevailed during the War. Prominent
among these sources are:
(1) the relief resulting from the decline in the birth rate and the con-
sequent fall in the number of claims for maternity benefit:
(2) the release of the Society from liability in respect of which it had
received reserve values, by deaths among male members of
military age; and
(3) the high rate of interest secured on investments.
In addition, the cost of Disablement Benefit has been below the provision
made in the financial basis of the Act, and it is probable that this experience
is at least partly due to the War.

It should be noted that the sickness claims during 1913 and 1914 were con-
siderably in excess of the valuation standard and necessitated the intervention
of the Insurance Commissioners. Subsequently the experience exhibited an
improvement, doubtless in part due to the temporary influence of War conditions,
and, on balance, a small profit has accrued in respect of this benefit.

7. Fluctuations from time to time in the sickness experience, in the rate of
mortality, and in other elements affecting the financial position of approved
societies are inevitable, and should invariably be kept in view when the distribu-
tion of surplus is being considered. The conditions under which the present
surplus has been produced, as explained above, emphasise the importance of
this point and lead to the conclusion, after proper weight is given to the pro-
visions of the Act respecting the Contingencies Fund, that £12,907 of the surplus
should be carried forward, leaving £9,693 as now available for additional benefits.
I certify, accordingly, that of the surplus disclosed by the valuation the sum of
£9,693 is disposable surplus to which the provisions of Section 37 of the Act
of 1911 apply.

8. Having regard to the amount of the disposable surplus as certified above,
the attention of the Society is directed to the provisions of Section 37 of the Act
of 1911, and to Appendix C. to this Report.

P. N. HARVEY,
Valuer appointed by the Treasury under
Section 36 of the National Insurance Act, 1911.

Government Actuary's Department,
Buckingham Gate, London, S.W. 1.
12th April, 1921.

Many, many years ago I tried to follow our industry and the Agreement and was a member perhaps before some of you came inside the Union, and have been studying it for thirty years. I cannot see, fellow delegates, what good it will do for us. We are all going to be on the same level. You are beginning at the wrong end. It is dictatorship with a vengeance. It is jealousy, and the man with no ability will be on equal term with the clever man. You cannot have two firms on the same wages, and you cannot have a shilling rise unless agreed to by the manufacturers, yourself and the trade union official. You cannot say I am worth so and so. It is no use thinking you get a merit rise. We have enough loafers in our trade and I've had to carry people on my back many, many times.

MR. LEN. SMITH (Council Member) supported the resolution. The position has been very clearly put by the mover and seconder, and these resolutions have been embodied in the new suggested terms sent to the Federation for discussion. We do not believe the present system under which we are working to be the best that could be got. We have stated clearly time after time that we wish each operation to be priced in accordance with the Terms of Agreement, but that we should have some control over the member, working in the industry.  To-day we have no control. Instead of instilling into the minds of trade unionists that they must race away, I contend that our present method with its development has not developed trade unionism, but rank individualism. We cannot see the unity we used to see in days gone by. We don't see men helping one another as we used to. We want to regulate the conditions so that all the people in the industry can be brought in without being dismissed. Instead of 50 per cent. drawing all the money and 50 per cent. having out-of-work pay, we believe by a modification in our terms we shall be able to take steps to prevent it. We don't say it is a perfect scheme. In the working out of that we shall find faults and try to remedy them. We have found out the evils of the present system, and we have put our finger on the spot which we feel operates against the operatives. We hear talk about regulating the individual. Some want regulating. The main principle which is at the bottom of our system lies a good way back in history. We do not agree the manufacturers should have the right to say whether he shall work day or piecework as he has to-day. Your 1895 Terms of Settlement stated plainly, and in your first clause of the present Agreement it says it is subject to Clause 2 Sub-section 5 of the 1895 Agreement, which gives the manufacturer the option to work either day or piecework.  We are trying to alter that principle, and in altering it we have put forward proposals that will give officers and branch executives power to meet the members and say how far each should go. Even in short periods with no restriction (although we have a great number of men walking the streets) in 35 hours men have been drawing nearly as much as they did in 48 hours. Other people are walking the streets. Isn't it better we should try and devise some scheme to regularise these conditions, or are we to cater for 75 per cent. of our members to do as much as they like, whilst the other 25 per cent. walk about the streets, or are we prepared to say you shall do so many and no more? You will find with your reduction in hours factories of any size have increased their output by one-third, and the wages have not increased so very much. We want to realise if we had control of these men they would not have done as they have done. Northampton are honest in their intentions, and want to build up an industry whereby we can level up, and not level down, until we get to the bosses' standard, and nothing less than the bosses' standard is good enough for me. We do not want to level down, but to set up a standard which should be worked to and not exceeded, nor anyone to receive less. We do not want to go back to district statements. We want a national statement. If this resolution is adopted as the policy of the Union we want to apply it all round and do all the good we can. We want these things to be fought out here, and you cannot control the industry until you regularise the output.

MRS. M. J. BELL-RICHARDS (Council Member): I have carried loafers on my back many, many times.

If they do not earn their wages the employer makes it up... if more is earned, the employees get it. If the employees earn more they do not get it under the suggested scheme. Assuming a man is capable of earning £5 10s. and the rate is fixed at £4 10s., is he to stop when he has done his quantity for 90s., or is he to spread out the work over the full week just to earn £4 10s.? What would happen is this-some men could not stop at that figure and would be working either for someone else or the employer.

MR. J. MANNERS (Council Member): I ask the Conference to remember a vote of the members has been taken upon this question, and the members have decided upon a certain thing. Is it competent for this Conference to alter it?

THE CHAIRMAN: It is not a matter of competence or we should not have allowed it to go on the Agenda.

MR. J. MANNERS (Council Member): There has not been an argument put forward apart from showing the selfishness of certain men. If we are going forward to make steps towards

A NEW WORLD,

we must eliminate a certain amount of selfishness. Is our present policy the best? If so, I have no complaint to make, but I would like us to consider whether it is in the best interests of the whole, and to see if it is the safest and soundest policy we can adopt. I come from a part of the country where there is a strong feeling upon the point. We have had manufacturers putting reductions on earnings into operation. They said, We only want so many pairs to go through the factory; when that is done you can go home. The fast man did his 50s. worth of work and went home. The slow man also did 50s. worth of work, but if the present method had obtained the fast man would earn £4 and the slow man 30s. I have heard of manufacturers who put their men on 38 hours and at the end of that time they did as much work as they did in 48 hours. The manufacturer told the men he wanted a reduction in output. We must appeal to the intelligence of our operatives and there is a time when restraint has to be put upon themselves. Is it easier to work for all you are worth instead of regulating your output? We are told if this principle of control of output goes into our next proposed terms it is quite possible the Federation will not meet us. paid. Time after time at the Trade Union Congress this thing has been put down, and I
hope the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives will not be the first to pass such a
resolution.

Previously badly organised, the Leather Industry can now claim to have reached
a fair stage of organisation, though there are still far too many Unions concerned,
as these number something like 18 (all of which deal with leather workers only).
In 1913 steps were taken to form a Federation of all Unions dealing with Leather
and Leather Goods; the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives were invited
to join this, but declined. Later, the Federation was formed under the name of the
National Leather Trades Federation and covers all workers in the industry from the
raw skin to the finished article, including harness and saddle, bag and portmanteau,
football and belt, in fact all leather and leather goods with the exception of boots and
shoes. The result of this has been to secure for the workers national recognition
from the nationally Federated employers, the Leather Producers Association, with
whom we have national agreements fixing rates of wages, terms of overtime, hours
of labour, and grading of all operations. Wages vary from a minimum rate for skilled
dayworkers of £4, and £5 for pieceworkers, to £3 8s. and £4 5s. in a few very small
country shops. The principal Union in this Federation is the Amalgamated Society
of Leather Workers, head office Leeds. This has about 40 branches with a member-
ship of about 12,000. It has six full-time officials (not including any office staff),
and the latest figures available show a worth of about 11,000. While not a wealthy
society, its funds reflect its activities, as they have preferred to use same in fighting
to improve or maintain conditions, in preference to working for a bank balance for
show purposes. The No. 3 Division, which extends from Bristol and the west, to
east as far as Sawston, Cambridge, from north of Lutsouth of Sheffield, has
passed resolutions in favour of amalgamation wit

taken as a Sub-Committee of the Federation are now meeting to draw up a scheme

this is going forward. Latest information (May 7th) shows this is progressing and will

and District a number of these members are drawing strike pay as a result of being
involved in a dispute with leather manufacturers. Further, in quite a number of
shoe shops we find men, who are dressing leather, in the Boot and Shoe Union, and in
some cases this leads to trouble over their wages, when they are working with men
belonging to our Union. At Church's, Northampton, and White's, Norwich, to quote
two cases. Further, cases can be given of men who are claimed to be leather workers
being claimed and organised by the Boot and Shoe Union, legging workers for instance,
It will be seen that so far as a large number of workers are concerned, they are quite
prepared to co-operate with the Boot and Shoe Union in securing the very desirable
end of one Union for the one Industry.

SPECIAL NOTICE TO MEMBERS.
Every precaution is taken by us to ensure accuracy in these Reports, our correspondents
being men on whom we can rely; should, however, any errors creep into them, upon the
same being pointed out to us, we shall be most happy to give the same prominence to the
correction as to the original matter. As these Reports are exclusively for the use of Members,
the information contained therein must not be divulged.

23RD JANUARY, 1922.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
THE STATE OF TRADE
continues about the same as last month, but trade was disturbed by the
holidays. The figures given by the Ministry of Labour in the Gazette are as
follows :-
BOOT AND SHOE TRADE.
In this trade employment continued very depressed during December, and there
were increases both in the numbers unemployed and in the amount of short time worked.
In some cases extended holidays were taken at Christmas. Employment was, however,
not quite so bad, in most districts, as in December, 1920.
The percentage of workpeople unemployed in boot, shoe and slipper making and
repairing establishments, as indicated by the unemployment books lodged at Employment
Exchanges, was 11.9 at the 30th December, as compared with 9.5 per cent. at the 2nd
December. In addition, 3.0 per cent. of the workpeople were claiming benefit in respect
of systematic short-time working at the 30th December, as compared with 2.4 at the
2nd December.
At Leicester employment was fairly good for some of the women workers, but other-
wise continued slack, with much short time. At Hinckley employment was good, and
better than in November. At Wellingborough it was quiet, and showed a decline. At
Higham and Rushden it continued fair. At Northampton, Kettering and Leeds there
was much short time, and employment was still bad. At Bristol it was bad, and worse
than in November. At Norwich it was fair; better than in November, and much better
than last year. There was a decline in the Rossendale Valley towards the end of the
month, owing to the completion of Christmas orders.
In Scotland employment remained fair, or good, at Maybole and at Kilmarnock,
but it was bad at the other principal centres.

REVISION OF NATIONAL AGREEMENT.
As fully stated in last month's Address regarding the proposed New
Agreement a copy of which appeared in the December Report-a Special
Delegate Conference was held in the Boot and Shoe Trade Hall, Leicester, on
Thursday the 29th ult., at 10 a.m., the General President being in the Chair
supported by all the Council members. The Press representatives were not
present, so that there could be a full and free expression of views regarding
the said agreement.
The General President and General Secretary laid before the Conference
the proposals, pointing out at the same time the real position of affairs and
assuring the delegates, although it was a great disappointment to have to bring
such a report, it was absolutely the maximum we could secure from the em-
ployers, and at the same time the minimum of re-adjustment of wages. The

---

8
Conference discussed the matter from to a.m. until 4 p.m., when the following
resolution was proposed and seconded :----
"
That this Conference having heard the statement of the Council
regarding the re-adjustment of Wages, after full consideration of the
same, hereby records its opinion that the Council have secured the
best terms possible under the conditions now existing, and suggests
to the members that they endorse the proposal."
Discussion resumed and kept on until 5.30 p.m., when a roll call vote
was taken upon the resolution with the following results :-

Inasmuch as it is not intended to publish any special report of the Con-
ference proceedings, references will be found on page 52.
We can only once more express our great regret that the vote is com-
paratively so small, especially having regard to the great issues that are involved.
The position is one of vital importance to the whole of the membership and
we cannot but think that those members who refrained from voting will,
upon reflection, see that they have a duty to perform in regard to their
membership.
We have had a special meeting to deal with and review the situation
thus created; also we have met the Employers' Committee. After full con-
sideration of the facts and the industrial position, we have decided under Rule
116 to take a second vote, which vote must be returnable not later than Feb-
ruary the 3rd prox. We strongly urge upon the whole of the members that
they record their vote, and further, in view of the serious situation that may
be created if the vote is against acceptance, we hope the members will give
a vote for endorsing the Agreement, assuring the members that we have secured
from the employers the maximum conditions.
The proposals will, under the special circumstances, operate as from the
second pay day in February and the second pay day in May instead of January
and June, which were the dates in the original agreement.

DEATH of MR. W. H. LOWE, J.P. OF LEICESTER.
It is with sincere and deep regret that we have to record the passing
away of Mr. W. H. Lowe, J.P., on the 22nd of December. Mr. Lowe
held the position of Branch Secretary of the Leicester No. 2 practically
since the commencement of the Branch, that is, since 1890. For a
number of years Mr. Lowe was also the Treasurer for the Union, which
carried with it membership of the Council; in addition to which offices
he was a Town Councillor for a period, and for a number of years a
Magistrate for Leicester, likewise Treasurer of the Leicester Trades
Council, in all of which positions he rendered faithful and willing service
to the community. His period of office has seen a marked improvement
in the status of the members. His death means the loss of a very valuable
officer, one who had an high sense of duty and who at all times was
anxious to give of his best for the betterment of the general position.
To the Widow and Family we have in your name tendered sympathy and
condolence in the great loss they have sustained; we hope that their
sorrow and pain may to some extent be lessened by the knowledge that
Mr. Lowe was so highly respected and esteemed. (Further references
to his sterling character will be found on pages 62-63.

sure, put matters on a better footing; a personal visit often being best to remove these
little misunderstandings.
Immediately after Christmas we held a Special Council Meeting to make the necessary
arrangements for the Special Conference at Leicester the results being already known
the Council felt that if any of the representative members could address them in any way
they would appreciate such help; the business of such Conference will in a short time
be placed in the hands of the members.
A visit to Stone has been made and a very successful meeting held, also an inquiry
re non-members; next day a visit was paid to Lotus Limited, who immediately agreed
with us to put up the resolution carried at the Joint Conference to the effect that it is
in the interest of all concerned that all operatives and employers should belong to their
respective organisations; should any Branch feel embarrassed by non-unionism will
they please ask either the firm or ourselves to take this matter up for them.
On the 4th we had a very good meeting at the Leicester Branch on the Terms, which
appeared very favourable, although the voting does not represent that view.
On the 5th I went to the District Trade Board Meeting held at Birmingham, and
although we had a very successful meeting of the Board, the Repairing Employers,
encouraged by the manufacturers, think that a reduction in wages inevitable; we
opposed the same with all our power, and the voting resulting in an equal number on
each side, the manufacturers can have any change in these rates placed at their door,
and so we learn that an injury done to one may also affect others.
I paid a further visit to Stone and Stafford owing to several girls failing to obtain
Unemployment Benefit at the time that they were entitled, our suspicion being that
they were being treated unfairly, but after investigation we are of the opinion that the
errors made were made in good faith and we have made arrangements that our Mr. Dunn,
of Stafford, will give any advice asked for by the Stone members.
I am sorry to report that owing to a motor accident I have been unable to continue
my duties for the past five days but am now resuming my work at once.
In conclusion, may I wish our Members a most Prosperous and Happy New Year.

Yours fraternally,

7. MECKLENBURGH STREET,
LONDON, W.C. 1.
January 17th, 1922.

241, Uppingham Road, Leicester.
14th January, 1922.
To the Members of the Executive Council.
I have examined the Receipts, Counterfoils, Vouchers and Bank
Books, together with the whole of the Account Books for the Half-year
ending 31st December, 1921.
The Total Funds standing to the credit of the Central Office of the
Union amount to £267,070 12s. 11d., being an increase of £18,562 5s. 8d.
over the half-year ending 30th June, 1921. The increase on the Sick
Fund is £16,541 17s. 2d. and this despite the fact that you have increased
the sick and funeral benefit rates. Only £2,298 10s. 4d. has been gained
by the Trade Fund, due no doubt to the depression in trade and the large
call on the Unemployment Fund. There is a loss on the Political and
Fidelity Funds.
The Deeds and Investments have been checked.
I have to tender my thanks to the General Secretary and the
clerical staff who deal with the books for the careful, able and efficient
manner in which they have been kept.
The work on the State Unemployment Section has grown consider-
ably and every detail is clearly shewn.
I certify the Accounts to be correct and in accordance with Law.
J. B. B. ROBERTSON,

59
trade after preliminary training under a qualified instructor. These youths are thrown
into the trade regardless of the question whether there is likely to be an opening for them
or, in the case of crippled boys, whether they have any prospect of an opening in for them.
to enable them to earn their own living.

One-Man Businesses.

Another great difficulty in the Repairing Trade is the large number of Repairers
who employ no labour and are known in the Trade as "one-man businesses." These
men can sell their labour at any price and work as many hours as they feel disposed without
coming under the Trade Board regulations, therefore, we have suggested to the Govern-
ment that all Boot Repairers trading with the public should be registered either with the
Trade Board or Home Office, to be dealt with under the Factory Acts.

I wish to draw attention of the Committee to the fact that the Boot and Shoe Repairing
Trade is essentially a Piece-work Trade. The great majority of the workers, about 85
per cent. are employed on Piece-work, and the Trade Board has drawn upa very exhaustive
list of minimum piece-rates for the Trade. In some parts of the country considerably
higher piece-rates than those are paid to the workers. Any proposal to take away the
power of the Trade Board of fixing piece-rates would seriously diminish the effectiveness
of the Board.

District Trade Committees.

The Trade Board has established 16 Trade Bcard Committees covering the whole
of England and Wales. These District Committees, since their establishment, have been
consulted as required by the decision of the Trade Board. On every occasion when any
variation of rates has been proposed, before issuing a formal notice of proposal to vary
the existing rates or to fix new rates for special classes of workers, the Trade Board have
asked the District Committees in the first place for their endorsement or otherwise. I am
in favour of continuing the policy of consulting these Committees to this extent. In
regard to proposals for commencing any new rate of wages, I am strongly of opinion that
it would be impracticable to give these District Committees power to fix rates independently
of the Trade Board. I am, of course, opposed to differential rates being fixed by District
Committees; I think that they can be best established on a National basis through the
medium of the Trade Board. Any proposal for the variation of wages or the normal
number of hours of work have to go before the country for two months to give an oppor-
tunity for objection to be lodged, and it takes from four to six months to bring about either
an increase or reduction in wages; therefore, I would suggest that this procedure should
be varied so as to make it possible to accomplish their objects in a period, say, of four weeks.

I may further mention that, in the year ending November, 1920, 1,411 visits were
made in connection with the working of the Trade Board Act in respect of the Boot and
Shoe Trade of these visits 1,311 were to employers and 40 to workers. The principal
objects which the firms were visited for was to secure payment of minimum rates.

I am in favour of members of the Trade Board having full powers in their various
localities to investigate violations of the rates as laid down by the Board and such investi-
gations to be reported to the Board, as now operates with regard to the question of permits.
As regards the system of appointed members, and having experience of the Board since its
inception, I have found that the system has been advantageous, and I appreciate the
guidance and assistance given towards the solution of the many difficult problems apper-
taining to the trade during the Board's existence.

C.W.S. BOOT TRADE.

The slump in the co-operative boot and shoe trade continues, and the boot sales of
the Co-operative Wholesale Society for the past three months, to be reported at the January
meeting, will show a downward tendency. In the Manchester district they totalled
£234,180, a decline of £221,796, when compared with the corresponding period of 1920.
From the Newcastle branch they were £110,365, as against £243,099 in the corresponding
three months of the previous year. In the southern area the sales were £109,216, as
compared with £235,710. Thus the decreases were 48, 54 and 53 per cent. respectively.

During the same period 421,714 pairs of boots were sent from the works at Leicester,
Derby, Leeds, Heckmondwike and Rushden, a decrease of 306,595 pairs, or 42 per cent.
The supplies from the five works and the fellmongering works at Pontefract and Grappen-
hall, with the tanneries at Grappenhall and Street, were £315,169-a falling off of £346,303,
or 52 per cent.-Shoe and Leather News, January 5th, 1922.

"PLAYING THE FOOL."
UNION BRANCH SECRETARY AND THE FUNDS.
That he had "played the fool," was the remark made with reference to John William
Duxbury, 20, Brown Lodge, Smithy Bridge, Rochdale, by his solicitor (Mr. J. A. Hudson),
when he was summoned before the magistrates at Rochdale County Police Court, for unlaw-
fully and wilfully withholding money to the amount of £97 14s. 3d. belonging to the local
branch of the Amalgamated Society of Leather Workers. Mr. H. P. Jones (Leeds) prose-
cuted on behalf of the Society.

Mr. Jones said that until January last year the defendant was president of the branch,
and was then appointed secretary. His duties included the payment of all money into the
bank, with the exception of that which was dealt with at branch meetings. He had also to
draw money for use on behalf of the Society by cheques signed by two trustees and himself.
Later he presented at the bank an authority purporting to be signed by the chairman and
himself, allowing him to draw cheques under his own signature. From that date he did
so. There was £175 in the bank to the credit of the Society at the beginning of last year,
and at the end of the year it had all gone. The defalcations were discovered by accident.
It was found at the bank that the account was overdrawn, and by an error a letter was
sent to the former secretary respecting the matter. That aroused suspicion, and an audit
was held, with the result that it was first ascertained that ₤65 175. 9d. had been drawn,
which, with the overdraft of £7 2s. 6d., made a total of £73 6s. 3d. During the whole of the
period in question the defendant, who was a single man, was in receipt of £2 10s. per week.
Further inquiries were made, and as a result the overdraft was found to be increased to £9
by a cheque not previously presented. There was a further item of £16 125. 6d. State
Insurance to be added, which made up the total. These cheques from the Government
had not been accounted for.

Mr. J. A. Hudson, for the defendant, said he disputed the £16 125. 6d., and admitted
defalcations to the total of ₤81. If an order was made for that amount he would agree to
it. The defendant, he said, was a good-living young man prior to going into the Army,
and was well-known as a member of a chapel and of a young men's class. When he went
into the Army he got into the officers' mess. There was no doubt he had played the fool.
He was sorry and was anxious to make amends.

After consultation Mr. Jones said his clients were willing to accept an order for the
payment by instalments of fi per month until the defendant got work, the amount to be
then increased to 12 per month. On these terms an order for payment was made.
-The Shoe and Leather Record, January 13th, 1922.

DEATH OF MR. W. H. LOWE, J.P.
A Loss to the National Union.
LOWE. On December 22nd, at 18, Harrow Road, William Henry Lowe, J.P., aged 66
years, passed peacefully away, after a painful illness.

With the passing of Mr. William Henry Lowe, J.P., on Thursday, Leicester has lost
one of her most highly-respected citizens, whilst the National Union of Boot and Shoe
Operatives, of which he was an esteemed and valuable official, will particularly mourn
his demise. Mr. Lowe, who was 66 years of age, had not enjoyed good health for a long
time.
During practically the whole of his life Mr. Lowe was connected with the Boot and
Shoe Union, and from 1891 up to about ten years ago he was treasurer of the National
organisation. By virtue of that office he occupied a seat on the Union Executive, and
thus had a share in forming the policy of the Union in days when matters were not always
too bright. But perhaps the deceased gentleman was best known as the secretary of the
Leicester No. 2 Branch of the Union. He was elected to that office a short time after the
branch was formed in 1890, and continued without a break until the time of his death.
The deceased was also one of the oldest members of the Trades Council and for many
years acted as treasurer to that body.
In 1904 Mr. Lowe was returned unopposed as a Liberal and Labour member for the
Westcotes Ward on the Town Council and performed useful work during his term of office.
He was defeated in a three-cornered contest in 1907, in which year he was made a Justice
of the Peace.
Those who knew the deceased gentleman intimately will agree that he had a dis-
position of exceeding kindliness. Members of his branch of the Union had a genuine
affection for him, and all appreciate the capable work he did so unobtrusively in con-
nection with arbitration on important matters which came up in the trade a number of
years ago. He was always a strong believer in conciliation, rather than in strife, and
undoubtedly the whole industry has benefited largely by the work of such as he. Never
seeking the limelight, his advice was nevertheless always sought, valued, and generally
proved acceptable. It was recognised that he was an authority on trade matters, par-
ticularly in regard to clicking. He also helped to establish the principle of a minimum
wage in the industry. The unemployed problem naturally attracted his attention, and
nothing gave him greater pleasure than seeking out methods of improvement in con-
nection with the lives and prospects of his fellow-workers. He took a very active part
in the work of the Police Aided Association for clothing destitute children.
In all parts of the city, and in a much wider sphere, the death of Mr. Lowe will be
unfeignedly deplored.
We greatly regret to hear of the death of Mr. W. H. Lowe, J.P., announced in our
obituary column yesterday. The city is much the poorer by his passing. A shrewd,
conciliatory, and earnest trade unionist, he will be greatly missed in the National Union
connected with the boot industry, and in other spheres his loss will be sincerely lamented.
At one time he took an active part in local and political affairs, especially in Westcotes
Ward, but of late, though his interest in them was unabated, he has been in relative retire-
ment through failing health. But old friends will have only kindly remembrances of him
as a genial comrade of kindly disposition, true to his convictions, but ever considerate
of the views of others. The city can ill-spare such men as William Henry Lowe.-Leicester
Daily Mercury, December 24th, 1921.

MONTHLY REPORT.

TRADE
27TH FEBRUARY, 1922.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
has slightly improved during the month. The figures given by the Ministry
of Labour in the Gazette are as follows :-

BOOT AND SHOE TRADE.
Employment in this trade was very slack during January, and showed little change
compared with December, though it was not quite so bad, taking the country as a whole,
as in January of last year. Short time, in various forms, continued to be common at all
the principal centres.
The percentage of workpeople unemployed in the boot, shoe and slipper making and
repairing trades, as indicated by the unemployment books lodged at Employment Ex-
changes, was 10.7 at the 31st January, as compared with 11.9 at the 30th December.
In addition, 2.6 per cent. of the workpeople were claiming benefit in respect of systematic
short-time working at the 31st January, as compared with 3.0 per cent. at the 30th
December.
Employment in London was bad, though better than in January of last year. At
Leicester employment showed a further slight improvement, but was still slack, on the
whole, with a large amount of short time. The partial destruction of a factory by fire
increased the numbers of unemployed at Northampton, where employment was still bad.
At Kettering very few firms were on full time; some were running only two or three days
a week, and some had closed down altogether. There was a decline at Hinckley and at
Wellingborough, and employment was very quiet at both centres; at Rushden it showed
an improvement, and was fair. Employment at Rothwell and at Desborough was fairly
good; at Stafford it was slack.
Employment remained bad at Leeds; at Bristol it was again depressed; at Kings-
wood it was extremely bad, showing a great decline both on December and on January of
last year. At Norwich employment was fairly good, few operatives being unemployed.
Employment continued fair at Kilmarnock, but declined at Maybole; at the remaining
principal centres in Scotland it was still bad.

A great part of the speeches of these gentlemen have been devoted to Labour
and the Labour Movement. It is quite clear to us that determined efforts
will be made once more to mislead the electors and to traduce what Labour
stands for, in the hope that the electorate will vote against Labour candidates.
For instance, the Lord Chancellor in a speech delivered on 2nd February said,
amongst other things, the following :-
In the first place I examine the pretensions of the party which, outside the Coalition,
has the greatest number of adherents, and which undoubtedly constitutes the only grave
political menace to the fortunes of the Coalition. I need not say I mean the Labour Party.
We have had the advantage, during the last few days, of reading elocutions proceeding
from Mr. Clynes and Mr. Henderson. Whenever it is desired to put anybody forward to
administer soothing syrup in large quantities to the public, Mr. Clynes or Mr. Henderson
modestly advances to the limelight. (Laughter.) I wish to give no offence to any of our
Liberal friends here when I say that these speeches would be a very pleasant Sunday
afternoon diversion at a Liberal club.
There is never a mention of the only doctrines on which the strength of that party
in the country depends. What does Mr. Clynes or Mr. Henderson say on the programme
for capturing London ?
What do they say on what I may call in a compendious phrase, "Poplar
Finance?" They dare not denounce it; they merely ignore it.
They are equally silent on the treacherous part Labour has played since the war.
When in every other land the question was being individually asked, "How can I con-
tribute, in these difficult and tragic days, to the reconstruction of the State," what has
been the part of the Labour leaders here? It has been one of consistent and abject
poltroonery.
If the leaders of the Labour Party had told the truth, if they had said that the
man who laid aside his tools and refused to play his individual part in the reconstruction
of the industrial life of the nation was a traitor to the commonwealth, we should not have
lost, as we have lost, hundreds of thousands of working days in the last three years, and
the whole condition of the country to-day would have been far different. (Cheers.)

REMEMBER THE FIFTEENTH !
Once again we feel bound to call the serious attention of Branch Secretaries
to the fact that the FIFTEENTH day of each month is the latest day for
returns reaching the General Secretary. If Branches fail to send off their
returns to reach the Central Office before the 15th of the month it tends to
upset the organisation of the work in the General Secretary's Office. We beg
to intimate that unless returns are in before the 15th of the month, the Secretary
has been instructed to put into force the Rules governing the same. Returns
Sheets MUST also bear the signature of both the Branch President and Branch
Secretary or they will reluctantly have to be returned for completion.

Stamp. Members and their families should wear only "Union Stamped
Footwear."

EMINENT SHOE MAKER DEAD.
Professor Sir Henry Jones, LL.D., Glasgow, who died on Saturday at the age of 70,
was one of Wales's most distinguished sons. He was the son of a Llangernyw shoemaker,
and in his early days Professor Jones served his apprenticeship at his father's shop, and
at the same time spent three days a week at school. "The proudest day of my life," he
once said, "was when my father asked me to put some toecaps on boots. The toecap
fashion was new at the time and the stitching had to be very fine." He arranged with the
Village policeman to call him at one a.m. every morning so that he could pursue his studies.
Even in his later days he still retained an interest in the shoemaking trade. --Shoe and
Leather News, February 9th, 1922.
