BRANCH REPORTS.

BARNSLEY. Trade is very quiet here at present, repairing being very
slack. We are pleased to say that we are now clear of sickness, and we hope
that we shall be a long time before any of our members are on sick pay again,
because doctors' charges are so high that there is very little left out of sick
pay after the doctor has been paid.

BELFAST. Trade continues to remain very bad both in the manufactur-
ing and repairing; we were hopeful last month that trade was going to improve,
but we have been sadly disappointed. We regret that the Masters in the
Belfast area, both in the top and boot manufacturing, would not agree to pay
to the rates agreed upon by the National Joint Conference. We are pleased to
report that they did agree to pay the full minimum rate to the men, but they
made a reduction of 4s. per week to the adult females, and in the case of girls
and youths they are paying on the 1919 Irish Agreement. At a local Confer-
ence the Masters contended that they were not bound by the National Joint
Conference Agreement seeing they had no Irish representation, but stated that
if a Conference of the Irish manufacturers and members of the Irish Branches
with the Council represented were arranged they would agree to pay such rates
as agreed upon at such Conference. We would call members' attention to
their arrears in respect of being able to obtain Union benefits: no member over
the eight weeks' limit can obtain benefit without doing the necessary probation.
it is no use blaming the officials, the responsibility rests with the members.

DERBY. - Trade here is still very bad; all the Trade Union firms are
making very slack time. We regret to state that a number of our oldest
hands, who have been loyal to the cause, have been dismissed from the
local branch of the C.W.S. through shortage of work, but we cannot help but
think injustice has been done for several of them are whole-hearted in the
Co-operative Movement and serve on the local Committees, while others have
reached the age when there is very little chance of obtaining another situation.
The Management promised to absorb these members (who are hand-lasters)
into various machine departments, but unfortunately for them (the workers)
they have been transferred to the local Labour Exchange instead. We do not
thoroughly realise the C.W.S. mode of selecting these dismissals, but we are
inclined to believe a better method might have been found by which the work
could have been equally shared by all. We looked forward with bright hopes
when the C.W.S. became established in Derby, but we hardly think we have
one member in our Branch at the present time but who will readily admit it was
a bad day's work for the members in general. Derby, similar to many other
small Branches, is not a centre, and once an operative gets dismissed it is a
poor outlook for him in his own trade.

EDINBURGH.-January has been the heaviest month's sickness ever
experienced by the Branch, but it now seems to be falling off. Trade here is
still very quiet, both with new workers and repairers. We have arranged to
have a meeting with one firm in regard to the New Settlement, as some of the
operatives did not receive the full 10 per cent. increase on the 1920 Agreement.
We are of the opinion that 5 per cent. cannot be deducted on present terms,
and hope the matter will be amicably settled. Our National Organiser (Mr.
J. Buckle) has put up a nice case for the retaining of Wages Trade Boards.
Could it not be possible to have the Employers' case also printed in Monthly
Report? The Half-yearly Financial Statement, we are pleased to read, shows
a gain on both Trade and Sick Funds.

HIGHAM AND RUSHDEN. - The month has seen an improvement in
trade in the District; but for the failure of one firm with factories in Rushden
and Higham Ferrers, the amount paid in Unemployment Pay would have been
considerably reduced. The sickness for the month has been considerable
owing to the influenza, Irthlingborough suffering exceptionally from the
epidemic. The services of Mr. J. Buckle, J.P., in the District were appreciated
by the members. The clear and lucid way in which he dealt with the Terms
and Alternatives influenced the vote considerably, and we are bound to state
that he did not spare himself in any way to rouse the members bound to state
sibility. Also in interviews with the manufacturers he assisted very much.

LEEDS.-Trade here is bad, with little prospects at present of a change
for the better. We would urge upon all members who are in arrears to make
an effort to reduce the same and thus be entitled to Union benefits should they
fall ill or are put on the unemployment list. We wish also to notify our
members that the Branch Monthly Meetings will in future take place on the
Second Tuesday in the month, instead of the First Tuesday.

LIVERPOOL.-We are not in a position to report much improvement
in trade although we are of the opinion that the worst has passed. We have
paid out during the month in benefits (Out-of-Work, Sick and Funeral) con-
siderably more than what we have received in contributions, having to send
twice to the Central Office for cash. We note the result of the second ballot
of the wages question has resulted in a majority in favour of acceptance,
equivalent to three to one, which shows the wisdom of the Council in putting
into operation Rule 116.

MAYBOLE.-Trade is very bad and sickness very heavy. Messrs.
Lees & Co. have dismissed about fifty workers and the outlook is very black.
We had Mr. Bleakley with us and had a good meeting on the New Terms or
Strike question, but through some dělay our votes were not at the Central
Office in time. We expect Mr. Bleakley shortly to go into the Payment by
Results, as some are working day wage and some piecework, which is very
unsatisfactory. It is hoped the members will give us every assistance on this
question as it is only by combined effort we can accomplish anything.

NORWICH.-Trade continues to improve in Norwich, the continuous
run on Turn-shoe trade being quite remarkable and equally welcome. The
factories of the city are becoming unbalanced, due to the shortage of operatives
in the closing room; we shall therefore be required to arrange some method
of attracting additional labour in this department in order to keep male opera-
tives as fully employed as the volume of trade will allow. Like most other
centres, Norwich has had its share of "flu," but we are pleased to report the
epidemic is waning.

PLYMOUTH.-Trade has been fair during the month but has not been
good enough to absorb any of our unemployed members who are still anxiously
waiting for a trade revival. We have been privileged with a visit from our
Council Member, Mr. Manners, who gave us a very lucid exposition of the
New Agreement, and the work of our Council, on behalf of the Union. His
speech was listened to with interest, and we hope Mr. Manners has carried away
pleasant recollections and a desire to come again and give us a helping hand
with the slow and difficult work of organising Devon and Cornwall. If the
repairers are to receive the full benefits of Trade Board legislation, then some
effort must be made to get into touch with them and explain the efforts which
our Union has put forth on their behalf, for the prevailing idea among boot
repairers is that Trade Boards and Trade Unionism has no connecting link.
This error must be removed and the search-light of reason directed to the spot
where the stepping stones of Trade Unionism mark the rugged path.

FACTS FOR WOMEN WORKERS.

Working Women and Education.

The Conference on the Higher Education of Working Women, held at Toynbee Hall
on January 11th, was a great success. It was the first time that a Conference of such
kind had been called and the result must have been very gratifying to those responsible
for the arrangements. There were 230 delegates present, representing 88 working cla
organisations and 20 other societies interested in education for women. The bod
represented included Trade Unions, Local Labour Parties, and branches of the Women
Co-operative Guild, as well as the Workers' Educational Association, the National Ad
School Union, &c., and the packed hall showed the intense interest taken in the subject.

Miss Margaret Bondfield, who presided, said that they had come together to conside
how to obtain education for working women and to get their views on the matter. Th
hoped that as a result of the Conference and the speeches that would be made there, wome
main purpose of education was to teach people How to think. not WHAT to think. She
would be stimulated to think for themselves and to work out their own problems.

TRADE BOARD ENQUIRY.
Slow Workers and the Minimum Wage.
On Wednesday last, before Lord Cave's Committee, evidence was given by Mr. W. A.
Willis. LL.B., deputy chairman of the Boot and Shoe Repairing Trade Board and other
Boards, who said he thought that no system of a national minimum could be satisfactory
unless it dealt with persons who were sub-normal and slow workers.
That was his opinion from the experience he had had on the Boot and Shoe Board,
where they had to deal with applications, not by the dozen, but by the hundred. They
were possibly people who came under the heading of physical and mental infirmity. That
would be a bigger business than he could appreciate. He did not agree that if the Trade
Board system was extended on existing lines it would put these sub-normal workers out
of employment ; in fact, he thought it would give them employment ; but he did agree
that if the present system was extended to all industries the sub-normal or slow worker
would be completely blockaded from getting a job. He certainly preferred legislation
trade by trade. The subject of district committees had been mentioned on their Board,
but it had been left over for further discussion. He thought the whole country might
be divided into, say, seven or eight portions. Then they would be able to deal with those
districts much in the same way as the building trade had dealt with their problems. He
saw no alternative to allowing the committee to fix the rate. He was saying this without
having heard the matter discussed as far as the whole of the retail distributive trades were
concerned, but he had heard it discussed on the Boot and Shoe Board. That trade was,
of course, essentially a making-up trade which was carried on in every village in the country.
and so far as that Board was concerned both sides objected to district committees having
any power to fix rates. He did not know whether there was absolute unanimity on the
employers' side, but one would have thought that the employers would rather have relished
the idea of district trade committees.
With regard to the Boot Trade Board there had been about 33 occasions when they
had dealt with rates of any substance at all, and of that number of occasions, on 26 there
was agreement, the appointed members had voted seven times, and only on three out of
these seven occasions, did the votes of the appointed members carry. Every man in the
boot and shoe industry was more or less skilled. The Board had no power to deal with
any man unless he was actively engaged in making or repairing; they could not deal with
porters and that sort of people.-Shoe and Leather News, February 9th, 1922.

CO-PARTNERSHIP WORKSHOPS.
Anchor Boot.
The sales for the second half of 1921 have been £13,384, less than one quarter those of
the corresponding period of 1920. This shows how great the trade depression has been,

All unions affected by this union-smashing effort of the employers are respectfully re-
quested to circularise their members immediately, warning them that to accept the em-
ployers' invitation to allow their union to be used for such a purpose, would be an act of
treachery to Trade Union principles.

Any member of the Amalgamated Engineering Union attempting to serve his own
interests by deserting his fellow workers in the hour of trouble must also take notice that
a betrayal of Trade Union interests in the direction suggested by the employers, would
be an act as unscrupulous as any workman could perpetrate.

It is quite evident that the Engineering Employers' Federation have decided to wage
war on the Amalgamated Engineering Union and other unions, with the object of their
complete destruction, and the Trade Union movement must be fully aware that success
attending this object will imperil the safety of all unions and completely destroy the power
of Trade Unionism in this country.

The General Council, therefore, appeal to all officials and Executive Committees of
the affiliated unions to take all necessary steps to warn their members against the opera-
tions of the Employers' Federation directed to secure the assistance of members of other
Trade Unions in support of their avowed object.

Yours sincerely,
THE GENERAL COUNCIL.
We feel confident that the statements contained in the circular will prove
to all the members the absolute necessity of solidarity in the ranks of Labour
at this crisis. We cannot imagine any Union becoming an agent for breaking
up, or in the slightest degree lending themselves to any policy that would weaken
the Engineering and kindred Unions. On the contrary, now is the time to
show to all, that any attempts made to create in the ranks of Labour a state of
suspicion, one to another, or to give countenance to the idea that because of
difficulties forced upon them, any other Union would open its doors to member-
ship from those already in membership with their legitimate Union is doomed
to failure and deservedly so. The Joint Council of the Trades Union Congress
and the Labour Party have been doing what is possible to bring about an
honourable settlement, and have approached the Government to have an enquiry
into the question. The Government refused to act, alleging that it might
prolong the dispute. We hope that this deplorable position taken up by the
Government will not be forgotten when once again an appeal is made for your
vote to return members to the House of Commons.

ANOTHER UNION J.P.
We are pleased to report that Mr. W. R. Townley has been added to the
list of Justices of the Peace for Northampton. We trust our colleague may
long be spared to enjoy his new honour.

GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.

FELLOW MEMBERS,
CHESHAM. With the patience of Job we have for the past six months endeavoured
to the best of our ability to persuade, entreat, and almost beg of the Boot and Shoe Manu
facturers of Chesham to meet us with the object of restoring the position which they
occupy to one of equality with the rest of the industry. Many meetings of the operatives
have been held, who are not used to trade disturbances, and who certainly are not desirous
of breaking away with the firms where they have been employed so long. The state of
trade in the industry generally does not warrant our straining the relationship that has
existed between ourselves and the employers, and the advantage taken by the employers
of Chesham is not commendable in any sense. I believe the Boot and Shoe Manufacturers
to-day, at least for the present, are only likely to give two half-pennies for one penny, lut
at the same time many other people are similarly situated. The operatives more so,
whose banking account is either non-existent, or they have drawn upon the savings that
they have been able to accumulate for the last few years, until nothing is left. In the
light of this position, we thought at least, being at one time members of the Federation,
the Chesham employers would have met us and talked the matter over; but no, they have
not even had the courtesy to answer our letters, and therefore, there has been no other
alternative than to advise our members to hand in notices, as we cannot advise any member
of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives to work for any other firms in Chesham,
with the exception of Messrs. A. J. Reynolds, The Co-operative Society, and Messrs.
Woodington. These three firms have not shown any antagonism to us up to the present.
We are therefore calling upon the operatives to carry out their resolution of three
months ago to stand by the Union, its Officers, and themselves, until the employers of
Chesham have reached a better frame of mind.
The Government this week have offered their services which we have received with
alacrity, but from reports gathered from that source, the employers appear to wish to make
a bargain with the operatives independent of the Union's Officers. This would mean
that they have a desire themselves becoming non-unionists, and have no sympathy with
their fellow manufacturers in other parts of the Kingdom, to persuade the operatives
to cut themselves adrift from the Trade Union and Labour movement. This idea of
going back to the "Robinson Crusoe" policy of isolation will not be encouraged by us
in any sense, and I am sanguine enough to believe that the operatives in Chesham will
believe that they are entitled to be treated as good and on as honourable a level as any
boot and shoe operative in any part of the Kingdom. To this end we shall direct our
energies, hoping we shall have the assistance of the whole of the industry, as we have up
to the present time, especially through the medium of that very friendly publication,
The Shoe and Leather Record, who have never failed to give advice in the interests of the
industry to all concerned, at times including ourselves. This trouble is extremely regret-
table, as we have a reputation of being conciliatory in all our doings, and may the day
be far distant when we depart from the policy of common-sense and take up that pro-
posed by the employers of Chesham of trying to prevent fellow-freedom of the individual
in the trade to which he belongs.
In accordance with the principles of Trade Unionism the Chesham operatives have
severed their connection for the time being with their employment, and until such time
as they receive the respect due to them from employers for whom they have worked so
long, the issue is plain, simple and strong. They refuse to discard their Local Officials
or the National Officials although they are requested to do so. They refuse to meet their
employers unless accompanied by their Local or National Officials, and they intend to assert
their manhood and hold fast to the principle of collective bargaining, and to be treated as
humans.
WELLINGBOROUGH. - The Wellingborough employers have been a great source of
disturbance recently, owing to the fact that the whole of them have taken up the attitude
respecting a position assumed and put into operation by four members of the Federation,
but up to the time of writing have not signified their intention to respect the Holiday
Fund. These four members, I understand at Rushden, are influenced very largely from
the view that no man ought to receive anything for which he does not work. We, on the
other hand, believe that we have to earn the holiday money that is paid annually by a
method in which other wages are earned, and therefore, when one remembers whatever
may be an individual view for the whole of the industry, almost without exception the
whole trade have agreed to adopt this policy. The Union have taken upon themselves
the responsibility of pressing those outside the Federation, to act in a similar manner.
We are, however, pressing the Federation to deal with these members, or we shall be
compelled to do so.
I visited Wollaston and Finedon, and as I said before re Wellingborough in connection
with these four members in the Rushden Town, are cited as the source of all the reasons
why others refuse to comply. We certainly hope the Federation at their meeting this

STAMPED FOOTWEAR. May I once more appeal to our members to endeavour to put
a little life into the Stamped Boot and Shoe, as there is a very good agitation going on at
the present moment for a pure article for the benefit of the public. Some of us believe
that this agitation will save the hard earnings of poor people of this country who often
buy shoddy boots and are literally robbed of the money that they pay for them. This
is a statement which ought to be made, and I hope it fits every manufacturer who is guilty
of putting in strawboard or compo insoles to any boot or shoe in this country for outdoor
wear. Indoor is another matter; persons may be able to walk about barefoot or in their
stockinged feet, but to give people compo and paper in their boots without their knowledge
is nothing less than a fraud, and everything I can do to crush these people I shall be willing
to do, and I hope I shall get the assistance of all others in a similar turn of mind. To my
mind the country never knew of a better or more genuine article than when the War-time
boot was made, and I may add for the benefit of those people who object to Government
Departments, that this was made under Government supervision. For that reason some
of us would like more Government supervision, who could, if they like, solve the unem
ployment problem by finding direct employment.

7. MECKLENBURGH STREET,

LIVERPOOL.--Trade is much the same as the previous month, but we
are hoping to see an improvement between now and Easter. The "flu" is
very prevalent just now, and has touched up some of our members. There is
no doubt but what we are passing through a critical time, many people have
to tighten their waist belt and imagine they have bad a good feed, and go on
looking for the silver lining that is supposed to fringe the dark clouds; longing
for the time when they will see a "land fit for heroes to live in." If we study
the different newspapers and periodicals we find that everyone is in difficulties,
either politically or financially. We note that some co-operative societies
have decided to pay no dividend on the past six months' trading, and they all
report a loss on trading due to the slump in prices. We assume the same
applies to what is termed the private trader; whilst the cry goes on, we must
lower the cost of production by reducing wages so as to compete in the open
markets of the world. Then, if we look at the political side, we find everything
seems on the balance ready to topple over any moment. The present Coalition
appears likely to split up into sections, each having an axe to grind, and looking
for a strong man to lead them. Even the Labour Party is not a united body,
because we have at least three sections: moderate, advanced, and extremists.
Some people are of the opinion that if we had a General Election and a change
of Government trade might improve, but that is a doubtful question as a lot
will depend on the result of the poll and the men who lead the van.

LONDON METRO.—There is no improvement in our conditions. Trade
generally is bad with the exception of Turnshoe making. For many of our
members the outlook is very black. The reductions under the National
Agreement have been accepted in a loyal spirit by our members, also the
employers, although some of the latter tried to add to their pound of flesh.
Mrs. Bray, through the Executive, desires to thank the following Branches
for their contributions to the W. Bray Fund :- The Council, Ayr, Bristol
No. 2, Bromsgrove, Chesham, Glasgow, Kettering No. 1, Kettering No. 2,
Kilmarnock, Kingswood, Leeds No. 1, Leeds No. 2, Leicester No. 1, Leicester
No. 2, Leicester Women's, Manchester, Maybole, Norwich No. 1, Norwich
No. 2, Northampton No. 1, Northampton No. 2, Waterford, Redruth, Stafford,
Wolverhampton, Hinckley, Rushden, Worcester and London Metro. The
total amount collected was £124 9s. 6d. The Executive also wish to take this
opportunity of thanking Mr. J. Buckle, J.P., for his services and great interest
that so helped to put us on a sure line for the future.

MAYBOLE.-We are sorry to again report trade very slack, and a good
many of our members being dismissed. This is unfortunate as there are no
jobs to be had anywhere, and will have the effect of reducing the funds and the
membership of the Union, which will be a serious matter.

PLYMOUTH.--Trade has remained quiet during the month, and unem-
ployment is assuming a serious aspect throughout the district. Probably few
towns have suffered more severely than our own during the past two years
of trade depression. When we contemplate what the condition of the Boot
Repairing trade would have been without the protection of a Trade Board,
we have a feeling of thankfulness for its stabilising effect, and the freedom it
has given us from the bickering, and heart-breaking struggle which would
have been inevitable to maintain a living wage, if such protection had not been
given. We congratulate our old friend, Buckle, upon the able manner in which
be placed our case before Lord Cave's Committee, and the evidence given by
Mr. Crabb for the employers was good to read. We do not forget that he (Mr.
Crabb) is a West-countryman, and once having nailed his flag to the mast,
will not lower it with the first shot fired.

THE MORALITY OF PRICES.
If businesss ever reaches the ideal we may see many changes in present-day methods.
For instance, there is certainly room for what for want of a better term we may describe
as "Morality in Prices." Always there appears to be a tug of war as between bayers
there is one continual struggle to pull prices down; on the other there is an equal and
and sellers without any fixed basis of selling price determined by cost. On the one side
fixed determination to keep them up, and the stronger placed side for the time being equal
it may be one and then the other.

But what is chiefly complained of is the wilful misrepresentation that
takes place, and in this respect the whole situation at the present time is
most unsatisfactory. The buyer goes his rounds in some cases deliberately determined
to depress prices below what he knows too well is a paying figure. To beat the producers
he tells fairy stories of having bought just as good a parcel at considerably less money
and if the producer is a fool, or a very unfortunate man, he believes the story: whereas
if he had investigated the circumstances further he would have found that misrepresenta
tions had been made that the money paid on the previous occasion was just as much
as the leather was worth.

On the other hand, it is also true that a good deal of leather has been changing hands
recently, not of the substance and nature demanded by the purchaser, or that the pur
chaser believed he was getting. Simply a question of price again.
On the producer's side there is room for improvement in the same direction. He
puts up his prices according to the strength of the demand, believing in a time of pressure
that the price to charge for his leather is just what the buyer in his panic is prepared to
pay, and prices are forced up unduly, as they are depressed in a time of slump, because
the buyer then uses the same argument from his side.
No man in the trade has any right to sell leather below what it has cost him, just as
he has no moral right to sell it at an extortionate profit.
" morality of prices" to-day, it is regrettable to have to confess, is not quite
Business morality during the war was admittedly not at a very high level. The
what it should be. Still, we all have an abundant fund of hope, and just as we believe
in many respects, the leather trade has got back some degrees to the old standard of
morality which was lost during the war, so may we hope that our thoughts expressed in this
summary fashion may help, in some small degree, to improve the " morality in prices. -
Shoe and Leather News, February 23rd, 1922.

PARLIAMENTARY AGENT'S REPORT
To the 23rd February, 1922.
Once again Parliament has assembled, but the length of the Session on this occasion
is a matter of great speculation. Rumours are current almost every day, sometimes it
is the resignation of Lloyd George that is to take place, at other times it is to be a dis-
solution. There is a strong feeling that the Election will be in April, but for definit
information upon the subject we must "wait and see."
Certainly matters are not proceeding smoothly for the Government, they are being
attacked from all quarters. It is a strange thing that this most wonderful of all Govern-
ments have satisfied nobody, and if only there were anything in the nature of agreement
among the discontents, then the end would be near indeed.
One thing seems to be pretty certain, that Labour in the House will not be able to
secure their downfall, as against us there is a consolidation of forces, no matter how much
they may differ upon other issues.
It is difficult to see how a different position was possible, having regard to how the
Coalition obtained office. Never in the political history of this country were promises
more readily made to the people, all sections were to have their troubles and difficulties
removed, the sun of prosperity was to shine upon all and surprise was expressed that the
wicked Labour Party would not throw in their lot and help bring about the new heaven
on earth.
Our difficulty at the last election has been fully shewn by the results that have followed
We were not opposed to the ideas that were put forward, nor were we against the sugges
tions that were made as to what was needed, our difficulty was to understand how such a
mixed and composite body as the Coalition could possibly usher in this new era. I say
mixed and composite but only so in regard to more or less minor interests, as so far as
the real essentials are concerned they are very solid and compact.
Who would dare to say now that we were wrong in our predictions, or that our fears
have not been completely justified. The last three years is strewn with wreckage, even
where attempts have apparently been made to give effect to promises, the Bills have been
withdrawn almost as soon as they were printed, and where they have become Acts, can-
cellation has taken place almost before the ink has dried upon their pages.
All this is the explanation of present chaos. Nobody appears to be satisfied because
nothing is right, and nothing can be while this Government remain in office. They are
hopelessly incompetent, they have no settled policy, they live from day to day, always in
a Micawber frame of mind hoping for something to turn up, and all that comes along are
the chickens that come home to roost.
The lack of appreciation of what is involved was clearly shewn in the discussion upon
the Labour Party's amendment to the King's Speech in regard to unemployment. Mr.
Clynes was drawing attention to the serious condition obtaining among thousands of the
people through the lack of employment, and was emphasising the awful state in which
many were suffering. Sir Alfred Mond, the Minister of Health, blandly rose and asked
"has anybody starved." Evidently this superior person, who is specially fitted to govern,
is of the opinion that someone must die before there is real evidence of want.
.
The reply of Clynes to the criticism of the Labour Party by Lord Birkenhead was
very effective, the noble Lord like many of his colleagues had discovered that Labour is
not fit to govern, but also like his colleagues he is not certain the people believe this, so it
is up to them to convey the necessary information. He evidently was not very confident
of his case so far as material facts were concerned, so he called us by harsh names, we
were "poltroons" and several other things, equally as bad. As a lawyer he appreciates
to the full the value of the policy of when you have no case, abuse your opponents.
A further answer has been given by the elections of Clayton and Camberwell. Another
is being prepared at Wolverhampton, and if only the Government will provide other
opportunities, further replies from constituencies can be given.
The question that perhaps above all others that has occupied the public mind
during the past few weeks has been the Geddes Report. There are parts of it we can
agree with, but apparently they are the parts that the Ministers concerned will not accept,
stand the better chance of being accepted, viz., Housing, Education, &c. This report
such as the cuts affecting the Army and Navy. Those that we must and shall oppose
completes the wreckage of the New England, that "grandeur of being belongs to the
past. The future is to be but a repetition of what obtained before the wonderful promises
will in the industrial field, and they hope to do likewise politically before the people are
were made, only more so. The economic condition enable these people to impose their
given a chance to pass judgment upon them.

But the chance may come soon, and it is up to all of us to see that the judgment is
sound and emphatic. The best way is to return Labour men and women to Parliament
and elsewhere. This is a task which belongs to everyone, none can escape their share of

To 20th March, 1922.

The feeling of uncertainty that pervades the political situation in the country is
also characteristic of matters in the House of Commons. Everyone is wondering what is
really going to happen, and the enquiry that frequently greets one as to when the General
Election is to take place, indicate what is uppermost in the minds of many. This is not
surprising, having regard to the number who have no hopes of returning, and the others
whose numbers are by no means insignificant who have grave doubts as to what will
happen when the electors get another chance.

Some of our members in Leicester are about to be given an opportunity to reverse
the decision of December, 1918. I sincerely trust they will rise to the occasion. This is
not a time for petty differences, it is a time for solid combined effort against the common
enemy. The events of the past few months can surely leave no room for doubt in the
minds of the workers, or of those who wish well of their country. Whatever else may
happen the Coalition must go, and every bye-election should point in that direction.
I look to the Boot Operatives of Leicester to deliver a smashing blow to the enemy, and
thus help to re-establish Labour in that City for parliamentary purposes.

The business of the House since the passing of the Irish Treaty (Agreement) Bill has
not been of an exciting character, though on the discussion upon the Geddes Report the
Labour Party played its part in opposing those recommendations which would have
placed further penalties on the backs of the workers. The discussion upon the Education
cut was instructive. The Labour Party, according to its critics, is composed of those who
seek by violence and such like to upset and destroy all that stands for sound and good
government, so much so is this the view held that special missions and newspaper agitations
have to be organised whereby the people and the country may be saved from the machina-
tions of the "scoundrels and poltroons" who compose the Labour Party.

Yet I listened to these words from the Member for Oxford, who has great qualifications
to speak upon education. He said, "Many of us have received, in the course of the last
few weeks, a very strong appeal from the teachers of this country not to curtail the ex-
penditure on education. Not the less does that arouse a difficult question for those who
like myself, are very deeply concerned as to the future of national education. I know
that this is a question in which hon. Members on the Labour Benches feel very keenly
indeed. I heard Lord Haldane in another place last week say, and I believe it to be true,
that the Labour Party, of all parties in this country, and at the present moment, are
keenest in regard to education, and I should like to add my testimony to their anxiety in
that regard. I know it to be true that they are keenly anxious on that question."

This is a striking contrast to most that is said of us, and what emerges from it is
that we, more than any other section, want to see an educated people, that we, more than
anyone, want the chance of an appeal to an intelligent electorate. But those who are our
critics know this, and they do not want an educated electorate. They want a gullible
people, who can be swayed by prejudice, who can be manœuvred into false positions,
in short, they stand to gain from ignorance, we from enlightenment.

On the supplementary estimates the Labour Members have by no means been silent
or inactive. The Minister of Health was severely criticised upon the attitude of his Depart-
ment upon Housing, Health, &c., but the so-called economy practised by him is to the
liking of the House, and it is useless to try and convince them it is wrong. I sometimes
think there is a tendency to judge and criticise the Labour Party, by the success or failure
in convincing the House by the speeches delivered. This is a mistake. The speeches
are alright, it is the audience that is wrong. It is labour in vain. The only way is the
Fisher way, "sack the lot."

The case of the ex-Service man was well put by Griffiths, Lawson, Guest, and others,
when the estimate was under consideration dealing with the work of the Appeal Tribunals,
a body that has the final word in deciding applications for pensions. A case quoted by
T. Griffiths is worth stating to show what is meted out to those who suffered in the war.
A soldier badly wounded at Loos, but who later resumed duty, was after discharge rendered
incapable of work as a result of his wounds. He got a pension, but died shortly after.
His wife then received a pension, but the case was sent up for reconsideration, and the
pension disallowed, not because of the facts as stated not being correct, but because the
man, in his anxiety, like thousands of others to get out of the army, had signed himself
out. "Their sacrifice will never be forgot by a grateful country."

To-day, as I write, the discussion is taking place upon the Engineers' lock-out; whether
it will be productive of good time will tell, but it is well that the workers' case should be
stated on the floor of the House of Commons. An enquiry under the Industrial Courts

countless arrests of Socialists, and of all those who were connected with them.
Twice over, the Bolsheviks have had the prison of Boutirky invaded, and the
prisoners beaten to death..."

And further on :

"The condition of State Prisoners, especially of Members of the Central
Committee of the Social Revolutionary Party, is, at present, more than
painful. They are kept in strict isolation. For some time interviews have
been refused them. Before the attack on the Boutirky Prison, the representa-
tives of the Red Cross were authorised to go there; now they have no longer
the right. In the Taganka Prison, the political prisoners are separated from
the others, in premises, the lower story of which is not heated; in winter it is
unendurable. In the provincial prisons, Ural, Jaroslav, etc., the situation is
even more awful. Certain prisoners, transferred on April 28, are not to be
found anywhere in the provinces, and their fate remains absolutely unknown.

"I am convinced that, in the conditions indicated, the larger
number of the political prisoners will die. There are many amongst
them who are now seriously ill. Unless there is intervention in
their favour they will certainly perish."

It is the duty of the International, both to itself and to its unhappy
comrades in Russia, to take the initiative in such intervention.

When, under the pressure of the famine, and in order to maintain itself
in power in spite of everything, the Soviet Government resolved to make
concessions, in fact and in principle, to the Capitalist States, concessions
which were the very negation of its programme, an initial condition was
imposed upon it, namely, the liberation of such foreigners, British, French,
Americans, as, for political reasons, it was detaining in its prisons.

The hour has now come to demand the same thing for State prisoners of
Russian nationality, whose sole crime is that of having remained faithful to
their ideals and principles.

Serious, definite, concordant, as are the accusations made in the Memo-
randum on Soviet prisons, we admit that they cannot be held to be definitive,
unless the Soviet Government persists in its silence or its refusal to furnish
the required explanations.

But it is the right and the duty of the International to demand these
explanations.

Is it true that there are in Russian prisons, thousands of men,
chiefly Socialists, whose only crime is that of being adversaries of
the Soviet Government? Is it true that these State prisoners, badly
fed and deprived of medical care, are submitted to a regime, which
is destroying their health and threatening their life?

Is it true that, in order to defend themselves from the merciless
treatment or arbitrary acts of which they are the victims, many of
them have no other resource than to have recourse to a hunger
strike as in the time of the Tsars?


---
and professional education of teachers. It would recognise the vital importance of maintaining amongst its teachers freshness of mind and intellectual alertness, and do all that is possible to prevent staleness which must be the death of real education.

What is needed to-day is a new conception of elementary or, as I prefer to call it, primary education. In the past elementary education was of a special kind devised for a special class (which incidentally formed the great majority of the people) and which was treated as something inferior. But the primary school ought to be in England what it is in America, the common school, and its equipment should be the best the nation can offer.

What can be more absurd than to insist on classes not exceeding 30 in secondary schools and to allow classes of 60 in primary schools, to provide playing fields for the former but not for the latter ; to have different standards of staffing and air space? When we obtain, as we ultimately must, universal secondary education, the primary school will no longer be engaged in the impossible task of trying to educate both the child of seven and the adolescent of 13. It will assume its proper place. It will become the universal preparatory school.

There are those who, whilst approving of compulsory primary education, do not regard universal secondary education as an essential of a democratic community. Many people hold the view that all children are not capable of profiting by a secondary education. In my judgment a universal system of secondary education is a fundamental need of democracy. Moreover, I do not accept the view that education of the secondary type ought to be confined to selected students. The Education Act of 1918 accepts the principle of compulsory education for all young persons. The law, therefore, has recognised the need for a system of universal education for all boys and girls up to the age of 16 (and ultimately 18), irrespective of their mental capacity, so that the question of compulsory adolescent education has been settled. What is in dispute is its character. An excellent primary school system does not dispose of the need for the education of boys and girls after this period of education has closed. Adolescence has its own education needs.

Secondary education is the appropriate type of education for adolescents, as primary education is the type suitable for children. The report of the Departmental Committee on Scholarships and Free Places-states that " practically all children except the sub- normal (put at 25 per cent. of the total number) are intellectually capable of profiting by full time instruction up to 16 or beyond." That it is proposed that there should be an immediate increase of free places from 25 to 40 per cent., and that secondary education should be freed by the abolition of school fees as soon as the financial situation allows.

If this were carried out if three-quarters of the children in elementary schools passed to secondary, there would be 24 millions in the latter. In actual fact to-day there are less than 300,000, and the accommodation even for these is not adequate. Let no one say the small numbers in secondary schools is because there is no demand for secondary education. In 1919 no less than 9,271 applicants for admission to secondary schools in England as fee-paying pupils were refused admission for want of accommodation, and a further 8,780 were excluded because no free places for these were available, though they had reached the intellectual standard demanded by the school authorities.

Until about 20 years ago, secondary education was frankly a class preserve, and the idea that it could be required by the children of working people was dismissed as ridiculous. But the foundation of a democratic system of public secondary education has been laid, there is now a steady stream of children from elementary to secondary schools. But we have not so far proceeded further than the foundations. We must abandon the old idea of elementary and secondary education as two different systems. They are two stages in a single course of development which ought to be indissolubly connected. Secondary education is not merely for gifted children, but for all normal children. This will take time but we must hold it before us as the objective of our efforts. It is well to remember that the well-to-do give their children a secondary education, often at expensive schools, irrespective of their ability.

It is impossible to exaggerate the actual value of keeping the whole juvenile population under educational influences during the perilous years of adolescence. What the community loses by throwing immature and ill-equipped young people to the mercy of economic forces and casting them into an environment which tends to sterilise intellectual interests, to dull the finer sensibilities, and only too often to coarsen the moral fibre, cannot be measured. If it be urged that the adoption of a system of secondary education would involve the community in considerable financial obligations, I would reply that the loss sustained by the present waste of human possibilities far outweighs the financial expenditure necessary to secure compulsory education for all.

With a universal system of primary and secondary education, we should have laid the foundations on which university and technical education should be built. So far as technical education is concerned its value largely depends upon whether or not they have had the advantage of secondary education, without which they would not possess the necessary background of knowledge.

MR. W. R. TOWNLEY, J.P.
The name of Mr. William Robert Townley, the president of the Northampton No. 1
Branch of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives, has been added to the Com-
mission of the Peace for the County Borough of Northampton.
The announcement that Mr. Townley has been appointed a magistrate will le received
with a good deal of satisfaction in the town, for Mr. Townley is recognised to be a shrewd
administrator and he will bring sound ability to the discharge of his new duties.
Mr. Townley, who is in his forty-sixth year, is a native of Northampton. His associa-
tion with the boot trade has extended over thirty-four years, and except for a period in
which he worked in Glasgow, all his life has been spent in the town in which he was torn.
Always a strong Trade Unionist, he was in 1913 elected vice-president of his branch
of the Boot and Shoe Operatives' Union, and four years later, on the resignation of the
late Mr. D. Stanton, J.P., he became president. He has been president of Northang ton
Trades Council, was one of the Labour members of the Military Service Tribunal, has
Served on the Borough Insurance Committee, and on the Court of Referees at the Em-
ployment Exchange. For two years he represented the Northampton District on the
National Executive of the Boot and Shoe Operatives' Union, and he has frequently repre-
sented his branch at the National Conference.- Northampton Echo, March 22nd, 192

SOCIALISTS IN PRISON.
Appeal of the Second International. Demands on Moscow.

A manifesto on Socialist prisoners in Russian Communist prisons was issued yesterday by the Executive Committee of the Second International.
The Second International, it says, appeals to-day to all Socialists to demand of the Moscow Government an account of the manner in which it is treating its political adver- saries in the prisons of Russia.

Since the early months of 1918 increasingly numerous and pressing complaints have been made on the subject of executions en masse, arbitrary arrests, measures of terror decreed by the Tche-ka, in the name of the new power.

Batch of Allegations.
On the improbable accusation of counter-revolutionary tendencies, tried Socialists, Mensheviks, or Social Revolutionaries such as Gotz, Vedeniapine, Timofeev, Eugenie Ratner, Dan, S. Marosov, D. Donskoi, who had been liberated from Tsarist prisons in 1917, have been once again cast into the same prisons under the supervision of the same warders who had charge of them during the Tsarist régime.

Since then evidence has increased and become more definite. On November 20th 1920, the Central Committee of the Social Revolutionary Party addressed to the Com- munist Party in Moscow an open letter on the starvation diet which more than 60 prisoners, accused solely of belonging to the Social Revolutionary Party, were forced to undergo at the Central Convict Prison of Jaroslav.

On May 6th, 1921, the Central Organisation Bureau of the Socialist Party addressed to the proletariat of all countries a special appeal to denounce the acts of violence practised on the prisoners in the too celebrated prison of Boutirky in Moscow, and in the prisons of Zara, Žerentoni, Sakhaline and Odessa.

Finally, in October of the same year, the Executive Committee of the Conference of members of the Russian Constituent Assembly published, in a " Memorandum on Russian Prisons," a résumé of letters, manifestoes and complaints, individual or collective, which constitutes the most formidable of charges against the present régime in Russian prisons.

Concessions Asked For.
When, under the pressure of the famine, and in order to maintain itself in power in spite of everything, the Soviet Government resolved to make concessions, in fact and in principle, to the capitalist States, concessions which were the very negation of its programme, an initial condition was imposed upon it: namely, the liberation of such foreigners-British, French, Americans-as, for political reasons, it was detaining in its prisons.

The hour has now come to demand the same thing for State prisoners of Russian nationality, whose sole crime is that of having remained faithful to their ideals and prin- ciples.

Serious, definite, concordant as are the accusations made in the Memorandum on Soviet Prisons, we admit that they cannot be held to be definitive unless the Soviet Govern- ment persists in its silence or its refusal to furnish the required explanations.

But it is the right and the duty of the International to demand those explanations.
Threat of Hunger Strike.

Is it true that there are in Russian prisons thousands of men, chiefly Socialists, whose only crime is that of being adversaries of the Soviet Government? Is it true that these State prisoners, badly fed and deprived of medical care, are submitted to a régime which is destroying their health and threatening their life ?

Is it true that, in order to defend themselves from the merciless treatment or arbitrary acts of which they are the victims, many of them have no other resource than to have recourse to a hunger strike, as in the time of the Tsars?

We urgently request all affiliated Parties to make known these questions, which the International is publicly putting to the Government of Moscow, and to put them in their turn. They will judge for themselves, according to circumstances, how their action can most usefully be taken, whether through the Press or in political meetings, or by interviews with those who represent the Soviet Government abroad.

In some form or another, however, their intervention is a matter of urgent necessity. It is a question of the liberty, possibly of the life, of thousands of human beings.— Daily Herald, February 25th, 1922.

£1,441 WAGES ARREARS.
"One of the Worst Cases of Sweating"-says Labour Ministry.
Arrears of wages amounting to £1,441 were alleged to have been due to employees
of the Redruth Brewery Company, whose manager, James Wickett, was fined £2 at Cam-

1922 and
The Fourth Special Period from the 2nd November, 1922, to the 1st
July, 1923.
(d) The payment during the Third Special Period of a maximum amount of 15
weeks' benefit divided (in the case of persons receiving "free" or uncovenanted
benefit) into aggregate periods of 5 weeks, each period to be separated from the
previous one by an interval of 5 weeks. This division will not apply in the case
of persons who are entitled to benefit in respect of contributions to the Unemploy
ment Fund.
(e) No benefit to be paid in respect of unemployment on any day prior to the 17th
April in the Third Special Period to applicants who have drawn 22 weeks' benefit
from the commencement of the Second Special Period and before that date.
(f) During the Fourth Special Period 12 weeks' benefit to be payable with discretion-
ary power to the Minister to grant two further extensions of not exceeding five
weeks each to applicants who have made certain contributions to the Unemploy-
ment Fund.
(g) The conditions for the receipt of benefit (other than benefit payable in respect
of contributions under the one-in-six rule) to be the same as those at present
operating in respect of benefit for the "further six weeks" in the Second Special
Period with the exception that instead of proof of employment being required
in each of not less than 20 weeks since the 31st December, 1919, proof would be
required as follows :-
(i.) that not less than 20 contributions to the Unemployment Fund have
been paid in respect of the applicant; or
(ii.) that, having regard to the opportunities of employment in the applicant's
normal employment, he has been since 31st December, 1919, employed
for a reasonable period in some occupation which is now insurable or
in the case of a person formerly engaged in War Service that he had
been so employed before becoming so engaged or had no opportunity
owing to his youth of being so employed.
(h) The combined contributions under the new Act to be equal in amount to the
combined contributions at present paid in respect of Unemployment Insurance
and Dependants' Grants.
FIVE-WEEK MONTH.
There being five Saturdays during this month, Secretaries are asked to
make up their returns and pay for the same accordingly.
GENERAL ELECTION.
Rumours are constantly heard that the Government are only waiting a
favourable moment to declare for a General Election. We urge upon all to
put their machinery in order so that whether it comes in the near future or
It is
is delayed for some time, the workers may be found ready for the same.
of no practical value to complain after an election if it turns out contrary to
what we desire. The workers constitute the overwhelming majority of the
electorate. See to it that the vote is so used as will ensure those Members
being returned who will bring into existence just and equitable laws whereby
the people will be enabled to live under good conditions.

The political world is still in an unstable position, members of the Govern-
mont, especially Mr. Winston Churchill, M. P. doing all that they can by
speeches, full of invective on the one hand, and appeals to fear on the other
hand, of the terrible things that will happen if the Labour Party should come
into power in this country. The trend of events both in the country and in
the House of Commons, clearly show the necessity of keeping fully efficient
the machinery of the Labour Party, and thus be prepared for any events that
may arise in the near future. The bye-election at Leicester during the past
month shows what can be done by concentration day by day. We felt it
necessary to take some share in the said bye-election, and the President spent
some time in the constituency, urging the workers to use their votes on behalf
of Labour, and the last few days of the contest found all the Parliamentary
Candidates of the Union also assisting. The result was indeed remarkable, as
will be seen by the following figures :---

This was no small achievement to have secured, and it shows that there
is an awakening amongst the electorate which we hope will continue to grow
until the majority of Members in the House of Commons belong to the Labour
Party.

INDUSTRIALLY.

The situation continues very unsatisfactory. The dispute affecting so many
thousands in the Engineering and Allied Trades still continues. This has a
real, if indirect, effect upon many other industries, increasing unemployment
and augmenting the suffering and sorrow of multitudes of people. We sincerely
hope our colleagues may speedily be successful in securing reasonable con-
ditions of employment and treatment such as is due from one person to another.

We have already granted the sum of £100-this being the limit in
accordance with Rule 257-to the A.E.U., and to enable us to assist the
A.E.U. and kindred societies in future, we ask for powers to make a loan
of £5,000 to any such society.

The wider position is still in a state of uncertainty. Many are turning
to the Conference of Nations at Genoa (where the General Secretary has
been present), and hoping that from the discussions which are there taking
place there may emerge some better and more humane methods of dealing
with the intricate problems that have become accentuated as a result of
the recent war. There is no sort of doubt in our mind that the outlook
of those in authority must be changed if any real and lasting benefit is
to accrue to the people as a whole. Equally we feel sure that the vested
interests will make a strenuous fight to keep as far as possible the real
power in their own hands. The persons at the Conference at Genoa have
therefore those opportunities that seldom come to men, viz., the power to
so make arrangements as will indeed make it possible for humanity to go

Once again we feel bound to call the serious attention of Branch Secretaries to the fact that the FIFTEENTH day of each month is the latest day for returns reaching the General Secretary. If Branches fail to send off their returns to reach the Central Office before the 15th of the month it tends to upset the organisation of the work in the General Secretary's Office. We beg to intimate that unless returns are in before the 15th of the month, the Secretary has been instructed to put into force the Rules governing the same. GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
EAST LEICESTER BYE-ELECTION. - Probably the most important feature I hav
to report this month is the magnificent way in which the members of the Union responde
to the call of the Executive of the Union and their local officers in the East Leiceste
Election. The employers in the town of Leicester, and all those interested in the trad
who do not belong to the wage-earning class, and who are not members of the Nationa
Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives, are taking their beating badly. When we kne
that the President of the Federation was about to contest the seat, we felt that, as h
opinions and ours differed so widely on matters concerning the welfare of the Union and
home affairs in general, and knowing also the dearth of direct Labour representative
there is in the House of Commons, and that already Mr. Marlow's class has no less tha
600 members there, we were determined to put our members upon their merits, with th..
result that we all threw ourselves into the fight. The Executive of the Union issued the
following manifesto :-

TO ALL BOOT OPERATIVES-MEN AND WOMEN-AND WORKERS GENERALLY.
You now have a splendid opportunity of sending to the House of Commor
another Labour representative. The Council of the National Union of Boot Operative
appeal to you to record your vote for Alderman G. Banton.

Do not be misled by statements about "Wage Cuts" and the Council of the
Union agreeing to the same.

Mr. Marlow and his colleagues of the Manufacturers' Federation were, and are
responsible for the "Cuts."

The Council members fought strenuously against the same.

Now is the time to strengthen the position of Labour. Let it be known that you
resent the onslaughts being made upon the workers.

Your votes will determine the issue; you are in the majority; give your vote
to the Labour Candidate, and thus strike one more blow for freedom and progress.

Signed on behalf of the Members of the Council of the National Union of Boot
and Shoe Operatives.

T. F. RICHARDS, General President.
E. L. POULTON, General Secretary.

They also advised their four Parliamentary Candidates, with their Member of Parlia
ment, to assist to the best of their powers. Needless to say this was done. The language
on the above manifesto is resented very largely by some of the employers, and as usual
they adopted any argument to try and lead us to believe that our interests would be best
served by another employer and another manufacturer being returned instead of giving
us an opportunity of getting representatives for ourselves. One little point I would like
to remind them of is this: that had the President of the Federation had any liking for
the Union, why did he choose to fight the seat at Wellingborough ?-the only place where
we have our one representative in Parliament for the Industry? It is no use my going
into more details-suffice it to say I attended no less than 25 open-air meetings, and con-
sequently our appeals were made directly to our own Boot and Shoe Members. The
Members of Parliament who came down to speak on behalf of Alderman Banton, M.P.,
J.P., went back rather sad because of the lack of enthusiasm, but as we said, we felt sure
that our members, when the facts were brought close home to them, would respond in no
uncertain manner. When one remembers that in 1918 Alderman Banton polled 6,697
votes, and on this occasion the Alderman polled 14,062 votes, which converted the previous
minority into a big majority of 5,352 over the Coalition Candidate--and the majority
over both candidates was 1,597-it shows that he is wholly, solely, and actually, refre
sentative of the East Leicester Division after 70 per cent. of the voters had gone to the
poll. This is indeed the greatest victory that the Labour movement has had in any part
of the country, and to the everlasting credit of the Boot and Shoe Operatives, that they
played such an important part in this election. To those friends of Mr. Marlow, for whom
upon Mr. Marlow as a representative of wage-earners in the British House of Commons,
we have the greatest possible respect, they must pardon us if we say we decline to look
soon, that the Labour Party will take control of the Government of the country, and
or any other men who hold a similar position. I am of the opinion, and hope it will be
endeavour to rescue it from the terrible condition that the upper middle commercial
classes have got us into at the present time.

BRANCH REPORTS.
BARNSLEY. Short time is still going on here in spite of the nasty weather
that we have had, but we hope to have a better report next month
BELFAST Trade continues to remain very bad. It is reported that
the firm of Williamson Bros. is going to close for an indefinite period; if the
report proves correct it will add considerably to our unemployed members
We are passing through a very trying time but we must not lose hope, and
trust there must lie in the future brighter and more prosperous times for the
workers.
BRISTOL We are pleased to report a slight improvement in trade, with
a few of our out-of-work members reinstated at their old places. We hope for
a further improvement, as we have a large number of good old members still
walking the streets idle, and who we hope have well learnt the lesson that if
they want a real and lasting better state of things they must back the Labour
Party, who are the only party with a policy to remedy these evils of recurring
unemployment. Sickness has been rather heavy and three deaths have taken
place within a few weeks. One of these is a very sad case. Our old shopmate
Arthur Downs, who was a highly respected and old steward of the Branch
went to work as usual at 8 a.m. in the morning, had his usual break for a snack
at 10.30, and was about to restart work when he fell down and expired in a few
moments without being able to utter a word to his son who was by his side
It cast quite a gloom over all. Here was one who was always ready to help in
his breezy way anyone who required help, gone in a moment. May God rest
his soul. To his Widow and Children we extend our deepest sympathy. The
Branch Officials and Committee attended the funeral. His body was borne
to the grave by his shopmates who worked around him. One of the principals
and Manager of the firm at which he worked were present, thus showing the
respect they had for one of their oldest workmen.
BRISTOL No. 2.- We are glad to show a lighter sick account for this
month and hope for a further improvement in this direction. Trade in those
factories which produce ladies' light footwear is fairly good, but in the Kings-
wood district, noted for heavy goods, the chronic slump still continues and the
immediate outlook is not cheering. We hope that the effort now being made
at Chesham will be crowned with success for the operatives, as we believe that
it is injurious to the industry for one centre to be on less favourable Wage
Agreements than the rest of the country.
CHESHAM.-After several months of negotiating, with a view of getting
a peaceful settlement and the National conditions again restored, all attempts
by conciliation have failed, and the only alternative left was for notices to be
handed in. This has been done and our members have responded to the call
splendidly, and if we exclude the staff hands we can say that practically the
whole of the boot operatives are out, and do not intend to again commence
work until the employers are prepared to recognise us and pay the same con-
ditions as obtain in other centres making a similar class of work. We have
with us Mr. J. Buckle who is doing splendid work and has at once become
popular with all the operatives, and they are quite prepared to follow him
wherever he may see fit to lead them. During the month we have been
addressed by the General President, the General Secretary, Mr. Len Smith,
Councillor Warren and Mr. Bleakley, and some very inspiring meetings have
been held. We have to report that another of our members has succeeded in
obtaining Local Administration Honour, Mr. A. Glenister, who soundly defeated
one of the local boot manufacturers.

LABOUR AND EDUCATION.
Paper by Mr. W. R. SMITH, M.P., J.P., read to Northants District
Council.
Continued from page 160 in last Month's Report.
The educational system of a democratic people, as I conceive it, would be based upon
compulsory primary and secondary education. But clearly education beyond these stages
must be left to individual choice or vocational needs. The fullest provision for technical
education up to and including university training must be made for those who have need
of it.
In building up such a system there will be many problems to face. I have no hesi
tation in expressing the view that the two chief questions which will confront us are those
of teachers and finance, the latter not being the least difficult.
To secure and retain an adequate supply of suitable men and women in the teaching
profession is one of the greatest tasks of educational administration. The number of
entrants to the profession is far from adequate. The reduction in the size of classes, a
reform long overdue, the raising of the school age, the development of various forms of
higher education will necessitate a larger body of teachers than we at present possess or
are likely to obtain. Notwithstanding the superficial attraction of what may
seem to many people short hours of work and generous holidays, and in spite of the security
of the teaching profession, the supply has not been sufficient in the past. No doubt
there are many reasons why this should be so, but the small public esteem in which the
profession has been generally held and the inadequate salaries offered in the past have
certainly been largely responsible. The teaching profession is a key profession in a demo-
cratic country. Its influence entitle it to high regard.
If we face boldly the problem of supply it can be met successfully. But we are still
left with the further problem of the quality of the teachers. No effort to improve the fitness
and proficiency of the profession can be too great. The intellectual standard required of
teachers has been raised considerably since 1870. The Article 68 teachers, whose sole
qualifications were that they were over 18 years of age and had been vaccinated have
passed. The rise of training departments in connection with our universities marked a
step forward as a recognition of the real status of the profession and of the need for univer-
sity education.
I am convinced that a generous scheme for the education of intending teachers would
amply repay the community. One of the features of the past has been the loyalty of
teachers and their devotion to their work. But with fuller opportunities for an adequate
training, the community would be assured of an even greater measure of loyalty and de-
votion and of willing service.
The proposals which I have made would necessitate increased expenditure. But a
halt has been called and it is sad to see the Minister of Education from whom so much was
expected, associating himself with the cry of economy. The fever of economy has entered
the bones of His Majesty's Government. There can be no defence of waste. Economy
is imperative always, and was never more imperative than now. But there can be no
economy in education. Every penny withheld from that branch of public service means
injury to the future. Educational economy is a form of national suicide. It is the greatest
form of waste. To limit expenditure whereby that which you do spend fails in its objective
is to waste largely the money so spent.
It may be that for the moment education is saved from the onslaught that was made
upon it, but the danger is not past. Their appetite may be satisfied for the moment,
but the wolves will become hungry again, and they may attack in greater numbers, and
any apathy on our part will render their efforts greater possibilities of success.
Consider the present position. Classes are admittedly too large; school buildings
are inadequate and often unsuitable; secondary school accommodation is below present
needs; thousands of schools are badly equipped. Obviously there is a need for increased
expenditure. To dam the stream of financial assistance is to perpetuate gross evils, to
postpone insistent and overdue developments and even to lower the present standard of
efficiency.
May I now give some attention to the much-talked-of Geddes' Report, but at the
beginning may I point out a danger arising from this form of procedure in public life.
It is in itself an admission of failure and incompetence on the part of the Government.
They have handed to others the responsibility of ascertaining what should be the policy
of the country. That is far too dangerous a method in regard to education, as indeed it
is to all forms of public service.

OVERCROWDING HORRORS.
Shocking instances of overcrowding were described at a recent meeting of the advisory
sub-committee of the Bradford Mental Deficiency Committee.
A case was reported in which a husband, his wife, a daughter (a mental defective),
and her husband all slept in one bed, the only one in the house. In another case a mother
and three children, one of them a girl of 14, slept in the only bed, and a boy, mentally
deficient, slept at the foot of the bed.
EIGHT IN ONE ROOM.
At an anniversary gathering yesterday afternoon of the West Central Club for Jewish
Girls near Tottenham Court Road, the Hon. Lily H. Montagu, hon. secretary of the club,
said the girls felt a sense of injustice about housing conditions. She knew of cases in
Central London in which eight or ten members of a Jewish family were crowded into a
single furnished room because they could get no other accommodation. Daily News,
April 10th, 1922.
ONE IN EVERY 28 GETS POOR LAW RELIEF.
Figures Higher Than For Any Period in Last 72 Years.
Remarkable figures of the number of people in receipt of Poor Law relief in England
and Wales during 1921 are given in an official return issued yesterday.
On December 31st-the last record in the return-the number was 1,366,569, one in
28 of the entire population. This is an increase of 798,700, on the last week of December,
1920, or 141 per cent.
Heavy though that figure is it is not the highest for the year. That was reached on
November 5th, when the total was 1,519,823, the greatest number registered on any day
in the 72 years for which complete records have been kept. - Daily Chronicle, March 25th,
1922.
