criticism has been levelled against that Department, by the action that he himself has
taken on one or two occasions. Personally, we on this side are hoping that the Trade
Boards will be continued. We believe that their establishment has been greatly for the
public good, and we believe that the decisions that have been given from time to time
affecting what are known as “sweated” industries have been extremely helpful, and have
been the means of considerably modifying some of the worst industrial conditions in many
industries in this country. The point, however, to which we desire to draw attention at
the moment is with regard to the action of the Ministry so far as the Grocery Trade Board
is concerned, and I think that one is entitled to ask for some explanation of the conduct
of the Ministry in regard to that trade. The Grocery Trade Board was established by the
present Minister in June, 1920. Evidently the right hon. Gentleman was formerly of
opinion that the Trade Board was necessary, otherwise he would not have brought it into
being. This Trade Board has met on many occasions, it has spent nearly two years
deliberating on matters submitted to it, has considered a large number of objections raised
to its proposals and has submitted rates to the Minister which he has referred back to
them on no less than three occasions, and then he has, in the end, as I understand it.
refused to register the decision of the Board. I understand his explanation of his refusal
to register or put into operation the decision of the Grocery Trade Board is that the dis-
tributive trade is a new field of wage regulations. It is rather strange that the right hon.
Gentleman did not have that in mind when he constituted the Trade Board. The industry
has not changed during the two years: the special circumstances or conditions attaching
to the distributive trade were just the same, apparently, in 1920 as in 1922. Then he
states that there were objections to the rates fixed by the Board; but surely that is nothing
different from what has obtained in regard to most of the rates fixed by other Trade Boards.

I am certain that any rate proposed by any Trade Board will provoke objection from
some individuals. A Trade Board is an organisation that, as far as possible, represents
the best elements of the industry, and naturally those who seek to evade what may be
considered just responsibilities will raise objections to any rates emanating from a Trade
Board. But why should a special exception be made in the case of the Grocery Trade
Board? The Minister is inviting criticism of a very deadly character when he first sets
up a Trade Board to deal with an industry, and, after it has held numerous meetings,
issued its proposals, met objections, and fixed a rate, finally refuses to accept the rate
fixed. My hon. Friend the Member for North Aberdeen (Mr. Rose) passed some very
strong criticisms upon the Ministry of Labour when the Unemployed Insurance Bill was
under consideration on Thursday, and I cannot help thinking criticisms of that kind are
fully justified when we find a Department acting in this manner. I know it will be urged,
as it has been urged, that one of the difficulties of the Minister is that he is understaffed.
To-day he has given us figures which indicate that, in proportion to the numbers registered
at Exchanges now, the staff is considerably smaller than when the numbers were in the
300,000 area. But surely it takes as much labour to keep referring these decisions back,
and refusing to register them, as it would to accept them and put them into operation.
There were 14 meetings of this Trade Board, and that means that there must be a staff
to make the necessary arrangements, the expenses of the meetings are being incurred,
and the correspondence must be as great when you are referring back rates, and finally
refusing them, as it would be if the Ministry treated this Board as it has treated most others,
and accepted its rates. Therefore, to us, it seems that the criticism that the Department
has not utilised its opportunities to the best advantage is, to a very large extent, justified.

It has been suggested that the appointment of the Cave Committee is another reason
why this decision was not accepted. Why is one Board specially selected? Why is one
Board held up in its functions while other Boards are allowed to continue to make modifica-
tions in rates by raising or lowering them? Why is this one to continue to pretend to be
acting and then find, in the last resort, that the Minister refuses to do anything to bring
into operation the result of its deliberation? The regulations prescribe that the Order
shall be made within one month after the rate has been submitted, unless objection has
been taken, and yet we continually find happening what happened in the case of the Boot
and Floor Polish Trade Board, where they fixed the rates on 10th January and made a
request that they should become operative as from the 24th, and nothing was heard of
them. Two months went by and then a deputation had to wait upon the right hon.
Gentleman before he would give effect to the decision of that Trade Board. One cannot
help thinking the Minister has been intimidated too much by what might be called political
agitations, and that he has hesitated to use his full powers in connection with some of
these Trade Boards for fear of criticism coming from that particular quarter. I do not
think that is fair to the industries concerned. It is not fair, or right, or proper to get
employers of labour and representatives of workpeople to be continually meeting and
deliberating on these matters, fully assuming that they will be treated as other people
have been, and then finding, merely because of some more or less political agitation, that
they are unable to see the final result of their work in the establishment of a rate. I hope,
therefore, the Minister will give us some reason why this action has been allowed, and an
assurance that so long as Trade Boards are an acknowledged part of the machinery for
dealing with difficulties in the industrial world this Department will not put obstacles
in their path.

ASSISTANCE TO WAR VETERANS.
A Government Decree of December, 1917, founded the Opera Nazionale dei Combattenti
for assisting Italian veterans of the world war on their return to civilian life. The organisa-
tion, placed under government supervision, was incorporated with an initial capital of
300 million lire of which the Treasury contributed 250 million. Its activities are threefold:
Social, financial, agricultural.
The social section works through 4 general offices, 72 provincial bureaus, and 112
corresponding bureaus, and spends L. 1,752,000 a year in completing the vocational training
of ex-soldiers, helping them to find employment, and organising them into co-operative
trade associations, of which no fewer than 1,137 have been formed. It assists ex-officers
by enabling them to complete their studies interrupted by the war, and by preparing and
helping them to start commercial undertakings abroad or in the Italian colonies. Over
10,600 officers have thus been assisted at an outlay of L. 8,000,000. Special grants are
made to enable members to specialise in lines of study connected with their professional
work. Thus grants have been made to study the foreign book trade, the foreign wine
trade, for courses in forestry, for studying the railway systems in the Black Sea territories,
for training for managing positions in the hotel and tourist trade, &c. The Opera has also
opened training schools for the professional re-education of artisans, model farms for
agriculturists, &c. In all, it has organised 197 different courses, frequented by 11,500
veterans.
The financial section, to which the management of the capital of the Opera is entrusted,
has as its field of action the provision of land, agricultural, and personal credit to members.
It is authorised to issue bonds secured by mortgage on its real estate holdings and on the
Treasury annuities assigned it, and to receive savings deposits. This work is still in the
initial stage, and has consisted mainly in loans granted to individuals, and to co-operative
associations on the life insurance policies assigned by the government in the last year of
the war to all men in the front lines. Acting through the Bank of Naples, the Savings
Banks, and similar institutions, it has so far made loans to individuals amounting to 137
million lire and to 900 co-operative associations for 18 million lire.
The agricultural section is empowered by law to purchase land, to obtain it in grant
from the Crown, the provinces, the communes, charitable associations, public and ecclesi-
astical bodies, and private owners, whose estates are subject to land reclamation. It can
contract for public works, and promote the formation of agricultural co-operative associa-
tions of veterans to whom it leases, on an improving lease, the lands forming part of its
patrimony. The Opera is now in possession of 100,000 acres of land, a large part of which
has been leased on trial for one year to co-operative associations or to individual veterans,
renewable if the results are satisfactory. Those estates on which improtant land reclama-
tion works have to be carried out with a view to transforming the mode of cultivation are
under the direct management of the Opera itself. The most important of these are the
estates of Coltano (7,500 acres) in Tuscany, and of Licola and Varcaturo in the province
of Naples donated by King Victor Emanuel to the Opera, and that of Sanluri in Sardinia.
Great drainage works are in course of execution, canals are being excavated, great pumping
stations built, and thousands of acres, until recently fever-breeding marsh, will be turned
anto fertile farm-lands, some of which will be worked by co-operative associations, while
thers will be held by freehold farms by Italy's veterans.
--From a Monthly Survey of Italian Trade and Industry. ROME-April 1, 1922.

SPECIAL NOTICE TO MEMBERS.

Every precaution is taken by us to ensure accuracy in these Reports, our correspondents
being men on whom we can rely; should, however, any errors creep into them, upon the
same being pointed out to us, we shall be most happy to give the same prominence to the
correction as to the original matter. As these Reports are exclusively for the use of Members,
the information contained therein must not be divulged.

MONTHLY REPORT.

22ND MAY, 1922.

FELLOW MEMBERS,
THE STATE OF TRADE.

Trade is still on the slow side, although in some instances improvement
has taken place; there are a very considerable number out of employment
and others on short time. The Ministry of Labour figures for the past month
are as follows :-

BOOT AND SHOE TRADE.

In this trade there was a further slight improvement during April; employment
was still bad in the heavy boot trade, but fair, on the whole, with operatives engaged in
the light boot trade. As compared with a year ago there was an improvement.

The percentage of workpeople unemployed in the boot, shoe and slipper making and
repairing trades, as indicated by the unemployment books lodged at Employment Ex-
changes, was 10.0 at the 24th April, as compared with 9.6 at the 27th March.

Returns received from firms employing 34,650 workpeople showed that in the week
ended the 29th April 26.0 per cent. of these employees worked, on the average, 12 hours
a week less than full time.

In London employment continued bad, but was slightly better than in March. At
Leicester employment showed a further improvement, and was fairly good on the whole.
At Hinckley employment continued bad, with much short time. At Northampton and
at Wellingborough there was a slight improvement, but most firms were still on short
time, and there was much unemployment; most firms at Wellingborough closed for a
full week at Easter. At Kettering employment continued bad, very few firms were on
full time, the average being about three-quarter time. There was an improvement at
Rushden at the end of the month, at which time most of the factories were working full
time. At Higham Ferrers and Ringstead there was little change, and employment was
depressed. At Stafford there was a further improvement, and short time had practically
ceased.

REMEMBER THE FIFTEENTH!
Once again we feel bound to call the serious attention of Branch Secretaries
to the fact that the FIFTEENTH day of each month is the latest day for
returns reaching the General Secretary. If Branches fail to send off their
returns to reach the Central Office before the 15th of the month it tends to
upset the organisation of the work in the General Secretary's Office. We beg
to intimate that unless returns are in before the 15th of the month, the Secretary
has been instructed to put into force the Rules governing the same. Returns
sheets MUST also bear the signature of both the Branch President and Branch
Secretary or they will reluctantly have to be returned for completion.

BRANCH REPORTS.

BARNSLEY. In last month's report we note that the sum of £100 has been granted to the A.EU. Society, and that steps are being taken, so that they may receive some more from a £5,000 fund for such cases. We wonder if the different officials that are in power now ever look at the way our Union members were treated by the same body in the lock-out of 1895. We fail to find where they sent anything to our Union officials, although they had 77.000 members and were well off financially. Some good trades unions did send something, but, as the General Secretary (Mr. W. Inskip) said, it was very small in comparison to what the Shoe Trade Union had done for other trades that were in trouble. We hope that those in authority will take notice of this and think about their own members' position, for some are in a position quite as bad as the A.Ε.U.

BELFAST. Trade with us was never worse than at present, very little is being done in the manufacturing end, and the repairing also continues quiet. We have been hoping for better times and of enjoying the improvement that was to come to the people after the war.

CHESHAM. We are pleased to report that after being on strike for eight weeks, our members are as united and determined to see the National Conditions restored again as they were upon the first week of the strike. Our friend, Johnnie Buckle, has worked wonders with our members, and whatever he calls upon them to do, everyone is willing to respond to his call. We are pleased to report that the firm of G. Barnes & Son has agreed to fall into line and his operatives are resuming work on Monday, May 15th. We are hoping that shortly one or more of the other factories will follow his example. We are pleased to acknowledge in reply to our appeal the following donations:- Stone £1, Wellingborough £3 3s., Kingswood £5, Nottingham £2, Plymouth fI, Hull 10s., Kilmarnock £2, Norwich No. 2 £10, Edinburgh 10s., Kettering £5, Bromsgrove £2, London Metro. £5, Worcester ₤I IS., Northampton No. 1 £20 Northampton No. 2 ₤20, Leicester No. 2 £10, Glasgow £5, Leicester No. 1 15. Street £6 14s. 6d., and Manchester £5. We are extremely grateful to all the branches who have so generously responded to our appeal and trust that in our next report we shall be able to report victory won.

CHESTERFIELD.--In sending our returns we have to state trade very bad, all the members making new work are unemployed as the firm of Dronfield and Co. have closed down till trade improves. The employers state they cannot compete with the cheap labour districts round here, Stoney Middleton being one of the places where the men are working far from the National Agreement. QUESTIONS DEALING WITH UNEMPLOYMENT AT
THE GENOA CONFERENCE.

The following statement has been issued by the International Labour Office of the
League of Nations. The Sub-Committee appointed by the Economic Commission of the
Genoa Conference to deal with labour questions has drawn up a number of resolutions
which include the following articles :-
The economic reconstruction of Europe can only be effected by means of intensified
production, which depends essentially on labour. In order to obtain the fullest effort
on the part of the workers and to avoid unfair and dangerous competition between nations,
the attention of all States is called to the importance of the conventions and recommenda-
tions adopted by the International Labour Conferences.
"In particular, the present crisis, which affects not only production, but also the
consuming capacity of the people, weighs heavily on the workers, both morally and materi-
ally. While it may be true that measures of economic reconstruction are alone capable
of finally remedying irregularity of employment, direct measures to deal with unemploy-
ment appear to be none the less effective for ensuring sustained effort and efficiency on
the part of the workers. In combating unemployment, it is recognised that, in the first
instance, the utilisation of all productive forces to the utmost should be undertaken.
Apart from any arrangements providing insurance and assistance against unemployment,
the following measures are recommended :--
(a) The systematic distribution of all the labour available by the national organi-
sation of employment agencies and by the international co-ordination of such agencies
(emigration and immigration) by means of agreements between the countries con-
cerned.
(b) Subject to the special conditions obtaining in each country, the placing in
agriculture of as large a number as possible of such of the unemployed in industry
as are capable of being employed in agricultural work.
(c) The systematic allocation of public contracts with reference to the occurrence
of unemployment in the districts particularly affected, as far as may be consistent
with the general interest.
(d) The development of public works in aid of unemployment, provided that they
are useful and productive.
In order to accelerate the effects of such measures :-
1. It is recommended that all States should ratify the Draft Convention relating
to unemployment adopted by the International Labour Conference at Washington
in 1919, and should carry out, as far as practicable, the recommendation adopted
by that Conference.
2. The International Labour Office is requested to collect and publish every
three months if possible, all information available on the experience gained by the
different countries in dealing with unemployment.
It is further recommended that all the States concerned should contribute to the
inquiry relating to unemployment decided upon by the International Labour Confer-
ence of 1921, special attention being paid by such States to the effects produced by
the exchanges on the state of the labour market.

PARLIAMENTARY DEBATES.
WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION.
MR. WALTER SMITH: I beg to move,
That, in view of the unsatisfactory state of the law relating to Workmen's
Compensation, and of the fact that the War Addition Acts expire at the end of this
year, this House is of opinion that a Government Bill to amend the Workmen's Com-
pensation Act, 1906, should be introduced and passed during the course of this
Session."
I hope that if, in moving this Resolution, I curtail my observations, it will not be
taken as an indication that we do not attach the greatest importance to this subject.
Rather do we desire that the fullest opportunity should be given to discuss the question.
and for that reason I shall be as brief as possible in introducing it. I can only hope that
the reply of the Minister will be of a satisfactory nature, because there is no doubt in our
minds that the matter is one of the greatest importance, and one upon which legislation
is long overdue. This question is most urgent, and for more than one reason. During
the period of the War, a special provision was made in regard to this matter, to meet
what was known and understood to be a war-time condition; and I think it will be recog-
nised and admitted that that war-time condition, so far as regards prices and cost of living
and the difficulties of life generally, has not passed away, nor will it pass away in any
permanent degree, so far as one can judge. The legislation that was passed to meet the
difficulty does automatically lapse at the end of this year, and that makes it imperative
that something should be done in order that the unfortunate people who suffer from these
accidents shall not be driven back to the pre-War position. I can scarcely imagine, in
whether it be fatal or otherwise, that any Member of this House would desire either to see
the case of the industrial worker who is unfortunate enough to have met with an accident,
dependants left exactly in the same position as in pre-War times either or, if the
accident be not fatal, to see the worker himself left exactly as he was before the war-time
that worker's dependants left exactly in the same position as in pre-War times either or, if the
legislation was introduced. I cannot conceive that any Member of this House would
suggest for a moment that a maximum amount of £300 as compensation for the loss
of a husband is adequate. It fails entirely to meet the needs of the case, and it is quite
evident, in times of industrial disaster, that there is generally expressed in the minds and
the actions of the people great sympathy with those who are its victims; and yet we have
to realise that, unless something is done in the way of legislation, all that a widow will
have to look forward to, as compensation for the loss of her husband, is a maximum
amount of £300. I think it will be admitted that the claim we are making for some
legislation is absolutely justified from that point of view.

There is another reason why we have a right to urge upon the Government the necessity
of introducing legislation upon this question. It is that the Government itself has recog-
nised the need for such legislation. Some time ago the Government set up a Departmental
Committee to investigate and inquire into this matter, and that Committee conducted a
very extensive investigation. They examined the question in all its aspects, and it is
now some time since they submitted their Report. It is true that that Report was not a
unanimous Report, for there was a dissentient minority who were in favour of more
extensive recommendations; but, as regards the main body of the Report, it was unanimous
as representing something to which all the Committee would subscribe. The minority
merely dissented because they wished for something more. In the Majority Report
there was a recommendation in favour of many extensions being made in the benefits
and advantages accruing to those who, unfortunately, were injured in industry, or to those
who might be left because their bread-winner had been taken front them. Therefore,
on a question of this description, first bearing in mind the fact that the war-time legis-
lation will lapse automatically at the end of this year, and, secondly, having regard to the
fact that the Departmental Committee, after considering the question fully, recommended
extensions of the amount that can be claimed and paid to persons who are injured, we claim
that we are justified in coming to the House with this Resolution and in asking for support
for it. I sincerely hope that that support will be accorded to us, and also that the reply
of the Minister will be satisfactory.
I should like to say that we would wish that there were less need for our making this
claim. We wish it were possible to say that the number of accidents occurring was diminish-
ing, and that the need for putting forward claims on behalf of workpeople and their
dependants was becoming less and less. Unfortunately, however, the opposite is the case.
The tendency is for accidents to increase rather than decrease, although one would have
to admit that last year the figures were in the opposite direction. I believe, however, that
the last returns available are explained by the fact that such large numbers were unemployed,
and that the reduced figures were not due to a smaller proportion of accidents on the
average of persons engaged in industry. I should like to draw the attention of the House
to the far-reaching character of this qustion, when viewed from the standpoint of the
number of people affected by it. Every year 500,oco accidents occur. That is an enor-
mous figure. Half a million people are either killed or injured in this country every year,

MISS BONDFIELD ADDRESSES BOOT OPERATIVES UNION CONFERENCE.
Education and Personality.
An educational conference at the Northampton Trade Hall, arranged by the Northamp-
tonshire District Council of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives, was
well attended on Saturday afternoon. The audience was composed of delegates from
many unions affiliated to the Trade. Council, from the Adult Schools, and Co-operative
Society. The Rev. H. Hurst, curate of St. James' Church, presided.
Mr. G. Chester, of Kettering, president of the Northamptonshire District Council &
the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives, said the Union had attempted to foster
an educational policy, and had been fairly successful. One or two classes had been estab-
lished and fairly well attended, and one or two conferences had been held.

Miss Bondfield.
Miss Margaret Bondfield, J.P., who addressed the conference on "Education and
Personality," congratulated the Boot and Shoe Trade Union on the splendid lead they
had given to the other unions in this area. They were keeping pace with other progressive
bodies in the country. As well as the recommendations of the Geddes report, there were
other checks to development which counted as cuts on education. They knew from
practical experience that there were innumerable instances where local authorities who
would have progressed had been prevented from so doing by the Board of Education who
One of the most shameful methods of checking progress was the attempt to shift
the responsibility from local educational enterprise on to the local rates. The Board of
Education had announced that their system of grants was to be limited to a maximum
expenditure. In other words there would only be the very minimum of sanction given to
any sort of development in local education.

Miss Bondfield spoke earnestly against the Government's proposals to make no further
provision of special schools and to shelve the provision of meals for school children on to
some other at present unnamed body. They of the Labour Party had thoroughly gone
into the question of the physical education of the children. It was absurd to talk of
pauperising the country; they held not a class view, but the larger community view
that the children should be properly fed. The mid-day meal in the school might become
-as it had done in Bradford-part of the ordinary school curriculum.
"A Retrograde Step."
With regard to the closing of the smaller schools, Miss Bondfield said quite a large
number of these small schools were denominational schools, and it was impossible to settle
the denominational question by Act of Parliament. "I can imagine," she added, "nothing
more mischievous at the present moment than to close denominational schools merely
because they contain only a certain number of children." The proposal to increase the
size of classes and reduce the number of teachers was a retrograde and reactionary step.
"Most of us in this room," said Miss Bondfield, "have had very little chance of
education outside the elementary schools, and it is because of that that we are the best
authorities to deal with the matter. There is another and a spiritual side of the matter
which gives us the advantage over other sections of the community. There is an inherent
simplicity about the man who does things with his hands, who really creates and fashions
things out of raw material. He is not a parasite on the community: he is earning his
living. The international standpoint comes more easily to him rather than the patriotism
that is more often a very shoddy kind of materialism. Every now and again we do get a
vision of what life would be like-not by ceasing to work, but by working under changed
conditions, with a greater equipment, a finer knowledge, and larger outlook. We feel
these things are our heritage, and hitherto we have had the door shut in our faces."
All over the world the workers were having the same attitude of mind towards educa-
tion. Inherently in them was the divine spark that led them to strive for something
higher and nobler than they knew.

An interesting discussion followed, after which thanks to the chairman and Miss
Bondfield were accorded on the proposition of Mr. W. R. Townley, J.P. (president of the
No. 1 Branch of the Boot and Shoe Operatives' Union), seconded by Mr. L. Poole.-
Northampton Echo, 24th April, 1922.

LABOUR PROBLEMS AT GENOA.
Production and Unemployment.
Some indications of progress made at the Genoa Conference in the discussion o
concrete questions of industrial production and labour conditions are contained in a
statement issued by the International Labour Office (League of Nations). This office has
been represented in a consultative capacity at the Conference by a small delegation drawn
from the three groups-Governments, employers, and workers-which compose its govern
ing body, presided over by M. Fontaine and accompanied by M. Albert Thomas (director
of the office) and some of the technical experts of his staff.

A few days ago the Economic Commission of the Conference set up a Sub-Commission
to deal with labour questions. At a meeting of the Sub-Commission the question of the
eight-hour day and, therefore, of the Convention adopted at the First International Labour
Conference, held at Washington, was raised by a resolution submitted in the name of the
International Trade Union Federation. The Netherlands' delegate wished the Genoa
Conference to reaffirm the Washington Eight-hour Convention.

The Sub-Commission, after discussion, drew up a number of resolutions which included
the following articles:
"The economic reconstruction of Europe can only be effected by means of intensified
production, which depends essentially on labour. In order to obtain the fullest effort
on the part of the workers, and in order to avoid unfair and dangerous competition between
nations, the attention of all States is called to the importance of the Conventions and
Recommendations adopted by the International Labour Conferences.

"In particular, the present crisis, which affects not only production, but also the
consuming capacity of the people, weighs heavily on the workers, both morally and materi
ally. While it may be true that measures of economic reconstruction are alone capable of
finally remedying irregularity of employment, direct measures to deal with unemployment
appear to be none the less effective for ensuring sustained effort and efficiency on the part
of the workers. In combating unemployment it is recognised that, in the first instance,
the utilisation of all productive forces to the utmost should be undertaken. Apart from
any arrangements providing insurance and assistance against unemployment, the follow
ing measures are recommended:

(a) The systematic distribution of all the labour available by the national organi
sation of employment agencies and by the international co-ordination of such agencies
(emigration and immigration) by means of agreements between the countries con
cerned;

(b) Subject to the special conditions obtaining in each country the placing in
agriculture of as large a number as possible of such of the unemployed in industry as
are capable of being employed in agricultural work.
(c) The systematic allocation of public contracts with reference to the occurrence
of unemployment in the districts particularly affected, as far as may be consistent
with the general interest;

(d) The development of public works in aid of unemployment, provided that they
are useful and productive.
In order to accelerate the effects of such measures:
"(1) It is recommended that all States should ratify the Draft Convention relating
to unemployment adopted by the International Labour Conference at Washington in
1919, and should carry out, as far as practicable, the recommendation on unemployment
adopted by that Conference.

"(2) The International Labour Office is requested to collect and publish every three
months, if possible, all information available on the experience gained by the different
countries in dealing with unemployment.

"It is further recommended that all the States concerned should contribute to the
International reporting to unemployment decided upon by the International Labour Conference
any matters relating to attention being paid by such States to the effects produced by the exchanges
of the labour market. "Labour Leader, May 18th, 1922.

SOUTH AFRICAN EMBARGO.

To be Continued for Another Twelve Months-The Effect on Imports of
British Boots and Shoes-Most Classes of Footwear in Regular Use
Excluded-Local Manufacturers' Tremendous Pull-South African Shoes
and Leather Displayed at Johannesburg.

(FROM OUR OWN CORRESPONDENT.)
JOHANNESBURG, April 15th, 1922.

Yesterday afternoon a deputation of over a score of manufacturers and others interested
in South African boot manufacturing businesses, with Mr. S. Collier at the head, waited
on the Minister of Finance at Cape Town and put their case before him. They asked for
more protection and a continuance of the embargo. The Minister of Finance, in reply
said:

"He would grant the demand for a continuance of the embargo, not because he
liked that form of protection, but because he considered it the most suitable as an
interim measure.

The embargo will therefore be re-imposed for twelve months, during which period
the import of footwear most commonly used will be absolutely prohibited, or permitted
only with such qualifications as the Board of Control advise.

Thus, unfortunately, there has happened just what my last letter doubtless suggested
1. Record readers was likely to happen, although in some quarters here an increased duty
was anticipated.

The Door Slammed.
The continuance of the embargo is a much greater evil than a 15 per cent. extra
tariff would have been. However, there it is, and the outlook for oversea producers has
been darkened by an unfair method of slamming the door. The Minister said he disliked
the measure asked for, and seemed to think it necessary specifically to express his feelings.

The embargo is unquestionably bringing grist to the mills of the local manufacturers
for the making of practically all men's boots retailed at about 27s. 6d.. and less is entirely
in their hands. This in itself is a tremendous pull.

The imports of boots and shoes into the Union underwent a heavy reduction during
1921, and every exporting country suffered more or less. But the chief sufferers were
manufacturers in the United Kingdom and America. The following figures give an idea
of the fall in imports during 1921 as compared with those for 1920:

FROM
1920. 1921.
United Kingdom ............ 3,017,000 pairs . 966,693 pairs
United States ...................... 591,000 pairs . 38,749 pairs
Switzerland ..................... 235,000 pairs . 87.963 pairs
Australia ....................... 233,000 pairs . 22,031 pairs

4,076,000 1,115,436

I expect to be able next week to give figures regarding locally produced footwear.
It is already known that the output has been greatly increased; indeed, under such a
form of protection it could not have been otherwise.

Some South African boot manufacturers deserve credit for the way they have improved
their factories and introduced modern machinery. Thus with the help of imported skilled
labour they have been able to produce vastly superior boots, and are now gradually bring-
ing their productions up to the level of imported goods. This, of course, applies to the
cheaper classes of footwear.

Locally Made Leather and Boots.
At the present moment at Johannesburg there is being held a large show with an
Industrial Section, at which locally manufactured goods are displayed. An outstanding
feature is the exhibit of Messrs. Searle Ltd., whose boot factory at Great Brak River is
one of the most up-to-date in the country. The company employ about 500 workers,
of whom fully 60 per cent. are white. Messrs. Searle seem to tackle every branch of the
industry, and their productions include turns.
Messrs. J. W. Jagger & Co., the well-known importers, also make a creditable show
with the products of their new Cape factory. The firm have a unique advantage in the
distribution of their goods, for they have a big connection throughout the whole of South
Africa, and many representatives " on the road."
The Maritzburg Tanning and Leather Co make an effective display of both vegetable
and chrome-tanned leathers, dyed goat and sheep skins in various shades being an out-
most varieties of bottom and upper leathers. Their chrome tannages are specially good.

KEEP ON DOING,
There is lots of joy in living if you strike the proper gait ;
If you always come up smiling in the face of every fate.
If you're keeping step and whistling some lively little tune,
You'll be living gay and happy as a sunny day in June.
Keep a level head, don't worry, help your brothers on the way;
Let the sunshine of good humour shine upon you ev'ry day;
Speak a cheerful word at all times, never "knock" your fellow man.
And you'll surely be rewarded-just keep doing all you can.
There is lots of joy in living if you live your life aright,
Lots of sunshine and of roses, keep your eyes turned to the light,
Look behind the clouds of trouble; there's a silver lining there,
And you'll find it if you're only living life upon the square.
Scatter good cheer like the thistle scatters seed before the wind,
And the petty woes and troubles soon will be left far behind.
Be a "Booster" every minute, help along your fellow man,
And you'll surely be rewarded, just keep doing all you can.

OPPORTUNITY.

With doubt and dismay you are smitten,
You think there's no chance for you, son?
Why, the best books haven't been written,
The best race hasn't been run,
The best score hasn't been made yet,
The best song hasn't been sung,
The best tune hasn't been played yet;
Cheer up, for the world is young!
No chance? Why, the world is just eager
For things that you ought to create;
Its store of true wealth is still meagre,
Its needs are incessant and great;
It yearns for more power and beauty,
More laughter and love and romance,
More loyalty, labour and duty,
No chance, why, there's nothing but chance!
For the best verse hasn't been rhymed yet,
The best house hasn't been planned,
The highest peak hasn't been climbed yet,
The mightiest rivers aren't spanned;
Don't worry and fret, faint-hearted,
The chances have just begun,
For the best jobs haven't been started,
The best work hasn't been done.
-Berton Braley in The P. B. News.

MONTHLY REPORT.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
19TH JUNE, 1922.
THE STATE OF TRADE
continues about the same as last month, although in some centres trade has slightly improved. The figures given in the Gazette of the Ministry of Labour, are as follows :-
BOOT AND SHOE TRADE.
During May there was a further slight improvement in this trade. Employment was still bad in the heavy boot trade, but fairly good on the whole in the lighter sections.
The percentage of workpeople unemployed in the boot, shoe and slipper making and repairing trades, as indicated by the unemployment books lodged at Employment Exchanges was 8.7 at 22nd May, as compared with 10.0 at 24th April.
Returns received from firms employing 35,200 workpeople showed that about 21 per cent. of these workpeople were on short time, losing 12 hours a week on the average.
The improvement affected nearly all the principal centres except Stafford and Norwich (where employment was already good before the beginning of the month), and the Scottish centres, in most of which employment was still very quiet. Much short time was, however, still reported, particularly at Kettering, and in districts where the principal production is heavy boots (notably Bristol, Kingswood and Leeds). On the other hand, a certain amount of overtime was worked by some firms at many centres towards the end of the month to complete urgent orders for Whitsuntide.
The exports of boots and shoes in May, 1922, amounted to 59,844 dozen pairs, or 831 dozen pairs less than in April, 1922, but 26,913 dozen pairs more than in May, 1921.

THE CHESHAM DISPUTE.
Considerable progress has been made at Chesham during the month,
all the firms except two having agreed to acknowledge the Union and the
National Terms of Settlement. As a consequence the operatives resumed
work on the 12th inst., and we hope, ere long, to be able to report a settlement.
This proves that loyalty on the part of members to the Union means security,
and any departure from National Conditions should be at once reported to
the Central Office.
HOUSING.
In another part of the report there are several references to the bad housing
conditions still obtaining in the various parts of the country. We would,
however, especially call attention to the shocking state of affairs at Earl Shilton,
Leicestershire, because this is one of the places where in 1913 our sickness
rates were so high that we were successful in getting the National Health
Insurance Commissioners to hold a special enquiry into the same. It will be
seen by reference to pages 328-329 that some of the conditions about which
we
complained nine years ago are still unremedied. We are again taking the
matter up with the Ministry of Health, and hope by the presentation of such a
we

discreditable state of affairs the Ministry will see its way to take drastie action,
and ensure the health of the people should not any longer be endangered by
such a disgraceful condition of affairs being allowed to continue.
In relation to the Northampton conditions it is reported there are over
ised to build another 86 houses. It is of special interest in this case to notic
1.400 applicants for houses, yet the Northampton Town Comcil is only author
remembers the wonderful promises made to these men from 1914 onward.
the extraordinary number of ex-service men requiring houses, and when one

the ordinary amenities of life as represented by a decent house to dwell in
Moreover, the housing conditions in the country generally are so bad that we
shall continue to bring this matter to your notice in the hope that everyone
also upon Members of Parliament to ensure proper housing accommodation
will do his or her part to bring pressure to bear upon the local authorities, and
being provided. This is an important fact, because if the hundreds of thousands
of houses needed were actually erected, it would find work not only for those
in the building and allied trades, but would have its effect upon many other
trades, and thus help to bring about the working of the industrial machine
in a more effective manner which politicians are constantly telling us is so
necessary; yet when the Labour Party point out the ways and means by
which it could be done, the same politicians always find excuses.
We shall lose no time in this connection, and have already tabled a reso-
lution for the annual meeting of the Labour Party to be held at the end of the
present month.
POLITICS.
Another attempt has been made by certain members of Parliament to
again cripple trade unions in their political work, and to confine the activities
of unions to the narrowest limits. We are glad to see that Mr. W. R. Smith,
M.P., has taken a prominent part in the debates upon the Trade Union Act
1913, Amendment Bill, and in addition, we as a Council, have appealed to the
General Council of the Trade Union Congress, and the Labour Party to use
every legitimate effort to bring about the defeat of the Bill.
MR. E. L. POULTON, J.P., IN AMERICA.
On Wednesday. the 31st May, our General Secretary, Mr. E. L. Poulton,
J.P., sailed from Southampton on the R.M.S. "Homeric," for America, and
during the month has been attending the annual convention of the American
Federation of Labour at Cincinatti, Ohio, U.S.A.
CIRCULARS.
Several important circulars have been issued to the branches during the
month, particularly in reference to the Holiday Clause in the National Agree-
ment, February, 1922, and answers should be sent thereto immediately.

JOHN GREGORY, M.A., Shoe Poet.

It is with sincere regret we have to record the passing away of
JOHN GREGORY, M.A., of Bristol, who has been a member of our Union
since its inception. Mr. Gregory has taken not only very great interest
in the industrial life of the worker, but attained considerable distinction
as a poet, thus adding one more to the distinguished roll of shoemakers
who have occupied outstanding positions in this and other countries.
We tender our sympathy to the relatives of the late Mr. John Gregory,
M.A., in the loss they have sustained. He was the first secretary to
the Bristol Branch.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION ACTS.
We make no apology for again reminding branch officers and also the
members, that lump sums are NOT obtainable by law, but only by agreement,
and if branches are anxious that a solicitor should be engaged to safeguard the
interests of any member, the Central Office should be at once notified of the
accident, together with the full name and address of the member, registered
number and details of the accident on the prescribed form.

DAILY HERALD.
At our meeting this week the question of the Daily Herald was raised
owing to the fact that a special meeting of Debenture Holders has been held,
and the Union with other Debenture Holders have been asked to agree that :-
(a) “ A receiver be appointed, and is hereby authorised to sell the goodwill
of the Daily Herald newspaper to the Victoria House Printing Co.
Ltd.," and

(b)  “That Debenture Holders do hereby release, surrender and forego
to the Company all monies due and owing or hereafter to become
due and owing to them under the Debentures and the Trust Deed,
including the Balance of guaranteed interest.”

This means that the Daily Herald request that the £1,000 Debenture

should be sent to reach the Central Office by the 15th July prox.

SECOND ANNUAL CONFERENCE.

The Second Annual Conference is now a thing of the past. An official
report of the proceedings will be issued in a few days. The principal matters
of interest dealt with were the revision of the National Agreement and
Political Question. In connection with the latter the following resolution
was agreed to :-

“This Conference of Boot and Shoe Operatives, representing 80,000 members,
views with the greatest suspicion and enters its strong protest against the Bill intro-
duced by Col. Meysey-Thompson, and which received a Second Reading in the House
of Commons on Friday, May 19th last, as being an attempt to deprive the Trade
Unions of the right to adopt political action as a means of securing the improvement
of working-class life. The opportunity of obtaining the solution of our social problems
by constitutional action, Trade Unions are thereby deprived by such proposed
legislation. This, together with the Bills previously introduced by Sir F. Banbury,
Mr. A. M. Samuel, Col. Archer-Shee, and others, constitutes an attack upon Trade
Unions that is unwarranted, and is evidence of class legislation which has for its
object the keeping down of the people, with the consequent domination of the power
of wealth and social influence. We therefore, whilst strongly condemning this
attempt to secure class domination, call upon our members to use every means in
their power by helping in the return of Labour representatives to the House of
Commons, whereby this attempt to crush Labour may be rendered impossible. We
further call upon the General Council of the Trade Union Congress and the Parlia-
mentary Labour Party to take every possible step to bring the danger prominently
before the organised workers of the country.”

We hope every branch of the Union will ask their local M.P. to oppose
the measure, and ask for a definite reply as to his intention on the Third reading
of the Bill.

UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE.

We beg to call the attention of all branch officers to the resolution passed
by a large majority at the Second Annual Conference, that branch executives
should see that the Unemployment Insurance Act be administered in the
interests of the whole of the members. We trust therefore, that those branches
who have hitherto only partly administered the Act will see that every member
has the opportunity to receive the State benefit through the Union.

Exchanges where the human touch is so often absent. So many of out members hold
the view that we had similar powers at our Annual Conferences as we enjoyed at the
Biennial ones, but such is not the case, and my appeal to the delegates confirms that view.
I question whether we shall hold any more Annuals after next year; there does not appear
to be the zeal for the same after the trials we have given them.
STAMPED FOOTWEAR.- May I once more appeal to our members to endeavour to put
a little life into the Stamped Boot and Shoe, as there is a very good agitation going on at
the present moment for a pure article for the benefit of the public. Some of us believe
that this agitation will save the hard earnings of poor people of this country who often
buy shoddy boots and are literally robbed of the money that they pay for them. This
is a statement which ought to be made, and I hope it fits every manufacturer who is guilty
of putting in strawboard or compo insoles to any boot or shoe in this country for outdoor
wear. Indoor is another matter; persons may be able to walk about barefoot or in their
stockinged feet, but to give people compo and paper in their boots without their knowledge
is nothing less than a fraud, and everything I can do to crush these people I shall be willing
to do, and I hope I shall get the assistance of all others in a similar turn of mind. To my
mind the country never knew of a better or more genuine article than when the War-time
boot was made, and I may add for the benefit of those people who object to Government
Departments, that this was made under Government supervision. For that reason some
of us would live more Government supervision, who could, if they liked, solve the unem-
ployment problem by finding direct employment.

HOUSING PROBLEM.

86 Houses for over 1,400 Applicants. Position at Northampton.
The housing problem at Northampton is as acute as ever, and with the end of the
building of houses subsidised by the Government in sight, it is clear that the emergency
can only be met by the Town Council embarking on building schemes of its own.
Under the subsidy scheme the Council was allowed to build 560 houses, of which
about 510 are finished, and about 500 are occupied. The Housing Committee had hoped
to obtain Government grant towards the building of another one hundred, but the Govern-
ment has cut the number down to 36.
With Government aid, therefore, Northampton can build only 86 more houses. At
present the committee's books contain the names of no fewer than 1,403 applicants for
houses, and of late applications have been received at the rate of from 30 to 50 per week.
The position is even worse than these figures suggest, for of the 500 houses which
are let, at least 200 contain two families, the committee having placed two families in houses
where there are no children or only one child.
The matter was before the Housing Committee at a meeting held on Monday night,
and the committee, believing that further subsidies are not likely to be forthcoming
decided that the time had arrived for preparing to deal with the problem without subsidy.
Government departments are to be communicated with immediately in order that no
time shall be lost in regard to holding inquiries that may be necessary, and the committee
are determined, with the sanction of the Council, to push matters forward with all possible
speed.
The nature of the applications in hand can be judged from the appended summary,
which was before the committee at Monday's meeting:
Ex-Service men with their wives and families occupying rooms, 571.
Ex-Service men and wives without children occupying rooms, 250.
Ex-Service men (single) anxious to get married, 61.
Ex-Service men, tenants of houses but under notice to quit from landlord, 122.
Not ex-Service men with their wives and families occupying rooms, 106.
Not ex-Service men and wives without children occupying rooms, 46.
Not ex-Service men (single) anxious to get married, 8.
Not ex-Service men, tenants of houses but under notice to quit rom landlord, 100.
Applications from persons residing outside the Borough, 73.-Daily Echo, Northamp-
ton, May 23rd, 1922.

BRANCH REPORTS.

BELFAST. - Trade continues to remain very bad here, and there are
no signs to give us any hope of an early improvement.

BRISTOL. - Trade here has been fair for the past month. We hope for
a continuation of the same. It is with deep regret we have to report first of
the death of one of our most esteemed stewards and committeemen in Mr.
J. Busteed. He has been a very active and live member, rendering at all times
most valuable help by word and deed to his shopmates and the Branch in general.
Our sympathy goes out to his widow and children: may they be sustained in
their time of trial in the loss of one who was an ideal father and shopmate.
Next we have to report the death of the veteran of the Branch, Mr. J. Gregory,
who has been a member since the formation of the Branch. He was nearly
92 years of age, and has been called for many years the Cobbler-Poet. He was
the first secretary of the Branch and rendered yeoman service for Trade Unonism
when it was far from being a popular gospel to preach, and did much to place
Trade Unionism and Labour politics on a firm foundation. To his bereaved
family we extend our sympathy, and may they take courage in the thought
that he did what he could for the uplifting of his fellow-men. The funeral of
each was attended by the Officers and a good number of members.

BRISTOL No. 2. - Trade in the Kingswood area is still very bad, but we
hope to see an improvement in the near future as it is about this time that buyers
place their orders for strong work. We think that no other centre has felt
the effects of the slump to such an extent as Kingswood. As a consequence we
find there has been evasions in carrying out the Holiday Scheme, but we hope
that with a revival of trade we shall get the scheme going again. We note
with pleasure that the trouble at Chesham looks like finishing with com-
plete success to the operatives. This should demonstrate to all the value
of being well organised, which is the only hope of being able to withstand an
attack on wages and conditions of labour. Pleased to report that we have a
short sick list and hope that it will remain so.

CHESHAM. - Six more firms have agreed to fall into line and pay all the
National conditions, including the Holiday Scheme. This only leaves two more
firms to be dealt with, one of which we hope to deal with in the course of a few
days. A partial resumption of work will commence at once, and our friend
Buckle will continue to negotiate with the employers until a complete resump-
tion of work can take place. We sincerely thank the following Branches for
their financial assistance which arrived after our last Monthly Report :-
Ayr, £2; Desborough, £5 5s.; Kendal, £2; Glasgow, £10; Stafford, £2; Aber-
deen, £1; Ipswich, £2 2s.

CHESTERFIELD. - Trade remains very bad at present though members
making New Work, after being closed five weeks, have now commenced work
again at the factory, are only working 16 hours per week. We hope things
will brighten up again soon and that all our members will be able to get em-
ployment, as I think the last two years have been the worst since we can re-
member in the above branch.

EDINBURGH. - Another Annual Conference has gone by with not much
real business being done. Cannot delegates get the larger issues always in
front. The employers are able to organise their forces better than the workers.
Is it small prejudice that is at the foundation of all the trouble? Trade here
is still very quiet in the manufacturing, but the repairing section seems to be
picking up a bit. Scottish Branches are having a meeting to try and find a

NOTTINGHAM. We have to report the death of one of our oldest
members, C. Holmes, who has been a continuous member, since the Union was
first started in 1874. The Secretary, President, and some of his shopmates
attended the funeral as a mark of respect. Trade is quiet with us, though
we have had very light out-of-work pay lately.
PLYMOUTH. - Lord Cave's Report on Trade Boards has formed the chief
subject of discussion at our Committee and Branch meetings, and we confess
that after careful consideration of this report, we look to the future with some
anxiety, for if the recommendations of Lord Cave are going to be given legis-
lative effect, then the usefulness of Trade Boards are going to be lessened
considerably, and the good work which has been accomplished since the passing
of the 1918 Act will be almost completely destroyed. We would call attention
to just one of the recommendations which seem to us to be of vital importance.
i.e. "That it be the duty of a Trade Board to fix a general minimum time-
rate for the general body of workers in the trade, such rates to be fixed with
reference to the lowest grade of ordinary workers in the trade." Here we have
the great fundamental basis upon which all the wage rates of the future may be
fixed by Trade Boards. Think what this means, comrades. You first find a
sweated trade, then proceed to find the wage of the ordinary worker, you try
to discover the various grades of ordinary workers. Having found the lowest
grade and the rates of wages paid, you fix your minimum accordingly, but
lest this should be too high and numbers of workers cannot earn the minimum,
then Lord Cave and his committee recommend that exemptions be granted-
most accommodating, ladies and gentlemen. But we doubt if even this dis-
tracted and distrusted Coalition Government will dare to stoop so low ; if so,
this must be the last nail in their coffin, and they must be sent away into the
wilderness to discover "Sunshine for all," which was promised so volubly
during the year 1919.
SOUTHAMPTON.-Trade slack, but there appears signs of a slight
improvement-may it grow in volume. It is weary work chronicling "Trade
Slack."
GREAT YARMOUTH. -No progress to report at Great Yarmouth.
SHOEMAKER AND ARTIST.
Pictures Shown at Arts and Crafts Exhibition.
Headed "The Art of the British Working Man," an article was recently published
in the Strand Magazine, paying a tribute to the pictorial work of Mr. Robert Mallett, and
reproducing a scene of his taken from Costessey. Mr. Mallett lives at 121, Marlborough
Road, Norwich, and is described as " a shoemaker earning on an average 22s. a week."
Visitors to the Arts and Crafts Exhibition in St. Andrew's Hall, Norwich, had the
opportunity last week of seeing a picture by Mr. Mallett, in the oils section. The canvas
measured about 30 by 28, and its subject was entitled "In a Wood near Norwich." The
drawing was plain and bold. The middle distance showed some gnarled oaks in full foliage,
and on the horizon was a little patch of colour, relieving what otherwise would be a too
pervasive greenery of leaf and grass.
"I always had a passion for painting," said Mr. Mallett, in an interview, "but not
till 1 was 24 did I really begin to take seriously to it. I have had some tuition
at drawing, but never at painting, being quite self-taught. I am 40 years of age.
I have five children, so you will see that mine is not a very easy lot. I have always felt
that I have never been able to do justice to myself, inasmuch as I have great difficulty
in finding the wherewithal to purchase my canvasses and accessories.
"I am very fond of nature, and my very limited leisure time is spent amongst the
various beauty spots about my native city. Costessey, about three miles from Norwich,
is one of my favourite haunts, and I consider it one of the prettiest villages in England."-
S and Leather Record, May 26th, 1922.
The wage named above refers to the wages paid in 1906.-E.L.P., Gen. Sec.]

TRADE UNION DEMONSTRATION.
A Two Hours' Open Air Meeting.
Under the auspices of the Chesham Trades Council and Labour Party a Trade Union
and Labour Demonstration was held on Saturday evening, and attracted a great deal of
attention, and so much interest that a large crowd stood for two hours and more in the
Broadway and listened with close attention to the six speakers. Mr. F. C Watkins,
President of the Chesham Labour Party, presided, and was supported by Mr. E. L. Poulton.
O.B.E... J.P. General Secretary of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives, Mr
1. Buckle, J. P., and Mr. D. McCarthy, Organisers of that Union, Mr. S. Maynard, Typo
graphical Association, and Mr. W. T. Moulder. Workers' Union. The hesham Towe
Silver Prize Band led the procession which preceded the meeting.

A Change in Ten Years.
Mr. Maynard said his first words must be of congratulation to the workers upon the
size and quality of that demonstration. Such a demonstration could not have been held
in Chesham ten years ago. When he came to Chesham ten years ago there was not a
Trade Union branch in existence in the town at least, none showed their colours, and
he was surprised at that fact

The Early Days.
Mr. Moulder recalled the early days of Trade Union struggles in Chesham, their
successes and their set backs. It was a struggle almost heart-breaking, he said, and some
of them looked back upon those days with mixed feelings. The attitude then was, "What
are we going to get out of Trade Unionism?"; to-day there was a much less selfish
attitude, as the support accorded to the boot workers showed.

A Great Change.
Mr. McCarthy said nobody was more surprised and pleased than he at the great change
which took place in Chesham. When he first came to Chesham there was plenty to dis-
courage him now he found plenty to encourage him, and he hoped the workers would
remain firm. There was no need for them to waver. The union would back them up.
We were living in a time when working people were recognised factors in business and not
so much stuff to be thrown here and there at the will of a few. The general sympathy
was behind any struggle for proper
could be assured that they had the people with them as well as their union.

After Twenty-Five Years.
Mr. Poulton was suffering from the effects of a chill contracted on the way home from
Genoa, but he spoke at some length, and the audience followed very keenly his local and
national references. As he stood upon that platform his mind travelled back to his visits
to Chesham twenty-five years ago, when, with an old shopmate of theirs, he preached
Trade Unionism and they both found it a rather uphill task. He was quite sure that were
William Valentine Butler alive he would rejoice that the seed then sown had after many
days borne fruit. It was a small beginning, but the harvest was larger than they anti-
cipated. As short a time ago as two years, few would have dared to say that Chesham
men and women would have stood so firmly and shown so much loyalty in a struggle
for the common rights. But despite all forebodings, the Chesham men and women had
shown a steadfast front, and having shown that they were prepared to help themselves
they had the union behind them. There was a time when the workers in Chesham were
heedless of each other they each played for their own hand and they lost the game.
What had happened since? They had come to realise their responsibilities to one another :
they had caught the underlying spirit of Trade Unionism: they were standing up for one
another, and as a result they were waging a successful fight. To put it that they would
gain the victory if they remained steadfast was to put it rather crudely. They had

No Desire for a Victory which would Crush Other People.
They had a firm desire and intention, and that they would develop to its logical conclusion,
but they had no desire for a victory in the sense of the conqueror crushing the conquered.
They were out for victory in the sense that they wished to secure that national agreements
should be carried out in Chesham as elsewhere, and the struggle would continue until
that principle was established. Those present had no doubt been present also at the
meetings held by Mr. Buckle. No doubt Mr. Buckle found it necessary to speak very

NATIONAL CONFERENCE OF LABOUR WOMEN.
DELEGATES' REPORT.

We attended the National Conference of Labour Women, held at Leamington on
the 9th and 10th May, there were 338 delegates in attendance. We were welcomed by
Mrs. Warwick. Mrs. Hill, of the Women's Section, Leamington. Mr. Peree Cole, prospective candidate
for Warwick, was then called upon and he explained in short debate what we women
can do for ourselves. Miss Margaret Bondfield presided over the Conference and reported
the increase in the individual sections and the wonderful way the women were working in
the movement, our one aim being co-operation and common sense to push forward for
absolute equality. The Conference was educational and interesting and much discussion
took place. The Conference recorded its regret for the failure of Great Britain to ratify
conventions adopted at the International Conference under the terms of the Peace Treaty
of Washington. Another resolution urged the recognition of the Government of Russia
and the restoration of International co-operative trade. Disarmament formed an interesting
subject and caused much discussion, delegates assenting that we should not encourage our
children with movements or toys of the militarist description. Much agitation arose over
Motherhood and Childhood endowment, the committee recommending equal provisions
for mothers and children whose livelihood is cut off through unemployment, illness or
desertion by the father. One speaker urged that the endowment be paid in money, pro-
portioned to the family income, others spoke in favour of it being paid in kind. After
several other delegates expressed their views on the subject, Miss Bondfield added it could
be discussed at the branches if the report was approved. There were great differences of
opinions. Resolutions were passed urging the unemployment grant to be increased to
for the women and increases for men, also the Conference regretted the attack recently
made on the Trade Board system, and the proposal of the Cave Committee to restrict the
scope of the Trade Board Acts. This was the final of the Conference, Miss Bondfield
thanking all delegates for their attendance.

Yours fraternally,
I. GUMSLEY. EDITH SHERWIN.
E. PHILLIPS. A. BILLINGTON.
E. ALI. A. SMALLEY.
A. OAKENFUL.

TUBERCULOSIS IN BOOT FACTORIES.

A question as to the prevalence of consumption in the boot and shoe trade was put
by Mr. William Langley, J.P., secretary of the Rushden, Higham Ferrers, Irthlingborough
and Raunds District Branch of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives, at a
meeting of the Irthlingborough Urban Council, on the presentation of the annual report
of the Medical Officer of Health. Dr. Elliott (the Medical Officer) said that consumption
was more prevalent amongst boot and shoe makers than was the case in many other
trades, but added that he believed that lately there had been manifested an improvement
throughout the country.

One of the councillors inquired if the Medical Officer knew of any factory in Irthling-
borough which caused a larger proportion of deaths from tuberculosis than in such sur-
rounding towns as Rushden, Wellingborough, or Kettering. In reply, Dr. Elliott said he
knew of none, and he expressed the opinion that a town sometimes struck an epidemic
of tuberculosis, which lasted for a few years and then died down. He believed that the
present anti-tuberculosis campaign at Irthlingborough would do good, but that the results
might not be seen in the immediate future. Shoe Trades Journal, 23rd June, 1922.

CO-OPERATIVE SUPERVISOR.

Mr. John Haigh, the present manager of the Co-operative Wholesale Society's boot
factories at Leeds and Heckmondwike, has been appointed as temporary supervisor of
the society's boot factories in the Leicester and Derby areas. This has, unfortunately,
become necessary owing to the early retirement of Mr. T. E. Hubbard, who has nearly
completed 50 years of faithful service to the C.W.S. at the Leicester boot works, and the
unfortunate illness of Mr. Hubbard's assistant, Mr. Frank Poynton. Mr. Poynton has been
stricken by a serious illness, which will incapacitate him from active duty for a considerable
time. Mr. Haigh is taking charge until such time as a new management and organising
force is engaged and installed. Leicester Mail, May 24th, 1922.

THE TRADE UNION ACT (1913) AMENDMENT BILL
The Bill to amend the Trade Union Act, 1913, which was given a second reading in
the House of Commons on May roth, is a challenge to the Trade Union Movement
The history of Trade Unionism is a history of struggle. From 1800, when Combina.
tions were forbidden, there was a struggle of a quarter of a century before the Combination
Laws were repealed. It was not until half a century later that collective bargaining was
finally recognised by the law of the land. In 1900 the Taff Vale Decision gave a staggering
blow to the Trade Union Movement. After an active agitation, the Trade Disputes Act
was passed in 1906. This Act had hardly been placed on the Statute Book before Osborne
Judgment temporarily paralysed the political Labour Movement, and it was not until
began proceedings against the Amalgamated Society of Railway Servants. The Osborno
1913 that the Labour Party was able to breathe freely. The Trade Union Act which
was then passed is to-day menaced by the Trade Union Act (1913) Amendment Bill
engineered by the Tory Party. If this measure were to be passed into law, the situation
woul be as serious as that created by the Osborne Judgment.
As the law at present stands, the onus is upon a Trade Unionist to declare that he
does not intend to contribute to the political fund of his Union. The Amending Bil
proposes that the onus should fall upon him of declaring his intention to contribute
According to the present law he may claim exemption; according to the new Bill, he will
active steps to be exempted from his automatic exemption. He can now contract out of
the trouble of contracting in.
It is laid down in the Bill that :--
(i.) It shall be competent for any member of the Union to give notice in the
form set out in the First Schedule to this Act, or in a form to the like effect, that
he is willing to be levied and to contribute to a political fund of the Union by sending
such notice to the secretary of the lodge or branch of which he is a member, or to
the general secretary of the Union; "
Moreover, it is provided that :-
(iii.) Any member who has given notice of his willingness to contribute to
the political fund of the Union shall on and from the first day of January next
following the date of such notice cease to be liable to contribute as aforesaid, unless
during the current year of such notice and before such first day of January he shall
send to the secretary of the lodge or branch of which he is a member, or to the
general secretary, a notice in writing of his willingness to renew such notice for the
ensuing year, and in that event his liability to contribute as aforesaid shall continue
for a further period of one year and shall then cease, unless again renewed."
Put briefly, no Trade Unionist will be liable to pay a political levy, unless he states
his desire so to pay in writing, and to renew his written statement each year.
But this is not all. The Bill imposes obstacles to the establishment of any political
fund at all. According to the Act of 1913, the funds of a Trade Union are not to be applied
in the furtherance of political objects, "unless the furtherance of these objects has been
approved as an object of the Union by a resolution for the time being in force passed on a
ballot of the members of the Union taken in accordance with this Act for the purpose
by a majority of the members voting." The Amending Bill alters this and requires that
there shall be a vote " of at least 50 per cent. of the members" and that " of the votes recorded
those in favour of the proposal exceed by 20 per cent. or more, the votes of those against the
proposal" to further political objects.
It will be seen that the purpose of the Bill is to strangle the political activities of the
Trade Union Movement. The method proposed is based less on the opposition of Trade
Unionists to the political levy than on the inertia of most people, and on the hindrance
which the complicated procedure of notice in writing will be to quite loyal Trade Unionists.
The arguments against the Tory Bill are obvious. It is class legislation of the worst
type, and it seeks to impose on Trade Unions conditions which do not apply to other
associations. It attempts to draw a distinction between industrial and political questions
which does not, in fact, exist. It would, if passed, put upon those who subscribed to the
political fund the onus of providing the means for a Labour Party which can promote the
workers' industrial interests in Parliament on such questions as Unemployment Insurance,
Workmen's Compensation, &c.; and, finally, it would complicate and render more difficult
Trade Union administration.
The Bill is an attempt to counteract the growing strength of the Labour Party. It
is significant that it should have been introduced into the present House of Commons,
with its huge Government majority of men, a considerable proportion of whom probably
never expect to sit in another Parliament, and into a Parliament elected on quite other
issues. It is doubtful, indeed, whether any single Member of the House of Commons ever
referred to the question in his election campaign.

After an hour or so in Earl Shilton one could cite numerous cases of families, big

thatched roofs on which grass is growing, and in at least one bedroom I saw it is possible
to lie in bed and while away the time by counting the stars, an occupation that would not
commend itself to many.
Earl Shilton is situate in one of the nicest and most elevated parts of Leicestershire.
The village population is increasing, and, under efficient local government, Shilton should
become an important industrial township, none the less healthy because of its industrialism.
Leicester Advertiser, May 20th, 1922.

Tellers.

85. Two delegates shall be appointed as Tellers, whose uling as to
numbers shall be final, except in cases of dispute, when the Chairman shall orde
a recount.

Door Keeper.

86. A Door Keeper (not a delegate) shall be elected at the commence
ment of the Conference, whose duties shall be to test all applications for
admittance to Conference, and also to keep the floor of the hall strictly for
delegates only, and also to regulate the granting of passes to members of the
public to the gallery, and to perform such other duties as may be required
of him by the General Secretary. Preference to be given to a local man, and
his pay shall be 15s. per day for any day or days required.

Voting.

87. The system of voting shall be by show of hands, the decision of the
majority to rule.

Limitation of Speeches.

88. Every latitude is to be allowed the Delegates for giving expression to
their views on the various subjects that may be brought before the
Conference: but in the event of the Chairman seeing that the business is not
making satisfactory progress, he shall have power to appeal to the Conference
to limit the time allowed to movers of resolutions to ten minutes, a seconder
to seven minutes, and any subsequent speaker to five minutes. No one shall
speak more than once on a question, except the mover of an original
resolution. Should the President be of opinion that there is no practical
difference among the Delegates, he shall have power to stop the discussion.

Amendment of Standing Orders.

89. Should any amendment of the Standing Orders of Conference be
proposed by any Branch, such amendment shall be forwarded at the same
time and under the same conditions as the amendments proposed to the Rules.
Notice of such amendment to be sent by the General Secretary to the
Delegates as early as convenient after receipt.

Delegates leaving Conference.

90. No Delegate shall leave Conference without the consent of the
President. Delegates absent one whole sitting without leave of absence shall
be named by the Chairman. The Conference shall decide thereupon what
action shall be taken with any such Delegate.
