UNEMPLOYMENT ACT.
10. NORWICH No. 1.-“This Conference places on record its profound for the that the partial administration of the Unemployment Insurance Act by the Branches of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Ope ates against the best interests of the individual member at the Union as a whole.
It, therefore, requests the Council to take the necessary steps to terminate the arrangement with the Government at the cathest possible date."

MARRIED WOMEN IN FACTORIES.
11. WELLINGBOROUGH.-'That this Conference is of the opinion that where Married Women (with husbands at work) are employed, the Council should endeavour to arrange terms with the Manufacturers' Federation on the following lines:-That in the event of trade depression so as to necessitate the running of short time in any factory, Married Women (with husbands at work) should be the first to stand down."

POLITICAL AGENTS.
12. WELLINGBOROUGH. "That in order to secure greater co ordination in the Political activities of the Union, the Political Agents employed by the Union should be asked to attend periodically the Council Meetings, or at other times when the Council think fit, when the Political policy of the Union is under discussion. Further, that Political Agents be asked to attend the Annual Conference for the day when political matters are being discussed."

SUPERANNUATION.
13. WELLINGBOROUGH.-"That this Conference is of the opinion that the time has arrived for the establishment of a Superannuation Fund for its aged members, and instructs the Council to appoint a Sub-Committee to make inquiries from those Trade Unions who already have a Supera nuation Fund, and to place before the next Conference a scheme which could be taken up by those members.desirous of so doing."

14. WELLINGBOROUGH.-"That the words 'At the Seat of Government' in the minute passed at the Edinburgh Conference relating to the Annual Conference be rescinded. Further, that all future Conferences be held away from Boot and Shoe Manufacturing Centres." (NOTE. This is out of order as rules cannot be altered until 1923. See Rule 70.)

OPENING OF THE CONFERENCE.

The Second Annual Conference of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives
opened at the Club Union Buildings, Clerkenwell Road, London, E.C. 1, on Whit-Monday,
5th June, 1922, at 10 a.m.
Mr. T. F. Richards, General President of the Union presided, and was supported by
Messrs. C. Bleakley (Edinburgh), A. J. Dobbs (Leeds), C. Mayes (Kettering), J. Manners
(Bristol), W. Hindes, J.P. (Norwich), Alex. Smith (Wolverhampton), T. Adnitt (Leicester),
W. Warner (Hinckley), E. Law (Northampton), Len Smith (Northampton), C. Bates
(Rushden), all members of the Executive of the Union, with Messrs. J. Buckle, J.P. and
D. McCarthy—organisers, and Mr. W. R. Smith, M.P., J.P., Parliamentary representative.
Chairman's Welcome.

THE CHAIRMAN : On behalf of the Union, I beg to give you all a hearty welcome to
this thirty-fourth Conference of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives, having
regard to all the Conferences held, and I hope your minds will be concentrated on the
membership, that we shall all do our best for those belonging to the organisation. You
will notice from the platform our General Secretary happens to be absent, owing to his
being a delegate to the American Federation of Labour. He sailed last Wednesday
morning. I shall submit a letter from him to you later. Our duty at present is the
election of a doorkeeper and tellers.
Election of Doorkeeper.

Upon the proposition of Mr. G. PARBURY, seconded by MR. T. ADNITT, Mr. James Cull,
of the London Metro. Branch, was unanimously elected doorkeeper, and the Chairman
asked Mr. Cull to take up the position.
Tellers..

Council's Address to Conference.
In the absence of the General Secretary, MR. J. MANNERS (Council Member) read the Address of the Council to Conference as follows:-

34, GUILFORD STREET,
LONDON, W.C. 1.
5th May, 1922.
FELLOW MEMBERS,

1.---UNEMPLOYMENT.
The past year has been full of anxiety, not only for those holding office, but for the people generally due in no small degree to the fact that unemployment has been the lot of millions of workers on the one hand, and millions of others have been, and still are pleading for the barest necessities of life to keep them alive. This deplorable state of affairs, we hope, will, within the near future, so arouse the people that they will put into office men and women determined to grapple with the reasons that have brought about such a state.

As a Union we have been, and will continue to do our best to help those who find themselves without employment in the industry. The amount expended in Out-of-Work Benefit for 1921 was as follows:-
For half-year ending June, 1921 £76,920 17 10
For half-year ending December, 1921 £19,536 17 11
Total £96,457 15 9

In addition to such payment, we have paid out under the Government Scheme for the half-year ending
June, 1921 £19,685 12 3
December, 1921 £20,074 19 10
Total £39,760 12 1
and for contributions of members paid by the Union during the same period the following amounts :-
Half year ending June, 1921 £1,534 19 8
Half-year ending December, 1921 £1,716 5 4
Total £3,251 5 0

making a grand total of £139,469 12 10, which sum is, though inadequate as a proper income to the members, nevertheless one which has been of inestimable benefit to the recipients. We stated in our report last year that we were discussing with the Employers' Federation the question of a joint scheme for dealing with Unemployment and Under-employment for the industry. The Government Schemes have, however, for the time being,


---
put a stop to any mutual schemes such as was contemplated. During the
Vear we have taken a vote of the members, and secured powers to pay the
contributions of all members who were not in receipt of any income.
The question of Trade Schemes has, however, owing to the Geddes'
Report, once more become prominent so much so is this the case that the
Minister of Labour has sent a letter to both Employers' Associations and
Trade Unions asking for their views upon Insurance for Unemployment by
Industries rather than by a Government Scheme. We have therefore been in
correspondence with the Manufacturers' Federation about the question, and
at the same time the General Council of the Trades Union Congress have
also sent out to Trade Unions asking them, before committing themselves to
any particular Scheme or Schemes, to consult with the General Council upon
the subject with a view to ensuring some common line of action being pursued
by the Trade Union movement as a whole.

2. SPECIAL SICKNESS SCHEME.

The above-named matter, which, by your vote at the 1921 Conference,
we were instructed to proceed still further with, has not made any headway,
the employers not feeling themselves in a position to deal with the question
whilst the present slump continues.

3. THE FEBRUARY (1922) INTERIM AGREEMENT.

The question of the revision of the National (1919) Agreement was fully
reported upon last year, the result being that the following instruction was
passed as a guide to the Council: -

"This Conference gives full power to the Executive Council to revise,
if necessary, and adjourn the time of meeting with the Manu-
facturers until such time as circumstances should appear more
favourable for negotiation, but that no reduction of present
conditions be discussed until a Special Conference has been held."

We met the Executive Committee of the Manufacturers' Federation upon
the proposed revision of the Agreement on 24th May, 1921, and, after
discussing the general position, the following resolution was unanimously
agreed to :-

"That this Conference of the Manufacturers' Federation Executive and
the Executive Council of the National Union of Boot and Shoe
Operatives, having considered the question to amend the terms of
the 1919 Agreement, and the revised 1920 Agreement, hereby
decide to adjourn the matter for six months. It is to be clearly
understood the existing Agreement will remain in full operation.
Each side agrees to submit amended terms within the six months
period."

By this decision we secured another six months wherein the 1919-1920
Agreements continued to operate.

In December, 1921, under the chairmanship of Alderman F. Sheppard,
O.B.E., J.P., of Bristol, we met the Committee of the Employers' Federation
to again discuss proposals for a new Agreement, and after several meetings
proposals were arrived at which, though not satisfactory to us, were we felt
convinced the maximum could obtain. Those proposals were submitted to a
special conference of delegates held at the Boot & Shoe Trade Hall, Leicester,
on 29th December, 1921, the delegates being the same as dealt with the

tion of clauses 8, 9, 10, 11 and 12 (a) of the said Agreement for which the follow-

December (1921) Interim Agreement.

    upwards), and 5 per cent. on Piecework earnings, shall take place on the second pay

18
4. AMALGAMATION.
In the matter of amalgamation with other Unions we have not been able
to make any headway. The Amalgamated Union of Boot and Shoe Makers,
with whose Executive we had a number of interviews, and a fair amount of
correspondence, ultimately took a vote of their membership, which vote was
not in favour of amalgamation.
Another Union, called the London and Provincial Union of Handsewn
Boot and Shoe Makers, was also approached. They, however, were not in
favour of amalgamation.
5. INTERNATIONAL.
In relation to International Federation, we have made some headway.
A Conference was held in Vienna, in July of last year, at which a number
of Unions from England, France, Germany and Austria had representatives.
The meeting was really one called by the International Shoe and Leather
Workers. At the same time, and in the same building, there was another
Conference of Unions catering specially for the Leather Industries. A Joint
Conference was held to discuss the advisability of one International for all
workers concerned with the Leather Industry. After full discussion of the
matter, it was agreed that such an International should be formed. Our
delegates at the Conference were Mr. W. R. Smith, M.P., J.P., and the
General Secretary. A small sub-committee was formed to draw up rules
and regulations as Standing Orders for the International Boot and Shoe
Operatives and Leather Workers' Federation.
The General Secretary was appointed upon this Committee, and Mr. Smith
accompanied him to the meeting in the capacity of visiting delegate. The
Sub-Committee met in August, 1921, and rules and regulations were drawn
up, which will be submitted to a full Conference to be held in Munich on
June 10th-immediately following this Conference of ours.
We hope that this Federation will be one of the means, not only of benefit
to the leather industry, but, by interchange of thought and wider knowledge
of the conditions of other countries, may bring about such complete under-
standing between the worker's as to render war between nations impossible.
6.-DANGERS OF SECTIONALISM.
The question has been raised upon more than one occasion within recent
date, as to whether the interests of all the members-male and female-can
be, and are efficiently attended to and dealt with by the Council or Branch
Officers. The special point raised is that officials generally are men, which
acts as a deterrent against the women members. In our opinion there is no
foundation for any such statement. We claim that the women members'
interests are fully and adequately dealt with. Further, in our judgment it
would be a retrograde step to begin to divide the membership of the Union
into separate watertight compartments. There is a further suggestion that
there should be unions for men and unions for women only, which in our
judgment is a policy that would not make for real progress, but rather increase
the difficulties by which the movement is faced from time to time.
7.-POLITICAL ASPECT.
The present position is far, very far, from being satisfactory, whether
looked at from a national or international standpoint. The state of the
world is not only unstable, but also, in many cases, as represented by
politicians, reactionary. The need for solidarity amongst the workers is
greater than ever. Attempts are being made, and that pretty constantly, to
m

make arrangements between certain nations, which, far from tending to mutual
trust and confidence, would only result in a policy indistinguishable from the
"kind of diplomacy" that obtained up to 1914. To such methods we must
offer unrelenting opposition, and insist that agreements and understandings,
which should only be made after full discussion in Parliament, and be
based upon mutuality, goodwill and faith in the bona fides of one
another for the settlement of any differences by arbitration. Nationally
the outlook is one of grave import. Unemployment is still rampant, waste
of money still goes on in connection with a militant policy. On the
other hand, in matters that would really help the people, there is cheese-
paring, and an apparent determination to cut down expenditure upon that
part of policy which would the better fit one for properly carrying out their
duties as citizens. Under such circumstances, and with such an atmosphere
surrounding us, it becomes increasingly important that upon all occasions, in
both local and national elections, advantage should be taken of the same to
ensure the return of those who are pledged to carry out the labour policy.
This will need work not only when an election is near, but a good deal of
spade work being carried on constantly, whereby the electorate may be fully
informed of the real position of affairs. We trust that, in these matters, all
will do and give their best to aid the cause and to increase the momentum
behind the policy; accelerating, by such methods, the bringing into actual
practice those measures which will give to all the peoples of the earth
freedom and liberty, on the one hand, and deliverence from those terrible
conditions industrially of which so many at present are victims.
We are,
Yours fraternally,

At this stage the Chairman read the following letter, the same being received with

FELLOW DELEGATES,
34, GUILFORD STREET,
LONDON, W.C.1,
31st May, 1922,
To my very great regret I shall not be with you at the Conference this year
other than in spirit. I believe this will be the first Conference from which I have
been absent for about thirty years. The reason for my absence is because of the fact
that I am one of the delegates representing the British Trade Union movement at the
American Federation of Labour Annual Convention. I feel confident, therefore,
although I may be absent from our own Conference, you will agree it is an honour,
not only to myself, but also to the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives, to
be one of those elected to convey the greetings of the British Trade Union movement
to our colleagues across the seas.
The matters referred to in the Address of the Council to Conference, and in the
various resolutions from the branches, are both many and varied, and I have no doubt
there will be not only discussion upon many of the points, but diverse views expressed.
The diversity of view is a matter of which I have upon many occasions stated it is a
good thing, because we are more likely to arrive at a satisfactory determination of
any particular subject, the main point being that in our differences we should always
give one another credit for being sincere in the view that is being expressed.

MR. D. MCCARTHY (Organiser) : The men at Chesham are to blame, not the Council.
The men accepted a reduction without letting their officials know. The thing had been
going on a fortnight before Mr. Poulton had word of it. I was sent down to enquire into
the position. I met the local officials, and was told the people had no hope and no spirit.
When I spoke to one or two of them they justified the position. They said in pre-war days
their conditions were lower than other parts of the country and were prepared for them to
come down now. I reported to Mr. Poulton and wrote an accurate account of it. I
returned in a few days and advertised a meeting, and we had about sixty present, but it
was not a representative meeting. There were men from the Co-operative factory and
the unemployed, so only about fourteen were present who were affected. I told Mr.
Richards about it and asked him if he would try and arouse some enthusiasm. We had
another meeting and after I had been from shop to shop to bill a meeting, only 65 came.
The whole of the Council went down, and I might say in passing that I cannot agree with
what Mr. Lyne said. I hinted that we might be prepared to do something, because they
were undermining the whole position of the Union. It was only by persistent effort
that we got the operatives. Some Council Members felt the members should be expelled.
Success only came by the persistent efforts of the Council. We gradually had better
meetings, until 130 of the people affected turned up. There was nothing left undone in the
way of advice or agitation, and I think the Council deserve credit for their work.
don't know whether it is possible to discriminate between employers' associations, but
think we have as hard a set to deal with as any other trade in the country. I remember
Mr. Marlow saying when we were pressing him : " I confess in the past we were too anxious
to keep wages low, but in the name of the Federation I don't think that will happen in
future." They carried a resolution in January, 1920, that it was in the best interests of the
trade that we should be well organised. They allow their foremen to oppose us, and in
the country managers and foremen refuse to allow the operatives to join the Union. One
of their monthly journals sneers at myself at want of success. You will get nothing from
them unless you hold the advantage. It was nothing short of bullying us. Facts and
figures they ignored altogether. They thought the matter could be settled in an hour
with 56s. for men and 30s. for women, with 10 per cent. off statements, and so on. Until
we have a bigger fighting fund we can do nothing. We should remain in our present position
if we keep increasing our benefits every time we put the contributions up, and never get
a fighting fund. I feel sorry for the weekly wage earners. Manufacturers admitted the
reduction would make very little difference in the price of the boots and shoes. Is there
any honour at all in the money-making game? Some of you may say it will not improve
our position by exposing weak spots, but I think they should be exposed. Whilst the Council
may not be deserving of the praise of Mr. Jex, still I think they did well.

MR. J. BUCKLE (Organiser): We had had a kind of inquisition this morning and fault-
finding too because a delegate expressed approval of certain matters which the Executive
brought before a delegate meeting. Why was it brought to that delegate meeting, specially
called? It was brought there because a certain resolution was introduced at a conference
twelve months ago. The Executive Council of the Union, having perhaps at the most
critical juncture of their career, with perhaps the greatest difficulty it was ever presented
with, had to negotiate-inch by inch--with circumstances against them, and eventually
secured a settlement with which the Executive did not agree. I venture to say, Mr.
Chairman, no executive officer was satisfied with the terms of agreement, but the time had
arrived when someone was ready to take responsibility for the future welfare of the organisa-
tion, of which many of us have been members for years. (Hear, hear.) They had to pass
1900-10, 11-14, and through all those years we were building up a constructive policy.
Some of us are aware that whilst we deplore the fact that there are two minimums for men,


---
we remember the time when there were five or six minimum wages for men. By negotia-
tion one by one has gone, and I hope after the next negotiations we shall have brought a
state of uniform circumstances adaptable to our industry. During this period, I think it is
kind for those of us who have taken responsibility, to say to us you were right. In accord-
ance with the rules, the Executive Council came before a special meeting, and took that
meeting into its confidence and said the Executive recommended-although not unanimous
-the Terms. They became your property and we acted upon that instruction. One of
the points which is very catching -and it has been raised here this morning-suggests
our course was to send it to an independent person for the purpose of deciding it. My
private opinion is that our case was so flimsy we should have lost. The Executive, by its
vast experience negotiated, and mitigated the severity which might have obtained by an
award given by an independent arbitrator. In 1920 we secured 125. for men and 105. for
women extra. The fight we put up was on the increase of the cost of living over the 1919
period, and inasmuch as that had faded away what case had you to submit to a legal-minded
gentleman for arbitration? My own opinion is, we reciprocate the kind expression towards
the platform by thanking the delegates for their common sense. The miners' strike is too
dreadful to speak of; the engineers' strike is too regretful to think of. The most skilled
men the world has ever seen will be reduced to 46s. per week, and they have to be 23 or 24
years of age before they get the minimum. Our Constitution is, we can do better by nego-
tiation, and instead of paying 3s. 6d. contribution, we have a fair standard (owing to the
methods adopted) whereby we can maintain that standard on a smaller contribution much
longer than any other organisation. The Executive Council negotiated to the best of their
ability and perhaps shewed as much energy and backbone as anyone could desire. We
attempted to negotiate that no possible reduction was arguable until the index figure of the
cost of living was at 70 over 1919. We argued at 85, 90, and the Sub-Committee which
did the negotiation had a troublous sea. Some can talk, but always shirk responsibility.
You had to accept it, because the Trade Boards and every Union and industry had wages
receding. The Executive had to face the proposition that in the industry we represented,
before the war the operatives were very improperly paid. Our men and women never had
a proper payment for the work they did. I am not going to pretend we can suit everyone,
and we should be fools if we attempted to try, and if this Executive of ours goes, and we lose
power, some of us will be able to criticise. The weak spot in the terms is that we have to
meet the employers in October. Some of us will not see parity. When it gets there the
negotiable circumstance leaves men 42 per cent. over pre-war conditions, and with all due
respect to the ladies-they have a right to go for us-and I have a right to tell them we
did something for them, and we must remember the women have never been as strong
as they are to-day. When par is reached, women's wages are 50 per cent. over pre-war.
That is the point, 50 per cent., and that was negotiable. When you take the other depart-
ments perhaps the average percentage of increase will be round about 52 per cent. It
reflects not against the Executive Council, but is in their favour for the work done irre-
spective of departments or sex. We have done all it is humanly possible to do. I want
to remind those people who felt at the time that we should have sacrified our funds, that
instead of having smiling faces to-day you would have been in mourning. Your trade
union is not responsible for export trade being reduced to its present position. It is not
responsible for finding trade, but it is responsible for seeing its members have proper
wages and conditions.

MR. W. JONES (Kingswood): How many Unions were invited to amalgamate?
THE CHAIRMEN: Several years ago I called together eight or nine Unions with a

bers. They asked about the funds. We have tried our friend Taylor, of Rossendale
Valley, but they would not join up unless they could keep their local autonomy. They
want freedom but to share our funds. We have had a number of private conversations
and communications and they have never taken the matter seriously. So far as we are
concerned the Amalgamated Society turned it down by vote. In relation to the London
and Provincial Union-who only have members in London, doing West End work-they
did not feel inclined to amalgamate.

International.

MR. W. KENDALL (Leicester): Seeing our General Secretary was appointed to go to Munich and is now on the way to America, what is the position ?
THE CHAIRMAN: Mr. Len Smith will attend in his stead, along with Mr. Walter Smith.

MR. G. CHESTER (Kettering) asked for a report of what has so far been achieved.

MR. W. R. SMITH, M.P. Our first association with the International Body was when remember Herr Simon attended the Norwich Conference in 1912, and then we became affiliated with the International Shoe Workers' Union. There should have been another friend Gribble went to Stuttgart, he being there for another purpose. The delegates will Conference in 1914, just after the outbreak of war, but no delegate could get across fortunately for himself. No further Conferences were held until 1919, when one was held at Zurich. We were invited to attend and appointed a delegate, but it was impossible to get there owing to passport troubles. Last year the Conference took place in Vienna.
At Zurich it was decided to consider the question of forming an amalgamation of all Leather Workers, making the International one. One of the reasons that this question looms rather differently abroad from what it does here is due to the fact that large shoe manu-facturers are leather dressers also. There is a closer association between the two on the Continent than there is in England. Viewing it from our standpoint, having regard to the fact that the Leather Workers are split up here, we approached the matter with some hesitation, and we submitted proposals. Both Mr. Poulton and I found ourselves in great difficulty in accepting some of the rules. We had drafted a set of our own-one was drafted by Simon, and one by the French organisation. Several points we took exception to, and eventually the meeting was postponed until August. Mr. Poulton and I again attended a sub-committee and we were able to secure some of the points to which we attach great importance, one was in regard to voting. They were in favour of an unlimited number of delegates and vote to be taken from the delegation present. We have never supported that policy, because a large organisation like ours with only two delegates could be outvoted by a small organisation who might have more delegates. It is difficult to say what is likely to accrue as the result of the work of this International, but the principle of the thing is one to which we must give support. Recent events show it must be to the advantage of the workers to have the common understanding between all workers as far as possible. The countries represented were England, Scandinavia, Belgium, Czecho-Slovakia, Austria, Switzerland, and Germany, and the hope was expressed we might have a better understanding to help the workers in times of distress. The French delegate, Roux, asked that a manifesto might be printed and signed by the representatives of the nations on the committee, declaring our policy as being against war, and he wanted to post them in France having regard to the situation as it existed then so that he could put them before the French people as showing the futility of war. The rules will be finally adopted at the Conference on Saturday of this week. Mr. Poulton and I addressed the meeting at Vienna in a hall which has a seating capacity of 2,000; at that meeting speeches were made which seemed to indicate that as far as it was possible to gather there was a feeling amongst organised workers that it was in the best interests of all to have no wars. The idea is good but I suggest we wait for a time to see how far it can be used as an instrument so far as our organisation is concerned. I hope it will be possible to circulate information in the Shoe Union and have been able to retain
In Germany they have 90,000 members in the Shoe Union and have been able to retain the 48-hour week. They are suffering so far as wages are concerned owing to the currency which makes their money so small as compared with our own. The German shoe worker is one of the best paid operatives in Germany. Their position is being continually disturbed owing to the rate of exchange which renders their advances valueless. When I was there first the Mark stood at 300 to the £, to-day it is 1,200, which means in relation to our own money the German mark has fallen four times. It does not have the same effect internally as it does externally. We were informed that they were having a trying and difficult time, but they hope to retain their powers and strengthen and establish conditions which would be satisfactory to themselves and advantageous to the workers of all countries.

MR. G. CHESTER (Kettering): Is this a separate International or a Sectional grouping of the Internationals ?

MR. WALTER SMITH: It is an Industrial Federation, but one of the conditions of membership is that Unions must be part of their own National Body and linked up with the International Trade Unions whose head office is at Amsterdam. There seems from the information obtained the possibility of overcoming some of the sectional difficulties. Austria taken by itself has practically a German population, and the movement is afoot to try and bring about an understanding between them and the Czechs. One of the Austrian-Germans on the Executive resigned to allow a Czech to go on, and the Inter-national Executive is composed of Simon (Secretary of the Saddle-makers and Leather Workers), one Scandinavian, one Frenchman, one Czech, and our General Secretary.

policy of the Union, the expense to be borne by the Union.

to general policy, with alterations in the constitution and rules of the Union."

The circular having been distributed, the following is a copy of the same :-
LEICESTER WOMEN'S BRANCH OF THE
NATIONAL UNION OF BOOT AND SHOE OPERATIVES.
January, 1922.
[The Leicester Women asked for this to be put in the Report for January, 1922.]
FELLOW MEMBERS,
We are pleased to report that 200 new members joined this month, and no machinists are out of employment. We have held two large mass meetings in connection with the New Terms. Our women expressed deep dissatisfaction at the lack of
effort made on their behalf by the Council.
The arguments put forth against resisting a reduction because we are only a Women's Branch and must sink our opportunities for the sake of the greater body is ridiculous and has no logic in it.
As already stated, we have no machinists out of work and our labour is wanted Many firms are advertising. The reason for this shortage, notwithstanding all enquiries made by the Leicester Boot Manufacturers, is because our shoe girls leave for better wages, and not for fun as is supposed.
We believe there are many employers who have no desire to interfere with their women's wages. We make a further claim. The difference between men's and women's wages is too great. Women in both the closing and shoe rooms are very essential to boot production. Yet we are in receipt of less than two-thirds of the men's wage, and although when wages are normal and prices down to 1914, the men will have advanced 25 per cent. and the women 38 per cent. over 1914 wages, the women will still be 15s. a week below the men's minimum.
Our Branch in the past has been compelled to follow other districts, but not this time.
Our Council member, Mrs. Bell-Richards, moved to exempt the women from this agreement, but got no support whatever. We cannot forfeit the strength we have for improving our position. The sex war in our Union is forcing women to look well after themselves first. We had to draft, compile, argue, and administer our four piecework statements (asked for and used by many branches of the Union), without either advertisement, glamour, or cost to the Central Funds. Some districts asked for our printer so as to be enabled to order direct. The Leicester Women are proud of their achievements and intend going forward not backward, as some have already done, and others are doing. We are starting a Women's Social Club in connection with our Branch for educational purposes, the need of combination and sex-consciousness. The employers of the city have only to grant us the reasonable concessions we are entitled to and there will be no disturbance caused by us.
From our mass meetings we have our instructions. As far as the women in the Boot and Shoe industry of Leicester are concerned, past history may repeat itself. Belonging to a great organisation is good when equal rights are conferred, but detrimental when it becomes the undoing of even a small section.
Our Mass Meeting of the 13th inst, confirmed the resolution of January 1st-
No Reduction.
Another Mass Meeting of the Women's Branch will be held next week.
M. J. BELL-RICHARDS, President.
MRS. GOODMAN,
MISS MUIR,
MISS TIMMS,
MISS SHERWIN,
MISS KING, Secretary.
Executive.

The Parliamentary Representative's Report to Conference.

MR. W. R. SMITH, M.P., presented his report as follows :—

The past year has not been one that enables the forces of labour to look back upon it with any degree of satisfaction. It has largely been a replica of the previous one, but on the whole worse, for it must be obvious that the further the present industrial depression goes the more difficult does the position of the wage earner become. The small savings become exhausted, the power of friends and relatives to extend the helping hand become less and less possible, the funds of trade unions are depleted, and the resulting poverty and misery reaches a level that is at once despairing and depressing.

One can only hope that the present condition of things will bring home to the minds of the people how futile, nay, how criminal war is, how little it contributes to the solution of any problem and how it leaves us with even greater troubles and difficulty than those which we had before ; that as a factor in human affairs it settles nothing, it solves no problem, it leaves humanity on a lower level, it degrades and destroys, and while it may give to a few wealth and position to the many it brings tragedy and disaster.

It is necessary to emphasise this, because if the world is to develop upon lines that lead to greater happiness and well being, if the mass of the people are to lead lives that will enable them to develop the best that is within them, if the poverty and misery of to-day is to be replaced by wealth and the joy of living, then Peace must be permanently secured. War must cease to be. If jealousies and antagonisms cannot be entirely eliminated at least the method of meeting them must be changed, and if for no other reason than that the Labour Party of all others stand for this policy it should and must be supported by the organised workers and the people generally.

This is a feature that stands out in the work of Parliament. The Labour Party is always insisting upon a policy that will carry us in that direction. We are for curtailing the forces that lead to war, and for the development of housing, in all that will take us to the higher level. In education, in public health, in all that will help to produce the healthy mind and body, the

pians for dealing with the question in face of the coming winter. In the
division we got 77 votes against 266.
In the October Session, which we had brought about by our demand that
Parliament should meet, the Government proposals were most inadequate.
On the second reading of the Bill which had been brought forward, we moved
the following reasoned amendment:
"That, whilst anxious to take every step calculated to relieve distress
during the present unemployment crisis, this House cannot assent to
the Second Reading of a Bill which provides inadequate assistance to
some working-class families and no assistance to others, which adds
to the burden upon certain industries and imposes a further tax upon
a section of the workers whilst exempting from direct contribution
other and wealthier classes of the community, and which fails to
recognise the full obligation of the State towards every citizen deprived
of the means of livelihood."
In the division 226 voted for the Bill and 70 for the Amendment.
The chief Amendments put down for the Committee and Report Stages
were as follows:-
1. To cover all dependents. (Ruled out of order.)
2. To provide the grant in respect of the dependent husband of a working
woman. (This was conceded.)
was con-
3. To cover children up to the age of 16 instead of 14. (What
ceded was that any child between 14 and 16 undergoing full-time
its,raction at school should be included.)

Alternative to the present Government. They urge each other to hang
together for fear they will hang separately. They launch a campaign of abuse
because they dare not adopt a policy of argument. They accuse us of a policy
of violence and of trading upon the ignorance of the people, but they seek to
prevent the will of the people being operative by making the Constitutional
settle more difficult, and they oppose our efforts to spread education among
the people.
They speak of the Red Army we are supposed to be organising, but
they know it is an educated democracy we seek to bring into being, and though
the task may be difficult we shall ultimately succeed.
Our greatest need to-day is unity of effort and purpose, and a concentra-
tion upon the education of the people upon the political economic needs of the
present and the future. The past is a monument of the inefficiency of those
who have been in power, and records the fact that it is they who move and
legislate upon class lines. I trust that our union will play its full part in the
task that lies ahead, and that its candidates will be among those who will
constitute the Labour Party in the next House of Commons.
I hope I may be pardoned for mentioning that last year I was elected on
a ballot vote one of the Party whips, and for suggesting that this indicates I
have earned the confidence of my colleagues in the House.

Thompson and had for its object the complete change of the policy of trade unions with
respect to trade unions taking on political action. In 1910 this question was fully dis-
cussed in Parliament. The whole standing of trade unions in relation to political action
was reviewed, and much time spent in debating the question, and ultimately an agreement
was reached by all sections in the House. So much so that after consultations had taken
place there was no division in the House upon the third reading. It had been debated,
and the Government accepted it; Mr. Bonar Law, then the leader of the opposition,
accepted it, and the Labour Party also gave its acceptance. Under the Trade Union
Act, 1913, we have to ballot our members as to whether they are in favour of political
action, and then get our rules endorsed by the Registrar. This Bill states we shall take a
ballot, but unless 50 per cent. of the members vote it is void; of those who vote at least
there must be a 20 per cent. majority. Further, if those votes are in favour, no member
can pay his contributions to the political fund until he has signed the form giving power
to take it from him. To-day, if a man wants to pay he makes no request at all, but if he
does not want to pay he contracts out, whilst under the Bill he must contract in. It will

for the safeguarding of our agreements on the other. The sum spent at

NATIONAL UNION OF BOOT AND SHOE OPERATIVES
APPROVED
SOCIETY, 281.
INCREASED BENEFITS
and
HOW TO GET THEM.
SIX POINTS.
1 Every member should realise that practically the only source of income of a Society is the individual contributions of its members.
2 Every stamp is essential if increased benefits are to be paid. A loss of one stamp per member per Half-Year means a reduced income of £2,400 per annum. This would provide sufficient money to pay another 2/- per week increased benefit.
3 Every member must insist on the Employer stamping his or her card EVERY WEEK ANY EFFECTIVE WORK IS DONE.
4 Every member must return their stamped card to the agent, no matter how few stamps may be affixed thereto, immediately upon receipt of same from the Employer. 500 cards are still outstanding for the Half-Year ending December, 1921. If you have one in your possession return it at once.
5 Every member should make it his or her duty to make every young person a member on reaching the age of 16 years. Upon the due observance of these simple instructions depends the possibility of increased benefits.
6 Every member below 18 years of age is entitled to a free transfer. A fee of 6d. is paid to every member introducing a new member to the Society.

On behalf of the Council,
JOHN W. MURBY, Manager.

REPORT OF THE AUDITOR.
241, Uppingham Road, Leivester.
To the Members of the Executive Council.
I have examined the Receipts, Vouchers and Bank Balances for the
period ended 30th June, 1922.
The Total Funds standing to the credit of the Central Office amount
to £264,603 7s. 3d., and but for the heavy cost of the Chesham Dispute
would have shewn an increase over last half-year,
I have examined all the Deeds and find them intact. There is a
new investment of £6,000 with Kingswood, bearing interest at 5% per
annum.
The State Unemployment Section shews a balance of £6,825 13s. 8d.,
this amount including the £5000 loaned from the Trade Fund.
My thanks are due to the General Secretary and the Staff for the
information supplied as required, and I testify to the excellent manner in
which the books are kept.
I certify the Accounts to be correct, and in accordance with Law.
JAS. B. B. ROBERTSON,
Corporate Accountant and Auditor.

FOREIGN POLICY.
"This Conference holds that the disastrous economic, political, and social conditions
which prevail throughout Europe are very largely the result of the mischievous policy
pursued by the Supreme Council and the Allied Governments since the Armistice.
"The Conference also holds strongly that in the following three main points Govern-
ment policy is chiefly responsible for the existing international situation :-
(1) The Peace Treaties have crushed and impoverished the peoples of Central Europe,
and, by hindering the revival of economic intercourse, have caused unemploy-
ment and depressed the standard of life in Great Britain and other countries.
Delay and indecision in regard to Reparations, and the ever-changing but always
fantastic claims made upon Germany, have been among the chief obstacles to
a return to normal economic relations. The repeatedly renewed threats to enforce
Payment by military measures maintain an unrest in Europe calculated to bring
about another great war.

it has not been reached. But it is desired that Trade Boards in fixing rates shall have
has been reached, nor that he will necessarily withhold confirmation in every case where
this recommendation of the Cave Committee in mind.

(5) MISCELLANEOUS.
These are the principal recommendations of the Cave Committee. There are, in
addition, a certain number of other recommendations of considerable, though less, import-
ance, most of which would require statutory amendment. No action, therefore, can be
taken upon these recommendations pending legislation.
Finally, attention is called to certain points of administration with regard to the
relations between the Trade Boards and the Minister of Labour which have been the
regular Departmental practice for some time and which will continue to be the practice of
the Department---

(1) There should be a regular practice of early consultation between the Department
and the Trade Boards as to the form in which the determinations of the Boards
are to be expressed.
(2) The Trade Boards should have facilities for obtaining at any stage legal advice
on questions relevant to their work, and should have an opportunity of
expressing their views themselves to the Minister's legal adviser.
(3) While the Minister is ultimately responsible for the enforcement of the Acts and,
subject to the Courts, for the interpretation of scope, arrangements should be
made to ensure the closest co-operation between the Department and the
Trade Boards in the carrying out of these duties.

Ministry of Labour,
th July, 1922,
(Signed) T. J. MACNAMARA.

ENCOURAGING "NOSEY PARKERS."
More Bright Interludes in House Committee. Trade Union Finance.

The Trade Union Act Amendment Bill was further considered by a Committee of the House of Commons to-day, Sir Watson Rutherford presiding.

Mr. Geo. Balfour moved to amend the clause by inserting words to secure that the amount paid by each member of a trade union towards the political fund shall be recorded on the card.

Mr. Swan, opposing, said it would be infra dig, and a piece of impudence to enforce such a demand.

This would enable the "nosey parkers" to poke their noses into other people's business.

Amendment withdrawn.

Taking the Law "a Hass."

Mr. Swan moved an amendment to leave out the words "and the source and nature."

He said that the insertion of these words would render the law "a hass."

Mr. Naylor, supporting the amendment, said that because the members of trade unions were working men they were to be suspect as to their political funds.

Mr. Balfour explained that the words did not affect voluntary contributions.

Joke About Sir George.

Mr. Sexton said it was most unfair to ask trade unions to disclose the source of all their political funds, and not to enforce the same principle in the case of other political societies.

For instance, a trade union might receive a contribution from the hon. member for Boroughs (Sir George Younger), in fact, he should not be surprised if the hon. gentleman became a Labour candidate—(laughter)-having regard to his sympathy with trade unions.

Temptation.

Sir George Younger: It is not intended to ask for the disclosure of funds except as raised by the levies made on the members for political purposes. If I gave you a contribution, you would not be obliged to disclose it.

Mr. Sexton: I don't expect we shall ever get a contribution from the hon. member. (Laughter.)

Sir George Younger: I may tempt you.

Mr. Cairns, opposing the amendment, declared that the "green-eyed monster" was behind these words.

Amendment Defeated.

They were prepared to disclose the source of all their income if other political associations were required to do the same.

Mr. Balfour said the promoters of the Bill were prepared, on the Report Stage, to insert words to meet the views of the Labour members, providing the amendment was withdrawn.

This offer was also declined.

On a division the amendment was defeated by 23 votes to 13.

"Road to Madness."

Speaking on a subsequent consequential amendment, Mr. Sexton declared that the promoters of the Bill were out to cripple trade unions.

"They will not succeed," he shouted.

"Those whom the gods wish to destroy they first drive mad, and the hon. member (Sir George Younger) is travelling in that direction." (Laughter.)

The amendment was agreed to and the Committee adjourned.—The Star, 12th July, 1922.

GERMAN SHOEWORKERS' CONFERENCE
on 12th June, 1922.

Report of visit to German Shoeworkers' Conference, held at Mannheim
The Conference was opened by Herr Simon, the President of Munich, giving
a hearty welcome to foreign delegates, stating in the course of his speech that
there was a desire to learn from each other, which could only be accomplished
and by this method, to get a better understanding among the workers.
Roux, France; Muller, Austria; Dessinet, Belgium; Roth, Italy, and
Czecho-Slovakia, and W. R. Smith, England, addressed the Conference. Roth
explained the conditions in that country. He stated that although the Govern-
ment, and the workers had obtained many increases in wages, the cost of living was
higher and higher, and was getting beyond them. The falling in the value of the
brought fresh difficulties, and they contemplated even greater ones in future. They
could not prevent it, but they hoped to meet it with courage, and with as much success
as they could. In the course of his remarks he said they had a Socialistic Factory
had been selling goods as cheap as possible, and had realised up to the present
of six million kroner. He asked as to what profits are being made by the capitalists.
He added that the boot and shoe makers were amongst the best paid workers in the country.
There were too delegates present, seven of whom were women, representing the
members. There are four classes of members, the contributions ranging from 1 to 4
marks, but owing to the increased cost of living they would have to be raised.
As an instance of the changing conditions following upon increased price, an application
for 40 per cent. increase upon an agreement which was renewed in March last, was now
the subject of negotiations with the employers on May ist, when it was largely conceded.
Herr Simon, in his Presidential Address, condemned unauthorised strikes, of which
it was understood there had been a number in some districts. He also emphasised that
all members, whatever their political views, must carry out the rules- the Communist
had been giving trouble and were somewhat strong in one centre. He also pressed the
need of political action being kept outside the Trade Unions.
These points were sharply debated, the Chairman of the Executive Committee urging
that the line which divided industrial questions from the political was a very narrow one.
The question of time versus piecework was discussed and the latter was endorsed by
a big majority. It was also stated that very little overtime was being worked, and it
was understood the workers did not seek it, evidently believing that the normal hours
are sufficient in a modern shoe factory.
The discussions at times were somewhat heated, but on the whole an excellent spirit
prevailed. The Conference very much reflected conditions similar to our own, and the
delegates were of a type that were largely comparable to those attending a Conference
in connection with our Union.
Each delegate wishing to speak has to do so from the rostrum, and not from where
he sits. The spirit manifested was good, and though it was not altogether easy to follow
all the debates, the help rendered us by Miss Bickel was most beneficial, and was much
appreciated. She was an excellent interpreter and it will not be easy to replace her.
It may be added that the hours of Conference were from 9 to 6 with 2 hours for lunch
on the opening day, and from 8 to 6 on other days, the Conference lasting the week.
W. R. SMITH, 
LEN. SMITH,
}
Delegates.

SUDDEN DEATH OF MR. A. E. MARLOW,
Heart Seizure in London this Morning. A Remarkable Public Career,

It is with profound regret that we announce the sudden death of Mr. A. E. Marlow
1. P. C. A. He had a heart seizure in London this morning and passed away at the Langham
Hotel, at the age of 52.

The sad news comes as a terrible shock to all Mr. Marlow's friends and to the general
public which valued so highly the work he has done in many capacities.
Mr. Marlow was in his usual health yesterday. Mr. and Mrs. Marlow went to London
last evening. He was expecting to attend meetings of the Boot and Shoe Federation
to day

During the night he suffered acute pain and thought it was indigestion. Later he
became unconscious and passed away in the early hours of the morning before a doctor
could arrive.
For many years Mr. Marlow was a very hard worker in connection with his own
businesses, as a leader in the local and national organisation of the boot trade, and as a
public man with many interests. Occasionally he had felt the strain, and he had been
advised to go slow." But it was not easy for a man of his temperament to go at half
pace he must either do a thing thoroughly or leave it alone.

Mr. Marlow was a native of Northampton. Born in December, 1870, he was the son
of the late Mr. John Marlow, the founder of the boot and shoe manufacturing firm of
Messrs. John Marlow & Sons, so that A. E. was born into the trade in which he played so
important a part after he came to manhood's estate. Mr. Marlow received his education
at Kingswell College, and at the age of fourteen entered his father's factory in Woodford
Street and started to master the whole process of boot and shoe making.

It was when he was close upon thirty that Mr. Marlow began to take a prominent
part in the boot trade. From the time he left school till 1899 he was with the firm founded
by his father. In 1899 he left to begin business on his own account, and built the factory
at St. James', Northampton, which he conducted with remarkable success.

War-Work.

Mr. Marlow quickly made his mark in the Northampton Manufacturers' Association,
and for many years he served the Association faithfully and well. He was its president
from 1913 until 1920, when he resigned and was succeeded by Mr. A. E. Tebbutt. Mr.
Marlow's period of office included the war years, and he played a great part in building up
the organisation which made it possible to meet the tremendous demand for boots for the
Allied Armies; while the trade at the same time found its full quota of men for service.
No industry responded better or more faithfully to the demands made upon it than the
boot and shoe industry, and the success with which the situation was tackled was due in no
small degree to the foresight, skill, and energy of two men, Mr. Marlow and Mr. Owen
Parker, then president of the Boot and Shoe Manufacturers' Federation.

When Mr. Marlow relinquished the Presidency of the Northampton Association,
his services were recognised by his fellow members by the presentation of his portrait
in oils.

He had not long given up the leadership of the local Association, when he was elected
President of the National Federation in succession to Mr. Owen Parker, and his death
creates a vacancy which the Federation will find it hard to fill with a man of equal ability.

"The Square Deal."
Mr. Marlow was a trusted leader of the trade. A man of keen observation and shrewd
judgment, tactful and always ready to see the other side of a question, he took a pro-
ininent part for years in the negotiations between the Federation and the National Union
of Boot and Shoe Operatives. The full value of such work is known only to them and to
those who met them in Conference, but it is admitted that much of the smooth running
of the trade during the last twelve or fifteen years was due to the wisdom and force of
character of Mr. Marlow. His motto always was "the square deal," and in pursuing
this he earned not only the esteem of his fellow manufacturers, but the respect and good-
will of those representatives of the men's Union who saw the most of him and knew best
the work he was doing.

In addition to carrying on the St. James' Works, Mr. Marlow was the head of the
large business carried on at the Mounts Factory; and on the reconstruction of Cave and
Sons Ltd., Rushden, sorne years ago, he became managing director of that important
business.

Other Activities.
Outside his trade and public work, Mr. Marlow was a very active man.
director of the Northampton Electric Light and Power Co. Ltd., and of its sister company,
He was a

MONTHLY REPORT.

FELLOW MEMBERS,
2IST AUGUST, 1922.

TRADE
has been somewhat quiet during the month, owing to the break caused by the
holidays. The figures for the month as given in the Gazette are as follow:-

BOOT AND SHOE TRADE.

Employment showed a decline in most of the Midland centres and at Norwich, but
an improvenient at Kingswood and at Leeds, in the Rossendale Valley, and in Scotland.
These variations were partly due to the turn of the season, as the demand for light boots
slackened with the approach of autumn, while the demand for heavy boots, though increas-
ing, had not vet reached its full dimensions. On the whole there was a slight decline
during the month; but employment was still much better than in July of last year, and
at some centres (particularly at Norwich, at Bristol and Kingswood, and in the Rossendale
Valley) the improvement on last year was marked.

Returns received from firms employing 37,127 workpeople showed 29 per cent, on
short time, to the extent, on the average, of ro hours a week.

The percentage of workpeople unemployed in the boot, shoe and slipper making and
repairing trade, as indicated by the unemployment books lodged at Employment Exchanges,
was 6.7 at 24th July, as compared with 7.4 at 26th June.

The exports of boots and shoes in July, 1922, amounted to 55,919 dozen pairs,
or 2,073 dozen pairs more than in June, 1922, and 29,456 dozen paits more than in
Jaly, 1921.

SILEBY. - I had occasion the other day to go with Mr. McCarthy to Sileby, where
we held an open-air meeting of the members, and those who did not happen to be members
in that village. Our meeting was not as well attended by a long way as we expected, and
we Trade Union officials wonder very largely why this apathy among working men, whose
only means is their labour, and whose income and rates of wages are governed and controlled
very largely and obtained for them by their Trade Union. We wonder why they should
risk themselves to be imposed upon by those employers who have no other object in view
only living wholly and solely for the profit they can wring out of working men and working
women.
I have also had occasion to attend once more the NORTHANTS LEATHER CORPORATION
who are cutting stock for the trade, and here we are met with a peculiar position. The
whole of the directors are Boot and Shoe Manufacturers, members of the Federation, and
yet they coolly, calmly and deliberately tell us they consider these auxiliaries to the trade
should be treated as other than a Boot and Shoe Manufactory. We, on the other hand,
have informed them seriously, politely, but determinedly, that the Executive of the National
Union look upon this firm as being subject to the National Agreement of the Boot and
Shoe Industry. This is only another instance of the elasticity of our manufacturers'
minds. The Executive of the Union have only one policy for auxiliary firms' branch
factories, and people who want to cater for the trade, and that is to bring all the power
and pressure they have to bear upon these firms respecting the National Conditions.
Owing to the illness of the Manager, we have had to leave this matter for a short time,
but the Executive are determined on that policy, and one marvels why the state of mind
these gentlemen can work themselves up to that they should calmly and coolly ask for
exemption. We cannot agree to any departure, but as soon as this is quietly and calmly
understood, the better for our relationship.

One does not wish to complain, but generally speaking this scheme is far better than
the dead minimum wage, that is whilst trade is fairly reasonable and that the agreement
is that no pieceworker can have less than the minimum rate. Thus we think we have
obtained practically all we are legitimately and reasonably entitled to.

NOTED DUNDEE ARTIST DEAD.
Romantic Career of Late David Sellars.
A romantic figure, well known to many in artistic and literary circles in Dundee, has been removed by the death of Mr. David R. Sellars, 124, Hilltown. Mr. Sellars, who lived practically alone for many years, had been in bad health for several weeks, and was taken to the Royal Infirmary only a week ago.
Born in Mussel- burgh in 185.4 of Dundee parents, Mr. Sellars spent his youth in Dundee, his parents returning to the city when he was three years old. While at school young Sellars distinguished himself sufficiently to justify his teacher marking him out as a future assistant. His father's death, when David was 11 years of age, marked the beginning of his varied and romantic life. He became a message boy to a grocer, and spent his time reading and drawing in the cellar, and sub- sequently he was employed in the office of the Dundee Advertiser, working from four to nine in the morning, and attending school during the remain- der of the day. After some time, Sellars began to learn the shoe- making trade, under the division of labour system. When he was about 15 years of age Sellars saved several persons from drowning, and was presented with the medal of the Dundee Humane Society, and later received parch- ments, &c., for deeds of bravery. In his teens and early twenties he showed a pre- disposition toward art and Trade Union matters, and held several important positions, being Organiser for Scotland when he was 23 years of age.
Parliamentary Candidate.
At one time Mr. Sellars, who was a fine platform speaker, was chosen by the Bootmakers' Society as their Parliamentary candidate for Northampton, but his love for his art was such that he would not go forward, and came back to Dundee as assistant art master at the High School about 25 years ago. Since then he devoted himself mainly to art and literature. He gained numerous prizes and certificates from the South Kensington Department, and he was a well-known exhibitor at Fine Art Exhibitions all over the country. Some of his early work was very fine, and was on view in London and Edinburgh.
Mr. Sellars was a contributor to the daily newspapers and various periodicals and magazines. He wrote many poems, and was known under the nom de plume of "Small Tingle."
For many years Mr. Sellars lived a retired life, still continuing his art work, and producing many fine pictures. Several years ago he was presented with his portrait in oils, together with a purse of sovereigns, by his friends and members of the Dundee Branch. The occasion was a memorable one. On acknowledging the gifts, which were made by Mr. D. H. McIntosh, ex-president of the branch, Sellars, being in his most humorous and reminiscent mood, charmed the company with his witty sallies of what occasionally took place at the council meetings at 17, Silver Street, Leicester, forty years ago.
"
His day's work is o'er; After life's fitful fever he sleeps."
His portrait in oils is an excellent piece of art, painted by Mr. David Bathie, Shoemaker and member of the Dundee Branch, which was highly commented upon by Mr. Alex. Smith, Arbroath.

HUGE SUMS IN RELIEF.
£233,250,000 Spent in Three Years. Official Figures.

Dr. Macnamara's Reply to Workless Marchers.

Dr. Macnamara, the Minister of Labour, gave some interesting figures yesterday as
to the money that has been disbursed by the Government for relief schemes since the
Fall of 1920. He was replying at Montagu House to a deputation from a party of unem-
ployed who had walked from Birmingham to London.

The following were the sums mentioned by Dr. Macnamara:
Government and Towns £50,000,000
Export Credit Scheme £16,250,000
Public Works £17,000,000
Relief £60,000,000
Insurance Benefits £90,000,000
Total £233,250,000

The deputation, who numbered twenty-seven, were headed by Mr. George Bridgen,
of the Birmingham District Committee of the National Unemployed Workers' Movement.
The case for the deputation was opened by Mr. Bridgen, who said that what they wished
to protest against was the "gap" system of unemployment benefits, ex-Service men's
grievances, Poor Law relief, and what he termed "the National question."

"Gap" Hardship.
Mr. Spencer, another member of the deputation, said that he failed to see why there
should be a gap system. He suggested that it should be done away with, and the unem-
ployment payment continued. A man on the Labour Exchange for five weeks, if single,
was forced into a Poor Law institution during the gap period if he had no money. He
could not see that the man should be forced into that institution at a cost of 25s. a week
when he could be kept out by the continued payment of 15s. unemployment pay.

A delegate named Waterall said that 15s. weekly was not sufficient to maintain a man,
nor was 5s. enough to keep a wife; while it was ridiculous to think that a child could live
on one shilling weekly.

The youngest member of the deputation, a youth of 19 named Ganley, spoke of the
unhappy position of the single men and women in receipt of relief-especially in the matter
of clothes. He urged that if the doles were decreased crime would increase. It cost
at least £3 a week for every youth in the Air Force and 15s. a week to keep him when out.
Either the first figure was too extravagant or the second was not enough.

Dr. Macnamara's Figures.
Dr. Macnamara, addressing the deputation, said that since the Fall of 1920 the Govern-
ment and the municipalities had between them put up between 40 and 50 millions for relief
work. That figure included special provision out of the Road Fund made by the Ministry
of Transport for road work.

Relief work under these schemes would continue, and they had a number of new
schemes before them for the purpose of meeting the situation in the winter. But relief
work could not provide for a large number of the community such as women, clerks, and
skilled artisans. There was only one way to meet their case-indeed, to meet the case
of all, and that was by getting trade restored. To that end they had established an export
credit scheme, which had already sanctioned 16½ millions, with the view to recovering the
foreign markets which were destroyed as the result of the war. That effort would be
continued.

Referring to a loan guarantee which had been inaugurated to provide work, such as
the electrification of railways, docks, and construction work, Dr. Macnamara said that
seventeen millions had been spent already in that direction. Since the slump developed
in the Fall of 1920, the Boards of Guardians had disbursed no less than sixty millions
by way of indoor relief for the aged, the sick and the destitute, and outdoor relief. An
appreciable proportion of that had taken the form of money grants, and grants in kind
to the unemployed. Since the Fall of 1920 the Insurance Act had furnished ninety millions
in benefits. The "gap" had been reduced to one week, and, added Dr. Macnamara,
"I cannot do more than that."-Westminster Gazette, August 18th, 1922.

HAND-SEWN BOOTS.
No More to be Ordered by War Office. Distress at Raunds.
For the time being, at any rate, the last word appears to have been said on the
subject of War Office orders for hand-sewn Army boots. Desiring to alleviate the distress
caused to many hand-sewn workers in Raunds by the cessation of the orders for hand-sewn
Army boots, Thrapston Board of Guardians recently asked Major Brassey to ask the
War Office to receive a deputation. Major Brassey did so, and a reply from the War
Ottice declining to receive a deputation was read at a meeting of the Board of Guardians.
The letter, which was from Colonel George Stanley, Parliamentary Secretary to the
Secretary to the War Office, stated:—
"With reference to your letters of the 20th and 21st inst., in which the Thrapston Board of Guardians desire to send on behalf of local bootmakers a deputation on the subject
of handsewn Army boots, this question has frequently received careful consideration
during the past eleven years."—Northampton Mercury, August 11th 1922

POOR CRICKET.
There is undoubtedly the makings of trouble in the Wellingborough district over
the dispute between the boot operatives and their employers about the holiday, for
The latest move is that the men's union have sent a formal request to the employers
asking that they will carry out the terms of settlement. This seems to be a preliminary
to more energetic measures, and it requires no special foresight to guess where things will
drift, if wiser counsels do not prevail quickly.
About the merits of the Holiday Scheme Fund we are not concerned ; we know there
are two opinions about it, and we are prepared to believe Wellingborough boot manufacturers
facturers have good grounds for objecting to it. We suggest, however, this particular
point is unimportant, if it be considered what principle is involved, and what repudiation
of the terms of settlement might mean.
Wellingborough manufacturers are members of the employers' association. The
executive of the association had powers delegated to them by the members to make certain
arrangements with the men's union. In such case there are always bound to be details
which will be disapproved of by individual members, both on the employers' and the
workers' side, but if collective bargaining is to continue, such dislikes must be suppressed,
and a signed agreement loyally carried out.
It should not be necessary to point out that it has been because collective agreements
have always been accepted as obligatory by individuals, that it has been possible to main-
tain industrial peace in the boot and shoe trade for so many years. If it were conceded
that individuals were at liberty to dissect an agreement to observe what suited them, and
to discard what did not, there would quickly be chaos in the industry, and such liberty
could not be confined to employers only. Loyalty to obligations is a good policy, and a
honour their bond, for it was signed by those they delegated to sign for them, and is as
profitable one in the end ; we appeal to the boot manufacturers of Wellingborough to
much theirs as if each had appended his individual mark.
Little good is ever obtained by repudiating representatives, and in this case to succeed
had previously reigned, and to sow the seeds of a bad harvest to be later reaped. —Shoe
in doing so would only be to create mistrust and suspicion where harmony and good-will
and Leather News, April 22nd, 1922.

BOOT REPAIRING WAGES.
Proposed Changes in Minimum Rates.
At the fourteenth meeting of the Boot and Shoe Repairing Trade Wages Board last
week certain changes in minimum piece rates were decided upon. The general effect of
them is that during the period in which the cost of living figures published each month
in the Ministry of Labour Gazette is not more than 90, but more than 70, the present rates
shall with certain exceptions be subject to a reduction of 7 per cent.; and for the period
during which the cost of living figure is 70 or below, the present rates shall be subject to a
reduction of a further 5 per cent., the present rates to become operative again in the event
of the cost of living figure again rising above 90.
The principal exceptions are in the case of the minimum rates for male indentured
apprentices and the general minimum piece-rates for making (other than surgical" extras").
In both these cases, the present rates will continue to operate unless and until the cost
of living figure falls to 70 or below.
In the case of the general minimum piece-rates for making (other than surgical
"extras ") the reduction provided for on a cost of living figure of 70 or below is 5 per cent.
If and when the minimum rates are confirmed by the Minister, notices will be issued
to all employers in the trade setting out the minimum rates, and the dates on which they
will come into operation. Thereafter, a notification will be sent the employers in the
trade whenever any subsequent change in the cost of living index figure involves a change
in the minimum rates.—Northampton Echo, July 26th, 1922.

THE GENERAL ELECTION.
Statements are again being made that a General Election is near at hand.
Whether such election takes place this year or early in 1923, we would like to
impress upon the members of the Union the necessity of being ready to take
their part whenever the appeal is made to the country. Let it not be for-
gotten that the workers are in an overw elming majority. If they do their
part, both by work and vote, the next Parliament will be of an entirely different
complexion politically, and in its outlook generally, from the existing one.
Do not be caught napping as you were in many instances in 1918, but so
work and act as to ensure men and women being returned to the House of
Commons who will make it their constant aim to secure the passing of such
legislation as will rid us for ever from the injustices which we, and other
nations, are acutely suffering at the present time.

LIVERPOOL.-Trade appears to be on the "mend," we only hope it
will "last." The Trade Union Congress, sometimes termed "The Workers'
Parliament," has just held its annual rally at Southport. Having casually
perused the various speeches as reported in the local Press we fail to find
anything very startling, the extremist section not being much in evidence.
We note the Congress has decided to take over the Daily Herald and make
it the official organ of the Trade Union and Labour Movement. We also note
change of Editor, which may prove beneficial.

LONDON METRO.-Trade is very bad, with an ever-increasing number
of unemployed. There is a great similarity to the big slump of two years
ago, but we hope we have reached bottom and that trade will take an upward
turn. The following resolution was unanimously carried at our September
Monthly Meeting: - "That this meeting of the London Metropolitan Branch
of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives strongly protests against
the action of the South African Government in reviving the Roman-Dutch
law. It further desires that the General Council of the Trades Union Congress
be approached in order that the workers may obtain equal representation on
the Committee of Enquiry into the recent Mining dispute."

MAYBOLE.-Trade has very much improved, nearly all our members
are started again; also pleased to say sickness very light. It is hoped that
members will do their best to keep their books clear and so build up an organisa-
tion that has done well by them in time of need.
