PARLIAMENTARY AGENT'S REPORT.
The House of Commons has suspended its labours until November 14th, 1922, when
they will meet again to give attention to those matters which in the judgment of the Govern-
ment are matters of importance to the people remain. Whether they will be such questions as
Unemployment, Housing will usually be productive of much sympathy, but little else will be forthcoming.
or not is safe to predict that at the moment such a blot upon our so-called civilia-
tion will be removed is
I have long reached the conclusion that it is useless to expect anything from this
Government, it is hopeless. It is lacking in all those qualities that are essential for the
handling of big social problems, its supporters are largely of the class that can only judge
National prosperity from the standpoint of dividends. The human side is beyond them,
and so we drift on while thousands of our fellow citizens struggle against poverty and
disease, which in a well ordered community need not exist.
All this would be bad enough if we could only see some way out, if there were only
Just a glimmer of light to give us some hope of a brighter to-morrow. But on the con
trary the clouds gather more heavily over us. We have been told so often it is our foreign
trade that we must seek to re-establish, and which is only possible under conditions of
peace, yet, abroad nothing is heard but the rumblings of threatening war, while at home
the late war is apparently forgotten, and our newspapers speak of the next war, and advise
what we must do in order to be ready.
All this is due to the fact that those who claim to have won the war have lost the
peace, it is idle to pretend otherwise. There is no peace. In the Near East the old question
of Constantinople again raises itself, and British warships are held in readiness for emer-
gencies, while Turkey, urged on by their success over the Greeks, are declaring they will
not rest until they have their Capital back, even if it means war with Great Britain. How
far this attitude is due to encouragement given by those who are supposed to be our Allies
it is difficult to say, but it is perfectly obvious that France and Italy are backing the Turks
very largely, while the British Government is to say the least of it sympathetic towards
Greece. What madness, how is it possible to establish peace when those who are supposed
to be working together are really pulling in opposite directions.
And so to sum up the situation, all this greatest of all Governments have to offer us
in regard to our problems at home, is a condition of muddle, disaster, and chaos abroad
But of course we shall be better off when our foreign trade is re-established!

There has been much talk during the last two years about stabilising the exchanges
and yet to-day the situation is worse than ever. Germany is fast following in the wake of
Austria. The Mark to-day is worth less than the Kroner was twelve months ago. It is
difficult to properly understand the meaning of it all. There is one remarkable feature
in connection with this question, namely, that the countries with the higher rates of
exchange, have a high percentage of unemployment, while those with low exchange
rates have a low percentage of unemployment. One is forced to the conclusion that
high international finance is largely responsible. The gambling that is going on must be
It is no doubt a good thing for some people, but for the mass of the people
enormous.
it spells disaster and ruin.
At times like the present we should be almost without hope were it not that we have
our own Party to give us courage for the future. That Labour is gradually but surely
gaining the confidence of the electors is evident from the results of the Bye-Elections,
while at its National Conferences it shows a capacity to grasp and appreciate these wide
issues that speak well for the future.
One is also glad to note that industrially, Labour is showing an appreciation of present
and future obligations. This was manifest at the Trades Union Congress recently held at
Southport. While their is still room for improvement in the Congress, yet there was
an indication that before long the lessons of the recent past will be learned by those who
have responsibility, and ultimately reflect itself in a closer welding together of the different
units. This is absolutely essential, if we are not only to make progress, but be able to hold
our own against the forces that are arrayed against us.
The possibility of greater unity was evident in the various resolutions that were
discussed. The common needs of all was the driving force that enabled so many to be
carried with unanimity. If only we can forget our narrow personal point of view and keep
ever before us the main principles upon which our movement rests, then the time is not
far distant when organised labour will be better equipped for its great work. Then we
shall no longer need to pass resolutions calling upon the Government to do this, that,
and the other, and which, had past Governments really governed in the interests of the
people, would have been done long ago, but we shall be doing our own work and in the
only way whereby the future shall give to all the possibilities of a full life.

FACTORY ACT OFFENCES.
Three Bristol Boot Manufacturers Fined.
At Lawford's Gate (Bristcl) Petty Sessions, last week, Messrs. T. W. Brain & Son,
boot manufacturers, North Common, were summoned for not fencing the flywheel attached
to an engine, as required under the Factory Act.
Mr. Joseph Owner, Inspector of Factories, said that some two-and-a-half years ago
Messrs. Brain laid down a modern gas engine with a single flywheel, running 200 revolution
a minute. It was placed in an engine-house, through which workers had access from on
part of the factory to the other. The flywheel had not been fenced.
Mr. Albert George Endicott, Inspector of Factories, said he had seen the flywheel.
and as it was not fenced, he considered it dangerous. A worker passed through the
engine-room while he was there.
Mr. Samuel Brain said the engine-room was not connected with the factory. As
soon as the Inspector said the flywheel should be fenced, it was done. A fine of I was
imposed, including costs.
Messrs. Walter Brain & Son, boot manufacturers, answered five summonses charging
them with employing young persons under 16 years (where machinery was used) who had
not been medically examined.
Mr. Owner stated that in regard to the five young workers the firm had no medical
certificates. This was essential where machinery was employed in order to ensure that
such employees had not defective eyesight.
Mr. Walter Brain deposed that some of the boys had been working only a few weeks.
A fine was inflicted of IOS. in respect of each of the five charges, including costs.
Mr. Chas. Neads, boot manufacturer, Oldland Common, was summoned for not keeping
his factory limewashed, &c., in accordance with the Factory Act. Mr. Owner said that
when inspected on April 13th it was found that the premises had not been limewashed
since August, 1919. The sanitary arrangements were also unsatisfactory.

Harry Higgs said it was through his neglect that the whitewashing had not been done.
He could not get men when Mr. Neads sent for him to do the work. It had since been
done. Fined 2, including costs. - Shoe and Leather Record, September 8th, 1922.

SCOTTISH CO-OPERATIVE BOOT TRADE.
The difficulties of co-operative trade during the past half-year were not confined to
England, as the half-yearly report of the Scottish Co-operative Wholesale Society for the
half-year just concluded shows a decrease of over 27 per cent. as compared with the corres-
ponding six months of 1921. so far as the total turnover is concerned. The sales for the
six months of this year were £8,468,578. Grocery suffered most; but the trade of the
boot and shoe departments showed a decrease of 18.3 per cent., falling from the £493,728
of the first part of 1921 to £403,303. Strangely enough, the society's own boot and shce
works revealed a greater decrease than the distributive departments, for the production
fell from 217,331 to 171,422, a decrease of just over 21 per cent., or £45.909. The
expenses of the boot and shoe factories were £63,108, of which £51,116 were for wages.
Power, light and heating took £2,431, and repairs were £2,814. The stocks were reduced
from 400,004 to £51,220, and there was a profit of £3,317 in the factory for the six months.
The manager of the whole of the boot trade of the society is Mr. J. J. Horn.

GERMAN TRADE UNIONISM.

German trade unionism has since the Armistice, says Mr. J. H. Thomas, stood not
only for sane Government but a constitutional policy. This in reply to the appeal from
German trade unionists to the urions of Britain. It is of interest, perhaps, to add to
Mr. Thomas's remark that during the same period the trade union movement in Germany
has made remarkable progress. Before the war the number of German workers whose
wages and working conditions were governed by collective agreement was 1,399,000,
according to figures given by the Reichs-Arbeitsblatt and reproduced by the Labour Gazette.
By the end of 1919 the number had grown to 5,986,000, and at the end of 1920 had further
increased to 9.561,000. There has also been a noteworthy expansion in the scope of
individual agreement. The following table summarises the positioni

Practically the whole of the agreements in force at the end of 1920 were without
recomse to strikes or lockouts. At the end of 1913 66.1 per cent. of the workers covered
by agreement belonged to four industries, ie., building, engineering, wood-working, and
clothing. In 1920 these four trades covered only 33.7 per cent., which illustrates the
growth of collective bargaining in other directions. The new groups" affected were
mining, transport, and other (largely salaried) employees. The growth of trade
unionism in the German mining industry is of importance in regard to the question recently
wised by France and demurred to by Great Britain of instituting Allied control of the
Nemce mines, Westminster Gazette, 31st August, 1922.

POLITICS.
The past month has once again seen the nation close upon the brink of
war; this in connection with matters in the Near East. The Government
of this country in our opinion has developed an extraordinary aptitude for
bringing into existence a condition of affairs whereby (instead of the policy
of trust and goodwill being engendered amongst the nations of the earth)
mistrust, suspicion and doubt becomes paramount, bringing in their train the
warlike spirit. The three bodies representative of Labour in this country, viz.,
The General Council of the Trade Union Congress, The Labour Party and the
Parliamentary Labour Party, at once took up the matter and by a series of
meetings and propaganda in the Press, made it quite plain that differences of
nations must be settled by methods other than war. It surely must by this
time have become quite plain to the people of this country that what is
imperatively needed is the "will to peace." It is of minor importance to
say we desire peace when the policy pursued is one likely to lead to war. The
world has had more than enough of the horrors of war. We are the more
convinced of this from first-hand evidence of the many Conferences that have

Dutch Labour and the International Labour Office.
The Permanent Court of International Justice, in nominating the Deputy-
Session of the International Labour Conference (Geneva, 1921), to decide
whether the Dutch Government, in nominating the industrial organisations for
requirement of the Peace Treaty that the appointments should be representative of the
the industrial organisations most representative of the workers’ delegate, had complied with the
opinion of the Court was that the Government had complied with.
This incident gives point to the following announcement
published in the Industrial and Labour Information of the International Federati
The negotiations between the Executive Committee of the Internationa
Catholic Trade Unions and the Netherlands General Trade Union Federation
the appointment of the workers' delegate to the Fourth Session of the Internation
of Trade Unions, the Federation of Christian Trade Unions, the Netherlands General
Minister of Labour is to be asked to appoint as workers’ delegate agn
Labour Conference (Geneva, 1922) have resulted in complete agreement. The
Netherlands Federation of Trade Unions (affiliated to the International Federation of
Trade Unions of Amsterdam) and to appoint technical advisers from the several
central trade union organisations.

International Labour Office. Governing Body Meeting.
The Governing Body of the International Labour Organisation of the League held a
short session before the General Conference which opened on the 17th inst. Sir Montague
Barlow, M.P. (Government Delegate), General Baylay (Employers), Mr. E. L. Poulston,
J.P. (Workers), and for Canada the Rt. Hon. James Murdock, Minister of Labour and
Mr. Tom Moore (Workers) represented the British Empire at this meeting.
The Governing Body took note of the announcement that Switzerland had ratified
the four Washington Conventions concerning unemployment, the night work of women,
the minimum age of admission of children to industry, and night work of children, and
that Finland had ratified the Genoa convention concerning the finding of employment
for seamen.
M. Fontaine, Chairman of the Governing Body, underlined the importance of the
official intimation that the Government of the United States, being desirous of co-operating
in a work which had for its chief object the protection of workers against disease, had
appointed Dr. Dorsett, of the Department of Agriculture, to co-operate with the Advisory
Committee on Anthrax set up by the International Labour Organisation.

A long discussion took place upon the demand that German and Spanish should be
added to the official languages, but it was decided by 13 votes to 6 to maintain the present
official languages which are English and French.

M. Michaelis (Italy) presented a proposal to place the question of "factory inspection
in different countries (practical results obtained, recommendations to be made)” on the
Agenda of the 1923 Conference. It was decided to place this proposal before the new
Governing Body that is to be elected during the forthcoming Conference.
The offer of land which was recently made by the Swiss Government to be used for
the erection of a building for the International Labour Office was cordially welcomed for
the Governing Body, and a sub-committee was set up to supervise the preparation of plans
and erection of premises.
The following members were appointed to represent the Governing Body on the
Joint Advisory Agricultural Committee: Count de Altea (Spain), for the Governmental
group, Herr Leipart (Germany) for the workers, and M. Jules Carlier (Belgium), President
of the Central Industrial Committee, for the employers.

The Fourth International Labour Conference.
Prominent figures in the world of industry, both employers and workers, together
with Government delegates, assembled in Geneva for the fourth general session of the
International Labour Conference of the League of Nations which opened on the 18th
inst. Over 50 States were represented. Hungary, which has just been admitted to the
League of Nations by decision of the Third Assembly, will attend the Conference for the
first time.
Each country is entitled to send four delegates: two delegates representing the
Government and one each for the employers and the workers. Each group is accompanied
by several technical advisers. The British delegates are Sir Montague Barlow, M.P.,
Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of Labour, Sir David Shackleton, Mr. James
President of the Shipbuilding Employers' Federation and Vice-president of the


---
National Confederation of Employers' Organisations. Mr. J. H. Thomas, Brigadier General Baylay,
President of the Trades Union Congress. Mr. Harry Gosling, Mr. John Turner, Sir Andrew Duncan,
Mr. Humbert Wollte and Mr. Bellhouse, will be among the Advisers present.

Case of Non-European Countries.
The first item deals with the revision of Part XIII. of the Treaty of Versailles with a
view to modifying the periodicity of the sessions of the Conference. At present the
Governing Body consists of twelve representatives of the Governments (eight of these
Governments being those of States of chief industrial importance), six members appointed
by the employers' delegates at the Conference, and six members appointed by the workers'
delegates at the Conference. A large number of States, particularly the extra European
States, desire to be directly represented on the Governing Body. The Asiatic and South
American States, for instance, hold only two seats, those of Japan and Argentina, though
India's claim to be considered one of the eight States of chief industrial importance, which
implies a seat on the Governing Body, has been endorsed by the recent decision of the
assembly of the League of Nations. A similar need for fuller representation is felt both
in workers' and employers' circles. This demand should be met by the proposal to increase
the number of members from twenty-four to thirty-two: (sixteen Government, eight
employers' and eight workers' representatives) with a definite provision that a certain
number of these seats shall go to the non-European States. It is interesting to note that
the amendment proposed to the Peace Treaty to bring about this change still retains the
United States as a member of the Governing Body, though, as at present, her place will
probably continue to be taken by a substitute country (Denmark), until such time as she
joins the Labour Organisation. Germany, though not belonging to the League, has been
a member of the Labour Organisation for over two years.

Periodicity of Future Conferences.
The Treaty lays down that the Conference shall take place " from time to time as occasions
The periodicity of the Conferences is likely to be a very keenly debated question.

Emigration Problems. The Ground Work.
The second item on the agenda is the communication to the International Labour
Office of statistics and other information regarding emigration and the repatriation and
transit of emigrants. The problem of emigration is essentially an international one.
Many aspects of it were considered last year by the International Emigration Commission,
composed of representatives of the chief emigrating and immigrating countries, members
of the Organisation, and presided over by Lord Ullswater, former speaker of the House
of Commons. Though at first it was thought possible to bring the decisions of this Com-
mission before the 1922 Conference, considerations have since appeared to render the
discussion of certain of these questions momentarily inopportune. Moreover, it seemed
unwise to attempt to settle the world problem of emigration during the present period
of economic and political uncertainty and without the co-operation of the United States.
The standardisation of emigration statistics and the collection of information regarding
emigration will enable the Conference at a later date to examine the wider aspects of this
problem with all the clements of success in its favour.
The meeting of this Conference will also be the occasion of a broad discussion of certain
of the main labour problems of the day.
A report will be submitted concerning the unemployment crisis, which is still acute
throughout the world. The International Labour Office, in accordance with the resolu-
tions adopted at the Third International Labour Conference (Geneva, 1921) and at the
International Economic Conference held at Genoa in April, 1922, has studied this question
and has investigated both the general causes of the phenomenon, and the preventive and
remedial measures adopted by different States. The position with regard to the ratifica-
tion of Conventions by the various national Parliaments, in particular, of the Hours
Convention, will also be brought to the notice of the Conference.
The efficiency of the procedure of the last Conference was in no small measure due to
the tactful and impartial chairmanship of that old parliamentary hand, Lord Burnham.
So great has been the appreciation of his qualities as Chairman at this international gathering, that, contrary to previous customs, he has been nominated again as President of
Conference this year.

INTERNATIONAL LABOUR.
Condition of Workers.
The whole of this morning's sitting (Monday) was taken up with speeches of
workers' delegates, with the exception of two speeches made by M. Stern and Madame
Kjelsberg, (Government delegates of Czecho-Slovakia and Norway respectively).
it may be said that the sitting was devoted exclusively to the Labour interview
The first speaker was Mr. YOSHIHARU TAZAWA (Japan), who spoke in Japanese
the speech being translated into English and French. He culogised the work of the Labour
Office, described the unsatisfactory condition of workers in Japan, and observed that
three years had elapsed since the Washington Conference decisions, which his Government
had not yet applied. He added that many women were employed in mines in Japan
and that the mortality was great.

MR. E. L. POULTON (Great Britain), in addition to the remarks already relegated
alluded to the refusal of Salvador to pay its contribution to the Labour organisation, and
in this connection said that the unpaid contributions in 1920 amounted to 7 per cent,
in 1921 to 19 per cent., and in 1922 to 45 per cent. Mr. Poulton deplored this, and added
that should the present state of affairs continue it would seriously endanger the work.ing
of the Labour Office. In reference to the ratification of the various conventions, Mr.
Poulton appealed to all those having influence with their Governments to get them to do
the needful Speaking of the United States, he hoped to see American delegates present
at the next Conference. In conclusion, Mr. Poulton referred to the favourable report
received from Persia regarding the improved conditions of workers in that country, which
he described as the brightest picture in the directors' report. He had suggested it being
issued in the form of a special paper.

MR. E. L. POULTON, in the course of his interesting speech, also referred to the dis-
proportion in the present representation at the Conference. For example, out of a total
of 100 delegates there were fifty-six Government delegates, twenty-two employers' dele-
gates, and the same number of workers' delegates. Thus, the last-named were seriously
handicapped when it came to a vote, as there were always seventy-eight representatives
of the owner side against only twenty-two workers' delegates. The workers' delegates
regarded this in a most serious light. Continuing, Mr. Poulton said: "We have not had
the opportunity of that higher education and wider knowledge that the Government
and employers' representatives possess. In my own case, I had to earn my own living
hefore I was ten years old, and have had to keep my nose to the grindstone ever since.'
Mr. Poulton then submitted that the spirit of the resolutions of the Washington Convention
were hardly being carried out, and appealed to Governments to see that another year the
workers were adequately represented. - Daily Telegraph, 24th October, 1922.

CORRESPONDENCE.

The Council do not hold themselves responsible for the views expressed by Correspondents.

ORGANISATION AND EMANCIPATION.
THE GENERAL SECRETARY, NATIONAL UNION OF BOOT AND SHOE OPERATIVES.
Everywhere the fact is recognised, and should be deplored, that the membership
of the British Trade Union movement is falling off to an alarming degree. This is held
in some quarters to herald a return to pre-war strength. If this is true, then the worker
and it is nothing less than a duty to those who fell "to make the world safe for democracy"
and their dependants, as well as for those who follow us, to do all we can to stop the rot
haronk pre war conditions to look forward to, which, to my mind, were terribly inhuman
and put new life into our trade union.

New Ideas.
To do this, it behoves us to concentrate our energies into certain channels. The
channels should be chosen judiciously, so that not only will we get back our old members
but also gain new ones. This being the case, we should look to those methods of pro
Paganda used in the past, compare them with those of other parties and find out and
develop for ourselves, those which are most applicable and have proved themselves most
successful.

Missions.
It is a well-known fact that the I.L.P. holds Mission weeks in which meetings and
demonstrations are held, tending to revive interest and increase the membership.
For us to do likewise, it would be necessary for each branch to form Speakers' and
Educational classes as a preparation. The nucleus for these classes could be obtained by
organising all the Shop stewards and other members interested of each locality into a
Committee. The W.E.A. and the Herald League would be pleased to arrange for lecturers
and teachers and after a few months we would have in every factory at least one mar
who had all the union's aims at his fingers' tips, with the ability to put them forward in an
interesting and convincing manner.
Then it would be possible for Mission weeks, organised meetings and the like to be
held very successfully.

Local Journals.
Some branches which cover a large area and have a considerable financial member
ship, would find it a profitable undertaking to run a branch paper. This could be supplied
to every member, who would then be in touch with all the social, economic and political
movements and activities in which his branch and union are interested. The initial
cost, providing the editorial work and articles were done voluntarily, would be surprisingly
small. The return would be enormous and after the first issue, the cost would be amply
covered (if provision was made) by advertisements.

It would be necessary first, however, to obtain the sanction of the National Council,
as there is no provision in the rules for this type of innovation.

Social Clubs.
Far too long have our members been without their own Social clubs. These could
include Literary, Dramatic, Musical (choral and instrumental), Social and Sports sections.

No difficulty would be experienced in obtaining good support if these were started
for large numbers of our members belong to working-men's clubs, cycle clubs, and sports
clubs, and would be delighted at the prospect of taking part with their shop mates and
fellow unionists in diversions which would get them to know and understand each other
better and bring about a finer fraternal feeling.

Guilds.
Finally, as the present economic system leaves very much to be desired, and as at the
best of times it can only, for us, provide the bare necessities of life, we should make efforts
to use our Trade Union organisation to improve upon it.

It is perfectly true that if every member of a Trade Union or similar society was also
a co-operator, a large number of our economic difficulties would cease to exist. But as we
can see no immediate prospect of this taking place, only good would come of our following
the lead of the Building, Clothing and Furnishing workers and start in business for our
selves. This could be done at the commencement as repairers and bespoke makers, as no
great capital would be required; and as it prospered it would be possible to make, in
competition with profit-making concerns, for sale through the ordinary trade channels.

an aggregate loss of £4,533 for the combined leather works of the society. Shoe and

LEST WE FORGET.

It is now a little over twenty-seven years since the formation of the Boot and Shoe
Workers' Union in April, 1895.
During this long period there have been quite a number of attempts made to start
rump factional movements in the vain hope to find some short cut to the industrial
millennium.

To attribute such movements to the hope of industrial paradise is charitable in the
extreme, for nearly every one of such movements was really instigated by itch for office
by individuals whose unfitness for such was proved by their willingness to lead a faction
in dividing the ranks of labour.

Be that as it may, it is a fact that every one of these factions has proved a failure
in that not one of them has been stable or dependable either in membership, finances or
leadership.

Such of them as are now in existence have empty treasuries and some of them are
obliged to economise by laying off their organisers at a time when they should be working
overtime.

Should any of these factions now be obliged to fight they must do so without funds
which means with empty stomachs and to almost certain defeat.

After years of bombast and pretentious claims they are now reduced to a condition
of impotence and are talking some of uniting, forgetting that adding zeros together still
leaves nothing as the result.

Lest We Forget! During all these years what union has always upheld the banner
of unionism in our craft? Which has never failed in membership or money or leadership
to meet every single obligation?

Our Boot and Shoe Workers' Union is the only one that has met the test. We stand
to-day solvent in principle and solvent financially, the one and only solid bulwark against
attacks that might be directed against the wages and working conditions of shoe workers.

Let us say to the membership that while your officers are proud of the condition of
this union in this time of crisis in union affairs, we realise that you have made that position
possible.
Your support, your loyalty, your contribution to the common strength, your adherence
to our laws and policies have helped us to make this union supreme in its field.

Lest We Forget. May the same principles guide us all in the future, so that our
experience in working together in the years that are gone may render our efforts doubly
for union progress and success in the years to come.--American Shoe Worker
September, 1922.

HOUSES BEYOND REPAIR.
Thirteen Families in Seven Dwellings "Unfit for Habitation."
Fulham Indictment.
Surprising disclosures are made by Dr. A. M. Hewat, Fulham's new medical officer
in his housing report, just issued.
Each house in a group of seven in one Fulham street, he declares, "is in a state so
dangerous or injurious to health as to be unfit for human habitation, being damp, draughty
and verminous, and having a leaky roof, and, in most cases, bulging walls, in addition to a
large number of other serious defects."
The Public Health Committee of the borough council have considered the question
of entering the property to do the repairs, and have passed a resolution stating that "The
cost will be so high that the Council would no ver be able to recover anything like the amount
expended."

Closing Order Urged.
The committee's report states: "The property is really beyond repair, and it is
absolutely impossible to get any repairs done. There are at present thirteen families
housed in the premises."
On the representation of the medical officer the committee recommend that the
council make a closing order "prohibiting the use of each of the dwelling-houses for
human habitation until, in the judgment of the council, each dwelling house is rendered
fit for that purpose."; further, "That a notice thereof be given to the owners and occupiers
as required by the Statute."

The committee's report adds: "We are hopeful of making arrangements for the
transfer of a number of these families into new flats now nearing completion, so as to cause
the least trouble and discomfort to the tenants." - London Evening News, October 17th,
1922.

22,000 PEOPLE IN CONDEMNED HOUSES.
Bradford to Build Without Waiting for Subsidy.
Appalling housing conditions were revealed at a meeting of the Bradford Corporation.
It was decided to build houses without troubling about the Ministry of Health subsidy.
Cases quoted were :--
Three girls sleeping in the same room as a mentally defective youth of 20.
Two married couples sharing one room.
Eight people-father, mother, married daughter, and her husband and four children,
aged 14 to 21-all living in one room.
Father (a consumptive), mother, and four children living in a cellar dwelling so damp
that the paper was hanging from the wall.
It was stated that about 22,000 people were living in houses that had been condemned,
and that 10,000 houses were needed. -The Star, October 13th, 1922.

GENERAL ELECTION.
The General Election is now a thing of the past, and whilst the
Party may be congratulated upon the increased number of Labour Members
returned to the House of Commons, it is nevertheless very disappointing that
the country, as a whole, should have sent so many members pledged to support
the Rt. Hon. Bonar Law, M.P., and his policy of "'e-dunno-where'fore."
We, however, accept the verdict of the country because the people had it in
their power, as we have stated so many times, to determine who shall repre-
sent them in the British House of Commons. Thus, whilst we regret the
decision and accept the same, we must still continue with the clarion call to
plod along and educate the people to the real position of the affairs. So far
as the four Union Candidates are concerned, we heartily congratulate Alderman
Alfred Hill, M.P., J.P., in his successful fight at Leicester West upon having
turned the great majority of 14,223 for the ex-Member into a minority of
4,792: the figures are:-

and are confident they will act with credit in carrying out the duties of a
Labour Parliament.

BRANCH REPORTS.

ARBROATH. - Trade in our district remains chaotic. For a long time now our members have hoped and hoped for trade revival working for a new social order would be better-but only disappointment followed. One is often forced to wonder how workers, as badly hit as our members have been, can live at all, and unfortunately the truth is that most are existing to-day by laying up a heavy burden against the future. The worst feature of the depression here is the fact that short-time workers have been subject to so many disqualifying conditions regarding Labour Exchange benefit that for the last twelve months very few of our members have managed to get the additional assistance of the "dole" to their scanty wage. Luckily this is altered again in the new "Fourth Special Period" of benefit which began on November 2nd, and the Branch is contriving to get all short time regulated in such ways as will yield the maximum amount of Labour Exchange benefit in addition. This is so important that secretaries who have members on short time should take notice, and if they fail to understand what is meant by the foregoing, explanations can be sent. We have been reading about the wages in the Shoe Trade being stabilised over certain periods, and it is the wish of this Branch that our Executive may manage such an advantageous settlement. Speaking of wages brings up a grievance that is keenly felt by clickers, finishers, and machine-room workers. Each of those departments have been run on piece-work for the past two years, and during such slack times the results have been revealing. Those workers have, by this form of pressure, only got employment for time varying between 9 hours and 18 hours per week; perhaps a fair average would be 14. And there seems no likelihood at all of such departments ever being needed for more than half time. We are following the Council's advice re supporting Labour at the polls, and active as well as financial help is being given to the Labour Champion in the Montrose Burghs. We have also agreed to promote, if possible, the circulation of the Daily Herald. Our help in those directions will be a prelude to our own fight for better trade conditions when circumstances make it possible for us to move.

BELFAST. - Trade still remains very quiet. The slight improvement reported has been maintained, but trade is still far from normal. Many of our members are still on the idle list. We regret to record the death of Shopmate, Thos. Magee, of the Derry Section. To his sorrowing widow and family we tender our sincere sympathy.

BRISTOL No. 1.-Trade has fallen off considerably on light goods here, but considering the season it might be much worse than it is. We are sorry to report the sudden death of one of our old and much respected members, Mr. Hy. Drew, who, in the old days when it was not fashionable to be a Trades Unionist, did real hard work for the Union. One by one the old stalwarts drop out, and it is up to our young members to fill the gaps in the same spirit as the old brigade did. Another old member, Mr. G. Belsten, has passed away, and although he has not worked at making boots for many years (being engaged in selling them), he took great interest in the Union up to the close of his life. One other member has passed away during the month. To the relatives of our deceased brothers we extend our deepest sympathy.

CHESHAM. - Trade here is about the same as last month. A few more of our members who came out on strike have been reinstated. We are watching with great interest the fight on behalf of Labour that our four Boot Operative lines are making, and trust before this report is published they will become M.P.'s.

INTERNATIONAL LABOUR CONFERENCE,
MR. POULTON (Great Britain): Mr. Chairman, I am not quite certain as to what
is meant by Sub Section (3), and, for the sake of clarity and to prevent any misunder-
standing, I should like to ask the reporter, through you, what really is intended by the
words "The Group Secretary shall report to the Office forthwith the results of all official
meetings." We workers have had a great many meetings during this present Session to
deal with matters arising out of, or in connection with, the agenda and its business, but
those matters are, I submit, not necessarily such as arise solely out of or in connection
with the business of this Conference. They must, on the contrary, necessarily develop
from time to time into business which might be said to be personal to the Group itself.
Ant I therefore to understand by this paragraph that, because we have a meeting
we have therefore to report to someone in connection with the Secretariat of the Office
as to the result we have come to ? I submit that we cannot do anything of the Office,
nor can the Employers' Group, nor can the Government Group. We should not, I venture
to say, report to someone else, what we have been doing in these meetings of ours which
have been officially called. I should like to know what really is intended, because we do
not want afterwards to be accused of failing to carry out the regulations. It is much
better that we should have it out here first of all rather than afterwards have it said "Here
is a Group. They have had an official meeting. We have had no information as to what
has been done." The Group say "This was not an official meeting. It is termed an
official meeting; but we refuse to recognise it as such."
THE PRESIDENT: The drafting of this particular Article is rather in the nature of a
joke, and at present it must not be taken too seriously. For example, the "Office" of
which a report must be made of the different acts under Sub-Section (1) a, b, c, d and e
is the Office of the Conference and not the Labour Office. Therefore, of course, that
must be defined, because otherwise the word "Office," used as it is in Sub-Section (3)
would be interpreted to mean the Labour Office. I pointed out that "The Chairman"
is meant to be the President of the Conference. Over and above that, however, I think
there is substance in the point which Mr. Poulton has raised, and for that reason there
must be a further definition of what is to be reported. It is clear that the Conference
does not wish to interfere in the private and internal matters of Groups, even if they
are holding official meetings. So, in order to carry out the clear view of the Conference,
I think the Drafting Committee must insert further words. By its acquiescence, I consider
that the Conference is of opinion that the Drafting Committee should go rather beyond
its usual function in this matter, and define more clearly the meaning of Sub-Section (3).

very near future, some practical results from this preliminary work which it is proposed
to undertake on behalf of the men, women and children who travel in various parts of the
world. I was also delighted to hear our two lady delegates speak in the way they did on
behalf of the women and children, and I venture to say that they have made a valuable
contribution to the proceedings of the Conference, and that they have proven the practical
value of having women here to speak upon these important matters. I think the appeal
which is made to us by the lady delegates can largely be met by the passage on page V.
of the Report of the Commission, where it states: "The Commission noted that a repre-
sentative of the International Labour Office had been invited to attend the first session
of the Advisory Committee on the Traffic in Women and Children," and it finishes up by
saying "the Commission is of opinion that a continuation of this collaboration is desirable.'
Personally, I should use a stronger word than the word "desirable." I should say that a
continuation of this collaboration is essential, because we want this inter-working of the
two departments, and not separate machinery set up by one organisation overlapping the
work of the machinery set up by the other organisation. They may both be doing prac-
tically the same kind of work, and yet, if we are not very careful, they may be doing it
upon different lines. Therefore I trust that this work will be continued by the one col-
laborating with the other, so that there will be a saving both of time and money, and so
that we can achieve those results which are most desirable.
In supporting the whole of the Report-because I take it that the whole of the
Report is before us at once-I should like to say a word upon Recommendations (1)
and (2), more particularly No. 1.
THE PRESIDENT: It would be more convenient, if particulars are to be entered

out of order.
MR. POULTON (Great Britain): The only point is that I did not want to get up again.

necessity of getting up again. A resolution mentioned in the Report as being put forward

DEATH OF MR. T. A. WATTS.
The death occurred suddenly on Saturday night of Mr. Thomas Amos Watts.
of Far Cross Bank, Kendal. Mr. Watts had been out in the evening and returned
to his home, where he lived alone, shortly before ten p.m. On Sunday morning
the milkman, getting no response to his knocks, informed Mr. Watts' niece, who
lives across the street. The house was entered and Mr. Watts was found to be in
bed, dead. A doctor found that life had been extinct for nearly twelve hours,
bed Watts apparently expiring directly after he had retired for the night. He had
suffered with his heart for many years, and had gradually become worse. He was
57 years of age. Born at Weedon, Northants, he came to Kendal at an early age
as a rivetter at Netherfield. Later he went to Maybole, but after a period of twelve
months returned to Kendal, where he became secretary to the Boot and Shoe
Operatives' Union. He had been president of the Kendal Trades Council for up-
wards of twenty years, and had also been instrumental in forming many trade
unions in the town. He had been a member of the Kendal Town Council for a long
period. He was a Justice of the Peace for both the county and the borough, was a
member of the Kendal Watch, Electricity, and Education Committees, and the
chairman of the School Attendance Committee. He was also a manager of the
Kendal Council School. His wife died eight years ago and he leaves a grown-up
daughter and adopted son. At the Kendal Police Court, on Monday, appreciation
of Mr. Watts' service and regret at his untimely end were voiced on behalf of the
magistrates and police by the Mayor, Mr. E. W. Wakefield, and Inspector O'Neil.
At the Mayoral installation on Thursday reference was also made to the loss which
the Council had sustained and a vote of condolence was passed. The flag at the
Town Hall was lowered to half-mast. The funeral took place on Thursday and was
agely arrended, the Mayor and Corporation and representatives of other
dfs being present, and members of the Kendal Borough Police Force acted as
The general mourners included over 200 employees of Netherfield.

is entitled to grants from the State and provident funds. A French worker in a
ditions as to age and continuity of employment required by legislation on the
mine is entitled to the State premiums respecting old age pensions, without regard
or has spent 30 years as a wage-earner in France, 15 of which have been spent in the
is to be on terms of equality with the French worker French worker in the Independent
by the French Government, and by the Independent Fund for miners' pensions.
Conventions between States providing for reciprocity of treatment of foreign
are already in operation in Argentine, Czecho-Slovakia, Italy, Luxemburg, the Nether-
lands and Poland, among other countries.

Russian Railway Situation. Critical Autumn Prospects.
"The critical situation of the Russian Railways is at present causing great anxiety
to the central authorities at Moscow," states an article quoted in the "Russian Supple-
ment" of "Industrial and Labour Information," the weekly publication of the Inter-
national Labour Office of the League of Nations at Geneva.
The article which appears in Economicheskaia Zhizn (Economic Life), an official
Soviet organ, continues "After a somewhat quiet summer, during which the volume of
traffic diminished considerably, the railways are faced with the problem of coping with
the requirements of the autumn traffic, which, like that of the spring, places a great strain
on the rolling stock available. Extra transit facilities are required for the transportation
of the large quantities of grain collected in the outlying districts as payment of the food
tax, as well as for transportation of seed grain to districts where the harvest has been an
entire or partial failure. The prospects for the accomplishment of these two essential
tasks are, however, not at all promising, owing to the great dearth of fuel and the large
number of unserviceable trucks.

"The best equipped lines have fuel reserves for five days, while the majority have
only sufficient for from one to four days. The number of serviceable trucks is inadequate
and decreases daily, while those still in use are liable to break down at any moment as no
repairs have been made in them for eight years. As regards locomotives, the position is
better, thanks mainly to the new engines imported from abroad. But it is significant
that the number of unserviceable locomotives remains practically stationary and reaches
the very high figure of 60 per cent."

Labour Conditions in the East. Japanese Action.
The Japanese Government has just informed the International Labour Office of a
series of measures which it has undertaken to amend its social legislation in accordance
with many of the decisions of the International Labour Conference of the League of Nations.

Japan has ratified the draft convention on unemployment and the draft convention
for establishing facilities for finding employment for seamen. The Government is intro-
ducing Bills to make amendments in existing legislation to bring it in conformity with the
Convention fixing the minimum age for admission of children to industrial employment
and the convention fixing the minimum age for the admission of children to employment
at sea. As soon as these Bills have been adopted by Parliament the Privy Council will
give its consent to these two conventions, and the Japanese Government will take the
necessary steps for their ratification.

As regards the convention concerning the employment of women before and after
childbirth, the Japanese Government states that certain provisions concerning the pro-
tection of women before and after childbirth have already been inserted in the Health
Insurance Act of 1926 which will come into force in the near future. As, however, social
Insurance legislation in Japan may be said only to have commenced with the passage of
the Health Insurance Act, the Japanese Government find it difficult to conform to the
greater terms of this convention but promise, at every opportunity, to develop and improve
legislation in this respect.

As regards to the draft conventions concerning the employment of women during
and governing the night work of young persons employed in industry, the
Government is presenting a Bill to Parliament amending its present factory laws
ut the prohibition so far as it concerns factories in Japan. It is
ed in the next session of Parliament.

DISPUTES.
There is no change in the position at CHESHAM, Messrs. G. Long & Sons
Ltd. still refusing to pay to the National Conditions.
THE STATE OF TRADE
for the past month continues about the same. The figures in the Gazette issued
by the Ministry of Labour are as follow:-
During November employment in this trade continued slack and short time was
prevalent at all the principal centres. A few districts showed a slight improvement, but
in the majority of districts there was little change, or employment showed a slight decline,
as compared with October. The improvement reported last month in Scotland was not
maintained, employment being slack in all the principal centres except Kilmarnock, where
it was fair.
The percentage of workpeople unemployed in the boot, shoe and slipper making and
repairing trades, as indicated by the unemployment books lodged at Employment
Exchanges, was 7.0 on the 20th November, as compared with 6.6 on the 23rd October.
Returns received from firms employing 37,537 workpeople showed about 46 per cent.
on short time at the end of the month, to the extent of about 12 hours a week on the
average.
The exports of boots and shoes in November, 1922, amounted to 80,000 dozen pairs,
or 2,744 dozen pairs less than in October, 1922, and 34,485 dozen pairs more than in
November, 1921.

Government Green Book Statement Handsewn List, for the purpose of adjusting any
specific anomalous item or items, whether unfavourable to employers or operatives, brought
before the Boards in accordance with the customary procedure; provided always that any
adjustments of existing Statements or any new Piecework Statements shall ensure the
average worker earning not less than 25 per cent. over the minimum wage in operation
for the time being.

ments, have regard to the grade when estimating the productive capacity of the average
worker.

to be adopted in giving effect to classes to and II either side of the Board may require
the Standing Committee of the Conference to advise upon such procedure, provided
always that the piecework rates to be finally fixed shall be determined in accordance
with the rules of such Board.

Freedom of Contract with Operatives under 16.
13. The employers shall retain freedom of contract with all operatives under 16
years of age.

GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
NATIONAL CONFERENCE (DECEMBER, 1922) AGREEMENT. The most
matter dealt with during the month was the question of the National Agreement. The
most of you are aware the matter should have been dealt with in October, but owing to
the General Election we did not meet until the 23rd November. It would be as well to
depart from the usual course-which is not our custom-and pay tribute to the oft
repeated statement, that with the determination on both the Employers side and the
Union's side to keep the peace is having its reward by better relations existing betwee
the two bodies. So far as this Conference is concerned it passed without a hitch or any
unnecessary heat. Of course we naturally put in for a shorter working week in order to
if possible, relieve the unemployment market, if only very slightly, but the employers
could not see their way to grant us any concession, so the hours will remain at 48. Many
other changes, such as lowering the age from 17-as the employers proposed to 14 did
not meet with their approval, but they agreed to reinstate the clause that young persons
shall come under our jurisdiction at the age of 16. The employers think that juveniles
at 14 and 15 years of age should be left for them to have freedom of contract, because
it is hard to tell what is the tendency of a boy or a girl in regard to what part of a factory
they prefer to be employed in. Girls have the choice of two Departments, whilst the
boys have the choice of five. An attempt was made by us to get the minimum wage at
21 years of age, but we did not meet with success, owing to the fact that the foreign trade
is so very small at present, and nothing which will interfere with it would be good for the
industry. We obtained a concession in the fact that when the cost of living falls below
70 points, the men in the Heel Building, Stock or Shoe Rooms Departments, will have the
same minimum rate as those in the Clicking, Lasting, Finishing, and Rough Stuff Depart-
ments, and in future there will only be one minimum for male operatives in the trade.
This we have sought to obtain for many many years. We intimated there was a feeling
amongst the girls that the Women's Minimum rates should be the same as for men. This
point was made clear and definite, and we had given the employers warning that our
women think when they do the same amount of work they should be paid the same wage.
We persuaded the employers to accept a new clause under that dealing with Women's
Exempted Operations. This will be found in the agreement and states that no adult
is permitted at these operations at less than the minimum rates unless they have a permit
to do so.

The Holiday Scheme is made part and parcel of the Agreement although with great
reluctance by some employers in various parts of the country. We have strengthened
the clause for Pieceworkers which allows 25 per cent. over the Minimum Rates by adding
the words "to ensure the average workers earning not less than 25 per cent. over the
Minimum Wage." By strengthening this clause we made it clear to the employers gener-
ally that so far as pieceworkers are concerned that point must be rigidly adhered to.
These remarks not only apply to the employers but also to our officials and members,
as this matter has been very loosely dealt with by those officials who do happen to be
members of the Executive Council. Much was made by the employers of "anomalies"
in the statements. We contend, and can prove, that where anomalies do exist and give
operatives a large amount of money, that these items should be readjusted so as to give
the more badly paid operative a better price. Other matters touching the agreement
are dealt with elsewhere, and I think this has been the most successful conference we have
ever entered into on behalf of our members.

There are three outstanding features. We are asking the Government to give power
by legal enactment to our agreements, in order to force them upon non-federated firms
and non-unionists. The second item is that at the end of the agreement will be found a
clause adopted by the Joint Industrial Council requesting Manufacturers and Operatives
to be well organised, and we hope that very shortly that all operatives in the trade will
belong to the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives. The third item is the question
of back pay from those firms who have not been paying to the Holiday Provision Scheme,
and it is my intention to ask for some penalty to be imposed upon employers who fail to
carry out the National Agreement.
In this connection I am still pressing employers at Wellingborough where back money
is owing by 23 firms and in Rushden area by 7 firms.

Lane, Leicester, where a young man was given notice, and ultimately discharged, for
claiming the Minimum rate of wages for the hours he was in the factory. My colleagues
in Leicester had interviewed the Management and secured 6 weeks' back pay, with the
result that this member found himself without employment. I volunteered to take the

BRANCH REPORTS.

ARBROATH.-Trade in the district of our branch remains very bad.
Instead of improving our factories are forced to go on even shorter time than
heretofore, and members are nearly losing heart. We try to think it a case
of night looking darkest just before the dawn, and hope the industrial darkness
will yield to life-giving rays of “money-moons." The Executive of the
Union have been busy preparing matter for the Conference Agenda, and are
submitting several proposals which we think will be for the welfare of the
Union. We are opposed to permanent officials being at conferences without
arrangements, with the addition of fixing all future conferences of the Union
standing election, and are also proposing to revert to the old biennial conference
to meet in Leicester. Apart from saving a great deal of expense on travelling
we think it more natural to meet in Leicester than in London, while there is no
point in the belief that delegates will devote themselves entirely to business.
Not that we deny beauty or attractiveness to Leicester-on the contrary we
admire the "stately factories” and other "architectural wonders," as well as
when nothing in the nature of scenery or beauty spots form a counter-attraction
situation and sylvan charm-but we expect the "call" of these to weaken
as delegates find themselves back for the "umpteenth time. We are trying
also to get Rule 68 amended to include the payment of expenses of such meetings
by the Union. It is a real pity to have such fine machinery, and not get any
benefit from it simply because branches cannot afford to pay to use it. Short-
time workers are being put on the same footing as those who are fully unem-
ployed. Three of our girls, although not wholly idle, were asked to take work
in a neighbouring city where machinists were wanted at 36s. per full week.
They refused on the grounds of domestic hardship and unsuitability of employ-
ment. Their benefit is being suspended meantime, but the Branch is to carry
the fight to the Court of Referees so that members may not be penalised wrongly.
Along with those cases is the case of a shopmate who was driven to give up his
employment, first by being overloaded with work and responsibilities, and
secondly by being interfered with by an unauthorised person. His benefit is
refused for six weeks, but we mean to fight the appeal, and the Court of Referees
may agree with us. Members are glad and grateful to have the strong help
of the Union in their work-day troubles.

BARNSLEY.-We hope that trade will be better next year, and that we
shall be free from disputes and sickness. Wishing all our members the Com-
pliments of the Season.

BELFAST.-Trade is very bad both in the manufacturing and repairing.
We were hopeful when we were able to report during the two previous months
that a slight improvement had set in, that trade was going to revive, but again
we have been disappointed, as we have so often been during the past two
years. We are almost at the end of the year 1922. A most gloomy and
depressed one it has been to the workers, many have not had one hour's work
during the whole year. We can only hope that the year in which we are about
to enter may be a bright and prosperous one for each officer and member of
the Union. We hope that our members will resolve to take a more active
interest in the workings of the branch. The branch meetings are held on the
first Monday in each month at 7.30 p.m., in the Typographical Hall, Frederick
Street.

BRISTOL No. 2.-Trade has slowed down considerably during the month
but we hope for a quicker revival than we had a year ago. Now the new
Government is in power, we hope that the “tranquility" we are promised
will percolate from the Cabinet down to the workers. We want them to

MAYBOLE. - We are sorry to report that trade has somewhat slackened time.
Nine clickers of T. Lees & Co. have been dismissed, and all the rest of the team are slack with the exception of J. M'Creath & Sons, who are still running full time. We are also sorry that sickness is on the increase. According to Provisional reports the Sub-Committee of the Union on the National Agreement quite ton have done very well in view of the reductions in other trades. As this is the last report of the year 1922 we wish all the officials and members the Compliments of the Season, and hope that next year may be brighter for all workers.

NEWCASTLE. - Trade here is very bad. In fact it has never been known to be so bad in the history of our oldest member. Still we are hoping for the best. Probably after the General Election and a change in the Government, things will take a turn for the better. After all it seems to be the general report of trade all over the country. We are pleased to see two of our Members have been returned as Labour Members at the General Election, Mr. J. Buckle and Alderman A. Hill, but were rather disappointed when it became known that Mr. W. R. Smith had been defeated at Wellingborough. We thank the Council for sending Mr. A. J. Dobbs, our Council representative, to Newcastle, on behalf of our members working at Messrs. Pearsons' Slipper Factory, where there had been a reduction in wages. Although his visit did not secure all we had hoped for, still we feel that he did his best, and in the near future his visit will have brought about the result we aimed at. We attempted to do some organising at another local slipper factory, but the result was very disheartening. We are very sorry to hear of the death of one of our oldest branch secretaries, Mr. T. Watts, of Kendal. A letter of condolence was sent to the Kendal Branch on the great loss they have sustained.

NORTHAMPTON No. 1. - Trade remains slack here with very little prospect of improvement apparently. We think we are inclined to rely too much on foreign trade instead of seriously tackling the Agricultural industry, a revival of which would stimulate all other industries. Sickness is fairly light just now with members. We wish officers and members a better New Year than has been their lot during 1922, and hope for a great year of Labour legislation to cope with the difficulties of the working classes.

It is with deep regret we have to report the death of one of our prominent members, Mr. William Johnson, age 54 years, after a short illness. He was of a quiet disposition, but was always in the forefront of working class organisations, being elected to the Northampton Town Council about 12 years ago as an avowed Socialist. He was also President of the Northampton Trades Council for several years, both of which positions he held with marked ability. We can ill afford to lose men of his level-headed character during the trying His interment was attended by the Branch times immediately in front of us. Officials and a number of old trade unionists and friends. Greatest sympathy is felt for his relatives in their bereavement.

NORWICH. - Trade in Norwich has become much worse during the month, discharges taking place on a large scale in many factories. The turn- shoe has eased up considerably with the prospect of remaining quiet till the New Year. We in Norwich offer our hearty congratulations to Alf. Hill and Johnny Buckle on their splendid victories in the election. We must also express our regret at the loss of the seat defended by our comrade, Walter Smith; verily the boot operatives of Norwich and Wellingborough have some- thing to answer for.

PLYMOUTH. - Compliments of the Season to all members. Trade has had this month and has occasioned still further discharges of our members.

WHY YOUR FOOD IS DEAR.
At the South Lincolnshire Fat Stock Show Dinners, held during the
past week, a point emphasised by Speakers was the tremendous differ-
ence in prices obtained by the producer and paid by the consumer.
It was pointed out that although wheat is now at its pre-war price,
the loaf is still Ninepence. Those who drink it are still having to pay a
high price for their beer, yet the farmer cannot sell his barley. Beef is sold
in the market at a certain price, and a few days later sold over the
counter at 100 per cent. more. -Reynold's Newspaper, 17th December, 1922.

SPECIAL NOTICE TO MEMBERS.
Every precaution is taken by us to ensure accuracy in these Reports, our correspondents being men on whom we can rely; should, however, any errors creep into them, upon the same being pointed out to us, we shall be most happy to give the same prominence to the correction as to the original matter. As these Reports are exclusively for the use of Members, the information contained therein must not be divulged.

MONTHLY REPORT.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
26TH FEBRUARY, 1923.
TRADE
for the past month has somewhat improved, the figures recorded by the Ministry of Labour Gazette being as follow:-

BOOT AND SHOE TRADE.
During January employment in this trade continued slack. In some districts it was slightly better on the whole than in December, but in others it was worse. Short time was still very prevalent at nearly all the principal centres.

There was a marked improvement at Stafford, and some improvement at Leicester and Northampton, as well as at one or two other towns. On the other hand, there was a decline in a number of districts, including the Leicestershire country district, Welling- borough, the Bristol and Kingswood district, the Leeds district, and Scotland.

The percentage of workpeople unemployed in the boot, shoe and slipper making and repairing trades, as indicated by the unemployment books lodged at Employment Exchanges, was 8.8 on the 22nd January, 1923, as compared with 8.3 on the 18th December.

Returns received from firms employing 31,500 workpeople showed about 34 per cent. on short time at the end of the month, to the extent of about 10½ hours a week on the average. At the end of the previous month, about 38 per cent. of the workpeople covered by the returns then received were on short time, to the extent of about 13 hours a week, on the average.

The exports of boots and shoes in January, 1923, amounted to 73,211 dozen pairs, or 6,609 dozen pairs more than in December, 1922, and 29,182 dozen pairs more than in January, 1922.
Nearest Telegraph Office:
Red Lion Street, London, W.C. 1.

day by day it will be seen how strenuously the Labour Members are
to compel, if at all possible, the Government to take a wider view of its obliga-
tions to the Nation. The European situation is also receiving close attention
both on the industrial and political sides by the respective National Committees
and the Parliamentary Labour Party. The following is a copy of a resolution
that we have passed recently, the resolution being the result of investigations
by the General Council of the Trade Congress and the Labour Party
Executive:
This meeting of the Council of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives,
appeals to the people to realise the gravity of the present international situation, and the
failure of the Governments to make and maintain peace among the nations.
"In the East we are threatened by a new war. In the West, the French troops have
invaded Germany's richest and most densely populated region, and imposed a new hunger
blockade upon the already underfed and overworked German people. Others also suffer,
because the invasion of the Ruhr strikes at the economic reconstruction of Europe, delays
the rebuilding of the devastated areas, and threatens our own people with greater unem-
ployment and misery. Meanwhile, the British Government, an idle spectator of the
impending ruin, is regarded by the French and Belgian people as an accomplice of their
Governments.
"This meeting of the Council of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives,
sends fraternal greetings to the working classes of Belgium, France, and Germany, and
joins with them in the strongest possible denunciation of this policy of violence, which
brings neither reparations nor security, and is making of the Rhineland and the Ruhr
the Alsace-Lorraine of the future. We send an expression of sympathy in their suffering
to the workers in the Ruhr Valley.
"This meeting calls upon the British Government :
"(1) To adopt a policy of active diplomatic intervention, if possible, with the
co-operation of the United States Government.
"(2) To remove all misunderstanding by making a public declaration that in their
view the action of the French Government is a breach of the Treaty of Versailles and
is one from which they formally and unmistakably dissociate themselves.
"(3) To support any proposal that the Ruhr situation, the payment by Germany
within the limits of possibility of the equitable reparations indispensable to restore
devastated France and Belgium, as well as the whole problem of the inter-Allied
debts, should be dealt with by the League of Nations under Article II of the Covenant;
and at the same time to propose that Germany be admitted into full membership
of the League with a seat on the Council.
"(4) To propose as part of a settlement the withdrawal of all the Armies of
Occupation, and to make it clear that in any event no general settlement which
includes French or Belgian occupation of the Ruhr can be accepted by the British
Government."
Article II of the Covenant to which reference has been made, states :-
THREATS OF WAR.
Any war or threat of war, whether immediately affecting any members of the League
or not, is hereby declared a matter of concern to the whole League, and the League shall
take any action that may be deemed wise and effectual to safeguard the peace of nations.
In case any such emergency should arise, the Secretary-General shall, on the request
of any member of the League, forthwith summon a meeting of the Council.
It is also declared to be the friendly right of each member of the League, to bring to
the attention of the Assembly or of the Council, any circumstances whatever affecting
international relations which threatens to disturb international peace or the good under-
standing between nations upon which peace depends.

DEATH OF MR. J. W. MURBY.

We have to record, and do so with very sincere regret, the passing
away of our colleague, MR. JOHN WILLIAM MURBY, Manager to the
National Health Insurance Department. Mr. Murby had been ill for a
very considerable time. We were, however, always hoping he would pull
through. Unfortunately he did not, despite all possible care and expert
advice. We have lost a valuable officer of the Union by Mr. Murby's
death. The work of the National Health Insurance Department calls
for careful and constant supervision, and in Mr. Murby we always felt
that the work of the Department was in capable hands, he having been
in the position for ten years. Mr. Murby will also be missed in the
political world, as for many years he was a very active member of the
I.L.P., and was constantly speaking on their behalf in various parts
of the country. In fact, we do not think it too much to say that Mr.
Murby's activities in this work and his great anxiety to bring into being
better conditions of living for the workers hastened his death. For ten
years he was a member of the Leicester City Council, and resigned upon
the Union headquarters being moved to London.
To the Widow and Daughter we tender our sincere sympathy and
condolences in this their great loss. We hope that the fact of the high
regard with which Mr. Murby was held by many who knew the great
amount of work he did for the people will be some consolation to them
in their sorrow and loss.
At the funeral, which was largely attended, the Union was repre-
sented by the General President, Mr. T. F. Richards; Mr. D. McCarthy,
National Organiser; Mr. T. Adnitt, Council Member; Mr. R. D. Mayes,
Chief Clerk in the Insurance Department; and the General Secretary,
Mr. E. L. Poulton, J.P.
Further references to Mr. Murby will be found on pages 110-III.

REMEMBER THE FIFTEENTH !
Once again we feel bound to call the serious attention of Branch Secretaries
to the fact that the FIFTEENTH day of each month is the latest day for
returns reaching the General Secretary. If Branches fail to send off their
returns to reach the Central Office before the 15th of the month it tends to
upset the organisation of the work in the General Secretary's Office. We beg
to intimate that unless returns are in before the 15th of the month, the Secretary
has been instructed to put into force the Rules governing the same.  Returns
Sheets MUST also bear the signature of both the Branch President and Branch
Secretary, or they will reluctantly have to be returned for completion.

TRADE UNION STAMP.
This is a matter which we have stated before rests with the members to
make a success. It is in the interests of members themselves that " Stamped
Footwear " should be increasingly purchased; therefore, push the Trade Union
Stamp. Members and their families should wear only " Union Stamped
Footwear."

GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
I have just returned from the Memorial Service of our Shopmate, Comrade and
Brother Officer, Mr. J. W. Murby, who after an illness of several months has passed away
to that home from which no traveller returns, and so passes away another of those who
fain would have lived to see the great change in human society for which he lived and
worked. We all are here to-day and gone to-morrow, therefore let us make the most of
that which comes to our hand, and when we are called upon to lay down our work for
the Great Reaper, we shall do as he has done, and be grateful that we gave to humanity
the best we had to give.
The Daily Herald's future has played no unimportant part of our thoughts during
the month, the Unions being asked to guarantee its future for the next five years. Those
Unions, who like ourselves elect their Executive for two years only, may find that any
new body may not feel bound by the acts of their predecessors, and may undo at one stroke
that which the present body may think to be both right and proper. Still, with this proviso,
we are willing to help the paper. Speaking for myself alone, the paper on its merits, on
its deserts, on its genuine power for good ought to need no pushing. To lose the paper
now is unthinkable, but circulation is its one and only sure future for existence. Let
us all privately and publicly help to sustain this priceless organ, without which even our
Labour Members in Parliament would have a very poor reception in the Press.
I learn that the LEICESTER WOMEN'S BRANCH are distributing four dozen copies
per day amongst their members. This is certainly a sure way of increasing the circulation
until such time as individuals will act for themselves. Read the Daily Herald. Posters
are being placed outside all our Offices, and also outside the offices of Political Agents,
and Herald Committees are being formed to further the claim of this superb journal.
Will all our members please do their best, not alone for the paper, but for our own move-
ment. By this means and method it will give to all readers strength and inspiration.
RAUNDS.—The attitude of one of the members of the Federation in Raunds, Northants,
has caused some amount of attention and one which will have to be dealt with by the
Union and the Employers' Federation. The firm of Messrs. Adams Bros. disputed a
price for Stitching the Egyptian Army Boot, and after disagreement at the Board it was
submitted to the Arbitrator who was dealing with the question of Hard-Cased Toe boots.
The Umpire decided in the Employers' favour respecting Hard Toes, and in our favour
respecting the Stitching, by increasing the price by 1d. per pair. The firm immediately
accepted the benefit of the Hard Toc award, but declined to pay the Stitching award unless
7½ per cent. was deducted in accord with the 1919 National Agreement, which is never
considered by New Prices. The firm pleaded for a re-hearing on a technical point. The
Government, with our advice and consent, allowed a re-hearing, and the Umpire confirmed
his award ; still the firm declined to pay. Some advise we stop the firm, we say "no,"
for two reasons; the firm is Federated and we may be mulcted in damages. Secondly,
we have no right to spend Trade Union money to compel members of the Federation to
Officers of the Federation agree that it is their duty to see their members are loyal to the
carry out their part of the National Agreement, and it is a real pleasure to learn that the
Agreement. (Will all Officers please note). The worst of the matter is that the men,
some sixty or thereabouts have no work, and have been waiting for this money for the past
that any one man can punish his fellows by such a stupid policy, especially after the
six weeks. We must have some quicker machinery than this. It is a burning shame
matter had been before the National Joint Standing Committee and advice given. My
reason for dealing with this at so much length is to warn the Trade that such ought not
to happen, especially after my three different visits to the firm and every conciliatory
method tried.
A meeting called by the GENERAL COUNCIL OF THE TRADES UNION CONGRESS and
attended by Mr. J. Buckle, M.P. and myself, for the purpose of considering the best way
to settle disputes in the Co-operative and Distributive movement, and we learned that
no less than one hundred and fourteen disputes had occurred, and were referred to the

General Council, although some of their members are occupied three and sometimes four

set up a small Committee to und a way out of the impasse. The Committee reported to
