backing should be had for the asking, and with colleagues on this sub-committee confidence
would be greater. However, in the end a small Committee was appointed to draw up an
amended scheme to the one submitted. I was appointed one of the seven chosen. The
demand for a change is coupled with the astonishing statement that the National Joint
Standing Committee of Co-operators and Trade Unionists have given awards below the
Trade Boards rates. This certainly will need some explanation at the forthcoming Trades
Union Congress. I still hold that our Co-operative movement must lead in wages and
never be behind. This should be universal and not confined to one area.

HOLIDAY FUND.- There are still a few small firms who have not yet met the claim of
the Holiday Fund, and since my last Report we have had to "strike" one firm, who agreed
to comply after the men had been out one week, and another firm who had refused to pay,
advised us they were paying as last Friday. We have satisfied ourselves that the firm
"struck" has also paid. Two other firms have agreed with us this week, and as we have
so many small firms to deal with the notice has been handed in to another of those whom
we hope will be as good as the rest before the notices expire. All our members appear to
be very anxious to obtain this benefit added to their own contributions, and holidays
made a little more pleasant.

A visit to the NORTHANTS DISTRICT COUNCIL had more than a passing interest. Presi-
dent Townley, of Northampton, opened up a discussion on the question of Daywork
versus Piecework. All appear in our industry to agree that Piece payment is the most
satisfactory, but that some think the wage should be set or limited to a certain amount of
work, and a very proper suggestion was made by the speaker that employers whilst having
the power to choose Day or Piecework, we, as a Union, ought to have at least a fair notice
that such change is about to take place in order that the system should bear its quota of
responsibility with the NATIONAL AGREEMENT. As an instance, at a recent dispute at
the C.W.S. Works, Duns Lane, Leicester, I had occasion to make enquiries at Knighton
Fields, and find that some of the girls are not getting the full benefit of the National Agree-
ment, although the Management admit they ought to have known, but because the Heads
of Departments fail to realise the operatives must suffer. We are claiming for at least
the back money for one week. Our members with their fear of discharge, fear of asking
for that due to them, often neglect to make the demand, the responsibility for which is
no more theirs than the employers, but with this big difference, the employers benefit at
the expense of the indolent, careless or frightened operative. We hope to educate our
employers to that standard that they will overlook their wages books each week and see to
it that the National Agreement is being carried out in its entirety, one half of the responsi-
bility being the Federation's and the other the Union's.

GENERAL FEDERATION OF TRADE UNIONS held their usual monthly meeting and
congratulated their Chairman, Mr. Alfred Shortt, M.P., on being called to the Bar, a
distinction that any worker should be proud of, but let us hope that the movement will
not give him the cold shoulder as was done to Clem Edwards and Fred Brocklehurst.

The Deputation to the MINISTRY OF LABOUR reported the success of their visit to the
Minister and the administration of the Unemployment Insurance Act. A sub-committee
was chosen to see the Minister of Labour and to deal with the subject matter of the Act.

EDUCATION AT KETTERING. - A very good Conference was held at Kettering addressed
by Mr. Mactavish, of the Workers' Educational Association, his subject being "Education
and the Working-class Movement." The Conference was arranged by the District Council
of Northants Boot and Shoe Operatives' Union. Some 80 delegates attended and listened
with interest. In the absence of Mr. Bradley, through illness, the General President was
asked to take the chair, and a very good address was delivered by the General Secretary
of the Educational Movement, who believed that the Education Minister could be and
should be more important to the nation than even a Prime Minister. Views were expressed
that our girls should go from the elementary school to the university and our boys be
compelled to win a wife by sheer ability and merit and affection, the children of such a
mother would be an addition to the race.

Above all things if you do not wear Stamped Boots, read the Daily Herald.

7, MECKLENBURGH STREET,
LONDON, W.C. 1.
20th February, 1923.

Yours fraternally,

ihards

General President.

use the axe, and at the next Council meeting we hope we shall have this circular

[NOTE.-It is quite apparent that the Chesterfield Branch has misread
Circular 296. The rules regarding Unemployed members are still operative,
but when members were suspended for an indefinite period, unemployment
benefit was not payable. Circular 296 gives an additional advantage, because
if members are bona-fide suspended for more than FOUR weeks, unemployment
benefit will be paid from the fifth week as against NO benefit paid previously.-
E.L.P., G.S.]
CORK.-Trade here unfortunately still remains very slack..
EDINBURGH.-Sickness with our Branch is on the upgrade this month.
By the suggestions put forward in last Report it looks as if the Union is going
to revert to Biennial Conferences. We, along with other centres in Scotland,
are mapping out an organising campaign. All Unions affiliated to local Trades
and Labour Council have formed a special committee for this work. They
in turn are divided into three sub-committees: (1) Organising; (2) Recreative
and Educational; (3) Daily Herald. The first sub-committee is starting
off with A.E.U., as they are about the hardest hit, having lost a large amount
of members since lockout. Let us hope this endeavour will meet with success.
We are pleased that Mr. W. R. Smith has given warning through his report
about the proposed amendment or abolishment of Wages Trade Boards.
This would be a serious matter for the boot repairers. Of course what can we
expect when the citizens returned to Parliament members who make no bones
about it that they are determined to lower wages at every opportunity. The
unemployed, who have drawn uncovenanted benefit for the 12 weeks' period,
are now at the Labour Exchange's Committee consideration whether further
benefit should be paid or not. We trust the unemployed will not fail to apply
to Parish Councils to keep them from absolute destitution. Edinburgh
members have been making enquiries of the Secretary why the Branch did not
send voting returns to Central Office. The only explanation is that with
New Year's holidays it is very difficult to have returns back from all sections
in time for counting same. In future we should like an extra week for taking
the vote. This would save worry to Scottish officials and give a larger vote.
HIGHAM AND RUSHDEN.-Up to 1st February, 1923, Messrs. Adams
Bros. had not paid the Award for Egyptian Army Stitching. We are awaiting
the reply of the General President in respect to future action in this case.
The operatives are naturally very dissatisfied with the delay.
LEEDS No. 1. We regret to report that trade here is not as good as we
would like it to be. We hope for a change for the better in the near future.
Mr. Dobbs and Mr. J. Buckle, M.P., gave interesting addresses at our Monthly
Meeting on the New Terms of Settlement, which were much appreciated by
our members.

LEICESTER No. 1. - We are pleased to report a slight improvement in
trade during the month.
LIVERPOOL. - Boot repairing is still quiet, although not much below
the average for this time of the year. The industrial magnates are prognosti-
cating a boom in trade in the near future. Let it be soon. We are looking
forward to the opening of Parliament with mixed feelings as to what the
Government programme will be like, more especially in regard to unemploy-
ment, the housing question, and Rent Restrictions Act, whether they will
adopt the majority report of Lord Onslow's Committee or adopt, a middle
course; that is where the Labour Party will come in. We note by the General
President's report in the Half-yearly Report that the Trade Board has been
considering the duties and definition of foremen. That is rather a vexed
question with some of our members and one that we should like to see clearly
defined, as at the present time it is possible to get behind the Act of Parliament
and so evade payment of the full rate per week, even though they have been
employed by the firm more than forty-eight hours, and it is not much use for
the workers to kick up a shine in these hard times as there are too many men
looking for work, and glad to step into their shoes, or in other words take their
situations when vacant on the employers' terms.
MAYBOLE. We are sorry to report trade still very bad, some of our
people are only making half time.
NEWCASTLE.-Trade here is still very bad, but according to all that we
read in the papers there must be an abundance of orders in the offices of the
local shipyards, and we expect before very long there will be an improvement
in all trades, and that our trade will benefit, as well as others. There is a
rumour going around that the local representative on the National Committee
of the Trade Board is going to propose another reduction in employees' wages.
If this is so, we hope that our representatives who sit on the same committee
will strenuously oppose any reduction whatever. According to the Govern-
ment official Gazette for last month the percentage above pre-war has not dropped
to warrant any interference with wages at the present moment.
PLYMOUTH.-Trade remains quiet. We regret to record the death of
one of our oldest members, Mr. J. Waterfield, who had been a loyal member
for over thirty years, and although never taking any prominent position in
the work of our branch, his loyalty to the Union and faithfulness to his
shopmates never wavered. Steadfast and unselfish, his example was always
helpful and good; his loss will be deeply felt by all members of the Plymouth
Branch. We have endeavoured to help forward the circulation of the Daily
Herald by purchasing copies and getting them into a few of the workshops
during the past month, for we realise what a great power the paper must wield
in moulding public opinion, which is likely to become more and more the arbiter
on all questions dealing with wages and conditions of employment, as the
people advance towards the goal of real democracy.
SHEPSHED. - Voting for New Agreement caused a large attendance of
our members at our January meeting, and it was generally admitted that the
Council had done their best for the trade. There is still a lot of feeling with
the men over 40 not being able to get Sick Benefit, but why did not these
members look to it when they had the chance. The Union was established in
1874, and they had all these years before them. Our President. Mr. J. W.
Smith, is to be nominated for the Whit Conference.
SOUTHAMPTON.—Trade fluctuating with tendency to improvement.

DEATH OF MR. J. W. MURBY.
Former Active Member of the City Council.
The Labour Party of Leicester has sustained a heavy loss by the death of
Mr. John William Murby, which occurred at his residence, 6, Aylestone Street.
yesterday, at the comparatively early age of 50.
He was a native of Leicester, and attended St. Martin's Church School till he
was 14. Then he entered the shoe trade, taking up clicking.
The deceased, for a number of years, occupied a seat on the City Council, being
one of the representatives of Castle Ward. He took a deep interest in all matters
appertaining to the gas undertaking, and he was a fearless and able critic, carrying
conviction by the intense sincerity with which he advanced his various claims.
He was an official of the Boot and Shoe Operatives' Union, the Insurance
Department being under his control. In this work he was equally painstaking and
successful, and his loss will be severely felt by that organisation. When the head-
quarters of the Union were moved to London Mr. Murby went with them, but
continued to maintain his home in Leicester.
He was an ardent politician and lost no opportunity of advancing the Labour
cause both in Leicester and in other places. At one time he was regarded as the
prospective Labour candidate for the Bosworth Division, but health and other
considerations induced him to withdraw:
At the 1918 election he was the prospective Labour candidate for Ilkeston
Division, but retired owing to illness. Early last year he was chosen to fight Mr.
Neville Chamberlain at the General Election, but again he had to stand aside because
of his health.
He was hon. secretary to the Leicester "Right to Work" Committee from
1910 to 1913.
Mr. Murby had been in failing health for some months, but his death will come
as a shock to many of his friends.---Leicester Mail, 9th February, 1923.
FUNERAL OF MR. J. W. MURBY.
Mayor's Tribute at St. Mark's Church.
Many representatives of the Labour Party were at St. Mark's Church this after-
noon to pay a tribute to their old colleague, Mr. John William Murby, of 6, Aylestone
Street, Leicester, who passed away after a prolonged illness on Thursday last. All
his working life Mr. Murby had been identified with the boot and shoe trade, and of
late years he had held the official position of manager of the Health Insurance Depart-
ment of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives ; while also from his youth
he had espoused the cause of Labour.
The service was conducted by the Rev. A. Linwood Wright, vicar of St. Mark's,
assisted by the Rev. J. Beddow. Boys of the day school acted as acolytes and torch-
bearers. A hymn was sung, an address was given by the Mayor, and Mr. Walton
Knight, the organist, played the Dead March in "Saul."
The principal mourners were Mrs. J. W. Murby (widow), Miss Elsie Murby
(daughter), Mrs. Murby (mother), Mr. G. Murby (uncle), Mrs. and Mr. Smith (sister
and brother-in-law), Miss E. Murby (sister), Mrs. and Mr. J. Lilley (sister and
brother-in-law), Mr. A. E. Nicholls, and Mrs. Cook.
The body was enclosed in a shell and oak coffin, with solid brass mounts. On
the breastplate was the inscription: John William Murby, died February 8th,
1923, aged 50 years.
The bearers were Councillors H. Hand, G. A. Kenney, J. H. Baum, and A.
Monk, Mr. P. Acton (Municipal Employees' Association), and Mr. T. R. Hill (vice-
president I.L.P.).

In the Congregation.
The Mayor and Mayoress (Councillor and Mrs. A. Sheriff), Councillors H. Carver
(High Bailiff), W. E. Hincks, W. E. Wilford, W. Oram, J. K. Kelly, and J. Minto,
Mr. J. T. Boulter, Mr. C. Harris, and Mr. W. J. Moore were noticed in the very
large congregation, in which also were many persons in representative capacities.

GROWING VOLUME OF INTERNATIONAL LABOUR LAW.
Results of the International Labour Conference.
A note on the results achieved by the International Labour Conference of the League
of Nations up to the end of last year has just been issued by the International Labour
Office. This note summarises the action taken by the various countries in execution of
the Draft Conventions and Recommendations adopted at these annual Conferences, of
which four have been held (Washington 1919, Genoa 1920, Geneva 1921, Geneva 1922).
The fifth Conference is expected to open in Geneva during the month of October.
A detailed account of the results which the growing influence of the decisions of the
Conference has achieved, states the note, would be of inconvenient length. Such results
are frequently outside the sphere of legislation proper and States which have not yet
adopted definite legislative measures have recognised nevertheless the importance of the
principles embodied in the Conventions and Recommendations, and in many cases pre-
paratory work is in hand and the way is clear for eventual ratifications.
Further, no account is here taken of previously existing legislation which may corres-
pond with the provisions of a Draft Convention adopted by the Conference at a subsequent
date. It should be noted that in a number of cases ratification of the Convention
in question has been delayed by constitutional or other internal difficulties.
A number of countries have informed the Office that their previously existing legis-
lation already conforms with the provisions of certain of the Recommendations.
The following figures summarise the results attained up to the present :—
Ratification.
Number of ratifications registered by the Secretary-General .. 63
Number of countries which have notified their adherence to the
Berne Convention on white phosphorous since the Washington Conference 11
Number of cases in which ratification has been authorised by the
competent authority but has not yet been communicated 16
Number of cases in which ratification has been recommended to the
competent authority by the Government but approval has not yet been
signified.. .. .. .. .. 89
Application.
Number of measures finally adopted by legislative authorities, and
measures of an administrative character, giving effect partially or wholly
to the provisions of the Draft Conventions or Recommendations .. 78
Number of legislative measures of all descriptions proposed but not
yet finally adopted, which are intended to give effect partially or wholly
to the provisions of the Draft Conventions and Recommendations .. 63
The States in which different Draft Conventions have been ratified include:—Bulgaria,
Czecho-Slovakia, Denmark, Esthonia, Finland, Free City of Danzic, Great Britain, Greece,
India, Italy. Japan, Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Roumania, South Africa, Sweden
and Switzerland.
REMOVAL OF RENT CONTROL IN ITALY.
International Labour Office Information.
A decree has recently been issued by the Italian Government, states Industrial and
Labour Information, the weekly publication of the International Labour Office of the
League of Nations at Geneva, removing all control regarding rent regulations as from
July 1st, 1923.
Since the beginning of the war, tenancies have been regulated by Decrees prolonging
existing leases in favour of tenants. The Government had only allowed small percentage
increases of rents varying according to the rental.
Landlords who desire to regain control of their houses or flats on July 1st, or who
propose to raise the rent, must notify the tenant before February 1st, 1923. Tenants
who do not wish to leave their flats or desire to contest the proposed increase, must appear
before an arbitration court. Arbitration courts will be instituted in the chief towns of
the various administrative districts (mandamenti). They will consist of a landlord and
a tenant with a magistrate (pretore) as chairman. There will be no appeal against the
decision of this Court.

WORLD LABOUR "PARLIAMENT."
Programme of Fifth Meeting Next October.
The fifth annual session of the International Labour Conference of the League of
Nations will open at Geneva, on Thursday, October 18th.
The programme for this Conference was discussed by the Governing Body of the
International Labour Office during its recent meeting at Geneva. In view of the general
movement which has taken place in the direction of establishing the eight-hour day and
in view of the increased leisure enjoyed by the workers, the Governing Body considered
that it would be useful to establish guiding principles, based on experience already acquired
in a number of countries, relating to the use of the leisure hours of workers and therefore
decided to place this question on the agenda.
Other questions to be discussed will be the determination of general principles for
factory inspection work; the consideration of practical schemes for equal treatment for
national and foreign workers who are the victims of industrial accidents in a country;
and the question of a 24 hours' weekly rest-period in glass works where the processes are
continuous.
The Governing Body decided to defer their decision as to placing on the agenda the
prohibition of night work in bakeries until their next meeting in April.

INTERNATIONAL LABOUR LEGISLATION.
The attitude of the Government towards the proposals for labour legislation adopted
at the Third Session of the International Labour Conference held under Part XIII. of the
Peace Treaty is to be the subject of a question to the Prime Minister in the House of Com-
mons to-day. Mr. J. G. Hancock, Liberal Member for the Belper Division of Derbyshire,
will invite the Prime Minister to state what action has been taken or will be taken in regard
to the Draft Conventions and Recommendations of the Conference, seeing that the period
provided for in Article 405 of the Treaty, during which they should be submitted to the
competent authorities for legislative or other action, has expired.
The provision of Article 405 to which reference is made is as follows:-
" Each of the Members (of the International Labour Organisation) undertakes
that it will, within the period of one year at most from the closing of the session of
the Conference, or, if it is impossible owing to exceptional circumstances to do so
within the period of one year, then at the earliest practicable moment and in no case
later than 18 months from the closing of the session of the Conference, bring the
Recommendation or Draft Convention before the authority or authorities within
whose competence the matter lies, for the enactment of legislation or other action."
As the Third Session of the Conference closed on November 19th, 1921, the normal
period of one year has expired and three months of the extended period have elapsed.
Seven Draft Conventions and Eight Recommendations are involved. They deal
with the following matters :-
Prevention of unemployment in agriculture.
Protection before and after childbirth of women wage-earners in agriculture.
Night work of women in agriculture.
Age of admission of children to employment in agriculture.
Night work of children and young persons in agriculture.
Development of technical agricultural education.
Living-in conditions of agricultural workers.
Rights of association and combination of agricultural workers.
Workmen's compensation in agriculture.
Social insurance in agriculture.
Use of white lead in painting.
Weekly rest in industrial undertakings.
Weekly rest in commercial establishments.
Minimum age for admission of young persons to employment as trimmers and
stokers.
Compulsory medical examination of children and young persons emploved at sea.

"
130
That the members of the Board have had many difficult problems to determine
everyone knows, and that their decisions have not on all occasions pleased everybody may
be taken for granted. But any one who has been in constant attendance on the Board
from the outset must have noticed the improvement which has taken place in the character
of the deliberations and in the relations between the two representative sections. Fuller
knowledge of each other, and fuller experience of each other's conditions and difficulties,
has engendered mutual respect and confidence. Serious points of divergence still arise
and must continue to arise, causing vigorous, and sometimes voluble, debate: but as a
general rule the discussion proceeds on no merely selfish lines, and it is controlled by a real
desire to arrive at conclusions which will be consistent with the best interests of all affected
by them. Except on very rare occasions these conclusions are reached by compromise
or agreement, towards the accomplishment of which the independent members may proffer
advice or suggestion." - The Shoe and Leather Record, 9th February, 1923.

ORGIES OF WASTE AT MONTE CARLO.

Centre of Luxury and Extravagance.
Monte Carlo seems to be the one spot on earth where everyone has not only everything
he wants, but masses of this world's goods to throw away.

To go to Monte Carlo after London is like stepping out of reality into a highly-coloured
novel. Everyone is spending money right and left, everyone is prosperous and care-free;
no one thinks of anything but pleasure and profit. It all seems rather unfair that all this
should be going on as if there had been no upheaval in Europe, when some poor devils are
having such a terrible time to make ends meet. I wonder. when I see these masses of
people, all of them from countries which have been as badly hit as our own by the war,
where they manage to get the money, which our fellows can't get hold of in sufficient
quantities for comfort, let alone luxury.

Scenes of Magnificence.
Never has Monte been more crowded, even in pre-war days. Visitors are content to
put up with indifferent lodging when the hotels are full, in order that they may be within
hail of the Casino. All available villas and flats are bespoken at lavish figures. Carnivals,
tournaments, balls, thés dansants, concerts, theatres, pigeon-shooting, riding, golt, every
form of expensive amusement is in full swing, in addition to the main attraction of the
town-the Casino.

Prices are higher than usual as regards accommodation, amusement, transport, and
club and hire fees-yet the demand is greater than ever.
The comparative quietness of the dress, possessions, and jewels of the women which
characterised Monte two years ago has disappeared, and in its stead the full splendour of
brilliant silks and priceless tiaras and rings, furs, and motors have once more made their
appearance.

Habitués of Monte Carlo, who have known her in all her phases, say that they have
rarely seen her look as prosperous as she does this year.
The famous Café de Paris is serving as many customers a day now as it usually does
in March, and the dancing room, in which your bill for a cup of tea and a cake amounts
to 15 or 20 francs a head, is filled to overflowing every afternoon. Rival cafés are springing
up like mushrooms: every hotel is engaging bands and dance orchestras: the motor-hire
and carriage proprietors are working overtime people who look as if they were in trade
or in quite a small professional way are engaging motors or carriages by the week, without
even inquiring the price of hire.

Bank Notes and Diamonds.
But, despite all the expenditure that goes on under the glorious health-giving sunshine
during the day-time, it is during the Monte Carlo night-the night of the gambler, the
dancer, the diner, the operagoer, and playgoer that one can really judge of the limits of
extravagance of which Monte Carlo of post-war days is capable. The restaurants are
filled to capacity with people of all classes and all nationalities, who think nothing of five
pounds a head for their dinner, preceded by innumerable cocktails and followed by in-
numerable liqueurs of the rarest and dearest brands. Then, as the diners disperse, the
theatres and concert and dance halls, all with expensive entrance fees, fill with marvellously
dressed crowds, who come in the cars which line the roads leading up to the town for a
distance of several hundred yards, without standing room between them.


---
Here is the text from the image:

Crowd of the Casino.
131

Then there is the real crowd-the crowd of the Casino. There are three principal
places where gambling is in full swing day and night in Monte the Sporting Club, patron
ised by the elite who gamble in thousands the public rooms of the Casino, in which
congregate a strange and incongruous medley of humanity, ranging from the millionaire
in full evening-dress to the small shopkeeper in his working clothes; and the Municipal
Casino, the players in which are all townsfolk who come as much to dance and drink and
see the variety show as to play "Boule," the only gambling game which is allowed there
The Grand Casino opens at ten in the morning, and the public rooms close at midnight
after which the salons privés of the Sporting Club remain open till two or three a.m.
trente-et-quarante tables; when the game is in full swing people are often standing six
deep behind the chairs, staking over one-another's shoulders. The sums represented by
the counters lying on a single table during one spin of the roulette would keep a man in
Park Lane for the rest of his life.

One man will sometimes stake as much as a thousand pounds with thirty-five chances
against him, and a curious feature of this year's play is that the even chances, those on
which you have one chance in two of winning, are far less patronised than those in which
the odds against winning are six, eight, or even thirty.

Behind all the glare and glitter there is a side which is not made too public. A gambler
is ruined; a shot rings out, or blood spurts from a stab. The Casino is prepared for it all.
A motor-ambulance, organised like a fire brigade, dashes to the scene; there is a little
temporary excitement, the blood is mopped up, and play goes on as usual. The body
is hurried away; and the rest is silence.

No Rates and Taxes.

What I have seen of Monte Carlo leaves me wondering what the man who has done
his bit and is up against it over here would say and do if he could see it all. There is no
discontent here, no jealousy, for the fortune of the man of ease is shared by the townsman.
Everyone shares in the colossal luxury which the place breathes. Otherwise there would
probably be a revolution !

Throughout the Principality no one pays any rates and taxes-the Casino is the pro-
perty of the Prince, and out of its profits come the upkeep of the palace, the Municipality,
the roads, the huge public gardens, the hospitals, the police, the soldiery, and everything
else for which the British ratepayer has to disburse out of his hard-earned wages.

The foreigner alone is taxed. If he wishes to share in the well-being and prosperity
which this people has worked up for itself, he has to contribute towards the upkeep of the
State, and a tax for this purpose is added to his hotel bill-a form of direct taxation by
means of stamps which costs nothing to collect.

Out of the profits of one building the upkeep of an entire State comes-and it is one

133
The belief exists amongst organised workers, that employers are determined to utilise
the present slump for the purpose of degrading conditions of employment to the lowest
possible point. The action of certain Employers' Federations fully justifies the impression
that they consider the reduction of labour standards the line of least resistance as a means
of cutting down expenditure and reducing the cost of production.

As one group of employers secures success, others follow, and the low standards
obtained in one industry are quoted in other industries as a reason why the worker should
submit to reductions without protest. The conditions of labour in foreign countries are
also being quoted to demonstrate to the British worker why his standard of life should be
reduced.

Organised labour will not adopt a policy which will hinder a revival of trade, but we
cannot accept a degradation of the conditions of employment as a means for securing
trade success, nor will the workers agree that trade prosperity secured by degrading their
conditions of life and labour is in any way a success.

We are satisfied that attacks on labour standards develop a serious state of labour
unrest and revolt. A trade revival without industrial peace is impossible, and industrial
peace is out of the question if attacks are made on organised labour for the purpose of
securing extensions of the normal working day or week.

United Resistance.
Accepting the responsibility for defending labour standards, the Trades Union Congress
General Council will encourage resistance to all attempts which may be made to degrade
the conditions of labour, and will use all the power at their disposal for the purpose of
securing a united and determined stand against any effort which may be made by an
employers' combination, however powerful, to restrict the opportunities of the workers by
extending either the normal working day or week.

On behalf of the Trades Union Congress General Council,
J. B. WILLIAMS, Chairman.
C. W. BÓWERMAN, Secretary.

HOUSES FALLING TO PIECES.
Scandalous Conditions Revealed. Stairways Collapse.
Terrible Plight of Evicted People.
GLASGOW, Saturday.-It is difficult to believe that such terrible housing conditions
as those here revealed could exist in any civilised country, and if anything were necessary
to stimulate the Health Ministry to produce a new building policy, surely this should be
enough.

Owing to the collapse of a stairway the dwellers in a tenement at Dale Street, Bridgeton,
have to reach their apartments by way of a ladder.

There are fourteen tenants, comprising about sixty people, both young and old.

Now, the tenants have been ordered to quit by noon on Monday, as the building is
on the point of collapsing altogether.

Words fail adequately to picture the plight of these people in this congested working-
class locality.

Gas Cut Off.
The gaping entrances to the flats stand exposed to the elements, and the gas has been
cut off for safety.

Nowhere to Go.
Apart from their perilous situation the tenants are indignant at being ordered out on
such a short notice. "Where are these kiddies to go on Monday?" was one woman's
comment, as she pointed to her family all huddled round the kitchen fire. "There's
nothing but the street for us if the authorities can't find us a house," she added.

The problem on Monday will be how to remove the furniture from houses which have
no stairway, and it is understood that the fire brigade will be called in to assist in hoisting
out the household contents.

On the other side of the muddy courtyard is another tenement where the sixteen
tenants were ordered out owing to a bulging wall, and other properties in the vicinity are
in an equally dilapidated state. - Reynolds' Newspaper, 4th February, 1923.

For this reason it is the duty of the proletariat in all countries to carry on the war against war and against every cause of war, using every means, direct and indirect, inside and outside Parliament.
For this purpose it is necessary to put an end to the division which exists in the Trade Unions and to invite the minorities to rejoin their national federations in order to restore the unity of the working classes.
Constant and energetic propaganda for peace must be organised among the people against militarist and imperialist forces.
This propaganda and this action have a double aim.
They must support all efforts tending to remove all factors which propagate the spirit of war.
They must serve to lead to real and actual disarmament and prevent all impending threats of war and direct the struggle against the influences which render war possible.
In order to realise these two aims the Labour movement must counteract all wars which may threaten to break out in the future, with all the means at the disposal of the Labour movement, and to prevent the actual outbreak of such wars by proclaiming and carrying out a general international strike.
By speech and written word the Labour movement, if possible in collaboration with non-labour organisations, must conduct propaganda for the idea of the brotherhood of the peoples, and against everything which sustains and encourages existing antagonisms.
In particular the Labour movement must devote its attention to the education of children and young people in an anti-militarist and anti-capitalist spirit, and, with this aim in view, must bring all its influence to bear on the present educational system.
It is of supreme importance that the Labour movement must exercise a more rigorous supervision of the Press. The Labour movement must devote its full attention and all its energy to establish and maintain its own Press in all countries and also to establish relations between the whole Labour Press.
Of equal, if not still greater importance, is the propaganda and organisation against the possibility of war and for the action to prevent it.
It is with this aim in view that the Labour movement must, on the basis of the Rome resolution, not only exercise supervision over the manufacture and transport of all war materials, but must also, by constant and energetic propaganda, by educating and instructing the workers themselves, and with the briefest possible delay, render the manufacture and transport of war materials impossible.
The Trade Union organisations shall combat all threats of war and demand recourse to arbitration (between all countries concerned) in all differences that may arise between nations.
In this connection the International Federation of Trade Unions should undertake the responsibility to decide upon and to effect the general strike and the economic boycott in accordance with the Rome resolution.
The Labour movement must do all in its power to bring about the establishment of a real and true League of Peoples in which the workers can have confidence and to the jurisdiction of which all differences between the nations can be submitted.
This propaganda for peace must be conducted in collaboration with all who accept the Rome resolution as the basis for the struggle.
The preparations for all definite action shall be in the hands of the Committee set up by the International Trades Union Congress at Rome and composed of the representatives of the International Federation of Trade Unions and of the International Secretariats of the workers in the transport, mining and metal industries.
The direction of all definite action shall be in the hands of the Management Committee of the International Federation of Trade Unions
World peace can only be finally established when the present system of capitalist production, which is based on the idea of personal gain is replaced by a system of pro-duction which shall serve the needs and interests of mankind in general.
The resolution was carried, only the Russian delegates voting against the same.

KINGSWOOD AND THE NEW AGREEMENT.
Non-Compliance to be Reported to the Federation.

A meeting of the Kingswood Arbitration Board was held at 22, Clare Street, Bristol, on Friday last under the presidency of Mr. S. Iles, chairman. The principal item on the agenda was consideration of the ratification of the National Conference (December) 1922 Agreement.

A lengthy discussion ensued, following which it was proposed from the operatives' side that the Agreement should be ratified. The manufacturers declined to vote, and retired to consider the matter. On their return the Agreement was further discussed, and eventually the following resolution was passed :-

That this Board instructs the Secretary to communicate with the federated manufacturers in the Kingswood and District Association, requesting that they shall forthwith carry out the terms of the National Agreement, December, 1922, including the holiday provision scheme. That in the event of any firm not complying by the week ending February 9th or 10th, such firm or firms to be reported at once to the Federation.

Owing to the time spent in discussing the Agreement, consideration of other items on the agenda was held over until the adjourned meeting on the 15th inst.

* * * *

The Secretary of the Kingswood Boot Manufacturers' Association has notified those members who are federated of their obligations under the National Agreement of December last. In particular, they are requested to adopt, as from next week, the Holiday (Provision) Scheme, and those who fail to do so will be reported to the Federation. It is to be hoped that there will be no defaulters, as the disorganised condition of the industry in Kingswood will not be amended so long as federated firms ignore their duty to their fellows. As to the non-federated concerns, means will be found of dealing with them when the Agreement is respected by those who are nominally bound by it. The question of outdoor working is admittedly a difficult one, but is not insuperable. There is no good reason why the lowest grades of goods made in the Kingswood area should not be produced under factory conditions, though a good deal of prejudice and tradition remains to be broken down before that consummation is reached. The advantages of employing outdoor workers is more fanciful than real, as the experience of other centres has shown. In any case there must be no slackening in the determination of the Federation to bring Kingswood into line with those districts in which modern - and decent - conditions are the rule. Shoe and Leather Record, 9th February, 1923.

MANY POTATOES WASTED.
Washington, Feb. 10th.-About 50,000,000 bushels, or more than 11 per cent. of last year's record crop of white potatoes, were wasted or consumed on farms or left undug, according to the department of agriculture.

Heavy production last year resulted in prices which made it unprofitable for many farmers, especially those in the central northwest, to dig their crop, some sections being able to obtain only 20 cents or less a bushel.-American Federation of Labour Weekly News. Service, roth February, 1923.

[One more example of the unjustified waste going on under the present system. Millions wanting food, yet, owing to proper facilities as between grower and consumer, such waste as named above takes place. - E.L.P., G.S.]

MINERS' LIFE THE MOST DANGEROUS.
£5,509,395 Compensation Paid to British Workers in a Year.
Which is the most dangerous industry?
From the statistics of compensation paid in cases of disablement, it would seem that
mining entails the greatest risk of accident.
The annual charge for compensation in the mining industry averaged in 1921 40s. 9d.
per person employed. For factory employees the figure was only 9s. 5d., and for railway
workers IIS. 8d.
During the year £5,509,395 was distributed among 285,746 persons eligible under
the provisions of the Workmen's Compensation Act and the Employers' Liability Act.
Taking establishment charges and other expenses into consideration, it is estimated
that the total cost of compensation in 1921 was about £8,500,000. Daily Chronicle,
31st January, 1923.
"CLASS UNITY" FIRST!
Mr. Clynes' Hint to Rank and file of Trade Unionism.
There was much loose talk to-day about "class war"; what was wanted first was
"class unity," said Mr. J. R. Clynes, M.P., addressing a meeting under the auspices of the
National Union of General Workers at Edmonton last night.
During recent years, said Mr. Clynes, trade unions had suffered more from ingratitude
than from anything else. Their ranks had been thinned by members who had forgotten
the benefits received from them.
The unions were not humiliated, however. Their records justified their existence,
and he hoped that trade unionists would some day apply to their unions the same spirit
that they did to football and cricket.
"I have often been called 'Moderate Clynes,' " he added, but he only wished that
all trade unionists would be as PROGRESSIVE AS HIMSELF, IN WHICH CASE THE MOVEMENT
WOULD BE FAR STRONGER THAN IT WAS AT PRESENT. --Daily Herald, 19th February, 1923.

What the “Shoe & Leather News”
thinks of
Boot Manufacturers who refuse
to honour National Agreements.

"NIGGLING” HOLIDAY FUND.

" We are very sorry that, after all that has gone before, there are still some firms in the boot manufacturing trade which are not taking the recent national settlement with very good grace. Where a number of people are concerned, we are perfectly well aware that no agreement ever could be made absolutely satisfactory to all, indeed, there is Biblical evidence that the covenants the Almighty made with the chosen people in ancient days were frequently quibbled over and sometimes broken. One may recognise the inevitability of this divergence of view, and at the same time question the wisdom of giving active expression to it.

We suggest to the few who are inclined to refuse recognition to the section of the agreement dealing with the holidays to ask themselves "Is it worth while?" The cost to the employer of putting the holiday scheme into operation is not great. Its incidence will hardly be felt on the costs of a year's trading. There is no principle at stake, so far as we see, though we heard one employer say it was against his principle to be forced to pay for something he had never received. If that can be called a principle, in its present application, the same man has broken it many a time by continuing to pay contributions to Unemployment and Health Insurance.

On the other hand, there certainly is a principle at stake in refusing to accept the whole agreement, and that one which we think should stand the highest of all-honour. Even the gambler is said to recognise that, and will pay a debt of honour when he pays nothing else. The trade, through its chosen spokesmen, has entered into a definite undertaking with its employees to do certain things, and it cannot afford to palter with its bond. The point needs no elaboration, for it is obvious that if agreements may be observed or disregarded at will, there can be nothing left but reversion to the old-time arbitrament of brute strength."

" Shoe and Leather News," 15th February, 1923.

If your firm is not paying the National Conditions, you should report the matter at once to your Local Official.

GOVERNMENT AND THE DOLE ALLOWANCE.
Unemployment Fund Exhausted. Labour Ministry's Plan.
The Government is faced with a dilemma arising out of the long-continued unemploy-
ment of so many workers.
Funds to meet the dole allowance are running short, and special provision will have
to be made if the present scale is to be continued.
Very serious difficulties are arising in connection with the Unemployment Insurance
Fund.
This fund, as is generally known, has not been capable of bearing the heavy burden
placed upon it by unemployment. Numerous people have already received far more
from the fund in benefits than they have paid in by way of contributions. The result is
that the fund has long been exhausted. Weekly contributions do not cover outgoings,
and a large debt has had to be incurred. Parliament some time ago sanctioned borrowing
powers to the extent of thirty million pounds. It is understood that sixteen millions
has already been borrowed and exhausted.
On inquiry at one of the Government Departments concerned it was ascertained
that this amount was taken from Post Office savings.

The Critical Date.
On several occasions Parliamentary sanction has been given, covering stipulated
periods, for the payment of benefits to those unemployed whose contributions to the Insur-
ance Fund were exhausted. The current period ends on June Ist. This does not mean
that everyone drawing benefits at present will continue to do so until that date. For these
pecial benefits are in turn spread over periods of weeks, and many individuals will find
their particular period lapse before June 1st, which is merely an arbitrary date on which
all and every special benefit must cease, unless provision be made to the contrary.

It is understood that the Ministry of Labour is in favour of a
further period of special benefits, which shall carry us into the
middle of October next.

For this purpose a Bill will have to be laid before Parliament. Further large borrow-
ings will be required to meet the continuing obligations. Probably another twelve or
fifteen millions will be needed, and by October 1st the borrowing powers of the fund will
be almost exhausted.

Present Cost.
It is true that unemployment is decreasing, but it can hardly be expected to disappear
altogether by October 1st.
Experience, in fact, shows that the reverse is the case, and that it increases during
the winter months. At present unemployment is costing nearly a quarter of a million
weekly in doles alone.- Reynolds' Newspaper, 11th February, 1923.

there is largely due to the fact that a certain number of manufacturers,
seeing a temporary advantage for themselves, by disregarding the pro-
visions of the Holiday Provision Scheme, have refused to pay, entirely
overlooking the graver consequences that may result from their action.
Individualism of this kind is essentially anti-social, and, in my opinion,
very injurious to the best interests of the country as well as our industry.
" All connected with the industry are deeply impressed with the
importance of developing export trade. We realise our population was
not self-supporting, and that without foreign trade the standard of living
was bound to decline. Much of the present trouble is due to the
working of the capitalist system, and it seemed the most
dangerous foe of the common people might well be the money
power wielded by great industrial and financial magnates."
We can only hope Mr. Bostock will be successful in bringing into line with our
National Agreements all boot and shoe manufacturers who may be transgressing
such agreements.
CLAIMS ON THE CENTRAL OFFICE FUNDS.
INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE.
A number of claims have recently been made by Branches either on the
Monthly Return Sheets or by letter, for payment of monies to members in the
shape of Dispute Pay or Unemployment Benefit, which upon the information
supplied to the Central Office, the General Secretary has been bound in accord-
ance with rule to reply in the negative. When such reply has reached the
Branch Officers concerned, another letter has been sent to the General
Secretary with a considerable amount of additional information over and
above that contained in the first application, which has warranted the
General Secretary in replying in the affirmative. We cannot too strongly
impress upon all Officers of the Union that when any claim is sent to the
Central Office for information sought for, all the facts and information
at their disposal must be sent along-not merely from the point of
view of supplying the Central Office with the same-but because of the fact
that if payments are required from the Central Funds, it is in the interests of
the local officials and the members to see that such information is supplied
in the first instance, and thus prevent trouble and delay, which has happened
in several cases recently because of vagueness in the first letter sent.
VOTING.
Voting for the position of Insurance Manager to the National Health
Insurance Department must take place on the April meeting night and the
votes counted on the 12th prox. and posted so as to reach the Central Office
not later than the 15th inst., otherwise they will be disqualified.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION ACTS.
MORE CASES SETTLED FOR UNION MEMBERS.
We are pleased to report that through the offices of our Solicitor, Mr.
Evan Barlow, a number of settlements have been made and reported during
the past month :-

T. P., of Leicester
E. A. R., of Leicester

£35 and 5 guineas costs.

£30 and 3 guineas costs.
£40 and 4 guineas costs.
£10 and 2 guineas costs.
£250 and 15 guineas costs.
It will thus be seen that several of our members in the Leicester branches
have been enabled to secure a reasonable sum for the incapacities caused by
accident whilst at their employ.
We would once again, however, call special attention to the fact that lump
sums are not obtainable by law, but only by agreement, the securing of which
we have been very successful in obtaining.
In addition to the sums named above, the members received Compensation
benefit in accordance with law during the period of their incapacity.

POLITICAL.
The political side of the Labour Movement is full of activity especially
as represented by the members in the House of Commons. To those members
who follow—and we hope all will within the near future—closely the political
situation, it must be apparent that the time of “tranquillity” which the
Prime Minister said the country needed is not allowed to take place so far as
it is within the power of the Parliamentary Labour Party to prevent it. At the
same time we cannot but express not only regret but profound disappointment
with the Government at the way in which they are handling matters, whether
it is Housing, Unemployment, or the complicated International situation;
all alike, are from the standpoint of the Labour Members unsatisfactory.
The Labour Party in the House are doing their best and fighting day by day
to secure the adoption of a more enlightened policy, but up to the present,
whilst the argument is with them, the weight of numbers is with the Govern-
ment, proving once more the necessity of increasing the number of Labour
representatives in the House. We are pleased to record the fact that since
our last report two Bye-Elections have been won by Labour, in constituencies
which were looked upon as “safe” Conservative strongholds. This should
encourage us to continue our propaganda, because it is evident it is beginning
to tell upon the electorate of the country, when, in such places as Mitcham
and Edge Hill, Liverpool, they have returned Labour Members to Parliament.

Another remarkable tribute to the growing power of the Labour Party has been shown during the past few days by the presentation to Mr. J. Ramsay Macdonald, M.P.. the Leader of the Party in the House of Commons, of a memorial wishing the Party success in its efforts to help the weak and the suffering. This memorial was signed by five hundred Clergymen. We cannot do better than repeat the words of Mr. MacDonald himself in replying to the deputation which waited upon him:-
"We will all cherish it, and it will mean not merely an act of grace done by the hand but an act of homage and friendship and of mutual character done from the hearts of old colleagues who are still young in spite of their years and only anxious to fight more valiantly than ever in the battle in which we are engaged."
Further references will be found on page - 20g
FIVE-WEEK MONTH.
There being five Saturdays during this month, Secretaries are asked to make up their returns and pay for the same accordingly.
POSTAGE RATES.
We regret once more to have to refer to the fact that a considerable number of letters are constantly being received from the Branches insufficiently stamped. This means not only a double payment having to be met, but incurs considerable loss of time in delivery, because the Postal Officials have to deliver this corres- pondence during the time that the Central Office is officially opened, so that the postman can secure the postage due on the said letters. We therefore appeal once more to the Branch Officers to see that their correspondence is sufficiently stamped and thus save both time and expense.
REMEMBER THE FIFTEENTH!
Once again we feel bound to call the serious attention of Branch Secretaries to the fact that the FIFTEENTH day of each month is the latest day for returns reaching the General Secretary. If Branches fail to send off their returns to reach the Central Office before the 15th of the month it tends to upset the organisation of the work in the General Secretary's Office. We beg to intimate that unless returns are in before the 15th of the month, the Secretary has been instructed to put into force the Rules governing the same. Returns Sheets MUST also bear the signature of both the Branch President and Branch Secretary, or they will reluctantly have to be returned for completion.

TRADE UNION STAMP.
This is a matter which we have stated before rests with the members to make a success. It is in the interests of members themselves that "Stamped Footwear" should be increasingly purchased; therefore, push the Trade Union Stamp. Members and their families should wear only "Union Stamped Footwear."

GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.

FELLOW MEMBERS,
My opinion has been asked as to the right of any section of employers asking
for a percentage reduction in Piecework Statements, and have given my opinion that
such claim, although some think Clause 10, Section (c) allows this. That is absurd for the
anomalies do not mean general reduction, and many questions were put to avoid any
above reason. Further, no employer put up at the Conference any claim for a general
reduction, but cited cases where juveniles and those on minor operations drew more than
experienced and capable operatives on key operations, but we cited some minor, very minor
operations where the operative in this case had given up the highest position in one room
to go to another firm to do the most minor of all operations in that department, and results
interfere with an operative who bordered on the line of a genius.
to the firm and himself were phenomenal, and the employer denied that they wished to
We remember when the Leicester Men's branches asked for an increase the employers,
without the permission of the Chairman, withdrew from the Board. We could not be
quite so bad as that. But our side should demand the Joint Standing Committee's opinion
on the matter.
Again I repeat my oft-repeated question: Does the Statement produce 25 per cent.
above the minimum to all normal or average physical operatives? If not, then the
anomalous surplus or increase can be put to the underpaid operation. The only just way
to settle anomalous operations.
HOLIDAY FUND. The work for the past month has been very fierce, owing to the fact
that there are some firms who do not understand the National Agreement, as it should
be understood. I am sorry to say that the complaints appear to me to be rather against
the employers in almost every instance, and not against the operatives. Many firms
have had to be visited, in Leicester especially, where there is a very large number of very
small firms, to get them to pay their quota and to adopt the Holiday Fund, but it is pleasing
to report that almost without exception these employers, whether willingly or reluctantly,
have brought themselves into compliance. In two instances, especially, notices have had
to be handed in, although it is only fair to say, to show that we have tried to adopt a
conciliatory policy as far as possible, that we have almost without exception paid three,
four and five visits to these firms before definite action has been taken. Our generosity
appears to be taken as a sign of weakness; it would be as well for employers to remove
this from their minds, and thus enable us to continue the peaceful policy that has hitherto
governed the Industry.
LONDON METRO.—I have had occasion to visit the London Metro. Branch and to make
some enquiries as to one of our firms, Messrs. Weber & Phillips, in the East End of London,
who are credited with making work so much cheaper than many other firms. This firm
has been a source of annoyance to the Branch and the Union for many years. They are a
Federated firm, but this aspect of the case has not before been dealt with. We have
advised that the firm should be taken to the Board and expected to play their part in
accordance with the National Agreement. My colleagues inform me, the Organisers
especially, that the firm and its staff endeavour to stand outside the factory, with the
ultimate result that the operatives are intimidated from either talking to Trade Union
Officials or joining the Union. Our appeal to the Secretary of the Arbitration Board,
Mr. Craig,, has caused the matter to be placed upon the Agenda of the Arbitration Board,
who have advised that an investigation shall take place on the spot.
Whilst in this connection it would be well if our members would at least show some
sympathy with officials who go time after time to a factory and fail to arouse the interest
of the operatives who are the only people likely to benefit.
MOUNTSORREL.-It would be as well to say that during the past month I have made
no less than four visits to Mountsorrel Wholesale School Boot Co., who, it is said, are making
work much cheaper than anyone else in the district. There may be a reason for this,
and that is, so I am informed, by the Manager and Directors, both of whom I saw on the
two occasions I went to the factory, that they confine themselves to the making of one
boot only, consequently the operatives are more expert than they are at some other firms,
and whilst at the same time some employers make 20, 30 or 50 different classes of goods
and are never willing to give a price for the operative changing his lasts or boots, yet at
the same time they do not think that we ought to give the one-boot shop any advantage
over them. This is to a certain extent most reasonable. but at the same time, we cannot
prevent operatives from being more expert on an operation which they are doing con-
tinuously, than the operative who is having to change his work at least every hour. At
this latter firm I am sorry to say that the operatives are not all members of the Union.
and before we can drive home to them all that we would require on this firm, we must
find some means or other to get the operatives inside our organisation. It is pleasing to
report that the employer himself has promised me that he will put up in the factory the
resolution which forms part of the last National Agreement, recommending our Union.


---
Being appointed, as I reported in my last report, a member of the TRADE UNION
AND CO-OPERATIVE ADVISORY COMMITTEE, I have spent the best of two days on this work
on the Drafting Committee and again at the Conference on the 23rd ult., where we have
been again elected to form a Standing Advisory Committee between Distributive Co-
operative Societies and the Trade Unions. We hope that this work will be beneficial
to all concerned, and although the Conference refused to give direct representation at our
request to the General Council, they have made the chairman their chairman, and the
secretary their secretary, so that in a roundabout way the object is achieved. But I am
afraid the Co-operative Union will not accept this.
WIGSTON. - Our recent handing in of notices at Messrs. A. E. Crane & Co., of Wigston
Magna, has culminated in the firm ultimately agreeing to pay before the notice expired.
The same may be said of Messrs. J. Freeman & Sons, of Leicester, who also had notices
handed in, and was prepared to pay before those notices became due.

KETTERING. - Our next great trouble has been with the Northampton Leather Cor-
poration, of Kettering, where for reasons best known to the Manager or Directors them-
selves, they tried to claim that as an auxiliary trade they did not come within the four
corners of the National Agreement. Quite six months ago, with my Kettering colleagues,
we waited on the Directors and informed them that was an impossible position. We have
endeavoured to get into touch on three or four occasions and personal visits have been
made, but owing to illness and other causes no satisfactory progress had been made until
this week, when we became so tired of what I should call "manœuvreing" that we called
a meeting of the men, placed the matter before them, offered them advice for them to place
the matter in our hands, which they very readily did, and we had no other alternative
than to hand in notices. This is likely to bring about an early meeting between the
Directors, Manager and ourselves, and I am hoping that before the coming week is out,
that this little matter will be settled. The trouble is the firm are prepared to accept the
National Agreement, they are also, so they say, prepared to accept the Northamptonshire
Pressroom Statement, but as we tell them, if they will only agree to carry out that portion
of the Statement which calls on them to hand back to the operatives at the end of the week
his costing sheets, then all will be well. On the other hand our old friend, the Manager,
Mr. J. W. G. Smith, informs us that a dayworker ought to keep no record of his work.
This is contrary to the many years of experience that we have had, and piecework, pure
and simple, I hope, will never again be tolerated in our industry.

At the present time we have had much correspondence, and are endeavouring to set
up an Arbitration Board for Derby, Nottingham, and Mansfield. Whatever one may
think about Mansfield, the fact should be known the firm there deliberately left the town
of Leicester. From that point they have a right to pay to Leicester Statements.

NOTTS. and DERBY are certainly not less important towns than Leicester itself. We
therefore claim that Leicester Statements should apply. These employers are adverse
to that order of things, and we have no other alternative than to carry out our resolution,
set up a Board of Arbitration for the three towns, and endeavour to come to an amicable
arrangement. From an organising point of view, this ought to be well for the Union.
I am having meetings at Nottingham and Derby next week. We called one this week
at Mansfield, and although we waited a long time, only three individuals turned up. My
next visit will be to meet the operatives at the factory gates when they leave off. It is
useless our endeavouring to conciliate our members to do their business in private, if they
will not come to the meetings. It will therefore be my bounden duty to call upon them
when they leave off work and conduct our business in the strect, or take a sufficient number
of them with us to the nearest place.

At the time of writing the firm of Adams Bros., of Raunds, who have declined to pay
to Alderman Sheppard's Award for Stitching, in which the firm claim 7½ per cent. deduction,
a most unreasonable attitude. The Umpire has heard the case on two occasions, and it
has also been before the Joint Standing Committee. Despite this procedure, however,
the firm still refuses to pay, and we therefore intend to still further prosecute the case.
Such refusal to pay, however, tends to bring Arbitration into bad repute.

We are still pressing the Rushden Association for the back pay for the two holidays
due to the operatives for Faster and Whitsuntide of last year, and in my last letter received
from them they suggest that the Holiday Scheme did not become operative until this year.
This is due to their forgetfulness that February 6th, 1922 saw the Holiday Fund in the
Agreement of that date mandatory and not permissive.

Keep pushing the Daily Herald and patronise the boot shops which sell Stamped
goods.

7, MECKLENBURGH STREET,
LONDON, W.C. 1.
20th March, 1923.

Yours fraternally,

M. Richards
General President.

BRANCH REPORTS.

ARBROATH. - Trade continues to avoid three of our factories, but in
Carnoustie the remaining one seems to have a business magnetism which
attracts all kinds of customers, and it is common talk of their having secured
a large American order within recent weeks. For the sake of our members
we wish the other firms could meet with similar success. The Branch has now
got information of the appointment of the Secretary to the Local Employment
Committee. This is a belated recognition of our position as a trade in the
smaller towns of Forfarshire, and it has long been a complaint of ours that
railwaymen, textile workers, iron workers, &c., had representation, but ours,
which is the third industry in this district, had no voice in the work of the
Committee. It may seem to some that the most important period of these
Committees has passed, but such an impression is premature in view of the
very considerable alterations and modifications suggested by the Bill before
Parliament at present regarding the whole question of Unemployment Insur-
ance. Whether the functions of the Local Employment Committees may be
increased or lessened, we are glad nevertheless to have established a claim for
representation of our industry, and to have secured the consent of the Ministry
of Labour to it. One thing which we are keenly conscious of is, that owing
to the fact of all the employees of three factories being on short time and on
Labour Exchange benefit accordingly, it has provided a bond to unite the
members closer to the Union than ever, because they all recognise the value
of having an organisation behind them if their rights are challenged in any
way, or if inquiries have to be made to clear up difficulties. We note with
approval the way in which our Council are keeping the position of the Daily
Herald before the membership, because working folk must have a paper to put
the truth about Labour disputes before the public. Many of our members
may reasonably enough object to some of the things done and said, and written
in the name of Labour, but few could successfully argue against the various
sections of organised labour maintaining one national journal which will
publish true accounts of questions affecting the well-being of our kin. We
are of those who pray for a Scottish edition of the Herald. At present the
edition sent to Scotland is only equal to the evening papers of the previous
day, and readers have to buy other papers to get the late news. This is a
serious matter for people working short time, and as a consequence hundreds
go without the Herald in the meantime. When this difficulty is surmounted,
the Daily Herald will be bought eagerly in Scotland, and shoemakers, as always,
will be prominent in the ranks of progressive forces using this powerful press
weapon for the emancipation of children, women and men of Labour.

BARNSLEY.—We are sorry to say that two of our members have been
on the sick list, one from an accident, and the other from lumbago. One of
them has commenced working again, and we hope the other will do so before
long. Trade is very bad here, what with new introductions of ex-service
men, and many that have decent jobs who reckon to be good trade unionists
at meetings, &c., who buy soles cut out and heels too, and put them on them-
selves. The Barnsley Co-operative Stores have never in their history been so
short of work in the repairing department, as they have this last year,
and at the present time they are not getting three days a week.

BELFAST.-We regret to report that trade, both in the manufacturing
and repairing, continues to remain in a deplorable condition, and there are no
signs which would lend us any hope for an early improvement. We would
urge upon the members the necessity of not allowing their arrears to exceed
the eight weeks' limit. Union benefits can only be secured by strictly com-
plying with the rules.

BRISTOL No. 2.—The heavy trade still languishes for want of orders,
and Kingswood at the present time is not the place for operatives to find work.
Mr. W. R. Smith has been with us during the month. His presence has been
very encouraging and helpful to our members as well as to the officers. His
efforts are heavily handicapped by bad trade, but his earnestness in pointing
out to members and non-members, that their only hope lies in unity and
organisation has not been without effect. Kingswood is a big job to tackle,
and will take a long time to set it on a level with other centres of our industry
where modern methods of manufacture are prevalent.

CHESHAM.—Trade here is very bad and there is no sign of improvement.
Our Branch have nominated Mr. P. Bradley to contest one of the seats in the
Labour interest at the forthcoming U.D.C. Election, and we hope next month
to report another Labour gain.
CORK.—Trade still bad.

DUNDEE.—The long-continued stagnant condition of our trade makes
it a dismal and cheerless subject to write on. There is, however, an editorial
in one of our trade papers, which creates a feeling of hopefulness, and an earnest
desire for its consummation, i.e., " There are distinct indications that we are
in the first days of a stage that will burst into immensely greater industrial
activity." Let us pray that it may come soon, and lift many of us out of the
" Slough of Despond." Another of our old officials has been laid to rest,
in the person of James Larg. "Jimmy," as he was affectionately called, did
yeoman service on behalf of the Union away back in the early eighties. Strenu-
ous, irritating and uncongenial, was the task imposed upon a branch secretary
at that period, a position which our late friend held for four years, some thirty
years ago. Since then, much water has run under the bridge; boot manufac-
turing has been revolutionised; the method of handling disputes, the work
of branch secretaries then, is now dealt with in a collective sense by our Boards
of Arbitration. It is singularly strange that the passing away of our old
friend, "Jimmy," marks the third obituary notice of our late branch secretaries
within seven months that have been my painful duty to record, namely,
D. R. Sellars, D. R. Ferguson, and now James Larg. Men's years are numbered,
and our late friends are now completed. The pale messenger beckons silently.
Whatsoever thing man has on hand, important or unimportant, he must
suddenly quit it and go. He has reached the end of his furrow.

EDINBURGH.—Trade is still very quiet in new work but the repairing
has shown some slight sign of revival. Members at monthly meeting were
sorry to hear of the death of Mr. J. W. Murby; he was a very efficient Officer
of the Union. In fact the Secretary has been complimented on the prompt
way in which claims have been paid. This goes to prove that workers, given
the proper facilities, can manage their own business. We had before our
members at last branch meeting the resolution from Central Office re "Inter-
national Situation," which we are submitting to the proper quarters. Rent
control is still occupying a good deal of the working-class attention at present.
The Government proposals should help to awaken the citizens to how the
present rulers are prepared to legislate to defend class interest. Edinburgh
Branch are putting forward Mr. C. Bleaklev as a nominee to Local Labour Party
as a probable candidate for the next Municipal or Parish Council Election.
This means, if accepted, that the members will need to do all in their power to
try and have him returned.
HIGHAM AND RUSHDEN.—Trade during the month has varied, some
few firms working overtime, others short time, and in two cases closed
temporarily.
HULL.—Trade here remains very quiet. The boom which was expected
to come with the advent of a strong Conservative Government has not yet


---


---
taking its toll, a toll that can only be paid by a sacrifice of human comfort
and happiness, many of our members earning as little as £1 per week, and
that continuously is enough to develop despondency. However, "hope
springs eternal in the human breast," and with a faith and optimism that has
forever characterised the pioneer, we go forward with the knowledge that
ultimately justice will triumph over oppression. Hats off to the Parliamentary
Labour Party for their splendid fight they are waging in the House.
PLYMOUTH.—There is no improvement in the repairing trade and while
few shops are working full the majority of our members are losing time. This
is not because boot repairing is a worn-out industry, for a casual glance at the
footwear of our adult population, and especially that of the children, will
convince one of the hundreds of boots and shoes requiring the skilful attention
of the repairer. Neither is it because prices are too high in general, for after
a tour of our town anyone may be struck with the diversity of prices charged
for repairs, in some cases slaughtered prices. These range from 6s. men's
soled and heeled, down to the rock bottom price of 3s. 6d. How this is done
at the price we do not pretend to know, but there it is, a fact patent for all.
But in spite of this our people are ill-shod, our children dangerously ill-fed
and ill-clothed, which will one day return in the form of a boomerang with
more tuberculosis, more sanatorium, and more rates and taxes. The truth is
the people cannot afford to pay for repairs even if they were done at cost.
SOUTHAMPTON.—Trade slack, but slightly improving.
STAFFORD.—We are pleased to report a marked improvement in trade
during the February month. By the death of Mr. J. W. Murby the Union has
lost a very valuable servant. To the widow and family we tender our deepest
sympathy in their sad bereavement.
STREET.—We cannot report any improvement in the state of trade,
the smaller firms finding it especially difficult to get orders. This has meant
further discharges among our members during the month, including, we regret
to say, the President of our Branch. The Turnshoe trade is exceptionally
slack and workers on this class of goods are having a very bad time.
GREAT YARMOUTH.—With reference to supporting the Daily Herald
we beg to make a suggestion to all branches that they should try and form a
paper club in the workshops and factories in which our members are employed.
If there was only one penny a week each collected on a shop by the Shop
President, that would in most cases help the Daily Herald as several could be
bought each day and passed round.

ENGLISH CITY OF HOUSEOWNERS.
Thrifty Leicester's Huge Savings.
By means of small deposits in old-established institutions, the workers of Leicester
added in the past year more than $3,000,000 to their savings.
For many years Leicester workers have been noted for owning their own houses,
which are freehold, and it is only the high cost which is holding up this movement. At
present more than 7,000 families want houses for themselves of the six-roomed type,
with private back gardens.

One institution in the city took £1,300,000 in deposits during the year, and it has
now over 25,000 accounts. Similar institutions have had a record year of savings, while
the Savings Bank has never handled so much money.
invested in War Saving Certificates through the operation of several hundred factory and
The Post Office savings banks have done equally well, and large sums have been
workshop saving societies started during the War. - Daily Chronicle, 3rd March, 1923.
