That statement is a statement which is very likely to mislead, particularly other portions
of the International Labour Office, who, we know, are not so well aware of the methods
by which we conduct business in this country as we are ourselves. You know quite well
that from time to time at these particular Conferences the workers look pathetically to
this country to take the lead and give that support to those matters which will enable
them later to use our example as a lever to get better conditions than those unfortunately
urged is that apart from the reluctance reluctance which I do not pretend to understand
obtaining. One of the strong reasons that you and your colleagues have from time to time
is the fact that certain trades in this country stand in the way. There is the position,
-which the Government has to make laws in keeping with the obligations entered into,
and there are regulations which make what we desire almost impossible. In fact, I do not
think it would be an unfair use of language to say it has been said that it is impossible.
On the contrary, I and my colleagues hold that, so far from it being impossible, even the
regulations of the Convention now-and there are plenty of special exemptions-are
wide enough in their scope, and there is all needed elasticity. That is what was mostly
urged in connection with this matter to meet those varying conditions which obtain in
this country. I would specially call your attention to the Articles I am not going to
quote them-I know you will have them handy-Articles 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 of the Convention.
In these Articles specially we submit that there is plenty of scope and plenty of room to
meet the varying industrial conditions obtaining here and yet confirm the Convention
itself. We also heard, as you remember, on more than one occasion of the railwaymen
as being one of the great cases. I hold here a statement made to your Convention on
behalf of the firemen of Mr. Bromley's union. It is as follows :-
The men concerned do not ask for Sunday duty or overtime and would be quite
satisfied with six days' duty and an eight-hour day; if the companies desire or the
exigencies of traffic demand that they shall work Sundays, or overtime on any day,
the men demand that they shall be paid for such Sunday duty or overtime in addition
to their guaranteed six days of eight hours each; anything less than this will simply
return them to the old bad conditions above referred to.
I have been talking to Mr. Thomas, whom I am certain represents an overwhelming
majority of the railwaymen, who are quite prepared to admit that it will take time to try
to get over the technical difficulties. It would be absurd for me to pretend that I under-
stand the technical difficulties alleged to stand in the way. Equally, however, do I submit
to you that the railwaymen say that there are no difficulties urged that from their stand-
point cannot be overcome and yet confirm the Washington Convention. Moreover, it
was not a very pleasant thing at the meeting last week to hear what we did. I am now

JOHN WHEATLEY, M.P., ON THE RUHR DEPUTATION.
Dealing with the situation of the Ruhr, Wheatley began by deprecating the suggestion
that the people in our country should neglect their own social conditions and concentrate
their whole thought on the condition of Central Europe. THE CONDITION OF THE
GLASGOW WORKING CLASS WAS A MUCH GREATER TRAGEDY THAN THE
CONDITION OF PEOPLES IN CENTRAL EUROPE. There was a tendency to
magnify foreign affairs, and to attribute unemployment at home and the poverty associated
with it mainly to political disturbances and the poverty of Europe. The tendency to
deflect attention to the far ends of the earth that should be given to domestic affairs had
induced himself along with Maxton, Kirkwood, and Stephen, to go to the Ruhr and get
first-hand information. They had gone to the Ruhr, as friends, with sympathy for their
German comrades and with frank and open minds and determined to tell what they saw,
whether it is against the policy of the Government or of the British Labour Party.
They had not found houses tumbling down about the people as had happened during
the past few weeks in Bridgeton; they found the standard of housing immensely superior
to Glasgow's, and nothing of the slums which they knew here. In the midst of all the
present difficulties they had seen working-class houses being erected-houses which would
compare favourably in external appearance with middle-class houses here. The people
were well-dressed; the children seemed well-dressed and comfortable. They had found
no apparent shortage of goods. He believed it might be true that the standard and
quality of food was lower than ours, but there were no signs of the extreme poverty and
starvation that they had heard so much of. Moreover, there was no unemployment,
and the criticism that the apparent betterness was due to the fact that the German workers
worked harder than we did was absurd. The miners in the Ruhr Valley worked seven
hours from bank to bank-an hour less than our miners did.
We at home were being misled as to the facts of the situation. IF THE EAST
END OF GLASGOW WERE ONLY TRANSPORTED TO THE CENTRE OF EUROPE
IT WOULD BECOME THE MECCA OF POLITICIANS AND PHILANTHROPISTS
WHO WERE BLIND TO EVERY MISERY AT HOME. He had every sympathy
with the workers in every country who were oppressed by Capitalism, but no class of
workers in Germany could compare in poverty to the people he represented in West-
minster.
Mr. Wheatley went on to say that Capitalism had no constructive policy for dealing
with the situation, and described the proposal already outlined in the Press, which he
and his colleagues had suggested for internationalising the Ruhr. The only right they
had to suggest it lay in the facts of the situation. Germany was in debt and admitted her
debt, and they held that the debt should not be paid by lowering the standard of life of the German
workers but by confiscating the wealth of German millionaires. The application of some
such collectivist or Socialist principle seemed the only way out of a difficulty created by
competitive Capitalism. - Forward, 3rd March, 1923.

chance of nominating for Executive positions. If a larger delegation is possible then we
should send at least another delegate. But it would be a great advantage if our branches
were given a chance to follow the preparation of the agenda in the way I have suggested,

Executive. I am sure other bodies would like a chance. If autonomy is granted to the
Scottish Labour Party, a great step forward will follow. At present a certain air of
unreality exists while it is known that all decisions in Scotland come before the National
Party for review. Financially the Party in Scotland is sadly handicapped, having only
a very small sum of money to work on. Apart from the Conference altogether, the Party,
under Mr. Shaw's guidance, is doing magnificent work. In the political, municipal,
parochial, educational, and county spheres of work its efforts are brilliantly applicable
to the issues of each, and with money in hand the machinery of Labour activities in Scot-
land could rapidly be made second to none. Even with all the difficulties to overcome,
the Executive Council in their annual report showed a record of accomplishment which
made one feel proud of those who had been in office during recent times.
JAMES P. REID.

SCOTTISH C.W.S. BOOT TRADE.

The slump in the trade of the Scottish Co-operative Wholesale Society Ltd. has not
been arrested, and the sales for the past half-year were 15 per cent. lower than in the
corresponding period a year ago. They were £8,507,477. There was £104,437 available
as profit, and the society members are receiving a dividend of 2d. in the £. In the sales
the boot and shoe department contributed £368,905, as compared with £464,363 in the
last half of 1921, a decrease of £95,457, or 20 per cent. The productions of the boot factory
were valued at £191,621, as compared with £200,546, a fall of £8,924, or 4 per cent. The
comparison, however, is slightly disadvantageous, as the last 26 weeks of 1922 are set
against the last 27 of 1921. For the complete year the total productions were £363,043,
a decrease of 13 per cent.; and the year's sales in the boot department were £772,200,
a decline of 19 per cent. The last half-year's expenses were £15,955 for distributive
wages and £56,140 for productive wages.—Shoe and Leather News, 1st March, 1923.

"NOT FIT TO DIE IN"
Story of Houses in Sheffield.
Startling facts came out at Sheffield to-day, when an inquiry was held by the Ministry of Health with reference to the City Council's application to effect an improvement scheme in connection with houses in the neighbourhood of Oborne Street.
Dr. Wynne, medical officer of health, said there were too many houses on the site and too many people living in them. The houses were so dilapidated that repairing and reconstruction would not make them fit for habitation. The average height of the living rooms was 7ft. 6in. The sanitary arrangements were unsatisfactory, and the living accommodation was indecent.
In answer to Mr. Lambert (for the owner), who commented on the small number of deaths in the houses, Dr. Wynne said: ""The mere fact of people not dying on property does not affect me. The houses are not fit to live in, and they are not fit to die in. When people get sick they are removed to an institution to die.""
Mr. Albert Green, sanitary inspector, said the sanitary arrangements were the worst he had ever met. There was only one water tap for the 22 houses.
For the owner, Mr. Lambert said more than 600 had been spent in repairing the property. The tenants could not afford the rents of Corporation houses. Westminster Gazette, 2nd March, 1923.
LONDON HOUSING REVELATIONS.
HOME WITHOUT A ROOF.
"Only the Sky Over Sick Child's Head," Says Inspector.
Houses at Battersea in which some of the rooms were without ceilings and where the occupants had no protection from the rain were described during an ejectment application at the South-Western Police Court yesterday.
An inspector of the N.S.P.C.C. said in one of the houses was a sick child.
"The sky alone is above the people living here," he added.
As the occupants were unable to find accommodation elsewhere the magistrate suspended the ejectment orders. - Daily Chronicle, 17th March, 1923.
LANDING AS "BEDROOM" FOR SIX.
Stepping Over Sleepers on the Way to Bedrooms.
A landing in a Willesden house, with four doors and a staircase leading off it, is the only home of an ex-soldier, his wife and four children.
This was revealed on Saturday when the man was summoned at the local police court for overcrowding.
The other four sets of tenants, it was said, had to approach their rooms at night by stepping over the recumbent forms of the ex-soldier's family.
An order for abatement was made. - Daily Chronicle, 19th March, 1923.
683,000 PEOPLE LIVING TWO IN A ROOM.
London Census Disclosures.
414,447 More Families Than Dwellings.
Urgent Need For Rapid Building. Fewer Children.
London, "that great province of houses," is the subject of sensational revelations in the new volume of the 1921 Census statistics issued to-day.
It is true that the figures were taken two years ago, but there is no reason to suppose that they have been seriously affected by the lapse of months.
The book is confined to the County of London, and its most important aspect is the housing question.
A New Term.
We begin by noting that to avoid the ambiguity of the old terms "house" or "tenement" a new official term has been introduced, viz., "structurally separate dwelling,"


---
which means any room or set of rooms having separate access either to a street or to a.
common landing or staircase accessible to visitors.
Now, the effect of this definition may be to minimise the seriousness of overcrowded-
ing, because every room in a tenement house in which the front door is left open to
visitors is counted as a "structurally separate dwelling."
It is pointed out that the enumerators found it difficult to distinguish between buildings
originally crected so as to form separate flats or "maisonettes," which were so popular
before the war and those which have been quite roughly converted since the war.

A Partition and a Door.
In some of these cases the only thing the landlord has done is to convert a two-
storeyed house into two flats by putting a wooden cover and a door at the top of the
staircase, and a new water supply upstairs.
The L.C.C. regulations require the use of fire-proof partitions in the conversion
of large houses into flats, but in these smaller house-divisions those regulations appear
For a triffing expenditure, therefore, the landlord is able to collect about three times
to have been set at nought.
the pre-war rent of the house.

Startling Figures.
With these explanations we come to the figures of the Blue Book. The number of
"structurally separate dwellings" occupied, which in 1911 was 678,000, came to 706.450,
while the number of empties fell from 47,000 to 18,000.
There were 345,000 more private families than there were dwellings in 1911.
In 1921 this excess had risen to 414,447-
But here again it is important to remember that these figures really understate the
amount of overcrowding, because the existing " structurally separate dwellings" in which
these families are housed may in many cases only mean one room or a two-roomed flat.

The rooms counted exclude bath-rooms, box-rooms, and so on.
It is noted that the average size of the family has dropped 9 per cent. since 1911,
this being due to the heavily reduced birth-rate and an increased death-rate.
Although this has had the effect of giving a larger proportion of the population the
housing advantages gained by small families, the result has been that the amount of accom-
modation left in the housing pool for the large families has been actually diminished.

WORST DISTRICTS.
We find that 529,000 families occupy fewer than three rooms per family; that 294,000
other families occupy four to five rooms per family; that 126,000 families occupy six to
eight rooms per family, and that 40,000 others occupy nine or more rooms per family.
Out of a total population of 4,484,000, there were 683,000, or about a-seventh,
who were living in dwellings which gave more than two persons per room.
Housing pressure appears to be greatest in St. Pancras, where there are 2.3 families
to each dwelling, and only 17.6 per cent. of the families are in undivided occupation of
separate dwellings.
The biggest families are found in Stepney, Poplar, Bethnal Green, Greenwich, and
Bermondsey; the smallest in Holborn, the City, Westminster, and Marylebone.

LEICESTER FAMILY FOUR IN A BED.
Obtain Possession Order for Larger House.

That four of the occupants of the house had had to sleep in one bed and the husband
on the hearthrug downstairs, was stated in a possession case at Leicester County Court
before Judge Dobb this morning, in which Henry Marriott, 20, Denman Street, sued
Wm. Alfred Timms, 53. Chester Street, for possession. Mr. R. T. G. Wright appeared
for Marriott, and Mr. Basil Edwards for Timms.

Mrs. Dilly said her father, Mr. Marriott, was at present a patient in the North Evington
Infirmary, and could come out if suitable accommodation was found for him. He owned
four houses, one of these being 53, Chester Street, which had the advantage of a large
bedroom, which could be partitioned, thus making an additional room, and improving
upon the sleeping conditions they experienced before plaintiff went into the Infirmary.
Defendant would find 20, Denman Street ample for the needs of his smaller household.

Defendant replied that his wife did washing, and their removal to Denman Street,
where there was no copper, would make this work impossible.

His Honour said it was desirable that Mr. Marriott should have possession, and
advised that the parties should try to come to a settlement.

The case was put back for a couple of hours, when Mr. Wright informed his Honour
that possession had been agreed upon in 14 days, providing a contribution was made for
a portable copper.

His Honour accordingly made an order on these terms. - Leicester Mercury,
20th March, 1923.

EXPLOSION SEQUEL.
Successful Claim Against Boot Manufacturers. Value of a Daughter.

A sequel to a fatal accident at Wilbarston, was heard at Market Harborough County
Court before his Honour Judge Dobb, yesterday, when Joseph James Panter Skelham,
bootmaker, of Wilbarston, claimed from B. Toone and Co., boot manufacturers of Des-
borough, for compensation, under the Workmen's Compensation Act, for the loss of a
daughter who was in the employ of the respondents. Mr. C. S. Bigg appeared for the
applicant and Mr. Sanderson, barrister, was for the respondents.

Mr. Bigg said applicant's daughter was employed at Messrs. Toone, the branch at
Wilbarston. She was lighting a stove in the factory when it exploded and she was fatally
burned. It was claimed that applicant and his family were partially dependent upon
this girl. Her wages averaged 17s. Id., but at the time she died she was earning 23s.
a week, and it was reasonable to suppose she would shortly have been earning £2 a week.
She had been taught boot closing, and in her spare time in the evening and on Saturday
afternoons she assisted applicant in his business. He had felt considerably the lack
of her services as he could not do closing himself, and he had to employ somebody to close
his uppers or have them closed before they were sent home.

Mr. and Mrs. Skelham gave evidence bearing out this statement, and other evidence
was given as to the cost of closing uppers.

Mr. Sanderson submitted that the work the girl did for her father did not constitute
her earnings however useful she may have been. Whatever she did in the house ought
not to be considered at all in connection with this claim with regard to her wages. She
was ill for two long periods. After deducting the contributions she had to make for insur
ance, the cost of her illnesses, and her own spending money, he suggested that the family
could not have been in any way dependent upon her earnings.

His Honour said he was perfectly satisfied with the evidence of the applicant and his
witnesses as to the extent of their dependence upon this girl. It had been submitted
that he should not take into consideration the services she rendered to her father in his
business. He thought, however, that point was disposed of by a case decided in the
House of Lords which had been quoted, and he must take into consideration not only
the actual earnings from her employers, but also the services she rendered to her father.
He thought the work she did for her father well earned her keep and the spending money
she received, and the father and mother therefore benefited to the full extent of the wages
which she obtained outside. He was entitled, too, to assume that there was a reasonable
probability that if deceased had lived she would have been contributing more substantially
to the household than she was doing just before her death.

He gave judgment that the applicant was entitled to recover the sum of 150.-
Leicester Mail, 13th March. 1923.

FACTORY PERILS.
Consumption and the Boot Industry. Interesting Lecture at Kettering.
Although not nearly so large as might have been expected, the company assembling
at the Kettering Corn Market Hall on Tuesday evening to hear Professor Collis lecture
on "Health and Tuberculosis in Industry" was representative and influential.
Mr. Owen Parker, M.P. (ex-President of the National Federation of Shoe Manufac-
turers) occupied the chair, and was supported by Mr. T. F. Richards (General President
of the National Union of Shoe Operatives), and others.

The Chairman said that the vision of those of them who happened to be engaged
in industry had widened considerably during the last few years. He could not conceive
of any industry being justified in its existence and in its development, that did not regard
with seriousness its obligations to all the human factors engaged in it.

Scourge of the Industry.

Professor Collis said tuberculosis had been the scourge of the boot and shoe industry
for long past. The more they came to study it the more did it become borne in upon
them that tuberculosis and health did not agree. "The better the health of the com-
munity," said the Professor, "the more certain is it that tuberculosis recedes." During
the period from the middle of last century the deaths resulting from tuberculosis had
dropped, in the case of men, by more than 50 per cent.; and in the case of women by
about 65 per cent. He felt perfectly confident that by 1950 it would become as rare as
smallpox was now.

Industry as it should be.

The object of industry, he said, was to provide the means of living healthily and the
means for healthy activity; the human body had to be used and exercised in all its functions
to maintain its health. "If you don't do a good day's work," was the Professor's next
dictum, " you can't have a good night's sleep; and if you don't have a good night's sleep,
you can't be a healthy person." One of the defects of modern industrial work was that
it was likely to lose its interest, owing to sub-division; and in few industries was that
tendency more apparent than in the manufacturing of boots and shoes.

In building a factory's machinery, he said, the endeavour should be to make it as easy
as possible for people to work rhythmically. The question of knowing how to work had
something to do with the problem of health. Turning again to tuberculosis, the lecturer
told his audience there was no royal road to clearing that disease out of the boot and shoe
industry. The trouble there was not due, as in some other trades, to dust; for chest
and lung troubles were less in evidence there than elsewhere.

Touching upon the important matter of ventilation, Mr. Collis said the latest figures
published related to 1910-12, and much good work had been done since then. When the
next reports were issued he confidently expected to find a great improvement. In those
old days ventilation and other conditions were not satisfactory.

Comparing general mortality figures in the shce trade with those in other industries,
the lecturer pointed out that between 1890 and 1910 the former only decreased by 23
per cent., as against the latter's 32 per cent. "It is our industrial life," the Professor
declared, "which is holding back the rapid extinction of tuberculosis."

Its prevalence in certain industries he attributed in great measure to the workpeople
engaged therein being so close together. Dust should never be brushed up dry. Phthisis
figures for the period 1890-1910 showed a fall in the shce industry of 25 per cent., and 36
per cent, in others. Dealing with sanatorium treatment, the Professor said it seemed a
pity that when a man was leaving one of those institutions-the disease having become
quiescent-there was no sort of "half-way" occupation available before he resumed his
strenuous work in the factory.

Curable Complaint.

Speaking in a more heartening strain the Professor said: "There is no more curable
disease in the world than consumption, if you only treat it properly; but we will never
do that so long as we take people straight back from the sanatoria to full-time work in the
factory." Industry had got to tackle that problem itself it could not be done out of
State funds. - The Northamptonshire Evening Telegraph, 7th March, 1923.

NO TIME TO WORK.

In America men spend so much time in being efficient that they have no time left in
which to do the work itself. - Mr. Sinclair Lewis, the American novelist.

CO-PARTNERSHIP WORKSHOPS.
Leicester Co-operative Printing Society Ltd.
We beg to submit the Sixtieth Half-Yearly Report and Balance Sheet. The Sales
for the half-year amount to £23,402 15s. 2d., a decrease of £1,333 16s. 9d. compared with
the corresponding period of last year. The total Sales for the year amount to £49,344
16s. 9d, a decrease of £2,407 19s. 8d. compared with the previous year. After providing
for Interest on Share and Loan Capital to the amount of £988 9s. 11d. and depreciating
Fixed Stock, Buildings, &c., £1,026 18s. 5d., we regret to report an adverse balance of
£1,123 14S. 8d. Deducting the balance profit of £80 5s. 2d. brought forward from last
half-year there remains a Net Deficit of £1,043 9s. 6d. to be carried forward.
The Committee regret very much to have to record this serious loss on the half-year's
trading, which is largely due to the decreased turnover, severe competition and other causes
arising from the general condition of trade in the country. Members are assured that a
thorough investigation of the productive and administrative costs of the various depart-
ments and branches is being made, and we are hopeful that by economising in every possible
direction better results will be forthcoming.
BOX DEPARTMENT.--The Sales amount to £5,347, a decrease of £1,131 compared with
the corresponding half-year. This decrease is due to a great extent to the serious depression
in the Boot Trade for which this department caters.
LONDON BRANCH.--Trade has been very good, especially during the latter months
of the period under review.
KETTERING BRANCH.-Trade very slack during the first portion of the half-year,
but a great improvement was shown in the last three months.
Chesham Boot.
The sales for the last half-year were £14,203, and the profit £420. As a loss had been
incurred in the first half of the year this profit was used to cancel it.
Northants Productive.
The sales for the second half of 1922 were £15,018, but owing to the slackening of trade
a loss of £232 is incurred. Interest on Shares was paid out of Reserves and this debt
cancelled also in the same way.
Higham Ferrers.
The sales for the second half of 1922 were £14,824, and the profit was £350. This
was used to pay Interest on Shares £238, and the remaining £121 was added to the Interest
Guarantee Fund.
Sileby "Excelsior."
The sales were £28,126 for the past half-year and the profit £1,923, of which £232
went to Shareholders in Interest and Dividends. Customers received (266, about 2s. in
the £ on purchases, and the workers £620, also about 2s. in the £. According to rule, £89
was allocated to Education Funds, £178 to the Provident Fund and the same amount to
Reserve.
Union Boot Society.
The sales for the latter half of 1922 were £11,689. The profit was £168, of which
£147 went to Shareholders as interest. The granting of certain donations and subscrip-
tions made a final deficit of £79.
Glenfield.
The sales for the past half-year were £12,851, and the profit was £1,048. Interest and
dividend on Shares took £244. Customers received £250, being dividend on purchases
at 4d. in the £ and workers £250, being Is. in the £ on wages. Then ₤25 was added to both
the Education and Provident Funds.

same being pointed out to us, we shall be most happy to give the same prominence to the
correction as to the original matter. As these Reports are exclusively for the use of Members,
the information contained therein must not be divulged.

MONTHLY REPORT.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
TRADE
23RD APRIL, 1923.
does not seem to improve to any extent in the sense of absorbing members in
the factories, judging by the amount of money being paid weekly from our
Unemployment Fund. This is a serious matter, not only from the standpoint
of the Union on account of the continued drain on the funds, but also to the
members themselves who are placed in the unfortunate position of having no
work to do, and we can only hope that we shall be able to report more favour-
ably in the near future.
Owing to a printers' dispute, the Gazette issued by the Ministry of Labour
has not yet come to hand. We regret, therefore, we are unable to print our
usual list of figures in connection with unemployment.

do not hesitate to take full advantage of the improvements secured by the

At Messrs. Allen & Prior a dispute has been in being for about 5 weeks.

LONDON. - The London Branch Officials, along with Mr. T. F. Richards
shall be taken with the firm of Messrs. L. & J. Weber & Phillips Ltd., who,
and Mr. D. McCarthy, have for some time past been considering what action
rather than comply with the National Agreement, resigned their membership

At a meeting of the Board of Conciliation and Arbitration for the

INDUSTRIAL AND POLITICAL.
The past month has seen a good deal of activity both industrially and
politically. Disputes have been threatened in connection with a number of
industries, whilst the one in connection with Agriculture has indeed a tragic
side when one remembers the inadequate sum of money offered to the men
in return for the labour given. We hope that with the backing of the other
Unions they may yet be successful in their efforts to resist the terms which
the employers wish to impose upon them. Should, however, circumstances
be too strong and the Agricultural Labourers have to bow to the circumstances
and resume employment upon the terms offered, it is not too much to say that
such a feeling of resentment will be engendered amongst the men that they
will take an early opportunity to throw off such conditions and not only demand,
but secure such conditions as will enable them to maintain a fair standard of
comfort in their homes.
POLITICALLY the Labour Party has been making things far from tranquil
during the month. They have shown constant vigilance, and it is indeed not

---
too much to say that the effect of the Labour Party in th House of Commons
has been to show up, in clear outline, the injustice the workers are the
victims of. We hope it will so enlighten public opinion upon many questions,
particularly the Land question, Housing, and Unemployment, thereby
making it impossible for the Government to ignore these great and vital
questions. We can only hope our colleagues in the House will be enabled,
by their persistency and the adoption of statesmanlike methods, to secure
by reason, if not, then wring from the Government, more ameliorative
methods to ease the present tense situation which must obtain in thousands
of homes daily.
THE BUDGET, 1923.
Once more the workers are doomed to disappointment owing to the
attitude of the Chancellor of the Exchequer in dealing with the question of
taxation on tea, sugar, cocoa and the breakfast table generally, or by his setting
aside money for social reform. As one daily paper set out on their front page
in large bold headlines, it is "A Mean Budget." The opportunity presented
itself for a determined Chancellor of the Exchequer, despite the heavy taxation
which obtains as a consequence of the War, of helping and assisting the nation
as a whole financially, but rather than that being done we find a number of
smaller proposals the majority of which will leave the workers untouched. We
would refer you to pages 251-253 for a detailed list of the proposals which the
Government suggest putting into operation during the next 12 months. We
can only hope the members will, after perusal of the same, be more and more
convinced of the absolute necessity of sending representatives to the House
of Commons who will see that the policy of the Labour Party is carried out,
and thus help to bring about a better state of affairs both industrially, politically
and financially.
We are glad to note that the leader of the Labour Party, Mr. J. R.
MacDonald, M.P., made the position quite clear that they, the Labour Party,
would propose a number of amendments to the Budget proposals on the lines
of the Labour Party programme. .
MANAGER TO NATIONAL HEALTH INSURANCE DEPARTMENT.
The result of the Voting for the above-named position will be found on
page 244; no one having secured a clear majority, Mr. R. D. Mayes (Leicester
No. 2) and Mr. C. Bleakley (Edinburgh) will go to a second vote to be taken
at the May meeting night. The votes must be counted on the 12th prox. and
returns posted so as to reach the Central Office not later than the first post
on Tuesday, the 15th prox., otherwise they will be disqualified. It will
be observed that we have not recorded the vote polled for Mr. A. G. Randall.
Kingswood. because of Mr. Randall's desire for his name to be withdrawn
from the Ballot Paper. The letter which Mr. Randall states was sent to the
Central Office, intimating his desire to retire, did not, and has not even now,
arrived, and as a consequence his name appeared on the voting paper. When
this became known Mr. Randall, we understand, wrote to the Branches asking

Here is the text from the image:

234
them to delete his name, and as a consequence only a few votes were recorded
for him, which does not affect the position at all. It should, however, be
distinctly understood that any member nominated for Union Office wishing
to retire must acquaint the General Secretary of the fact so that he can give
instructions for the necessary action to be taken rather than nominees writing
to the Branches themselves.

A GREAT TRADE UNION EXPERIMENT.
The beginning of May will see a development of Labour journalism which
will mark an epoch in the Trade Union and Labour movement. The significance
of the forthcoming effort is very little realised by the Trade Unions, and not
at all, so far, by the general public. For the first time, a systematic attempt
will be made to utilise the Trade Union machinery of the country and to transfer
from Capitalist to Labour organisations the immense power, to say nothing
of the material resources, represented by the modern daily Press.

The Herald has made many appeals to the Trade Unions. It has never,
until now, been able to appeal on the ground that the paper is the property
of the Unions; run by them, they being responsible for it. For this has
recently become a fact. And it is a fact which changes the whole situation.
For Trade Union machinery can now be used in a way in which it would not
have been possible when the paper was not Trade Union property.

The Joint Committee appointed by the General Council of the Trades
Union Congress and the Executive Committee of the Labour Party, have been
considering how the new relationship of the Unions to the paper can be best
turned to account.

The possibilities of the thing have been stated by various writers. There
are, at a moderate computation, five million workers organised in Trade Unions.
If each accepted it as a bit of loyalty owed to his Union to “take our own
daily first," that would mean a potential newspaper circulation of several
millions, sufficient, that is, to make half a dozen large newspapers financial,
successes virtually the day that they started. What is so terrifically costly
about the establishment of a newspaper is not the machinery. It is the gaining
of circulation—running at a loss, that is, during the usually long period when
there is not sufficient circulation for the paper to pay. If Trade Unionists
took their own papers, the really big circulations of the country would be
those of the Labour dailies. Think for a moment what the gain of power and
influence would be if half a dozen of the largest dailies in the country were
Labour-owned and Labour-controlled !

Well, it is this preliminary “act of loyalty” which the Trade Unions
and the Labour Party have now undertaken to organise, in a systematic way.

THE ENLARGED “DAILY HERALD.”
The first step, of course, is to bring into being a paper which, as an organ
of news and entertainment, will compare with existing daily newspapers.
This, to be quite frank, the Daily Herald has not been in the past. It had not

WATCH PARLIAMENT. “RABBIT HUTCH" BILL TO-DAY.
Parliament is to give its time to-day and to-morrow to a discussoin of one of the
nation's most crying needs-the provision of new houses in order that people may have
room to live.
The form which this discussion will be obliged to take, is a debate on the Govern-
ment's "Rabbit Hutch" Bill !
We criticised this Bill very unfavourably, when it first appeared; and further reflection
has not sweetened our feelings about it. We agree with the opinion expressed in the
current number of The Builder-a technical organ not chargeable with party bias-" it
will be rightly considered that any Government that can contemplate such a measure
is a public danger."
The Bill fixes a minimum and a maximum size for the new houses. The maximum
size rules out a parlour, unanimous as is the desire of working people to have one; it can
at most include three small bedrooms. The minimum size will barely allow for two,
that the inhabitants can " swing a cat in."
Has it not long since been agreed on all hands, that three bedrooms is essential for
the decent housing of a mixed family?
It is a shabby, undemocratic Bill. It flouts alike the science of Public Health and
the decent feeling of common people. No self-respecting Cabinet could adopt it.
The question is not one of parties or of persons. It is a great human question, in
which the electorate are directly and vitally interested.
Public opinion can win. Nothing else can. It will be a poor showing for our
democracy if the electors sit down tamely under such a contemptuous challenge to their
direct interests, both public and private. - Daily Chronicle, 23rd April, 1923.

FELLOW MEMBERS,

told me in London on the 12th inst., that they were paying out that night. Although
our Branch on my advice had paid out, arrangements had been made for the men to hand
Arbitration to those who have little confidence, and even some of those who proffer con-

their amounts over to the Officials. This has been a long job, too long to encourage

working under protest the same shall be dealt with within twelve days.
I am still pressing the Employers for the Back Pay for the Rushden and Welling-

ROSSENDALE VALLEY UNION.—Delegates to the Southport Trades Congress will
remember that the Delegate from the Rossendale Slipper Union, taking advantage of a
debate, charged our Union with blacklegging. An attempt was made by one of our
delegates to defend the Union, but such a large assembly refused to be drawn into a con-
Council to take the matter up and a hearing was granted last week by the Disputes Com-
troversy, as many have told me since. But the charge remains, and we asked the General
mittee. We put up the following case:-
The Secretary of the Society having wired us in July that the dispute was satisfactorily
settled we hold it the acme of meanness to have sprung a complaint on an assembly two
months afterwards. During such time they could and should have complained, had they
thought we were guilty, but the facts are that a certain firm sent work to Northampton,
Uppers only, and we were at once, both myself and Mr. Len Smith, advised to stop this
blacklegging. I saw the lady who had taken the work out, and found that the people
were working daywork on a minimum of nine girls, only two belonged to our Union.
My colleagues in Northampton, four out of the six, at one time or another made themselves
acquainted with the particulars and came to the conclusion that the work was sent for the
purpose of getting it done better, Rossendale Valley work being poor in quality, low in
grade. The fact that the Union calls itself a Slipper Union indicates that we, as a Union,
have never feared their competition and ability, and as a result are satisfied that it would
be next to impossible for Northampton to blackleg a town who are accustomed to make
all leather uppers at all times. One gentleman, who was their greatest asset, told a Govern-
ment Official in our hearing that they did not pretend to be Shoemakers in the general
sense as they were capable of making shoes out of envelopes. An opponent had since
written saying he was prepared to either prove the charge or withdraw it. Council
thought the matter should be pressed to the General Council of the Trades Union Congress,
and with Mr. Lyne, we put the case before the Committee, and although the absurd pro-
position was put up that these women get 70s. against our women's 40s., we produced the
wages for Northampton and Rossendale Valley as published by the Board of Trade Gazette,
and showed that the town that claimed our rates was from 25 per cent. to 50 per cent.
less than them for the last fourteen months, and had actually received less wages per
head, per week. They said that maybe short time would make a difference; we say that
as their stuff is all cheap—none cheaper—there is a greater public demand for such, than
for our better and costlier stuff. The Committee did not fail to hint that his method of
approach was not good, neither was his treatment at Southport, and we have now had the
findings of the Committee, who after putting our case and the Rossendale charges, register
the result as follows:-
"Looking to the fact that the dispute was settled at least four months before the
matter was raised at the Southport Congress, and that no definite details could be given
of any cases arising since the settlement in May, your Committee did not consider it
necessary to record any decision; but recommended that in the event of any further
cases arising between the two organisations, they should agree to deal with them promptly
and in a friendly spirit." I have sent to the Secretary, Mr. C. W. Bowerman, M.P., a
letter asking him to postpone reporting to the General Council, if possible, until after the
21st, that is, until after the Council of the Union has considered the Committee's lack of
of Mr. Taylor, the Secretary of the Rossendale Slipper Union, for his unfounded charge

FELLOW MEMBERS,
At the meeting of the Council on 26th March it was agreed to that I should spend
the month from that date organising in Leicestershire and London. The Easter holidays
were longer than usual owing to slackness of trade, and little could be done in the way of
organising during this period. I don't know how many members may be gained to the
Cosby Section as a result of our efforts, but 16 were added to them before Easter. The
gains in propaganda work counts for something else as well as increasing membership.
Members are reminded of their obligations in regards to working to agreements, and seeing
that they are faithfully observed.

With the President of the London Metropolitan Branch I visited ten factories-some
of them twice trying to win the defaulters over to the Union. Besides this work we
saw employers over special grievances of members and held shops meetings at night to
deal with complaints. At one meeting we held the President and Secretary of the Branch
were present, and the subject was the changing from piecework to weekly wages. The
members were given instructions to take the piecework rates strictly as their basis of
reckoning, and they pledged themselves to do so. There is an awful fear over our members
going through. I wish that
in claiming their rights on account of the bad times we are
some of the rich Anti-Socialists who speak of the tyranny that will be imposed on the
workers if Socialism comes had to work and live on their wages in a boot factory for one
year.
D. MCCARTHY.

The past month has not been one of great activity in Kingswood, as what with the
state of trade, which is bad, and the holidays intervening, the opportunities for any move-
ment have been greatly restricted. But we have kept things on the move as far as possible.
There is one matter about which satisfaction can be expressed, that is, we have got through
the first skirmish in a satisfactory manner. After being out for about five weeks the
workpeople have resumed work at Allen & Prior's on terms which can be said to be com-
pletely satisfactory. There was a certain amount of regret felt that we should have had
trouble at this firm, which in the past had always conformed to our conditions, and one
hopes now that matters are adjusted, we shall find everything working smoothly in
future.

There has also been a slight improvement in regard to the Holiday Scheme. The
Federation have tackled the question with the result that it has been agreed to put same
into operation for April, May and June, during which time we are expected to bring into
line every non-Federated firm.

While I suppose we are compelled to welcome this as a slight advance, yet it must be
obvious to all concerned that the months named, are almost the worst so far as trade is
concerned in this district, and that it is idle to think we can do all we would wish under
such conditions. But while this is so, I think I am but stating a fact when I say, that so
far as the Union is concerned there will be no looking back on this question. Whatever
the effort needed, whatever the cost may be, we shall face it and we shall win. All we ask
of our friends on the other side, who have equal responsibility with ourselves in this question,
that they will give all the active support possible, to the efforts we are making.

One thing is certain at the moment, we have convinced some of the Employers here
we are in earnest, and this has had its effect in a way satisfactory to us.

I may perhaps add, when at home during the Easter Holidays, my advice and assist-
ance were sought in connection with the Agricultural Labourers' dispute in Norfolk. This
I gladly gave, as I am certain these men have the good wishes and support of every member
of our Union. They are making a splendid 'fight, the determination shown by both men
and women being of the highest order.

It would be a splendid thing for the whole movement if these people, the lowest and
worst paid, were to be the ones to successfully resist the attack made upon the wages of

16th April, 1923.

WALTER R. SMITH.

BRANCH REPORTS.
ARBROATH. It becomes tiresome to state month after month that
trade is bad, but in the interest of truth an accurate report is of more con-
sequence than an attempt to put a rosy complexion on the industrial situation
obtaining in this locality. If any member of the Union is finding their
bank book growing into uncomfortably large dimensions then this district
can be recommended as affording most suitable conditions for reducing it again
to proportions which remove the need for burglar-proof safes or other protective
devices of similar purpose. A swollen balance soon wilts and withers when
subjected to a spell of the leisurely life of the shoeworker on the East Coast of
Scotland. It can hardly be wondered at that good trade here- if ever it is to
happen-suggests terrors scarcely less real than those confronting the operatives
as things are. Given a change for the better the difficulty of knowing how to
apportion the weekly income without incurring the wrath of landlord, grocer,
tailor, milkman, &c., &c., all of whom will no doubt think they should come
first in the reckoning is one of those problems which will produce more grey
hairs than any other experience yet encountered. We have often cause to
regret the legacy of the past, but in this instance the legacy will be a hydra-
headed monster of the most forbidding appearance, and its name D.E.Β.Τ.,
will make D.O.R.A. shrink into insignificance. Emigration is still active
here and more and more members are finding it possible to avail themselves
of this "open-door"-let us hope to fortune--and the pity of it is the young
and the gay and the best are those who find it easiest to go. God speed to
them, and may their hopes receive a rich reward. Those who are left must
face the future with the best heart possible, and somehow a compensation
may materialise which will soften the blows of fate. The ordinary work of the
branch proceeds as best it can under such depressing conditions, but luckily
no disputes or other troubles arise to add to other worries. All the Union
conditions are faithfully observed by all our manufacturers, or if some small
irregularity crops up, the best spirit is always shown in having it discussed
and corrected. Long may we remain as free from trade troubles, and
long may manufacturers of the better sort do as Mr. H. J. Bostock did the
cther day when he administered that well-merited rebuke to the "bolshevist
bosses" of Kingswood. Our members were pleased with the way our
Council gave prominence in their last month's Address to such a remarkable
utterance, and if such leadership continues we feel sure the Boot and Shoe
Manufacturers' Federation will some day or other be making unconditional
grants of funds to the National Union in order to provide greater strength
to us in the work of making our industry the freest from selfisli and inhuman
exploitation.
BARNSLEY. - Trade still keeps very bad here, men on short time.
We are pleased to say that we have a clean sick list once more, and hope
to remain so.
BELFAST.-Trade continues to remain very bad.
CHESHAM. - Trade here is very bad, in fact men who have spent their
whole lives in the trade cannot remember anything approaching the slack
time we are now experiencing. Our local manufacturers are complaining
about the unfair and cutting competition they have to meet from the Kings-
wood Area, and we are watching the Council's efforts to bring some of these
manufacturers into line. We regret to report Mr. P. Bradley, our nominee,
was unsuccessful at the poll in our local U.D.C. election, but we have the
consolation of a Labour gain of two seats upon that body.

some years on the Branch Executive and an earnest trade unionist. He was
taken ill about the time of the 1921 Conference and had to return home before

LEICESTER No. 1.-We are pleased to report that we have had the

LIVERPOOL.--Boot repairing has shown marked signs of improvement

the workers are quite justified when they get below what is reasonable and fair
in resisting the same to the best of their ability.
MAYBOLE - We are sorry to report trade very slack, most of our members

they would like.

NOTTINGHAM.—Trade still very quiet. We had a special meeting
early in the month and the General President attended for the purpose of
explaining the desire of Council to set up a District Board for Derby, Mansfield
and Nottingham. After a general discussion and a number of questions bad
been answered, it was agreed to fall in with Council's view, and our President,
Mr. A. Goodwin, was elected for this town.
PLYMOUTH.—Trade is still quiet and although there is very little
prospect of immediate improvement, there are signs that the slump has reached
zero, and with the coming of Spring the trade barometer will begin to rise
gradually to a more comfortable and congenial level. We do not anticipate
any more discharges through slackness of trade, or any further extension of
short time, neither do we desire or anticipate many more of our members
appearing under the doleful heading of "Members Scratched," but will look
forward with confidence to a list of recruits and veterans appearing under the
heading "New and Re-entered." The last two years has been a real testing
time, but we are pleased to report that the spirit of comradeship has never
been better displayed or the value of our Union membership so indisputably
demonstrated. This has meant food for the present and hope for the future.
SHEPSHED.—Trade is getting worse. One of the three firms here has
closed down for a period, the factories being full of stock.
SOUTHAMPTON.—Trade has a tendency to improvement. It is very
slight up to the present, but yet sufficient to make us a little more hopeful.

NOTICE TO BRANCH SECRETARIES.

WAR AGAINST WAR.

Will all Branch Secretaries who have not remitted cash nor
returned the postcards, kindly do so AT ONCE to enable the
Account to be closed.
E. L. POULTON,
General Secretary.

THE WORKERS AND WAR.

"Working folk do not make war—they have never done that—and I wish sometimes
that working folk would declare that they would take no part in warfare on any account
whatever," said Mr. Ben Turner, M.P., in the House of Commons on 21st March. It is
a hopeful sign for future world peace that working folk in this country and throughout
the world are declaring that they will never again take part in warfare on any account
whatever.
The No More War Movement in this country, which is the British section of the War
Resisters' International, is composed of men and women who have pledged themselves
never to take part in war, whatever the ostensible object may be. Members of the Move-
ment are also pledged to " strive for the removal of all causes of war, and to work for the
establishment of a new social order based on co-operation for the common good." The
Chairman of the Movement is George Lansbury, M.P.
All interested in this vital question should write to the Secretary, No More War
Movement, 304, High Holborn, London, W.C. I.

LABOUR MOVES REJECTION OF HOUSING BILL.
Mr. Chamberlain's Views on Parlours. Indignant M.P.'s.
Mr. Neville Chamberlain, the Minister of Health, rose amid Ministerial cheers, to move
the second reading of the Government's Housing Bill.
"Great masses of our people," he said, "are unable to find separate dwellings. They
are herded together without privacy, without comfort, without almost the ordinary
decencies of life.
"The effect of this overcrowding are far-reaching and constitute a perpetual danger
to the physical and moral health of the community."
These conditions, he went on, are responsible for much unrest and social discontent
although he was bound to say that one must be filled with admiration for the patience
with which, for the most part, these evils were borne. (Hear, hear.)
Every consideration of humanity must impel them to the conclusion that there was
no question more urgent, none that cried more loudly for immediate attention, than this
of housing.
The important thing, he said, was that they should begin their work upon lines which
were capable of growth and development, and as far as possible try to avoid artificial
devices which could not go on indefinitely.
"Only a Beginning."
He asked the House, therefore, to regard this Bill, not as a solution of the housing
problem, but as a beginning of a solution; not as an end in itself, but as a starting apparatus
which would put the engine in motion.
The arrears in house building which had accumulated during a period of 13 years
could not possibly be wiped out in the short period covered by the Bill.
They must not merely reinstate the small builder, but restore or replace the machinery
by which alone he was able to carry on his operations. Private enterprise was beginning
once more. During the last six months upwards of 12,000 of such houses had been com-
pleted, and another 16,000 were in course of erection.
It was perfectly true, added Mr. Chamberlain, that most of those houses were of a
superior class-(Labour cries of "Oh!")-suitable for middle classes.
The present process, he admitted, was bound to be a slow and gradual one, and there
still remained a considerable margin which for some years to come it would be impossible
for private enterprise to cover.
Coming to the provisions of the Bill, Mr. Chamberlain said he had been criticised
for giving too much and for giving too little; but the local authorities whom he consulted
were satisfied, and, as they said, it was up to them to see it carried through.
He was afraid, proceeded the Minister of Health, that he himself was responsible for
the confusion that had arisen by the introduction of the word "parlour" house, because he
spoke of a subsidy house as a "non-parlour house."
It appeared to have been thought that he had some prejudice against the parlour,
as such, that he desired to deprive children of a room for studying, and sweethearts of a
room to court in-(laughter)-and generally to lower the standard of working-class accom-
modation. He very much doubted whether the activities of sweethearts would be hindered
through the absence of a parlour.
There was considerable interruption at this point, Mr. David Kirkwood and some
other Labour members expressing their indignation at the tone of Mr. Chamberlain's
remarks.
The member for Dumbarton interrupted several times, and was shouted down. The
Speaker also intervened.
When the Minister lightly remarked that a room 1oft. 6in. by 9ft. 3in. was "big
enough for courting," Mr. Kirkwood sprang to his feet and, amid considerable noise from
the other side of the House, exclaimed: "What does he mean? What kind of language
is that?"
Mr. Chamberlain said hon. members would have ample opportunity of expressing
their views later. He gathered from their observations that the space allowed was insuffi-
cient to permit the inclusion of parlours in the houses contemplated. (Labour cheers.)
That was not so, because houses were being built to-day which came within the
limits which did provide parlours.
Passing on to the subsidy provisions of the Bill, Mr. Chamberlain said he was convinced
that under them they would get a number of houses built in the course of the next few
years.
The powers it was proposed to give local authorities to facilitate building without
State assistance were explained in detail, as well as the other clauses of the Bill.


---
Appalling Conditions.
Mr. Wheatley (Lab., Shettleston), in moving the Labour amendment, said the Minister
did not understand the gravity and extent of the housing problem, and had no sympathy
with the people (Ministerialists: Oh, oh!) - whose needs he was endeavouring to provide
for.
The problem was really a financial one, and was intertwined with the problem of
wealth and poverty.
There was in Glasgow a waiting list of 20,000 families who had never known what it
was to have a home of their own, but led a sort of vagrant life in furnished lodgings. Slums,
though condemned, could not be cleared, because there were no other homes for the people.
The standard of housing in Glasgow was abominably low. Sixty per cent. of the
families lived in two-apartment dwellings, and three families had to share the sanitary
accommodation. In Lanarkshire it was even worse.
"I was one of eleven," he continued, "who lived for years in a single-apartment
dwelling in Lanarkshire, and I could shock even hon. members opposite by a narrative
of what life under those conditions meant."
Surely the time had come not merely for a beginning of a solution (Mr. Chamberlain's
description of his Bill), but for a solution itself.
How the Shortage Arose.
The housing shortage did not originate with the war. There had been a scarcity
since 1910, and it was due to the operations of rings and combines in the building trade.
Between 1910 and 1913 the cost of building rose 60 per cent.
He considered that the price of land was not the main factor, though he would like to
see the abolition of private property in land, because it enabled private persons to prevent
the satisfaction of the people's needs.
Rings and combines were the inevitable result of the competitive system: they were
the combination of the survivors in the struggle, and would not be destroyed under
Capitalism. How could they expect a monopolist in, say, chemicals, to destroy a com-
bination in cement?
The remedy to which the country would be driven, even at the cost of shedding a
Conservative Government, would be the manufacturing and merchanting of building
materials by the State.
You will have to produce homes for heroes by the same methods as you produced
shells for heroes."
Passing on to the financial aspect of the Bill, Mr. Wheatley expressed the opinion
that 5 per cent. would have to be paid on the capital for housing. That would mean a
burden of £25 a year on the smallest type of the houses to be provided.
Not Enough Labour.
There was not enough skilled labour in the country to build the houses that were
needed. That was because the operations of the rings, having restricted building, many
skilled men had emigrated.
The right remedy would be to assure the youths who were ready to enter the trade
that there would be plenty of work for them in providing the houses that were needed.
Yet this Bill was to operate merely for two years.
There was no need to stimulate the local authorities in this matter. He only wished
the Government was as enthusiastic for housing as were even the Conservative members
of the local authorities throughout the country.
Drawing towards the close of a speech which was as forcible as it was comprehensive,
Mr. Wheatley argued that it would be necessary to charge the tenants of the houses that
would result from this Rill £10 a year to cover rent and rates- "and yet," he exclaimed,
"you have reduced many of the working classes to an income of not more than £100
a year!"
He objected to the Minister's proposals on slum-clearing. The owner of slums should
not be better treated than the vendor of bad meat. He should be compelled to clear
them at his own cost.
"The houses," he declared with warmth, "will be miserably small. The Minister
must have shocked even his own supporters when he talked of rooms roft. 6in. by 9ft. 3in.
These houses will never be homes; they will be slums. He has proceeded on the assump
tion that the working classes have no friends and do not want a place to entertain them.
The Minister was laying down a standard for 50 years to come, and asking Parliamen-
tary acceptance for the permanency of class distinctions.
"Why should you object to the preaching of class war? What do you do in all your
legislation?" (Labour cheers and Tory protests.)
"All these proposals emanate from people who believe in their souls that this country
is a spent force, and that all you require is a temporary measure to house people till they
can be shipped overseas; but fortunately for Britain, and for the human race, the control
of this country and the British Empire is passing rapidly out of the hands of those who
can bring in a measure like this."
(Loud Labour cheers.)
---

---
"I do not think the Government has ever been convinced of the terrible circumstances
under which the mass of our population is living," said Mr. Rhys Davies (Lab., West-
houghton).
What the Census Revealed.
The London County Council had conducted a census in London, which showed that
2.433,136 persons had less than one room each to live in.
On the very night that the census was taken, it was found there were 18,969 empty
houses in London, with 101,554 vacant rooms.
The Minister of Health ought to have inserted a clause in the Bill to deal with the
atrocious system that allowed the landlord to hold houses vacant, free of rates, in the vast
majority of cases.
Sir Alfred Mond (N.L., Swansea, W.) approved of the general lines of the Bill, but
regretted Mr. Chamberlain had not produced a bolder scheme.
Sir Kingsley Wood (U., Woolwich, W.), while considering that this was an excellent
Bill in many respects, made the stock allegation, that the men engaged on building work
had in many cases curtailed output. Where only 300 bricks a day were laid instead of
000, it meant, declared the speaker, attempting to prove by mere assertion, that the
workers who had to occupy these houses had to pay no less than is. 6d. a week increased
rent.
"It is not mere sympathy the Labour Party wants," declared Mr. Kirkwood (Lab.,
Dumbarton). "We want houses, not rabbit hutches."
While medical authorities were fearing that pestilence would arise because of inadequate
housing accommodation, the Minister of Health had had the brazen audacity to propose
in cold blood the type of house proposed under the scheme.
"If this," Mr. Kirkwood went on, in loud, scornful tones, "had been a zoo of wild
men who had never been near civilisation they would know just as much about the lives
and ideals of the people whose houses are being discussed.
"These things are as foreign to the gentleman who made those statements as if he
had come from Borneo!" (Loud laughter.)
The Minister of Health had said that these houses were for " a certain class:"
"That's my class, sir, and I am as good as he is, mentally or physically. I make
that challenge to the entire class that he represents. We are not going to take this lying
down any longer from the Government of this country. The day is past.
"We stand on an equal footing with all the right honourables and gallant gentlemen
that ever filled the House of Commons, and they will have to remember and not talk in
that flippant manner, because it's not going to be tolerated."
In Clydebank and Dumbarton they were not content with £6 for 20 years; they
wanted ₤12 for 60 years.
They were not asking for sympathy or brotherly love. Could there be " brotherly
love" between the man who could not get shelter for his children and the men who had
two or three hundred apartments in a house?
The Minister of Health was the man of the moment who was supposed to be going
to lead this Government out of the wilderness of Sinai and into the plains of Palestine.
It was all Dead Sea fruit'
He asked Mr. Chamberlain to go over the Bill again to see if it were possible to grapple
with this problem in the way Mr. Lloyd George grappled with the munitions problem in
the early days of the war, having always in mind that fundamental principle that every
father and mother in the country should have a home. Otherwise, it was the end of the
road, and of the Tory Government and any other Government that stood betwixt the
people and better houses.
Mr. Macpherson (N.L., Ross and Cromarty) said the Bill would receive no support
from Liberal Scottish members unless there was a reconsideration of the subsidy and a
guarantee that every house to be built in Scotland should have a larger space for parlour
houses.
Exceptional Praise.
A speech that brought exceptional applause from all parts of the House came from
Mr. J. Stewart (Lab., St. Rollox.)
"We should scrap this bad house for a better house," he declared, proceeding to
show how bad housing had affected the development of the people in Glasgow.
"Watch the places where the people are who work only when an employer will engage
them. Watch the height of the boys on the corner-a little over five feet, something in
keeping with the stature of myself and of the same physique. Watch the women-flat-
chested, without any development.
"Then come to Saucichall Street or Buchanan Street, well-to-do places, and you
will see an entirely different type of woman- well-developed, because they are living
under decent conditions, giving them an opportunity to develop.
"That is the price you are paying." - Daily Herald, 25th April, 1923.

"FEARFUL TAX TO PUT UPON THE PEOPLE."
Sugar Deputation to the Financial Secretary.
Mr. Lander's Telling Speech.
An unanswerable case for reduction of the sugar tax was put to the Financial Secretary
to the Treasury last week by a deputation of co-operative representatives, who stated
the claims of the consumers.
The deputation waited upon the Financial Secretary to the Treasury (Major A.
Boyd-Carpenter, M.P.) at the House of Commons, on Wednesday, 21st March, 1923, at
4.30 p.m.
Mr. A. V. Alexander submitted that from actual co-operative experience and from
their actual trading returns, the people who are most urgently in need of relief in regard
to taxation to-day are the working-classes, whose standard of life has been so depressed
on account of enormous wage reductions and unemployment.
The burden of a tax like that upon sugar (25s. 8d. per cwt. as compared with Is. Iod.
before the war) was surely out of all proportion to the position of the wage-earners and
their purchasing power.
Mr. Lander said they had great hopes last year, and had been informed that this
was one of the taxes which would receive consideration and be reduced. He gave figures
which showed, with a consumption of sugar amounting to three million cwts., and the
consumption in the factories of another quarter-of-a-million, they had paid tax amounting
to £3,511,993. It meant that the present tax upon sugar added about 80 per cent. to the
value of the imported article. It was an extraordinarily high figure for any one com-
modity to bear. It put up the value to the consumer. It enabled the refiner to take not
only a profit on the imported article, but a profit on the tax - to the disadvantage of the
consumer. It became in that way doubly onerous. It made a tax on the raw material
and a tax on the merchant. He wished to emphasise the point that it bore the heaviest
on the working classes of the country, and they were the people who could least stand the
heavy burden that was put upon them.
Further, it would be interesting to note that prior to the war, 1913, including the
tax, which was then Is. Iod., the standard price for granulated sugar was running
in the neighbourhood of 15s. 9d. per cwt. for the whole of the year. To-day, the
quotation for the same sugar, with a 25s. 8d. tax upon it, is 61s. wholesale. That
is 400 per cent. over 1913.
People realised that sugar is an essential food. The fact had been proved by the
consumption. One would have thought that people would not have bought it at its present
price, but sensible people buy those things which are essential and necessary. He showed
that in 1914 the consumption of foreign sugar per head of the population was 96 lbs. per
annum. It fell during 1916 and the following war years. (He would add that the co-
operative movement were entitled to consideration for helping the Government during
that difficult time in handling sugar). In 1922 the consumption had come back to 91 lbs.
-only 5 lbs. difference! It was a fearful tax to put upon the people, which represented
17s. 6d. per head of the whole of the entire population of the United Kingdom. That
was what the sugar tax meant to-day.
With Reference to Industry.
Everyone was anxious to get over the present time of unemployment. What was
happening in the industrial world so far as sugar was concerned? It entered largely
into the production of many articles which are necessary. For the purposes of illustration,
he would mention jam. Jam was a good food. They had national authority for that,
because the Government during the war were tremendously anxious that the people
should do two things-eat more bread and eat more jam. What was the position of jam
to-day? Everyone knew of the losses which had been taking place. The Co-operative
Wholesale Society had four factories at the present time, and had increased their factories
at the request of the Government during the war. The price of jam was affected very
seriously by the price of sugar, the largest constituent in the making of jam. At the
present time the jam factories were either closed down or on short time, and carrying
large stocks. That would affect the agricultural problem. The fruit question and the
agricultural question would be affected if the price of sugar was so high that neither jam
manufacturers nor the housewives could afford to make jam. The consequence of this
is that we have people going to the Labour Exchanges and on the streets looking for
work.


---
259
Major Boyd-Carpenter's Reply.
Major Boyd-Carpenter, in replying, admitted all that had been said with regard
to the value of sugar as a food. There was this, however, to be said, that among all the
competing interests who are pleading for a reduction of taxation, there is still the necessity
of carrying on the finance of the country. To take d. off sugar would mean a
loss of six millions revenue or more; to take 1d. off would mean twelve-
and-a-half millions; and to abolish it altogether would mean a loss of
over thirty-five millions, and he did not think that even the most
generous-minded Chancellor could contemplate that figure with equa-
nimity, I can assure you that the Chancellor is anxious to get a collective opinion from
all interests concerned, and in his final judgment, he will give weight, not to particular
interests or political considerations, but he will consider, first, what is feasible; second,
what is right; and third, what gives most adequate relief with the limited amount of
surplus at his disposal, if there is any. - Co-operative News, 31st March, 1923.
MR. POULTON AND THE EIGHT-HOUR DAY.
Mr. E. L. Poulton, J. P., who has just returned from Geneva, where he has attended
the Quarterly Meeting of the International Labour Office in connection with the League
of Nations, has again been prominent in his efforts on behalf of the workers generally.
At the outset, Mr. Poulton raised the question of the British Government not carrying
out the Agreement made at the Washington Convention relative to the eight-hour day
and moved a resolution thereon. The matter was discussed for a session and a half, and
ultimately Mr. Poulton withdrew his resolution when one of his French colleagues, M.
Jouhaux, suggested that a Special Commission be appointed, consisting of nine delegates,
three from the Governments represented at the International Labour Office, three from
the Employers' side, and three from the Workers' side, and Mr. Poulton was elected as
one of the Workers' Representatives. This Committee will discuss and make suggestions
to meet the objections which have been found to obtain in the carrying
out of the eight-hour clause.
The Annual Conference usually held in Geneva in October will be of short duration
this year on account of the financial situation of the Office. In addition to the Directors'
Report, items will be dealt with in reference to the Inspection of Factories and "Safety
First " in factories at the October meeting, and a larger Convention will be held in May,
1024. It was decided that, at the meeting to be held later on in this year, the question
of night work in Bakeries and Anthrax should also be dealt with.
LISTENINGS IN.
During 1922 the C.W.S. estimate the amount of duty paid to the Government, directly
and indirectly, and included in the price of sugar, jams, sweets, canned fruits, tea, coffee,
tobacco, and dried fruits as £7,685,326, or 41.94 of the value of the trade, or 8s. 5d. in the £.
*
8s. 5d. in the £
is the rate of tax paid by the people on their food. In 1922 the C.W.S. paid
£7,685,326
in taxation on such everyday necessaries as sugar, sweets, jam, tea,
coffee, cocoa, tobacco, and dried fruits. The value of these articles sold
by the C.W.S. was £18,324,022, so that out of every £1 spent 8s. 5d.
goes in taxation.
*
*
Co-operators pay even more income tax than other people. They pay the ordinary
dues as they are liable, and, in addition, they pay at the highest scale on the land and
property they hold collectively, even though their individual incomes are below the limit.
*
*
As for dividend on purchases, donations to hospitals, education grants, and so on-
well, that is not income and that is the point which the amateur tax-gatherers don't
or won't see.
*
The poor man buys insurance by weekly payments. The rich man saves money by
paying his cheque quarterly. Why not tax him on this extra "income"? We can.
imagine what the F.R.I. would say about it.

AN INSANITARY VILLAGE IN LEICESTERSHIRE.
One of the most insanitary of the big villages in Leicestershire, viz., Earl Shilton,
has neither a sewerage nor a sewage disposal system, nor has it any creditable system of
sanitation. The consequences are that preventable diseases have been endemic in it for
the last quarter of a century. Yet neither the Hinckley Rural District Council, in whose
area it lies, nor the Leicestershire County Council, both of which bodies are somewhat
diffident in sanitary administration, appear to recognise that the responsibility for the
high death-rate which prevails lies on their shoulders. According to the Leicester Mercury,
the Rural Council is frequently "tinkering " with the drainage of the place, and quite
recently were indulging in an " improvement scheme " which revealed the fact that house
drains in many cases had been laid into the public road and not connected to the main
drain, and that sewage springs periodically burst out. The sewage of the village is dis-
charged on to a field without any systematic treatment, and not only pollutes the stream
The Hinckley Rural District Council should act as other Sanitary Authorities do, and
obtain the advice of sewerage engineers to help them to deal with the existing insanitary
condition, failing which the Ministry of Health will, we are confident, feel it their duty
to intervene.-Municipal Engineering and Sanitary Record.
[The above is strong evidence for the justification of the Council in taking the action
they have done, for a long time past, in connection with the Earl Shilton district, and its
bad and inadequate insanitary arrangements, with its consequent effects upon the health
of the people. We can only hope this one more testimony, coming from such a source,
will have the effect of inducing the Authorities to take proper steps to deal with this
important question in an adequate manner.-E.L.P., G.S.]

INDUSTRIES OF BELGIUM.
Boot and Glove Industries.
In the boot industry, after complete stagnation during the early part of 1922, the
situation showed gradual improvement, and although, in the latter part of the year,
business was slow and only orders for immediate delivery were given, the position on the
whole may be described as satisfactory.
In this market the home industry has to meet strong foreign competition. The total
value of the import trade was 15.1 million francs, the principal sources of supply being
France (164 tons), Germany (120 tons), the United Kingdom (112 tons), United States
(21 tons), Switzerland (15 tons) and Austria (12 tons). The export trade was valued at
only 2.8 million francs, the principal markets being France, the Netherlands, the United
Kingdom, Norway and the Congo.
In contradistinction to the boot industry, the glove industry has an important export
trade, and goods were exported to a value of 9.3 million francs, as compared with imports
valued at 2.2 million francs. The bulk of the exports were absorbed by the United King-
dom and the United States, whose shares amounted to 6.3 and 2.7 million francs respectively.
France, the Netherlands and Italy also took small consignments. The import trade was
principally in French hands, the trade with Germany and the United Kingdom being
comparatively small. - The Financier, 17th April, 1923.
