MONTHLY REPORT.
28TH MAY, 1923.
TRADE
has slightly improved during the month. The figures recorded in the Gazette
issued by the Ministry of Labour are set out hereunder :-
BOOT AND SHOE TRADE.
Employement during April showed an improvment in most of the Midland centres,
but a decline in the Bristol and Kingswood district, and in the Leeds district. Taking one
district with another it showed little change as compared with March, and was still slack.
Short time was still prevalent, especially in the heavy boot trade.
Employment at Leicester continued fair, and was better than in April of last year.
At Northampton it showed an improvement, but was still slack. It was bad at Welling-
borough, and worse than in March. At Kettering it was poor, with much short time.
At Stafford it was very fair, some overtime being worked. At Norwich there was much
variation as between one firm and another; on the whole there was a slight improvement.
There was a decline in the Bristol and Kingswood district and in the Leeds district, where
employment in the heavy boot trade was very quiet. Employment continued fair in the
shoe and slipper trade of the Rossendale Valley.
at Glasgow, where it was described as fair.
In Scotland employment continued bad, except at Kilmarnock, and with some firms
The percentage of workpeople unemployed in the boot, shoe and slipper-making and
repairing trades, as indicated by the unemployment books lodged at Employment Ex-
changes was 8.5 on the 23rd April, as compared with 8.6 per cent, on the 26th March.

The exports of boots and shoes in April, 1923, amounted to 64,507 dozen pairs, or

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION CASES.
We have pleasure in reporting that for one of our members, J., of
Northampton, we have secured during the month the sum of £200 for the
loss of his Thumb.
A further case, in London, has been settled during the month, A.L., of
the London Metro. Branch, having secured through the efforts of the Union
Solicitor, Mr. Evan Barlow, £50 and £5 5s. towards the costs.
We would again remind members that lump sums are NOT OBTAINABLE
by law, but only by agreement. Despite the many statements made through
the Monthly Reports, members have still an erroneous idea upon this subject.
ARBITRATION.
A further step in connection with the formation of Boards of Conciliation
and Arbitration has been made. A Board governing the districts of Mansfield,
Derby and Nottingham was brought into being on the 24th ult. Mr. T. F.
Richards, General President of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives,
was elected to the chair. Mr. Harold Royce (Mansfield Shoe Co.) was elected
---

secretary. The rules governing the Board were agreed to and ordered to be
vice-chairman, and Mr. J. Harding (Messrs. Seymour & Harding) was appointed

A further meeting was held on the 8th inst., when rules were adopted.
We trust that as a result of this Board being constituted the members in the

Board of Conciliation and Arbitration for the Midland Counties Boot
Heel Manufacturers' Association, Leicester. I.R. 242/1923.
The following Award has been given by Mr. George Sedgwick, J.P., of
Leicester, during the month, and registered by the Ministry of Labour, on the
25th ult.:-
Award on the claim by the National Union of Boot and Shoe Opera-
tives against the Midland Counties Boot Heel Manufacturers' Association,
with regard to the operation of Sorting Lifts and Top-pieces as governed
by an Agreement signed 12th December, 1922.
Terms of Reference.
Claim by the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives that the
operation of Sorting Lifts and Top-pieces for quality or substance, or both,
is an operation governed by the Minimum Wage Rate of the Agreement
entered into between the National Federation of Boot and Shoe Manu-
facturers and the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives, signed on
12th December, 1922.
A dispute having arisen in reference to the above question between
the parties aforesaid, the Minister of Labour appointed me (the under-
signed) as Arbitrator to determine the disputed matters.
Having heard the representatives of both sides, and having fully
considered the evidence and information placed before me, I do now
award as follows :-
That the operation of Sorting Lifts and Top-pieces for quality or
substance, or both, is an operation governed by the Minimum Wage Rate
of the Agreement entered into between the National Federation of Boot
and Shoe Manufacturers and the National Union of Boot and Shoe Opera-
tives, signed on the 12th day of December, 1922, and that all the workers
employed in such operation by the Midland Counties Boot Heel Manu-
facturers' Association, shall be paid the full Minimum Wage Rate, as
stated in the before mentioned Agreement, except such workers as may
become subject to the provisions as stated in paragraph 15 of the said
Agreement, dated December, 1922.
(Signed) GEORGE SEDGWICK,
Arbitrator,
22, West Avenue, Clarendon Park, Leicester.
Dated this 21st day of April, 1923.

THE THIRTY-FIFTH CONFERENCE OF THE UNION
was held during Whit-week. We hope that as a result a still better under-
standing of the many and varied questions with which we are confronted
from time to time has been arrived at. Appended is a resumé of the vital
decisions reached :-
An additional Organiser to be appointed.
Benefit to be paid to "Suspended" members under certain defined
conditions.
Withdrawal from the General Federation of Trade Unions.
Conferences of the Union to be held biennially in future instead of
annually.
Persons between 40 and 50 years of age to join the Union for trade
purposes only.
Persons over 50 years of age to join on special terms.
Special Conference for the Jubilee of the Union next year.
NONE of the above matters will operate until after the Ist September,
1923.
An official report of the proceedings of the Conference will be issued during
the month, price one penny each, which we hope the members will read, as
important questions were dealt with at the Conference.
NATIONAL AGREEMENT (DECEMBER) 1922.
Now that the cost of living is down to 70 points, the alteration made
in the National Agreement (December) 1922 comes into cperation. We would,
however, call special attention to the fact that there will be ONLY ONE
minimum for male operatives, which is a factor for which we have been
striving for many years past and is a great point in our favour.
RESULT OF VOTING.

Health Insurance Department will be found on page 293. The total votes
cast were:-

We regret once more to have to refer to the fact that a considerable number
of letters are constantly received from the Branches INSUFFICIENTLY STAMPED.
This means not only a double payment having to be met, but incurs considerable
loss of time in delivery, because the Postal Officials have to deliver this corres-
pondence during the time that the Central Office is officially opened, so that
the postman can secure the postage due on the said letters. We therefore
appeal once more to the Branch Officers to see that their correspondence is
sufficiently stamped and thus save both time and expense.
REMEMBER THE FIFTEEΝΤΗ!
Once again we feel bound to call the serious attention of Branch Secretaries
to the fact that the FIFTEENTH day of each month is the latest day for
returns reaching the General Secretary. If Brarrches fail to send off their
returns to reach the Central Office before the 15th of the month it tends to
upset the organisation of the work in the General Secretary's Office. We beg
to intimate that unless returns are in before the 15th of the month, the Secretary
has been instructed to put into force the Rules governing the same.
Sheets MUST also bear the signature of both the Branch President and Branch
Secretary, or they will reluctantly have to be returned for completion.

IS LEICESTER HEALTHY ?
Striking Statement by Councillor Wilford. "Insidious Canker."
"Health Work in the City" was the subject of an interesting address given by Councillor W. E. Wilford (chairman of the Health Committee of the City Council) to the members of the Leicester Trades Council last night.
For many years, said the councillor, the citizens of Leicester had been told that as far as the city was concerned, "all was well." The city had been boomed to the skies as the healthiest and cleanest place in the country, but those behind the scenes had enter- tained doubts, and of late those doubts had been justified and realised. Leicester may, on the surface, appear very pure and fine, but underneath there was a very insidious canker, which, if not stopped, would produce disease and death in their midst.
There were two great defects in the housing conditions in Leicester. The first was the sink and tap facilities. In the city there were thousands of homes where those facilities were not provided. The other defect was the bad lavatory accommodation.
Shocking Housing Conditions.
In some parts of the city the housing conditions were shocking. Healthy and moral lives were almost out of the question. The Health Committee were handicapped by the fact that since 1914 they could not condemn a single house as unfit for human habitation.
Tuberculosis was the greatest scourge of the present day, although cancer seems to be growing. The number of cases of tuberculosis, however, seemed to be increasing instead of diminishing. The greatest difficulty the committee had to contend with was being notified of the disease early enough to prevent it. Forty to fifty per cent. of the cases that were notified were advanced.
Councillor Wilford was heartily thanked for his address.— Leicester Mail, 2nd May, 1923.

GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
We are again confronted with a claim from some of the employers that they are
meeting with a great amount of competition from quarters they cannot name, and they
feel it to be the duty of the Union to remove these obstacles. If that was, and is, the
object of their joining the Employers' Federation, then they certainly were expecting more
than we are likely to satisfy them with. We, as a Union, are bound by the terms of settle-
ment, and up to the present pride ourselves that no section of the industry enjoys any
immunity from these terms. Any Employers' Association in the Federation can be
approached the firms in question. Any Employers' Association in the Federation can be
supplied with up-to-date information of our activities in any area in which they may be
interested, and we feel sure that they will have no reason to complain with our activities
and work for the benefit of the whole of the industry. With fifty permanently employed
officials we certainly cannot be called lackadaisical in our methods knowing, as we do, that
any unfair competition by any employer not federated is more detrimental to us with our
membership seventy-four times greater than is that of the Federation, and this in itself
would never have been what is is had we permitted the best of employers and firms in the
trade to have been undermined by unfair competitors, but even in a matter of this kind
we often fail to get the support of the grumbling manufacturers who complain in generalities
only. In this particular we cannot take them seriously. Were we to accept from our
members general complaints, unspecified, then we should always be harrassing some firm
or other without any tangible result. We can only accept complaints when specifically
stated as to who when, and where the firms are situated, and without this the employers
would save their time and ours not to trouble us with complaints.
In the above connection one of my colleagues and myself were asked to meet a number
of employers in a certain district, but they could not give us any tangible information,
only that the statement in one area was they thought not quite so good as theirs, and they
had to admit that their conditions were not so advantageous as the complained of district.
Oh, for the lack of logic, when some manufacturer is a better organiser than the grumbler;
in fact some of them would do well to make themselves acquainted with each individual
department, and by making the Production side a complete study.
Loyal members of the Federation would do well to assist the Union, who is no respector
of persons amongst the firms working to the Agreement, and we should like in the Welling-
borough district a better spirit to be shown than to withhold the dues owing to the opera-
tives for periods that some less loyal, now ex-members, of the Federation adopted.
There is certainly a difference between a man whose representatives will not consent
to sign an agreement, and the man who refuses to agree and is not bound because he is
unfederated and has not been represented, and who pays for the first time, as compared
with those who having paid suddenly, cease for a period in the hope that the gap will not
have to be paid for.
Our duty is clear. We must act justly to all men, and we pride ourselves that our Union
to the best of their ability do this, and we shall press our claim to the highest tribunal
in our industry.
The Joint Standing Committee of the Union and Federation, whose duty it is to inter-
pret the terms of settlement, have been called together for the purpose of interpretation,
and it seems very strange that in both the instances referred to them neither of these claims
have been made before. Although both clauses have been in existence unchanged since
1919, and in one case a Chairman's note gives the explanation which is not admitted by
the employers' side to be good evidence. Both the items under discussion were endorsed
by the 1920 Agreement, also by the 1922 Agreement, and was again endorsed on February
Ist, 1923.
This brings me to the view that in future we must act on the advice given me in 1911
by Lord Buckmaster, that no matter what may be the opinions of Conferences the only
sure way is to have our Agreements down in writing and made as plain as possible.
Further, we must see to it that we have a saving clause that either side not complain-
ing or asking for an interpretation of any clause within three months of the signing of such
document must stand by the letter of the Agreement until the same is again amended by
the National Conference.
LEICESTER. Several firms have been visited respecting the Holiday Scheme, and all
those visited and seen have made satisfactory arrangements to meet our demands. It
may be well to say these firms are very small and trade with them has not been of the best.
NORTHANTS LEATHER CORPORATION has again been visited and the position discussed.
We are of the opinion that the offer of the firm now is sufficient to meet our demands
and preserve the position intact.

MOUNTSORREL has again been visited. Men and women were met outside the gates
and refused to stop and listen to the Union's representatives on their duty they and our-
selves owe to the working-class movement. This cannot be permitted to go on, and
have already asked our Organiser, Mr. D. McCarthy, with myself, to hold some Sunday
meetings. We both know what it is to do a bit of work for the Socialist movement and
are prepared to do the same for Trade Unionism. This is our own call, our own choice.
consequently it should be done as an extra, and we intend taking Rothley, Mountsorrel,
Sileby and Syston. We believe that we shall be able to create a Trade Union feeling
in these villages that has not and which does not at present exist.

at the Chamber of Commerce, Nottingham, when the following officers were appointed
with unanimity: - Chairman, T. F. Richards; Vice-Chairman, Mr. Harold Royce; Secre-
tary, Manufacturers' Association, E. Harding. Business: - A copy of the suggested

(Mansfield), G. F. Goodwin (Nottingham), and W. Blissett and H. Herberts (Derby),

The rules were then submitted, slightly altered and signed. The Chairman then sub-
mitted the Female Agreement for the perusal of the Board. Before the next meeting
each side to nominate two at least of their number to form the nucleus of a Committee
with power to call witnesses, to draw up Statements for the District, and to consider at the
next meeting what statement shall be taken as a basis for this purpose. We hope by this
Board's work to influence the district, such as Melbourne and perhaps other parts of Derby-
shire. We have already nominated our respective members for the Committee, and await
the employers doing the same.
The General Federation, continuing their instructions, have received an invitation
to meet the General Council of the Trades Union Congress on May 23rd at the House of
Commons, but as the House will not be sitting the meeting will take place at the Caxton
Hall on the same date, and owing to our Conference being held at this time it will not be
proper for me to attempt to attend such meeting.
STREET. - A visit to Clark's, of Street, has been paid by me owing to the lack of co-
hesion on one part of the factory, which ought to be making better time on a class of goods
very much in demand. This weakness was at once seen, and let us hope that the local
officers and ourselves will not have to complain of any lack of confidence, as our action is
solely for the men's welfare.
GLASGOW-With Mr. Buckle we visited the City and saw the Directors of the S.C.W.S.
and appealed to them to allow us to take the case of the operatives on piecework. relin-
quishing a 5 per cent. given voluntarily three years ago to which the operatives clung.
Although they have been credited with having the best statements in the kingdom, they
claimed that as the gift was due to their own spontaneity, we ought not to press them.
We saw the operatives in the mess room after leaving-off time. We explained the matter
fully to them and asked would they accept our advice? They asked a few questions
and then got up and walked out, totally ignoring two of their officers, who had travelled
300 miles to try and help them. Such is the reward from some members.
RUSHDEN. Complaints having been made concerning a firm in the area by or through
other members of our Union, caused an investigation to be made on two separate occasions,
one to find out whether the rumours were true by holding a meeting of the operatives
who had no complaint to make, but who found themselves in such a position that any
unnecessary complaint could easily make matters worse instead of better. The second
visit was to see the firm who supplied us, untrammelled, with all the information one
wished for in such a manner that we shall be able to give an accurate account of the position.
ADVISORY COMMITTEE of Trade Boards has held a meeting of those appointed to
advise the Boards on the question of the Registration of Outworkers, and the Committee
met at the Labour Ministry, Whitehall, and agreed that the first step was to get all out-
workers registered with power for all Boards to have access to the addresses of all out-
workers, and by this means prevent the sweating that takes place in all industries. For
this reason we want the power to be extended to any Trade Union that these lists of out-
workers should be supplied them on application.
The Daily Herald, I hope, is becoming the daily paper that all our members will
ultimately take, read and act thereon. Its real value to our movement, compared with
other papers, is 3d. per copy.

BRANCH REPORTS.
ARBROATH. - In Arbroath trade is remaining so bad that one firm has
discharged seventeen operatives, and it looks as though this factory may have
to "close down" either temporarily or, perhaps, altogether. The other factory
in this town is just managing to keep in touch with a small stream of experi-
mental orders which may, however, develop into a good-class trade as time
goes on. In Carnoustie, one factory is also reducing workers, but curiously
enough the remaining one of our group is still able to keep on full time. Indeed,
for months ahead the operatives here are sure of regular business, and they
congratulate themselves on such a beneficent stroke of prosperity. One thing
is the relaxation of the regulations of the Labour Exchanges. The old "Con-
tinuity Rule" produced anomalies such as no one could defend. The idea of
receiving benefit for six days in a fortnight if the worker got his working time
arranged four days one week and two days the following, but got nothing if
he worked three days each week, always suggested administrative sense gone
mad. The new "Three-in-Six Part Rule" removes this absurdity, and alto-
gether the short-time worker stands a chance of working to better advantage
and obtaining idle benefit for his lost days. There is one development in con-
nection with Labour Exchange Local Employment Committees which demands
close attention. In dealing with applicants for Idle Benefit, Rota Committees
are authorised to request "documentary evidence" that applicants are "gen-
uinely seeking" employment. This is leading to serious results, because it is
not always conceded that an assurance from an applicant's Union Secretary
is sufficient, and claimants are practically forced to go hither and thither
seeking a start whether at their own trade or industry or outside of it, in order
to get vouchers stating they had sought work. One can easily guess what this
may lead to, and accentuates the menace of the unemployed on the doubtful
security of the man in a job. With such an army of unemployed driven to
run round the various workshops every week or so, it needs no stretch of imagi-
nation to picture employers planning to use them to cut further the wages of
those inside or, at any rate, demanding a greater docility in view of this "knock-
ing at the door." All this makes one marvel at the obtuseness of those who
oppose the demand for affiliation to Trades Councils, Trade Congresses, and
Labour Party of the Organised Unemployed Committees. These Committees
are keeping the unemployed from being the most reactionary forces in modern
industrialism, and yet there are those who sneer at them as being "communistic"
or "bolshevist." Some of the leaders may be, but the work they do must
be done by somebody, or else the unemployed in the large cities would become
the recruiting ground for scabbery or, even worse, for Fascism. Better by far
to appreciate the Organised Unemployed Committees for good work done,
and be in a position to control and regulate and work with the men outside
the factory gates, so that those inside may not be endangered by competition
of an unscrupulous character. The times call for the closest co-operation and
unity amongst workers, idle and employed alike, as a safeguard against the
boss class.
BELFAST. Trade continues to remain very bad, and there are no signs
of an early improvement.
CHESHAM. -Trade here is still very bad.
CHESTERFIELD. - In sending our returns we have to state trade bad,
as most of our members have been out of work since Easter through the firm
of Dronfield & Co. closing down.

DESBOROUGH. - It is with deep regret we have to report the passing
away of one of our oldest members, viz.. Alfred Murkett. At one time he held
the position of President of the Branch, and for many years was active in Trade
Union work. To his sorrowing wife and children we tender our deep and
sincere sympathy.
EDINBURGH.-Trade still very quiet. Under the auspices of Trades
Council a special campaign is being waged to try and bring back defaulting
members into Unions, also to augment numbers in several Unions which have
been heavily hit since the slump in trade. At present this Committee are
approaching all workers under Town Council to become members of their various
craft unions. Sub-Committees, dealing with the educational side of Trade
Unionism, are arranging lists of speakers who will attend Branch meetings and
give lectures on various aspects of the Labour Movement. Edinburgh Branch,
taking advantage of this scheme, made arrangements for Mr. Doull, of E.T.U.,
to lecture on the Housing Problem, but unforseen circumstances intervening
agreed to fill the breach, taking as his subject Wages. Members gave a very
attentive hearing, and at the finish there was a good deal of discussion. In
the Winter months we hope to arrange several of these lectures to try and
bring out the members in larger numbers to Branch Meetings. Along with other
sections of the working class we joined in the May-Day Demonstration. When
will the workers demand the first of May as being made a statutory holiday
with full pay? The Daily Herald. We are pushing the Prize Scheme, and up
till the present a goodly number have started buying the paper, but thousands
more could do the same. Then Labour would have some chance of coming
into its own. Stalwarts must keep pegging away. Before this appears in
print the Annual Conference will be past. Now we sincerely hope that the
business done will all be for the good management of our Union. We are
sorry to report the death of one of our Dunfermline members. The Branch
extends its sympathy to widow and family.
HIGHAM AND RUSHDEN. - We are sorry to report that trade is worse
in our district this month, both Sickness and Unemployment again being heavy.
We have settled this month two compensation claims. One slight accident
for £25 and costs, and one in which four fingers of right hand were crushed, for
£300 and costs in addition to over £50 weekly payments, proving again the
advantages of the Union's help. Messrs. Adam Bros., of Raunds, have now
paid the Umpire's Award in the hand stitching of the Egyptian Army Boot,
amounting to £187 75. 7d. We wonder what chance the workmen would have
had if the Union had not been behind them in this case.
KINGSWOOD.-We are unable to report any improvement in trade,
and this depressed condition of the local industry reacts upon the moral of the
operatives. Full use has been made of the services of Mr. W. R. Smith, Organiser,
and the difficulties (quite peculiar to Kingswood) have given full scope
for his abilities. A revival of trade will present the opportunity so anxiously
hoped for and enable us to emphasise the observance of the National Agreement
in its entirety throughout the district.
LEICESTER.-We are pleased to report that sickness during April was
much lighter than during March. As regard the Out-of-Work Fund, this shows
a steady decline in payments for the month as compared with the previous
month, and a decrease of roughly £35 per week compared with the corresponding
month of last year. We can only report trade as fair, there being a number
of our members working short time still. We are also pleased to report that we
joining new members rapidly, and trust we shall continue to do so. We
are having a "Showcard Day" during June, when all members are requested

NORTHAMPTON. - Trade is a little better, and we are pleased to say the

NORWICH. Trade in Norwich has shown some slight improvement during
the month, the turnshoe section having the advantage of the change. Although
the corner of depression seems to have been turned, yet we still have a great
number of operatives unemployed, a number we are pleased to report that is
steadily getting smaller as the days go by. The great event of the month, so
far as the shoe trade is concerned in Norwich, was the visit of the General
Secretary, Mr. E. L. Poulton, J.P., on the occasion of the unfurling of the new
Banner. A most enjoyable evening was spent, the outstanding item of the
programme being the splendid speech of the General Secretary. A speech of
force and weight, one could not help feeling the inspiration to help the National
Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives to become even yet a greater force than has
at present been secured. When on a similar occasion, at Northampton, we
Leard of Mr. E. L. Poulton's sudden illness we felt concerned for his health,
and we voice the wishes of every Norwich operative in hoping for a speedy
return to robust and sound health again.

PLYMOUTH. - The new Trade Board Bill has appeared at last and,
although we are not yet in possession of a copy, a summary of its provisions
has been published in the press sufficient to give us an insight into the Govern-
ment's intentions. The Bill apparently contains all the objectionable features
of the Cave Report, and allows little or no opportunity for the extension of the
Trade Board system to industry, but we notice that it is claimed by the Govern-
ment in their memorandum to the Bill. "That it will give encouragement to
the voluntary development of satisfactory organisation by enabling represen-
tatives of employers and workers to come together and agree on rates of wages."
This is a rather important admission by the Government and should be ex-
ploited to the full, and if the Government is really sincere, why rule out from
the scope of the Bill all trades other than those deemed to be sweated? Why
not encourage and make provision for all workers and employees to enjoy the
benefits of this beneficent system of collective bargaining and have it optional
to the parties concerned to apply for and claim legal sanction for their agreed
minima? Three million workers already enjoy the legal protection of Trade
Boards; another million at least is asking for it, and yet a mere handful of
employers can stay the legitimate desires of the people.
SHEPSHED. - Trade does not improve much here, factories only working
half time.
SOUTHAMPTON. - Trade has a slight tendency to betterment.

and given considerable assistance in the adjustment of a few local difficulties.
Situated as we are, far away from the great centres of our industry, it is always
a great encouragement both to officials and members to have a national officer
among us even for a brief period.

WHAT THE VICAR OF ECTON THINKS OF THE LABOUR PARTY.
Further colour was lent to the idea that Mr. W. R. Smith will be the prospective
Labour candidate for the Wellingborough Division by a remark made at a meeting by
Mr. F. T. Curzon, secretary of the Earls Barton Labour Party.
Having referred with regret to Mr. Smith's defeat at the last election, Mr. Curzon
added, "I might say that I hope in a few days to be able to announce that he will be
fighting in this division again.
he will, we shall have to do our duty as workers and trades unionists."
And if Mr. W. R. Smith stands again, as I hope
This statement was made at the social and dance of the Earls Barton Labour Party,
held in the Public Hall, at Earls Barton. The particular attraction arranged
for the occasion was a visit from the Rev. Canon A. W. Jephson, Rector of
Ecton, who, in a comprehensive address, stated why, although he was not a member of the
Labour Party, he looked to the Labour Party as the only one likely to solve the difficulties
with which the country is at present beset. "The Labour Party," he contended, "can
improve the condition of the people of this country materially, and can do it with justice
to all. But not by beating others down. I believe in justice to all-and we shall get it
through the Labour Party."

What She was Going to do.
He went on to speak of the failures of the Coalition Government, and deplored the
fact that the wages of the Agricultural Workers should be raised in January only to be
dropped in August. He told how, when the wages were put up to 42s., he spoke to a
labourer's wife and innocently inquired, "I suppose you are going to save money now,
are'nt you?" "No, I aint," the woman promptly replied, "I am going to feed the
children properly for the first time in their life."
After the applause had died down the Canon added. "I'm bound to say I felt ashamed
at having put the question."

DEATH OF MR. MARTIN LEADER.
Pioneer in Boot and Shoe Union.
The death of Mr. Martin Leader, which took place yesterday, at Melton Mowbray,
recalls the early days of the Leicester Branch of the Boot and Shoe Operatives' Union
practically financed for the first
existence.
Mr. G. Sedgwick, J. P. (secretary of the Leicester Branch until 1886) is one of the
few a Mercury representative he observed that at the time he knew Mr. Leader the latter was
branch secretary of what was then a branch of the Amalgamated Cordwainers' Union
"When the present Boot and Shoe Operatives' Union was formed here," Mr. Sedgwick
proceeded, "Mr. Leader, with others, was in the forefront of the pioneer work. He
continued as secretary of the newly-formed branch, and for many years indeed he was the
man who had to do with the settling of labour disputes between Leicester employees and
their employers. During that time he was remarkably successful; in fact, he was almost
the branch in himself."
Mr. Leader, whose age was 80, is to be buried at Belgrave Cemetery to-morrow.—
Leicester Mercury, 4th May, 1923.
BEWARE OF THE DOG.
Slipper Maker Sues Boot Manufacturer.
Under the Workmen's Compensation Act, Abraham Fineberg, slipper maker, 9, St.
Thomas Square, Hackney, E., sought compensation at the Shoreditch County Court,
on the 26th ult., against his late employer, Mr. Shinbaum, boot manufacturer, 5, Eleanor
Road, Hackney, E.
The applicant said that after being employed by the respondent for a day, he was
told that his work was not good enough, and was dismissed. When he was paid by the
respondent's daughter he asked for his tools, and she sent a young woman with him into
the factory to get them. Whilst there the respondent's dog attacked him and bit
his hand.
The defence was that as the applicant was paid his wages when dismissed on the
Friday he should then have taken his tools away with him. He had no right in the factory
the next day. It was alleged that it was not known he was on the premises on the Saturday
until he screamed when bitten by the dog. He gained access to the place by pulling a
bobbin on the back street door, which was the usual thing for the employees to do.
Judge Cluer held that the applicant should have taken his tools away when dismissed,
and that the injury on the following day was not caused, therefore, in the course of his
employment. Judgment was entered for the respondent, with costs. — Shoe and Leather
Record, 4th May, 1923.

NATIONAL UNION OF BOOT AND SHOE OPERATIVES.
REPORT of the Parliamentary Representatives of the
Union to the Thirty-Fifth Conference, 1923.
FELLOW DELEGATES,
HOUSE OF COMMONS,
WESTMINSTER, LONDON, S.W. 1.
9th May, 1923.
In presenting this report, it is with great pleasure and satisfaction
that we are able to record the fact that the Labour Party has gone many steps
towards reaching the position when its members in the House of Commons
to be proud of, when we remember that but so short a time back the Party
will be called upon to take up the reins of Government. Surely we have much
which was looked upon by some as being quite insignificant, has now to be
recognised as the official opposition of H.M. Government as we had 142 Labour
Members returned at the Polls last November. While taking satisfaction in
character of that Party, and when some of us seem inclined to become impatient
ment is in power, possessing all the qualifications associated with the traditional
at what is apparently little progress, it is well to remember that numbers
count, and that Division Lobbies tell the tale.
It is undoubtedly true that judged by the standards of real progress the
Government of to-day is profoundly lacking, but this should be a constant
challenge to the opposition to display constant and determined effort to mitigate,
as far as possible this lack by well directed and constructive criticism.
Parliament opened on 23rd November, 1922. The election of Speaker
having taken place, the first business the House had to consider was the passing
into law a Bill which has given to Ireland her freedom after long years of
coercion and force. We hope the foundation has been laid for Ireland to
ultimately become a happy and prosperous Nation.
The past few months has been a very strenuous time. The Party has put
up vigorous opposition, and has somewhat altered the atmosphere and outlook
upon many important questions appertaining to the well-being of the com-
munity. The Party has been responsible for raising the question of the
Occupation of the Ruhr and the dangers that may accrue, and they have
repeatedly suggested that some method should be employed with a view to
having the Reparation question settled on what could be regarded as a fair
basis, so that the reconstruction, economically and otherwise, could take
effect. The Government has simply taken up a non-interference attitude
upon the matter. So strong has the feeling become, that official deputations
have gone over to the area concerned with a view to investigating the matter
from time to time, in order to get a good grasp of the situation as regards
France and Germany.

HOUSING.
There is going on in Committee an animated discussion of the Housing
Bill, the proposal to give State money only to "non-Parlour" Houses. The
houses may either be two-storeyed, with a minimum of 550 and a maximum of
780 superficial feet. These measurements will be calculated in accordance
with rules laid down by the Minister of Health.
The Plan A has a total available area of 754.66 square feet, Plan B 808.82
square feet, and Plan C. 836.00 square feet. These are official plans and are
well within the maximum allowed under the new scheme. It will be seen
from a study of these plans that every available inch has to be utilised. The
planning has to be very carefully thought out. The architectural problem
involved, demands greater cleverness in design, so as not to waste any space
on passages or corners. The essential measurements laid down by the Ministry
is: 180 feet should be allowed for the Living Room, 150 feet for the first
Bedroom, 150 feet for the second Bedroom, and a minimum of 65 feet for the
third Bedroom. In addition, room will have to be found for the Scullery and
usual offices. The Bath may either be placed in the Scullery or in a separate
compartment, or either on the first or ground floor. Undoubtedly there are
powerful arguments in favour of the Parlour House, notably that a Parlour
provides privacy for the younger generation-in case of sickness or death a
parlour is invaluable. Much is being made of the so-called disregard of the
Middle Classes. A study of the full text of the Government Bill shows that
their needs have been considered. The proposed amendment of the "Small
Dwellings Act" extends the limit on the market value of houses in respect
of which advances may be made from £800 to £1,200. It will also be of direct
assistance to the skilled artisan class that local authorities may guarantee
the repayment to a Building Society of any advances made to any of its members
to build or acquire houses. Money may also be advanced to persons or bodies
building houses.
A generous limit has been placed on the estimated value of such houses,
for the advance or guarantee can be given on such value up to £1,500: for
£1,200 under the Small Dwellings Acquisition Act, and £1,500 for houses
financed by Building Societies and other bodies.
EDUCATION.
Here again we have evidence of the fact that the Government are retro-
grade and reactionary. Wherever possible, economy has been applied regard-
less of consequences. The promise held out in the Fisher Act made impossible
of fulfilment, and the vision which was opened up by the possibilities contained
therein gradually receding, until a position almost of despair has taken the
place of hope. The cry for economy has been seized upon by certain public
bodies, no doubt glad of the opportunity to curtail expenditure until the
children of the workers are becoming the victims of the inefficiency brought
about by what we must regard as false economy which must inevitably result
in a lowering of the standard to which all progressive people would aspire.
After a war that was to end war, we are still confronted with the appalling
fact that for the year 1923-24 that whereas provision is made in the Estimates

FINANCE.
As a consequence of the prosecution of the late war the country has to
constitute a burden for generations to come and lead to permanent high prices.

At the last General Election the Labour Party foreshadowed a Policy which

of the community something will have to be done to lift the load, or we shall
sink lower and lower beneath its weight.
BUDGET.
Mr. Baldwin, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, introduced his first new
Budget on the 16th April, 1923, and it is a most remarkable fact that
whilst there was a surplus of £100,000,000 brought forward from the
previous year, still the reduction in taxation, as far as its effect on the vast
majority of the working class population is concerned, reductions are con-
spicuous by their absence. The employing and capitalistic classes were again
favoured with reduction on the Income Tax, Postal and Telephone Rates,
and without doubt the Budget stands out as one of the most capitalistic and
"favoured-class" pieces of legislation of modern times. The interest on the
National Debt alone absorbs over £300,000,000 per annum, and whilst this
vast amount of interest is payable it is not at all likely that reductions of
taxation on the essentials of life will be seen. The Party put up a strong fight
for the reduction of duty on Tea, Sugar, &c., but without avail. And so we
look in vain for the promise of that sort of legislation that will usher in the time
so glibly spoken of by the late Prime Minister; whether we look at home or
abroad the same disappointment is experienced.
In our preceding remarks we have dealt with what may be regarded as the
Home Policy; and now perhaps in a few words we may be allowed to bring
to your notice the failure of the Government in the field of Foreign Policy.
In this respect the experiences of the last few years seems to stand for nothing
so far as improvement goes. The same old jealousies, suspicions, and pre-
judices, seem to be operating. Men of responsibility are talking about the
next war as if it had already been decided that the same was inevitable. The
race for armaments is again starting, leaving one to infer that nations, who,
but a short time back were our Allies, now, if not our actual enemies, are having
to be watched and treated, if not as probable, yet as possible ones, or why the
frantic talk of the French superiority in Air Forces, or the huge expenditure
to be incurred in the Pacific which can only be justified by the fear of an Eastern
Power. Ah well while the great mass of the people seem to be satisfied,
which must be the explanation of the present Government's majority, we
suppose things will remain pretty much as they are, but some day surely the
eyes of the people will be opened and they will discover for themselves the
right path.

CIVIL SERVICE.
Another question which has occupied the attention of the Party is that of
the Lytton Entrants to the Civil Service, on which question the Government
were defeated on roth April, on the Motion that a Committee of Enquiry be
set up to investigate the conditions obtaining in the service. The actual
grievance is that the overwhelming majority of the Lytton Entrants to the
Clerical Clerks are ex-Service Men, and started at the rate of £70, £80, or £85
per annum, in other words, although they are men of all ages, the majority
married and have families to support, and with anything up to seven years
temporary service, had to start at the same rate of pay appropriate to a boy of
18 years of age. The strong feeling of the House with regard to the disgraceful
conditions obtaining, and the Government taking up an attitude which was
regarded as an unreasonable one, and the unsatisfactory arguments of the
Minister for that Department when the Division was taken, the Government
were defeated, and after an adjournment of the House, the Government con-
ceded to the opinion of the House, and a representative Committee to investigate
and report on the conditions of employment was appointed.
PRIVATE MEMBERS' MOTIONS.
Private members have a system of balloting and those who head the list
are given a paper with a list of Motions to choose from. Those members who
are lucky enough to head the list fix on a particular Motion and are allowed
to move it in the House; for example, Mr. Snowden's Motion on "Failure of
Capitalistic System."
Motion made, and question proposed, "That, in view of the failure of the
capitalist system to adequately utilise and organise natural resources and
productive power, or to provide the necessary standard of life for vast numbers
of the population, and believing that the cause of this failure lies in the private
ownership and control of the means of production and distribution, this House
declares that legislative effort should be directed to the gradual supersession
of the capitalist system by an industrial and social order based on the public
ownership and democratic control of the instruments of production and dis-
tribution." Debate adjourned.
MOTHERS' PENSIONS.
That in the opinion of this House, pensions adequate for the proper
upbringing and maintenance of children should be paid to all widows with
children or mothers whose family breadwinner has become incapacitated,
such pensions to be provided by the State and administered by a committee
of the municipal or county council wholly unconnected with the Poor Law."
Rejected by: Ayes 184; Noes 248.
ACCIDENTS IN MINES.
That this House deplores the heavy loss of life and the large number of
non-fatal accidents in mines, and is of the opinion that legislation to improve
and strengthen the provisions of the Coal Mines Act, 1922, should be introduced
and carried into law without delay in order to secure the fullest protection
possible to those engaged in this dangerous industry." Agreed to without
Division.

NATIONAL MINIMUM WAGE.
"That in view of the practically universal acceptance of the principle

Unionists. We may rely upon it that our position is to be challenged. We
question whether the Prime Minister will be able to restrain the rank and file
of his own Party in their aggressive opposition to Trade Unionism. Already
a motion has been carried to amend the Trade Union Act re the Political posi-
tion; also as recently as the first day of the month (Labour Day) a Bill was
introduced having for its object the repeal of the Trade Union Act, 1906. To
be in the House and to hear the frenzied applause which is given every time
anything is said against Trade Unionism it is quite easy to discover the spirit
of antagonism which prevails, and which has for its object the weakening of
our position. To be forewarned is to be forearmed, and it is hoped that when-
ever the attack comes we shall be found prepared and sufficiently strong enough
to maintain our hard-won position.
May we be allowed to say that we consider it to be a very great honour
to be allowed to represent our fellow workers and citizens in Parliament.
Conscious as we are of our own limitations, we sincerely hope that our presence
there will be of some, if little help, and service, in helping to make things better
for us all.
Fraternally yours,
JOHN BUCKLE.

PARLIAMENTARY DEBATES.
UNEMPLOYMENT BENEFIT.
MR. ROBERT YOUNG asked the Minister of Labour whether he is aware that J. D.
Walmsley, Earlestown, Lancaster, was disallowed benefit from December 22nd, 1922,
referred to was an attempt to increase his income by sales of the Daily Herald; that his
income from this source ranged from 3s. 1d. to 13s. 6d. per week ; that in no case did he
to January 22nd, 1923, on the ground that he was not unemployed ; that the employment
earn the equivalent of 3s. 4d. per day; and whether, under these circumstances, he can
explain why benefit was disallowed?
MR. BETTERTON: The limit of 3s. 4d. a day referred to in the question applies only
to the earnings from a subsidiary occupation carried on by the applicant before he became
unemployed. In general, under Section 7 (2) (a) of the Unemployment
Insurance Act, 1920, any day on which any sum is earned cannot be
counted as a day of unemployment. The particular case referred to has been the
decision under the Act is final, and who has
confirmed the disallowance of benefit.-Parliamentary Debates, 27th, March, 1923.

COST OF LIVING INDEX FIGURES.
MR. HANNON asked the President of the Board of Trade whether, seeing that the
present cost of living index figure is based upon statistics of family budgets collected
nearly 20 years ago, and that the index figure does not accurately represent the present-
day cost of living, he proposes to proceed to the collection of the statistics of family budgets
which will fairly represent the cost of living at the present time ?
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Sir M. Barlow) : I have been asked to reply. The Ministry
of Labour cost of living index number is always carefully defined as indicating the average
increase in the cost of maintaining unchanged the pre-War standard of living of working
class families. For the purpose of such a calculation the use of pre-War budgets is strictly
correct. When working class conditions become more normal, it will, I think, be desirable
that a new index number shall be calculated designed to show the changes in the cost of
maintaining a normal post-War standard of living; but before this could be done a new
inquiry into working class expenditure would almost certainly be necessary. I propose
to take up the consideration of an inquiry of this kind as soon as conditions become more
normal. Parliamentary Debates, 24th April, 1923, vol. 163, No. 44.

COST OF LIVING (RENT).
COLONEL NEWMAN asked the Minister of Labour whether he is aware that for large
sections of the community any increase in rent is allowed for in the cost-of-living figure
on which their wages or salaries are based, thereby making the cost of living higher for
those other sections of the community whose assessments for Income Tax on their houses
is about to be increased with no compensating rise in salary or income; and is it his inten-
tion to remove rent from among the items on which the cost-of-living index is based?
SIR M. BARLOW: The official index figures are designed to indicate the average increase
in the cost of maintaining unchanged the pre-War standard of living of working-class
families, and the exclusion of so important an item as rent would seriously impair the
validity of the statistics for this purpose. I do not know whether the hon. Member realises
that as the percentage increase in rents is less than the general average for other items,
the effect of excluding rent would be to raise the final index figure. - Extracts from Parlia-
mentary Debates, Wednesday, 9th May, 1923, vol. 163, No. 55.

SCOTTISH TRADE UNIONS CONGRESS.

DELEGATES' REPORT.
The Twenty-sixth Annual Meeting was held in Dundee on the 18th April, 1923, and
following days. The delegates numbered 174 and represented 240,000 members, which
was considerably better than the previous year. Congress received a civic welcome from
the Lord Provost and Magistrates, and while greeting the visitors to Dundee, Lord Provost
Spence in solemn mood urged them not to cry for the moon. Some delegates may have
thought even the moon would be a desirable place compared with old "Mother Earth"
at present, but no resolution appeared on the agenda calling for the performance of
astronomical feats. The Report of the Parliamentary Committee was a document well
worth perusal. From beginning to end it demonstrated how much alive the Committee
were to the interests of Trade Unionists, in their handling of all the problems arising in
the course of the year. The action taken in connection with the infamous Circular 51 of
the Education Department, which was meant as a deterrent to Education Authorities
feeding and clothing necessitous school children, was much appreciated, as was also their
persistent efforts to force the Divisional Controller for Scotland, Ministry of Labour, to
adopt better procedure to be observed by Rota Committees in their work of examining
applicants for Unemployment Benefits.

Rota Committees were adopting the objectionable practice of demanding documentary
evidence from applicants that they were genuinely seeking employment, and the Parlia-
mentary Committee had striven hard to get officialdom to issue instructions to the effect
that a certificate from his or her Union Secretary be regarded as sufficient proof of the
search for work.

While seeming to agree to this reasonable request, the number of qualifications and
reservations made it very unsatisfactory. Congress stood solidly by the Committee in
their efforts to reach a settlement free from ambiguity and also unfairness. The efforts
of the Committee to establish a sound relationship between Trade Unionists and Co-
operative bodies also met with hearty approval, and all the delegates realised, although
the task was difficult, it was nearly the most worth while accomplishing. It will indeed be
a happy day when both organisations reach an understanding which will obviate labour
troubles finally between the respective members. Other parts of the report are worthy
of comment, and only considerations of space forbid.

The agenda consisted of resolutions of the kind made familiar to those attending
conferences, and very little of an original nature emerged in the discussions.

Hours of Labour, Control in Industry, Control of Credit, Amendment to Shop Acts,
Self-Government for Scotland, Public Ownership and Control of Railways, Old Age Pen-
sions, Housing, Adult Suffrage, Industrial Disputes, Unemployment Insurance, Trades
Boards, Entertainment Tax, Fair Wage Clause, Blind Persons Act, Facist Movement,
and a series of proposals on Unemployment, were all discussed, and the standing resolutions
agreed to.

If any subject created more than usual interest, it was the question of Facism in
Scotland, but both the delegates and the Press were inclined to link the whole thing up
with light-hearted banter. Robert Smillie, to mention one name, treated it with proper
seriousness, and his speech was a wise combination of warning and advice based on a
thorough estimation of the forces that create Facisti propaganda. The fraternal visitors
helped to brighten the proceeding each day, and without exception all delivered interesting
and informative addresses.

Mr. Agnew, of the Co-operative Movement, and Messrs. Campbell, McShane, and
Kinnon, of the Organised Unemployed, held the attention of Congress during the first day
with rousing and effective speeches. Arising out of the latter speeches came the demand
for affiliation, and owing to the vigorous efforts of a majority of number delegates in favour
of accepting affiliation of the Unemployed Committees, the President lost control of the
proceedings for a time. After order was restored, it was found that standing orders
prevented such a course being followed however, and affiliation will come up again next
year.

Mr. Ben Shaw and a speaker on behalf of Co-operative Insurance spoke on the second
day, and without exaggeration this latter subject was a revelation to all in the hall. Here
is a financial weapon of the most powerful description, which confers extraordinary advan-
tages on its members, and yet is terribly neglected by those who should support it. But
on Friday came the greatest treat, oratorically, of the week. Mr. Saklatvala, M.P., was
present on behalf of the All-India Trades Union Congress, and his speech roused Congress
to such a pitch that the ovation on concluding was continued to the extent of being an
encore. Finely phrased, light and shade delightfully blended, packed full of facts and
figures, and all delivered with the easy assurance of the practised orator. But it was the
magnetism of the man which produced the effect. Delegates and gallery alike will long
remember the inward stirring of soul produced by the magical eloquence of this gifted

3-5
and while India and its peoples will remain an enigma to most Britishers there can be no
doubt but what Mr. Saklatvala will exercise a powerful influence in convincing the leaders
of labour in this country of the need for understanding between the common people of both
nations with a view to restoring India to its rightful position in the march of civilisation,
A deported member of the I.W.W., of America, also spoke, and evoked the strong
sympathy of Congress by his description of the blackguardly methods adopted by the
U.S. Government to suppress the class-conscious leaders in the workers' movement there.
Mr. C. M. Lambert won the confidence of the meeting for his plea to protest to the President
of the States against such barbarous treatment of trade union officials.
First place in our summary of impressions must be given to a drawback experienced
by the Boot and Shoe delegates. As our branches never see the notice calling for resolu-
tions to the agenda, no proposals are sent in by our Union. This allows others to be called
upon for all the speeches, and as a consequence delegates from our Union get no oppor-
tunity of proving their worth. Where this acts against the Union is in the appointment
of Executive Council members. On three occasions a Boot and Shoe nominee was put
to the vote of Congress, the last occasion being for an executive seat, and only a handful
of votes were secured. It can be stated positively certain conversations proved it-
that this was due to delegates being in ignorance of the Union and of its delegates. It is
certain that if we took a larger share in putting forward matter for the agenda, and sought
to show that our delegates were as trustworthy as any of the others, a position on the
executive could be won and held. The value of that position is apparent to those who are
acquainted with the important work performed during the year by the Congress Executive,
and it is not in an envious spirit this is written, but rather because the traditions of the
Boot and Shoe Union demand such ambitions among its representatives.
Throughout the proceedings it was heartening to see the way in which the young men
stood by the ideals of Labour. A few of the older ones still make the mistake of trying
by sound and fury to spread the belief that they are still terrible fellows to fight, but it is
only a matter of time when the new political school of trade unionists will win the day.
Congress has been lucky in the choice of secretary, Mr. Wm. Elger, who is incompar-
ably efficient. Still a young man, it is easy to predict for him a big career in the trade
union movement. Questions, explanations, references to past correspondence or events,
found him ready to supply in the most succinct form and with most admirable address
just what was required at the moment. Although only appointed last year his work and
conduct was that of a veteran in experience.
All the arrangements for the comfort and entertainment of delegates exceeded expecta-
tions, while the public meetings found huge audiences gathered in Dundee's famous Caird
Hall-which is surely second to none. While in Dundee your delegates got in touch
with the local branch of our Union, and a meeting was convened by the Secretary. Mr. Alex.
Brown. Age deals lightly with Alec, his spirit and joy in life still remaining as exuberant
as of yore. The Dundee members, in spite of trade vicissitudes, are keenly interested in
the affairs of the Union, and a very profitable evening was spent in their company.
If anything is needed to add the final touch of pleasure to a Congress week, it is
secured in the meeting with friends in our own Union and in having a heart to heart
talk with them.
JAMES I'. REID.
CHRIS. BLEAKLEY.
£5,000,000 AWARDS.
What Workmen's Compensation Costs Yearly.
"The cost to industry of compensation following accidents to the workers amounts
to a sum of about five million pounds yearly," said Lieutenant-Colonel J. A. A. Pickard,
general secretary of the British Industrial "Safety First" Association, on the 5th
May, 1923.
"Add to that the legal, medical, and other expenses, the indirect cost of lost time,
both of man and machine, and you get a sum, estimated at 50 per cent. higher, which
constitutes a very heavy charge on production.
"Prevention is better than cure," he continued, "and international experts have
agreed that some three-quarters of all industrial accidents could be prevented by the
exercise of greater personal care on the part of the worker and better organisation on the
part of the employer. In this country that is not yet sufficiently realised."

LABOUR WOMEN'S CONFERENCE AT YORK.
DELEGATES' REPORTS.
1OTH MAY, 1923.
York was visited by about 500 delegates to the National Conference of Labour Women
which commenced in the Festival Concert Room under the presidency of Mrs. Harrison
Bell, Chairman of the Standing Joint Committee of Industrial Women's Organisations.
The Conference discussed several important questions, including that of the dismissals
of Married Women Teachers, upon which there was some plain speaking, and also differences
of opinion.
An official welcome to the delegates was given in the afternoon by the Lord Mayor
(Alderman J. B. Inglis, J.P.), who was accompanied by the Lady Mayoress. The Lord
Mayor heartily welcomed the delegates, and said that it was his duty to do so although
he might not agree with them on many points. They had a lot of differences of opinions,
but some good always arose from such differences. It would be a bad job for the country
and for the City of York if they had not any difference of opinion, and he was proud and
pleased to say that he numbered many friends aomng the Labour Party in the city. Why
should they not have differences of opinion? Everyone had a right to their thoughts
in regard to political and social subjects and they ought to agree to differ. He did not see
why they should not be able to agree to differ. Another reason he was glad to be present
was because the power of women was much greater to-day than when he was a boy. The
women had so much power and influence for good or evil that they must all feel it was for
the good of the community that they should take up their part in connection with the
various spheres of life. Every woman was a centre of influence, and it was for them to
see that that influence was exerted for good. (Applause.)
PRESIDENT'S ADDRESS.
Trade Union Amendments Acts.
Mrs. Harrison Bell, in her presidential address, said since the last Conference at
Leamington Spa organisation had proceeded apace, 20,000 new members having been
added to the party. The women of the party were bringing a new influence to bear
and a new and clearer light was shining on old problems, so that plans could be made to
remedy them as soon as opportunity occurred.
The C.W.S. Strike.
The Standing Orders Committee recommended the following emergency resolution
in reference to the strike amongst C.W.S. employees: - " That this Conference regrets
the action of the C.W.S. in imposing reductions of wages and worse conditions of labour
without consultation with the Union concerned. It feels that the present strike is likėly
to bring discredit on the workers' movement and urges the C.W.S. to agree without further
delay to submit the whole of the questions at issue to the Joint Committee of Trade Union
ists and Co-operators for arbitration."
Miss Simmons (National Union of General Workers) moved the resolution, which was.
submitted in view of the fact that there is a meeting of the parties, and said they deprecated
reductions of wages without consultation of the unions. Mrs. Adamson (Lincoln) seconded,
and two co-operators spoke in support, hoping that it would be the means of a settlement
of the dispute. The resolution was carried.
The Two Shift System.
Miss Helen Firber (Bristol) moved a resolution protesting against the hardships
inflicted on women and girls by the two-shift system, and reminding the Government that
this measure was placed on the Statute Book in the face of widespread trade union opposi-
tion, and demanding that it should be repealed. The resolution was carried.
Elections on One Day.
A resolution that all Parliamentary and Local Government Elections should take
place on Saturday, and that all Municipal Elections should be held in May instead of
November, was carried.
Parliamentary Candidates.
Miss Harkness (Glasgow Trade and Labour Council) moved :--" That this Conference
urges the Labour Party to take every opportunity to secure full adult suffrage on the
basis of one person one vote at the age of 21 years."
Miss Harkness characterised it as an insult that a woman should not have the franchise
under 30 years of age. The Prime Minister was returned to Parliament because plural
votes were in operation by which some persons had two or three votes.

sidered that many women under 30 had much more sense than people over 30. (Laughter

Mean Economies.
Proceeding, the President said that they viewed with apprehension the proposals for
economy which embraced the stint of milk and treatment for infants, cutting off supplies
for school meals, and increase of size of classes, and in instituting such mean economies
the children just before they reached the highest salaries scale provided by the Burnham
as to try and oust men and women head-teachers who had given 40 years to the service of
Committee so that their pensions might be less, promoting at the minimum rates to fill
the vacancies thus created with persons over 18 who had been certificated, and who may
not even have had six months' training. Could meanness go any further ? (Cries of
"No.")
The Conference met 30 minutes earlier on Wednesday than was originally contem-
plated.
Mrs. Turner (North Bucks) moved a resolution congratulating the Agricultural
Workers in Norfolk in their magnificent fight for better conditions for themselves and their
families. The resolution continued: "The Conference views with alarm the terms of
settlement, which it considers absolutely inadequate to procure a decent standard of living
for workers and will also prove an added menace to the town dweller. It therefore presses,
campaign in the countryside by the National Labour Party, and urges that the
in view of the vital importance of agricultural industry, for a vigorous propaganda
Parliamentary Party be asked to declare Labour's agricultural policy in the House of
Commons."
Miss Saward (Workers' Union), speaking as a daughter of an agricultural worker now
earning 27s., seconded, declaring that low agricultural wages threatened the conditions
of workers in every industry. Since 1918 farmers, landowners and the Government had
allowed three million acres to go out of cultivation, but had encouraged land-workers to
emigrate so that they should not remain to kick up a row. The resolution was carried
unanimously.

MRS. A. SMALLEY,
Leicester.
I attended the Conference of Labour Women held at the Festival Concert Rooms,
Museum Street, York, on the 7th, 8th, 9th of May. Mrs. Harrison Bell presided. There
were 518 delegates made up as follows: 320 from 210 Women's Sections of Labour Parties,
114 from 78 Trades and Labour Councils, 49 from Trade Unions, 35 from Fabian, Co-
operative, and other societies, the Trade Union numbers showing very clearly the little
interest shown towards the education and advancement of women trade unionists.
On Monday, 7th May, we were entertained at a reception by children from Germany.
Mr. Brown, Assistant-Secretary of the International Federation of Trade Unions, also
spoke to us on the coming Women's International at Cologne, in August. We have to
thank the National Executive of the English Labour Party for its help and financial
assistance, which makes it possible for English Women to take a great part at this Con-
ference. Many women in our Union who believe that the workers' grievances can only
be permanently solved by international agreements, and understandings, are hoping
that the Council of our Union will rise to the occasion when asked for a delegate to represent
us at this Congress.
Tuesday morning session was given to Labour Women's Organisations to discuss
and educate themselves in such matters as District Councils, and the Constitution of
Women's Sections generally in the Labour Party. I attended this as a visitor, and found
it very helpful from an educational standpoint. By ballot vote four women were elected
represent the Labour Party on the Standing Joint Committee of Women's Organisations.
On Tuesday afternoon the Lord Mayor of York opened the Conference and welcomed
the delegates to York, as did also the Chairman of the York Labour Party, and the President
of the Women's Section of the Labour Party.
Emergency resolutions were moved on the following questions: —Agricultural
Labourers (great was the discontent among the labourers' wives on the award accepted
of 25s.). The Irish Deportation. C.W.S. Dispute at Pelaw and Silvertown, also Trade
Boards. The Labour Party's Interim Report on Motherhood and Child Endowment
was passed after much discussion. Resolutions protesting against the discharge of married
teachers, or any other married women on the ground of marriage, was, after a long discussion,
mostly between industrial and labour delegates, carried by a large majority. The resolu-
tion on Unemployment among women. Education for Peace. The French Occupation
of the Ruhr. The Penal System. Women Police. Housing and Rents. Education
and Feeding of School Children, and the position of the Equality of Women in Industry.
All were discussed from a woman's point of view, and decisions arrived at.

its own business in a way that was a credit to Labour. With every woman who attended

Leicester.
Report of the National Conference of Labour Women, held in the Festival Concert
Rooms, at York, on 8th and 9th May, 1923.
The Conference opened at 2.30 on the 8th, Mrs. Harrison Bell in the chair.
said he considered it a great honour to be asked to do so.

The first business was a welcome to the delegates by the Lord Mayor of York, who
the country to-day was of great importance. Woman had so much influence and it was
the country if there were no differences of opinion, and he thought the power of women in
Mr. Hartley, Chairman of the
food to also welcomed the delegates. He, too, said a great deal to-day depended on the
women of the country. Whether the parliament of the country was good or bad depended
very largely on them. The Chairman of the Women's Section in York also joined in the
welcome and said the people in York would that day be realising the new spirit dawning
in the land. The Women's Section in York was making great progress having already
over 500 members.
The President of the Conference suitably replied.
Mrs. Harrison Bell, in her address, said how pleased she was to say that since the last
Conference in Leamington they had enrolled 20,000 new members. It had been a year
of anxiety in the Trade Unions, but although members had lapsed there were still many
more in the Unions than in 1914. In her opinion they were all there still and only waiting
for employment to be able again to pay into the Union.
Mrs. Adamson (Lincoln), said we ought to pay a tribute to those women candidates
who, though defeated, set up such a good fight at the last Parliamentary Election.
Adult Suffrage was then discussed. Miss Harkness (Glasgow) moved: "That this
Conference urges the Labour Party to take every opportunity to secure full Adult Suffrage
on the basis of one person one vote at the age of 21."
Miss Atkinson (Nottingham) seconded, and said in her opinion women under 30 had
much more sense than those over 30.
Mrs. Palmer and Mrs. Bell (Wimbledon), in supporting, said they thought the salvation
of the country lay in the younger women, who were quite as capable of reasonable opinions
as men of 21 years. Resolution carried.
A good discussion took place on the question of Married Women Teachers. A married
teacher delegate said she did not think the L.C.C. were against married women teachers
because they were married. The real reason was to discharge experienced teachers
drawing large salaries. She said there would be plenty of work for single teachers if we
could demand that classes in all schools should be only the size of those in secondary
schools. This resolution protesting against the action of the L.C.C. in discharging these
teachers was put to the Conference and carried.
The next discussion was on the two-shift system for girls. In moving the resolution
condemning the same, the delegate said it was detrimental to the health of these girls,
especially in the districts where housing conditions were bad, and girls were unable to get
their proper rest. This resolution was carried.
A resolution that all Parliamentary Elections be held on Saturday, and all Municipal
Elections in May instead of November was discussed. Swansea Women's Section said
they found it difficult in November to get the women out to vote. Weather was often
bad, and in their opinion May would be a much better month.
Mrs. Nicholls (Northampton Labour Party) supported the resolution dealing with
Saturday elections, and said in many cases the men, and especially railwaymen, were away
at work all the week, and therefore unable to record their vote at all. Resolution carried.
WEDNESDAY MORNING.
The first business of the Conference was an emergency resolution recommended by
Standing Orders Committee. Mrs. Turner (North Bucks) moved the resolution con-
gratulating the Norfolk Agricultural Workers on their magnificent fight for better conditions,
but viewed with alarm the terms of settlement, which were inadequate to provide a decent

living and urged the Labour Party to organise a Propaganda Campaign along the country-
side. This was seconded by a daughter of an agricultural worker whose mother was

A protest was made against the Irish deportations without trial. It was an outrage

Miss Symonds presented a report on the work done last year for the education of

The International situation was then discussed. A protest was made against the
Germans in the Ruhr working under French military rule. The League of Nations was
denounced as a fraud. What was really needed was a League of ALL Nations.
A report was read by Dr. Marion Phillips and accepted on Motherhood and Child
Endowment. The Conference was sure the committee were doing all they could to put
up a scheme regarding the same, worthy of the Party they represented.
An emergency resolution was moved by Miss Susan Lawrence, urging the Parliamentary
Labour Party to fight against the Government's measure regarding Trade Boards.
Miss Mary Quayle (Transport Workers) seconded, but it was opposed by Miss Carlin
(Dockers' Union) and Miss Manicum (Workers' Union), who both said in their opinion
Trade Boards made it very difficult to organise women workers. Two other delegates
protested against such views, and said although the Trade Boards were not perfect, they
were a great help to the workers and must be retained. Resolution was carried.
The Conference asked for the Abolition of Capital Punishment and also demanded a
force of Women Police in all large towns.
The next discussion was on Unemployment.
Mrs. Malone moved the resolution dealing with the foreign policy which called for the
re-opening of trade with Russia. Trade agreements this last two years had kept peace
with them. Barrow-in-Furness delegate said if trade agreements were broken there would
be more unemployment than at present. Other resolutions on unemployment asked
training with maintenance, and Dr. Marion Phillips recommended the Conference to ask
our Labour Representatives to press for an immediate grant from Government of £100,000.
The full support of the Conference was given to this appeal.
Other sections of the resolution asked for the unemployment insurance and relief to
be made more adequate, protesting against the gap in relief when girls who had anyone
else in the family working were unable to draw any relief at all. It was no fault of the
girl being out of work, and the Government should supply full maintenance.
Bolton Women's Section moved the Government be called upon at once to build
suitable houses for the workers with lower rents. Barrow seconded, saying the housing
conditions there were terrible, ex-Service men were in cellar dwellings and there were
many bad cases. They protested against the non-parlour dwellings; in these dwellings it
was difficult for a child in a large family to be able to study as much as he or she needed.
Mrs. Harkness (Glasgow) said their scheme of direct labour had saved that city some-
thing like £40,000, and we should demand that local authorities be given power to carry
on the work.
There were several other resolutions to discuss, but these, with the other business,
were referred to the Standing Joint Committee of Industrial Women's Organisations for
their consideration.
N. RICKETT,
Northampton No. 2.
NINE IN ONE ROOM.
The sanitary inspector at Higham Ferrers (Northamptonshire) reported that one
bedroom in a cottage was occupied by two brothers, ages 20 and 9, and seven sisters,
ages 19, 16, 15, 12, 7, 6 and 4. The only other bedroom was occupied by the parents and
a baby.
At the same meeting the Council had an old house to let, and the tenant of the cottage
referred to was one out of about 30 unsuccessful applicants. - Westminster Gazette, 9th
May, 1923.
