WOMEN'S ADVICE ON FACTORY INSPECTION.
Need at Next International Labour Conference.
meeting.
The importance of the presence of women at the Fifth Annual Session of the Inter-
national Labour Conference of the League of Nations, which will be held in Geneva next
October, is urged by the Director of the International Labour Office, M. Albert Thomas,
in a letter he has addressed to Governments in connection with the arrangements for this
This Conference will discuss general principles for the organisation of factory inspec-
tion, as it is felt that the time has now arrived for crystallising the results obtained by
experience in the chief industrial States possessing efficient services of factory inspection
and for indicating by what means the supervision exercised by such services may be
extended to countries which at present have less effective safeguards for the administration
of factory laws.
By the terms of the Peace Treaty each of the four delegates, which each of the 54
States members of the International Labour Organisation is entitled to send to the Con-
ference, may bring two advisers, the special stipulation being made that "when questions
specially affecting women are to be considered by the Conference, one at least of the
advisers should be a woman."
In drawing the attention of Governments to this portion of the Treaty the Director
also refers to the following clause among the principles " of special and urgent importance
which all industrial communities should endeavour to apply, so far as their special circum-
stances will permit":
"Each State should make provision for a system of inspection in which women
should take part, in order to ensure the enforcement of the laws and regulations for
the protection of the employed."
The first session of the Conference which met in Washington in 1919 recommended,
in view of the decisions reached regarding certain aspects of women's employment, "that
each States member of the International Labour Organisation which has not already
done so should establish as soon as possible, not only a system of efficient factory inspection,
but also in addition thereto a Government service especially charged with the duty of
safeguarding the health of the workers, which will keep in touch with the International
Labour Office." Notification has been received from Great Britain that this recommenda-
tion has already been applied in this country.
WORLD CARE OF THE DISABLED.
Meeting of Experts at Geneva.
A meeting of experts from all parts of the world on questions connected with disabled
ex-Service men will be held at the International Labour Office of the League of Nations
at Geneva, on Tuesday, July 31st, to discuss the question of finding employment for dis-
abled men.

"The national was thus kept in his country, which no longer opened its gates, by the formal obstacle of passport arrangements, which are still almost everywhere in force. Similarly, in countries of immigration measures have been taken almost everywhere to guard against a fear of invasion which has possibly been rather exaggerated. The Three Per Cent. Immigration Act in the United States sufficiently illustrates this tendency from any one country to three per cent. of the number of persons of that nationality resident in the United States in 1910; it restricts considerably the emigration of peoples who take a principal part in present-day emigration, such as Italians, Poles, Hungarians, and Jews.
# Restrictive legislation, however, does not explain the whole situation. The tendency noted is too general to be referred to a particular set of circumstances. Another factor, the economic factor, has been involved, but its effects are often very ill understood. Immigration depends on economic conditions in the countries towards which it is directed; at a time of depression a country of immigration will close its doors; it will cease to ask for immigrants and the stream of immigration will automatically dry up. Again, when a country of emigration is hard hit and the prosperity of its people suffers, individuals are unable to find the necessary money to pay their expenses. Poverty keeps a population stricken class; on the contrary, the possession of certain means is indispensable if emigration is to take place.
"Towards the end of 1920 and during 1921 countries both of emigration and of immigration suffered from a very severe economic crisis. In the countries of immigration unemployment and the fear of an excessive influx of immigrants caused restrictive measures to be hastily taken in the countries of emigration, at any rate in those where the exchange had fallen severely, the unforuntate population was unable to get together the money required for passage and settlement, payment for which is always calculated on a gold basis!"

SHOE UNION AND LABOUR NEW BANNERS.
Unfurling by Miss Bondfield and Mr. E. L. Poulton, J.P.
A "Labour" May Day celebration meeting was held at the Northampton Town Hall on Tuesday evening. There was a fair attendance. Mr. Emmett Law (President of the Northampton No. 2 Branch of the Boot and Shoe Operatives' Union) occupied the chair, supported by Miss Bondfield, J.P. (Prospective Parliamentary "Labour" candidate), Mr. E. L. Poulton, J.P. (General Secretary of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives), Mr. F. O. Roberts, J.P., M.P., Mr. W. R. Townley, J.P. (President, Northampton No. 1 Branch), Mr. W. Pitts (Secretary of No. 1 Branch), Mr. S. Thompson, J.P. (Secretary No. 2 Branch).

A number of children, trained by Miss I. Smith, gave charming old English folk dances.

Mr. E. L. Poulton, J.P. (who was present to unfurl the handsome new banner of the No. 1 and 2 Branches of the Boot and Shoe Operatives' Union), in the course of his address, said in 1892 when their old banner was unfurled, the Northampton No. 1 Branch had a membership of 4,285. It had now 5,597 members, and those figures would have been higher but for the agreement between the two branches that all the women should be transferred to the No. 2 Branch. In 1892 the No. 2 and the old No. 3 Branches had just over 900 members. To-day they were in the proud position of being able to say that the No. 2 Branch had grown to 7,046 members. Thus they had in Northampton nearly 13,000 members of the Boot and Shoe Operatives' Union, and the Union had more influence than many people imagined. In 1892 the Union as a whole had just over 42,000 members, and at the present time they had over 75,000. (Applause.) They had ₤40,000 in their central fund in 1892, and at present together with the Branch funds they had ₤368,000, and they had established an out-of-work fund out of which they had paid their members nearly $200,000 during the period it had been in existence.
Mr. Poulton went on to say that the war they were engaged in was a war against unjust and inequitable conditions, and amid applause he unfurled the new banner.

On one side of the banner is a figure holding a flag inscribed "Emancipation of Labour," and inviting the workers to march towards the rising sun of the "Co-operative Commonwealth," and underneath the picture are the words "Workers of all lands, unitel you have a world to win, you have nothing to lose but your chains." The other side of the banner bears the words "Northampton Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives, Northampton No. 1 and No. 2 Branches." In the centre is the figure of St. Crispin, the patron saint of shoemakers, and illustrations of various operations in the boot trade. At the bottom is inscribed "May the Trade be trodden underfoot by the Whole World."
Miss Bondfield unveiled the banner of the "Northampton Labour Party (Women's Section!" The motto on the banner is "What the Parents Sow the Children Reap." -
Northampton Chronicle, 2nd May, 1923."

EDUCATION AND THE BOOT AND SHOE TRADE.
Address by Mr. A. C. Boyde.

"Educational Extension" formed the subject of a very interesting address by Mr.
A. C. Boyde, M.A., LL.B., Director of Education, at Harleston Road P.M. Schools on
Friday night.
Mr. Boyde said when he came to Northampton two and a half years ago Northampton
and the whole country was bubbling over with enthusiasm for education, but since then
there had been a serious slump in education, chiefly because of the financial state of the
country. The country had spent over £300,000,000 a year on what is at best a luxury-
he would not name it, but it costs a penny a pint less now than it did a month ago.
£20,000,000 is to be given back to those who drink this luxury, but at the same time the
expenditure on education is to be reduced by £3,000,000. Those who decided to do this
had not a proper view of the relative values of the things under consideration.
When spending money like business men the thing to consider was not how much
are we spending, but are we getting value for our money. If we are getting value for our
money the more we spend the better, and that should be our attitude towards education.
The purposes of education are to produce sound bodies, keen brains, and model men
and women. or, as it is put in the education text-books, to produce a physical, mental,
and moral man. If we attained to those ideals it will be very difficult to argue that we are
spending too much on them. The position we have to face to-day is much too serious
to allow of any check on education.

The Resources of Science.

He was quite satisfied all the resources of science have not been applied to the boot
and shoe industry as they could have been. The Education Committee started a senior
day course for youths of 18 and 19 years of age from the boot and shoe trade. Scholar-
ships of the value of £40 were given, £20 by the Education Committee, £10 by the manu-
facturers, and £10 by the Trade Unions. About ten youths went through the first year's
course, which ended last August. The second year's course should have begun in Septem-
ber, but not a single candidate presented himself from the whole boot and shoe trade.
On the leather side, on the other hand, the number of students joining the classes had been
very satisfactory.

A reason for the dearth of students from the boot and shoe trade was that by attending
the course they were losing a wage of about 36s. a week for one of about 16s., but the chief
reason was that there is no conviction in the industry that science is of use in boot and
shoe manufacture. Mr. Blakeman had estimated that no fewer than 300 young people
entered the boot and shoe trade in Northampton every year, yet, in spite of the fact that
their wages were paid, only 66 boys turned up for the time-off scheme, which catered for
boys and girls between the ages of 14 and 16.

Yet on the engineering side 74 attended under the scheme, and the engineering trade
in Northampton was not nearly so large as the boot and shoe trade. On the commercial
side 207 had taken advantage of the time-off scheme. The great need is for a competent
person to convey to the young people the conviction that it will profit them and their
trade if they will give up their time to the courses. - Daily Echo, Northampton, 5th May,
1923.

GENERAL FEDERATION OF TRADE UNIONS.

SPECIAL REPORT ON DUNDEE
On the High Rate of Expenditure on Disablement Benefit to Women
Members in Scotland.

A careful examination has now been made of all these claims. At the end of June
there were 123 women in Scotland receiving Disablement Benefit, and of these 110 are
attached to the Dundee Branch, and 13 to other Branches.
A careful examination of the medical evidence and visitors' reports does not indicate
the presence of any malingering ; in fact there is clear evidence that the majority of cases
may be termed chronic, and unlikely to ever resume work. Nearly one-half (60) of the
members are receiving monthly certificates from their doctors, and a further 12 are in
various institutions. Of the 123 cases mentioned, 72 of the members are over the age of
50, and the average age of all the members is 50. There are six members, not more than
23 years of age, who are suffering from Tuberculosis.
The average duration of incapacity of the 123 cases under consideration is 109 weeks
4 days.

With regard to the use of Regional Medical Officers, we have always referred cases
where the visitor's report-or the nature of incapacity-has indicated the least possibility
of the member being capable of work. During the last 18 months, 27 of the 123 members
in question have been referred to the District Medical Officers, but, until the last few days,
last few reports received from the District Medical Officer, however, there have been
there was not a single case in which benefit could be justifiably suspended. Among the
three cases in which benefit has been suspended pending a further local report, which has
not at present come to hand. Of these three cases, one failed to attend for examination,
another is declared capable of light work, and the third is certified as not incapable
of work.
The bulk of our women members in Scotland are ordinarily engaged on heavier work
than the women members in England, and this has a direct bearing on the rate of expendi-
ture on both Sickness Benefit and Disablement Benefit. Furthermore, heavy work
causes incapacity much more frequently during pregnancy. Taking 100 consecutive
claims for Maternity Benefit, it was found that in England approximately £100 was ex-
pended on Sickness Benefit before the date of confinement, whereas in Scotland the amount
was £273.
The only prospect of any diminution in the average rate of expenditure is by way of
deaths and the age limit (there are 21 members over 65), or an increase in the younger
membership.

Sickness Amongst Scottish Women.
I have called attention to the difference between the benefit cost per head of women
members in England and Scotland, the comparable figures for incapacities arising out of
or incidental to, pregnancy being £100 England, and £273 Scotland. Recent comparisons
show that the ratios are rising in Scotland, and that these tend more seriously to depreciate
the stability of the Benefit Account.
W. A. APPLETON.

Housing Conditions.
Occupied houses in Dundee numbered 42,256, and, as the population numbered
168,315, the average number of persons per house is 3.98. In 1911, in the area now
included within Dundee, occupied houses numbered 41,229, and the average number
of persons per house was 4.28. The 42,256 occupied houses contain 111,064 windowed
rooms, and the average number of persons to each 100 such rooms is found to be 152;
in 1911, in Dundee as then constituted, this average was 169, while in the area annexed
to the City during the inter-censal period it was 95, and within the area now included
within the City it was 161. Using this proportion as a test of the housing condition
of the population these figures show that crowding is less now than in 1911, either in
the City as then constituted, or in the area included within the City. The number
of persons per 100 windowed rooms in the portion of Dundee within the Dundee
Parish is 152, and within Mains and Strathmartine Parish, 131.

Coroner on 321
PANEL DOCTORS INDICTED.
"Penny-in-the-Slot" Treatment. "Scamped Work."
The experiment of trying to provide 15,000,000 people with medical attendance on contract
lines has had ten years' trial and has proved a failure.
This was one of the remarks made yesterday by Dr. Edwin Smith, the North-East
London coroner, at the resumed Shoreditch inquest on John Edward Cox (22). He died
in the local infirmary, and complaints were made by his father of the treatment his son
had received at the hands of Dr. Hemsted, his panel doctor.
At the outset the coroner said he thought there was no doubt there had been neglect
in this case.
Mr. Charles A. Davis, solicitor, on behalf of Dr. Hemsted, said he had a certificate
from a doctor at Brighton stating that Dr. Hemsted was unable to attend the inquiry as
he was confined to bed.
The coroner said he did not propose to adjourn the case again as there was no question
of criminal neglect. The letter the doctor had sent to the Court showed that he was
decidedly hazy about the case. He said that when Mr. Cox called at the surgery he was
suffering from bronchitis, and he told him to go to hospital as he himself was too ill to
attend him.
Although he gave him a prescription for infusion of rhubarb, or something of that
svt. as a matter of fact the patient was suffering from strangulated hernia and died four
days later.
Mr. Davis pointed out that the patient died four days after his visit to the surgery
and medical men had stated that anyone attacked with strangulated hernia died within
48 hours.
Inadequate Treatment.
The coroner said he did not, as one who had been a medical practitioner for 25 years,
agree to that: but there was another aspect of the case, for it represented a class all too
often met with, namely, that of panel patients receiving totally inadequate attention.
It was common knowledge that at a typical panel consultation the patient announced
what seemed to him to be his most prominent symptom, a cough, or a pain, and so forth,
and instantly got a prescription for something supposed to fit his condition.
There was no time for any but the most perfunctory investigation, for the waiting-
room was full of other patients to be seen, and the patient was hurried from the surgery,
almost before he had entered it.
The underlying cause of the symptoms must be missed in an immense number of cases
where recognition of the early stages of the trouble was all-important.
The human machine that was out of order did not lend itself to this lightning
diagnosis and penny-in-the-slot style of treatment.
It was also claimed that the system was a step forward to better things. That was
nonsense. The panel system was a retrograde step, not too strongly described as a disas-
trous blunder and a miserable failure.
It put a premium on scamped work and inefficiency, for it could not be denied that
on the whole the worst work was being done by the men drawing the largest incomes.
In the end a verdict of "Death from natural causes" was recorded by the coroner.—
Daily Herald, 12th May, 1923

DOGS IN SILK CAGES: PEOPLE IN DENS.
Powder and Luxury for Pets. Puppies v. Men.
Great care was taken of the dogs yesterday at the annual show of the Ladies' Kennel
Association, at Richmond.
The claims of colour were not forgotten, and a bulldog with a green collar was housed
in a cage lined with green silk.
In the toy dog section silk of varying hues lined the cages, bordered with silk of another
shade harmonising with the colour scheme.
Dainty hair brushes, combs, hair-dressing powders, and thermos flasks with warm
water were laid out in front or beside the cages, and the proud owners of the favoured
animals were in constant attention upon their pets.
DREADFUL OVERCROWDING IN POOR AREAS.
A case was in Blackpool, were an ejectment order was granted against a tenant of one
room rent 6s. In it there lived and slept five persons.
In a possession case yesterday, at the Thames Court, it was stated that there were no
fewer than 24 occupants in a house of five small rooms, and that in one room there were
eight people. The magistrate (Mr. Disney) said it was one of the worst overcrowding
cases he had heard for a long time.
DIED, LOOKING FOR WORK.
Sixty-three years old, and out of work, William Henry Jackson, a Mexboro' insurance
worker, was yesterday found dead from exhaustion on a country road at Kirton Lindsay,
near Brigg, Lincolnshire. He had been tramping the country looking for work.
-Daily Herald, May 17th, 1923.
TRAGEDY OF THE OPEN ROAD.
Old Man's Body Found in a Hovel.
A gruesome discovery was made by a Hillmorton labourer, named John Alfred Cashmore,
on Sunday. He was walking past a hovel near the Watling Street Road when his attention
was attracted by what seemed to be a bundle of rags.
On investigating he found the dead body of a man, apparently 65 years of age. There
was nothing to show the cause of death, which, it is believed, occurred some days previously.
The man had evidently undergone considerable hardship, and the body was in a terribly
wasted condition.
A ticket found in one of his pockets bore the name of Joseph Williams. The body
was removed by the police to the Red Lion Inn, Hillmorton, to await an inquest. —Leicester
Mercury, May 15th, 1923.

MOVE FOR WORKERS' BETTERMENT.
Labour's Appeal for Ratification of the International Labour Conventions.
The policy of the Government with regard to the draft conventions and recommenda-
tions adopted by the third and fourth sessions of the International Labour Conference,
held at Geneva in 1921 and 1922, was under discussion in the House to-day.
Some of the proposals are already law in this country.
As to the others, the Government is prepared to give effect to two conventions-one,
prohibiting, with certain exceptions, the employment of persons under 18 as trimmers or
stokers; and the other which makes compulsory the medical examination of children
and young persons employed on ships.
The Rejected Proposals.
The Government was strongly criticised during the debate for deciding to take no
action in regard to those which prohibit the employment in agriculture of children under
14 during school hours, the employment of white lead and sulphate of lead in internal
painting of buildings, and the employment of males under 18 and all females in industrial
painting work involving the use of these substances.
A recommendation to prohibit the employment of women as agricultural workers
during certain periods before and after childbirth was also rejected by the Government,
and this decision also was the subject of severe strictures.
The view of the Labour Party was that the Government should, as in honour bound,
ratify all the conventions and adopt all the recommendations.
To the Minister of Labour's resolution approving the Government's policy the Labour
Party tabled an amendment substituting for approval a declaration in favour of ratifying
the conventions and recommendations.
SIR M. BARLOW, the Minister of Labour, moving the resolution approving the Govern-
ment's policy, said the 1921 conference was concerned mainly with the question of agricul-
ture. It adopted seven draft conventions and eight recommendations and these were
laid on the table of the House in March, 1922.
After explaining these in detail, Sir Montague said the Government found itself in
some difficulty with regard to ratification, because on some points attention would have
to be directed with a view to amendment.
Ratification Urged.
MR. CLYNES (Lab., Platting), moving the Labour amendment, said he thought the
House should at least go to the length of supporting those decisions which their representa-
tives at the international gathering had not opposed.
"We cannot have the full results of this beneficent and promising work," said Mr.
Clynes, "if these great assemblies are not fully encouraged to work with the confidence
that their decisions will not be merely respected, but will be put into effect by the Govern-
ments and the peoples represented.
"Public money is frequently used for research work and other scientific purposes,
and the Labour Party says that some of it should be used for this helpful work of human
betterment, of which large masses of the population in all countries are greatly in need."
Mr. Clynes expressed special disappointment that they had not had unqualified
acceptance from the Minister of Labour of the maternity Convention.
He urged the Government to say definitely whether a Bill was to be introduced this
session to deal with the question of trimmers and stokers. If not they would have to wait
until the end of 1924, long before which time the Government itself might have come to
an end. (Laughter.)
Danger of Delay.
DR. MACNAMARA (N.L., Camberwell, N.W.) hoped the Labour members would set
their faces against ratification with reservations. There might be reservations until
there was nothing left.
As to the convention dealing with the age of children in agriculture, he pointed out
that the existing Scottish law provided certain exceptions which made it impossible for
us to ratify it as it stood.
He understood that the matter was to be referred to the International Labour organisa-
tion. So far so good, but he appealed to the Labour Minister not to leave the matter
there. Let him get an early reply so that they might know where they were.

INSIDIOUS ATTACK ON LABOUR.
Tories and Trade Union Levies.
The political organisation of the Labour and Trade Union movement is being made
the object of insidious attack.
The idea is to injure its financial resources. Money is essential to any political move-
ment, and the first object of Labour's opponents is to restrict the system of political levies
common to the Trade Unions.
The movement began in Conservative quarters in the last Parliament, and has now
been revived in this, but with interesting developments.

A Bill has been introduced in the House of Commons by Colonel Archer-Shee, a
Unionist, under which no political levy could be collected
by a Trade Union unless and until the member had first signified in writing on a prescribed
form his willingness to subscribe such a levy. This form must be filled up annually, other-
wise the levy cannot be collected.
A Subtle Point.
The subtle point of this change is this-that whereas now a Trade Union member is
called upon to pay the political levy-after a ballot has decided that it shall be made-
unless he signs a form releasing him from doing so, in future under this Bill every Trade
Unionist would be required to sign a form indicating his willingness to pay.
Leaders of the Labour movement calculate that, for a time at least, this provision
would very materially affect the political income of the movement.
The placing upon the individual Trade Unionist of the onus of signing once a year
a declaration of his readiness to pay a political levy would mean a loss of income, not
through lack of sympathy, but through forgetfulness, and would necessitate special
organisation to get the forms signed and collected.

Government's Proposal.
But the move goes farther than this. The Bill-which is, of course, a private member's
measure-is badly placed in the Parliamentary ballot for the right to introduce private
Bills, and the Government has been asked to give it special facilities.
The Government's reply is an indication that it will shortly invite Labour leaders
to discuss the political levy with them "in the hope that some arrangement may be reached
by which the position of members of Trade Unions who desire to contribute to any political
party may be assured."
The form of the reply has roused a suspicion in the minds of Labour representatives
that what the Government have in mind is a suggestion that a compromise might be
effected whereby the right should be given to Trade Unionists when asked to pay political
levies to stipulate which political party such levies shall be paid to.
opponents.
The effect of this would be that any Trade Union member could demand that his
political levy should be paid to the Conservative Party, and the organisation machinery
of the Labour movement would thus be used to provide funds for its political
Astute Move.
If Labour suspicions are well founded-and it is believed that they arc-it is a decidedly
astute and "cool" move.
Labour, it is declared, would never consent to any such proposal, and if the alternative
is that facilities will be given to the Bill referred to, then the Bill will be fought tooth and
nail.--From an exclusive article to Revnelis's, 29th April, 1923.

NEW ZEALAND FEDERATED BOOT MANUFACTURERS' INDUSTRIAL
ASSOCIATION OF EMPLOYERS (Auckland Branch).
BOOT TRADE. - First-class Machinists, light work ; wages, £3 or more, according to
ability. - NORTHERN BOOT LTD., Federal Street.
MR. T. F. RICHARDS,
AUCKLAND,
9th March, 1923.
President, National Union of Boot & Shoe Operatives.
DEAR SIR. - At a meeting of our Association held in December last, the matter of
scarcity of labour occupied the greater part of the session, and on the suggestion of Mr. W.
Gilbert, it was decided that it would be advisable to write, soliciting your assistance in
inducing suitable labour coming to New Zealand.
There are many advantages offering here to industrious operatives, male and female.
There is practically no unemployment in the Shoe industry, and as to machinists there is an
unsatisfiable demand; some of our members have been advertising continuously in the
Press, and offer £3 5s. per week and upwards to good hands.
Although we are working under an award in this Dominion, for both sexes, there are
really very few who are on the minimum, and then only on account of age or other dis-
ability. The minimum here is £4 6s. weekly for males. Females £2 5s., many of the
judges the conditions of work and living are of a much higher standard than the English
factories work five days only. I may say that according to the opinion of competent
standards, food being cheaper and as Mr. Gilbert may have told you food is purer and of a
higher quality than in your big cities.
With regard to the housing conditions, of course there is a shortage of houses, as is
generally the case all over the Empire, but there are literally many thousands of houses
going up and in Auckland particularly the suburbs are increasing in a wonderful
manner.
We can confidently say that this is the most favoured spot in the British Dominions.
I believe I am not overstating the situation when I say that a man has an infinitely better
chance of betterment here than the old country. I could instance many cases of men who
have started and are carrying on successful businesses here though only a few years in the
Dominion.
Although there have been many additions to our population by emigration, they all
find shelter and soon adapt themselves to the conditions here. There are more workmen
here owning their own homes than could possibly be in the Home Country, a far greater
proportion.
Now, if you could use your influence to induce some of the surplus labour to come
along to New Zealand, they would, I am sure find congenial employment, under climatic
conditions that are unsurpassed.
Benchmen and Machinists for preference; there are advertisements appearing con-
tinuously in the daily papers for hands of every type.
Mr. Gilbert is enthusiastic in advocating the enlistment of English workers, he having
had a good deal of experience as President of the Employees' Union, and is now a partner
in a flourishing business.
I wrote some time ago to you, but cannot understand why I have not received a reply
so have taken the precaution of registering this letter as I can only conjecture the first
has gone astray.
I am, Sir, yours faithfully.
W. J. RATTRAY,
Secretary, New Zealand Boot Manufacturers' Association, Auckland Branch.
Address letter: - W. J. RATTRAY, c/o Kelly & Rattray, 46, Belgium Street, Auckland,
New Zealand.
「The above is a copy of a letter I have received from New Zealand. Any member
desirous of going to New Zealand I would suggest first of all he should get into touch with
the Trade Union Officials there, and my idea of inserting this letter in the Monthly Report
is to give any intending emigrant to New Zealand useful information. - T. F. RICHARDS.

KINGSWOOD BOOT MANUFACTURERS.
The annual meeting of the Kingswood and District Boot Manufacturers' Association
was held on Monday in Bristol, Mr. G. E. Britton presiding. The secretary reported
a balance in hand of £29 15s. 8d. Mr. G. E. Britton was thanked for his valuable services
and re-elected President, and other appointments were Executive Committee, Messrs.
G. E. Britton (chairman). G. F. Bryant, E. E. Pratt, A. Lovell, and A. F. Moon; Arbitra-
tion Board, Messrs. G. E. Britton, G. F. Bryant, E. E. Pratt, W. J. Edwards, F. Cook,
H. Sheppard, A. F. Moon, and F. Wilshire; reserve members, Messrs. A. H. Miles, O.
Lovell, O. Edwards, and A. H. Jay; secretary, Mr. W. T. Ling; hon. auditors, Messrs.
H. G. Fussell and R. C. Bird. Messrs. Allen and Prior, Kingswood, were elected members
of the association. - Western Press, 2nd May, 1923.

5
STANDING ORDERS.
ANNUAL MEETINGS.
RULE 80. Annual Meetings of the Conference shall be held on Whit Monday
and subsequent days.
TIME OF CONFERENCE MEETING.
RULE 81. On the first day of Conference the Delegates shall assemble at a
place provided for the purpose, at Ten o'clock a.m. prompt, and
shall proceed to the election of Door Keeper and Two Tellers, and
shall also consider the President's Address and Council's Report; after
which the Conference shall adjourn at 12.30 p.m. and re-assemble at
2 p.m. and proceed with the business of the Conference and adjourn at
5 p.m. On Tuesday and each succeeding day, the time of meeting
shall be 9.30 a.m., adjourn at 12.30 p.m., re-assemble at 2 p.m., and
adjourn for the day at 5 p.m.
DELEGATES' QUALIFICATION.
RULE 82. The Conference shall consist of Delegates who have been elected
in accordance with General Rules 71 and 77, which read as follows:-
"Delegates shall be elected in accordance with the number of Financial
Members returned in the December Report previous to the date on which
the Conference is to be held. All Permanent Officials shall attend the
Conferences by virtue of their office, over and above the maximum of
representation. The basis of representation for delegates shall be one
delegate for every 1,000 financial members, with a minimum representa-
tion of not less than fifty delegates (one-third to form a quorum)."
"The latest date for sending in amendments and additions to Rules, or
Standing Orders of Conference, shall be January 15th, in the year in which
the Conference is due to be held, and they shall be published in the
January Monthly Report. Nominations for delegates shall be taken on
the February Monthly Meeting Night, and voting for same on the March
Monthly Meeting Night."
The Council to attend by virtue of their office.
PRESIDENT OF CONFERENCE.
RULE 83. The President of the Union, by virtue of his office, takes the chair
at all Conferences.
STANDING ORDERS COMMITTEE.
RULE 84. A committee of five persons shall be elected from the Delegates
of the Conference, whose duty it shall be to examine the Delegates
Credentials, and report thereon. They shall also be at the service of
the Conference to consider any questions or matters that may be
relegated to it with a view to reporting thereon during the sitting of
Conference. For such extra services they shall receive additional
pay, to the amount of 10s. each.


---
Here is the extracted text from the image:

6
TELLERS.
RULE 85. - Two Delegates shall be appointed as Tellers, whose ruling as to
numbers shall be final, except in cases of dispute, when the Chairman
shall order a recount.
DOOR KEEPER.
RULE 86. - A Door Keeper (not a delegate) shall be elected at the commence-
ment of the Conference, whose duties shall be to test all applications
for admittance to Conference, and also to keep the floor of the hall
strictly for Delegates only, and also to regulate the granting of
passes to members of the public to the gallery, and to perform such
other duties as may be required of him by the General Secretary.
Preference to be given to a local man, and his pay shall be 15s
per day for any day or days required.
VOTING.
RULE 87. - The system of voting shall be by show of hands, the decision
of the majority to rule.
LIMITATION OF SPEECHES.
RULE 88. - Every latitude is to be allowed the Delegates for giving expression
to their views on the various subjects that may be brought before
them; but in the event of the Chairman seeing that the business
is not making satisfactory progress, he shall have power to appeal
to the Conference to limit the time allowed to movers of resolutions
to ten minutes, a seconder to seven minutes, and any subsequent
speaker to five minutes. No one shall speak more than once on a
question, except the mover of an original resolution. Should the
President be of opinion that there is no practical difference among
the Delegates, he shall have the power to stop the discussion.
AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS.
RULE 89. - Should any amendment of the Standing Orders of Conference be
proposed by any Branch, such amendment shall be forwarded at the
same time and under the same conditions as the amendments pro-
posed to the Rules. Notice of such amendment to be sent by the
General Secretary to the Delegates as early as convenient after
receipt.
DELEGATES LEAVING CONFERENCE.
RULE 90. - No Delegate shall leave Conference without the consent of the
President, and Delegates absent one whole sitting without leave of
absence shall be named by the Chairman. The Conference shall
thereupon decide what action shall be taken with any such
delegate.

8
EXISTING RULES.
RULE 32.—Persons over 40 years of age wishing to join the Union shall join
for trade purposes only, but may join the National Health Insurance
Department for sick purposes. Persons joining under this rule shall
be entitled fo £6 funeral benefit.
RULE 33.—Operatives of 50 years of age or over shall be allowed to
join the Union on the following scale: Entrance fee, 6d.; contri-
butions 5d. per week, 3 1/2d. to go to the Central Fund and 1 1/2d. to
branch (females 1 1/4d. and 3/4d.); the member to receive for the above
contributions all trade benefits, with the exception of out-of-work
pay, out-of-work contributions, and funeral pay. The benefits
allowed being strike, dispute, lock-out, travelling, bond-note and
legal assistance in connection with trade matters.
RULE 36.—A full financial member (male or female), with not less than five
years' continuous membership, leaving the United Kingdom with a
clearance card for employment abroad, and returning within five
tinuous member of another Union connected with our craft, shall serve
a probation of six months before becoming entitled to either sick,
funeral, or out of work benefit.

12
EXISTING RULES.

RULE 205. - Compensation shall be given to financial members for loss of tools
by fire, at the discretion of the Council. The application to be made
through the Branch Committee.

RULE 209. - Any member who has belonged to the Union thirteen weeks, any
is clear on the books, shall be entitled to a Bond Note of £5, and and
branch wishing to give Bond Notes of greater amount or additional
Bonds, or Bonds to members who have not belonged to the Union
thirteen weeks, can do so, but on their own responsibility.

RULE 210. - If a member has made away with work, and the Union has made
it good, all expenses so incurred shall be placed as a book debt
against such member, who must repay it, serve twenty-six weeks'
probation, and be clear on the books before becoming entitled to
trade or sick benefits, the probation to date from the time he makes
his first payment towards the book debt. The Council shall have
power (on the application of the branch) to mitigate the amount as
they may deem fit.

RULE 211. - The Union to be at the cost of prosecution under this law, and no
Bond Notes to be issued but those supplied by the Council.

RULE 212. - In all cases where the parties so entrusted should abscond with
the work, or any portion thereof, the employer must make applica-
tion for them at their addresses, and should the employer fail to
recover the property he must be prepared to prosecute or the Union
will not indemnify him.

RULE 213. - All Bond Notes to be returned by the members to the Secretary
who issued them, or a note from the employer to show that all the
work has been finished up properly.

RULE 214. - The Union will not be answerable to employers for any work kept
out above fourteen days, unless the said employer notifies the same
within fourteen days of that date.

RULE 215. - Should any branch allow a Bond Note to remain in the possession
of an employer after the member to whom it was issued has con-
tracted a debt of 13s, including trade and sick contributions, fines
and levies, such branch will be held responsible for all claims made
on security of such Bond Note.

RULE 216. - All bills from employers for work made away with, and the Bond
Notes upon which the claims are made must be forwarded by
the branch officers to the Council when making their claims to the
Union.

RULE 217. - Members out of employment and entitled to benefit shall receive
3s. per day or 18s. per week for any ten weeks they remain out of
work during any 12 consecutive months.

EXISTING RULES.

RULE 236. - Male members declaring on the sick fund shall receive 2s. per day
females, and youths under 18 years of age, to receive 1s. per day
or 12s. per week for twelve weeks in any twelve consecutive months
6s. per week during the same period, provided it is drawn continuousy.
But should a member declare on the sick fund oftener than once
during such twelve months, the whole amount previously drawn, if
coming within the twelve months previous to the date on the
declaring-on certificate, shall be reckoned against him. Example:
a member drew one day's pay on the 29th May, in any year,
and declared on again on the 29th May the following year, that day's
pay shall be counted. Members who may have received their full
amount in such twelve consecutive months, shall not be entitled to
any further sick benefit until after the expiration of 52 clear weeks
from the date of receiving his or her last sick pay. The total amount
of sick pay to be drawn by any full male member shall not exceed
£40; half-pay members, £20; females not to exceed £20, whether
continuous members or not. A member working for a longer period
than three hours in a day is not entitled to any payment from the
Sick Funds for such day.
Suppose
RULE 252. The General Secretary shall keep a banking account of £500 of
the Union Funds and shall find security to that amount.
RULE 253. The Council shall have a banking Account of £3,000, and shall be
empowered to draw on the said account. Cheques must be signed
by the General President and General Secretary.
RULE 255. In the event of the sick fund being reduced below an amount
equal to 7s. 6d. per financial member, the Council shall have power
to lay a levy of 1s. per quarter per member, and 6d. per quarter per
female or youth member, until the fund is restored to an amount
equal to 7s. 6d. per financial member. The only exemption shall be
members paying for special trade benefits. Sick levy must not be
paid from the branch funds, but directly by each individual member
of the Union.
RULE 263.-Any member engaged on Union business after his working hours
shall be paid at the rate of 1s. 6d. per hour.
RULE 294. --Any members whilst on the sick funds found out of their homes
after nine o'clock p.m., between the first of April and the first of
October, and seven o'clock p.m. between the first of October and
the first of April, shall be fined to 2s. 6d. for each offence. Any
member not suffering from bodily infirmity, but unable to follow his
usual employment, may, by permission of the branch officials, obtain
exemption from this Rule.

EXISTING RULES:

RULE 23. To make provision for the Union being represented in Parliament
by Members, who shall pledge themselves to work for the realisation
of the Union's objects, and carry out the decisions of the Trade
Union Congress.

RULE 25. To administer the National Health Insurance Acts, 1911-1920, and
Amendments thereto.

RULE 48. - Any member or members bringing a clear card of more than twenty-
six weeks' standing from another society, shall be admitted free, and
forthwith entitled to a Bond Note. He shall, however, serve
the necessary probation of twenty-six weeks for trade, and fifty-two
weeks for out-of-work, sick and funeral benefits.

RULE 55. The President and Secretary (who must reside within a radius
of fifteen miles of the seat of government) shall be elected every two
years by a general vote of the Financial Members of the Union.
For the election of the Council, who shall also serve for two years
the Union shall be divided into twelve Districts (see Constitution for
division of districts, Section 3, Rules 26, 27 and 28), and each district
shall elect its own representative, who must be a Financial Member
of one of the branches in the district.

RULE 57. Two Organisers shall be appointed by the vote of the whole
country. They shall act under the direction of the Council. They
shall be elected every two years, at the same time and in the same
manner as the Union officers.

RULE 58. A manager for the business of the Union under the National
Health Insurance Acts shall be elected every two years by a general
vote of the Union. He must be a Financial Member of the Union
and over 21 years of age. The salary of the manager shall be £400
per annum. The nominations and method of election for the said
official shall apply as in the case of election for the Union officers.
The duties of the manager shall be to manage and control the
business of the Insurance Department, to see that the business is
carried out in accordance with the Insurance Acts and the rules of
the society. The manager of the Insurance Department shall be
subject to the control of the Council and act under their instructions.

RULE 99. He shall attend the Trade Union Congress and the Annual Meeting
of the Labour Party, by virtue of his office.

RULE 100. He shall also attend the Trades Union Congress and the Annual

RULE 108. The duties of Parliamentary Agents when elected to the House of
Commons shall be to pay strict attention to all questions brought
before the House affecting the Union, and the interests of labour
generally. They shall from time to time publish particulars of such
questions in the Monthly Report. When not engaged in the House
of Commons they may be employed as organisers by arrangement
between themselves and the Council. It is understood that for active
and consultative purposes their services shall be at the disposal of the
Council. Parliamentary Agents shall pledge themselves to and carry
out the labour programme as laid down from time to time by the
Annual Conferences of the Union; otherwise they shall cease to hold
office. When elected to Parliament they shall attend the Annual
Conference and give in their report. Should a Parliamentary Agent
be elected to the House of Commons who was a full time national
official before the election to the House, and fails to secure re-election
to the House of Commons, he should act as organiser for the Union
until the following Conference, when his position would be
determined.
RULE 70. A National Conference of Delegates from each and every district
in the Union shall meet annually for three days, on Whit Monday,
Tuesday, and Wednesday, to discuss matters of policy connected
with the Union, and every third year the conference shall be
extended to six days to deal with suggested alterations, amendments
or additions to rules, the expense to be borne by the Union. Except
that if any rules need alteration in Part II. the Conference may
deal with the same at any Annual Meeting.

GENERAL SUGGESTIONS.

56 THE COUNCIL. -New Rule.- "Five women members shall be elected annually
to attend the Annual Advisory Conference of Women in connection with
the Labour Party (Women's Section). Voting to be confined to the
British Trade Union Congress districts."

57 ARBROATH. - New Rule. - "That the Industrial Policy of the Union be to
establish day-work regulated by quantity statements, as against piece-
work with unlimited output, and that a new rule be framed to emphasise
the principle."

58 NORTHAMPTON NO. 2. - New Rule. - "The abolition of all Minute Notice Con-
tracts, and that the term of employment shall be a week's notice on
either side."

59 ARBROATH. - New Rule. - "That full reports be published of the proceedings
of conferences with Employers when the Council are negotiating new
Terms of Settlement."

90 ARBROATH. - New Rule. - "That the Council be instructed to prepare and
institute a superannuation scheme for the members, and that the necessary
changes of Rules be made accordingly."

91 HIGHAM AND RUSHDEN. - New Rule. - "Contributions to be paid by Union
for members with no income."

92 KETTERING NOS. I AND 2. - Workers' Educational Trade Union Committee. -
"This Conference presses on the Executive Committee the necessity of
at once considering the desirability of linking up with the Workers'
Educational Trade Union Committee, and thus affording to the members
of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives similar educational
facilities as are enjoyed by the Iron and Steel Trades Federation, the
Union of Post Office Workers and other organisations."

93 KETTERING NOS. I AND 2. - Hours of Labour. - "This Conference urges the
Executive Council, in its negotiations with the Employers' Associations,
to continuously and strenuously press for the realisation of Object II
in the Rules of the Union, feeling that the fulfilment of such rule will go
far to absorb the unemployed in the Boot and Shoe Industry."

94 The following Resolution to be passed at the Conference held in London during
Whit-Week, May 21st to 26th, 1923:-

"That the Council take the necessary steps to amend the Rules in
accordance with the various resolutions passed; to register the
same with the Registrar under the necessary Acts of Parliament,
and that the new Rules should come into force on and from
Saturday, September 1st, 1923."

33
Opening of the Conference.
MONDAY.
Morning Session.
THE Thirty-fifth General Conference—and the Third Annual Conference of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives opened at the Imperial Hotel, Russell Square, London, W.C. 1, on Whit-Monday, the 21st day of May, 1923.
The General President of the Union—Mr. T. F. Richards—took the chair promptly at 10 o'clock a.m., and was supported on the platform by Messrs. C. Bleakley (Edinburgh), A. J. Dobbs (Leeds), C. Mayes (Kettering), J. Manners (Bristol), W. Hindes, J.P. (Norwich), Alex. Smith (Wolverhampton), T. Adnitt (Leicester), A. W. Lyne (Northampton), Len. Smith (Northampton), W. Warner (Hinckley), C. Bates (Rushden), and E. L. Poulton, J.P. (General Secretary).
In addition there was present on the platform, Messrs. D. McCarthy and W. R. Smith J.P. (National Organisers), together with Mr. J. Buckle, M.P., J.P. (Parliamentary Representative of the Union).
The Chairman's Welcome.
THE CHAIRMAN: On behalf of the Executive Council of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives I offer you a very hearty welcome to London, and hope on this occasion as on all others, we shall concentrate our minds and intelligence for the benefit of the members whom we loyally and steadfastly represent.
Some of you are possibly aware that our General Secretary met with a very serious set-back in his health in the early part of this month. As a Council we considered the matter yesterday, and whilst we should like to see him take a prolonged rest, he informed us he had consulted a medical man and thanks to a small respite our General Secretary feels a little better. He has agreed to take another rest after this week, and we hope it will bring him back to health and vigour again. Let us hope and pray that.our wishes will fructify in this direction.
We do not intend to take advantage of the presence of the General Secretary this week, and as a Council we decided to do all we could—including Mr. Bordoli—to try and relieve the General Secretary as much as possible in connection with his duties.
Mr. E. L. POULTON thanked the Chairman and the delegates for their kindness.
Election of Doorkeeper.
Upon the proposition of Mr. J. Woodward, seconded by Mr. Albert Mason, it was unanimously decided that Mr. H. C. Robbins, of the London Metropolitan Branch, should act as Doorkeeper.
Tellers.
The following delegates were nominated for the position as Tellers:—Mr. H. Cramp- horn (Leicester), Mr. R. White (Edinburgh), Mr. W. Langley (Higham and Rushden), Mr. H. Fraser (Norwich), Miss E. Sherwin (Leicester Women's). Mr. D. Astley was also nominated, but declined to go to the vote.
Upon the names of the nominees being put to the vote the CHAIRMAN declared Mr. W. Langley and Miss E. Sherwin the two Tellers elected, the voting being:—
Mr. W. Langley  62   Mr. H. Fraser  16

36
The Chairman's Address.
Mr. T. F. RICHARDS: You will find the Council's Address is very elaborate and
gives many things I wished to raise. Further, we have now two Members of Parliament
instead of one, and I don't want to trespass upon the political situation. I should like to
say that I don't mind how many M.P's this Union can boast of, but I do think when you
once have a Member of Parliament he should be retained come what may. We never
ought to lose a seat once it has been captured, and although it may bring comfort to some
minds that our friends Buckle and Hill have taken the place of Mr. Walter Smith, it is no
(Hear, hear.) Once Labour has won a seat it ought always to be ours
for ever and a day. I look at the matter most seriously. When a person has served and
given four years of his life for the benefit of the workers and an organisation, and then
another person can come into that constituency only three weeks before the election and
win the seat, it passes my comprehension. It is not to the credit of our members, and I
hope our friends in the Wellingborough Division of Northants will endeavour to see that
in future they vote in the right direction. Further than that, if the Union had done
nothing in this division one might understand it. The work done by the Union for the
members there is and has been enormous, and it is not pleasurable to find that we only
have two Members of Parliament when we ought to have more. That seat should never
have been lost.
Another matter I should like to dwell upon is our National Agreement which we fixed
up last December. I don't wish to boast, but so far as the employers are concerned, we
did not find them so antagonistic upon the last occasion as has been the case in many
instances. When you consider our position and compare it with other industries it com-
pares very favourably indeed with what those in other trades are getting. (Hear, hear.)
I hope when we get to that part of the report we shall find someone who will confirm this,
and although we did not carry the whole of the country with us-taking the vote as a
whole it was a good one—and if there are any of the minority present perhaps they will
voice their views as to what they think we should have obtained. I think we will now turn
to the Address of the Council, and any other points I wish to raise will be dealt with upon
the particular paragraphs.
The Council's Address.
The Address of the Council to Conference was, upon the proposition of Mr. George
Parbury, seconded by Mr. J. Wheeler, taken as read. Appended is a copy of the Address:
2nd May, 1923.
FELLOW DELEGATES,
1.-THE NATIONAL (DECEMBER, 1922) AGREEMENT.
Since our last Conference, we have effected another national agreement
with the Employers' Federation in connection with working conditions for the
trade. The Agreement is as follows:—
CONFERENCE AGREEMENT.
Uniformity in Labour Price of similar classes of Goods.
1. Subject to Resolutions 1 and 5 (d) of the Terms of Settlement it is
desirable that a uniform system of prices should obtain, and that the general
outline or ground-work of such system should be arranged on a broad basis,
so that the essential conditions and prices can be applied or adapted to the
same class of labour and materials in all areas producing similar classes of goods.
Basis of Piecework Statements.
2. Where general or shop statements do not at present exist, the Local
Arbitration Boards, at the request of either side, shall proceed forthwith,
upon the ratification of this Agreement, to prepare piecework statements
for their respective districts (subject to Clause 1). All manufacturers and
operatives shall accept such statements in their entirety as a basis of payment,
but the system shall be termed a daywork system, and the wages of the opera-

---
Here's the extracted text from the image:

37

tives shall be regulated and adjusted weekly according to the amount of work
done at the prices fixed by the statements for each operation or process,
provided that no adult operative shall be engaged at less than the minimum
wage rate without the written permit of the Union or the Local Arbitration
Board in cases where the minimum wage is applicable, and provided also that
when operatives, whether on full or short time, have been supplied with a full
quantity of work, and have been granted reasonable facilities for the proper
performance of their work, and do not earn the minimum or agreed wage rate
at the statement prices, they shall be paid only for the actual work done at
the statement prices. In cases where circumstances arise that prevent the
operatives earning the minimum or agreed wage rate owing to bad materials
or special care required in the performance of their work, such cases shall be
subject to special adjustment between the employer or his representatives,
and the operatives or their trade union officials.
Non-Restriction of Output.
3. It is understood that operatives use their trade skill and productive
ability to the best advantage and fullest capacity provided they are paid the
full rate of wage for all output.
Regulation of Conditions of Employment.
4. (a) Where operatives attend at the factories on the instructions of
the employers or their representatives, work shall be found for them for at
least half a day, except when short time is being worked, and in that case
operatives, whether engaged on day or piecework, shall be informed overnight
if their services will not be required on the next working day, and shall be
informed before the mid-day interval if they will not be required to attend
in the afternoon. If no such intimation is given, and operatives attend at the
factories, work shall be found for them for a period of not less than four hours
in the morning and three hours in the afternoon, or they shall be paid for the
four hours and three hours respectively at not less than the minimum or agreed
wage rate.

(b) This clause shall not apply in the case of machinery breaking down in
any factory after the operatives have entered, or in the case of illness or absence
of any operative which interferes with the organisation of the factory, in which
cases the operatives shall be allowed to leave the factory at once. It is under-
stood that employers and their representatives will take all reasonable pre-
caution to avoid the necessity of sending operatives away from the works on
account of breakdown of machinery or disorganisation of the factories.
Uniformity of Organisation.
5. All operatives shall be subject to the same organisation and discipline
in regard to attendance at the factories during working hours.
Hours of Labour.
6. The ordinary working week shall be one of 48 hours.
Period of Training.
7. A person under 18 shall not be eligible for the minimum wages specified
in the succeeding clauses unless and until he or she has had twelve months'
experience in the trade. During this period of probation a young person shall
receive an advance in wages at the end of six months. When the twelve
months' probationary period has elapsed, he or she shall be paid at the minimum
rate applicable to his or her age.

Strikes and Lock-outs.
22. The Conference re-affirms Resolution 8 of the Terms of Settlement
of 19th April, 1895, which is as follows:-
"No strike or lock-out shall be entered into on the part of any body
of workmen, members of the National Union, or any manufacturers
represented on any Local Board of Arbitration."
(a) Where grievances exist they shall be investigated immediately by
representatives of the Local Manufacturers' Association and of the
local branch of the Union concerned, with a view to adjustment.
(b) Where any strike or lock-out takes place and is continued beyond
the period of three days allowed by the Agreement of 31st March,
1910, the right of the Federation or the Union, as the case may be,
to claim upon the monetary guarantee under that Agreement and the
Trust Deed, may be exercised by application to a National Umpire
appointed in accordance with Clause 9 of the Trust Deed and on the
recommendation of the Minister of Labour for a forfeiture either
(a) by way of fine or penalty or (b) by way of damages or compensation
for loss sustained, and in any case where the latter alternative is
adopted the amount of such loss shall be assessed by a committee of
three representatives of the Federation and three representatives of
the Union, and in the event of their disagreement the question shall
be referred to the National Umpire.
Joint Standing Committee.
23. A Standing Committee of three representatives of the Federation
and three representatives of the Union, with the Chairman of the Conference,
shall be appointed to deal with all matters arising out of or in connection with
the Terms of Settlement of 1895, so far as they are now operative, and any other
National Agreement between the Federation and the Union and this Agreement,
including any disputes that may arise as to the interpretation of such agree-
ments, provided that due regard is paid to the authoritative decisions that
have already been given under the above-named agreements.
Conflict with Local Arbitration Boards.
24. Anything in this Agreement which is in conflict with existing local
awards or agreements shall be remitted to the parties by whom such agreements
were made, or to the Local Arbitration Board. Failing agreement by the
local authority, the matter in dispute may be remitted to the Standing Com-
mittee, acting in an advisory capacity with a view to obviating the necessity
of a reference to the Arbitrator for such local board.
Responsibility for Observance of Agreement.
25. Both parties to this Agreement undertake to use such means as are
at their disposal to ensure its due observance by all employers and workers,
whether members of their respective organisations or not.

We feel, however, that the present is not an opportune time to ask for an
increased contribution for such a scheme, and it is quite clear that there
must be a very considerable increase in contributions if a scheme is to be
incorporated in the Rules. We do not, therefore, feel warranted in recom-
mending the adoption of a Superannuation Scheme.

3.—COUNCIL MEMBER—No. 6 DISTRICT.
It will be observed that District No. 6 is still vacant. This we very much
regret, it is however no fault of ours that the vacancy continues. In our judg-
ment it is a very mistaken policy, that because of some disagreement that one
district may have upon a small portion of our policy that they refuse to send
a representative to take part in the executive work of the Union. In our
judgment such action tends rather to weaken than strengthen, and we can
only hope that the LEICESTER WOMEN'S BRANCH will see their way to
reconsider their decision, and take their full share of the work of the Union as
a whole.

4.—UNEMPLOYMENT.
We regret to have to report that unemployment and underemployment
has been above the normal, and as a result the call upon the Trade fund has
been somewhat serious. The rate of pay which was settled by the Edinburgh
Conference has increased the liability upon the fund, and this will be better
seen by the following series of tables :-

The result of the payment from the Trade Funds of such a large sum of
money has had the effect of reducing the balance, although it may be said
that the reduction is not a serious one. The position, however, of the fund
would have been an entirely different one had we not conserved our funds
during the period of the war, and the fact that we have explicit rules govern-
ing the claims for unemployment benefit. We are fully aware that it is held
that unemployment benefit should be paid even for odd days off; this,
however, would mean a very much higher contribution than the present one
to meet the increased liability, but in our opinion the present is not an
opportune time to increase the contributions. Although, as stated above, we

NATIONAL UNION OF BOOT AND SHOE OPERATIVES.

Benefit, the Council at their meeting to-day have again considered the matter,
and eventually the Council unanimously decided that no benefit can be
Owing to certain irregularities as to the payment of Unemployment

The Council are, however, prepared to consider the claims of certain

NO benefit will be payable until after the fourth consecutive week of
suspension, holiday periods not to be reckoned, and payment will then only
be allowed from the commencement of the fifth week. The Officials must,
even then, be quite satisfied that the suspension is a bona fide suspension
before any benefit is allowed.
Yours faithfully,
E. L. POULTON,
General Secretary.
This policy was endorsed by the branches, and we venture to suggest that
it has been of considerable help to the members, who, owing to unfortunate
circumstances, are forced out of employment.
Upon further consideration of the question of suspension from employ-
ment and the unfortunate position in which many members find themselves
owing to the fact that although, technically, it may be said they have not
received a full discharge in accordance with Rule 223, the method adopted of
"suspension" really means that the member is unemployed. It is clear to
us from the evidence we have before us from month to month at the meetings
of the Council, that it is impossible (financially) upon present contributions to
grant benefit to members immediately they are suspended. We do, however,
feel that something must be done to try and meet such a position, and we
therefore now recommend to the delegates in Conference that we insert a rule
in the Rule Book upon the following lines :-

The question of INSURANCE BY INDUSTRY for unemployment is a
matter which has engaged our attention for some time. The trade union
movement is divided upon the subject; nevertheless, for ourselves we lean to
industries only, because in some industries the contribution would be high and
the view that it should be made a national matter rather than one for
the rate of benefit low owing to the heavy rate of unemployment, whilst in
others such as workers under Government and municipalities who are in
regular employment-would escape their full responsibilities and should pay
backing up the General Council of the Trades Union Congress and the Labour
to a national fund. Along with other Unions we have done our part in
Party in striving to bring about a more enlightened and humane policy towards
those who find themselves without work. We hold strongly to the view,
even if it is done at a loss, that it would be much better to give the workers
some employment rather than pay them for doing nothing. All kinds of work
are needed to be done to put the nation in a satisfactory position, yet the
Government steadfastly resist any of the schemes put forward by the Labour
Party. We can only hope this constant refusal of the Government to adopt
such a policy as outlined time after time by the Labour Party will so open the
eyes of the electorate that within a short period of time they will return a
majority of members to Parliament in favour and determined to carry out the
policy of the Labour Party.
In the STATE UNEMPLOYMENT SECTION of the Union's work, the
sum of £84,739 1s. 4d. has been paid out from March, 1921, until the end of
December, 1922, through the Central Office. As a result of experience we have
found out that when the forms are properly filled up there is very little
trouble in dealing with the claims which are promptly dealt with. The pay-
ment of the State benefit to the members through the branches of the Union
is of considerable advantage to the members in receipt of unemployment
benefit, the benefit from the Union and the State being made at one and the
same time. Further, we venture to suggest that the fact of signing the
unemployment books at the branch offices rather than at the Employment
Exchanges is also of advantage to the members.

7.-POLITICS.
The Political situation both nationally and internationally is very serious.
In our opinion the Government signally fails in rising to its responsibilities
in dealing with problems which are before the nation. Whether it is
Unemployment, Housing, or Finance, the situation is equally unsatisfactory.
Internationally, timidity, rather than courage seems to be the guiding policy
of the Government. We know the Prime Minister has said "tranquility" is
desired. Tranquility there cannot be whilst so many millions of people are
constantly on the verge of poverty. It is fortunate that we have at the
present time in the House of Commons a strong Labour Party. We venture to
say the past few months' work of the Party in the House of Commons has been
very valuable to the nation as a whole. It is not always the amount of work
accomplished or shewn in black and white as Laws of the Land which count,
but things prevented being done very often are of equal value, and we venture
to say that had there not been a strong opposition such as the Labour Party,
bad as things are to-day, they would have been worse without such representa-
tives being present to fight for and on behalf of the workers.
With pleasure we record the fact that two of our colleagues were returned
to Parliament in November, 1922, in the persons of Mr. John Buckle, M.P.,
J.P., for Eccles, and Alderman Alfred Hill, M.P., J.P., for the West Division
help forward humane administration in laws whereby the lot of the workers

8.—OBITUARY.

We exceedingly regret we have to report the loss of some of our
colleagues who held official positions in the Union.
Mr. W. BRAY, LONDON METRO. BRANCH, was, from the
point of view of his being secretary to the Branch only in office a
short time, although for many years Mr. Bray had taken an active
part in the work of the Union in endeavouring to consolidate the
general position.
In the person of Mr. WM. H. LOWE, J.P., LEICESTER No. 2
BRANCH, he was amongst the first members to join the Union, and
was the first secretary to the Branch, and held such position from
1890-1921. He was for a considerable number of years Treasurer of
the Union, which position carried with it a seat on the Executive
Council. In both positions the late Mr. Lowe rendered yeoman
service both to the Union as a whole and the Leicester members in
particular. In addition, Mr. Lowe was for a time a member of the
Leicester Town Council, Treasurer to the Leicester Trades Council, and
a Justice of the Peace, so it will be seen that he lead a very busy life
on behalf of the movement and such men can be ill-spared.
We have also to report that we have lost by death Mr. W. J.
MURBY, Manager to the National Health Insurance Department of
the Union from 1913 until February, 1923. In Mr. Murby we had an
officer who could be thoroughly relied upon, and one who did his work
in a courteous and efficient manner. For many years Mr. Murby had
taken an active part in politics, especially in connection with the
I.L.P., for whom he addressed meetings in all parts of the country.
For many years Mr. Murby was also a member of the Leicester Town
Council. Mr. Murby never spared himself in striving to help the
working classes of the country, whose interests he had so much at
heart.
Mr. THOMAS A. WATTS, J.P., who was Secretary to our
Kendal Branch for 32 years, died in November last. He was for
many years a tower of strength in the Kendal district and was an
officer of great tact and discretion. He was a member of the Kendal
Town Council until his death, manager of one of the public schools,
and a magistrate both for Kendal and Westmoreland.
To the relatives of our departed colleagues we have tendered, in
your name, the sympathy and condolences of the members, resting
assured that their services were fully appreciated, and we can only
hope the result of their work will continue to act as an inspiration to
others to carry on and to still bring about greater success in the work
they have been compelled to lay down.

9.—CONSUMPTION.

For a very considerable period, a number of our members have been
under the special treatment of Major C. H. Stevens, of Wimbledon, for the cure
of consumption. The treatment is of such a character that the members need not
pay a visit to London, their case being dealt with by correspondence between
themselves and the Major. During the period there have been 75 members
under treatment, and the reports to date show on the whole a very consider-


---
Here's the extracted text from the image:

52

able benefit has resulted to the great majority of members treated. We feel
the time long enough to state that in our opinion the remedies which Major
Stevens has applied are of such a character as to warrant us in saying that
with care and attention to the instructions given from time to time by Major
Stevens, there is a reasonable prospect of members being restored to health and
strength again.

We have had before us the reports of the members and branch officials
as to the progress made, and these reports bear out the statements made
above.

Having regard to these statements we feel fully justified in asking for your
full assent to our continuing to send suitable patients for treatment. The finan-
cial arrangements made by us are of such a character that the money paid to
Major Stevens has proven to be well spent, £645 for 75 cases over a period of
18 months. We would remind the membership that although this is not in
the rules, it is really a very substantial benefit granted to those members of
the Union, who unfortunately need special treatment for this dread complaint.

10. THE UNION'S JUBILEE.

We would remind the delegates to the Conference, that in February next,
the Union will have been established fifty years-years of great and grave
importance, and despite the slowness with which we move, a great deal has
been done to soften on the one hand, and improve on the other, the conditions
of the workers in the industry. It is equally true that a great deal has to be
done before we can attain to anything like what can be regarded as a satis
factory position. By reference to the report of the Union for 1874, we find
there were Thirty Three Branches with a membership of 4,195. To-day we
have Seventy Two Branches and 75,000 members 20,000 of whom are women.
In 1874 the Funds of the Union stood at £67 15s. Otd., whilst to-day the total
funds of the Union are £372,043 14s. Od., thus shewing remarkable progress so
far as the Union's finances are concerned. We venture to say that if the
present was the time to give in a report relating to the past years, it would be
found that the Union had made very great progress in many ways. We feel
some special recognition of the fact of having 50 years of history now behind
us should be taken note of, and we, therefore, propose to make certain
suggestions on the floor of the Conference itself, relating thereto.

11.—MATTERS INTERNATIONAL.

So far as the Boot & Shoe Workers' International Union is concerned,
although we are keeping as closely in touch as possible with the said body,
we cannot at present report any great progress. As a matter of fact, a
meeting of the Executive of the International was called in the early part of
this year, but it was found impossible at the last moment—to have the
meeting in consequence of the disturbed state, particularly of Germany, which
was brought about by the action of France in the Ruhr. This we sincerely
regret, and we are hoping that within the very near future normal conditions
will prevail and thus enable the work to proceed in this connection.

Upon the wider sphere of the International position, it becomes more and
more apparent that one of the great needs of nations is for a better, clearer
and closer understanding between the peoples, whereby not only may we be
able to prevent war taking place, but such a policy being pursued both
economically and industrially as will enable the workers to be for ever released
from the circumstances which make for many millions one continuous round
of anxiety and dread of what may happen from day to day.


---
12.-IN CONCLUSION,
having regard to the abnormal circumstances by which not only our own
industry, but throughout the world generally, finds itself surrounded we feel
justified in claiming that we have successfully held our position in the midst
of very grave difficulties which we have had from time to time to face, such as
the last national agreement. There is, however, an obligation not merely
upon the national and local officers of the Union, but upon the membership
generally to do all they can to strengthen the organisation and to maintain a
sides. We have no sort of doubt that the times ahead of us will be strenuous
live interest in the work of the Union both on its industrial and political
times, and will require a great deal of endurance and steadfastness if we are
to go forward. We appeal to the membership in all parts of the country to
help those whom they put in office from time to time, to do all they can not
only to strengthen the position, but so mould public opinion as to secure such
a series of laws being passed in the near future which will make for the general
uplifting of mankind.
Yours fraternally,
T. F. RICHARDS, Gen. President.

RULE 108.—The duties of Parliamentary Agents when elected to the House of Commons shall be to pay strict attention to all questions brought before the House affecting the Union, and the interests of labour generally.
