Mr. G. CHESTER (Kettering) asked if the General Secretary would give an explana-
tion as to why all the interest was allocated to the sick fund instead of being divided
according to rule.

THE GENERAL SECRETARY: You all know there is such a thing as income tax.
My duty is to safeguard the funds of the Union and keep them intact, rather than let other
people have them. If that is done in a straightforward honest way I submit it is my duty
to report such method to the Council, and I prefer to discuss this matter with Mr. Chester
privately.

Mr. W. R. SMITH (Organiser): I am in a position of being unable to let the
statement of the General Secretary go by unchallenged, but feel unable to discuss it fully
for reasons he has stated. I challenge any contradiction that there is any risk whatever
from a financial standpoint of the income tax being lost unless it is placed to the sick fund.
I can give you any number of instances of unions who suffer no injustice because they do
not allocate the interest to the sick fund. Your trade fund has gone down in an alarming
degree. If this question had been dealt with on the basis of interest being allocated
differently there is a difference of between forty and fifty thousand pounds due to the
trade fund. Your sick fund would have been down by that amount. This, to me, is a
most important point. When we are reviewing in the light of past experiences, the right
and correct thing to do in future in regard to the interest is to see that it is allocated accord-
ing to rule. As a matter of fact your trade fund is considerably less than it was a year ago,
although your total funds are higher. Having regard to what was emphasised this morning
by Mr. Jex, it does appear to me you are running some risk unless this matter is altered.
The matter has been dealt with in quite a constitutional manner. It is definitely laid
down that funds from which you pay out-of-work benefit income tax is recoverable.
£18,000 was paid out in out-of-work benefit last half year, and does anyone believe that a
fund which is used for such a purpose must be charged with income tax. As the matter
has been raised I would ask this Conference in the interests of our members-to see
that the allocation of the interest is revised.

THE GENERAL SECRETARY: I hope we shall view this from its proper per-
spective. To sit and listen to Mr. Walter Smith one would think it was an enormous
amount that the Trade Fund has lost. It is approximately £5,000 per annum.

Mr. W. R. SMITH (Organiser): If you started from the point when the proportion
was altered it is a considerable sum. Once the contributions were divided into one quarter
to one fund and three-quarters to another. Now it is half and half.

THE GENERAL SECRETARY: I would remind the Conference that it is
only a few years ago that we had to borrow £10,000 from the Trade Fund to
place to the credit of the Sick Fund, to put it in a better financial state. This
was not repaid until 1921. There is no sort of feeling with the General Secretary
and his colleagues upon this matter. The only thing I desire is to safeguard-as far
as it is possible to do the whole of the funds of the Union. If the position has
been altered from the standpoint of the Treasury I cannot argue that position any
longer, but I am not aware that it has been altered. At the time we acted as we did, we
took the best possible advice it was possible to take. Within the last six months two
big unions have applied to me to know how we get our income tax back. I made the
suggestion to the Council and it appears upon the agenda, that to try and meet the altered
circumstances you should transfer d. per week of the full male contributions to the Trade
Fund because the fund seems now to be in a comparatively healthy state as compared with
the position when we had to borrow the £10,000. It is purely a matter of book-keeping at
the Central Office. By adopting the suggestion of the Council you will be able to transfer
between five and six thousand pounds annually-on our present membership-which will
balance the amount of interest which is not now allocated to the Trade Fund. If there
is any loss on the Trade Fund because it receives no interest, that loss will be reduced.
I submit that is a better way than running any risk of losing monies by not being able to
recover the income tax. Mr. Smith has drawn attention to the fact that the Trade Fund
is lower than a year ago, whilst the Sick Fund is higher. You all know we have had an
abnormal slump during the past two years and in one year alone £96,000 was paid out in
unemployment benefit. It is a record of which we should feel proud. We can also show
a balance in hand in the Trade Fund of £157,744, whilst many unions have suffered a
reduction in their funds, and in addition have had to reduce benefits. The reduction in the
Trade Fund is mainly due to the humanitarian methods of the Council in allowing sus-
pension benefit and not because it has received no interest. I quite appreciate the friendly
criticism given by Mr. Smith, and the Council purpose to meet the difference by the transfer
of monies, but having regard to the strain put upon the Funds I think we have every
reason to congratulate ourselves. (Applause.)

Politics.
Whilst dealing with the question of politics Mr. J. Buckle, M.P., J.P., was called upon
to give in the report of Ald. A. Hill, M.P., J.P., and himself, which was as follows:
HOUSE OF COMMONS,
WESTMINSTER, LONDON, S.W. 1.
9th May, 1923.
FELLOW DELEGATES,
In presenting this report, it is with great pleasure and satisfaction
that we are able to record the fact that the Labour Party has gone many steps
towards reaching the position when its members in the House of Commons
will be called upon to take up the reins of Government. Surely we have much
to be proud of, when we remember that but so short a time back the Party
which was looked upon by some as being quite insignificant, has now to be
recognised as the official opposition of H.M. Government as we had 142 Labour
Members returned at the Polls last November. While taking satisfaction in
the triumph of the Labour Party, let us not forget that a Conservative Govern-
ment is in power, possessing all the qualifications associated with the traditional
character of that Party, and when some of us seem inclined to become impatient
at what is apparently little progress, it is well to remember that numbers
count, and that Division Lobbies tell the tale.
It is undoubtedly true that judged by the standards of real progress the
Government of to-day is profoundly lacking, but this should be a constant
challenge to the opposition to display constant and determined effort to mitigate,
as far as possible this lack by well directed and constructive criticism.
Parliament opened on 23rd November, 1922. The election of Speaker
having taken place, the first business the House had to consider was the passing
into law a Bill which has given to Ireland her freedom after long years of
coercion and force. We hope the foundation has been laid for Ireland to
ultimately become a happy and prosperous Nation.
The past few months has been a very strenuous time. The Party has put
up vigorous opposition, and has somewhat altered the atmosphere and outlook
upon many important questions appertaining to the well-being of the com-
munity. The Party has been responsible for raising the question of the
Occupation of the Ruhr and the dangers that may accrue, and they have
repeatedly suggested that some method should be employed with a view to
having the Reparation question settled on what could be regarded as a fair
basis, so that the reconstruction, economically and otherwise, could take
effect. The Government has simply taken up a non-interference attitude
upon the matter. So strong has the feeling become, that official deputations
have gone over to the area concerned with a view to investigating the matter
from time to time, in order to get a good grasp of the situation as regards
France and Germany.
```

UNEMPLOYMENT.
The Government have failed to bring forth any policy which will help to
solve this pressing problem. True it is, arrangements have been made to
provide certain monies for Relief Work, and a further extension of Uncovenanted
Benefit in connection with the Unemployment Acts, but this has been done
very largely under duress, for it is inconceivable to think of any Government
leaving something like a million and a half of unemployed men and women to
starve. But when we come to Policy, the only idea seems to be that of emigra-
tion. What could have been done if only half of the energy that was exerted
for the prosecution of the War had been exerted on behalf of the Unemployed
in the time of Peace, and if the suggestions of the various Labour organisations
had been acted upon, one feels that the situation would have been vastly
different ?
HOUSING.
There is going on in Committee an animated discussion of the Housing
Bill, the proposal to give State money only to "non-Parlour" Houses. The
houses may either be two-storeyed, with a minimum of 550 and a maximum of
780 superficial feet. These measurements will be calculated in accordance
with rules laid down by the Minister of Health.
The Plan A has a total available area of 754.66 square feet, Plan B 808.82
square feet, and Plan C 836.00 square feet. These are official plans and are
well within the maximum allowed under the new scheme. It will be seen
from a study of these plans that every available inch has to be utilised. The
planning has to be very carefully thought out. The architectural problem
involved, demands greater cleverness in design, so as not to waste any space
on passages or corners. The essential measurements laid down by the Ministry
is: 180 feet should be allowed for the Living Room, 150 feet for the first
Bedroom, 150 feet for the second Bedroom, and a minimum of 65 feet for the
third Bedroom. In addition, room will have to be found for the Scullery and
usual offices. The Bath may either be placed in the Scullery or in a separate
compartment, or either on the first or ground floor. Undoubtedly there are
powerful arguments in favour of the Parlour House, notably that a Parlour
provides privacy for the younger generation-in case of sickness or death a
parlour is invaluable. Much is being made of the so-called disregard of the
Middle Classes. A study of the full text of the Government Bill shows that
their needs have been considered. The proposed amendment of the "Small
Dwellings Act" extends the limit on the market value of houses in respect
of which advances may be made from £800 to £1,200. It will also be of direct
assistance to the skilled artisan class that local authorities may guarantee
the repayment to a Building Society of any advances made to any of its members
to build or acquire houses. Money may also be advanced to persons or bodies
building houses.
A generous limit has been placed on the estimated value of such houses,
for the advance or guarantee can be given on such value up to £1,500: for
£1.200 under the Small Dwellings Acquisition Act, and £1,500 for houses
financed by Building Societies and other bodies.
EDUCATION.
Here again we have evidence of the fact that the Government are retro-
grade and reactionary. Wherever possible, economy has been applied regard-
less of consequences. The promise held out in the Fisher Act made impossible
of fulfilment, and the vision which was opened up by the possibilities contained
therein gradually receding, until a position almost of despair has taken the
place of hope. The cry for economy has been seized upon by certain public
bodies, no doubt glad of the opportunity to curtail expenditure until the

FINANCE.
As a consequence of the prosecution of the late war the country has to
face huge financial liabilities, which if dealt with along the old lines, will
constitute a burden for generations to come and lead to permanent high prices.
At the last General Election the Labour Party foreshadowed a Policy which
sooner or later will hold the field. It may be that it will not be called a Capital
Levy, but whenever the question is properly dealt with, it will be in a way
that will work out on the lines advocated by the Labour Party. This huge
indebtedness cannot be allowed to remain where it is, crushing out the life
of the community-something will have to be done to lift the load, or we shall
sink lower and lower beneath its weight.
BUDGET.
Mr. Baldwin, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, introduced his first new
Budget on the 16th April, 1923, and it is a most remarkable fact that
whilst there was a surplus of £100,000,000 brought forward from the
previous year, still the reduction in taxation, as far as its effect on the vast
majority of the working class population is concerned, reductions are con-
spicuous by their absence. The employing and capitalistic classes were again
favoured with reduction on the Income Tax, Postal and Telephone Rates,
and without doubt the Budget stands out as one of the most capitalistic and
"favoured-class" pieces of legislation of modern times. The interest on the
National Debt alone absorbs over £300,000,000 per annum, and whilst this
vast amount of interest is payable it is not at all likely that reductions of
taxation on the essentials of life will be seen.
for the reduction of duty on Tea, Sugar, &c., but without avail. And so we

In our preceding remarks we have dealt with what may be regarded as the
Home Policy; and now perhaps in a few words we may be allowed to bring
to your notice the failure of the Government in the field of Foreign Policy.
In this respect the experiences of the last few years seems to stand for nothing
so far as improvement goes. The same old jealousies, suspicions, and pre-
judices, seem to be operating. Men of responsibility are talking about the
next war as if it had already been decided that the same was inevitable. The
race for armaments is again starting, leaving one to infer that nations, who,
but a short time back were our Allies, now, if not our actual enemies, are having
to be watched and treated, if not as probable, yet as possible ones, or why the
frantic talk of the French superiority in Air Forces, or the huge expenditure
to be incurred in the Pacific which can only be justified by the fear of an Eastern
Power. Ah well while the great mass of the people seem to be satisfied,
which must be the explanation of the present Government's majority, we
suppose things will remain pretty much as they are, but some day surely the
eyes of the people will be opened and they will discover for themselves the
right path.

**DEPORTATION.**

There has also been the question of Deportation raised, the outcome of which is that a deputation has been appointed to visit Ireland and the Free State Government. The keen debates that have taken place from time to time in the House proves this: that the Government are not out to do anything substantial unless forced by the untiring efforts of the opposition. There is no doubt the opposition of the Labour Party is a real live wire, and is creating an impression both inside and outside of Parliament.

**CIVIL SERVICE.**

Another question which has occupied the attention of the Party is that of the Lytton Entrants to the Civil Service, on which question the Government were defeated on 10th April, on the Motion that a Committee of Enquiry be set up to investigate the conditions obtaining in the service. The actual grievance is that the overwhelming majority of the Lytton Entrants to the Clerical Clerks are ex-Service Men, and started at the rate of £70, £80, or £85 per annum, in other words, although they are men of all ages, the majority married and have families to support, and with anything up to seven years temporary service, had to start at the same rate of pay appropriate to a boy of 18 years of age. The strong feeling of the House with regard to the disgraceful conditions obtaining, and the Government taking up an attitude which was regarded as an unreasonable one, and the unsatisfactory arguments of the Minister for that Department when the Division was taken, the Government were defeated, and after an adjournment of the House, the Government conceded to the opinion of the House, and a representative Committee to investigate and report on the conditions of employment was appointed.

**PRIVATE MEMBERS’ MOTIONS.**

Private members have a system of balloting and those who head the list are given a paper with a list of Motions to choose from. Those members who are lucky enough to head the list fix on a particular Motion and are allowed to move it in the House; for example, Mr. Snowden's Motion on “Failure of Capitalistic System.”

Motion made, and question proposed, “That, in view of the failure of the capitalist system to adequately utilise and organise natural resources and productive power, or to provide the necessary standard of life for vast numbers of the population, and believing that the cause of this failure lies in the private ownership and control of the means of production and distribution, this House declares that legislative effort should be directed to the gradual supersession of the capitalist system by an industrial and social order based on the public ownership and democratic control of the instruments of production and distribution.” Debate adjourned.

**MOTHERS’ PENSIONS.**

"That in the opinion of this House, pensions adequate for the proper upbringing and maintenance of children should be paid to all widows with children or mothers whose family breadwinner has become incapacitated, such pensions to be provided by the State and administered by a committee of the municipal or county council wholly unconnected with the Poor Law."
Rejected by: Ayes 184; Noes 248.

POSITION OF PROFESSIONAL WORKERS.
“ That in view of the worsening conditions of middle-class professional
workers, and of the advantages resulting from the recognition of the organisa-
tions of manual workers and the practice of collective bargaining, this House
is of the opinion that local authorities, banks, insurance and shipping com-
panies and other employers of professional and clerical workers should follow
the example of the Government in recognising the organisations of these
workers.” Agreed to without Division.
OLD AGE PENSIONS.
“ That in the opinion of this House, the recommendation of the Depart-
mental Committee on Old Age Pensions in favour of the repeal of the provisions
of the Old Age Pensions Act as to calculation of means should be adopted and
the Old Age Pensions Acts amended accordingly, thereby enabling applicants
for, and recipients of, the old age pension to derive the full benefit of their
thrift and personal provision for old age and receive assistance from friends,
employers and organisations without reduction of, or disqualification for, the
full pension.” Rejected by : Ayes 208 ; Noes 230.
We deeply regret the fact that our two colleagues who were nominated
for Wellingborough and Wells Divisions respectively, were not successful in
securing election. We hope, however, that whenever a General Election comes
along, the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives will have its full quota
of representatives in the next Parliament.
Our concluding words are in the nature of a warning to you all, as Trade
Unionists. We may rely upon it that our position is to be challenged. We
question whether the Prime Minister will be able to restrain the rank and file
of his own Party in their aggressive opposition to Trade Unionism. Already
a motion has been carried to amend the Trade Union Act re the Political posi-
tion ; also as recently as the first day of the month (Labour Day) a Bill was
introduced having for its object the repeal of the Trade Union Act, 1906. To
be in the House and to hear the frenzied applause which is given every time
anything is said against Trade Unionism it is quite easy to discover the spirit
of antagonism which prevails, and which has for its object the weakening of
our position. To be forewarned is to be forearmed, and it is hoped that when-
ever the attack comes we shall be found prepared and sufficiently strong enough
to maintain our hard-won position.
May we be allowed to say that we consider it to be a very great honour
to be allowed to represent our fellow workers and citizens in Parliament.
Conscious as we are of our own limitations, we sincerely hope that our presence
there will be of some, if little help, and service, in helping to make things better
for us all.
Fraternally yours,
JOHN BUCKLE.
ALFRED HILL.

Continuing Mr. J. BUCKLE, M.P. said: I wish to thank the very many people
for their congratulations received from all parts of the country. I deeply regret that our
colleague, Mr. Walter Smith, did not win his election in Wellingborough, nor did Mr. Len.
Smith, at Wells. Had we had the four years' experience of Mr. Smith it would have been
of distinct advantage. Ald. Hill and I decided that in view of the fact that we expect
to get a very large number of representatives of the Union in Parliament before very long,
that it was better for us to have a joint report as this would also save a great deal of time.
(Applause.)
ALD. A. HILL, M.P., J.P. After the exhaustive and detailed report of Mr. Buckle
there is not much for me to add. I should like to emphasise the sincere regret in not seeing
our colleagues returned along with us. We very much regret the fact that our friend
Mr. W. R. Smith was not re-elected for Wellingborough. You can quite imagine what it
is like going into a strange place like the House of Commons quite a stranger, how very
much nicer it would have been to have had a guide who had had four years' experience.
There are times when I feel very lonely and isolated for the simple reason that I am the
only Labour man returned either for the City or County of Leicestershire. Buckle is
come up to expectation the fault will not be ours. I think the Labour Party is to be con-
gratulated upon the outcome of the questions concerning deportation. If you had been
in the House of Commons when Mr. Patrick Hastings, M.P., raised the matter and seen
assumed delight of the Attorney-General, you would have thought that the result would
have been quite different. It looked as if there was no chance of that gentleman making
a mistake. Of course he had the backing of the Government, and upon this occasion
they let go. The other night when the Attorney-General had to take his gruelling, and
Bridgeman, the scapegoat of the Attorney-General, had to admit a blunder had been made,
they were in quite a different mood. It is to the credit of the British constitution-
notwithstanding the weight and power of the Government-that the Law Lords allowed
no prejudice nor bias to over-rule them, and they decided the Government was in the
wrong. You know the result. If it had been decided otherwise who would have been
safe from arrest ? As we have pointed out in our report there is a large and powerful
number amongst the Government supporters who are attacking the trade unions. There
would have been nothing to prevent trade union leaders being arrested later on. One
other point I wish to emphasise is that we must offer a prayer to be saved from our friends.
These men get up in the most friendly spirit and say they are anxious for the welfare of
the men and women who belong to a tyrannical trade union. They are not only trying
to save the trade unionists from their false leaders, but also the co-operative movement
from being over-run by bolshevists. The only friend the working man has to-day appears
to be on the Government benches. Rightly or wrongly the majority of the people in
Leicester West returned me as their Member of Parliament. When one remembers the
great number of boot and shoe operatives there are in the Division there is no reason why
we should not have won. I am unable to understand how the boot and shoe operatives
allowed anyone else to be returned to Parliament for Wellingborough.
I wish to thank you all for the confidence placed in me; firstly, by the Council in allow-
ing me to go forward as a candidate, and I very much appreciate their action in providing
me with a railway contract. Secondly, I wish to thank the people of Leicester, and right
along the line I have met with the greatest friendship and the helping hand has been
extended to me both in Leicester and at the Central Office.
Mr. A. PEAT (Leeds) asked why there was no mention in the report of the Parlia-
mentary representatives dealing with war pensions ?
Mr. J. BUCKLE, M.P.: Being new Members of Parliament we have to feel our way.
Members are allowed to ballot and if they are the fortunate ones they move a resolution
similar to those I have read out to you, but we have not overlooked pensions at all.
THE CHAIRMAN : This is only a report and it does not pretend to contain every-
thing, but I am sure both Buckle and Hill will bear the matter in mind.
ALD. A. HILL, M.P.: It is very rarely we have a chance of dealing with the situation
of war pensions until it has been turned down by the House of Lords Tribunal. Upon
nearly every occasion that Minister of Pensions tells us that regulations are sent to the
General Council dealing with ex-Service men upon which Council there are four repre-
sentatives of the British Legion. You will understand, therefore, we have a tough job on,
but if you feel there is anything we can do we shall be prepared to do it. We shall do all
in our power for the ex-Service men.
Mr. J. BUCKLE, M.P.: Thirty hours per week has been spent upon this question
alone. I have forty-five cases at present before the Minister of Pensions. One fortnight
I had over six hundred letters, and one hundred and nine of them were from ex-Service
men, so you will see we are doing all we can.
The Conference then adjourned at 12.30 a.m.

Afternoon Session.
The Conference resumed its first day's sitting at 2 p.m., Mr. T. F. Richards presiding.
The Roll was called and all the delegates answered to their name.
Mr. W. R. TOWNLEY, J.P. reported that it was pleasureable to note that the

Beer v. Tea and Sugar.
Mr. H. C. ATTEWELL (Northampton): The Parliamentary Agents' Report is
not couched in that tone of language with which Ald. Hill made his separate report. Upon
the question of Ireland it states in the report that Parliament passed a Bill which gave
to Ireland its freedom. If that is the opinion of the Labour Party of this country it is
not the opinion of the Northampton Branch—at any rate not the opinion of myself.
There can be no freedom in any part of the British Empire until countries are represented
by their own representatives instead of being dominated by this country. Ireland to-day
is seething with revolution because we allowed our people to say they must be allied to
the Empire. I contend that this is an absolutely rotten policy. The question of deporta-
tion has gained more sympathy since this document—referring to the Parliamentary
Agents' Report—was published. There is no credit due to the Labour Party for the
presentation of the case on deportation. It is due to the judges of this country. The
Labour Party raised the question in Parliament and came up to a stumbling block. There
is no credit to the Labour Party in the grand finale concerning deportees. The question
of deportation has been put before the Government upon numerous occasions, but what
did the Labour Party do when they came to the stumbling block? Why, let it stop at
that. Then we have the question of the Egyptian and South African deportees. If there
is any part of the British Empire which wants to govern itself we, as the working people
of this country, should be prepared to see that they can govern themselves. The question
of Reparations is also mentioned. I would like to have seen it put down that we are
against Reparations. In order to curry favour with a few of the people who do not under-
stand the position, the official Labour Party say we should have as much in reparations
as they can afford. The whole Treaty of Versailles should be scrapped.
The price of beer was reduced in the Budget of this year, but the price of sugar and
tea were not. We, as workers, are pleased to have this reduction on beer, even if that is
all that can be got. Wives of the boot operatives also like a drink of beer. There is now
a good saving on beer, more than would have been saved on sugar and tea, and the Labour
Party would do more good in trying to get a further reduction in the price of beer than in
trying to get a farthing off sugar.
Mr. D. MCCARTHY (Organiser): If you sat in the House of Commons and watched

to a section, but if Ireland had been left complete they would have accepted the position
sooner or later. There are some of our friends who give considerable time to education,

people are denied proper access to secondary schools and this ought not to be. I heartily
support what the Labour Party has done and is doing.

if we cannot govern ourselves.

Consumption.
Mr. J. GREAVES (Leicester): I have a daughter under the treatment of Major
Stevens. Five weeks ago she was taken to the sanatorium and I wrote and told him,
and now she is taking the medicine in tablet form, and indeed I am very grateful for what
he has done.
Mr. A. PEAT (Leeds): I served in the army for three years and eight months.
I was diagnosed as suffering from tuberculosis. I consulted a chest specialist and was
granted a war pension. I was examined later by the D.D.M.S. and sent to a sanatorium
and got worse. After being there for some time they decided I had not contracted the
disease in war service and I was discharged. I walked about for eighteen months and
gradually got worse, and the doctor said it is no use you bothering here any more. I went
to the branch office and Dobbs said, "Would you like to try this new treatment?" I said
"Yes." I felt worse during the first week and went back to the sanatorium; then I
gradually began to get better and better, and since then I have been at work for the past
thirteen months and never had a day's illness. I have not seen a doctor since then either.
I have never come across any medicine which gives me more ease or relief. It is a
terrible complaint and you are soon despised and rejected. I hope the Conference will
continue to allow the Council to let members have the treatment.

In connection with the final paragraph in the Council's Address THE CHAIRMAN
said: I have had to report several employers recently, but I am glad to know that the
Employers' Federation is not composed of employers of that character. At the present
time we have four most important matters before us, and there are four responsible officials
of the Federation who are trying to evade their responsibilities, so we must not agree to
anything without getting advice. Your local officials will have to advise you and if they
cannot, then they must send to the Central Office. Advice is cheap enough. By this
means manufacturers will understand our agreements are not merely paper agreements,
but that they must be loyally carried out by all. I am pleased to say about 80 per cent.
of the manufacturers are already doing so, and amongst the leading manufacturers we get
from them their support in trying to enforce the agreement upon all.
Mr. A. STOTT (Heckmondwike): I beg to complain of the fact that there is no
reference in the report as to the present organisation of the trade. We have run up
against the employer who is trying to undermine the position of the existing agreement.
The Council should inform us at this stage what information they have at their disposal
with a view to our taking stock to see how far the agreement is carried out. The value
of the agreement to-day is very much worsened than when it was signed. I understand
an employer has the right to revert back to daywork conditions. That is the insidious
part of the attack upon the operatives. I am told by employers that it has met with
success in various parts of the country, and whilst I have no information to the contrary
I should welcome enquiry. Whilst the employers are trying to scrap the question of
piecework it is quite obvious that in any factory the operative may be called upon to do
his piecework quantity for the day rate wage. The bulk of the piecework conditions were
established in a period of trade almost unprecedented. During the two years which have
recently passed I suggest the policy pursued by employers has been to secure improved
workmanship, and in consequence the operative has lost wages. I hope this Conference
will give its mentality to this problem.
THE CHAIRMAN: What you have said contains nothing new. In 1895 it was
decided that we must accept either daywork or piecework. That is not the position to-day
-only on paper. Our policy to-day is when you go on day labour you have a set wage
and earn that wage according to the quantity statement. Where is the difference? The
man or woman limits the work done according to the wage they are to receive. I don't
think at the present time there is enough work for all our operatives to work full time.
It is not a wise thing to put something into an employer's head. I could name many
cases of firms who have gone on the day labour system but in all instances instructions
have been issued that the quantity must be limited. We are all of the opinion that piece-
work is the right system, and we only differ on the point as to whether an operative should
earn as much as he wishes or limit his wages. The employers got their point in 1895.
This is what they fought for and won, and whether they will give it up now is another
matter. They say they get better work, and there is no scamping when operatives are
on day wages. We believe in good work and good time, and in everybody acting fairly
the National Agreement, to write to the Central Office and let us know.

TUESDAY.
Morning Session.
The Conference resumed its deliberations at 9.30 a.m. on the 22nd May, 1923, Mr.
T. F. Richards, General President, presiding.
Upon the Roll being called it was found that Mr. H. Sanders (Higham and Rushden)
was absent, but he arrived later and explained the reason for being late.
The Minutes of the proceedings of the Conference for Monday were read and unani-
mously endorsed, the Chairman signing the same.

Item 23 to stand by itself.

The Standing Orders Committee also submitted a resolution dealing with the
Russian Trading Agreement
which Mr. W. R. SMITH (Organiser) proposed, viz:-
"This Conference of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives representing
75,000 members, views with great apprehension and alarm the possibility of the
Trade Agreement between this country and Russia being cancelled, leading as it must
to a rupture between the two countries.
"It declares that such policy will not only be detrimental to the people of this
country, and accentuate the problem of unemployment, but also will greatly add
to the danger and possibility of War. We therefore call upon the Government to
take steps to submit the points in dispute to a conference, whereby they may be
adequately examined, and adjusted upon an amicable basis satisfactory to both sides.
"We strongly condemn the action of the Government, and Secretary for Foreign
Affairs in particular, in issuing ultimatums without the consent of the people of this
country, and further pledge ourselves to support the General Council and the Parlia-
mentary Labour Party in any action they may take."
The delegates who have followed the discussions of the Russian position will remember
that it was promised that negotiations would go on for a few weeks. It was stated by all
parties in the House of Commons that they did not want war between this country and
Russia, and that war must be avoided at all costs, and although the Government stated
they did not desire anything like that, it was clear from the ultimatum that negotiations
may be broken off, and in that event there would be an elment of hostility which would
point in the direction of war. I believe this country feels we have had sufficient of war.
In submitting this resolution I would like to say it is not a new question. It has been going
on between the two countries ever since the Great War finished. It is a question upon
which the Labour Party has very pronounced views. One of the questions which was
passed at the Conference of 1920 dealt with unemployment, and if this country is to succeed
then we must develop our foreign trade. As a nation at this moment we live largely
upon our exports We have become a manufacturing nation. In regard to coal, iron,
steel, cotton, wool and boots and shoes we manufacture more than we can consume, and
this surplus must be disposed of if we are to try and solve the question of unemployment.
We felt the position so keenly a few years ago that a Council of Action was set up and they
were partly responsible for the abandonment of the policy of war.
This resolution states
it views with alarm and apprehension the possibility of a breach with Russia. I would
like to make it clear that we do not endorse everything that has been done in Russia.
(Hear, hear.) It does not mean we endorse what their Government has done. We ought
to recognise the form of government that any country creates by the people living there.
There is in this policy something else we should strongly condemn. We cannot permit
questions of dispute between nations to be settled by ultimatum. I am not going to say
Russian Government. It may be they have carried on propaganda in a way beyond their

That being so the Labour Party began to feel some steps must be taken in view tune

THE GENERAL SECRETARY: We established this fund some years ago because
we felt we should have the benefit rather than the insurance companies. Upon the whole
it has proved beneficial. We have not had many calls upon the fund, but we have had
some, and this fund has helped those branches who found it necessary to claim upon it.
The Council felt, having regard to the amount of money paid into the branches that the
officials should be properly covered by this insurance, as they have to look upon the matter
from the business point of view, and the amount of money received by some Branches
and the amount they pay to the Fidelity Fund is not comparable. In some instances
the Council feel that branches have not paid sufficient to the fund having regard to their
income. It is not so much one individual, but the Council feel that there should be some
parity between the amount of money paid in weekly, and the amount they pay
for the insurance of the officers. Some branches still have the idea that it is optional
whether they pay or not. This fund is obligatory, and sometimes we have had to write
asking for the premium. I hope this will not occur again as it increases
the amount of correspondence from the Central Office and also the branches.
THE CHAIRMAN: It is simply a case of protecting the members and the funds.
The few claims we have met have been considered satisfactory.
Mr. W. LANGLEY (Higham and Rushden): What is the position of those branches
who have about forty shop presidents and collectors?
THE GENERAL SECRETARY: We have always given a very wide interpretation
to this matter. We have dealt with it from the point of view of men or women who handle
money on your behalf. Some shop collectors, presidents and clerks are insured by
branches under the scheme. If a shop president collects £12 weekly he could be insured
on the 2s. 6d. scale. If, say, he only collects 12s. 6d. weekly it would be for
your local executive to decide whether to insure him or not.
Mr. F. C. JEX (Norwich): Could the General Secretary tell the Conference the

THE CHAIRMAN: The fund to-day is £497 15s. 7d.
THE GENERAL SECRETARY: We hope there will not be any calls upon the
fund. It must, however, be viewed from the point of view that there might be. Some
branches will not pay any more under this scheme, whilst others will pay 100 per cent.
more. We feel some branches have paid an inadequate sum for the amount of money
paid into the branch weekly.
ALD. A. HILL, M.P. (Leicester No. 2) thought the premium was excessive.
THE CHAIRMAN: I know two instances where the whole of the fund would
have been exhausted if we had paid all they claimed as the liability. We have created

Mr. W. LANGLEY (Higham and Rushden): The resolution states "each official

THE CHAIRMAN: We agree the Secretary should be insured for the sum paid
weekly into any particular branch. If a shop president collects say £12 weekly he would
only be insured for that amount. Insurance for shop presidents is optional.
We have power in our rules to protect shop presidents, but it must be done by the
member first. I think you ought to pass this, and if you feel it is unfair later on then it
could be altered with the next revision of rules. I am told the rates of premium are
favourable with those charged by any insurance company.

Ballot Papers.
Mr. H. ATTEWELL (Northampton) proposed Item 9:--
9 Northampton. -Rule 189.- Add "Ballot papers to contain no other matter
except For' or 'Against,' any question to be voted upon."
The object we had in view in Northampton when this matter was discussed was the
question of balloting which has now become a most important subject. They thought
that this particular addendum was wanted. In so far as 99 per cent. of our ballot papers
are issued by the Council in the proper way and conform with rule. We do not wish to
lay any particular charge against the Council, but we hope they will give us a ballot paper


---
84
similar to that given us by the capitalistic classes, and have no side issue printed on the
ballot paper. No particular advice should be placed upon the ballot paper. Some weeks
prior to an agreement being voted upon, the Northampton Branch hold a series of meetings
whereby those questions are placed before the members. The Council, as is their invariable
rule, have separate leaflets printed which members can read, and then when members
go to the poll their mind is made up. At the present time it is in the power of the Council
to place upon the ballot paper some advice which may be contentious, and as the men

ment, or a Strike." We do not grumble at at that, but what we ask is that all ballot papers

Mr. A. BIRT (Northampton) seconded the resolution. Our members think that

Mr. J. GREAVES (Leicester): I am not surprised that this resolution should

THE CHAIRMAN: One feels in a quandary when advanced men come forward

to have another resolution before this one is discussed, and that is that all members should
write a précis on the Union's rules and regulations. They ought to understand the economic
side of the workers. If members do not come to branch meetings to be educated, what

Party, the National Labour Party, the A.S.P. or the Communists, have ever committed
themselves to a "yes" or "no" policy without understanding the question they are
voting upon. The best men oppose the referendum unless they can get all the people
there. The only thing we can do is to put the whole of the circumstances on the ballot
paper and the alternative. I am surprised to hear people grumble with the last ballot
paper because we asked people to vote for or against a strike. If the strike had come
off, our critics would have been on the Council like a load of bricks. I don't think
any of my colleagues differed upon the form of the ballot paper. I think it would be
unwise on your part to ask members to vote " yes " or "no." Yes or No on what?
You cannot put other men's views unless you are honest yourself. To say we are to hide
ourselves behind the rank and file is not manly.
Mr. H. ATTEWELL (Northampton): I definitely complained of misunderstanding,

Fire Claims-Loss of Tools.
Mr. T. H. VALLANCE (Leicester No. 2) asked the question No. 11 ;—
11 Leicester No. 2.- Rule 205. -To ask question re Employers' Liability.
The necessity for asking this question arises out of a fire in Leicester over twelve
months' ago. In the early days of April last year, the firm of Messrs. Howard, Freer & Co.
was burned out. Our members put in their claims for loss of kit. The branch officers
went through these claims very carefully and reduced them considerably. Mr. Poulton
replied to say the claims for compensation would be placed before the Council in due course,
and informed us that aprons were not considered to be kit so far as a shoe operative was
concerned. Later we heard from Mr. Poulton who told us to go and see the firm, and we
did not like it, going cap in hand as if for charity. We should like to know whether there
is any understanding between the Federation and the Union as to manufacturers finding
```

---
kit, and if so, how long that understanding has been in existence, and were the branch
officials notified? Where does the matter stand now? We ought to delete this rule if it is
to be looked upon as charity.

THE CHAIRMAN: If there is such an elaborate question to be asked it ought
surely to be put upon the Agenda. (Hear, hear.) The power is always in the hands of
the questioner to make it as long or as short as he thinks fit, and it would save trouble
if it had been put down on the Agenda. So far as the rule is concerned, Rule 205 says:-

RULE 205. Compensation shall be given to financial members for loss of tools
by fire, at the discretion of the Council. The application to be made through
the Branch Committee.

Even in your Secretary's time on the Council we decided what was to be considered
as kit.

THE GENERAL SECRETARY: I am sorry Mr. Vallance used the word "charity."
We feel there is a moral obligation upon all employers to recognise the necessity of finding
kit for all operatives. When we put the matter before the Joint Industrial Council some
years ago they were sympathetic towards the matter, and a resolution expressing the desire
Mr. Vallance asks if branches were notified. The answer is " yes,"
through the Monthly Report. In this particular case now raised I have the series of
letters here which deal with the case, and as the Leicester Nos. 1 and 3 branches had secured
the money for their members, the Council thought that strengthened our case.

(COPY.)
LEICESTER NO. 2 BRANCH,
SHOE TRADE HALL, LEICESTER,
19th May, 1922.

MR. E. L. POULTON, J.P.

DEAR SIR,-Re the claim for kit at Messrs. Howard, Freer & Co., I have been in
touch with the Principal and he has agreed that he is prepared to meet the claims in
a reasonable manner, as soon as he knows his own position with the Insurance Com-
pany, but whether the Company admit the claim or not, he will.

(Signed) A. HILL, Secretary.
This policy has been adopted for some time past and has met with success. We
hope members will carry out Rule 7 and insist upon kit being provided for them. We
know some members prefer to find their own kit. Surely we have a right, without using
the word charity, if members have lost kit in a fire, to ask the firm to reimburse the member
for that loss. The Council deal with every case upon their merits. We have some extra-
ordinary cases and claims sent in under the heading of tools. We have had claims for
topcoats, boots, spectacles, tea jugs, so you will see the Council have to use their discretion
in the matter as to what comes within the four corners of the rules. I know the Council
have incurred some hostility in the matter. The rule does not say we shall honour all
claims sent in, and I assure you, as the person who is responsible for passing the claims on
behalf of the Council, those claims are all dealt with on one basis. There is no sort of
desire to favour one part of the country from another. The fact that we have generally
satisfied the majority of the members is sufficient proof that we have carried out the rule.
If you want aprons and overalls, then you must make it more explicit as to what does come
under the rule. In some cases it would mean a very considerable expenditure if we passed
the claims as sent in-one which I think was not intended when the rule was passed.
When you have claims for £1 for topcoats, 15s. for overalls, and other items, you will see
that when forty or fifty people are claiming the cost would be heavy. We have struck
out those kind of things and shall continue so to do unless you instruct us otherwise.

ALD. A. HILL, M.P. (Leicester No. 2): The General Secretary has over-stated
the question. Leicester No. 2 Branch does not want the Council to willingly back every
claim that is handed in. The Leicester No. 2 Branch Executive examined all the claims.
Are we right in asking for the rule to be carried out? It got about that the employer
in this instance was going to pay. We sent three or four letters to the Central Office,
and as many to the employer. I challenge the General Secretary to prove that we ever
sent in an excessive claim. We want to know if members are not entitled to this benefit,
have we a legal claim on the employer?

Mr. T. VALLANCE (Leicester No. 2) said he wished to withdraw his remark
when he used the word "charity."

THE CHAIRMAN: The difference between the non-federated and the federated
employers is that one takes instructions from headquarters and the other does not. We
feel our members ought not to take their kit into a factory. I know they have done it
because they prefer to use special kit. We had a meeting with the Federation and agreed
must not get upset because you had to wait a bit. We had an Umpire give an Award
and it took us five months before it was carried out, and not until the employer had been
seen three times, but we got it in the end.

17 Kettering No. 2. - Rule 219, Line 4 - After "months" insert: "This shall
not apply in cases where the ten weeks' benefit is extended in all over
eleven months. In such cases the complete periods of benefit ending
twelve months prior to the date of again declaring on shall not be reckoned
against the member."
Item 17 was moved by
Mr. J. E. CHAPMAN (Kettering No. 2) for the purpose of calling attention to
an anomaly which exists. As the rule at present stands it is possible for a man to be out
of work 62 weeks out of 105, and only draw one stretch of benefit. Another man in the
same house out of work 62 weeks, can draw two stretches of benefit. As a Branch we feel
we are up against this anomaly, and ask for it to be removed, as I am sure you will realise
our difficulty.
Mr. W. G. COLTMAN (Kettering No. 2) seconded.
THE GENERAL SECRETARY: The delegates will have some difficulty in follow-
ing the technical points. My experience has been somewhat difficult, and the experience
of most branch secretaries also, in carrying out this rule when the Central Office is appealed
to, but because two men in one house in Kettering have drawn at different periods benefit
and we cannot go into it unless the details are given. I hope the Conference will vote
against this resolution because of the ingenuity which may be brought forward, and will
make us more difficulties.
Mr. G. CHESTER (Kettering): I have several cases in Kettering, too. Here is
one: In January a member drew 2 weeks' benefit; March, 4 weeks; July, 1 week;
December, 2 weeks; all in 1921, and after receiving nine weeks' benefit in eleven months
comes on again in October, 1922, and I understand by the Central Office ruling that nine
weeks count against him. Mr. Chapman has the letters from the Central Office and can
producethem if necessary.
Mr. E. TEBBUTT (Wellingborough): I am pleased this matter has been raised.
It appears either the Central Office is wrong or the Branch. Several instances were given
and explanations given.
Mr. G. PARBURY (Leicester): A man can draw so many weeks in 12 months.
If in January and the next month or so a man drew 9 weeks out-of-work pay, and another
week in December of the same year, that world all count against him. That is rule.
How would you alter it? I cannot understand why the resolution is here.
THE GENERAL SECRETARY having obtained the details of the Kettering cases,
named them as follow:-
I have the details of the case before the Conference which are as follow:-
9th August, 1920 .. Benefit drawn 2 weeks.
3rd January, 1921 .. 2
4th July, 1921 .. 4
1st August, 1921
8th August, 1921 .. 1
Total, ten weeks. The Central Office rules that this benefit came within the twelve
months' period, and was right.
DELEGATES: Agreed.

Unemployment Benefit to Suspended Members.
THE GENERAL SECRETARY proposed the following New Rule, which had been
referred back from the Address of the Council to Conference :-
Any member who may be suspended from work for more than twelve con-
secutive working days shall be allowed to declare upon the Out-of-Work
Fund of the Union, payment from such Fund to the member to commence
as and from the thirteenth working day upon which the member is not
employed; it always being understood that the officials must themselves
be satisfied that the suspension is bona fide before benefit is allowed under
this rule. Holidays are not to be counted as entitling a member to claim
benefit under this rule. In the event of a member resuming work, and again
being suspended, he must serve a further probation of twelve consecutive
working days before again being entitled to re-declare upon the Out-of-Work
Fund under this special rule.
Note. For the purposes of the paragraph relating to non-payment for holidays
the following is the method for calculating the same :-
Easter, three days. August, one week.
Whitsuntide, three days. Christmas, one week.
For Scotland-The July Holidays, one week.
The New Year Holidays, one week.
We are hoping, but that hope seems against hope, that the position regarding
employment would become again normal. Meantime many of our members are out of
work or suspended, owing to an understanding with the manufacturers operatives were
not dismissed wholesale, but were suspended. The existing rule is very explicit and
allows of no two interpretations. We have had as you are all aware-various methods
to try and meet these members of ours who have been suspended from work, and
although the amount of money paid out in unemployment benefit has been tremendous, still
the position has not been fully met. The present position is such that at the monthly
meetings of the Council reports are presented and requests made that something should be
done for those members who go into the branch offices morning after morning to see if
there are any jobs for them, or if there is any proposal whereby they may receive benefit
from the Union. The Council desire me to say that they appreciate to the full the loyal
and sympathetic way in which the branch officers throughout the country have tried to
meet the position. This is not merely lip service. The Council know you must have had
a very unpleasant job to have to refuse these members benefit. The Council highly
appreciate the fact, however unpleasant it has been, that you have all tried to meet the
situation. I hope you will, therefore, accept my word upon this matter. The Council
have given very careful thought and consideration, not only to the items on the Agenda,
but to the position generally to see if anything could be done for members who may be
suspended for indefinite periods. It is much better frankly to tell the members that the
contributions are not sufficient to give additional benefits, rather than do a thing and then for
it to break down. The Council of the Union boldly faced the position and told the members
the position we should be placed in. There are one or two resolutions on the Agenda
which we should like to see carried. It needs no words of mine to say the Council would
like to be in a position-and would be eager to be able to grant all cases which come before
them-rather than have to say no. To be enabled to say yes rather than no, would mean
the members must pay a higher rate of contribution. When we discussed the matter we
felt the present was not an opportune time to ask for any increase in the contributions.
Many members in all districts, and the branch officials know better than I do, that although
some of the members are at work, they are working such short time that it is hard for them
to take some risks and liabilities when they are faced with a set of circumstances similar
to meet all their dues and demands. An Executive Council has always to be prepared
to those with which we are faced to-day, and this resolution was drafted a great number
of times, before it was finally decided upon in its present form. We would rather do this

than boast of a big account at the bank. You know that it has always been my ambition
as General Secretary, to see our Union the strongest in the country, so far as our worth per
head is concerned and general efficiency. I hope I have never forgotten, although one
endeavours to help our unfortunate members. I know some of the delegates will be
likes to see a big fund, that we must not rest content until we have used our best
disappointed having regard to some of their resolutions, yet I hope you will accept this
position. It is not this week, nor next week that long-sighted men ought to take, but of
many days ahead of us. I have therefore pleasure in moving this resolution and hope
it will be unanimously carried.

Daylight Saving.
Mr. A. BIRD (Norwich) proposed Item 34:-
34 Norwich No. 1. Rule 294. Add " Members to be allowed out of their homes
till 10 p.m. during the operation of the Daylight Saving Act."
The need for the operation of this particular rule has been shown to the officers and
members on account of the fact that Friendly Societies in Norwich have granted relief to
their members, and we ask that a similar extension be granted on the Union side.
Mr. H. FRASER (Norwich) seconded the amendment.
THE CHAIRMAN: What chance would a sick visitor have if a man is out. He
has no right to find a man at home only after hours. It will make it very difficult if sick
visitors have to start their work after 10 o'clock at night.
Mr. J. GREAVES and Mr. H. WILLIAMS (Leicester) opposed the amendment
to the present rule.
Mr. F. C. JEX (Norwich): Although I am not pressing this item personally, I should
like to say the sick visitors themselves raised the matter at the branch meeting. Early
in the week the Chairman said the Union was created for the benefit of the members and
not branch officers, and now you have a chance to vote in that direction.
The resolution was lost.
The Conference adjourned for the day at 12 o'clock noon.
On Wednesday afternoon the delegates travelled from Russell Square, London, and
had a most enjoyable motor trip to Windsor, as the guests of the General Officers and
members of the Executive Council, acting for the Union. Upon arrival tea was provided
at the Thames Hotel, Windsor, and despite the inclement weather, many of the
delegates visited historical places of interest, including Windsor Castle, whilst other
delegates enjoyed themselves at an impromptu concert at the Hotel.
The return journey to London commenced at 8 p.m., and upon arrival home, all
expressed their pleasure with the delightful outing.

Political Agents.
41 The Council. - Rule 59, Line 2. - Add "financial members of the Union."
Mr. A. J. DOBBS (Leeds) proposed Item 42:--
42 Leeds. Rule 59, Line 2. - Delete all words after "Union," up to and including
"success" on fifth line, and insert the following:-" Who shall submit
all offers received from constituencies to the Council. The Council shall
have power to place any Agent in a Constituency where they think there
is a reasonable chance of success. In the event of any Agent refusing
to contest a Constituency selected by the Council, he shall resign his position
as Agent."
We have had a big discussion in Leeds over this question, and I hope you will discuss
it in the spirit in which it is brought forward. There is no bitterness intended towards
anyone, and no personal attack is made on anyone. The time is fast coming when the
⚫economic pressure upon our members would be so great that they would have to choose
between carrying out the national agreements and starvation. We say something will
have to be done to relieve the pressure which is continually being put upon the working
classes. The best method of doing that is through political action. As the Labcur Party
grows, so we want to see the number of Labour men in the House of Commons grow, and
eventually have a Labour Government who will give us laws for the advancement of the
people. Our rules say we shall have five Parliamentary Agents, and under certain cir-
cumstances seven. We need not be concerned about the other two, because they are not
affected by this resolution. The rule says we shall have five Parliamentary Agents. The
result shown in the last election was such that we really only had three agents. I am not
blaming our General President nor General Secretary for not accepting constituencies.
I do not think we could expect them to do so under present circumstances. I don't think
any sensible man would, with a position such as the one they hold, accept an offer to go to
Parliament. We ought, however, to make a provision that we should have our five
Parliamentary Agents, all of whom are prepared to stand for Parliament. If the General
President and General Secretary have decided not to stand for Parliament, then
they should retire from that position and not act the dog in the manger policy.
I was asked pointedly how it was that two of our agents could not find
stituencies. I knew they could. As a matter of fact the General President has
made no secret of the fact that he had many offers. I don't say they were all
satisfactory. We do not want men to accept a position and then not go on with it.
They should be prepared to carry out the rules. I don't think it is necessary for me to
say much more about it, as it is a question as to whether we believe in political action or not.
I have never hesitated to say I am prepared to spend as much money as we can afford on
political action, as I believe it is political action in which we shall have to make our stand.
I am longing for the time when we can get a majority in the House of Commons, amongst
whom our Union has its full share. Members who have been elected as Parliamentary
Agents of the Union should either carry out the rules or resign and give others a chance.
Mr. J. WALSH (Leeds) seconded. I cannot add much to what friend Dobbs has
said. Our Parliamentary Agents should have a reasonable chance in any constituency.
There may be constituencies where there is little chance of success in any constituenc
mer would succeed. I hope all the points raised will be replied to We have been told
Nothing is too good for me, and I don't see why it should be too good for other people.

not at 25s. a day, nor 21s. per day, but at 11s., and I did my own work for three years
at the office as well. I did my speaking at street corners and did not follow another
candidate. I got elected. It cost £750 to elect me and the delegates immediately lowered
it to £500 so that I should not be re-elected. It had the desired effect. All the Council
members of that day did all they could for me and did good work. When the time came
and I was beaten by 400 votes, my Agent told me beforehand that I should lose by that
number, as the other people had put that number of latchkey voters on the list, and my
Agent only had twelve bob a week. During that three years the work had an effect upon
me. I did not have to send for a doctor, but I lost my hair and many of the delegates
will remember it. I went bald-headed to Parliament due to hard work. When I had been
in Parliament four years I finished seventeenth on the list for Divisions, and so you will
see I paid some attention to the work, but during the recess my greatest trouble was to
find some work to do. Some of my friends in Northampton grumbled because I took

London, and promised to ring him up whilst the deputation were on their way. He
promised to consider it, but I told the members of the deputation that if they could not
persuade this other gentleman I would consider the matter. He accepted it, and had
almost a walk-over. In two other constituencies I was on the point of taking, but the
local people thought we should not win until the next time. I told them I was not out

Mr. A. J. DOBBS (Council Member): I am pleased the discussion has been

I thought it was time our rules regarding the political agents was

matter of fact if on being sent to Parliament it makes our men better, and gives them more

our minds was, as I said before, to see that all our men were prepared to go into the political
arena. We must use the political weapon to make our individual organisation effective.

and good. Why not have the full number of Parliamentary Agents and tack on the national
officers? Our agents ought not to refuse others the right of standing, and I will be quite
frank and say I disagree with Rule 67. Has any officer of our Union the right to accept
an office which he never intends to use? I don't think there is any need to raise the per-
sonal side, because if I disagree with a man I do not hesitate to tell him, but I have no
animosity against him. I don't want to make the position of our general officers more
difficult. Even now the treatment of the Parliamentary Agents is better than in the
past, still I am not satisfied that we treat them sufficiently well. I feel sometimes we have
been too mean and too near with our national officers. It is not my fault, but the
fault of the members who frame the rules. Are you satisfied with the present position ?
If not, then I ask you to vote for the resolution number 42, and I appeal to you with every
confidence.

National Health Insurance Work.
THE CHAIRMAN suggested the Report of the National Health Insurance Depart-
ment should be taken as read, this being unanimously agreed to.
National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives.
NATIONAL HEALTH INSURANCE DEPARTMENT.
COUNCIL'S REPORT.
34, Guilford Street,
Russell Square, London, W.C. 1.
May, 1923.
Fellow Officers and Delegates,
1) It is with extreme regret that we have to put on record the
passing away of Mr. John W. Murby, the Manager of the Insurance
Department, since the last Triennial Conference. For 10 years
Mr. Murby was Manager of this Department - years of change, years
of experience in the evolutions through which National Health matters
have passed. A zealous Trade Unionist, he was always interested
in that which made for the uplifting of the lowest, and any question
having the welfare of the workers as its ultimate aim, found his strong
support. A keen politician, he spent himself, without stint, in the
pursuit of his ideals, and it is almost certain that, but for the break-
down of his health, he would have reached a position of national
influence for his Party. In connection with the decease of Mr. Murby,
a grant has been made to Mrs. Murby of £100, being three months'
salary. We feel sure that this step will meet with the approval of the
delegates.
2) In accordance with Rules 50 and 67, Part 2, and the Com-
missioners' Regulations 408 A.G.D., 1912, the Report of this Society,
and the Cash Statement showing amounts received and disbursed
covering three years ending December 31st, 1922, is herewith

presented. During this period the sum of £85,808 16s. 2d. has been

£18,340 7s. 5d., making a total of £104,149 3s. 7d. December 31st,
1922, marks the completion of 10 years' benefit payment under National

pounds has been paid away by this Society in Benefits and Administra-

(3) The Cash Statements relating to the three separate years, 1920,
1921, and 1922, together with the Audited Cash Statements for the
years 1918, 1919, 1920, and 1921, are appended to this report and
should provide some interesting perusal. It is a matter for congratula-
tion that the Administrative expenses of the Society have been kept
at the lowest possible figure compatible with efficiency, the sum of
no less than £8,741 standing to our credit as Surplus on the Adminis-
tration Account. Unfortunately, however, the heavy Sickness to
which our members are subject nullifies the effect of this saving by
the fact that on Valuation the Surplus on Administration is auto-
matically turned over to the Benefit Fund Account, thereby helping to
reduce the adverse balance, caused by - as stated above - the heavy
sickness rate which has obtained. It is a matter of constant anxiety
to those responsible, to devise some means of keeping our Sickness
incidence down to the lowest possible figure, consistent with the
determination to perform our true function as a medium through
which distress caused by Sickness can be alleviated.
(4) Intimation has been received from the Ministry that this Society
will be Valued for the second time, as at December, 1923. The report
of the first Valuation was submitted to the Annual Conference, held
in May, 1921, and for nearly two years our members have had the
advantage of increased benefits as a result of the Surplus shewn at
that Valuation, on our total Funds. It is stated on good authority
that the result of the second Valuation will be, if anything, better than
the last, speaking nationally.
(5) Appended to this Report will be found a Table shewing the num-
ber of Contributions and Cash Values received during the three years
ending June, 1922. Our gross membership is 43,253, being members
who have passed through the Society since its inception; our nett
membership is 32,500--25,290 men and 7,210 women. It is pleasing
to note that during this period of generally decreasing membership
of Approved Societies, this Society has held its own, and although
shewing no nett increase over last year, new entrants have kept our
membership practically stable.

(6) A Table is also shewn in the Appendix giving particulars of
our Investments. It will be seen that the sum of £77,081 14s. 1d.
has been invested in securities selected by the Society, and £63,933
in securities selected by the Ministry of Health, making a grand total
of £141,014 14s. 1d. Reserve Values also standing to the credit of
the Society, but which are gradually being redeemed, amount to
£118,000. These figures prove that our Society is in a sound healthy
financial position, and though it has been found impossible to provide
for a larger Surplus increase of benefits as compared with some
Societies which have the advantage of healthier occupations and a
smaller incidence of Sickness, there is room for congratulation on
our position.

(7) The question of a Joint Card for Health and Unemployment
Contributions is one that has occupied the minds, both of the Ministry
and the Managements of Societies, for a considerable time. No
decision, however, has yet been arrived at. Many arguments can be
adduced both for and against the suggestion. The matter is at present
down for the consideration of the General Council of the Trade Union
Congress.

(8) Your Executive express the hope that every effort will be made
on the part of officials and members, to extend the growth of the
Approved Society of our Union. We would point out the advantages
to our members of being able to draw their Sickness Benefits from
one source. Every effort is made to settle claims for benefit as soon
as received, without any vexatious delay, and our procedure in pay-
ment of benefit is such as to ensure prompt settlement of claims.

(9) In conclusion, we would urge each member to do their part
in making known to their fellow workers the advantage of joining
up with them in our Approved Section, and thus making it a still more
effective and efficient Society in helping the members in their time
of need.

Yours fraternally,

THE COUNCIL.

THE CHAIRMAN: We have with us this afternoon Mr. R. D. Mayes, our new
Insurance Manager, who was recently elected by the members. Let me add that with
the exception of the General Secretary, Mr. Mayes is the oldest member connected with
its inception, and was in our Leicester No. 2 Branch office for six months prior to his taking
up a position in the Central Office, and in addition his activities in the trade union world
are well known to all of us in the City of Leicester. I wish to congratulate Mr. Mayes
upon his election.
Mr. R. D. MAYES (Manager) thanked the Chairman and the delegates for the
reference made to him.
The Report of the work of the Department was then considered seriatim, Items
1 to 6 being accepted without discussion.
In connection with Item 7 the Chairman stated that the Union had played an important
part, and on Item 8 he impressed the desire of all shop clerks taking members into the
Approved Section as soon as they reached the age of 16 years.
Mr. J. GREAVES (Leicester): You expressed the idea that we should make our
Approved Society stronger, and that we want members for the Society. In the election
just completed I noticed very particularly that many of our members, not approved,
had a vote. To me this seemed a peculiar position.
THE CHAIRMAN: I don't differ with you at all, but the Government made that
part of our understandings. They did not like the idea of dissecting members and we had
to obey their wishes. The rule is very clear upon the point. I know some of my colleagues
felt the Manager should be the controlling authority, but the Government turned it down.
Our General Secretary is responsible to us in every sense, and the Government hold him
responsible for the work in the Department. Some of us on the Committee of Manage-
ment do not come under the régime of insurance, but we were told owing to the position
we hold on the Industrial side that we should be expected to take this additional office.
Mr. W. KENDALL (Leicester): I should just like to say that many members
where I work who are not approved with us did not vote.
Mr. D. ASTLEY (Leicester): That cuts both ways. We have a young man who
has just been elected Secretary to the Foresters' Approved Society, yet he belongs to our
Approved Society.
Mr. W. KENDALL (Leicester): When a youth attains the age of 16 we cannot tell
by his looks, but the C.W.S. have his age because of paying him the scale, and when we
approach him to approve through us we are often too late. We are at a great disadvantage
compared with the firm.
Mr. J. P. REID (Arbroath): Do we have any members in our Approved Society
who are not members of the Union?
THE CHAIRMAN: No.
Mr. J. ROBERTSON (Glasgow): There are a goodly number of members in
Glasgow who joined us when State Insurance was first introduced; they left the trade,
but are still members with us.
THE CHAIRMAN: That is quite permissible.

DEAR SIR, I have your letter of yesterday s date to hand. The question raised in the
same is one that has occupied the attention of my Executive for the last ten years.
Many efforts have been made by this Society to call the attention of those responsible
for the condition of things in the Earl Shilton and Barwell District. Representations
were made, within the first few years of the introduction of National Health Insurance,
to the Local Government Board, and have been repeated time after time, and as
recently as January of the present year, communications have been sent to the
Ministry of Health on the same subject. The question of Housing is one that enters
very largely into the difficulty surrounding the matter. Unfortunately our protests
have borne very little fruit, beyond evoking the reply that certain houses have been
built recently in the district. Our protest is naturally respecting the insanitary
condition of houses already existing.
Regarding your request for Statistics, I may say that although the Union has a
large membership in the district, the Friendly Societies have such a strong hold,
that the Approved Society has a comparatively small number of members residing
there.
This being so I am afraid any figures supplied would be based upon such a small
number of persons, that they would be of very little use to you. Suffice it to say
that this district has always been regarded by this Society as its blackest spot. I
trust you will be successful in your efforts to call the attention of the proper authority
to the state of affairs that exist.
Any further assistance that you think it is possible for me to render I shall be
pleased to provide.
MR. T. CREW, A.F.I.,

You will see, therefore, that we never lose sight of the matter. In reply to Mr. Astley

list it does not follow that they have the worse average of sickness benefit. The member-

Mr. W. JONES (Kingswood): I read the report to which Mr. Parbury referred

a more active chap who is more bitter against the landlordism than Astley. He has been
on the Board of Guardians and the local Council for years, and if there was a firebrand
that name applies to Astley. I don't want to deprive him of any criticism, and will read
you an extract from the Municipal Engineering and The Sanitary Record, for 22nd March,
1923 -
One of the most insanitary of the big villages in Leicestershire, viz., Earl Shilton,
has neither a sewerage nor a sewage disposal system, nor has it any creditable system
of sanitation. The consequences are that preventable diseases have been endemic
in it for the last quarter of a century. Yet neither the Hinckley Rural District
Council, in whose area it lies, nor the Leicestershire County Council, both of which
bodies are somewhat diffident in sanitary administration, appear to recognise that
the responsibility for the high death-rate which prevails lies on their shoulders.
According to the Leicester Mercury, the Rural Council is frequently "tinkering"
with the drainage of the place, and quite recently were indulging in an "improvement
scheme" which revealed the fact that house drains in many cases had been laid into
the public road and not connected to the main drain, and that sewage springs periodi-
cally burst out. The sewage of the village is discharged on to a field without any
systematic treatment, and not only pollutes the stream most seriously, but the con-
ditions constitute an offensive nuisance to the neighbourhood. The Hinckley Rural
District Council should act as other Sanitary Authorities do, and obtain the advice
of sewerage engineers to help them to deal with the existing insanitary condition,
failing which the Ministry of Health will, we are confident, feel it their duty to intervene.
However, the Council will not lose sight of the matter.
