RULE 60. Should exceptional circumstances arise in a constituency whereby
it is apparent that a member of the Union might be returned to Parliament,
it shall be within the power of the Counil to support a member or members
even though not one of the Union's Official Agents; it being understood
that this power shall only be put into operation after full inquiry by the
Council as to the real position and also being satisfied that the circumstances
fully warrant giving such support. Not more than two candidates shall be
given support to under the above-named circumstances. Any member
being supported at an election under these conditions shall not be deemed
to be one of the Official Parliamentary Agents. If therefore at an election
the member was not successful, it must be understood that he would not be
put upon the-Union Official List of Parliamentary Agents.
We have administered the rule according to the spirit in which it was passed. We
have no power to make favourites of anyone. We pointed out the position to Mr. Hill
long before he was nominated for the position, and he agreed to accept the situation, and
expressed the hope that his people would stand by him. Mr. Hill undoubtedly feels his
position is strengthened by his retaining the position of secretary to the Branch. I went
down to two of their branch meetings, and Mr. Hill made it very clear that he had no
intention of resigning from the secretaryship of the Leicester No. 2 Branch. You will
make positions less secure in the future if you pass this resolution.

Mr. R. WHITE (Edinburgh) seconded the resolution.

THE GENERAL SECRETARY : I don't think this resolution will take a lot of
time, because in spirit we agree with it. Just because they had a few cases in Arbroath
where certain curriers earn more than our men does not prove that we should alter our
rules. Our people in that part of the country were against piecework, and the majority
of them did not get more than the minimum. As a matter of fact the Leather Workers'
Federation was brought into existence owing to the goodwill of the Council, at meetings
held in my office in Leicester, which was offered to them gladly, and without charge.
Judging from reports I am afraid that Federation is not so active as we could wish for.
We have attempted to come to an understanding with other unions. We thought we had
accomplished it with the Amalgamated Society of Boot and Shoe Makers, but their
members voted against it. We opened up negotiations with the Rossendale Valley Union,
but here again it was refused. At the moment we are about half way with the negotiations
with a Union in London, and I am hoping we shall be successful.

THE CHAIRMAN : Mr. Reid need not have quoted the curriers, as our boot repairers
to-day have a minimum wage of 72s. We made an attempt to get several unions to
amalgamate. I personally tried several years ago, but without success. A Union with
200 members wants the same representation as a Union 50,000 strong. That was some
of the trouble we had with the Amalgamated Society. They wanted us to take over
1,800 members with two permanent officials, but eventually we split upon the question
of superannuation. Whilst amalgamation may be a good thing, you must not forget
that it will bring about additional work for your present officials. The people who amal-
gamate ought only to want the same amount of attention as our present members, and not
demand sole attention. We have tried all and sundry, including leather workers and
saddlers, and I don't think it ought to be us every time that should make the overtures,
although we should not put any obstacles in the way of amalgamation.

The Resolution was lost.

It was then decided that the Chairman should put the rule into operation dealing
with the Limitation of Speeches. The Chairman read rule 88, as follows:-
RULE 88. - Every latitude is to be allowed the delegates for giving expression
ference; but in the event of the Chairman seeing that the business is not
to their views on the various subjects that may be brought before Con-
feaking satisfactory progress, he shall have power to appeal to the Con-
ference to limit the time allowed to movers of resolutions to ten minutes,
a seconder to seven minutes, and any subsequent speaker to five minutes.
No one shall speak more than once on a question, except the mover of
an original resolution. Should the President be of opinion that there is no
practical difference among the delegates, he shall have power to stop the
discussion.

Mr. G. CHESTER (Kettering) proposed the alteration to the present rule. I want
to say in all seriousness to this question that most of us have been emphatic during the
week as to how the trade union movement should be developed. The trade union move-
ment in the past has been somewhat different from what it is at present. In future we
must prepare to educate the members. We have so far specialised upon industrial matters.
I want this Conference to feel, if possible, the necessity of having organisers to help forward
the political objects of the Union. If the trade union movement is the real live body
that it pretends to be, then we must have someone amongst us constantly who will be able
to educate our members. This kind of work has been attended to by most branch officials.
I think all branch officials will agree with me that when an outside official is billed to attend
our meetings there is a much larger meeting than when it is just the ordinary n onthly
meeting. The attendances usually are very poor and yet we nearly always get a good
response if an outside official of the Union comes along. We realise our present organisers
are engaged upon industrial matters, and also our head officials in the main dealing with the
present-day position. We realise the industrial activity of this Union is their chief aim,
but we suggest that an additional crganiser be elected who will deal with the political side
of the Union's work. We want someone—perhaps a woman could deal with the question
better than a man—who has had some experience in the work so that our members may be
educated to take an interest in all matters affecting the movement. I appeal to you,
therefore, to pass this rule.

members.

Mr. G. CHESTER (Kettering) proposed Item 64.
64 Kettering Nos. 1 and 2.- Rule 106.- Delete Rule and insert :
(a) The duties of two of the Organisers shall be to act as Organising
Agents, Investigators and Dispute Managers, if necessary, when called
upon to do so by the Council. They shall give full particulars in writing
to the General Secretary. They shall also be at the service of the Council
for any other duties to which they may think fit to appoint them. They
shall be in attendance at the Council Meetings. They may take part
in the discussions upon matters relating to organising, disputes and
investigating, but shall have no vote at the Council Meetings. They
shall, by virtue of their office, attend the Conferences of the Union. They
shall report to the General Secretary, daily, where they may be found.
They shall do their best to organise all working at the trade, including
repairers, and shall also push the Trade Union Stamp by attending all
meetings and gatherings where such advertisement would be likely to help.
(b) The duties of the third Organiser shall be, as far as possible, specially
confined to visiting branches in a general supervising capacity. He shall
lecture at Branch and specially convened meetings on Educational and
Political matters. He shall seek the general establishment of Rules
68 and 156 in all centres, and strive for the fulfilment of Rule 155. He
shall be subject to the same general conditions as applied to the other
Organisers.
I feel that there is sufficient scope for the additional organiser who will now be appointed
to be put to this position in the Union. The Conference seems to be up against it, but I
feel there is an absolute necessity for this class of work to be done, and we find the necessity
for such work more and more.

Richards) presiding.
Upon the Roll being called it was reported that all the delegates were present.
Renewed Discussion on Organising.
Mr. W. PITTS (Northampton): In view of the decision arrived at this morning,
I do not think it is necessary for this question to be put to the vote. To bring forward
such a resolution and state the duties of a new man is altogether wrong, and the suggestions
of Mr. Chester are unthinkable. Undoubtedly there is plenty of work to do on the educa-
tional side, but where will the advantage come to the Union, if this man only looks after
the educational side. If members desire to improve their educational facilities then ther
can get to know all they want from the public libraries. To carry this resolution will
stultify the hands of the Council, and will not help forward the principles laid down this
morning.
Mr. G. CAMPBELL (Kettering): If there is any need for such a man as this,
time shall be taken up teaching, but simply states that he shall work in a certain capacity.

Mr. F. C. JEX (Norwich) supported the resolution. In 1918 the Norwich Branch
suggested that we should meet for three days instead of six, and that was beaten. Finally,
in 1920, the Conference accepted the position. I am bound to confess that I am dis-
appointed with the change, and think the proposal of the Council would meet the position
better. I hope the Conference will accept the position whatever may be the outcome,
ALD. A. HILL, M.P. (Leicester No. 2) opposed the resolution. Our Norwich
friends made a mistake in trying to crush into three days what it has usually taken six.
I tried to discover from the General Secretary in what way the experiment had failed
He simply said it had failed, but that is quite a different thing from bringing the evidence
to prove his case. There was a feeling, very widespread, in our Union, that as things were
moving rapidly it was necessary for the Executive Council to meet the rank and file more
frequently, so that they could get into closer touch than had been the case. I agree that
every two years is too frequent to upset the rules. No sooner have you one set of rules
from the printer than you begin to revise them. I question whether any evidence can be
brought of any other Union altering its administrative rules so often as we do, although
they may meet annually. I differ with the General Secretary ard think the experience
has been justified. We shall come up to the situation when our members will be wanting
to get into definite touch with the policy of the Union as expressed by the Council. Surely
we shall not be in the position we are to-day for ever. Some day the clouds must break
and give us a vision of progress. I hope the majority of the Conference will adhere to the
present position.
THE CHAIRMAN: Higham and Rushden moved that we should have Annual
Conferences and that was accepted at Edinburgh.

Mr. J. FOUNTAINE (Northampton No. 2) then proposed Item 74.
74 Northampton No. 2.- Rule 70, Line 2.-Delete "annually," and substitute
"every two years." Also Delete (Line 4) "third year the" and sub-
stitute "alternate."
I am glad the Council's resolution has been carried. This resolution, like others
from Northampton No. 2, comes out of a decision made at the monthly meeting. The
result was that we felt we were not justified in spending the amount of money that we do
on these Conferences. We onght to be out for economy. The delegates who work in the
factory and come to these conferences are twitted with the fact that they come out for a
week's holiday. This is the second conference I have attended, and I am not only out for
economy, but for keeping up the reputation of the Union. I propose that at one biennial
meeting we should have a meeting for three days, and the next one to alter the rules.
Last year was my first experience and I was told we should have the slaughter of the
innocents at the end of the Conference. If we can have the slaughter of the innocents
on Friday, let us slaughter them on Monday. (Laughter.) I am not out to take away
the efficiency of the Conference, but if you can alter your rules in five days, then three
days should be sufficient to discuss policy. These are the views of the most active members
in one of the most active branches in the country, and I hope you will all support it.
Mr. T. PENDRED (Northampton No. 2) seconded the resolution.
Upon the same being put to the vote, only seven delegates voted in its favour, THE
CHAIRMAN declaring the same lost.

Now we have come to the real slaughter of the innocents. Our people in Arbroath

the ballot box occasionally along with the rank and file.

Voting.

Mr. A. G. RANDALL (Kingswood) moved Item 84.
84 Kingswood and District. - Rule 91. - Delete, and insert: "All Union
Elections shall be by ballot, but in all cases the Voting Papers and the
names of all candidates shall be uniform. No votes will be counted at
any time unless given by the members in person, at such places as the
Branch may appoint for voting. Voting shall take place on one and the
same day, except in the case of Branches having Sections. Members
shall be supplied with a Ballot Paper after the Branch Officers or others
appointed for the purpose have satisfied themselves that the member is
financial and registered, and being not more than 8 weeks in arrears,
the member's card shall be date stamped when ballot paper is issued.
After members have recorded their vote, they shall deposit their paper in
a box provided to receive it, or return the paper to the person appointed
to receive it, who shall be responsible, and shall see the papers deposited
in the Ballot Box. Such Ballot Box shall be sealed after the votes have
been recorded, and not opened until the day of counting, and then only
in the presence of the elected scrutineers. All votes to be counted on one
and the same day in each District, the Council to fix the same in the
Monthly Report. Council be asked to suggest amendment to induce
larger numbers of members to vote."
Our members feel that the present position is not a satisfactory one.
If delegates
will consult the figures recently issued in connection with the position of Insurance Manager,
they are very disconcerting to see such a small number have taken any interest in the
vote. Our members in Kingswood think this can be improved by adopting the method
in our resolution, so as to get to the bulk of the rank and file to enable them to record their
vote. It is done in some unions, and we think if the ballot papers were left with the mem-
bers and returned to a responsible official later in an envelope for the purpose, the result
of the ballot would be much better. We do not think the present position a good one.

Mr. W. PAIN (Kingswood) seconded. As one who has cast the votes occasionally
I think our present system of voting is not a favourable one. When we go into the polling
station we are faced with a ballot paper not knowing any of the qualifications of the
nominees. The more conscientious members will not vote because they do not know the
men whose names appear on the ballot paper. It is our endeavour to try and create a
new system so as to give every one a chance to vote. When we had to take the voting
for the national officers last year, the ballot paper had twenty-eight names on it. No
one had seen the names until they came along to vote. If the ballot paper had been given
out two or three days before the vote had been taken, we should have had a much better
ballot. Take the ballot for this Conference. We were grouped with one of the Norwich
branches. No one in Norwich knows me, and so nearly all the Norwich members voted
for their nominees. The same thing obtained in Kingswood. If this Conference will
improve our system of balloting it will be a good thing.

THE CHAIRMAN: I think the delegates should be very careful in their state-
ments. You say our members do not know whose names will appear on the ballot papers.
Monthly Report. You don't want your branch officers to give you the pedigree of every
That is not our fault. Members have facilities and opportunity of seeing them in the
individual, surely. We have had to investigate a few cases and you cannot be too careful.
I have known branches poll more votes than they had members. We should be very
careful. This proposal will allow any particular individual to get votes for his pals,
and put a premium on the ballot box. A vote has been taken quite recently: how is it
that all the interest seems to be in one quarter of the globe? I don't want us to send an
electioneering agent into every factory.

Mr. T. H. VALLANCE (Leicester No. 2): If this is passed we shall have more

shop president brings in from a shop near by 35s. per week, so it is safe to say there are
between 35 and 40 clickers in the shop. We pay 5s. for the rent of a room; 5s. for poll
clerk, and for the last few votings we have not averaged five votes. We have been down
to as low as three, and one of those three was the polling agent, so the two votes cost us 5s.
each. If you passed this resolution you would get more votes, but if people are not interested
enough at present to enable them just to cross the road to vote, then we ought to do
nothing to bring about what I think would amount to corruption.

Piecework v. Daywork.
Mr. J. P. REID (Arbroath) proposed Item 87.
87 Arbroath.-New Rule.-" That the Industrial Policy of the Union be to
establish daywork regulated by quantity statements, as against piece-
work with unlimited output, and that a new rule be framed to emphasise
the principle."
In formally moving this resolution I wish to say that we discussed it two years ago
when it was passed by a narrow majority. I should like to see it added to our rules.
Mr. J. T. OSBORNE (Bristol) seconded. We have discussed this matter several
times at our branch meeting. We have some factories in Bristol where men have to produce
a certain number of boots for a given wage. There are others working piecework pure and
simple. Our branch feels that more operatives would be employed if this resolution was
carried. I don't suggest it will be carried, and some of my members have told me they
do not agree with it. In fact I think we shall be up against something if it is carried.
Mr. J. WHEELER (Leicester): I consider there is a great deal to be said upon
this resolution. Many of our members, and some of the delegates present do not under-
stand what is meant by daywork regulated by quantity statements. Assuming a firm
give notice to go on daywork, after they have been working piecework, then we should
say the men must earn their wages according to statement. Jus: prior to coming to this
Conference a firm reported such a thing had happened, but we gave them the advice I have
just given. I am convinced something will have to be done in the way suggested by this
resolution. We have a firm in Leicester working on the Conveyor system. I don't think
there is another firm in England working like it.
THE CHAIRMAN: Nor in Europe.
Mrs. M. J. BELL-RICHARDS (Leicester Women's): And we don't want it
either.
Mr. J. WHEELER (Leicester): I should like the delegates to visit that factory
and see how it is worked. They have a trolley system each operator working on six-pair
lots. The man releases the lever and sends it on to the next man.
Those men were earning
anything from £5 to £8 per week. The most extraordinary thing about it is the firm
select the best type of young man for the purpose, because they must be active. Recently
they wanted an edge setter and the Manager said he did not want a man who could only
do from 12 to 14 dozen per day, but he wanted a man who could do 20 dozen, so you will
understand that man could earn from £1 to 30s. daily. I suggest the Council should try
and make some arrangements to try and prevent this thing happening. As far as the
factors are concerned, if they could not get their work as quickly as they desired, then the
men would be able to work slower
after the busy time the men are put off. Piecework lends itself to unemployment, because
Mrs. M. J. BELL-RICHARDS (Leicester Women's) opposed the resolution.
When we were compiling our piecework statements they were based on the large quantities
done by low-paid day labour. Can you control all your operatives and get them to work
according to statement. I know some districts are organised to quantities. In Leicester
recently one or two firms have gone on daywork, but we have been watching them. The
young flapper on daywork cannot go slowly. As a result the pieceworker has to suffer.
We have a good deal healthier membership to-day on piecework than we had on daywork.
The unlimited output may be a danger. Piecework pure and simple is the thing. We
know that some time ago the operative worked very quickly and arranged with manu-
facturers to work three days and have three days off, and when men earned £5 in three
days and women from 12 to 13 in the same period, they came on our Suspension Fund
spread it over the operatives all well and good, but you will not do it by passing this
for out-of-work pay.
Mr. T. RABBITT (Wellingborough): The Council will have to concentrate
upon this subject. Piecework is all right if you can control the operatives not to earn
two men's wages. In our district men were put on piecework and they speeded up, and

Mr. A. W. LYNE (Council Member): Most of the delegates are agreed to-day,
although they were not two years ago. Two years ago I suggested that we should go
back to daywork regulated by quantity statements, but in the light of recent experience
cue is bound to admit that to go back to daywork without any variations in the wages
is too dangerous. If we could deal with the whole of our members who are receiving less
than they earned there would not be a dissentient voice. We should have this question
before us as something to aim for. Realisation has become effective if those who take an
active interest in the work tackle their own members. It is easy when you get your mem-
bers together to be able to prove the disadvantages of doing more work than they are paid
for. The manufacturers would not have approached our men in Northampton were it
not for the fact that they could earn big wages. Our men are using this resolution for
propaganda. We must compel the manufacturers to reckon the work done at not less
than the minimum wage rates, and not more than a maximum wage. No fixed wage,
important that the quantity statements should be worked to.
Mr. C. BLEAKLEY (Council Member): I don't think there is anyone in this
Conference who agrees with the conditions under which our people have been working.
None of us want to go back to the old daywork system. Men have been trained to a posing
to-day and they have to keep pace with the machinery. Our funds have suffered on accounn
of the pace with which they had to work. If we could convert our members to workout
reasonable pace we should be justified in doing so. We should continue our propaganda.
Mr. Buckle has told us before that he has visited factories where men have earned 30s.
a week more than they have drawn; that must be stopped. We think men ought not
to work at top speed. If the price per operation is fair then our men should receive the
full benefit.
Mr. A. BIRT (Northampton): I don't think Mrs. Richards is right in stating
people are healthier on piecework. Still, the fact remains that it does not pay an operative
to be on the sick. He loses too much money because he has been drawing £4 or £5 a week,
which is considerable compared with his sick benefit.
Mr. W. KENDALL (Leicester): What are those people doing to allow a man to
do 15 worth of work and only get £3 for it? The manufacturer has the right to say
whether men shall work day or piecework. We ought to be the people to say whether
they shall do so or not. The men where I work are very fair. If anyone is away ill the
others try to pull his work in. Our lasters in their own interests thought it better to have
a limited amount, and agreed to do so. One man, however, still went the pace, although
at that time we agreed to fix the amount at 11d. per hour. The Branch meeting fined
this man f1 and when the man wanted sick pay, Mr. Poulton had to tell the branch that he

FELLOW MEMBERS,
MONTHLY REPORT.
25TH JUNE, 1923.
THE STATE OF TRADE
continues about the same as last month. The figures given by the Ministry
of Labour in the Gazette are as follow:-
BOOT AND SHOE TRADE.
There was a temporary slight improvement in the state of employment at most
centres of the boot and shoe trade in the middle of May owing to pressure of orders for
Whitsuntide; but this was not maintained, except to a small extent at some centres,
and employment at the end of the month was slack on the whole, with short time working
still very prevalent. The Whitsuntide holidays were extended at many centres.
Employment at Leicester continued fair, only a small amount of short time being
worked. There was a further slight improvement at Northampton, but short time was
still worked and about half the factories closed for a whole week at Whitsuntide. At
Wellingborough employment was still bad. Apart from a temporary improvement
before the holidays, employment at Kettering continued poor; there was much unemploy-
ment, and those who remained in employment were working only about three-quarter
time, on the average. Employment at Stafford continued fair, full time being worked.
There was no marked change at Norwich. In the Bristol and Kingswood district employ-
ment remained poor, though there was a temporary improvement before the Whitsuntide
holidays in the light footwear trade. At Leeds employment continued very quiet in the
heavy boot trade; in the light footwear trade it was fair. Employment in the slipper
trade in the Rossendale Valley continued fair.
In Scotland employment was bad at all the principal centres.
and repairing trades, as indicated by the unemployment books lodged at Employment
The percentage of workpeople unemployed in the boot, shoe, and slipper making
Exchanges, was 7.9 on the 21st May, as compared with 8.5 on the 23rd April.

DISPUTES.
A strike occurred at the factory of Messrs. R. E. Tricker & Co.,
Northampton, on the 19th inst., some 43 operatives being affected. The
dispute arose upon questions affecting wages and piecework statements. The
firm refused to negotiate with the local officials. As a result the operatives
ceased work upon instructions of the local officers. The following day the
head of the firm, Mr. E. Barltrop, called at the Central Office, and had a long
interview with the General Secretary, who made suggestions with a view to
an early settlement by the local officers. As a result of the efforts of the
General Secretary, the local branch officers met the principals of the firm, and
conceded a 4s. weekly increase to male operatives, and 2s. to 6s. to the women
operatives, over and above the minimum rate of wages. In addition quantity
statements are to be prepared; these to come into operation during the early
part of August.

**349**

**POLITICAL MATTERS.**

The position still remains, as we stated last month, in a very unsatisfactory
state. The Government, in its method of dealing with national and inter-
national affairs, would seem to be constantly in a very timid frame of mind.
We do not pretend to agree with the Russian method of government so far as
any attempt to apply it to this country is concerned, that being the business of
the Russian people. That is no reason why we should not try to come to some
agreement so that trade can begin to move without hindrance between the two
countries, and points of differences between England and Russia could surely
be settled at this time of day by having a conference of representatives of the
two Governments.

Then there is the matter of the Deportees and Ireland. The members
who have followed this question, and we hope all of them have, will have
noticed the attempts of the Government to widen the scope of their Bill which
would have had the effect of narrowing, if anything, the liberties of the freedom
of the subject, and giving greater power to the Officials. Thanks, however, to
the strenuous fight put up by the Opposition, especially the Labour Party,
very considerable improvements were made in the Bill during its passage through
the House of Commons.

We regret we cannot report any progress in connection with the Housing
question, or the further fulfilment of the Government's obligation regarding
international affairs.

At the risk of being told we are constantly harping upon these things,
we again repeat the necessity for a strong and ever-growing opposition in the
House of Commons to fight the Government's policy. This can most effectively
be brought about by constant interest in matters political and creating a healthy
atmosphere in all parts of the country, so that whenever the opportunity pre-
sents itself we may increase the number of those who are determined to bring
about so far as it lies within their power, such a reorganisation of society as
will give opportunity to the people as a whole to be free from cares, anxieties
and worries which the present system inflicts upon multitudes day by day.

We would particularly call attention to the constant attempts being
made to undermine the method by which funds are raised for political matters.
This is done, we know, under the guise of the great concern that certain indi-
viduals have for the welfare and liberty of the members of a union. We trust
no members will be misled by this camouflage, especially having regard to the
small amount of contribution paid by the members to the political fund. There
are also regulations for those members conscientiously opposed to this payment
for them to contract out, and we have never put any pressure upon a member
who so desires to contract out.

These attempts at trying to restrict the workers in their corporate capacity
from political work, which in reality is behind the whole business, is such as
calls for our whole-hearted opposition, and we feel confident the members will

ATTEMPTS TO PAY LESS THAN THE MINIMUM RATES.
By reference to page 250 of the April report it will be seen the peculiar
to pay the minimum rates of pay agreed to between the Manufacturers' Federa-
views that are held by certain people in KINGSWOOD as to their obligations
tion and the Union on the one hand, and the prices fixed by the Boards of
Arbitration for the district on the other. The dangerous policy that was
pursued in this case of subsidising a man's wages from the local rates, and thus
enable the employer to escape his responsibilities, will be seen by all.
We have had our attention called to another case from IPSWICH, where
a boot operative drowned himself in consequence of certain work being offered
to him below the proper rate, which he refused, presumably because of the
offer made to him, and for the time being, the local Employment Exchange
withheld his State benefit. At the inquest the son of the deceased said his
father's money had been stopped by the local Exchange because he had refused
a job of making canvas shoes at the rate of 2s. 6d. per dozen. A juryman,
who had knowledge of the trade, told the Coroner that a good workman could
earn 7s. 6d. daily at the work offered to the deceased, whilst the representative
from the Employment Exchange intimated that the deceased was interviewed
in respect of a vacancy for a boot laster, but did not think he could do the
particular work offered. The suspension of his benefit was only temporary,
and due to a discrepancy in the statements filed at the local Exchange.
It should be noted that this person was not a member of the Union, but
the case proved once more the necessity for belonging to a Union, and thereby
be enabled to have these matters attended to by the local officials. We felt
that the matter was such as to ask our Mr. W. Hindes, J.P., to make enquiries
into the whole affair, and we trust good results will follow.

GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
UNION'S CONFERENCE.-The most interesting event during the month has been
the Whitsuntide Conference, where the delegates took very seriously into consideration
the untold suffering that falls upon the more unfortunate members of our Union, through
no fault of their own, nor yet their employer, the members often having to "stand off"
through lack of employment. The Union's attitude has been all along to endeavour, to
the best of their ability, to save the distress amongst its members, and for this purpose
granted, after placing the facts before the members, some very large sums of money.
They have now come to the conclusion that with our method of settling disputes without
resorting, only in very extreme cases, to the weapon of strike, that the accumulated funds
could be better utilised by stretching the benevolent side of our Union to such an extent
that we may be more generous with the Unemployment Benefit than has hitherto been the
case. Although this new regulation cannot become operative until September, we feel
that we may be more generous with the Unemployment Benefit than has hitherto been the
sure the members will appreciate the wisdom prevailing whereby members without income
case. Although this new regulation cannot become operative until September, we feel
members will not feel that we are asking too much if we ask for an additional contribution
for this particular purpose. One is convinced that it would be a very good thing had we
work, and if at the end of two years we find that we are spending too fast, perhaps the
at the end of two or three years we might be in a position to make more definite and more
got a larger and more permanent scheme than the one already in existence. Perhaps
drastic proposals: for the time being we must await the turn of events.
Personally, I am very sorry to see the Conference decided to withdraw from the
General Federation of Trade Unions, although that organisation appears to be likely to
join up with the Trades Union Congress. Personally, I hope the time is not far distant
when there will be one organisation for all workers.
The Conference also came to the conclusion that Annual Conferences were not as good
as Biennial ones held in previous years. They have therefore changed to the old position
which worked so well. It might be interesting just to mention that next year the Conference
will be held at Stafford, where we hope to celebrate the jubilee of the Union's existence
of 50 years. It is too early yet for any of us to say what form this will take, but we think
it will be made a very memorable occasion.
Speaking of the Conference generally, discussions were very good, debates ran rather
high, and voting on some matters very close. Everything considered, a very good Con-
ference indeed.
BACK TO THE UNIONS CAMPAIGN. In addition to the above we have spent a whole
week in Leicester and Leicestershire, where a Trade Union Week has been held on the
suggestion of the General Council of the Trades Union Congress. Dinner-hour meetings,
evening meetings, or open-air meetings were addressed by numerous speakers, including
myself and our Mr. McCarthy. At the end of the week the officials of the Leicester Branch,
with Mr. McCarthy and myself, held Sunday morning meetings at Anstey, Rothley and
Mountsorrel, all well attended, and in the evening a demonstration-one of the best ever
held in the City of Leicester-took place in the Market Place, in which we played a part.
We are fully persuaded that good will result, as Trade Unionism has had a fillip by the
work put in.
MANSFIELD, DERBY AND NOTTINGHAM BOARD OF ARBITRATION has again taken up
our time, and we have held several meetings of employers and operatives in obtaining
information for the drafting of Statements for this part of the district. There is a variety
of work, Children's, Women's, Canvas and Fabric, all of which have to be provided for.
We are meeting the employers again this week with one or two of the several sub-committees,
for the purpose of considering the type of statement which will be most applicable for this
work. Whilst in some districts employers are endeavouring to introduce Day Labour,
yet in other districts employers are doing their utmost to adopt Payment by Results,
but as the employer has the choice of working either daywork or piece, we maintain our
right to advise all operatives whether on one system or the other, to work strictly to state-
ment, and we fully believe this will be carried out. We have been invited to meet some
employers who feel that competition in other parts of the country are pressing upon them
to such an extent that they claim that they cannot get into the market. We have pointed
work, they are likely to be much more successful than those firms who make a variety of
goods. We are of the opinion that specialisation seems to be more and more the order of
the day, and it is only by acute organisation that employers in the future will be able to
maintain the position that they have held in the past.

UNIONS AND POLITICS.
"Is the trade union movement superior or subordinate to party politics?" asks
M. Edwards, 90, St. Paul's Road, Kennington, referring to the discussion at last week's
conference of the Boot and Shoe Operatives on the subject of affiliation to the Federation
of Trades Unions.
"The G.F.T.U.," he adds, " is the Help One Another' society in industrial welfare.
Its active operations must be less spectacular than political controversies and elections,
but is it not the best conception of trade-union brotherhood to which membership can be
had irrespective of political opinion?"-Daily Herald, 5th June, 1923.

in the report of the Comptroller and Auditor-General on the accounts of the Fund for
A big increase both in Unemployment Fund contributions and benefits are reported

Contributions Trebled.
Contributions during 1921-22 showed an increase on the previous year from £13,483,118
1,42,431,769, and payments of benefit from £34,126,201 to 153,060,622.
This increase was due mainly to the further extension of unemployment insurance
under the Acts of 1921 and 1922.
Over 15 Millions Deficiency.
The report states that after the realisation of the investments remaining with the
National Debt Commissioners at the close of the 1920-21 account, it became necessary
to obtain from the Treasury advances out of the Consolidated Fund for the purpose of
discharging the liabilities of the Unemployment Fund. At the close of 1921-22 the total
deficiency on the fund was 15,386,188 15. 7d.

ORGANISERS' MONTHLY REPORTS.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
After our Conference I went to Leicester with the General President, Mr. Richards.
to take
perature, and it was surprising how people stood for hours listening to the speakers. There
were no indoor meetings. On our platforms we had Engineers, Bakers, Brass Workers,
Hosiery, General Workers and Shoe Workers represented. There was an eagerness on
the part of all to put in as much effort as possible that week for our common cause.
I went to
just outside. The Council member and local Secretary, Mr. Alex. Smith, and I, seemed
the girls when apparently
Inside set in motion to counteract our efforts. For the time being this
counter move has checked our work. We have placed the details before the local Board
of Arbitration for the matter to be judged on rules governing both sides.
I spent a few days at Manchester and helped the local Secretary in organising a shop
where things were getting loose owing to the want of a collector. At another firm where
some new work was introduced the women could not earn the proper wages. We got a
promise that the Manager would go into the prices with the operatives concerned, and try
to adjust them. This firm is well organised and the representatives of the Union are always
well received by the management.
I spent two days at Stafford. The males are highly organised here, and we are
hopeful of getting the females up to the same standard. When visiting a shop here with
Mr. Dunn, I was pleased to hear the head of the firm say that he would not think of sus-
pending or discharging a Shop President because of his position as such. He looked
bound up in the whole procedure governing the Federation and the Union. Much un-
upon the Shop Presidents as a necessary part of the machinery of our Union and as generally
pleasantness would be avoided if all manufacturers in the industry took this statesman-
like view of things.
23rd June, 1923.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
D. MCCARTHY.
The past month has been divided with the Union Conference, Kingswood, and a visit
to Frankfort to attend a meeting of the E.C. of the International Shoe and Leather Workers.
The Conferences of the Union that have been held in London, have been rather
unfortunate in regard to the places in which we have met. The one this year, at least so
far as the morning sessions were concerned, being the worst of all. It will be worth while
getting away from London, if only to have a decent hall in which to meet.
The impression left on one's mind is that on the whole the Conference was an improve-
ment on the two previous ones.

met with some keen criticism, and perhaps rightly so, as it contained a new principle in

who would argue that experience has not justified the step taken. If only there could be

The position at Kingswood does not show great improvement. Trade picks up very

workers who need heavy footwear, is having its effect on Kingswood boot operatives.
It demonstrates the folly, when a nation has nothing left but its home market, of curtailing

**355**

employer wanted to withhold that which was due to his workpeople. It was the last
straw, so to speak, and they told him they were stopping work. He tried a little bluff,
but when he saw he was up against it, to use his own words, he meekly submitted. More
of this spirit by the workers would help enormously. The absence of it gives to the un-
scrupulous employer the encouragement to further infringe upon the rights of his work-
people, and one success leads him to further effort. There is nothing in our National
Agreement or local statements that the operatives can afford to give up. The situation
for the time being may be difficult, but a little courage now will save a deal of trouble
later on.

Let the officials help, and when they have taken up a grievance see that they have the
backing of those for whom they are acting. There is nothing worse in Trade Union
activity for an officer, local or national, to be let down by the members. In the meantime,
so far as Kingswood is concerned, our policy is to go steadily forward.

The visit to Frankfort was in many ways interesting. It is evident that the workers
generally place great value on the eight-hour day or 48-hour working week, and it was
with pleasure one learned that its application is general on the Continent; in Germany the
hours are 47, and that in several countries it has been given the force of law. It is also
of interest that in Germany the legal enforcement of agreements, which we are seeking,
is in operation. Instead of being a pious opinion at the end of an agreement, it is an
established fact.

There were many evidences as to the effect on the working class in Germany of the
Ruhr occupation. When I was in Munich last year the reports from Austria and Germany
showed almost a complete absence of unemployment. Now, some factories are closed and
the remainder almost entirely on short time. It was stated that over 90 per cent. of the
boot operatives of Germany were either out of work or on short time. With industry
depressed like that, how absurd it is to speak of getting reparations.

Further results of the occupation are shown in the rapid falling of the Mark, and when
it is understood that the price of bread and other foodstuffs follow the Mark, the position
of the workers can readily be understood. A wages agreement loses its value before a
week has passed, in fact a day may be sufficient, so much does the situation change.

When will Europe return to sanity? The question that one is continually being asked
is, “When is trade going to improve?” To which I have always replied, "Not until
Europe becomes settled, and most people agree." And yet so far as Government policy
is concerned, how slowly we move in that direction.

It is pleasing to know that organised labour in practically every country is against
this imperialistic militarist policy that holds Europe in its grip; and it is encouraging
when one finds a resolution condemning the occupation of the Ruhr drafted and moved by
a French comrade, which was the case at Frankfort. Once again it may well be that it
is from the working-class movement a solution of the problem will come.

During the visit one had the opportunity of looking over a boot factory and also of
addressing a meeting of shoe operatives. I will endeavour to write about those experiences
next month.

18th June, 1923.
WALTER R. SMITH.

ARBROATH. We end the month with trade as bad as ever, and at the
time this is written, with an intimation of a further cut on the wages. That
puts the lid on with a bang, and the majority of our members will now receive,
after all the deductions, less than £1 per week short-time wages. Truly a
"It never rains but it pours " is an old
axiom, and we are feeling uncomfortable about its truth. We have frequently
noted the fact that one of our group of factories is on full time, and at the
moment it appears we may be in trouble with the management of this firm.
In common with other factories in Scotland, after Basic Statements were
compiled, the finishers and clickers of this place fixed up prices, mutually
agreed upon, and have been working to them for nearly three years. Instead
of posting notice of the " cut " in wages this firm adopted the idea of telling
the pieceworkers they would have to go back to set-wages, but that the best
workers would get 25 per cent. over the minimum rates. Naturally the
members are resenting this departure as they apparently are not to be allowed
any voice in the arrangement, other than being given the privilege of sending
a deputation to hear the decision of the firm. Nor do they feel the complaints
made by the firm about the unsatisfactory results of piecework to be well
founded seeing it has taken such a long time for this to be discovered. A
plentiful supply of orders and a retrospect of twenty months' full time, hardly
support the assertion that the clicking and finishing have been suffering in
quality as the outcome of piecework. But then Scotland produces a distinct
type of employer who usually makes rules or processes, even of logic, obey his
desire rather than their own course. Another factor which weighs with the
operatives is the partial and practical compulsion which made them yield to
the demand for payment by results. On the East Coast of Scotland the men
were unanimously against it, but events in which the employers forced the
pace overcame that opposition. "To be driven out of" what they had to be
"driven into," as one member put it, is just what human nature does not like.
However, we are doing everything possible to prevent a rupture, and our
Carnoustie shopmates may reach a settlement without serious difficulties.
Our branch was fortunate in getting an early report of the Annual Conference
from the Secretary, who was one of the delegates. The Council did well in
putting forward their proposal re Suspension Benefit, but we wish they had a
bigger contribution to work on, so that the waiting period could be eliminated.
All our suspensions are within the limits of the waiting period, and so we can
never expect to get the benefit, even although our suspensions, though short,
come so frequently as to make us lose more time perhaps than those who may
get it. In closing we give our thanks to Conference for their decision re District
Advisory Councils, as we are convinced the Scotland District will derive great
benefit from the activities of this method of uniting and co-ordinating the
work, the thoughts, the aspirations and ideals of the sons of St. Crispin.
BELFAST.-Trade still continues to remain very bad, both in the manu-
facturing and repairing. Again we would remind members that Union benefits
can only be paid in strict accordance with the rules.

Government. Also we secured 58s. minimum for males and 36s. for females.
EDINBURGH.-Pleased to report the repairing trade fairly busy this
month. We, along with other unions. have been busy during our "Back to the

LEGAL CASES AFFECTING LABOUR.
Workmen's Compensation.
AWARD FOR TOTAL INCAPACITY-WORKMAN UNABLE TO STAND FOR MORE THAN TWO
HOURS CAPACITY TO DO LIGHT WORK.
The appellant in this case was a painter who fell from a ladder and suffered a fracture
of the left ankle in February, 1920, as the result of which three operations became necessary.
He remained in hospital until the middle of 1922, when an agreement was entered into to
pay him ₤1 155. a week. He received this weekly payment until October, 1922, when the
respondents made an application to the County Court Judge to review this amount. An
award was made by the Judge of f1 a week for partial incapacity, finding that the only
incapacity at that time was the workman's inability to stand on a ladder, and that he
tras capable of doing any form of light work. The appellant appealed from this decision
on the ground that he was totally incapacitated and that there was no evidence that be
could do any fohat heigas totally incapacitance was that the appellant was incapablert
Working for more than two hours while standing. Held, that on the evidence the Court
of Appeal could not say that the County Court Judge was bound in law to say that the
appellant was totally incapacitated. The appeal was therefore dismissed.-(Court of
Appeal. Fowler v. Minter.) -Labour Gazette, June, 1923.

Successful War on Microbes.

"It will be understood that as a general rule when bacteria are inoculated under the
skin of a rabbit, for instance, this animal will develop in itself a power to destroy them,
"The immunity may be produced by the inoculation of dead bacteria, as well as of
living bacteria, and in man the former method is always used, owing to the danger of
producing serious illness with living bacteria.
Destroying of Bacteria.
or to a diseased person to cure it.
"This method of immunising may be applied to a healthy person to prevent disease,
"The smart manner in which immunised persons are enabled to destroy bacteria is
not known. In some cases the microbes are dissolved, and disappear from the blood.
while in others they are eaten up, and destroyed by phagocytic cells in the blood.
Harmless Process.
constitutes the well-known 'opsonic' theory.
"This latest method of defence has been familiarised by Sir Almroth Wright, and
"Its application takes the form of inoculating into an infected patient a dose of the
infecting microbe previously killed.
"This killing process makes the method harmless, and it is the process used by the
Inoculation Department for the last eighteen years with a variable degree of success.
Coating of Fat.
"To be successful, the microbes have to be digestible by the tissue of the patient.
In 1921 Captain Douglas showed that the indigestibility of some microbes was due to a
coating of fat which surrounded them.
"Unfortunately he found that with most bacteria the coat of fat was stuck so hard,
that he could not dissolve it off. and so he was not able to apply his new idea to the treat-
ment.
Dr. Dreyer's Work.
bacillus.
"At this point Professor Dreyer came upon the scene, and began work on the tubercle
"He took a culture, pickled it with formalin, and found he could defat the bacillus
and make it digestible.
"He tried this defatted bacilli upon the treatment of disease in animals, and used four
guinea-pigs for the purpose. Three he treated, and one he left alone. All were diseased.
"The three gradually improved to normal, but the fourth got gradually worse. One
of the three was killed, and it was found that all the tuberculosis inside it had disappeared.
Test on a Man.

weeks of his treatment the benefit from the tubercle inoculations was greater than from
other forms of treatment.

will become normal in temperature, put on weight, and improve in health, and finally
become arrested and cured as a result of the treatment." - Pall Mall Gazette, 15th June,

Confusion on the Rent Law.
Mr. Neville Chamberlain's new Rent Bill-the text of which was issued vyesterday-
contains the following as its main proposals :----
Rent restriction is to continue in force until 24th June, 1925.
restriction then ceases to apply, and the landlord can fix the rent at whatever figure he
There are two exceptions to this. If before that date a house becomes vacant the
may choose.
The second exception is that if a landlord grants a lease or makes an agreement for
a fix the rent without
Acts will no longer apply to that case. If the Bill passes, long-term agreements the
suddenly boom!
Nor is restriction to apply to licensed premises.
A clause has been inserted making it illegal for landlords to sell furniture to a tenant
at more than the value of the furniture, and no one will regret that that form of trickery
is scotched.
The provisions dealing with repairs and sub-letting are also important.
The sanitary authority's certificate that the house is not in a reasonable condition
will be a good defence to a claim by the landlord for rent or proceedings for eviction.
Where, on the contrary side, a house is sublet at a profit rental, an amount not exceed.
ing to per cent. of the net rental may be charged by the landlord.
New Reign of Terror-How Bill Provides Opportunities for Speculators.
"The general principle of the measure is very bad," said Mr. Dan Rider, secretary
of the War Rents League, interviewed last night. "It does not preserve control for two
years."
By decontrolling every house that became empty after the Bill was passed owners
and speculators were encouraged more than ever to obtain possession of such houses,
because they could charge any rents and premiums and throw any burdens upon the
tenants.
"The Bill will open up a reign of terror," he said.
Agents would be able to exercise their well-known coercive powers of persuasion to
get tenants to contract out of the benefit of the Act. So that in two years time there
would be very few houses under the Act.
The whole trend of the Bill was to enable landlords to force their tenants to buy
their worn-out houses at inflated prices.
As to the provision that any new buyer of a house could claim possession, not only
for himself, but for his children, and even his employees, or those who were going to be
his employees, that meant that no one but a relative or a workman of the owner's would
have a chance of any home under the Bill.

LABOUR WOMEN'S CONFERENCE AT YORK.

DELEGATE'S REPORT.
The Annual Conference of Labour Women was held at the Festival Concert Rooms,
York, on 8th and 9th May, 1923, Mrs. Harrison Bell being in the chair. There were five
hundred delegates present, a large increase upon the previous years.
The Lord Mayor of York gave us all a very hearty welcome, and said he felt it an
honour to do so. No doubt there was a great many differences of opinion there, and
although he did not agree on all their points, a great lot of good often arose from these
different opinions, because the power of the women was very important and they should
use their influence for the good of the country. Mr. Hartley, Chairman of the York Labour
Party, and Mrs. Mackereth, President of the Women's Section, also gave a hearty welcome
to all.
Mrs. Harrison Bell suitably replied and thanked them on behalf of the delegates.
She also stated in her address that there was two thousand more members who had joined
us since last year.
An emergency resolution was sent to the C.W.S. in regard to their workers, that they
should submit all their questions to the Joint Committee of Trade Unions and Co-operators
for arbitration. The question of Married Teachers proved very interesting discussion,
opinions being well divided; also the giving of the vote to women at 21 years of age.
It was impressed upon all delegates to urge all the Labour Members in the House to strongly
support any resolutions in favour of the vote as it would prove a great interest and support
to the Labour Party of this country. That there should be a Women's Labour Day as
well as a May Day. That Municipal Elections should be held in May instead of November,
and that voting should take place on Saturdays. There was a good discussion on the
Agricultural question. and many points were brought forward which were very interesting
and of an educational character. The debate on Irish Deportation brought forward
statements of how the deportees were treated. Then International Peace. There would
be no question of Peace while the country was ruled by the economic war makers. That
the Labour Party try to abolish the two-shift system amongst girls, as being detrimental
to their health. That until the unemployed can find a suitable job the Labour Members
should fight for full maintenance for the same. That Continuation Classes should be
formed for the younger people to prevent so much juvenile unemployment amongst those
who have left school. That there should be Trade Boards for Domestic Servants and not
district wages. That the trade unions organise their women to safeguard them, as that
is the only barrier between the worker and employer. There was a good discussion on
the Housing question. It was stated that it was a most shameful fact that large houses
were only occupied for three months of the year, and allowed to stand empty for the rest
part of the year, while the poorer class were housed together in the condition that they
are to-day. The question that there should be more women serving on the benches of
our children's courts, and more women police caused a deal of discussion, and that Capital
Punishment should be abolished.
The report of the year's work was taken paragraph by paragraph. Proposals 9, 10,
and 11 were left for Standing Orders Committee to deal with. The Conference finished
at six o'clock Wednesday evening, Mrs. Harrison Bell thanking all delegates for their
attendance. The York Section presented Dr. Marion Phillips and Mrs. Harrison Bell
with a large bouquet of flowers.
ANNIE BILLINGTON,
Wellingborough.

NEW BUILDING FOR WORLD LABOUR OFFICE.
Plan Judging by International Jury.
About 70 plans have been received in the competition among Swiss architects for
plans for the new building to be erected at Geneva as a permanent home for the Inter-
national Labour Office of the League of Nations, and these are being judged during this
week by an international jury of architects.
The decision to build an office was taken at the Assembly of the League of Nations
last year when many strong comments were made by members of a committee of inquiry
on the unsuitability of the present accommodation-a building outside the town of Geneva
which was originally a school and not easily or completely adaptable to the work of the
Office. Such a decision, however, was rendered more easy to take by the generous offer
of the Swiss Federal Council to present a site for this purpose, situated a short distance
from the office of the League with a frontage on the edge of the lake.
Mr. E. P. Warren, F.S.A., F.R.I.B.A., is serving on the jury of architects, the other
members being M. Maurice Brincourt (France), M. Piacentini (Italy), and M. A. Guyonnet
(Switzerland). Their work of selection began at Geneva on Monday, 28th May, and they
hope to make known the result of their deliberations in about a week.

The lack of uniformity in the labour regulations of the various States, and particularly
those relating to child labour, led as early as 1906 to attempts to control child labour by
Federal legislation. In 1916 and 1919 Federal Acts were passed which attempted to secure
this control, but in both cases they were declared unconstitutional by the Supreme Court.

The question is therefore being discussed in the United States of passing an amendment
to the Constitution which would give immediate and direct power to Congress to legislate
on the subject of the protection of child labour.

WOODEN HOUSES.
Would it Pay to Build them in England?
Interest in the question whether wooden houses should be erected to overcome the
present shortage of working-class dwellings in the city continues. The Mail has gathered
two other representative opinions, and they will be read with interest.
Councillor H. C. Snow, in an interview, said: "To your question, Why not build
wooden houses in this country? I will put another: 'Why build wooden houses in this
country?'
"Your question seems to be re-opened owing to the visit of certain Canadian gentle-
men to Leicester. Now, I have lived in Canada for several years in and amongst wooden
houses, and my reply is: 'Why build houses of wood-which is not a local material in this
country-when our local material is of a better and more substantial character?'
Wooden houses are not built in new countries necessarily from choice, but because
wood is the cheapest, and because it is sometimes the only local material available. In
urban districts, where these wooden houses are put up in quantities, there are generally
no proper roads, no proper sanitation, or other services, and the conditions of the people
in those areas become appalling.
"Now, when I went to Winnipeg in 1889 nearly all the houses and buildings, and even
the hotels, were constructed of wood. There was no drainage to the houses, no street
drainage; middens were in the backyards, and the principal products were diphtheria and
typhoid fever.
Not a Paying Proposition.
"Coming home to our own conditions, our first needs when laying out a building
estate for numerous people to live on are proper roads and access, proper drainage, water
supply, and other public services which should be brought into the homes of the people.
"When you have got these main factors of civilisation, which are the primary cost
of the development of the estate, it would not pay either individuals or Corporations to
attach them to wooden shanties of a temporary character, because the whole question
of producing houses for the working classes is based upon the principle of cheap finance.
This character of building is no asset, no security as an erection, and cannot be financed
on sound lines either privately by long mortgages or publicly by proper loans.
"Furthermore, it is well-known that in new countries where these buildings are
temporarily erected, they generally become infested by vermin, and it is impossible to get
rid of the vermin without destroying the buildings.
"So that for a country like our own, where the prevailing building material is of a
substantial character (brick or stone), having gone to the expense of the necessary pre-
liminary services and development, it is a sounder and better-paying proposition to proceed
on substantial lines and build not for a few years but for generations.
"I will say nothing about the risks of fire. They are apparent to all, and the frequent
disasters which one reads of as occurring in Western towns, they being burnt out, are mainly
owing to the inflammable character of the wooden buildings.'"
Mr. W. Keay's Views.
Mr. William Keay, president of the Leicester and Leicestershire Society of Architects,
invited to give his opinion as to the advisability or otherwise of building wooden houses
in Leicester to meet the shortage of dwellings, in an interview with a representative of the
Leicester Mail, said: "I agree with Councillor H. W. Hallam absolutely. There is nothing
from an economic or hygienic point of view better than a brick wall. Wooden houses
are not to be compared with brick.
"Here in Leicestershire you have a clay that makes excellent bricks and you can put
up a brick building almost as quickly as a wooden one.
"I should not recommend the building of wooden houses for one moment." -Leicester
Mail, 2nd June, 1923.
A man sent his Irish servant with a present of a live hare to a friend. The hare
managed to escape, but the servant made no effort to catch it; all he did was stand and
gaze after it with a satisfied grin on his face. "You may run, and run, and run, you
blubbering beast," he shouted, "but it's no use, for you haven't got the address." -Shoe
Workers' Journal, June, 1923.

INTERNATIONAL FEDERATION OF TRADE UNIONS.
International Trade Secretariats.
FOOD AND DRINK INDUSTRY.-At a meeting of the Executive of the International
Union of Federations of Workers in the Food and Drink Trades, held at Basel, on 22nd
and 23rd April, it was resolved that the decisions of the Union Executive must, if in accord
with Congress resolutions, be binding upon the affiliated organisations. It was also
decided to submit to the next Congress of the International Trade Unions proposals for
the declaration and practical realisation of international boycotts. Another resolution
embodied a refusal to admit to affiliation unions who are already affiliated with Moscow,
although working alliances may be concluded with such unions.
TRANSPORT WORKERS. - The International Transport Workers' Federation numbered
on 1st January, 1923, 2,217,972 members, 80,000 of whom are women. The respective
numbers of the different sections are :- Railwaymen, 1,225,000; seamen, 50,000, and other
workers, 942,972.
National Federations.
DENMARK.- The Danish Federation of Trade Unions numbered on 31st March,
They belong to 52 different unions.
232,574 members, of whom 38,056 are women. During the past year the membership has declined by 72,796.
FINLAND. - The Finnish Federation of Trade Unions numbered on 1st January,
48,176 members, of whom 8,714 are women. During the preceding year the membership
decreased by 413. The average wage of the male worker in Finland has risen from 5.63
to 5.94 Finnish marks, and that of the female worker from 3.15 to 3.19 marks. The
Trade Union Congress is now being held.
General.
HOTEL AND RESTAURANT WORKERS. - The Executive of the German Union proposes
to convene an international congress next Autumn of the International Union of Hotel,
Restaurant and Bar Employees.
POTTERY WORKERS. - The International Federation of Pottery Workers will hold an
international conference in Berlin on 4th June. This will be the first since the outbreak
of war.
DOMESTIC EMPLOYEES. - Two Austrian unions of domestic employees decided in
March last to amalgamate under the title of "Union of Persons Employed in Domestic
Work, and of all Cleaners and Domestic Workers."
Italy.
THE CAUSES OF THE ITALIAN TRADE UNION DEBACLE. - An honest critic, writing of
the disasters of the Italian Trade Union Movement, attributes them to the lack of courage
of the leaders, who allowed themselves to be led instead of leading, and to their failure to
keep in touch with the rank and file of the movement. He points out that trade unionists
have accustomed themselves to take much and give little; they need to build up a "trade
union conscience." Great numbers flocked to the trade unions after the war: the member-
ship of the General Confederation of Labour rose from 350,000 to two millions; but
there was a shortage of experienced leaders, and those improvised to meet the pressing
need of the moment have in many cases proved inadequate. Many of these have now
abandoned the movement and those that remain must now seek to educate themselves.
FASCIST TRADE UNIONS AMONG ITALIAN EMIGRANTS. - The Fascist Corporations
are initiating a campaign for the formation of Fascist trade unions among Italian workers
who have emigrated to foreign countries. Suckert, the director of this propaganda,
urges that Fascist trade union nuclei must be created, with bourgeois secretaries, to protect
the interests of the workers, see that their wages are not below those current in the country
of immigration, encourage further immigration, prove that fascism is not anti-proletarian,
and facilitate the political action of Italian Fascists in foreign countries.
HUNGARY. -The Hungarian Government has introduced a very reactionary Bill
regulating trade unions and strikes. Even passive resistance is regarded as an aggression
on the freedom of labour. In many branches of industry, such as the railways and shipping,
the water, gas and electricity supplies, and hospitals, strikes are prohibited absolutely:
in others, compulsory arbitration must precede a strike. Trade Unions may only deal
with purely economic matters; and they may not publish any journals, nor give lectures
on any but purely technical subjects. No contributions may be levied beyond those
prescribed in the rules, and all accounts must be annually submitted to official inspection.
Lists of members of the executives, and, if desired, of all members must similarly be sub-
mitted. In case of any breach of the law, the trade union may be suspended; and respons-
ible leaders are liable to heavy punishment.

International Trade Secretariats.

INTERNATIONAL UNION OF FEDERATIONS OF WORKERS IN THE FOOD AND DRINK
TRADES. On 26th March the Executive of the American Bakers' and Confectioners'
Union decided to affiliate with the above international. The American Union has a
membership of 35,000, and is in favour of the legal prohibition of night-work and Sunday
work in bakeries and confectionery factories.
INTERNATIONAL CONGRESS OF BUILDING GUILDS. The Third International Congress
of Building Guilds met at Hamburg on 28th May. Representatives were present from
Germany, Palestine, Spain, Holland, Sweden, Czecho-Slovakia, Austria, and Hungary;
Italy, France and England being prevented from sending delegates. The reports showed
that German guilds are well organised, and have not yet suffered from the economic
depression which has hit especially hard those of Holland, England, Czecho-Slovakia,
and, since its currency recovery, Austria. Italy's once flourishing guilds are almost
impotent, and some have removed to France. Hungary has been unable to begin practical
work. As for Spain, although she was represented at the Congress, nothing has as yet
been done in that country; at a National Building Conference, which has just been held,
it was, however, proposed that building guilds should be founded, and that they should
be financed from a fund drawn from banking sources. The International Congress resolved
to interchange information of experience, establish economic inter-relations and set up
an international credit depot.
National Federations.
THE CZECHO-SLOVAKIAN FEDERATION OF TRADE UNIONS.-The annual report of the
Federation for the year 1922 shows that it suffered much from economic conflicts and
communist rivalry. At the beginning of the year, it comprised 55 unions, with a total
membership of 650,000; at the end it had only 49 unions, with 400,000 members. Seven
new unions affiliated with it during the course of the year and eight seceded. Owing to
heavy disbursements to the unemployed, the balance sheet of the federation shows a deficit
of 800,000 kronen.
FINLAND. The Congress of the Finnish Federation of Trade Unions which took
place at the end of May was attended by 77 delegates, of whom 47 were Communists and
20 Social Democrats. The report showed that wages have been raised to the level of the
index.
GERMAN TRADE UNIONS AFFILIATED WITH THE I.F.T.U. At the end of March, 1923,
the membership of the German trade unions affiliated with Amsterdam was 7,863,961,
of whom 1,646,338 were women. At the end of June, 1922, it totalled 8,150,862. The
largest of the constituent unions are (1) the Metal Workers, numbering 1,585,276 at the
end of March; (2) the Factory Workers; (3) the Textile Workers, numbering at the same
date, 719,743 and 713,321 members respectively.
THE GERMAN WOOD WORKERS' UNION.-This Union holds its Annual Congress at
Cassel in the middle of June.
THE GERMAN FIREMEN'S UNION is convening for 6th July a meeting of its district
representatives to discuss reorganisation, and to consider what measures can be taken
to prevent the threatened lengthening of the working day.
SWITZERLAND. The Swiss Federation of Salaried Employees' Unions, which has
existed for five years, numbers 50,000 members.
CANADA.- The trade unions of Canada number 276,521 members, of whom 206,150
are "international," or linked up with the trade unions of the U.S.A.
General.
WOMEN'S WORK IN GERMANY SINCE THE WAR. In general, the industrial work of
women in Germany is more extensive than before the war. Women are retaining the
cigar-making which they first took over during the war; and also in some districts, the
tending of the semi-automatic machines used in making small hardware goods. They
also hold their ground in all those branches of industry in which they have always been
dominant, namely, the textile industry, cleaning, laundry work and typing.
INCREASE OF UNEMPLOYMENT IN GERMANY. The official figures for persons in receipt
of unemployment benefit on 1st May, 1923, was 321,638. On October 1st, 1922, the
number was only 21,028.
VARIETY IN WORKING HOURS IN U.S.A. There is in the U.S.A. great variety in the
length of working hours. In most of the steel concerns, two shifts only, of 12 hours each,
are worked. The pottery industry is in a transition stage from the two to the three-shift
system; the chemical industry, with the exception of the sugar refineries, has adopted
the eight-hours' shift, as have also paper mills and rubber works. The public utility
services are also moving towards the eight-hours' day.
INDIA. The first "all-women strike" was announced as having broken out in some
Madras spinning mills at the beginning of May.

MIDDLEMEN MAKE FOOD DEAR.
Striking Report on Garden Produce. Six Stages of Profit and
High Rail Rates.
Before the consumer gets his fruit and vegetables it may have had as many as 16
to 20 different handlings, and have had the attentions of six intermediaries.
Middlemen are essential, but to-day there are too many of them. Railway freight
charges in this particular industry are too high, and the retailer does not adjust prices to
conform with big reductions in the wholesale prices.
This state of affairs in the fruit and vegetable markets is revealed in a second interim
report issued yesterday by Lord Linlithgow's Departmental Committee. The first report
dealt with milk and milk products.
The main points of the report are:—
(1) Unless the fruit and vegetable industry in many districts is to perish the railway
rates cannot be maintained even at 50 per cent. above 1914 rates.
(2) Retailers as a whole are not profiteering, but there are cases of such profits (gross)
as 331 per cent.
(3) The chief complaint against the retailer is that he does not adjust prices to conform
with big reductions in wholesale prices, preferring restricted demand and a large margin
to a large turnover and a small margin.
Growers' Profits Low.
86 per cent.
(4) Growers' percentage of profit in the most favourable circumstances did not exceed
(5) Middlemen are essential. Direct consignment from grower to consumer can never
develop on a large scale.
(6) Covent Garden is wholly inadequate as a central wholesale market.
(7) Producers are urged to consider the possibilities of co-operative marketing, and
the Government is asked to devise credit facilities.
(8) Well-packed and well-graded supplies are the most effective form of advertise-
ment. Marketing is "the other half of production."
Less Jam being made.
(9) The sugar duty should be reduced as soon as the market's condition ensures the
fall to the consumer, so that surplus fruit can be more largely used in jam-making. The
canning of fruit by home manufacturers should be extended.
The Committee recommend: Quicker handling on rail of soft fruits; installation of
Post Office telephones in railway station offices for use of growers; railway companies
should adopt cash-on-delivery system for suitable consignments; fixed local market
porterage charges; licensing of commission salesmen.
They state that street vendors are a safeguard to the consumer, and that owing to
high prices the consumption of jam per head has greatly declined.-Leicester Daily Mercury,
22nd June, 1923.
SUCCESSFUL MUNICIPAL BANKING.
Despite a year of serious depression, Birmingham's municipal bank has had remarkable
success, according to the recent annual report.
After making ample provision for depreciation, the bank has a surplus on the year's
working of £9,692, which has been placed to the reserve fund.
In the twelve months the total sum taken by deposits was £1,950,916, and the deposi-
tors' balances, rising from £746,984 in 1920 to £2,883,942 last year, place the bank amongst
the six largest savings banks in the country.
The amount per depositor in the bank averages £28, and it is stated that there are
many evidences of care being taken in making withdrawals by depositors who have become
unemployed or are working short time.
The report states that the bank is reaching a class of depositor for whom no provision
had previously been made, and it has been found that 99 per cent. of the depositors have
less than £300 standing to their credit.
