THE LABOUR OFFICE.
More Conciliatory Attitude of British Government.
The decisions of the Governing Body of the International Labour Office, which has
been sitting in Geneva for the last two days, have been awaited with some anxiety by the
staff of the International Labour Office and all those interested in its future.
The attitude of the British Government and employers' delegates at the last session
in April and the attacks on the office which have since been made in certain English papers
have caused considerable unrest and apprehension.
It was feared, and everything pointed in that direction, that the criticisms levelled
against the organisation were politically inspired. Many of them could equally well have
been applied to the Secretariat of the League of Nations, but in no case was this done.
The decision of the Governing Body of the International Labour Office to budget
for a figure £4,000 less than that provisionally adopted at the April meeting disposes of
the rumours set on foot from the first sitting that no further economies would be agreed to.
The attitude of the British Government delegate from the beginning was also more
conciliatory. He stated, to everybody's relief, that the Government disclaimed any
responsibility for the recent attacks on the Labour Office in the British Press, although
rumours had reached me in Geneva that the Ministry of Labour had had a share in pro-
voking them. He declared that the Government would continue to support the office.
This declaration should hardly be necessary when one considers Great Britain's
share in the foundation of the League of Nations and its Labour branch.
The results of this session of the Governing Body are more satisfactory, in the opinion
of Mr. Poulton, the British Workers' delegate, than those of the last session. It remains
to be seen, however, if the organisation will be allowed to continue its activities in peace.—
Daily Herald, 19th June, 1923.

18 Months for Man who Earned £20 a Week.
“You are an excellent workman, but in regard to your treatment of women no words

With this comment the Recorder at the Old Bailey to-day passed sentence of 18
months' hard labour on Alfred Frederick Spinks, aged 49, for bigamy.
Mr. J. F. Eastwood, prosecuting, said prisoner lived with his wife for nine years.
Owing to his brutal treatment she left him.
In 1920 he " married" another woman, and two years afterwards deserted her for a
third woman.
Counsel added that Spinks was one of the most expert boot-cutters in England and
earned from £17 to £20 a week. He was the inventor of the block toe, which made his
services in great demand.
A detective said the legal wife stated that two of her children died of semi-starvation
owing to the man's neglect. - The Star, 30th May, 1923.

MONTHLY REPORT.

23RD JULY, 1923.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
TRADE
continues about the same as last month, the details reported in the Ministry of
Labour Gazette being set out hereunder :-

BOOT AND SHOE INDUSTRY.

During June employment remained slack on the whole, with much short time working.
In the industry as a whole there was a slight decline as compared with May.
Employment at Leicester declined, and only a few firms were well employed at the
end of the month. There was no marked change at Northampton, where employment
was quiet. At Wellingborough it continued bad. At Higham and Rushden it was fair;
some short time was worked, but it was not general. Apart from a slight improvement in
the middle of the month, employment at Kettering remained poor. At Stafford it was
again fair, full time being worked. At Norwich there was a decline; there was much
short time and unemployment, and employment was not nearly so good as in June of last
Year. In the Bristol and Kingswood district employment was still quiet, but there was a
marked improvement during the month. Employment at Leeds was bad. In the slipper
trade in the Rossendale Valley employment remained fair.
In Scotland employment was bad at Arbroath, Dundee, and Maybole, but fair at the
other principal centres.
Returns from firms employing 41,807 workpeople in the week ended 23rd June showed
that about 40 per cent. of these workpeople were on short time in that week, to the extent
of 12 hours a week on the average.
The exports of boots and shoes in June, 1923, amounted to 90,425 dozen pairs, or
2,002 dozen pairs more than in May, 1923, and 37,179 dozen pairs more than in June, 1922.

The contention of the Union is that Clause 13 is limited in its operation to Time Rates,
and does not include freedom of contract to fix Piecework Rates for such operatives
different from those authorised by the Local Board of Arbitration.
interpretation which ought properly to be placed on Clause 13, having regard to the other
I have carefully considered the evidence and contentions submitted to me, and the
provisions of the Agreement, and I adjudge and determine as follows:-
1. That Clause 13 does not confer upon employers freedom of contract with operatives
2. That the firm in question are not entitled, without the sanction of the Leicester
under 16 years of age who are employed by them on Piecework.
Roard of Arbitration, to employ operatives under 16 years of age at Piecework

Dated 9th July, 1923.
W. ADDINGTON WILLIS.
NATIONAL CONFERENCE (DECEMBER, 1922) AGREEMENT.
(The Northamptonshire County Boot Manufacturers' Federation).
Re The Interpretation of Clause 19 relating to Overtime.
AWARD.
A difference relating to a claim for overtime rate of pay was submitted under Clause
23 Standingsted under Clause
considered the matter on 15th May and 6th June, 1923. The representative members of
con Committee were unable to agree upon a decision and, acting upon the instructions of
their Federation and Union respectively, submitted the difference to me, the Chaim of
of the Committee, for my determination as Umpire.
The difference arises upon the claim that if an operative is prevented by genuine
illness from working a full normal week of 48 hours, he is still entitled to demand overtime
rate of pay for time worked on any day during that week beyond the usual daily hours.
The question to be determined is not whether it would be right, proper or equitable
that in such circumstances an operative should be allowed overtime rate, but whether he
is entitled to it under the terms of the Agreement which the parties have made.
Overtime shall only be paid to an
Clause 19 (a) says (so far as now material):
operative who has worked the full period of a normal week of 48 hours, unless an inter-
ruption in the normal week has occurred for which the operative is not responsible.
Does this mean every interruption for which the operative is not responsible, so as to
include all interruptions personal to the operative or caused by his domestic, private or
public affairs, of which illness is but one of many instances? There can be no justification
for saying that it applies to only one or some of these instances.
Or does it mean some interruption for which the operative is not responsible which
occurs in or in connection with the working of the factory whereby the operative is pre-
vented from working a full week?
After very careful consideration of the case and of the contentions submitted to me
and of the terms of the Agreement, including a comparison of the overtime clause in the
1914 Agreement, as requested by one of the representatives of the Union, I have come to
the conclusion that the second interpretation is the only reasonable one.
I therefore adjudge and determine:
That the expression
"unless an interruption in the normal week has occurred
for which the operative is not responsible," as used in Clause 19, paragraph (a) of the
National Conference (December 1922) Agreement, does not apply to an operative
whose failure to work a full working week has been due to his illness, and that such
operative is not entitled to claim overtime rate during that week unless and until he
has worked a full period of 48 hours.
Dated the 11th day of July, 1923.
(Signed) W. ADDINGTON WILLIS.

HALF-YEARLY STATEMENT OF ACCOUNTS.
The statement of accounts for the half-year are published herewith, details
of which appear in a later section of this report. Upon the whole, having
regard to the abnormal conditions of the world's trade, this having its effect
on the boot and shoe industry, as well as other trades, we think we may con-
gratulate ourselves upon having passed through another half-year so success-
fully as we have done. It is true that upon the Trade Fund there is a loss of
£2,297 IOS. IId. This, however, is fully accounted for owing to the large
amount of money we are constantly paying out for unemployment benefit,
which amounted to £23,144 15s. 9d., or £4,610 35. 5d. more than was paid
out for the half-year ending December, 1922. It will therefore be seen that
had it not been for this, we should have been enabled to have reported a saving
on the Trade Fund.
The Sick Fund has considerably increased, and upon the whole the funds
at the Central Office are larger than in the previous half-year.
It may appear to some of the members that the aggregate amount of money
we have in hand is rather large. What should be remembered is that we
have a large membership too, and having regard to the financial obligations
to the members, the Central Fund is not yet in a fully satisfactory state.
We would further remind the members of the fact that our present financial
position is due very largely to the methods by which the industry is governed in
settling its business by arbitration methods, thus enabling us so successfully
to meet our financial obligations. Those methods of arbitration have brought
many benefits in the way of obtaining conditions in the industry, and rates of
wages.

THE LABOUR PARTY IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
The Labour Party is continuing its strenuous fight in the House of
Commons, meeting, it is true, with constant defeats in the Lobby Divisions;
revertheless, the case of Labour is day by day not only kept to the front, but
it is more and more apparent that if we are to be delivered from the present
ieplorable conditions whether in this country or abroad, and to put matters
more humanitarian lines, then we must see that the Labour Party is returned
power.
The position internationally is indeed a serious one, France still standing
hat for her full pound of flesh in regard to reparations. One cannot help but
fed that her method of dealing with the matter is one, which instead of being
in the best interests of the people, will cause irritation, distrust and ill will.
it is also very significant that the British Government, despite the poverty
they never tire in telling us) to which the country has come, have decided

to a naval base at Singapore. This surely is not the way to bring about

fraternity and goodwill, which should be the aim of all those in civilised
a state of opinion whereby we can pass

As showing the strong feeling upon the position of France and the Ruhr
appeared in the Pall Mall Gazette for the 6th inst. This paper cannot be said
Crisis, we beg to call the attention of the members to the following article which
to support the policy of the Labour Party, but the article in most unmistakable
terms clearly points out the unreasonable attitude the French Government
are taking up, as will be seen from the following:-
"The days are slipping by and there is no indication that France is prepared
On the contrary, there is every

going their own way regardless of the economic needs of their friends and
neighbours. Such an association as France proposes is not an Entente, it is
a humiliation, and opinion in this country is rising strongly against her.
"We are tired of waiting for our Allies to see reason, for it may well be
contended that if they cannot understand by now that their policy in the Ruhr
is doomed to failure, how can they be expected to understand it in time to save
the whole of Europe from economic chaos ?
"The French Government and people must be warned that if our Govern-
ment decides that we have waited long enough for that fertile co-operation
which is denied us, and determines upon an independent policy of our own,
it will have the country solidly at its back. Loath as we shall be to see the
Entente which promised so much for civilisation broken and ended, we all
recognise that even the warmest friendship may be pressed too far.
"This country wants peace, and is determined to have it. A distracted
Europe at our door is an intolerable nuisance, and if France will not assist us
to put things straight then we must act alone, considering only our own interests,
which are bound up in a rehabilitated Europe."

ARBROATH. - Our trade barometer still points to "bad, no-change."
It often happens that a busy period is experienced in Scotland before the mid-
summer holidays, but here we are on the brink of the annual vacation without
trade showing any temporary spurt. One could moralise over the change
which has come over the fortunes of Scotland's workers in recent years. Our
national prosperity rests on the conditions of industrialism in Glasgow, and as
these continue to be very bad, the rest of Northern Britain reflects the same
results. If the huge population of the second city could only get full employ-
ment, in a short time the outlying towns and cities would soon show increased
industrial and commercial brightness. It also has a marked effect when the
mid-summer stop is reached. Visitors reach to every part of Scotland when the
West is busy, and so money circulates in all directions, but this year again it is
only the fortunates who can find enough in their purses to change from the
daily round. The sad shrinkage in the purchasing power of the common
people over such an extended period tells emphatically of the failure of Capital-
ism to meet the elementary needs of life, and everybody should give attention
to the programme of the Labour Party which outlines a more natural, a more
humane, and a more sensible industrial system for our nation to base its social
welfare on. Last month we wrote of an employer in our district who wished
to take clicking and finishing departments off payment by results, and put
them back on fixed wages conditions. Despite several visits of our Council
Member to this firm, and despite the Managing Director having had an inter-

BRANCH REPORTS.
ARBROATH. — Our trade barometer still points to “bad, no-change.”
It often happens that a busy period is experienced in Scotland before the mid-
summer holidays. but here we are on the brink of the annual vacation without
trade showing any temporary spurt. One could moralise over the change
which has come over the fortunes of Scotland's workers in recent years. Our
national prosperity rests on the conditions of industrialism in Glasgow, and as
results. If the huge population of the second city could only get full employ-
these continue to be very bad, the rest of Northern Britain reflects the same
ment, in a short time the outlying towns and cities would soon show increased
industrial and commercial brightness. It also has a marked effect when the
mid-summer stop is reached. Visitors reach to every part of Scotland when the
West is busyv, and so money circulates in all directions, but this year again it is
only the fortunates who can find enough in their purses to change from the
daily round. The sad shrinkage in the purchasing power of the common
people over such an extended period tells emphatically of the failure of Capital-
ism to meet the elementary needs of life, and everybody should give attention
to the programme of the Labour Party which outlines a more natural, a more
humane, and a more sensible industrial system for our nation to base its social

LIVERPOOL.-Trade with boot repairers in this district generally is
fairly good. We have nothing particularly to report because we never get
more than about half dozen members turn up at our monthly meetings lately.

rates of wages, and the fact that it is national and uniform in operation removes

NORWICH.-Trade bad, slight signs of improvement.
NORTHAMPTON No. 1.-Trade remains quiet here but a slight improve-
ment on previous month, but it seems we shall never have the continuous run
of good trade we used to have at this time of the year. We must hope for a
better winter trade, but that seems rather doubtful in view of the enormous
reductions in wages that have taken place in all industries, which kills the home
market which is much more important than the export trade. We are busy
at the time of sending off our returns with the special Trade Union effort,
and meetings are being held all over Northampton and county, outside factories
and all kinds of works, including breweries. We don't know what our Pro-
hibitionist friends will think of the idea, but we hope the various organisations
will have an increase of members as a result. We have had a dispute at a small
firm which thought it could ignore the Trade Union officials and make their
own terms with their workpeople because it employed a number of outworkers.
After they definitely refused to see the local officials, we had no alternative
but to call upon all the men and women to cease work. This quickly brought
the employer to a reasonable frame of mind, and the matter was settled within
2 week much to the advantage of the workpeople.
NOTTINGHAM.-Trade has fallen off considerably around here. Most
of our members are only working three days a week on new work, and in the
repairing shops short time each day is general. We have rather heavy sickness
for the time of the year, but this has been mainly due to the weather which
has been so changeable.

LABOUR PARTY CONFERENCE.

Delegates' Report.
The Labour Party Conference was held this year in the Queen's Hall, London, from
June 26th to the 29th inclusive, and was attended by about 900 delegates. Mr. Sidney
Webb presiding.

Apart from many resolutions dealing with the internal work of the Party and the more
effective machinery to deal with the ever-increasing influence of the Labour Party, we think
it may fairly be said that the outstanding feature of the Conference, apart from the very
decisive vote rejecting the resolution proposing to admit the Communist to the Party,
and also the equally emphatic vote against the Party Whips being sent to Mr. J. T. Newbold,
M.P., were the increasing appreciation of the fact that more and more regard must be paid
to the practical side of the work, and the policy that must be pursued, when it is borne in
mind that the Labour Party has now become the official Opposition in Parliament, and
might within the very near future be called upon to assume the position of forming a
Government.

Whilst in no way abating or dropping the ideal for which the Party stands, there
certainly was shown a determination to appreciate its proper value and the responsibility
which attaches to a Party holding the position in the country now held by the Labour
Party.
Amongst the more important resolutions passed were the following: —
Foreign Policy.
This Conference welcomed the establishment of the new Socialist and Labour
International, renewed the protests of the Party against the Ruhr occupation, expressed
the opinion that the last offer of the German Government should be taken as a basis
for negotiation, renewed the repeated declarations of the Party on the reparations
question — including inter-Allied debts and withdrawal of the armies of occupation —
called for a world conference to revise the peace treaties, expressed alarm at the
possibility of a division between the French and British peoples — especially at a new
race in air armaments — and advocated full recognition of the Soviet Government.

Education.
The Conference specially condemned in a lengthy resolution
(a) The discontinuance of the reduction of the size of classes, and, in many cases,
the actual increase of the numbers under each teacher.
(b) The failure to overtake the arrears of school building.
(c) The arrest of the development of Special Schools.
(d) The severe limitation in the provision of meals for children found hungry
at school or suffering from lack of food.
(e) The reductions in the number of free places at the Secondary Schools, and the
allowing and even encouraging of an onerous increase in the fees.
(f) The continued suspension of the National Scholarships to the Universities.
(g) The continued and even increasing employment of untrained and unqualified
teachers.
(h) The penalising of the entire teaching staff, first by the unwarranted deduction
of 5 per cent. towards the cost of superannuation; and, secondly, by permitting
Local Education Authorities to press for substantial reductions below the agreed
Burnham scales.
(i) The failure to organise a national system for the training of teachers, they
heavily penalising those Local Education Authorities whom it encouraged to
Training Colleges.

THE LABOUR PARTY CONFERENCE.
The Twenty-Third Annual Conference of the Labour Party opened at the Queen's
Hall, London, on Tuesday, 26th June, and continued for the three following days. There
were approximately 900 delegates present. Mr. Sidney Webb, M.P., presided.
In the Chairman's address Mr. Webb claimed that the problems of the day could be
satisfactorily solved on the principles put forth by the Labour Party. Whatever might
or suffered from lack of education would not now be made by any person of candour
have been the case in past years the accusation that the Labour Party was inexperienced

Europe to the other. Never, perhaps, in all history had there been so impressive a
a real peace. The Labour Party held that the treaties failed because, almost from end to
end, they ignored economics and morality.

by owning or those who lived by working. It was this that was at the back of the almost
The struggle was as to who should be financially losers by the war—those who lived
nearly twice the produce of this year's income tax. The Labour Party must go on asserting
that there can be no financial security, and, indeed, no complete restoration of industrial
prosperity in this country, so long as one million pounds has to be taken out of the product

A War Debt Redemption Levy, on fortunes exceeding £5,000 in graduated

both him who does and him who suffers it, and futile to both." Violence persuaded no

A resolution was then taken, brought forward by the Executive Committee, that the
position taken up by the Annual Conference in Edinburgh in June, 1922, rejecting the
application of the Communist Party for affiliation be endorsed. After discussion a card
vote was taken with the following result :-
For affiliating the Communist Party 366,000
Against . . . 2,880,000
Majority against 2,514,000
A further vote was taken upon a recommendation that the Labour Party Whip be
sent to Mr. Walter Newbold, M.P., with the result that by an overwhelming majority
the same was defeated.
Other important matters dealt with during the week was the question of Foreign
Policy which was proposed by Mr. J. Ramsay MacDonald, M.P., who begged the Conference
to entertain no illusions about the difficulty of the task of achieving international peace.
" Do not let us live in a fool's paradise," he exclaimed. "Given a war situation,
you will be in it whether you want to or not." Unless the policy of stifling armaments
prevailed, the harvest of armaments would be reaped.
Therefore, he desired the Conference to send to the French workers a hearty resolu-
tion of friendship and fraternity, and an appeal for joint action to suppress militarism
and imperialism.
The maintenance of the Capital Levy as the centre stone of the whole fabric of the
Labour Party's financial policy was reaffirmed, the resolution endorsed calling for a reduc-
tion of armaments, the Taxation of Land Values, the Abolition of Food Taxes, and the
Entertainment and Corporation Profits Taxes.

Meaningless Heroics.
The Barrow Labour Party submitted a resolution calling for protests against the
"crimes committed by the British Government against subject races in the interests of
the expansion of the Empire and for Imperialistic and capitalistic ambitions."
The delegate who moved the resolution denounced those Labour leaders who were
"always supporting the British Empire."
Mr. Ramsay MacDonald trounced the speaker for this attack, declaring the resolution
to be meaningless heroics. On every conceivable occasion, he said, Labour had taken
its stand against Imperialism, militarism, and oppression of the subject, and here was
Barrow, of all places in the world, decrying its efforts though it did nothing to help. Mr.
MacDonald asked why did not Barrow send a Labour Member to the House?
The resolution was carried.
Other resolutions of importance passed during the week dealt with matters affecting
Rating, Emigration, Milk, Unemployment, Housing, and the New Trades Board Bill.
Some of the resolutions affecting these matters appear on the report of the delegates to
Conference appearing on pages 454-455.
During the week the delegates were entertained at a Garden Party at the offices of
the Workers' Union, Golders Green, whilst on another occasion the London Labour Party
invited the delegates to pay a visit to the County Hall, which is the new Headquarters
of the London County Council, which is claimed to be the finest building of its kind in the
world.
WHAT THE "NEW LEADER" THINKS OF MR. SIDNEY WEBB'S
ADDRESS TO THE LABOUR PARTY CONFERENCE.
Mr. Sidney Webb's opening address was filled with close reasoning, with quiet
yet memorable phrases and with the spirit of service and hope. He spoke before the
fateful decision to double the air force was known, but his broad survey is the best com-
mentary upon it. From that " factory of inefficiency " in Versailles came the rivalries
no less than the oppressions of the victors. While he stated firmly the duty of resistance
to this Allied policy, he carried us forward into a wide positive programme of international
organisation, in which every item calls for thought and action. The main emphasis in
the address was laid upon the fundamental ideal of democracy. VIOLENCE IS TWICE
ACCURSED, TO HIM THAT USES AND TO HIM THAT SUFFERS IT. Moreover, as he shrewdly
reminded us, with the Italian precedent before us, the violence of angry property is apt
to be more efficient than that of a revolutionary mob. Here lies our chief difference with
the Communists. WE CAN GO NO FASTER THAN WE CAN CARRY A MAJORITY OF THE
ELECTORATE WITH US BY PERSUASION It must, we would add, be not only a genuine
numerical majority; it must also have within it powerful elements of intelligent con-
viction. SNATCHED MAJORITIES ARE NOT ENOUGH, AND THE BEST SIGN OF THE PARTY'S
GROWTH is that in the Whitechapel and Morpeth by-elections, Mr. Gosling and Mr. Smillie
achieved absolute majorities where their predecessors had won only by the splitting of the
opposition vote. A PARTY WHICH AIMS AT FUNDAMENTAL CHANGE MUST HAVE BEHIND IT,
IN QUALITY AND EVEN IN NUMBERS A FAR GREATER MEASURE OF SUPPORT THAN AVAILS
FOR A PARTY WHICH MERELY DEFENDS AND ADAPTS THINGS AS THEY ARE. We shall have
against us, when we make our first essay in Government and attempt any fundamental
change, not the Lords alone, but in the main the Civil Service also, AND THE VAST POWERS
OF FINANCE AND THE PRESS, with their infinite scope for sabotage. THE ANSWER TO SUCH
FORCES MUST BE NOT NUMBERS ONLY, BUT ORGANISED INTELLIGENCE, AND A DEMOCRACY
WHICH CAN USE THE INDUSTRIAL AS WELL AS THE POLITICAL WEAPON.
CANADA AND SHOE WORKERS.
We have received a letter from the Secretary of the Boot and Shoe Workers' Union
of America, Mr. N. L. Phillips, of the Labour Temple, Toronto, Ontario, that some firms
in Canada are hiring shoemakers from Leicester to whom they have promised steady work
at good pay and advancing cost of transportation, and that this was brought to the notice
of that Union by an operative who was brought over under these conditions last February.
The firms are only paying 40 cents per hour, which is not one half of that Union's minimum
rate and he is finding it next to impossible to live and is enduring a great deal of hardship.
They are going to take his case up and help him all they can, and ask that this shall be given
as much publicity as possible. They urge all English shoeworkers to view with suspicion
all advertisements for Shoeworkers in Canada, and that all those who contemplate going
to Canada should write to the Boot and Shoe Workers' Union at Toronto, who will be glad
to give the facts of the Shoemaking business in Canada and also help them all it can.

Report of Executive Council Meeting of International Shoe and
Leather Workers, held at Frankfort, 6th June, 1923.
All the members were present except Mr. Poulton, Mr. Smith, the reserve member,
attending in his place. Herr Simon presided and Lex acted as Secretary.
The first business was the Secretary's report for period from 1st July, 1922, to 30th
April, 1923. It dealt very largely with the position of the German workers resulting
from the occupation of the Ruhr. The rapid falling of the Mark, which is shown by the
fact that prior to the occupation they were 45,000 to the £, while to-day they are 480,000
to the £, is a serious matter for the workers, as the price of bread and other foodstuffs
largely follow the Mark, and this makes changes in wages necessary almost every week.
Unemployment has greatly increased, some factories had closed down, while of those
that were open at least 75 per cent. of the operatives were on short time. It was stated
that over 90 per cent. of the shoe workers in Germany were either out of work or on short
time.
The following two paragraphs are worth quoting from Simon's report.
" I will not enter into details about the excesses of the French and Belgian soldiers.
I will not enumerate the verdicts of murders that have been committed against German
workers and citizens in a time of peace, all these lamentable facts are sufficiently well
known. I only want to point out that these conditions will contribute to aggravate the
world's crises, and that not only the workers of Germany, but of the entire world, will be
doomed to misery and privation."
"The German workers know that the damages of the war in France and Belgium
have to be made good again. They have always fought with all their forces for the fulfil-
ment of the reparations of these damages. But these reparations can only be paid, if the
economic life can come to a peaceful evolution."
The report further dealt with the activities of the International in regard to reports
issued, and the work of the Secretary in connection with various International gatherings.
Arising out of the report a resolution was passed unanimously condemning the Ruhr
occupation, the terms of the resolution being drafted by Comrade Roux, of France.
A financial statement covering the period since the last Conference held in August,
1921, was presented. It is difficult to explain same, as the figures being in marks, and
received at different periods, the value of the contributions varied considerably from the
time they were sent. There was a balance of 7,326,843 marks, while other fairly substantial
assets exist in other currencies, including 1,545 in American dollars, and £376 in English
notes. The expenses of the meeting would be about six million marks.
The agenda for the Congress to be held in Dresden on 16th September was dealt with.
Reports from the various countries were asked for, to be sent in by 1st August, so they
may be translated for the Congress.
It was agreed that a separate discussion should take place on the question of the
eight-hour day. Mr. Smith was asked to undertake the introduction of same, but owing
to our delegates not having been appointed, Mahler, of the German Leather Workers,
was given the task.
A letter was read from Moscow asking for the affiliation of the Russian workers in
the leather industry, and failing affiliation that they be permitted to attend as guests.
Simon added that he had seen a representative of the Russian Union in Berlin, and also
Yusefowitsch in Hamburg. He informed them the matter was one to be decided by the
E.C. It was also suggested by the Russians, that there should be consultation in regard to
future wars.
After some discussion it was decided not to accept their affiliation, nor to permit
them to attend as guests. Only Vesely, of Czecho-Slovakia, spoke in favour of affiliation,
but he did not vote for it. It was mentioned that negotiations were taking place between
Amsterdam and Moscow, and it was felt that any decision as to the merging of forces
should be left to them.
Simon stated that the position in Russia was changing, and that the workers were
struggling to maintain the eight-hour day, but some were working 10 hours. There were
at that time strikes at Odessa. The workers were strongly criticising their leaders.
A resolution was passed protesting against the dissolution of the Shoe Workers' Union
by the Government in Czecho-Slovakia. This, it was understood, had taken place because

A. J. DOBBS.

A VISIT TO A SHOE FACTORY IN GERMANY AND A MEETING
WITH GERMAN SHOE WORKERS.

I stated in my report last month that I would give our members an account of a visit
to a German Shoe Factory, and a description of one's experiences in addressing a meeting
of German shoe workers.
In its general features a German factory differs little from our own. The sub-division
level. The machines used are practically the same, and when I say that the British United
of labour, with the various mechanical devices, bring things down largely to a common
Puller-over and Consol were in use it will be evident to all how true this is. The idea
governing in this factory was to get the best machine no matter where it was made.
The firm whose factory we visited was one of the best in the country, both from the
standpoint of class of trade, and in the relationship that existed between the firm and its
workpeople. Let me say here, that every operative was a member of the Union. They
had achieved what the Americans call 100 per cent. efficiency.
The factory without being in any way elaborate, was well built (it was nearly new)
and spacious. In its general arrangements it was well planned, the operatives having
plenty of room in which to work. Due regard seems to be given to the health of the workers.
There was a large dining room below, with a stove in which food could be kept or made
hot. The operatives are allowed to put their food in the oven half an hour before meal
time so that when it is required it is just right for eating. Evidently many take their food
at the factory, and in some cases the wives bring the food and place it in the stove or oven
and take away the empty vessels of the day before. A long double wash basin is provided
so that the workers can wash before leaving the factory, while ample provision is made for
clothes without hanging over one another or even touching.
The trade is purely retail, consisting of ladies' and men's goods, a large quantity
being welted, which by the way were made on the bed-laster. They run about 450 samples,
and have just over 400 customers. The styles generally were unsuited to British trade.
Goods are exported; we were shown some that were for Switzerland, and some golf boots
for England. A good number were substitutes for turnshoes, made on the tackless principle,
the uppers being solutioned down; they looked exceedingly well, and we were told the
wearing qualities were good.
The methods of handling work were well thought out, and all work has to be com-
pleted in 32 days, that is, from the time the order is issued from the office to readiness for
dispatch. The instock system is only in use in connection with a few of the cheaper
lines. In every room there are fixed in several places five coloured electric bulbs, and
each of the managerial staff has a colour or colours allotted to him. Should he be required
at the office, a bell rings and his coloured light comes on, and he at once goes to the telephone
and ascertains what is wanted. If it is an urgent matter such as a trunk call then the
bell rings twice.
I have stated the class of work was good. Never have I seen finer upper leather
dose that difficulty would be had in getting sufficient for shoe tongues. One cannot
imagine the clickers claiming for faulty material.


---
The method of cutting is somewhat strange to us. The knife used by the clicker looks to be some 9 or 10 inches long when new and has no handle. It is bound round with leather, and when used is held as we should a pen. I never saw a single operative holding as we should. On stout material and linings it is held butcher fashion. How strong the knife proper is.
Another interesting feature was in regard to the press knives. The knife proper is of the same depth as those in ordinary use here, but there is a sort of bridge constructed over them, with a short stem leading up to a plate on top. The operative holds the knife by the bridge or stem, and the plate forms a complete protection to the hand. This is looked upon with so much importance that a law has been passed making their use compulsory. The knives on revolution presses are constructed the same, though of greater depth. The idea seems to be that prevention is better than cure.
The hours worked are 47. This obtained throughout Germany in the Shoe trade. I may perhaps add that the 48-hour week is enforced by law in the country generally. The hours were worked so as to give one and half hours to dinner. It is interesting to note that the German workers refuse to work longer hours on the five days so as to have a short Saturday. Evidently sport has not got them in its grip yet, nor allotments.
The rapid falling of the Mark makes it difficult to speak about wages. At the time I was there the rate was 2,500 marks per hour, which in our values is very low, though in pre-war terms it would be £125. Changes in wage rates have to be made very frequently under present conditions, and it must be exceedingly difficult to keep pace with the changing rates of exchange, and as the price of food largely follow the mark the position is bad indeed.
One has often wondered how business is possible with this changing of values, but I ascertained that when any material is bought, it is entered up on terms of the dollar, so that the change in the value of the mark is easily met, the dollar being the basic rate of value to-day. By this means leather or any material purchased some time ago can easily be measured in present day prices.
Another illustration can be given of the effect of the exchange rates. Before the war the cost of lasts was 2 ¾ marks, at the time of my visit it was 32,000 marks. The manager informed me that a new style for the season required 7,000 pairs of lasts, which at present prices meant a capital outlay of 224,000,000 marks. They were meeting this position by grinding or scouring down old lasts, which besides effecting an economy, also provided work for some who otherwise would have been displaced. I may here say that the factory had little more trade than represented half their capacity. As the firm had last-making machinery this economy could be better and more easily effected.
A practical illustration of the effect of the Ruhr occupation was given to me. Some of the machinery used was manufactured in the occupied area. This applies to a number of machines that were used for lift cutting, and one of these had been standing idle for four months because a part that was broken could not be replaced. Nothing could be obtained from these areas, and one can only conclude that had it been a pivot machine, there would have been a danger of the whole factory being stopped. The thought that naturally arises is, how can any reparations be paid while industry is paralysed in this fashion.
One other incident is worth recording. When we entered the lasting room a number of the men were standing together arguing in an excited manner. As the manager was with us we wondered what would happen. He took little notice of them, but said to me that it was very disturbing to him when trade was such that he could not give the men a full week's work, and being on piecework their earnings were small. I suppose he thought I was still puzzled about something, for he turned and said, you know what they were arguing about, don't you? I said I did not. Oh, he said, one of them has had more than his share of the work and the others are after him about it.
After we had looked round the factory we wended our way to the hall where a meeting was to be held. It was a building that appeared to be quite 100 yards long, and from 30 to 40 wide. It was largely built of wood, one side being entirely of glass looking out on to what seemed to be pleasure gardens with fields beyond.
The appearance upon our arrival just before five o'clock was not very encouraging. There were only a few people present of both sexes, some of whom were enjoying a meal in which a dark-coloured bread seemed to loom somewhat largely. I thought to myself the workers here are like those at home and bother little about the affairs of their Union. But we had not been seated on the platform very long when workers of all ages and either sex poured into the hall, which was soon full to overflowing. The seating was not sufficient, and a raid was made upon the spare chairs upon the platform, and also upon those in the gardens outside.
Order was soon obtained, and the chairman opened the meeting. He had not got very far when from different parts of the hall men rose and spoke with evident heat. As I had already been called upon and was on my feet for the purpose of speaking, I thought


---
it was some kind of protest against me addressing them. I soon found such was not the
case, but due to some of those holding Communist views wanting to have the meeting
run according to their ideas. Herr Simon soon obtained order again, and I proceeded to
speak. I was limited to ten minutes so had to condense what I wished to say. I was
listened to with great respect, and received with great enthusiasm. I was followed by
Comrade Roux, of the French Union, who also had a splendid reception. The speeches
were interpreted, and the audience cheered us both, Roux especially so.
It was a manifestation of the fact that the workers have no quarrel with each other.
Our Governments may fall out, the big financial interests may manœuvre and scheme in
the interests of their class, but the workers the world over have more to gain by friendship
and goodwill than by hatred that must ultimately lead to war.
The meeting was an interesting experience, the German workers take more interest

FELLOW MEMBERS,
The Vienna Women's Conference.
It has come to my knowledge that the Council of our Union have not considered
it worth their while to send a delegate (from our many thousands of women members) to
the working Women's Conference in Vienna, the only International Working Women's
Conference of Labour Women. I wish to say how disappointed I am that our Union
should be so blind to the interests, not only of our women in this country, but to the help
and inspiration we may be able to give to the working women in other countries who are
worse off than ourselves. When I call to mind that our President, Mrs. Bell-Richards,
was the means of getting a ten minutes' rest pause for all workers embodied in a Convention
at Geneva, in 1921, I feel we should not hesitate to get the real working women's opinion,
whoever it may be, on the things that vitally affect us as workers-ills that from experience
we are able to talk about and remedy. Once again let me say how sorry I am that our
Executive of Labour men should not have considered the question more fully.
Yours, a Fellow Member,
E. A. TIMMS,
Leicester Women's Branch.
17th July, 1923.

THE WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BILL.
The Government's Scheme.
The introduction of the Workmen's Compensation Bill into the House of Commons
is an event of some importance to all Approved Societies, as well as to the employed clasess
committee stage, but in general it should be able to secure a speedy passage, seeing that
throughout the Kingdom. The Bill in its details has been exciting some criticism in the
it is founded on the recommendations of the Holman Gregory Committee, to which reference
differs from that Committee's scheme, since the Government did not find themselves
obliged to adopt every recommendation blindly and abdicate their own responsibilities,
has frequently been made in these pages. There are certain points, of course, on which it
On the second reading debate, Mr. G. Locker-Lampson, Under-Secretary for the
insurance. I do not say for a moment that the principle of compulsory insurance is
" In the first place, one of the recommendations was that there should be compulsory
machinery and additional cost, and I think at present it would be inopportune to introduce
wrong, or that it is impracticable, but it involves the creation of a great deal of additional
it. It also means a very radical alteration at a time when reconstruction is going on in
Home Office, stated :-
industry as a whole.
"As to State supervision of rates of premium, the object, of course, was to secure
that a reasonable proportion of the premiums paid should go in respect of compensation.
The Bill proposes that this should be very largely carried out by voluntary agreement
with the Accident Offices Association. The loss ratio which the total amount paid by the
companies under the association in any year in respect of compensation, including reason-
the companies in that year is to be not less than 60 per cent. during each of the next three
years. After those three years it is to be 62 per cent, or such other proportion, not less
compensation falls short of or exceeds the above loss ratio, the companies will be bound
than 60 per cent., as may be agreed upon, and further, if the amou amount paid in respect
to make a corresponding rebate or will be entitled to make an additional charge, as the
case may be, to the employers before the next premium is paid. The Committee recome
mended that 70 per cent. should be paid in compensation, but circumstances have very
largely changed since the Holman Gregory Committee reported. In the first place, there
has been a very large fall in the premiums owing to the immense quantity of unemployment,
and secondly, we are not adopting compulsory insurance. Thus, in future, the percentage
payable in compensation will, after three years, be not less than 624 per cent. instead of,
as I believe it was in 1921, no more than about 37 per cent. of the whole of the premiums
received.
"In regard to total and partial incapacity, the Committee recommended a figure of
628 per cent. in all cases up to a maximum of £3 a week. The Bill adheres to the original
50 per cent. under the Act of 1906 as regards the higher-paid workmen, but it raises the
maximum to 30s. a week instead of £1, and in regard to the lower-paid workers who earn
a weekly wage under 50s., it fixes the proportion on a varying scale between 50 per cent.
and 75 per cent. In regard to partial incapacity there is a similar scale adopted for the
lower-paid workmen. So that in all these cases the lower the wage the better the benefit."
Every Approved Society worker has an interest in this Bill, for no one can have failed
to experience doubts, or proofs, that National Health Insurance has borne burdens which
employers should bear in respect of Workmen's Compensation. Piecemeal legislation
has touched National Health Insurance rather severely, and a reform of Workmen's
Compensation and its administration was long overdue when the present Bill was framed.
The decision to throw over the experience gained in the health scheme and reject the idea
of compulsory insurance of Workmen's Compensation risks may have been a sound one as
regards the practical difficulties, but it is to be hoped that the inequities as between Sickness
Benefit and Workmen's Compensation will nevertheless be redressed.—The Insurance
Magazine, July, 1923.

MINISTRY OF HEALTH.
Vote on Supply. Vaccination.
MR. A. HILL (Leicester West) : The subject we have been discussing to-day is one on
which, on a number of points, we see, perhaps, almost unanimous agreement. Had it
not been that the Minister made some reference to the question of vaccination, I do not
know that I should have attempted to get the attention of the House. But as I come
from the City of Leicester, I feel that I must say something on this question in the interests
of my constituents. I do not know whether I misunderstood the right hon. Gentleman,
but the impression was certainly conveyed to me that the Ministry were at least con-
sidering the advisability of revising their policy. I can assure the right hon. Gentleman
that the people of Leicester are as emphatic in their opposition to vaccination to-day as
ever they were. If there be any departure from the present situation with a view to doing
away with the privilege of exemption, and with the idea of making vaccination once again
compulsory, then I can assure the Ministry that there will be united opposition. The
Minister will discover that among his strongest opponents will be found some of the most
ardent supporters of the Government as a whole. This question, in past years, has been
looked upon as vital in our city of Leicester, and for many years it was the deciding factor
in regard to the personnel of the board of guardians. We have long ago discarded vaccina-
tion, and we feel as safe as any city in the land. (An Hon. Member: “What of
Gloucester ?") I did not know that Gloucester was an unvaccinated city. My impression
is that Gloucester believes in vaccination to a much greater extent than does Leicester.
We, in Leicester, have always "banked" on good sanitation. We have been ably led

This Convention has already been ratified by a considerable number of The Washington countries, though not yet, I regret to say, by this country. The question is of something Conference was merely one part of a very great movement of immense social importance which took place for the shortening of the working hours in 1919-20. The movement is one in which we think this country ought to take the lead instead of lagging behind and the vention.

I need not say much about the reasons that render such a Measure as this necessary. Most hon. Members will agree that there are few darker and blacker pages in our industrial history than the hardship, exhaustion, ill-health, irritation, ruin of family life, and denial hours-the unnecessarily and scandalously long hours to which generation after genera- in times past. And even if some economic loss were to follow, we might fairly say that we are prepared to put up with some diminution of production, and compensate for it by a better distribution, rather than permit injurious from a human and social point of view. As a matter of fact, we are not faced with that alternative. We have official and unofficial the continuance of a system so injurious from a human evidence, evidence of the employers themselves and the most enlightened employers at that-to prove that the shortening of the hours need not necessarily be followed, and has not in fact been followed, by a diminution of output. In many cases quite the con- trary. It is quite true that there has been some advance in this matter. Something has been gained. I think it is hardly an exaggeration to say that the gain in the case of their working hours is almost the one and only gain that has been secured by the working classes since the war. There are about 2,000,000 of the workers of the country who are working 48 hours or less per week. That, however, does not alter the position of the millions who are still working more than 48 hours per week, particularly in the unorganised trades, and among the women workers. And it does not alter the fact that though the situation is not so difficult at the moment, it is highly probable that when trade improves the conditions will become much more serious, and that attacks upon the hours of labour, of which there are already sinister signs, will become much more determined and much more widespread than now. In my constituency, with the textile workers especially, the danger is felt to be a very real danger indeed. The thought of returning to the old working hours of 55 and 56 per week is one that haunts their minds like an evil dream. It brings back what, to them, is a vivid and hateful memory. It is against such evil possibilities that I propose, by this Bill, to erect a legal barrier which will not easily be broken down.

Question, "That leave be given to introduce a Bill to limit the hours of employment," put, and agreed to.

Bill ordered to be brought in by Mr. Charles Buxton, Mr. Clynes, Mr. Duncan, Mr. Greenwood, Mr. John Hodge, Mr. William Robinson, Mr. Thomas Shaw, Mr. James Henry Thomas, Mr. William Thorne, Mr. Tout, Mr. Turner, and Mr. Robert Young.

The indemnity shall be paid for the days during which the seaman remains

to two months’ wages.
Though this Draft Convention has so far been ratified only by two States Bulgaria
and Estonia, its ratification has been recommended to Parliament by the Governments
of Belgium, Chili, Denmark, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Poland and Spain, while
Bills to give effect to it are before the Argentine and French Parliaments.
The British Government has not yet ratified the Convention, but in the House of Com-
mons on 8th November, 1921, the then Minister of Labour (Dr. Macnamara) stated that
they were prepared to accept it, postponing formal ratification until it had been carried
into effect by an amendment of the existing legislation. He quoted the Merchant Shipping
Act, 1894, which provides:—
“Where the services of a seaman terminate before the date contemplated in the
agreement by reason of the wreck or loss of the ship… he shall be entitled to
wages up to the time of such termination, but not for any longer period.”
Dr. Macnamara added that the President of the Board of Trade proposed to introduce
a Merchant Shipping Bill when the pressure of Parliamentary business permitted, which
would, among other provisions, bring the law in this country into line with the Convention
of the International Labour Conference.
WORLD STUDY OF INDUSTRY.
Some Statistical Problems.
The work of the International Labour Office of the League of Nations in collecting
and distributing information on world labour problems will be carried a step forward
by the decision of its Governing Body to call a conference of representatives of official
labour statistical services at Geneva on 29th October, 1923.
One of the first problems before the International Labour Office has been to overcome
the lack of uniformity in the information supplied to it by the different countries on
industrial and labour questions which makes effective comparison from the international
point of view difficult and sometimes impossible. The exact idea of what is an unemployed
person, for example, varies from State to State. Figures produced with regard to wages
are based on different standards in different countries.
Last year the Chief of the Research Division of the Office visited the labour ministries
at Berne, Berlin, Warsaw and Prague, with the object of discussing the greater standardisa-
tion of information. The compilation of statistics on every aspect of labour and industrial
problems was studied—unemployment, hours of work, wages, cost of living, retail and
wholesale prices, industrial fatigue, industrial hygiene, housing, welfare work and the like.
The conference of statisticians in October is expected to facilitate this movement
towards standardisation by discussing:—
(1) Classification of industries and occupations for the purpose of labour statistics;
(2) Statistics of wages and hours of labour;
(3) Statistics of industrial accidents.
WORLD EMPLOYMENT POSITION.
General Situation Improves.
“The improvement in the general industrial situation which was noticed last month
still continues, according to the latest information received,” states the International
Labour Review, the monthly publication of the International Labour Office of the League
of Nations, in its general survey of the employment situation.
UNITED STATES.—A heightened industrial activity still continues in the United States,
with a few indications that in certain quarters the limit of expansion has been reached,
especially in the iron and steel trade. The volume of employment based on returns from
some 5,000 establishments increased by 2 per cent. in the month of March and the aggregate
wages bill by 5 per cent. Wages are still rising and workers in the steel trades received
a general rise of 10 per cent. in April.
CANADA.—In Canada the situation has improved in certain trades, owing largely
to better weather conditions. The lumber, pulp, and paper trades, for instance, are
particularly active. A shortage of labour exists in some trades due to the continual
exodus to the United States. In the manufacturing trades a slight decline in employment
has been experienced.
UNITED KINGDOM.—In the United Kingdom the number of unemployed, though
high (11 per cent.), is lower than at any point during the last two years. Employment
was good in mining, and in the tinplate, carpet, and worsted trades, but bad in the cotton

INTERNATIONAL LABOUR LEGISLATION.
Annual Reports to be made.
By Article 408 of the Treaty of Versailles, each State which is a Member of the Inter-
national Labour Organisation agrees to make an annual report to the International Labour
Office on the measures it has taken to give effect to those Conventions of the International
Labour Conference to which it is a party.
In the case of four of the Draft Conventions adopted at the Washington (1919) Session
of the Conference, and three of those adopted at the Genoa (1920) Session, the latest date
for their enforcement by States which ratified them was 1st July, 1922. Annual reports
for these Conventions are thus due for the period ended 30th June, 1923. The Director
of the International Labour Office has accordingly issued to the various Governments
copies of the prescribed forms for their reports, with a request that these may be in the
hands of the Office by the end of next month.
The Draft Conventions concerned deal with: -
(1) The employment of women before and after childbirth;
(2) Night work of women;
(3) Juvenile employment in industry;
(4) Night work of young persons ;
(5) Juvenile employment at sea;
(6) Unemployment indemnity for shipwrecked seamen; and
(7) Employment agencies for seamen.
Of the above Conventions those relating to night work of women, juvenile employment
in industry, night work of young persons, and juvenile employment at sea, have been
ratified by Great Britain, and the necessary reports will therefore be due to Geneva from
the British Government.

INTERNATIONAL LABOUR CONVENTIONS AND JAPAN.
Considerable progress has been made in Japan in the sphere of labour legislation
as a result of the adoption of Draft Conventions by the various sessions of the International
Labour Conferences.
By an Act of 8th April, 1921, Japan gave effect to the Unemployment Convention
which includes provisions for the establishment of free public employment exchanges.
By the Employment of Seamen Act, 1922, Japan gave effect to the Convention which
provided for the abolition of private fee-charging agencies for finding employment for
seamen and the substitution of public employment offices.
In virtue of the Japanese Act respecting the prohibition of the use of white phosphorus
in the manufacture of matches, promulgated in April, 1921, the Japanese Government,
in accordance with a Recommendation adopted by the Washington Conference, has
adhered to the International Convention adopted at Berne in 1906 on the prohibition of
the use of white phosphorus in the manufacture of matches.

GENERAL PRINCIPLES FOR THE ORGANISATION OF FACTORY
INSPECTION: THE FORTHCOMING INTERNATIONAL
LABOUR CONFERENCE.
The Governing Body of the International Labour Office has decided to place only
one question on the agenda of the next Conference, which will be held in Geneva in October,
1923. This question is "General Principles for the Organisation of Factory Inspection."
In deciding to place this question on the agenda, the Governing Body, was guided by
Article 427 of the Treaty of Versailles, which lays down the following principle as one of
the questions of special and urgent importance for the regulation of conditions of labour:
"Each State should make provision for a system of inspection, in which women should
take part, in order to ensure the enforcement of the laws and regulations for the protection
of the employed."
In the last paragraph of the Article the High Contracting Parties declare that in their
opinion the principles mentioned in Article 427 are well fitted to guide the policy of the
League of Nations, and that "if adopted by the industrial communities who are Members
and safeguarded in practice by an adequate system of such inspection,
they will confer lasting benefits upon the wage earners of the world." It will thus be
seen that the Treaty of Versailles does not merely propose the institution of a system of
factory inspection in every country as one of the most important and urgent measures
for the regulation of conditions of labour, but actually regards such a system as a necessary
condition for the successful application of all the other principles laid down in Part XIII.
As the Treaty itself proposed the question of factory inspection as one of those to be dealt
with by the International Labour Organisation, it was inevitable, as the Director pointed
out in his report to the Third Session of the Conference, that the Organisation should at
some time or other discuss it.
The importance of instituting organisations for enforcement and supervision which
are approximately equal in effectiveness in all countries is increasingly felt as a larger
number of the International Labour Conventions are ratified. Such an organisation
would remove one of the most serious objections which have been made to the system of
international legislation set up by the Peace Treaty, namely, that the international Con-
ventions do not in practice have the same effect in the different countries which ratify
them because they are not observed to an equal extent. If the Conference were to lay
down definite principles as regards this question, the Conventions would be more com-
pletely and effectively enforced, and increased validity would be given to one of the most
important arguments in favour of international legislation, namely that it prevents unfair
competition.
The International Labour Office has now sent to all the Governments a questionnaire
dealing with the general principles for the organisation of factory inspection. The ques-
tionnaire is preceded by a detailed account of the purpose of factory inspection, the duties
and powers of factory inspectors, and the system of organisation in the majority of
countries. The report states that the Governing Body does not desire to ask the Con-
ference to lay down strict regulations for the organisation and work of the factory inspection
system in all countries. It is rather proposed to study the lines on which the system has
Leen instituted and the actual daily work of the inspectors in each country, with a view
to ascertaining the fundamental principles for the satisfactory organisation of a system
for supervising the enforcement of labour legislation.

THE REVIVAL OF APPRENTICESHIP,
The decline of apprenticeship in recent times has been observed in almost every
country as large-scale industry has developed. This has resulted in a shortage of highly-
skilled workers, while the workers now produced as skilled are often inadequately trained.
In some countries it is thought that this situation is partly due to the fact that modern
systems of apprenticeship are a survival of the older systems, but do not offer the same
guarantees for supervision, thorough training, and opportunities for employment at the
termination of the contract. Attempts are therefore being made to revive apprenticeship
and to adapt it to the large-scale production which appears to be an essential character-
istic of modern industry.
The International Labour Review publishes an article giving an account of the various
attempts of this kind which have been made in the United States, Canada, South Africa
and Australia, principally in the printing, railway and building industries. The Appren-
ticeship Act of Wisconsin, for example, lays down that the State is to be a third party to
the apprenticeship contract in order to secure its observance and protect the interests of
the apprentices. The form of the indenture is laid down in detail by the Act and the
regulations issued under it. Copies of each indenture must be sent to the Industrial
Commission, which is an official body entrusted with the preparation and application of
labour legislation. The Commission keeps in touch with employers and apprentices.
All trade agreements affecting apprenticeship require its approval. It also supervises
the execution of the standard schedules of instruction which have been drawn up for the
principal trades by joint committees of employers and workers. It is the sole authority
which may permit the annulment of an indenture. The Act further lays down on the
basis of statistical investigation the number of apprentices to be admitted to each industry.
Previously the only limitation was on the number of apprentices to be engaged by each
employer. The rates of pay are also fixed on a statistical basis.
An interesting innovation has been introduced in New South Wales. Boys can be
apprenticed to a group of employers, as well as to an individual. In this case the members
of the Employers' Association are jointly, but not severally, liable for the performance of
the contract, and the apprentice may work for any member of the Association. This
helps to ensure that the apprentice receives as thorough a training as possible, and, especially
in a highly-organised trade, largely overcomes the difficulty caused by the apprentice's
desire to move from one establishment to another.
In addition to the action taken by the public authorities, the article also mentions
some interesting attempts made by certain large undertakings, particularly the railway

LABOUR-OWNED BAKERY.
Experiment Proves a Success.
In Bermondsey there is a bakery which serves more than 50,000 houses each day.
In this bakery the turn-over is more than £150,0oo a year, the hundred-odd employees.
get 12s. 6d. above trade union wages, for a 44-hour week, and three weeks' holiday in the
vear.
It is run by the Bermondsey branch of the Independent Labour Party, Dr. Alfred
Salter, Labour M.P. for Bermondsey, being the founder and secretary of the concern.
When he was asked by the Westminster Gazette what was the customers' side of the
picture he said emphatically: "We give them the best bread on the market at about a
penny less than anybody else, besides is. discount in the pound."
Start Without Capital.
The Labour bakery was started in the summer of 1914 without a penny of capital,
on borrowed money. To-day it has paid off nearly all its mortgages, has buildings worth
13,000, and has been visited by a deputation from the local Master Bakers asking it to
raise its prices.
Dr. Salter declares that the great lesson this concern teaches is that vital distributive
services can be run at enormously decreased cost if they are properly organised in areas.
He holds that bread, milk, and similar commodities ought to be supplied in the same way
es letters are distributed by the Government.
"We have whole streets," he said, " where practically every house is supplied by us;
mother borough you would find five or six distributors' vans in each street."-West-
sch Gazette, 25th June, 1923.

"AMBIGUOUS LANGUAGE."
Alderman Hill, M.P., and Decisions on Ex-Service Men's Pensions.
Alderman A. Hill, M.P., asked the Minister of Pensions in the House of Commons
yesterday if he was aware that dissatisfaction existed amongst ex-Service men owing to
decisions given by the assessment tribunal committee: seeing that the papers declaring
such decisions are worded in language which is ambiguous, would he take measures to so
consider the reversing of the regulations which set aside the final awards, so that the men
might receive the amounts due to them after winning the appeal, and so do away with the
periods of waiting which take place under the present system.
Major Tryon replied that steps had been already taken to make clear the meaning of
a decision by a tribunal setting aside a final award by incorporating an explanatory note
in the official forms on which those decisions were announced.
The Minister added: I should like to take this opportunity of again explaining that a
final award is simply a final decision by the Ministry as to a man's degree of disablement.
If the tribunal set aside a final award, their action merely implies that, in their opinion,
the case is not, at the time, suitable for a final decision. It does not necessarily mean
that the tribunal disagree with the rate at which disablement has been assessed, nor does
it imply that any further compensation is immediately payable. In such cases the effect
of the tribunal's decision is merely to restore the man to the position he was in before a
final award was declared.

TRADE BOARD PROSECUTION.
Breach of Regulations Costs £58.
At Old Street Police Court, on Wednesday last week, Abraham Smith, of 36, Brushfield
Street, Spitalfields, was summoned that on 17th March he unlawfully failed to pay wages
at not less than the minimum rate fixed by the Boot and Shoe Repairing Trade Board
(Great Britain) in pursuance of the Trade Boards Act, 1909 and 1918, to Frederick Henry
White, being one of the said workers. There were further summonses for furnishing to
William Jackson, an officer appointed under the provisions of the Trades Boards Act,
information in respect to the payment of certain wages due to White, knowing the same
to be false, and for producing a record of wages with respect to the payment of White
which was false in a material particular.
Hyman Smith, of 36, Brushfield Street, was summoned for causing to be produced
to Mr. Jackson a record of wages due to White, knowing the same to be false.
Mr. Kemp, barrister, who prosecuted, said the Act only applied to certain scheduled
trades, and the summonses had regard to the boot and shoe trade.
Mr. Clarke Hall: It is apparently a recent addition to the schedule ?

SHOE TRADE CUSTOM DISPUTE.
Foreman Gets Damages Against Employer.
At Leicester County Court, to-day, judgment was given for £9 19s. in a case in which
Albert Feddament, 4, Harvey Lane, claimed for damages in lieu of notice from Bert
Gamble, boot manufacturer, 3, Elton Street.
Plaintiff contended that he was a staff man, and should have a month's and not a week's
notice.
Claimant said he was engaged in March, 1918, as an operator, at £4 10s. a week.
Shoe operatives' wages were afterwards reduced and witness was only paid £4 6s. Sub-
sequently defendant asked him if he would take charge of the room, and he agreed to do
so, but not officially. At the beginning of this year defendant called him to the office
and said he could not pay for a foreman, trade being bad, and witness agreed to act as
working foreman at £4 4s. a week, a month's notice to be given on either side. On May
th witness asked for an increase in wages but, the following day, defendant not only
fused the increase, but gave witness a week's notice.
Replying to Mr. H. G. Bennett, for the defence, witness agreed that notices were
hibited stating that all employees were subject to a week's notice, but he contended
t he was a staff man, and should have a month's notice.
For the defence Mr. Gamble gave evidence that plaintiff was only entitled to a week's
A foreman clicker, employed by defendant, said that he considered he would
be entitled to a week's notice.
is Honour gave judgment in claimant's favour of £9 19s. and costs.—Leicester
th, 26th June, 1923.

MONTHLY REPORT.

27TH AUGUST, 1923
FELLOW MEMBERS,
STATE OF TRADE.
The state of Trade during the past month has upon the whole been quiet,
the figures extracted from the Gazette issued by the Ministry of Labour
being as follow :-

BOOT AND SHOE INDUSTRY.

There was a slight improvement at some centres in the middle and at the end of July,
principally with firms which had received urgent orders in preparation for the holiday
season. The improvement, however, was not general : on the contrary, the net effect
of the changes at the different centres was a slight further decline; and short time was
worked to a considerable extent in nearly all districts. There was much variation as
between one firm and another; some firms, even in centres where work was generally
slack, being temporarily busy on urgent orders.
Among workpeople covered by the Unemployment Insurance Acts, the number
registered as unemployed (including a due proportion of those working systematic short
time in such a manner as to qualify for benefit) was 15,047 at 23rd July, 1923, compared
with 12,820 at 25th June, 1923.
Employment in London was very bad, and worse than in June. At Leicester and at
Hinckley it was slack, and worse than in June; short time was general. At Northampton
some firms were busy while others were suspending workpeople; on the whole there was
not much change. Employment was very bad at Wellingborough; very few firms were
working full time. In the Higham, Rushden and Irthlingborough district employment
was better than a year ago; but short time was worked by some firms. Employment
remained slack at Kettering, though there was an improvement at the end of the month :
the average time worked was reported to be not more than three-quarters of full time.
At Stafford employment declined, and was rather slack; at Norwich a further decline
was reported, and employment was bad. There was a further improvement in the Bristol

ment was very bad, and short time was general.
In Scotland an improvement was reported at Maybole, Ayr and Aberdeen; but
employment remained quiet at Glasgow and bad at Dundee and at Arbroath.

POLITICAL AND INDUSTRIAL SITUATION.
Parliament has adjourned until November next. It cannot be said that
the Session which was brought to a close on the 2nd inst. was distinguished
by any outstanding measures which would bring permanent relief to the people
of the country, or to the speedy solution of the difficulties in connection with
the international position. It is quite true that a number of speeches have
been made expressing regret at the situation, and the desire to see a better
time, but the fact remains that there was very little done to relieve the situation
so far as real legislation is concerned.
We still have with us the vast army of unemployed, although to those
who have eyes to see there is a tremendous amount of employment could be
found in this country, apart altogether from the question of the export
trade. It is indeed a significant fact that even the great employers of the
country have been moved to send a letter to the Prime Minister condemning
the Government schemes to relieve unemployment, as being inadequate. This
letter was signed by Sir Allan M. Smith, M.P. (Chairman) and Mr. P. J.
Hannon (Secretary), and the attention of the Prime Minister is called to the
fact that upon the 25th July, 1923, they addressed a letter to him offering
in outline of constructive policy, as they contend that the proposals of the
Minister of Labour are "quite inadequate, and certain facts postulated by
im in his speech are likely to mislead the casual reader." The letter
ncludes as follows :-
"
"The problem is urgent and does not admit of a single day's delay.
We are approaching our fourth winter of unemployment with, in addition,
the cumulative effect of the last three winters."

NATIONAL AGREEMENT (DECEMBER) 1922.
Some confusion appears to exist regarding the application of the several
rates and adjustments of piecework statements in connection with the above-
named Agreement. The question of the application of the Repairing (Trade
Board) Rates must not be confused with the Agreement relative to the manu-
facturing side of the industry. We, therefore, print below the Clause affecting
the operations of the Minimum Wage and Graduated Scale Rates and adjust-
ments of Piecework Statement Rates.
8. THE MINIMUM DAY WAGE RATES as set out in the Interim Agreement, Feb-
ruary, 1922, and based upon the index figure of the cost of living are confirmed, or
varied and confirmed, as under. Changes are to become effective on the first pay day
in June or November, and are to be based upon the Board of Trade Index figures
for the preceding April or September.
This means the Board of Trade Index figures for the month of September,
published in the October issue of the Labour Gazette, will be the determining
factor for the wage rate in November.
REMEMBER THE FIFTEENTH!
Once again we feel bound to call the serious attention of Branch Secretaries
