GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
Trade during the last month, wherein one has to meet employers, it is very
depressing to learn from most of them that trade is in a parlous state. No orders, no
prospects, hope being the only asset the trade seems to possess at the present time, and
with the New Unionism spirit, which we all meet with when organising, certain people
refuse to assist in the Unions unless they can get something more out of them than what
they have paid in. Although I have been confronted at open-air meetings recently with
the query: " Was 56s. enough to live on ?" "Why is it that the shoe operative pays is.
per week contribution and the building trade a Holiday Fund ?" "What benefits do they give?" So far as the
trade is concerned, wherein do they suffer as compared with other industries, and what
part has the questioner taken to improve the position? The "something for nothing
non-Union workshop, and even some more enlightened quarters where it is least expected.
spirit needs no advertisement. It will find its way out at every street corner and in every
shoe factory is outside the pale of our Union-it passes my comprehension. I am afraid we
My trouble at the present time is to conceive why any man or woman working in a
can only continue our work of organising, and hoping that some day that these people
will see the light.
EARLS BARTON, Wellingborough, has had trouble at Barker's. The firm wish
to put the men on day labour, hoping by that means, they say, to get better work.
This may be true, but the operatives hold the other view, and we share it with them,
that when day labour is called for after working piecework, we have only one idea-and it
is better for the employers to know it-that we, or at least I believe the object is to get
piecework quantities at day labour minimum, and from my point of view such firms are
suspect. Then when these firms find that the men are not more remunerative they wish
to return to piecework; but this can only be condoned when such firms have satisfied us
the fundamental principles of the terms of settlement, and in this respect I trust the local
and the operatives that they are in a position to carry out to the satisfaction of ourselves
and, therefore, not so strong as in ordinary times, and the temptation to stretch the terms
officials will keep a sharp look-out because, owing to bad trade, employers are very nervous
is very great. Indeed, we visited one firm that admitted making up stuff described as
"muck," and when we asked the question "Why so?" the answer was that it was to
oblige a customer. We replied we cannot alter our prices or condone such to oblige cus-
tomers who are prepared to palm off upon the public stuff described as "muck," and it is
not creditable to any firm to be prepared to make up such stuff which is only being used
to gull the public, and to take a mean advantage of the poor. In this connection I am
convinced that as a Union we must expose "shoddy"; the employers having failed to
tackle the same.
WELLINGBOROUGH have purchased a splendid building for new offices in Church Street ;
spacious, quiet and very roomy. The Branch are to be congratulated on making a move
so beneficial to their large and, I hope, growing membership. Here they will be able,
under pleasant conditions and surroundings, to do their work and administer to the require-
ments of our members there, who, I believe, will be pleased to know that they are members
of a Branch that caters for them in so pleasant a manner.
A meeting of our side of the Board of Arbitration for the County of LEICESTERSHIRE
was held, when we appointed our officers for the ensuing year. Mr. D. Astley was invited
to act as Chairman, the idea being that it is much nicer for the successful working of the
Board to change our Chairman and Vice-Chairman occasionally so as to give all members
the chance of filling the position.
The GENERAL FEDERATION OF TRADE UNIONS held their usual monthly meeting, and
we are sorry to learn that the trouble between the boilermakers and their employers is
still in progress. Our appeal to the Ministry of Labour and interview have borne no
fruit, as we knew it would not. There have been times when Unions have said, "Hands
off," and we are not surprised when employers take up the same attitude, and whilst
private employment exists this policy is likely to continue. We have several Unions
who say that they do not believe in compulsory arbitration, and if we say that, how can
e deny the employers the same right?
We have also had a dispute at the firm of J. W. BLACK, OF SOUTH WIGSTON, but as
Chairman of the Company has a business at Kettering we journeyed there, saw the
inciple, and we hope we have persuaded him, although somewhat reluctantly, to agree
hour suggestion to make the reduction no more than the increase; he complied, although
could not imagine a state of mind that wanted to take more off the wages than they
on, that is why we say alertness must be our motto.

ORGANISERS' MONTHLY REPORTS.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
My last report was given on 24th July. On 25th July I went to Messrs. Ward,
The "Queensville" Boot Works, Stafford, and asked permission to speak to the females
in the closing room. One of the partners took me to the machine room straight away
and asked the forewoman to stop the machinery for me to speak. I can remember our
Branch Officers many years ago asking the Management of the C.W.S. Boot Works, at
Leicester, for the opportunity to speak to the workers on the premises after working
hours, but this was never granted. It is a pleasure to record of a private firm stopping
the machinery for five minutes to allow me to speak to the machinists. On the 26th I
went to Stone to consult with the Secretary there on a plan of organising. On the 27th
I spoke at a heel-making firm at Stafford; we made some members here. On the 28th
I saw one of the heads of Messrs. Bostock, "Lotus" Ltd., over speaking at their works
at Stone. I was granted the privilege of speaking in three departments after the August
holidays. In answer to a message from Mr. Poulton, I went to London on the 29th to speak
on the "Back-to-the-Union" Campaign. The first meeting was at Clapham Common. There
were two platforms and the attendance was good. The evening meeting was at Putney
Bridge. This was a fine meeting. Many trade union banners were in evidence and made
a circle for the meeting. I should say that the London trade union officers in charge of
the work received me right well and thanked our Union for my presence.
After the holidays I went to Stone and spoke on three occasions in the turnshoe
department to the men, in the closing room and stock room. Mr. R. Dunn, Secretary of
the Stafford Branch, accompanied me. We were given ten minutes in the firm's time
this report will appreciate the generous feeling shown to us by Messrs. Bostock in allowing
I know that the Council of our Union and the members who read
us to speak inside their great works at Stafford and Stone. Speaking for the local officials

in the spirit the resolution agreed on over three years ago, that it was in the best interests
members as a result of our propaganda; about 40 new names were brought in to-day for
Mr. Dunn to add to the Stafford Branch. This evening we are speaking to the females

It is difficult to understand the apathy and indifference that far too frequently is
shown in regard to industrial conditions. It is not satisfaction with present conditions
that give rise to it, for complaints are frequent enough, in fact, these very people are the
distinct and separate from themselves. The Union is strong or weak according to how
ones that ask "what is the Union going to do about it?
the workers make it strong or weak. And in this respect mere membership is not suffi-

This is absolutely essential. Every happening or attempt to vary the conditions at

beginning than it is after a period of time, when perhaps it will be claimed that the work-
people are satisfied, and have endorsed the change. If infringements or attempts at same
were reported at once on every occasion, our difficulties would not be so great as they are.
Nothing is gained by neglect, and members should understand that it is just as much a
responsibility of theirs to report as it is for the official to investigate when the report is
made.
The Union is like a machine, every part must be working accurately if the best results
are to be obtained, and everyone who holds a card is a part of the machine.
Of course it is all to the good if we have none outside the ranks, and I am pleased
to say that some members are being made. The difficulty is to understand why they are
outside. The record of the Union, both in regard to the conditions of labour in the factory,
as well as to benefits, justify one in saying, that instead of people pleading they cannot
afford to belong to it, it should be the other way, that they cannot afford to be outside the
Union and its beneficent influence.
There is no doubt that in some districts our task is greater than in others, and to say
the least of it Kingswood is not one of the easiest, but I am fully persuaded that in time it
will be in line with the rest of the country. We have got things on the move, the successes
art have come to us have awakened interest in others, and workers are asking why they
ould not have the full advantage attached to our agreements. The eyes of the operatives
turned in our direction and we will show that the Union is a power for good in the
fustry, and that not even in Kingswood shall the worst type of employer set the pace,
determine how the boot operative shall work and live.
Just, 1923.
WALTER R. SMITH.

keep the National Union in the van of progressive forces fighting to advance
or defend the best interests of all workers, we are serving the real interests of
our class.

CORRESPONDENCE.
The Council do not hold themselves responsible for the views expressed by Correspondents.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
51, ST. GEORGE STREET,
NORWICH,
8th August, 1923.
It will be remembered that at the Conference of the Union held in London during
Whit-week a resolution was carried instructing the Executive Council to discontinue
affiliation with the General Federation of Trade Unions. The resolution emanated from
Norwich, and was moved by myself with a speech, may I say, that did at least attempt
to present the true position of the Federation in its relationship to the British Labour
Movement.
Now, whatever may be our personal opinions on the matter, it certainly does not
warrant the General President misrepresenting the position in the way he does in his
report as published in the July Report.
He states:
GENERAL FEDERATION OF TRADE UNIONS.-During the month a most interest.
ing Annual Meeting of the General Federation of Trade Unions at Bridlington was
held, where, on all hands, very profound regrets were expressed that our Union,
bring about affiliation with the Trades Union Congress, should withdraw on the
commercial and capitalistic policy is contrary to the spirit of any kind of Trades
ground that having paid £30,000 in we have had only £800 out. This non-unionist.
penny in the Trade Unionism, the kind which is too shallow to be of any good
nineties, and savours
to the movement.
May I congratulate the General President on a fine effort at "Gutter Journalism,"
for surely the pages of our Report have never before contained such dishonest and libellous
statements against the delegates assembled at Conference.
I stated the Federation had failed to rise to the needs of the modern movement,
that it in fact was obsolete machinery and operated only to overlap and interfere with the
work of the Labour Party (Political) and Trades Union Congress (Industrial).
The examination of the case against the Federation was conducted from a quite
proper standpoint, viz. :-Is the Federation functioning to the general benefit of the
Labour Movement? The answer was a very decided NO, even from those who did not vote
for the resolution.
Our case is that every effort should be given to strengthen the Labour Party politically,
and that all interests should be consolidated in making the Trade Union Congress the main-
spring in industrial organisations.
Much can and will be done if some of the fourth and fifth rate Labour Leaders will
subordinate their assumed importance to the welfare of the wider movement. The time
has come when the Congress must do the work the Federation has refrained from doing,
viz.:-Co-ordinate and consolidate the interests of the 5,000,000 members whom they
operate for.
Much more was said, and on those lines the discussion ranged, although I incidentally
mentioned that the financial comparisons would not win for the Union much glory. To
pay in fees during a period the sum of £23,000 and receive in return £755 in fighting dis-
putes that cost £21,000 was, to my mind, not quite the right way to organise our financial
resources.
No, Mr. Richards, the Federation will not do, its only credential is its title. What
useful purpose it might have served has been prostituted by some of its leaders ("Top-
notchers "), and because we, the smaller fry, dare raise our voices against a continuance
of these things we become subject to abuse and misrepresentation (ever the weapons of
the incompetent) from men such as Mr. Richards.
Again I say the decision to withdraw was not prompted by financial reasons, and
Mr. Richards knows that to be true. I hope, therefore, when Mr. Richards meets his
friends of the Federation he will do our Union a service by stating the true facts of the case
and incidentally win for himself respect from those who differ with him.
Yours very truly,
FRED C. JEX,
Branch Secretary, Norwich Branch.

Now a trade union is a voluntary association of persons to obtain and retain fair
vires) and having objects in restraint of trade, they are illegal bodies.
others guilty of embezzling their funds. The Act of 1871 gave trade unions just enough
Up to 1871 the members of a trade union had no legal redress against its officials or
legislation to hold land or property to enable them to carry on their proper business;
while not enough to expose them to actions at law. (This Act only applied to unions
registered.)
But in 1901, in the famous Taff Vale case, a judgment was given which made the
funds of a union liable for the actions and injuries caused by its servants, agents or officials.
This judgment was followed by others in the next seven years which made trade unions
liable for £22,000.

As a result of much agitation another Act called the Trade Disputes Act (1906), was
(picketing). This Act absolutely reversed the Taff Vale decision, by making union funds
union may be sued for civil wrongs, they cannot be taken to law for watching or besetting
free from liability for actions of injurious nature by union servants, agents or officials.

While the Act of 1906 made it possible for unions doing as the members wished with the
funds, it prevented them from doing anything outside the objects. If they wished to do
something outside the objects, after obtaining a unanimous vote of the members, they
could apply for power from the Registrar of Trade Unions and Friendly Societies.
If the union's representatives did not first obtain a unanimous vote, objectors could
get an injunction to restrain by applying to the Courts. A case in point is that of Mr.
Osborn, a member of the Railway Servants' Union. He objected to being compelled
the political candidates for whom the political fund was instituted. The judgment to
restrain was upheld by the House of Lords.
political fund, on the ground that his
It was followed by the Act of 1913, which gave members of a trade union or similar
society the right to contract out of the political, or any other special fund which was not
in existence, and which they did not accept or agree to pay to on joining. This did not
affect their right to draw all other benefits from other funds to which they subscribed.
On the face of it this power to contract out is very fair. It seems so fair that the
desires of the movers of the new Bill to reverse the position and make those who wish
to subscribe, contract in, can only be interpreted in one way. That is, they think, by doing
so they can weaken the financial support the trade unions give to the Labour Party, and
forestall the time when Labour shall come into its own.

Summary.
(1) Trade Unions are not liable to be taken to law for crimes—" Nobody to be kicked,
or soul to be damned."
(2) Unions are free from actions for civil wrongs. They must manage their own
domestic affairs.
(3) Breach of contract or change in objects, gives members right to restrain and
contract out.

by short-sighted employers of labour, has long since won its rightful place in the world
of industry. Even by those who were most bitterly opposed to it it is now accepted as
indispensable to the modern system of collective bargaining, which on one side ensures
fair treatment for many who are individually unable to command it, and, on the other,
introduces an element of stability in the cost of labour." -The Times, 8th August, 1923.

DEAR MR. POULTON,
Geneva has sent me a copy of your letter of 30th June, and of their reply, together
with the statement accompanying that reply.
I am delighted to learn that there is a prospect of your broadcasting a statement on
the work of the International Labour Office. The wireless affords an excellent medium
for publicity, and when I heard Mr. Clynes broadcasting a few days ago on the League of
Nations, without a mention of the Labour Organisation, I thought what an excellent
thing it would be if someone who could speak with authority on the subject were able to
give a short talk devoted to our work.
I have read the statement prepared by Geneva. It certainly contains most of the
facts though I fancy you will agree with me that they are presented in a rather uninteresting
way. From personal knowledge of a few owners of wireless receiving sets, I should say
that they prefer to have their information presented in a fairly popular manner, or, at any
rate, with some sort of " colour" or "life." I have no doubt you will realise what I am
trying to indicate and will easily clothe with flesh the rather dry bones of the Geneva
statement. I am only writing to endorse the implied offer of Geneva of any help which
this office can give you in the preparation of the material or text of your pronouncement.
In particular, I think you may be glad to have the enclosed copy of a pamphlet we have
produced on "The I.L.O. and the East," which is brought approximately up to date by
the accompanying communiqué issued a few days ago relating to action in China (see pages
477-478 in July Report). If there are any points on which you think we might help you
please do not hesitate to let us know. I personally, am going on leave for two or three
weeks at the end of this week, but Mr. Robbins will gladly supply you with anything
you need.
Yours sincerely,

WORLD INFORMATION OFFICE.
Governments Greater Use of International Labour Office.
The steady increase in the use which is being made by Governments of the Inter-
national Labour Office of the League of Nations as a world information department on
industrial and labour questions is revealed in a statement which has just been issued by
that Office on information supplied during the last six months.
Among the requests from Governments which were answered in that period were the
following :-
UNITED STATES (Bureau of Labour Statistics, Department of Labour): Collective
agreements between employers' and workers' organisations in the Piedmont building
industry.
NORWAY (Ministry of Social Affairs): Arbitration in various countries.
POLAND (Social Attaché Polish Government to the International Labour Office):
Output in various occupations and in various countries, international organisations and
central labour organisations in various countries, legislation for the protection of com-
mercial employees Czecho-slovak, Danish and Serbian legislation concerning health, old
age and accident insurance. Social and economic results of the eight-hour day.
ITALY (Ministry of Labour): Representation of trade unions on advisory bodies
dealing with labour questions.
INDIA (Bombay Labour Office): Hours of work in the textile and metal industries
and for dockers and railway and tramway workers, Norwegian Compulsory Arbitration Act.
CHILI (Labour Office, Santiago de Chili): Statutory protection of maternity.
KINGDOM OF THE SERBS, CROATS AND SLOVENES (Ministry of Social Policy): Legisla-
tion in various countries concerning the protection of seamen.
FRANCE (Ministry of Commerce and Industry): Number of spindles used in the
worsted industry in different countries.
GERMANY (Federal Ministry of Labour): Social insurance institutions in various
countries.
These individual answers, of which the variety is noteworthy, are in addition to the
regular study made by the International Labour Office of current labour questions through-
out the world, the results of which are published in Industrial and Labour Information,
its weekly journal, and the International Labour Review, its monthly periodical.

```
A WAGE BAROMETER.
e and Fall since 1914.
Under the title of "Wage Changes in Various Countries, 1914 to 1922" (Studies and
rts, D.10; 25.) the International Office of the League of Nations has just published
dy of the variations in the wage level since 1914 in the chief industrial countries of
forid.
spite of such obstacles as fluctuations of exchange, lack of uniform statistical
al, and variations in the standard of living of the workers in different countries,
```

---
532
an effort is made not merely to trace the movement of money wages but, by comparing
these changes with those of the general level of prices, to estimate the combined result on
the real wages of the workers, and further, by comparison with the level of wages in 1914.
to determine how far money wages have been adjusted to the cost of living.
The study is a continuation of an earlier report covering the period 1914 to 1921.
In that study the period was mainly one of rising prices and wages during the war and in
the post-war industrial boom. Indications were also given as to the tendencies of moncy
it is to this period that attention is mainly directed, and, as there are signs of a cessation
of the period of falling prices, it has been possible to cover the greater part of the period
of " deflation" which has been common to most countries outside Central Europe,
In the present study,
Figures are given for the United Kingdom, France, Belgium, Sweden, Norway.
Denmark, the Netherlands, Italy, Germany, Austria, Bulgaria, United States, Canada,
South Africa, Australia and India.
The chief general conclusions may be summarised as follows:-
According to the level of real wages, the above countries may be divided into three
main groups :--
(1) Those in which real wages are definitely higher than before the war, viz. Sweden.
Norway, Denmark, the Netherlands and Australia;
(2) Those in which the level is about the same as, or only slightly higher than, in
1914, viz.: The United Kingdom, France, Belgium, Italy, the United States,
Canada and South Africa;
and Bulgaria.
(3) Those in which real wages are lower than before the war, viz. : Germany, Austria
There is a general tendency for real wages to fall during periods of rising prices and to
rise when prices are falling. In other words there is a " time lag" in adjusting wage rates
to changes in the level of prices, and this acts against the workers when prices are rising
and in their favour when prices are falling.
There appears to be a tendency for wage rates to continue to rise after the rise in prices
has ceased to continue to fall after the cost of living has ceased to fall. Thus at the present
time, in a number of countries in which prices rapidly fell during 1921 and the beginning
of 1922, there has been a general tendency for this movement to cease, and a certain stabilisation of
prices is observed. In a number of these countries, however, reductions in rates of wages
continue to be effected for a further period and real wages suffer decline.
In the earlier study it was shown that there was a general tendency during periods
of rising prices for the relative differences between the wages of skilled and unskilled
workers, of men and women, and of professional workers and manual workers to be dimin-
ished, so that in many cases there was less inequality between the wages of these groups
in 1921, than in 1914. These changes are maintained in Germany and Austria where prices
continued to rise during all or most of 1922, and in these countries the relative differences
between the wages of skilled and unskilled workers are now very small. In countries
where prices have fallen, there appears to have been a reversal of the above tendencies
which operated when prices were rising. Thus in periods of falling prices there appears
to have been a tendency for the lower paid or unskilled workers to suffer greater pro-
portionate reductions than the higher paid or skilled groups.
WHITE PHOSPHORUS IN MATCH-MAKING.
Prohibition Effects on Italian Industry.
Interesting details of the effect of the prohibition of the use of white phosphorus on
the match-making industry in Italy are given in a report of the Senate Committee on a
Bill to convert into an Act the prohibition decree of 23rd December, 1920.
A Convention on this subject was adopted in 1905 at Berne and between that date
and 1914 it was adopted by thirteen countries, including Great Britain. The First Inter-
national Labour Conference of the League of Nations, held at Washington in 1919, recom-
mended that each country which had not already done so should adhere to the Berne
Convention, the result being that exactly the same number of States (thirteen) have done
so between 1919-1923 as did between 1905-1914.
The use of white phosphorus in the match industry has been entirely prohibited in
Italy since January, 1921, says the Report, and during the two years the decree has been
in operation it has been noted that the alteration of equipment has not given rise to the
difficulties and the inconveniences that had been feared. There are at present 90 factories
in the industry, employing about 8,000 workers and including nearly 20 small undertakings
employing on an average not more than five workers. As a result of the prohibition of
the use of white phosphorus there were more or less long periods of suspension of work
when the Decree first came into operation, but no factory has actually been closed down.

```text
man was studied by the meeting of experts on the subject, just held at the Internatio
Labour Office of the League of Nations at Geneva, is revealed by the resolutions adopt
which are given in full below.
This meeting was attended by experts from thirteen countries, including Lt.-

of Labour; General Sir A. H. Russell (New Zealand); Brig. Gen. J. S. Wylie (S

The following were the resolutions adopted :---
```

Essential Provisions to be included in all legislation, regulations or
agreements, relating to employment for disabled men.
1. Persons entitled to benefit.
(1) All legislation, regulations or agreements should be applicable to all disabled men
in receipt of pensions, whatever methods of compensation are adopted by the pensions
legislation.
(2) All legislation, regulations or agreements should be of a permanent character.
(3) The experience acquired in safeguarding the employment of the war-disabled
could appropriately be applied for the benefit of disabled workers and other disabled
persons.
2. Undertakings covered by legislation, regulations or agreements.
(1) All legislation, regulations or agreements should be applicable to all undertakings
in which the minimum number of workers employed reaches or exceeds a certain figure
to be fixed in each State.
(2) Undertakings subject to such legislation, regulations or agreements by virtue
of the number of persons employed therein should, however, be able on application to
obtain exemptions, when it is proved that the employment of disabled men in such under-
takings is impossible or particularly difficult. Such exemptions should be granted by
authorities entrusted with the application of such legislation, regulations or agreements,
in which the associations comprising disabled men and the trade organisations affected
should be represented.
(3) Undertakings subject to such legislation, regulations or agreements which obtain
Nemptions should be liable to the payment of a compensatory tax or charge, the produce
of which should be applied for the benefit of the persons entitled to the benefit of such
legislation, regulations or agreements.
Percentage of disabled men to be employed.
All such legislation, regulations or agreements should fix a general percentage of
Sled men to be employed. Such percentage should, in each State, be calculated
ving regard to the total number of wage-earners, the number of disabled men entitled


---
536
to benefit and the variations from the general percentage which it may be necessary to
allow to certain undertakings or certain classes of undertakings.
(2) Variations from the general percentage should be allowed to undertakings applying
for the same, when it is proved that it is impossible or very difficult for them to attain
the general percentage, Such variations should be granted by the authorities entrusted
with the application of such regulations, legislation or agreements, in which the associa-
tions comprising disabled men and the trade organisations concerned should be represented.
4. Administrative organisation of employment agencies.
(1) In countries which, in conformity with the decisions of the International Labour
Conference at Washington, have established a general and complete system of public
employment agencies, under the control of a central authority, with provision for the
joint consultation of employers and workers, it would be desirable to entrust the application
of such legislation, regulations or agreements to such public employment agencies.
(2) Such public employment agencies should, wherever necessary and particularly
in the larger towns, establish special sections for finding employment for disabled men.
Such sections should act in close co-operation with any government department dealing
with disabled men and with the associations comprising disabled men.
(3) The Committees administering the public employment agencies should include
representatives of any government department dealing with disabled men and of the
associations comprising disabled men, who should be directly entrusted with the application
of the legislation, regulations or agreements relating to the employment of disabled men.
(4) The action of the public employment agencies should be supplemented, wherever
it is considered necessary, by the action of any government department dealing with
disabled men and of the associations comprising disabled men.
(5) In States possessing both a system of public employment agencies and a general
system of social welfare institutions for the benefit of all classes of disabled persons, what-
ever be the origin of their disability, such institutions, which possess great experience of
the medical and vocational aspects of the problem of the disabled, might be entrusted
with finding employment for disabled men. Such institutions should, in the matter
of finding employment, act in close collaboration with the public employment agencies.
5. Wages of disabled men.
(1) The amount of the pension of a disabled man should not have any effect on wages,
but wages should be fixed independently of the pension.
(2) In principle, the wages of a disabled man should be equal to the normal current
wages of ordinary workers carrying on the same vocation in the same district, and should
be subject to the additions of every kind payable to ordinary workers according to the
same methods of calculation.
Nevertheless, in countries in which, owing to the economic situation, the employment
of all disabled men on full wages is not possible, and in very exceptional cases in which,
notwithstanding the efforts made to secure adequate vocational re-education and vocational
guidance, the vocational capacity of the disabled remains appreciably reduced, it is
admissible that such disabled men should not receive the whole of the basic wages of
ordinary workers, but subject to the following reservations :-
(a) Such reduction shall not apply to cost of living bonuses and increments
on grounds of seniority, or to any payment based on other considerations
than output.
(b) The conditions in which and the limits within which such reductions of
wages may be allowed shall, in each State, be the subject of provisions
contained in legislation, regulations and agreements, and agreements of
service involving such reductions shall be subject to approval by authorities
including representatives of the associations comprising disabled men and
the trade organisations concerned.
(c) The associations comprising disabled men shall be empowered to take legal
proceedings for enforcing the penalties and damages imposed by the general
labour legislation and the legislation, regulations or agreements, especially
applicable to the employment of disabled men.
6. Dismissal.
In all such legislation, regulations or agreements, disabled men shall be specially
protected against wrongful dismissal, both by the provision of a period of notice and by
providing for the submission of disputes between a disabled man and his employer to one
of the authorities entrusted with the application of such legislation, regulations or agree-
ments in which the associations comprising disabled men and the trade organisations
concerned shall be represented.

THE RURAL WORKER.
International Meeting in Geneva.
The first session of the Joint Advisory Committee on Agriculture, set up by the Inter-
national Labour Office of the League of Nations, and the International Institute of N-
culture, opened in Geneva yesterday (Wednesday, 22nd August).
The Committee, which was created for the purpose of ensuring collaboration bet-
the two organisations on questions affecting the agricultural worker, consists of the
representatives of the Governing Body of the International Labour Office and three repre-
sentatives of the Permanent Committee of the International Institute of Agriculture
and has the assistance of a number of experts chosen from national and international
bolies representative of practical agriculturists, among them being Mr. Rowland R. Robbins,
C.B.E., Chairman of the Labour Committee of the National Farmers' Union, and Mr.
R. B. Walker, General Secretary of the National Union of Agricultural Workers. Sir
Thomas Elliott (Great Britain) is one of the representatives of the International Institute
of Agriculture.
France, Belgium, Germany, Italy, Poland, Japan, Spain, and Norway.
Other countries, from which members of the Committee and experts are drawn, include
The questions put before the Committee by the International Labour Office for ex-
amination at the present session are: -
(1) Vocational education of agricultural workers;
(2) Workers' co-operation in agriculture;
(3) Prevention of anthrax infection in flocks;
(4) Agricultural aspects of items on the Agenda for the International Labour
Conference of 1924, including the development of facilities for the utilisation
of workers' leisure, and equality of treatment for national and foreign workers
as regards compensation for accidents.
The Committee will act solely in an advisory capacity. Any conclusions it may reach
will be of the nature of recommendations, and it will be for the Governing Body of the
International Labour Office, which meets next October, to take the necessary decisions
with regard to any action of the Office based on these recommendations.
FACTORY INSPECTION.
Problem of International Uniformity.
The fifth session of the International Labour Conference set up by the Peace Treaty,
which will be held in Geneva in October, will be devoted to the examination, from the
international and national points of view, of "General Principles for the Organisation
of Factory Inspection."
It may be recalled that among the principles for regulating labour conditions men-
tioned in Article 427 of the Treaty as being particularly important and urgent is included
the following: "Each State should make provision for a system of inspection in which
women should take part, in order to ensure the enforcement of the laws and regulations
for the protection of the employed." It was felt by those who drafted the section of the
Treaty by which the International Labour Organisation is established, that it would be
useless to adopt a programme of international labour legislation unless some adequate
system existed in each country for its application and supervision on appreciably similar
bases. One of the most serious objections hitherto raised against the scheme of legislation
instituted by the Treaty is that Conventions of the International Labour Conference may
perhaps not be applied with equal strictness in all the States which ratify them, and it is
partly in order to remove this objection that the coming Conference is to be invited to lay
down fundamental principles on which the supervision of the enforcement of labour legis-
lation in all countries might be organised.
In accordance with the regular procedure now followed in connection with the Inter-
national Labour Conference, a series of questions on the subject to be discussed has been
addressed by the International Labour Office to all the States which are members of the
organisation. These questions, which are preceded by a survey of the chief problems
involved in the subject, are designed to elicit exact information as to the views taken by
the various Governments of the object and scope of factory inspection, the nature of the
functions and powers entrusted to factory inspectors, and the methods by which factory
inspection should be organised and conducted.
Reports embodying the replies to this questionnaire will be prepared for distribution
to the delegates attending the Conference, and the ground will thus be cleared for the
examination of common general principles which might be accepted by all States and
embodied in a formal Recommendation of the Conference for submission to Parliaments.

LEICESTER COUNTY ARBITRATION BOARD.

Appointment of New Officers.

The annual meeting of the County Arbitration Board of the Boot and Shoe Trade was held at the City Hall, Leicester, Mr. George Geary in the chair, when Messrs. G. Ward, H. Harvey, H. P. Atkins, G. A. Burton, W. H. Keywood, J. H. Bott, J. Riley, G. A. Denman, R. Starmer, J. W. Hunt, and J. Palmer, representing the manufacturers’ side; Messrs. W. Warner, J. H. Osborne, D. Astley, T. Adnitt, G. Parbury, A. Needham, W. Woodward, G. Smith, F. Leader, F. W. Burchnall, C. Hurst, Mrs. M. J. Bell-Richards, and Miss S. A. Peberdy, representing the operatives’ side; and H. A. Flavill (secretary) were present.

The stockroom statement prepared by the Joint Committee appointed by the Board was adopted, subject to the Committee agreeing upon a few suggested amendments.

The additions to the county finishing statement fixing prices for randing wood heels and crowing on heels were confirmed and the decision of the Finishing Committee in establishing two different classes of standard shaped heels for which extras are to be paid for shape was approved.

The thanks of the Board were given to Mr. G. Geary (chairman) and Mr. W. Warner (vice-chairman), for their past services. Mr. D. Astley (Earl Shilton) was appointed chairman of the Board for the ensuing year. Mr. G. Geary (Barwell) vice-chairman, and the district enquiry committees were re-elected for the ensuing year.

Mr. H. A. Flavill was re-appointed secretary for the ensuing year.

AND YET IT IS SAID “WE ARE POOR!”

Dress-Designing Beauty Visits London. Her 500 Frocks.

Miss Caroline Nunder, the famous New York dress-designer, who dresses all the prettiest and wealthiest women of Long Island and Newport—the Mayfair of New York—has arrived in London.

The envy arises out of the fact that every year Miss Nunder wears 500 gowns of her own design—and none more than once.

She acts, indeed, as her own mannequin, wearing the models at theatres and dinner parties and dances and selling them next day to the women who have seen her wearing them.

Could any woman ask for more ?

Miss Nunder, who is 24 years old and extremely pretty, with fair bobbed hair and large hazel eyes, receives £10,000 per annum.—Evening News, 15th August, 1923.

The craze for jewels at Deauville is said to be positively alarming. A diamond dress —silver satin covered entirely with small diamonds—is one of the novel and brilliant costumes; and it is said that no ultra-fashionable feminine visitors to Deauville can be truly happy without a four-inch depth on both arms of “all-round” diamond and sapphire bracelets set in platinum. One woman had ten on one arm, twelve on the other!

" WANGLING " THE DOLE.
Unemployed Men Fined for Fraud.
"These frauds upon the Employment Exchange have got to be stopped," observed
Mr. J. L. Ward, who presided at the Town Hall this morning. Two summonses for fraud
were heard, Mr. Simpson prosecuting, and each defendant was fined 40s.
John Haywood, of 19, Thornton Lane, was summoned for obtaining unemployment
benefit and making a false representation that his wife was not employed."
The evidence called by Mr. Simpson was that defendant had been on the unemployed
list for some months. On 25th May he claimed for six days for himself and his wife, and
received £1 4s. On the back of the receipt was the statement signed by defendant that
his wife was not in work. Actually she was engaged in regular employment by Messrs.
Miller & Co., Granby Street, as a washer-up and kitchen hand.
Defendant offered to pay the money back, pleading ignorance, and saying he was
told by some men it did not matter whether his wife received anything or not.
The second defendant was George Harry Widdowson, 60, Paget Road, who was
summoned for obtaining benefit when employed by the Leicester Distress Committee.
It appeared that on 18th August last year defendant certified that he was not employed
by the Leicester Board of Guardians. On the 25th he received £1 from the exchange,
and it was ascertained that on the 22nd and 23rd he was employed by the Leicester Distress
Committee and earned 6s. 8d. for the two days.
Mr. Simpson remarked that when the summons was issued a year ago defendant
Defendant said he got work at Upringham, that was why he went away. Pleading
ignorance, he said he told the Distress Committee he was receiving unemployment benefit.-
disappeared.

HOUSING. The imperative need was once again shown for active work
in connection with this question. We give herewith a case reported in the
Leicester Mercury of 7th September, 1923, which shows a disgraceful condition
of affairs. Whilst it may be said it is an exceptional case, the fact remains
that hundreds of thousands of new houses are required, and that at once, to
meet the barest necessities of the situation.
A shocking case of overcrowding has just come to light in Nuneaton, a man,
his wife, and three children living and sleeping in one room. In the other part of
the house, which has two rooms up and two down, live five adults and two children.
The victim of these conditions is an old " contemptible," Mr. George Bateman,
who went to France with the 1st Division in 1914, and served throughout the war.
He has lived in his present circumstances for six months. Unable to find a house
or get furnished rooms, because landladies said "No children," he took this single
room as a last resort at a rental of 5s. a week.
Mr. Bateman, who is an ex-Quartermaster-Sergt. in the R.A.M.C., said there
is just sufficient cubic space in the room to equal that required for one patient in an
isolation hospital.
Mrs. Bateman said she had been to see the Council about getting a house, but
they could do nothing for her.
The sleeping arrangements constituted a problem, which was solved in this way:
The husband and wife sleep on two chairs, the two young children (aged four and
three) on the table, and the baby (12 months) in the pram.
Mr. and Mrs. Bateman are a respectable couple, and their position is extremely
painful to them. Mr. Bateman says he has been looking for a house without success
since April, 1919, and has spent a lot of money advertising for rooms. As soon as he
mentioned children, he states, his quest was hopeless. - Leicester Mercury, 7th Septem-
ber, 1923.
The serious position of the Herald also took up some considerable time,
and ultimately a resolution was passed instructing the General Council to carry
on for another three months; meantime cash is needed if the resolution is to be
acted upon. We have paid our share of contributions for 1924 and 1925 in
accordance with the authority given us at our own Conference this year, and
we hope that those Unions who have not hitherto responded will at once do
so, and thereby assist in saving the Herald. The other great need in
connection with the Herald is increased circulation. This is your paper, we
urge you to purchase the same daily and induce others so to do. We must
keep in being a daily paper. This is an easy matter to do if each do their
duty. It is a good pennyworth apart altogether from being a Labour paper.
Therefore our advice is buy, buy, buy, and thereby increase the influence of
Labour locally, nationally, and internationally.
The Congress recorded its full appreciation of the work of Mr. C. W.
Bowerman, P.C., M.P., who, under the age limit, now retires from the Secretary-
ship. For many years Mr. Bowerman has been actively engaged in the work
connected with the General Council, and the severance is bound to be felt.
The work has grown immensely since Mr. Bowerman has been secretary. In
Mr. Bowerman the Congress always found a courteous, affable and energetic
secretary. We hope he may live many years yet to render service to a cause
he has served so long. For Mr. Bramley, his successor, we hope that the work
may, under his guidance, still further increase in usefulness and influence, and
thereby help the workers to a better and more enduring status in life than the
one at present obtaining.

GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
Perhaps the most important work of the month can be attributed to the TRADE
UNION CONGRESS, held at Plymouth, and attended by 702 delegates, representing 4,369,000
odd members, and compare this with 1913, but I think it would be best for us to compare
the above figures with the Congress held at Cardiff in 1921, only two years ago, when there
were 810 delegates, representing 6,000,417 members. These figures make the first figure
look small as we have lost nearly one-third of the membership, including a number of
Unions-several officials of which I knew well-and have had to learn that much of the
loss during the past twelve months has been due to the resolution passed at Southport,
taking over the responsibility for the Daily Herald. This is a real pity, because unless
papers, but as the Chairman said in referring to the Daily Herald: "What does it matter
we do have a paper the Labour Members certainly will not get much help from the other
whether we have a paper or not. does not the failure lay with
or words to that effect.
Think of it, Fellow Members, after twelve months trial with the Trades Union Congress
drastic changes, but with the exception of a new and very capable Editor the personnel
and the Labour Party Executive behind it, many of us thought there were going to be
make for popular feeling and economy, and that portion of the movement that has openly
opposed Labour Candidates, should receive no more encouragement even by those who
were prepared to cave in to the attitude exhibited towards those who for a quarter of
a century had laboured hard to produce a movement with men behind them of adminis-
When most friends of the paper expected an alteration that would
trative capacity and ability.
Many Unions, including ours, had guaranteed several years' fees in advance, and yet
the prospects were unsatisfactory, and the paper has already been given a further three
months' life. Some of us have done much for the paper and accounted for many readers
and subscribers, and have at all meetings reminded our audiences of the value of our own
Press. Yet, in spite of all, on to-day's figures, not one in twelve are taking the paper.
One often wonders what kind of conscience those men have who will allow their money
to be used for political purposes and yet fail to take a journal, the only Daily that deals
absolutely with the problems that most concern the wage-earning section of the com-
munity. Personally, I shall still do all I can, both financially and physically, to save the
salvation lies in the two Executives referred to taking sole control and changing both name
with eight of the leading papers to compete with, and which have
ionaires behind each of them, how can Labour compete with their hands tied by lack
capital and support. There is still another three months to show the movement that
we cannot allow this our only Daily to die, in addition £12,500 must be found before the
end of this month. If those Unions who have not paid their fees in advance will only
do so, then the storm may be weathered, but final success can only come by loyalty to
the movement by taking the paper. One wonders what each of our 142 M.P.'s think of
their security if their constituents consume other literature. How can their prospects
look in such a light? As one great Internationalist tells me, who looks upon the British
Trade Union movement as by far the finest in the world, whilst all Continental countries
have Labour papers, and many of them, this country lacks even one with safety. He
really cannot understand it. Neither can anyone else, unless we agree with the Chairman
of Congress, that if the movement wanted the paper it would have it, and could not
be denied.
UNEMPLOYMENT BY INDUSTRY.-Personally I was sorry that the resolution was
carried discouraging the principle of Unemployment by Industry, meaning of course the
adoption of a scheme to be agreed to between the Manufacturers' Federation and the
Union, a subject upon which, as an Executive, we have already given adherence, and a
policy, to my mind, that should be tried until we can secure a Labour Government, when
the administration could be done on more sympathetic lines than at present. The policy
of sending workers to the Labour Exchanges for their benefit has been the means of
estranging and weaning them from their Trade Union, and accounts for more leaving the
Unions than we are aware of. Once let the worker think the officers are disinterested in
his welfare and he quietly abandons the organisation as being of no account. There are
those officials who would like to be relieved of this irksome duty, but the taking up of
this and National Insurance has had the effect of strengthening many Unions, but since
a few have abandoned the Unemployed administration, trade union membership has gone
down with a rush, and after so many years hard work we do not feel elated or sanguine
enough to find some personal excuse, and those who often meet with the non-unionist
wonder why these people remain unorganised and without the tangible benefits granted
through membership.

ORGANISER'S MONTHLY REPORT.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
During the past month I have been organising and helping at Stafford, Stone
and Wolverhampton. We had a "Back to the Union
September 10th to 15th. Several unions sent national officers to speak and the meetings
generally were well attended. The firm of Messrs. Edge, near Wolverhampton, have
withdrawn from the Federation with the view, no doubt, of permanently running their
business on non-union lines. The leading operatives may get wages that might appear
all right, but fair piece rates will be ignored. Boy labour will be uncontrolled and the
Graduated Scale of Wages for Juveniles will be just what the firm choose to pay. The
Stafford Board, with the Chairman of the Federation, have done their best to try to get
Wolverhampton and Stafford branches with myself, were deputed by the Board to see
way we have been treated at Stafford and Stone. I pointed out in a letter to Messrs.
Edge that the most prosperous manufacturers in the industry and the men who were
held highest in esteem as citizens were the men who worked to the National Agreements.
Manufacturers who are good organisers and pay close attention to details can get on without
looking all the time at taking advantage of the workers' wages and conditions.
In my last report I mentioned that Mr. Dunn and I were allowed to speak in the
closing room at the "Lotus" Works. As a result of that meeting the girls formed a
Shops Committee and the Management have agreed to consult with this Committee on
matters that may arise from time to time. I had a unique and pleasant experience yester-
day, 20th September; I got permission to speak in the closing room at the branch factory
of the "Lotus," in George Street, with the view of getting the girls to elect a Collector
and a small Committee to assist her. In a few minutes the business was done and all
seemed pleased.
We have joined nearly 300 members at Stafford and Stone. Taking into account
the short time being worked this, I think, may be considered satisfactory. Stone is nearly
100 per cent. strong, and excepting the two heel-making works, where trade is very bad.
Stafford is about the same. I have been assisting Mr. Dunn over prices for Clicking, Edge-
setting and Closing, and several small matters. With the exception of the Clicking prices
everything was settled satisfactorily. The Stafford Board must deal with the clickers'
case if the firm in mind persist in going on as they are.
STAFFORD, 21st September, 1923.
D. McCARTHY.

```text
BRANCH REPORTS.

ARBROATH.—Our local trade is taking a worse turn, and all the employees
are being paid off from one of the Arbroath factories. Part-time is bad enough,
but when a works closes down altogether the position becomes harder for tho
affected. Up here it becomes inevitable that men must transfer homes it work
is to be got at the trade, and this entails a small upheaval of an expensive
life in many cases, men, and in some instances women, are forced to face a future
quite impossible to get temporary work until things get better, and so, late in
description. All industries are suffering in this part of the country, and it is
of change and uncertainty. Whether they will find new employment in any
other part of Scotland is doubtful, and permanent unemployment may be their
lot. In this connection we are faced with a very troublesome problem. Labour
Exchanges keep offering any employment of which they get notice, and members
are penalised if they refuse. It may be work in Aberdeen or Dundee, and
without considering whether it is work the applicant can manage or not, the
Insurance Officer disallows benefit, and the claimant or the official of Union
must attend the Appeal Court of Referees to prove the reasonableness of the
refusal on the part of the member. Just now we have a spate of disallowances,
and our official has his hands full trying to get justice done to the idle members.
If members were all free agents without family responsibilities, they could start
a nomadic life and go hither and thither as wanted, but modern life is too
complex to permit folk leaving their moorings in this haphazard way without
any guarantee of permanent settlement. In Carnoustie our troubles are
growing instead of diminishing. Regarding the men's question of earning their
wages according to statement, we cannot too strongly insist on our members
acting loyally to the Union. Not only are their own conditions at stake, but the
conditions throughout Scotland, and a betrayal in one part leads to defeat else-
where. We must secure the National Terms, and all the power of the Union will
be behind us if we act correctly and courageously. No member need fear or doubt
if the instructions of the officials are faithfully carried out. Our women mem-
bers in Carnoustie are not being paid according to the National Terms, and this
must cease. In fact it becomes a question as to how much "back pay" should
be claimed. In future every member must claim the rate applicable to his or
her age, and any refusal to pay must be dealt with immediately. We are
accused of seeking to cause trouble because we are inquiring closely into the
conditions of our members, but our only object is to give to each member the
rights they pay for. Our members sometimes ask what the Union does for
them, and when one does get busy the employer wants to know why the D-1
he can't be left alone. But our members must get all the conditions they are
entitled to by the National Terms before we can afford to sit down in ease.
It is up to the members themselves to see their rights secured and maintained,
and surely federated firms cannot refuse to honour their own agreement. We
shall never seek to cause unnecessary dispute or bickering in our factories,
and shall be only too glad to work in harmony, but harmonious relationships
between employer and worker can only be built on honesty and truthfulness,
which would make both sides agree immediately to carry out always the precise
meaning and spirit of National Terms for our industry when mutually accepted
by both responsible organisations.

BARNSLEY.—We are pleased to say that members are now working
full time, and seem likely to continue doing so now the worst months of the
trade for this year have passed.
BRISTOL No. 2.—Glad to report that trade has shown an upward ten-

those firms who stood outside the Holiday Scheme, and we hope to report
```

Interesting statements and greetings were also tendered from America, Canada and
the Co-operative Congress. The question of the action of the directors of the Co-operative
Wholesale Society was also a matter which threatened to bring about a very serious
position between the Co-operative and Trade Union movement. Happily this was averted.
The Joint Committee of Trade Unionists and Co-operators, under the chairmanship of our
colleague, Mr. E. L. Poulton, J.P., met at Plymouth, and after a very prolonged sitting of
the Committee until 10.30 p.m., they came to certain decisions which the Co-operative side
of the Joint Committee proceeded with to Newcastle-on-Tyne to meet the directors, the
result being on Thursday, the 6th inst., a telegram was received by Mr. Bowerman stating
that the directors would submit matters to arbitration, thereby avoiding any open rupture.
It is sincerely to be hoped that the result will be not only settlement of outstanding differ-
ences, but a spirit of goodwill on all sides whereby adjustments can be made from time
to time without any friction.
The Secretary, Mr. Bowerman, owing to age limit, retires this year. Fitting tribute
was paid to his many and varied services to the movement extending over many years,
and a retiring allowance of £300 was unanimously accorded him.
Mr. F. Bramley, the Assistant Secretary was, by vote, selected to succeed Mr. Bower-
man. We hope his tenure of such office may result in still further extending the usefulness,
prestige and power of the Trade Union movement.
In our judgment the time has arrived when the Standing Orders should again be
revised so as to reduce the numbers attending the Congress-the Congress is too large and
too many subjects are attempted. It would be, in our opinion, much more effective to
have a smaller representation and fewer subjects dealt with. Another matter we feel
ought to be dealt with, and that with a strong hand, viz., the washing of "dirty linen"
with the Press present. If such a process is to be indulged in, which we much regret,
it ought to be done in "private" session. We have left till almost last, the question of the
least important, the question of the Daily Herald. It is indeed a very great disappointment
after the Southport vote and the tremendous amount of work put in during the year to
increase the circulation of the Herald, to find such a poor response has been made. It is
easy to find fault with the Herald and point out its shortcomings. Making, however,
full allowance for the same, the fact remains that the Herald is our paper; run in the
interests of the Labour movement, giving more information upon labour questions and
political and economic questions that directly affect the workers' lives than do other
papers, and therefore ought to be supported by the workers.
After full discussion in two private sessions the Congress, while giving every credit
for the work done by the Directorate and the Executive of the Labour Party and the
General Council, felt that one more effort must be made to keep the Herald going, and not
close it down as suggested by the Council, this decision being due to deficient lack of
support by the rank and file and the exchequer being empty. A resolution was therefore
passed calling upon the Unions to send in cash and at once to ensure the continued existence
of the Herald. We may here say that we, as a Union, have done our share in paying up,
as we have paid our fees for 1924-1925. We sincerely hope the cash will be forthcoming,
and what is of equal importance, that the circulation will go up rapidly. Buy the Herald,
and induce your friends to buy the Herald.
Unity and concord are words very much used in the movement. The General Council
during the year reported upon action taken both to increase unity and promote concord.
dunen, however, this part of the report was dealt with it seemed as if all the forces of
disunity and inharmonious chords were let loose at once. It is indeed to be deplored
that so much energy is used during the year upon these subjects, and then when put to the
test it ends in recriminations. We can only hope that ere long real power will be given
to the General Council to deal with this matter in a way which will prevent any unseemly
squabbles taking place in Congress itself. Despite, however, this unpleasant aspect of the
week's work, we believe good work was done at the Congress, and which will show itself
in the not distant future. We record with pleasure that our Colleagues, Mr. E. L. Poulton,
was returned unopposed to the Council, and Mr. T. F. Richards again returned as a member
of the General Purposes Committee.
The Plymouth Branch of the Union entertained the delegates of the Union to Congress
to an enjoyable evening, when a very good entertainment was given and highly appreciated.
A good spirit was shown between the delegates and the officials and members of the Branch.
We also feel it a compliment to our Plymouth Branch that the Branch President, Mr. T.
Smale, was appointed Secretary of the Congress. Mr. Smale is also Secretary to the
Plymouth Trades Council.

INTERNATIONAL LABOUR OFFICE NEWS.

RURAL LABOUR PROBLEMS.

International Discussion at Geneva.

Agricultural education, co-operation, the prevention of anthrax, and the profitable
utilisation of leisure were the chief subjects discussed by the Joint Advisory Committee
on Agriculture, set up by the International Labour Office (League of Nations) and the
International Institute of Agriculture, at a meeting just held in Geneva.

The meeting was attended by three representatives of the Governing Body of the
International Labour Office, and three representatives of the International Institute of
Agriculture, including Sir Thomas Elliott. K.C.B., Counsellor of the British Embassy in
Rome. The Committee were assisted by a number of experts representing the principal
agricultural organisations of various countries, and including Mr. Rowland R. Robbins,
chairman of the Labour Committee of the National Farmers' Union, and Mr. R. B. Walker,
general secretary of the National Union of Agricultural Workers.

Technical Training for Landworkers.

The Committee first considered the question of the vocational education of agricultural
workers. This problem has already received close attention from the International Labour
Office, and was the subject of a Recommendation adopted by the International Labour
Conference of 1921 for examination by the Governments of all the States which are members
of the Organisation. The Recommendation urged that each State should "endeavour
to develop vocational agricultural education, and in particular to make such education
available to agricultural wage-earners on the same conditions as to other persons engaged
in agriculture."

Further, each State was urged to supply regular reports to the Inter-
national Labour Office on steps taken to develop technical education for landworkers.

After a general discussion of this question, the Committee requested the experts to
consider in detail the points on which Governments should be invited to report, and to
indicate in broad outlines the nature of the information which should be supplied. The
experts duly submitted to the Committee a questionnaire designed to elicit the fullest
possible information from Governments, and this was adopted by the Committee with a
recommendation to the Governing Body of the International Labour Office that it should
be forwarded to Governments with an intimation of the Committee's approval. By this
means it is hoped to bring together all available information showing what is being done
in the chief agricultural countries to promote agricultural education both in ordinary
schools and in special institutions.

Agricultural Co-operation.

The second subject considered was that of workers' co-operation in agriculture. This
problem, also, was dealt with in a Recommendation of the 1921 Conference, which invited
Governments " to encourage the creation of agricultural workers' co-operative societies
for the working and purchase or renting of land," and, to this end, "to take steps to increase
agricultural credit especially in favour of co-operative agricultural associations of land-
workers established for the purpose of agricultural production." In this case, again,
Governments were urged to present periodical reports to the International Labour Office.

During the discussion of this item, it was made clear that in the opinion of the Com-
mittee there was need for an extension of facilities for the acquisition by agricultural
workers, through co-operative methods, of access to land and equipment for its cultivation,
as a means not only of securing stability for the worker on the land but of promoting
increased production from the land. As in the case of agricultural education, the Com-
mittee agreed on the terms of a questionnaire to be addressed to Governments with regard
to co-operative undertakings in agriculture, their extent, methods and results. The
Committee further indicated its desire for continuous and effective collaboration between
the International Labour Office and the International Institute of Agriculture in the study
of this question and in the preparation of proposals for the encouragement of co-operation
in agriculture, each body keeping the other informed of the action it took and the results
of its investigations.

The Prevention of Anthrax.

Thirdly, the Committee examined the question of the prevention of anthrax infection
in flocks, in conformity with a resolution adopted by the Advisory Committee of Experts
on Anthrax which met in London last December and dealt with some of the problems of
this disease, from the point of view of safeguarding the health of workers engaged in
handling wool, hair, hides. &c. The report of the last-mentioned Committee will be laid
before the International Labour Conference next June. In the meantime, the repre-
sentatives of the International Institute of Agriculture have undertaken to lay the question
before the assembly of the Institute, and to take steps with a view to calling the attention

The Next Step.
A full report of the proceedings of the Committee, which is of a purely advisory
character, will be presented to the Governing Body of the International Labour Office
at its meeting next October. In the meantime it may be stated that the first session of
this mixed committee is regarded as having completely justified the action of the two
international bodies which created it. The proceedings throughout were of the most
cordial nature, and revealed a desire for co-operation between the two institutions which,
it is believed, is of good augury for their future fruitful collaboration.

INDUSTRIAL PRODUCTION OF THE WORLD.

Report of Geneva Enquiry.
The International Labour Office (League of Nations) announces the publication in
French of the first volume of a report containing information, collated and analysed,
concerning industrial production throughout the world.*

INDUSTRIAL DISEASES.
International Meeting of Experts.
to assist the
International Labour Office of the League of Nations in dealing with questions affecting
the health of the workers, will meet in Geneva to-day.
The Committee, which was set up in accordance with a resolution adopted by the
International Labour Conference at Washington in 1919, is composed of medical inspectors
of factories and others possessing technical and scientific knowledge of industrial hygiene,
drawn from about a dozen countries, and including Dr. T. M. Legge (Chief Medical Inspector
of Factories, Home Office), and Dr. S. Miall (Director of the Brimsdown Lead Co. Ltd.).
The Committee will be invited to advise the International Labour Office on two
questions :-
and skins;
(1) The protection from anthrax of workers engaged in the handling of hides
(2) The compilation of a list of the principal industrial processes to be considered
as unhealthy.
As regards anthrax, it may be recalled that considerable progress has already been
made in the direction of safeguarding the health of wool-workers by the disinfection of
wool from infected or dangerous countries; but, in the case of hides and skins, according
to the opinion of a special committee which studied the matter last December, it is imposs-
ible at the present time to secure complete disinfection, though various processes have
been tried and some have given interesting results. The problem, therefore, is two-fold:
To discover a satisfactory process of disinfection, and, pending that discovery, to devise
measures, by regulations or otherwise, for the protection of workers occupied in the mani-
pulation of hides and skins. The experts will be asked at this week's meeting (1) to make
suggestions for the organisation and co-ordination of research in different countries into
disinfection processes, for joint consideration by the International Labour Office and the
Health Committee of the League of Nations, and (2) to indicate what provisions might be
made for minimising the risk to the workers during the actual handling of hides and skins,
for the sterilisation of the effluents of tanneries, and for the use of serum against anthrax.
As regards the preparation of a schedule of unhealthy processes, this involves not
but the collection and study of all the available scientific and statistical information
merely the careful examination of the dangers to health involved in various processes,
relating to each process. The list is already in an advanced stage, but before it is published
the experts forming the present Committee are to be asked to examine it in detail and to
collaborate in ensuring its scientific completeness and accuracy.

GOOD NEWS FOR CONSUMPTIVES.
A Proved British Remedy at a Cost of Sixpence Per Day.
REMARKABLE CURES AT BLACKBURN.
A Twenty-Five Years' Boycott. The Story of a Great Wrong.
A FREE GIFT TO THE NATION.
This new treatment (Umckaloabo) constitutes an entirely new and really
efficient weapon in the fight against tuberculosis, and its use, once
it has become general, might contribute largely to the eradicating
of this terrible scourge.- Dr. SECHEHAYE, Geneva.
The treatment of tuberculosis has received a good deal of attention in the Press
recently. This has been brought about by the fact that the Insurance Committee of the
Lancashire County Council, with commendable enterprise, proposed to provide over
£100,000 to make what is known as the Spahlinger serum available for persons suffering
in the county from this hitherto incurable malady.
Before this could be done, it was necessary to obtain the consent of Mr. Neville
Chamberlain, the Minister of Health.
Mr. Chamberlain announced to a deputation that waited upon him from the County
Council, that although he was convinced there was a sound prima facie case for these
remedies, he was not prepared to take the responsibility of authorising the expenditure
of public money upon them at the present stage of their development.
Dr. Spahlinger is a Swiss physician, residing at Geneva. He has been engaged on
this treatment for sixteen years.
It takes Dr. Spahlinger about four years to produce the complete serum. It is the
result of a combination of 22 different serums, each of which, it is stated, attacks some
one symptom associated with tuberculosis, and altogether is the result of very delicate
and exact experiments.
Although Dr. Spahlinger estimated that it would be the end of 1924 before the com-
plete serums and vaccines could be ready, he stated that the first of the 22 forms could be
available by next December.
The Lancashire Insurance Committee are spending very large sums in sanatorium
and other treatment of tuberculosis, and they are convinced that this method should be
tried. They did not guarantee it as a cure, but considered that it was very promising.
Sanatorium Treatment "A Tragic Failure."
The treatment of tuberculosis is costing our nation nearly £2,000,000 per year. This
is principally spent in sanatoriums. The ratepayers of Blackburn alone have to provide
every year nearly £8,000 for consumptive treatment.
The true effectiveness of this so-called remedy is tersely summed up in the following
paragraph reprinted from the Medical World of 16th July, 1920 :-
"Dr. Dickinson, Adviser to the Insurance Committee of Newcastle, has issued a
'Survey of Sanatorium Treatment,' of which most of our readers will have heard if they
have not read it, its figures being such as to appear incredible without the data he gives.
Briefly, in only 14 out of 1,086 cases had the disease been arrested, and only eight of these
were bacillus-free for a certainty, whilst of a further series of 1,162 cases but 81 are now
at work or fit for work. The only possible conclusion is that sanatoriums, in spite of all
the vast expenditure upon them, are, for the working classes at least, a tragic failure."

name of Umckaloabo, by Mr. Charles H. Stevens, 204, Worple Road, Wimbledon, London,
for use in tincture, capsule, and lozenge form.

Examples of the Cure.
A number of medical men gave evidence for Mr. Stevens. I can only find space for a
summary from the evidence of one of the gentlemen. All the others are in the same
strain.
Edward Ferdinand Grun, L.R.C.P., M.R.C.S., medical officer of the second district
of the Steyning Union, said that he was living at Southwick, Brighton, and in practice
there. He had had to deal with a good deal of tuberculosis. He had written a book on
ther Koch's treatment of tuberculosis. At the time he wrote the book he was a doctor
with Dr. Wodehouse, at the Hospital for Incurables at Putney. Dr. Koch's work was
exciting great interest and he was instructed to go and investigate the treatment. He
did so and wrote the book on his return. He was the author of a number of letters to the
Lancet. In 1908 he received a circular about Stevens' Consumption Cure. He wrote
to Mr. Stevens, who told him about the mixture and furnished him with some very striking
During the whole of his 30 years' practice he had lost many dear friends
from tuberculosis, and in 1908 one had just died. He thought it his duty to try and see
whether it was of any use. He obtained samples from Mr. Stevens, and having obtained
the consent of patients used the mixture. He was very surprised by the extraordinary
results of its use.
results of its use.
beneficial results.
A patient had asked for relief and he was ordered to go and see her. He found her in
a very bad state. She was expectorating a great deal. Her temperature was 103; she
could not take her food. He gave her a supply of the mixture. Her symptoms improved
almost at once and at the end of 14 days before the next meeting of the Guardians her
husband managed to send her away. The name of the woman was Hudson. He used the
mixture again in the case of a lad who was at school at Shoreditch Grammar School. He
had a cavity at the apex of the lung and a bad cough. The witness said he had treated
this boy with various remedies, but he got so bad that he was unable to go to school. He
put this boy under the treatment. The result was that in three months there was no
mischief in the lung and no tubercle, and there had been no subsequent relapse.
Another patient he had treated with the mixture had come with him to the court
had been certified by four medical
witness also examined him. About April, 1908, he had a very bad attack, and the disease,
which had been more or less latent, became acute. He put him under the treatment
and he got better. He lost his cough and he put on weight. He had been working as the
captain of a yacht and all this wet summer he had been sailing round the coast.
