---
There was a man named Hersee, who was a gardener, who had been in his employ-
a man of good physique. All of a sudden he was taken in with acute galloping phthisis.
A man of 11 to 12 stones, in a month he weighed seven stone. The witness came home
from abroad and found him in a very serious condition. He treated him with the remedy,
and he greatly improved, but unfortunately, he was subsequently attacked by influenza,
and died of pneumonia.

There were other cases where he had used the mixture, but of course he saw a great
number of patients and he did not keep notes of them all.

On the whole, he was of opinion that the treatment had been extremely beneficial,
and in any future cases he should have he should recommend its administration. Mr.
Stevens made no charge to him for the medicine. Doctors were supplied with it free of
expense. He had used the mixture since 1908 and had noticed no difference in its outward
characteristics or in its taste.

Miraculous Cures at Blackburn.

In the end the jury failed to agree. Mr. Stevens brought a second action against
the British Medical Association, and lost his case.
I came to the conclusion that Mr. Stevens had been badly treated, and wrote him to
this effect. I also promised to give his treatment a trial if any of my relatives or friends
were smitten with this terrible malady. This I did in 1914, and have since supplied the
remedy to several persons who had tuberculosis, the results in every case being most
satisfactory.
A Singular Coincidence.
Before dealing with the Blackburn cures, I want to explain why I am giving publicity
to Mr. Stevens' treatment of tuberculosis at the present time. On the same day as there
appeared in the Press a report of the action of the Lancashire Insurance Committee, I
received a translation from the Swiss Medical Review, published at Berne, and dated
21st March, of a paper read at a Medical Conference held at Geneva. It is a rather singular
coincidence that whilst Dr. Spahlinger was developing his cure for the treatment of tuber-
culosis, another eminent Genevan physician, Dr. Sechehaye, should have been using the
British cure for three years with great success. By putting the welfare of his patients so
very much above any professional prejudices he may have against a treatment introduced
by an unprofessional man, Dr. Sechehaye in no way lessens his esteem for the honourable
profession of medicine. It is possible that his courageous action may have some influence
with the British medical profession.

202 Cases Treated in Three Years.

Dr. Sechehaye, to whom I have already referred, in his paper given before the con-
ference of medical men at Geneva, dealt with the results obtained in 202 cases he had
treated over the past three years. These would fill several columns of this journal, and
I can only quote one or two general observations as follows:

“ Amongst the cases cured or in the course of being cured, some are of a very grave
character; white tumour of the elbow with fistula, osteoarthritis of the shoulder, in which
ankylosis could be avoided, white tumour of the knee with abscesses and fistula, not open
supperating coxalgia, tuberculosis of the foot with complete caries of the ankle bone and
of the calcaneum, &c.

“ The time between the commencement of the treatment and recovery was from
5 to 8 months, even in the case of patients who had been bedridden sometimes for several
years.

“Results are particularly favourable in cases of tuberculosis with predominating
bronchitic tendencies in children. Last winter, Umckaloabo, often after fruitless attempts
with Thiocol preparations, really worked wonders by bringing about in several cases of
this kind a prompt and thorough transformation.

“Another striking fact is that the slightest tendencies to a relapse are overcome by
a resumption of the treatment. The most frequent causes of failure have been unfavour-
able economic conditions with unhealthy living accommodation, hard work and cares,
insufficient nourishment, alcoholism, and, in rare cases, gastric trouble.”
After dealing exhaustively with the 202 cases he had treated, Dr. Sechehaye gave

The Blackburn Cases.
In recording the cases at Blackburn which have come under my notice, I refrain in
the interests of the persons concerned from publishing their addresses, for they would be
certain to be inundated with inquiries. I shall be pleased to give the names and addresses
to representative persons.

A Bad Case Cured.
Early in 1914 a young married woman in Blackburn, an ardent Sunday-school worker,
was compelled to give up her class owing to her having been smitten by tuberculosis.
It was stated that she had lost one lung, that the other was also seriously affected,
and that she also had the affection in the throat. I believe tuberculosis of the throat
has never been cured by the ordinary medical treatment.
I offered, if her husband was agreeable, to arrange for Mr. Stevens to treat her by
tinued the treatment at her own expense for another three months, when she was cured,
correspondence for three months. This was done, and at the end of that period she con-
and has had no further trouble.


---
Mr. Stevens, in a number of testimonials sent out, refers to this as "an easy case".
It cannot have been very easy seeing that the young woman treated had been in the
Blackburn Royal Infirmary for six weeks, that her foot had been in plaster of Paris for
seven months, and that after a consultation between three medical men it was decided
to recommend her to have her foot amputated.
As superintendent of the Sunday-school she attended, I was asked to go and see her
before she underwent the operation.
I did so, and found that she was anxious to try the Stevens Specific. I arranged to
get her the medicine if her doctor did not object. Fortunately for the young woman, he
consented. The following is the record of the case as sent out by Mr. Stevens:
1916. December 11. Miss - wrote: "I have received the medicine. My com-
plaint is all in my ankle. I have been in hospital for six weeks, and had it in plaster
for seven months. It is very swollen."
1917. May 11. "I am still improving and able to walk about. My foot is still swollen,
but very little to what it was. All my friends are surprised how well I have done
since I started to take your medicine. Am only sorry I did not know of it before."
1917. August 8. "I am now able to work; this I owe to your medicine."
1917. October 24. "I am still able to follow my work, and never feel anything wrong
with my foot."
This young woman is to-day strong and well, and has never had the slightest return
of the trouble. She declares that Umckaloabo saved her foot from being amputated.

Tuberculosis Bone.
The next case I know nothing about, except what I found in Mr. Stevens' testimonials,
simply suppressing the address and name, which are given.
On October 19th, 1917, I received the following letter:
"Dear Sir, - Having heard of your marvellous cure of Miss - , I have a daughter
thirteen years old suffering from a tubercular bone in her thigh. She has been going to
the Royal Infirmary for eighteen months, and on crutches ever since she had her leg in
plaster of Paris. She can't bend it, and I should like your advice."
(Some medicine was sent for her by return post.)
1917. December 11. "I am quite satisfied with your treatment for my daughter. She
is going on fine, getting fuller in the face, eating a lot better, and no pain; only when
we feel it (the leg) the pain comes on again."
1918. January 27. "She is still on the mend, and can bend her knee a little without
pain."
1918. April 9. "She is still on the mend."
1918. October 28. "She seems to be doing very nicely; can go about without crutches
and walk very well, only the stiffness has not gone out of her leg yet."
1919. March 16. "Still improving."
1919. April. "Gave up treatment."
1921. March 3. "We have only your treatment to thank; she is doing fine, and has
started work. Use this letter if it be of any service to you."

An Ex-Service Man Cured.
In the early part of this year a young married man who formerly resided in Blackburn
called to see me about Mr. Stevens' treatment for consumption. He was one of four
strong, healthy brothers who went to the war. Three of them were killed on the battle-
field, the fourth being wounded and gassed. This developed into tuberculosis, and he was
pensioned off and advised to take a small farm in the South of England. For two years
he had been under treatment, but gradually grew weaker, and had to engage a man to
look after his place while he tried if residence in Southport would benefit him.
He took Umckaloabo for two months with the consent of his doctor, when he dis-
continued the treatment and returned to his farm.
Writing to me last month he said: "I can now rise at 6.30 a.m., and, with a rest
for an hour after lunch, work in the open until it is dark (which I do every day). A year
ago I was not supposed to do more than four hours a day of light work. I have no boy
to help me now, and I have reared over 500 chickens this year."

summoned for obtaining unemployment benefit by false representation. Mr. Keefe, who
appened to preseente on behalf of
ant war paid 21., the pension which he would have been entitled had he been unemployed
f of the Ministry of Labour, said that on March 16th defend-
throughout the year as a boot worker, for the firms of Barratt & Co. Ltd., and the Saxone
Co. Ltd.

signed application from defendant.
George Albert Gutteridge, of the Norwich Employment Exchange, said that he paid
the defendant 255. on receiving from him a signed form, on March 16th.

WANTED-MEN.
There's the chap with the "Can't," and the chap with the "Won't,"
And the chap who's betwixt, more or less;
There's the chap with an "Aye," when it ought to be "Nay," and
The "No," when it ought to be "Yes."
There's the chap who's too weak to get up when he's down-too
Bluffed to strike back when he's hit,
And the chap who bobs up when he ought to stay down; and the
Chap who does nothing but sit.
There's the chap who is brave when he's nothing to fear, and
The chap who's afraid without shame.
But the world wanting men has no patience with these-what it
Wants is the fellow dead game!
What it wants is the chap with the "Can" and the "Will," and the
"Get up" and "Hustle" and "Do";
And the chap who " comes back," with a smile on his face, when the
World thinks he's beaten clean through;
The chap who'll back down when he knows he is wrong, and the
Chap who'll stand pat when he's right,
And the chap who keep faith when he pledges his word, and will
Back up his stand with a fight;
The chap who forever puts right above wrong, and honour o'er
Riches and fame;
Ah, he is the chap that the world's looking for-the trustworthy
Fellow-dead game!
-" Exchange," Shoe Workers' Journal.

66 IN THE MELTING POT."
Affairs of a Kingswood Boot Manufacturer.
At Bristol Police Court yesterday, Messrs. Jay Bros. were summoned under the
Factory Acts for failing to keep a register. There were two summonses, and Mr. H. W.
Brown, who appeared for defendants, pleaded guilty to both charges.
Mr. James Owner, H.M. Inspector of Factories, explained that Jay Bros., a boot
manufacturing firm at Kingswood, failed to keep a general register showing the names
of young persons employed, dates of lime-washing, particulars of accidents, &c. The other
summons referred to a register of names and addresses of people who were doing work in
their homes, of whom Jay's employed 41, so that they could be visited by the inspector
to see that their working conditions were all right. Jay Bros.' factory at Bolton Lane
came within the city boundary in 1921, and since then witness and his predecessor had
written to them several times, and witness had interviewed Mr. Walter Jay three times,
but he could not get him to produce the register.
Forms as Greek or Latin to Proprietor.
Mr. Brown said he had known Mr. Jay for 40 years. He could not write his own
name, and could no more fill up the forms referred to than he could translate a Latin or
Greek book. There were thousands owing, the firm was bankrupt, and its affairs were
in the melting pot. If the justices saw fit to inflict a fine, Mr. Brown could only pay it
himself.
Answering Alderman Whitefield, Mr. Owner said this was not the first time he had had
trouble with Mr. Jay. He had complained to him personally on four occasions, and sent
four times for offences under the Factory Acts, the last occasion being in 1919, when he
two letters to him. In the last 20 years he had been before the Lawford's Gate magistrates
was fined 40s. for having an unfenced fly-wheel.
The magistrates (Mr. A. G. Verrier and Alderman William Whitefield) imposed a
fine of 20s. in each case. —Bristol Times, 28th August, 1923.

REPORT AND BALANCE SHEET OF THE LEICESTER CO-OPERATIVE
PRINTING SOCIETY LIMITED.
We have pleasure in submitting the 61st Half-yearly Report and Balance Sheet
half-year. After providing for Interest on Share and Loan Capital which amounts to
pared with the corresponding period of last year, but an increase of 1,201 Over the previous
The Sales for the half-year amount to £24,003 175. 8d., a decrease of f1,338 3S. IId.com.
of £1,043 9s. 6d. brought forward from last half-year, and the remaining balance of
fo86 5s. 8d., and depreciating Fixed Stock, Buildings, &c., £1,069 125. 8d., there is a
balance profit of £304 5S. 2d. This amount has been deducted from the adverse balance
£739 45. 4d. written off the Reserve Fund.
Considering all the circumstances, the Committee regard the result of the half-year's
work as very satisfactory. It is a good recovery from the position at the end of the previous
half-year, and testifies to the effectiveness of the reorganisation and measures of economy
which have been instituted. The prevailing depression in trade, which naturally reacts
on our own industry, is still making it very difficult to obtain the amount of work needed
to keep the works fully employed, but during the greater part of the past half-year we were
fortunate in having a steady flow of orders. At the commencement of the half-year
management generally have proved to be very valuable and to have fully justified the
Mr. H. S. Halford was appointed as Works Manager and Estimator at the Leicester Printing
Works. Mr. Halford's services in the direction of close supervision and assistance in
having installed a Rotary Offset Machine and accessories, thus bringing this department
appointment. We have made an important addition to our plant in the Litho Department,
thoroughly up to date.
LONDON BRANCH. - An important development is taking place here. The owners of
the premises we occupy at present now require them for their own purpose, and we have
been compelled to seek fresh quarters. After considering many propositions we have
securedad. It is admirably adapted for our purpose, although too large for our sole use
for the time being. We are subletting the upper floors and utilising the basement, which
will provide the necessary accommodation and improved conditions for working which
we have been needing for so long. The trade has been well maintained here and the better
facilities in prospect will be helpful from every point of view.
BOX DEPARTMENT. - The continued depression in the Boot and Hosiery trades is
making business very difficult to maintain, but we are glad to report that on the whole
trade has been well maintained. The Sales for the half-year amount to £6,235, a decrease
of £1,061 compared with the corresponding period of last year, but an increase of £888
over the previous half-year.
PRODUCTION OF FOOTWEAR IN DENMARK.
1922 Figures Below those for 1913.
The total production of boots and shoes in Denmark during last year amounted to
2,217,000 pairs, valued at approximately 30,000,000 crowns, says the Chamber of Commerce
Journal. This compares with 2,315,000 pairs in 1921, 3,557,000 pairs in 1920, when
production attained its maximum, and 2,400,000 pairs in the last pre-war year.
Sales have been somewhat greater than production. During 1922 Denmark imported
footwear, principally from Germany, to the amount of 790,800 kilos., as compared with
574,900 kilos. in 1921. Converting Danish production into weight, the total during last
year was 1,257 tons, as compared with 783 tons imported. The value of imported footwear
last year amounted to 13,200,000 crowns, c.i.f. Danish harbour or station. - The Shoe and
Leather Record, 31st August, 1923.

A TESTIMONIAL TO MAJOR STEVENS' TREATMENT.
DEAR MR. POULTON,
NORTHAMPTON,
29th August, 1923.
I am writing to you to discontinue taking Mr. Stevens' treatment for a time,
as I am feeling myself again now. I thought it such a pity to take it when I am feeling
allright. I have been taking it for three years altogether, as I had been taking it for some
time before the Union took it up. I wish to thank you very much for the benefit I have
received and should I fall ill again, I hope you will be able to see your way to let me continue
treatment again.
I once again thank you very much.
I remain, yours truly,
MRS. F. E. B.
£500,000,000 TURNOVER.
What the C.W.S. Bank does Yearly.
The Red Lion Square branch of the C.W.S. Bank, through which much of the trade
union business of its clients has been transacted in London, is to be removed next week,
along with the offices of the Co-operative Insurance Society, to premises in Kingsway,
formerly known as West Africa House, and in future to be known as Clare House, they being
on the site of the old Clare Market.
There are 8,187 trade unions and trade union branches now banking with the C.W.S.,
in addition to 1,029 Co-operative societies and 3,458 friendly societies, clubs and other
working-men's organisations. The bank has a turnover of £500 millions a year. - Daily
Herald, 30th August, 1923.

STATE OF TRADE.
22ND OCJODE 192
The state of trade during the past month continued quiet, and the demand
made upon the Union's Unemployment Fund was higher than of late. The
figures recorded by the Ministry of Labour Gazette are set out hereunder:
BOOT AND SHOE INDUSTRY.
Employment during September remained very slack, and much short time was again
worked. Some districts showed a slight improvement; others, including several of the
principal centres, a decline. On the whole, there was not much change as compared
with August.
Among workpeople covered by the Unemployment Insurance Acts the number
registered as unemployed was 14,785 on 24th September, as compared with 15,644 on
27th August.

VOTING FOR ORGANISER.
The Council at their meeting this week had before them many letters
of complaint relative to a letter which appeared over the name of Mr.
James Gribble, of Northampton in the Northampton Echo for the 5th of
September, 1923, in connection with the recent vote for the third Union
organiser.
After careful consideration, the Council unanimously passed the fol-
lowing resolution :-
" That the Executive Council of the Union learned, with surprise,
that in connection with the recent voting for organiser, Mr. James
Gribble, of Northampton, should have written to the local press showing
preference to one of the candidates, and thereby showing bias as to the
way members are to vote. The Council deprecate such action, and
trust that NO member will adopt such a policy, as it is both unfair,
and likely to prejudice the position and create endless confusion and
ill-feeling."
THE SUSPENSION BENEFIT.
This is the first month wherein the new rule granting benefit to suspended
members has been payable, but we are as yet unable to give the number of
members who have drawn benefit, as the records cannot be completed until
the end of the month. Meanwhile, we wish to impress upon officials and
members the fact that the rule must be fully complied with before payment is
made. The rule relative to this benefit is as follows :-
216. ANY member who may be suspended from work for more than
TWELVE CONSECUTIVE WORKING DAYS shall be allowed to declare upon
the Out-of-Work Fund of the Union, payment from such Fund to the
member to COMMENCE as and from the THIRTEENTH WORKING DAY upon
which the member is not employed; it always being understood that the
officials must themselves be satisfied that the suspension is bond fide
before benefit is allowed under this rule. Holidays are not to be counted
as entitling a member to claim benefit under this rule. In the event of
a member resuming work, and again being suspended, he must serve a
further probation of twelve consecutive working days before again being
entitled to re-declare upon the Out-of-Work Fund under this special rule.

WINTER PROSPECTS-UNEMPLOYMENT.
The present position of affairs, whether looked at from the industrial,
itical or economic standpoint, is very unsatisfactory. There does not appear
be any real trust or confidence between the nations such as is necessary
ring about more stable and promising state of affairs than at present obtains.
far as the British Government is concerned, we cannot but express our
great disappointment at the lack of vision and courage at present shown
Ministry. The newspapers-without regard to party colour-are daily
up the question of unemployment, but what is missing is the putting
ing schemes which will need the skill and labour of the great armies of
es who are vainly asking for work. Promises are made and statements


---
616
I that the Government is seriously considering the question. This
whilst men and women are starving for the want of the bare
ole output at present upon the vital question-" seriously
We have upon more than one occasion called attention to
the programme of the Trades Union Congress and the Labour Party, who have
muatic of life.
hemes drawn up for dealing with this question, and we wish to refer to several
points in that programme. Firstly there is
HOUSING.
Apart from finding employment for hundreds of men, and they in their
turn by spending wages finding employment for others, there is the great
scandal attached to this question of the bad housing of millions of people in
all parts of the country, yet at the present moment Health Weeks are .being
held in cities and towns whilst the main thing which would help to materially
improve the health of the people is proper housing accommodation. Houses
are lacking because of the timidity of the Government to deal with such a vital
issue.
Then there is the question of canals, afforestation, reclaiming of foreshores,
making of new roads, improvement of existing roads, all of which would find
work of a useful and beneficial nature to the nation as a whole. We are
driven to the point time after time to find the will is lacking in the present
Government to seriously tackle these great questions. It is, therefore, incum-
bent upon all workers to not only keep a live interest in the various trade
unions, but to also spread abroad the fact that if these matters are to receive
that treatment which the seriousness of the position calls for, men and women
must be placed in authority-both nationally and locally-who will not shrink
from dealing with the vested interests which stand in the way, and whose power
is so great at the present time. It may be said (and with truth, that difficulties
would be found in putting these schemes into operation. Difficulties have
always to be met when great reforms are adopted. We hope, however, no one
will be dis-spirited because of the need for great courage and determination
being necessary in connection with such matters. We must keep pegging
away and convert public opinion to our views. There is one other serious
question to which we wish to refer, and that is the question of
WAR.
We are all well aware of the phrase "War to End War." War will not be
ended until the overwhelming majority of the people have the will to peace
and make known to those in authority, in no unmistakable manner, that war
between nations should be brought to an end for all time, and in its stead
reason shall be brought to bear to settle differences which may arise between
nations. One has only to read their newspaper from day to day to see how
near nations are to a militarist outbreak. It is the more imperative, therefore,
that all those who believe in peace and goodwill should use their energy and
influence to not only prevent war, but to bring into being an era of peace. trust
and confidence between the nations.

GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.
FELLOW MEMBERS,

We are at present aware of advice being given by some that absolute freedom prevails
in the employers' choice of the above. We deny that. Such can only be done after due
notice, or in a general sense only after due consideration and with the approval of the
local board. Clause ro, Sub-section C. deals with anomalies only, and any attempt to
do more than this should be immediately reported.
LEGAL FORCE OF AGREEMENTS. - The Trade Press has dealt many times with the
action of the Trades Union Congress at Plymouth and the confirmation of the National
Agreements by passing such legislation as to enable such Agreements to have the full
force of law, and although some even of our members may hold diverse views on the matter.
none of us can dogmatise either way, but after many years of voluntary effort many of us
think that the non-unionist has too much of the good things provided for him by his less
selfish comrade, who thinks a little pressure will do the "pay for nothing" person a lot
of good. It was in this manner we entered into the spirit of a scheme for the Industry
and paid part expenses for same being drafted, and it ill becomes big unions who are con-
tinually asking the Government to give their own industry special treatment, and to find
the finances for such a purpose and yet deny another industry legal enforcement only of
their conditions.
Already on one important point we stand alone as the only Union in the world which
has a monetary guarantee between both sides as a guarantee against Lock-outs or Strikes
before resorting to Arbitration. We are perhaps the only Union in the world that had
help from the Employers' Federation for Strikers' children during a dispute, and like the
Cotton Operatives, we are one of the few, who, under proper safeguards, believe in and
practise Piecework or Payment by Results.
Therefore, it is nothing new that we should have a different point of view to many
other Unions who prefer other means and methods of working, which they are welcome to
adopt, but must allow others similar freedom, which means that they would not present
adopt National Agreements for legal enforcement, whereas we should; and with my
present experience of Trades Boards should prefer that power than our adherence to the
Voluntary Registration of Agreements.
The TRADE BOARD held a two days' meeting at Whitehall, where we have been review-
ing the past D 22 and D 23 Lists to correct anomalies, grant permits and to revise prices,
if necessary, but after being warned that the wages paid to Managers and Foremen was
about to be challenged, it was, after postponement from one day to the next, allowed to
go unchallenged to the country. A careful review of the prices and conditions as reported
on previous occasions will bear comparison with prices and conditions generally in the
majority of trades. This may not receive the "puff" that some other work gets, but it
is the greatest feat known in our industry, the reason for its success being the work of both
sides aided by three independent gentlemen who hear all the discussions and evidence,
and act as mediators in the finding of agreement between us, in which they have been
unusually successful.
In connection with the above I have had to approach a large firm of multiple shop-
keepers as to the payment of Trade Board rates by one of their Managers in a town 100
miles from the Chief Office. My complaint was that the Ministry had been dealing with
the Manager instead of the Directorate, and further, instead of the Ministry advising
conciliatory means on the report and advice of a Special Committee, including the Chair-
man, they were considering the effect of a prosecution; here was the bold, bald idea of
resorting to force before trying conciliation. I knew many of the Directors, paid the firm
a visit and saw one of the Principals, who has investigated the matter and has recom-
mended a course we are about to follow in a few days. We have no fear but of a settlement
satisfactory to all concerned, and in the meantime the Ministry is taking the case up again
and paying special visits.

ORGANISERS' MONTHLY REPORTS.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
Since my last report I have been organising at Nuneaton and assisting Mr. W.
Warner, at Hinckley, and Mr. Alex. Smith, at Wolverhampton. There are three factories
at Nuneaton, and owing to the fact that a great many of the operatives do not reside
there, it is a difficult matter to organise them, get meetings of them, or to make them
solid and united. We made some members, but our aim is to unite the three shops and
to make one man responsible for the financial side of the business. At one factory the
employer gave Mr. Warner and myself an opportunity to speak to the workers inside the
factory. I believe that we have got all in, with one exception, at this place. If the
promises given to me at another factory are realised we shall have all in there.
For many years our Union has worked systematically towards the equalising of con-
ditions in every branch of the trade, but to me it seems that the factors and the shop-
keepers are the great obstacles in the way of our making it impossible for any manufacturer
to carry on business unless he observed the agreements of the trade. Primarily, the non-
unionists are to blame. The factors and shop-keepers are outside all trade union control.
When they buy boots it is all a question of price. The matter of fair wages and conditions
concerns them not. A manufacturer severs his connection with the Federation, takes
advantage of the bad times we are going through, reduces wages and throws aside every
standard of fair dealings, but he is the darling of the factors and the shop-keepers if he
comes along with cheaper goods than he previously sold. The producers in the boot and
shoe trade have cause to curse the non-producing side of the industry. Pity it is that
the Federation and the Union don't more effectively unite to check those everlasting
squeezers and grinders of the people who produce the goods.
D. MCCARTHY.

The past month has largely been spent in the Kingswood area, and one is pleased
to report further progress having been made. We may not have achieved all we would
have liked in this area, but it is certainly no longer the black spot it was regarding the
conditions contained in the National Agreement. But while that may be so, there is
only one thing that can give a guarantee for the future and that is the National Union of
Boot and Shoe Operatives receiving the confidence and support of the operatives engaged
in the district. Unity and solidarity among the workers irrespective of sex or occupation
is the one thing needed. In view of this, the fact that both branches are making new
members is helpful and encouraging.
In the light of experience one is inclined to the opinion that it may be rather more
difficult here than in other centres, to maintain the influence of the Union. There are
too many of the old features and conditions of the trade in existence. On the common
or cheaper lines of heavy work much outdoor labour is employed, with the result that the
whole family is engaged on the work, and the total earnings appear to give a measure of
satisfaction, even if they do not reach our minimum figures. Then again this system
makes it easier for new firms to start, with the result that competition becomes keener,
and unhealthy trading develops.
It is perhaps true to say that the heavy work made in this district lends itself to
adulteration as readily as any, and it is carried to its utmost limit in the Kingswood area.
This is the most pernicious of all forms of competition, and in the long run it is no use to
anyone. It degrades those who make it whether employer or worker, and it is a fraud
on those who buy the goods so produced. One illustration of the extent to which adultera-
tion is carried on as told to me may be worth recording.
At a town in South Wales, a woman entered a shop to purchase a pair of boots for one
of her children. She was shewn a pair of Kingswood production. In examining them the
woman commented on the fact that the hobs were not properly hammered down. The
shopkeeper stated that could easily be put right and proceeded to pull them on a last
kept handy for such a purpose. He gave one blow with the hammer when to the surprise
of both shopkeeper and customer, the hobs not actually struck by the hammer flew out.
When the former recovered from his astonishment he found the woman had vanished,
and in place of a sale he had lost a customer who probably would never enter his shop
again, and further he was in possession of a quantity of boots that he dare not offer to
anyone again.
These boots were made by a firm well known in Kingswood. A firm that has always
sought to evade our conditions, a firm, who, in my opinion, by this method of manufacture
has robbed both his workpeople and the public. The only satisfaction obtained from the
whole business is, that he has never made any headway as a manufacturer, thus proving
that this kind of trading brings with it no satisfactory results. It would be well if this
form of business could be abolished, and one would like to see the matter considered from
the standpoint of legal enactment. Its destruction would be helpful to the employer
who seeks to produce a good article, it would be a good thing for the worker, the shop-
keeper, and the public.

BRANCH REPORTS.
ARBROATH. - During the month trade has continued bad, and the firm
of Colin Grant Ltd., has closed their factory for the time being. It seems a
pity that one of the best factories in Scotland - from a building point of view-
and enterprise somewhere in the trade willing to carry on the Gold Medal fame
should go out of business, even temporarily, when surely there must be capital
of this firm which has been established over forty years. But such things are
outside the control of humble officials, and our mournful position is that nearly
forty members-men and girls - are signing the branch books. Such con-
ditions look bad for the winter months, and with more stringent regulations
applying at the Labour Exchanges, our members are in for a bad experience.
The new circulars sent to Exchanges indicate the official view of the appalling
distress felt throughout by workers. Further efforts are to be made to cut
down the expense, and many may be denied benefit during the new "benefit
year" who got it regularly before. Those who have to claim uncovenanted
benefit are to suffer most, and a stern fight should be made in every part of
the country to force the Government to either provide work or give adequate
relief payments. The whole trend of the new regulations is in the direction
of assuming it to be a person's own blame if he or she is out of employment
for any length of time. This unwarranted assumption should be exposed
mercilessly, as it cannot be laid to the blame of anyone that work cannot be
got. Labour Exchanges are too busy paying out benefit and taking the daily
signatures to be able to help folk to find work, and in any case in view of the
appalling dearth of jobs, how can it be otherwise than that some remain idle
all the time. This futile pretence of blaming applicants for not finding jobs
when such a vast number have been without regular work for fully three years,
and while all industries are rocking on their foundations yet, may easily provoke
disorder, and yet who could complain if it so happened. If this rotten form
of administrative impertinence is allowed to pass unchallenged, the only
alternative for the older and less assertive workers will be to take in each
other's washing and so earn stamps, to prove their genuine desire to work.
This useful and highly enlightened practice would salve the official conscience,
and all would be well! We have had a visit of Mr. T. F. Richards, General
President, and good meetings were held in Carnoustie and Arbroath. Mr.
Richards spoke very well, and created a deep interest as he outlined the wide-
spread activities of the National Union. National Terms, Trade Boards,
Trade Union Congress and Labour Party, International relationships, &c.,
were each laid under review to indicate the scope and nature of the work which
confronted a national organisation, and even the humblest member could
appreciate the incessant activities of National Officers. Such a visit brings
home to all the bond of work and the bond of principle, and we wish a regular
form of visitation by our officers could be designed. Mr. Richards lives Union,
and exudes Union in all he does, and we can only hope to have him back.
While with us he dealt very effectively with our trouble in Carnoustie, and
we have every reason for thinking that is over now. Mr. C. Bleakley, our
Council member, accompanied the President, and the best thanks of the branch
are his for the disinterested work he has performed for us. Let us close by
sending greetings to the new Scottish Advisory Committee, and wishing it
a long and useful life.

that our members are sticking to their work well after so much short time
has had to take place. Our Secretary has been at a convalescent home at

NORTHAMPTON No. 1.-Trade here remains quiet; very few firms
on full time, several small firms have closed down for an indefinite period;
some have gone into bankruptcy, which all adds to the number of permanent
unemployed. Speaking generally the only prospective avenue of creating
employment is by the national organisation of agriculture. This it is estimated
would employ an additional million men, and put this country in a more
staple condition, instead of always looking for export trade as the only hope.
During the month our Vice-President, Mr. Len. Smith, has been elected as a
National Organiser, and we hope he will have a successful time, and thus
assist in getting the membership up to the 100,000.

UNEMPLOYMENT BENEFIT SUSPENDED.
Miners who Refused Jobs Away.
A point of interest as regards unemployment insurance benefit has been raised at
Blaina, says the South Wales News of Ist September.
At a meeting of the Blaina District Miners' Council on Thursday evening, Mr. Dunn,
miners' agent, according to a supplied report, dealt with cases which had been submitted
to the chief insurance officer in London for observation.
He explained that a number of unemployed married men were asked to accept work
in the Mountain Ash and Aberdare districts. They did not refuse to go, but said they
were willing to accept work if accommodation could be found in these districts for them-
I selves and families. Such accommodation could not be found, only lodgings for the men
themselves.
As the men did not go their unemployment benefit was suspended. By an agreement
between the Ministry of Labour and the Miners' Federation he, the agent, had placed the
case before the chief insurance officer.
The chief insurance officer, in disallowing the benefit, gave the right to appeal to the
Court of Referees.
The council considered the matter and decided to carry the case to the umpire for
final decision.
trict, which was about one-third the number of unemployed twelve months ago. Insurance
Mr. Dunn also reported that there were now only 592 unemployed in the Blaina dis-
cette, 29th September, 1923.

The Report of the Secretary referred largely to the position in Germany, and the
largely increased since the occupation of the Ruhr. Boot and Shoe operatives were badly
hit in this respect. In May 16 per cent, were out of work, and 70 per cent. on short time.
some working as little as eight hours a week, while 30 per cent. worked less than 30 hours.
"The German workers have accepted the duty
that Germany had to perform the reconstruction of the damaged districts and to pay
reparations up to the extreme limit of its capacity, but the possibility for reparation
payment is destroyed when the most important territories of industry and of raw materials
are occupied by a foreign army, and divided from their country. Ten thousands of
railwaymen as well as railway officials, were expelled from their dwellings and deprived
workers. Peaccable workers, even school children, were brutalised and menaced with
of their property, and often submitted to hard penalties of imprisonment, sometimes to
imprisonment for life, because they were unwilling to become traitors to their fellow
shooting, because they did not perform the orders of the French authorities. There is
probably in history no example of a conqueror who brutalised in the same manner the

There have been acts of sabotage, we condemn energetically, but they have been

making an appeal to the conscience of the world to prohibit those acts and at last establish

The effect of the depreciation of the mark was shewn. At the end of August the
wages varied from 400,000 to 700,000 marks per hour, while at the time of our visit it
had risen to as much as 5,000,000. The difficulty evidently was to get wages to rise
equally with prices, and consequently famine revolts, plundering, and irregular strikes
had taken place.
The report further showed that through the Secretary useful work had been done,
though we regret to say that an attempt to settle a dispute at Ballys', in Switzerland,
was not successful. The financial statement showed the funds to be in fairly satisfactory
condition. There was a lengthy discussion upon the report, some of which was irrelavent,
but it was adopted after the closure had been applied.
A resolution dealing with the conditions for affiliation was submitted by Simon on
behalf of the E.C. We opposed this on the grounds that the conditions established at
Vienna two years ago were adequate for our purpose. The resolution was carried. The
question of the admittance of the Russian Communists was strongly opposed. They
asked to come on the grounds of unity within the movement, and the need for a united
front. But it was pointed out by some delegates that Communists had taken the place
of Trade Unionists on strike, while a paper had just been started by them that attacked
Trade Unionism, and in some places articles by Fascists in support of their cause were
published in the Communist Journals.
A report on the eight-hour day was presented by M. Roux, France, from which it
appeared that such had been established in a large number of countries, some by law and
others by collective bargaining by the Unions. He pointed out that attempts had been
made by employers' organisations to destroy the eight-hour day, but had failed. In
Germany the organised employers had offered 500 million gold marks towards reparations
if the Government would make some concession on the eight hours. The Unions ener
getically apposed these proposals. He urged we should not be content with the eight hours,
but should at once prepare to establish the 44-hour week.

CONFERENCE ON FACTORY INSPECTION.
Delegates for Geneva.
The Ministry of Labour announces that the fifth general conference of the International
Labour Organisation created by the Treaty of Versailles will meet at Geneva on 22nd
October, to discuss "General Principles for the Organisation of Factory Inspection."
The Government have appointed as their delegates Mr. H. B. Betterton, M.P., Parlia-
mentary Secretary to the Ministry of Labour, and Sir Malcolm Delevingne, Assistant
meder-Secretary, Home Office, and, in agreement with the National Conferedation of
Employers' Organisations and the General Council of the Trades Union Congress, have
nominated Mr. James Lithgow (ex-President of the Shipbuilding Employers' Federation,
lice-President of the National Confederation of Employers' Organisations) and Mr. E. L.
Poulton, J.P. (Secretary of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives and member
of the General Council of the Trades Union. Congress) as employers' and workpeople's
delegates respectively.
The following advisers have been appointed :-
For the Government Group. - Mr. O. C. Allen, Ministry of Labour; Mr. Gerald
Bellhouse, Chief Inspector of Factories, Home Office; and Miss Constance Smith, Deputy
Chief Inspector of Factories, Home Office.
For the Employers' Group.-Mr. J. B. Forbes Watson, secretary of the National
Confederation of Employers' Organisations.
For the Workers' Group. - Miss Margaret Bondfield, chairman of the General Council
of the Trades Union Congress, secretary of the Women Workers' section of the National
Union of General Workers; and Mr. A. Conley, secretary of the Tailors' and Garment
Workers' Trade Union.
A further adviser for the employers' group will be appointed. Mr. A. L. Kingham, of
the Ministry of Labour, Montagu House, Whitehall, S.W. I, is secretary to the delegation. -
The Times, 12th October, 1923.

BOOT AND SHOE REPAIRING TRADE BOARD.

The 18th meeting of the Boot and Shoe Repairing Trade Board (Great Britain) was
held at the Office of Trade Boards on Wednesday and Thursday, 19th and 20th September,
1923. Mr. W. Addington Willis, the Chairman, presiding. The following members of the
Board were present:—

Appointed Members: Mr. W. Addington Willis, Professor G. W. Daniels and Mr.
W. G. Campbell.

Representatives of Employers: Messrs. J. Bachop, W. T. R. Beckett, J. L. Beckley,
H. L. Burrows, J. Coombes, H. Crabb, J. Hoyle, A. King, T. Malone, W. B.
Noble, F. Park, J. Pollitt and H. Treadwell.

Representatives of Workers: Messrs. C. Bleakley, P. Brennan, J. W. Dickson, A. J.
Dobbs, J. Gay, A. J. Gwyther, J. Jagger, M. McGill, A. T. Morris, W. Orchard,
J. T. Osborne, W. Renwick, T. F. Richards, F. Swain, and W. J. Webb.

Mr. R. Wilson and Mr. J. Gulland for the Secretary of the Trade Board.

The Board received intimation from the Ministry of Labour of the appointment of
Professor G. W. Daniels as Deputy Chairman of the Board, and of Mr. James Coombes
as a representative of Employers on the Board.

The Board also received intimation from the Ministry of Labour that they had decided,
with a view to giving more adequate representation to the various interests of the trade,
to appoint one additional representative of Employers and Workers to the Board.

Proposed Variations of Minimum Rates.

The principal business before the Board was the consideration of the proposed varia-
tions of the minimum rates of wages. This question was fully discussed at the meeting
of the Board held on 18th, 19th and 20th July. The principles upon which the proposed
variations should proceed were decided at that meeting, and the question of adjusting the
proportionate increases or decreases, in accordance with the rise of fall of the Cost-of-
Living figure, on the lines of the decisions of the previous meeting, had been referred to
the Administrative Committee for consideration.

The Administrative Committee submitted Draft Notices of Proposals to the Board
for approval. After full discussion the Draft Proposals were, with certain amendments,
approved by the Board, and the Secretary was instructed to issue the Notices of Proposal
at the earliest practicable date. The principal features of the new proposals are as follow:

General Minimum Time Rates.

The Board propose to fix two principal General Minimum Time Rates:—
(a) For workers who are wholly or mainly employed in making bespoke hand-
sewn leather footwear (including bespoke hand-sewn surgical work), or who are wholly
or mainly employed in performing any of the operations in the making of bespoke
hand-sewn leather footwear (including bespoke hand-sewn surgical work) on the
sectional system.
(b) For workers employed on all other work (except the special classes of workers
employed as power sole-stitchers, pressmen, and foremen and managers for whom
special minimum rates have been fixed).

The proposed minimum rates for the workers referred to in paragraph (a) above are
5s. per week of 48 hours above the minimum rates payable to the workers referred to in
paragraph (b) above (except the special classes).

The Board propose to fix a graduated scale of payments for all workers for various
periods until the Cost-of-Living figure is 30, but this scale does not vary the General Mini-
mum Time Rates at present in operation, in respect of the workers referred to in paragraph
(b) above for the periods when the Cost-of-Living figure is more than 70.

The effect of the Trade Board's proposals may be illustrated by stating that on the
basis of the present Cost-of-Living figure of 73 the minimum time rate for bespoke hand-
sewn work (including all operations in connection with the making of bespoke hand-sewn
surgical boots) would be 65s. per week of 48 hours, and the rate for repairing and for making
bespoke pegged work and bespoke rivetted work would be 60s. per week of 48 hours.

It is proposed to make a variation in the existing rates for learners by taking 1s.
from the weekly rates for the years between 15 and 17 and adding it to the weekly rates
between the years of 19 to 21.

General Minimum Piece Rates.

With regard to the General Minimum Piece Rates the Board propose certain per-
centage reductions (a) from the piece rates for repairing, and (b) from the piece rates for
making, for periods dependent upon the Cost-of-Living figure, ranging from the period
when the figure is more than 90 to the period when it is not more than 30.

in any other
The Board agreed to amend the definition of an indentured apprentice so as to provide
that the indentures of apprenticeship shall be in the Trade Board's form or "
form approved by the Board" The object of this amendment is to give the Board wider
powers in dealing with applications for the registration of apprentices whose indentures
are in the forms which have long been used by recognised Associations and public bodies.
Inspection and Enforcement.
The Board received a report from the Ministry of Labour on Inspection and Enforce-
ment in the Trade for the period from 1st April to 30th June, 1923. The total number of
inspections made during the period was 49. The total number of complaints received
during the period was 47, of which 26 were investigated. Arrangements have been made
for the investigation of 39 outstanding complaints. The Roard also received a special
report on the inspection of a number of firms in London employing outworkers.

LABOUR MINISTER ON WINTER WORK PLANS.
50 Millions to be Spent—and Perhaps Much More.
Apcal to Builders.
Cabinet Committee's " Constant" Efforts.
Sir Montague Barlow, the Labour Minister, in an important speech in the City to-day,
announced that unemployment schemes involving an expenditure of 50 millions are being
initiated, "and as far as possible put in hand immediately," by the Government.
The expenditure, he added, might work out at a "considerably higher figure."
Sir Montague gave the following details of this program :---
Roads and Bridges
Unemployment grants (additional)
Trade facilities
Railway Companies (approximately)
£14,000,000
10,000,000
12,000,000
15,000,000
Some allowance must also be made for Public Utility Companies who received assist-
ance from Lord St. David's committee.
Sir Montague indignantly repudiated Mr. Clynes's charge that the Government had
not carried out the pledge it gave in August, and stated that the Cabinet Unemployment
Committee was in almost constant contemplation of the problem.
HOUSING PROBLEM.
Builders asked to Reconsider Their Position.
Emigration Schemes,
Sir Montague Barlow said unemployment was the most distressing, the most paralysing
problem that faced any statesman to-day. We had been carrying this terrible burden
for three years. It was true that the figures were about 80,000 better than this time last
year, the total of wholly unemployed last week being 1,251,600, compared with 1,330,000
on 9th October, 1922, but he was quite willing to admit that this figure did not represent
the total of unemployment in the country.
An August Pledge.
Sir Montague claimed that the Cabinet Unemployment Committee had carried out
the pledge he gave on 1st August to continue its operations and enlarge its plans as necessity
might require.
"I wish to repudiate with all the strength in my power," he said, "the charge which
Mr. Clynes has thought good to make against the Government, and incidentally against
myself, of breach of faith, and of not carrying out the pledge which I gave to the House
of. Commons.
"Our Socialist opponents, including Mr. Clynes, are anxious to secure power and the
control of government in this country. But I would suggest to them in all sincerity,
that in that pursuit of power they will not find it worth while to make such charges as these
of which I cannot but think Mr. Clynes himself is secretly ashamed."
Mr. Clynes.
He had read the agenda of the Trades Union Congress at Plymouth five weeks ago,
and the chairman's speech, but he found no mention of unemployment. Mr. Clynes was
present. Did he introduce the subject of unemployment? Did he propose plans?
"Not a word did he utter, so far as I can discover," said Sir Montague.
Dealing with a suggestion that the Government "should press on with infinite zeal
a vastly extended housing policy," Sir Montague continued :-
"I am glad to say that the Government policy is progressing steadily. I see that
380 local authorities have initiated building schemes.
"But I put it to the building operatives and their leaders in all seriousness and in all
friendliness whether a time has not come to reconsider their position. At any rate it is
clear that until the acute shortage of skilled labour is eased it is obviously useless for the
Government to bring forward a greatly extended program of building."
Empire Development.
Turning to the Government's unemployment proposals, Sir Montague referred to the
Imperial Conference, to which—and to the development of relations with the Dominions—
they were looking for much help and success in future, " not only in the redistribution of
our man power, but in the strengthening and organisation of our markets.

Crown Colonies, along what I may call the Lord St. Davids hoe, for the

send out the best of the young life of the community to form replicas of the home com-

Training here or in the Dominions is essential. I believe it is practicable."
Railway's 10 Millions.
Referring to the efforts of great companies to help reconstruction, Sir Montague
singled out the Great Western Railway, which is spending ten millions, and referred to
it as " an excellent example of what an energetic industrial undertaking can afford."
Other Companies.
Similar programs were also being undertaken by other railway companies, and he
hoped to be able to announce further progress on another occasion.
"So far as I can gather, not less than about five millions' worth of work is being put
in hand by the various railway companies along the lines I have indicated probably
more," he added.
Three "Trunk Lines."
Sir Montague then referred to "the three trunk lines of the Government effort"—
unemployment insurance, trade development, and relief schemes.
England was at last beginning to realise the greatness of unemployment insurance—
our sheet anchor."
Export Credits.
"As to (b) trade development, under the heading of export credits scheme and trade
facilities provision, here again there is ample provision, both for the individual trader who
desires to export, and to have his risk shared by the Government, and also for the public
company which desires to enter on big constructional development.
"The export credit program still allows of some £16,000,000 or rather more of risk
being undertaken in proper cases.
Trade Development.
So far as trade facilities were concerned there had been big developments since August.
10 to 12 millions in round figures, and this will bring the total State guarantee up to the
figure of about 30 millions out of 50 available, leaving 14 for other schemes of develop-
ment as they come along."

LABOUR:
The Coming Power
A VOICE IN THE PRESS.
Is there another newspaper in the country, has there ever been
a newspaper so widely cherished as the "Daily Herald"? Is there
a newspaper proprietor anywhere who would not appreciate the
unique advantage which the "Daily Herald " has in the matter of
personal service among its readers ?
The letters which pour into the Herald Office by every post give
evidence of widespread interest in the details of the paper's circula-
tion figures. In every Parliamentary division the units of the Labour
Movement have now been informed of the quota or proportion of new
readers which are required as the local share of the 500,000 circulation
that is required.
Yet, with all this interest and goodwill, with all this general
feeling of benevolence towards the Herald, it is still necessary to tell
its friends in the plainest possible English that all previous efforts
must be redoubled and renewed if the paper, the only one of its kind,
is to be preserved for the future.
Many of the understanding ones, who are the outposts of this
great idea of an independent Labour Press, have become tired, and
have given up the struggle in despair. But in many places the warfare
against prejudice has been renewed at the right moment and is
achieving its rewards at last.
After long silence, the arguments and persuasions of years are
beginning to have their effect.
The amount of willing service in the form of canvassing must,
in the aggregate, represent a volume of pressure upon wavering
minds which, if it be continued long enough, will undoubtedly have
rich results.
The "Daily Herald" wants more readers and is getting them;
the question is, will it get them quickly enough to save this great
enterprise from an untimely death, as its proprietor, LABOUR,
approaches the threshold of power:
Only personal effort can avail.

WHAT MR. McCURDY THINKS OF THE "YES,
WE HAVE NO BANANAS" GOVERNMENT.
The questions of Unemployment, and Security for the Worker, were the subjects of
a special address, delivered by Mr. C. A. McCurdy, K.C., M.P., at the Northampton Town
Hall, on 6th October, 1923.
Mr. McCurdy, who was very heartily received, said that the Government were so
busy taking off their hats to Poincare or rubbing themselves where he last kicked them,
The trouble of the Conservatives was not that they had no remedy for trade depression,
for unemployment, and for the distressed agriculturists. On the contrary, they had a
golden remedy for all these evils. They had been telling them so for years. “Tariff
Reform means work for all." "Tariff Reform means two jobs for every man." Their
difficulty was not that they had no remedy, but that they could not screw up their courage
to apply it. They felt bound by the pledge of Mr. Bonar Law, and that pledge meant that
if they were to give the country the remedy in which they believe, they must first ask the
permission of the electors.
Mr. Baldwin and his colleagues were on the horns of a horrid dilemma. Either they
must withhold from the British manufacturer their golden remedy for bad trade, or they
must take the chance of themselves joining the ranks of the unemployed. (Laughter.)
Either they must stick to their fiscal principles or stick to their places.
One and a quarter million unemployed are asking the Government what
their policy is for coming winter. The only answer they got was, "Yes,
we have no policy to-day."
The farmer asked whether the Government wanted him to continue
arable farming, or what was their policy for British agriculture, and the
only answer they got was, "Yes, we have no policy to-day."
The whole country was asking: What is the Government's foreign
policy? Are they in agreement with France, or are they in profound
disagreement, and what is now the policy of the Government with regard
to the French occupation of the Ruhr? And they get no answer from
anybody. This was a “Yes, we have no Bananas" Government.
(Laughter.)
The Government relief works will find occupation for not more than 300,000 men.
That will leave more than one million out of work. Was there really nothing useful that
these men could do?
How to Pay our Debt to the United States.
A Vast Re-Housing Scheme.
France was building new and modern factories, improving her waterways and railways,
overhauling her industrial plant. Yet one million men on these islands stood looking
idly at one another. There was abundance of productive work waiting to be done. He
would give them one example-the re-housing of our slum population would not merely
pay for itself, it would in the course of the next 10 years be producing an annual profit
sufficient to pay off the debt of this country to the United States of America. Four years
ago the cost of building was prohibitive, a cottage which could be built to-day for £330
was then costing £1,200. There was a good excuse then for caution and delay before
embarking on a bold re-housing policy. There was no such excuse to-day. Three millions
of our people, men, women, and children, are festering and rotting in slums. Glasgow,
for example, was rotten with rickets, and out of a population of 1,000,000, 600,000 were
living in one room or in two-roomed tenements.
What was this condition of affairs costing us? Not merely in terms of immorality,
health, crime, and unhappiness, but in terms of cash? At the lowest possible estimate
the total direct material loss in England and Wales from sickness and disability, including
loss of wages, was £150,000,000 a year. Tuberculosis alone, that product of the slums,
costs us £90,000,000 a year.
The President of the British Medical Association had pointed out that if the abolition
of the slums and the removal of three millions of our race from these hotbeds of disease
reduced our national sickness bill by only one-third, the saving would be £50,000,000 a
year. What would it cost at present prices to rehouse three million people? He had

What the "Northampton Daily Chronicle" thinks of Mr. McCurdy.
Mr. McCurdy says that whether it is unemployment or agriculture or France and
foreign affairs the Stanley Baldwin Government have no policy, and he even suggests
they seem to have no time to attend to the unemployed. It is, he declares, a
we have no bananas" Government. And why is Mr. McCurdy moved to pay these left-
handed "compliments ?" He was elected to Parliament by the Conservative vote of
Northampton, and he has never formally broken off from the "understanding" then
existing. Moreover, he will not be again elected for Northampton unless he has the
Conservative vote. Wouldn't it be better form to say the least for him to speak a
little more respecfully of the Government and give them credit for honesty of purpose.
There would still be room for him to offer his political or economic wares and there
would also be a far greater readiness among Conservatives to sympathetically examine
them.
In view of the above-named statements, it is quite plain that with proper manage-
ment, the outlook for the return to Parliament of a Labour Candidate is much more
promising than it was in 1922. It is to be hoped that all sections of workers in North-
ampton will realise the great opportunity they have, and when the appeal is made to them,
I hope they will put their X against the person running in the Labour interests, and thus
ensure the return of the first Labour Candidate for Northampton. - E. L. POULTON, General

GOOD NEWS FOR CONSUMPTIVES.
Continued from page 586 in September Monthly Report.
Snatched From the Grave.
My last case is of a very remarkable character. It relates to a gentleman who for
many years hold an important position with a Blackburn firm, afterwards receiving a
responsible appointment in London.
Mr. Stevens says this patient was in an advanced condition of pulmonary consumption
when commencing the treatment, having a large cavity in each lung. His general con-
dition was very poor. His normal weight was 13 stone, but when he began taking the
remedy he was only 8½ stone.

cure:
Writing me on the 23rd ult., the gentleman enclosed the following account of his

"I have ample cause to feel grateful to Mr. C. H. Stevens, of Wimbledon, for his
wonderful discovery for the cure of that terrible scourge, consumption.
"Three years ago I was attacked at the age of fifty-six by this malady, and by force
of circumstances obliged to continue at my work. I got weaker and weaker, lost weight
to an alarming extent, and finally collapsed, being on the verge of death.
"Before my collapse I consulted three specialists, who in each case advised sanatorium
treatment.
"Finally, I entered one of the most famous hospitals in England for the cure of
consumption. I was in such a weak condition that I was put to bed immediately, and
remained there as a bed patient during the whole five months I was in the hospital.
"I was especially well treated and well looked after, but at the end of the five months
the medical superintendent asked for an interview with my wife, and informed her—
unable to do anything further for me, which was tantamount to indicating that my case
was hopeless.
"After leaving the hospital, which I did in such a weak state that I was removed in
a vehicle, although feeling better for the long rest and the ample, wholesome food, all the
symptoms of the fell disease were upon me.
"The outlook seemed very bad indeed. I did not quite know what took place at the
interview which my wife had with the medical superintendent, but the impression left
on her mind was that I had not long to live.
"Just at this time, when black despair was looming upon my household, my old
and valued friend, Mr. T. P. Ritzema, informed me of the wonderful cures of consumption
which had been effected by Mr. Stevens, and strongly advised me to try the treatment.
I did so, and have cause to bless the man who gave the advice and the man who discovered
the wonderful Umckaloabo cure.
"The treatment is very simple, and the directions easy to follow.
"From the very first I experienced relief. After a few days there was a sense of
cleanness and sweetness of the palate and throat, to which I had long been a stranger.
"The disease had been allowed to get such a terrible hold upon me that it seemed a
miracle when definite and not to be disputed improvement began to take place. Progress
was necessarily slow at first, but week by week, and month by month, the improvement
went on, and life began to open up anew fresh hopes for the future; visions of a return
to health and strength and a return to work and happiness!
"These dreams and visions have become crystallised facts, and to-day, I have so far
got back to health that I am about to make application to my old firm for reinstatement
after an absence of over two years.
"It is undoubtedly the duty of those who guide the destinies of our nation to take
up and use Mr. Stevens' treatment. The nation has at its disposal a curative agent which
is thoroughly effective in curing and eradicating this terrible scourge from our land."
Boycotted for Twenty-five Years.
It is twenty-five years since Mr. Stevens took up this treatment, having himself been
cured of tuberculosis by the use of Umckaloabo. Had he been out to make money by his
discovery he might have formed a wealthy syndicate, gone in for a big advertising campaign,
and made a fortune. On the contrary, for the first nine years he gave the preparation
away. He then took up the sale of the article for a living, continuing to supply it to poor
people free of charge.

An Offer to the Nation.
In view of the large sum of money that the Lancashire County Council was willing
to provide for experimenting with the Spahlinger treatment, I asked Mr. Stevens on
what terms he would be willing to sell his treatment to the nation.
Although I believe that he is a comparatively poor man, he replied that if the Ministry
of Health put Umckaloabo to the test and found that it was a specific for consumption,
he would be willing to make the nation a present of it, together with his stock-in-trade,
on condition that it was supplied to panel patients and used in the national sanatoriums.
A more generous offer was never made to any people.
WHAT OF CANCER?
Hitherto a vast sum of money has been spent in endeavouring to find a cure for
cancer as well as for tuberculosis. This has been largely, if not exclusively, expended in
endeavouring to find a serum with which to inoculate patients suffering from these scourges.
The specific for tuberculosis discovered by Mr. Stevens, and which, according to Dr.
Sechchaye, may contribute largely to eradicating this terrible scourge, belongs to the
vegetable kingdom. It seems to entirely clear the system of tubercle. Is there any
reason why the vegetable kingdom should not be explored for a specific to cure cancer?
“And the leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations."
The medical faculty seems to be obsessed with the idea that there can be no cure
for either cancer or tuberculosis except through a serum injected into the blood of those
who are overtaken by these terrible scourges, although it has not yet been proved whether
cancer is caused by bacilli or not. Any person who brings forward a new serum is hailed
as the deliverer of the people. This was the case in the year 1880, when Dr. Koch, a
German physician, was able to isolate tuberculosis and at a later period-produced
tuberculin, which was received throughout the world as an absolute remedy for the disease.
Unfortunately it turned out a dismal failure. The remedy for the white scourge has
apparently been found in a plant grown in the British Empire, and all that is necessary is
for the medical profession to prescribe it to deliver the human race from the destroyer.
Mr. J. A. Speed, secretary of the Lancashire County Council Insurance Committee,
speaking recently in Manchester on the treatment of tuberculosis, said: “Whether it
was the Spahlinger healing OR ANY OTHER they wanted its benefits and wanted it now.
The digging must be done and CONSUMPTIVE PATIENTS MUST BE SAVED. Waiting was
no use.
The Lancashire County Council need not wait another day for a remedy, much less
until the end of next year to make experiments with the Spahlinger treatment. Mr.
Stevens will be pleased to send the Council a supply of his specific free of charge, so that
it may at once be put to the test in the Lancashire Sanatoriums.

KINGSWOOD BOOT OPERATIVES.
Success of a Recent Campaign. Future Prospects.
The annual rally of the Kingswood and District Nos. 1 and 2 Branches of the National
Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives was held last evening at the British School, Kingswood.
Mr. J. Manners, a member of the National Executive of the Union presided, and the chief
speakers were Mr. T. F. Richards, general president: Mr. E. L. Poulton, J.P., general
secretary of the Union and Mr. W. R Smith. Messrs. Poulton and Smith have recently
returned from a national conference of shoe and leather workers in Germany.
The Chairman said that 90 per cent. of those working in the trade locally were receiving
the benefits of the holiday scheme. He felt that achievement was something to be proud
of because for many months they had been faced with adverse circumstances as regards
the trade. It was only in the last few months that they had been able to make any appreci-
able headway. Locally interest had been taken in the quest of the cut in wages, which
became operative in June, being restored.
Mr. T. F. Richards expressed appreciation of the work done locally on behalf of the
Union by Mr. W. R. Smith, Mr. J. Manners, and Mr. A. G. Randall. It had been felt in
the past that in the Kingswood trade the economic conditions were in a bad way. That
reflected itself in many employers who naturally preferred, through bad trade and other
causes, to make an escape from obligations by not paying to the holiday scheme, which
was an organised agreement made by organised bodies of Employers and the Union. The
Union embraced at least 80 per cent. of those engaged in the trade. No loophole would be
allowed the employer by the Union to escape his responsibility. They did not want to
make trouble for the employer. They started on a campaign many years ago with the
sole intention, as far as possible, of endeavouring to see that the labour cost of the boot and
shoe operatives should be as stationary and as fair nationally, irrespective of districts, as
was the price of leather, machines and taxes of the country. He did not think any em-
ployer in Kingswood or any other part of the Kingdom would impugn or tell them they
had endeavoured on any particular occasion to take a mean or contemptible advantage.
The very fact that their agreement of 1895 remained solidified to-day, and from that time
till now a general upheaval in the boot and shoe industry had not taken place, was an
example to other industries. They had endeavoured to have a working agreement which
and the majority of the employers. Time was when the boot and shoe operative was looked
upon as of lower status than he was to-day. Many people would rather wear boots without
nails than those with nails, and they had arrived at a transitory stage. They might find
that lighter grades would be made in course of time. They had competitors. They would
remember the struggle made with their greatest competitors at Chesham. The conditions
in Chesham now were such that they had no complaints to make. The success at Chesham
had defended Kingswood. If the cost of living at the end of September was officially
shown to be over 70 per cent., then the last "cut" would be restored in their wages.
(Applause.) The prospects between themselves and the employers appeared to be of a
satisfactory character. The speaker appealed for greater support of the Union in the
future.

manufacturers were desirous that every manufacturer should pay to that scheme. By
support to their local officers they should see from time to time that the scheme was
honoured. He felt strongly upon the question of hours. Whatever economists might
say here or in other countries, they might make up their minds that the workers were going
to have shorter hours, also on the Continent and in America. Mr. Smith and himself
had just returned from Germany, attending a national conference of shoe and leather
workers. One of the principal matters discussed there was the maintenance of the eight-
hour day. Emphasis was particularly laid upon the necessity of that, and the Boot
Operatives' Union hoped to see the number reduced lower and lower as they found the
means of producing boots and shoes and other articles by machinery faster and faster.
When machinery turned out goods at a faster rate the workers ought to be entitled to
benefit. They should be entitled to that from a humanitarian standpoint, and also with
the view of having greater opportunities to improve themselves and fit themselves to
discharge their duties as citizens. It was somewhat pathetic to note the way the Continental
workers were looking to England to bring about a more satisfactory state of affairs. He
appealed to them to build up their organisation, to make it increasingly useful to themselves.
He felt sure they had the same sort of spirit as people in other parts of the country. Because
they had fallen on bad times and the days were dark do not let them get dispirited. Let
them display the qualities and courage shown on another field during the war, and on the
industrial field do their part towards bringing about a better state of affairs.
Mr. A. G. Randall, J.P. (local secretary of the Union), said that although 90 per cent
were receiving the benefit of the holiday payment scheme, they should not be satisfied
until the remaining 10 per cent. were benefiting. They were looking with anxiety to the
winter. As a season's trade it had been disappointing. It was hoped to make some pro-
vision for the winter in the district outside their own funds. The Union during the past

Has England no policy? Do you people see nothing but an easy life?"
Undoubtedly, the first effect of the speech here was to stiffen the sections hostile to
the League. I have studied the speech, and its mischief lay in what it did not say more
than in what it did say. Mr. Baldwin really does not know the circumstances with which

representatives here, but his last words, spoken as we shook hands, were:
and your Government have not done well. You have a great opportunity if you
only had the wisdom to take it."
It is plainer than ever to me that in these days it is being determined for us whether
the next generation will, or will not, find itself again involved in a world war. There is
no alternative between a League of Nations, with peace, and a Balance of Power,
with war.
And if the League of Nations is to have a ghost of a chance there must be
a British policy, pacific but firm, friendly but clear as to aim. That we have
not got, and that is the great danger which now besets our Country. - Extracts
from the Daily Herald, 4th October, 1923.
