UNEMPLOYMENT.
Mr. Baldwin on Taking Risks.
We live in times, said Mr. Baldwin yesterday, when risks must be taken. Yes, but
what sort of risks? By far the greatest risk of all is the risk of doing nothing, and if this
was the risk that Mr. Baldwin had in mind, he is entitled to congratulate himself. But of
any other sort of risk, we can see no sign in the Government's policy. Prod it anywhere
and you find it soft, yielding and spongy.
The one question that is relevant, namely, whether France ever intends to get out of
approaching the time when whatever we do it will make no difference to the fact. Our
the Ruhr, and if not what we propose to do about it, is never mentioned. We are rapidly
chief textile industry will be the spinning of words, while others make the facts.
Or take that other aspect of the problem, the relations of capital and labour. We not
only need the old closed markets to be reopened, but if we are to compete successfully in
them, we need to get back our old power to produce more cheaply and better than our
competitors. That is impossible without close and sympathetic co-operation between
capital and labour. You must have a constructive labour policy which will increase
industrial output; you cannot increase output without an incentive to the worker; and
your incentive must be part of a considered policy that will remove the prime heresy of
labour in our time, that you can make work for others by doing less yourself. We can
imagine England under the right leader being rallied by such a policy into a great industrial
revival which would rival the triumphs of the past. But as for this Government, we cannot
discover that it has any labour policy at all.
Mr. Baldwin yesterday seemed to be addressing himself to the third part of the pro-
blem-emigration, and the development of the under-populated lands in the Dominions.
But here, too, there seems to be a conspiracy to shirk the real issues. The Government's
policy crumbles into dried currants, and one section of the Liberal party is treating the
currants as though they were granite boulders, heaving and sweating as though the great
fiscal controversy of the early years of the century were upon us again. We have expressed
our opinion on these proposals about currants. The issues seem to us comparatively
trivial in their present form. Our suspicion is that Mr. Baldwin, so far from having a
policy that will accomplish anything, is really occupied in doing nothing at all that matters.
The sterling of British statesmanship is no sooner touched by this Government than
it breaks up into small coinage and unconsidered trifles.
Unemployment insurance ought to be standardised and brought up to subsistence
level, and the guardians would thus be relieved of a disagreeable and onerous responsi-
bility. At the same time, the enduring remedy for unemployment is NOT UNEMPLOYED
BENEFIT, BUT WORK. It is distressing and disappointing to find that, with Christmas
getting nearer and nearer, NOTHING IN THE FORM OF A CONSTRUCTIVE POLICY IS FORTH-
COMING FROM THE GOVERNMENT. France has organised a flood of constructive and pro-
ductive enterprises in the months during which our rulers have been painfully devising
sops and remedies. Why have we not done the same? If a cure for the worst disease
that attacks the industrial worker has been found in France it can be found here.--Daily
Chronicle, 13th October, 1923.
SUPPRESSION OF TRADE UNIONS IN GREECE.
H.M. Commercial Secretary at Athens transmits a translation of the text of a "Re-
volutionary Decision" of the Greek Government, dated 20th August, 1923, by which all
legally recognised trade unions and trade union federations are declared to be non-existent
on and from the date of the Decision, and are to be dissolved by Royal Decrees on the
advice of the Greek Government. The public prosecuting authorities are to take over all
trade union archives, books and registers, and their funds are to be deposited, under the
care of the same authorities, with the National Bank of Greece, in an account in favour
of the Workers' Provident Fund. Legally recognised Workers' Benefit Societies are
excluded from the scope of this Decision. - The Labour Gazette, October, 1923.

DOLES FOR THE "DISTINGUISHED."
Living on Glamour of Ancestry. Mystery Pensions.
Doles to the "Distinguished" cost the British people for the year ended 31st March
last £366,456, according to official statements issued yesterday.
The pensions for naval and military services totalled £12,270. For the most part
they are not pensions for naval and military services rendered by the present recipients.
Lord Rodney and Baroness Rodney have £1,000 each because the first Baron Rodney,
born in 1718, distinguished himself by victories at sea at the Battle of Cape St. Vincent in
1780, and other naval engagements. There is no evidence that the family has ever been
anywhere near the poverty line.
Earl Nelson, though not a direct lineal descendant of Horatio, benefits because of
Horatio's part in the Trafalgar victory. It was computed in 1913 that collateral relatives,
personally unknown to the public, who could have no claim but what they derived from
accidental fact of bearing Nelson's name, had collected altogether over £500,000.
"Pretty Well Paid."
Yet Nelson himself was pretty well paid. Apart from his pay as a naval officer and
prize money, which at the Battle of the Nile alone amounted to over £3,000, while an estate
grant by the King of Naples produced an annual sum of £3,000, Nelson was also presented
with £10,000 by the East India Company, and in the latter part of his life he had Govern-
mental pensions, English and Irish, of £4,000 a year.
Viscount Hardinge draws £3,000 a year by virtue of a pension for that amount voted
to the first Viscount and his next two successors to the peerage. The first Viscount fought
at Ligny, where he lost a hand, and in India.
A Mysterious £2,000.
Exactly why Lord Seaton draws £2,000 a year is not clear. But he served in the South
African War and the Great War himself, and many of his ancestors were warriors whose
names were conspicuous.
Under the head of political and civil pensioners only two names figure in the financial
accounts of the United Kingdom - Lord George Hamilton, £2,000, and the late Viscount
Chaplin, £1,200. Both of these will not figure in next year's accounts.
The total amount drawn by Lord George Hamilton was £44,000.
Lawyers draw £56,000.
Among the pensions for judicial services there are £5,000 to Earl Loreburn, Viscount
Haldane and Lord Buckmaster. Earl Loreburn is an ex-Lord Chancellor. He was in
office 6 years. Viscount Haldane was Lord Chancellor for just under three years, and
Lord Buckmaster one year and seven months.
Two Irish peers, Lord Shandon and Lord Glenavy, have £3,692 each.
Others on the law list are Lord Trevethen, £3,322; Lord Wrenbury, Lord Phillimore
Viscount Mersey, Sir A. M. Channell, Sir M. Ingle Joyce and Sir E. Ridley, £3,500. All
were adequately paid when " in harness" in law courts.
The total pensions for judicial services in England amounted to £56,422.-Daily
Herald, Wednesday, 3rd October, 1923.
The above-named list shows how well certain people are looked after by the Nation.
What a contrast when the recipients are working people; the smallest amount of
income from any small savings due to thriftiness on their part are taken into
account and the allowance reduced accordingly. Another example showing the
need of a Labour Government.-E. L. POULTON, General Secretary.
ATTACK ON HOURS?
M.P.'s Warning to Boot and Shoe Operatives.
A warning to operatives in the boot and shoe trade, that an attempt to destroy the
48-hour week was being contemplated by the Federation of British Industries, has been
made by Mr. John Buckle, M.P., at a meeting of the union at Higham Ferrers, Northants.
He knew that the union was very strong, but it was necessary to rope in those who
had accepted the advantages obtained by the union's efforts.
Before the Boot and Shoe Operatives' Union was formed, said Mr. Buckle, men had
to work 60 hours a week for 18s. to 20s. The rapid growth of the union had com
rate of 56s., shortly to be increased to 6os., in accordance with the cost-
scale, for a 48-hour week.-Daily Herald, 15th October, 1923.

WOMEN AND WORLD LABOUR PROBLEMS.
Many women will attend the fifth annual session of the International Labour Con-
ference of the League of Nations which opens at Geneva on Monday, 22nd October, and
which will study "General Principles for the Organisation of Fractory Inspection."
To this Conference each of the 56 States which are members of the International
Labour Organisation is entitled to send four delegates, two representing the Government
and one each the employers' and workers' organisations, and each delegate is allowed two
technical advisers. It is in the capacity of technical advisers that most of the women
will be present.
In the lists of official representatives already received at Geneva there appears the
name of Mme. Betzy Kjelsberg as full Government delegate for Norway. Mme. Kjelsberg,
who is a Government factory inspector, has already attended the two preceding sessions
of the Conference in 1921 and 1922 as delegate.
Among technical advisers for Government delegates appear the names of Mme. Julie
Arenhold (Denmark), factory inspector and civil engineer; Mme. Letellier (France),
Departmental Inspector of Labour, who attended the 1921 session in the same capacity;
and Mme. Marguerita Sarfatti (Italy).
It is also stated that Miss Margaret Bondfield, who has just been elected first woman
chairman of the Trades Union Congress, will attend this session as a technical adviser
to the British Workers' delegate, Mr. E. L. Poulton, O.B.E., J.P., General Secretary of
the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives.

MONTHLY REPORT.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
TRADE
19TH NOVEMBER, 1923.
during the month has showed no improvement, no less than 2,336 of our
members drawing benefit from the Union's Unemployment Fund. The figures
issued by the Ministry of Labour are as follows: -

BOOT AND SHOE INDUSTRY.
Employment during October continued slack on the whole, and showed little general
change, an improvement in some districts being counterbalanced by a decline in others.
Short time working was still very prevalent.
The percentage of workpeople unemployed, as indicated by the unemployment books
lodged at Employment Exchanges, was 9.8 on the 22nd October, compared with 10.3 on
24th September.
In London employment remained bad generally. There was a slight improvement
at Leicester, but short time was still largely worked. At Northampton employment
was slack; most of the factories were working short time. At Kettering some firms
were on full time, and few were working less than three-quarter time; employment was
slightly better than in October of last year. At Wellingborough there was a further
improvement, and very little short time was worked. Improvements were also reported
at Hinckley and in the Rushden district; in the latter district employment was good,
and some overtime was worked. At Desborough employment declined, and much short
time was worked. Employment also declined at Stafford and at Stone.
At Norwich there was not much change, and short time was largely worked. At
Bristol employment was still quiet; at Kingswood the gradual recovery from a condition
of extreme depression was maintained. A slight improvement was reported at Leeds,
though short time was still largely worked.

at Leicester, but short time was still largely worked. At Northampton employment
was slack; most of the factories were working short time. At Kettering some firms
were on full time, and few were working less than three-quarter time; employment was
slightly better than in October of last year. At Wellingborough there was a further
improvement, and very little short time was worked. Improvements were also reported
at Hinckley and in the Rushden district; in the latter district employment was good,
and some overtime was worked. At.Desborough employment declined, and much short
time was worked. Employment also declined at Stafford and at Stone.
At Norwich there was not much change, and short time was largely worked.
Bristol employment was still quiet; at Kingswood the gradual recovery from a condition
of extreme depression was maintained. A slight improvement was reported at Leed,
though short time was still largely worked.

THE GENERAL OUTLOOK.
The general outlook is not at all a bright one, many members still receiving
unemployment benefit, whilst a still greater number are working short time.
This policy is one pursued for many years by the Union, and upon the whole
is much better than the operative being out of work entirely. Nevertheless,
the spending power of those on short time must necessarily be reduced, and
taking the whole country through, having regard to operatives unemployed as
well, the home market is essentially restricted, and after all that ought to be
the basis of our well being and prosperity. We would therefore call the serious
attention of the members to the position in which we find ourselves to-day
owing to the action of the Government. The Premier, Mr. Stanley Baldwin,
has made a number of speeches latterly, which all go to prove-whatever word
may be used that at the back of the mind of the Government, the idea of
---

---
"Protection" is prominent. We are aware of the fact that when people are
short of work, or have no work at all, a specious case can be built up and state-
ments adduced which are designed to show that we should be better off under
Protection. In this respect, however, experience is readily available, and the
history of our own and other countries shows that protection, apart from being
a real help to the worker, tends to make his position worse. We hope, there-
fore, that our members will not be misled by any will-o'-the-wisp which is being
attempted to be put into the forefront for what appears to be an early General
Election. We are, therefore, pleased that the General Council of the Trades
Union Congress and the Executive of the Labour Party have taken an early
opportunity at a gathering held on the 1st inst., to welcome the return of Mr.
J. Ramsay MacDonald, M.P., from his voyage in the East, to secure from
M.. MacDonald, as leader of the political side of the movement, a clear statement
that the Labour Party will not allow itself to be drawn into an argument
merely of Protection v. Free Trade, but their battle cry will be Protection". the
Labour Policy, which policy puts in the forefront adequate methods of dealing
with the unemployment question. This question becomes more and more
serious because of so many boys and girls leaving school with no chance of
getting a good training in any particular trade or calling.
At a joint meeting of the General Council of the Trades Union Congress
and the Labour Party held prior to the meeting referred to above, the following
resolution was unanimously passed :-
"This meeting of the General Council of the Trades Union Congress
and the National Executive of the Labour Party calls upon Trades Unions,
Trades Councils and other affiliated organisations, local Labour constitu-
ency bodies, and individual members,
to resist to the utmost the specious policy of Protection, and to press
upon the electorate Labour's policy of work and wages, with the
provision of adequate maintenance for the reserves of industry, to
be secured by international reconstruction and co-operation, national
reorganisation and development, and the putting into operation of
Labour's general programme to meet the crying social and economic
ills which assail the urban and rural populations alike.
" This is the only real alternative to Protection, and upon that we
stand."
This resolution was followed by a splendid speech from Mr. MacDonald,
in which he gave a very good outline of the Labour policy, which policy the
Party has been constantly bringing to the front as an alternative to the many
makeshift schemes the Government have from time to time brought forward.
We hope the members availed themselves of the opportunity of reading the
special report of this speech in the *Herald* of the 2nd inst., thereby being enabled
to see for themselves the practical proposals the Labour Party have for dealing
not only with unemployment, but the world position.

THE GENERAL ELECTION.
The General Election has been precipitated upon us, but the call has found
the Labour Party ready. On Tuesday, the 13th inst., the Prime Minister, the
Rt. Hon. Stanley Baldwin, M.P., announced to the House of Commons that he
the Tory Government would appeal to the country upon the question of
Protection. We appeal to all our members and the workers generally - who
had advised the Crown to dissolve Parliament on Friday, the 16th inst., when
candidate in their respective divisions, and thereby return to power men who
are in the great majority - to so use their influence and vote for the Labour
understand the working-class difficulties. The General Election at this moment
was not of our seeking, but we are confident that the policy of the Labour Party
is the policy for the workers and also for the best and highest interest of the
Nation generally. A majority for the Labour Party in the next House of
Commons means real headway will be made to bring about better conditions
in the lot of the workers both at home and internationally. During the past
twelve months the Government have done nothing tangible, although they
have made many, many promises, and now that the opportunity has come we
trust the workers will take full advantage of the same by voting Labour, and
thus help on the millions of workers throughout the country.
So far as the Union is concerned, we shall have candidates at Eccles,
Daventry and Norwich. In the first named Mr. J. Buckle, J.P., will again
champion the cause of Labour, whilst at Leicester West, which has been
represented by Ald. A. Hill, J.P., the latter will not contest the Seat, he having
retired from the campaign on medical advice, which we very much regret
indeed, he having in the short period during which he was a Member of
Parliament, been assiduous in his duties in fulfilling the position of a M.P., not
merely from our own standpoint, but for the constituency as a whole. We
trust Ald. Hill will speedily be restored to his normal health and strength again.
In connection with LEICESTER WEST, we felt that Ald. Hill, having won
the Seat by such a handsome majority and the Union having spent a very
considerable amount of cash upon the constituency, the Union would have
been given the first choice of another candidate. To our surprise, although
we held our meeting a week sooner than the usual time, owing to the Election
being sprung upon the country, the Executive of the local Labour Party had
a meeting on Friday, the 16th inst., and decided that they could not wait
until Monday, the 19th inst., and selected a candidate immediately. Thus
the position passes from us. We feel we have a right to express our disapproval
of such procedure, especially, as previously stated, we not only won the seat,
but had a full time agent in the Division, thus keeping the Party machinery
in being, at our expense. More may be said of this next month.
In the DAVENTRY Division of Northants our Mr. Len. Smith has been
selected as the Candidate; at Norwich our Mr. W. R. Smith, J.P., has been
selected as one of the two Labour Candidates, this being a two member con-
stituency.

REMEMBER THE FIFTEENTH!
Once again we feel bound to call the serious attention of Branch Secretaries
to the fact that the FIFTEENTH day of each month is the latest day for
returns reaching the General Secretary. If Branches fail to send off their
returns to reach the Central Office before the 15th of the month it tends to
upset the organisation of the work in the General Secretary's Office. We beg
to intimare that unless returns are in before the 15th of the month, the Secretary

ORGANISERS' MONTHLY REPORT.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
MANCHESTER,
21st November, 1923.
During the past month I have been organising at Nuneaton, Market Harborough
and Manchester. Also I had to deal in an arbitration case at Leicester where I represent
our side as an arbitrator. The manufacturers' side claimed that for the building of heels
that leather layer lifts should be the same price per gross as lifts made of board or pulp.
We claimed that the leather layer lifts were not as uniform in substance as the pulp lifts,
and that the operator had to use judgment in selecting lifts as though they were leather.
The Umpire's decision is that when leather layer lifts are as uniform in levelness as pulp
lifts the price shall be the same, but judging on the samples of lifts and leather layer board
submitted by our side and the employers, the price shall be the same as for leather lifts.
At Nuneaton I had the help of Mr. W. Warner, Secretary of Hinckley Branch, and I
am pleased to report that we made some progress towards uniting the factories there.
We had a good meeting and joined about 50 members. At one firm where the Holiday
(Provision) Scheme was not being carried out we got the employer to agree to it. There
are two small heel building factories at Nuneaton and the workers are poorly paid. All
sense of honour and fair dealing are ignored in regard to prices when compared to the
Leicester prices for heel building. At the firm of Smith's the workers are all juveniles
and unable to defend themselves. I am of the opinion that if their parents understood
the true position of things that no matter how hard up they may be they would not allow
their girls and boys remain there. Some of the girls said if there was any chance of getting
anything elsewhere they would leave the place. I presented the employer with a copy
of the Statement and showed him where he was wronging the youngsters as well as the
trade. Messrs. Asher's, of Leicester, run the other shop. There are not many employed
there, but so far as I could learn the conditions are not much better than at Smith's.
I paid a few visits to Market Harborough. There are more men getting the minimum
wage here now than there were when Mr. E. Law and I were there over twelve months ago.
The workers are to blame here as well as the employers for the full conditions of the Agree-
ments not being carried out. Mr. Looms, senior, told me that if I could get a meeting of
the workers and take their conditions down, that he was prepared to go into anything
that I considered unfair. I told the men and women of this promise, but it seemed to
have little effect on them, as I could get no one to volunteer to take contributions or agree
to a meeting.
At Manchester I have made a little headway in organising the repairers, having
secured over 20 members. Some of the men think that because they are working under
Trade Board Awards the Union is of no use to them. They overlook the fact that it was
the trade union movement which secured them the position they now enjoy.
Last night I attended Mr. J. Buckle's nomination meeting at the Eccles Town Hall.
It was a fine meeting and the approval vote in Johnnie was carried out
I hope that our candidates and the Labour Candidates throughout the country may
triumph. The devil's cause has been too long enthroned in power.
D. MCCARTHY.

GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.
TBLLOW MEMBERS.
devoted to the welfare of the Union.
GENERAL ELECTION. - Owing to the sudden change in the political world, I have
Iween asked by my colleague for LEICESTER WEST if I would permit my name to go forward
as Candidate for that Division, as Ald. Hill, J. P., is retiring owing to ill health. In
have decided to retain my position as General President of the Union, rather than undergo
view of the rule that prohibits a national officer from being a Member of Parliament I
similar experience which I had in 1910. Consequently, my time will be wholly
KETTERING. - During the month I have, upon several occasions had to visit a Kettering
tirm who do not feel inclined to adopt the National Agreement in the same sense as it is
usually accepted. The employer in this case, who has only recently owned the particular
factory in question, which is situated in South Wigston, had deducted from the operatives'
wages-dayworkers in the Press and Heel Building departments-4s. upon each occasion
whereas the original advance was only 8s. and 7s. respectively. The firm have an idea
that because the business is not paying, they have a right to deduct from wages so long
as they pay more than the minimum rates. This is a policy we cannot accept, and as a
consequence we are now pressing the firm for payment, or to refer the case to arbitration.
The firm is non-federated so arbitration is our forte, and the policy we hope to pursue,
and thus avoid friction. The matter will be placed before the Executive Council at their
next meeting as to whether this policy is to be pressed to its logical conclusion, and I do
not doubt that we shall receive their hearty support.
WELLINGBOROUGH, Four visits have been paid to Wellingborough and Leicester
local management do not understand the National Agreement, and the policy which has
in connection with the C.W.S. factories. Friction has occurred owing to the fact that
hitherto prevailed between the Union and the C.W.S. Management. Although for some
reason or other there was exceptional shyness upon the part of the girls engaged in coming
to meetings to enable us to get the facts, after several attempts I am pleased to say at
present that everything we expect from this firm appears to be in good working order,
and we have no doubt about the future.
SOUTH WIGSTON. I have visited the firm of Messrs. Crane & Co., where, owing to
considered when the first award was given respecting South Wigston that Leicester prices
the class of work done-children's and sizes-they wonder whether the business was
should apply to that town. With two of my colleagues from Leicester we saw the head
of the firm and are going very carefully into the matter because this business is solely for
children's and sizes' work. The employer's statement is that he feels the effect of com-
petition only about a quarter of a mile from his firm. My two colleagues are going through
the Statements with him and will report at an early date as to what course should be
taken, when, if necessary, the opinion of the Executive of the Union will be taken as to the
next step.
TRADE BOARD. I have attended a Trade Board meeting for the Midland area at
Birmingham. Under the presidency of Professor Daniels, of Manchester University, we
went through the new proposals now before the country, and I am pleased to report that
after careful consideration the Board as a whole-both employers' and employees' repre-
sentatives came to the conclusion that the proposals in themselves were very reasonable
and would meet with the unanimous support of that body.
NORTHANTS DISTRICT COUNCIL has met during the month at Desborough, and which
I attended. One of our colleagues, Councillor A. W. Lyne-although he was not a coun-
cillor at that date-gave a very interesting report of his visit to Germany, in which the
members showed very enlivened interest to hear a report from someone who had been
to the country under discussion. It gives one a much different idea from what we read
in the Press from time to time, and it is very evident from Councillor Lyne's report that
speaking of Germany generally, they are in a very bad way. Let us hope that the new
Government will get us out of the slough which we are in at present, including the whole
of Europe. If I were asked to forecast a result of the Election, I should surmise that the
halance of power will be with the Labour Party. Although I doubt that they will be
strong enough to form a Government. Let us hope someone will arise to pacify the
country and put it upon a better footing than it is at present. My own opinion is that
the Labour Party's programme, being so unselfish in its entirety, is the only foundation
upon which the country can permanently build.

NORTHAMPTON
I have also attended a very interesting meeting at Northampton
to explain and defend the attitude that the Union has taken upon the subject of reverting
back to the minimum of 60s, and leaving the Stock, Shoe Room and Heel Building Rooms
Our explanation was and is that had we accepted the proposition made to us, we should have suffered-generally speaking-because in the Leicester area, nearly all
those operatives in these departments are working on very good piecework statements.
and secondly we should have been altering an agreement within the space of two years
set for its allotment, and I am pleased to say that my colleagues in Northampton look
upon the matter in the same light as myself. When one considers that the Council had the
matter before them and did not see their way to enter upon such a doubtful proposition
in surrendering the statements, they allowed the matter to slide without taking it at all
seriously. I promised the operatives and am sure my colleagues will agree with me-
that at the meeting of next October when the Agreement is again considered, that we shall
give one minimum for all males, and I trust that this will be the
stepping-stone for one minimum for males and females.
LEICESTER WOMEN'S BRANCH.-I attended a meeting of the Leicester Women's
Branch at their request, and dealt with the Agreement affecting women and the Women's
Branch. We had a very good meeting and much interest was shown in the discussion
and application of the Agreement. As many of them are pieceworkers, or working on the
policy of payment by results, there were no difficulties in the way, but the meeting was
called for the purpose of letting them understand how the matter stood, and to also find
out whether there were any prospects of any firms likely to throw obstacles in their way.
None have been reported up to the present.
GENERAL FEDERATION OF TRADES UNIONS.- I have also attended meetings of the
General Federation of Trade Unions, when the Boilermakers' strike was considered once
again. As many of our members will know that Mr. A. Short, M.P., Chairman of the
General Federation of Trade Unions, is a boilermakers' representative in the House of
Commons, any help or assistance the General Federation of Trade Unions could give
would be willingly given. They felt, however, the matter was too delicate for them to
in any sense probe, but their help was at the disposal of the boilermakers. We were hopeful
that a meeting between the boilermakers and the employers would be held at an early
date. In any case we were satisfied that no pressure could be put upon the Ministry of
Labour to which the Minister would respond by asking for his interference.
During the month I have been called upon to give advice respecting one of our branches
who own property and the disposal of a small portion of it. I was surprised to find that
the solicitor of the other side who were purchasing the strip of land from the Branch in
question, wanted to know upon what authority we had to sell land, &c., &c., and under
what Acts of Parliament we were registered. Unfortunately for us, we are sometimes in
the hands of legal advisers who ought to know better, but upon this occasion, the original
Deeds had been drawn up that we were registered under the Friendly Societies' Act, whereas
as a matter of fact we are registered under the Trade Union Acts 1871-1918. I began
to wonder whether we should not take the necessary powers, although if my memory
served me correctly we have powers under the Trade Union Act to own property, and
consequently this was borne out by investigation. Consequently when the fact was made
known to the purchaser's solicitor, he ceased making enquiries as to who were our trustees,
when were they elected, had we appointed others in their stead, and so on and so on.
I did not hesitate to tell the legal gentleman that in my opinion it savours of several daily
newspaper attacks upon trade unions. I am assured that nothing of the kind was intended.
RUSHDEN was visited on the roth inst., when we met 77 collectors of the branch. A
musical programme was supplied by members of the branch and I, with the General
Secretary, was called upon to say a few words of encouragement upon the organisation of
the union.
THE ELECTION. In conclusion, I hope that the results of the election will show a
good sterling number of Labour members in the British House of Commons, who I am
sure will do all they can to bring about an improvement in our own country and Europe
in particular.
THE "DAILY HERALD." The Daily Herald will again be to the fore, and perhaps
this journal will show to the workers of this country-whether of brain or muscle-that
without a Labour paper justice cannot be done to the great working population.
I hope you are still wearing "Stamped" boots.

BRANCH REPORTS.

ARBROATH. - Trade is still bad with us, and to all appearances no
chance of improvement can be expected before the Spring. That phrase
seems to mock one when the past experience is taken into account, but as an
end must be reached sometime, one hopes it will be each succeeding trade
period. To temper the bad times comes the welcome news that the last wages
cut is to be restored. This removes the grudge, largely felt, which existed
because of the last cut, and for a time at anyrate we are free from that worry.
In Scotland we do not get the advantage of a much cheaper living in spite
of apparent falls in the National standard. Full inquiries such as conducted
by the Union of Postal Workers in Scotland have revealed that the average
cost of living in this country exceeds the Board of Trade figures considerably.
Why that should be is not very clear, although an explanation might be found
in the fact, that shop-keepers and other distributive merchants combine
together so skilfully as to defeat the normal incidence of rise and fall in market
prices. It is a curious reflection on "economic law" or purpose to find the
cunning intelligence of a section of the community, thwart or divert such from
its objective. Unemployment is becoming the burning question in public
affairs in this town. For the past three years our Town Council has evaded
its duty to provide helpful work, but at last we seem to be driving it into a
corner. Our members have taken a prominent part in establishing organisation
amongst those signing at the Labour Exchange, and since this was done we
have been able to extract promises from Parish Council, School Authority,
and Town Council that everything possible will be done to relieve the acute
distress this winter. Each suceeding winter sees the lot of the unemployed
intensified in its misery, as all resources have been used up, and the primary
need of food is added to by the need of boots and clothing and fuel. Relief
above the bare subsistence level is demanded, and the only sensible policy is to
provide some kind of work with a wage to
The Scottish Advisory Committee has now got started to work, and the first
agenda of proposals has been considered. These showed an urgent desire to
help those members in the Repairing Trade as well as those in the New Work
side of the industry. We are glad that there is a strong likelihood of our being
able to establish one Arbitration Board for Scotland in place of the three
District Arbitration Boards. The weakness of District Boards has been revealed
in the two districts with the small branches of the National Union. These
have practically ceased to function, because the small employers are afraid of
yielding concessions which the larger firms may refuse. In any case it would
be distinctly better to make Scotland uniform in its consideration of, and its
decisions on, all matters referred to arbitration. As a Branch we regret our
Council could not take a more drastic step in dealing with the Edinburgh
protest against Gribble's letter on the last Union vote. It is a pity they
couldn't have declared the vote null and void, as a decision of that kind would
stamp out a practice which only needs acquiescence to develop into an un-
mitigated evil. As the rules do not support that procedure sufficiently, it
is up to some Branch to move when the time comes. As a General Election is
imminent, let us express the hope that the National Union takes its proper
place in the coming fight, against the monstrous doctrine that Protection
will meet our nation's needs. There is no worse economic heresy than the
view that fiscal juggling will establish sound industrial prosperity.
BARNSLEY.-Trade is still good here, and men are fully employed.
We hope it will continue all the winter, for it has been very bad for the last
few years, but there is every prospect of it continuing good, and full employ-
ment for those engaged in this district.

CHESHAM. The improvement in trade previously reported has been

CORK. Trade during the month still remained bad.
EDINBURGH. Trade here is still very quiet. We have been successful
in having arrears paid up to a few of our members. Having attended a District

which we believe should be added to Statement. Also some alterations in
piece-workers should have two breaks in 10 points when the time rate is only
figures in regard to sliding scale. Our members cannot understand how
operative every to points. Hand-sewn makers have forwarded a suggestion
which in our opinion goes to the root of the whole question of the apprentice-
ship, whether it should be according to years worked, or as per schedule accord-
ing to age. The Scottish Advisory Committee have again met and a very

good suggestions for discussion which will certainly help the members of
Committee to meet the arguments which are oftimes levelled at officials when
negotiating with employers. Edinburgh Branch at monthly meeting believe
the vote for organiser. Scotchmen generally like a straight fight and no stabbing
that Council have done all in their power in connection with our protest regarding
in the dark. Edinburgh has just passed through a Municipal election but have
not been able to add the Labour representatives in Town Council. One of
our Shopmates was a candidate for the Unemployed, and under the circumstance
had a very good vote.
HIGHAM AND RUSHDEN.-Trade remains fairly good right through
the district, although a number of older operatives are out of work, but gener-
ally speaking we are in as good a position as most districts. The visit of Mr.
John Buckle, M.P., has been a help to us, although the meetings were not
attended as well as we hoped they would be, the weather spoiling the dinner-
hour meetings.
KINGSWOOD AND DISTRICT.-Trade generally throughout the
district is fair, some firms experiencing a falling off of orders. A mild excite-
ment was caused locally when a small manufacturer, a local Councillor, asserted
that the Heavy trade of the district was booming. Subsequent experience has
proved that this statement was more optimistic than wise. We also disagree
with those persons who assert that the day of the heavy boot is gone for ever.
We believe that when the unemployed army is absorbed into industry, an
increasing demand will be made for good strong honest boots, and a reaction
will set in against shoddy death traps, which bring neither pride nor profit to
manufacturer or operative.
LEEDS No. 1.- We regret to report that trade here is not as brisk as we
should like it to be, and as a consequence our members in the majority of cases
are not as fully employed as we should like them to be. We would strongly
urge upon those members who are fairly well employed to see that they have
a clear Union card, and thus be entitled to Union benefits should they need them.
We wish to draw the attention of all our Approved Health Insurance members
that we do not make any grants for either dental or eye treatment, but that
we do pay increased financial benefits in sickness, disablement and maternity
benefits. We are pleased to report that Mr. A. J. Dobbs, our Branch President,

PLYMOUTH. - Following the Trade Union Congress, Plymouth has once
more been the centre of national and political interest. The great Unionist
Party gathered here from all parts of the country and presented us with no
mean view of its wealth and power, but we were interested mostly in the
programme adopted by the organisation, and more particularly with the
speech of the Prime Minister, outlining the immediate and future policy of
his Party. Very few of our members indeed were fortunate enough to hear
him, the price of a ticket being far beyond us, but we claim that our interest
in the future of our country and the programme of the Government is just as
keen and intelligent as that of those who bedecked with dazzling jewels and
beautiful furs, arrived in smooth-running motor cars, albeit the show seemed
not for us. However, we must say that the Premier appeared to be the very
essence of sincerity and goodwill, but whether or not his great discovery of
Protection will prove to be a panacea for the terrible scourge of unemployment
remains to be seen. His declaration of the Government's intention to build
several light cruisers was welcome news to a dockyard town, and hope long
deferred has revived once more. We wish all members a Merry Xmas and a
Happy New Year.

PROVISIONS OF THE AWARD.
The members of the Joint Board of Conciliation and Arbitration for the
Boot Trade in the County District of Northampton having failed to agree on

His Award is as follows :-
THE AWARD.
(1.) The provisions of this Award shall apply to all cases in which
work is given out in quantities of three pairs or under, and shall be in
substitution for :-
(a) The extras provided "for quantities of three pairs or under "
in "Extras 5" of the Clicking Statement, 1919.
(b) The extras provided under the heading "Samples and
Specials" and "Samples and Odd Pairs" in the Lasting Statement,
1919; and
(c) Any extras corresponding to the above now being paid in the
closing and finishing departments.
(2.) The extras to be paid for quantities of three pairs or under, shall
be as follow:-
CLICKING. Where patterns and materials are not found for the operative:
100 per cent. on Statement prices. Where patterns and materials are found
for the operative: 65 per cent. on Statement prices for a single pair; 50 per
cent. on Statement prices for two or three pairs.
CLOSING.-50 per cent. on Statement prices for a single pair; 25 per cent.
on Statement prices for two or three pairs.
LASTING. If all the proper materials (e.g., heels) are found for the opera-
tive: 50 per cent. on Statement prices for a single pair on all operations;
33 per cent. on Statement prices for two or three pairs on all operations.
If all the proper materials are not found for the operative: An extra 10 per
cent. to be added.
FINISHING. On edge paring or trimming and edge setting: 60 per cent. on
Statement prices for a single pair; 33 per cent. on Statement prices for two
or three pairs. On all other operations: 33 per cent. on Statement prices
for a single pair; 25 per cent. on Statement prices for two or three pairs.
(3.) This Award shall come into operation at the commencement of the
full pay week which begins on or next the 30th day of October, 1923. -Kettering
Evening Telegraph, 31st October, 1923.

CHILDREN'S HERITAGE OF HEALTH.
Neglect Due to Bad Environment. Preventable Physical Defects.
After the first year of life the young child has to bear a heavy burden of environmental
neglect.
Bad housing, poverty, and the absence of hygienic supervision are the main factors
in this neglect.
The chief Medical Officer of the Board of Education, writes to this effect in his annual
report, which was issued yesterday.
With regard to the care of children under five years of age, the report says: "It
may be safely assumed that from 80-90 per cent. of children are born healthy, and with
the potentiality of leading normal and healthy lives.

Heritage of Healthy Birth.
Whatever be the facts of parentage, the tendency of nature is to reassert the right
of each new generation to the heritage of healthy birth." It adds:--
"After the first year of life the young child has to bear a heavy burden of en-
vironmental neglect, associated with bad housing, poverty, and absence of hygienic
supervision. As a result, the school medical service is faced with the hard issue that,
out of an infant population born healthy, 35 to 40 per cent. of the children who are
admitted to school at five years of age bear with them physical defects which could
have been either prevented or cured."

Effects of Unemployment.
The report also states that the improvement in the physical condition of the children,
which occurred during the war and was maintained during the two years of prosperity
after the war, has not been lost in the past two years of "unparalleled conditions of un-
employment and financial restriction."
"If it be asked why has unemployment not affected the health of children more
than appears to be the case," says Sir George, "I think the answer is that (a) there has been
an increased sense of responsibility among the parents for their children's welfare; (b)
there have been forthcoming various monetary aids of the nature of relief, insurance,
and union payments, and these have in part made up for loss of wage; and (c) there has
been the supervision, assistance, and nurture of the school medical service."--Leicester
Daily Mercury, 1st November, 1923.

SOME OTHER THINGS TO REMEMBER.
What of the toll of human life and suffering? The casualties in the Great War
were more than half the population of England. Upwards of nine millions were killed.
Approximately one-tenth of the killed were British.
It brings home the magnitude of these losses to reflect that it would take the Legion
of the Dead nearly two months, without stopping day or night, to march past the Cenotaph
four abreast. It would take nearly six days for the British section of this Legion to do
their part.
In America it is officially stated that they have produced a liquid of which approxi-
mately three drops applied to the human skin cause death. Several thousands of tons
of this can be manufactured in a day. A fleet of aeroplanes equipped with it could anni-
hilate the population of a city in a few hours. A pilotless aeroplane controlled by wireless
has been perfected. Next we shall have a pilotless tank controlled by wireless, or a
pilotless submarine. Torpedoes directed by wireless exist already.
Do not forget that at the present time there are more men under arms than there
were in 1914. What for? Do you want War? Do the workers of other countries want
War? They do not, any more than we do. Our duty then is to clearly support PEACE,
and a peace policy. Make it so clear to Kings, European Presidents, Statesmen, Diplomats,
that differences between nations must be settled by reason, and not by force, and thus
bring into actual practice the time when-
No strife shall rage, nor hostile feuds
Disturb those peaceful years;
To ploughshares men shall beat their swords;
To pruning hooks their spears.
E. L. POULTON, General Secretary.

DOLE FRAUD.
Leicester Man Goes to Goal.
At the Leicester City Police Court on November 21st, 1923, before Mr. J. L. Ward
and other magistrates, John William Harrison, a shoehand, of 37, Elmdale Street, was
summoned for obtaining benefit under the Unemployment Insurance Act by making false
representation on 28th September.
Mr. Simpson, prosecuting, stated that Harrison applied for unemployment pay last
June. An arrangement was made so that he received the pay through his trade union,
the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives. From June to September he was in
receipt of the pay, and then it came to the ears of the authorities that the defendant was
being employed and was working as a china rivetter. He was having work regularly
from two china merchants in the city. He and his brother together were carrying on the
business.
Mr. Simpson produced an invoice written on a bill head, on the top of which was
printed "A. and J. W. Harrison, makers of rush and cane chair seats, glass and china
repairers, &c., 37, Elmdale Street."
On 28th September, for the week ended two days earlier, defendant drew 24s. unem-
ployment pay and similar amounts on 5th, 12th and 19th September. He also received
from one of the china merchants £7 3s. od. for work done from Ist to 27th September.
Witnesses were called to prove that defendant had received unemployment pay.
Defendant, in the witness box, told the magistrates that previous to 1921 he and his
brother were in partnership. Then he was sent to prison for an offence and the business
failed. When he came out of gaol he started in the boot trade and was thus employed
until June. Since then he had simply fetched the work and money from the various
places and handed it to his brother, who was still doing it. They made the mistake of
still having his name on the bill heads. He did not help his brother.
Albert Harrison, 12, Bakehouse Lane, assured the Bench that his brother (defendant)
had not done any of the china rivetting work "since his last sentence." Witness gave
his brother a few shillings for fetching the work and taking it back, but it was never
more than 5s. a week.
Three previous convictions were proved against defendant, one of which was for
attempted warehouse breaking.
Harrison was sent to prison for a month with hard labour in connection with this
case.-Leicester Mail, 21st November, 1923.

FAST TRAVELLER.
We like a story that was very popular with the Army in France.
It is the tale of a negro who was beating it for the back areas as fast as he could go,
when he was stopped by a white officer.
"Don't delay me, suh," said the negro. I's gotta be on my way."
"Boy," replied the officer, "do you know who I am? I am a general."
"Go on, white man, you ain't no general."
I certainly am," insisted the officer angrily.
"Lordy!" exclaimed the negro, taking a second look. "You sure is! I musta
been travelin' some, 'cause I didn't think I'd got back that far yit."

THE CAPITAL LEVY AND WHAT IT REALLY IS.
One of the Originators of the Proposal Explains How it Would Work.
Press and the Rothermere section particularly is attempting to create a bitter prejudice
What is the Capital Levy? How will it work? What is its purpose? The Tory
against the policy of the Capital Levy.
In the article below, Mr. Pethick Lawrence gives a concise explanation of what the Capital
Levy really is, what its objects are, and how it would be levied.
The writer, it may be mentioned, is one of the originators of the proposal, and the author
of an explanatory pamphlet on the subject, published by the Labour Party.
While Liberals and Tories are fighting over again the tariff battle the Labour Party
will go to the country on its full programme of reform. In the front rank of this programme
is reduced taxation. We stand for reducing the flat rate of the income-tax, for raising the
exemption limit, and for giving larger allowances to people with children. We stand for
abolishing the corporation tax and the entertainments tax.
Above all, we stand for abolition of the taxes on food. Tea, sugar, and all the
other foods of the people must not be made artificially dear by taxes as they are
to-day.
Their continued existence is a scandal, because they press most heavily on the poorest
people and those with large families who find it hardest to make ends meet and keep the
wolf from the door.
Neither the Liberal Party nor the Tory Party have the means to bring about these
reductions in taxation. The only Party that can have the means is the Labour Party
and the only way is the Capital Levy.
The Capital Levy is an emergency measure for redemption of a great part of the
National Debt. It is intended to be applied once and once only, and its proceeds will
be kept separate from the annual revenue and used exclusively to redeem debt.
When this is done an immense cut will be effected in the annual interest which
has at present to be paid out of annual taxation.
The Levy will not be imposed upon companies, corporations, or businesses, as such,
but upon individuals, who will have to make a return giving the value of their total wealth.
and will be assessed on this, just as is the case with the executors of a deceased person,
for the purposes of the estate duties.
No person whose total wealth falls short of £5,000 will be subject to the Levy.
This is true whatever the nature of the wealth possessed, whether it be a small holding,
or furniture, or stocks and shares, or war bonds, or savings certificates, or other
Government, Colonial, or Municipal stock.
If a person's total wealth exceeds £5,000 he or she will become liable to tax, but the
rate at which he will have to pay will be graduated, so that a man with £6,000, £7,000
or even £10,000, will only have to contribute a very small amount.
Against this he will obtain reductions in taxations of all kinds, in Income-tax
and in indirect taxation, which will fully compensate him for his share of the Levy.
Those with great wealth will have to bear a heavier proportion, but this is only just,
because if they had been taxed adequately at the time, the vast war debt need not have
been incurred.
Some traders are afraid of the Levy because they do not understand it. They think
that they will have to hand over a great sum in cash to the Government, but this is not the
case.
If their business is a company and their private wealth consists of shares in it, they
will be able to discharge their liability by handing over some of their shares.
If their business is a private firm they will have the option of paying the Levy in
instalments spread over 15 or 20 years which they can meet out of income, and which
will be set-off by the reduction effected in income-tax.
The working capital of the country does not consist of money, but of things-land-
and houses and factories, mines and forests and railways, machinery, plant and so on.
The Capital Levy will not reduce these in any way.
It will merely bring about a transference in some of the title-deeds of these things.
Consequently the Capital Levy will not reduce the output of commerce or th
employment of labour. On the contrary, by reducing annual taxation and see

Staggering!
We believe that in the event of the authors of the crisis securing an electoral majority
for their Protectionist policy they will deal a staggering blow to the economic and financial
stability of the nation.- From the Tory Glasgow Herald.

Protection Fails.-I.
Protection has failed to keep out imports.
Protective duties of 33 per cent., imposed by Mr. McKenna, the Liberal, and erst-
while champion of Free Trade, are in force on cinema films, watches and clocks, musical
instruments, and motor cars and parts thereof.
In 1922 (which is the post-war year showing the lowest aggregate imports) the number
of clocks imported was 3,741,126 against 2,413,926 in 1913; the number of musical instru-
ments was 408,048 against 175,445 in 1913; the number of motor-cars was 14,361 against
6,820 in 1913; and the number of motor chassis was 8,527 against 7,958 in 1913.
The only cases in which the quantity of 1922 imports was less than 1913 are those of
watches (2,700,342 in 1922 against 3,535,523 in 1913) and motor-cycles and tri-cars (976
in 1922 against 1,725 in 1913).
The latter case is probably due to the increasing popularity of motor-cars. The
reduction in imports in this case is certainly not the result of the McKenna duty, for in
1920, when the duty was just as much in force as in 1922, the number imported was 4,305
against 1,725 in 1913.
Protection Fails.-II.
Protection has failed to prevent unemployment.
At the end of December, 1921, the percentage unemployed in all insured industries
was 16.2 per cent.; the percentage unemployed in the construction and repair of vehicles
(chiefly motor vehicles) was 20 per cent. In December, 1922, the percentage unemployed
in all insured industries was 12.2 per cent., and in the construction and repair of vehicles
was 14.1 per cent.
The Ministry of Labour has now ceased to give percentage figures; but the numbers
unemployed in the construction and repair of motor vehicles and aircraft rose from 21,255
in August, 1923, to 23,662 in September.
In the manufacture of watches, plate and jewellery, &c., the percentage unemployed
in May, 1923, was 11.4 per cent., while the percentage for the manufacture of miscellaneous
metal goods (including musical instruments) was 8.9 per cent. At the same date 11.5
per cent. were unemployed in the manufacture of glass (other than optical and scientific glassware).
The percentage unemployed in all the insured industries at that time was 10.5 per cent.
The figures for the protected industries were, therefore, generally above the general average.

GUILTY.
A country school board was visiting school and the principal was putting his pupils
through their paces.
"Who signed Magna Charta, Robert?" he asked, turning to one boy.
"Please sir, 'twasn't me," whimpered the youngster.
The teacher, in disgust, told him to take his seat; but an old tobacco-chewing country
man on the board was not satisfied, so, after a well-directed aim at the cuspidor he said:
"Call that boy back. I don't like his manner. I believe he did do it."

REPORT OF THE STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE OF INDUS-
TRIAL WOMEN'S ORGANISATIONS, January - October, 1923.
INTERNATIONAL WORK, - The International Federation of Working Women. The
Committee continued during this year to represent in this country the International
Federation of Working Women, but before the meeting of the Biennial Congress at Vienna
in August, 1923, the Committee went very thoroughly into the whole situation and received
a report from the Federation secretariat to the main principles of which agreement was
only Trade Union women, and that the representation in this country should therefore
in Great Britain the General Council would give it hospitality in its offices and would give
of the Federation, put this matter before the Women's Group and the General Council
agreed to a report from them under which it was resolved that if the Secretariat remained
assistance through the staff of its Women's Group as had been previously done by the
Federation that it should endeavour to secure the development of the Women's Depart-
ment of the I.F.T.U. into a Women's Section. These matters were discussed in detail
by the S. C. which appointed a special committee to consider and report upon them,
and the delegates sent from Great Britain had instructions to press for this develop ment
and to urg. that if the I.F.T.U. would undertake this work of forming a Women's Section
with a Women's Advisory Committee and a Biennial Congress of Working Women, the
Federation's identity might be absorbed in that larger organisation. The British delega-
tion to the Congress consisted of all members, who were as follows:-
Dr. Marion Phillips, Miss Edith McDonald. Mrs. F. Harrison Bell, Miss Madeleine
Symons, Miss Margaret Bondfield, Miss Julia Varley, Miss Dunch, Miss Vera Chinn,
Miss Edith Howse, Miss Ward, Miss Florrie Moss.
Dr. Marion Phillips having intimated her intention of not continuing the work of
International Secretary, it was agreed that the British delegation should put forward the
name of Miss Edith McDonald, then acting as Assistant Secretary for that office, if the
Secretariat remained in Great Britain. It was decided at Vienna that it should so remain,
and the proposals with regard to the future of the Federation were adopted on the lines
which have been described. Miss Margaret Bondfield was re-elected British Vice-Presi-
dent. Mrs. Harrison Bell. Treasurer, and Dr. Marion Phillips was made a Consultative
Member of the Secretariat: Mlle. Burniaux (Belgium) has taken the place of Mrs. Robins
(U.S.A.) as President. The full report of the Congress presented by the delegates was
adopted by the Standing Joint Committee, and it is understood that a Report of the
Congress will soon be available in book form.
INTERNATIONAL CONFERENCE OF SOCIALIST WOMEN, HAMBURG, MAY, 1923. The
British Labour Party sent two delegates to this Congress, Miss Susan Lawrence and Dr.
Ethel Bentham. Mrs. Sidney Webb attended as a Fabian delegate and Dr. Marion
Phillips as secretary to the delegation and as a fraternal delegate on behalf of the I.F.W.W.
The work of the delegation was discussed with the S.J.C., and a report submitted by them
on their return. The Conference met on Sunday, 20th May. Its two main purposes
ofere to consider what organisation should be established in the future to link up Socialist
women of all countries, and also to report upon the conditions specially affecting women
in the different countries. The result of the discussion on future arrangements was
inconclusive and was finally left in the hands of the Præsidium of the Conference to see
what arrangements could be made with the new International formed at Hamburg in the
following week, but the feeling of a large majority was against having any separate inter-
national organisation for women in the Socialist parties even as part of the International.
The Conference was well attended, about 90 delegates being present, and there were many
interesting speeches upon the position of Socialist women in different countries. Reso-
lutions were also passed dealing with Women's Suffrage, an International Women's Day,
Education and Peace, and Motherhood and Child Endowment.
Dr. Marion Phillips, who was one of the Præsidium, has continued to act as the corre-
spondent for Great Britain with the Austrian women Socialists, who initiated this Congress,
and who are continuing their endeavours to develop a women's side to the work of the
new International on the restricted lines laid down by the Conference.

dealt with in a letter of protest to Sir Montague Barlow early in the year, and questions
were also prepared upon this subject which were asked in the House of Commons. Informa-
tion was collected as to the position of unemployed women and circulated to members of the

PENAL REFORM AND POOR PERSONS DEFENCE. -This subject has occupied a great
deal of the attention of the Committee. A report upon it was presented and adopted by

Prisoners Defence were the result of joint meetings between the Sub-Committee of the
S.J.C. and the Labour Party Advisory Committee on Legal and Judicial Matters.

before the House of Commons, were put forward, which will be dealt with by the Labour
Party in the coming session. The Committee made an enquiry from Labour women
magistrates as to the conditions of nursing in prisons and some useful information was
obtained. The whole question of penal reform will continue to occupy close attention.
The case of Mrs. Wright, who drowned her child when in very great despair, was taken
up by the Committee and help was given in getting signatures and a petition for her reprieve.

KEEP ON DOING.
There's lots of joy in living if you strike the proper gait;
If you'll always come up smiling in the face of every fate,
If you're keeping step and whistling some lively little tune,
You'll be living gay and happy as a sunny day in June,
Keep a level head, don't worry, help your brothers on the way;
Let the sunshine of good humour shine upon you ev'ry day;
Speak a cheerful word at all times, never" knock" your fellow man,
And you'll surely be rewarded-just keep doing all you can,
There is lots of joy in living if you live your life aright,
Lots of sunshine and of roses, keep your eyes turned to the light,
Look behind the clouds of trouble; there's a silver lining there,
And you'll find it if you're only living life upon the square.
Scatter good cheer like the thistle scatters seed before the wind,
And the petty woes and troubles soon will be left far behind.
Be a Booster" every minute, help along your fellow man,
And you'll surely be rewarded, just keep doing all you can.
-Exchange,

WHAT LABOUR WILL FIGHT ON WHEN ELECTION COMES.
Ramsay MacDonald Defines the Real Issues and Lays Down Clear
Constructive Policy. Straight Questions for Mr. Baldwin.
Labour's Programme ". Protection.
It was a smallish room in which the gathering was held, and for the most part Mr.
MacDonald spoke in a conversational tone. But every now and then his voice to e, every
Never was a party leader more emphatic or more genuinely in earnest, never did a
and when all his hearers broke into loud applause on hearing his declaration :-
Party gathering approve more vigorously a declaration of policy, than when he declared,
now and then some emotion-pity, or anger, or sarcastic disdain thrilled in his tonee
The issue on which we shall fight is not Protection versus Free Trade. It is Pro-
tection versus the Labour programme.
That was the core of the speech. Ranging over a wide field, touching at all important
points the situation created by Mr. Baldwin's speeches, it was all a disscitation upon that
text. Every part of it fitted in with that declaration and formed a mosaic of which the
central pattern was a firm resolve not to lose the initiative, not to let the adversary choose
the battleground, not to take up a merely negative attitude, but to make a positive offer
in reply to the Prime Minister's challenge.
Protection Fallacy.
Protection, said Mr. MacDonald in a closely-reasoned and very skilful analysis of the
problem of unemployment, would not help us to find markets for our manufactures. On
the contrary, it would add to the difficulty of finding them.
We could not sell our goods at present because other countries, owing to the political
chaos in Europe, which so deplorably affected the rates of exchange, produce more cheaply
and could undersell us.
The Tory remedy was to make our goods dearer still !
Nothing appreciable had been done by the present Government to help in reducing
that chaos to order. As for its dealing with the workless, it was a scandal and a disgrace.
The leader's voice shook with indignation as he pronounced this condemnation. A
few moments before it had sunk to a sad whisper as he spoke of "your friends and my
friends" in the ranks of the unemployed.
Here, we felt, was the only spirit in which this terrible disaster could be combated
with any hope of success. Tories and Liberals speak of unemployment as something
remote from themselves, from their own lives and families and friends. The deep murmur
which responded to Mr. MacDonald's parenthesis proved its truth. All these men and
women were burning to cure unemployment because it is a real disaster to them, because
it does touch their friends, their relatives, their daily lives.
Real Remedies.
And how could it be cured? By developing our own country. How could we reduce
the taxation which weighed so heavily upon families of small means? By combining
economic wisdom with moral rectitude, imposing a Capital Levy and paying off a large part
of our debt. How could we increase production? Turn the unwilling into the willing
producer by producing, not for private profit, but for common use.
Those were the issues on which Labour would fight. Those were the only remedies
which offered any hope of improvement.
Protection would leave our difficulties and problems as they were. It would expose
us, in addition, to all the evils of "lobbying" in favour of particular industries-such
intriguing and bullying and bargaining as they had seen in connection with the Safeguard-
ing of Industries Act.
Into the working of that measure Mr. MacDonald called for a searching inquiry,
prophesying that it would knock the bottom out of Mr. Baldwin's case for Protection.
He pleaded, too, for more inquiry into "the terrible thing called Socialism." Few of
those who trembled at it knew anything at all about it.
Pioneers of Socialism.
They did not know that all the saints and seers of the nineteenth century-Carlyle,
Ruskin, Robert Owen, Shaftesbury-had been pioneers of Socialism. Not a single great
name could be shown in opposition to the principle that common interests, and not private
interests, must come first. That was Socialism, and he never felt more confident of its
Power to build up a new social stricture in which all might be contented and of which all
could be proud.

SUNLIGHT AND BETTER HEALTH.
There is no longer any need to emphasise the general advantages of exposure to sun-
by cutting off the supply of a few simple and universally available factors, directly causes
light. But if we consider its effects in detail we are driven to conclude that civilisation.
diseases which require the most elaborate treatment to arrest or cure.
light and Health " (Nisbet, 5s. net), Dr. C. W. Saleeby traces the various discoveries with
regard to one of these factors. We find that not only are tuberculosis and rickets curable
by light but that their development is prevented by its agency in conditions under which
they would otherwise certainly appear. Sunlight and artificial light are, therefore, not
only antiseptic but also stimulative to the vital powers, calling up their maximum resistance
against disease. The range of its beneficent power is already proved to be so great that we
are justified in assuming that the mere general effect of increased sunlight would be the
arrest or rout of the majority of diseases and an immense increase in health and energy.
This conclusion is not weakened in the least by the fact which Dr. Saleeby makes clear
that the specific action of sunlight in the cure of disease is still unknown. But if it be
true, what can be said of the dilatoriness and cowardice of the Government in dealing
with the evil of smoke, which effectually cuts off the sunlight from those members of the
population whose mode of life places them most in need of it? Cologne, Düsseldorf,
and Essen, when working at full pressure, were smokeless cities. Even Pittsburg has cut
off over 85 per cent. of its smoke. In this country alone do we tolerate an evil which
directly saps the vigour of everyone and produces disease in numerous people. The
Committee on Light of the Medical Research Council work in vain if their findings are to
have so little influence on policy. This is another case in which we should naturall
expect the Ministry of Health to act; but up to the present we see no sign of any adeqint
attempt to deal with the smoke evil. - Westminster Gazette, 12th November, 2

PATHETIC.
A big burly man called at the rectory, and when the door was opened asked to see the
rector's wife, a woman well known for her charitable impulses.
"Madam," he addressed her, in a broken voice. "I wish to draw your attention to
the terrible plight of a poor family in this district. The father is dead, the mother is too
ill to work, and the nine children are starving. They are about to be turned into the cold.
"How terrible!" exclaimed the lady. "May I ask who you are?"
The sympathetic visitor applied his handkerchief to his eyes.
"I'm the landlord," he sobbed.-American Legion Weekly.

ILLUSTRATED.
Two tourists in Spain could not speak the language, and consequently had some
difficulty in making known their wants. At a wayside inn they tried to obtain roast beef.
Nobody could understand them.
"What are we to do?" asked one of them, despairingly.
"I know," said the other, a ray of hope appearing. "I'll draw a picture of a cow.
Then they'll understand."
He made a rough sketch of a cow, put a "2" underneath it, and handed it to the
waiter, who instantly smiled to show that he understood, and went off to execute the order.
A few minutes later he returned with two tickets for a bullfight.

A ROBOT'S ROUNDELAY.
Hush-a-bye, baby, on the tree top,
When you grow up you can work in a shop;
When you are married your wife can work too,
So that the rich will have nothing to do.
Hush-a-bye, baby, on the tree top,
When you are old your wages will stop,
And when you have spent what little you save,
It's rock-a-bye, baby, off to the grave.

MONTHLY REPORT.
17TH DECEMBER, 1923.
There is practically no improvement in trade over what was reported in
last month's issue. The number of members who received Out of Work Benefit
during last month is 2,531. The Union's Out of Work Fund has proved to
be a very great advantage to those of cut members, who have unfortunately
from time to time found themselves out of employment. The figures recorded
by the Ministry of Labour Gazette are set out hereunder :-
BOOT AND SHOE INDUSTRY.
Employment during November continued slack on the whole, but improvements
were reported in some districts, and less short time was worked than in recent months.
The percentage of workpeople unemployed, as indicated by the unemployment book
lodged at Employment Exchanges, was 9.6 on the 26th November, as compared with
9.8 on the 22nd October.
In London employment remained bad. There was a further improvement at Leicest
although a good deal of short time was still worked. There was not much change
Northampton, where employment remained moderate on the whole, with much sho
time; at Kettering there was a slight further improvement, though short time was s
largely worked. At Wellingborough employment continued to improve, and there
very little short time working; a few factories were even reported to be working overti
Overtime working was also reported in the Rushden district, where employment contin
good. At Hinckley a further improvement was reported, while at Desborough emp
ment remained bad. General slackness continued at Leeds, but a slight improve
was reported. An improvement was reported at Stafford.
All Trade Unionists should have their Repairs done
by Repairers who use the TRADE UNION STAMP.

There is practically no improvement in trade over what was reported in
last month's issue. The number of members who received Out of Work B to

NEW MAGISTRATES.
It is with pleasure we record the fact that two more of our colleagues,
Councillor J. Gribble and Councillor A. W. Lyne, both of Northampton, have
been made Magistrates during the last month. We congratulate our colleagues
and feel confident they will carry out the duties connected with the office in a
manner creditable to themselves and the movement.

THE GENERAL ELECTION.
Once more the nation has been called upon to elect representatives for the
members to be ready at all times for an election, believing as we did that such
House of Commons. For many months past we have impressed upon the
an appeal would not be long delayed. We cannot but think that among the
reasons for having an election so soon after the 1922 election is, to make it
increasingly difficult for the Labour Party to find money to fight elections.
The Party, however, with great courage, have risen to the occasion, and
there was no lack of Labour candidates in all parts of the country.
So much so, it would have been easy to have secured an absolute majority
of members had the electorate so used their powers as to send more Labour
Members to the House. This, however, has not taken place, although 191
Labour Members (including six Co-operative Members) were returned to the
House of Commons, out of a total of 615 Members.
THE UNION'S CANDIDATES.
So far as the Union is concerned we had three Candidates in the field:-
Mr. John Buckle, J.P., for the Eccles Division of Lancs.; Mr. W. R. Smith, J.P.
for Norwich; and Mr. Len. Smith, for the Daventry Division of Northants.
In the Eccles Division, Mr. Buckle had two candidates fighting him this
time-Conservative and Liberal-the Conservative being a formidable opponent
owing to his great local influence and also that he was a representative for
Eccles until Mr. Buckle won the seat in 1922. The fight was a strenuous
one, but we are delighted to report that, thanks to the whole-hearted support
of a band of workers, led by Councillor M. Rogerson, our Agent for the Division,
added to the way in which Mr. Buckle placed his views before the electorate,
Mr. Buckle was again returned for the Division. The figures are as follows :-

LEICESTER WEST.
It will thus be seen that in a number of districts where our trade is pre-
dominant Labour Candidates have been successful. These stuces are a
source of gratification to us and we hope as opportunities present themselve
other constituencies will likewise return Labour Members.
In our November issue we inserted a paragraph commenting upon the
method adopted by the Leicester Labour Party, the seat in Leicester West
having passed from us. We also expressed our disapproval of the procedure
adopted, as we had not only won Leicester West, but kept a full time agent in
the Division. Although the methods adopted were not just to the Union, we
refrained from taking any further action, because we desired the seat to be
retained for Labour, and as showing our sincerity in the matter, Alderman
A. Hill, J.P., in addition to taking the chair at one of Mr. Lawrence's meetings,
issued a special appeal to the electors to support Mr. Lawrence.
As a Union, although the services of Councillor J. H. Baum, our full time
Agent in the Division, would have been of great service to Mr. Len. Smith in
the Daventry Division, we agreed that Mr. Baum should continue in the position
of Agent in Leicester West. We claim we have shown a spirit of goodwill
and patience in connection with such a matter, although we had and still have
every reason to complain of the way in which we have been treated. We can
only hope that no such an unfortunate occurrence will happen in the future,
but that there will be full compliance with the procedure laid down by the
Labour Party, and full consultation with the Union in the selection of the
candidate, especially when, as in the case of Leicester West, we have been
paying an agent for some considerable time and thus giving full financial
responsibility to keep the machinery in order.
DAVENTRY.
In the Daventry Division of Northants we felt that a circular issued by
Captain Fitzroy, the Conservative Candidate, was worded in such a way that
if it was not absolutely over the line then it was very close to being contrary
to the law regarding such cases. We therefore took the matter to the Chancery
Division of the High Court on Tuesday, the 4th inst. The case was heard
by Mr. Justice Astbury, and it is interesting to record a remark made by the
Judge :-" It seems to me this is a most improper circular to have issued.
But I do not know that that is enough to give me jurisdiction to stop it."
The fact that we took the matter up so promptly had a very beneficial
effect upon the said candidate as is shown on page 743 of this report of a state-
ment published by Mr. Fitzroy.
