The position created by the election shows that no Party has a clear
majority. As a result it has been, and is, the cause of all sorts of rumours
being circulated as to which Party will take office, or whether the Rt. Hon.
Stanley Baldwin, M.P., will carry on, and go to the country again in a
short time.
At the time of going to Press the position is one of great uncertainty, and
one which is calling for full consideration, especially from the point of view of
the Labour Party and their acceptance of office. The decision as to the policy
to be pursued under such circumstances clearly must rest with those whom
we have elected to represent us in the House of Commons, having regard to
the circumstances by which they find themselves surrounded. We therefore
trust that whatever decision may be arrived at that it will be loyally accepted
by the Party as a whole, because it is quite clear that the circumstances are
such as to prevent the Party fully carrying out its policy should they decide
to take office. The situation is one which will put to the test the principles
underlying the Labour Party, and we appeal especially to our own members
to do their part in keeping alive full interest in the movement and the objects
for which we stand, so that when another election comes, whether in the
immediate future or not, it will find us fully prepared, and with such machinery
placed at our disposal as will materially increase the number of members on
the Labour side of the House of Commons.
Further references will be be found elsewhere in this issue.

FELLOW COLLEAGUES,
11th December, 1923.
As reported last month, in my report, I have definitely decided that
my work as General President is more important than that of a Parliamentary
Agent, and as has been explained before I decided to relinquish the latter
position.
Yours fraternally,
T. F. RICHARDS,
General President.
To the Members of the Executive Council.
FELLOW COLLEAGUES,
7th December, 1923.
I have been considering for a considerable time past the position
of my being one of the Parliamentary Agents, and the rules bearing upon the
same, more especially bearing in mind the discussion which had taken place
at the Union's Conference this year. It is quite clear to me that if I consented


---
729
upon to resign my position as General Secretary to the Union, but with our
present procedure this would also mean cutting me off from my Industrial
work in connection with the movement generally.
matter.
This I am not prepared to do, believing as I do, that I have been of one
use to the general movement. The decision of the Conference and the state-
ment in the rules make it quite plain that I ought to declare myself upon the
I have given very careful consideration to the matter and have now come
to the conclusion that it will be best for me to retire from the position of one of
the Parliamentary Agents of the Union, and ask you to accept this resignation.
This would have been done in time—if I had known we were going to have a
rush election—to enable the Union to take a vote to fill the vacancy created.
My reason for not resigning sooner was because of the fact that the next Union
voting will not take place until February, and I did not wish to put the Union
to the expense of having a Ballot Vote to fill this one position, hence my
reason for not resigning until now.
Yours faithfully,
E. L. POULTON,
General Secretary;
FIVE-WEEK MONTH.
There being five Saturdays during this month, Secretaries are asked to
make up their returns and pay for the same accordingly.
GREETINGS.
We wish every member the Compliments of the Season, and trust that
1924 will be brighter and happier than 1923 has been.
REMEMBER THE FIFTEENTH!
Once again we feel bound to call the serious attention of Branch Secretaries
to the fact that the FIFTEENTH day of each month is the latest day for
returns reaching the General Secretary. If Branches fail to send off their
returns to reach the Central Office before the 15th of the month it tends to
upset the organisation of the work in the General Secretary's Office. We beg
to intimate that unless returns are in before the 15th of the month, the Secretary
has been instructed to put into force the Rules governing the same. Returns
Sheets MUST also bear the signature of both the Branch President and Branch
Secretary, or they will reluctantly have to be returned for completion.
TRADE UNION STAMP.
This is a matter which we have stated before rests with the members to
make a success. It is in the interests of members themselves that "Stamped
Footwear " should be increasingly purchased; therefore, push the Trade Union
Stamp. Members and their families should wear only "Union Stamped
Footwear."

GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
It is with great pleasure that one has to record the wonderful suc of the
Labour Movement at the Polls. To those who have been associated with the oldest of
Socialist movements-the Socialist League-it is a great relief to feel that the workers
are being aroused, and have given the Labour Party a much heavier vote than they did
last year. With one hundred and ninety-one members (including six Co-operative
members) receiving the Labour whips
upon to form a Government, they should do so, and thereby prove to the movement
that they are prepared to carry out (if permitted) the promises they have made to
the electorate, and should at once abolish all taxes on food as the election literature
has shown all parties agreed on paper on this matter; amend the Old Age and War-
time Pensions, and amend the Unemployment Benefit Act, and make them more
adequate, remove anomalies and bring in the Agricultural Labourer and Domestic
Servants; advance loans to local bodies for housing and road widening on garden
city or other lines, and pay as per present arrangements, sixty per cent. from State
funds; open up trade with Russia; press France to deal justly with Germany by an
international conference; beg all industrialists to prefer arbitration in labour disputes:
apply the Sankey Award to the mines and miners, and supply the Parliamentary Debates
at Id. each to the general public.
Members will be aware ere this of the retirement of Ald. A. Hill from Parliamentary
work, and the Local Labour Party, for reasons best known to themselves, refused to allow
the matter to be postponed for three days whilst the Executive of our Union were consulted
as to a candidate. Although the rules of the Labour Party demand that all component
bodies shall have the right of nomination, our Union was denied this right. I learned that
Mr. Hill had decided to retire on the 14th Nov., when he asked me could he say that I
would go into nomination, and I replied next day that I should stand by the Presidency
of the Union. The following day the Executive of the Leicester Labour Party decided
on a candidate, and thereby refused the Council of the Union the opportunity of proposing
a nomination, which had we been permitted to nominate, we could then have had no
ground of complaint. As it is there is a very grave breach of faith by not observing the
general rules of procedure.
The result of the Leicester elections is everything to be proud of, as also are all the
other wins and efforts of the Party. My contribution to the local Press two days before
the election was as follows:-
"This country has tried Liberals and Tories. Both agree in their hearts that to settle
the Unemployed problem by giving all men and women work would not help them to
govern the country to their liking, and may even lose them power and pelf: the workers of
the country may prefer to govern themselves. After so many years, surely the time has
arrived when another party, hitherto untried, should be given a chance. Let us hope that
no boot and shoe operative can in his or her heart vote for either Liberal or Tory
on the 6th."
My political activities on invitation took me to the DAVENTRY DIVISION OF NORTHAMP-
TONSHIRE, where Mr. Len. Smith was a candidate. I am sorry he has not won, although
we expected the sitting member was well entrenched, and it was very largely an agricultural
area. Still, Mr. Smith's supporters thought he had a very good chance, and the meetings
in the shoe areas were very enthusiastic, and I believe very loyal at Daventry and Long
Buckby. I also addressed meetings at FINEDON and IRTHLINGBOROUGH, and attended a
very large and enthusiastic meeting at Rushden in the WELLINGBOROUGH DIVISION, and felt
from the tone of the meetings that Mr. Cove was bound to win as the Tories were running
a candidate this time, instead of being content to back the Liberal. Mr. Cove is now the
M.P., and I trust he will well nurse the constituency for matters point to this being a
short-lived Parliament.
DESBOROUGH was another most solid and enthusiastic meeting for Mr. Perry, the
Co-operative candidate, and the solidarity that was manifest at the meeting was a good
augury that here was another seat won for Labour, and as Mr. Perry has been elected
we are pleased to know that Labour has been true to itself.
The last three days was spent with Mr. Buckle, at ECCLES, and the many meetings
addressed made one feel that in spite of a third candidate, a Liberal being in the field, none
of Mr. Buckle's supporters felt any dismay, and in the end the majority was larger than on
the last occasion, which means that the Liberal made no difference. The whole result
has made the Labour Movement very proud of its achievements and bids fair for the future.
Disputes have been attended to at various places, such as Crick's, LEICESTER, where
the firm had not advanced the clickers the amount due on the last rise, but as trade is
so bad and the men, although on day labour, are working dead to Statement, the employer
---

732
the per cent. has been added to the Statement there is no advantage being taken by
the atm, but if they get more trade he will have no objection to giving the extra right
way.
We have also visited the form of Crane's, South Wigston, where one half of the recent
trouble has been sottled, and the firm advised that the other portion must be strictly
adhered to, and we shall advise the men accordingly. It is these (come in at the war-time
period) shops that are giving the most trouble, but constant and persistent attention will
ultimately bring them into line.
WELLINGBOROUGH. We have three firms here who are causing us some very close
attention, all of the same order as those just referred to. One of them, who is making
the lowest priced man's boot I have heard of, is paying wages not satisfactory to
us, and
we are, even at great risk, claiming the proper rates, and shall press them to the full. We
cannot protect non-unionists who will make their own terms not caring a jot for their
fellows, and encouraging firms just as neglectful to take labour below its market value.
The other two firms have not yet met our requirements on the Holiday Scheme.
whether the business will continue for several reasons. We intend holding meetings of
one having postponed the matter owing, he says, to bad trade, and the other is doubtful

who fear the unemployment period. If many people who speak ill of the unemployed
person had our experience, they would soon find that the working people of this country
as a whole prefer remunerative employment to the Employment Exchange, and it is only
as a last and desperate resource that they appeal to the Branch Officials for advice and help
when employers put the men to the test of doing as they wish-ignore our Agreements or

At RUSHDEN an ex-member of the Union, now an employer, has taken this line not
for the first or second time, and we are bound to press this gentleman by all reasonable
means to comply with our Agreement even if we have to resort to stronger measures,
which we prefer not to do, as such action cannot improve any business or establish peace
and concord.
The GENERAL FEDERATION are getting their usual crop of disputes, and the experience
of other Unions are much akin to our own in all businesses. The suicidal policy of lower
wages has a great tendency to reduce living to a mere existence. Employers of labour
need lessons in political economy.
I visited FINEDON and made inquiries into the question of a case which had been
before the Magistrates at Wellingborough, and where the complainant's wages was reported
as 52s. per week; the Employers' Federation wondered whether this was general. My
investigation, after seeing officials and firm proved that the man was being taught a
machine of which he was without any experience, and himself forfeited his situation,
and the cost of the labour performed by the man during a very short time, viz., two weeks,
was 30 per cent. less than the Statement called for, the quantity and operation being taken
into account. On this firm of Parker & Cooper's, we found that the firm had not tried
to get cheaper labour than Statement calls for.
The Highfields Shoe Co., Finedon, was also visited for a similar reason to the above, viz.,
men receiving less than the minimum, and here we found men engaged on junior operations
such as lower priced labour could perform, and we are bound to consider value if firms
are generous to some men on some operations, because they would rather have an operation
done by an expert, or are prepared to pay a little more than Statement, it is not our wish
to prevent a member from receiving the benefit.
We also visited the firm of Norton & Langley, Finedon, who are struggling young men,
having been in business since the war, and have worked overtime without the extra of
time and a quarter. We were not satisfied with the attitude of the firm on the point, and
arranged for a meeting of the operatives. Such has been held and all instructed to refuse
to work overtime.
I went to WOLLASTON and saw Messrs. Phillips Bros., and afterwards felt that, owing
to much illness and breakdown in machinery, that the firm had not exceeded the overtime
clause of the Agreement. In the same place, at the firm of Nutt & Rice (another firm of
recent growth), the employers argue these men have made no claim, consequently they
accept the position as being satisfactory. A meeting of the operatives is here essential
as the firm refuse to pay time and a quarter as they cannot afford it, they say. We advise
no overtime and must instruct the members accordingly. A meeting was afterwards held
at Irthlingborough, after we had made another visit to Finedon to get the final attitude
of the firm of Norton & Langley, with the above result, that we must act through the
membership.
The operatives from Perkins & Bird did not turn up in such numbers as we have the
right to expect, but we got information from the men, women and girls as to the attitude
we are to assume when we meet the firm, who had withheld for one week the 24 per cent.

BRANCH REPORTS.
ARBROATH. Trade is failing to pick up with us yet, and even our best
factory in Carmoustic has started to put members on short time. Very little
which was quite unexpected. When we were interesting ourselves in some of
as vet, and affecting two departments only, but it seems to show a decline
the conditions of this place a few months ago, there seemed to be plenty of
orders with the firm, but our hopes have gone beyond the facts. Whether as
the result of our efforts or not, three girls and two men have been discharged
here, and the unfortunate thing about it is that the members in Carnoustie
have not taken steps to compel an inquiry. Mr. Richards and Mr. Bleakley
to slip, and matters will be worse another time. We are alarmed to think of
any future effort which may be made to investigate into conditions when
members can be punished with impunity, and no protest be forthcoming.
to say that such a spirit will not make our Union as influential as it ought to be.
This was not the spirit which built up the National Union, and we venture
No member can afford to stand back and wait on another raising the question
of elementary rights. If we cannot all go in for justice, there is something
wrong, and our Union is the weaker accordingly. Our members were very well
pleased to get the increase owing to the increase in the cost of living, but we
find a difficulty in getting all the young folk to report their ages in order to get
proper wages. There seems to be a diffidence-quite unusual and quite
uncalled for among the youths and girls, and we must insist on our members
to keep all the young workers up to the scratch in this matter. When the age
is not handed in it simply means a present to the employer, which they neither
expect nor need. The hurry-burry of the General Election has caused great
excitement here, as elsewhere. Labour was faced by a united enemy in this
area. In spite of pretended differences Tory and Liberal agreed to work
together to defeat Labour, and unfortunately they succeeded. The would-be
champion of "sane and steady" government in the person of the Liberal
Candidate, broke down before the fight was well begun, but although safe
in the seclusion of the hospital he got the majority of the votes cast. This
is the second time this brilliant advocate of "sane and steady" government
has collapsed before the guns of Labour, but each time the sickly sentiment
of the electors has overcome judgment, and the working class candidate has
gone down. We are glad the National Union had a share in the fight, although
we cannot understand the curious happening on the withdrawal of Alderman
Hill, at Leicester. It was clearly our seat, and a nominee of ours should have
been put forward. Where are our young bloods who shine at our Conferences ?
When the older leaders held back, surely some of our men with youth on their
side could be given a chance. Congratulations to Mr. J. Buckle for his win at
Eccles, but double greetings to Mr. W. R. Smith for his magnificent come-back
at Norwich. His amazing victory there proves he should never have lost
Wellingborough, while the success of his successor at Wellingborough com-
pletes what must remain a mystery. Hats off to Norwich, and may the electors
there never prove as fickle as W. R.'s last constituency. Could the Union
not prepare itself for the next election, which cannot be months ahead, by
having at least five candidates prepared to fight if the chance is offered them.
We have the men, we have the money, and we could get the constituencies
if necessary. The next fight, and the next, will find a dearth of candidates
unless the Unions are prepared to fight for political as well as economic emanci-
pation.

NORTHAMPTON. - Trade remains quiet here, no influx of trade;
new industries, little prospects except slump. Wealth production rather
than effective demand, less earnings, less purchasing power (Capitals win).
Miss Margaret Bondfield elected M.P. by good majority, great hope of practical
measures to deal with unemployed problem. A great step towards new order of
society, bound to come someday, let us hope soon. Congratulations to Mr.
J. Buckle, M.P., Mr. W. R. Smith, M.P., and Mr. Fred Gould, M.P. Wave of
enthusiasm on our side for the grandest and greatest step in human history
(Socialism). Make haste, but don't get panicky. Best wishes to Officers and
Members for a more prosperous New Year.

NORWICH. - Trade in Norwich was slightly worse during November
taking the city through (although an improvement was observable in two
factories), consequently a larger number of claims for unemployed benefit
were registered with the branch. Just a few firms are running very well, and
at full pressure, while the major portion seem quite unable to maintain a steady
trade for long at a time. The result is that a portion of the operatives are
doing exceedingly well, whilst the greater number are finding it difficult to
earn sufficient to enable them to live. Just one of the many illustrations
shewing the inability of capitalist-owned industry to serve the human needs
of its people. We must "wait and see" what 1924 has in store; certainly if
political force has any bearing on social life the new parliament should encourage
us to hope for an improvement in the coming months. Hearty congratulation
to Johnny Buckle on his second victory, with hats off to Northampton and
Norwich on their fine achievement with Bondfield and Smith. The shoe
operatives of both towns have certainly risen to their responsibilities, an can
feel much satisfaction with a result to which they have so largely contributed.
Wishing officials and operatives as happy a Christmas as the times will allow.

NOTTINGHAM. - Trade is very quiet in this part, most of our members
only working three short days a week, while in the repairing short time is also
the rule, with no signs of a change for the present. Our members find great
difficulty in keeping up payment of their contributions.

PLYMOUTH. - Since our last report we have witnessed one of the most
stirring election campaigns ever experienced in the old town of Plymouth.
In each of the three divisions, Sutton, Drake and Devonport, the Conservative
Party has been challenged and the fight was fast and furious. The retiring
members were well entrenched with three local papers behind them, one blazing
away every morning at sunrise, another at sunset, while the third was brought
up once a week to do the long range firing ; the ammunition they fired did not
appear to be British manufacture, some being labelled Russian and some German.
Yet, it was designedly created to produce a great psychological effect, fear of
the Capital Levy hitting the poor man with a few pounds to his credit, fear of
a reduction or a complete loss of their service pensions, fear of the Bolshevicks
who had served their fellow men, good and true, for nearly half a century
as town councillors or trade union officials, and last, but not least, the fear
of the working man of one of his own class. This is more widespread than
most Labour men realise and can only be removed by more education, more
charity and service consecrated to the well-being and uplifting of our fellow-
men. It is regretted that we did not send at least one Labour man to West-
minster and secure a fair representation of opinion from the old town that once
stood four-square for the rights of the people and defied all the forces of class
and privilege hurled against it. But that was before the time of daily news-
papers, when men formed their own views upon politics and did not get them
handed out ready made by two noble gentlemen, made of paper.

SHEPSHED. - There is a slight improvement in the trade here, and it is
to be hoped that it will keep so.

THE POLITICAL SITUATION.

PARTY IN DEADLY EARNEST.
The Labour Movement yesterday threw down another challenge to the Government-
a challenge on behalf of the great army of Unemployed.
At the Joint Meeting of the General Council of the Trades Union Congress and the
National Executive of the Labour Party the attention of the Tory Cabinet, which is
awaiting defeat, of the Liberal Party, which is manœuvring for position, of the Labour
Movement, whose leaders are ready to take office, and of the electors throughout the
country, was drawn sharply once again to the issue on which Labour fought the Election.
The joint resolution, embodying the challenge, runs :-
"In view of the rejection, by an overwhelming vote of the electors, of the Govern-
ment's 'solution' for the problem of unemployment, and the declared intention of
the Government not to meet the newly-elected Parliament before January 8th,
"This joint meeting of the General Council of the Trades Union Congress and the
National Executive of the Labour Party, mindful of the intense suffering now experi-
enced by large numbers of the workless and their dependents, requests an immediate
public announcement of the Government's plans for dealing, adequately and effectively,
with the problem that continues to be the gravest confronting the nation."
This resolution embodies the deep feeling throughout the movement that failure to
deal with the present appalling situation is little less than criminal.
Labour is too conscious of the misery and sadness of an army of men, women, and
children, willing to work, and yet prevented from so doing, to countenance delay or hesi-
tancy in meeting their needs.
For full three years the official figures of this army have never been
less than 1,000,000. At times they have risen to over 2,000,000, and to-day
they stand at 1,194,700.
To these "official" figures have to be added many hundred thousands of those not
covered by the Insurance Act, those wearied with the constant search for work and driven
to despair, those on short time or casually employed.
The total of those who to-day are directly affected by the breakdown of Capitalism,
the chaos at home and abroad, is not less than 2,000,000.
"This joint meeting registers its complete confidence in Mr. J. Ramsay
MacDonald, M.P., as Leader of the Parliamentary Labour Party, being
sure that should he be called upon to assume high office he will in all his
actions consider the well-being of the nation in seeking to apply the principles
of the Labour Movement."
Only through the application of those principles can there be any real betterment
of the lot of the workless; only with their full application can there be any permanent
cure. Daily Herald, 14th December, 1923.

**TRADE BOARD MINIMA.**
Magistrate and Non-Unionist. Employer Fined.

"I wonder if any of these men belong to their trade union. Do they know that by
Act of Parliament they are entitled to a minimum of £3 a week?"
This comment was made at Tower Bridge Police Court yesterday by Mr Waddy
when hearing summonses under the Trade Boards Act.
Charles Henry Hoskins, boot repairer, of Peckham, was stated to have advertised
for "a partner with £50." Three men made agreements to work for £2 a week and 25
per cent. of the profits. For some weeks they got the £2, eventually the money was
reduced to odd sums and the men in despair, gave up. They were owed £17 3s. 2d.,
£18 0s. 8d. and £24 1s. 4d. respectively.

**Magistrate's Rebuke.**
One of the men said he did not know about the £3 minimum. He did not belong to
a trade union because he was a disabled soldier and a learner.
Mr. Waddy: You tell me you don't know, but I know what workmen trade unionists
talk about when together; but you chose to take £2 a week and a chance getting 25 per
cent. of the profits. You might sue in the County Court, but I see no reason for these
men make these agreements with their eyes open.
Later, the magistrate said: "These summonses give rise to a question of considerable
public importance. The Statute under the Act has fixed a minimum wage, and these
men entered into a partnership agreement in one sense, and, I think, there is no doubt
that both workman and employer knew the meaning of the Act.
"I am asked to make an order on the employer to repay the difference between the
wages he paid and the minimum, and this seems to me inequitable. If they had received
their money and 25 per cent. of the profits they would have said nothing. The business
fails, and they now ask for the balance of wages they would have been entitled to under
the Act.
"With regard to defendant, the point is different. He was under statutory obligation
to pay the minimum, and he knew it was illegal for him to make such a contract, and that
it was a direct breach of the law. Defendant must pay a penalty of 40s. and 21s. costs
on each summons, £9 3s. in all, or in default 21 days' imprisonment."
Time was allowed defendant to find the money. - The Daily Herald, 28th Nov., 1923.

**TRADE BOARD MINIMA.**
Mr. T. F. Richards, General President of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Opera-
tives, writes relative to a report under the above heading which appeared in our issue of
the 28th inst., where a Boot and Shoe Repairing employer was fined under the Trade
Boards Act, that in the evidence of one of the employees it is reported that the reason
"he did not belong to a Trade Union was because he was a disabled soldier and a learner."
Mr. Richards wishes our readers to know that so far as the National Union of Boot
and Shoe Operatives is concerned, no bar has ever been placed upon disabled soldiers
becoming members, and doubtless if the employee named in the report had made applica-
tion to one of their seventy-one branches, he could not only have become a member of the
Union, but received invaluable advice upon matters relative to Boot and Shoe Repairing
and the Trade Boards Act. Many thousands of Boot and Shoe repairers in various parts
of the country are already members of that Union.
(The above was sent to the Daily Herald on the 28th November, 1923.-T. F. RICHARDS,
General President).

**CHANGES IN COST OF LIVING: STATISTICS FOR 1st DECEMBER, 1923.**
Summary: Average Increases since July, 1914.
All Items included .. 77 per cent.
Food only 76

During November there was a further advance in the average level of retail prices of
food. Eggs, butter, sugar, potatoes and milk were dearer at 1st December than a month
earlier. On the other hand, fish and bacon were cheaper, while the remaining articles of
food included in the statistics showed no substantial changes in prices, on the average.
As a net result of all the changes recorded, the average increase over the level of
July, 1914, in the retail prices (in Great Britain and Northern Ireland) of the articles of
food included in these statistics rose to about 76 per cent. at 1st December, as compared
with about 73 per cent. at 1st November. The Ministry of Labour Gazette, December, 1923.

CHARGE OF IMPEDING THE DUE EXERCISE OF THE FRANCHISE.
SMITH v. FITZROY.
(Before MR. JUSTICE ASTBURY.)
Serjeant Sullivan, K.C., and Mr. L. R. Lipsett moved, ex parte, before Mr. Justice
Astbury, this afternoon, on behalf of Mr. Len. Smith, Labour candidate for the Daventry
Division of Northamptonshire, for an injunction to restrain Captain E. A. Fitzroy, the
Conservative candidate for the division, from impeding the due exercise of the franchise
by the publication of a circular contrived to mislead the electors.
SERJEANT SULLIVAN said that the defendant had issued to the electors an address,
which contained a copy of a ballot paper, on which the defendant's name was printed
in very prominent letters, and below there was written: "Do not sign your name or put
any other mark than a X. which must be placed in the space to the right of Captain Fitzroy's
name, as shown above, or your vote will be lost." Counsel read an affidavit by the plain-
tiff's solicitor, who stated that the voters of the division included a large number of persons
in a humble position and of limited education, who were likely to be deceived by the unfair
and misleading terms of the document and that unless the circulation was restrained
incalculable harm would be done to the plaintiff in the constituency.
MR. JUSTICE ASTBURY asked what jurisdiction he had to grant the injunction.
SERJEANT SULLIVAN said:- Under the ordinary jurisdiction to restrain an improper
act to the detriment of the person applying.
In answer to a further question, he said, that he had no authority on the point, but
election law, was like any other part of the law of the land, and his Lordship had ample
jurisdiction to restrain a circular which would exercise undue influence. It did not require
a precedent to restrain a wrongful act.
MR. JUSTICE ASTBURY said that he had no general jurisdiction to restrain people from
committing wrongful acts. He had no doubt that the circular was an improper one, and it
might result in a risk of the election's being declared void. But this application was made
when only one day remained before the election. It appeared that the circular was
issued about 20th November, and he was not satisfied that it had not come to the plaintiff's
notice shortly afterwards, and the plaintiff might have made the application at once.
He declined to grant an injunction at this time, which would be of no use to the plaintiff,
but the plaintiff could go to the Court of Appeal if he wished and try to persuade them
to grant the injunction.
Solicitors.-Messrs. Kenneth Brown, Baker, Baker, and Co.-The Times, 5th Decem-
ber, 1923.
To the Electors of the Daventry Division.
Fox Hill,
West Haddon, Rugby,
5th December, 1923.
Yesterday evening my attention was called to a report in the Evening Paper that
Mr. Len. Smith had applied to the Court for an Injunction to restrain me from issuing
to the Electors any more copies of my Election Address, on the ground that the Instruc-
tions as to how an Elector should record his Vote for me, so that there should be no chance
that it would be lost, were misleading.
This report was the first information that I received that Mr. Smith had any intention
of taking this course, and consequently I had no opportunity of being represented in
Court, or of informing the Judge.
(1) that my first intimation that objection had been taken to anything in my
Election Address was sent to me on Saturday morning, 1st December, by Col. Kerr's
Agent.
(2) that immediately I was aware that a different construction to that intended
had been put upon the words referred to in the Address, I gave instruction (at Col.
Kerr's request) that a statement making the meaning still clearer should be read
at each of my public meetings, and a letter to every Elector to that effect has been
issued with the least possible delay.
From the report of the proceedings in Court, it would appear that the Judge (Mr.
Justice Astbury) made comment on the words about which the complaint was made, of
which no doubt political use will be made.
I must leave it to the Electors of the Daventry Division to form their own opinions
as to whether I have on this or on any other occasion intentionally done anything to
mislead them, and further to form their opinion as to the methods that have been adopted
by my opponents to endeavour to lead them to this conclusion.
E. A. FITZROY.

PROSECUTION OF EX-INSURANCE AGENT FOR MAKING A
FRAUDULENT CLAIM FOR OUT-OF-WORK BENEFIT.
John Williams, of 13, Gainsborough Road, Liverpool, was summoned at Dale Street
on November 1st, 1923, at the instance of the Incorporated Insurance Industry Unemploy-
ment Insurance Board, for having made a false representation for the purpose of obtaining
out-of-work benefit.
Defendant, in the first instance, pleaded not guilty.
Mr. Paxton, prosecuting on behalf of the Board, said that this was a first prosecution
of its kind by the above-mentioned Board, which administered the Insurance Industry
Unemployment Insurance scheme approved by the Minister of Labour under Section 18
of the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1920. Defendant, recently employed by the United
Friendly Insurance Co. Ltd., applied to the Board for unemployment benefit, and in his
formal application alleged that he was not in receipt of sick pay nor a member of an approved
society, whereas in fact he was a member of the Hearts of Oak Benefit Society, and had
been in receipt of sick pay for some time before the application was made, and was still in
receipt of such pay at the time of the application.
It appeared that defendant admitted that he had been in receipt of sick pay at the
time of the application.
On the advice of his solicitor, defendant withdrew his plea of not guilty.
Mr. H. J. Davis, defending, urged that defendant did not realise the connection
between sick pay and unemployment insurance benefit.
The magistrates stated they were quite satisfied that the defendant knew perfectly
well what he was doing, and that he had deliberately made a false representation for the
purpose of obtaining benefit. They fined him £5, allowing him, on his application, one
meath to pay. - National Insurance Gazette, December 15th, 1923.

THE BOILERMAKERS' DISPUTE.
Success has crowned the efforts of the General Council of the Trades Union Congress
in regard to the overtime and nightshift agreement. It has been a long and difficult
to settle the disastrous dispute between the boilermakers and the federated employers.
task, requiring in the three mediators appointed by the General Council, Miss Margaret
Bondfield and Messrs. E. L. Poulton and Fred Bramley, a high degree of diplomatic skill
and delicacy of touch. There has not often been an industrial dispute in which the issues
were so complicated and many-sided; it involved inter-union relations of a very important
character as well as the relations between employers and employed. The autonomy of
unions, the sanctity of agreements, the principle of Trade Union federation, and the unity
of the organised industrial movement were all brought into discussion. Where the official
negotiators of the Ministry of Labour, and the unofficial mediators representing the civic
authorities in the towns chiefly affected by the prolonged stoppage, failed to secure a
settlement, the spokesmen of the Trades Union Congress succeeded. They succeeded
because they worked with a single eye to the interests of the workers directly concerned
and of the whole Trade Union Movement whose welfare they had at heart. The terms
of settlement were signed by Mr. John Hill and Mr. Mark Hodgson on behalf of the boiler-
makers, and by Mr. Leonard Roper and Sir Charles Sanders on behalf of the Shipbuilding
Employers' Federation. Here we have only to congratulate the Trade Union Movement
on the ending of a dispute which has lasted for many months, and which at times seemed
to baffle all efforts at a solution which would leave the Trade Unions most directly con-
cerned with their essential unity unimpaired. Not only has unity been maintained,
but we believe it has been strengthened; and certainly the wisdom and practical states-
manship of the General Council of the Trades Union Congress has been proved.-The
Labour Magazine, December, 1923.

Parliament—that there must be provided First Aid Equipment in all factories,
the clause in the Act being hereunder:
FIRST-AID EQUIPMENT.
A First-Aid box or cupboard must be provided in every factory, and
where more than 150 persons are employed, one such box or cupboard
must be kept for EACH 150 PERSONS, fractions to be reckoned as 150.
The number of boxes required must be calculated on the largest number
of persons employed at any one time.
Each box or cupboard must be placed under the charge of a responsible
person, whose name must be stated in a notice affixed in every workroom.
Where an ambulance room is provided, and arrangements are made
for the immediate treatment of all injuries occurring in the factory, the
Chief Inspector of Factories may issue a certificate exempting the factory
from the above provisions to such an extent as he may decide.
The carrying out of the requirements of this Clause in the Act should be
of considerable help in minimising the danger to health owing to any accident
which befalls an operative. Should the above paragraph not be carried out
in any factory where our members are working, we hope they will report the
matter to the branch officers to enable them to secure compliance with the law.
THE NEW PARLIAMENT,
as members are aware, met on the 8th inst., and proceeded to the election of
the Speaker, the Rt. Hon. J. H. Whitley, M.P., he being unanimously re-
elected. The House opened for the business on the 15th inst. The position
is one of constant change, surrounded by a good deal of complexity. If one
was not aware of the circumstances of the recent election, and the result to
the Conservative Party, one might easily imagine from the reading of the
King's Speech that the Government was likely to remain in office for a con-
siderable time, and that they were really going to deal with a great many
subjects, when as a matter of fact it is as certain as things can be that within
a few hours from the time of our going to Press with this paragraph, that the
Conservative Government will be defeated, and a new Government will have
been called into being. The new Government so far as one can forecast will
be a Labour Government. It is true the Labour Party in the House does not
command a majority of votes therein, nor does the Liberal or Conservative
Party. This will undoubtedly add to the difficulties of a situation, which in
itself would not be an easy one, but a situation which we are fully convinced
Mr. J. Ramsay MacDonald, M.P., as leader of the Labour Party, will surmount
and overcome, backed up—as he will be—by the Party as a whole, with the
members in the House, and millions of the masses outside. We bespeak for
our colleagues full consideration under the abnormal circumstances under
which they will take Office, because whilst we have no doubt that all will be

REGISTRATION.
The time for registration for the new voting list of burgesses has once more
arrived, and we beg to urge upon the members their duty to see that their names
appear upon the voting lists published from time to time in all districts, so that
when members are called upon as citizens to exercise their vote they will not be
precluded from so doing. This is an important matter, because it has been
found upon more than one occasion when persons have been to vote, their
name did not appear upon the Register. We know of instances where not
odd cases, but considerable numbers were omitted from the list, and were thus
deprived of exercising their vote. The lists may be examined at places of
worship, local post offices or town halls, and if it is found that your name does
not appear thereon, application should at once be made to the Local Labour
Party to enable the matter to be put right.

DEATH OF MR. GEORGE STANDEVEN.
It is with deep regret that we record the death of MR. GEORGE
STANDEVEN, Secretary to the London South Branch for over 28 years.
Mr. G. Standeven has been a member of the Union for over 40 years,
and was a quiet, unassuming member, always anxious to do what he could
to help forward the work of the Union, and so improve the conditions of
the workers generally. Mr. G. Standeven died on the 16th inst., and to
his family we offer our sincere sympathy.
The funeral took place on Tuesday, 22nd January, and we were
represented by the General Secretary, Mr. E. L. Poulton, J.P.
Now that another Union stalwart has joined the Great Majority we
trust his life work will have so influenced the younger generation as to
induce them to carry on the work which Mr. G. Standeven has had to
lay down.
DEATH OF MR. J. SPEIGHT.
Shortly after the telephone message was received at the Central
Office intimating that Mr. G. Standeven had passed away, Mr. J. Wescoe,
of Leeds, telephoned to say that MR. J. SPEIGHT, Secretary to the Leeds
No. 2 Branch, died suddenly on the 16th inst., he having been at work
in the factory on the 15th inst. Mr. Speight was Secretary to the Leeds
Branch for about ten years, and was at one time the Leeds representative
on the Executive Council. Mr. A. J. Dobbs represented the Council
at the funeral.
To Mrs. Speight and family we have sent our sympathy, and trust
that the example of Mr. Speight will act as an incentive to the younger
members to carry on the work.
DEATH OF KENDAL PRESIDENT.
MR. J. T. ROOKE, the President of the Kendal Branch, has also
passed away during the month. To his relatives we tender our sincere
sympathies. Further references will be found on pages 49 and 63.

GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.

FELLOW MEMBERS, The article this week by the Labour Correspondent of the Daily Herald, in
Saturday's issue, again brings to the front the wisdom of the Trade Union element of this
country in making their purchases at only well-known fair houses, who have the reputation
of giving fair conditions to their employees, whether resident or non-resident. If this
was done, a well-known multiple firm with business premises in nearly all towns, and
whose recent principal was reputed to be a millionaire (at one time in the City of Leicester)
and was alleged by a girl over 20 years of age to be paying a wage of ros. per week
For that reason the writer has never entered one
of their premises. For the above reason we ought to make the fact known that we have
a Trade Union Stamp for all houses making honest goods, and as only fair and honest
houses already have our Stamp, we should make it part of our Union Stamp Contract
that the houses using the Stamp are fair business people, and by this means revive the
demand for Trade Union Stamped articles. Further, as the employers have failed to come
to an agreement as to a Standard Shoe, then the operatives and the general public ought
seed sowing shoe off the market. One wonder how far the and multiple shopkeeper
to take a hand and see whether they cannot at least drive the pocket picking, consumptive
is responsible. I have an inherent suspicion of the non-producing factor.

Trade is on the whole rather quiet so far as business is concerned, but the usual crop
of troubles await us, mainly due to the awkward position in which War Time firms made
their appearance, with a few who came into being since the War. This makes those who
have to build up a reputation, get and hold a good type of operative, give confidence to
their customers in so short a space of time, makes their task a colossal one, and no wonder
that temptations are great to take orders at almost any price and expect to get their
material and labour on similar conditions. This is sufficient to keep the Officials of the
Branches and Union alive to the situation, and these gentlemen, in their anxiety to get on,
are prepared to accept the offer of that weak operative whose strength is so weak as to
in their illgotten employment; anybody could employ men for a week or so if they were
permit himself to offer himself at less than Union rates. These few men are shortened
prepared to sell their labour at less than cost, but such a method would be short-lived,
and we should and must claim loyal adherence to the National Agreement that governs
both bodies, and an Agreement which has worked better and been respected more than
any previous Agreement, proving that we are gradually, if slowly, connecting the non-
federated firms to respect the Terms of Settlement equal with the federated firms. In this
we are very successful, but should like to be able to record the fact that there is no trouble
with federated employers. As a matter of fact the few who have businesses either in
another area, or an auxiliary business, we find these few members as hard as brads. In
fact they would have liked to have ignored the National Terms and put up a case asking for
complete exemption, but as we impose, according to our strength, successfully these con-
ditions, and gradually but surely all our employers are coming to the conclusion that our
vigilance will not permit the wages bill to be reduced, and it is not to the credit of any
section of manufacturers that any attempt to reduce wages should be made in face of the
National Agreement that makes no provision, only on certain terms and lines. Any
attempt to depart from that must first of all get the consent of the Joint Standing Com-
mittee.

SOUTH WIGSTON. At the time of writing I have just completed a settlement of a
case at J. W. Black, South Wigston. Rather than strain the relations that exist, and
taking into consideration bad trade and the fact that the employer has businesses in three
other towns where he is looked upon as a fair employer. I should certainly have advised
the strongest pressure possible, but as the men had been lax and slow in making their
claim, we feel that we ought not to pull the chestnuts out of the fire for those who put
them in. This case has caused four personal visits, besides numerous letters, and an offer
of arbitration that was declined. I earnestly ask all our members to be prompt in their
demands and to let the Officers know immediately. We can then claim, otherwise members
may find that there may be a claim by the Union against them for a dereliction of duty.

RUSHDEN. The firm of Nicholson's, Rushden, was visited by Mr. C. Bates and myself
prior to Christmas. The firm refused to pay, and at the end of the week handed the men
a week's notice to apply separately on December 26th. I wrote to the firm telling them
otherwise we should have to advise them not to apply for work until the firm settled
that we hoped some settlement would be arrived at before the men left for the holidays.
Result: The employer decided, as he was putting in machinery, to pay up all
dues and demands, and start as many as possible after the holidays and give the seven
men for whom he could not find a place at present a legal week's notice. The men have
been met and we are in hopes that some of them may get a start in a few weeks. The
change in the firm is certainly due directly to the men's loyalty not to give up the Holiday
Fund.
WELLINGBOROUGH. Another firm, Odell & Dixon, had intimated that he was not
grace owing to the illness of his partner, and we are having to take the necessary steps to
enable him to comply with the Terms and the slightest inconvenience to all concerned.
TRADE BOARD. For two days in December we attended the Central Trade Board
Meeting at Whitehall, for the benefit of the Hand-sewn Making and Repairing Operatives
of the country. What with making out and agreeing to prices, passing the Registration
of Apprentices, granting permits to those crippled persons not capable of doing work
equal to the normal operative, seeing members of the Ministry and advising on questions
non-unionists on the District Trade Committee, we were kept fully employed, if only to
see that the well known opposition to Trade Unions makes no headway. I have already
seformed the Minister that if he appoints non-unionists I shall advise that our men do not
ict with them, and have asked Mr. Brennan, of the Amalgamated Society of Boot and
Shoe Makers, and also Mr. Orchard, of the N.U.D.A.W. and the Co-operative Employees,
sho also have many members working at the Trade, and they have all joined with me in
sending on a vigorous protest. We appear to gain a foot and lose two if these natural
enemies of Trade Unions, who appear to be strong at present, are in the Ministry of Labour.
FINEDON. The Highfield Shoe Co., of Finedon, has again been visited and matters
are far from satisfactory. We have already made many claims for adjustment and are
sorry that the firm do not appear as yet to locate the seriousness of the situation, but as
we informed them they will comply with all our National Conditions before we withdraw
our attention. There is a lot that wants putting right, and as they have had our case
for a week now, we must press for compliance.
NOTTS, AND DERBY BOARD.-The Mansfield, Nottingham and Derby Statements
have all been printed, proofed, and checked, and visits have been paid to Mansfield and
Leicester for this purpose, and a Board Meeting is to be held on the 17th inst. at Nottingham
for the adoption of these Statements and their application to the branches for which they
have been compiled.
GENERAL FEDERATION OF TRADE UNIONS. On the 20th December I attended my
last meeting of the General Federation of Trade Unions, and with my deep regret severed
a connection that was of a very laudable nature and character, and after the many many
years (more than thirty) when the Movement thought, and still think, that united action
is a power, and that we have rendered help and succour to those worse off than ourselves.
We are proud and rejoice in the fact that we have measured our regard for many years by
the financial help we have given, and prefer this to the recommendation suggested and
implied that we have paid more than we have drawn out.
Once again may I appeal, strongly appeal, to all our members-women and men,
girls and boys-to think of the future before us, of the prospects of Labour having a chance
to place their well considered humane plans for the redemption of mankind, stripped of
boastfulness, cant or arrogance, but based on the one plan and plane of equality in treat-
ment to all, friend or otherwise.

BARNSLEY. There seems good prospect of our members starting the
New Year with plenty of work, instead of as last year. Working short time
was their prospect last year, and it continued as such for some months. We
hope to have a better year as regards sickness, having had four members on
during the year on the sick fund, but we are clear at the present, and hope
to continue so for a long time.

BELFAST... We regret that we have nothing of an encouraging nature
to report. Trade still continues to remain very quiet, especially in the manu-
facturing end. We are very much disappointed that the workers in the
Repairing trade do not appear to appreciate all that our Union has secured
for them in the way of increased wages and improved working conditions.

CHESHAM.—Trade here is getting quiet again. Several members have
been discharged through lack of orders and a good number are working short
time.

EDINBURGH. — Trade here has been far from satisfactory during the
month. Our largest Repairing Factory—St. Cuthbert’s Co-operative Society—
which employs over 50 hands are removing to new and up-to-date premises.
They are installing a new plant of the latest machinery, not only for Finishing,
but also in conjunction with Benching as well. The Directors originally
intended putting all on a weekly wage basis, but owing to certain information
coming along that the representatives of the old Hand-sewn Body had arranged
a settlement and fixed prices for those machines with Birmingham firms,
which had been well advertised throughout Scotland, with a frenzied desire to
establish same conditions here, St. Cuthbert's offered to adopt these prices
in conjunction with their machines, but the Special Committee which had been
appointed to deal with the matter along with our Council Member, C. Bleakley
(who has been of considerable assistance to the Committee throughout these
negotiations) absolutely refused to consider the figures named. We were
then asked by St. Cuthberts to submit another Statement, which we very
soon did, but this was immediately turned down, and not until after several
meetings were we able to arrive at a figure which is undoubtedly an improve-
ment on the Birmingham Statement. We are giving same a three months'
trial together with a 46½ hour week against the present 48 hour week. We
appeal to other Branches in Scotland or England to accept nothing of this
Statement. We know that several firms in Scotland are anxious to have
prices fixed for this work. Reports to hand say that good money can be made
on the Birmingham Statement which has an hourly guarantee rate given.
If wages can be earned why do employers not give a weekly guaranteed wage.
They would lose nothing in the transaction according to their information.

GLASGOW.-Trade with us is fair, the factories on restarting after the
holidays are running full time. Members working on the Repairing are having
a very bad time of slackness.

HIGHAM AND RUSHDEN. - Trade remained fairly good right up to end

ployer. At Finedon trouble was experienced at one firm. Shops meetings

KETTERING. - December witnessed a striking and significant spectacle
in the boot and shoe trade in Kettering - that of three or four firms working
overtime. The event was so unusual a happening during recent years as to
warrant some comment in this report. Did the circumstances arise merely
out of the Christmas rush, or was it the upward turning point in the sloth of
one to think that the latter may be the actual fact. There is a better and
much brighter spirit prevailing, and out of it one can at least hope that 1924
will be generally much better for our members than the last two or three years
have been.
ELECTION. - The success which attended the recent Parliamentary Election
in this Division reflects considerably on the political sagacity and high purpose
of the members of our Union. We are by far the largest organised body of
workers in the constituency, and everywhere our members were to the fore
striving to attain the splendid victory which resulted. The necessity for
political activity inside the Trade Union movement was, however, never more
evidenced. On all sides one heard this and that doubter questioning the policy
of Labour or of the Labour Candidate on this or that question, and determining
a vote on a simple fractional issue. As Trade Unionists we have one practical
principle before us: "The attainment of a status in Society which shall give
us security from want, and freedom to obtain from life the maximum service
and joy." The realisation of our principle, we have bitterly learned, can only
be obtained by strong workshop organisation and in and by national legislation.
It is pure folly, then, to believe on the one hand in Trade Unionism, and, on
the other hand, to permit a petty issue of minor importance to split our influence
on the political field. Let us look to the big thing always, the small jobs will
then complete themselves. However, congratulations to all our members
who did the thing well.

OPENING OF THE TECHNICAL SCHOOL AT KETTERING.

What Ald. Bostock said at the opening of the Technical School
at Kettering on Saturday, 12th January, 1924.

Ald. Bostock said one often heard people ask what they had to do with the people
who came after them. He believed that we had everything to do with the people who
came after. We were the inheritors of the past; we were not owners, but trustees, and
it was up to us to see that that inheritance of ours was passed on, wider and larger, to
those who came after.

Making Life Worth Living.

One of the great drawbacks of the industrial era had been the extent to which, in the
pursuit of wealth, we had been indifferent to the waste of human life, and our disregard
of the conditions which made life worth living. When the factory system was introduced
child life was exploited, and towns were allowed to grow up badly planned. Even now
we disregarded the smoke evil; but there was a greater evil than that in that nine out of
every ten young people of the country went uneducated during the really critical years
of their life. We gave them the key of knowledge, but did not teach them how to use it.

A school such as they now had at Kettering was of inestimable value to any neigh-
bourhood. Technical education was very important, and was, indeed, invaluable to
those who were not content to remain at the bottom, but aspired to be managers and
foremen.

It was important to-day to see they made good use of their leisure. We were living
now in times of revolution. He was not one of those who feared revolution: there had
been many silent revolutions in English history. But power was passing into the hands
of democracy, and if that power was to be properly used we must see that it went, not to a
partially educated, but to a fully educated democracy. In that scheme of education
the new school would play its part.

Trade Command.

The educational work being done at Kettering was part of a process that was giving
them a better command of a trade when, as a trade, they had been lamentably ignorant
of the materials they used."

PARLIAMENTARY AGENT'S REPORT.
Since the last report appeared above my name, much water has flowed under the
bridges, many changes have taken place, and once again I find myself a member of the
Labour Party in the House of Commons. While always viewing the political situation
with interest and anticipation, it did not seem but a short time ago that the country would
pass through a General Election before 1923 had passed out.
The fact that such has happened does but emphasise the uncertainty of politics,
and calls for the greatest of effort at all times whereby we may not be caught unawares
by any sudden development. There is nothing that is more difficult to forecast than a
future political situation, and in few matters appertaining to national life are the possi-
bilities more prolific.
With these in mind it is pleasing to reflect upon the success of the Labour Party in
the recent General Election. We hoped for much, but few amongst us thought we should
do so well. Not because we did not deserve the success that has come our way, but
because of the many forces and influences that are against us. Our own Daily Herald
is a solitary oasis in a desert of journalism. Everything possible was done to misrepresent
us in the eyes of the electors. If the people were not frightened at the coming of the
Labour Party that certainly was not the fault of the Trust Press.
We must learn from this election the importance of a strong Press of our own, and
while one is glad to note the improvement in the position of the Daily Herald, we must
not rest until we have not merely one paper, but a powerful Press of our own circulating
in all parts of the country.
So far as my own contest was concerned, we had a very good fight. The local move-
ment feel very proud of the achievement; they have reason to be, for it was a splendid
result, and it was well worked for by all sections of the movement. But though we are
satisfied with what we have accomplished, there are those who feel very sore and are already
talking of what will happen the next time. It is up to us to see that the next will be a
repetition of the last. But I have reason to know these things are somewhat uncertain.
The happenings since the election have been both amusing and instructive. At one
time we were a helpless, hopeless crowd, too incapable for words, deficient in ability,
lacking in experience. It was a huge joke to imagine that Labour could ever become the
Government of the country. But now that the Party has faced the situation with courage
and sagacity, those who belittled us before, now turn and beg for a Coalition of others
against us, whereby we may be prevented from taking office, and put into operation the
changes which are long overdue, and which are possible within the limitations of the
situation in which we shall find ourselves. As has been often stated before, it was not
because of our shortcomings that these people opposed us, but because they fear the
advent of Labour, and the attack it will make against the ranks of class interest and
privilege.
If, as appears almost certain, Mr. MacDonald is called upon to form a Government
within the next few days, it is well that it should be understood it will be under circum-
stances that can hardly be termed favourable. I suppose it is true to say that were we
free agents, we would not seek it. As MacDonald said at the Albert Hall on the 8th of
this month, "it is a bankrupt estate that we have to take over." We shall come into
office following upon the most hopeless bungling in our political history. There is scarcely
one phase of the situation that can be termed satisfactory, either at home or abroad.
But we have never hesitated to claim for our Party that at least it is equal to any
other, and that it could and would govern if the opportunity presented itself. We are the
heirs in succession as far as parties in the House go, and because of that, we shall accept
the responsibility of office if the present Government is defeated, and resign.
But this will call for the best that is within us, and the movement in the country
must trust those whom it has selected to fight its battles in the House of Commons. Under
any circumstances it would be difficult, but under present conditions it will be doubly so.
It is well to remember we shall be in office, but not in power, that there is no guarantee
that any of our proposals will be carried in the House; but while that may be so, it is well
to understand that there are other ways in which things can be done, and it is safe to say
that every effort will be made to secure ample reforms within the limitations imposed
upon us.
There will, at any rate, be one great advantage, we shall be gaining experience which
will be useful when the time comes for Labour to be in power as well as in office. With
a generous confidence from the movement outside, and loyalty inside, we shall hold our
own and lay the foundation for greater things later on.
It is not without some regret that I pass once again from the industrial to the political.
The former sphere always appealed to me, and just now the field for work is fairly wide,

with credit to themselves and advantage to our members. It will be my endeavour in
the years ahead may be more fruitful to the people for the coming of Labour
my new sphere to render the best service that my abilities will permit, in the hope that
will always be in the forefront of the fight for the cause of the people
I thank those branches who sent me congratulatory messages, and I hope our Union

THE WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION ACT, 1923.
The New Workmen's Compensation Act came into operation on 1st
January, 1924.
COMPENSATION ON DEATH.
The maximum compensation payable to dependents in the case of fatal
accidents under the 1906 Act, is £300.
Under the New Act the maximum compensation payable in the case of
fatal accidents for a widow without children remains at £300, but where children
are left under the age of 15 years further compensation is added on a sliding
scale, but the whole compensation payable to the dependents on death must
not exceed £600.
The minimum compensation payable in the case of death has been raised
from £150 to £200, and in no case can it be reduced below this limit by deduc
tions for payments made to the workman.
The amount payable when no dependent whatever is left is increased
from £10 to £15.
TOTAL INCAPACITY.
The New Act repeals the War Addition Acts which increased the maximum
weekly compensation from £1 under the 1906 Act to 35s. Od. under the War
Addition Acts.
The New Act now substitutes 30s. Od. for £1 a week as the maximum
payable to a person totally incapacitated, that is, he is entitled to half his
average weekly earnings not exceeding 30s. Od. a week, but in case his weekly
compensation is less than 25s. Od. an additional payment must be made repre
senting one-half the difference between the actual weekly compensation, and
the sum of 25s. Od., or the average weekly earnings whichever is the less.
For example:—A workman earning 30s. Od. a week, would be entitled
to half this amount, namely, 15s. Od.; plus half the difference between this
figure, that is 15s. Od.; and 25s. Od., in short, another 5s. Od. So he would
be entitled to £1 per week, that is 66% per cent. or two-thirds of his wages.
Compensation shall be payable under the Principal Act if the injury
disables the workman for more than three days, but shall not be payable in
respect of the first three days, unless the incapacity lasts for four weeks
or upwards.
The 1906 Act provided that if the workman was disabled for 14 days
the compensation would include the whole period of two weeks, thus covering
the first three days, which are now excluded unless he is totally incapacitated
for at least four weeks.
PARTIAL INCAPACITY.
Compensation for partial incapacity is also increased. If for total in-
capacity the weekly compensation payable was 25s. Od. or more, the com-
pensation for partial incapacity is to be one half of the difference between
the average pre-accident weekly earnings and the average of what the workman
is earning or able to earn in some suitable employment or business after the
accident.
If, however, the maximum amount of compensation payable during total
incapacity is less than 25s. Od. the same percentage is to be applied for partial
incapacity as that applied for total incapacity.
To give an illustration:—
A workman earns 30s. Od. a week. He receives during total incapacity
£1 a week compensation—that is, the 66% percentage referred to in the example

of 30s. Od., that is, two-thirds of 15s. Od., which equals 10s. Od.
Under the Principal Act compensation is not payable to persons employed

ACCIDENTS “ARISING OUT OF” THE EMPLOYMENT.
Numerous decided cases in the Courts show that no compensation is
payable if the workman's injury has been due to or caused by his action in
contravention of regulations or the orders of his employer or to his acting
without instructions. After 31st December, 1923, an accident so caused will
be deemed to "arise out of and in the course of his employment," if the act
was done for the purposes of and in connection with the employer's trade or
business, and the result is death or serious and permanent disablement.
EVAN BARLOW,

BATHS OF PARAFFIN WAX.
Rheumatism Cure at Leeds Tannery.
The treatment of rheumatism by immersing the affected limbs in hot liquid paraffin
wax has interested a number of institutions, which have installed baths.
Perhaps the first person to introduce the treatment into this country was a layman,
Mr. W. L. Ingle, the governing director of Messrs. W. L. Ingle Ltd., tanners, of Churwell,
Leeds, and added interest is now given to the subject by the installation of a new bath
at the firm's works.
Mr. Ingle first read of wax bath treatment in a French paper, and it was purely a
philanthropic motive, and the fact that he had the wax at hand, which led him to put up
the first bath in the country.
Since then many cases have been treated at the works free of cost, Mr. Ingle being
happy to have been the means of relieving pain.
The principle is a simple one-merely that of heat treatment. It has been found
that patients can endure a much higher temperature in the liquid wax than in water,
and that whereas the heating effects are lost almost immediately with water, the stimulus
to circulation caused by the wax bath continues for five or six hours.
In an interview Mr. Ingle said :-
"We use a large quantity of paraffin wax for waterproofing leather in our works,
so that when I first read of a bath of this material, which was being used with success in
Paris, I decided to try one in Leeds.
"Since then numbers of cases have been dealt with here, and some wonderful cures
have been effected; on the other hand, there have been numbers of disappointments.
For example, we find that it is no use in arthritis cases.
"From among others I recall two special cases. One was of a man who, through
rheumatism, had lost his situation. He had had to sell his furniture, and got down and
down until he and his wife lived in a common lodging-house. He was brought to the
works on crutches, but after his bath he carried them away under his arm. He persisted
in the treatment until it made a new man of him, and he got his home together again and
found work.
"The other was of a man who, through rheumatism, found himself and his wife and
ten children in one of the workhouses in this city. The authorities allowed him to come
here and take baths, and now he and his family are out of the workhouse and in their
own home.
"The treatment was also given with benefit to soldiers during the war, though at
first I had some difficulty in getting the military authorities to accept my offer. The
matter was clinched, however, when American officers brought two ambulance loads of
men to the works."

24th December, 1923.
DEAR SIR.-Replying to your letter of 21st December respecting the application of
melted paraffin for the hands and feet. Usually a cheap galvanised pail is obtained for
the purpose, and it requires about 18 lbs. of wax. The wax is semi-refined paraffin,
118/120° melting point. The pail containing the wax is placed either on a gas stove or
in an oven, and heated slowly until it is melted. The temperature should be about 125
Fahr. The feet or hands are immersed in this for about twenty minutes. The treatment
may be repeated daily, if required, but generally about twice weekly is sufficient. The
advantages of the wax treatment over hot water are, first, a much higher temperature
can be borne of the melted wax than of water, and secondly, the increased circulation
that is set up after the wax treatment continues for five or six hours, whereas after hot
water an immediate reaction takes place. We supply the wax at 21/2d. per lb., which is
about the cost price. The wax can be used repeatedly, because no germs can live in it.
This matter was tested by the Military Authorities when they adopted it for the treatment
of wounded soldiers. Any of your local members can come up to our Works and give it
a trial free of charge.
Yours faithfully,
W. L. INGLE.

PARLIAMENTARY DEBATES.
BENEFIT GAPS.
MR. STEPHEN asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of Labour what
steps he proposes to take to abolish the gap under the Unemployment Insurance Act;
and what he proposes to do in the meantime to obviate the distress among the many
thousands of people on the gap, and in consequence in absolute want.
MR. BETTERTON.-The "gap," which is of three weeks' duration is a provision laid
down by Act of Parliament, and cannot be abolished without legislation. The Gap does
not apply to covenanted benefit, and only those who have drawn uncovenanted benefit
continuously from the 18th October onwards are at present affected by it. After the gap
a further 14 weeks of uncovenanted benefit is available.-Extract from Parliamentary
Debates, Vol. 169, No. 6, Thursday, 17th January, 1924.

DAILY HERALD CIRCULATION PROGRESS.
BY GEORGE LANSBURY, M.P.
(Reprinted from the Daily Herald, 29th December, 1923).
Very often this page has been used by me to tell our readers of the difficulties connected
with the publication of this paper. To-day, at the end of 1923, it is possible to give a
more hopeful story.
Those friends who, in the autumn, were writing obituary notices or prophesying our
early decease have been gravely disappointed, and what they supposed to be a decomposing
corpse has become a very healthy young thing, destined daily to grow in wisdom and
stature. As was said of Mark Twain by Mark Twain, "The news of our death was grossly
exaggerated."
400,000 Reached.
Of course, there are dangers and pitfalls ahead. As the song says, we have still
" a long, long way to go," but with your continued help it is now certain we shall arrive.
We shall need money, all the money that unions can raise, if we are to develop as we should
is their paper, and that all who support other papers in preference to their own are, whether
do. We have still to raise millions of trade unionists to the fact that the Daily Herald
they know it or not, acting the part of blacklegs.
For all this, we are entitled to rejoice that, after years of effort, we are now steadily
and surely winning our way to success. New advertisers are coming in daily as those
whose business it is to advertise are finding the Daily Herald a first-class medium for
advertising.
Our circulation, which at the end of August was 290,000, is to-day 378,000, an
increase of 88,000. Our advertisement revenue has increased at least 75 per cent., and the
number of unsold returns has also decreased. On one or two days during and after the
election our print was over 400,000. In many districts thousands of these were bought
by election agents for sale or free distribution. This circulation was, of course, not normal,
and is mentioned to show how much was done by our friends during the electoral fight to
assist our work. Two weeks ago we were printing 373,000; to-day the figure, as stated
above, is 378,000.
500,000 Should Come Soon.
In addition to increased sales and advertisement revenue, we have ruthlessly cut
down our expenses. All our costs are down. It may be said with perfect truth we are
working at high pressure with a minimum staff in every department, consistent with
loyal observance of trade union rules and conditions.
The net result of our efforts during the past three months is that, leaving out of
account expenditure incurred in paying out notices and other charges, which would have
been payable had the paper ceased to exist, we have been able to get through this three
months without drawing on the General Council for the full amount of its guarantee.
Our actual requirements amounted to £4,380, as against £12,500 allocated to us by the
Congress. For the first time during the twelve years of its life the paper has been published
for some weeks without a subsidy from anybody.
We are all very thankful that we have arrived at this position, and, in putting these
facts before our readers, I would like to repeat again and again the thanks of all connected
with the paper to those who made this possible. Especially would we all like to thank
our ever loyal friends of the Miners' Federation for their action at Plymouth, and our
friends on the General Council and the Labour Party Executive Committee. In saying
this, I am voicing not only my own sentiments, but also those of Arthur Henderson, our
chairman, and all my colleagues on the Board of Directors.
It is certain also that the Leader of our Party, J. Ramsay MacDonald, will join the
directors and the staff in urging on all concerned the need for still greater effort. In life
account expenditure incurred in paying out notices and other charges, which would have
we cannot stand still. We must move onward and still onward.
is the figure we want to reach before the Labour Prime Minister takes his place on the
Treasury Bench. Then we must press on until we reach a million, and so onwards until
we are able to say that all his words and those of his colleagues reach the home of every
worker throughout the three kingdoms.
And Why Not 1,000,000 ?
Five thousand
How shall this be done? Only the same old way. Talk about our paper; make
people understand it is an ordinary newspaper with all the news contained in other papers,
but is also the official daily mouthpiece of our mighty Movement. Buy extra copies


---
whenever you can afford to do so. Get a friend to buy one from you every day. A thing
paid for is always more valuable than a thing received free. Help the secretary of your
Labour Party to organise a house-to-house canvass of all those who voted Labour at the
last election.
Do not leave the job to someone else. Take for your slogan, "One million readers
for the Daily Herald."
However hard and difficult a job this may appear to be, take comfort from the thought
that three months ago our obituary notices were written that today, because of the
enthusiastic, devoted work of people like you, while not yet quite out of the wood, we are
out of immediate danger and therefore the task before us is lighter, more hopeful than
ever, and, as is always the case, they succeed who believe they can succeed. Faith and
