At the County Court, Northampton, to-day, before his Honour Judge Savoley-Hill
Mr. A. M. Troup (Messrs. Phipps and Troup) applied on behalf of Arthur William
Mason, 35, Queen's Road, Northampton, for compensation (under the Workmen's Com-
pensation Act) for injury sustained while in the employment of Messrs. W. R. Davies & Co.,
railway wagon builders and repairers, 1, Tithebarn Street, Liverpool. Mr. W. W. James
(Messrs. Heygate and James, Wellingborough) appeared for respondents.
It appears that the applicant was a wagon repairer, and on the 20th of June last year,
whilst engaged at respondent's premises at the Castle Station, Northampton, he was
chopping a bolt to remove it from a piece of iron, and a fragment struck him in the eye.
As a result his eye had to be removed, and he was claiming compensation for permanent
partial incapacity. The average weekly earnings of the applicant were 50s. during the
months previous to the injury.
Mr. James suggested that, seeing that the standard rate of pay was now 48s. instead
of 50s. a week, compensation should be in proportion to 48s. The man was now earning
30s. a week.
Mr. Troup said that the drop in wages had already taken place at the time the man
The average for the twelve months previous to the injury was still
50s. During the last week he was earning £3 4s. 6d. on piece work.
sustained his injury.
His Honour referred to the case of Tones v. Rimley Iron Co., and said that the words
which appeared to be material were that the Arbitrator must still give compensation
estimated on the average earnings of the workman in the best manner available to him.
The best available basis upon which to come to a decision in this case was on the wages
for the year June 1922-23. There was a small matter of 2s. between the parties. It
was a matter, perhaps, of more importance to applicants than to respondents, but he was
not going to decide the case on that. Justice had to be done whether the case was between
and a pauper. Although there had been a drop in wages, the best
evidence he could act on was the average wage plus the fact of the last week's earnings.
He came to the conclusion that the proper standard rate of wages was 50s. a week. He
awarded compensation at the rate of 10s. from September 12th, this being half the difference
between 30s. and 50s.-Northampton Chronicle, 9th January, 1924.

FOOD.
During December there was a fall in the average prices of eggs and bacon, partly
counterbalanced, however, by advances in the average prices of butter, milk, fish, sugar
and potatoes. The other articles of food included in the statistics showed relatively
little movement in prices.
As a net result of all the changes recorded, the average increase over the level of
July, 1914, in the retail prices (in Great Britain and Northern Ireland) of the articles of
food included in these statistics fell to about 75 per cent. at 1st January, as compared
with about 76 per cent. at 1st December.

UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACTS.
Decision Given by the Umpire.
CASE NO. 6006, SECTION 7 (I) (iii). - SUITABLE EMPLOYMENT, NOT UNABLE TO OBTAIN-
JOB LOST BY DELAYING APPLICATION FOR IT FOR ONE DAY.
The applicant, who had last been employed in his usual occupation as joiner for two
weeks ending 11th August, 1923, was on Monday, 13th August, offered local work as joiner
with a building contractor at the standard rate of wages. The offer was made at 10 a.m.,
and the applicant was told that if he went to the job at once he would probably be able
to start work in the afternoon of the same day.
The prospective employer, who had asked the Employment Exchange to supply
engaged because it was not known that he had been sent by the Exchange. If the applicant
men, stated that the applicant applied for work on Tuesday, 14th August, but he was not
had produced his Introduction Card from the Exchange and had reported for work as
instructed, he could have started on the Monday afternoon. There was no vacancy for
him at the time of the employer's report.
but he had to see a friend about another possible job on that day. When he went for the
job on Tuesday he forgot to produce his Introduction Card and was rejected.
Recommended by the Court of Referees that the claim for benefit should be allowed
on the ground that a disallowance of the claim would impose hardship on the applicant.
The Insurance Officer declined to accept the Court's recommendation. His view
was that the applicant, who had been employed for only seven weeks since September,
1922, should have gone to the job offered at once. Through the delay of one day he
had lost his chance of obtaining work.
Decision.-" On the facts before me my decision is that the claim for benefit should
be disallowed. If the applicant had applied for the job at once, as he was instructed to
do, he would probably have secured it. He does not satisfy me that he was unable to
find suitable employment." - The Ministry of Labour Gazette, January, 1924.
MR. JOHN ROOKE, KENDAL.
Mr. John Rooke, a former member of the Kendal Town Council, died suddenly yester-
day from heart disease.
Mr. Rooke was highly esteemed in Westmorland, and by his kindly disposition and
broad-mindedness had made himself popular with all classes.
At the time of his death he was president of the local branch of the National Union of
Boot and Shoe Operatives, and was vice-chairman of the Netherfield Workers' Committee
the Westmorland County Hospital.
In early years he was a well-known Rugby football player. He was an ardent Church-
man, and a member of the Kendal Parish Church Choir. Aged 62 years, he leaves a widow,
two sons, and one daughter. - Yorkshire Post, 8th January, 1924.

INTERNATIONAL LABOUR OFFICE NEWS.

LABOUR CONDITIONS AT SEA.
International Meeting in London.
A joint international commission of shipowners, seamen, and representatives of the
International Labour Office of the League of Nations, will meet at the Ministry of Labour,
Montague House, on Monday, 17th December, to consider questions affecting the con-
ditions of life and labour of seafarers.
Mr. Arthur Fontaino (French Government), as President of the Governing Body of
the International Labour Office, will preside over the Commission, which will be composed
of the following members:---
Representing the International Labour Office: M. Lococq (employers, Belgium); and
Mr. E. L. Poulton, J.JP. (workers, England).
Shipowners' Representatives: M. Deckers (Belgium); Mr. Cuthbert Laws (Great
Britain); M. Nordborg (Sweden); Mr. Robb (Canada); and M. Hori (Japan).
Seamen's Representatives: Herr Döring (Germany); Signor Giuliotti (Italy); Mr.
Havelock Wilson (Great Britain); M. Nilsen (Norway); and M. Rivelli (France).
The Commission was created more than three years ago to assist the International
Labour Office in dealing with questions of maritime labour. Its constitution and functions
were laid down by the Governing Body of the Office in March, 1920, and those of its
members who represent shipowners and seamen were appointed by the International
Labour Conference at Genoa, in July, 1920, the nominations being made by the ship-
owners and seamen's delegates respectively. Two meetings have already been held:
at Geneva in November, 1920, and at Paris in March, 1922.
At next week's meeting the Commission will receive a report from M. Albert Thomas,
Director of the International Labour Office, on action taken as a result of decisions of the
previous sessions. This report will include a survey of the progress made in various
countries in connection with the ratification and application of Draft Conventions and
Recommendations of the International Labour Conferences of 1920 and 1921 affecting
juvenile employment in ships, unemployment indemnity for shipwrecked sailors, hours
of work in the fishing industry, &c.
Reports will also be presented on social insurance for seamen, the regulation of dock
cargoes, and the international codification of laws affecting seamen.
Discussion will be raised on the questions of the international regulation of hours of
work in the mercantile marine, the prevention and treatment of venereal disease among
seamen, and the compilation of statistics of shipwrecks and accidents at sea.
The Commission will also be asked to advise the Governing Body of the International
Labour Office on the question of placing on the agenda of a future meeting of the Inter-
national Labour Conference the subject of the inspection of labour conditions in ships.
In this connection the Commission will be invited to express its opinion on the desirability
of holding-not before 1926-another special session of the Conference, comparable with
that of 1920, to deal solely with problems of maritime labour.
It is anticipated that the session of the Commission will occupy two days.
INTERNATIONAL LABOUR ORGANISATION.
A YEAR'S PROGRESS.
Steady progress has been made in 1923 by the International Labour Organisation
of the League of Nations in its various fields of activity. The following brief summary
surveys the more important events connected with its work during the year.
Factory Inspection.
The Fifth Annual Session of the International Labour Conference was held in Geneva
in October, 122 delegates attending from 42 countries, the largest number up to the present
time. Dr. ADATCI, Japanese Ambassador at Brussels, presided, and among the distant
countries represented were South Africa, Australia, Brazil, Canada, Chili, China, Cuba,
India, Japan, Siam and Venezuela, while for the first time the Irish Free State sent dele-
gates. The Conference devoted its time to discussing "general principles for the organisa-
tion of factory inspection" and a detailed Recommendation touching every aspect of this
question was unanimously adopted.
Progress of the World Labour Law.
Ninety-two "ratifications" (formal signature as a treaty) of decisions adopted Ly
the Conference have been received up to 31st December, and sixteen have been authorised


---
65
in various countries but not yet formally communicated, as against sixty-three "ratifica-
tions" and sixteen authorised at the beginning of the year. The grand total of measures
in the various countries for ratification and application of decisions was 511 at the beginning
of the 1923 Conference as compared with 324 in 1922.
Reforms in the East.
Striking progress has been reported from the East during the year. Important
changes in Indian mining legislation were embodied in an Act passed in February which
contained sections, relating to hours of work and the employment of children, to give
effect to decisions of the first Session of the International Labour Conference as far as they
affect India, and the legal enactment of the weekly rest day, a decision thereon having
been taken at the third Session. Japan has ratified a decision of the second Session
regarding the employment of seamen and ratification of the Convention fixing the minimum
age of children employed at sea has been approved in principle by the Japanese Privy
Council. The first steps towards State regulation of labour conditions have been taken
in China. Special labour sections have been created at Peking in the Departments of
Agriculture and Commerce, Communications and the Interior, and provisional factory
regulations have been promulgated dealing with hours of work, minimum age of children
and maternity benefit for women workers.
Disabled Ex-Service Men.
Important resolutions concerning the employment of disabled ex-Service men covering
questions of wages, tenure and other conditions of work, were adopted by a committee of
experts from thirteen countries which met at the International Labour Office in Geneva
during August. This was the second meeting of such a committee, the first having been
held in the previous year, following requests from important national organisations con-
nected with the disabled, to consider questions relating to medical treatment and the
provision of artificial limbs.
Agricultural Questions.
In the same month was held the first session of the Joint Advisory Committee on
Agriculture set up by the International Labour Office and the International Institute
of Agriculture at Rome to ensure effective collaboration between the two organisations
on questions affecting the workers. Three representatives attended from each, and among
the experts also present were Mr. Rowland R. Robbins, C.B.E., Chairman of the Labour
Committee of the National Farmers' Union, and Mr. R. B. Walker, General Secretary
of the National Union of Agricultural Workers.
Industrial Health.
Experts from nine countries were present in Geneva at a sitting of the Advisory
Committee on Industrial Hygiene held in September. The question of organising research
in various countries into processes for the disinfection of hides and skins infected with
anthrax was carefully examined and the Committee also studied the work undertaken
by the Office in connection with the study of unhealthy processes.
World Labour Statistics.
Representatives of official labour statistical services in different parts of the world
met in conference at Geneva at the end of October. This meeting was prompted by the
feeling that if statistics could be drawn up in such a manner as to render them inter-
nationally comparable, the scientific study of labour questions from the world point of
view would be greatly facilitated. The conference discussed the classification of industries
and occupations for the purpose of labour statistics; statistics of wages and hours of
labour; and statistics of industrial accidents.
Conditions at Sea.
The Joint Maritime Commission, which assists the Office in dealing with questions
affecting seamen, met in London in December and discussed such questions as social
insurance for seamen, dock cargo regulations, international codification of the laws affecting
seamen, and the prevention and treatment of venereal diseases among seamen. The
Commission consists of five representatives each of shipowners and seamen and two of the
Governing Body of the International Labour Office. An unanimous tribute was paid
to the value of the scientific research work done by the Office in preparation for this meeting.
World Unemployment.
Two subjects have claimed the particular attention of the Office during the year.
Firstly, the collection and comparison of information on world unemployment has been
steadily continued, in co-operation with the Economic Section of the League of Nations.
Secondly, the question of social insurance and the present world position with regard
to it is being examined in detail preparatory to the discussion of general principles of
social insurance at a future session of the Conference.

L. AND J. WEBER AND PHILLIPS.
Lower prices are presumably the cause of the small decline of £2,804 in net profit
shown in the accounts of L. & J. Weber & Phillips, the wholesale boot and shoe manu-
facturers, for 1923. In having earned a net amount of £46,663 the company has done
quite well, and can comfortably continue to pay a dividend of 15 per cent. on its share
capital, which distribution absorbs £27,900. The directors are again putting £10,000 to
reserve and increasing the balance forward (subject to corporation profits tax) from
121,004 to £26,701. In the trade circumstances a fall of £20,961 in stocks, to £31,618,
is scarcely surprising. Creditors have come down from £35,295 to 19,479, at which
figure they are within £3,628 of the debtor total. The cash position is a strong one, the
holding being only a trifle smaller than before at £55,503, in addition to which the company
has a War Loan investment of £60,303, the latter showing an increase of over £20,000.
In comparison with other asset items, goodwill at £60,586 looks to be somewhat high.
It represents more than 21 per cent. of the total assets. Financial News, 14th January,
1924.

HE WHO SERVES.
He has not served who gathers gold.
Nor has he served, whose life is told
In selfish battles he has won,
Or deeds of skill that he has done,
But he has served who now and then
Has helped along his fellow men.
The world needs many men to-day;
Red-blooded men along life's way,
With cheerful smiles and helping hands
And with the faith that understands
The beauty of the simple deed
Which serves another's hour of need.
Strong men to stand beside the weak,
Kind men to hear what others speak,
True men to keep our country's laws,
And guard its honour and its cause;
Men who will bravely play life's game
Nor ask reward of gold or fame.
Teach me to do the best I can
To help and cheer our fellow man;
Teach me to lose my selfish need
And glory in the larger deed
Which smooths the road and lights the day
For all who chance to come my way.
--Guest.

A NOTE OF WARNING.
ALIENS SWINDLED.
New York, 8th December. - In the last few years foreigners have been swindled out
of $12,000,000 by a gang of real estate sharks who sold undeveloped marsh lands within
a 50-mile radius of this city, according to testimony before the state legislative committee
that is investigating immigrant exploitation.
The sharks would supply free tickets for a Sunday inspection trip to a tract of land.
Each guest would draw a lot, but was charged $49.50 to cover legal fees for transfer of
property. The figure of £49.50 was set to keep within the petty larceny limit of $50.
Miss Marion K. Clark, chief clerk of the alien division of the state labour department,
restified that aliens in mines and labour camps in this state are living under conditions
that amount almost to peonage. She stated that the victims are without legal protection
because the state bureau of immigration, established in 1910 by the Hughes committee,
was abolished by the legislature in 1911.
STATE PROTECTION FOR ALIENS URGED.
New York, 8th December.— "With all the education in the world you can not make
good Americans out of aliens who have been disillusioned and embittered," said State
Industrial Commissioner Shientag in suggesting the creation of an advisory council to
protect aliens.
A state legislative committee has uncovered methods by which aliens are wronged.
They are fleeced by swindlers and are robbed in labour camps, employment agencies and
by steamship agents.
"The problem of how to deal with our immigrants, of how to protect them against
fraud and exploitation, is as difficult as it is important," said the commissioner. "Our
own citizens, many of them highly educated, lose millions of dollars every year as the
result of stock and land swindlers alone. It is apparent therefore, that the immigrant,
helpless and ignorant of our ways and language, is subject to even greater exploitation."--
American Federation of Labour Weekly News Letier, 8th December, 1923.
FOOT IN THE COGS.
Accident at Kingswood Factory. Foreman Fined.
A serious accident which occurred at the premises of Messrs. Edwards & Co., boot
manufacturers' of Wood Lane, Kingswood, on 16th October, 1923, led to the appearance
of the foreman, Albert Victor Stone, aged 35, at Lawford's Gate Petty Session, yesterday,
charged with an infringement of the Factory Act. Mr. W. J. Robinson pleaded guilty on
behalf of the defendant.
Mr. J. Owner (Factory Inspector) said it was incumbent on the occupier of every
factory clearly to fence in dangerous parts of machinery. In the factory was a guillotine
ranging machine, and Messrs. Edwards & Co. had complied with their statutory obligations
by providing fencing round the machine. The defendant engaged a boy Box, and had
occasion to use the ranging machine. The boy stood with his body closely adjacent to
the running shafts of the cogwheels, and his right foot became involved in the cogwheels.
The act was committed without the knowledge of the employers. Defendant was a man
who bore a good character, and except for this error of judgment he had not given his
employers the slightest trouble, and was told that he would not lose his employment.
The defendant was exceedingly sorry for what had occurred. He had been accustomed
to that kind of machinery for the past 12 years.
Machine Fenced.
The Chairman, Mr. Kossuth Robinson, said he had received testimony from the other
magistrates as to the good character of the defendant and taking the facts into considera-
tion they would only fine him £5 and costs. The Chairman went on to suggest that possibly
some change might be made in connection with the machinery. One of the Bench (pre-
sumably Mr. A. G. Randall) was an expert in leather machinery and he would like to have
a conversation with Mr. Owner when an opportunity presented.
Mr. Owner stated that immediately after the accident the firm had the whole of the
back of the machinery in question fenced and it was now possible for a workman to stand
at the back in perfect safety. - Western Daily Press, 18th January, 1924.

MONTHLY REPORT.
25TH FEBRUARY, 1924.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
STATE OF TRADE
has slightly improved during the month, the figures given in the Gazette issued
by the Ministry of Labour being as follow:-
BOOT AND SHOE INDUSTRY.
Employment during January was again only moderate on the whole, but the improve-
ment which was noticeable during the larger part of the previous month was fairly well
maintained. In many districts a considerable amount of short time was still worked ;
but conditions were generally better than in January of last year.
The percentage of workpeople unemployed, as indicated by the unemployment books
lodged at Employment Exchanges, was 9.5 on 28th January, 1924, as compared with
9.8 on 21st December, 1923.
In London employment was still bad, though slightly better than in the previous
month. A further improvement occurred at Leicester, and employment was fair; there
was less short time working than in the previous month, and overtime was reported in a
few cases. At Northampton, however, a considerable amount of short time was still
worked, and employment remained only moderate. At Kettering there was no marked
change as compared with December, and employment remained generally moderate,
but at Desborough less time was lost and employment improved. In the Wellingborough,
Higham and Rushden districts employment remained fair on the whole. Although short
time was worked in a number of factories a few workpeople were on overtime during the
month. At Hinckley a slight decline in employment was reported. There was practically
no change at Leeds, but at Stafford employment again showed a slight upward movement.

PARLIAMENTARY AFFAIRS.
In last month's Report we stated, amongst other matters, that within a
few hours from the time of going to press we felt certain a new Government,
and that a Labour Government, would be called into being. Such declaration
has fully materialised, and we now have as the head of the Government the
Rt. Hon. J. Ramsav MacDonald, P.C., M.P., whom we heartily and sincerely
congratulate. Mr. MacDonald has taken upon himself the arduous and difficult
task, not only of Prime Minister, but also that of Minister for Foreign Affairs.
It is quite evident that Mr. MacDonald has endeavoured-in forming his Govern-
ment-to give consideration to all sections of thought in the Party, and the
ministerial appointments show-especially those appointed who were not
members of the Labour Party-not only tolerance, but a sincere desire to
make the Cabinet a national body.
It is indeed matter for congratulation
that we have at last a Labour Government in office. Whilst we know the
Labour Party does not command a majority of the votes in the House of
Commons, nevertheless we feel confident their tenure of office will be distinctly
advantageous not only to Great Britain but also to the workers on the
Continent. Already one sees the evident determination of Mr. MacDonald to-
if possible-bring about a settlement of European Affairs, and thus accelerate
the pace by which nations will be able to devote themselves to those internal
matters which so loudly call for attention. In connection with the appoint-
ments in the Ministry, we rejoice exceedingly that one of our colleagues-
Mr. W. R. Smith, M.P., J.P.-has been appointed Parliamentary Secretary to
the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries. Mr. Smith's knowledge of agricul-
ture is extensive, and his ability has been shown upon more than one occasion
by the way with which he has handled agricultural problems, especially those
relating to the National Union of Agricultural Workers. We heartily and
sincerely congratulate our colleague, and hope he will have good health, and
thus be enabled to successfully cope with the strenuous work in front of him.
At the same time we look upon the honour thus conferred as an honour partly
belonging to the Union, in that one of its members has been appointed to
a high position in the State.
We beg to repeat part of what we said last month :-" It is incumbent
upon all members of the Labour Party to do their part in defending those of
our colleagues in the House of Commons, especially at the present time, resting
assured that if support is forthcoming, the present is only a beginning to a
fruitful and beneficial period, not only for the people of this land, but for those

QUARTERLY BALANCE SHEETS.

In spite of repeated applications certain Branches have failed to forward
to the Central Office, the Quarterly Balance Sheet. It is clearly laid down
in Rule 127 that the Branch Secretaries shall ". . . prepare a Balance
Sheet once a quarter, or more often if required, such quarter to end
on the last Saturday in February, May, August, and November, and
under the heading of Offences and Penalties, Branch Secretaries, says :-
"Failing to send a Quarterly Balance Sheet to the General Secretary
to be fined 2s. 6d." If, in future, the Rule 127 is not strictly adhered to,
we shall have no alternative but to enforce Rule 302.

BANKING.
Quite recently cases have come to our knowledge where Branch Secretaries to save trouble, loaned monies to the Branch for Union Benefits, and then paid all the Branch Contributions to their own personal Banking Account.
This-with the change of Branch Secretary brought about complications, and we wish to make it IMPERATIVE that ALL Union monies MUST be banked in the name of the Union. Branch, and thus obviate any unnecessary trouble.
We are sure, upon reflection, it will be seen that this is not only the better way, but also the proper way of dealing with Branch Funds.

REMEMBER THE FIFTEENTH!
Once again we feel bound to call the serious attention of Branch Secretaries to the fact that the FIFTEENTH day of each month is the latest day for returns reaching the General Secretary. If Branches fail to send off their returns to reach the Central Office before the 15th of the month it tends to upset the organisation of the work in the General Secretary's Office. We beg to intimate that unless returns are in before the 15th of the month, the Secretary has been instructed to put into force the Rules governing the same. Returns Sheets MUST also bear the signature of both the Branch President and Branch Secretary, or they will reluctantly have to be returned for completion.

TRADE UNION STAMP.
This is a matter which we have stated before rests with the members to make a success. It is in the interests of members themselves that "Stamped Footwear " should be increasingly purchased; therefore, push the Trade Union Stamp. Members and their families should wear only "Union Stamped Footwear."

TRADE UNION BUTTONS AND BROOCHES.
A fresh supply of buttons and brooches has recently been secured and can be had upon application, price 6d. each, cash with order. Secretaries please note, when ordering buttons or brooches, cash should ALWAYS be sent with order.

STREET. - The girls at Messrs. C. & J. Clarke's Ltd. struck work because they were
informed that all girls who failed to earn their wages at the employer's price would be
discharged, and as they had left the factory, and we were informed that the men had been
warned that they would be stopped, unless the girls returned, this caused me to immedi-
ately depart for Street on Saturday morning, the 16th inst., reaching there at 4 o'clock
in the afternoon. We held a meeting lasting three hours, when the girls unanimously
decided to take the advice given them and return to work on Monday morning, the 18th
inst., at 8 o'clock, and we would see the firm and place before them the whole of the com-
plaints, and to this end the two local officials with the three representatives from the
Closing Room, on the Menday morning sojourned to the factory and met four members
of the firm, to whom we conveyed the minds of the operatives, and as they claimed they
had discharged no one for several years, they felt that the present girl, only sixteen years
of age, who had been complained of on several occasions, was not fitted for the
industry, and therefore they must part. We are sorry for this, but cannot do other
than accept the inevitable, I have made two visits to this place in Somersetshire, the
two visits having occupied seven days, the distance and railway facilities making the
journey a long one.

NORTHAMPTON ADVISORY COMMITTEE met at Rushden on the 19th ult. and received
a very good report, which I hope will be included in our Report. With deep regret the
Resignation of the Secretary, Mr. S. J. B. Barnes, J.P., Desborough, who has been a very
good officer, was received. Mr. G. Chester was pressed to assume the position, and can
only do so, he says, if he can get relief from other work.

FINEDON. - The Highfield Works has again received a further visit from us, and
many advances obtained with a very definite promise to try and end matters at the end
of the next few weeks.

EARL SHILTON has again been visited owing to the competition of some firms in that
district being charged with unfair advantages on Labour costs. We again interviewed
the men and the firm, and set up prices that gives an adequate return to the men at a cost
to the firm at not less than Leicester prices; this should at least save Leicester firms.

BURTON-ON-TRENT was then visited and a factory found some hundred and fifty
yards long, with approxmately 180 girls and men employed on White Canvas Louis Heel
work beautifully made and finished for such a class of shoe. Such work is a credit to the
firm. Some of the operatives belong to us, and the others we hope to influence later,
but all depends whether they are members of the Rossendale Slipper Union or not. If so,
then we may find it not to our wishes that we should tamper with them.

EARL SHILTON was again visited, and the ro per cent. deducted from the operatives'
wages was, at our request, removed, and the other matters referred to the head of the firm,
who is away in South Africa.

THE TRADES UNION SPECIAL COMMITTEE, set up by the General Council for the settle-
ment of disputes between Co-operative Societies and the Operatives Union, met at the
Eccleston Square Offices with representatives of the Co-operative Union, and we have
endeavoured to find a way out of the difficulties, and after several hours we have not yet
found agreement, We are likely to meet again to further consider the troubles on these
matters. This cost us two days' serious work, and I am afraid will cost many more until
unity is found.

"DAILY HERALD." - May we again beg of all our members, male and female, old and
young, weak and strong, to read the Daily Herald, the best newspaper in the country
for Workers, and may all those workers wear only Trade Union made Boots.

THIRTY-SIXTH CONFERENCE
(1924).
JUBILEE YEAR.
Agenda.
1. COUNCIL'S ADDRESS.
2. KETTERING NO. 1 BRANCH. "This Conference, believing that Education
is essential to the full development of the Trade Union movement,
recommends this Conference to discuss the problem in its widest
aspect, and to determine that, as soon as the Educational Policy of
the Trade Union Congress is issued, this Union will do everything
possible to develop such policy amongst its members."
3. LEICESTER NO. 1 BRANCH. "To ask the Council to meet the Manufacturers' Federation with the view of altering the age when members
become entitled to the full Minimum Wage from 23 years of age to
21 years of age; also the Graduated Scale to be altered accordingly."
4. LEICESTER NO. 1 BRANCH. "That owing to the increase in the amount
of work involved in the administration of the State Unemployment,
Branches shall receive not less than 6d. in the pound."
5. LEICESTER NO. 1 BRANCH. " That the Executive of the Union press the
employers to consider the wisdom of curtailing the Juvenile Labour
in our trade to one male person under 19 years to every five persons
over 19 years, as we are convinced that on the basis of 1 to 3, the
industry has been incapable of absorbing the Juveniles when they
have passed into the Adult stage."
6. LEICESTER NO. 1 BRANCH. "This Conference asks the Council to press
for the abolition of Overtime, or claim double time for same."
7. LEICESTER NO. 1 BRANCH. "This Conference asks the Council to strongly
press for a reduction in the hours of labour from 48 per week to 44
per week."
8. NORWICH NO. 1 BRANCH. "That the Executive Council do approach the
Home Secretary with a view to securing legislation demanding a
reasonable standard of light, air, and general cleanliness in all workshops and factories used for the manufacture of boots and shoes."
9. STAFFORD BRANCH. "That this Conference instructs the Executive
Council to arrange an Educational Scheme with the National Council
of Labour Colleges under which free classes and Correspondence
Courses would be available for our members, such scheme to be paid
for by an allocation of 3d. per member per annum from the funds of
the Union."

FELLOW MEMBERS, 25TH FEBRUARY, 1924.
ORGANISER'S REPORT.
was with me some days and we made things so lively at two factories that the police came
to see what was the matter. We had a peculiar experience, from a trade union point of
view, at a meeting of clickers from a shop in Bethnal Green on 23rd January. The Council
were prepared to support the clickers in demanding the London Statement prices. Mr.
Mason and Mr. Woodward, of the London Metro., and Mr. Bleakley and I appealed to the
men for over two hours to pluck up courage and give us permission, by their vote, to see
their employers and make a demand for the Statement. Our logic and eloquence only got
us one out of twenty-five in favour of the resolution I moved. None voted against and Mr.
Mason declared the resolution carried. The proprietors were written to and asked to give
us an interview. This was granted. On 4th February Mr. Mason and I visited the firm
and had a long meeting with the directors, the outcome of which was an advance of 6d.
a dozen on several lines on outsides, and 1d. a dozen on fittings. They further agreed
to meet us again in May with the view of considering the Statement. I can imagine
what these clickers would say if they asked their local or national officers for advice and
help if they got as cold a response to their appeal as they gave us. We got increases for
them against their will. Their only excuse was that there were other shops as bad as
I thought
the trade, and not to use some employers arguments who aim at the standard of the poorest
paid shops. We held many meetings of other shops where the position of the clickers
was nearly similar to the one mentioned, but I am pleased to say we had the unanimous
support of the men in these shops. On five lines we got advances of 6d. a dozen and 3d.
on six others at a shop in Hackney. This firm is to be seen in May on the full acceptance
of the Statement. In 1920, when the Clickers' Statement was first applied, the majority
of the clickers were getting good weekly wages and they did not trouble about protecting
themselves by seeking to get this excellent Statement applied to all the factories in London,
hence the present trouble.
The bosses' Statements are meant to be good dividend-making instruments, and the
trade union ones are intended to make happy and healthy homes.
In a recent report I pointed out that while we had a voice with the manufacturers in
fixing conditions of labour, we had no understanding with the big factors and multiple
shop-keepers. There are certain factories in London where the conditions are very low,
and the operatives of any calling where wages are low and the workshops ugly and mean,
they gradually become in outlook and character something like their conditions. They
are scarcely able to respond to appeals for a higher manhood. I noticed from time to time
that the motor lorries of some noted multiple shop-keepers called at a few of these poor
factories and took cases of boots with them. Unbridled competition is a scourge and those
who talk loosely of trade unionism being played out do not realise the mischief they are
doing. Trade unionism has never been applied to the full extent in any industry yet.
I paid a visit to Manchester over a firm's prices for Closing not giving the machinists
the agreed wages, and also to claim some back money for irregular deductions made last
year. This business is not yet settled.
D. MCCARTHY.
"THE LABOUR WOMAN."
The Labour Woman for February contains a very striking article on the life of women
tramps. This is one of a series of three dealing with Casual Wards and based upon informa-
tion from a woman who has been on the road for some time. It is to be hoped that this
very startling description based on first-hand experience will have some result in drawing
the attention of the Ministry of Health and the Poor Law Authorities.
The picture of Labour's three women M.P.'s taken on the Terrace of the House of
Commons is the special illustration for this month, and Miss Susan Lawrence's maiden
speech on the Feeding of School Children has been included because, as the Editor points
out, it marks the historical occasion on which the House of Commons was first addressed
by a Labour Woman M.P.
This monthly journal is increasing its circulation very rapidly, and during the first
two months of 1924 has put on four thousand copies. Price 2d.

BRANCH REPORTS.
ARBROATH. The members here are still on short time, many not even
averaging half time. Rumour has it that the factory in Arbroath which closed
this time she so often is, because there are members who may find it extremely
difficult to get employment at the trade again unless we have this place started
once more. The one-factory town is a menace in other ways, and all members
are interested for their own sake. While the dearth of business reflects itself
in an excusable apathy regarding industrial matters - we suppose members
over the country feel the uselessness of striving for an extension of trade union
desires when work is scarce - yet we find an atmosphere of enthusiasm regarding
things political since the election kindled the fire of hope. It is not too much to
revival. If the Labour Government can vitalise the League of Nations struc-
hope that through political influences may come the long awaited industrial
ture, open up the markets of Europe by means of a sensible and virile foreign
policy, there can be little doubt but trade will show a remarkable improvement.
We are on the threshold of stirring times, and history will awaken envy in future
generations when they read of the happenings of our day. And yet we treat
it in prosaic fashion. Apart from the newspaper headlines - and these are
that has occurred in our political institutions during those recent months.
wonderfully quiet - a stranger would little understand the momentous evolution
Where are the terrors and exaggerated anxieties which the opponents of Labour
helpful schemes from the new Government to meet the clamant evils of to-day.
pretence it was. Already everybody seems to have settled down to await
the Banbury crowd may yet be placing carpets for them to enter on. We are
apply, and so instead of Coldstream Guards to clear them out of Parliament,
of those who wish immediate attention to anomalies in Unemployment Insur-
ance benefits. Every friend of the idle worker should demand abolition of
gaps, and further, it should be still regarded as an emergency payment and not
tested on the rights of claimants measured by contributions, past or pro-
spective. The volume of idleness is far too great to deal with as they have been
dealing with it since the new benefit year began. Our members have had so
much to do with Labour Exchange benefit that it is natural we should wish
helpful alterations introduced into its administration. After a considerable
amount of trouble we have at last secured a representative of the Court of
Referees for our area, and along with this has come a widening of panels which
has permitted four workers' representatives being appointed. In view of former
neglect it is a big step forward, especially if the old regulations continue,
whereby so many are disallowed benefit in order to let the Court test the validity
of claims. Our experience was that our Court failed utterly to bring out
important and essential information in many cases, just because the panels
were obsolete, and too much was left to the discretion of the neutral chairman.
We also know of a great deal of injustice arising unnecessarily in connection
with claims, simply because so many claimants are ignorant of what to do.
Our own official is constantly approached by textile, iron, and casual workers
for help on this or that question, and when suspensions or disallowances are
not seen to, equity is a bad second. May the Labour Government continue
till wrong is made right.
BARNSLEY. - Trade has fallen off here very much lately. The reason
is that many of the country people are doing their own straight jobs and
repairing, and working at their own work, and bringing the rougher repairing
to the Co-operative to do, thus robbing the workmen at the Co-operative

BELFAST. - We are unable to report any improvement in trade.
BURNLEY. - We are sorry to report the death of Mr. Daniel David

CHESHAM. We regret to report trade very quiet, a number of members
signing the out-of-work book, and the future not at all hopeful.
CHESTERFIELD.-Trade is bad, most of our members are working
9 till 4. This is about the run in Chesterfield, about four months full time
and then the other eight months short time and out of work, which is, for most
of our members, a bare existence from year end to year end. Some of our
members have not got a start at all since the firm closed down last Easter.
There is no prospect for these members at all.
EDINBURGH.-Trade still very quiet. One of our shops has been given
an ultimatum re our accepting what is termed the Birmingham prices for
working in conjunction with benching in repairing, or else time rates. The
members concerned, also the Branch, have decided to accept nothing less than
we have been able to obtain from St. Cuthbert's Co-operative Society, which
is the largest repairing shop in the district. Owing to negotiations still being
held we think it advisable meantime to say nothing further, but trust our
representatives on Administrative Committee of Wages Trade Board will
uphold the position which Edinburgh has secured. Edinburgh and District
are trying to have a Labour weekly newspaper started. Well, according to
the members which claim to represent Labour interest on public bodies, this
adventure has certainly some field for propaganda. Let us hope it will succeed.
We offer our congratulations to Mr. W. R. Smith on the position he has attained
in the first Labour Government.
HIGHAM & RUSHDEN.-Trade remains fairly good. One small firm
at Finedon has ceased work, but generally trade is fair. The trouble at the
Highfield Shoe Company, Finedon, is nearer settlement. This we expect to be
finally cleared up by the next visit of the General President. Show Card days
have been held at several factories, the Branch Officials acting as scrutineers.
This method has resulted in bringing into line a few non-unionists at the
factories dealt with. We heartily congratulate our friend, W. R. Smith,
upon his promotion.
KINGSWOOD & DISTRICT. - We regret to report trade very quiet, and
no immediate prospects of improvement. Our sick list is also very heavy,
due largely to a mild form of influenza. We are continually on the move,
as attempts are made to encroach on the wage conditions of the operatives.
We propose to make application for an organiser when a suitable oppor-
tunity presents itself. At present a number of factories are almost closed for
lack or orders.
LEICESTER No. 1.- We are pleased to report a slight improvement in
trade.

LIVERPOOL. We are having a quiet time lately in so far as the repairing

LONDON METRO. Pleased to report there is an improvement in trade,
but principally in the machine shops. Our hand workers have had a very
trying time for the last twelve months, and the outlook is a very poor one for
them. London could do with the spirit that used to be shown in defence of
Statements, for where there is a charter of wages and conditions, it is up to the
men to observe them, and not, as in several shops in the East End, refuse to
work to Statement, because their poor employer, if he had to pay would not
be able to undersell fair-paying houses and they, perhaps, would experience a
slackness between the seasons instead of working seven days a week with a bit
of overtime thrown in. We had Mr. Bleakley and Mr. McCarthy with us for
a few days, and think that our Scotch friend was rather surprised at what he
saw and heard. It is with regret that we have to report that one of our oldest
members, Mr. J. Gibson, has passed away. He was for many years a trustee
of the branch, and one of the fighters of days gone by. The branch is the
poorer for his passing.
LONDON SOUTH. At the Monthly Meeting held on 6th February, 1924,
there was a large attendance, the best for some time. A vote of condolence
was taken for the late Secretary, Mr. G. Standeven, who has served the Branch
faithfully for many years, and has worked hard for its members and kept
them together. We, the members of the South London Branch, know that
in the loss of Mr. G. Standeven a valuable asset of the Branch has gone. The
new Secretary elected is Mr. J. Rawlings, 111, Gloucester Road, Peckham,
London, S.E. 15, who will be only too pleased to hear from old and new members,
and at the same time trusts that all members will rally round and attend the
meetings and take part in the business of the Branch, and not be members in
name only, but become active members, and thereby let others know that there
is a branch in South London.
MAYBOLE. We are sorry to have to report trade very bad, most of our
members working short time. We are pleased that the firm of J. Lees & Co.
have arranged to work three days each week, and so allow the members to
sign three days at the Labour Exchange. The Secretary attended the Scottish
Advisory Committee meeting at Glasgow, on Saturday, when the business was
relating to introduction of machinery into repairing shops and fixing of prices
for operations. We feel that much good will be done with this Committee.

most firms losing time. Some departments more than others. Let us hope
260 people out of work. There can be no doubt that society has got to be
that the Spring trade will give us a lift up. One firm ceased business throwing
before poverty caused by unemployment can be eliminated. Sickness is heavy
reorganised on the basis of communal ownership of the material means of life.
just now, but not so bad as about two years ago.

NORWICH. - Trade in Norwich has shown considerable improvement
during the month, especially in the machine-sewn section. Claims on un-
employed fund have diminished accordingly, and we hope, judging by the present
improved position, to show a much reduced claim for February. Taking advan-
tage of the trade spurt the officials have tightened up organisation in one or
two weak spots, and have secured one hundred and thirty new members in
the month of January (mainly females), as a result of organising meetings.
While trade holds good - we intend to continue this work and so make Norwich
completely solid (100 per cent. membership we are aiming at), enabling us to
withstand the encroachments employers make when the cycle of bad trade
comes once more. Norwich feels mightily pleased with MacDonald's first
efforts at Labour Government, and we hope the Union may share the additional
pleasure at knowing of Walter Smith's recognition in the first Labour Adminis-
tration. Throughout the country shoe operatives recognise his sterling worth,
and we earnestly wish the same degree of success in his new sphere as has
characterised his official association with our Union.

NOTTINGHAM. - Trade has slightly improved. Members on new work
are now employed about three-quarter time, while in the repairs there is little
change to report.

PLYMOUTH.- Trade is still on the quiet side here, but with the accession
of Labour to the Seat of Government a change is manifest. The spirit of gloom
no longer broods o'er the murky waters, but a ray of sunlight flits around.
There is a bright hope of things to be, and a keen expectancy of springtime
and fragrant flowers. The reins of Government, held strong in the hands of
Labour for the first time in the history of our nation, with its Ministers hailing
from the pit, the factory and the ploughtail, has captured the popular imagina-
tion. The spirit of faith and hope once more beckons us onward and upward
to freedom and peace. True, the Slough of Despond has left its mark, the
burden is heavy and the hill called Difficult, but from the Delectable Mountains
we have already caught a glimpse of the Celestial City, and by the help and
co-operation of all who believe in building the New Jerusalem in England's
fair and happy land, the foundation stone may be true and firmly laid. If
fate is kind to the new Government and Mr. Asquith continues to guide his
Liberal team with that spirit of true magnanimity which characterised his
attitude to Labour taking office, then we believe the hand of fate holds peace
and prosperity for the humblest as well as the highest members of the com-
munity. Success to the new Government.

SOUTHAMPTON. - Trade still slack.

STREET. - Trade here is not what we would like it to be, although the
large factory is working three-quarter time generally, but we are looking for
improvements which seem long in coming. We are glad to report that we have
had a visit from Mrs. M. J. Bell-Richards during the month to investigate
conditions of employment and rates paid in our Closing Department at the
large factory of Messrs. C. & J. Clark Ltd., as we could not get the firm to
recognise certain things that are contained in the National Agreement. We
are certain that with her help we shall be able to bring our Closing Department
up to a standard of comfortable working and a decent wage at the end of the
week, which is more than they have received for some little time. Our best

ANNUAL REPORT
Of the Northamptonshire Joint District Council of the Boot and Shoe
Trade, as presented to the Annual Meeting, held at Rushden,
18th January, 1924.
In compiling a record of the history of the growth of movements or organisations,
the feelings of the historian are affected somewhat by the perusal of the records he is
examining. At times he is thrilled with pleasure, anon moods of depression are his.
Actually his thoughts, as he sifts the records of the past, are touched and tinctured with
a mingling of both experiences. Pleasure is his, as the records reveal performances, that
give him an indication that hopes are being realised, that the organisation is doing the
things for which it was brought into being. On the other hand there are moments when
depression overtakes him, as he discovers, that in some directions progress is not being
achieved. When this is the case, he must search for causes that indicate where progress
has been hindered, and where the work of the organisation has been retarded.
So much by way of preface to my third Annual Report. I will now endeavour to tell
you the story of the past year.
Statistics.
I will deal in the first place with the statistics of the organisation, things dry in them-
selves, but when clothed with their implications, either give us thoughts for encouragement,
or cause feelings of depression. Let me say at once, that my reading of our figures is an
encouraging one, because they indicate growth.
In the eight branches that form the four districts that together make up the Joint
District Council, we have 29,900 members, more than one-third of the membership of the
Union. These figures show an increase of 272, not very large, but when compared with
the 1,842 reduction of last year, they show that the tide has turned and is with us. Daventry
Higham and Rushden, Kettering No. 1, and Kettering No. 2 branches all show a slight
increase. Kettering No. 2 having the best record with an increase of 261. On the other
hand the Desborough, Northampton No. 1, and Northampton No. 2 branches show a
small decrease, while strange enough, the figures for the Wellingborough branch are exactly
the same as last year.
Let us hope that when the report is given next year, that all branches will show an
increase.
Perhaps the most noticeable feature which gives greatest cause for encouragement
is to be found in the fact that we have 388 more probationers than last year.
The actual figures of the district are as follow :-
Males. Females. Probationers. Totals.
September 30th, 1922 ... 18,867 9,470 1,291 29,628
November 24th, 1923 ... 18,896 9,325 1,679 29,900
These figures show an increase of 29 males, a decrease of 145 females, while probationers
show an increase of 388. The net increase being 272, as compared with a decrease of
1,842 last year. Certainly it gives more pleasure to record the increase than it did to
chronicle the reduction.
Formation of Another District Council.
Another pleasurable incident I have to record this year is that another District Council
has been formed. Scotland has now followed in the wake of Northamptonshire, largely,
I believe, through the persistence of our friend Reid, of Arbroath, coupled with the fact
that the Union in Conference last Whitsuntide decided to pay the expenses of District
Councils. We congratulate our Scottish friends on their wisdom in following us in the
formation of a District Council, and can only hope that similar good results will follow
their decision.
Further, may we express the hope that other districts will forget something of the
bias of local feeling, give the question the earnest consideration it deserves, judge of the
work and possibilities of the usefulness of District Councils as shown in our Annual Reports,
then decide to do likewise. Because, whatever our United Council may not have done,
it has splendidly vindicated itself in this connection, that it has given us in the Northamp-
tonshire branches a better understanding of one another's local circumstances, and a keener
appreciation of each others difficulties.
I well remember that when we first met together, the chief occupation seemed to be
to try who could best score off another district, until some began to get heartily sick of
the whole business. At this time we were in danger of shipwreck.
To-day, however, with the growing influence and wisdom of tolerant minds, together
with the gathering experiences of the results of our mutual help, we have emerged almost

During the year under review, the operations of the National Agreement have resulted

ordinary Trade Agreements I do not know.
I will now deal with the attempts we have made as a Council to try and carry out the
objects for which we were formed, viz., to establish and develop Educational, Political.
and Industrial policies throughout the Union.

I will deal in the first place with the Industrial side of our work. Two of our mectings
At Wellingborough, Mr. W. Townley, of Northampton, opened a discussion on "Day-

result wages were much higher, the consequence being that manufacturers began to agitate


---
119
In the first place they asked for a reduction of 30 per cent., this was reduced in steady
stages down to 20 per cent., 15 per cent., and finally 5 per cent., while now even this has
partly disappeared in some directions, while it has considerably increased in others.
The contention of the manufacturers to impose a flat rate reduction has been contested
all along in accordance with Paragraph C, Clause 10 of the National Agreement, where it
speaks about revisions in the following language: " Local Boards of Arbitration are
recommended to exercise their powers of reviewing, on the request of either side, existing
piecework or quantity statements, for the purpose of adjusting any specific anomalous
item or items, whether favourable to employers or employed."
Many meetings have been held, but upon this position we are determined to stand,
with no thought of yielding in the slightest degree, for as an historic person said upon a
celebrated occasion, "We can do no other." Somebody will ultimately have to give a
ruling as to what this Clause really means, but we shall never agree that anomalies exist
only on one side.
Educationally.
I am afraid that in this direction we have hardly done as well as in previous years.
and the present indications are such, that from the point of view of Educational Classes
we shall do worse this season. In other directions, particularly in the form of Educational
Conferences, we hope to do much better.
Three educational classes have been held during the year, one at Kettering, where
Mr. George Chester conducted a class of 23 on "The Law relating to Trade Unions."
At Rushden, Mr. Arthur Allen dealt with the subject of " Political Theory " to a class of 14,
while at Northampton a class was held at which the subject of "Economic Science"
engaged the attention of 26 students, the tutor being Mr. P. Cowen, M.A.
In regard to the present season, classes are being held at Rushden and Northampton
with an approximate attendance of 42.
It is just one of those strange things in life that we cannot understand, why so few
people are personally interested in the question of educational achievement. If men
and women would but realise the incalculable difference that an educated and cultured
mind adds to the fulness of life, then many more would avail themselves of the oppor-
tunities that come to them. Be that as it may, and deeply though we may deplore the
lack of real interest in education, we are very glad that even the small number attended
the classes arranged by our branches. To these, at any rate, we trust has come something
of the joy of acquisitive knowledge, which in the days that are coming will reveal itself
in well-ordered minds, that will be able to grapple and deal with the great problems that
await us. Labour is slowly but surely coming into power, and we shall want all the applica-
tion of intelligent minds to the difficult problems around us, if we are going to live up to
even the suggestion of our reiterated ideals.
In furtherance of our educational efforts, an educational conference was held at
Kettering in February, when our General President, Mr. T. F. Richards, introduced to
a very good attendance of delegates, Mr. J. M. Mactavish, General Secretary of the W.E.A.,
who gave a lecture on " Education and the Working-class Movement." The lecture was
thoroughly appreciated, and we were well rewarded for our efforts to arrange it.
The idea behind these lectures is to stimulate Adult Education in the Trade Union
and Working-class Movements. Possibly several will be arranged in the coming year.
Already we have arranged for Mr. W. G. Cove, M.P. for the Wellingborough Division, to
give a lecture on 9th February.
In educational matters, as in many other things, we have to keep pressing on in the
work, regardless of setbacks or indifference, realising that it is only in persistent endeavour
that we shall be able to realise our ideal of securing an educated democracy and an intelligent
people.
Political Work.
At our previous meeting held at Desborough, we agreed to hold the Annual Meeting
on the first Saturday in December. Had nothing intervened, I am afraid that my remarks
on this head would have been very brief indeed. Instead, however, of meeting together
at our Annual Meeting, we were in the throes of a General Election.
Mr. Baldwin, the Conservative Prime Minister, had seen some of the actual effects
of unemployment in the country. Then, presumably, he had had a vision of the world
put right by the magic influence of Protective Tariffs, and like the honest man he says
he is, thought the country should have an opportunity of saying whether they could see
the vision in exactly the same way. He therefore dissolved Parliament, and, like a knight
errant of old, went forth to slay the giant of unemployment, armed with a Tariff in one
hand by means of which he was going to keep manufactured goods out of the country,
while in the other hand he held an enormous money bag, that was going to hold the monies
that would considerably increase the revenue of the country as a result of the imposition

Politically we must go on with our educational work, steadily building such a demo-
cracy, that the time will come when the causes that result in want will never be tolerated,
that hungry children and homeless men and women will never be allowed, and when
idleness shall be exorcised from the earth.
Let me now conclude my report with just a personal note, which to me is the most
difficult to express. For twelve years I have been Secretary of the branch at Desborough,
nearly nine of which I have been a full-time official. Seven of those years I have filled
the post of Secretary of the old Northants Advisory Committee, and the Joint District
Council, and to-day is the last of my official connection with you. I have certainly tried
to take my part in the stirring times of the last few years, and although I may not have
been as brilliant as I would have liked, at the same time I have done my best. For twelve
years I have breathed the very spirit of Trades Unionism, and I believe that in the Industrial
and Political development of the future it will fill a great and important part. To all of
my friends I have an affectionate regard that has grown with the passing years, and all
that I can quite feebly say to express my thoughts, is, that I have been privileged to
associate with you. Many of you I am deeply indebted to, you have helped me much.
I want to thank you, and to express the fervent hope that the sun will shine upon your
work, and that under its beneficent and warming influence you may see the harvest of a
glorious fruition.
STEPHEN J. B. BARNES,
Secretary.

INTERNATIONAL LABOUR OFFICE NEWS.
HOURS OF WORK AND REPARATIONS.

Miss Bondfield at Geneva.
The Governing Body of the International Labour Office, whose meeting Miss Bondfield
is attending as representative of Great Britain, discussed on the 30th January the problem
of promoting a more general ratification of the Washington Convention on Hours of Work.
in order thereby to arrest the tendency in various countries to prolong the working day.
The question was examined thoroughly and dispassionately in all its aspects, including
the relation of the recent extension of the hours of work in Germany to the Reparations
Problem

During the discussion Miss Bondfield referred to the fact that the present Minister
of Labour was Chairman of the Committee on Hours of Work at the Washington Con-
ference, and said:

"That in itself may I think be taken as a guarantee that the British Government
will leave no effort untried to secure further consideration of this question and the
ratification of the Eight-Hour Day Convention. The British Government recognises
that this is not merely a national but an international question, and that it is of vital
importance to get stabilisation for the life of Europe. The British Government
will endeavour to remove the reproach under which some of us feel we have lain in
this matter of what we regard as our duty in view of statements made at the Washing-
ton Conference on behalf of the British Government."
Miss Bondfield added that the Government would endeavour to promote practical
means to secure simultaneous ratification of the Eight Hours Convention by various
countries.

"SAFETY FIRST."

Another paper by Lt.-Col. J. A. A. Pickard, D.S.O., General Secretary of the British
Industrial Safety First Association, discusses "Safety and Protection in Industry," and
reaches the conclusion that the value of the "Safety First" movement has not yet been
fully realised in this country. By some it is thought to be a campaign of cranks, but the
roll of its followers quickly disproves this fallacy. It numbers among its members most
of the leading and progressive undertakings, and it should not be impossible that, in a
not too distant future, every industrial undertaking worthy of its name should follow in
their footsteps. As a national humanitarian movement it is one in which all interests
should harmoniously pull together in the common aim of lessening one of the heaviest
burdens imposed upon civilisation.

PROTECTION OF LIFE AND TRADE.

Mr. Stevenson Taylor calls attention to the economic advantage of standardising
internationally the Safeguarding of Industrial Machinery. In this country agreements
have already been made between the Factory Department and representatives of employers,
operatives, and machine makers with regard to the safeguarding of dangerous parts of
the machinery used in certain industries. Similar agreements might be made by the
makers of other classes of machinery, so that every maker would only supply machines
with standard forms of safeguards. This would eliminate the bogey of competitive prices
based upon the cost of the guards so far as the makers in this country are concerned, but
it would not eliminate the competition by machine makers of other countries. This is
therefore a matter for international agreement and worthy of consideration. Moreover,
the standards of safeguarding machinery vary in different countries; this involves addi-
tional trouble and expense to machine makers, because different types of guards and other
fittings are required on similar machines. Mr. Taylor argues that although standardised
safeguarding for all dangerous parts of the vast number of different machines now in use
may be an impossible ideal at the present moment, a beginning might nevertheless be made
with the more obviously dangerous parts.

Other papers contained in the pamphlet issued by the International Labour Office
relate to "International Co-operation in the study of Industrial Fatigue" (by Mr. D. R.
Wilson, Secretary of the Industrial Fatigue Research Board), and to Industrial Disease
and Injurious Processes, by Professor Collis, of the People's League of Health, and Dr.
Legge, Senior Medical Factory Inspector.

The International Labour Office points out that though the Conference before which
these papers were read was national and not international, the importance of the subjects
comprising as they do much information upon the subjects of industrial hygiene and
safety.

THE EIGHT-HOUR DAY.
Austrian Approval of International Convention.
Steady progress has already been recorded this year in the ratification by the different
States which are members of the International Labour Organisation of the League of
Nations of the Draft Conventions adopted by the annual sessions of the International
Labour Conference, and news has just been received that a committee of the Austrian
National Assembly has unanimously recommended the ratification of the Convention
adopted at Washington in 1919 on the question of the eight-hour day and forty-eight
hour week.
At the meeting of the Governing Body of the Office at the end of January the repre-
sentative of the Polish Government announced the ratification by the competent authorities
of his country of thirteen Conventions, while the Italian Government representative
announced the forthcoming ratification by Italy of all the Conventions adopted by the
International Labour Conference, with the exception of that on the eight-hour day, which
has been submitted to Parliament.
Japan has ratified the Convention dealing with the minimum age of employment of
children in agriculture, the main provision of which prohibits the employment of children
under fourteen years in agricultural work, save outside the hours fixed for school attendance.
Effect has also been given in Japan to Conventions fixing the minimum age of employment
at sea at fourteen and making annual medical examination of youths under 18 employed
at sea compulsory.
The Danish Government has been authorised by Parliament to ratify the Convention
on the minimum age at sea, and also the Convention fixing the minimum age of young
persons employed as trimmers and stokers in ships at eighteen; the latter Convention
has also been approved by the Finnish Parliament and will be ratified this year.
INDUSTRIAL PRODUCTION OF THE WORLD.*
International Labour Office Report.
The International Labour Office (League of Nations) announces the publication in
French of the second volume of a report containing information, collated and analysed,
concerning industrial production throughout the world.
The report, which will be completed in four volumes in French, embodies the results
of an inquiry into production throughout the world undertaken by the Office in accordance
with instructions given by its Governing Body in June, 1920, the initiative having been
taken by Mr. Pirelli (Italy) on behalf of the group of employers' representatives.
The second volume deals with the general movement of production in the period
from before the war until 1921 or 1922, and the corresponding movement of the average
output per worker. The two succeeding volumes will deal with the explanation of the
crisis of production and with the remedies proposed and experiments made.
This volume contains 1,356 pages, with 665 tables and 330 diagrams. Nearly a
thousand pages are required for the survey of the general movement of production. This
survey covers a considerable number of articles classified under the following heads :—
mineral, fuel, ores and metals, chemical products, agricultural products for industrial
purposes, agricultural products for food purposes, agricultural implements, manufacturing
industries, building.
The comparisons which are made are based on statistical data relating to the various
countries which are published in the report. The method adopted in making these com-
parisons consists in giving first of all for the whole of the period under consideration a
general account of the movement of production, and then in following the movement of
production for each of the four following groups of countries: belligerent countries of
Central and Eastern Europe; belligerent countries of Western Europe; neutral European
countries; extra-European countries. Finally, an effort is made to indicate the changes
which have taken place in the case of each of the countries.
The articles which are taken into account include the following :—coal, oil, iron, copper,
lead, zinc, aluminium, mercury, silver, gold, manures, sulphur, rubber, cotton, wool,
silk, linen, hemp, jute, beetroot, sugar cane, sugar, wheat, rye, maize, rice and ships.
The part of the work dealing with the output per worker is divided into three sections
concerning respectively :—problems of method; output per worker in various countries;
supplementary information on output in agriculture.
* Inquiry into Production: General Report, Volume II. Published for the International
Labour Office (League of Nations) by Berger-Levrault, Paris (25 French francs);
obtainable from the International Labour Office, Geneva (12.50 Swiss francs).

TABLE TALK.
This is the time of the year when butter is at its highest price. In comparing prices
it should be remembered that there is more of butter and less of water in best Danish
than in any other.
Blended butter is now in much demand. Blended butter is not a mixture of butter
and margarine as some suppose. It is all butter. "Blending" simply means mixing
butters from different parts of the world to produce standard qualities. But a C.W.S.
blend should be insisted upon.
During the last six months of 1923 the C.W.S. sold about 1,000,000 pounds weight
more tea than in the last six months of 1922. The English and Scottish Societies thank
own societies.
The most disturbing new year fact for the housewife was the continued increase in
the price of sugar. The Statist, reviewing the situation, sees no hope of lower prices for
some time to come. Apart from the high sugar tax, the reason for high prices is the state
of Europe, which last year again resulted in a poor production of beet sugar.
Looking at food prices generally, while sugar, potatoes, rice, butter, and lard are
"up," there are rather lower wholesale prices, as compared with a year ago, for bacon,
ham, dried fruits, oatmeal, and flour. Where the difference is not enough to affect the
retail price, co-operative members get the benefit at the quarter end, through the dividend
on purchases.
There are 249 directors of public companies in the present House of Commons, and

Lords there are 425 directors. Of these, 70 are associated with the Federation of British
Industries.

DISPUTES.
For some time past the General President and also Mr. Len. Smith (National
Organiser), along with the local officers, have been trying to get the firm of
Messrs. Odell & Dixon, of Wellingborough, to honour the National Agreement.
The firm refused to comply, and the matter having been in hand since last
November we felt compelled to declare a strike, and notices were handed in on
the 1st February, 1924. After the operatives had been out on strike ten days
the Ministry of Labour intervened, and negotiations were re-opened with the
firm. Certain offers of the firm were conveyed to the operatives by Mr. Len.
Smith. Ultimately it was agreed that the arrears due under the National
Agreement and adjustments in wages should be paid from the second pay-day
in November, 1923. Having, therefore, secured compliance with the Agree-
ment the strike was closed, and the operatives returned to work on the
eleventh day.
Whilst we may regret that such a course had to be adopted to secure
compliance with the Agreement, nevertheless we are determined so far as it
lies in our power, even if extreme measures have to be taken to ensure
National Agreements being honoured both by federated and non-federated
firms. A letter upon this subject appears on page 156.
It does not follow because under our methods of arbitration that the
activity of the Union is slack. On the contrary, the National Officials, as also
the Branch Officers, are constantly dealing with adjustments of wages due to
altered methods of manufacture, or new patterns of boots and shoes that come
into the market. The great advantage to the member is that these adjustments
nearly always take place under the machinery by which the trade is governed
without loss of time, and therefore, without loss of wages to the
member.
DAYWORK METHOD OF EMPLOYMENT.
We would call the members' special attention to the following copy of
a circular which was issued on the 12th inst.:-
We beg to call your attention to an important point in connection
with the policy and procedure of the Union regarding daywork methods
of employment.
Some employers appear to be under the impression that once daywork
is the method of employment, the piecework statements are not the basis
for measuring the wages paid. It cannot be too clearly pointed out that
the policy of the Union has always been, that if daywork is the method
by which wages are paid, then the amount of work done for the wages
paid MUST be based upon the quantities' statements which have been
drawn up from time to time by the Boards of Arbitration, and which,
therefore, can easily be applied as to the output when on daywork.
