GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
SHODDY FOOTWEAR.-The time seems to have arrived when each industry should
at least see, as far as they possibly can, that we give the public value for money. In this
connection one is constantly brought up against the " shoddy" that is being palmed on
to the general body of working men and women, whose income is so small that they are
practically compelled to take articles at a price to suit the size of their purse, and generally
the caterers for the lowest-priced article are the bugbears in the trade, and bring a certain
amount of contempt on the industry where we see cards and advertisements emblazoning
goods at prices for the finished article less than the labour cost alone of an honest product.
Rumour has it that it is bankrupt stock; or is purchased at a great sacrifice? One
wonders who does the sacrificing, the workers, the employer, the multiple shopkeeper,
or the factor, and we also wonder how far these firms are interested in the welfare of the
trade.
It has been my lot to get an expression of opinion from many members of the trade,
both Manufacturers and Repairing Employers, and all without exception are unanimous
in their statement that the most honest article produced by our trade during the past
twenty-five years was the War-Time Boot and Shoe, when all had a fair living, all con-
sumers had an honest article, and even the Government of the day, who supervised the
production, were content with the effort made to give value for money.
It is very disturbing to find that some very notable firms are placing orders with
firms who do not recognise or pay our National Conditions in their entirety, and although
we are very reluctant to create a disturbance, yet we must protect the National Terms,
and it is being fast borne in upon me that we shall soon have to consider whether the time
is not over-ripe when we should name and advertise those firms we can trust to be loyal
to our National Terms, and also give a written guarantee with every pair of boots or shoes
sold, that they are of a certain standard of quality and free from adulteration. This
method of guaranteeing an article is already done, and for a number of years the firms
adopting such a course have no regrets. The Labour Government could help us by making it
illegal to cover up or hide the insole of any boot or shoe and an Industrial Tribunal to check
adulteration and protect the public from men of a poor type rolling in wealth in a few
years, whilst operatives who cannot pocket their conscience, go on working day by day,
and they and their children are trapped into Consumption by wearing " shoddy boots,
bought as " shoddy," and sold as though they were honest goods. Oh! that our advocacy
of factories of our own and multiple shops we advocated in 1892 had been listened to with
more sympathy and respect; we could have worked out our own salvation. To those
members who know nothing of this effort, we shall have a résumé of the attempts to become
our own employers given in the early future.
PIONEER BOOT WORKS, NORTHAMPTON. -I am sorry to learn that the Pioneer Works,
Northampton, of which Mr. James Gribble is Manager, have decided to give up business;
this will still leave sixteen boot and shoe factories owned and controlled by the workers
employed and their friends and the Union's branches.
NATIONAL AGREEMENT BREACHES. -Little by little we are straightening out the
departures made by some firms from the strict letter of the National Agreement, and it
will be most pleasing when we can rely upon the members of the Federation seeking advice
from their own officials, before making or attempting drastic changes, without incurring
the risk of troubling the Union official. The attempt recently of some firms trying to
start Juvenile Factories or Departments is entirely impossible, and yet we are told the
responsibility is ours! True, we are perfectly willing to accept all the responsibility and
to give the employer who would like to introduce such a system, the following information-
that this firm could not guarantee that our industry has not more boys to adults than any
other industry; that already we are creating blind alley employment; that if we agreed
to the suggestion it would outrage the National Agreement, Clause 17, and when the
boys become adults in five or seven years, can any firm guarantee employment or promise
the boys that they will not become the indirect cause of their fathers' discharge ? Industry
is never parochial but national and international.
CO-OPERATIVE EMPLOYEES. Several more meetings have been held in connection

BRANCH REPORTS.
ARBROATH. — Our members are still on short time and there seems to
be little hope of spring trade in our district. What we wrote last month
about the re-opening of Colin Grant's Ltd., in Arbroath, still remains at the
“rumour” stage. We also learn with regret — a selfish regret, really that
the S.C.W.S. are seeking power to spend a large sum on the extension of their
present factory at Govan. Inquiries have been made in the past by the
Directors of that body as to what facilities they might have in opening a factory
in our part of Scotland, and we had strong hopes of their acquiring the above-
mentioned factory in this town. We were confident they could run it with
success and profit in every way by such an enterprise. The proposition of
the Directors to confine their shoemaking developments to Govan kills the
one hope of our industry being saved up here. " The writing is on the wall,”
extinction of the trade in new work. Be it long or be it short, we have had an
interesting history, and without doubt the few remaining factories on the East
Coast of Scotland will make a strong effort to overcome their difficulties yet.
Naturally we want them to succeed, although as indicated, we sense it to be
a struggle against the inevitable. How far employers are to blame for the
increase of their own difficulties remains a moot point, but recently we sug-
gested their policy was at fault. We have no reason to change our opinion,
and events in our quarter serve to confirm our statements. It would be well
spent time if employers in Scotland would confer more with their workers,
and encourage suggestions and statement of views. An unwise kind of secrecy
seems to stand in the way of this. Employers will not believe their employees
are capable of co-operating with them on such matters as factory management,
or that they could offer helpful advice as to how their business should be
conducted. A Whitley Committee should operate at every factory of any
size, and it would be up to both sides to prove their respective worth. Failing
such machinery, several factors of recent growth are likely to produce trouble
in two of our factories, and we are deeply concerned about it. The Agenda
of our Jubilee Conference contains useful matter. Proposals which do not
interfere with rules are difficult to devise, and it is well to have our large branches
in a position to put forward such practical suggestions. Kettering's resolution
should meet with a warm welcome. The importance of educational work
cannot be ignored, and it certainly behoves our Union to emphasise and vitalise
the policy of the Trade Union Congress, as and when declared. Stafford
Branch can afford to accept the above policy, and the champions of real educa-
tional work within the Union's ambit, should join forces in order to reach a
profitable agreement. Leicester Branch will rally many friends on the points
submitted in its name, and ultimate success will attend those demands. If
carried at the Conference by a strong vote, our Council may be relied upon to
make a stern fight for the inclusion of those intended for insertion in the National
Agreement. We wish our Jubilee Year to be marked by a great advance.
Fifty years of endeavour on the part of workers in any industry deserves
fitting reward, and the National Union can look back over an unique historical
period. We trust the Council are contemplating issuing a survey of the Union's
work, coupled with a description of the transformation of the industry itself
in those restless and progressive years. Such a souvenir would enlighten the
public, and also stimulate the members as to difficulties overcome, and others
to be met. We can say our fifty years are past, and who knows what the next
fifty have in store? How long will it be before our Union is managing the
Boot and Shoe Industry of Britain on behalf of the Government, and for the
good of all the people?

CHESTERFIELD.—Trade is still very bad and the firm here has been

We have had Mr. A. Smith down over the matter, and when he left here everyone

DUNDEE.—With the passing of the month of February, no one associated
with the boot trade in this centre will feel a pang of regret, as the conditions
of trade prevailing at present are exceedingly bad. The one and only boot
factory extant in Dundee, and that a bantling, has found it necessary to dis-
charge a fourth of their employees. Truly, over the portals of the city might
now be written, "Ichabod," so far as boot manufacturing is concerned. Yet.
there was a time, not far distant, when our good town could boast of four
fair-sized boot factories, employing several hundreds of workers. Such are
the changes which relentless time brings in its train. As a consequence of the
stagnant condition of trade, our unemployed register is on the upward grade
numerically. It is pathetic to hear some of our members who have had long
periods of unemployment, speak of the dire effects it has upon their manhood:
the deterioration; the moral fibre is weakened; the physique and mentality
is worsened; that, briefly put, he is not the man he was. Economically his
value as a productive unit is very much lessened, and when we take into con-
sideration the million and a half of unemployed men, the annual loss to the
nation must reach a fabulous sum when measured in terms of money.

HIGHAM & RUSHDEN. - We heartily congratulate Mr. Bates, our
Branch President, on his twenty years' service in that office. In reviewing the
twenty years, we see that wonderful advances have been made in the interests
of the workers of our trade. Twenty years ago our membership was 708, now
7,820. Branch funds then £700, now £12,200. Wages and conditions have
improved. Clickers were paid 26s., Lasters and Finishers 27s., Pressmen 22s.,
Closers IIS., I2S. and 13s. No minimum in Shoe Room. Now National
Conditions obtain. We are also pleased to note that Alfred Crouch was on
the Committee then, and is now a member of Committee. There is no doubt
the result is largely the work of Mr. Bates and Mr. W. Bazeley, J.P., our late
Secretary, so far as the organisation of the Branch is concerned, with the help
of Messrs. Richards, Poulton, W. R. Smith, Buckle, and J. Gribble. Trade
remains fair in the district. Several factories have been visited for Show Card
days, in addition to the ordinary dispute and wage enquiries.
LEEDS No. 1.-Trade here is not as good as last month. Our sick and
out-of-work lists are much heavier than last month. During the past month
influenza has been very bad here, but we are hoping that with an improvement
in the weather our sick list will be considerably reduced. We would once
more urge upon our members that when declaring on sick, that as far as possible
the member's Union Contribution Card should accompany the doctor's note.
We would also urge upon our members who are in arrears with their contribu-
tions, that an effort be made, if at all possible, to reduce such arrears, and thus
be entitled to all Union benefits should the same be needed.
LEICESTER No. 1. - Trade is a little better than last month, but we still
have a good number of members unemployed. We are pleased to report
that our President, Mr. T. Adnitt, and Secretary, Mr. G. Parbury, were returned
by overwhelming majorities in the recent City Council Election. We desire
to congratulate Mrs. M. J. Bell-Richards on her splendid fight in the Humber-
stone Ward.
LEICESTER WOMEN'S.-The Leicester Women's Branch have to report
a two weeks' organising campaign, which has been very successful from an
educational point as well as added membership. The Branch invited the
services of Mrs. Harrison-Bell, of the National Labour Party Executive, and
for two weeks we have held dinner-hour meetings every day, also evening
meetings indoors. A meeting was held one Sunday afternoon at which the
General President, Mr. T. F. Richards, spoke on loyalty to our Union. Friday,
the 14th, we finished up with a Social Gathering, Dance and Whist Drive,
which was crowded with our own members. Our President, Mrs. Bell-Richards,
having had an invitation to fight West Humberstone Ward for a seat on the

LONDON SOUTH. - On 5th March a very large gathering for the usual
monthly meeting took place. Mr. Owen, the President, took the chair, and
after the minutes were read, a discussion took place on the Repairing Machinery
at Freeman, Hardy & Willis, and the members that work at the above-named
firm have decided not to work in conjunction with machinery under any
circumstances on a statement that is less than the three firms that are working
in conjunction in London - namely, Mansfield's, Hart's, and Lyn's - which
they consider is plenty taken off for the process, considering that pre-war
employers contended that a penny to do it by hand was an exorbitant price.
Furthermore, according to Statement, they are only stopping 1½d. for work
prepared for machinery in rivetted class over 2's, under 2's, 1½d. They also
hope that the repairers throughout the country will send in their opinions by
letter to the Board of Trade (Mr. Popplewell, 1 Whitehall Gardens, Whitehall).
If not, by reading the suggested statement, they will find out that they will be
losing their minimum if they accept the terms that are in the clause, where it
states the employer should guarantee 1s. 3d. per hour for five hours' work on
full day, four hours on a half-day, less percentage according to price of living.
They will be worse off than before the war. Sorry to have to announce the
death of Mr. A. Pearson. A vote of condolence was taken on behalf of the
family.
MAYBOLE. - Trade is very slack and sickness very heavy, also funeral
claims heavy. Since our last report we have lost two members, 130935 Mary
Watson, and 40402 Thomas Baird, late Secretary to this Branch for many years.
His death was very sudden; he died sitting on his chair listening to a wireless
concert. Mr. Baird was a quiet, unassuming man, a faithful servant to this
Branch during his term of office, and an honest man. He was laid to rest on
Friday, 7th March, and his funeral was attended by representatives of the
Town and Parish Council, the Elders of the Parish Church, all of which he was
a member or ex-member. The Secretary represented the Branch. To both
of these families we tender our deepest sympathy.

NORWICH. - Trade in Norwich has continued to improve during the
month and prospects seem to be brighter than for many months past. Fancy
M.S. is forming the larger proportion of our trade just now, although Turnshoe
is improving.
PLYMOUTH (REPAIRING). We were interested in the Burnley report
for last month and the questions put forward for discussion, but we find our
selves unable to give any considered judgment upon the matter before further
information is available. We desire to know how many boot repairers the
Union is catering for, and what branches are wholly or mainly repairing branches.
We have often thought how useful this information would be to an organisation
such as our own. In general this does not appear difficult to obtain, and would
be most interesting to repairing branches. At present we read the different
reports and are unable to tell whether manufacturing or repairing is being
referred to, except when the subject is specially mentioned; even then we
know not whether the branch is wholly or mainly employed in repairing.
Possibly the Council would know, if so, some arrangement should be made to
pass the information on for the benefit of members. This may be done by
placing the word "repairing" after the name of the branch as now appearing
in this report, or placing Repairing Branches under this heading. The Branch
Reports should be one of the most useful and interesting features of our Monthly
Report, and it is a matter to be regretted that every branch does not send in a
report each month.
STREET.-Trade here is worse now than it has been previously, especially
in the Turnshoe Department, where nearly all the operatives have been sus-
pended. This we cannot understand when the work done in that grade is of
the finest and is very high-class, both in design and workmanship, and we are
looking forward to a revival of that class of goods in the near future. We are
glad to report that we have had two more visits from the General President
and Mrs. M. J. Bell-Richards, and we are glad to report that as a result of the
latter's visit there is a decided improvement on some of the operations in the
Closing Department of the large factory, due to the suggestions of Mrs. Richards.
The operatives are in some cases earning higher wages than before. We had
a stoppage of the girls in that department on 16th February, owing to a girl
being discharged, and the threat used that unless some of the other operatives
did not earn the minimum rate they would have to go also. This was dealt
with by the General President, and the girls returned to work on the Monday
morning pending an interview with the firm, who at that meeting gave us the
assurance that there would be no more discharges until each and every case
had been fully discussed and gone into. There are other cases here which will
occupy the time of our National Officers and Mrs. Richards for some little time,
although it may be done by correspondence seeing we are so far away from the
large centres, and we do not want other branches to think we are monopolising
the time of our National Officers, but we know we shall get their very able
assistance. We are glad to report also that we have our worthy Secretary,
Mr. J. H. Hooper, J.P., back in Street again, but not able to start duties yet
as he needs some amount of recuperation. But still we are pleased to see him
amongst us again, and are hoping for him to have a complete recovery soon.
WELLINGBOROUGH.-Trade has shown a considerable falling off
during the past month, again bringing forward the problem of the elderly
operative. One of the tragedies of our modern industrial system is the fact
that the cry of "too old at forty" still holds the field. What a blot upon our
industrial advancement, that when a person has given the best of his life
and skill to industry his reward is the scrap heap. Here is a problem for our
leaders and politicians. We must still press for pensions at an earlier age than
70, in order to in some part help solve the problem. Our branch is still showing
renewed life and activity. We now have twenty-one shop presidents, which

LONDON BRANCH. The new development, of which a preliminary announcement
was made in our last report, is now an accomplished fact, and in the early part of the half-
year we removed to our new premises in Gough Street, Gray's Inn Road. Events have
more than justified this important step, and already we have found it necessary to purchase
additional machinery to cope with the steadily increasing volume of work. It will be
noted that some of the preliminary expenses involved in the removal and fitting up of the
new building and the legal costs and commissions in connection with the sub-letting have
been written off the current expenses of the half-year.
KETTERING BRANCH.-Considering the small staff here the number of orders which

for the larger orders which are transferred to Leicester.

for December, both for wholly and partially unemployed, chiefly in the building, textiles,

SOME QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS.

1. WHAT HAPPENED IN THE GREAT WAR?
NINE MILLION MEN were killed.
MILLIONS MORE were crippled and maimed.
WOMEN AND CHILDREN were starved to death in their thousands.
FLOURISHING CITIES were levelled to the ground.
GREAT TRACTS OF FERTILE LAND were devastated and made barren.
HUGE AREAS OF COUNTRY are now lying idle: WHOLE POPULATIONS
are destitute and ravaged by disease: FAMINE has been raging throughout the Central
States of Europe.
OVER 30,000 MILLIONS OF MONEY absolutely wasted.
2. Is ANYONE TRYING TO STOP THIS HAPPENING AGAIN?
YES. THE LEAGUE OF NATIONS.
When peace was signed in 1919, Great Britain and more than forty other nations
made a League to work together for the good of all, and to prevent war. There are now
fourteen more members of this League of Nations, including Austria, Hungary and
Bulgaria, who were against us in the war.
Fifty-four nations altogether, over three-quarters of the world's population.

3. WHAT HAVE THEY AGREED TO DO IN ORDER TO PREVENT IT?
(a) To try to reduce their armies and navies so that they will not be afraid of each
other, and will save the money to spend on better things.
(b) To make no more treaties or alliances in secret.
(c) To settle disputes by arrangement. Never to go to war till they have talked
things over for nine months.
(d) To protect small and weak nations, and not to bully them or make money out
of them.
(e) To end injustice and to fight disease throughout the world.
(f) To stand together so that no nation in the League dare break its word.

4. WHAT THE LEAGUE HAS ALREADY DONE.
(a) Stopped one War; and prevented four others.
(b) Registered and made Public over 300 Treaties.
(c) Insisted upon a strict account of all Mandated territories.
(d) Repatriated 400,000 Prisoners of War.
(e) Successfully fought Famine and Epidemics in Europe.
(f) Suppressing Traffic in Opium and Drugs.
(g) Suppressing traffic in Women and Children.
(h) Conventions signed to simplify Custom formalities and provide better treatment
in Ports and on Railways.
(i) Restored Austria and now restoring Hungary.
(j) Assisted Greece in Repatriation of a million refugees.
(k) Strongly supported humane Labour conditions all over the World and helped
Social Progress in every possible way.

5. WHY HAS NOT MORE BEEN DONE YET?
Because public opinion-YOUR OPINION-was not mobilised and made to tell.
THE LEAGUE OF NATIONS UNION provides you with an opportunity of "pulling
your weight" for peace and a better world outlook.
If you desire better things-as there is no doubt you do-then join the League of
Nations Union and help to form a strong Public Opinion which is the greatest Weapon
of the League.
The League of Nations is a Machine-and a very Great and Wonderful one-but
that is You and I, have to provide the DRIVING POWER to make it work.
If we all lend a hand we shall have a glorious result.
THE LEAGUE IS ABSOLUTELY NON-POLITICAL AND NON-SECTARIAN.

COMMERCE AND CONSCIENCE.

We are not by any means prepared to contend that in all commercial transactions
and relationships there is an absence of what is termed conscience, but in very many it
can doubtless be said that the faculty or attribute is well stretched, if not non-existent.

If the ruminations and ramifications of business life (in all trades) were scrutinized
and analysed thousands of instances would be found daily wherein as the final result
unsuspecting men are the prey of "clever" dealings.

Let us take as an example some recent happenings within our knowledge in connection
with certain classes of leather. In citing them we simply aver that the effects are un-
economic, unsound, and to the detriment of the industry dependant upon the commodities
in question.

During the past few months and particularly the last few weeks-there has been an
increasing shortage, for instance, in the supplies of sheep leathers-whether in the pickled,
crust or finished state-and sensational advances in prices have resulted.

To the users of these materials this fact alone, even in its natural form, has been
serious enough.

But with the opportunity-as has always been the case-the vultures have
swarmed the markets and accentuated the difficulties. Speculators scoured
every warehouse and bought up all available supplies-holding again for big
second, third, or even fourth profits on original costs.

Illustrative of this point we are informed on good authority that in a number of recent
transactions as many as three and four profits (and by no means small ones) have been
taken on the same parcels of leather in one day between merchants within a few hundred
yards of each others' warehouses-and even then the goods have not found their
way to the ultimate consumer. Prices have often by these means been raised twenty
per cent. and more against the next buyer.

Be that as it may, we are convinced that when by such methods prices have in many
cases been doubled in a short space of time those methods should by some means be broken
down.

By whom and how is it to be done?

These reflections lead us to wonder how it is so generally the case that, on a rise in
the market, a known and positive scarcity of the particular class of leather, and almost
certain further advances in prices, the shoe manufacturers (or the leather dressers, as the
case may be) allow the speculating merchants invariably to steal a march on them and
manipulate the market to their injury in the way we have described.

But-we shall be told- "business is business" and it is up to anyone to make a profit
wherever and however possible-conscience, economics or the final welfare of the trade
do not enter into the question. Well, perhaps so! Yet, we frankly deem it a pity that
such conditions can continue to obtain in our trade.

Are our methods obsolete?

Think of the absurdity of one specific transaction (and there are many such) where a
considerable parcel of leather sold three times in one day was actually booked to the fourth
party before it was bought from the first. The offer was made from A to B, from B to (
and then from C to D-each time, of course, carrying a profit. When D ordered the goods
the transactions were carried out in reverse ratio-by 'phone-in comparatively a few
minutes. Meanwhile, of course, in the process of the operation the price had been enhanced
by fully 15 per cent.

Does not the possibility of such incidents and their recurrence clearly indicate that
there is a screw loose somewhere ?

Is it that there is a lack of intelligent and efficient "touch" between supply and
demand-between the producers' and the consumers' markets ?

We have no desire to moralise regarding the "iniquities of profiteering," or attack in
any way the legitimate operations of the "middle-man" (who, in the general way, we are
convinced, functions to the total good of trading), but there can, we believe, be only
harm resulting from such processes of merchanting which allow it to be possible that several
middle profits are extracted before the material reaches the ultimate user, who, after all,
is faced with the hardest task of all, namely, producing and marketing the finished article for
sale to the public at competitive prices against the manufacturers of the whole world.

For that reason we shall be pleased, if by any alteration in existing conditions these
uneconomic factors can be eliminated.

STATE OF TRADE.
28TH APRIL, 1924.
Trade has fallen off during the month, the claims on our Out-of-Work
Fund being considerably higher than of late. As a matter of fact, in round
figures, we have been paying from the Union's Out-of-Work Fund at the rate
of £1,000 per week for many weeks past. To this extent the Union is helping
to keep intact the homes of those members who, but for such assistance, un-
doubtedly would find their economic difficulties much greater than they do
now. We would also point out to the members that in this connection, they
might quite well do some good organising work for the Union in pointing out
the distinct advantages that accrue to those in membership with us. We
desire to increase the membership to such an extent as to be able to say the
whole of those who are eligible to join the Union, are included in its member-

SICKNESS.

heavy for a considerable time past. Here again is shown the advantage of
belonging to such an organisation as ours, the cash payment being of help at
a time when money is necessarily badly wanted to procure those essential
things to ensure restoration to health.

(Mr. T. F. Richards), the General Secretary (Mr. E. L. Poulton, J.P.), with
Mr. J. Buckle, M.P., J.P., and Mr. F. Gould, M.P., waited upon the Home

Department including some, if not all, of the resolutions passed by the Joint
Industrial Council in 1919, in any new Factory Bill which it was understood
was to be introduced in the near future in the House of Commons. He also
asked that the Department should appoint additional factory inspectors,
preference being shown for men with a practical knowledge of the trade. Mr.

GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.

FELLOW MEMBERS.
SHODDY FOOTWEAR. The general unanimity with which the Press has referred
to Shoddy in our trade goes far to show the will to demand purity of product, or at least
value for money. If the industry is to have manufacturers of " margarine" boots and
shoes, then the sum should be advertised and marked as such, and wrapped up in paper
We are fully aware of the difficulties of making an all leather
the use of pulp heels is not so well known to the general public, and often, when used in
than leather. The demand for lightness calls for wood heels which are fairly well known:
boot and a solid leather boot, and a leather and boot comprised of many materials, other
's, women's, or children's boots and shoes, is wholly out of place,
the life of such goods never guaranteed by the manufacturers or shopkeepers and dis-
ing men's,
hard wearing
tributors. The greatest sinners in this respect are the multiple shopkeepers, who in many
cases do no manufacturing, of very little themselves, but buy very extensively, unmindful
as to the rates of wages paid, or the conditions under which they are produced, and when
their attention is called to the matter, reply with that lamentable excuse
"sweater" is encouraged, the
don't buy this stuff our competitors will," and so the
sweated" still suffer, and the genuine trader is deprived of business because he, with
his small business, is determined to deal with firms of standing and repute who are proud
of their business, and are willing to give a guarantee with their goods.
It is to be hoped that those in any industry who wish to protect and help their fellows
will, where such a policy would be of service, issue a white list advertising the firms we
look upon as fair, and ask the general public to only deal with those houses whose names
appear on the list. As an illustration we could at once recommend to the public that the
co-operative movement, with its sixteen productive factories and its eight C.W.S. factories,
is practically immune from this taint or taunt, with the exception of the ladies' fancy
goods, made principally for evening dancing and dry weather wear.
We hope to be able to send a deputation to the Board of Trade in the near future
to ask for help in the matter, and to adopt other methods of bringing the same before
the public

IN THE MEANTIME, TO ALL PURCHASERS OF BOOTS AND SHOES, SEE THE INSOLE BY
LIFTING THE SOCK BEFORE PURCHASING, AND INSIST ON A LEATHER INSOLE. Without
of consumption, kidney diseases, rheumatics, and all other ailments due to shoddy footwear;
once soaked, never dry, and a damp foot assured as long as the boots last.
HOME OFFICE. A deputation from the Council waited on the Home Secretary, the
Rt. Hon. A. Henderson, to place before him the result of many visits we had made to the
Home Office and the result of much time and discussion we had had with Mr. Williams,
Dr. Collis, Professor Hill and Professor Moore, on that dread disease, Consumption or
Phthisis, in our industry, finding as we do that we hold a most unenviable position in
industrial diseases, being among the worst of all trades affected, and anxious to control
to some extent the health of the operatives who, for the best part of the day, and the greater
part of their lives, are often working in an atmosphere described by the Medical Research
Committee attached to the Home Office as injurious to health. We want a sufficiency of
light, air and ground floor space-no operative to be closer than four feet or more; all
firms to be registered as fulfilling these requirements, and no license granted unless all the
Home Office requirements are met; all workshops, in homes or outside, to be registered
in a similar manner; the abolition of underground workshops andm an yother matters
in keeping with the improvements we are entitled to, as the present Factory Act is more
than twenty years old. We merely sounded the Home Secretary on what we should like
to see, fully mindful of his knowledge of the subject. He thanked us for further interesting
him in a subject he has always had at heart, and hopes when the Bill is drafted, we will
help him to get amendments likely to conform with our wishes. Ultimately we asked him
whether on the question of Phthisis the Home Office was the authority, or the Minister of
Health; the Home Office whilst the operative is in the factory we were told, but they
seemed in doubt We have already written the Minister of Health asking him to receive
a deputation on the point. We think that this good work of healthy homes can easily
be undone by unhealthy workshops. As we have had no reply yet, we await developments.

TRADE BOARD. We have asked by letters (and through some thirty-three thousand
circulars issued last month) for information respecting the help, if any, that the Rounding
and Channelling Machines would be to our members, and whether the prices we tentatively

ORGANISERS' REPORTS.
22nd April, 1924.
During the past month I have been to Manchester, Lancaster and Cork. The
trouble at Cork is over the claim of the Lee Boot Company there for the piecework prices
of the Green Book for heavy work. Northamptonshire for men's and boys' light work, and
Leicestershire for women's and girls' work. The operatives contend that a shop like theirs.
doing a variety of trade from heavy nailed to ladies' fine work, is not suited for the applica-
When I went to Cork the previous month, 13th March, I found that the factory had been
closed this year up to then, and that only six weeks had been worked from August to
arbitration. The firm declined the offer. A temporary agreement was come to on 20th
In January of this year the operatives suggested that they submit their differences to
March on the lines that the pressmen and machinists work on weekly wages and that we
get piecework rates fixed for the heavy trade in a month, and for the light work within
two months. The majority of the operatives started work on 24th March, and others
Christmas, 1923.
The firm contended that orders could not be got on the old prices.
were taken on as soon as work was ready for them.
We submitted revised prices to the firm on 15th April, but these were declined because
they did not correspond in detail with the printed prices of the districts mentioned. With
the exception of the Roughstuff department the difference between us was small, and I
The question is going to arbitration now, and the pity of it is that this was not accepted
in January. Needless suffering might have been averted. The Cork Branch is 100
per cent. strong in organisation, and has a spacious clubroom of its own, where the members
are free to go and have games and discussions. When in work a penny a week is paid
by each member towards the upkeep of this. I might say that the wages earned at Cork
on the revised prices of 1919 only gave on the average of what the Council looked to obtain
officers to obtain for their members. My thanks to colleagues at Leeds, Wolverhampton
and Northampton, for information sent to help us at Cork.
D. MCCARTHY.
During March I have been building up and consolidating the organisation in the
Wellingborough area. The Shops President system is now operating successfully and
will be the means of keeping the organisation together, especially in the large firms. The
difficulty here, as in most centres, is the small firms who engage a very few operatives
and are ever on the look out for cheap labour. Long spells of unemployment force men
into taking wages that otherwise they would not look at, and there are certain manu-
facturers who are always prepared to take advantage of this circumstance. In discussing
this position with several of these people one complaint is general, viz.:-some other
manufacturer is making boots cheaper than they are; orders can only be obtained if a
certain price is reached. One manufacturer (who is a fair firm) was perfectly honest
about it; he pointed out that his materials cost him the market price; a certain quality
was demanded, nothing could be taken out on that side, so therefore when it came to
getting down to the price the buyer offered, there was only one point at which he could
reduce costs, and that was labour. Factors by their attitude are indirectly producing
sweated labour, and are an additional enemy to the Union by beating down the manu-
facturers to an economic price, the manufacturers in turn beat down wages and make it
difficult for the National Terms to be fully applied. This side of the problem will eventually
have to be dealt with.
Several visits have been made to Olney, where conditions are not anything like what
they should be. Trade has been very bad for about three years, and as a consequence
many of the operatives have allowed their membership to lapse. With a revival of trade
the membership is steadily being built up again; conditions are also improving. Still,
there is room for further improvement, and with continual visits, and added interest,
there is no reason why a full membership should not be obtained again, and also proper
conditions put into force.
Special attention has been paid to a large firm in Wellingborough who do a variable
trade in Closing, comprising Legging, Strap, Fancy Bag Work, &c., in addition to Upper
Closing. The minimum at this firm is regarded at the maximum; there are about 250
girls working there, and a large number are non-members. Meetings have been held
outside the factory, and evening meetings have been called, but I am sorry to have to
report that very little progress has been made; apathy and indifference is the bugbear,
and only by continual propaganda can the importance of being organised be brought
home to these operatives.
LEN. SMITH,

LIVERPOOL. Trade is showing signs of improvement, although nothing
to boast about yet. We note in the March Report certain repairing branches
are inclined to kick over the traces if the scale as suggested for working in con-
junction with machinery, viz., the rough-rounder and channeller comes into
force. We are not surprised, as the proposed cuts are too drastic and devoid
of reason and commonsense. We do not object to labour-saving machinery,
but we are not out to boom it up at our expense. In reply to our request for
copies of the latest Trade Board orders, the Secretary informs us that they are
not now available for free distribution, but may be purchased from H.M.
Stationery Office, Imperial House, Kingsway, London, W.C.2, for threepence
each copy, and that they are sent out to employers of labour for the purpose of
being posted up in the workshops. They may be purchased from H.M. Station-
ery Office direct or through any bookseller dealing in this class of literature.
On the other hand, if a branch official of a trade union requires copies to post
up in his office he has to dip into the branch funds. We assume this is part
of the economy stunt. What appears to be required is a sharp axe to cut the
red tape.
MANSFIELD.—Trade here is rather good. We have had several visits
from the General President (Mr. Richards), also one from Mrs. Bell-Richards,
on account of putting the Piecework Statement in. Although this work is
rather slow, with the help of the Officials it will be made all right, hoping
to benefit our Union members and also satisfy the masters.
MAYBOLE.—Trade is very slack. Most of our people are only working
three days a week and on the Labour Exchange for three days, and conse-
quently some of our members are falling into arrears. Sickness is still very
heavy, but showing signs of abating.
NORWICH.—Trade has been exceedingly busy during the month, many

provision for new labour. Consequently our claims have dropped to nearly
half by the end of the month. This tendency is very satisfactory, especially
so as the turnshoe section is showing progressive improvement, and additional

PLYMOUTH (REPAIRING) Trade slack during the month. Some of
our members have been on the unemployed list. Fortunately our unemployed
benefit is good, and many of our members have realised the advantages of
union membership during the past four years. But there is another aspect of
the question which seems to us to call for serious reflection, and we should be
interested to hear something of the experiences of other branches, especially
repairing branches, upon the same question. We find the same thing happening
again and again: our members becoming unemployed claim their unemploy-
ment benefit, sign the book regularly until benefit is exhausted (nine pounds
to our organisation, for we find it very rare a member returns to the trade as
written off from Union funds), then something happens much more detrimental
an employee. He generally finds a little shop in a back alley and becomes
what is known as "a one-man business." No one can blame him for this.
Really his effort is commendable and, more often than not, inevitable, but we
invariably lose our member, and that is where the rub comes. Now we think
something might be done to keep these members organised; certainly they
may be still classed as workers, seeing they all work for the public, while many
of them are no better off than a journeyman in regular employment, or a fore-
man paid the Trade Board rate. But our Union contributions and benefits do
not exactly meet their case. We are quite aware that the employers endeavour
to organise these men, and probably that is all to the good as there is a danger
of these people seriously affecting the trade, but do they not rightly belong to
us ?

SOUTHAMPTON. Trade very slack, the shipyard workers' strike having
a depressing effect on trade of all kinds.
STREET. We regret we are unable to report any improvement in the

receiving sickness benefit owing to the influenza epidemic.

PHTHISIS IN BOOT AND SHOE INDUSTRY.
Principal Union Officials visit the Home Office.
HOME SECRETARY'S REPLY.
At the request of the Executive Council of the National Union of Boot and Shoe
Operatives, a deputation consisting of Mr. T. F. Richards (General President), Mr. E. L.
Poulton, J.P. (General Secretary), Mr. J. Buckle, M.P., J.P., Mr. F. Gould, M.P., and
Mr. Ernest Bordoli (Confidential Clerk), waited upon the Secretary of State for Home
Affairs-the Rt. Hon. Arthur Henderson-on Friday, the 4th April, 1924, at 10.30 a.m.,
at the Home Office, Whitehall, London, S.W. 1.
Mr. W. R. Smith, M.P., J.P., was prevented from attending owing to being engaged
on work connected with the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries.
In addition to the Secretary of State for Home Affairs, there was also present from
the Home Office-Sir Malcolm Delevingne, Mr. R. Bannatyne, C.B., Dr. Legge, C.B.E.,
and Mr. C. G. Markbreiter, C.B.E.
MR. RICHARDS: I hope you will pardon us for the brevity of our case. We are well
aware of the gentleman we are addressing, and know the Secretary of State has full know-
ledge of the facts, otherwise we may have gone more fully into detail.
I have known the Secretary of State firstly as a workman, councillor, and during my
brief period in the House of Commons always found him interested in the subjects about
which we have called to-day.
The object of the deputation is to impress on the Department the vital necessity of
incorporating in the proposed new factory legislation, the series of resolutions, the outcome
of a special Conference of representatives of the Boot Manufacturers' Federation of the
United Kingdom, and representatives of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives,
held at the Home Office in 1917.
This deputation, however, consisting exclusively of representatives of the National
Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives, particularly desires to emphasise, that although in
agreement with the resolution whereby it is proposed to increase the cubic capacity now
provided in the present factory Act of 250 cubic feet per operative to 500 cubic feet per
operative, that the Home Office will agree to secure a clause in the new Factory Act, whereby
there shall be a minimum space of 4 feet between every operative working in a boot factory
at a machine or bench.
We are emphatic in this recommendation because the Medical Research Committee
in its investigation, having special regard to the boot and shoe industry and the prevalence
of Phthisis, reports on page 6 of its report, as follows :-
"The air space as measured by cubic capacity per person always exceeds as
minimum of 250 cubic feet required by Section 3 of the Factory Workshops Act,
1901, and was found in 100 factories of varying sizes to average 800 to 900 cubic
feet per head."
In the same report it is stated that although the cubic feetage provision in the Factory
Act was in almost every case exceeded there seemed to be a general congestion in the
departments.
Again expert evidence was quoted conclusively proving that for operatives to sit
within three feet of each other constituted a danger zone as far as the disease of Phthisis
was concerned.
This deputation also wishes to impress upon the Home Office the necessity in the
proposed new factory legislation to make provisions whereby it shall be compulsory for
all boot and shoe operatives to be employed in factories. Our reasons for making this
suggestion are because we have knowledge of the fact that there is still a large number
of boot operatives employed in small workshops in connection with their homes, where
factory legislation is evaded, and our great desire is to see that the new proposed factory
legislation eliminates from our industry all conditions which tend to sweating and creating
unhealthy conditions of labour.
This deputation also wishes to strongly urge on the Department the necessity for some
provision being made in the new factory legislation whereby it shall be compulsory for
every employer of labour in connection with the production of boots, shoes and slippers,
or preparing or manufacturing parts in connection with the manufacture of boots, shoes
or slippers, to register or otherwise secure a license to use as a factory any particular
building for the employment of labour under the Act.

MR. POULTON: I wish to substantiate the statements of the General President.
I believe you already have the report from the Joint Industrial Council, as follows:-
1.-LIGHTING.
(a) Natural:
1. In any new works, underground workrooms should be prohibited.
The definition of the term underground workroom was left to the Home Office.
2. As regards existing works, no underground room should be used as a workplace
after a period of three years unless a certificate has been given by H.M. Inspector of
Factories that it is suitable for that purpose, that in the event of exception being taken by
the owner, occupier, or any operative employed in such factories to the withholding or
otherwise of such a certificate, the case shall be referred by that party to the J.I.C. which
shall be required to investigate and report its opinions to the Chief Inspector of Factories,
Home Office, and further that the Home Office shall take no official action in the matter
pending the receipt of such a report.
3. All windows must be kept clean inside and outside.
(b) Artificial:
Artificial lighting should be adequate and the light should be so placed and shaded
as to prevent, so far as practicable, the rays of light from impinging directly on the eyes
of the workers.
2.-CLEANLINESS.
(a) Walls and Tops:
The legal requirements should be strictly enforced and in view of the number of
existing regulations and the difficulty of strict enforcement, this Council asks that if the
staff of Inspectors is inadequate for the purpose, the Home Office will seriously consider
the advisability of appointing additional inspectors for the boot and shoe trade.
(b) Floors:
in good condition.

MR. GOULD I can only speak from the practical side, having only recently left the
boot factory. Our industry is subject to specialisation of machinery. Accumulation of
dust comes into the factory, due to the fact that the absence of proper inspection enables
a firm not to have the fans cleaned out as often as they should be. Very often I have
leave their machine for five or ten minutes to get a breath of fresh air, due to the
clogging of the fan and causing bad ventilation. The cuttings from the clicker's bench
and pressman's bench fall to the ground and are all too frequently spat upon. These
bits are picked up by boys or men, and used by other people in the making of the boot.
You come into contact with the spit and accumulation of dust, and there is the danger
of infection.
Until we have fresh legislation that compels manufacturers-particularly in the
heavy nailed trade in Kingswood and district-from using wash-houses and back kitchens
for making boots, these dreadful conditions are likely to continue, and I hope you will
give us powers to control it. That is one of our problems. I hope you will give attention
to the matter.

FELLOW OFFICERS,
for Union Officers, which complaints, upon investigation, have been found to be such as
So many complaints have come to hand recently as to the manner of Voting
say that the following method must in all cases where Voting is necessary for Union
to prove that the Rules have not been adhered to the Council therefore instruct me to
If not, there will be no other course left open but to deal
ing the Vote recorded, or if necessary to disfranchise the Branch for a period not exceeding
with any Section or Branch who fail to conform to Rule in this matter, by either disallow.
positions be strictly carried out
12 months, or order a new Election:
(a) The member must be a Financial member that is, he must have paid 26 Weeks'
Contributions apart from his Entrance Fee.
(b) No Member, though Registered, must be allowed to vote if he is in arrears with
his Contributions more than eight weeks.
(c) Branches can have more than one Polling Station, all of which must be apart
from any Factory.
(d) No Voting Papers must be sent to any member.
(e) Members must come in person to the Polling Station.
(f) Members must produce their cards before being supplied with a Voting Paper.
(g) The person in charge of the Polling Station and Ballot Boxes must examine
the card to ascertain if the member is entitled to vote according to Sections
A and B; if he is not he must NOT on any account be allowed to Vote.
(h) If the member is entitled to vote, he shall be handed a Voting Paper by the person
in charge of the station, who shall date stamp their card to show that the member
has voted.
(i) Voting Papers must not be torn out of the Ballot Book until an applicant applies
for one to record his vote thereon.
(j) The unused Ballot Papers must be returned to the Branch Secretary, who shall
keep the same until at least the next Monthly Meeting of the Branch.
(k) The Ballot Papers used for Voting must be kept intact by the Branch Secretary
for a period of three months after the vote has been declared by the Council.
(l) The person in charge must see that a member who has a Ballot Paper for voting
purposes deposits the same in the Ballot Box before he leaves the room.
Yours fraternally,
(Signed) E. L. POULTON,

EDUCATION AND DEMOCRACY.
Report of an Educational Conference held at Irthlingborough, 9th February, 1924,
arranged by the Northants District Council. Mr. W. G. Cove, M.P., for the Wellingborough
Division, gave a lecture on "Education and Democracy."
Mr. W. Taylor, headmaster of the Irthlingborough Council School, presided, and
delegates were present from all branches of the Boot and Shoe Union in Northants, together
with Mr. T. F. Richards, General President, and representatives of other Trade Unions.
Local Labour Parties, Co-operative Societies, Co-operative Guilds, and Working Men's
Clubs.
Mr. W. Langley, J.P., welcomed the delegates to Irthlingborough.
The Chairman added his welcome to the delegates and said that the large number
present spoke well for the interest that was being taken in education by people of all sects
and all shades of political opinion. He wanted the rising generation to be something more
than "receivers and repeaters" of bald facts. Rather they should be "thinkers and
utterers." Knowledge was power and ignorance a curse.
(Hear, hear.)
Mr. Cove, who had a cordial reception, said: My ideas of the practical teacher have
been revolutionary. I have not been satisfied with the methods which have been imposed
on the educational system of this country. I believe that we thought too much about
need for self-government, for the shouldering of responsibility by any class of working
people, that need is quite as present in the teaching world as in any industry in this
country. We have not trusted the craftsman enough-we have not trusted the
enough as far as education is concerned. You have not given the teacher a chance with
all our discoveries in methods and principles, our development along the psychological
line all those scientific principles have been cut across by one simple thing, and that is
great classes of 50 or 60 scholars in the elementary schools of this country
would say to Mr. Trevelyan, as Minister of Education, that the most effective reform, the
most revolutionary reform that he could initiate in the elementary schools of this country
would be to reduce the 60 to 20 or 25. (Applause.) But my subject is "Education and
Democracy." I am not an expert on democracy. I have suffered the ills of democracy.
I am afraid democracy is thought of, in this country, more from the point of view
of form than of content. Democracy is not merely the right to vote; not merely the
constitutional right to have your representatives on your local councils, or a Parliament
elected directly by the people. That is only the form democracy might take, in my
judgment. Further, frankly and honestly, I cannot envisage a true democracy which is
merely political in its expression. I see the industrial aspect in democracy. (Hear, hear.)
True democracy must at least consider not only the political freedom to vote and so on-
there should be not only representative government in the political sense, but it must
include control by the workers in some evolutionary degree over the conditions of work they
perform in the factories, workshops and mines. (Applause.) That is the industrial aspect.
There must be the intelligence to vote as well as the right to vote. There must be going on
behind that an intensive individual culture of the sense of citizenship along educational
lines. I believe that one of the curses of modern democracy is its inertness, passivity, sitting
down to observe-not the activity that the chairman mentioned, "thinkers and utterers,"
but the "receivers and repeaters." We are subject in this country to the difficulties of
our individual citizens not being active enough, not mentally virile enough. Before we
can have an effective democracy we must have an active individual composition of that
democracy. It must be alert, critical, constructive. Democracy not only has these
sides, but it also has the material side. Before you can have a democracy there must
be some material security, economic security. There must be underneath all our endeavours
this fact that man has not to face poverty which prevents him becoming educated, which
makes him wonder whether he will get his meals to-morrow. We have developed to the
point in human society where, for the mass of the people, the adventures of life must be
adventures in the realm of mental things, not in the realm of getting on, or making money
or getting social position, but in creative activity in the arts and sciences. I am firmly of
opinion that the experiences of our youths will not be limited by the house or the home
in which they happened to be born. You have no more right in democracy to prevent a
child entering into the heritage of our literature, of enjoying beautiful pictures, of appre-
ciating the glories of music, than you have to deny the right of food, clothes, and shelter.
(Applause.) These things must be open to the appreciation and enjoyment of all individuals
provided that the personal self-effort is forthcoming. Therefore you must not limit
experience to the homes. True democracy is not the fickle victim of the herd instinct
and mass suggestion. Are we free from that in this country? What is the meaning
of your "trusted" Press ?
How is true democracy to be achieved? It cannot be achieved if you have classes of
60, nor by mere drill. It can be achieved only by education having this philosophy under-
lying it, that the human and personal being is one whole, body, mind and soul, and that

he is chasing a golf-ball, or when he is chasing a profit? Is the banker best satisfied with
himself when he is figuring interest or when he is hip-deep in the stream, figuring trout?

and such articles, is of very little value as an indication of what life, as the workman
understands it, really costs.
An index of the nature of the one in question will prove many things on paper which
are of little value, if the people whose wages are reduced by its agency find that serious
hardship results. Without a doubt this has taken place in most industries during the last
year or so, and the standard of living throughout the whole country has suffered as a
consequence. Trade as a whole has not improved greatly through its workings, not even
export, and the home market has been greatly weakened through lack of purchasing
power all round. It apparently escapes our statisticians that, when the working class is
reduced to bare necessities, most of the manufacturing trades of this country languish as
a consequence.
We have pointed all this out before at one time and another and have endeavoured
to show that this lack of appreciation of actual conditions and the consequent absence
of foresight engendered cannot do other than bring about labour dispute after labour dispute.
It is absolutely useless to attempt the building up of commercial prosperity on anything
but enduring foundations and these are not to be obtained while labour, which is the first
primary essential of all production, is not only uncertain, but justly restless.
It has been our earnest desire without exercising any partiality whatever to show
that from any aspect whatever, the present rate of general earnings is not a safe one for
industry in this country. We have a vast reservoir of the finest labour in the world which
presents the greatest potential commercial possibilities if handled with all due consideration,
but during the last twelve months or so the pressure exercised on it by economic con-
ditions has been so great that not even those in full employment have been able to live
their usual lives. This is not reasonable and the trading associations which have upheld
continued wage reductions as the great panacea for all trade evils are likely to find them-
selves in the position of again having the unreasonableness of the workers to deal with
unless something is done to mitigate conditions. Already we see that strike agitation
is gaining ground, and than this there can be nothing more suicidal to business interests.
We again say that general stabilisation of wages on a generous basis
is not only advisable but necessary if this year's trading is to proceed
prosperously. The Shoe Trades Journal, 4th April, 1924.

MEDICAL EXAMINATION OF YOUNG PERSONS IN FACTORIES.
The Home Secretary has appointed a Committee to inquire into the working of the
provisions of the Factory and Workshop Acts for the medical examination of young
persons as to their fitness for employment in factories, and to consider :-
(a) Whether the existing requirement of a certificate of fitness, limited to a
particular factory, should be modified; whether any other changes should be made
in the examination and certificate, and what arrangements should be adopted for
the future.
(b) What measures should be taken for linking up the examination of young
persons under the Factory and Workshop Acts with their examination under the
school medical inspection service, and, if considered desirable, with other public
health services of the country.
(c) What arrangements could best be made for providing medical supervision
of young persons (where such supervision is considered necessary by the Department)
during employment in factories or processes where the conditions of work are unfavour-
able to health or physique.
The Committee consists of :---
Mr. Rhys J. Davies, M.P., Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State, Home Office
(Chairman).
Mr. Gerald Bellhouse, C.B.E., Chief Inspector of Factories.
Dr. R. Wallace Henry.
Mr. J. Moore Murray, secretary to the Warrington Education Committee.
Mr. Sydney W. Pascall.
Mrs. Rackham.
Mr. W. J. Tout, M.P.
Mr. A. H. Wood, of the Board of Education (Medical Branch).
The Secretary of the Committee is Miss R. E. Squire, O.B.E., of the Home Office.--
The Ministry of Labour Gazette, April, 1924.

THE PIONEER BOOT WORKS.
Readers of Justice will be sorry to learn that at a special meeting of the shareholders
of the Pioneer Co-operative Boot Works held on Saturday, 15th March, it was decided
to wind up the affairs of the society. The necessity for this step is due to the fact that the
trade of the Pioneer Boot Works is far from sufficient to enable it to keep going with its
increased powers of output since 1919.
The origin of the Pioneer Boot Works was a suggestion made by certain Northampton
comrades in 1904 that a trade in boots and shoes might be of financial advantage to the
S.D.F. The suggestion was acted upon, a certain number of boots were produced and
sold, and the profit on the sales handed to the S.D.F. The one on whom the burden of the
beginning of this effort fell was comrade James Gribble. He had been out of work prior
to this beginning being made for the S.D.F., and at first he devoted his time and labour
voluntarily to the attempt. So successful was he that in five months a little over £100
was sent to the Central Office of the S.D.F. The following year the Pioneer Co-operative
Boot Works was instituted, and registered in January, 1906, as a Co-operative Society.
Gribble was then definitely appointed manager and operations were carried out at a shop
in Wellingborough Road, Northampton. In 1907 the progress of the Pioneer Boot Works
was such that it had to move into more commodious premises in Clare Street, where there
was not only a small factory but ground behind on which the factory could be considerably
extended. The whole property was bought outright in 1912.
In about 12 years it is
computed that £3,000 had been sent to the S.D.F. headquarters and £3,000 to various
branches and clubs.
With the divisions in the British Socialist Party caused by the war, it was found
necessary to change the operations of the Pioneer Boot Works to those of an ordinary
Co-operative Society, and this change was made in 1917. The war would have undoubtedly
brought considerable business to the Pioneer Boot Works had it been large enough to take
advantage of the opportunities presented. As it was its powers of production at that
time were totally inadequate to meet the demands of its ordinary customers. During
1917 and 1918 it was inundated with orders, less than half of which it was able to execute.
This led to the acquisition of machinery and the extensions of the factory in 1919 and
1920: but before this development could be completed the slump in the boot trade set in,
and since then the Pioneer Boot Works has gradually come to the position wherein it had
the capacity of producing 1,000 pairs of boots a week and at most could not dispose of more
than 500. All attempts to obtain wholesale trade, though successful in one or two quarters,
were rendered almost hopeless by the general depression in the trade and the closing down
of smaller factories due to the fact that the powers of boot production were greatly in
excess of the effective demand for the goods. Seeing, therefore, that to continue on these
lines could only mean that the shareholders would eventually lose whatever money they
had put into it, the Management Committee of the Pioneer Boot Works were reluctantly
compelled to advise the winding up of the Society.
The one above all others who will feel the closing down of the factory at Clare Street,
Northampton, is our old comrade James Gribble. For the last 20 years he has devoted
his energies to promoting the Pioneer Boot Works in which he has been as successful as
it is possible for any human being to be. But the economic circumstances of the boot and
shoe industry to-day are such that Gribble himself has been the first to recommend the
course that has been taken.—Justice, 3rd April, 1924.

FOOD.
During March there was a substantial fall in the retail prices of several of the principal
articles of food, largely owing to seasonal causes. The price of eggs fell to an average
of 1½d. each at 1st April, as compared with 2½d. at 1st March and 3½d. in December. The
price of milk was reduced by 1d. or 2d. a quart in many towns. The average price of butter
fell during the month by over 2d. per lb., and that of cheese by 1d. per lb. There were
also smaller but appreciable reductions in the prices of fish and bacon. Potatoes showed
the only appreciable increase in prices during the month.
As a net result of all the changes recorded, the average increase over the level of
July, 1914, in the retail prices (in Great Britain and Northern Ireland) of the articles of
food included in these statistics fell to about 67 per cent. at 1st April, as compared with
about 76 per cent. at 1st March.—The Ministry of Labour Gazette, April, 1924.

DEATH OF "ANSTEY" MOORE.

An Ardent Labour Worker.
The Leicester Labour movement has lost one of its oldest and most ardent supporters by the death on Tuesday last of Walter John Moore. He had only been ill for six days, and died suddenly from heart trouble.
"Anstey" Moore, as he had been known to his friends all his life, was 58 years of age. His life was spent in service for the Labour movement. He joined the I.L.P. in the early nineties, and has rendered yeoman service in Labour's cause. He was a member of the Board of Guardians for many years.

Trade Union Worker.
A boot and shoe worker, he was actively connected with his union, and was a member of the local Arbitration Board (Finishing Committee).
His work for Labour was sustained to the last, and he acted as agent for Coun. Adnitt in the recent by-election in the Latimer Ward.
A man of strong and earnest character, who has been a familiar figure at Labour gatherings for a generation, "Anstey" Moore will be sadly missed by his many colleagues in the trade union and Labour world.- Leicester Pioneer, 4th April, 1924.

RUSHDEN'S "CHIEF."
Urban Council Honours Mr C. Bates for the Second Time.
At Rushden the "man of the week" is Mr. Charles Bates, who on Wednesday evening was for the second time in his career appointed Chairman of the Rushden Urban Council.

Though distinctly popular among all sections of the public, the appointment gives an especial degree of pleasure to trade unionists, since for no fewer than 20 years Mr. Bates has been president of the Rushden and District branch of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives. In that responsible office he has established himself as a labour leader of the finest type-one in whom courtesy, reasonableness and earnestness are both apparent and actual. Few trade union officials have a longer or more creditable record of service in the interests of the workpeople and of industry itself.
Mr. Bates can claim 22 years' experience of Urban Council work-and decidedly useful work it has been.
Mr. Bates is naturally proud to think that during his twenty years of service as president of the Rushden Branch of the Boot Operatives' Union the membership has risen from 700 to eleven times that number, and that the funds have increased from £700 to £12,000. His share in the work of forming branches throughout the district, in the memorable events of 1905 (when the Union secured a minimum wage of 28s. and a 56-hours week), and in the negotiations which have resulted in steady improvement in working conditions and wages, is a story in itself.
Patience and good humour have helped Mr. Bates to achieve a great deal in the interests of the boot operatives. The same qualities will enable him to serve the town equally well.- Northants Evening Telegraph, 19th April, 1924.

ORGANISER'S REPORT.
(Continued from page 215.)
During the past month I have been endeavouring to improve the membership in the
London area. I find that the Clickers are the best organised section, and the result is
that this section have good working conditions, both as regards Statements and general
earning capacity. The Clicking Statement is worked to in practically all the factories, and
the few exceptions where it is not being worked to in its entirety are being dealt with.
So far as the Closing Department is concerned, there is a need for sustained efforts, many
shops where a large number of girls are employed, having no members of the Union.
Varying methods have been tried in order to induce them to join, but the results have
been small up to the present moment. Inquiries have been made as to their wages and
conditions, and the evidence proves there is 100m for improvement. With the Making
and Finishing Departments, where the organisation is fairly good, the whole of the em-
ployers work on similar lines, good wages being paid to operatives on the most important
operations, whilst those engaged on less important, either get the bare minimum, or
graduated scale, and in some instances less. Many meetings have been held for the
purpose of gathering information on these points, also in relation to the application of the
Holiday Scheme. I find there are three large factories where the scheme has not at present
been put into operation. These are being dealt with. But the most disturbing factor is
that the firms supplying the orders have a reputation for fairness and good working con-
ditions in their own productive factories, the National Agreement being fully observed.
Why do these people place their orders with firms who they know are breaking the Agree-
ment? The Union will have to adopt some method whereby the public can be informed
upon this matter. Some form of advertisement might be useful.
So far as membership is concerned, steady progress is being made, about 100 joining
during the month, and given time I feel this can be considerably improved upon. More
assistance should be given by those who are already members, and who are in continual
contact with their shopmates. With a greater interest taken, and conversation, the work
would be made easier, and much better results would be obtained.
LEN. SMITH.
INTERNATIONAL FEDERATION OF TRADE UNIONS.
LEATHER WORKERS (FRANCE): The National Federation of Leather Workers held
its ordinary Congress at Paris on 6th April. It now comprises 71 unions and its member-
ship is steadily, though slowly rising. In spite of the fact that 79,318 frs. have been paid
out as strike pay. the funds of the federation amounted to 50,076 frs. In 32 localities
the leather workers succeeded last year in securing improved working conditions without
a strike. Of the 16 strikes, 10 were successful. The Federation places in the forefront
of its programme the maintenance of the eight-hour day, and the principle of paid holidays.
LEATHER WORKERS (SWEDEN): The Swedish Boot, Shoe and Leather Workers'
Union raised its membership in 1923 from 8,278 to 9,064. The number of branches has
also increased from 53 to 56. Unemployment among the members is decreasing, although
it cannot be said that the normal standard of employment has yet been attained.

MONTHLY REPORT.
FELLOW MEMBERS, 26TH MAY, 1924.
THE STATE OF TRADE
has slightly improved during the past month. The figures recorded in the
Gazette issued by the Ministry of Labour are as follow:-
BOOT AND SHOE INDUSTRY.
Employment showed no marked change during April, and on the whole was only
moderate. For some days before the Easter holidays factories in a number of districts
were busier than usual, and overtime was worked; but during the greater part of the
month short time was worked in most centres. A considerable number of factories closed
for extended holidays at Easter.
The percentage of workpeople unemployed, as indicated by the unemployment books
lodged at Employment Exchanges, was 10.2 on 28th April, 1924, as compared with 9.5
on 24th March, 1924.
Returns from firms employing about 42,000 workpeople in the week ended 12th
April, 1924, showed that nearly 31 per cent. of these workpeople worked short time in that
week, to the extent of about II hours each on an average.
There was a further improvement in employment in London during April. At
Leicester there was not much change, employment being fair generally, and very good
with women workers; some overtime was worked, more particularly during the week
preceding the holidays, but a few factories were still reported as working less than full
time. A good deal of short time was still worked at Northampton, and employment
was only moderate; though most of the factories were busy immediately before the
Easter holiday. At Kettering there was a slight improvement before the holidays, but a
number of factories were still working less than full hours, and some closed down for a
week or ten days at Easter. In the Hinckley district, at Wellingborough, and in the
Higham and Rushden district employment was generally slack, with much short time.
There was general slackness at Leeds in the heavy boot section; short time was general,
and the holidays were extended by many firms; those engaged in the light boot trade,
however, were well employed. At Stafford employment was fair, and showed an improve-
ment.
At Norwich employment continued good; a large proportion of the operatives were
on overtime, and practically no short time was worked. In the Bristol and Kingswood
district there was a further decline, and employment was considerably worse than last
year; there was much unemployment, and short time working was general throughout

THE BUDGET.
Although it is some weeks since the Budget was introduced in the House
of Commons, we make no sort of apology for reviewing it here, inasmuch as
this being the first Labour Budget, it will be of historical value to look back
upon as to what such Budget contained. It must be remembered that the
Labour Party had only been in office three months when the Budget was
introduced, and to that extent it is the more creditable that upon its financial
side there has been such a real attempt to reduce taxation, especially for the
section of the community whose income is the lowest.
The total cost of the reductions in taxation proposed will be £34,050,000 this
year and £40,443,000 in a full year.
The following are the reductions :--
SUGAR.-11d. per lb. from to-day.
TEA.-4d. off standard rate per lb., and consequently 31d. off Empire grown
tea from 5th May.
COCOA.-11d. per lb. from 29th April.
COFFEE.-2d. per lb. from 5th May, and Chicory 2d. per lb. from 5th May.
EXTRA DRIED FRUIT DUTY. - Abolished.
ENTERTAINMENTS.-No tax up to and including 6d. admission, reduction of
tax up to and including Is. 3d. admission. The tax up to the Is. 3d. price will be :
7d. seats one penny, 8d. seats three-halfpence, 8d. to Is. 1d. seats twopence, Is. 1d.
to Is. 3d. seats threepence.
SWEETENED MINERAL WATER AND HERB BEER TAX.-Abolished.
INHABITED HOUSE DUTY.-Repealed 30th June.
CORPORATION, PROFITS TAX of 2½ per cent.-Repealed.
MCKENNA DUTIES.-To expire on 1st August.
Income-tax concession to widowers, with children, who keep housekeepers.
A Bill has been introduced to restore the powers and efficiency of the Land
Valuation Department, originally set up under the 1909 Budget.
Concessions are made in the licence costs of motor vehicles. There is to be a
reduction of 11d. local telephone call rates to 1d. and 21d. rates to 2d., and a slight
reduction in trunk calls between the hours of 7 a.m. and 2 p.m. up to a 35-mile radius.
The Deadweight Debt of the country, Mr. Snowden announced, stands at
£7,680,484,000, and the interest costs annually £305,000,000.
The Labour Party is to be congratulated upon the way with which it has
dealt with its first Budget. We can only hope they will continue, not only
in office, but in real power, and thereby have further opportunity for placing
the burdens of finance upon the backs of those best able to bear the same.
The Party in the House has again been dealing with problems that not only
affect the welfare of the people of Great Britain, but which have a vital bearing
upon the relations of this country and those of other nations. The constant
attempts of the Prime Minister to deal with for instance the situation in
France and Germany which is one of the very great difficulties and beset with
all kinds of pitfalls. It does, however, appear that real headway has been
made to come to a better understanding with France so as to make easier a
settlement of the Ruhr position.
