EDUCATION.
We would also call attention to the more humane policy which is being
pursued by the Ministry of Education, and to the necessity of using to the
utmost the powers which are already very large in the interests of the children.
As the Minister of Education the Rt. Hon. C. P. Trevelyan, M.P.-recently
stated:
“All our people outside the House should do all in their power to appoint members
upon the local education authority with a progressive type of mind. If this is done.
a better opportunity of fitting themselves for fulfilling their duties when later on they
so many reforms can be brought about under the existing laws and give the children
have to take their part as men and women."
FACTORY ACTS.
Another matter upon which we feel very strongly is the question of the
Factory Act to which we fully referred last month, and which has been raised
several times in the House of Commons since. The Home Secretary has
now introduced a Bill to deal with many of the matters that from time to
time labour organisations have placed before the Home Office, and amongst
them subjects we ourselves named. In this connection we would call special
attention to the following answer given on the 15th inst., in the House of
Commons:—
LORD HENRY CAVENDISH-BENTINCK asked the Home Secretary how many
workshops and factories have not been visited by His Majesty's factory inspectors
for more than a year, and how many for more than two years ?
MR. HENDERSON : The figures for 1923 were, in the case of factories, 24,005.
and 1,776; in the case of workshops, 59,948 and 35,280.
On the same day the answer was supplied, a discussion took place in the
House of Commons itself, regarding the lack of inspectors of factories. During
the course of the debate it was shown that there are now fewer factory inspectors
than during the war. It was stated that there were 205 factory inspectors
for 283,542 factories; which means each inspector has to deal with 1,383
factories. No wonder so many factories are not visited during one, or even
two years. When one remembers the number of hours the workers have to
spend in factories, it does indeed become largely a mockery to talk about
"efficient factory inspection" under such circumstances. We, therefore,
urge all members to use their influence in their various districts, not only to
create a live opinion upon these matters, but to as far as possible use such
influence with their Member of Parliament as to insist upon an adequate staff
of inspectors being appointed to deal with this important work.
TRADE BOARDS.-CAVE COMMITTEE.
On the 7th inst., Mr. Betterton asked the Minister of Labour whether he
proposes to introduce legislation to give effect to the recommendations of the
Cave Committee. The following reply quoted officially from the Parliamentary
Debates will, therefore, be of interest to our members :-
MR. SHAW: I have no immediate intention of introducing legislation of the
character referred to.
Following is the reply :—
It is presumed that the recommendations of the Cave Committee to which
reference is made in the question are those concerning (i.) the establishment of district

HOUSING.
We sincerely hope that the Government will not only be able to produce
the plans, and that speedily, but that they will put the same into operation
and erect houses as quickly as possible, and thereby not only find employment,
but help to remove the great scandal and menace to the health of the people.
Evidence is constantly coming to hand as to the bad social conditions owing
to the lack of houses. The following examples were received at the Central
Office on Monday last :-
"Man, wife, and three children (aged 3, 2 and 9 months), another child expected

very close, and in spite of cleanliness, children all look pale and sickly.'"

whom are children. One member of the household has never been to bed for four
years, but sleeps on the couch downstairs. Applicants have been married eight
years and never had a house to themselves, and as the family increases it is very
difficult for them."

REMEMBER THE FIFTEENTH!
Once again we feel bound to call the serious attention of Branch Secretaries
to the fact that the FIFTEENTH day of each month is the latest day for
returns reaching the General Secretary. If Branches fail to send off their
returns to reach the Central Office before the 15th of the month it tends to
upset the organisation of the work in the General Secretary's Office. We beg
to intimate that unless returns are in before the 15th of the month, the Secretary
has been instructed to put into force the Rules governing the same. Returns
Sheets MUST also bear the signature of both the Branch President and Branch
Secretary, or they will reluctantly have to be returned for completion.

TARIFFS.
The Dublin correspondent of the Shoe and Leather News writes in the issue of the
8th inst:-
" I heard on good authority that many shops had put on the 15 per cent. new tax
on all goods in stock. One would not be surprised if this were so. Indeed it was rather
to be anticipated."
*
*
*
*
*
"The Manager of Messrs. Winstanley says the tariff is not premature, but inadequate."
"Another Irish manufacturer says the tariff is not big enough to protect Irish goods."
*
*
*
*
"In all Ireland the average family is seven-father, mother and five children. In
families who will be hit by the tariff that is the well-to-do, the independent and rich
who can afford to buy Irish goods the average family is only four-leaving the average
man who cannot buy the untaxed article, saddled with the obligation of buying boots
for ten-with the full tariff on each pair. He can only afford to buy the more popular
imported article."
*
*
*
That is the point I have been trying to make to all those who are interested in this
question-before and since the imposition of the tariff on boots. By those interested
I mean those who will have to pay. The man in South Africa does not have to pay this
tax! Neither does the native of Central America! The rich man in Ireland will not have
to pay it! None of these, then, are interested, except in so far as the tax may benefit
themselves. The man who pays the tax, the hard-working Irish farmer and labourer
with a large healthy family, struggling along on 30s. or £2 a week he is the only one
compelled to shoulder the entire tax and he is the last to be consulted, if indeed he is
consulted at all by any of the super-patriots in Ireland.
*
*
His only hope then is to emigrate! Perhaps this is the result looked for in the present
policy!
*
*
*
*
Sir James Crockett says, "it is perverted patriotism to impose a tariff upon goods
which cannot be produced in the country, as the inevitable result is increased prices to
the consumer."
*
*
*
[It would appear, therefore, that already the tariff has resulted in preventing that
goodwill so necessary between the peoples of the two countries; instead, it has accentuated
difficulties and is driving the peoples apart.-E. L. POULTON, General Secretary.]

GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
SHODDY FOOTWEAR. There is still great need for all concerned to interest
themselves in saving the general public from the imposition of adulterated articles, which
lust obtain money from innocent persons, and then inflict a punishment by introducing
some foul disease into the persons concerned. Although we shall have the prejudice of
one judge going so far as to say there is no such thing as adulteration in boots: it will
be our duty who think there is, to enlighten this mistaken legal divine, and we may perhaps
persuade the makers of all Boots and Shoes to stamp theirs as "Warranted all Solid
Leather" or if adulterated " except the inside middle stiffening and heel" which are
composed of pressed paper. In fact no one has any right to sell the public something
it does not expect, and it is very pleasing to find that the Conference of the National
Federation of Boot Trades Associations, who met this week at Plymouth, had this subject
up for consideration and have very wisely decided to set up a Special Committee with a
view to legislative action. They are also willing to co-operate with our Union as soon
as we can make it convenient to arrange a meeting. We therefore, can depend upon their
help, and we may also get the help of the Employers' National Federation later when we
on the outsole for the purpose of protecting the public. There is a guide to help us in
have, as a Union, decided upon the course of action most likely to bring about the elimina.
tion of adulteration in Boots and Shoes, unless properly described in large legible characters
tions, held on 9th December, 1920, and such specification could be used as a groundwork.
or guide, and some such should be given as a warranty or guarantee with every pair of
Boots or Shoes sold, as one is compelled to hear that the multiple shopkeepers, who do
not manufacture, but buy all their goods, often although many of them occupy positions
of trust and power-are the most guilty and often the prime movers in the introduction of
this course of deception which is a real art to them. Many of them are Justices of the
Peace, who often sit in judgment on others; whereas an enlightened public would certainly
require an improvement in their business methods. Let us hope that we may contribute
towards, and to hasten, such an end at no distant date.
HOME OFFICE. - Another visit to the Home Office has taken place on this occasion
as part of a deputation on behalf of the Hand Sewn Boot and Shoe Making and Repairing
Board, and on this occasion we were received by the Under-Secretary, Mr. R. J. Davies,
M.P., in the absence of the Home Secretary. Our visit was to :—
1. Ask for access to the list of Outworkers obtained by the Local Health Authorities.
2. To ask for Factory Acts to apply to Outworkers.
3. That wages lists for pieceworkers be hung up in Workshops.
4. The prohibition of Underground Workshops.
5. The registration of all workplaces for health reasons.
6. Apply the Shop Acts to Boot Repairers.
The Under-Secretary said they would do their best to help us, and that the new
Factory Bill would meet most of the points mentioned, but he could see great difficulties
in applying the Shops Act.
MINISTER OF LABOUR. — A deputation met the officials of the Ministry of Labour
owing to the Minister being busy. This is a great mistake for Labour Ministers to be too
busy, as some of us do not believe in leaving the running of the Department to officials.
These people have already in the Government Departments tried, and have been successful
in some instances, by being able to control Ministers. Labour men must be wary. We
went to first object to the limited experiment of putting boys to Boot Repairing for an
hour per day, as the idea would only lead boys to think they could repair boots and would
cause a few of them to take ultimately the work of able-bodied men.
We advised two
members of the deputation to visit at least the two towns where this system is being
carried on by the Local Authority.
MINISTER OF HEALTH. - We have found that the Minister of Health had the power
referred to him by a special Order in Council, as far back as May, 1921, to take control
of Infectious Diseases, and we are, as a consequence, pressing the Minister to see the same
Deputation from the Council of the Union that saw the Home Secretary on this subject,
so vital to our industry, the health of the operatives being of most profound interest.
TRADE BOARD. —We have spent another three days on this work, and find that we have
a very large congregation who contribute nothing to organised labour, which gets these
people the benefit they enjoy, and as recent events prove, there are many who belong to
the organisations who are still discontented with all that has been done for them. This
kind of appreciation has the effect of easing off the representatives' interest for the work,
and as a consequence, the grumbler gets less and less. We have sent out a trial statement,
and the evidence supplied by the men to the officials of all the Unions affected has been

ADMIRALTY. A deputation of our Union members and M.P.'s waited on the Parlia-

all they could by taking the position into their most serious consideration.
WAR OFFICE. The same members of the deputation went to the War Office and met
Mr. Lawson, who received us very courteously and has promised to do his best to distribute
the orders as we wished, and to, if possible, give annual contracts and endeavour to meet
more regular employment and not cause overtime. He was extremely sympathetic,
and we hope for good results, but we must not expect the Government to order boots
they don't want. The Tories did that last year, so that the Labour Ministers cannot
even give a reasonable contract because of the stock already in hand.
BURTON-ON-TRENT. We have been to the firm of Eatough's at the request of the
Manager, and have fixed up the price for Pulling-Over and Consol Lasting. We find that
the Pulling-Over and Consol men belong to us, and the others belong to the Rossendale
Valley Union. We are sorry for this and hope that the strained relations now existing
between the two Unions will be assuaged, and not rendered more aggressive. The last
letter from Mr. Taylor to me was indeed written in a very good spirit, and, we hope, may
heal our differences later on.
Will all our members please be loyal to the Trade Union Stamp and those making
honest goods, and be loyal to the Labour Movement by taking the Daily Herald-your

KINGSWOOD AND IRISH TARIFFS.
The Kingswood Branch unanimously passed the following resolution at
their May meeting:-
"That this meeting of Kingswood boot operatives views with alarm the proposal
of the Government of the Irish Free State to impose a tariff on imported boots and
shoes, inasmuch as Kingswood supplies large quantities of strong boots to Ireland,
and the loss of this business to Kingswood will intensify the already large percentage
of unemployment among Kingswood boot operatives. Therefore this meeting urges
His Majesty's Government to make strong representations to the Government of the
Irish Free State with the object of maintaining the present commercial relationship
of reciprocity, and this failing, to use its best endeavours to get a substantial modifi-
cation of the proposed tariff on boots and shoes."

ARBROATIL. Our trade conditions remain bad, and our members suffer
accordingly. Not only so, but the cost of living gives us serious concern too,
as the drop of five points last month seems to point to a similar experience
or less during April we lose the four shillings again in June. We suffer by not
last April figure was 74. and this past April has been computed at 73. Recently
the workers have been somewhat startled to find this " cost of living" basis
for wages is fundamentally wrong. Since the Budget introduced helpful
reductions on foodstuffs they can all realise that instead of securing any
advantage by such means, it will only react against their wages. Beneficial
legislation designed to relieve the worker of a grievous load, is to miss the
worker altogether, and be the means of pulling down his wages still further.
We hope our Council will put up their strongest case against continuing this
arrangement when the National Agreement is under consideration, and instead
of basing wages on the cost of living, aim at wages based on value of work done
plus the ability of the industry to pay. Our industry can pay good wages,
although in its eventful history it has not been distinguished in this respect,
We don't think it would be a hardship on employers to make them pay a much
ruthlessly any improvement in their employees' wages, yet go out of their way
to pay fancy wages to experts called from far-off parts ? We have had this
experience frequently in our district, and it is generally an insult to the other
workpeople employed. It may be a legitimate effort to improve the productive
capacity of a factory, or to introduce better principles of manufacture, but our
considered opinion of all that has been tried in this direction is that the money
has been wasted. There are few things more provoking to workers than to
have their qualities overlooked, and strangers welcomed and applauded on the
slightest grounds. If instead of spending large sums on management, staff,
and would-be instructors, manufacturers did a little more to give their rank
and file workers a good percentage more than the dead level of a minimum,
we are confident their efforts would be rewarded more satisfactorily. It is not
by showering money and appreciation on a few ornaments at the top, that the
necessary harmony and enthusiasm permeates the employees in a modern fac-
tory. All must live, and all are beginning to feel a greater desire for a better
life, and the finest encouragement workers can get is the tangible appreciation
of better remuneration. Our industry can pay better all over the country,
and we hope to see better wages established in our next Agreement, and not
on any mere "bread and butter" basis. Let each Council member absorb
the inspiring address by Mr. W. G. Cove, M.P., which was reproduced in last
month's Report, and which ought to be read and re-read by every member.
Life means more than work; life means more than gaining a bare existence
from toil; real life expands and blossoms in leisure, and when that leisure is
comfortable, growth and happiness are quickened. Our Council will have
every member behind them in striving to the utmost to get such terms as will
ensure satisfactory remuneration and satisfactory leisure. The old cry of
killing the industry can be ignored to-day. The boot and shoe industry will
never succumb because its operatives are well paid. It could go under if
profits (not regulated by cost of living) are its sole object. Material ambitions
cannot endure, and employers will never succeed who have sordid views.
Let our fight be for "Bread and Roses," particularly for the "Roses," as we
have hitherto only got the thorns.

PLYMOUTH (REPAIRING).-Trade is still quiet with us. We were pleased
to find an outline of the Unemployment Insurance Bill No. 2 in our MONTHLY
REPORT, and we beg to draw the attention of members to the effort now being
made to abolish Refunds. Our members do not view this proposal to negative
their right to these compulsory savings with very much favour, neither do
we see the necessity for such a proposal, and why a Labour Government should
contemplate confiscating the workers' compulsory savings is beyond our
comprehension. We can understand other Governments doing this in the
"good old days
of the past, but why borrow the trickery of old parties.
True, the maximum amount standing to a worker's credit when his hair is
turning grey may not be a very bounteous sum, but it belongs to the persons
insured or their personal representatives, expressly stated in the Act of 1920,
and we well remember it being used as a "little sugar to sweeten the medicine."
We congratulate the Government on their splendid efforts, nationally and
internationally, but we do not intend to adopt the attitude of closing our eyes
and trusting blindly to their goodness. Here is a little matter touching the
workers' pockets; paying sixpence per week from the age of sixteen years
to sixty would mean something like fifty-seven pounds, plus 2½ per cent.
compound interest. Probably our Labour Minister would tell us that the worker
who never made a draw upon the unemployment funds would be fortunate
indeed. Undoubtedly he would be, but that is not the point. The insured
worker has a legal claim and his rights should be defended. We did not under-
stand the Capital Levy to commence just here, but were under the impression
that it started higher up the scale. If this Bill becomes law we hope the
Chief Office will make a point of advising all old members how and when to
make their claim.
WATERFORD.—Having been on short time since Christmas we are glad
to report an improvement in trade, hoping for an increased membership in
the future.
WELLINGBOROUGH.-Trade at present in our district is very bad,

all we can as a Union to stamp out the manufacturer of shoddy footwear.
Mr. W. A. Wyman, our Secretary, has received many congratulations upon
his recent marriage.

Dear Sir,
I understand that on Friday the Industrial Council's
Bill is down for its second reading. I hope you will make it
convenient to be in your place, and vote for the Bill. The
principle set out in the Bill is of vital importance to the Boot
and Shoe Industry, and several times resolutions have been
passed by the Executive of the Federated Associations of Boot
and Shoe Manufacturers, and the Executive Council of the
National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives, approving of
the same.
On the 12th December, 1922, it was unanimously resolved
that "This National Conference of Boot Manufacturers and
Operatives urges upon H.M. Government the desirability of
giving to National Agreements voluntarily entered into and
approved by Joint Industrial Councils the same validity as
awards under the Trade Board Acts, 1909 and 1918, with
the object of ensuring the observance of fair conditions of
labour by all engaged in the industry."
I trust, therefore, that you will be able to see your
way to vote for the second reading of the Bill.
Yours faithfully,
E. L. POULTON,
General Secretary.
The above is copy of letter sent to ALL Members of Parliament,
and the progress of the Bill will doubtless be watched with interest.
E.L.P.

ANNUAL CONFERENCE OF LABOUR WOMEN, LONDON, 13th-14th MAY.
DELEGATE'S REPORT.
This Conference was to be held at the Guildhouse, Eccleston Square, but owing to
the large number of delegates it was found that it would be impossible, so they had to
find a larger place, and it was held at the Holborn Empire, Holborn, London.
This year there was one thousand and eight delegates. On Tuesday morning there
was a private business meeting for members of the Women's Sections and Co-operatives.
On Tuesday afternoon the Conference started for all delegates at the Holborn Empire.
Mrs. Harrison Bell occupied the chair, supported by Dr. M. Phillips, and other members
of the Labour Party.
A very cordial welcome was extended to all delegates present, and we also had greetings
from fraternal delegates from abroad. Those present represented Holland, Belgium,
Australia, New South Wales, Perth, and Western Australia. France and Austria sending
telegrams with good wishes for the Labour welfare and success.
There were 99 resolutions sent, and owing to so large a number the Standing Orders
This was put to the meeting and the adoption of this resolution was carried.
Then Dr. M. Phillips brought forward the Report, and it was decided to take it para-
Committee decided to group them up that related to the same subject.
graph by paragraph.
Then there was the subject of Education, and a most interesting discussion took place.
No time limit being placed on the speakers it took up a large amount of time. The subject
was opened by Miss Susan Lawrence. She expressed the opinion that we wanted to educt
public opinion. There was a great and growing demand for education of the children.
There were not the schools and there were not the teachers, as half of the children of London
were without schools.
Mrs. Lowe, of London, said if we could only get the proper enthusiasm we should get
the people's support. Education should be elementary till they are 11 years old, purely
elementary up to a certain point; after that every child should have a course of economics,
and also give them complete household and advanced technical education.
Mr. R. Davies (Home Office) said he was pleased to have been there to hear their
views on education. Some of the speakers' views were that primary schools should be
abolished, and that it was a vital need to give the children a good education. We also
had Mr. Morgan Jones to say a few words to us on education.
Penal Reform was the subject of a short discussion. Emigration of Children was
brought forward, and it was suggested that young children should not be allowed to
emigrate unless full investigation was made in all cases to see how they were being treated.
We were doing them a great injustice in allowing them to go until their welfare had been
ascertained.
In regard to the working women of this country we should organise in our trade
unions, and endeavour in our homes to get members, as men are fighting for the expulsion
of the women. We must stand up for our rights, and men and women must confer together
to discuss the question of not standing in each other's way. We must also reorganise
to make our factories better for the children.
The Housing question then arose. Houses should not be built with less than five
rooms and rent not more than nine shillings a week.
There was a lengthy discussion on Maternity and Birth Control, therefore making it
impossible to get through all the propositions on the agenda.
On Tuesday evening there was a vast meeting of delegates at the Royal Albert Hall
to hear some of our Labour Members. Mr. R. MacDonald and Miss M. Bondfield were
accorded a most hearty welcome. Other Parliamentary Members were present to speak.
The London Labour Choral Union, led by the Camberwell Band, gave us a very good
programme of singing, altogether making a very enjoyable and pleasant evening.
(MISS) A. BILLINGTON,
WELLINGBOROUGH BRANCH.

IDEAL FACTORY.
NEW C.W.S. BOOT WORKS AT NORTHAMPTON.
Credit to the Organisation.
The new boot works erected by the C.W.S. at Northampton were formally opened on
Wednesday morning. The works are intended to supply retail societies with men's and
boys' boots, and when fully equipped will be able to turn out 15,000 pairs a week. The
architects' department at Leman Street, London, has been responsible for the plans, and
the building department has carried out the constructional part of the work.
Mr. L. Tysoe (manager of the Rushden works) has been entrusted with the super-
vision of the new factory; whilst the management will be in the hands of Mr. H. E. Tysoe
junior.
The factory is pleasantly situated in Ardington Road and is, from an architectural
point of view, consistent with the salubrious and residential quarter of the town. It has
been fitted with the best machinery that can be produced for the manufacture of boots-
an important detail that has had the personal supervision of Mr. Tysoe, senior. The local
operative is famous for his workmanship, and with the best machinery at his disposal
he may be relied on to give co-operators the quality, style, and finish they so much desire
in their boots and shoes.
The whole of the work is carried through on the ground floor, with saw-tooth roof of
northern lights.
The interior of the factory is particularly attractive and inviting to the craftsman.
Brightness has been considered to the smallest detail. The roof and top window frames
are white, with a light frame work of girders painted green. Steel shafts, separately
driven by electric motors, run at equally measured distances across the mill, and in juxta-
position with these are steam-heated pipes with aluminium coating. Everything seems
to have been done not to obstruct, but to reflect, the light.
The factory is electrically driven and lighted, and approaches that condition to which
engineering ingenuity is tending—that is, to make even a large floor of industrial operations
dustless and noiseless. One may add that whilst every means has been provided for
emitting light, all that engineering skill can provide in dust extraction has been applied.
Leather "fluff," which flies from any machine where grinding is in process, is swallowed up
by a system of suction into huge pipes and carried into a cyclone on the roof, and thence
deposited into boilers where it is consumed by fire. The cleanliness of the atmosphere,
light-emitting windows, must suggest to visitors
a remarkable advance in workshop conditions.
Nothing has been overlooked to safeguard the physical health and safety of the worker.
Where there are stone steps you will find them bearing a mixture of carborundum, a silver
substance which prevents slipping and makes them easy to ascend or descend. Other
similar details have not been neglected.
The frontage of the factory is lined with a stretch of green turf and variegated shrubs.
At the back of the building is an acreage of land on which Mr. Tysoe has already planted
a border of poplar trees, and recreational facilities will be provided later. Add to these,
bright dining halls, tea and rest room, and lavatories with all-time attendants, and one is
driven to the conclusion that the ideal factory has come before the ideal home, as far as
the artisan is concerned.
OPENING CEREMONY.
NORTHAMPTON, Wednesday.
In the presence of a representative gathering of directors and officials, Mr. G. Thorpe,
J.P. (president of the C.W.S.), formally declared the premises open to-day.
Mr. Wilkins (director), who presided, on behalf of the board, expressed his satisfaction
at the large attendance. He explained that when the present site was obtained some
residential property owners were worried at the idea of a boot factory being erected there.
A promise had been made that the Board would put up a presentable factory and one which
would not be an eye-sore to the district. This had been observed.
boots were famous throughout the world, and the directors hoped with this new under-
taking to make a definite step forward as far as this factory was concerned. Mr. Wilkins
referred to efforts made in recent years by improved methods to stop dumping of cheap
lines of American boots on the British market.
In asking the President to open the factory Mr. Wilkins referred to Mr. Thorpe's
approaching retirement. The directors had a big lump of admiration for the Chairman,
who was one of the most consistent workers it had been his privilege to be associated
with during the troublesome period through which the co-operative ship had been passing.
During the past five years Mr. Thorpe had successfully piloted it through. His colleagues
were pleased he was permitted to remain until smooth waters were reached.
Northampton

BOOT REPAIRING TRADE BOARD.
Report on Inspection and Enforcement of Orders.
A report has been issued by the secretary of the Boot Repairing Trade Board, giving
figures in connection with the inspection of workshops and the enforcement of the orders
in regard to wages and hours of employment for the three months ended 31st March last.
At that date the number of boot repairers on the Board's list was 29.410.
During the period under review, 58 firms received a visit of inspection for the first time
and twelve firms were re-inspected where irregularities had previously been discovered.
the total number of inspections being seventy. Of these, 39 were firms employing fewer
than two workers, excluding two firms employing no workers; 25 employers two to five
workers; one employed six to ten workers; and three employed eleven to twenty workers.
No firms in the twenty-one to one hundred or over one hundred sections were inspected.
The total number of workers employed by the firms inspected was 175.
The total number of complaints received during the period was 58, and 61 complaint
including 31 outstanding from 1923, were investigated, of which 28 were dealt with by
correspondence. Arrangements have been made for the investigation of the 30 complaint
outstanding, of which two are outstanding from 1923.
The number of firms visited during the period in the course of (a) routine inspection
and (b) as the result of complaint were 37 and 33 (twelve received in 1923) respectively.
The number of firms on whose premises it was found notices were not posted were (a) 12
Records of time were not kept in (a) 23 cases and in (b) 17 cases, while it was
found that the records kept were inadequate in one case under (a) and one case under (6).
In regard to wages, it was found that records were not kept by twelve firms under (a
and eight firms under (b), while the records of wages kept were inadequate in one case
under (a) and one case under (b).
In the course of routine inspection two firms were found to be underpaying workers,
the total arrears claimed being £2 16s. 44d. The whole of the arrears were paid, the
number of underpaid workers involved being two. In response to complaints, it was
found on inspection that twelve firms were underpaying workers, the total arrears claimed
being £290 16s. 91d., the number of workers involved being twenty-five. Of these twenty-
three workers received £195 14s. 7d. as payment for arrears.
Of the arrears outstanding
£80 8s. 84d. is due from three firms, who are paying by instalments. The remainder
£14 13s. 54d. due from two firms was claimed only recently.

PRESENTATION TO MR. S. BARNES, J.P.
A large gathering at the Assembly Room of the Working Men's Club, Desborough,
took place on 24th May, 1924, to make a presentation to Mr. S. J. B. Barnes, J.P., who
after 12 years' zealous service as secretary to the Desborough Branch of the National Union
of Boot and Shoe Operatives, has retired.
The gifts to Mr. Barnes were a handsome hanging clock in oak case, with Westminster
chimes, and a barometer.
After tea Mr. Reuben Cox, president of the branch, called on Mr. W. R. Smith, M.P.,
as an old friend, to make the presentations.

Tributes.
This Mr. Smith did in a very suitable speech, remarking on the great work Mr. Barnes
had done, and the esteem in which he was held.
Mr. Poulton and Mr. Richards spoke in a reminiscent mood, referring to their pleasant
associations with Mr. Barnes. The former, who gave an account of the movement's
progress from its inception, said in the 12 years in which Mr. Barnes had held office as
secretary the branch at Desborough had made great headway.
Councillor W. Whymant, the new secretary, also spoke.
In a very fitting reply, Mr. Barnes (who was accompanied by Mrs. and Miss Barnes)
referred to the old stalwarts who in days gone by had done a great deal for the Union,
Later there was another very enjoyable function, when Mr. R. Coe, the president of
the branch, again presided.
Congratulating the branch on the work it had accomplished, Mr. Poulton said it had
had its ups and downs in the 31 years that had elapsed since it was inaugurated.
Although Mr. Barnes had officially retired, he would still assist the branch in helping
to bring about the happier times which some of them dreamed of and hoped to see before
they passed away. (Applause.)

Aim and Object.
“We are looking forward,” said Mr. Richards, “to the time when we shall be one
great human family. Our policy, aim, and object are to see a brotherhood of man and a
universal feeling in the world.” (Applause.) Their motto as boot and shoe operatives
was “May our trade be trodden underfoot by the whole world.”
Mr. W. R. Smith, M.P., made references to the work already accomplished by the
Labour Government, and intimated that they would press for the 48-hours week, more
houses, and also deal with European affairs.

APPRECIATION OF UNION OFFICIALS.
The Management Committee of the General Federation of Trade Unions on the
30th April, 1924, presented to Mr. T. F. Richards, General President of the National
Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives, the Federation's Gold Medallion, and desires by this
presentation to express its appreciation of the loyal, consistent and disinterested service
which Mr. Richards has rendered during his twenty years' official association with the
Federation as Auditor and Member of the Management Committee.

BOOT TRADERS AND REGISTRATION.
"Shoddy" Footwear Condemned.
The annual conference of the National Federation of Boot Trades Associations, at
Plymouth yesterday, adopted a number of resolutions which dealt with the question of
registration.
Government Measure.
The Secretary (Mr. John Hoyle) said that there was approaching the Committee
stage in Parliament a Government measure for dealing with factories and workshops,
the first for nearly twenty years, and last week a deputation interviewed the Minister
with a view to securing in the bill a clause that would provide for the registration of every
place used as a workshop. The provision would cover the case of a man working for
profit in his own private house.
"Shoddy" Footwear.
The President (Mr. F. F. Sprackling) moved that the council should take action to
protect the public against the ill-effects of shoddy footwear by setting up a special com-
mittee of inquiry with a view to legislative action. If they did not take it up as a trade
it would be taken up by the medical profession, and they could not deal with it without
the assistance of practical workers. It was not only the shoddy boot, but often the
adulteration of leather which caused the mischief to children's feet, and he hoped that
soon there would be nothing but pure leather used.
The resolution was carried.- Western Morning News, 9th May, 1924.

INTERNATIONAL LABOUR OFFICE NEWS.
"EQUAL PAY FOR EQUAL WORK."
A Committee appointed by the Swedish Government in 1921 to investigate the wages
and old age pensions of female employees of the State has recently presented its report
in a volume of nearly 300 pages.
The Committee suggests a common wages system for male and female employees,
with provision for the application of the family-wage principle. Taking as starting point
the principle that the work done by women in the service of the State should not be more
expensive than that done by men (i.c., equal wages for the same amount of work), the
Committee finds that a certain difference in the wages paid to male and female employees
(1) the rate of sickness among the female employees has been proved to be greater
is justifiable on the following grounds :-
by more than 40 per cent, than that of the men ;
(2) women occupy a special position as regards old age pensions, having regard to
longer average life ;
(3) the ratio between the quantitative output of work of men and women, and
(4) certain other factors, such as the liability of men to conscription and the impossi-
bility of the State ignoring wage conditions on the general labour market.

NEW RULES FOR TRADE UNIONS IN CHINA.
Interesting evidence of the changes in industrial and social conditions which are
being realised in China is afforded by the issue of draft regulations by the Chinese Govern-
ment authorising the organisation of workers into trade unions. Some of the more import-
ant provisions are the following:-
Workers engaged in the same occupation may organise into unions for the purpose
of securing their economic well-being and promoting their common interests. Trade
unions are legal personalities. They encourage mutual assistance among their members
and endeavour to secure an improvement in conditions of employment, they investigate
conditions of labour, make proposals to the Government with regard to labour legislation,
and answer all enquiries of the Government offices. Trade unions may establish branches.
In order that a union may be formed a proposal must be signed by at least 10 workers ;
the proposal, which must contain draft statutes for the union, is to be submitted for
approval to the appropriate local administrative authority. Workmen engaged in national
industries or public services must in addition secure the approval of the government office
in charge of the industry or service. In applying to the Government for permission to
organise a trade union, the promoters must submit, with the application, their own names,
and particulars of their age, native place, occupation, and address.

"SAFETY FIRST" IN WORLD INDUSTRY.
An American Record.
Details of the progress of the safety movement in industry in various countries are
given in the latest number of Industrial Labour Information, the weekly publication of the
International Labour Office of the League of Nations, from which the following extracts
are quoted :-
UNITED STATES.-Employees of the Delaware and Hudson Railroad, working in the
locomotive repair shops at Colonie, are claiming the world's railway shop safety "record."
The 1,035 men employed in these repair shops worked a total of 200,000 hours in the month
of January without a single "reportable" accident (an accident which causes a loss of
more than three days' work), and with no loss of time from accidents.
The railway company officials state that the great success resulting in this claim for
a safety "record" is due to a five-year active safety campaign by officials and men.
JAPAN.-The International Labour Office has recently received evidence of the interest
taken in questions of industrial safety in Japan. An organisation exists, known as the
"Safety Society of Japan" (Nippon Anzen Kyeki), the object of which is to promote
safety in factories and mines and also the safety of the general public.
The society, which works in close co-operation with the Social Bureau, is endeavouring
among other things to set up safety committees in the mines and factories. It is at present
devoting its attention to Marunouchi, an important business district of Tokyo. The
managing director, Mr. T. Gamo, hopes, however, in the near future to organise branches
in Osaka and Kobe.

ACCIDENT COMPENSATION FOR ALIEN WORKERS.
Information as to the possibility and scope of an international agreement on the
question of equality of treatment for national and foreign workers as regards workmen's
compensation for accidents is contained in a report just issued by the International Labour
Office of the League of Nations.
The possibility of arriving at such an agreement, says the report, appeared to be
considerably enhanced in consequence of the increasing extent to which the régime of
equality of treatment in respect of workmen's compensation has been established during
the last generation, either independently of or by means of special treaties between State
and State, and of the not insignificant similarity at any rate as to fundamentals which
exists between the laws on the subject in the different countries. The replies of Govern-
ments which have been received to a series of questions on this subject very largely confirm
this impression.
These replies, which have come from twenty-three Governments and four provinces
of Canada, are printed in the report and, in the light of them, the International Labour
Office has outlined a Draft Convention for discussion at the sixth annual Session of the
International Labour Conference which opens at Geneva on 16th June.
it undertakes to grant to workers who are nationals of any other State which has ratified
The main provision of the proposed Draft Convention is that a country which ratifies
the representatives of such workers, the same treatment in respect of workmen's com-
and who suffer personal injury by an industrial accident happening in its territory, or to
pensation as it grants to its own nationals, and not to make any discrimination against
ceased to reside in its territory. Special agreements are suggested to cover workers
these workers of their representatives by reason of the fact that they do not reside or have
temporarily or intermittently employed in such territory.

be discussed at the Sixth Annual Session of the International Labour Conference of the
The development of facilities for the use of workers' spare time is one of the questions
-the International Labour Office containing the replies of various Governments to a
eague of Nations which opens at Geneva on 16th June, and a report has just been issued
ries of questions as to the possibility and scope of an international agreement on the
bject.
Before it was possible for the Office to consider what should be included in the pro-
certain whether the Governments considered the question of the use of workers' spare
sals to be submitted to the Conference as a basis of discussion, it was necessary to
ne, which is a problem of an entirely new character, sufficiently ripe to be dealt with by
Recommendation indicating general principles and suggesting methods by which pro-
able utilisation of spare time might be promoted.
A large majority of the Governments have replied in the affirmative on this point.
ney recognise that owing to the differences of custom and tradition in the various countries
adoption of definite measures cannot be formally prescribed; but they consider
at identical problems are everywhere involved, and that the discussion might therefore
ad to the adoption of a Recommendation. This would, at any rate, as one of the Gerefore
ents points out, create some form of moral obligation for the Governments and the
mployers' and workers' organisations.
On the basis of these replies the International Labour Office has outlined a Recom-
endation for discussion by the Conference among the provisions of which are the
lowing :-
Each State Member of the International Labour Organisation should consider the
eans of so arranging the working day as to make spare time as continuous as possible
ternation of shifts, shortening of mid-day breaks, adjustment of working hours to the
ason and the like), further, by means of a well-conceived transport system, the time
ent by the workers between their homes and their work should be shortened as much
possible.
Among the institutions which may assist individual development and contribute to
e general progress of the community, those are recommended which have for their object
e improvement of the workers' domestic economy and family life (workers' gardens,
otments, and the like); the development of physical health and strength by means of
mes and sports; and the encouragement of technical and general education (libraries,
ading rooms, lectures, technical courses, educational courses, and the like)..
Attention is also drawn to the necessity of safeguarding the individual freedom of
e workers against any tendency towards obliging them to use any particular institution,
e most practical and successful institutions being those which have been started and
veloped by the workers themselves.

WORLD UNEMPLOYΜΕΝΤ.
Report to International Labour Conference.
Great interest attaches to the report on world unemployment which will be presented
by the International Labour Office of the League of Nations to the Sixth Annual Session
of the International Labour Conference which opens in Geneva on Monday, 16th June.
The report is the result of a resolution adopted at the Fourth Session in 1922 that the
International Labour Office should actively continue its work as regards the collection of
information and international co-ordination in the matter of unemployment. The reso
lution also stated that the permanent documentary inquiry of the Office should be made
to bear on the respective movements of production and consumption of the various classes
of goods; that a special investigation should be made of the causes and remedies of
seasonal unemployment and that, in collaboration with the Economic and Financial
Section of the League of Nations, the Office should make a special study of the problem
of crises of unemployment, their recurrencies and the fluctuations of economic activity,
to collate and compare, in particular, the results of the investigations made in various
countries, and to make known the measures taken with a view to sustaining economic
activity and thus stabilising the labour market.
It will thus be seen that the International Labour Office is studying not only the
particular problems raised by the world unemployment which resulted from the economic
disorganisation following the war period, but also the general question of unemployment
when world industry is in a normal state.
taining a survey of the world crisis of unemployment from 1920 to 1923.

POSITION OF THE WORKER IN RUSSIA.
Changes in the Last Six Years.
Very interesting details of the changes in the position of the Russian worker during
the last six years-all the information being taken from Soviet sources
publication just issued by the International Labour Office of the League of Nations, called
“Industrial Life in Soviet Russia, 1917-1923.”
are given in a new
The fundamental differences between the present system and that existing before
1921 are carefully demonstrated not only from the point of view of the State regulations
issued, but also from that of the actual conditions of labour prevailing. This dual method
of treating the subject is of importance when it is realised that there is still a considerable
margin in Russia between laws on conditions of labour and their application.
Since the inauguration of the new economic policy in 1921 the system of labour
legislation has been transformed. The new Labour Code starts from principles which
differ completely from those which were at the base of the former system. Compulsory
labour is, practically speaking, abolished. The engagement and dismissal of workers has
been declared free. The conditions of labour are determined by free agreement between
the parties, and the value of work is determined by the laws of supply and demand. The
central power defines itself to fixing a minimum wage, leaving to the parties concerned
the duty of determining the actual remuneration of labour by collective agreements.
introduced into Russia two years ago have exerted a far-reaching influence," says the
Conditions of work in Russia are at present governed less by the legislation
of the executive authorities, in spite of the considerable change in the principles of such
legislation, than by economic and social conditions, and in particular by the growth of
private capitalism side by side with State capitalism.'
volume.
The fullest details of this remarkable transition must be essential not only to the
student of economics but also to the political observer who is desirous of understanding
the present position in Europe.
TRADE UNION FAMILY ALLOWANCES.
A Belgian Experiment.
The Belgian Confederation of Christian Unions has established a fund for the payment
of family allowances to permanent members of the unions, states Industrial and Labour
Information, the weekly publication of the International Labour Office of the League
of Nations.
Under the scheme which came into operation on 1st April, the unions are to affiliate
to the fund all members who have reached 21 years. Family allowances will be paid in
respect of all children under 16 years of age, beginning with the third. For this year
the allowance is fixed at 500 francs per child per annum. Payments are being made
monthly by postal cheque sent direct to the members entitled to them.
In addition to these regular allowances, a birth bonus of 200 francs will be paid in
respect of each child, irrespective of the number of children in the family.
The unions will pay to the fund 275 francs per member per annum, this figure being
fixed on the basis of statistics of membership.

BOOTS AND HEALTH.
Dr. Ethel Bentham and the High-Heeled Girl.
Bad boots are one of the most prolific causes of ill-health, said Dr. Ethel Bentham,
Labour candidate for East Islington, in a speech at Highbury last night.
"It is really an exception," she added, "to find an adult foot that is not more or
less deformed.
"It is enough to make one weep to see the bulgy, swollen ankles and
misshapen calves and flattened toes of the high-heeled girl of to-day."
Unsuitable footwear accounted for one-third of the disabilty of women.
-Daily Herald, 26th May, 1924.

MONTHLY REPORT.

23RD JUNE, 1924.
TRADE.
There is little improvement in the state of trade compared with last
month, the figures given by the Ministry of Labour Gazette being as follow :-
BOOT AND SHOE INDUSTRY.
Employment was moderate on the whole during May, but was slightly better than
in the previous month. In some centres short time working was still prevalent, though
to a less extent than in April. Compared with May, 1923, conditions generally showed an
improvement.
The percentage of workpeople unemployed, as indicated by the unemployment books
lodged at Employment Exchanges, was 8.3 on the 26th May, as compared with 10.2 on
the 28th April.
Employment in London again showed a slight improvement. At Leicester it was
fairly good on the whole; although some short time was worked, the majority of factories
were running full time. At Northampton employment was somewhat better than in
April, but a considerable amount of short time was still being worked. At Kettering
short time was still worked in some factories, and, taken as a whole, employment was only
moderate. It was estimated that about three-quarters of the firms were on full time at
the end of the month. Employment continued slack at Wellingborough and bad at
Hinckley, and the majority of workpeople were on short time in these centres. In the
Higham and Rushden districts, however, although short time was still being worked,
employment improved, and was generally fair. It was still poor in the Raunds district.
At Leeds there was a further improvement in the light boot and shoe scction of the trade,
and employment in this section was very good; but at factories producing heavy footwear
employment continued quiet. A considerable improvement was reported at Stafford,
where employment was very fair. The slipper factories in the Rossendale Valley were
reported to be working full time.
Employment was again good at Norwich, and showed a further improvement; full
time was general and overtime was worked at a number of factories. At Kingswood
there was an improvement; but employment at Bristol was still only moderate, and much
short time continued to be worked. Conditions at Street were fairly good, and better
than in April.
The majority of operatives were fairly well employed during May at Glasgow, Edin-
bargh, and Kilmarnock; but at Maybole and Arbroath employment continued poor,
and a good deal of short time was worked.

MANCHESTER DISPUTE.
It will be recalled that quite recently a dispute occurred upon the firm
of Messrs. Gregg & Co., the operatives ultimately returning to work pending
further negotiations. The case was heard in London towards the end of last
month, Mr. W. Addington Willis (Chairman), Mr. O. Parker, J.P., and Mr.
G. Sedgwick, J.P., being the members of the Court appointed to hear the same.
An adjournment was made and the next hearing held in Manchester on the
4th inst. Mr. A. J. Dobbs represented the Union and placed the Union's
position before the Court.
The Court met in Manchester as stated above, and both sides gave
evidence, after which the Court adjourned, and we now await their decision.

JUBILEE YEAR CONFERENCE.
The Jubilee Year Conference of the Union was held on the 9th-11th inst.
at the Borough Hall, Stafford.
The Mayor of Stafford (Mr. J. Wheeldon) welcomed the delegates on behalf
of the Corporation and citizens, whilst Mr. Ingle sent a welcome on behalf
of the Labour Party. The General President suitably replied to the same,
and on behalf of the Union presented the Mayor with a copy of the Souvenir
"Fifty Years." The Conference, as is well known, was largely one to celebrate
the Jubilee of the Union. No alteration of rules was discussed. Mr. George
Sedgwick, J.P., who held the office of general secretary from 1878-1886, was
present, whilst the old "war horse," Mr. Harry Moreton, was prevented from
attending owing to illness.
In his presidential address, Mr. T. F. Richards said since the Union was
formed at Stafford in 1874, it had grown in membership from 4,207 to nearly
80,000, and its funds now totalled over £100,000.
They had had 29 years without a national conflict, and both employers and
employed were determined that there should be no conflict if it could be avoided.
They were one of the only Unions in the world which had a mutual
guarantee of £1,000 with the employers against strikes and lockouts.
Dealing with the subject of shoddy footwear, the President said most
poor men and women bought boots and shoes, guided by price rather than value.
They hoped that shortly the Board of Trade would help them in the pro-
duction of a boot, such as once existed in the war-time boot, made under
Government control, and to Government specifications.
That was, if he dared to say so, a socialised product, which was killed by
the distributors refusing to distribute for 124 per cent. and demanding 33
per cent.


---
315
A special committee was to be formed, with a view to legislative action in
this matter.
A good discussion upon the political situation took place, and the absolute
need for strengthening not only the industrial, but also the political work of
the Union, thereby increasing the usefulness of the organisation.
On Wednesday, the 11th inst., the delegates and friends inspected the
many departments of the Lotus Shoe Works (Messrs. Bostock's, of Stafford),
which was a revelation to many, showing as it did, what can be done in a large
up-to-date factory. The visit was much appreciated as also were the remarks
of Mr. Bostock, who stated that he desired for a better understanding between
employers and employed, to make the burden of work as pleasant as possible.
A full report of Mr. Bostock's speech appears on page 338.
We have more than Fifty Years' work behind us. The future is unknown

will be more fruitful than the past, and those that live to see the Union reach
its century may still see greater benefits accrue to the Union and the services
of mankind generally.
CONSUMPTION.
As is well known we have for many, many years past followed up the
question of the excessive rate of mortality of shoe operatives, due to con-
sumption. Although some improvement has been made during the past few
years, those members who die at 45 years of age and under still shows a high
death rate of members from phthisis. It is the more necessary that we should
ensure full compliance with any Acts of Parliament which have a bearing
upon the health of the members. If, therefore, there are evasions of the existing
Acts, we hope all members will at once report the same to their local officers,
so that the inspectors may be apprised of the same. We make no apology
for repeating what we stated last month regarding the lamentable lack of
efficient inspectors, and thereby neglect of oversight which is so necessary to
ensure full compliance with the law in factories. We appeal to the membership
not to lose sight of this matter, but to push the matter at their local Labour
Party meetings, and thus bring pressure to bear upon the Government to
increase the number of Inspectors, and thus bring about an improvement in
the condition of affairs.
POLITICAL.
The political situation, especially as represented by the British House
of Commons, is still full of interest. Parliament having re-assembled, there is
no doubt in our mind that real fighting will begin, and it is therefore the more
incumbent upon those of us outside the House to render every assistance to
those members in the House of Commons, and influence, if possible, members
of other parties to vote for the Bills which the Government will present.

LONDON DISPUTE.
The firm of Messrs. Jackson & Joseph do not work to the National Agree-
ment, although the National Officers, with London Metro. Officers, have tried
patiently for two years to bring the firm to recognise the agreements arrived
at by the Federation and the National Union. About twelve months ago they
left the Federation.
On 4th February, 1924, Mr. A. Mason and Mr. D. McCarthy met the heads
of the firm. A claim was made for the London Clicking Statement, the adoption
of the Holiday Scheme, the Graduated Scale of Wages, the Minimum Wage
at least for Females of 20 and over. The heads of the firm agreed to meet
them in May to see if an agreement could be fixed up.
On 2nd June, a letter was received from the firm, to the effect that their
workers were all satisfied, and refusing any further negotiations with us.
We appeal to all of you who believe in Trade Unionism and standing by
National Agreements, which gives Manufacturers and workers in various
districts a fair deal, to come with us and take their stand with the Union for
justice and fair play.

GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.

FELLOW MEMBERS,
SHODDY. In addressing you this month I am pleased to report that the interest
taken in the elimination of Shoddy Footwear still finds a place in the minds of the general
public through a very sympathetic Press, who in many instances urge us to proceed with
this matter until some action has been taken to either eliminate the same, cause it to be
altogether discarded, or a description given with each pair. As the matter now stands,
and having gained a fair amount of publicity and notice, it appears the time has arrived
for our Union to consider the matter in all its aspects; not only is it a question of the
construction of the boot or shoe that is being considered, but in addition, the Tanners
are taking some interest in the question as to the purity of the articles that are to be
utilised in the production of a boot or shoe. This is very interesting, when we find that
there is material on the market which is loaded with various substances, not with the
intention of bettering the article, but in the main making the most of the material for the
benefit and profit of the producer, as in shoddy footwear produce, in other words, shoddy
leather. In this connection one is reminded that in Australia, and recently in South Africa,
there are already existing in these two colonies prohibition against the use of varilum or
other deleterious compounds in leather, which is likely to weaken its usefulness.
We are hoping that not only the Boot and Shoe Trades Association, whose support has
already been proferred, will give us their invaluable help, but that we may get the support
of the Employers' Association in a matter of this kind. Even if we went no further than
make a demand that all boots and shoes for men, women and children, should be no less
in quality than a trades specification yet to be agreed upon. The idea that a warranty
with the goods denoting their composition appears to gain favour, and when one realises
that some of the paper insole shoes are sold at considerable profit, or are purchased at less
than half price than they are sold to the public, it gives one a very disturbed feeling that
those who have any power at all do not appear to endeavour to bring about some reform
in this direction. In my remarks in one or two newspapers, which I made at Stafford
there is a misprint, which in itself becomes elusive to us. I said that ink, heel ball, and the
paper sock, covered up a number of sins. A translation has appeared in some papers
translated by anyone who really understood the subject. I hope I may in my next report
be able to say that we have made further progress in this connection.

EARL SHILTON. - Eatoughs Ltd. have again been visited and our request pressed for
the adopted Rossendale Valley conditions, owing to the fact that they construct a shoe, such
as we do not make in this district, of a slipper character, and most of his work is also
Veldtschoens, but the employees are all members of ours. They have had a system of
paying from 1½ per cent. to 2½ per cent. on earnings as an annual bonus to remunerate
the workers, and this bonus was looked upon as being equal to our Holiday Scheme. It
was not paid last year, so that we have no other alternative but to press for our National
Agreement, all the operatives in the meantime having become members of ours. We hope
in a very short time to be able to report that the operatives at their Burton-on-Trent
factory, who at the present moment are in two Unions, i.e., the Rossendale Valley and
our own, and the employees also at Syston factory will become members. We shall then
be in a position to claim the application of the National Award in both cases.

At the request of the CO-OPERATIVE WHOLESALE SOCIETY, we attended the opening
of their new factory at NORTHAMPTON, which is destined to produce, they hope in the near
future, 20,000 pairs of boots per week. It is a very nice building, being the latest addition
to the industry, and like most of the new factories in our industry - to the credit of the
employers be it said, independent of their activities and actions with us is the last thing in
factories, and if work can be made a pleasure to men and women, certainly this factory is
everything that one could desire. One is not surprised at finding the best in the co-operative
movement, because this is part of our own movement. It is to their credit to say that they
as individual employers build some very beautiful factories, thereby showing that their
sole object in our industry is not to ignore the sources from which their income and wealth
comes.

DESBOROUGH. - It has also been my pleasure with my colleagues, to attend a pre-
sentation, a report of which appeared last month, to Mr. S. J. B. Barnes, when he was
presented with a clock and a barometer, as a memento for his many years services as
Secretary to the Desborough Branch. Be it said that Mr. Barnes, although he has trans-
ferred his life and work now to the manufacturing of boots and shoes, having thrown in
his lot with his brother, all of us who know and respect him, cannot do otherwise than
wish him well in his new sphere of life, believing that he is not likely to give us any trouble
in the future, but may be able to give us, as he has done in the past, some assistance, owing
to the knowledge that he has, not only as a clicker, but of the closing room, which helped

NORTHANTS ADVISORY COUNCIL. At our usual meeting of the Northants Advisory
Council at Kettering, a very interesting discussion took place on the subject of Boy
which was opened by Mr. W. R. Townley, of Northampton Branch. At the previous
meeting Mr. Langley, of Rushden, Mr. R. Poole, of Wellingborough, and others took a line
of his arguments, and endeavoured to eliminate them, for the benefit of all concerned.
I am perfectly satisfied in my own mind that this subject is of vital importance, as to what
we shall do with our boys, and it is very evident that greater restriction will have to be
put upon juvenile labour coming into the industry, not so much to protect our own industry,
as to protect the boys coming in. The same may, in a very short time, apply to girls,
because every operative who has to work for his or her living feels that they must enjoy
their own economic independence, if such is possible. Our members will not be surprised
therefore to learn that the shoe operatives of this Council consider there are three very
important things. One is, limit the boy labour in the industry; two, try to encourage the
Government to give subsidies to parents for keeping the children at school for a longer
period; and three, lower the pensionable age of persons who are compelled to retire from
business. A very interesting discussion took the whole of the afternoon, and as is usual,
tea was taken later. It was my pleasing duty to have the honour of presenting, on behalf
of the whole of the branches connected with the District Council, who had subscribed for
a presentation in the shape of a very nice gold watch to Mr. S. J. B. Barnes for his eight
years' Secretaryship, which gave me great pleasure owing to the kind feeling and respect
in which I hold Mr. Barnes. Mrs. M. J. Bell-Richards had been requested, and made a
presentation of a gold wristlet watch to Mrs. Barnes in a very appropriate manner. Mr.
Barnes responding, on his and Mrs. Barnes' behalf, said he felt overwhelmed with gratitude
and respect with which he had been held, and thanked us from the bottom of his heart
for our good wishes, and hoped he would ever retain that golden opinion. These matters
are too infrequent in our Union, and it is nice to find that at last there are times when the
feeling of comradeship and loyalty comes out and the services of those recognised who have
endeavoured to do their very best.
MANSFIELD.-We are still in contact with Mansfield in endeavouring by instigations
to the firm, and the holding of meetings of the operatives, to get them on a proper footing.
We are improving the position considerably. On the last occasion there were many
members who did not turn up, and it was only the operatives who were really in need
that found it convenient to come to the meeting. This is often the case as soon as our
members get a satisfactory state of affairs. In the workshop they fail even if only asked
once in three months to come to a meeting to come along at the proper time. One is
doubtful whether we are improving the membership by doing so much. If an officer
makes the slightest error, he is reminded quickly. However, our work must go on, whether
the members appreciate it or not, and we hope soon to have this firm, as many others,
working to our satisfaction.

STRIKER WINS CLAIM.
Overtime Rates for Boot and Shoe Operative.
A case of considerable interest to trade unionists came before the Old Street magistrates
yesterday, when H. Galliphant, a boot finisher, sued Messrs. Jackson and Joseph, of
Princelet Street, E., for money due to him for overtime.
Galliphant explained that a dispute had occurred in the works of Messrs. Jackson
and Joseph, owing to trade union conditions not being complied with. He ceased work
on Wednesday, 4th June, following instructions from his union officials. During his three
days' work previous to this, he declared, he worked seven hours' overtime, for which he
was paid at ordinary rates instead of at ordinary rates plus 25 per cent.
had offered to pay him the amount claimed, but this he had refused.
Since the summons had been issued, said the claimant, a representative of the firm
The magistrate, Mr. Watson, awarded Galliphant the amount claimed and costs.
proceeding, and the works are now being picketed.- Daily Herald, 18th June, 1924.

effect that the firm was not paying. This interview was neither pleasant or profitable,
and Mr. Vallance has placed the matter in the hands of the Union, as the local Executive
are determined to deal with this firm.
J. H. BAUM.

FOOD.
During May there was a further fall of d. per lb. in the average retail price of granu-
lated sugar and of d. per lb. in the average retail price of tea, the total decrease since Ist
April being 2łd. in the case of sugar and 3d. in that of tea. Fish, milk and cheese also
were cheaper, on the average, at the end of May than at the beginning of the month. On
the other hand, bacon was slightly dearer, and the prices of potatoes continued to advance.
The prices of meat, flour, bread, butter, margarine and eggs showed no appreciable change,
on the average, during the month.
As a net result of all the changes recorded, the average increase over the level of
July, 1914, in the retail prices (in Great Britain and Northern Ireland) of the articles of
food included in these statistics fell to about 60 per cent. at 31st May, as compared with
about 63 per cent. at 1st May. The Ministry of Labour Gazette, June, 1924.

BRANCH REPORTS.

ARBROATH. Our trade is still remaining bad, and it seems we are
destined to go through this year without much change. It is a pity that
fashion is more and more gripping the footwear trade, because a large section
of the public who were content formerly with normal wear, now seek the new
fancy leathers, and in the latest styles. Fashion is a fickle mistress, and
manufacturers who attempt to lead have an anxious time straining ever after
new effects. The old controversy as to whether fashion leads the makers or
the makers lead the fashion can be left out, because in some subtle way both
statements are true, and industry conducted on competitive lines can never
escape from the chaos and wastefulness of this compelling urge towards novelty
and unless something like normal employment is restored to the people of this
country many more businesses will go under. While purchasing power lies in
In the meantime small manufacturers are at their wits' end to know what to do,
few hands, comparatively speaking, such trades as ours will fluctuate according
to all manner of whims and caprices, but let better trade return to the main
industries, and the old-time commonsense trade will be experienced again.
It was touch-and-go, however, and the prospects for November are not bright.
Our members are delighted to learn there is not to be a cut in wages this June
before then. This "cost-of-living" basis for wages will more and more go out
although of course our Council will be again reviewing our National Agreement
of favour because it cannot meet the growing aspiration amongst workers for
a better standard of living. It is all very well to say it serves better for the
moment than any other proposal, but while it cannot be left out it should only
be used as the lever for a demand on a higher plane. The "cost of living"
for many a day was an argument only one of many-which was used to advance
the demand for a higher standard of life for the workers, but in those later
years, owing to numerous exigencies, the demand itself became the common
one of "an adequate wage to meet the cost of living." That served a purpose,
and may still do so, but nothing can prevent the old and truer demand again
being voiced for wages to meet the cost of living, to meet occasional holidays,
to enjoy a few recreations together with entertainments on a modest scale, and
provide against the inevitable "rainy day" as well. That claim on life is
natural and will grow stronger as time passes, and it is up to every Union to
prepare the way for the "fuller life" wage claim. It has often been argued
that bare necessities or "Fodder" should not be included in the wages at all.
A reasonable average amount should be earmarked to every worker as "upkeep
allowance," which would generally cover food, clothing and housing. And
then the wage-the real wage-would be the surplus demanded for adequate
relationships with life in its broad aspects. Visionary it may be meantime, but
young democracy will translate that vision into concrete form yet, and the
sooner the better. We hope that our Branches will discuss the new Agreement
prospects fully, and send in all suggestions to Council. Our Union should be
seething with ideas and views upon such problems, and, although often extrava-
gant, a very efficient policy is often the outcome of extreme demands hammered
out in debate. Our Jubilee Conference will be past ere these lines appear,
but our earnest wish is for its success. May the spirit of its founders be in the
hearts of the delegates, and may the best traditions of trades unionism be
maintained on such an occasion. The greatest monument to mark our Jubilee
year would be an improved National Agreement to brighten the lives of the
members and workers in the trade.

CORK.-Trade continues to show an improvement, due to the tariff on
imported footwear into the Free State. We would advise Branch Secretaries,
if any of their members are looking for work over here, to communicate with
the Secretary before accepting employment, as this will save an amount of
unnecessary trouble.
DERBY.-Trade in Derby is bad at the two Union shops. The C.W.S.
clickers have, most of them, been off about three weeks, and it does not appear
they will get a start before the holidays. Some of us were very much interested
with the opening of a new C.W.S. factory at Northampton, and we hope it
will be for the benefit of the operatives in that district. Some of us think
who are in the Co-operative Movement, that it is better for the C.W.S. to start
a new factory than to buy one, the same as they did at Derby, where there was
a capacity for and employees for 12,000 pairs a week when they only have
orders for about 5,000, which has meant about 100 have had to leave or have
been stopped this last four years, which means in a town like Derby that they
cannot find a market for their craft.
DESBOROUGH.-Trade here is quiet, for whilst some are working
overtime others are very short indeed, and we have more members unemployed
than we have had for some considerable time. On 24th May we had a Tea
and Social Evening, which was attended by our General President, General
Secretary, and Mr. W. R. Smith, M.P. We took advantage of the occasion to
make a presentation to our late Secretary, Mr. S. J. Barnes, J.P., consisting
of a handsome clock and barometer. This duty was ably carried out by Mr.
W. R. Smith, M.P., supported by Mr. T. F. Richards and Mr. E. L. Poulton, J.P.
Mr. Barnes suitably acknowledged the presents and wished us every success.
At the evening meeting the same gentlemen addressed a good attendance and
were well received. The Labour Choir also gave selections. We hope that as
a result of their visit there will be a good effect in our membership.
HIGHAM AND RUSHDEN.-We are pleased to state that trade has
improved during the month. Even in Raunds an improvement has been
noticed. We are grateful for the assistance rendered by the deputation to the
War Office and Admiralty, consisting of the General President, General Secretary,
Mr. C. Bates and Mr. Harvey (of Raunds), and also Mr. F. Gould, M.P., and
Mr. W. G. Cove, M.P. We are also pleased to report that we are back to 8,000
membership.
KINGSWOOD AND DISTRICT.-We are glad to report some signs of
improvement in trade, and trust that the improvement will be maintained.
We note with satisfaction that the Industrial Councils Bill second reading
was carried by 236 to 16, and we sincerely hope that sufficient influence will
be brought to bear with the object of getting the Bill "starred" for its third
reading this session. The very effective speech made in support by our colleague,
F. Gould, M.P., speaking, as he did, from personal knowledge and experience,
has been much appreciated by all those who believe that Trade Agreements
