should have the backing of the civil law, and thus give an opportunity to bring
the light of publicity to bear upon the unfair employer.
LIVERPOOL.---Boot repairing has been fairly good during the past month.
The world and his wife is off to Wembley and must have decent looking boots.
Members will note on page 274 of the May Report that we have had a flying
visit from our old friend, Mr. D. McCarthy. Note his comments re the Mersey
Dock and Harbour Board. In connection with this case we have been supplied
with a copy of the Section "9" Trade Boards Act, 1909. "Any shopkeeper,
dealer, or trader, who by way of trade makes any arrangement, express or
implied, with any worker in pursuance of which the worker performs any work
for which a minimum rate of wage has been fixed under this Act, shall be
deemed for the purposes of this Act to be the employer of the worker, and the
net remuneration obtainable by the worker in respect of the work after
allowing for his necessary expenditure in connection with the work shall be
deemed to be wages." At present the matter is sub-judice, so we reserve our
comments. In the Shoe Trades Journal, 6th June, under heading Versatile
Shoemakers, we note the following interesting paragraph: "Between Paramul
and Sofala on the Mudgee-Bathurst Road (N.S.W.), Mr. Tom Williams has
cultivated 200 acres of land, and while the young crops of wheat, oats and barley
are growing, he and his sons mend boots from Orange, Bathurst, Lithgow
and Mudgee. The scheme is simplicity itself. Mr. Williams visits a number
of towns, collects the boots and them does the jobs at the farm with up-to-date
machines. There are twelve in the family, so that both the industry and the
farm can expand quite a lot yet. Regular boot repairers in the various towns
the idea. They are thinking of
farming in their spare time." A good example, we should think, of the kind of
colonist the Empire needs. Working shoemakers are something like sailors
in that they are usually able to turn their hand to anything. In their own
phrase, they are "never beaten." Possibly those in the Colonies excel in this
direction, as it will be supposed that in some parts the exigencies of existence
would make for the development of the attribute.
NORWICH.--Trade continues good, much overtime being worked during
the past month. Claims, therefore, both to sick and unemployment benefits,
are much lower than has been the case for some long time past. The Norwich
Branch marked its Jubilee year on 29th May by having the General President
visit the city to officially open its new premises. For many years the local
officials have been compelled to work in offices that neither provided healthy
conditions for the occupants, nor suitable convenience for its members, and at
long last alternative building accommodation has been secured and adapted
to modern requirements. The Norwich members were pleased to hear the
General President unstintingly bestowing praise on the officers and congratula-
tions on the members. At least, we in Norwich now own offices and meeting
hall that corresponds somewhat with the standing the Union has secured in
the industry.

SCOTTISH TRADES UNION CONGRESS.
DELEGATE'S REPORT.
The twenty-seventh annual meeting of the Scottish Trade Union Congress was held
at Town Hall, Ayr, on Wednesday, 16th April, and following days. The delegates num-
bered 200, representing approximately 350,000 trade unionists, this being a decided im-
provement on last year. The chair was occupied by Mr. T. Wilson, Shop Assistants'
Union. Congress was welcomed by the Chief Magistrate, and also representatives of the
Trades and Labour Council of Ayr. The report of the Parliamentary District Committee,
or General Council, was presented and represented a document worthy of the movement,
demonstrating, as it did, minutely, the valuable work and the able manner in which the
many problems have been handled and dealt with during the year. There were seven
amendments to the Standing Orders and fifty motions from affiliated societies, besides
three from the General Council itself, which you will agree was quite a formidable agenda
for the time at our disposal, and consisted mainly of the following: Control of Industry,
Control of Credit, Trade Union Access to Wages Books, Accidents in Mines, Central Clearing
House, Daily Labour Newspaper in Scotland, Amalgamation of Trade Unions, Six-hours
day, National Scheme of Superannuation, Old Age Pensions, Trade Boards, Unemployment,
Housing, Workmen's Compensation Act, 1923, Lighting of Workshops, Labour College,
National Council, Education, Public Ownership and Control of Railways, and many others.
A resolution was agreed to demanding a closer relationship between the Soviet Govern-
ment of Russia and the Labour Government of this country. A Back-to-the-Unions
Campaign had been undertaken during the year. Meetings both in and outdoor were held
up and down the country, over a quarter of a million leaflets being distributed. It was
agreed to vote 150 as an annual subscription to the Scottish Labour College. This will
give the Council, or rather entitle them, to three representatives upon the National Execu-
tive of the Labour College. The speeches and debates were of a very high standard and
augers well for the future, as many of them were given by comparatively young men and
women. It was decided that Dumfries would be the next place of meeting, and 1924
Congress ended with "Auld Lang Syne."
C. BLEAKLEY.

PRESENTATION TO MR. ERNEST BORDOLI.
Union's Confidential Clerk Honoured.
Appreciation of Central Office Staff.
A number of delegates and friends attending the Jubilee Conference of the National
Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives were entertained to tea by the Leicester Women's
Branch, on Tuesday, 10th June, at the Vine Hotel, Stafford.
Amongst those present were:-Mrs. M. J. Bell-Richards (President of the Leicester
Women's Branch), Mr. T. F. Richards (General President), Mr. E. L. Poulton, J.P. (General
Secretary), and Mrs. Poulton, Mr. J. Buckle, M.P., J.P., and Mrs. Buckle, Miss A. Muir
(Secretary of the Leicester Women's Branch), Miss E. Sherwin (Assistant Secretary), Miss
E. A. Timms, Miss P. Billings, Miss Westbrook, Mrs. Goodwin, Mr. and Mrs. H. Poulton,
Mr. E. Bordoli (Confidential Clerk), Mr. W. E. Goldsmith Mr. C. Masters, Mr. L. Angell, of
the Central Office Staff, together with Miss A. Billington, Mrs. Bordoli and Mrs. Masters.
After a most enjoyable tea, Mrs. M. J. Bell-Richards, on behalf of the Leicester
Women's Branch, presented to Mr. E. Bordoli, Confidential Clerk, a Gold Watch with the
inscription :-
" Presented to E. Bordoli by the Leicester Women's Branch of the B.S.O.,
June, 1924."
Mrs. RICHARDS, in making the presentation, paid tribute to Mr. Bordoli's services
which he had rendered to the Leicester Women's Branch since the early days of 1913.
She recalled the fact that the services of Mr. Bordoli were performed when the Leicester
Women's Branch were really in need of help. He gave his services with a free heart,
without expecting any reward, and his special knowledge stood them in great stead.
Mrs. Richards, on her own part, said she and the officials of the Branch felt for a long
time past that some recognition was due to Mr. Bordoli for the way in which he had
always assisted the Branch, and felt that the time had now arrived when they could show
their appreciation of the work done for them. She further intimated that whenever she
called at the Central Office, she admired the spirit and comradeship amongst the whole
of the members of the Central Office Staff, and she was deeply indebted to them all.
Mr. T. F. RICHARDS, General President, heartily endorsed the statements expressed
by the President of the Leicester Women's Branch and members of the Central Office
Staff generally, and was delighted that the presentation had been made as an appreciation
of the services rendered both to the Branch and the Union generally. Mr. Richards said
Mr. Bordoli had always been very loyal to the Union.
Mr. E. L. POULTON, General Secretary, reviewed the early days of the Branch, and said
that he was greatly pleased with the spirit of comradeship amongst the members of the staff
and paid tribute to their loyalty, intimating that in Mr. Bordoli himself he had a colleague
who was trustworthy and anxious at all times to help forward the movement. He was
confident that the watch would be much appreciated by the Chief Clerk, and expressed
pleasure in being able to add this testimony. When he had to be away from the office,
he knew the work was in good hands, which was a great relief to him to feel this was so.
Mr. J. BUCKLE, M.P., J.P., said he and Mrs. Buckle were honoured and deeply touched
in being asked to be at the gathering. He had dared to say in the country, and even at a
conference, that the Central Office Staff were second to none of any Trade Union Staff.
The work was done efficiently at a minimum cost. He naturally did not come into contact
with Mr. Bordoli as much as other officials; nevertheless, Mr. Bordoli was always courteous
and anxious in the extreme to do all he could to put forward the Union's work. It was
a splendid appreciation of his work, and he was proud to bear testimony to it.
Mr. BORDOLI, in his reply, thanked Mrs. Richards and the Leicester Women's Branch
for their kind thought, and said he was deeply moved by their action. The present, which
came as a complete surprise to him, would be greatly appreciated, and all he had done
was done in the interest of the Union generally. He was deeply grateful to the references
made to him, and the Office Staff generally. He felt that the honour which had been
conferred upon him was undeserved, as always his endeavours had been, and would be,
to support not only the work of the Women's Branch, but of the Union generally. He
reviewed the work of the Union and its branches in 1913 as compared with the present
day, the Head Office staff being increased from two to nine members, the work having
increased considerably. In conclusion Mr. Bordoli once again expressed his heartfelt
appreciation of the thought which had prompted the Leicester Women's Branch to make
such a magnificent gift for the work he had done, and assured Mrs. Richards that the
confidence in him would never be misplaced.
Mr. Bordoli was congratulated by his colleagues of the Central Office Staff, who said
they felt that the honour done him was well merited, and extended to him the congratula-
tions of the staff generally.
An enjoyable musical evening was then spent.

NORTHANTS JOINT DISTRICT COUNCIL.
PRESENTATION TO MR. S. J. B. BARNES.
Following the Quarterly Meeting of the Northants District Council, a presentation
was made to Mr. and Mrs. Barnes, on behalf of the Operatives' Section of the Board of
Conciliation and Arbitration for the County District of Northants. Mr. E. Law, of the
Northampton No. 1 Branch, presided at the function. The present to Mr. S. J. B. Barnes
took the form of a gold watch and chain and bore the following inscription :-
"PRESENTED TO
STEPHEN J. B. BARNES, Esq., J. P.,
BY THE
NORTHAMPTONSHIRE BRANCHES OF THE
NATIONAL UNION OF BOOT AND SHOE OPERATIVES
IN GRATEFUL COMMEMORATION OF HIS
EIGHT YEARS' SERVICE ON
THE BOARD OF CONCILIATION AND ARBITRATION FOR THE
COUNTY DISTRICT OF NORTHANTS,
MAY 31ST, 1924."
The presentation was made by the General President, Mr. T. F. Richards, who, in
a very lucid and appropriate speech, commented on the excellent work which Mr. Barnes
had done upon the Arbitration Board in his capacity of Secretary of the Operatives' side
for a number of years. This work entailed a considerable amount of personal sacrifice,
and a considerable knowledge of the requirements of the trade. Mr. Barnes had shown
marked ability in the way in which this work had been performed, and, on behalf of the
Northamptonshire Branches, it was with very great pleasure that he presented the token
of esteem.
The present to Mrs. Barnes which consisted of a Gold Wristlet Watch with the in-
scription,
"PRESENTED TO
MRS. S. J. B. BARNES
IN GRATITUDE FOR SERVICES RENDERED
TO THE NORTHANTS BRANCHES OF THE
NATIONAL UNION OF BOOT AND SHOE OPERATIVES,"
was made by Mrs. T. F. Richards, who characteristically spoke at some length of the
sacrifices and work rendered to the movement by its women members.
She was particularly pleased to be present and to make the presentation to Mrs.
Barnes because of the distinct recognition which the Northamptonshire Branches had
given directly to the work and influence of women. A good deal, she affirmed, had yet
to be done in bringing the women's outlook and position on an equality with the men, but
more and more, it was asserted, the province and function of women and their equality
of work and service was being recognised and appreciated.
Mr. Stephen Barnes, in reply on behalf of himself and wife, thanked the Branches
for the presents, and claimed that in all his work he had tried consistently to do the best
that was possible for the members of the Union. He had looked for no reward, but he was
exceedingly gratified, that on his leaving the work, he and his wife should have been
honoured in this way.
Many aspects of his work were then touched upon, and considerable emphasis laid upon
the early struggles in the formation and development of his own branch.
Appreciative thanks were then passed to Mr. and Mrs. Richards for being present
and taking part in the function by Mr. W. Langley, of the Rushden Branch, and Mr. Geo.
Campbell, the President of the Kettering No. I Branch.

NEW BRANCH OFFICES.
Opening of Headquarters at Norwich.
Mr. T. F. Richards, General President of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Opera-
tives, opened the new headquarters of the local branches of the Union, at St. Mary's
House,
Mary's Alley, Pitt Street, Norwich, on the 29th May, 1924. The place has been exceed-
ingly well adapted to its new purpose. On the ground floor is a well-equipped separate
and well-lighted assembly room, which affords comfortable accommodation for 200
people.
At the opening proceedings the chair was taken by Mr. W. Hindes (president of No 1
Branch), and among others supporting him were Mr. T. F. Richards, Mr. F. C. Jex (secre-
tary), and Mr. A. H. Folkard. Mr. W. R. Smith, M.P., and Mr. Segon (president of No. 2
Branch) were unavoidably prevented from attending.
Mr. Hindes said they had met to commemorate the opening of that new building and
also the 50th year of the existence of No. 1 Branch of the National Union of Boot and
Shoe Operatives in Norwich. The boot and shoe operatives of Norwich, or, as they were
called in the cld days, rivetters and finishers, had a union prior to the starting of the
National Union. The two branches of the Union in Norwich to-day had a membership
round about 8,000. In a survey of the history of the Union in Norwich, Mr. Hindes said
the local organisation established an arbitration board before the national body adopted
such a step. (Applause.) The local organisation had every reason to be proud of what
they had done in securing better wages and improved conditions inside the factory.
(Applause.) He hoped the time was not far distant when as a Union they would have a
bigger control than they had at present over their industry.
Mr. Folkard gave some statistics relating to the growth of the local Union. In 1894,
when the original organisation of clickers and pressmen went over to the National Union,
they only numbered 76 members. The amount paid during the last five years in out-of-
work pay was £8,167 2s. 5d. and sick pay £2,544 2s. 11d. From the very beginning of the
organisation of boot and shoe workers in Norwich he had never ceased to hold office.
(Applause.)
Mr. Richards then declared the new offices open. In his speech he hoped the improved
conditions which the Union had brought about had not caused any suffering to the general
community. (Applause.) They had not been over-rabid in their demands, but had
simply followed up economically what they considered they were entitled to. (Hear, hear.)
He considered one of the best things the Union ever did was the obtaining of one week's
holiday with pay. (Applause.) They were not out solely for getting increased wages.
That matter was not the be-all and end-all of their activities. Although consumption
among boot and shoe operatives was decreasing it was not going down fast enough. (Hear,
hear.) The Union wanted to secure healthier surroundings for the workers, better work-
shops, more sanitation, and more light. (Applause.) He congratulated Labour in
Norwich on returning two Labour representatives to the House of Commons, and trusted
they would go on increasing their representation on the local bodies.
On the motion of Mr. Folkard, seconded by Mr. Jex, a hearty vote of thanks was
passed to Mr. Richards.

NOTICE.

GOVERNMENT CONTRACTS.

Contractors for Government work are required
in the execution of their Contracts to observe and
fulfil the obligations upon Contractors specified in
the Resolution passed by the House of Commons
on the 10th March, 1909, namely :-

"The Contractor shall . . . pay rates of wages and observe
hours of labour not less favourable than those commonly recognised
by employers and trade societies (or in the absence of such recog-
nised wages and hours, those which in practice prevail amongst
good employers) in the trade in the district where the work is
carried out. Where there are no such wages and hours recognised
or prevailing in the district, those recognised or prevailing in the
nearest district in which the general industrial circumstances are
similar shall be adopted. Further, the conditions of employment
generally accepted in the district in the trade concerned shall be
taken into account in considering how far the terms of the Fair
Wages Clauses are being observed. The Contractor shall be pro-
hibited from transferring or assigning, directly or indirectly, to any
person or persons whatever, any portion of his contract without the
written permission of the Department. Sub-letting other than that
which may be customary in the trade concerned, shall be prohibited.
The Contractor shall be responsible for the observance of the Fair
Wages Clauses by the Sub-Contractor."

This notice must be prominently exhibited, for the
information of the workpeople, on the premises where work
is being executed under a Government contract.

MR. RICHARDS ON SHODDY FOOTWEAR.
Let us leave the vexed questions of colours and fashions and turn to a subject which
more nearly concerns every shoe retailer in the country that of Shoddy Footwear, and
inextricably bound up with that aspect of the shoe trade.
Everyone will agree with Mr. T. F. Richards, the President of the National Union of Boot
and Shoe Operatives, that shoddy boots and shoes are not made by shoe manufacturers
because they are "bad at heart." But one does not feel inclined to agree with the opera-
tives' President's further assertion that it is because they are careless of the wearable
qualities of the articles. He added that they were careless of the quality because their
minds were centred on dividends to their shareholders. Whether a shoe manufacturer is
in business on his own account, or is the managing director of a company, he has got to
make a profit, or his business would cease to exist. He has to supply the public need, as
expressed through the retailers, and when that demand is for cheap shoes the manufacturer
has got to make them, or get out of business. His customer says: "I want a boot at a
certain price. If you can't make it I must go elsewhere." Does Mr. Richards suggest the
price; you must go elsewhere"? Let us see where Mr. Richards leads us—or rather
leads himself and the boot and shoe operatives.

Will Mr. Richards Order "No Shoddy Shoes"?
It may be assumed from his pronouncement that the Union is strongly averse from
the making of shoddy footwear. Why, then, does it permit its members to take part in
their manufacture? We will agree that it is not because the operatives employed in
factories where shoddy footwear is made are bad at heart. But as you can't make fish of
one and fowl of another it is because, according to Mr. Richards, they are careless of the
wearable qualities of the articles they help to produce. "It is a libel on the boot and shoe
operatives," I shall be told, but Mr. Richards is responsible for the libel, and not I, because
I do not believe it. If the operatives in question said: "We will not make shoddy foot-
wear," however, they would be presumably in the same position as their employer. He
would reply: "Then, if you are backed up by your Union, I suppose I cannot get other
operatives for
his Union to order "No operatives are to assist in making shoddy boots," and as the Union
in the trade, no more shoddy boots would be made,
and the public would have to pay more for their boots.

The Wicked Retailer Again!
This is the logical outcome of Mr. Richards' pronouncement. It is the only consistent
course he can adopt. But what is the lame conclusion he arrives at as to the responsibility
for the manufacture and sale of shoddy boots? It is the greed of the retailer! What he
wants is that reliable boots shall be made at the same cost to the public as they now pay
for shoddy, but that while the manufacturer would get more for them, as he would have to,
or he could not make them, unless the tanners gave him the leather or he stole it, or unless
the operatives consented to operate for considerably reduced wages, both most improbable,
or say impossible, contingencies, the retailer should distribute them at 12 1/2 per cent. gross
profit instead of 33 1/2 per cent.
Looking a Long Way Ahead!
"The war time boot," says Mr. Richards, which the trade "agreed was the best
civilian boot known in our time, made to specification under Government supervision,
a Socialised product, was killed by the distributors, who refused to distribute at 12 1/2 per
cent. and demanded 33 per cent." This is a perversion of the fact. While everyone else,
boot manufacturer, operative and factor, got their recognised profit, the retailer was asked
to forego his. They looked forward very shortly, Mr. Richards went on, to the Board of
Trade helping them in the production of such a boot. If that means that "they" are
looking forward to the Board of Trade stepping in and forcing the retailer to distribute at
12 1/2 per cent., then " very shortly" is surely a very loose figure of speech, for undoubtedly
they" are looking forward a long way! I should like to hear the opinions of Mr. John
Hoyle and Mr. Henderson Neal as to the probable length of this vision!
-Shoe and Leather News, 19th June, 1924.

"TIRED OF SHOES."
Why Dr. Ethel Bentham Shows Impatience.
"I am sick and tired of shoes," said Dr. Ethel Bentham, Labour candidate for Isling-
ton, when asked by a Weekly Dispatch representative to enlarge on her statement that
"bulging, swollen ankles, misshapen calves, and flattened toes" are the products of
ill-fitting and tight shoes.
"The modern fashionable shoe, I honestly believe, makes it nearly impossible to
find a perfect foot to-day.
modern-
1924.
Nearly every foot is deformed by the cramping and compressing of the foot in the
But there I am again-shoes, shoes, shoes!" - Weekly Dispatch, 1st June,

"THIS MISERY OF BOOTS" - H. G. WELLS.
I am delighted to see the protest made by Dr. Ethel Bentham against the footwear
of the woman of the present day.
Much illness, bad temper, broken-down nerves, and scamped work are directly attribut-
able to the discomfort the average woman suffers from her feet. No male, secure upon
his square toes, can possibly realise what she endures.
Why do bootmakers like women to wear uncomfortable shoes? Is it that in cutting,
the sole too narrow and the toe bent inwards, there is a certain saving of leather which
makes for larger profits?
I always ask for shoes cut as men's are, wide across the big toe joint and with a straight
line from the arch of the instep to the end of the big toe. Over each new pair of shoes
I have had to fight a battle. It is the same with the shoes of my four children.

Yet "No Complaints!"
Till lately I was a rich woman, and rich women can afford to pay for what trades-
people consider their phantasies. So I have paid extremely heavily, in money, time, and
trouble to prevent my feet and my children's feet being deformed by bunions-the inevitable
result of the high heel and the toe slanting inwards. But poor women cannot pay for
these things.
The result is that the feet of the nation's children are now so deformed that people
who write articles in the Daily Mail do not even notice that there is anything to criticise,
and consider Dr. Ethel Bentham a crank because she has called attention to the facts.
They don't know what undeformed feet are like.
The only females in this country who have normal feet are those of the very privileged
classes; and they are the only people for whom normal footwear is made.
During the war, the boots supplied to girls who worked on the land under Government
auspices were all cut with the slanting toe. One girl-in an agony-spoke to me about it,
and I wrote to headquarters. The answer came back that "mine was the first complaint."
I am told that there is a place in Mayfair, instituted by Madame Pavlova, where
beautiful and well-built footwear is sold. But it is, of course, prohibitive in price. It
must be until bootmakers are driven by their clients to supply proper footwear.
There is a fortune waiting for the bootmaker who will start making pretty, becoming.
normal shoes. Daily Herald, 9th June, 1924.

you, Sir, to remind the audience that I am President of the Federation. I am now address-
ing you in a private capacity and not as a member of the Federation, and anything I say
now is not to be used against me in evidence. (Laughter.) We are pleased to be associated
with you. It is a very remarkable history of the Union you've issued. Fifty years of
hard work which has placed the industry and its organisation in a high position. I am
satisfied that that state of affairs could not have been brought about unless the Union
had had as officers and leaders people who commanded the respect not only of their con-
stituents, but of the people with whom they negotiated. It was a very happy thing
for the shoe industry that it had not got away from the stage when masters and men, or
employers and employed, met together in their daily work and knew each other. You
may think we are hard-perhaps some of us are-but some of you are pretty tough nuts
(laughter), yet we are able to meet together and settle our differences. There is a great
deal of work still to be done by the Union and the Federation acting together. The Federa-
tion is being asked to accept responsibility to finance the Research Association and Science
in our trade. We ought to discuss the conditions that make work pleasant and put them
into force. In our factory we have two "rest" intervals-one at 10 a.m. and one at 4 p.m.
Some feared the output would fall as a result. I never had any anxiety myself, and I am
glad to say our people are satisfied that if we gave up the "rest" periods it would be fatal.
In our factory we have tried to get cleanliness and as much light, sun and air as possible.
In our factory we don't always have rain, and people say what a clean town it is. We live
in a charming part of England, engaged in a necessary industry. I believe in your debates
you have talked about tuberculosis. This is a disease which can to a large extent be con-
quered by living under better conditions and getting more sunlight. Everyone of us should
do all in our power to urge forward smoke abatement bills, and so try to promote better
surroundings. Mr. Richards, I could talk to you for many hours longer, but after three
days I imagine you have had as much talking as you wanted. I should, however, like to
say what a pleasure it has been to me and my fellow directors and everyone in the factory
to show you round the factory, and we are proud to let you see the things we have remedied.
I thank you very heartily for the honour done us by coming to our factory. (Applause.)
MR. T. F. RICHARDS: I know Mr. Bostock does not wish us to pass him a vote of
thanks, but on your behalf wish to say how very much we appreciate his kindness. (Cheers.)
MR. R. DUNN: It would be indiscreet for me to let this occasion go by without
saying a word. This is a red letter day for Stafford. I wish England had more employers
like the Lotus people. They are splendid people to deal with. It is nothing but fair to
say how much we appreciate what these people do. (Applause.)

IMPORTANCE OF FOOT COMFORT.
"People seem only just to have discovered the enormous importance of foot comfort
to the general health," said Mr. Sinclair Bunting, lecturing to Birmingham mothers on
Thursday last.
"Change your shoes and stockings frequently," he said, and, if possible, never wear
shoes,
which are practically airtight, should be avoided by all sufferers from tender feet."
He further advised them not to wear very high or very low heels. Moderate heels,
he said, with a good base, were best, and never to change suddenly from very high to very
low heels, as the sudden change will do more harm than wearing the high heels - Shoe
and Leather News, 19th June, 1924.

LUNACY ACT.
MR. BUCKLE, on 5th June, 1924, asked the Minister of Health, whether, in the case
of the additional London County Council Asylum about to be opened in the neighbourhood
of Epsom under the name of West Park Mental Hospital, he will say whether it is intended
for the care and treatment of certified patients: what accommodation it will afford
and whether voluntary boarders are to be admitted?
Answered by Mr. Greenwood.
The answer to the first part of the question is in the affirmative. The institution will
provide accommodation for 1,732 patients.
My Rt. Hon. Friend regrets that the law does not allow voluntary boarders to be
admitted for treatment in public mental hospitals.
MR. BUCKLE, on 5th June, 1924, asked the Minister of Health, whether he is aware
that the majority of early cases of nervous breakdown cannot be proved to be dangerous
or unfit to be at large, and that they are in consequence in no sense lunatics and cannot
be classified among those whose treatment comes under the purview of a Royal Com-
mission on Lunacy; and, in view of the fact that no legislation is needed in order to make
provision for their benefit, will he take steps to supply without delay this need by the
allocation, where desired, of a grant to the health committees, as distinct from the asylums
committees, of local authorities, to enable and encourage the provision of appropriate
hospitals for early cases which shall be free from detention and unconnected with lunacy
administration ?
Answered by Mr. Greenwood.
Many early cases of mental illness are clearly certifiable under the Lunacy Act and
could not be detained for treatment unless they were certified without contravening the
provisions of that Act.
The question of providing facilities for treatment without certification will be con-
sidered by the proposed Royal Commission, and my Rt. Hon. Friend proposes to await
their report before considering what action should be taken.
AGRICULTURAL WAGES BILL.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Noel Buxton) introduced the above-named Bill
on Monday, 2nd June, 1924, when it secured a second reading.
During the debate Mr. W. R. Smith (Parliamentary Secretary) said: "We have no
cause for complaint in regard to the general tone of the debate. There seemed to run
through all the speeches an agreement that some form of machinery is needed to deal
with wages in the agricultural industry. There seemed also to be agreement that even
when wage decisions have been reached, through whatever machinery may be ultimately
established, the rates should be compulsory and capable of being legally enforced. . . .
I think this House has a right to ask in what material way the Wages Board machinery
failed during the years of its existence. The Wages Board was in existence for over four
years.
There were five minimum rates of wages fixed by the Agricultural Wages Board.
The first was a wage of 30s., fixed by mutual consent; the next was a wage of 42s., also
fixed by agreement. The next was 46s., and it is quite true a majority vote decided it,
but, strange to say, although the farmers at that time said they could not pay the wage,
yet I have since read an article in the Press, the weekly notes of a farmer who speaks with
some authority, who stated when he was objecting to paying 30s. a week in the spring of
last year, that it was different when the 46s. was fixed. He said, 'we paid it then willingly,
because we could afford to do it, but the farmers on the Wages Board said they could not
afford to pay it. That is my point. The first three rates were fixed by mutual consent;
the next was fixed in face of the opposition of the farmers, who stated the industry could
not stand that wage, and then afterwards a farmer in the public Press admits they paid
it readily and willingly, because the industry enabled them to do so. . . . We have had
to engage more inspectors to see the farmers paid the proper wages to their men. The
Wages Board alone recovered from farmers in this country over £40,000 in arrears of wages;
as much as £100 was obtained by one of the unions in arrears in respect of wages from
one man."
The Vote was put and there voted 245 Ayes; 214 Noes.

AGREEMENT IGNORED.
Union Withdraws Boot and Shoe Operatives.
Protracted negotiations between the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives
and a firm in Spitalfields having failed to produce any result, a crisis has arisen owing
to the refusal by the firm to recognise the national terms of agreement.
The Union has accordingly been compelled to instruct its members to withdraw from
the firm, and to place an embargo against other members working for it.
Large retail factors have also been asked to discontinue placing orders until the firm
complied with the national agreement.
Mr. Dan McCarthy and Mr. Len Smith are dealing with the matter, and hope to
achieve good results, not only in the Spitalfields area, but in other parts of London where
the sweating of boot and shoe operatives is prevalent. — Daily Herald, 7th June, 1924.

SHOEMAKER'S SON WHO IS A "KING."
Matty Island, one of the Solomon group, is ruled over by a European "king" who is
the son of a shoemaker. The islanders and cannabalism are not strangers, and the "king"
has before now been near to being an item on the menu of his subjects.
Christen Nielsen Oertoft was the "king's" original name—he is a Dane—but when
after the war, the Solomon Islands became British, he changed his name to William P.
Leonard. — Evening News, 10th June, 1924.

SHOES MADE FROM OLD FILMS.
Mary Pickford may be on your Dancing Pumps.
No city in the world, probably, observes the old adage "Waste not, want not" more
carefully than does London to-day.
Old films, for instance, are boiled down and, after a certain proportion of silver has
been extracted, the residue is used for making patent leather.
Thus your shiny shoes or dancing pumps may contain a tiny fragment of a portrait
of Pola Negri or Mary Pickford. — Evening News, 4th June, 1924.

INTERNATIONAL LABOUR OFFICE NEWS.
WORLD LABOUR CONDITIONS.
Delegates from all Lands at Geneva.
Delegates from all parts of the world will gather at Geneva on 16th June for the

ARTIFICIAL LIMBS.
Valuable International Studies.
A remarkable volume containing descriptions of the various artificial limb-fittings
at present in use in different countries, classified according to the type of amputations
and the method of manufacture, will be published early next week by the Internation
Labour Office of the League Nations.
The volume which is called "Artificial Limbs: Appliances for the Disabled." is
amply illustrated and contains about three hundred pages. It should be of the greatest
value not only to those interested in the problems of ex-service men disabled in war, but
also to persons injured in industrial and other accidents, and marks a great step forward
in the international comparative study of measures for the better welfare of workers
throughout the world.
The preparation of this work arose out of a wish expressed by an international con-
ference of representatives of disabled soldiers and seamen held at the International Labour
Office at Geneva in 1922 for the collection and dissemination of all available information
concerning the best type of artificial limbs and orthopædic instruments, and especially
those designed to enable the maimed to earn their livelihood by industrial or similar
employment. It was particularly desired that this information should be made as widely
available as possible.
The International Labour Office therefore entrusted the task to Dr. Florent Martin,
director of the Technical and Scientific Institute of Artificial Limb-Fitting at Brussels,
and the volume is published under his name.

very large extent, and sometimes even to enable the disabled man to follow a trade as

MINE-WORKERS IN CHINA.
Proposed Reforms.
The steady progress which is being made in the State regulation of working conditions
in China, which started with the issue of factory regulations in March last year, is carried
still further by drafting of regulations dealing in detail with conditions in mines, according
to information received by the International Labour Office at Geneva and printed in its
weekly publication, Industrial and Labour Information.
These provisions apply to all mines employing more than 50 underground workers.
The mine-owners are to be represented by the chief engineer who is to deal with questions

of ventilation, the presence of gas or water, and the use of explosives in the mines. No
women or children under 12 are to work underground, while in certain circumstances
limited to ten per day. The shafts must be properly supported and each pocket must
the employment of children under 17 may also be prohibited. Hours of work are to be
have at least two openings for the passage of labourers. Safety lamps are required in all
mines where the presence of coal gas is suspected.
The regulations also deal with payment of wages, hours of work and general labour
conditions of women and children, as well as of men. They do not, however, contain
any provisions with regard to wage rates, and it is unlikely that any special provisions
to make the fixing of a uniform minimum wage possible or desirable for the whole country.

DO FIXED PRICES MEAN MORE WORK?
Lessons of the World Unemployment Crisis.
"The acute unemployment suffered throughout the world from 1920 to 1923 is closely
connected with the periodical crises which have afflicted the working classes and humanity
as a whole for a century" is one of the important conclusions reached in a report by the
International Labour Office of the League of Nations, which will be presented to the
Sixth Annual Session of the International Labour Conference, opening in Geneva on Monday
next. The report is the result of an inquiry into the world unemployment crisis under-
taken by the Office at the instruction of previous sessions of the Conference.
"True, the great questions of international relations," continues the report, "result-
ing from the war and the Treaties of Peace, have gravely affected the national economy
of many countries, and continue to do so, resulting in the complication and aggravation
of unemployment."
The result of the inquiry seems to indicate, however, that apart from certain exceptions,
the available statistics show scarcely any correlation between changes in unemployment
and fluctuations in foreign trade. In many countries the period of most intense unem-
ployment was accompanied by a greater volume of exports than at some other date, for
instance, 1920, when industry was very active and unemployment only moderate.
On the other hand, there has been a close correlation between unemployment and
price fluctuations, which had already been recognised by most economists as one of the prin-
cipal characteristics of the economic cycles and periodical crises of unemployment before
the war.
The report proceeds to show how nations are not so closely inter-related from the
economic point of view, as before the war, and how the disappearance of a universal currency
standard has led to the movement of prices in each country following an individual course.
While, before the war, periods of general depression tended to become more or less simul-
taneous throughout the world, it would now seem more exact, instead of speaking of a
world crisis of unemployment, to describe the calamitous period of 1920 to 1923 as one
of a series of national crises. The conclusion is therefore reached, states the Report, that
crises of unemployment are a direct consequence of the instability of prices.
Further, in each country, the influence of the home market on industrial activity
would seem to be more important than that of foreign markets, whence it follows that
the restoration of the purchasing power of the mass of consumers is the most important
condition for the recovery of trade.
True, the instability of prices is not an ultimate cause; for it is the effect of numerous
causes, among the most important of which are variations in the volume of currency and
credit and the conditions of the exchanges. These factors themselves raise the important
problems at present dominating international policy (interallied debts, reparations, &c.)
which have a powerful influence on the individual financial and monetary policy of most
countries.
If the recurrence of unemployment crises in different countries is to be prevented,
an effort would have to be made, if the above suggestions are well-founded, to stabilise
prices; but perhaps such stabilisation would not be possible in certain countries without
first settling the important international political problems which have interfered with the
financial stability of these countries.
Thus, at the end, one comes back to the fundamental idea "that the achievement by
each country of stability in the value of its currency is an essential prerequisite of economic
reconstruction."
The details of this inquiry will be published in a full report, "Unemployment, 1920-
1923," by the International Labour Office, the above extracts being taken from the brief
report which is being submitted to the delegates attending next week's conference.

been working on certain evenings of the weeks as a waiter and assistant at a club. A

Recommended by the Court of Referees that the claim should be disallowed. The
Court formally disallowed the claim, and expressed a desire that the Umpire's decision
should be obtained. They were of opinion that the case hinged on the question whether
the applicant's average of remuneration exceeded 3s. 4d. per day.
The applicant's Association appealed to the Umpire.
Decision.- " On the facts before me my decision is that the claim should be disallowed
until 7th March, 1923.
"The applicant having ordinarily followed the occupation of working at the bar of the
Working Men's Club in addition to his usual employment and outside the usual working
hours of that employment is entitled to be considered as unemployed on those days in
respect of which he does not receive remuneration exceeding 3s. 4d.; but on any day
in respect of which he receives more than 3s. 4d. as remuneration for his work at the club
he must be deemed to be not unemployed.
"It appears, however, that as from the 14th July, 1922, until the 7th March, 1923,
the applicant did not apply in the prescribed manner, and his claim must be disallowed
for that period, but after the 7th March he will be entitled to claim in respect of days on
which his remuneration did not exceed 3s. 4d. per day." The Ministry of Labour Gazette,
June, 1924.

STANDING ORDERS.

BIENNIAL MEETINGS.
RULE 80. Biennial Meetings of the Conference shall be held on Whit Monday
and subsequent days.

TIME OF CONFERENCE MEETING.
RULE ST. On the first day of Conference the Delegates shall assemble at a
place provided for the purpose, at Eleven o'clock a.m. prompt, and
shall proceed to the election of Two Tellers, and shall also consider
the President's Address and Council's Report; after which the
Conference shall adjourn at 12.30 p.m. and re-assemble at 2 p.m. and
proceed with the business of the Conference and adjourn at 5 p.m.
On Tuesday and each succeeding day, the time of meeting shall be
9 30 a.m., adjourn at 12.30 p.m., re-assemble at 2 p.m., and adjourn
for the day at 5 p.m.

DELEGATES' QUALIFICATION.
RULE 82.-The Conference shall consist of Delegates who have been elected
in accordance with General Rules 71 and 77, which read as follows:-
Delegates shall be elected in accordance with the number of Financial
Members returned in the December Report previous to the date on which
the Conference is to be held. All Permanent Officials shall attend the
Conferences by virtue of their office, over and above the maximum of
representation. The basis of representation for delegates shall be one
delegate for every 1,000 financial members, with a minimum representa -
tion of not less than fifty delegates (one third to form a quorom)."
"The latest date for sending in amendment and additions to Rules, or
Standing Orders of Conference, shall be February 15th, in the year in which
the Conference is due to be held, and they shall be published in the
February Monthly Report. Nominations for delegates shall be taken on
the February Monthly Meeting Night, and voting for same on the March
Monthly Meeting Night."
The Council to attend by virtue of their office.

PRESIDENT OF CONFERENCE.
RULE 83.-The President of the Union, by virtue of his office, takes the chair
at all Conferences.

STANDING ORDERS COMMITTEE.
RULE 84-A committee of five persons shall be elected from the Delegates
of the Conference, whose duty it shall be to examine the Delegates"
Credentials, and report thereon. They shall also be at the service of
the Conference to consider any questions or matters that may be
relegated to it with a view to reporting thereon during the sitting of
Conference For such extra services they shall receive additional
pay, to the amount of 10s. each.

THIRTY-SIXTH CONFERENCE.
JUBILEE YEAR - 1924.
RESOLUTIONS.
1. COUNCIL'S ADDRESS.
2. KETTERING No. 1 BRANCH-" This Conference, believing that Education
is essential to the full development of the Trade Union movement,
recommends this Conference to discuss the problem in its widest
aspect, and to determine, that, as soon as the Educational Policy of
the Trades Union Congress is issued, this Union will do everything
possible to develop such policy amongst its members."
3. LEICESTER NO. 1 BRANCH. - "To ask the Council to meet the Manufac-
turers' Federation with the view of altering the age when members
become entitled to the full Minimum Wage from 23 years of age to
21 years of age; also the Graduated Scale to be altered accordingly."
4. LEICESTER NO. 1 BRANCH. - "That owing to the increase in the amount
of work involved in the administration of the State Unemployment,
Branches shall receive not less than 6d. in the pound."
5. LEICESTER NO. 1 BRANCH.-"That the Executive of the Union press the
employers to consider the wisdom of curtailing the Juvenile Labour
in our trade to one male person under 19 years to every five persons
over 19 years, as we are convinced that on the basis of 1 to 3, the
industry has been incapable of absorbing the Juveniles, when they
have passed into the Adult stage."
6. LEICESTER NO. 1 BRANCH.-"This Conference asks the Council to press
for the abolition of Overtime, or claim double time for same."
7. LEICESTER NO. 1 BRANCH. - "This Conference asks the Council to strongly
press for a reduction in the hours of labour from 48 per week to 44
per week."
8. NORWICH NO. 1 BRANCH. - "That the Executive Council do approach the
Home Secretary with a view to securing legislation demanding a
reasonable standard of light, air, and general cleanliness in all work-
shops and factories used for the manufacture of boots and shoes."
9. STAFFORD BRANCH. - "That this Conference instructs the Executive
Council to arrange an Educational Scheme with the National Council
of Labour Colleges under which free classes and Correspondence
Courses would be available for our members, such scheme to be paid
for by an allocation of 3d. per member per annum from the funds of
the Union."

MONDAY, 9th JUNE, 1924.
Conference Opened.
THE Thirty-sixth General (Jubilee Year) Conference of the National Union of Boot
and Shoe Operatives opened at the Borough Hall, Stafford, on Whit-Monday,
9th June, 1924.
The General President of the Union-Mr. T. F. Richards-presided, and the Con-
ference opened at eleven o'clock a.m. In addition to the General President, there were
also present the members of the Executive Council: Messrs. T. Adnitt, J.P. (Leicester),

The Chairman's Address.
General Secretary.
on behalf of the Union, and to contrast the delegation with that of 50 years ago. This
It is pleasing to me to have the honour of welcoming you all here as delegates
delegation consists of 53 permanent officials, 2 Parliamentary Representatives, and one
unofficial, 68 delegates, or 123 all told, covering a membership of 77,243. Compare this
with the 25 delegates who represented the Conference in 1874 with a membership of 4,207
only. In addition to this, we have now seven branches owning their premises and offices
valued at over £30,000, whilst the funds in hand of all the branches of the Union total
£102,744 5s. 2d., which is used for branch purposes only.
We meet to-day to commemorate 50 years' existence of our Union and to summarise
a few of the yearly milestones we have passed from 1874 to 1924. We are fully aware
that prior to that date there were in many towns local unions who practically stood alone,
unmindful and indifferent as to the fate or future of their fellow craftsmen in other towns,
and so on the 29th December, 1873, they decided to form a National Union. There
gathered together in this town of Stafford, 25 delegates from the following towns: Leicester,
Nottingham, Northampton, Leeds, Chester, Worcester, Manchester, Hull, Stone, Nantwich,
Birmingham, Newcastle, Bristol, Glasgow and Norwich, who laid the foundation stone for
our Union, and these magnificent men founded the National Union of Boot and Shoe
Rivetters and Finishers, as it was then known. Even when the present President joined
there were not 7,000 members in the Union after 11 years of its existence. It has been
my pleasure to know personally, every Gercral President and General Secretary except
living General Secretaries, and Mr. Poulton and I are the only two delegates present who
one-Mr. H. Horsfall. The present General Secretary and Mr. G. Sedgwick are the only
ference decided to have a permanent General President, Mr. J. Judge being elected. He
were here in 1892. It is gratifying to know that in this town in the year 1892 the Con-

held the position for a few months only, being appointed in September, 1892, and retiring
in May, 1893, and sent a letter to the Council explaining that he did not appreciate being
made a "social outcast." I hope those who think an organiser's job is easy will remember
this. At a later date, in addition to the General President and General Secretary, the
Conference in 1918 decided to have four permanent Organisers, but owing to the outbreak
of war the Council felt it would be unwise to take the risk, which caused them to ultimately
take the responsibility of two only; but in 1923 a third organiser was appointed, thereby
showing that this part of our work is of premier importance. But we cannot stop there.
The work of the Union proper will be found in the Souvenir, but there are still some items
not included which may bear a little elaboration. To my mind the two outstanding
features in our work was in the first place the demand for indoor working, and in Leicester
this matter was entered into with zest, zeal and spirit, which brooked no delay. Here
we had a large body of men whose education was never more than elementary, determined,
come weal, come woe, their homes should be workshops no longer, and although these
men enjoyed more personal freedom than most industries, they were prepared to change
home employment for factory life, and to once and for all save themselves, their women
and children, from the degradation of waiting outside a factory for hours or even days,
as though they were begging for work. The employers on the Board of Arbitration met
the officials of the day in a fair and honourable manner, and with a very few exceptions
was accepted, and in a very short time, and so Saint Monday became a thing of the past,
and to the everlasting credit of the Lasters and Finishers of Leicester, they sacrificed
their own freedom for the benefit of the wives and children of their shopmates. The
next great event of our history was the lockout of 1895, which cost the Union sixty-two
thousand pounds. Their fellow trade unionists contributed £1,049 1s. 10d. It would
serve no useful purpose to in any way reiterate the feelings engendered by both sides
during the six weeks that that struggle continued-suffice being to say we both won.
And as a proof of that we have had 29 years without a National conflict or anything likely
to create any such feeling. We know each other's measure, and we also know there are
employers on the other side high up in the confidence of the Federation who are imbued
with the same spirit as ourselves, that it would not be to our credit to be unable to settle
our troubles by any other means than that of wordy warfare, fought out by us, responsible
for both sides, without either a stoppage in the industry or the imposition upon our wives
and children that they should take part in the conflict.

The objects of our Union are unique as Clause 20 indicates-The socialisation of the
means of production to be controlled by a democratic state in the interests of the entire
community, and the complete emancipation of labour from the domination of capitalism
and landlordism; with the establishment of a social and economic equality between the
sexes. No one will be surprised that we are meeting in Stafford to-day, because Stafford
is the home of high-class ladies' shoes, second to none in the world. Its operatives or
journeymen, as known in the olden days, were just as well known for their superior crafts-
manship.as their forefathers were in all towns and villages, as the only craftsmen who were
a trouble to the Parson and the Squire, and it was therefore to their everlasting credit
that the Shoemakers of Stafford should send one of the first two Labour members to
Parliament in the person of Mr. Alexander MacDonald-a miner-he being elected in
February, 1874; the other Labour M.P. being Mr. Thomas Burt-also a miner-he being
elected for Morpeth at the same time, the very year of our Union's birth. But where,
oh where! is Stafford to-day? This is not all. Stafford has played its part in political
affairs, but we must not forget the neighbouring town of Wolverhampton, who sent the
first member of our Union-T. F. Richards-to Parliament in 1906 (who, by the way, was
born in Staffordshire), and then, lest we forget, let us remember that the President of the
Employers' Federation, Mr. H. J. Bostock, is also a native of Stafford, and a gentleman
in whom we have explicit confidence. Is it not therefore most fitting that Stafford was
chosen to celebrate our Jubilee year. We cannot stop here. Our Union in 1918 had then
a second member in Parliament in the person of Mr. W. R. Smith, sent by the Wellingboro'
Division of Northants; and in 1922 two other members, Mr. J. Buckle for Eccles, and Mr.
Alderman Hill for West Leicester were returned, and yet again in 1923 we saw Mr. W. R.
Smith returned for Norwich with another Labour member, Miss Jewson, for which we
ought to be proud that our members stood by their own; Mr. J. Buckle re-elected for
Eccles, whilst another of our members, Mr. F. Gould, was returned for the Frome Division
of Somersetshire, and has since been elected as one of our Parliamentary representatives,
but the greatest feat of all was the advent of the Labour Party's strength from our first
Labour Party in the House of Commons, of 29 members in 1906 to 192 elected in 1923,
and within a few months of the Conservative Government being unable to function the
Labour Party were called upon to form a Government on the 23rd January, 1924. In
this connection one of our members, Mr. W. R. Smith, was asked to assume the office of
Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries. Mr. Smith has
spent many years with the Agricultural Labourers' Union, and was its President from
1911 to 1923. He was chosen by the Agricultural Labourers' Union to represent them on
the Agricultural Wages Board. We all hope that the Agricultural Labourer will some day
wake up and claim his own. We may help to remove obstacles from his path, but his
destiny is in his own hands, and to this end we may rely upon it, that if the Labour Party


---
cannot help him, then no one else will. In the past the minds of the members of late
governments have been directed by their own personal or private business positions;
their wealthy friends advice and attachment has not been lost upon them; they have
been "nobbled" by newspaper editors, and influenced by the flattery of their immediate
friends, and so ofttimes subordinated themselves to their advisers-a danger Labour men
must observe. All men are prone to this, and many may fall victims, especially those
who have neither the time or inclination to study a subject for themselves. The first
Labour minister set a good and wise example when he took office, intimating that he would
only do so on one condition that he be allowed the right to appoint his own secretary.
This was granted and both the Minister and the Department were an immediate success.
The Labour Party took office on the 23rd January, 1924, and immediately made it known
to Russia, Germany and France that they were anxious to uphold the rights of all European
peoples, to bring Peace to all nations. Among many other things in their brief spell of
responsibility, they have tranquilised bankers and business men who have already signified
their intention to help rather than to hinder the Government. They have promised to
remove the means limit for Old Age Pensions; they have removed the gaps in connection
with State Unemployment Benefit taken away the restrictions to single persons;
removed the stigma from ex-service men in asylums; given relief to Poplar; introduced
a housing scheme; removed many restrictions and taxes from the breakfast table; set
the officials on the track of income-tax dodgers; introduced permanent relief for agri-
cultural labourers; propose raising the meagre income of those needing work by increasing
the unemployment benefit by 3s. per week; and are making an effort to relieve the parents
of very young workers to avoid blind-alley employment. In addition, they have coin-
menced schemes of afforestation foreshore reclamation, and have given their word to
mothers; make lawful the 18-hour working week (which I hope will also include mothers;
and take definite action in respect to land values and to grant votes to women at 21 years
of age.
Coming to our own industry, we have been more fortunate than some. We are the
only Union in the world to have a monetary guarantee against lockouts and strikes, and
so general has the belief become amongst our own members, and so cordial have been the
relations between the employers and ourselves, that we united in asking the Government
of the day to impose the conditions agreed upon by the majority, upon the minority at
least as a minimum. We were informed a fortnight ago that Mr. F. Murrell, the Liberal
Member for Weston-super-Mare, had secured an early place in the ballot and had given
notice to introduce the "Industrial Councils Bill." Having been introduced, it received
the second reading on the 30th May last, and carried by 236 votes to 16. We wired all
the shoe representatives in the House of Commons, and sent a letter to every member of
the House, urging them to support the Bill. We are not favourable to compulsory arbitra-
tion for any trade, but we are in favour of compelling the minority to have not less than the
minimum enjoyed by the majority, nor to accept worse conditions, because they pull
down for personal reasons, and do not build up for the public good. Should this Bill
become law, as we hope it will, we trust that in Committee such safeguards will be found
as to make its application not less favourable than the Trade Board Acts, which, with
very slight reservations, work exceedingly well; the main reservation is the small number
of inspectors to administer the Act. Some of us often feel we are almost asking too much
from so few inspectors to keep in order those employers and operatives affected, under
the control of over forty Trade Boards, when there are only thirty-five inspectors to do
the whole of the work. The handsewn boot and shoemaking and repairing board has not
less than 30,000 employers on their list to look after, and this in itself is more than any
meagre staff can accomplish.

SHODDY.
The Cordwainers' Company was founded in 1272, and their object is as stated
in their Charter granted in 1842-" To end all fraud and deceit in the Craft." That
Company and its objects appear to have fallen into decay, because some of us have known
hidden there. It has been said that there is fraud in all trades except brushmaking,
the virtues or the crime of heel ball; ink; and paper socks and the many sins that lie
and in that they put the little ones in the middle. It is for this reason that many of us
think the time has arrived when the general public ought not to be bamboozled by making
payments for articles that are not what they seem, and have no description or guarantee
as to their composition. Most poor men and women, especially when buying boots and

As a Union we are prepared to accept help from any other section of the industry,

recently appointed a committee for the purpose of holding an enquiry into the question

on the health and purses of the poor. The only two methods to prevent this appear to
me to be (1) To issue a white list of retailers who deserve the support of the movement,
and to get the support of the Board of Trade to insist that every retailer gives a written
document of the materials used in the production, this to be given with every pair of boots,
then (2) Bring the matter before the Trades Union Congress, Labour Party Conference,
supply every trades council, labour party and co-operative organisation with this white list.
Since the Suspension Benefit scheme came into operation in September last, the Union
has paid out the sum of £6,155 4s. 3d. for members who have unfortunately been suspended,
thus proving once again the great assistance our Union has been to members during times
of distress.

THE MAYOR OF STAFFORD (Mr. J. Wheeldon) to address the Conference.
Mr. President, Ladies and Gentlemen: I am pleased to be present to extend to you a
very hearty welcome, and hope you will have a successful conference. I understand
this is the Jubilee Year Conference, and that you have been in existence for fifty years.
I congratulate you upon the good work you have done. You have set a good example
to many other organisations by being able to settle your differences without disputes.
The day has come when matters should be settled without resorting to strikes (hear,
hear), and the day should not be far distant when nations ought to settle disputes without
war. (Hear, hear). You have done many things to shod the foot of man; most of my life
has been spent in trying to put something into the head. I have been engaged in educa-
tional work all my life, and retired from school a year last September, and later came
into political life and asked to accept the position as Mayor. You say "there is nothing
like leather." I suggest "there is nothing like education." It is efficiency which tells.
I believe in some of your centres you have classes of those engaged in the industry, and
those who attend - if they feel so inclined - can obtain details and experience of the trade.
We have classes of that kind, and they are doing good work. In this town one large
firm is sending down, voluntarily, a number of boys and girls for instruction in the day-
time, in addition to the evening classes. That is all to the good of the worker. I don't
know how many of you have visited Stafford before, but it has improved during the past
forty-five years, and compares very favourably with any other industrial district of the
country. There are many ancient buildings here, and you may have a salt or fresh water
bath. I wish you all success, and hope your conference may tend to promote peace
between employers and employees. (Applause.)

Council's Address.
THE GENERAL SECRETARY read the Address of the Council to Conference
as follows:
FELLOW DELEGATES,
1.—OUR JUBILEE.
26th May, 1924.
Our first words to you, as delegates, must be words of congratulation, seeing we are
assembled together in connection with the work of the Union. The National Union of
Boot and Shoe Operatives has been in existence over fifty years, the official birthday being
on the 2nd February, 1874. During the past fifty years both industrial, economic, and
social conditions have very materially changed, and upon the whole for the betterment of
mankind, We are well aware of the great amount of distress existent at the present time,
due largely to the World War, and the effect of which we shall continue to feel for many
years. Making, however, full allowance for the awful happenings arising out of and in
connection with the War, we are firmly convinced that very considerable improvements
have been made in the lot of the worker. We do not propose to go further into this matter
in our Address to you, because the Jubilee Souvenir (a copy of which each delegate has
received), deals fully with those matters, which are not only of interest to our trade but
to the country generally.
2.—TRADE.
The state of trade since our Conference in 1923 has, to some extent improved, but
not to anything like the amount as to find work for all those employed in the industry.
This is reflected in the amount of money we have been called upon to disburse as Unem-
ployment Benefit as follows :-

Four months ending April, 1924

STATE UNEMPLOYMENT BENEFIT.—We venture to say that it is distinctly advan-
tageous to the members to have drawn their State benefit through the agency of the Union,
and we hope that all branches will make arrangements for their members to have State
benefit through the Union in accordance with Rule 26.
In this connection we note that a resolution appears upon the Agenda asking for an
increase in the amount paid to the Branches for administrative purposes. We would point
out, however, that if such an amount as asked for was agreed upon, it would take the
WHOLE OF THE ADMINISTRATION MONEY allowed for this work. We feel con-
fident the delegates will see that it is not possible to concede the amount named in the
resolution in view of the fact named above.
3.—NATIONAL CONDITIONS.
The work of the Union has been carried on without friction so far as the Employers’
Federation is concerned, the machinery for dealing with differences that call for adjust-
ment having been found equal to the demands put upon it. A few non-federated firms
have given us some amount of trouble. Here, however, thanks to the methods adopted,
due to our many years of experience, we have been enabled to not only deal with firms
who were not complying with the national agreement, but to secure compliance with the
same, and this at a minimum of loss of time to the members, which in itself is a point that
should not be lost sight of as to the value of the Union to its members.
4.—THE NATIONAL AGREEMENT.
When we were negotiating with the Employers in November, 1922, it will be recalled
that amongst our requests was one for a reduction in the hours comprising a working week.
We pressed this point very strongly, and although upon that occasion we were not success-
ful in our claims, nevertheless, we left the impression upon the Employers’ minds that we
shou’d continue to press for a reduced working week when next our demands were submitted.

5.-FACTORY ACTS.
At our meeting in January, 1924, we decided to approach all the Members of Parlia-
ment connected with the boot and shoe industry to use their best endeavour to see that the
recommendations drawn up by mutual consent of the Joint Industrial Council representing
the boot and shoe industry-of which both the Employers' Federation and ourselves are
the sole members and representatives of the Home Office, in securing the proposed
Report of Recommendations in any new Factory Act likely to be introduced.
follows:-
The Recommendations which were arrived at on the 4th December, 1919, are as
JOINT INDUSTRIAL COUNCIL.
Report of Recommendations affecting the Health of Workers as revised by the Sub-Com-
mittee on December 4th, 1919.
1. LIGHTING.
(a) NATURAL.
(1) In any new works, underground workrooms should be prohibited.
The definition of the term underground workroom was left to the Home
Office.
(2) As regards existing Works, no underground room should be used
as a workplace after a period of three years unless a certificate has been
given by H.M. Inspector of Factories that it is suitable for that purpose,
that in the event of exception being taken by the owner, occupier, or any
operative employed in such factories to the withholding or otherwise of such a
certificate, the case shall be referred by that party to the J.I.C., which shall
be required to investigate and report its opinions to the Chief Inspector of
Factories, Home Office, and further that the Home Office shall take no
official action in the matter pending the receipt of such a report.
(3) All windows must be kept clean, inside and outside.
(b) ARTIFICIAL.
Artificial lighting should be adequate, and the light should be so placed
and shaded as to prevent, so far as practicable, the rays of light from im-
pinging directly on the eyes of the workers.
2. CLEANLINESS.
(a) WALLS AND TOPS.
The legal requirements should be strictly enforced, and in view of the
number of existing regulations and the difficulty of strict enforcement, this
Council asks that if the staff of Inspectors is inadequate for the purpose,
the Home Office will seriously consider the advisability of appointing addi-
tional inspectors for the Boot and Shoe Trade.
(b) FLOORS.
(1) In order to facilitate cleaning, the floors of all workrooms should
be maintained in good condition.

FIRST AID EQUIPMENT.
(126.) A First-Aid Box or cupboard must be provided in every factory,

(128.) Where an ambulance room is provided, and arrangements are made
for the immediate treatment of all injuries occurring in the factory, the Chief
Inspector of Factories may issue a certificate exempting the factory from the above
provisions to such an extent as he may decide.
This being of considerable importance to all workers we hope that if our members

not complied with, they will at once send full details to their branch officials when the
matter will be dealt with.

11.-POLITICAL MATTERS.
The past twelve months has been a period wherein history has been made very rapidly
indeed. No one, we venture to suggest, would have thought at our last Conference, that
before the year was out the then Prime Minister, the Rt. Hon. Stanley Baldwin, M.P.,
with his big working majority in the House of Commons, would have forced a General
Election. Yet, as we know, such an election did take place, and with very different results
from those anticipated by the then Prime Minister and his friends.
It is not for us to go minutely into the why and the wherefore of the reasons for the
procedure adopted; it is enough for us to know that the result was to bring into office a
Labour Government, and thereby bringing into practical politics many of the questions
which had been the "plaything" of the older parties-housing, unemployment, and inter
national matters-including an open and frank talk with France, the eight hours day and
ever, must not expect that the whole of our programme can be carried out at once, having


---
23
regard to the fact that the Labour Party, although in office, does not command a majority
of the votes in the House of Commons. Nevertheless, the outlook for labour will, as a
result of such accession to authority, be a very considerable improvement in the sphere
of those questions which so vitally affect the lives of millions of our fellow citizens.
It is especially gratifying to know that our colleague, Mr. Walter R. Smith, M.P., J.P.,
has been appointed to a post in the Labour Government, viz., that of Parliamentary
Secretary to the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries.
We felt at the time of his appointment that he would justify the honour conferred
upon him, and the months that have passed since his appointment fully confirm our views
having regard to the manner in which he has handled the business connected with the
office he holds.
In addition to Mr. W. R. Smith, M.P., J.P., being returned to Parliament as the
Senior Member for Norwich, we are very pleased to record the fact that Mr. J. Buckle,
M.P., J.P., was re-elected for the Eccles Division for a second time, and the secretary to
our Midsomer Norton Branch-Mr. F. Gould, M.P.,- whilst not being a nominee of the
Union, won the Frome Division of Somersetshire for Labour.
Mr. Len Smith was the candidate for the Daventry Division of Northants, but we
regret that he was unsuccessful. Nevertheless, a good fight was put up and Labour's
views were brought very prominently before the electorate.
The General President-Mr. T. F. Richards and General Secretary-Mr. E. L.
Poulton, J.P.-having retired from the position of Parliamentary candidate, two other
members were elected to fill the positions-Messrs. D. McCarthy and F. Gould, M.P.
Seeing that Mr. Gould was already a member of the House of Commons, we consulted
with him as to his position in the Frome Division, and as a result of our conversation, we
decided to recommend that £100 per annum be granted to Mr. F. Gould, M.P., until the
next General Election.
A resolution dealing with the Political Fund will be submitted to you during the
Session for your endorsement.
12.—REVISION OF NATIONAL AGREEMENT.
Our Agreement with the Employers' Federation is nearing the time when the same
can be once more reviewed. We have given careful consideration to the outlook in the trade,
and as a result of our survey we have sent along to the Manufacturers' Federation certain
proposals.
We hope, when we meet the appointed representatives of the Employers, that our
request for the above-named revisions of the Agreement will be acceded. The delegates
and members may rest fully assured that no effort will be wanting on our part to ensure
success being attained. Meantime, a great deal can be accomplished by the members
themselves to talk about the proposals and to back them up in their several districts.
13.—CONCLUSION.
In conclusion we feel that it may confidently be stated that with all our handicaps
and shortcomings, the half century which has now elapsed since the Union was started,
has been a period wherein very considerable improvements have been secured, and the
way made much easier for the younger generation—who will soon take our place—to
accomplish greater things in the next half century; this, because of the sacrifices made by
not only officials, but of the membership as a whole.
We therefore trust that the days to come may be both brighter and fuller of the real
joys of life than any of the days that are now behind us.
Yours fraternally,
T. F. RICHARDS, General President.

the Government used to play with the districts which made goods for them, and shift
the orders about without regard to the operatives working in a particular district. As

THE GENERAL SECRETARY: I should like to correct the impression in regard
to the Agreements. Mr. Attewell talked of 21 and 23 years of age. It should be stated
that in 1914 there was not a national minimum, nor could we establish one. We had to
agree to this :-
"From the commencement of the first working week on or after 1st January.
1915, there shall be an increase of 1s. per week at 22 years of age and over, in all
existing minimum wage rates for male operatives, and from the commencement of
the first working week after 1st December, 1915, there shall be a further increase of
Is. per week at 23 years of age and over, in all such minimum wage rates
At the same time we established a minimum wage for heel-building departments
this for the first time in our industry, and also a minimum for the closing departments.
It was not until 1919 that we actually established a National minimum. The Council
will remember that at that time (1914), we could not enforce a National minimum rate,
and at the same time felt we could not ignore the additional shillings offered. A vote of
the members was taken and the Agreement accepted.
