Factory Acts.
Paragraph 5 and Resolution 8 were next dealt with.
8 Norwich No. 1 Branch. "That the Executive Council do approach the
Home Secretary with a view to securing legislation demanding a reasonable
standard of light, air, and general cleanliness in all workshops and factories
used for the manufacture of boots and shoes."
Mr. F. C. JEX (Norwich): This resolution was drafted before we knew a Bill
was to be presented to Parliament. The Norwich members wanted the Executive Council
to take an opportunity of paying more attention to the matter. They tabulated the
resolution, not so much because of the circumstances under which the industry is governed
at the moment, but for the time when we have better trade. During the war we found
men of all grades anxious to invest their capital. We have information that all from
dentists to bricklayers put their spare cash into six new firms in Norwich. Houses which
had been condemned long ago, were equipped and used as factories. The operatives
had good wages, but their hygienic conditions of working were deplorable. Owing to the
lack of power we found it nearly impossible to control these factories. Now, in many
instances, these conditions have passed away because many of the manufacturers have gone
out of business, or two or three have united and chosen the best place for the time being.
The time is coming when our industry will have a boom; then you will see speculative
capitalists anxious to put money into the boot and shoe industry. We feel steps should
be taken to secure legislation which will make it necessary for a certificate to be obtained
from the Medical Officer of Health before factories can be used. I know it will incur
expense, and more professional examiners being appointed, but whether that is so or not,
as to whether we shall want more permanent staff or ornaments if you like it must
be done. I agree our Council have done much, but we want the Council to know the members
in the country are at the back of them. We are concerned with all the general conditions
surrounding the life of the operatives, in addition to the question of wages. They are the
things which lengthen the life of the operatives. We commend the Council upon the steps
they have already taken, and hope they will go still further.

(2) The foregoing provision shall not apply to any underground room used only

or any part of which is so situate that half or more than half the whole height thereof,
measured from the floor to the ceiling, is below the surface of the footway of the
adjoining street or of the ground adjoining or nearest to the room.
(4) Any certificate issued under this section may be withdrawn by the inspector
for the district if such alterations are made in the room as in his opinion to render-
it suitable.

PHTHISIS IN THE BOOT AND SHOE INDUSTRY.
Principal Union Officials visit the Home Office.
HOME SECRETARY'S REPLY.
At the request of the Executive Council of the National Union of Boot and Shoe
Operatives, a deputation consisting of Mr. T. F. Richards (General President), Mr. E. L.
Poulton, J.P. (General Secretary), Mr. J. Buckle, M.P., J.P., Mr. F. Gould, M.P.,
and Mr. Ernest Bordoli (Confidential Clerk), waited upon the Secretary of State for
Home Affairs the Rt. Hon. Arthur Henderson-on Friday, the 4th, April, 1924,
at 10.30 a.m., at the Home Office, Whitehall, London, S.W.I.
Mr. W. R. Smith, M.P., J.P., was prevented from attending owing to being
engaged on work connected with the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries.


---
In addition to the Secretary of State for Home Affairs, there was also present
from the Home Office Sir Malcolm Delevingne, Mr. R. Bannatyne, C.B., Dr. Legge,
C.B.E., and Mr. C. G. Markbreite, C.B.E.
MR. RICHARDS: I hope you will pardon us for the brevity of our case. We are
well aware of the gentleman we are addressing, and know the Secretary of State has
full knowledge of the facts, otherwise we may have gone more fully into detail.
I have known the Secretary of State firstly as a workman, councillor, and during
my brief period in the House of Commons always found him interested in the subject
about which we have called to-day.
The object of the deputation is to impress on the Department the vital necessity
of incorporating in the proposed new factory legislation, the series of resolutions
the outcome of a special Conference of representatives of the Boot Manufacturers'
Federation of the United Kingdom, and representatives of the National Union of
Boot and Shoe Operatives, held at the Home Office in 1917.
This deputation, however, consisting exclusively of representatives of the National
Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives, particularly desires to emphasise, that although
in agreement with the resolution whereby it is proposed to increase the cubic capacity
feet per operative, that the Home Office will agree to secure a clause in the new fac-
now provided in the present factory Act of 250 cubic feet per operative to 500 cubic
tory Act, whereby there shall be a minimum space of 4 feet between every operative
working in a boot factory at a machine or bench.
We are emphatic in this recommendation because the Medical Research Com-
mittee in its investigation, having special regard to the boot and shoe industry and
prevalence of Phthisis, reports on page 6 of its report, as follows:-
"The air space as measured by cubic capacity per person always exceeds
as minimum of 250 cubic feet required by Section 3 of the Factory Workshots
Act, 1901, and was found in 100 factories of varying sizes to average 800 to 900
cubic feet per head."
In the same report it is stated that although the cubic feetage provision in the
Factory Act was in almost every case exceeded there seemed to be a general congestion
in the departments.
Again expert evidence was quoted conclusively proving that for operatives
sit within three feet of each other constituted a danger zone as far as the disease of
Phthisis was concerned.
This deputation also wishes to impress upon the Home Office the necessity of
the proposed new factory legislation to make provisions whereby it shall be com-
pulsory for all boot and shoe operatives to be employed in factories. Our reasons
for making this suggestion are because we have knowledge of the fact that there is
still a large number of boot operatives employed in small workshops in connection
with their homes, where factory legislation is evaded, and our great desire is to see that
the new proposed factory legislation eliminates from our industry all conditions which
tend to sweating and creating unhealthy conditions of labour.
This deputation also wishes to strongly urge on the Department the necessity
for some provision being made in the new factory legislation whereby it shall be
compulsory for every employer of labour in connection with the production of boots,
shoes and slippers, or preparing or manufacturing parts in connection with the manu-
facture of boots, shoes or slippers, to register or otherwise secure a license to use as a
factory any particular building for the employment of labour under the Act.
This deputation wishes to express its great dissatisfaction with the inadequacy
of the department staff of inspectors for the enforcement of the Factory Act. The
deputation has knowledge of the fact that scores of boot, shoe and slipper factories
are never visited by a factory inspector unless it is in the case of following up an
accident which has been reported.
The deputation, therefore, sincerely hopes that the department will take imme-
diate steps to increase its staff to enable it to thoroughly administer the law.
In the appointment, however, of any additional factory inspectors the deputation
seriously suggests that the time has come when expert practical men who have been
thoroughly trained in the industry should be alone appointed, in connection with that
industry is concerned a special staff should be created to thoroughly administer the
industry; in other words, this deputation wishes to recommend that as far as its own
Acts, and that staff should consist exclusively of men who have worked and gained
their knowledge in the factories.
In connection with this recommendation this deputation suggests that in the
appointment of inspectors the ordinary Civil Service examination should be dispensed
with, and the persons appointed should be appointed on the sheer merit of their
practical experience and knowledge of the industry.
---

---
37
In conclusion, we would respectfully remind you that we speak as a deputation
on behalf of the workers of an industry which has been singled out by the Medical
Research Committee owing to the fact that the death rate from Phthisis is abnormal,
statistics showing that boot and shoe operatives dying from all causes between 20 and
45 years of age over 50 per cent. die of consumption.
We are anxious that these important matters should be brought to your know-
ledge. It would be like taking coals to Newcastle to try and educate you upon the
subject. At a number of meetings we have held with the boot employers, resolutions
them. We trust you will give this matter your serious attention. Reports were
were passed in this connection, and we certainly hope you will have time to consult
ment look upon the matter seriously. We hope you will not overlook us when legis-
issued in 1915, 1920 and 1921, through the Home Office which show that your Depart-
lation is brought in.

Factories that it is suitable for that purpose, that in the event of exception being taken
by the owner, occupier, or any operative employed in such factories to the with-
holding or otherwise of such a certificate, the case shall be referred by that party to
the J.I.C. which shall be required to investigate and report its opinions to the Chief
Inspector of Factories, Home Office, and further that the Home Office shall take no
official action in the matter pending the receipt of such a report.
3. All windows must be kept clean inside and outside.
(b) Artificial :
Artificial lighting should be adequate and the light should be so placed and shaded
as to prevent, so far as practicable, the rays of light from impinging directly on the
eyes of the workers.
2.-CLEANLINESS.
(a) Walls and Tops :
The legal requirements should be strictly enforced and in view of the number of
existing regulations and the difficulty of strict enforcement, this Council asks that
if the staff of Inpsectors is inadequate for the purpose, the Home Office will seriously
consider the advisability of appointing additional inspectors for the boot and shoe
trade.
(b) Floors:
1. In order to facilitate cleaning, the floors of all workrooms should be main-
tained in good condition.
2. Unless efficiently cleaned daily by a mechanically operated Vacuum Cleaner,
the floors of all workrooms should be thoroughly swept by a damp method at least
once in every 24 hours.
The floor of all Clicking and Closing Departments should be washed at least once
in every six months and if practicable the floors of other departments should be treated
in the same way.
3. Floors should not be swept while the operatives are present in the workrooms.
WASHING ACCOMMODATION.
Ample and suitable Washing Accommodation (including Soap and Towels) should
be provided.
FIRST AID EQUIPMENT.
Unless a suitable Ambulance Room is established a properly equipped First Aid
Box for every 150 workers should be kept in a convenient position.
PURITY OF AIR.
Gas and Oil Engines should be separated from workrooms.
INFECTION FROM Consumptive WORKERS.
Spitting on the floors or walls of factories or workshops should be prohibited.

THE SECRETARY OF STATE: Mr. Richards and Gentlemen, -I am very pleased
to have had this opportunity of hearing the case which you have submitted to us this
morning, and can say your visit comes most opportune from the standpoint that we
are about to introduce a Factory Bill. I was very pleased to hear Mr. Poulten pay his
tribute to the officials of this Department, for during the time I have been associated
with it I have had it very definitely confirmed what I knew before, that any matters
affecting the health and safety of the workers, the officials devote themselves, and
are devoting themselves to protect the interest of the workers with commendable
zeal. I am rather glad Mr. Poulton, coming with the weight of his experience in the
organised labour movement, should be prepared to give his testimony, and I am
quite sure his colleagues also take that view of the work which the officials of the Home
Office have been doing for a long time past. Perhaps the coming of a Secretary in-
terested in so many of these questions as I am will enable them through the coming
Factory Bill to give expression to some of the laudable ideas which are at the back
of their minds. I can assure the deputation that the points which have been brought
before us will receive-and are already receiving-the most careful consideration.

It is over twenty years since we had a comprehensive Factory Bill, and naturally
it is the desire of all in the Department to avail themselves with the improvements
and developments with regard to the health, ventilation and space as far as we think
Parliamentary circumstances will permit, and of course always bearing in mind
you can carry some of the changes advocated without interfering with the continuance
of an industry. The work that is done outside factories is a very important matter.
It used to be a very familiar phrase twenty years ago when I first went to the House of
Commons-"the out-worker." I well remember being on the Select Committee,
presided over by the late Sir Thomas Whittaker, when we received evidence of the
most appalling nature so far as out-workers were concerned. Although I knew a
good deal about it before that Select Committee, it was the information I obtained
there that made me so strong to get a change in connection with the chain makers
at Cradley Health, which resulted in our getting an amendment-which I moved
myself carried and included in the Sweated Trades' Bill. Both the officials and I
are tackling these questions with sympathy and practical experience. Any new
point which may have been made this morning will be made a note of by Sir Malcolm
Delevigne and will receive careful consideration. If they are not already in the new
Bill and it is possible to secure their inclusion, I shall be only too delighted to see they
are included. As the Bill goes through the House your own representatives--and
officials outside the House will be in a position to try and secure their inclusion
and they will be able to consult Mr. Davies or myself as to any amendments they wish
to make.

The case you have presented appeals to me very sympathetically.

JOINT EDUCATION COMMITTEE. 2ND INTERIM REPORT, 1922-23.
SUMMARY OF RECOMMENDATIONS.
Secretary.
1. That the time is not yet opportune for giving full effect to paragraph (b) of
the Southport Congress resolution, but that the General Council, through the Joint
Education Committee shall continue its efforts by consultation with representatives
of working-class educational bodies for the purpose of co-ordinating such activities,
and with a view to giving full effect to the provisions of the Southport resolutions.
2. That the General Council call a conference of representatives of affiliated
Unions which have provided or contemplate the provision of educational facilities
for their members with a view to developing a united purpose and policy in Trade
Union educational work.
3. That pending the General Council being able to submit a practical scheme
of educational work as required by paragraph (c) of the Southport Congress resolution,
the Council be empowered to create a special educational fund by (a) a grant from the
Trades Union Congress funds up to a maximum of £1,000 per annum, and (b) by such
voluntary grants as may be obtained from the affiliated Unions by the Council. The
fund thus created to be available for assisting such working-class educational institu-
tions as may be approved by the General Council.
4. That special consideration be given by the Joint Committee to the educational
needs of women Trade Unionists.
5. That the recommendations with regard to the question of education for young
workers be endorsed.

DEAR MR. POULTON,
73 SWINTON STREET,
LONDON, W.C.1.
11th April, 1924.
I understand that your Union has decided to undertake adult educational work
for the benefit of its members, and in that connection I want to suggest for the con
fideration of your Executive Council and yourself, the question of linking up with
the Workers' Educational Trade Union Committee.
As I think I have previously explained to you, that body originated a few years
ago from a decision of our Confederation to adopt some educational scheme for our
members.
It is true that prior to that, a great many of them attended W.E.A. and other
classes, but my Executive came to the conclusion that one of the important develop-
ments of progressive Trade Union work, must be to afford opportunities through the
Trade Union for the members to learn more about trade union history and that of the
working-class movement as a whole, to get some idea of political economy and social
science and any other matter that would tend to produce thinking men and women
to broaden their outlook and make them more loyal and useful members of the Trade
Union Movement.
In this matter it seemed to us that to get a real interest taken in a policy of that
kind, the responsibility must be accepted by the Union itself, and the members must
know that the educational facilities were those provided by the Union.
We, of course, knowing that a great deal of educational work was being done on
the Continent, particularly in Germany, hoped the idea would develop into the Trades
Union Congress taking a more active part in this aspect of Trade Union work.
We considered the possibility of establishing a scheme of our own, but we found
that the difficulties were considerable and the cost out of proportion to the advantage
obtained, and we consequently consulted some of the prominent men in the W.E.A.
and asked them if they could advise a scheme which would be under Trade Union
control and would meet the needs of our members. The result was that they sub-
mitted a scheme to our Executive Council under which the W.E.A. undertook to put
its existing machinery at our disposal, we providing funds and controlling the policy
and finance. The scheme was accepted by our members right throughout the country
after discussion at our Divisional Council meetings.
Since then a number of other Unions have come in, such as the Railway Clerks,
Postal Workers, Engineering and Shipbuilding, Draughtsmen, and the Society of
Operative Printers and Assistants.
The work is controlled by a Central Committee consisting of representatives
appointed by the Executives of the Unions concerned, and on which the W.E.A. is
also represented, and it is that Committee that is called the W.E.T.U.C.


---
Here is the text extracted from the image:

46
Then the country is divided into a number of divisions, and there are local com-
mittees consisting of representatives of the Unions concerned in the scheme, with a
secretary who is usually the Divisional Secretary of the W.E.A.
While the scheme provides for the fullest amount of educational work, such as
lectures, week-end schools, one, two or three-year classes, summer schools, and so on.
Of course we proposed to develop that so that our best students in the three-
year classes would have scholarships at Ruskin, Central Labour, or whatever other
recognised Labour Colleges we decided on for that purpose, and the value of this is,
of course, that students would have to do a considerable amount of ground work
before getting a scholarship instead of, as at present, often going straight to Ruskin
and similar colleges without any previous education.
However, the slump in trade came at the end of 1920, and, as a result, we have
had to very much limit our activities.
Any individual Union joining the Committee can decide precisely how much it
will spend; it can also decide as to how it can spend it independent of what any
other Union on the Committee may do: that is to say, one Union may desire to
expend more on week-end schools than on summer schools: it may decide to spend
more on classes and so on. What we have found, however, is that we get the best
advantage from co-ordinating our activities, and when each Union has indicated
what it proposes to spend on any particular branch of the work, then say, we take
week-end schools, where all the Unions have members in the same divisional area.
These schools are held jointly, each Union providing to send such number of students
as it is disposed, and so you have members of the different Unions brought together
not only for such social intercourse as these schools provide, but also to discuss to-
gether the lectures that are given. Further, it creates a strong fraternal feeling
as between the rank and file of different Unions, and you get all the different opinions
expressed to the general advantage.
When the Central Committee has decided its scheme of work according to the
expenditure its component parts are going to incur, then the local Committees are
informed and they have to make arrangements accordingly. Whatever expenditure
is incurred is reported to the Central Committee which, of course, has not merely
the right of criticism, but also of control in such matters.
The W.E.A. is simply the instrument by which the machinery is applied. The
Unions absolutely decide on policy and on the extent of the educational work, and
entirely control the financial position.
I am sure your Executive could not find a more suitable medium for carrying
out any educational work they desire. The mere fact that you may have members
in divisions in which other Unions have not, does not in the least degree affect the
situation. The arrangements are made so as to provide for the maximum advantage
to the members of each Union, and what a particular Union does, is entirely at the
discretion of its own Executive who instructs its representatives on the Committee
as to the extent of their commitments.
I may say we have arranged our programme for the 1923-24 period, but if your
Executive decided to join the W.E.T.U.C., it is not too late for some modified arrange-
ment which would be suitable to your Organisation.
If there is any other point you want an explanation on, I shall be glad to supply
it. Meanwhile I hope the matter will have your consideration and that of your
Executive Council.
Yours faithfully,
(Signed) A. PUGH.

faction. It will be recalled we were elected to Parliament in December last and at the
fall of the Baldwin Government took office at the end of January of this year. The Party
has much to be proud of, and we have now 193 Labour Members in the House of Commons,
and whilst not being in the majority, nevertheless, the Labour Party has been enabled
to put into operation several of the matters it has preached from the platform for years
past. The last few months have indeed been strenuous ones, the Party being faced with
an experienced Opposition. During its term of office the
FIRST LABOUR BUDGET.

of the community whose income is the lowest. The principal items in the Budget are :-
The total cost of the reductions in taxation proposed will be £34,050,000 this
year and £40,443,000 in a full year.

employment. At the time of going to Press a Bill is before Parliament to considerable
it must be remembered that until the Party has a majority in the House its full program

The following will give a resumé of the activities regarding unemployment:-
No. 1 BILL (which became an Act on 21st February) to remove the gap of three week
which, under the Unemployment Insurance Act of 1923, was imposed after th
receipt of 12 weeks uncovenanted benefit in the period commencing on 1st
October, 1923.
No. 2 BILL was introduced on 3rd April and proposes considerable amendments
existing Acts (in respect of periods and rates of benefit, rates of contribution
inclusion of juveniles between 14 and 16, refunds of contribution, &c.).
No. 3 BILL was introduced on 4th April, and has received the Royal Assent. It
extends the existing maximum of 26 weeks' Benefit payable up to 15th October
1924, to 41 weeks for the same period.
48 HOURS WEEK.
In connection with hours of employment the Minister of Labour is to introduce a
Bill to supplement the terms of Washington Convention of 1919, but it has not yet been
possible to introduce the actual Bill into Parliament. When this becomes law it will be
of considerable benefit to many millions of workers throughout the country.
PENSIONS.
The first administrative action of the Ministry of Pensions was to issue special instruc-
tions to treat all claims with the utmost sympathy and consideration, and that, in accord-
ance with the principle of working agreed with the Treasury, every man should have the
full benefit of the doubt.
In the old days, when a Final Award was set aside, the Ministry took no action unless
the man appealed on deterioration. The Minister has now arranged that in all cases
where the Award is set aside, the man should be immediately re-boarded with a view to
the issue of pension, if possible.
The Minister has arranged, with the sanction of the Treasury, that as from the 1st
April last there should be no change of entitlement in any case more than a year old, unless
there has been actual error of diagnosis or obvious error of fact, or fraud. This applies
to all pensions.
When the Minister took office approximately 80 per cent. of the pensions had been
reviewed, and he found himself precluded from discontinuing the review. But immediately
action was taken to give every dependent the right of appeal and, in many instances,
the pension has been restored to the original sum. Seven hundred ex-service men have
been transferred from Poor Law charges and are now under the administration of the
Ministry of Pensions.

In regard to Pensions, through the Pensions Minister, Mr. Fred Roberts, the Govern
ment has brought about a change in the whole of the conditions under which pension
have been granted. The first thing they have done is to wipe out that stigma placed on
the ex-service man who has been classified as a pauper lunatic. The next step of a definite
benefit of any doubt. This is perhaps of more importance than appears upon the surface
character was that instructions have been issued that the ex-soldier should be given the
you can get a disability of 20 per cent. you are not entitled to a pension, but receive a final
Perhaps those who have had connection with the Pensions Department will know unless
award. This shows how past Governments have dealt with claims of ex-service men.
Ex-soldiers have had their disability assessed at one point below the 20 per cent., which
means they get six or twelve months' award, and their pension has gone for ever. Under
our arrangement they get the benefit of the doubt, which means they get a pension instead
of a final award. There was a difficulty in dealing with the question of dependants. The late
Government insisted on reviewing them, and when we took office we found 80 per cent.
had had their pensions reviewed, and it was impossible to stop it. The Pensions Minister
stated in every case where pensions had been reduced, they had the right of appeal for
reconsideration, and many allowances have been restored-if not to the full amount, at
was granted to a mother where the son had been killed, and the mother died, the pension
ceased. That has been altered, and now the pension automatically goes to the other
parent. There has been quite a number of things of that description done.
In relation to Housing, the Government of the day have established a definite under-
standing with the building industry. The Government has agreed to put into
operation a programme covering fifteen years. It gives a guarantee for that time, and in
return the building industry has given a guarantee to the Government that they will so
organise their forces to supply houses so that at the end of fifteen years 2,000,000 working-
class houses will have been built. This means that it is only a question of a few years
when there will be no one in this country in the working class who wants a house, but
that they will be able to get one.

Now think of what we have done, and what we have in hand, and I hope that at
the next election we shall get your support and see that we are returned by a large majority.

WEDNESDAY AFTERNOON-11th June, 1924-was spent inspecting the works
of Messis. Lotus Ltd. (Bostock's), Stafford. The extent of the works and the wide range
of work executed, was a revelation to many of the delegates, as also was the provision
made for dealing with any cases of sickness; likewise the playing fields, gymnasium and
concert hall for the use and benefit of the operatives.
After tea, provided at the Brook Hall, Mr. T. F. Richards presided at an informal
gathering, supported by Mr. H. J. Bostock, J.P., and Mr. E. L. Poulton, J.P.
Mr. T. F. Richards (President of the Union) spoke of the appreciation of the delegates
of the hospitality extended to them by the firm, and asked the company to bear in mind
the fact that Mr. H. J. Bostock was President of the Employers' Federation (applause)
the Federation with which they had so much trouble. (Laughter.) He was delighted
to think that they had had an opportunity of going over the Lotus Works, and for the
delegates from all parts of the Kingdom to have seen what was being done in Stafford.
"Treacle Borough" was well known in Leicester, and as a consequence they knew
Leicester had been built up by Stafford men.
They looked upon Mr. Bostock and the
as one of their best friends. (Applause.)
Mr. H. J. BOSTOCK: Mr. President, ladies and gentlemen, it was unkind of
you, Sir, to remind the audience that I am President of the Federation I am now addressing
ing you in a private capacity, and not as a member of the Federation, and anything I saw
now is not to be used against me in evidence. (Laughter.) We are pleased to be associated with you. It is a very remarkable history of the Union you have issued. Fifty
years of hard work, which has placed the industry and its organisation in a high position.
I am satisfied that that state of affairs could not have been brought about unless the Union
had had as officers and leaders people who commanded the respect, not only of their constituents, but of the people with whom they negotiated. It was a very happy thing for the
shoe industry that it had not got away from the stage when masters and men, or employees
and employed, met together in their daily work and knew each other. You may think we
are hard - perhaps some of us are but some of you are pretty tough nuts (laughter)
yet we are able to meet together and settle our differences. There is a great deal of work
still to be done by the Union and the Federation acting together. The Federation is being
asked to accept responsibility to finance the Research Association and Science in our trade
We ought to discuss the conditions that make work pleasant and put them into force. In
our factory we have two "rest" intervals-one at 10 a.m. and one at 4 p.m. Some feared
the output would fall as a result; I never had any anxiety myself, and I am glad to say our
people are satisfied that if we gave up the "rest" periods, it would be fatal. In our factory we have tried to get cleanliness and as much light, sun and air as possible. We are
only just beginning to realise to the full the health of our citizens. Happily, here in Stafford,
we don't always have rain, and people say what a clean town it is. We live in a charming
part of England, engaged in a necessary industry. I believe in your debates you have
talked about tuberculosis; this is a disease which can to a large extent be conquered
by living under better conditions and getting more sunlight. Everyone of us should do
all in our power to urge forward smoke abatement Bills, and so try to promote better
surroundings. Mr. Richards, I could talk to you for many hours longer, but after three
days I imagine you have had as much talking as you wanted. I should, however, like to
say what a pleasure it has been to me, and my fellow Directors, and everyone in the factory
to show you round the factory, and we are proud to let you see the things we have remedied.
I thank you very heartily for the honour done us, by coming to our factory. (Applause.)
Mr. T. F. RICHARDS: I know Mr. Bostock does not wish us to pass him a vote
of thanks, but on your behalf wish to say how very much we appreciate his kindness.
(Cheers.)
Mr. R. DUNN: It would be indiscreet for me to let this occasion go by without
saying a word. This is a red-letter day for Stafford. I wish England had more employers
like the Lotus people. They are splendid people to deal with. It is nothing but fair to
say how much we appreciate what these people do. (Applause.)
E. B.

MONTHLY REPORT.

FELLOW MEMBERS,
2IST JULY, 1924.

TRADE.

There has been a slight improvement in Trade during the past month.
The figures recorded by the Gazette are set out hereunder :-

BOOT AND SHOE INDUSTRY.

Employment during June was moderate and showed little change, on the whole,
compared with May, but was, in general, better than in June of last year. Short time
was still largely worked in many centres, and many factories closed down for the whole
of Whitsun week.

The percentage of workpeople unemployed, as indicated by the unemployment books
lodged at Employment Exchanges, was 7.7 on the 23rd June, as compared with 8.3 on the
20th May.

Returns from firms employing over 38,000 operatives in the week ending 28th June,
1924, showed that about 23 per cent. of these operatives worked short time in that week
to the extent of about 10 hours each on an average.
Employment in London remained fair. At Leicester there was a slight decline;
Northampton a slight improvement. Employment was fair on the whole in both dis-
tricts, but some short time was still being worked. At Kettering employment was only
moderate, and after the Whitsun holidays the majority of factories worked only three-
quarter time. At Wellingborough employment was quiet, and the majority of the
operatives were working short time. Conditions remained fair in the Higham and Rushden
districts, systematic short time, but employment continued brisk at factories producing
light footwear. At Stafford employment was very fair, with very little short time. Em-

THE SPITALFIELDS DISPUTE (LONDON).
The strike at Messrs. Jackson & Joseph is still in being. During the
month a number of meetings have been addressed by the General President.
National Organisers, local officers, and help has been offered and accepted
from several Labour M.P.'s, including our Mr. J. Buckle, M.P. and Mr. F.

by the Union, despite efforts made by the employers to get them to return
to work. Members must not seek employment at this firm. We trust that we
may be able to report a successful issue later. We understand an appeal has

THE BOOT TRADE.
Award to Deal with Slackness and Unemployment.
As a result of the deliberations of the Northamptonshire Board of Arbitration, sitting
at Kettering on 13th June, the following new Award, signed by Mr. W. Charles Cattell,
has been made :-
Standing Off.
All operatives standing off work at the wish of the employer, through slackness of
trade, shall accept same for a period of not longer than four weeks in the first instance.
If the employer cannot re-engage the operative after the expiration of the first four weeks
he shall have power to authorise a further period of not longer than four weeks' suspension,
making eight weeks in all. If the employer cannot re-engage the operative after the
expiration of eight weeks he shall, at the end of the eighth week, terminate the engagement
by notice, or pay its equivalent in wages.
It being understood and agreed by the Board that if, during the above period of four
to eight weeks it is desired by either party that the employment be terminated, both
employer and employee are entitled to a week's notice.
No employee can be deemed to be temporarily employed in the restricted sense now
used after such employee has worked 48 hours, except in the case where an operative is
employed as a substitute for a regular employee who is ill.
Notice.
All employees, after working 48 hours, must receive one week's notice, or give such
notice before such employment can be terminated.
All such employees are thus entitled to the stoppage of holiday payment and unemploy-
ment and State Insurance contributions.
Exceptions as to the stoppage of holiday payment can only be made in the case of
operatives employed in substitution of an employee who is ill, and then only for the period
of the first weeks of such employment.

TAMWORTH.—It has been my purpose to visit a TAMWORTH firm who get their clicking

ing the operatives at Wilnecote (Tamworth),

LEICESTER - A case of importance has had to be investigated where a firm are endeav-
ouring, apparently, to utilise male labour to defeat the attitude adopted by the women
in the conduct of their business. Three men have been engaged to do the Stock Room
work, hitherto done by girls. The firm have conceived the idea of putting the Stock
Room on day labour; after failing to get the work done at their own price, two of the girls
have been discharged, to my mind, as a deterrent and to frighten the other girls, all of
whom, including the men, have been advised by me, to work at the price set down in the

```text
statement. This policy of calling in men has been done before when there has been a
glut of work. The operatives think this will be the case again in a very short time, the
distasteful part being the discharge of the two girls, who immediately got other and better
employment. But here is a principle -ought we to allow one operative to be set off
against another? This ought not to be permitted, and the Union must consider the
matter on its merits.
TRADE BOARD. Two more days have been spent on this work, which meets with no
satisfaction from some of those who benefit by the work done. Of the six members repre-
senting the workers' side, two belong to our Union, three belong to the Amalgamated and
one to the N.U.D. & A.W. These latter four are all Hand Sewn Makers and Repairers.
In this goodly company Mr. Buckle and the General President find themselves, with men
of experience, and when we ask our members who are supposed to know, we get no data
as to hourly or weekly quantities except from one Branch, but whose
figures are confronted with the employers' figures, not only from these two firms but from
London gave us no earnings. These members give us their opinion, which we advance,
four other towns and cities from which we had no evidence, and only one figure. Even
but it is figures that tell the tale, and yet in spite of that, we got an 8 per cent. advance
on a price that has been tried deliberately for a period before these prices can be accepted.
The District Committee will have an opportunity of amending this, and if they can, then
we hope they will improve our work. We have had a further enquiry into the "making
longer" of shoes, and this matter has hung fire a long time. The department got a wrong
impression, and now we are informed that the likelihood of a settlement is close at hand.
The men have already drawn two large sums in back money, and feel sure the firm will
do the honourable thing on this occasion when the facts are drawn to their attention.
STREET. We have had a deputation from Street, and it has been my pleasure to take
them round the factories of the C.W.S., Knighton Fields, Palfreyman Bros., J. Rawson &
Sons, Equity Shoe Works, and T. Roberts & Sons, of Leicester. Many things were seen
that do not exist in any isolated firm, unless it is much up-to-date. Each and every
firm have methods of their own which are always sub-rosa with us as officials, and the
kindly way in which the principals at the firms received us, and showed us all we wanted
to know, impressed our visitors that Trade Union Officials and Employers in the Shoe
Industry are not on bad terms by any means. The Management of the C.W.S. and Equity
Co-operative Society were equally courteous, and will entirely remove the impression
made that any difficulties exist in seeing a Leicester factory.
STRIKE. -At the request of the Organisers I have addressed an open-air meeting of
Jackson & Joseph's men outside Spitalfields Church. The men who are out are worthy
of support, and the pity of it is that men and women can be found to serve a firm who
decline to be ruled or controlled, and who we invite to submit their claims to arbitration
to one of the Directors of their own customers. By the general run of the trade, this is
why I am pleased that the Bill which would allow Unions and Federations to impose the
same condition on the minority as governs the majority should become law, and those
Labour members who voted against the measure ought not to prevent someone else having
an opinion as well as themselves on what is good and what is bad. We are hopeful that
the Bill will become law and that no trade need have it unless they wish. At the same
time I must here correct a statement I believed to be true, viz.: "That we are the only
Union in the world who have a monetary guarantee." I have been informed that the
Dyers' Union and the Dyers and Finishers, of Bradford, and the General Workers' Union,
of which the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of Labour is an official, have an
agreement in the Bradford area of a similar amount of £1,000 each side, as a guarantee
to observe the bond-a copy of which I have. I therefore wish to correct the impression
and to take off my hat to my friends who have done better than we have, because they
have a guarantee that all employees must belong to one of the Unions involved. We hope
to improve our agreement. This would cost nothing.
Wear Stamped Shoes and read the Daily Herald! You will be the better for doing
both.
7 MECKLENBURG STREET,
LONDON, W.C. 1.
15th July, 1924.
Yours fraternally,
W. F. Richard
```

BRANCH REPORTS.
will be at Wembley during the mid-summer holidays in July. Few of us
ARBROATH. Our trade is still very poor, and very few of our members
ever thought to live through a time when the talk of holidays would jar so much
as it does in these modern times. To maintain the custom in the face of holidays
all the year round savours of burlesque, and many of our members can only

LONDON METRO. We are pleased to report that trade still continues

feeling the effects of the stoppage. One of the trade papers has published
Jackson & Joseph's statement of the position, and why negotiations ceased.
They first state that the men were satisfied with their job. Well, when their
employees came to the Office with patterns of fancy shoes and complained of
the price paid, that certainly did not show that satisfaction existed. They
state that the men could not obtain a better situation in any London factory.
From the work point of view they are right, for there is not a firm in London
or in the trade, that insist on their employees working six full days and over-
time, and have them in on Sunday to keep their hand in so as they will be fit
for work on Monday. They state that they are not fighting the Union or
Federation, but meeting the wishes of their employees. If that is so, why have
we had to interview the firm at the employees' request on the price paid for
clicking and fitting cutting, and the Holiday Provision Scheme. They state
there is a large percentage of Union members still carrying on. That is not so.

MR. E. L. POULTON ON 48-HOURS WEEK.
Address to the International Labour Conference.
On Tuesday, the 24th June, 1924, Mr. E. L. Poulton, J.P., General Secretary to the
National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives, and the British Workmen's representatives
to the International Labour Conference now being held in Geneva, addressed the meeting
on the 48-hours week and said:-
"It is increasingly difficult to find new matter in connection with this great question,
which we now have before us for the sixth time, in addition to many times on the Go-
Director's Report that ratification had been secured for this very important reform
instead of having to ask again from this tribune that every nation should adopt it
Body. As workers, we were hoping that before 1924 we should be able to read in the
ever, we intend as workers to keep this matter in the very forefront of our programme,
nations of which they form the units; although on the one side we have somewhat sadly
believing that it is not only of great interest to the workers as workers, but also to the
point of our international work, it is nevertheless with pleasure that we note the French
to lament the fact that so little progress has been made in this connection from the stand-
Minister of Labour stated a few days ago the intention of their Government to bring
before the French Chamber at the earliest possible moment a Bill to ratify the Hours
Convention. That, at any rate, is encouraging.
"In the Director's Report it is stated that Great Britain is one of the countries which
is holding back the question of ratification. I hope that the British Government is going
to take its courage in its hands and put the Bill through, in accordance with the decisions
arrived at in 1919 in Washington. One of the principal reasons, or one of the alleged
reasons, for not ratifying this particular convention, is that each nation is waiting for
some other nation to ratify it. I hope that game of battledore and shuttlecock is not
hand labour more and more, and men are more and more becoming victims of the system
going to continue. The workers are determined to have it settled. Machinery is displacing
and women employed have to increase their physical pace to keep pace with the iron
because they have to keep pace with the machines. I know in my own industry the men
machine, whatever the capacity of that machine may be. Therefore, I say the human
factor is one which not only calls for consideration but which also calls for action in the
way of shorter hours of work, as methods of production are improved.

"Surely it is much better that the workers should work under just and humane con-
ditions, that they should work under conditions in which they feel they have no injustice
to put up with, rather than have rankling in their breasts, indignation, and a sense of
injustice because of the apparent neglect of Governments to fulfil their obligations.
"About eight days ago, it was my pleasure to go over one of the biggest factories in
the United Kingdom. That factory had a maximum working week of 48 hours, but the
head of the factory thought it would be advantageous both to the employer and to the
employee if shorter hours were to be worked, so as to give the workers rest both in the
morning and in the afternoon. The workers there have, therefore, been given a ten-
minute rest in the morning and ten minutes in the afternoon, making 100 minutes altogether
in the five full working days, or practically two hours out of the nominal 48. That em-
ployer told me there had never been cause to regret the action, and that it had not had
any effect on the output of the factory, because of the advantage accruing to the workers
by giving them this period of time off, although it really meant a working week of 46
hours.
"I feel bound to appeal in strong language, and to ask the members of this Conference
to go back to their countries and tell their Governments of the feeling here, in order that
next year we shall be enabled to see in the Director's Report that ratification has been
secured, and which the workers prize so highly in their several spheres."
DAILY HERALD
CANDID; CLEAR; CONCISE.

"AS OTHERS SEE US.”
Non-Stop Industries.
Thirteen years without a strike, a record claimed for the shipping industry, is no mean achievement in these troubled days.
It is not, however, the best. The boot and shoe operatives can beat the sailors with plenty to spare, for their industry has maintained peace for 20 years.
It is probably unique in that the Union and the Employers' Federation have a mutual guarantee of £1,000 against any stoppage. The Star, 11th July, 1924.

CITY POLICE NEWS.
" A Pleasure to be Prosecuted," says Mr. Evan Barlow.
Leicester, Saturday. Magistrates: Mr. W. A. Toller (in the chair) and Mr. A. H. Baddeley. Messrs. J. and E. Glover, boot manufacturers, Lichfield Street, were summoned by George Frederick Sedgwick, H.M. Inspector of Factories, for contravention of Section 1 of the Factory and Workshops Act with regard to limewashing. It was stated that the limewashing in question had not been done for four years, whereas it should have been done every 14 months. A letter had been sent to defendants bringing the matter to their notice, but the limewashing was not carried out.
Mr. Evan Barlow, who represented the defendants, said it was a pleasure to be prosecuted by the son of the former worthy Factories Inspector, Mr. G. Sedgwick. Defendants had no desire to avoid their obligations.
The magistrates imposed a fine of 40s. - Leicester Mail, 21st June, 1924.

LEGAL QUERIES ANSWERED.
"DELTA" (Leeds). If you can earn the same wages with one eye as you did with two you have no claim for further compensation at present, but if later on you cannot earn as much as you did before, as a result of the accident, you will be entitled to weekly compensation for partial disablement. You cannot claim a lump sum.-Herald, 26th June, 1924.

RUSHDEN CHOIRMEN APPRECIATED.
Adult School Songsters on East Coast.
"Ordinary working men, at it daily in a boot and shoe factory! Why, you ought to be earning a living, every one of you, as professional vocalists!" This was one of the tributes paid to the Rushden Adult School Prize Male Voice Choir, on the occasion of a week's singing visit to Cromer and Sheringham-and it was a tribute, too, paid by a musician of high standing in the country. Conducted, officered and manned almost entirely by boot and shoe operatives, the choir's standing in the musical world is rising year by year, and their receptions at Cromer and Sheringham were enthusiastic in the highest degree, many requests being made to them to come again next year.
The conductor of the Choir is an old member of the Union, and much work is done by the Choir, particularly in respect to charitable cases.

MEDICAL EXAMINATION OF YOUNG PERSONS
FOR FACTORY EMPLOYMENT.
The Committee appointed by the Home Secretary
to inquire into the working of
the provisions of the Factory and Workshop Acts for the medical examination of 
persons as to their fitness for employment in factories" have presented their report.
The medical examination of the boys and girls who are to enter industry is two-
fold; there is the medical examination for factory employment by certifying surgeons
under the Factory Act, and the medical examination during school life by medical officers
of the Local Education Authority under the Education Acts. The evidence given to the
Committee respecting the working of the first-mentioned system was conflicting, but on
the whole unfavourable and the Committee record their opinion that the failure (as
such they regard it) is due to inherent defects of the system itself. They therefore
recommend that the examination and certification of young persons should be amended
as follows:—
(1) The age for examination should be raised from 16 to 18 years.
(2) The examination should be required in all factories and workshops, except
such as the Home Office may, by Special Order, exempt.
(3) The form of the certificate should be positive instead of negative, i.e. it should
be to the effect that the young person is physically fit for employment in the factory.
(4) The surgeon should be able to grant, at his discretion, a qualified certificate
to which conditions may be attached respecting the nature of the work on which the
young persons may (or may not) be employed, the remedial or other measures which
are to be taken in regard to the young person; or the certificate should be conditional
upon re-examination within a stated period on account either of the physical state of
the young persons or of the industrial conditions.
(5) The certificate should be obtained within 14 days after the young person
has started work in the factory, and should include a statement to the effect that the
surgeon has seen the young person's school medical record.
(6) The examination should be conducted at the factory.
(7) The surgeon should have the duty of acquainting himself in every factory
where he examines young persons with the process upon which they are, or are proposed
to be, employed, and of recording in the register the date of his visits.
(8) The standard of examination, the form of certificate and the nature of the
conditions which may be attached to qualified certificates should be prescribed by
the Home Office, which should supervise the work of the surgeon.
(9) A retaining fee should be paid to the surgeon out of public funds for the
purpose of covering the examination of processes referred to in (7) above, the making
of an annual report, and the re-examinations referred to in (4) above. The fee for
examination on entering employment in a factory should continue to be paid by the
occupier.
(10) The title "Examining Factory Surgeon" should be substituted for "Certify-
ing Factory Surgeon" to mark the change effected in the duties and responsibilities
by the above amendments.
(11) On the application of the occupier of a factory who employs a medical officer,
the Central Authority should have power to appoint him to be examining-surgeon
for that factory for the purpose of examination of young persons, as in the case of
charitable institutions under the Factory Act, 1907.
In regard to linking up the examination of young persons under the Factory Act
with that under other public health services, the Committee are of opinion that the Councils
of Counties and County Boroughs in England and Wales, and the District Committees
and Town Councils in Scotland, should at once be invited to submit schemes for taking
over the examination and certification of young persons, which should be regarded as one
of the specialised services of the Local Authority, like the school medical inspection.
If the voluntary trial made by Local Authorities proves successful, the whole of this work
should, in the opinion of the Committee, ultimately be transferred to the Local Authorities.
The Report is signed by all the members of the Committee; but certain reservations
are made by Sir Gerald Bellhouse, H.M. Chief Inspector of Factories, who doubts the
necessity for raising the age for examination from 16 to 18 years, and disagrees with the
proposal to pay a retaining fee to examining surgeons out of public funds.
An appendix to the Report shows that 1,681,158 young persons were examined for
fitness by certifying surgeons during the five years 1919-1923, of whom 54,056 were rejected.
Statistics as to the number conditionally certified are not available for the years 1919 and
1920, but the number so certified during the three years 1921-23 was 22,847, as compared
with 28,560 rejected outright in the same three years.-The Ministry of Labour Gazette,
June, 1924.

FELLOW MEMBERS,
MONTHLY REPORT.

25TH AUGUST, 1924.
TRADE
during the past month has somewhat improved though not to the extent we
either desire or wish. We hoped it would improve to such an extent as to
absorb the whole of those who are at present unemployed. It must not,
however, be forgotten that the capacity of the Trade for making boots and
shoes is so great that the question of a reduction in the hours of labour must
never be lost sight of. The figures recorded by the Gazette are set out
hereunder :-
BOOT AND SHOE INDUSTRY.
Employment during July remained, on the whole, moderate. It was, however,
distinctly better than a year ago. A good deal of short time was still worked in various
centres.
The percentage of workpeople unemployed, as indicated by the unemployment books
lodged at Employment Exchanges, was 7.5 on the 28th July, as compared with 7.7 on the
23rd June.
Returns from firms employing nearly 38,000 workpeople in the week ended 26th July
showed that about 29 per cent. of these workpeople worked short time in that week to the
extent of about eight hours each on an average.
Employment in London showed little change. At Leicester employment was gener-
ally quiet, with some factories working short time; but it was much better than in July
of last year. At Northampton employment was reported as fairly good, especially during
the last week of the month, in preparation for the trade holidays in August. At Kettering
employment was poor, though in this centre also there was an improvement at the end of
the month. Employment at Wellingborough remained quiet, and half of the factories
in this district were working short time; but in the Higham and Rushden districts employ
ment was fair, and most of the factories ran full time. Employment was reported as bad
at Hinckley. The heavy boot factories at Leeds remained slack, with much short time,
but operatives producing light footwear were again busy. Only a little short time was
worked at Stafford: but employment, although fair, was not so good as in the previous
month. Employment in the slipper trade remained good at Rawtenstall.
There was a further slight improvement at Bristol and
There was little change at Norwich; employment was good, full time being usually
worked, and some overtime.

POLITICAL.
The first session of the Labour Government has now ended. It has been
asked in the past "Can Labour Govern?" We have always maintained that
Labour could govern, and have pointed to the state of affairs the various
countries have been brought to from time to time by other parties than the
Labour Party, adding that Labour could at any rate govern as well as those
who have had the control of the countries for hundreds of years.

GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.

FELLOW MEMBERS,
SHODDY. We are bound to again turn our attention to the question of Shoddy
Footwear and to complain of those retailers who take advantage of the poor by assuming
to be their friends, and who seek their suffrages for public office and take upon themselves
public work with all its responsibilities. In some instances they have received honours
from the King, and are called upon to shield, by their acceptance of office, anyone from
chicanery or fraud, and it is to the credit of those pure-minded men who refuse to stock
shoddy or paper-stuffed boots or shoes, that they receive the support of a good type of
customer. We are now called upon to ask those manufacturers who send boots and shoes
to our Colonies to be made aware of the inquiry recently held in New Zealand, when these
goods obtained from Great Britain were pulled up and examined by experts in the presence
of five Members of Parliament, and the Secretary of the Labour Party. We are well
aware that such an inquiry was held in several towns and cities, and could mention the
to that found in New Zealand, where, we are informed they-being a young democratic
sitting Members and the Labour Party Secretary would reveal a state of things similar
colony-want value for money without deception, and as one of the men engaged is an
old shopmate of mine, one need not wonder that those who claim Labour principles, and
are. prepared to act up to them, cannot stand idly by and see boots bought as "all leather"
and when pulled up are found to contain (after being warranted all leather) composed of
that flimsy kind which we used as boys on a piece of string to carry bricks with. Very
in ignorance, and a strong plea was made to the danger to health. This is a worthy
strong criticism was offered to those who send to New Zealand the shoddy rubbish purchased
subject for the Health Committees of our large towns, and the Minister of Health ought
to advise all public bodies of the danger of putting into office those guilty of gulling the
public. The Inquiry Committee of New Zealand are asking the Legislature to pass a law
leather. This Committee strongly emphasised the fact that to their mind a genuine
article could be placed on the market at 1s. per pair more than the shoddy price. As all
these productions were purchased by the Union of Shoemakers, we shall be able, probably
in a very short time, to turn again to this subject. In the meantime, will all those inter-
ested bestir themselves to compel the "Shoddyites" to mark in plain language the com-
position of their pocket-picking boots and shoes.
The Sub-Committee of our Union, owing to several reasons, have not yet met, but hope
to do so in a few days.

GOVERNMENT AND HANDSEWN BOOTS. We have at last received a reply from the
War Office, through Mr. J. J. Lawson, M.P., Financial Secretary, in which he says that
after very careful consideration and the objections to Handsewn Boots being so strong,
that their purchase could not be justified, and that the matter has been considered since,
and the Machine-made Boot preferred, and owing to heavy orders being placed by the
late Government last winter, was also another factor. This reply causes me to remember
a few things about the placing of orders, an old trick of the Tories who always place large
orders when they are leaving office, the object being to show how good they are, and when
other Parties do anything for the public these petrified hangers on of office shriek bribery,
bribery and corruption-they being experts, understand. Concerning the objections to
Handsew Boots, I am bound to again approach the Financial Secretary, and say that I
invited Mr. Haldane, then Secretary of State for War, to test the Handsewn Boot which
they were buying in 1906 at 10s. 5d. per pair, to test them with two platoons of men in
one regiment-Handsewn versus Machine-made. No! he refused, he being like a few
others, machine mad. My plan was a three years' trial, each man to have two pairs
Handsewn boots for a platoon of 60 men, and two pairs Machine-Sewn for a platoon of
60 men, boots to be repaired by regimental cobblers until both pairs had been thoroughly
worn out-cost and comfort to be fully recorded. I should bank on the Handsewn boots.
I fully accept the suggestion that had we wanted six million pairs for the last great inter-
national crime, we certainly could not have had them made Handsewn, but we claim
Handsewn to be the best and cheapest for European wear, and it would find much employ-
ment and pay better than out of work benefit, although we do not ask the Government to
do as they are about to do with the Sugar Refining Factories, and as they do with the
Shipping Companies in subsidising ships for prospective use, but no subsidies for the
private soldier, not even employment at his own industry.

THE SPITALFIELDS' DISPUTE. - The Ministry of Labour for the City of London had
arranged an interview with Messrs. Jackson & Joseph, at Clement's Inn, and asked the
General President to meet these gentlemen, with Messrs. McCarthy and Smith. We
spent two and a half hours trying to arrange a settlement, the firm alleging that their
business was progressing favourably and that they had been chosen for attack, whilst

Branch. ALL Branches ought to immediately inform the Central Office when they fail
to impose the National Conditions; such actions give colour to those who advocate the
centralisation of funds.

class corporation," my answer is "No closer than the profession take some trainers into

ORGANISER'S REPORT.
During the past month I have been engaged in the Midland District. I have visited
a few firms in Leicester with reference to the organisation of women, chiefly lapsed members
and good work has been done. I have devoted considerable attention to the Sileby Dis
trict. This is rather a difficult district. The conditions are fairly good, and nearly the
whole of the firms adopt the National Scale and Holiday Fund, but in the firms that I
visited there would not be more than 25 per cent of our members. I have no complaint
to make with regard to the meetings, and I have found no opposition to any views that
have been put forward. It is simply a matter of sheer apathy, indifference, timidity and
selfishness. In view of the holidays I have taken full advantage to press home the Holiday
Fund, which they fully admit was due to the work of the Union. I made a special effort
at Bray's where the conditions are quite good, but somehow or other they are under the
impression that if they joined the Union it would mean a reduction in their earnings.
I had very good meetings here and our members were well satisfied with the effort that i
made. Good meetings have been held at the School Boot Company, Mountsorrel. I have
visited this firm five times, and also canvassed them personally. The girls here are indebted
to the Leicester Women's Branch for the excellent conditions under which they work.
and some of them have promised to join. I have personally interviewed the whole of the
men working at Parker & Barlow's, we have a number of Leicester men working heme
and are all in the Union, but the men who reside in the district are very reluctant to join,
saying that they are waiting for a majority to join. I have met the operatives on four
occasions working at R. Willett's, Sileby. The manager here has not got a very good
name in the district, and I am under the impression that influences are at work in the
factory which prevent the operatives from joining. I had good meetings and canvassed
each man personally, but with very little success. Mr. Leader, the Secretary, has rendered
me yeoman service, but our rate of progress is exceedingly slow, but our members are grate-
ful to the Union for the efforts that we have made to arouse interest in the work on the
Union.
I visited Burton-on-Trent, met the operatives at Eatough's; we are making a little
progress here. I had occasion to meet the management with reference to one of our
members, and with the difficulty removed with reference to the other Union, I think the
progress will be assured. Structural operations are still going on for the accommodation
of W. Hill's, from Leicester, and it will be about two months before they commence business
here.
I have again visited the Wilnecote School Boot Company at Twogates (Tamworth).
The conditions of this firm have depreciated since my last visit. About 100 persons work
here but there are only about 12 men, chiefly youths. Girls are still working in the lasting,
finishing and press room, and I had no difficulty in having a meeting with them. From
information that I gathered the girls in the machine room had been put on piecework.
The rates of wages formerly paid on daywork were 8s., 16 years of age; 14s. over 18;
18s. over 20. Under the piecework rates they are now earning on an average between
the ages of 18 to 20, about 7s. 6d. per week, over that age ros. 6d. per week. Youths up
to 20, 15s. 6d. per week. I made a comparison on one operation and found according to
statement prices the firm were paying 2 d. per dozen for work, as against rold. I kept in
touch with the operatives for three days, and received quite definite promises that they
would join, but owing to the advent of the holidays, and the prospects of 12 days' holiday,
I am meeting them again. I think it would be almost impossible to find worse conditions,
and they expressed regret that they did not join on my former visit. Fortunately I was
able to obtain information which will enable the Union to adopt other methods to deal
with this firm, and if the operatives will only keep to their present intentions I am confident
that these shocking conditions can be considerably improved.
J. H. BAUM.

```text
BRANCH REPORTS.
ARBROATH. — We have had our annual holiday period and trade is still
bad in our district. The increased benefit at the Labour Exchange will soon
be helping to ease the position of the short-time worker, but constant vigilance
is required to protect the rights of members who are compelled to sign the
register. A great deal of trouble arises with short-time workers at holiday
times, and a great deal of money is lost through ignorance of regulations,
although the most of it is recovered later on. An important point has emerged
in this connection. Dock Labourers and Preserves Workers have contested
successfully the stoppage of six or more days as holidays when twelve other
consecutive days have not been signed, on the ground that they have never had
customary holidays of that kind. This has led to us lodging a claim on similar
alike. Two of our indirect claiming members lost six days' benefit simply
grounds, and a test case will be heard for our direct and indirect claimants
because they accepted casual repairing, even although they had less than
thirty days' work for the past year. Other difficulties arise in connection with
days preceding, and immediately following, holidays, if not signed for at the
time, and a great deal of trouble is experienced in recovering these omissions.
A number of our permanently unemployed members got a shock at the beginning
of the new period by having a day deducted for the last day in July. It certainly
looked a scurvy business to withhold a day from those who had completed
their 41 weeks on the 30th July, and it was an unexpected mistake of the Labour
Government to start their new scheme on the Friday when the Labour Exchange
week commences on the Thursday. We hope the Scottish members of our
Union are watching closely the new development in day school education
North of the Tweed. Following upon a circular issued some time ago (the
famous Circular 44) we have the Scotch Education Department creating
Advanced Divisions as alternatives to the Intermediate Higher Grade Course
which was given in the Academies and Secondary Schools of Scotland. This
would be a step in the right direction if accepted in the right spirit by adminis
trators, but we are not far wrong in stating that it is being used to the detriment
of a large number of children of humble parents. Since the war the workers
have been sending their children more and more to the Secondary Schools,
and a building problem has resulted. Now our educationists see a chance of
turning away large numbers to those Advanced Divisions in the Elementary
Schools, and under the pretext that the courses of study are "just as good
many are being diverted unfairly from the best course. No doubt in time
the Advanced Divisions can be made very effective, but at present no satis-
factory equipment exists for Science and Art Teaching, and the scarcity of
Chapter V. teachers make it improbable that the teaching can be higher, for a
few years at any rate, than the old and fatuous supplementary classes. Mem-
bers should watch jealously the actions of Education Authorities in developing
and equipping those Divisions both with apparatus and qualified teachers,
so that children of working-class parents will not be prejudiced, and miss the
best and most valuable period of their educational life. At present the watch-
word is cheapness, but the electors should demand efficiency at whatever cost.
Education of children cannot be prostituted to save a few pockets.
```

HIGHAM & RUSHIDEN. Pleased to report a falling off in sickness and
unemployment during the month (with the exception of the unemployment
caused by Messrs. Sanders & Sanders fire). The Blucher Statement has been
scrapped by the County Board and the old Black Work Statement of the Army
District has also been formally and respectfully buried by the Joint Standing
Committee governing Government Contracts, which means that the only
Statements now in existence in the District are the Northants County State-
ments and the Army Red Book. We have granted £2 2s. od. to the Rushden
Builders now on strike.

KINGSWOOD AND DISTRICT.--Trade shows signs of improvement in
this centre, and the figures published in the Half-yearly Report again show
the substantial sums paid to the Kingswood membership during the past
half-year. We are sometimes inclined to wonder if our operatives fully realise
the value of this side of our Union's activity. Certainly the stability of our
financial resources is the wonder and envy of less fortunate organisations,
and should stimulate the operatives of our district to a higher respect for
the Union which has proved its ability to establish decent standards of wages
and conditions. We have voted £5 to London Metro. and wish the officers in
charge a speedy and satisfactory settlement. With trade improving in this
District comes the question of overtime, and we are determined that all opera-
tives who refuse to insist on payment of time and a quarter, will be dealt with
as working against the interest of the Union.

LEEDS No. 1.--We regret to report that trade here, especially in the
Heavy and Medium work, is not good, but on lighter work we are much better.
During the month Mr. Wright, our Solicitor, has been successful in settling
two cases of Compensation after much time and inconvenience, viz., R. W.,
35193, £20; and J. P., 34933, £27 IOS.

LEICESTER No. 1.--We have to report a considerable falling off in
trade, every week showing an increase in the number of discharged and sus-
pended members. Some manufacturers appear to have a tendency to discharge
or suspend members at the first signs of decreasing trade. This matter was
discussed at our August Branch Meeting, and a letter has been sent to Mr.
T. W. Smith, Secretary of the Leicester Federation, asking that manufacturers
carry out the following resolution, passed at a meeting of the Board on 30th
August, 1923: "That with a desire to limit the amount of actual unemploy-
ment during the present period of slackness of trade, manufacturers be advised
to work uniform short time, either departmentally or over the whole factory,
in preference to discharging or suspending operatives." We trust this will be
carried in the interests of the members. A sum of £15 has been granted by

PLYMOUTH (REPAIRING). This month we have to report that thanks
to the Finance Act and the Labour Government the Plymouth Co-operative
Society find it no longer necessary to deduct twopence for a receipt stamp
from our members who happen to earn two pounds or more. Thus ends one
of the chapters in our history which has caused a good deal of annoyance and
unpleasantness. The decision of the Society came at a most opportune moment
when the Branch had decided to make one more effort to remove the grievance,
but before saying goodbye to the old imposition we wish to thank all those who
helped to expose its injustice and bring the question to the notice of those in
authority. It is nearly five years since our Branch first took up the matter
with our Co-operative Committee, and we have been slowly hammering away
ever since. Many methods were adopted to call attention to these deductions,
letters were written to the Society, the Trades Council discussed the matter,
it was raised on the District Trade Board Committee, and on the National
Board by our General President (Mr. T. F. Richards). Our local Member of
Parliament was also interviewed upon the matter and the question was raised
on at least two occasions in the House of Commons, but nowhere did we find
any attempt to justify the action of the Society, while their Committee actually
expressed regret at not being able to accede to our request for the discon-
tinuance of the practice. However, looking back over our efforts of the last
four year we do not think they were in vain, for someone must have heard
our cry and brought relief. We trust that the jingle of the twopence will sound
all the more musical in the pockets of our members because of the efforts they
put forward to obtain. it.

It is to the credit of the public and the Press that no one of any consequence

who at that time dealt in shoddy, but certain things happened which caused them
falls back on the old, weak, decrepit, worn thin idea, the curse of all movements.
