his action will also tend toward the prevention of exports of boots and shoes which are
action was taken to protect the public against the fraud of shoddy footwear. Furthermore,
destroying the good name for quality in our most important markets, built up at great
expense and trouble by British manufacturers. Readers of our Editorial Comments:
things should be allowed to continue.
In view of this demand of a prominent Labour representative for legislation to protec:
the boot buyer, we are glad to note the question is at last receiving the attention of the
manufacturing side. In the annual report of the General Purposes Committee of the
Boot Manufacturers' Federation mention was made as to what could be done in the matter
of misleading advertisements. Apparently the question is beset with legal difficulties
as it was stated that "the only course open was to communicate with the proprietors of
the paper which published the advertisement, place the facts before them, and induce
them to discontinue the advertisement, although the paper in such a case would probably
require an indemnity from the Federation against a possible action for refusing to insert
the advertisement." Most reputable newspapers, we are inclined to think, require little
persuasion to discontinue misleading advertisements, although, of course, in the case of
standing contracts the question of possible damage must be considered. However, we
hold the opinion, if definite evidence was produced, that any given advertisement was
misleading, it would be at once discontinued with the majority of the leading daily or
weekly papers. At any rate, we frequently refuse advertisements which we consider
against the best interest of the commercial world. It appears to us that the Federation's
reasoning is open to criticism, and that they will have to adopt quite another line if they
wish the public-and, we might add, the leather trade-to believe they are really in earnest
to purge the trade of shoddy.
In the report quoted we also note the statement is made that "so far as the purchaser
was concerned, if he could show that he bought shoes, and had been defrauded by the
advertisement into believing that they were of a quality which they did not possess, he
could bring an action for the return of his money." Fancy that! But as it is usually
the poorest who are defrauded in the matter of footwear, it is manifestly absurd to tell
them that they can take action. Those of us who have had experience of law and lawyers
will appreciate the joke, but at the same time we cannot congratulate the Boot Manu-
facturers' Federation on their help or advice as far as protecting the wearers against
shoddy shoes goes. "Legal opinion," sapiently concludes the paragraph, "was that in
matters of this kind the public must protect itself, and that the Federation could not act
in the Courts as its guardian." As in actual practice the public can do nothing of the
kind, it is all the more reason why such fearless men as Mr. T. F. Richards should return
to the charge again and again, and, what is more, that he should have the hearty support
of British leather producers.

WHO PAYS THE DUTY ON TAXED GOODS?
ANOTHER PROOF.
A South London shoeseller writes:—" I am now convinced that an import duty is a
tax on the consumei, a point on which I formerly felt some doubt. A customer of mine
in Dublin ordered last week a pair of men's boots, price 16s. 6d., which were duly sent,
the postage being 9d. He now forwards me details of the Customs charges—namely,
duty 2s. 7d., and Post Office fee for Customs clearance 6d., making the cost of the boots
20s. 4d. in all. I am not afraid of losing his custom on account of these charges, but he
tells me that several of his friends who would otherwise send their orders to me will not do
so in view of the higher cost owing to the import duty. I enclose the label showing the
Customs charges on the parcel I sent." Our correspondent may be assured that any
prospective customers will pay the import duty, whether they buy footwear from him or
from a Dublin shoe dealer. For when a wearer in the Irish Free State demands shoes of
the character our correspondent deals in they must be imported. In the case of goods
imported in bulk lots the Post Office fee for Customs clearance is not chargeable, but there
is no escaping the charge of 2s. 7d. on a pair of boots invoiced at 16s. 6d.
* * *
When the duty of 15 per cent. came into operation a few months since it was feared
in some quarters that the exports of footwear to the Free State would be reduced per-
manently. For it was predicted that British shoe manufacturers who previously traded
with Irish buyers would establish factories across St. George's Channel. No move in
that direction is yet apparent, and it seems that the large quantities of shoes which were
rushed over in order to evade payment of the duty are nearly absorbed, for our Dublin
correspondent reports that representatives of British firms are now securing good orders
from old customers, and that the trade has now reached the normal level. The tariff,
in Ireland a good deal of worry, as the Customs authorities are
responsible for the holding up of consignments which would formerly have gone through
promptly. That, however, is what invariably happens when import duties are levied.
The Free State Government is evidently obtaining considerable revenue on the imports
of boots and shoes. -The Shoe and Leather Record, 8th August, 1924.

TRADE BOARD DEPARTMENT.
MISS JEWSON asked the Minister of Labour how many inspectors and investigator
since he took office and will he ask the Treasury for a further grant, in view of the bad
are employed in the Trade Board Department; by how many have these numbers increased
wages and conditions of many workers ?
MISS BONDFIELD: As the reply is necessarily a long one, I propose, with my hon
Friend's consent, to circulate it in the Official Report.
Following is the answer:
The total number of inspectors sanctioned for the Trade Board Division of the Ministr
of Labour is 60. Of these, three are headquarters staff engaged in general control, and
three are engaged from headquarters on special inquiries. Forty-eight officers have
either been allocated, or are in process of being allocated, to seven divisions in which
inspection has been decentralised, and the remaining six inspectors will be appointed
later. The total inspectorate, including the headquarters staff and special inquiries
officers, sanctioned when my right hon. Friend assumed office, was 30; though, in addition
10 officers were working as Trade Board inspectors on loan from other Departments of
the Ministry. Further, as part of the decentralisation of inspection, provision has been
made for secretarial assistance in each division.
With regard to investigation, which is carried out not by the Trade Boards Division,
but by the Statistics Division, for the general work of investigation (including that in
connection with the Trade Boards Acts) carried out by them, the total number of officers
sanctioned is 28 (including four officers in control). This figure compares with the total
staff of eight in post at the time mentioned in the question.
With regard to the last part of the question, we shall carefully watch the progress
made in the work as the result of this increase in staff, with a view to seeing that it is ade-
quate for the present work or any further work which may devolve upon it.

HOURS OF INDUSTRIAL EMPLOYMENT BILL.
A "Bill to Limit the Hours of Work in Industrial Undertakings" in Great Britain
was introduced in the House of Commons by the Minister of Labour on 14th July.
The object of the Bill is to give effect to the provisions of the Draft Convention adopted
in November, 1919, at the first meeting of
Labour Organisation, establishing the principle of an 8-hour day and a 48-hour week,
subject to certain qualifications, in industrial undertakings. The Ministry of Labour
Gazette, August, 1924.
BRITISH FOOTWEAR IN CANADA.
Imports Three Times Fifteen-year Average.
MONTREAL, 28th July. - The Shoe Manufacturers' Association of Canada points out
that during the fifteen-year period 1899 to 1914 the value of British imports of shoes
averaged 178,114 dol., compared with 660,765 dol. for the fiscal year ended March, 1924.
The Canadian manufacturers also state that British competition up to the present has
been principally in a few lines-particularly in heavy walking boots of fine and cheaper
grades and in felt slippers. They say that in one or two of these classes the British manu-
facturers have already captured probably as much as one-third to one-half of the entire
trade, and that this competition is spreading to other lines. (Reuter's Trade Service.) -
Shoe and Leather News, 14th August, 1924.

FEWER INDIAN CHILD WORKERS.
Results of Recent Legislation.
The effect of the application of decisions taken at the annual s
national Labour Conference of the League of Nations on the questions of the mai
of child workers and the limitation of hours of work is shown by a report on the
of the Indian Factories Act for the year 1922, extracts from which are quoted in Ladeni
and Labour Information, the weekly publication of the International Labour Othe
In spite of the inclusion of a number of new factories by the coming into
in July, 1922, of the Indian Factories Amendment Act, the number of children emplos 1
for child labour from 9 to 12, states the report. In cotton spinning and weaving taill
decreased from 68,113 in 1921 to 67,658 in 1922, owing to the raising of the minito a
and jute mills, which usually employ about three-fourths of the total number of factit
children, the increase in the number of males in 1922 was 10 per cent., whereas the winter
children was not followed by a corresponding increase in the employment of women
of females increased 5 per cent.
It may be concluded from this that the exclusion of
Statistics of the average weekly hours worked in factories throughout India have been
published for the first time. They show that, while the majority of the factories probably
worked up to the maximum of 60 hours permissible under the amended Factory Act, a
considerable proportion worked appreciably shorter hours. In the case of men, more
than a quarter of the factories making returns were observing a week of not more than
38 hours, and in the case of women the proportion was considerably higher.
It is noteworthy that the number of accidents reported during the year 1922 was

down the movement again began to extend in countries in which a high degree of indus-

agreements concluded during this period and the legislation passed regulating labour
conditions laid down restrictions on the length of the working day and thus secured on
behalf of the worker a margin of spare time. This margin the workers sought to use in
part to better their own economic conditions.

RED INTERNATIONAL OF LABOUR UNIONS.
The Opening of the Third Congress of the Red International of Labour
Unions at Moscow, on 8th July, 1924.

On 8th July the Third Congress of the Red International of Labour Unions was
opened at Moscow. Even the opening speeches show how great is the yearning for unity
in the R.I.L.U.

Losowsky (President of the R.I.L.U.) said: “The strength of the revolutionary
Trade Union Movement lies in the fact that it is permeated through and through with the
Communist spirit.”

BUCHARIN, speaking in the name of the Fifth Congress of the Communist International,
said: "What we have to do is to awaken a furious hatred of the yellow trade union leaders,
to produce manliness, perseverance and political far-sightedness enough to shrink from
nothing, to utilise every opportunity to destroy the present yellow leadership, and to
win the trade unions for ourselves."
THAELMANN (Germany): "We must look facts in the face. Next to the profiteers
IS THE AMSTERDAM INTERNATIONAL, which still has in its ranks (both in respect of organisation and of ideas) a large part of the world proletariat. Our business is to destroy its
influence on the working classes.

"We must examine our experiences in the past campaign, if we are to destroy the
influence of the Amsterdam lackeys on the working classes, and thereby win over the
workers organised in trade unions.

"In our fight to secure the daily needs of the working class, we must convert the
trade unions into organisations which are capable of being a powerful weapon against
the bourgeoisie IN THE CIVIL WAR which must INEVITABLY RESULT FROM THE ARMED
INSURRECTION OF THE PROLETARIAT.
"Every economic conflict which breaks out in the course of the imperialistic developments of world capitalism is an important political battle. To bring this experience
within the reach of the masses organised in trade unions is to go halfway towards the
victory of the revolutionary idea in the trade unions, and towards dealing a death-blow
to the Judas policy of the Amsterdammers.
DR. NANSEN ON LIES.
Double Standard of Morality Wrong.
Dr. Nansen, speaking at the World Congress of Women University members at
Christiania, said: “We must acquire new ideals—the old ones were not good enough,
and we must acquire an international frame of mind that will work for humanity.
“Hitherto we have had two varieties of morality, one for the individual and another
for the State. It is asserted that these two varieties of morality are indispensable to
humanity; that is a lie; there is no reason why national morality should not be the same
as individual morality. Whether a statesman or an individual lies, it is a lie all the same.
Lies and the two varieties of morality are what have created the misery of the past.”
Herald, 7th August, 1924.

[One more example of what is termed “business lies." As Dr. Nansen states, it must
be part of our business to destroy such false standards.—E.L.P., G.S.]

A TRADE UNION VETERAN.
Joe Wescoe's 70th Birthday.
A very pleasing and interesting little function took place at the Leeds Trades' Hall
the other evening. It was the seventieth birthday of Mr. Joe Wescoe, Secretary of the
Leeds No. 1 Branch of the Boot and Shoe Operatives' Union. A smoking concert was
arranged and many of his old friends gathered and congratulated him on the occasion.
Mr. T. S. Briggs, President of the Trades' Hall Club, presided, and he, together with
Messrs. Braily, Dobbs, Willans, and others expressed their very hearty congratulations.
A pipe and tobacco pouch was presented to Mr. Wescoe as a small token of their esteem.
Mr. Wescoe, who has been for 32 years the secretary of his trade union branch, as well
as senior trustee for the Club for a period of 22 years, suitably acknowledged the gift and
the congratulations and expressed his best wishes for the United Trade Union and Labour
movements. He had during his period of service seen many changes and some considerable
progress. He pleaded for a spirit of unity and toleration, which he said was the proper
line to take to secure more and greater progress.—Leeds Weekly Citizen, 25th July, 1924.

BOOT AND SHOE INDUSTRY.
In this trade employment during August continued moderate, and was not so good
as in July; short time was again prevalent. Compared with a year ago, however, there
was an improvement at almost all centres.
The percentage of workpeople unemployed, as indicated by the unemployment books
lodged at Employment Exchanges, was 8.7 on the 25th August, as compared with 7.5
on the 28th July.
Returns from firms employing about 36,900 workpeople in the week ended 23rd
August showed that about 28 per cent. of these workpeople worked short time in that week
to the extent of about 12 hours each on an average.
Employment in London continued depressed in the manufacture of medium weight
goods, but there was some improvement in the light dress and dancing shoe trade. At
Leicester employment continued slack, with much short time, and was worse than a
month earlier. At Northampton employment continued fairly good, the general improve-
ment previously reported being maintained. At Wellingborough employment was
described as very poor, with a large amount of unemployment and short time, particularly
in men's occupations; there was also much unemployment at Kettering. A slight improve-
ment was reported in the Higham and Rushden districts, and employment was fair. At
Leeds employment continued slack with makers of heavy and medium boots, and was
worse than in the previous month. At Stafford there was a considerable amount of short
time and unemployment, partly due to seasonal slackness, and employment was con-
siderably worse than a month earlier. Employment in the slipper trade of the Rossendale
Valley continued good, but showed a slight decline.
At Norwich employment continued good, and skilled workers especially were well
employed, although overtime was not so general as previously. In the Bristol and Kings-
wood district employment was fair and somewhat better than in July; while at Street it
continued good.

THE TRADES UNION CONGRESS.
was held in the City Hall, Hull, this year, Mr. A. A. Purcell, M.P., being the
Chairman. Despite statements to the contrary, the Congress was, in our
a very successful one, not only from the point of view of the number
of resolutions dealt with, but the spirit shown, and determination to as far as
possible ensure unity of working amongst, and in connection with the various
Unions that form the Congress. This was more especially shown in the resolu-
tions dealing with the question of fewer unions; the policy of unity of action
between unions and the increased powers given to the General Council to help
any union which may find itself in difficulty regarding conditions of labour
or any new agreements into which they desire to enter. The Congress was
also noted by the fact that for the first time there were fraternal delegates
from Russia. The whole of the delegates from other countries dealt with the
question of the desirability and necessity of an understanding being arrived
at between all the unions so that greater effectiveness could be given to the
movement for improved conditions of labour in whatever country such move-
ment may be taking place. We secured the assent of Congress to two of the
three resolutions submitted by us-Housing and Compulsory Workshop
Accommodation-but in relation to the resolution dealing with

POLITICAL.

work as to ensure when the appeal is made—the Labour Party securing
a largely augmented membership in the House of Commons.

GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.

On the question of shoddy shoes we are not putting forward the
claim that shoes are "shoddy" because they are not composed of all leather, because we
are aware that there is leather and leather. Our claim is first and foremost to protect the
public for the honour and credit of our industry, which at present does not hold so high a
position in the minds of the poorer portion of the community, as it would if we could
persuade a sympathetic Government to adopt a descriptive label, tab or warranty of some
kind indicating in plain language the composition as to what the component parts of the
shoes are made, as most people nowadays can read; the onus would then rest on the
purchaser if they bought a pair of shoes such as I have before me--a "Basil" Upper, Canvas
and Paper backed insole, with a split middle and outsole, to be sold at 5s. These goods.
sold to an inexperienced person, is nothing short of a criminal offence in the eyes of all
and under the pretence that they are part of a
honest people, as under no circumstances are they worth the money, especially when they
are palmed off to the public as though
consignment of goods purchased from some reliable source. These goods are sandwiched
in, to the amazement of other shoe dealers, who complain of such mean tactics that they
would not descend to adopt. In this connection one wonders why the Government should
permit firms to advertise the fact that certain goods are rejects from the War Office, or
the Navy, or from the Government Contractors. The latter may easily be true, but the
former is sometimes true. In a large number of cases such goods were never made for
or intended for these Departments, as only those are genuine that either have the name of
the manufacturer or the firm where made, or have a private mark of the Department.
We hope that the Government will, for the benefit of their reputation, irrespective of what
Party may be in office, insist on all manufacturers who make shoes for either the Army,
Navy or Air Force, adopt the old method of stamping all such goods with the name and
address of the maker. Such a method would not be an inner step in shoddy goods, it would
be in keeping with our old advocacy in regard to house property, that all owners' names
should be placed in a prominent place where anyone could see who were the owners, and if,
as we are informed, it is a useful thing to advertise, why not stamp the source of origin,
or attach, by a label, the same information. Surely we are all interested in protecting the
public from wilful and malignant imposition.

ORGANISERS' REPORT.
During the past month we have been keeping in close touch with men on dispute at
Jackson & Joseph's. This dispute is now in its thirteenth week and the men are deter-
mined to return to work until the full Terms of Agreement are put into operation.
We have been in communication with as many boot factors as we can possibly find who
are not
We are very pleased to report that many of these firms have sent
hase dealings with this firm, asking them to refrain from purchasing goods while the
favourable replies, and we hope by this method to put the necessary pressure on, not only
conclusion
to bring the firm to a reasonable frame of mind, but also to bring the dispute to a favourable
Unfortunately there are few well-known firms who have not thought it
advisable to adopt this policy, and these firms by the continuance of this attitude, are
only prolonging the dispute, but are assisting Jackson & Joseph's to undermine the National
Terms of Agreement. We wish to point out that we are in possession of evidence, carefully
compiled to prove that the conditions and wages existing on this firm are of such a nature
and character which makes it utterly impossible for other firms, even in this area, to
approach within 25 per cent, the prices of the goods produced by the firm in question.
In visiting a large number of firms in this district we are continually confronted with
the impossibility of producing goods at such a low rate. No wonder, when we come to
consider the hours of working and general conditions obtaining. The week before the
strike commenced, and many weeks previous, the number of hours worked were from
00 to 65 hours weekly, always including Saturday afternoon and Sundays. The prices
paid for work done in the clicking room alone, exclusive of extras, was upwards of 25 per
cent. below London Statement. We feel that all possible pressure should be brought
to bear to end such a disgraceful condition of affairs, as the tendency is to lower the
standard of the whole industry.
Up to the present we have explored every possible avenue to end this dispute, and we
are convinced that the continued pressure that is being applied is having its effect. The
principals of the firm are not at all happy in the circumstances in which they find them-
selves. With the object of furthering our investigations we have visited a number of
federated and non-federated firms, and the information obtained proves there is still
room for improvement. The National Agreement is broken in some way by almost every
firm visited. The operatives are not without blame in this direction, many of them
objecting to the Holiday Scheme being applied, thereby making the work of organising
more difficult and full of disappointments.
Despite these difficulties we are endeavouring to visit each shop in turn in order to
encourage more active interest in the affairs of the Union, and although this work is by
necessity very slow, we feel that this is the only method that can be adopted in an area
where men reside miles from their place of employment.
To sum up, we feel that London, from the point of view of our industry, is a place
where continued vigilance is required, and concentrated activity is absolutely necessary.
We would again call attention of all branches that the dispute at Jackson & Joseph's is
in its thirteenth week, and while thanking them for past donations, ask for continued
financial support.
LEN. SMITH.
J. H. BAUM.

FOOD.
Between 1st August and 1st September there was a further fall of about 2d. per 7 lbs.
in the average retail price of potatoes, but otherwise all the articles of food covered by
these statistics showed an appreciable upward movement in price, except meat, sugar and
margarine, the prices of which showed little or no change on the average. The greatest
increases were in the average prices of butter (1 d. per lb.), bacon (1 d. per lb.) and eggs
(d. each). As a net result of all the changes recorded, the average increase over the level
of July, 1914, in the retail prices (in Great Britain and Northern Ireland) of the articles
of food included in these statistics rose to about 66 per cent. at 1st September, as compared
with about 64 per cent. at 1st August. - The Ministry of Labour Gazette, September, 1924.

NATIONAL CONFERENCE (SEPTEMBER, 1924) AGREEMENT
The Incorporated Federated Associations of Boot & Shoe
Manufacturers of Great Britain and Ireland and tho
National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives.
NATIONAL CONFERENCE
Of REPRESENTATIVES OF THE FEDERATION and THE NATIONAL
held at 7 Tavistock Square, London, W.C. 1, on 18th and 19th September 1924.
COPY OF AGREEMENT arranged by the Conference.
On the motion of Mr. H. J. Bostock, seconded by Mr. T. F. Richards, it was unani-
mously resolved :-
"This National Conference again urges upon H.M. Government the desirability of
giving to National Agreements voluntarily entered into and approved by the
Industrial Councils the same validity as Awards under the Trade Board Act, and
the object of ensuring the observance of fair conditions of labour, by all engaged
in the industry, and requests the Government to give facilities for passing into law
the Industrial Councils Bill read a second time on 29th May, 1924."
CONFERENCE AGREEMENT.
Uniformity in Labour Price of similar classes of Goods.
1. (a) Subject to resolutions 1 and 5 (d) of the Terms of Settlement it is desirable
that a uniform system of prices should obtain, and that the general outline or groundwork
of such system should be arranged on a broad basis, so that the essential conditions and
prices can be applied or adapted to the same class of labour and materials in all areas
producing similar classes of goods.
Notice of alteration in System.
(b) Manufacturers shall, before changing the method of working from piecework to day-
work, or vice-versa, give four weeks' notice of their intention to the operatives, and also notify
in writing the local branch secretary of the Union.
Basis of Piecework Statements.
2. Where general or shop statements do not at present exist, the Local Arbitration
Boards, at the request of either side, shall proceed forthwith, upon the ratification of this
agreement, to prepare piecework statements for their respective districts (subject to
Clause 1). All manufacturers and operatives shall accept such statements in their entirety
as a basis of payment, but the system shall be termed a daywork system, and the wages
of the operatives shall be regulated and adjusted weekly according to the amount of work
done at the prices fixed by the statements for each operation or process, provided that no
adult operative shall be engaged at less than the minimum wage rate without the written
permit of the Union or the Local Arbitration Board in cases where the minimum wage
is applicable, and provided also that when operatives, whether on full or short time, have
been supplied with a full quantity of work and have been granted reasonable facilities
for the proper performance of their work, and do not earn the minimum or agreed wage
rate at the statement prices, they shall be paid only for the actual work done at the state-
ment prices. In cases where circumstances arise that prevent the operatives earning the
minimum or agreed wage rate owing to bad materials or special care required in the per-
formance of their work, such cases shall be subject to special adjustment between the
employer or his representatives, and the operatives or their trade union officials.
Non-Restriction of Output.
3. It is understood that operatives use their trade skill and productive ability to the
best advantage and fullest capacity provided they are paid the full rate of wage for all
output.
Regulation of Conditions of Employment.
4. (a) Where operatives attend at the factories on the instructions of the employers
or their representatives, work shall be found for them for at least half a day, except when
short time is being worked, and in that case operatives, whether engaged on day or piece-
work, shall be informed overnight if their services will not be required on the next working
day, and shall be informed before the midday interval if they will not be required to attend

DUNDEE. - The position in Dundee from a trade point of view, permits
of no exultation. It moves, but exceedingly slow. It gives us pleasure,
however, to state that a section of our branch - Blackford - has shown a spirit
of enterprise in having secured an American order for their noted gents' brogue

Mr. Taylor, the manufacturer. A picnic and presentation of more than passing
notice took place on a recent Saturday, the occasion being the jubilee of the
firm of Messrs. Jas. Carmichael & Sons, curriers, and tanners, and until recently,
boot manufacturers, Tay Street, Dundee. A party of seventy left the city in
char-a-banes for Birnam, an ancient and beautiful country town, noted for
its Royal Forest, which figures in " Macbeth." In consequence of a continuous
downpour of rain, the Institute there became the rendezvous. Here the party
made merry in dancing, recitations and songs, which I learn, were rendered
in a highly creditable manner. The memorable item in the programme
however, came on after an excellent tea had been served. Mr. Yeaman, one
of the firm's oldest employees, in a well-set speech, presented Mr. Jas, Car
michael, senior partner, with a golfing bag and a set of golf balls. Mrs. Jas
Carmichael became the recipient of a chaste afternoon tea service of Royal
Crown Derby China. Mr. Carmichael, in returning thanks, was in a happy,

business. Becoming tired of conjugating verbs, his father harnessed him to

very quickly changed his opinions of life at school. This, however, did no harm
as he remarked, but rather had a chastening effect, it being the lowest rung
of the ladder. It afforded him great pleasure in referring to the very happy
relations that existed between the firm and the employees, that during all
these years there had been no serious rupture. Mrs. Carmichael, in a charming

THE FIFTY-SIXTH TRADES UNION CONGRESS.
DELEGATES' REPORT.
The Fifty-sixth Trades Union Congress was held in the City Hall, Hull, from the
Ist to 6th September, 1924, Mr. A. A. Purcell, M.P., presiding.
The Congress was officially welcomed by the Mayor and Sheriff and representative
from the Hull Trades Council and Labour Party.
The President's Address to Congress whilst citing many of the things accomplished.
was also a plea for breadth of outlook and co-operation between the various forces that
are making for a better and brighter world, and the outlook generally to be such as will
bring into line not merely the various British elements of the Labour Movement, but also
those of other countries, especially naming Germany, Russia and India. Mr. Purcell
concluded his address as follows:-
THE FORWARD VIEW.
"It is becoming increasingly clear that deep down in the hearts of our class
and women who are coming to take our places in this movement stand out much
there exists a determination to end the present state of things. The younger men
against the evils we have permitted to continue, nationally and internationally.
more saliently as rebels against the existing order, protesting and demonstrating
"We must not grow weary or tire in our energy and enthusiasm in our efforts to
secure the co-operation of the younger generation in the work of remoulding and
rebuilding our great movement on an all-inclusive plan, giving the opportunity to
them to develop administrative skill, gifts of organisation, and power of leadership.
capable of changing the existing structure of capitalist society and bringing into being
Our aim is not merely to build big unions, but to create an instrument of solidarity
service a place, an opportunity and a life free from the horrors of poverty, ignorance,
a Workers' State which will guarantee to all who are ready and willing to render
insecurity, and disease."
The resolutions passed were of very great importance to the movement, and marked
a stage forward to bring about that understanding which will enable the trade union
movement as a whole to make real headway. For instance, what will be known in future
as THE CHARTER is really a consolidation of many resolutions that from time to time have
been passed by the movement, and now form a composite resolution so that one may see
at a glance what the movement stands for.
INDUSTRIAL WORKERS' CHARTER.
"That this Congress reaffirms the decisions of past Congresses with regard to
necessary and rundamental changes in our social, economic, and political systems,
and decides to formulate the said decisions in an industrial workers' charter, and
pledges itself to secure by every legitimate means the fulfilment of the objects con-
stituting the charter which, subject to such additions as Congress may from time
to time approve, shall be as follows :-
1. Public ownership and control of natural resouces and of services-
(a) Nationalisation of land, mines and minerals.
(b) Nationalisation of railways.
(c) The extension of State and municipal enterprise for the provision
of social necessities and services.
(d) And to make proper provision for the adequate participation of the
workers in control and management.
2. Wages and hours of labour-
(a) A legal maximum working week of 44 hours.
(b) A legal minimum wage for each industry or occupation.
3. Unemployment-
(a) Suitable provisions in relation to unemployment with adequate
maintenance of the unemployed.
(b) Establishment of training centres for unemployed juveniles.
(c) Extension of training facilities for adults during periods of industrial
depression.
4. Housing-
Provision of proper and adequate housing accommodation.
5. Education-
Full educational facilities to be provided by the State from the elemen-
tary schools to the universities.

HOUSING.

The annual Housing Conference was held prior to the Trades Union Congress at Hull
and attended by many delegates from all parts of the country. It was overwhelmingly
proven that there is as great a need, if not greater, for the erection of houses as was the
case two years ago. The question of building houses affects the moral, health and domestic
questions, and we are running great risks not only from a health point of view, but of
reducing the standard of our lives by overcrowding. It is therefore incumbent upon us
to continue to bombard local authorities, M.P.'s and the Minister of Health, and constantly
remind them of this vital necessity of building houses for the people to dwell in.
The following instances recorded during the month show a shocking state of affairs

Gravel Pit as Home.

At Depwade (Norfolk) District Council yesterday the inspector reported that a man
and his wife and child were living in a gravel pit at Needham. Their covering was sack
over poles, but they had got a feather bed. The owner of the pit charged 3s. a week for
the use of the pit.
The chairman said there would be more straw stacks after the harvest, which would
make better accommodation than this. – London Daily Mail, 9th September, 1924.
* * * *
The scandal of exploiting the homeless by charging exhorbitant rents for what are
styled "Furnished Rooms" is mentioned by the Medical Officer for Oldham.
In his annual report he quotes a case of a derelict house, formerly an Inn, let by the
owners for £40 per annum, yielding a total rental for so called "Furnished Rooms" of £408.
No wonder that, as the doctor says, those engaged in this very profitable business
are always on the look out for additional houses to convert into furnished rooms.
The profits quoted by the doctor are by no means exceptional. The house is larger
than those generally converted into furnished rooms, but the rent per room is not more
than the average.

Dr. Wilkinson gave another instance where a house rented at £27 per year brought
to the tenant 54s. per week from furnished rooms, and still allowed him a kitchen and
bedroom for his own occupation.
A health inspector gave instances of tenants of four-roomed cottages letting off three
of the rooms and getting 16s. per week rent from the sub-tenants though they themselves
only paid 6s. rod. to the owner of the house.
A two-roomed back-to-back cottage was let at 5s. per room and there were many
cases of rooms being let off at 12S., 13S. and 14s. a week. The so-called furniture generally
consisted of a dilapidated bed, with a minimum of clothing, a rickety table, and a broken
chair or form.—E. L. P., Gen. Sec.

At the recent Conference of representatives of the Union and the
Federation, on the motion of Mr. H. J. Bostock, seconded by Mr.
T. F. Richards, it was unanimously resolved—

"This National Conference again urges upon H.M. Government
the desirability of giving to National Agreements voluntarily entered
into and approved by Joint Industrial Councils the same validity
as Awards under the Trade Board Act, with the object of
ensuring the observance of fair conditions of labour, by all
engaged in the industry, and requests the Government to give
facilities for passing into law the Industrial Council's Bill read
a second time on 29th May, 1924."

A DOCTOR ON THE EIGHT-HOURS DAY AND ITS BENEFITS.
La Journée Industrielle, the journal of the French industrialists, contains a leading
a singularly unprejudiced book on "The Life of the
article, speaking in highly appreciative terms of the work of Jacques Valdour, a French
doctor, who has recently published
Worker." Valdour is a zealous student of social reform, and he spends his holidays working
incognito as a factory hand, and living in the ordinary workers' quarters. He has some
interesting things to tell us about drunkenness; he declares that it has much decreased
since the war: during the whole of last summer he saw scarcely ten cases of drunkenness
in the largest working-class districts of Paris, and the number of public-houses is fast
declining. He traces this change to the beneficial influence of the eight-hours day, which
has caused no less than 300,000 Parisian workers to move out into the suburbs and buy or
build small houses there. All these workers, says Valdour, have given up drinking, and
have returned to their families.

TRADES UNION CONGRESS-THE LABOUR PARTY.
The Anglo-Russian Treaties.
One of the first acts of the Labour Government was to carry out its avowed policy
tions with Russian representatives have been pursued with the object of framing a series
of according diplomatic recognition to the Russian Government. Subsequently, negotia-
of Treaties by means of which assistance may be rendered to Russia to re-establish her
industries.
Many of the politicians, aided by their representatives in the Press, are conducting
a campaign of violent misrepresentation of the present proposals. In view of these activi-
Labour Government as a PRELIMINARY TO DISCUSSION BY THE HOUSE OF COMMONS, steps
ties against the ratification of the two Treaties which have been signed on behalf of the
should be taken to bring the true facts respecting the Treaties before the public generally
The main points to be emphasised in respect to the present proposals may be summarised
and the rank and file membership of the Labour and Socialist Movement in particular.
as follows:-
(a) The two Treaties already signed MUST BE RATIFIED BY THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
before they can become operative.
(b) Certain machinery provided in them will be set up to settle the claims of bond-
holders, small claimants, and ex-property owners.
(c) When satisfactory agreements have been arrived at, these agreements will be
EMBODIED IN A THIRD TREATY.
(d) Upon the SIGNATURE OF THE THIRD TREATY the British Government will "recom-
mend Parliament to enable them to guarantee the interest and sinking fund of a
loan to be issued by the Government of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics."
(c) The loan CANNOT BECOME OPERATIVE UNTIL THE THIRD TREATY HAS BEEN
RATIFIED.
Time and time again, in days gone by, the British Democracy has headed national
opposition to the excesses of Czardom. It has defended the right of asylum in this country
for Russian refugees. At a decisive moment it successfully raised its emphatic voice
against a new war with Russia. While it opposes the suggestion that the Russian form of
Government is necessary under our Parliamentary system, it recognises that the entrance
of Russia once more into international relationships with this country and the world at
large is as imperative to the interests of Britain as to Russia.
We call on every active spirit in our ranks to let the man in the street and the woman
in the home know the true facts of the case, and so put power and moral force behind the
Labour Government to secure an overwhelming vote when Parliament is called upon to
ratify its Russian policy.
FRED BRAMLEY, Secretary.
Signed on behalf of the General Council of the Trades Union Congress,
J. S. MIDDLETON, Acting Secretary.
On behalf of the Executive Committee of the Labour Party,

BOOT REPAIRING TRADE BOARD.
Report on Inspection for Second Quarter of Year.
The Boot Repairing Trade Board (Great Britain) has issued a report on inspection
and enforcement for the period 1st April to 30th June, 1924, in the course of which it is
stated that on 30th June last the number of firms on the Trade Board list was 29,021.
During the period under review 77 firms were inspected for the first time, the number of
firms previously discovered being 11, making total
inspections during the three months 88.
Of the firms inspected, 10 employed fewer than 2 workers (excluding 5 firms employing
no workers), 18 employed from 2 to 5 workers, 4 employed from 6 to 10 workers, 1 employed
between 11 and 20, and 1 employed between 21 and 100. The total number of workers
employed by the firms inspected was 100.
The total number of complaints received during the period was 63. Of this number,
57 were investigated, 18 being dealt with by correspondence. Arrangements, it is stated,
have been made for the investigation of the 36 complaints outstanding.
The activities of the inspectors are not confined to the investigation of complaints
received. A number of inspections are undertaken on the initiation of the Department.
designated "Routine Inspection," and in the following details, the routine inspections
are prefixed (A) and the inspections undertaken after the complaint has been received
are prefixed (B).
The number of firms inspected during the three months was (A) 49, (B) 39; total, 88.
The number of firms on whose premises it was found current notices were not posted
was (A) 8, (B) 9. The number of firms where it was found time records were not kept was
(A) 27, (B) 20. In (A), 12 firms were found to have kept no records of wages paid, and in
the case of 3 the wages records were inadequate. In (B), 9 firms were found to have kept
no wages records, and one had kept an inadequate wages record.
The number of firms found to be under-paying workers was (A) 6, (B) 14. The total
arrears claimed from these firms were (A) £21 9s. 10d. and (B) £205 13s. 9d. The total
number of workers under-paid was (A) 8, (B) 18, the total number of workers to whom arrears were
paid being (A) 7, (B) 15. A note is added that the arrears outstanding under (A), due
from one firm, are being paid by instalments. Of those outstanding under (B), £46 4s. 5d.
from one firm, is being paid by instalments. Action is being taken to secure pay-
ment of the remainder, which is due from two firms, and was claimed only recently.
The number of adult time workers employed by the firms visited was 86, 83 male and
3 female. It was found that 8 adult males were being under-paid, the arrears claimed
totalling £115 1s. 5d., of which £22 11s. 3d. has been paid. This was under (B), no under-
payments in this section being discovered in the course of routine inspection.
The number of learners employed by the firms visited totalled-male 44, female nil.
In (A), 6 juveniles were found to be under-paid, the arrears claimed being £19 17s. 3 d.,
of which £12 4s. 4d. has been paid. In (B), 5 learners or juveniles were found to be under-
paid, the arrears claimed totalling £27 12s. 4d., of which £13 19s. 4d. has been paid. Piece-
workers employed by the firms visited were found to total 69, all males, of whom, in (A),
two were found to be under-paid, the arrears totalling £1 12s. 7d., all of which has been
paid; while in (B), 5 were found to be under-paid, arrears totalling £63, of which £51 11s. 1d.
has been paid.
The number of firms inspected in the different divisions into which Great Britain is
divided for the purposes of the Trade Board were :-Scotland (A) 10, (B) 2; North-Eastern
(A) 3, (B) 1; North-Western (A) 1, (B) 5; Midlands (A) 11, (B) 8; South-Western (A) 11
(B) 6; London and South-Eastern (A) 4, (B) 17; total (A) 49, (B) 39. Of the inspections
undertaken, 70 occupied one day or less, 14 occupied two days, and 4 occupied three days.
The report under review concludes with "General Remarks," which are devoted to
particulars of two summonses, one at a Police Court and the other at a County Court.

BOOT REPAIRERS' WAGES.
Increase of 3s. a Week from September 1st.
The cost of living figure having reached 71, the time-rate wages of boot repairers are
to be increased on 1st September by 3s. per week, bringing them up to 60s. Notification
of the increase will be issued in the course of a few days by the Boot Repairing Trade Board.
The alterations to be made in the existing schedule of piece rates will indicate a reduction
of 7 per cent, on the previous standard instead of as formerly 12½ per cent.; the piece
rates will be those shown in column two instead of those given in column three.

DUBLIN.
From Our Own Correspondent.
Since September opened retailers have been unanimous in their compla
(1) taxes and (2) high prices. It is not because there is little business
and traders are missing sales because the public either cannot or will not reale
turnovers are not generally satisfactory; it is because the pinch of the test dr
Until September cheap summer shoes kept ladies' departments going togethe
plimsolls for children, but now, with the winter season approaching, more suletantu
"experimental" tariffs are of grave domestic concern.
The Press generally are very critical of the "Statistical Tax," which from 1st September
has been levied on all parcels imported by post or rail. The tax is chargeable on each
article (descriptions specified) contained therein, so that several sixpences may be charge
able on the same packet. Although this tax is not levied on dutiable goods, it is being
freely discussed by the boot trade, because laces, grindery, leather, rubber heels, window
tickets, stationery, paper and string, &c., are all affected, and this, of course, adds to the
bootman's burden.
The trade is with the Irish Times in the belief that "it is high time that the business
community of the Free State should assert itself and protest against the further Balkanisa-
Of course, this tax, like the 15 per cent. tax, promises a substantial revenue because
44.2 per cent. of the number of consignments imported by sea in September last were
under £10 in value; 45.2 per cent. of those imported by rail were under £5, and 55.4 per
cent. of those imported by road under £3. The Shoe and Leather Record, 19th Septem-

IRISH FREE STATE STATISTICAL TAX.
Protest by Dublin Merchants.
At a meeting of the committee of the Dublin Mercantile Association held last week,
a resolution was adopted expressing the opinion that the statistical tax of 6d. recently
imposed on import trade was injurious.
It was stated that the tax, which was hitting the boot trade severely, would cost
firms anything from £100 to £500 per year, which would require a pro rata increase in turn-
over of £2,000 per year-an increase that was not likely to materialise.
Commenting on the tax the Irish Times (Dublin) writes: "Nobody wants this tax.
The public is irritated by it. The business community declares that it is defeating its
ostensible purpose; and, of course, it adds considerably to the already absurdly com-
plicated system of classification in connection with the Customs frontier. As a revenue
producer its value is likely to be negligible. It may bring a little more business to local
distributors; but, WHEN ALL IS SAID AND DONE, its chief result will be a further increase
in the cost of living."The Shoe and Leather Record, 19th September, 1924.
One more example of the burden of "Protection," viz.-increase in cost of living-
E.L.P., Gen. Sec.j

INTERNATIONAL LABOUR CONFERENCE.
The General Council of the Trades Union Congress has published a 24-page booklet,
and circulated it to the Congress delegates at Hull, giving the full report of Mr. E. L.
Poulton, J.P., the Workers' representative for Great Britain, of his work at the Inter-
national Labour Office, Geneva, which report deals with the 48-hours week; night baking;
unemployment; glass workers' weekly suspension; workmen's compensation, &c.
Mr. E. L. Poulton's Initiative.
A feature of the speech delivered by M. Albert Thomas, in the name of the International
Labour Office, was the high appreciation he expressed of the work done at Geneva by the
British Trade Union representative, Mr. E. L. Poulton, J.P. It was through Mr. Poulton's
initiative, he said, that the I.L.O. had been able to raise industrial standards in backward
countries to a higher level.

MONTHLY REPORT,
27TH OCTOBER, 1924.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
TRADE
during the month has shown a slight improvement; the figures recorded by
the Ministry of Labour Gazette are as follow:-
BOOT AND SHOE INDUSTRY.
Employment during September remained moderate on the whole, and a good deal of
short time continued to be worked. There was little change compared with the previous
month, but a general improvement compared with September of last year.
The percentage of workpeople unemployed, as indicated by the unemployment books
lodged at Employment Exchanges, was 8.5 on the 22nd September, as compared with 8.7
on the 25th August.
Returns from firms employing about 38,400 operatives in the week ended September
27th showed that over 34 per cent. of these operatives were on short time in that week
to the extent of about 12 hours each on an average.
Employment in London was generally bad; but an improvement was reported in
departments making men's boots. At Leicester short time was fairly general, and em-
ployment on the whole was slack and worse than in August. It remained fair at North-
ampton, though some short time was worked. At Wellingborough employment, although
only quiet, showed a slight improvement on the previous month, women workers being
in demand. There was not much change at Kettering, where short time and unemploy-
ment were still prevalent. Some factories, however, were working full time. Most
factories at Higham and Rushden worked full time, and employment continued fair.
At Leeds employment in the heavy boot department remained slack, and short time was
general; an improvement, however, was reported. At Stafford employment was very
slack. Employment in the slipper trade of the Rossendale Valley improved slightly,
but a large amount of short time was still worked.
Conditions were not so good as in the previous month at Norwich, and employment
was only fair. In the Bristol and Kingswood district, on the other hand, there was a
further improvement, and employment was fair. At Street employment remained fairly
good.

NATIONAL (SEPTEMBER, 1924) AGREEMENT.
The full Agreement was published on pages 509 514 of the last REPORT
and the more important changes in the Agreement were set forth in ouw Addre
last month. We venture to say an impartial examination of the Agreement
and the advantages we have secured are such as to fully warrant not only

markets of the world are not yet normal. We confidently appeal to member
ance of the proposed Agreement, especially when it is considered that the
such an important matter affecting as it does-the members as a whole.
not only to record their vote in its favour, but to poll in large numbers upo
Meeting night. Votes to be counted on the 12th prox., and the results posted

THE GENERAL ELECTION.
We have during the past few months, repeatedly urged upon the members
the necessity of keeping the political machinery in good working order, because
in our judgment an election might be precipitated upon us at any time. This
has now become a fact, and before this REPORT is in the hands of the members
it will be known whether the workers have returned a Labour Government to
power. The General Election was not of our seeking, but we are confident
upon this occasion that the policy of the Labour Party is the policy of the
workers, and also the best for the Nation generally. A majority of Labour
M.P.'s in the next House of Commons will mean real headway being made
to bring about better conditions in the lot of the workers. The work of the
Labour Party during the past few months is sufficient evidence to show what
will be done once they are returned to power.
So far as the Union is concerned, we shall have candidates at ECCLES
FROME and NORWICH. In the first-named division, Mr. J. Buckle, J.P.,
will again champion the cause of Labour; at Frome, Mr. Fred Gould, J.P.,
will be the Labour candidate; and for Norwich, Mr. W. R. Smith, J.P., will
again be cur nominee. The great and outstanding need is work. We are
fully satisfied that the work our colleagues have done oit behalf of all
sections of the community during their membership of the House of
Commons is of such a character as to fully warrant their re-election to
Westminster. Their services have always been given to the community
freely, and we very sincerely hope that the electorate in the various
divisions will return our colleagues by large majorities to the House of
Commons to enable them to continue their work for the benefit of the
people as a whole. Therefore,
WORK AND VOTE LABOUR,
Both in the General Election and Municipal Borough Elections.

DEATH OF COUNCILLOR T. ADNITT, J.P.

It is with sincere regret that we have to record the fact that Councillor
T. ADNITT, J.P., of Leicester, passed away on the 19th inst. after a short
illness. Mr. Adnitt was elected Vice-President of the Leicester Branch
in 1919 and President of the Branch in 1920, and was a member of the
Council of the Union from September, 1921, until September, 1924.
Mr. T. Adnitt did useful service in many connections and he will be
missed from our work. We trust his good work will enable the younger
generation to take up the sword that Mr. Adnitt has had to lay down.
The funeral took place at Leicester on the 22nd inst., and
was attended, on behalf of the Council, by the General President
(Mr. T. F. Richards), Mrs. M. J. Bell-Richards and Mr. D. McCarthy,
Organiser.

THE LABOUR PARTY CONFERENCE.

During the month the Twenty-fourth Conference of the Labour Party
has been held in the Queen's Hall, London. The Conference was indeed a
momentous one, as during the sitting the Prime Minister decided to dissolve
Parliament and appeal to the country. Many resolutions were passed dealing
with housing, unemployment, &c., whilst it was decided by an overwhelming
majority not to accede to the request of the Communist Party and allow them
to affiliate with the Labour Party.

The Conference really resolved itself into the commencement of the
Election Campaign, the feeling of the delegates being very intense that every
ounce of energy must be put into the Election, and thereby not only repel the
attack upon the Party, but make further steps forward when dealing with the
many questions by which the real interests of the people are at present being
held back. The Prime Minister gave a magnificent speech to rally the forces
of progress against reaction, and we feel confident the effects of the Conference
generally will be felt for many days yet to come, as an incentive towards still
more determined effort being made to place the Labour Party in a majority
in the House of Commons.

We regret that Mr. W. R. Smith, J.P., failed to secure re-election upon
the Executive Committee. The General Secretary, Mr. E. L. Poulton, J.P
was elected a member of the Conference Arrangements Committee for nex
year, whilst the General President, Mr. T. F. Richards, acted as Teller to th
Conference.

PARLIAMENTARY AGENTS.
Mr. D. McCarthy, one of the Union's Parliamentary Agents, has tendered
to us his resignation from that post as he feels unable to face the strain necessary
for parliamentary life. We do not intend to fill the vacancy at the moment
but propose to do so when the various nominations are taken for the national
conferences in February next.
HISTORY OF THE UNION.
It will be recalled that the "Fifty Years' History of the Union" was
presented to the delegates to the Union's Conference, and also a copy has
been sent to each Branch. It has come to our knowledge that there is a
desire on the part of some of the members to secure a copy if a cheap
edition could be printed. We have made arrangements to issue such an
edition at Is. per copy. To enable the order to be placed immediately,
please send to the Central Office stating how many copies you will require
of this most interesting and valuable record of the work of the Union.

BALANCE SHEETS.
We beg to call serious attention to the fact that THIRTY-FOUR
branches failed to send in their balance sheet for quarter ending August, in
accordance with Rule 127. As a consequence unnecessary trouble and
expense is caused by having to make application for the same, and unless
balance sheets are remitted AT ONCE, we shall have no alternative but to
put Rule 302 into force.

THE "DAILY HERALD."
We trust that all our members will take every available opportunity to
push the Herald, the only daily paper owned and controlled by the movement.
By purchasing the Herald daily a full report of the political world as seen by
Labour can be read.

REMEMBER THE FIFTEENTH!
Once again we feel bound to call the serious attention of Branch Secretaries
to the fact that the FIFTEENTH day of each month is the latest day for
returns reaching the General Secretary. If Branches fail to send off their
returns to reach the Central Office before the 15th of the month it tends to
upset the organisation of the work in the General Secretary's Office. We beg
to intimate that unless returns are in before the 15th of the month, the Secretary
has been instructed to put into force the Rules governing the same. Returns
Sheets MUST also bear the signature of both the Branch President and Branch
Secretary, or they will reluctantly have to be returned for completion.

TRADE BOARD PROSECUTION.
Repairer Fined and Ordered to Pay £19 Arrears.
At the South Western Police Court, before Mr. K. McMarshall, on Friday last, Walter
Sidney Crick, boot repairer, 12 Ritherdon Road, Balham, was summoned for failing to
pay Walter Henry Clifton, an employee, the minimum wages fixed by the Boot Repairing
Trade Board. There were also two summonses against him for failing on 28th April
and 21st May to post in the workroom a schedule of the minimum rates.
The defendant, who pleaded guilty, said: "I did not know anything about it. I have
been in the business only 18 months."
Mr. Kemp, prosecuting for the Ministry of Labour, said that on 28th April an Inspector
visited the defendant's premises and found that Clifton was not being paid the minimum
rates and that no schedule of rates was posted. The defendant gave as his reason that he
did not think it necessary, and that he knew someone else who was not paying the rates.
Mr. Kemp added that Clifton was a pieceworker, and that for the week ending 17th
May he was underpaid 9s. He received £2 18s., and an underpayment of 9s. on that
amount was a considerable sum. As there was no schedule of rates posted in the shop,
Clifton was not able to tell what was due to him. On 28th April the defendant promised
to post the schedule. On 21st May the Inspector found that the schedule was not put
up properly. It was tacked down at each corner, and the rates relevant to Clifton's work
were not visible. The fact was significant, because another adult worker whose rates
were set out on the first sheet of the schedule was properly paid. A man who paid less
than the minimum rates was indulging in unfair competition with others. On the defend-
ant's conviction he (Mr. Kemp) proposed to ask for an order for the payment to Clifton of
the arrears due to him.
Mr. Victor Andrew Goddard, an Inspector under the Trade Boards Act, said he had
calculated that from May, 1923, to the date of the summons Clifton had been underpaid
£19 4s. 2d. The defendant carried on a good class business, and charged his customers
top prices.
The defendant stated that Clifton was not an ordinary workman, but a friend who
worked as he liked. Clifton had a perfect right to look at the schedule if he wished.
The magistrate said the defendant was warned on 28th April. He imposed a fine
of £5 for not paying the minimum rates, fines of 20s. on each of the two summonses for not
posting the schedule, and £2 2s. costs, and ordered the defendant to pay £19 arrears to
Clifton. The Shoe and Leather Record, 3rd October, 1924.

BRANCH REPORTS.
ARBROATH. - Trade is still failing to pick up with us, and the winter
months will make life more trying than ever. Since our last report we have
now got a decision in our test case re customary holidays. This has gone
against us, but the reasons for the decision should be noted. The argument by
the Umpire is not given in our case, but can be seen in the current issue of
the Labour Gazette in a case stated by dock labourers. In spite of the fact that
many dock labourers in different parts of the country are exempt from the
holiday rule because it is held that docks are not shut down for customary
holidays at all, this case, No. 7712, was turned down by the Umpire on very
shallow grounds. We would urge all officials of the Union to read carefully
that report, because it will show the Government attitude which we must
oppose. The Umpire, a comparatively new man by the way, rejects a number
of definite opinions of his predecessor, and goes back to an early view that the
12-day rule should apply generally, and not be limited to absolute customary
holidays of shop, or workshop, or factory. A volume of protests could soon
clear this pious view out of the way, and establish a better and fairer practice.
Just the other week our members lost one day's benefit because of the statutory
autumn holiday, even although they have not worked on a Monday for four
years. We say without hesitation that no holiday should be kept off a part-
time worker unless it deprives him or her of employment. When the worker
would otherwise have been employed, it would be unfair to expect benefit,
but when a holiday is part of idleness it should be paid as such. Our members
are interested in the New National Agreement, but before supporting same they
are to have it elucidated by a Council Member. The main objection to it falls
on the qualification to the boy question, namely, exempting heel-building,
preparing and stock rooms. In our experience this vitiates entirely the con-
cession secured. But we will reserve judgment until we have heard an ex-
planation by one who was there. We have to report this month the dismissal
of our Secretary from his employment because he insisted on his right to attend
a sitting of the Court of Referees. Although every member of the Union
employed in this factory could confirm the fact that no work in the place was
urgently needed at the time, a curt refusal to permit the Secretary's attendance
was given by the management. The sorry thing about it is the fact that the
firm which employed him agreed to represent the Employers' Panel in order
to allow our Union to be on the Workers' Panel, and yet no provision was to
be made to put it into practice. This opens up the big question of workers'
rights in connection with government organisations, and more will be heard of the
matter. Our relations with this firm have been cordial enough, and it is a
great pity they should countenance any action likely to impair these, yet there
is no justification for the arbitrary interference of one who is comparatively
a stranger to the detriment of good feeling. It is our earnest wish that some
satisfactory arrangement may be made to provide our Secretary with a modest
living to enable him to continue his helpful work on behalf of workers of all
descriptions.
CHESHAM.--The improvement in trade previously reported is main-
tained, and we are pleased to report our sick and unemployment claims for the
month are very small. During the month one case of accident, with legal
assistance provided by the Union, has reached final settlement, the sum
obtained being £35, in addition to weekly compensation from the time of acci-
dent and legal expenses.

NORWICH. Trade in Norwich continues fair, although unemployment
has steadily increased during the month. The additional numbers unem-

Apart from seasonal failure, condition of trade is generally satisfactory, the

PLYMOUTH (REPAIRING).-By the time this report appears in print
the great fight will be over and the verdict known, but if the Government be
judged by its success in diplomacy and the establishment of goodwill among
nations, then the verdict must be one of complete confidence, for it is here that
the spirit of Labour has been moving the hearts of men to higher and noble things.
When the Conservatives gave up the seals of office the Ship of State was moving
fast into the rapids of international strife, while the dark clouds of despair
gathered around, but thanks to tactful and courageous handling by Labour the
ship has been pulled into smooth running waters and the hope of glorious
sunshine. When we contemplate how with the stroke of the pen treaties
and agreements have been made in the past, interfering with trade and ulti-
mately forcing the wages of working men down to starvation level, then it is
we realise that the voice of the toiler must be heard and the hand of Labour
guide the pen. Nationally, we believe Labour will increase its strength, for
although the anti-labour Press is united against us, its power is already beginning
to wane, with the Daily Herald giving the truth every day and the contempt
and exposure coming from Labour platforms, the people no longer look upon
the views expressed as gospel truth, but are beginning to see that more often
than not the Press is on the side of those "who toil not, neither do they spin,"
and "against" those who live by the sweat of their brow. What the result
of the election will be we cannot tell, but those who have an abiding faith in the
progress of humanity will know that whatever the number of Labour men re-
turned to Westminster, the cause of right goes marching on.

STAFFORD.-Trade in this centre is very slack, and we sincerely hope

WATERFORD.-Trade continued good for the past month.

THE 10-HOUR DAY IN GERMANY.
To the Editor of the Shoe and Leather News.
Sir,-On page 7 of your issue of 2nd October there is a statement about the
day in Germany. The statement is so drawn up that it would appear that the
day is a recognised working day in the shoe trade.
I beg to state that at a meeting of the International Boot Operatives
held very recently, where there came under review the various methods of c
of pay, and hours of labour in many countries, it was distinctly stated that the
boot operatives have made a new agreement with the employers of Germany, To
a 48-hour working week in the shoe trade, as also to some extent increasing the ro
wages. This agreement I have a copy of, and, as a matter of fact, as I am dictatar
letter the same is in my hands.
There is, therefore, no sort of doubt about the shoe trade having maintained a 14-1
working week.
You finish up your statement as to what the League of Nations has to say abeer
throwing overboard the Washington Agreement. Upon this point I beg to state that the
matter has constantly been before the governing body of the International Labour Office,
and the statements made at such meetings are that if there is any departure from the
48-hour working week it is only temporary, and, as a matter of fact, a good many of the
statements made relative to the hours of work in Germany are not in accordance with
facts.
It is clear, however, that in the shoe trade the hours of working are as stated above..
Yours faithfully,
October 4th, 1924.
E. L. POULTON, General Secretary,
National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives.
[We are glad to receive from so well-informed a correspondent as Mr. E. L. Poulton
the assurance that, so far as the shoe trade is concerned, there is a new agreement retaining
the 48-hour week. This, of course, does not alter the fact that the law in Germany which
established an eight-hour day has been revoked, and that it will now be legal to work
extended hours. We are glad to be assured that the governing body of the International
Labour Office is alive to the importance of the risk of throwing over the Washington
Agreement. We do not, however, like even a permissive temporary departure from the
48-hour week in Germany. - Editor, Shoe and Leather News.] -Shoe and Leather News,
9th October, 1924.

COUNCILLOR T. ADNITT, J.P.,
Passes Away after a Short Illness.

After a very short illness the death has taken place of Councillor Thomas Adnitt,
J.P., President of the Leicester No. 1 Branch of the Boot and Shoe Operatives' Union
As recently as Wednesday, 8th October, he was at the Shoe and Leather Fair in London.
On the following Friday he was taken ill, and had to keep at home. Serious symptoms
developed, with the result that he passed away early yesterday morning.
Born 56 years ago, Councillor Adnitt had been associated with the life of Belgrave
from his earliest days. With the keenest interest he watched the village grow into the
large and important suburb of the city of to-day; indeed, he played no small part in its
development, first throwing himself into its religious, social, and recreative affairs, and
later entering more fully into its public work.

His City Council Work.
Aspiring to represent Belgrave on the City Council, he was elected on that body as a
member of the Labour Party in November, 1912. He served for ten years, and was then
defeated at the polls by Mrs. Swainston on the question of school grouping. In the fol
lowing year, however, he was returned to the Council by Latimer Ward on the death of
Councillor N. C. Perkins. While interesting himself in Corporation affairs generally, he
specialised in the work of the Watch, Health, Sanitary, Water, and Distress Committees.

His pushfulness was seen in his activities as a worker in the shoe trade. He secured
a seat on the executive of his branch (No. 1) of the Shoe Operatives' Union, then became
vice-president, and, five years ago, succeeded to the presidency vice the late Mr. T. Orton.
He sat on the executive council of the Union for several years, and helped in the negotiation
of the last two wage agreements. He retired from this national position last August.
Recognition of his public service took the form, a few months ago, of elevation to the
position of Justice of the Peace.
Considering his physical disability, it was remarkable what a large and varied amount
of work Councillor Adnitt got through. He showed much devotion to duty, and his
colleagues and indeed all who knew him-held him in much esteem. He lost a son in
the war, and leaves a widow and daughter. - Leicester Mail, 20th October, 1924.

Funeral Service.
Many manifestations of esteem and regret were seen at the funeral of Councillor
Thos. Adnitt, J.P., of 65 Marfitt Street, Leicester, which took place to-day.
Prior to the interment at Belgrave Cemetery, an impressive service was held at
Belgrave Hall, conducted by the Rev. T. Bernard Jones (pastor).

Minister's Tribute.
The Rev. T. Robinson, in an address, said he knew full well there were many present
who could speak of the late Councillor Adnitt's work on the City Council, and as president
of No. 1 Branch of the Boot and Shoe Operatives' Union; while others could speak of
his presidency of the Leicester Trades Council. Others could bear witness to his active
and abiding interest in the Adult School movement, and to his splendid service rendered
on behalf of Belgrave Hall.
He was a local preacher, a teacher of young men, and a class teacher, and was always
ready to help young people. These things he accomplished in spite of a great infirmity,
and in spite of the great personal sorrow in the loss of his son, who was killed in the war
and who was organist of that Sunday School.
Whatever he undertook, Councillor Adnitt did it with great enthusiasm and con-
centration, while his sincerity and integrity earned him the love of all with whom he came
into contact. He was a man of great faith, hope and charity.

The Mourners.
Among the chief mourners were Mrs. Adnitt (widow), Miss Adnitt (daughter) and
Mr. and Mrs. Workman.
Representing the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives were the Council:
Messrs. T. F. Richards (General President), D. McCarthy (Union Organiser), and Mrs.
M. J. Bell-Richards (Council Member), W. Warner (Hinckley) and W. Wyman (Welling-
borough).

ONE NEVER KNOWS.
One never knows
How far a word of kindness goes ;
One never sees
How far the smile of friendship flees.
Down through the years
The dead forgotten reappears.
One kindly word
The soul of many has stirred.
Man goes his way
Until life's end
And tells with every passing day
"Once unto me he played the friend."
We cannot say
What lips are passing us to-day.
We cannot tell
Whose prayers ask God to guard us well.
But kindness lives
Beyond the memory of him who gives.
-Edgar A. Guest, in Seattle Star.

MR. T. F. RICHARDS STILL ON THE WARPATH.

SHODDY

With acknowledgments to "Shoe and Leather Record."

"LEATHER AND LEATHER."

The Public and Shoddy Shoes. Guineas v. Shillings.

"Malignant Imposition" must End.

Shoes for my lady at eight or nine guineas a pair are being shown at the Shoe and
Leather Fair this week, and "shoes" for the community at 5s. a pair are mentioned by
Mr. T. F. Richards, General President of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives,
in his last monthly report to the members of the organisation.

My lady's shoes were described in the Daily Herald on Tuesday-black satin with
inlays of gold, and ostrich feather trimmings.

Mr. Richards describes the 5s. shoes thus: "A 'basil' upper, canvas and paper-backed
insole, with a split middle and outsole."

The selling of these goods to an inexperienced person he characterises as "nothing
short of a criminal offence in the eyes of all honest people."

"There is nothing like leather " is one of the slogans of the industry; but in explaining
that the Union does not claim that shoes are "shoddy" because they are not composed of
all leather, Mr. Richards says there is "leather and leather."

Protecting the Public.

In order that the public may not be duped, Mr. Richards throws out the suggestion
that all manufacturers should be compelled by the Government to indicate, in plain
language, by a label, tab, or warranty, the composition of the component parts of shoes.

Referring to the large number of goods that are advertised as rejects from the Army
or Navy supplies, which in many cases is to be doubted, Mr. Richards expresses the hope
that the Government will insist that all manufacturers who make shoes for the Forces
shall stamp them with the name and address of the maker.

"Surely," he concludes, "we are all interested in protecting the public from wilful
and malignant imposition."-Daily Herald, 9th October, 1924.

Mr. Poulton Explains Clauses to Wellingborough Operatives.
Mr. E. 1. Poulton, J.P., the General Secretary of the Boot Operatives' Union gave
the quarterly meeting of the Northamptonshire Joint District Council at Wellingborough
an able résumé of the new Factories Bill and its relation to factory hygiene. He had for

the General President Mr. W. G. Cove, M.PP. Mr. G. Chester, Kettering; and many
well-known members of the Union.
and it was one upon which the Home Office always welcomed a deputation of workers
Mr. Poulton said the subject before them was assuming an international character
particularly when they desired to bring about an improvement in factory life. This new
Factories Bill was the result of many years' agitation, not merely on the trade union and
political side of the movement, but amongst many outside, who had been convinced of
the inadequacy of the existing Acts of Parliament. The last Act was passed in foot,
but anybody who had been connected with the trade since then would agree that the
Factory Acts wanted overhauling and bringing up to date. Circumstances had been
too strong against them moving in that direction hitherto.

stitute for the 250 cubic feet air space for individuals no less than 400 cubic feet. In some

improvement in certain of their factories. The clause as to the provision of an adequate
supply of soap and clean towels for the workpeople raised a smile, and Mr. Poulton said
there ought to have been these facilities provided years ago, as was done in America.

of an agitation by men like themselves, but there was a chance in the Bill to make that
drying of clothes were provided for in the Bill, and the speaker dealt in detail with the
Seats for female workers and suitable accommodation for the storage and

that although many improvements had been made in these matters during the past few
