MORTALITY IN THE SHOE TRADE.
There has recently been published a Blue Book giving a return of the mortality among
men in certain occupations in the three years 1910-1912. The report is a very full one,
and although not exhaustive, the great majority of trades are included. An obvious
criticism of any deductions made from the figures is that they are twelve years old, and this
criticism carries very much weight in matters relating to the shoe trade. The delay in
completing the returns and the publication is partly accounted for by the war, but that
does not fully satisfy the curiosity for the reason of so long a delay.
They are not altogether pleasant reading, for they show that consumption levied a heavy
toll.
The figures we quote are all comparative, that is, they tell nothing in themselves,
but, in the words of the report, "They bear the same ratio to each other than the death
rates would."
The compilers take what they call a standard of population. That is a sample of the
general male population which may be taken to represent the average, and so the com-
parisons of any trade with this standard population show how that trade or profession
compares with the average. The number of deaths between the ages of 25 and 65 in the
standard population would have been 790. Among Shoemakers it was 820, but
among the Shoemakers of Northamptonshire and Leicestershire only, it
was only 736. Where the difference lies may be seen below.
From consumption alone the deaths in the shoe trade were very much higher than
that of the standard population. They were amongst shoe operatives as a whole, 222;
Northamptonshire, and Leicestershire only 235; and in the standard population only 142.
In these years the shoe trade had a very bad record. The following corresponding figures
showing deaths from phthisis taken at random from certain other trades for purposes of
comparison: Miners, 87; agricultural labourers, 71; doctors, 65; schoolmasters, 70;
ironfounders, 148; watchmakers, 187; bricklayers, 128; furriers, 182; curriers, 190;
saddlers, 154; printers, 210; tailors, 187; brewers, 181; hotel keepers, 198; general
shopkeepers, 185. In not many industries is there a higher death rate. The worst of
all is that of the tin miners, where the figure is 684. Other trades which are worse than
the shoe trade include lead miners, 335; stone getters, in sandstone counties, 415; file
makers, 434; potters, 282; tobacco manufacturers, 239; hotel servants, 294; barmen,
434; hawkers, 420.
Apart from phthisis, the figures show that the shoe trade is a healthy one. The deaths
The standard population from alcoholism and cirrhosis of the liver were four and 13;
xive operatives show even greater sobriety than that, for the figures were only two and
-No.amption Daily Echo, 29th September, 1924.

INTERNATIONAL LABOUR OFFICE NEWS.
WORLD LABOUR CONDITIONS.
Meeting of the I.L.O. Governing Body.
The Governing Body of the International Labour Office of the League of Nations met
at Geneva on Thursday, 9th October, and discussed a number of important questions.
Among the items on the agenda was the fixing of the date for the 1925 Session of the
International Labour Conference. This Session will discuss generally social insurance
and also an international agreement on workmen's compensation. The 1924 Session,
which met last June, provisionally adopted Draft Conventions on equality of treatment
regarding accident compensation for national and foreign workers; on the weekly rest
in glass-manufacturing processes where tank furnaces are used; and on night work in
bakeries. These, together with a recommendation on equality of treatment, will come
before the 1925 Session for final voting and, as the Governing Body fixes the agenda of
the Conference, it will be for next week's meeting to decide formally to place these questions
on it.
The Governing Body will also discuss the agenda for the 1926 Session, having before
it the recommendation of the Joint Maritime Commission, which recently met at San
Sebastian, that the subjects (1) of international codification of regulations regarding
seamen's articles of agreement and (2) of labour inspection at sea should be included
therein.
Other questions will be resolutions referred to the Governing Body by the 1924
Session, and decisions of the Assembly of the League which affect the International
Labour Office.
The Governing Body consists of 24 persons, 12 representing Governments and six
cach the employers and workers. The British representatives are: Government, Miss
Margaret Bondfield, M:P., Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of Labour ; Employers,
Vice-President of the
and Workers, Mr. E. L. Pouiton, Secretary of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Opera-
tives.

ARMY AND NAVY BOOT "REJECTS."

Mr. T. F. Richards, the President of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives
once again tackles the question of shoddy shoes in his September report. And good luck
to him! This time he tells us that shoes are not necessarily shoddy because they are not
composed of all leather and in this we agree with him. He advocates a descriptive tal
or label to show just what the shoes are made of; judging by his description of one
"chamber of horrors," called a shoe, the time is ripe for this, although we rather fancy
ever, here is his description of a shoe he has before him: "A basil upper canvas and
paper-backed innersole, with a split middle and outsole to be sold at 5s." Mr. Richards
thinks the sale of such goods to inexperienced people is nothing short of a criminal
offence.

Another fraud he draws attention to is the advertising and selling of boots which are
supposed to be rejects from the War Office, Navy, or Government contractors. He
states that in a large number of cases such goods were never made or intended for these
Departments, and he advocates the stamping of rejects with the name and address of the
maker. "Surely," he concludes, "we are all interested in protecting the public from
wilful and malignant imposition." Whatever view the shoe trade may take we feel Mr.
Richards has the support of the leather trade in his efforts, at all events. -The Leather
World, 9th October, 1924.

JOIN UNIONS AT ONCE.

No Exceptions made by C.W.S. Important Ruling.

All C.W.S. employees of whatever class must join their respective trade unions or be
dismissed was the resolution adopted on Saturday at the divisional meeting of the Co-
operative Wholesale Society held in Manchester.

This important ruling has arisen out of a resolution passed by the members of the
C.W.S. in 1919 to the effect that all employees should be members of their respective
trade unions.

For various reasons this resolution has not been completely carried out, and at a recent
general meeting in Manchester and Saturday's divisional meeting a definite ruling was
sought in regard to the 1919 resolution, with the result stated.

It had been recommended that managers, buyers, heads of departments, principals,
and confidential assistants and employees over 60 years of age be exempted from the scope
of the 1919 resolution regarding trade union membership, but, after discussion at Saturday's
meeting, the recommendation was lost, 1,531 voting for it, and 1,562 against.-Daily
Herald, 13th October, 1924.

WHEN A WORKER ARRIVES LATE.
Ground for Discharge if Man has Contract of Service.
Weck-End Off Sequel.
An interesting and important decision concerning employees was given by Judge
Cluer in the Shoreditch County Court to-day.
A cabinet-making foreman entered into an agreement for twelve months serve at
45 12s. 6d. a week. In August his wife went for a holiday, and he asked for, and was
granted, a long week-end. The following week he again had a week-end off, it was alleged,
without asking for it, but did not arrive at his place of business until 10 a.m. on the Monday
instead of 8.
Drawing too Fine a Line.
His employer decided that he had broken his contract of service, and he left, but he
was now asking for £50 damages as compensation for his dismissal, it being suggested
that it was drawing a fine line if a man in a responsible position had to turn up to the
minute on a Monday after a week-end off.
Judge Cluer, in giving judgment for the defendant, said the plaintiff could have got
up early and walked, and it was ground for discharge if he had a contract of service and
arrived late. Business was business, and it could not be carried on properly unless the
employees strictly adhered to their part of the bargain. -Evening Standard, 23rd October,
1924.

FOOD.
Between 1st September and 1st October there was a further advance in the general
level of the retail prices of food. All the articles included in the statistics showed an
upward movement in price except meat and margarine, the average prices of which showed
no appreciable change. The most important increases were those in the prices of eggs
(d. each on the average), milk (d. per quart) and butter (Id. per lb.).
As a net result of all the changes recorded, the average increase over the level of
July, 1914, in the retail prices (in Great Britain and Northern Ireland) of the articles of
food included in these statistics rose to about 72 per cent. at 1st October, as compared
with about 66 per cent. at 1st September. - The Ministry of Labour Gazette, October, 1924.

STATE OF TRADE.
24TH NOVEMBER, 1924.
There is a slight improvement in Trade during the month, and the
figures recorded in the Gazette issued by the Ministry of Labour are as
follows :-
BOOT AND SHOE INDUSTRY.
Employment showed a slight decline on the whole as compared with September,
and was only moderate. Short time was still being worked to a large extent in many centres.
Compared with October, 1923, there was a fairly general improvement.
The percentage of workpeople unemployed, as indicated by the unemployment books
lodged at Employment Exchanges, was 10.0 on the 27th October, as compared with 8.6*
on the 22nd September.
Returns from firms employing nearly 40,000 operatives in the week ended 25th
October showed that over 36 per cent. of these operatives worked short time in that week,
to the extent of about 14 hours each, on an average.
Employment remained bad in London. At Leicester it was still slack, and short
time was fairly general. At Northampton employment remained fair, although short
time was still worked at some of the smaller factories. At Wellingborough employment
was quiet, though somewhat better than in September; there was some unemployment
among male operatives, but on the other hand there was some demand for female workers.
Employment remained moderate at Kettering; there was a good deal of unemployment
and some firms were working short time; employment was, however, better than in October
of last year.
In the Higham and Rushden district there was an improvement, and full
time was mostly worked, and at Finedon there was even some overtime.
There was no marked change in the depressed conditions at Leeds, and a great deal of
short time was again worked, especially in the heavy boot trade. There was much slack-
supper trade of the Rossendale Valley there was a slight seasonal decline, and a good deal
f short time was worked.
Short time was worked in some factories at Norwich, but employment, although
Conse was still fair for the time of year, and noticeably better than in October of last
the Bristol and Kingswood district there was a decline; many factories, however,
prin full-time working. At Street employment was fair, but not so good
September.

```text
ENFORCEMENT OF AGREEMENTS.
Members are aware, that apart from our rules as to securing enforcement
of Agreements, the Agreements between the employers and ourselves are
such as to put an obligation upon both sides to see that the Agreements are
fully carried out. This work we claim we are constantly doing, and with
(financial) benefit to the membership. During the past month, an unusual
case has occurred which has created some comment as to the method of the
Union when dealing with employers. The case referred to is that of the
Wilnecote School Boot Co. Ltd., Tamworth, which company went into voluntary
liquidation. At a meeting of the creditors held at Leicester, on the
22nd ult.,
Mr. Watson said, "The decision to wind up became
necessary on account of labour trouble. It appeared that
when the company had taught their employees how to do
good work the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives
made certain demands. The operatives were members of
the General Workers' Union, but as they did not transfer
to the National Union the latter, it was alleged, made repre-
sentations to the Co-operative Wholesale Society Ltd., who
were the company's largest customers. Whether or not
pressure was brought to bear on the Co-operative Wholesale
Society was not clear, but the fact was that orders from
the Society ceased."
Several creditors strongly criticised the action of the
National Union.
It will be seen that several creditors criticised the action of the Union
regarding the matter. Our position is very clear, however, because we might,
and other manufacturers ought, to complain very strongly indeed of people
who start boot and shoe manufacturing and attempt to undersell their com-
petitors by a disregard of the duly accredited statements that have been
entered into between the Boot Manufacturers' Federation of Great Britain
and ourselves as representing the Union. As a matter of fact, we have always
been prepared to consider any special circumstances connected with any firm,
with a view to doing what is just and equitable. In cur judgment it is cause
for complaint by us that this firm attempted to disregard Agreements entered
into-and which we endeavoured to see carried out our only desire in these
matters is to see that the selling prices of goods should not be determined
by undercutting of wages. Further references to this matter will be found
on page 627.
```

REMEMBER THE FIFTEENTH!
Once again we feel bound to call the serious attention of Branch Secretario-
to the fact that the FIFTEENTH day of each month is the latest day for
returns reaching the General Secretary. If Branches fail to send off their
returns to reach the Central Office before the 15th of the month it tends to
upset the organisation of the work in the General Secretary's Office. We beg
to intimate that unless returns are in before the 15th of the month, the Secretary
has been instructed to put into force the Rules governing the same. Returns
Sheets MUST also bear the signature of both the Branch President and Branch
Secretary, or they will reluctantly have to be returned for completion.

GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.

FELLOW MEMBERS.

GENERAL ELECTION. We are sorry to have to report that the General Election
in which we spent many days, has not reached our anticipations, even so far as our repre-
sentatives are concerned. It is a source of deep regret that we have lost in the Eccles
Division, our member, Mr. J. Buckle, J.P., who had successfully repelled the attacks of
the enemy on two occasions, but who on this occasion, fell a victim to the vitriolic utter-
ances of his opponent and the Russian Letter. He was always a very dutiful represent-
ative, and I think, after the good work done by the Labour Government in increasing the
financial position of the Unemployed, Old Age Pensioners, and bringing peace to Europe,
Labour members are entitled to expect from the rank and file of their own order. We
these matters in themselves should have obtained a renewal of that confidence which
do not expect others to be so considerate, or so desirous of making permanent, so far as the
Union is concerned, the position of the average working man or woman. We are also
sorry to report the fact that our other member, Mr. W. R. Smith, J.P., who occupied the
distinction of being Parliamentary Secretary for the Board of Agriculture, was unable
in the field. On this occasion the Liberals and Conservatives combined, and when one
world for some time felt that the vote obtained at the last election was with three parties
to win in the town of his birth, viz., Norwich, but some of us who have known the political
considers seriously that is an important factor in the situation, and it is a most remarkable
achievement to have got within 5,000. Mr. Smith's local assistance and his activities
for many years in the labour world warrant certainly greater confidence, but as we are
also human, we must not expect too much, because there are so many working people
to-day whose lot in life is anything but rosy, and they are often prepared to risk a change
in their position. Personally, I am very pleased to see that the Labour Party itself has
so long as it is a change under the delusion that it is going to bring them some improvement
added over a million votes to its voting strength and its adherents, in spite of all the
vilifications with which they have had to encounter. I am sanguine enough to believe
that the time is not far distant when there will be a further opportunity given to our
representatives, when there is little doubt that they will be returned with great majorities,
and thus enable them to finish the work so well begun. In this connection I should also
like to refer to Mr. F. Gould, J.P., of Frome, who, although only a candidate of the Union,
is an ex-Member of the House, and had taken part in bringing about the improvements
above referred to. Mr. Gould being so well known in the district to which he has devoted
much of his life, and considering the large number of people with whom he has come in
contact from time to time, it certainly was a great surprise that the people who had already
given him a very short trial and in a short space of time preferred another member. Here
again, we believe the time is not far distant when he will place his services at the disposal
of his fellows, and I hope receive that reward to which he is legitimately entitled. It
would be as well if all our members were to exercise themselves in the question of politics,
which to most of us forms part and parcel of the Government of our lives, and it would be
well if all can be induced to show a more vigilant interest. Many people attribute the
failure to the fact that the women had become frightened; to this I do not subscribe.
I take the contrary view and say that our working-class women are thinking women.
and those who have stood loyally by the Labour movement and who are helping to increase
the voting strength of the Labour movement as the results of the General Election show.
Let us hope that at the next election, in spite of the threatened attitude the present Govern-
ment is likely to take towards Trades Unions, that we shall resist all their efforts to interfere
with our liberties. They would be well engaged if they put their own house in order
first before turning their attention to those Unions who are rendering yeoman service by
utilising their funds for the benefit of their members, and thereby easing the rates and
taxes of the Kingdom. My own particular part in the recent contest was spent in Leicester,
Leicestershire, Eccles, and Wellingborough.

LEICESTERSHIRE COUNTY BOARD. It has been my duty to attend the Leicestershire
County Board where our relationships in Leicestershire are so good that we have not met
for several months. The appointment of officers was duly recorded, and Mr. Denman, on
behalf of the Manufacturers, was put forward as Chairman for the ensuing year, and as
is our custom we unanimously supported that gentleman's nomination, and prevailed
upon our old friend, Dan Astley, of Earl Shilton, the past year's Chairman, to take the
position of Vice-Chairman for the coming year. The only matter of any importance was
the notice given to adopt a Pressman's Statement for the County, the same being presented
by the No. 2 Branch of Leicester, endorsed by our side, was referred to a sub-committee
by the Board for consideration and report. This matter will come up in the usual way,
and will be dealt with upon its merits.

HIGHAM AND RUSHDEN. - It has been my pleasure, with my colleague, to attemi the
Annual Gathering of the Higham and Rushden Branch in their Hall, on the 8th in-t.
a policy that has become an annual affair and a social which bids fair to keep Shop Presi

STAFFORD. It was my pleasure to also attend the Monthly Meeting of the Stattord
Branch, and a very goodly number, for the size of the branch, turned up to the meeting
The organising of Stafford was dealt with, and intensive organising was the subject taken.

to call in the factory of Lotus Ltd., in order to visit the Department at the request of the
Council of the Union. One is always pleased to go to the Lotus factory, the courtesy
shown to a Trade Union Official is most marked; anything one wishes to see is immediately
placed at your disposal without any embargo, and although it is not my duty as an official
to advertise methods of manufacture which are entirely of an organising character and for

LEICESTER. I have also had the pleasure of being shown round the Brockton Heel

again here what a method of management can do in an auxiliary branch of the industry,
which most people look upon as being of a minor character, but where the men employed
earn as good wages as ever they do in the more experienced part of the craft.

are making headway. They have a Manager who has a knowledge of the productive side
of the boot and shoe making, and who puts forth his very best energies from the original
point of view to keep the firm going. New machines are being installed, and they appear

ORGANISERS' REPORTS.
During the past month we have been very busy with the firm of Messrs. Hertz & Son.
The position here was that so far as piecework operatives were concerned there was no
restriction in working hours-7 o'clock in the morning to 10 p.m. was quite a common
occurrence, and always Sunday labour. The first climax came when a penny per pair
reduction was put to the men at a meeting held by the employer in the factory. A vote
was taken when a majority voted in favour of acceptance. We at once called a meeting
of the operatives, the whole of them attending. After two and a half hours animated
discussion, a majority decided to resist the reduction, and instruction was given to the
officials to enforce the 48-hour week, and in all circumstances resist Sunday opening of
the factory. An interview was arranged with Mr. Hertz and the proposals laid before him.
He agreed to withdraw the notice of reduction, and also put up notices in each depart-
ment, stating the hours of working, and instructions to the doorkeeper would be given
to open and close the door according to the posted notice.
A fortnight later 22 lasters were discharged on the plea of shortage of work. A
meeting of those discharged and those still at work was held. It was a lengthy and wordy
meeting, and after a considerable time a resolution was unanimously carried that those
still employed should continue to work at the old prices, and accept no reduction. A week
later information was received that a reduction had been offered and accepted by those
working. A meeting was called and the rumour was found to be correct, but the men
concerned claimed that they only accepted the Id. per pair reduction on the understanding
that this should be confirmed by the Branch Committee. A deputation was elected to
attend committee, when they would receive instructions as to what action to take.
We have also been engaged in assisting the Sew-Round Branch in organising out-
workers. We spent the whole of one day when the men were shopping their work, and
interviewed each one.
impression is that with a little more persuasion all these can be organised. We attended
About 100 were seen, of whom half were members, and our general
the executive and monthly meeting of this Branch.
We have had several meetings of Meltzer's operatives in the Finishing and Clicking
Departments. Interviews were arranged and many difficulties were cleared away by
frank discussion. The only difficulty now existing is the pricing of fancy styles in the
Clicking Department. An early interview has been arranged.
A meeting was held of the operatives working at Wachman's and 15 operatives
joined. We have visited in the dinner hours, the firms of Lipman's,
We also interviewed the men working at Lynn's, a repairing shop, and 16 promised to
join, one volunteering to act as Shop President.

s, Chissick's and Cohen's.
The strike at Jackson & Joseph's is still proceeding, and after 22 weeks the men are
still firm. We feel that the pressure which is being imposed is having its effect, and that
we are now within reasonable distance of a settlement.
LEN. SMITH.

```text
BRANCH REPORTS.
ARBROATH. — Trade is no better here, and our members are duly anxious
about the future. We have had great excitement during the election, a Labour
candidate not only fighting the Montrose Burghs as formerly, but one was also
entered for the County Division for the first time. This gave our Carnoustic
members a chance to strike a blow for Labour, and right well did they help.
The candidate was put forward by the Railway Clerks' Association, and a very
excellent fighter he proved to be. Although an agricultural constituency.
which has shown an equality between Liberalism and Toryism in the past,
the Labour candidate persuaded nearly four thousand electors to vote his
ticket. Had the election been fought on clean lines, the Labour vote would
have been much greater, but the power of the Press, and the influence of all
the well-to-do wirepullers in the division, scared many from voting as their
conscience dictated. The unscrupulous misrepresentations of the Russian
Treaty, and later by the " Red Plot," was bound to succeed with such a short
time at the disposal of Labour. Any idea that the Capitalist Class will ever
allow themselves to be voted out of existence has got a rude shock this election.
Those who argue, and there are many, that force will yet be the only power to
subdue them, have their arguments greatly strengthened now. One likes to
think it could all be done constitutionally, but when you find the master class
turning like a vicious animal at bay when very little danger is in the air, one is
left to wonder what would happen if there was a serious danger of their power
being destroyed. A first step towards depriving the Capitalist Class of their
sharpest and most venomous claw would be the nationalisation of the Press.
That these great organs should be left in the hands of wealthy individuals to
use in any way they think fit to poison and inflame the minds of the public is
to incur the danger of the very forces of revolution which everyone deplores.
We regret the defeat of our three candidates, and the regret is the greater when
we realise that small opportunity will emerge to let them go back for a long time
to come. Again will be seen the point we make about the Press. When the
orthodox parties staged their Punch and Judy Shows, the different Liberal and
Tory papers would attack according to needs of the occasion, but when we are
left in the position of the combination majority as it is, and with only one small
daily newspaper to tell the truth, and that paper only read by a handful of
people, when will the people ever get a chance of change. The future is dark
and one can only hope for brightness in a collapse or rupture in capitalistic
forces which have in the past brought about progress even when intelligence
was muzzled and in chains. May truth prevail against the forces of evil.
BRISTOL No. 1. — We are sorry to report trade as bad, with very little
prospect of the improvement we have so long been hoping for. The General
Election has come again, and we are sorry to report we were only able to hold
one seat out of five in Bristol. The only consolation we have is the increased
solid Labour vote, the aggregate being much larger than 12 months ago. We,
in common with other parts of the country, suffered from the effects of the
poison gas let loose by our opponents. Whilst it has given us a set-back for
the time being, we must plod on, feeling assured that in the very near future
truth will prevail, and Labour will come into its own as a result of honest
plodding work. We much regret that our three agents were unsuccessful in
their fight. We, in Bristol, mourn with Kingswood at the loss of our comrade,
Geo. Jones, who was a real stalwart in the Union's cause. To his widow and
family we extend our deepest sympathy. Our Secretary should have repre-
sented the Branch at the funeral, but was prevented at the last moment owing
to urgent Guardians' work.
BRISTOL No. 2. — We can only report that trade is rapidly declining,
for members working only three days a week. The immediate
```

---
outlook is not encouraging. We deeply regret that our three
results, which came as an unpleasant shock. We deeply regret that our three
colleagues were among the defeated and sorrowfully realize that at present
we have no representative in the House. We feel the Party will be weaker
through their absence. All the forces of wealth, backed by a powerful Press
were arrayed against us. We emerged from the onslaught forger in number
but more determined in spirit to carry on until the result of the poll reflects
the judgment of the people rather than that of inflamed passion and panic
generated by base misrepresentation. The voting for the New Agreement
shows a big majority in favour. Regret was expressed that we had not been
able to get a greater restriction in the number of boys. What we desire is that
all those who are admitted should have opportunities to become efficient in
their trade, and be assured of being able to earn a living in the industry.
CHESHAM. Trade here remains good. It was with the deepest regret
we learned of the defeat of all the Union's candidates after the recent election,
but we can, as supporters of Labour, feel pleased with the increase of the
Labour vote.
CHESTERFIELD. Trade is fair. We have still some of our members
unemployed, and our sick list is heavy at the time of writing. We were sorry
to see all our three representatives defeated in the General Election, and also
to see the numbers of the Labour Party reduced when we were hoping for
something better. In a great many instances the Labour vote was consider
ably increased. Mr. G. Benson increased his vote here by over 6,000-last
election 6,000, this time 9,000 - and the Tories supported Mr. Kenyon, the
Liberal. We are improving and next time we shall win.
CORK. Trade remains good.
DAVENTRY. There is an improvement in trade, which we hope will
continue. The Council Member for the district (Mr. W. R. Townley) addressed
a special meeting of the Branch on the 13th inst. and explained the New Terms
of Agreement to the members, who accorded him a very hearty vote of
thanks, and the view was expressed that it was the most successful meeting
the Branch had held for several years.
DERBY. Trade in Derby has greatly improved since the last report,
all the firms being practically on full time.
DUNDEE. It is very gratifying to be in a position to report that the one
(and only one) shoe factory in this large city of ours is busy, viz., the Angus
Shoe Manufacturing Co. Ltd. The repairing section of the trade may be defined
as being in the doledrums. There has just passed beyond our Ken, for all time
coming, one of our oldest members, William Sievwright, a man who did yeoman
service in the cause of trade unionism. He occupied the position of Branch
President for several years, also the vice-presidency of the Dundee Trades
Council. Some twenty years ago he was largely instrumental in bringing into
being the Dundee and District Master Boot Repairers' Association, which
earned for him the sincere thanks of that body. The welding together of the
employers into a concrete organisation resulted in better wages and a con-
siderable improvement in conditions generally for the employees, which testified
to the sagacity and foresight of him, whose death it is our painful duty to
chronicle in this report. Several members at our last monthly meeting paid
warm tribute to the memory of our late friend and shopmate. The Secretary
was instructed to send an expression of sympathy to the family of the deceased,
and that it be duly entered in the minutes of the Branch. The tragic and
painful suddenness of the death of Mr. E. D. Morel, senior M.P. for the City
of Dundee, has cast a gloom over the town, especially in labour circles. Just
a short fortnight ago he was returned with a large majority. In his triumph
death stalks in. "Whatsoever thou hast in hand, availeth not, thy task is
finished." Exeunt.


---
EDINBURGH.- Trade remains much about the same in this district.
After a long period the Branch seems to be going to have some results of our
organising in a factory which has, up till now, refused to become members
of our Union. If the conditions are as stated by the employees, well, they want
some overhauling. We have not been successful in having either of our can
didates returned as members of the Town Council. But we have this consola
tion, that a very good fight has been put up and that the Union will, whenever
they get the chance, again nominate the two members. Well, Edinburgh has
not done so bad in having a Labour gain at the General Election. The Labour
Party must keep pegging away until there is not only Members of Parliament,
but a general desire on the part of all the working class to have better con
ditions on which their lives depend. We were sorry when results came through
to see that our colleagues, J. Buckle, F. Gould, and W. R. Smith, had not been
returned to the House of Commons. They only fall to rise again in greater
strength for the next fight. Our New Agreement seems to be meeting with
general approval of the members. It is not all that could be desired, but still
there is slight improvements.
HIGHAM AND RUSHDEN.- Trade continues fairly good in the dis
trict generally. Finedon, several firms being on overtime; Irthlingborough,
not so busy, three firms working short time er reduced staff; Higham and
Rushden, fairly good; Raunds, Ringstead and Stanwick, no improvement,
while Irchester, Wollaston and Bozeat trade has improved. The whole of our
district is seething in election excitement at the time of writing this report
(28th October, 1924). It is remarkable at the number of our own members
whose names are on the list of assentors to the Conservative candidates' papers.
It convinces us that it is exceedingly difficult in England to break from the old
traditions, and yet we are told of Red Revolution. It seems almost impossible
to rouse the great majority of our members to see that the Members of Parlia-
ment they too often support are also the men they pay trade union subscriptions
to be protected against. Parts of our Branch lie in three different Divisions,
viz., Wellingborough, Peterborough and Bedford. The General Secretary's
addresses at Ringstead and Rushden were much appreciated. The Branch
President has been very busy assisting generally.
KINGSWOOD.- Trade is still fairly good, and we trust this will continue
for some time. Since our last report a General Election has swept over the
country like a tornado. Some constituencies, like the five "Wise Virgins,"
had their lamps trimmed and burning; others, like the "Five Foolish Virgins,"
were unready and there was much wailing and gnashing of teeth. The mag-
nitude of the turnover can now be surveyed in the calm that follows the storm,
and though the casualties are heavy new ground has been gained, new converts
made, new enthusiasm fired. Consolidate your defences against the day.
The tide (like day following night) never fails, but returns again fresh and
strong to bear us firm in faith to our goal-the Co-operative Commonwealth.
We record with deep sorrow the loss of our colleague and friend,
Councillor George Jones, who died 1st November, as the result of a chill
contracted during the election campaign. He was held in the highest
esteem by all sections of the community, and the attendance at his
funeral which our General Secretary attended-was a remarkable
tribute to a good and useful citizen. A close and personal friend for
many years is able to estimate the true worth of a departed friend,
and now George has gone we can realise that the Union is the poorer
for his untimely death. The district has lost a trenchant champion for
all that was worth while his family have lost a kindly father, and his
widow a husband who was a lifelong lover. Faithful and chivalrous,
he was a bonny fighter, and every inch a man.


---
LEICESTER No. 1. It is with deep regret that we have to report the
death of our President. Councillor Thomas Adnitt, J.P. The Branch has
suffered a great loss. A letter of sympathy and condolence has been sent to
the widow and daughter. The Branch was represented at the funeral by
G. Parbury (Secretary), J. Wheeler (Vice-President), A. Worth (Assistant
Secretary), M. Parker (President's Assistant), J. T. Collin, G. Knight, J. Greaves,
H. Cramphorn, G. Brooks (Committee), W. Bailey and F. Wigston (Staff).
H. Widdowson (Anstey), W. Elliott (Oadby), H. Taylor (Wigston), F. Burchnall
(Enderby), S. Bruin (Blaby), representing the Section Secretaries. Trade is
still very bad, in fact we have never had such a long spell. There is no sign
of improvement. We are pleased to report that our Secretary has again been
returned to represent the Wyggeston Ward on the Leicester City Council
by a large majority. He has also had the honour of being appointed High
Bailiff for the City.
LEICESTER WOMEN'S. The Leicester Women's Branch have to
report that trade is still slack, much short time being worked in our Closing
Rooms. Our Branch regrets the result of the General Election, in so far that
we have lost our three members, Mr. J. Buckle, J.P., Mr. W. R. Smith, J.P.,
and Mr. F. Gould, J.P. We did our best by sending our women out to help,
and in the financial part as far as we were able. However, the future is ours,
and we are looking forward thereto. Our Social, Dance and Whist Drive held
on the 13th November, was a huge success, the Trade Hall being crowded
with mostly young members of our Branch.
LIVERPOOL. The boot repairing trade has shown a marked decline
during the past month. The elections are over and, like a tornado, have
swept the country, with the result that a lot of good men have lost their seats.
Such are the fortunes of battle, and we have to bow to public opinion for the
time being whether we like it or not, and hope for the best. Nil desperandum.
This being the last report that will be in the hands of members before
Christmas, we wish all officials and members the Season's Greeting.
N.B. We have a new stock of Union Buttons and Brooches, which can
be obtained from the local secretary at sixpence each.
LONDON SOUTH. The monthly meeting was held at the Club House
Stores, Newington Butts, the chair being occupied by the President, W. Owen.
A fair number of members attended, when the report was accepted, as also
was the correspondence in connection with the size longer and toe caps; the
men of Freeman, Hardy & Willis receiving 6d. per pair above the price they
have been having, but are still in doubt as to the price. The above sum has been
fought for by the General President, and he is still doing his best for the men
for a further advance, as he considers that there is still some misunderstanding.
He also wishes that the members would take a little more interest in their
trade affairs and not accept any statements that might be offered to them,
but always refer to statements that are official and the ones that they are
supposed to be working to. This would save time and trouble and members
would get things settled more promptly.
MAYBOLE. Trade is very slack, some of our members only getting
16 hours' work in three days, and three days at the Labour Exchange. The
Secretary, who has been on the Town Council for five years, was again nominated
and stood for election last week and was second on the poll with 712 votes.
We are indebted to the members for the part they played, but for them the
result would have been impossible. Since then the Secretary has been made
a Baillie the first Labour Baillie in Maybole. We are sorry to see that our
good friends, Messrs. Buckle, Gould and Smith, were unsuccessful at the General

NORTHAMPTON No. 1.—Trade remains quiet here in spite of the
election is over and the Tory pack are in full armour in the Commons. We
rumours of extraordinary good trade. But the usual cries are about most of
will the people realise there is no hope under capitalism for either regular work
or a comfortable existence for the mass of workers, and that the only hope of
permanent improvement is by the workers using their political power alone
with their industrial organisation to substitute Communal Ownership of the
means of life with production for use in place of the present chaotic
private ownership with production for profit.
NORWICH No. 1.-Trade during the month declined in Norwich with
marked tendencies, although claims for the month do not support that view.
Returns for the current month will greatly emphasise the state of trade, and in
that particular, for the worse. Many operatives are signing the out-of-work
book with little or no prospect of securing work until the New Year. There
is, however, scope for consolation to those unfortunate members in the know-
ledge that we have at last a great Conservative Government anxious and willing
to deal with the poverty problem. What an unfortunate election for the
National Union! Three men, good and true, fighting, but to lose their seat-
Eccles, Frome, Norwich-what a tale-to say nothing of Northampton. Well, in
Norwich we faced a combination of forces as great as any in the country, and in
spite of all arrayed against us the Labour Party increased its solid party vote
by four thousand. We are confident that in the near future Norwich will
rise true for Labour, even though we have to fight Liberals and Tories joined
together under the banner of Anti-Labour. Expressions of regret to Johnnie
Buckle and Fred Gould.
PLYMOUTH (REPAIRING). The election is over. Locally our parlia-
mentary representation is unchanged. The excitement has died away, and we
are all in a position to review the past and speculate concerning the future.
Looking back over the past we can safely say that on no previous occasion do
we remember the anti-Labour forces so united against us, or the Press of the
country so overwhelming hostile and unscrupulous in their attack. Whether
the Labour leaders acted wisely or not in accepting the challenge on such an
issue as the Campbell case and the Russian Treaty, which were open to so
much prejudice, misrepresentation and misunderstanding (for we find that
some of our own candidates did not understand the Treaty), will always remain
a controversial point. We had always supported the acceptance of office
largely because of the possibility of choosing our own time and programme for
an appeal to the country, hoping that on the presentation of Labour's own
Budget early in 1925 would be the most favourable opportunity. However,
the battle was joined on an issue not entirely of Labour's own seeking or crea-
tion, but on the shifting sands of bitterness and hatred flung up by the back-
wash of the Old Brigade-Liberals and Tories. Upon this shingle Labour
endeavoured to build its castle of peace and goodwill; the attempt failed
lamentably and Labour has been given the task of criticising and looking on.
Let us hope that our criticism will be more generous and helpful. Let our sense
of British fair play remain untarnished by the lying and deception which has
befouled the name of English journalism during this election. Already we
see signs of doubt and misgivings among the scribes, for unwittingly they have
knocked out their sparring partners, the Liberals. Henceforth the fight must
be in earnest between Labour and privilege. We quote from one of our local
papers who fought with surprising bitterness: - "The Conservative success
was beyond all expectation, and in a mood of introspection and analysis, which
marks the reaction from the election fever of the last few days, we cannot

LEICESTERSHIRE ARBITRATION BOARD.
Mr. G. A. Denman Elected Chairman.
The annual meeting of the Leicestershire County Arbitration Board was held at the
City Hall, Leicester, on the 5th inst., under the chairmanship of Mr. D. Astley. There
were also present Messrs. G. Geary, G. A. Denman, J. H. Bott, W. Harvey, H. Leader,
H. P. Atkins, T. J. Bellamy, J. A. Smith, J. W. Hunt and J. Palmer, representing the
manufacturers, and Messrs. T. F. Richards, A. Hill, G. Parbury, M. A. Parker, W. Warner
J. H. Osborne, A. Needham, W. Woodward, F. Leader and F. W. Burchnall, representing
the operatives, and Mr. H. A. Flavill, secretary.
Sympathetic reference was made to the loss sustained by the Board by the death
of Mr. T. Adnitt. A vote of condolence was passed with his widow and daughter.
The decisions of the Finishing Statement Committee authorising a reprint of the
complete Finishing Statement for the Operatives' side, and fixing the extra for scouring
heels with aluminium plate insertions at 5d. per gross pairs were confirmed by the Board.
Mr. G. A. Denman was elected chairman and Mr. D. Astley vice-chairman for the en-
suing year. The secretary, Mr. H. A. Flavill, was re-appointed. The members of the
district inquiry committees were also re-appointed the operatives' side to fill the vacancy
caused by the death of Mr. Adnitt. The financial statement for the past twelve months
was presented and adopted, and the compilation of a piecework statement for the press
department was referred to a joint committee consisting of the chairman and vice-chairman,
with five members from each side. -The Shoe and Leather Record, 14th November, 1924.
MR. T. F. RICHARDS ON STRIKES.
Mr. T. F. Richards, of the Boot and Shoe Operatives' Union, made a very sensible
speech about the futility of strikes the other evening. We agree with most of his points.
Where is the practical sense in working for peace abroad, as Trade Unions profess
to do, and organising for industrial strife at home?
Every strike punishes the working people more than it hurts any employer.
As Mr. Richards says, strikes lead eventually to the Conference table. Why not
begin there, and stick there until a settlement is reached ?
If war between nations is wrong, so is war between capital and labour. Leicester
Mail, 13th November, 1924.

RUSHDEN BRANCH ANNUAL RE-UNION.
Mr. W. G. Cove, M.P, and the principal officers of the National Union of Boot and
Shoe Operatives were the chief guests at a tea and social held at the Trades Hall, Rushden,
on Saturday, 8th November, 1924.
Mr. Charles Bates, president of the Higham and Rushden Branch, welcomed the
guests, making special mention of Mr. R. D. Mayes (head of the Insurance Department)
and Mr. Cove, who, he said, had "come back to the fold." The Wellingborough Division
seemed to be the only bright spot in Northamptonshire, but he did not doubt their friends
in the other districts had done their best.
Giving figures to show the rapid growth of the Higham and Rushden Branch. Mr.
Bates said that 21 years ago they had 783 members and 140 probationers, and the funds
amounted to £700. The minimum wage for lasters was 27s., and the operatives worked
50 hours a week. In 1922 the membership was 7,600, in 1923 it was 7,685, and the present
total was 8,050. The funds had increased by £3,663 in the last three years, and the
minimum wage was £3.
Mr. Mayes (manager of the Insurance Department) said the Approved Societies had
two sets of enemies, the doctors and the Health Insurance Committees, and both would
gladly see them pass out of existence. Of all trade unionists only one-eighth or one-tenth
had insured through their own unions' approved society. The Boot Union had 32,000
members approved through its society, and the operatives had close upon £200,000 invested.
In the Rushden and Higham Ferrers district 2,400 out of 8,000 members were approved
through the Union. He would like to see that proportion grow.
Mr. T. F. Richards, the General President of the Union, said he was pleased to be
there, if only to congratulate them on their good sense. He had always had a sneaking
regard for East Northants-even when he was their nominee. (Laughter.) He was glad
that their friend Cove had retained his seat; it was quite as pleasing to the Union as it
was to Mr. Cove. He was glad that all the things that had been said had not had the
effect of driving them from their steady goal. Trade union men were making members
and adherents, and it was delightful to think that they had added one million members
to their 4 million voters. The 5 million voters were solid trade unionists and
Labour men.
When one thought of the big struggles the members of other unions and federations
had had, they were pleased to think that their own policy of arbitration and discussion
had borne good fruits. The employers had agreed, in the last negotiations, that when dar
or piecework was to be started upon, at least they would have a month's notice. Reason
had got to be given if they could not earn, by their piecework prices, 75s., and he must
say that when they had had to investigate these matters the employers had generally
given a good reason if the pieceworkers had not been able to earn the amount mentioned.
The Union were anxious to get back the minimum rate of wages at 21 years-a point
they let slide during the war. In the recent agreement the employers hedged, but did
give the minimum wage at 22.
Mr. E. L. Poulton (General Secretary) said the Labour people of the Wellingborough
Division managed to resist the "slide" in the district, and maintained the position intact.
A certain thing happened during the contest which lost them a good many seats, but the
people in the Wellingborough Division were able to stop the stampede. Sir Robert Horne
had given them notice of what he thought those tyrannical trades unions were.
Sir Robert would have a tough job if he thought he could upset them. Sir Robert
had already said what he hoped the Government would do with the trades unions of the
country. In the new Parliament Mr. Cove would find still more scope for his ability if
the Government endeavoured to put new burdens upon the people. It was rumoured
that the Government would bring in new schemes in connection with insurance. They
were not going to agree quietly to being "improved" off the face of the earth.
When the boot operatives had a 56-hour week the pressman had 22s. a week. That
same man to-day, if he was on piecework, must have at least 75s. for 48 hours. They
had also done a great deal to increase the status of the men engaged in the industry. They
had taken great pride in the fact that the unofficial understanding with the employers for
a shortage of work there should be general short time rather than discharges. He wanted
years past had been that discharges must be kept to a minimum, and that if there was
to bear his testimony to the way the employers had carried that out.
Mr. Cove said he was very glad to get into touch with the local trade union movement.
He did not believe that anybody could be an efficient representative in Parliament unless
unionism. He had had experience of another union whose methods of conciliation
were similar to those of the Boot Operatives' Union. He referred to the National Union
of Teachers.

LEGAL CASES AFFECTING LABOUR.
Workmen's Compensation Acts, 1906-1923.
APPLICATION TO REDUCE WEEKLY COMPENSATION-REFUSAL TO UNDERGO OPERATIOS.
An application was made at the Hanley County Court for the diminution of the
unreasonably refused to undergo an operation. It was stated, that the respondent met
weekly amount of compensation being paid to a collier, on the ground that the man lad
with an accident in November, 1922, which resulted in a rupture, and he had not worked
since, but was drawing compensation and Unemployment Insurance benefit. The collier
objected to the idea of being operated upon, and told the firm that he would not conser
the matter unless the surgeon gave a written guarantee that the operation woul
success.
His employers contended that this was an unreasonable attitude to take up.
Judge Ruegg, K.C., said: "I have been asked over and over again to stop com-
pensation on the ground of a man refusing to undergo this very operation and in every
case I have refused. It means that I am being asked to say that every miner who is bad!
ruptured and does not submit to an operation ought to have his compensation stopped.
It will be a long time before I say that." His Honour added that he could not encourag
these applications to stop compensation because workmen refused to submit to an opera-
tion. Florence Iron and Coal Company v. Whittaker.-Hanley County Court. September
9th, 1924. Ministry of Labour Gazette, November, 1924.
UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE BENEFIT.
It was reported that the applicant had been drawing benefit from 10th April to 30th
October, 1922, and from 1st April, 1923, to 16th February, 1924, periods during which
he had in fact worked as a theatre attendant. His claim for benefit was therefore disallowed
under Section 7 (1) (ii) in respect of these periods, on the ground that he was not unemployed.
The applicant admitted that he had been employed during the periods referred to,
but a representative of his Association submitted that the applicant was entitled to benefit
for the second of the periods because the work as theatre attendant had by that time
become an additional occupation from which the applicant derived only 195. per week,
or less than 3s. 4d. on the daily average.
as theatre attendant
The Umpire's decision shows the essential dates and other information in the case.
Recommended by the Court of Referees that the claim for benefit should be disallowed
in respect of both periods. The Court held that the occupation
had not by 1st April, 1923, become an additional occupation within the meaning of the Act.
The applicant's Association appealed to the Umpire and attended an oral hearing
of the case.
Decision." On the facts before me my decision is that the claim for benefit should
be disallowed." - Ministry of Labour Gazette, November, 1924.

```text
ORGANISER'S REPORT.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
Since my last report I have been organising mainly at Barwell. The weakness
in this area has been due to the want of Shop Presidents and the absence of accurate
information on the position of each factory in organisation. Mr. Dan Astley and I have
been trying to put things in the first state of order by getting factories to elect Shop
details that make for success or otherwise in the trade union movement. The records
of our Union prove beyond doubt the value of Shop Presidents to good organisation.
Our experience at Barwell and Nuneaton recently justify our faith in them. At Hall &
Geary's, Barwell, we elected a Shop President on 31st October. Eight members joined
President, but when we did get one he joined about a dozen members the first week. This
new members when he started. At Nuneaton Mr. W. Warner and I had a meeting of the
seven joined with him, and since then (7th November) many more have joined. At the
workers at a factory there. A Shop President was elected and the day following twenty-
firm of Leader's, Barwell, it was difficult for us to get anyone to take on the job of Shop
has been our general experience with the newly elected Shop Presidents.
25th November, 1924.
D. MCCARTHY.
```

WAGES IN THE FRENCH BOOT AND SHOE
INDUSTRY.
The manufacture of boots and shoes is one of the important industries of France,
employing approximately 220,000 workers. While there is no census showing the number
and capacity of plants, it is certain that there are more than 600 factories engaged in this
a day.
About two-thirds of these are of small capacity making fewer than 100 pairs
Under normal conditions there is a lack of labour in French boot and shoe factories,
particularly in the more skilled occupations, and workers engaged in this industry are,
in consequence, relatively better paid than others. The wages of competent workers
range from 160 francs to 250 francs a week, the average being probably about 200 francs.
The labour cost on a pair of boots, the retail price of which is 100 francs, amounts to about
11 francs, while the cost of material is from 45 to 50 francs. Although the greater part
of the material manufactured is made on American lasts and with American machinery,
the average daily production per worker is stated to be much lower than in the United
States. Ministry of Labour Gazette, November, 1924.
CHANGES IN COST OF LIVING: STATISTICS FOR 1st NOVEMBER, 1924.
Summary: Average Increases since July, 1914.
All Items included ..
Food only
..
FOOD.
..
80 per cent.
79 "
During October the average level of the retail prices of food continued to rise. The
most important increases in prices affected eggs (1d. each on the average), potatoes (1d.
per 7 lbs.), flour (nearly 1d. per 7 lbs.), and bread (between 1/4d. and 3/4d. per 4 lbs.). Milk,
butter, bacon, tea and cheese were also dearer on 1st November than on 1st October.
On the other hand, sugar was cheaper at the later date by about 1/4d. per lb. The prices
of meat, fish and margarine were approximately the same at both dates.
As a net result of all the changes recorded, the average increase over the level of
July, 1914, in the retail prices (in Great Britain and Northern Ireland) of the articles of
food included in these statistics rose to about 79 per cent. at 1st November, as compared
with about 72 per cent. at 1st October, 1924, and 73 per cent. at 1st November, 1923.---
Ministry of Labour Gazette, November, 1924.

CONFERENCE AGREEMENT.
Uniformity in Labour Price of similar classes of Goods.
1. (a) Subject to resolutions 1 and 5 (d) of the Terms of Settlement it is desirable
that a uniform system of prices should obtain, and that the general outline or groundwork
of such system should be arranged on a broad basis, so that the essential conditions and
prices can be applied or adapted to the same class of labour and materials in all areas
producing similar classes of goods.
Notice of alteration in System.
Manufacturers shall, before changing the method of working from piece.

operatives, and also notify in writing the local branch secretary of the Lion

Regulation of Conditions of Employment.
4. (a) Where operatives attend at the factories on the instructions of the employers
or their representatives, work shall be found for them for at least half a day, except when
short time is being worked, and in that case operatives, whether engaged on day or piece-
work, shall be informed overnight if their services will not be required on the next working
day, and shall be informed before the midday interval if they will not be required to attend
in the afternoon. If no such intimation is given, and operatives attend at the factories,
work shall be found for them for a period of not less than four hours in the morning and three
hours in the afternoon, or they shall be paid for the four hours and three hours respectively
at not less than the minimum or agreed wage rate.
(b) This clause shall not apply in the case of machinery breaking down in any factory
after the operatives have entered, or in the case of illness or absence of any operative
which interferes with the organisation of the factory, in which cases the operatives shall
be allowed to leave the factory at once.

**Strikes and Lockouts.**
22. The Conference re-affirms Resolution 8 of the Terms of Settlement of 19th April,
1895, which is as follows:-
"No strike or lockout shall be entered into on the part of any body of workm
members of the National Union, or any manufacturers represented on any loc
Board of Arbitration."
(a) Where grievances exist they shall be investigated immediately by representative
of the Local Manufacturers' Association and of the local branch of the Union
concerned, with a view to adjustment.
(b) Where any strike or lockout takes place and is continued beyond the period of
three days allowed by the agreement of 31st March, 1910, the right of the Federa-
tion or the Union, as the case may be, to claim upon the monetary guarantee
under that agreement and the Trust Deed, may be exercised by application to a
National Umpire appointed in accordance with Clause 9 of the Trust Deed and
on the recommendation of the Minister of Labour for a forfeiture either (a) by
way of fine or penalty, or (b) by way of damages or compensation for loss sustained,
and in any case where the latter alternative is adopted the amount of such loss
shall be assessed by a committee of three representatives of the Federation and
three representatives of the Union, and in the event of their disagreement the
question shall be referred to the National Umpire.

**Joint Standing Committee.**
23. A Standing Committee of three representatives of the Federation and three
representatives of the Union, with the Chairman of the Conference, shall be appointed to
deal with all matters arising out of or in connection with the Terms of Settlement of 1895,
so far as they are now operative, and any other national agreement between the Federation
and the Union and this agreement, including any disputes that may arise as to the inter-
pretation of such agreements, provided that due regard is paid to the authoritative decisions
that have already been given under the above-named agreements.

**Conflict with Local Arbitration Boards.**
24. Anything in this Agreement which is in conflict with existing local awards or
agreements shall be remitted to the parties by whom such agreements were made, or to the
Local Arbitration Board. Failing agreement by the local authority, the matter in dispute
may be remitted to the Standing Committee, acting in an advisory capacity with a view
to obviating the necessity of a reference to the Arbitrator for such local Board.

**Responsibility for Observance of Agreement.**
25. Both parties to this agreement undertake to use such means as are at their disposal
to ensure its due observance by all employers and workers, whether members of their
respective organisations or not.

```text
THE POOREST TOWN IN
ENGLAND.
13,000 out of 35,000 on Dole
or Relief.
A Tragedy of Bright Air.
Out of a population of 35,000, more than
13,000 people in Jarrow are in receipt of
parish relief or the unemployment allowance.
These figures illustrate the tragic plight to
which the town has been reduced by trade
depression. Jarrow is now the poorest town
in the North Country.
With its air no longer smoke-laden and
grimy, it has also become the brightest town:
but it is a tragic brightness, for the atmosphere
is clear and clean because the works stand
silent.--Daily Chronicle, 3rd November, 1924.
The lunch hour provided a curious scene.
Fat hampers were brought up, cage-doors
were opened, and dogs and their owners
partook of dainty meals of chicken and other
tasty dishes
Manchester Evening News, 23rd Oct., 1924.

a period in view of the proved wealth of the country which could deal with the unemploy-
ment problem in such a way as would ensure upkeep for those out of work.--E.L.P., G.S.]
```

SANITY IN TRADE UNIONISM.
BOOT AND SHOE INDUSTRY.
For an industry to have been free from a national stoppage of production, either
by a general strike on the part of the operatives or a lockout by the employers for a period
approaching 30 years, is a record of sanity in industrial relations upon which both the
employers and the operatives' organisations are to be congratulated.
It was in November, 1804, that the last national strike in the boot and shoe industry
began, and the fight was waged until April, 1895, when a settlement was effected between
the Federated Association of Boot and Shoe Manufacturers and the National Union of
Boot and Shoe Operatives at a joint conference held at the Board of Trade. There have
been many difficulties to arrange many adjustments to make as an outcome of changes
in machinery and methods of production; there have been local disputes to settle. But
all these things have been done through the conciliation machinery which has been brought
into existence, and is now so long and well established, to regulate wages, hours and
conditions of work.
What is the explanation of these agreements being honourably observed by both
employers and operatives? It is true that when the Board of Trade strike settlement
was effected on 19th April, 1895, a clause was inserted that "No strike or lockout shall be
entered into on the part of any body of workmen, members of the National Union, or any
clause in 1910 setting up a guarantee fund for the observance of the agreement. To this
Arbitration," and to this was added
fund the Federation and the National Union have both deposited £1,000.
But I firmly believe that the spirit of confidence which has been created, the feeling
which has been engendered on both sides of the conciliation table that they must " play
the game," is a far greater and more binding obligation than the legal power by which
observance can be enforced.
The Operatives' Gain.
The operatives have gained substantially by the agreement, and wages and working
conditions in the boot and shoe industry are a model upon which those of other trades
could be fashioned to the real advantage of the workers. When the agreement was
originally made in 1895 the minimum wage of the boot and shoe industry ranged from
26s. to 30s. for a working week of 54 hours. Under the new agreement, which is to be voted
upon by the operatives at their November meetings, the minimum wage rates for male
operatives are to be:-

will be 50s. per week for a working week of 48 hours. In the case of female operatives the

In the boot and shoe industry much of the work is done at piece rates. This agree-
ment contains a clause which has obviously been framed to afford protection to those
operatives who, by their skill, dexterity and energy, are giving of their best.
Thus the minimum wages to be earned at piecework rate is not less than 25 per cent.
above the minimum day wage rate. This brings the minimum wage of the adult male
pieceworker to £3 15s. per week and of the female worker to £2 5s. per week, with the
same proportionate increase of the earnings at all the earlier ages.

What is the advantage to the employer of these agreements? There can be no
question that they have resulted in establishing excellent relations between the workers
and their employers. A basis of remuneration has been fixed by mutual agreement

DAVENTRY'S NEW MAYOR.
Councillor I. H. Johnson's Good Work.
Councillor Isaac Johnson, J.P., C.C., one of the Labour members, was unanimously
elected Mayor of Daventry, at the meeting of the Town Council on Monday.
Mr. Johnson's election was proposed by Mr. E. T. Browning, who thought the member
would be all agreed that Mr. Johnson was a gentleman who deserved his very high honour
Mr. Browning had worked with Mr. Johnson for a considerable number of years, and had
found him straightforward, conscientions, fearless, and yet courteous to his opponents.
the support of the whole Council. This was the 350th year since a Bailiff or Mayor was
Mr. Johnson was of a minority party, and they were glad to know that he was to receive
first appointed in the Borough; certainly it was the first occasion upon which one of the
political faith of Mr. Johnson had been elected. Mr. Johnson early in his career grasped
the idea of self-help, and seeing its value, attached himself to the Friendly Society move
ment in the Ancient Order of Foresters, and had served in all the offices in the town in the
Order. In the Co-operative movement, Mr. Johnson held the office of president, and from
these he went into the Trade Union movement. Mr. Roche seconded, and added his
testimony to the excellent work of Mr. Johnson.
Mr. Johnson said that the honour was one of which he was proud, but nothing gave
him greater pleasure than the support of the whole Council, and especially the support of
Mr. Roche. He thought he could claim to be the first of the rank and file - by that he
meant a wage earner - to occupy the position. Looking down the list of Mayors one found
most of them were men of position and influence; what he might lack in that way he hoped
to make up in work and usefulness. - Northampton Echo, 11th November, 1924.

THE UNION'S SOUVENIR.
A quarto souvenir volume for the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives, and
produced by the Leicester Co-operative Printing Society Ltd., is a credit both to this
association and to the printer. The pages place on record the history of the Union, and
there are many illustrations, including portraits in half-tone, and reproductions of emblems
in colour. The whole is admirably produced. Colour is used to advantage, such as in
the red rule borders, and the whole is provided with a tasteful gold blocked cover and
attractive end papers. - British Printer.

BENEFITS OF THE EIGHT-HOUR DAY.
An interesting summary of the benefits accruing to the community from a shorter
working day is given in a letter addressed to the Press by the Czechoslovakian Minister
of Social Affairs in discussing the attack by German employers on the eight-hour day.
"Since the introduction of the eight-hour day in our country," he declares, " there
has been a decrease in the use of alcohol, an improvement in the standard of housekeeping.
and a rapid increase in the membership of workers' athletic clubs, educational unions,
and so on." - Labour Press Service, 30th October, 1924.

SECURITY OF EUROPE.
The Next War.
Lord Grey of Fallodon, speaking at Newcastle-on-Tyne on Saturday at a meeting
arranged by the League of Nations Union, said that there was less risk to-day than ever
that the League of Nations would be made a party question. Neither the League nor
foreign politics had been made a matter of party politics during the last year.
"I associate myself with the tribute paid the other day by Mr. Baldwin to Mr. Ramsay
MacDonald," he continued, "for the part he has taken in bringing about the London
Agreement on the German reparation question. (Cheers.) The question of reparations
was a great obstacle to getting Germany into the League. That obstacle, I hope, has been
removed, or has been put into the way of being removed, by the London Agreement
which was brought about under the Labour Government, and I hope that by that means
the way has been cleared for Germany to enter the League. I would also like to say
that the late Government did make the League of Nations one of the cardinal principles
of its policy and devoted much thought to the development and strengthening of it.'
The purpose of the League, he continued, was to give a sense of real security to the
nations of Europe so that they might feel it unnecessary to depend on armaments for
same competition in armaments as before 1914, and the same result in another great
European war. If Britain wished to use her influence to secure future peace she must
make it clear that she stood for something. (Cheers.) Rightly, British public opinion
had declared that it would have nothing to do with separate entangling alliances. If
Brithin meant to make the League of Nations 2 reality she should say "We will not stand
for separate alliances. There is one thing only for which we are prepared to stand, and
that is the Covenant of the League of Nations. (Cheers.).
The next war would be a concentration of bombs and poison against the great centres
A population. It would be a victory over civilisation itself, and civilisation could not

```text
The British Labour Movement is strongly opposed to compulsory arbitration
By M. CHARLTON,
Leader of the Australian Labour Party.
The Labour Party in Australia was formed as the result of the seamen's
1890, compulsory arbitration being made a prominent plank of the platform
In 1900, Mr. Wise, the Attorney-General of the then Government, which w in a
minority and had to depend on the Labour Party, passed the first Arbitration Act
The Act provided for the settlement of all disputes by the Court, which ou
employees, penalties being provided for strikes and lockouts.
a judge, as chairman, and a representative of the employers and a representative of
More Trade Unionists.

It was necessary for industrial unions to register before they could invoke the aid of
As a result of this legislation workers were encouraged to organise, and it soon became
apparent to those unorganised that, whilst the conditions of organised labour were im
proving by awards of the court, their standard remained as formerly.
In consequence, large bodies of shop employees and clerical workers formed union
and registered, thereby improving their conditions.
boards were appointed to expedite action.
Owing to the large number of claims lodged, the court became congested, and wages
At a later date the Commonwealth Parliament passed an Arbitration Act, which,
owing to the provisions of the Federal Constitution, could only deal with disputes which
extended beyond the boundary of more than one State.
This Act has done much to improve the conditions of the workers in the larger unions,
which are inter-state, such as the shearers. They have received substantial increases.
Fewer Stoppages.
During the war period an Industrial Disputes Act was passed by the Commonwealth
Parliament to deal with miners' grievances. Substantial increases in wages were given.
There have been disappointments in the working of arbitration in Australia, chiefly
owing to the congestion of business, which has occasionally caused a cessation of work.
It has never been claimed by the strongest supporters of arbitration that it
would completely prevent strikes and lockouts. It has, however, considerably
minimised them, and has materially assisted in raising the standard of living.
In addition, since the advent of arbitration the membership of trade unions has
greatly increased.—The Daily Herald, 7th November, 1924.
THE SPITALFIELDS DISPUTE.
It is regrettable that the National Union should find it necessary to intervene between
a shoe manufacturer and his customers. But the action taken recently by that body
is fully approved by the Boot Manufacturers' Federation; it is, in fact, supported by that
organisation. Certain members of the Union were withdrawn a few months ago from a
the National Agreement. They preferred to ignore the arrangement which ninety-five
per cent. of the boot manufacturers in the country deem quite satisfactory. The men
are, of course, receiving strike pay, and we learn that the Federation has raised a special
fund out of which the sum of five shillings a week is to be paid for each of the strikers'
children. It is possible to set at defiance for a time the Federation and the Union, though
that attitude cannot be maintained indefinitely. And now that the largest buyers of shoes
are unwilling to obtain supplies from what they regard as tainted sources, the end cannot
be far distant.—The Shoe and Leather Record, 31st October, 1924.
```
