LATE MR. A. G. H. JONES.
Funeral of Kingswood Councillor. Representative Congregation.
There was a full muster of Kingswood councillors at the funeral of one of their number,
the late Mr. A. G. H. Jones, at Hanham Road Congregational Church, yesterday afternoon,
who said that while the late Mr. Jones did not take an active part in the work of the church,
The service was taken by the Rev. Enoch Jones (pastor of Whitefield Tabernacle),
he was a faithful and consistent member.
Councillors Line Church Approach.
The members of Kingswood Council lined the approach to the church. There were
present Messrs. W. S. Rudge (chairman), A. G. Randall (vice-chairman), and others.
Members of the Kingswood Fire Brigade acted as bearers, Captain S. Peese being in
command.
Boot Operatives' Representatives.
Representing the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives were Mr. E. L. Poulton,
J.P. (London), general secretary; Kingswood and District branch, Messrs S. Iles, C.C.,
president: A. G. Randall, secretary; W. E. A. Payne, G. Gay, F. Britton, G. Brent
(Paulton): Bristol and Kingswood No. 2 Branch, Messrs. J. Manners (secretary), n
Peacock, F. Gardiner, A. Monks; Kingswood and District Boot and Shoe Trade Arbitra
tion Board, Messrs. J. Manners, S. Iles, S. Peacock, and A. G. Randall. Mr. G. E. Britton,
past chairman of the Arbitration Board, and president Kingswood Manufacturers' Associa-
tion, was unavoidably prevented from attending. Representing Thornbury Division
Labour Party, Messrs. S. Iles, C.C., president; J. H. Alpass, A. G. Randall (treasurer)
M. Giles, E. C. Parker, J. H. Lacey, and H. Clements (secretary, Kingswood Labour Party):
U.A.O.D., Messrs. W. Payne, past-president Bristol and West of England District: A. G
Randall, and S. Iles.
The wreaths included flowers from the Kingswood and District Branch of the National
Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives, Bristol and Kingswood No. 2 Branch, Chairman,
Vice-Chairman and members of the Kingswood Council, the Thornbury Divisional Labour
Party, Kingswood Labour Party, Messrs. G. F. Hutchings & Co., Bristol, boot manufac-
turers; "Fellow workmates," and the Kingswood Philharmonic Male Voice Choir.
The interment took place at the Kingswood Wesleyan Cemetery, Mr. H. Painter
carrying out the funeral arrangements.
Colleagues' Tribute.
At a meeting of Kingswood Urban District Council, last evening, the chairman, Mr.
W. S. Rudge, referred to the loss the Council had sustained since the last meeting in the
death of Mr. Jones, whom he characterised as one of the ablest of their citizens, who had
a great heart, was broadminded, tolerant, and public-spirited. Although Mr. Jones was
not a native of Kingswood, he had great love for the district, in which he was a pattern
to many who had been born there. Mr. Jones differed from several of the councillors
politically, but they felt he was sincere in his political views. He was the soul of enthu-
siasm in anything he undertook, and Kingswood was the poorer by his loss, especially
the young people. Mr. Jones believed in doing well everything he was engaged in. His
diligence was amazing, and his resolutions were an example to them all. The Chairman
moved a vote of sympathy with the widow and family, which was carried by members
standing.
The Chairman expressed gratification that every member of the Council was present
at the funeral.-Western Daily Press, 6th November, 1924.
MULTIPLE SHOE FIRMS.
While it is possible for a firm to reduce labour costs by underpaying their operatives,
that is a policy which has its disadvantages. We understand that a London firm, who
seceded from the Federation in order to evade the conditions set forth in the National
Agreement, have discovered that some of their most important customers are no longer
willing to do business with them. One of the largest multiple firms in the kingdom, it
is stated, has decided to place no further orders with the manufacturers in question, with
the result that they find it difficult to keep their factory running at full capacity. Attention
may also be called to the statement made by Mr. James Manfield. It was alleged that
his firm were purchasing shoes from a concern which do not conform with trade union
hours and wages. Mr. Manfield admitted that his company formerly obtained certain
goods from the firm alluded to, but the last delivery from that source was received four
months since. And he added that no more orders would be placed. The Shoe and Leather
Record, 31st October, 1924.

SIR ARTHUR WHEELER.
Some of His Impressions of America.
Sir Arthur Wheeler. Bart., returned to Leicester this week from a visit to America.
In the course of a brief conversation we had with Sir Arthur Wheeler this morning, we
father that he had been greatly impressed by what he had seen in the United States.
"There is NO MORE HUSTLE in America than there is in this country, PERHAPS NOT
SO MUCH," said Sir Arthur, "and THEIR GENERAL EFFICIENCY IS BY NO MEANS GREATER
THAN OURS, and yet there is something in the 'push and go' of America which impres
one, and which is a good tonic for the average Englishman.
"Their adaptability is greater than ours, largely because they are not so embedded
in tradition as we are.
"For instance, everywhere in America I SAW WOODEN HOUSES. The best of people
live in delightful villas built of wood, yet we in this country are held up for houses because
of the inability of our people to face the new conditions which obtain.
"It is not as though the climate in America was better than the climate here.
matter of fact, in the winter it is much worse, but yet houses of wood are quite comfortable
commonplace substitutes for the bricks to which we pin our faith in this country.
Leicester Mail, 30th October, 1924.
One is glad to have the testimony of Sir Arthur to the fact that the "old" country
is not the sleepy, inefficient place that is sometimes stated. Regarding houses built of
wood, it is indeed strange that no serious attempt is made to erect houses of wood. It is
not, however, the workers' fault. - E.L.P., G.S.].
WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION.
At the Holsworthy (Devon) County Court on the 15th inst. Judge Higgins, when
hearing the case of a servant girl suing her employer for compensation to her right hand,
said "he should not allow the girl compensation if it were found that she neglected or
refused, any practical aid towards her restoration to a normal state."

WILNECOTE SCHOOL BOOT со.
At the meeting of creditors of the Wilnecote School Boot Co. Ltd., it was stated that
the liquidation of the concern was due to labour trouble. Regarded as an explanation,
the statement is unconvincing, seeing that the loss on trading in the nine months since the
company was formed accounts for £1,739, the turnover during that period having been
$10,500. The company, it would seem, has never made a profit in spite of the fact that
the efforts the were in observance of the agreement were ineffective
the operatives employed were not paid in accordance with the National Agreement, and
In the circumstances, it is not surprising that the National Union informed the Wholesale
Co-operative Society Ltd., who were the principal customers of the company, that the
factory was being worked under unfair conditions, with the result that no further orders
were placed by the Co-operative Society. This precipitated the collapse of the Wilnecote
concern, but on the facts as reported, it is evident that the company was already insolvent
and could not have continued trading. Its downfall was due not so much to labour
trouble, as to selling its output at prices which did not cover the cost of production.
The Shoe and Leather Record, 31st October, 192.4.

Every precaution is taken by us to ensure accuracy in these Reports, our correspondents

MONTHLY REPORT.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
TRADE
22ND DECEMBER, 1924.
has slightly improved as compared with the previous month, the figures recorded
in the Gazette being as follows :-
BOOT AND SHOE INDUSTRY.
Employment during November was only moderate on the whole, and much short
time was again worked. It showed little change as compared with October.
The percentage of workpeople unemployed, as indicated by the unemployment books
lodged at Employment Exchanges, was 9.7 on the 24th November, as compared with 10.0
on the 27th October and 9.6 on the 26th November, 1923.
Returns from firms employing over 38,000 operatives in the week ended 29th November
showed that 35 per cent. of these operatives worked short time in that week to the extent
of about 11 hours each on an average.
Employment in London showed a slight improvement and was better than in Novem-
ber of last year. At Leicester conditions were still slack, but showed an improvement;
there was an increased demand for workers. Employment was quiet at Northampton
and showed a decline; some short time working was reported. There was a further
slight improvement at Wellingborough, but a number of firms were still unable to work
full time. A good deal of short time was worked at Kettering, though some of the larger
factories were able to maintain full-time working, and there was even some overtime;
employment was generally moderate and about the same as in October. Employment
was poor, and worse than in October, in the Higham and Rushden district, and short
time was worked by some factories. Employment at Irthlingborough and Raunds was
very bad.
Employment declined at Leeds and was generally bad; in the heavy boot section
short time was generally worked, but fair conditions again prevailed with makers of light
footwear. There was much short-time working at Stafford, and employment generally
was very slack. At Norwich employment was fair and much better than in November
of last year. A further decline was reported in the Bristol and Kingswood district, where
employment was generally poor. At Street employment was fair, but not so good as in
the previous month. The seasonal depression in the slipper trade of the Rossendale
Valley continued, and employment declined.

SPITALFIELDS DISPUTE.
The Spitalfields Dispute at Messrs. Jackson & Joseph continues, but
we are hopeful of coming to an agreement within the near future

NON-OBSERVANCE OF AGREEMENTS.
We would once more impress upon the whole of the membership the
absolute necessity of at once reporting to their officers any breaking away from
or non-observance of, the Agreements which have been entered into nationally
and locally so far as wages, hours and conditions are concerned. It is the
more essential that this should be done at once, because of the fact that
certain employers are making complaints of non-observance of conditions,
these complaints when followed up are found to be of such a vague character
owing to the unwillingness of employers to give names of firms which they
allege are not carrying out Agreements. We have stated upon many
occasions that we are always willing to deal with real cases in such a way
as will show that we, as a Council and Union, are determined that Agreements
should not be broken if we can prevent it. We would remind employers,
and especially those who indulge in this grumbling—although they refuse
information to enable us to deal with cases—that there is an obligation upon
the employers as well as the Union to carry out the Agreement, and that
we should assist one another in the enforcement of the same.
Clause 25 of the National (September, 1924) Agreement, states: —
25. Both parties to this Agreement undertake to use such means
as are at their disposal to ensure its due observance by all employers and
workers, whether members of their respective organisations or not.
We hope, therefore, that there will be a full appreciation of this fact by
the employers, and that in future they will do their part to secure full observance
of the conditions, and thus remove unfair and unjust competition of people
who might otherwise be inclined to cut prices by non-adherence to the National
Terms.
ANOTHER J.P.
Our colleague, Mr. A. J. Dobbs, has been appointed a J.P. for the City of
Leeds. We beg to heartily congratulate him upon this honour, which in our
judgment is well deserved, and we are quite sure he will carry out the duties
of such office in a manner both creditable to himself and with honour to the
organisation of which he is a member.

at the commencement of this month, we had passed the £1,000,000 sterling

This is indeed a very large sum to have paid out, more especially having regard
to the fact that the employment benefit has only been paid for a comparatively
short period. Not only does this sum of money represent help at a time of
need, but it also means that in very many cases it has enabled homes to be
kept together, and has given both to men and women fresh heart and encourage-
ment to keep a cheery outlook, because of the help granted through the agency
of the Union in their times of stress,

There is, moreover, the wider question which is often overlooked, and
which we venture to say some day will receive adequate recognition at the hands
of the historians, i.e., the great help nationally and the good – socially
upon the lives of the people which trade unions have so beneficently rendered
in providing means for out-of-work benefit, sick and funeral pay. This work
constantly goes on without any flourish of trumpets, but nevertheless it is a
work which has helped tremendously the working classes of the country to
maintain their homes intact and to preserve manhood and womanhood from
degradation.

POLITICAL.

The political situation is now somewhat clearer, due to the fact that on
the 9th inst., the King's Speech—otherwise the policy of the Government was
declared, whereby we are able to judge of some things which may take place
within the next year or so. First the Government declare that the Treaties
which were before the last House of Commons are to be thrown on the scrap
heap, and that they do not intend to ratify such agreements with Russia.
The Government also state that they propose to proceed with the plans for
increasing the naval base at Singapore. Thus upon two matters there is a
reversal of the position adopted by the Labour Government. It is also evident
from speeches that have been made—particularly by one of the Under Secre-
taries of State—that although it is not named in the King’s Speech, trade
unionists will have to be very much alive and tenacious of their rights; par-
ticularly on the political side, because of the fact that a number of members
on the Government benches are opposed to the existing conditions by which
trade unions have the right and authority to carry on political work,
nationally or locally. In this connection there is a great deal of misunder-
standing and wrong views held as to the amount of money that unions con-
tribute for this purpose. Cases have come under our notice regarding the
amount of money we are authorised to place on one side for Political purposes;
and when it has been explained as to how small the same is - threepence per

quarter per full male member both surprise and astonishment has been
expressed thereat. Other cases have been brought to our notice where it was
the intention of a member to ask for exemption from payment to the Political
Fund, but when the small amount was mentioned to them they withdrew their
opposition because, whilst there may be some members who take a different
view from the great majority, we are confident that the local work done throughı

It would also appear from one or two phases of the King's Speech that any

will be based upon a contributory basis from the people themselves. Here
again great vigilance will be needed and all the support possible required for
members of the Labour Party who are in the House of Commons, so that they
can speak effectively and also with the full knowledge that they have the
authority and influence of the general membership of the Party and trade
unions behind them in any action they may be called upon to take from time
to time in the House of Commons itself.
Meanwhile, we would again impress upon the members the absolute
necessity of keeping the machinery in good working order in each district.
A good deal can be done locally through the existing parties if opportunity
is taken of them to send to local authorities men and women who are supporters
of the Labour programme. There are a great many laws already which are
not taken full advantage of, and which we hope with increased local activity,
will be used to their utmost in the interests of the country as a whole.

GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
The proverb says "Eternal vigilance is the price of liberty," and in this sense we
again revert to the question of "Shoddy," and its effect on the community. In this
connection we hope to see some very drastic changes, and the help of the Employers'
Federation (although they have members who manufacture this stuff), yet there is in any
industry an overwhelming number of employers who are proud of their callings, and have
a great deal of respect for a genuine article and a good reputation for fair dealing; but
there are others, whose object in life is a cash result. They don't ever introduce, if they
can help it, the human aspect as some of my advisers in public life have been advised to
express themselves, freely say, "Ah, it don't pay," and whilst men or women live by that
alone it matters not a jot whatever their political opinions are. They are a clog on the
wheel of progress and suffer as much from some kind of fear as does the man who is in some
cases afraid to ask for his price for fear he should get the "sack." Therefore, if we are
to improve the industry by purifying it, then all sections must throw in their lot. We
have nothing to lose by letting the public know that our object is not only avoidance of
disturbances, but good conditions for the operatives and a sound and solid article for the
consuming public, and when we recall the outstanding fact that in our industry, without
counting the eight shoe factories belonging to the C.W.S., we have in this England of ours
no less than sixteen shoe factories owned and controlled by the members of the Union
and their friends, and to the best of our knowledge every man, woman, boy and girl over
sixteen years of age are members of our Union. This gives us an insight into the troubles
that employers have in their business by being able to get first-hand information respecting
all aspects of the industry. Not one of those factors on principle produce any shoddy.
If working-class factories can produce honest goods, so ought others.
We are pleased to see that the Employers' Federation have agreed to a specification
for an All-Leather Boot, or what should be understood to be the minimum of what one
should be, although I am sorry to see the sectional heel unlimited. To my mind this
should be confined to not more than two lifts thick. The "ALL-LEATHER" BOOT SPECI-
FICATION of the Employers' Federation, appears on page 656.
Should I think read Outsole and Toppiece.
OUTSOLE OR TOPPIECE . . . . . Leather.
INSOLE . . . . . . . . . Leather, grain or split, single or two whole piece.
MIDDLESOLE . . . . . . Leather, grain or split, single or two whole piece.
STIFFENER . . . . . . . Leather, grain or split, single or two whole piece.
HEEL . . . . . . . . . . Leather lifts, whole or sectional.
The Employers' Committee considers that it is not necessary that toe puffs, shanks
or bottom fillings, should be all leather, as other suitable materials are available, and say
further:-
BOTTOM FILLING . . . . Leather, felt or cork composition, such as Besto.
SHANK . . . . . . . . . Leather, felt, wood or combination made of steel and
board.
TOE PUFF OR BOX . . . . Leather, felt, celluloid or canvas.
The Employers' Committee recommends members to limit the use of an ALL LEATHER
Stamp to boots complying with the above specification on orders placed and accepted
after 1st December, 1924.
The above marks an important step forward, and in addition I am informed they are
seriously considering whether some mark, informing the public that their goods have been
made under "National Conditions" might be helpful. I am bound to say truthfully
that the non-federated are mainly the producers of Shoddy, and they, like the non-unionist,
want the world for themselves.
ALL TO JOIN THE UNION.
The Federated Employers for their own safety would be well advised to start no
non-unionist for the simple reason that if he got a majority, then the Union could not be
responsible for the conduct of such non-members, we having had recent experience upon
this point speak with definite knowledge when two firms left the Federation for the deliber-
ate purpose of evading the National Conditions.
In addition to the above they should refrain from purchasing from these Shoddy

WHITE LIST.
Could we do as we were able to do with the Government during the war, to only deal

FACTORS SHOULD REFUSE TO DEAL
with those firms who had the reputation to pay less than our rates and evade our National
Conditions. If so we should make a remarkable step forward as we know of one big factor
in Leicester who has refused to take any goods from a firm who are evading our National
Conditions. Another factor in Leicester advertises his goods largely and is buying from
a non-Union centre whose conditions are deplorable.
THE SPITALFIELDS DISPUTE.-At the request of the Ministry of Labour we have had
two interviews with Messrs. Jackson & Joseph's, Spitalfields, and the dispute still con-
tinues. The firm have entered into an agreement with some twenty of their key men,
and are not prepared to discharge operatives who have accommodated them through the
strike. There appears only one way for us and that is to let the firm have that reputation
they deserve of being a firm where National Conditions cannot be accepted and our members
prohibited from going.
Another firm in London is in a similar position, but the organisation is so poor that
action cannot be taken to compel these firms to play the honourable trade game.
MOUNTSORREL and SILEBY have had several visits this month. We have a firm in
each place without a member, although numerous attempts have been made by the usual
dinner hour meeting to organise these people, yet they appear devoid of thought of the
present or future, and can only blindly accept anything done for them without the simplest
thanks. I am of the opinion that our Organisers should work together in two's in these
difficult districts-to my mind the most successful way without interfering or depending
on any local efforts.
OUR SHODDY BOOTS COMMITTEE has met and decided to have some Shoddy Boots
dissected by the Research Department of the Manufacturers' Association, and approach
the Manufacturers' Federation and the Repairers' Association in order that we may get
their views with the ultimate object of a massed attack on the Shoddy man.
WOLLASTON.-At the request of the Higham and Rushden Branch we held a meeting
at Wollaston for organising and educational purposes. We cannot boast of the size of
the attendance, the general view being expressed that the Union has done so well that the
members are requiring to be spoon fed. Let us hope this is wrong, but we cannot imagine
our members paying is. and 6d. per week for nothing to see what they are getting for
their money after and during the threatened attack by the Tories on the Unions, they are
not even ruffled with the prospective danger lurching in the way.
COUNCIL MEETINGS.-We considered the position of the Eccles, Norwich and Frome
Parliamentary seats, and advised continuance and with the same Candidates, if the local
people so desire.
ORGANISING.-We now have five Organisers who can do an enormous amount of work,.
and my old wish of four Organisers in 1914 is at last consummated. If the names, ages,.
wages, and occupation of all factories in the industry were obtained, and they ought to be,
the present staff of organisers could not do that work once round under five years, and as
local officers spend a much busier time now than ever before, the organiser brings a fresh
mind to bear and is able to rectify the daily wrongs he finds as he proceeds. If he feels
lonely, the Repairing side of our industry will allow him to fill up his time.

Shop and have six months' training of two hours per day, four days per week, or one day

maintain the handsewn boot as voted by the Marines themselves to be the best boot for
comfort and wear, and it would be worth while if the Army and Navy did this in Govern-
ment Workshops, and save the awful spectacle cf turning on the streets so many young
men who could be adequately and remuneratively employed by the services for service
work only, but until this becomes an accomplished fact, we are prepared to make provision
for these men to continue their training under some employer at rates commensurate with
their lack of being fully qualified men, and in this connection we are willing to help.
The Inspectorate for Trade Boards is very interesting.
In 1919 the number of firms per Inspector under Trade Boards was 408 to 1.
In 1920 the number of firms per Inspector under the Trade Boards was increased
to 818 to 2.
In February, 1922, the number of firms per Inspector under the Trade Boards was
966 to 4.
In January, 1924, there was a Staff of 39 Inspectors, which meant every Inspector
was responsible for 4,830 firms. As five Inspectors were engaged solely at Headquarters,
this left only 34 Inspectors for actual inspection.
In January, 1923, the number of firms on Trade Board Lists was in all trades 188,405.
And between Ist January, 1922, and March, 1923, 4,723 firms only were inspected, repre-
senting about 2 per cent. At this rate if every firm is to be inspected once only, it will
take fifty years to go round once, but the Ministry of Labour brought the 39 Inspectors
up to 60, which will permit inspection amounting to not more than 4 per cent.
COMPETITION AMONG UNIONS.
One Shoe Union for All.
We have had occasion to again complain of some of our members on one firm clearing
their cards and joining another Union. We complained, and ultimately took the matter
to the Disputes' Committee of the Trades Union Congress, and found that these men had
joined the other Union in such a manner that that organisation did not know the facts
or they would not have taken them, as the officials of both bodies work amicably together
on other matters. We are determined not to allow the greed of a few disgruntled men
from that good fellowship continuing. It so happened that five out of the six did not find
the haven of Trades Unionism until they were over fifty years of age, and at sixty years of
age they have transferred. We can well afford to let them go, and we feel sure such attempts
in future will be refused if we only inform the other Union in time.
The time has arrived when all Shoe Unions should be rolled into one whatever the
cost, whatever the inconvenience. There are already a body whom both could appeal
to to act as mediator between us if we cannot agree, and I trust when next we make this
attempt we should be determined to amalgamate for unity's sake.

General President.
INTERNATIONAL FEDERATION OF TRADE UNIONS.
What the Employers think about Improving Working Conditions.
Various employers' organisations have recently held conferences to discuss questions
which affect the workers. The two chief questions discussed have been working hours
and workers' insurance.
AN INTERNATIONAL CONGRESS OF MASTER BAKERS, which met at Brussels, con-
demned the draft agreement compiled by the Geneva Conference for the prohibition of
night work in bakeries, and passed a resolution to found an International Union of Master
Bakers, to fight this Agreement.
A GENERAL MEETING OF DANISH EMPLOYERS' ASSOCIATIONS formulated the demand
that the management of factories must be left wholly in the hands of the employers, and
diminished Parliament not to pass legislation regulating working hours.
A GENERAL MEETING OF THE FRENCH UNION OF EMPLOYERS' ASSOCIATIONS in the
TEXTILE INDUSTRY demanded that more work should be done in order to increase output,
and thereby cheapen production. It also demanded that social insurance should be
developed only gradually, and should be guided in its development by the experience
and desires of the industrial and commercial associations.
THE ASSOCIATION OF FRENCH INDUSTRY AND AGRICULTURE protested against the
present institution of the eight-hours day, which, it declared, places French industry at a
great disadvantage compared with most of its strongest competitors. The Government
must amend the existing regulations establishing the eight-hours day.
THE ASSOCIATIONS OF THE FRENCH PRINTING PRESS-OWNERS consider that, in view
of the financial difficulties of the country, the time is not suitable for the introduction of
the proposed social insurance. They also object to the compulsory employment of war
wounded.
THE ITALIAN INDUSTRIALISTS' ASSOCIATION disapproves of the general establishment
of the eight-hours day, and demands that international labour legislation shall be restricted
so as to prevent its hampering the increase of production in Italy.
THE POLISH NATIONAL UNION FOR INDUSTRY, MINING, COMMERCE AND FINANCE
demands the modification of the existing regulations on the subject of working hours,
paid leave, and holidays for festivals.
THE ROUMANIAN MANUFACTURERS' ASSOCIATION declares that the only benefit to be
obtained through labour legislation is the establishment of the practice of free negotiations
between employers and workers; the State must not interfere with these negotiations.
THE NATIONAL UNION OF SWISS EMPLOYERS' ASSOCIATIONS demands that efforts
shall be made to lengthen the ordinary working week to 52 hours on the basis of Article 41
of the Swiss Working Hours Act.
In every country, therefore, the employers' organisations are combating the eight-
hours day, and the advancement of the workers towards improved conditions; and
always one country complains that another is ahead of it in exploiting the workers, and
that for this reason it cannot compete with its wicked neighbour. Obviously there is
only one remedy for this. When every worker on the face of the globe enjoys the benefit
of the eight-hours day, there will be an end of all this unfair competition based on long
working hours. Why do not the employers grasp this simple fact, and turn their energies
to spreading the gospel of the eight-hours day among their own ranks ?
[The above extracts show the absolute need for keeping our machinery in an high
state of efficiency and also that the workers should become active members of their trade
unions.--E.L.P., G.S.].

BRANCH REPORTS.
ARBROATH.-Trade is still bad in this district, and our festive season
will be like the weather, very variable. It seems inevitable that an extended
holiday will be given to a large number of our this season, with
all its consequent hardships. If this additional period is added to the holiday
it will bring us again in contact with the customary holiday rule of Unemploy-
ment Insurance. We still think it a shame that this rule should be used to
stop benefit to claimants even when the customary holiday does not deprive
short-time claimants of work. It is a pity we cannot get a united front by all
the large unions on such a matter, because it requires only this pressure to have
it altered. Another matter which is clamant is the offer of potato-picking to claimants as a test of their genuine desire for
work. Throughout Scotland this work is paid for at the princely wage of 45
45. 6d. and 5s. per day, while frequently you have to find your own form of
conveyance to the fields which may be a few miles away. Many claimants
draw considerably more benefit than would be paid for a week at potatoes.
It is not insurable work, and although it is used by the Ministry of Labour as
a "test," there is another point that the same Ministry decides against a claim-
ant when he has been working for any length of time at non-insured employ-
ment. The unions must join in protesting against such underpaid and unprofit-
able uninsured work being offered their idle members who are drawing extended
benefit, and their being penalised when it is refused. A very large number
have been punished severely in this district over their refusal to accept this
scandalous alternative. Arising out of disallowance of benefit by the Chief
Insurance Officer, if upheld by the Court of Referees, is the further evil of an
extended penalty at the option of Local Employment Committees. When
such difficulties confront a large number of idle workers, the work of using
existing machinery is very great and very unsatisfactory, as can be judged
when a Court of Referees may have as many as 35 cases to deal with at a sitting.
No full or fair hearing is possible in the time allowed the Court. There are
two other points being dealt with just now which should interest trade unions
and officials everywhere. One is a Divisional Office decision to refuse benefit
unless a claimant has at least twelve stamps to his or her credit. Regulations
at present allow a discretionary power to waive a definite number if oppor-
tunities have not existed, especially for young persons just starting insurance,
for securing stamps. These regulations are to be scrapped if this decision is
allowed to pass, and branches should join in upholding the practice of " waiving"
the definite number of stamps in exceptional circumstances. The other point
is serious to a greater degree. Central Office of the Ministry has sent out an
instruction to refuse benefit to any claimant returning from abroad until they
have had work of an insurable nature since their return. Many young men in
the Iron Trades and Building Trades, forced to go abroad and then in turn
forced to come home, have large reserves of unexhausted contributions, and
yet they are to be refused benefit until they have found work of sufficient
duration to prove they are normally insurable. It is terrible, and a flaming
protest should be sent to the Ministry in order to have this decision cancelled.
Every town will have many cases of this kind at the present moment, and serious
hardship will be inflicted if the decision stands. The fight is being taken up
by some Labour Exchange Committees, but the unions should use every effort
to press home the protest. Unemployment Insurance may yet be the rallying-
ground for the unions and produce that united front which is often spoken of-
The one union for all workers.

Dance in the Art Galleries on the evening of Friday, 21st November, the first

gathering of the Saxone Shoe operatives, both male and female. About 210

harmony being proceeded with. Mr. Geo. Clark, Managing Director, occupied
the chair, and was supported by Messrs. C. Bleakley, Council Member, W. F.

Glasgow, representing the Shoe and Leather Record, and W. Henderson, Presi-
dent, J. Campbell, and A. Flanagan, Secretary. The speeches were lucid and
crispy, educative and interesting, special reference being made to the process
of building up the trade in Kilmarnock, the great changes that had taken place

development of high speed, highly productive labour-saving machinery, and
in face of that, paradoxical as it may seem, the expansion and growth of the
excellent programme of music and song was gone through with the customary
National Union, not only in Kilmarnock, but throughout the country. An
votes of thanks to the chairman, speakers and artistes, and last, but by no means

Prosperous New Year than 1924 has given us, and hope that by the time
these lines are read many of our members will have secured work again.
PLYMOUTH. During the month we have lost one of our members,
John Proctor. He was at work a few days before his death and passed away
quite suddenly. Although he never interested himself in Trade Unionism
or Labour Politics, being more inclined to Conservatism, he was, nevertheless,
a man of exceptional tastes, and every spare moment in the workshop was
employed in reading some musty old volume of recent purchase; almost
every second-hand bookshop in the town was visited by him, and his know-
ledge of English History would have put many a secondary school pupil in the
shade. Later years he studied Greek and was often to be seen, sat upon his
bench with paper and pen in hand attempting a translation of some old manu-
script. He also had some knowledge of music and was well acquainted with
many biographies of the old composers. To the widow and family we extend
our sympathy. The funeral was attended by our President and Secretary,
together with sixteen of our members. We wish all members a Happy New
Year.

Reprint of Circular No. 325. issued in March, 1924.
NATIONAL UNION OF BOOT AND SHOE OPERATIVES.
34 GUILFORD STREET,

December, 1924.
FELLOW OFFICERS AND MEMBERS,
DAY-WORK METHODS OF EMPLOYMENT.
I beg to call your attention to an important point in connection
with the policy and procedure of the Union regarding day-work methods of
employment.
Some employers appear to be under the impression that once day-work
is the method of employment, the piecework statements are not the basis for
measuring the wages paid. It cannot be too clearly pointed out that the
policy of the Union has always been, that if day-work is the method by which
wages are paid, then the amount of work done for the wages paid MUST
be based upon the quantities statements which have been drawn up from
time to time by the Boards of Arbitration, and which, therefore, can easily
be applied as to the output when on day-work.
For instance, supposing an employer pays an operative (male) 62s. per week.
such 62s. should be measured by the statement as to the number of pairs or
operations to be done for this wage. It has not been unknown that some
employers have expected that for the 62s. paid, the amount of work done
would be nearer 70s.
So far as women operatives are concerned, it has also been known that
some employers expected for 37s. per week paid as wages, 45s. worth of work
as judged by the Statement. The same method must also apply to Youths'
wages on the Graduated Scale, which are governed by the piecework and
quantities statements. I trust NO MEMBER will be under any misappre-
hension that the output MUST be regulated by the statement according
to the wage paid to an operative on day-work.
Yours faithfully,
On behalf of the Council,
E. L. POULTON,
General Secretary.

INTERNATIONAL BOOT AND SHOE OPERATIVES
AND LEATHER WORKERS' FEDERATION.

INTERNATIONAL SECRETARIAT.

Re-affiliation of the American Boot and Shoe Workers' Union with
the International Federation.

Since the end of the Great War the International Secretary made repeated effort
to bring about the re-affiliation of the American Shoe Workers' Union having been affiliated
with the International Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives before the war. During the
past years these efforts had had no success. At the last meeting of the International
Council, on 23rd July, 1924, this question was again discussed and the members were of
unanimous opinion that the efforts to bring about the affiliation of the American Union
had to be continued. Colleague Poulton, General Secretary to the National Union of
Boot and Shoe Operatives, England, was charged to use his influence to reach this aim.
Poulton and Simon's united efforts have had now the desired result. On 30th October
the Secretariat had a letter from the American brother Union where the American comrades
declared their re-affiliation with the International. As the different affiliated Unions
will be interested in these negotiations the respecting correspondence will be herewith
notified:

MR. E. L. POULTON,	BOOT AND SHOE WORKERS' UNION,
General Secretary,	246 SUMMER STREET, BOSTON.
National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives,	18th August, 1924.
34 Guilford Street, London, W.C. 1, England.

DEAR MR. POULTON,

Your communication of 28th July, 1924, relative to the matter of the Boot and
Shoe Workers' Union becoming affiliated with the Shoe and Leather Workers' Inter-
national, has been referred to me upon my return from a brief vacation.

The question of re-affiliating with the Shoe and Leather Workers' International
has been discussed at several of our Board meetings during the last few years, but
no definite action has been taken.

In view of the fact that our General Executive Board is scheduled to meet begin-
ning Monday, 8th September, 1924, we have decided to submit your communication
to the Board for such action as they may desire to take, and the decision of our General
Board will be immediately communicated to you.

Trusting, &c.
Fraternally yours,
(Signed) C. L. BAINE,

BETTER BOOTS.
The Value of Goodwill in Industry. A Thoughtful Lecture.
"Shall we not work for greater efficiency and a greater measure of goodwill because
of a certain knowledge of the necessity of each individual to the other. Then will come
a greater satisfaction in labour, and all is labour whether employer or employed. Let
each man know his best is expected, is appreciated, and that his best is a sound policy
for all concerned."
These were the concluding words of an exceedingly interesting lecture by Mr. E. T
Hawthorne, of Messrs. William Timpson Ltd., Kettering, on "What of To-morrow?"
at a meeting of the Northampton and District Boot and Shoe and Allied Trade Managers'
and Foremen's Association, held at the Black Boy Hotel, Northampton, on Wednesday
evening. Mr. G. Macready (president) was in the chair.
Mr. Hawthorne said some people might argue that the workman had lost his indi-
viduality, that he was a drop in the ocean, that his view-point was no longer of any
importance. But were these the facts? A HEALTHY TRADE UNION WITH LIVE, LEVEL-
HEADED OFFICIALS WAS THE FINEST POSSIBLE THING FOR THEIR TRADE OR ANY OTHER
TRADE. He suggested that rather than losing status the individual had more status under
the present order of things.
What would be their factory methods and organisation of the future? It was safe
to say that specialisation of individuals in the various details of management, supervision,
and operation had come to stay. The future would demand greater efficiency and larger
co-operation between the units that made up a manufacturing concern. The work of
employer, manager, foreman, and operative would not be less arduous, but it would be a
combination of first-class organisation, better working conditions, and last, but not least,
a closer mutual understanding between all grades which would lead to a much larger
measure of mutual satisfaction for all those concerned. What industry needed, and
THE
what industry was getting was men with vision, men with the ideal of service and a square
deal. No man asked for more.
THE SAME APPLIED TO THE WORKMAN.
INEFFICIENT EMPLOYER WAS GOING. SO HE OUGHT. THE UNSATISFACTORY MANAGER
AND FOREMAN WAS GOING TOO, AND RIGHTLY SO.
He ought not to be expected to ask for less.
What was to be the future of the managers and foremen themselves in the industrial
life of the future? One thing was certain. Foremen, managers, and executives would
be required as long as they had industry. But what of their functions? THE OLD ORDER
THE FOREMAN WHO DROVE IS GIVING WAY TO THE ONE WHO COULD LEAD.
The foreman of the future would be chosen more and more according to his knowlgdge
of men.
WAS CHANGING.
The result would be found in a better product.
"
Mr. Hawthorne went on to emphasise the great responsibility which was theirs.
Do you always give a sympathetic ear to any complaints that may arise? Do you
You may say you are not appointed
always see that justice is done? Will your men ever come to you and ask your advice
in their private difficulties and personal worries ?
for that purpose. I say that if they do come to you you are to be congratulated on having
the confidence of your subordinates, and such a thing is the finest motive force extant.-
Northampton Echo, 11th December, 1924.

FINAL MEETING OF PIONEER BOOT WORKS LTD.
Presentation to Councillor J. Gribble, J.P.
tive Boot Works Ltd., which has been voluntarily liquidated, came definitely to a close
This was the last meeting of shareholders in the company, called to pass the last report,
At a meeting held in Kingsway Hall, London, on Saturday last, the Pioneer Co-opera-
to adopt the last balance sheet, and to decide the custody of the books and papers belong-
ing to the company.
Councillor James Gribble, J.P., who founded the business and has been its manager through-
Mr. H. W. Lee, editor of Justice, was in the chair, and among those present were
out, Mrs. Gribble, Mr. J. F. Green (ex-member of Parliament for Leicester), Mr. F.
Davey (secretary of the company), and Mr. D. Barratt, of Northampton.
The report and statement of affairs were presented by Mr. Gribble, who has been
acting as liquidator. It showed that not only had all creditors been paid twenty shillings
congratulate themselves. A resolution that the report be adopted was carried, as was
result on which Mr. Gribble said, amid applause, he thought they had every right to
also a resolution that the books and papers be left in the custody of Mr. Gribble.
Rising at the close of the formal business, the Chairman said the meeting so far had
gratification. That was to make some recognition of the splendid services of Mr. Gribble,
not been a pleasant occasion, but he now had a duty to perform which gave him the greatest
not only to the company throughout its existence, but during the process of liquidation.
When the notice of the final payment was sent out, a suggestion was made that some
testimonial should be given to Mr. Gribble. The response had been as encouraging as it
was fitting, and he had the greatest possible pleasure in handing to Mr. Gribble a cheque
for £115 17s. 6d. as a tribute from the shareholders in the company. (Applause.)
Mr. J. F. Green said he claimed that the company had been a success even though
they were winding it up. It had given splendid service to the movement. As they had
made up their minds that they could not carry on, it was better to wind up when they
could pay twenty shillings in the pound than to hang on and in the end have to miserably
fizzle out. (Applause.) He knew the meeting would endorse every word that had been
said about the services of Mr. Gribble. Mr. Kay and Mr. Davey also spoke.
Mr. Gribble, who was visibly moved, said the kindness he had received the whole
way along had been quite a revelation to him. He had been very much touched not only
by the kindness he had received from his old comrades in the Socialist movement, but also
from his old colleagues of the Boot and Shoe Operatives' Union. It made him feel that his
work had not been in vain. The cheque would be very handy (laughter), but he did not
value it because of that so much as because it represented the gratitude of practically all
the shareholders in the company. They had accomplished what they set out to do up to
a point. They had contributed a great deal of money to the support of the movement,
and that was what the Pioneer Boot Works was started for. In the end they had been
crushed out through no fault of anyone, and they had wound up in an honourable manner.
If he could not have paid everyone twenty shillings in the pound, it would have been the
greatest blow of his life. He had been proud of his work for the company, and he was
proud to have their confidence to the last. (Applause.)

Now the Tory Government has reluctantly been compelled by the Labour Cabinet to its Attorney-General to the effect that in Stanley Baldwin about a week ago rose in the House to say with the primness that the instruction given was to be instituted without its knowledge or sanction. This was the ground upon which the Tory Party conducted its election campaign on the Campbell case. Challenged by Mr. MacDonald and his colleagues on the Front Bench, the Tory Government does not only that it is the duty of an Attorney-General to inform himself of all the relevant facts regarding such prosecutions, but also to take account of the views of the Government or the appropriate Minister before coming to a decision. Mr. Baldwin, in fact, has grudgingly acknowledged that the Labour Cabinet did nothing improper or unusual in defining the procedure in regard to political prosecutions. Labour has been justified out of the mouths of its enemies: and there we can leave it. — Labour Press Service, 24th December, 1924.
LOBBY NOTES.
(By Our Lobby Correspondent.)
Perhaps no better Minister than Mr. Churchill could have been selected by the Government to shatter the illusion that the removal of the McKenna Duties had brought about the ruin of the motor industry.
In an official statement circulated on Tuesday, he reported that the number of motor-cars imported into this country during the six months from May to October this year was 7,055, or only 22 more than during the corresponding period of last year. Moreover, during the same comparative period the number of imported chassis actually decreased from 5,418 last year to 5,268 this year.
The fact that the motor trade has not been ruined is also apparent when another angle of view is adopted. According to the official figures, the number of unemployed in the motor industry on 20th November, 1923, was 21,489. By 24th November this year the number had been reduced to 17,398. Further, the number of workers engaged in the industry has grown from 193,020 in November last to 201,790 in November of this year.- C.E.L.
Labour Press Service, 24th December, 1924.

I wish for peace at twilight,
And happiness at dawn;
The help of God as slow I trod
The way that leads me on.
For strength to aid another,
Who needs the aid of me;
The gift of smiles through weary miles,
And blest humility.
For some place in the future
To serve or to command;
And to the ends some gallant friends,
Who love and understand.
For mind forever open
And soul with courage high
To see the light and do the right,
When life has cast the die.
For hopes within my power
To better me and you;
And then the will to keep them still,
And faith to see them through.
-HENRY GILLEN.

A PICKET ASSAULTED.

Mr. Joseph Bound Over to Keep the Peace.
At the Old Street Police Court, on Saturday, Mr. Joseph, of Messrs. Jackson & Sons,
boot manufacturers, 11 Princelet Street, Spitalfields, E., was summoned by Mr.
Gibbins for having assaulted him outside the factory on 22nd November.
Mr. Hornby, who defended, said his friend, Mr. Thompson, had had an opportunity
of speaking to him on the matter. His client would be prepared to be bound over to
the peace towards the complainant and pay 21s. costs. Both his friend and his client
would like to say something on the case.
Mr. W. H. Thompson, who appeared for the complainant, said the matter had arisen
out of an unfortunate dispute between the firm and the National Union of Boot and Shoe
Operatives. His client was acting as a picket on behalf of the Union, and had no desire
to be vindictive. He only wished to say that the Union endeavoured to conduct the
disputes in the spirit in which they ought to be conducted, and wanted employers to un-
stand that they had a right to expect similar conduct from them.
Mr. Hornby said that if the case had been gone into he should have had indisputable
evidence that there was a push and nothing more. His client said that in picketing those
concerned came rather too close to the premises, and he hoped in the future that they
would endeavour not to annoy the firm more than they could help. In paying costs,
it did not necessarily mean that the defendant should have been ordered to do so.
Mr. Watson (to defendant): You are bound over to keep the peace for six months
and pay 21s. costs. —The Shoe and Leather Record, 5th December, 1924.

WAGES IN THE BOOT-REPAIRING TRADE.

Minimum Rates to be Fixed.
At a recent meeting of the Boot and Shoe Repairing Trade Board (Great Britain,
it was resolved to fix certain general minimum piece rates for male and female workers
employed on work preparatory to rounding and channelling machines, in accordance
with the proposals contained in the Notice of Proposal D. (27) issued by the Trade Board
on 6th September, 1924. The Board have requested the Minister of Labour to confirm
the rates as fixed and to bring them into operation under the Trade Boards Act on 5th
January, 1925.
Due notice will be sent to all employers in the trade as soon as the minimum rates
have been confirmed by order of the Minister of Labour. In the meantime information
in respect of the minimum rates may be obtained from the Secretary, Office of Trade
Boards, I Whitehall Gardens, London, S.W. 1.
The Trade Board have not yet varied the general minimum time rates and overtime
rates for male apprentices in accordance with the proposals contained in their Not
D. (27), but will resume consideration of the question of making the proposed variat
at their next meeting.—The Times, 2nd December, 1924.

TRADE UNIONS IN CHINA.

How they are Developing.
Details of the growth of trade unions in China are given in the latest number of
Industrial and Labour Information, the weekly publication of the International Labour
Office of the League of Nations.
China may, from the point of view of trade union organisation as it exists at present
be divided into three zones-the North, the Yang-tze-kiang Valley and the Kwang-tung
province, says Industrial and Labour Information.

THE NORTH. - In the North the movement for the organisation of the workers is
comparatively feeble; though, the railwaymen of the Peking-Mukden and Peking-Sui-
yuan lines have powerful trade unions.

THE YANG-TZE-KIANG VALLEY. The great river Yang-tze-kiang waters the two
industral provinces of Hu-pei and Kiang-su. The first is served by the river port of
Hankow, the other by Shanghai on the estuary.
The workers of Hu-pei have made considerable efforts to organise themselves, and
towards the end of 1922 they set up a workers' federation including 24 trade unions and
about 40,000 members.
About the same time the workers on the Peking-Hankow railway formed themselves
into a trade union with 11 local sections.
At Shanghai, according to a report of the Economic Information Office of the Chinese
Government, 47 trade unions were created in 1922, and out of a total of about 120,000
Chinese workers engaged in industry in the district, about 80,000 are members of trade
unions.
The workers' organisation movement also included 30,000 coolies, 50,000 dockers,
and about 5,000 drivers.

THE SOUTH. - But the greatest progress has been made in the South, in the province
of Kwang-tung. This may be partly due to the support given to the trade union move-
ment by Dr. Sun-yat-sen, whose advanced tendencies are well known.
There are 200 trade unions at Hong-kong and 300 at Canton, and some of them are
very powerful. The most important and active is probably the Mutual Assistance Society,
a Socialist organisation which endeavours mainly to co-ordinate the work of the trade
unions and publishes several papers for this purpose.

This was the society which conducted the great seamen's strike at Hong-kong from
November, 1921, to March, 1922. At that time it succeeded in collecting $20,000, and
was able to pay every striker, whether a member of the union or not, strike pay varying
between 45 cents and Ș1 per day. It also succeeded in producing sympathetic strikes
among the workers of Hong-kong and Canton. The seamen were successful and obtained
a wage increase and also the recognition of their trade union, which in 1923 had about
30,000 members.

National Developments.
At the present moment the trade union movement is tending to overstep the bounds
of districts and to constitute itself as a national organisation for the whole of China.

CHILD LABOUR IN THE EAST,
Child Labour in Shanghai.
published a report which throws a striking light on conditions of child labour as they
The Child Labour Commission appointed by the municipality of Shanghai recently
exist in Shanghai.
The report sums up the result of the investigation, so far as concerns mills, factories,
and similar places of industry, in the following words -
The commencement age varies with the nature of the employment, but it can be
asserted that, generally speaking, the child begins to work in the mill or factory as soon
as it is of any economic value to the employer. The Commission have seen very many
children at work who could not have been more than six years of age.
"The hours of work are generally twelve, with not more than one hour off for a meal.
The children frequently have to stand the whole time they are at work. In many industries
day and night work is the rule, there being two shifts of twelve hours each.
"In many cases the atmospheric and dust conditions are bad. The sanitary arrange-
ments in the majority of mills and factories leave very much to be desired.
"The contract system of employment is common.
contractor supplies the requisite labour and is paid on production. This system is obviously
open to grave abuse. In some instances the children employed receive no money and their
Under this system the native
conditions of life are practically those of slavery."
The Commission recommends that regulations should be made prohibiting the employ-
ment of children under 10 years of age, rising to 12 years within four years.

THE EIGHT-HOUR DAY.
The Eight-Hour Day in Canada.
The results of a recent enquiry made by the Canadian Department of Labour to ascer
tain the present position of the eight-hour day movement in industrial undertakings in
Canada have been made known to the Select Committee on Industrial and International
Relations by the Assistant Deputy-Minister of Labour.
The enquiry showed that 54.22 per cent. of the employers of firms making returns
work an eight-hour day, or 48-hour week, or less.
The enquiry was based on returns received from employers having fifteen or more
employees in the various industries, excepting agriculture and fishing. Information
was received from 5,263 employers having 690,317 employees.
It is interesting to note that the industry in which the highest proportion of employees
was working a 48-hour week or less was transportation, with 91.5 per cent., and the
industry in which the smallest proportion of the employees worked a 48-hour week and
less was logging, with 19.23 per cent.

THE PROGRESS OF INTERNATIONAL LABOUR LEGISLATION.
Rapid progress continues to be made in giving effect in the national legislation of
various countries to the decisions of the International Labour Conference.
Up to 15th November, 1924, ratification of International Labour Conventions had
taken place in 141 cases.
It is interesting to note that the Conventions which have been ratified by the largest
number of countries are the Unemployment Convention (17 countries), the Convention
prohibiting the night work of women (13 countries), and the Convention prohibiting the
night work of young persons (13 countries).

CLITHEROE HOUSING COSTS.
Direct Labour Contracts.
In a report to Clitheroe Corporation on housing costs, the surveyor (Mr. A. R. Blezard),
who is in control of the Town Council's building scheme, states that when tenders were
asked for 20 houses of Class B type (three rooms upstairs and three down), the highest
price received was £1,313 per house, and the lowest tender £1,255. The Building Guild
estimated the cost at £1,020 per house, but the Government declined to accept any of the
tenders and approved of the Corporation's plan to proceed by direct labour, providing the
cost did not exceed £950 per house. Mr. Blezard now reports that the 20 houses have
been completed for less than £700 each.
For houses of Class A type (two rooms downstairs and three up) the tenders ranged
from £492 10s. to £650 per house. Again, the Ministry of Health declined to accept the
tenders and allowed the Council to construct the houses by direct labour, with the maxi-
mum cost fixed at £400. The surveyor states that 20 are almost complete and the price
of the finished dwellings will be under the figure sanctioned by the Government.-The
Times, 9th December, 1924.
[Yet another example of the saving to the community by direct labour being em-
ployed.-E.L.P., G.S.].

IN DARKEST LONDON.
Seven Living in One Small Room. Baby Suffocated.
A verdict that a child's death was due to the bad housing conditions under which the
family were living was returned at a Southwark inquest on 4th December, 1924.
Five children, their mother and father, had been compelled to
sleep in one room so tiny that it would not hold a cot.
There were five similar houses, four of them being occupied by families
Walk Sideways.
Asked by the coroner whether the stairs were substantial, Mrs. Butler said, "The
coroner's officer had to walk upstairs sideways."
Sergeant Gunns, the coroner's officer, describing his visit to the Butlers' rooms, said
Six people standing upright would fill the downstairs room.
By sitting on the stairs one could almost reach the stove.
Before he could go upstairs he had to pull back the chest of drawers and clamber
over them, thus reaching the narrow, winding staircase.
The coroner remarked that in the matter of overcrowding, Southwark was infinite,
worse than the East End.

"HULLO !"
When you see a man in woe,
Walk right up and say "Hullo!"
Say "Hullo!" and "How d'ye do?"
"How's the world a-usin' you?
Slap the fellow on his back,
Bring your hand down with a whack.
Walk right up, an' don't go slow.
Grin, an' shake, an' say "Hullo!"
Is he clothed in rangs? Oh, sho!
Walk right up and say "Hullo!"
Ragin is but a cotton roll,
Jest for wrappin' up a soul;
An' a soul is worth a true
Hale, an' hearty "How d'ye do?"
Don't wait for the crowd to go,
Walk right up an' say "Hullo!"
We've big vessels meet, they say,
They saloot an' sail away,
Jest the same are you an' me,
Lonesome ships upon the sea,
Each one sailing his own jog
For a port beyond the fog.
Let your speakin'-trumpet blow;
Lift yer horn an' cry
"Hullo!"
Say "Hullo!" an' "How d'ye do?"
Other folks are good as you.
W'en you leave your house of clay,
Wanderin' in the far-away,
W'en you travel through the strange
Country to'other side the range,
Then the souls you've cheered will know
Who ye be, an' say "Hullo!"
—S. W. Foss.

of airmen's high-legged boots out of sheep
skins. This new type of protective foot-
wear proved to be extremely successful
and my firm was kept busy on these until
the close of the War.
In the boom years which followed,
factories were stacked with orders and
everybody was fully employed.
On my return to civilian life I immedi-
ately interested myself in Union affairs. I
was elected part-time President of the
Wellingborough Branch in November,
1918. In common with other branches,
there was a great increase in membership
and it became necessary for another full-
time official to be elected. In July 1919
I was elected as the first full-time Branch
President.
My long years as a Trade Union Official
had commenced-years which have been
full of adventure, disappointments and
triumphs, but with it all an intense feeling
of satisfaction.
By 1921 the boom had petered out and
the industry entered into the years of un-
precedented unemployment. Looking
back over those years, one realises the
fortitude and courage with which both
employers and operatives faced those
tremendously difficult times. I am con-
vinced that the industry was saved from
complete collapse because we had a
National Agreement in operation. What
would have happened if it had been a free
for all is difficult to contemplate. It was
not, of course, without difficulty that the
agreements were enforced, especially in
some districts, but the fact that there was
an Agreement enabled the Union, some-
times with assistance from the Federation,
to insist on its observance
With the national spending at its lowest
ebb, the demand was for the cheapest
product. Piecework, which had grown
during the War and the boom years, was,
in many instances, being replaced by day-
work in the mistaken idea that this would
cheapen production. This led to numer-
ous disputes and much heart burning
among our members. Still trade did not
improve and unemployment and short-
time working was widespread.
The records of the Union show that,
from 1920 to 1939, £1,210,999 was paid
out in unemployment benefit; in the peak
year, 1921, £96,457 was paid. In addition,
the Union, acting on behalf of the Ministry
of Labour under the State Unemployment
Acts, paid £3,633,233 State benefit. Few
homes escaped the tragic consequences of
unemployment.
Many firms closed down, but still the
industry survived and fought back to get its
share of trade from the purchasing public.
The industry is under a deep debt of
gratitude to the leaders of both sides of the
industry, who, by their foresight and
tenacity, guided the industry through those
difficult years.
My work as a branch officer, in common
with my colleagues, was an exacting one.
Many small firms, which had commenced
business during the War with a certain
measure of success when trade was good,
now found themselves in difficulties. They
had not the background or foundation of
the older established firms, and unfortun-
ately many of them had tried to meet the
situation by adopting methods outside the
National Conference Agreement. This
led to many arguments and minor disputes,
and their actions would have undoubtedly
undermined the structure of the industry
had not the Union taken firm action.
The best elements within the Federation
were sympathetic to the Union and gave
moral support which had a great bearing in
restoring confidence in the negotiated
agreements.
During these eventful years the industry
had spasmodic periods of trade revival,
but these soon passed and the bad times
reappeared. It is true, of course, that
individual firms maintained a fairly even
rate of production; when one looks back
and realises more fully the difficulties they
were up against, it is to their credit that
they were able to do this in view of the
general situation.

Disappointments, Disputes and
Achievements

IN DECEMBER, 1929, I WAS ELECTED AS A
National Organiser of the Union. I
commenced my new duties by working in
the Leicestershire and Northamptonshire
districts. It will be readily understood
that, to induce non-members to join the
Union was no easy task, especially when
trade was so bad. Factory gate meetings
were the then accepted method of organi-
sing. You usually got a sympathetic
hearing although, at times, vocal opposition
was in evidence. Gradually but surely,
opposition was broken down and you had
the satisfaction of handing in to the local
office a batch of names of new members.
My advent as a National Organiser
coincided with another serious recession in

GENEROSITY OF NORTHAMPTON FIRM.
On page 60 will be found the outline of a scheme which has been put into
operation at Messrs. Crockett & Jones, Northampton, whereby considerable
financial assistance will accrue to the employees of the said firm. We are
glad of this recognition of the fact that there is some responsibility owed one
to another as members of the community apart from that of bare employees.
We feel confident the workpeople of Messrs. Crockett & Jones, whilst fully
appreciating all the firm has done, will see in the scheme, not merely help for
themselves, but one more fact of the necessity of rendering to one another
that assistance which, from time to time, is required to help along the pathway
of life, one of the most effective being membership of the Union.
THE POLITICAL WORLD.
Although Parliament is not sitting, it does not mean there is no need for
doing political work. There is a good deal of activity going on in various
parts of the country, and we would urge upon the membership how necessary
it is to keep fully in being, the local organisation, and to constantly carry on
the work of informing the public of the necessity at all times to send men and
women both to the House of Commons and local councils, who are in sympathy
with the aims, objects and ideals of the Labour Party.
