GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.

FELLOW MEMBERS,
SHODDY. The Shoddy agitation has drawn the attention of one of our leading
daily papers, and they have been at some trouble to visit various people interested in the
industry, and will no doubt express their views of a trade which during the great lament-
able war, did their duty to both friends, Allies, and to the public. When requested to
make a war-time boot (and the Government of the day were prepared to assist the general
public by putting on the market an honest and unadulterated article at a price as reason-
able as possible), every effort was made, but the distributive section of the trade som
refused to accept the recommendation of the Committee and distribute at 12½ per cent.,
but demanded and got their usual 33⅓ per cent., irrespective of the wants, requirements,
or poverty of the munition workers, for whom this class of boot was made. Some of the
largest firms of boot manufacturers were prepared to distribute on the Committee's terms,
and when the Chairman put the question in the event of the retailers refusing to distribute,
how would the public get the goods? he was advised that the Co-operative Movement
would be able and undoubtedly willing to help. The interested persons had visions
immediately that the Co-operative Movement would immediately become known-as
they are to-day-the most genuine and reliable distributors in the nation. Think of it-
5 per cent. for manufacturers, retailers demand more than six times that amount for
their share of the spoils. To my mind this and the other parties, the factors, are the only
departments of the shoe industry where legitimate and beneficial economies can take
place in the interests of the public. The enormous profits and dividends made and paid
call for drastic improvements in the industry. The question has been put to me again,
"Why don't the Union order its members not to make
Shoddy;" such a statement must be answered because it has been asked by grown men.
Answer One.- Ought the operative, bound as he is willing to be by the Terms of
Agreement which has been in existence for thirty years, to interfere with the Management?
Answer Two. - Can the Union itself agree on what is Shoddy, and impart that know-
ledge to its members?
Answer Three. Ought that to be the perogative of the Union?
Answer Four.- Is not the simplest, safest, and best way to stamp the shoes as they
do in the City of Leicester for the Australian market- "Warranted Solid Leather Outsole
and Insole, Wood Heel"? We should then be able to eliminate the practice now made
by those one would describe as "Shoddy Dealers," who are known to the trade, although
for the crimes committed in their name.
stock, and then sandwiching in a line of rubbish of the pick-pocket kind. Until each
industry takes up the purification of their own industry, they may be held responsible
Rumour has it that one factor who advertises
largely, is said to be buying stuff from a non-union centre where hours and wages don't
matter so long as men get work, and the employers persuade the "natives" that if they
join the Union they will lose their work, so give a Is. rise for a few months, then take it
again, and by this means keep the operatives in constant fear. We hope to be able to
give the opinion of the Medical Profession on the danger to health of the Shoddy goods
we wish to see marked down, or rightly named, as this form of espionage must cease.
LEICESTER WOMEN'S BRANCH. This Branch had cause to carry a resolution of protest
against a federated firm who prosecuted a young woman for leaving without notice. The
facts are, as this young woman was on short time, she wished to leave; she asked per-
mission, and was refused. She was then advised to leave, as such an attitude on the part
of the firm was unreasonable. In Northants the law of the land is carried out, a full week's
work or a full week's money on either side. Leicester Branches only claim for the same
time as the factory is making when a member is discharged, and they expect no obstacle.
If, when working short time, an operative asks permission to leave, they should be per-
mitted. I have a case in mind where an employer put out a paper-"Wanted: an
Operative." One applied. "Are you out of work?" "No!" says the operative, "I want
to better myself and intend leaving." He was promised the situation. After he left, his old
firm objected to another employer setting one of his workmen on unless the man was
thrown out of work first, or allowed his late employer to give him a rise to keep him. I
know an employer who has a workman who was bought in three times by one firm:
apparently his worth was only recognised each time he got a better berth offered him.
What a pity commercialism only moves when pushed. Leicester Branches ought to have
a better understanding on this subject, as the Women's Branch have expressed their
determination to contest all such cases, and had the operative informed the Branch they
would have sought legal assistance. The Leicester No. 1 Branch also passed a strong
resolution on the subject, and do not permit the employers to enforce on their members
the right to refuse a reasonable request to leave a firm when working short time, and my
indictment against this firm, or any firm, is that had the Employment Exchange fund
been used to pay this young woman to stand by for the convoni


---
13
not have prosecuted, but as the Union funds were at stake only, no respect for the Union's
funds were regarded as of any importance. This matter cannot be left where it is.
SPITALFIELDS DISPUTE. -This strike still continues, and additional attempts have
been made to bring about a settlement. We are in the following position :-Some twenty-
three agreements are already in existence prohibiting the holders from calling in either
the Trade Union representatives, or the Employers' Federation representatives, in case
of dispute between the firm and the signatories, and we want the reinstatement of the
strikers who have been reduced to nineteen. To leave the accommodators in, is a big
s'ice of over-generosity on our part, and we want an opportunity to organise the rest of
the firm before we agree to settle. All this must, even if modified, be reduced to writing
by the Ministry of Labour and a real settlement made that will not jar on the nerves of
anyone interested. There are others in London whom the settlement will affect, if well
settled.
ADVISORY COMMITTEE OF TRADE BOARDS.-We have held a further meeting of this
Committee and have appointed deputations to the War Office and Admiralty with a view
of asking them to extend the training time from six months to at least twelve, to those
men who are leaving the service at the end of their period, and to where possible allow
them to remain as Hand-Sewn Makers, on similar lines to the men engaged at Eastney
Barracks, where they employ some fifty men in the Hand-Sewn shop. It would at least
find more employment by paying out more wages and keep many of these men from being
thrust into an already overstocked human market. We also find a big difference on policy
and scope with the legal department of the Ministry, who have taken so narrow an attitude
that may have such far-reaching results as to jeopardise any benefit we, or the Trade,
may have received from Trade Boards, and the enemy is already being helped by those
unions who have experienced the apparent weakening of the Boards which appears to be
very obvious since the advent of the Tory Government. Prepare yourselves, fellow
members. In railway trains and other places you hear the rumbling of "what are they
going to do with the Trade Unions"?
TRADE BOARDS' EXECUTIVE. - A meeting of this body has been held at Eccleston
Square, in the General Council Room, and the report of the work of the Executive Council
carefully examined, because one Board in the Distributive Trade had deliberately broken
the 48-hour week by extending the hours. One Union has been compelled to withdraw
their representatives from that Board rather than be responsible for extending hours of
labour. Had these employers shown any wisdom they would be well advised to shorten
the hours and give employment to those now receiving payment without working.
BARWELL. I attended a meeting there to try and remove the impression that when
we ask our members for names, ages, and wages, that we have specially sought some
individual firm for treatment. I think they ultimately agreed that it was the wisest course
when some imputation has been levelled at a district, that a couple of representative firms
should be taken until we are able to take others. Our five organisers will be a long time
taking this evidence from the 800 factories connected with the Federation, as a week is
required to take one firm if each department has to be summoned to a meeting, and the
evidence then obtained, but the Leicester method of filling up cards by the operatives
from the worker to the Central Office is most reliable.
MESSRS. JOHN Clemson LTD., Derby.-Owing to the operatives on this firm falling
in membership, we called a special meeting, specially warned, to be held not five minutes,
walk from the firm; so few turned up that I drafted a circular to each operative informing
them that there were more out of the Union than in, and as the governor belonged to the
Federation, I felt sure he would be disappointed to know the true state of affairs on the
firm. I simply hoped we should be able to be content with the progress made by the
end of the month without going any further.
C.W.S., DERBY ----We have had to call the attention of the Management of this firm
to the small earnings of the Turn-Shoe Department, and the fact that although the Manage-
ment had signed statements as far back as August, 1923, there were girls working contrary
to the National Terms, in wages, hours, overtime, and conditions, with the result that
a 10 per cent. increase has been given and the shortcomings in the Management minimised.
This is very unfortunate when a firm with a reputation admit nearly all the complaints
made on behalf of the operatives, and then would look upon you as the culprit. If they
will attempt this on a National Officer, what chance has a local one with them ?
MANSFIELD.-Two visits have been paid to the firm of Messrs. Faire Bros. who have
somewhere about 130 employees at wages far below the scale, many of them being on
piecework. They cut Slipper Soles, Insoles, and make Stiffenings. We have organised
about 100 of them, and we have appointed four Shops' Presidents. Now the test comes;
will the Management do as they did before, call the girls into the office one by one and
induce them to leave the Union; the firm won. I have promised them help before Easter
if they prove their loyalty to the Union.
BURTON-ON-TRENT has been visited four times. Having no local Secretary, a hall
had to be obtained, bills printed and distributed. Not many came to the meeting, although
Mrs. Bell-Richards was advertised as an inducement to the girls to attend. We are

SPITALFIELDS DISPUTE.
Negotiations have been carried on during the month by the General
President, the General Secretary, and the Organisers, and a settlement has
been arrived at whereby the National Conditions have been observed.
OURSELVES V. N.U.D.A.W.
From time to time we have had to complain because members of our
Union have been accepted into membership of the National Union of Dis-
tributive and Allied Workers without any consultation with our officers.
Quite recently we had a case before the General Council of the Trades Union
Congress regarding the matter, and as a result of the negotiations we have
entered into an agreement which should obviate any friction between the
two organisations in the future. Appended is a copy:—
[COPY.]
TRADES UNION CONGRESS GENERAL COUNCIL.
MEMORANDUM OF AGREEMENT between the National Union of Boot and
Shoe Operatives and the National Union of Distributive and Allied
Workers.
MUTUAL. PROTECTION OF MEMBERSHIP.
In pursuance of negotiations which have taken place between the
National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives, the National Union of
Distributive and Allied Workers and the Disputes Sub-Committee of the
General Council of the Trades Union Congress, it is mutually decided
that the following undertaking shall be entered into :—
" That the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives and the
National Union of Distributive and Allied Workers hereby agree that
neither Society shall in the future take members from the other
without consultation and agreement with the Society concerned."
Signed, this Third day of January, 1925:
On behalf of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives :
T. F. RICHARDS,
General President.
On behalf of the National Union of Distributive and Allied Workers :
J. HALLSWORTH,
Industrial General Secretary.
On behalf of the General Council of the Trades Union Congress :
FRED. BRAMLEY,
Secretary, T.U.C.

If there should be any cases occur in future where members transfer from
membership of the Union to the N.U.D.A.W., branch officers are requested to
at once send along particulars to the General Secretary, so that the matters can
be dealt with along the lines named in the agreement above.
GENEROSITY OF NORTHAMPTON FIRM.
On page 60 will be found the outline of a scheme which has been put into
operation at Messrs. Crockett & Jones, Northampton, whereby considerable
financial assistance will accrue to the employees of the said firm. We are
glad of this recognition of the fact that there is some responsibility owed one
to another as members of the community apart from that of bare employees.
We feel confident the workpeople of Messrs. Crockett & Jones, whilst fully
appreciating all the firm has done, will see in the scheme, not merely help for
themselves, but one more fact of the necessity of rendering to one another
that assistance which, from time to time, is required to help along the pathway
of life, one of the most effective being membership of the Union.
THE POLITICAL WORLD.
Although Parliament is not sitting, it does not mean there is no need for
doing political work. There is a good deal of activity going on in various
parts of the country, and we would urge upon the membership how necessary
it is to keep fully in being, the local organisation, and to constantly carry on
the work of informing the public of the necessity at all times to send men and
women both to the House of Commons and local councils, who are in sympathy
with the aims, objects and ideals of the Labour Party.

ANNUAL RETURNS.
A full return of Income and Expenditure for the Union (Council and
Branch combined) has to be sent to the Registrar of Friendly Societies in
compliance with the different Acts of Parliament covering Trade Unions
Branch Secretaries are requested to help me by completely filling in the form
already issued, and send it back to the Central Office NOT later than
30th January, 1925.
HISTORY OF THE UNION.
There are still a number of copies of the "Fifty Years' History of the
Union" in stock, and members desirous of securing a copy should place their
orders at once. They can be purchased through the branch officers at 6d.
per copy, and all members desirous of learning about the work of the Union
should not fail to obtain a copy of this most interesting and valuable record
of the work of the Union.
FIVE-WEEK ΜΟΝΤΗ.
There being five Saturdays during this month, Secretaries are asked to
make up their returns and pay for the same accordingly.
THE "DAILY HERALD."
We trust that all our members will take every available opportunity to
push the Herald, the only daily paper owned and controlled by the movement.
By purchasing the Herald daily a full report of the political world as seen by
Labour can be read.
REMEMBER THE FIFTEΕΝΤΗ!
Once again we feel bound to call the serious attention of Branch Secretaries
to the fact that the FIFTEENTH day of each month is the latest day for
returns reaching the General Secretary. If Branches fail to send off their
returns to reach the Central Office before the 15th of the month it tends to
upset the organisation of the work in the General Secretary's Office. We beg
to intimate that unless returns are in before the 15th of the month, the Secretary
has been instructed to put into force the Rules governing the same.
Sheets MUST also bear the signature of both the Branch President and Branch
Returns
Secretary, or they will reluctantly have to be returned for completion.
TRADE UNION STAMP.
This is a matter which we have stated before rests with the members to
make a success. It is in the interests of members themselves that "Stamped
Footwear " should be increasingly purchased; therefore, push the Trade Union
Stamp. Members and their families should wear only "Union Stamped
Footwear."

GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.

FELLOW MEMBERS,

SHODDY. The Shoddy agitation has drawn the attention of one of our leading
daily papers, and they have been at some trouble to visit various people interested in the
industry, and will no doubt express their views of a trade which during the great lament-
able war, did their duty to both friends, Allies, and to the public. When requested to
make a war-time boot (and the Government of the day were prepared to assist the general
public by putting on the market an honest and unadulterated article, at a price as reason-
able as possible), every effort was made, but the distributive section of the trade soon
refused to accept the recommendation of the Committee and distribute at 12 per cent.,
or poverty of the munition workers, for whom this class of boot was made. Some of the
but demanded and got their usual 334 per cent., irrespective of the wants, requirements,
largest firms of boot manufacturers were prepared to distribute on the Committee's terms,
and when the Chairman put the question in the event of the retailers refusing to distribute,
how would the public get the goods ? he was advised that the Co-operative Movement
would be able and undoubtedly willing to help. The interested persons had visions
immediately that the Co-operative Movement would immediately become known-as
they are to-day-the most genuine and reliable distributors in the nation. Think of it-
5 per cent. for manufacturers, retailers demand more than six times that amount for
their share of the spoils. To my mind this and the other parties, the factors, are the only
departments of the shoe industry where legitimate and beneficial economies can take
place in the interests of the public. The enormous profits and dividends made and paid
call for drastic improvements in the industry. The question has been put to me again,
as put by a journal some time ago, "Why don't the Union order its members not to make
Shoddy"; such a statement must be answered because it has been asked by grown men.

Answer One.-Ought the operative, bound as he is willing to be by the Terms of
Agreement which has been in existence for thirty years, to interfere with the Management?
Answer Two. Can the Union itself agree on what is Shoddy, and impart that know-
ledge to its members ?

Answer Three.- Ought that to be the perogative of the Union ?

Answer Four.-Is not the simplest, safest, and best way to stamp the shoes as they
do in the City of Leicester for the Australian market"- " Warranted Solid Leather Outsole
and Insole, Wood Heel" ? We should then be able to eliminate the practice now made
by those one would describe as "Shoddy Dealers," who are known to the trade, although
not to the public, with enticing people with a genuine line of misfits and samples and surplus
stock, and then sandwiching in a line of rubbish of the pick-pocket kind. Until each
industry takes up the purification of their own industry, they may be held responsible
for the crimes committed in their name. Rumour has it that one factor who advertises
largely, is said to be buying stuff from a non-union centre where hours and wages don't
matter so long as men get work, and the employers persuade the "natives" that if they
join the Union they will lose their work, so give a Is. rise for a few months, then take it
off again, and by this means keep the operatives in constant fear. We hope to be able to
give the opinion of the Medical Profession on the danger to health of the Shoddy goods
we wish to see marked down, or rightly named, as this form of espionage must cease.

LEICESTER WOMEN'S BRANCH. - This Branch had cause to carry a resolution of protest
against a federated firm who prosecuted a young woman for leaving without notice. The
facts are, as this young woman was on short time, she wished to leave; she asked per-
mission, and was refused. She was then advised to leave, as such an attitude on the part
of the firm was unreasonable. In Northants the law of the land is carried out, a full week's
work or a full week's money on either side. Leicester Branches only claim for the same
time as the factory is making when a member is discharged, and they expect no obstacle.
If, when working short time, an operative asks permission to leave, they should be per-
mitted. I have a case in mind where an employer put out a paper" Wanted: an
Operative." One applied. "Are you out of work? " "No!" says the operative, "I want
to better myself and intend leaving." He was promised the situation. After he left, his old
firm objected to another employer setting one of his workmen on unless the man was
thrown out of work first, or allowed his late employer to give him a rise to keep him. I
know an employer who has a workman who was bought in three times by one firm:
apparently his worth was only recognised each time he got a better berth offered him.
What a pity commercialism only moves when pushed. Leicester Branches ought to have
a better understanding on this subject, as the Women's Branch have expressed their
determination to contest all such cases, and had the operative informed the Branch they
would have sought legal assistance. The Leicester No. 1 Branch also passed a strong
resolution on the subject, and do not permit the employers to enforce on their members
the right to refuse a reasonable request to leave a firm when working short time, and my
indictment against this firm, or any firm, is that had the Employment Exchange funds
been used to pay this young woman to stand by for the convenience of the firm, they dare

GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
SHODDY. - The Shoddy agitation has drawn the attention of one of our leading
daily papers, and they have been at some trouble to visit various people interested in the
industry, and will no doubt express their views of a trade which during the great lament-
able war, did their duty to both friends, Allies, and to the public. When requested to
make a war-time boot (and the Government of the day were prepared to assist the general
public by putting on the market an honest and unadulterated article, at a price as reason-
able as possible), every effort was made, but the distributive section of the trade soon
refused to accept the recommendation of the Committee and distribute at 12 per cent.,
but demanded and got their usual 33½ per cent., irrespective of the wants, requirements,
or poverty of the munition workers, for whom this class of boot was made. Some of the
largest firms of boot manufacturers were prepared to distribute on the Committee's terms,
and when the Chairman put the question in the event of the retailers refusing to distribute,
how would the public get the goods? he was advised that the Co-operative Movement
would be able and undoubtedly willing to help. The interested persons had visions
immediately that the Co-operative Movement would immediately become known-as
they are to-day-the most genuine and reliable distributors in the nation. Think of it-
5 per cent. for manufacturers, retailers demand more than six times that amount for
their share of the spoils. To my mind this and the other parties, the factors, are the only
departments of the shoe industry where legitimate and beneficial economies can take
place in the interests of the public. The enormous profits and dividends made and paid
call for drastic improvements in the industry. The question has been put to me again,
as put by a journal some time ago, "Why don't the Union order its members not to make
Shoddy"; such a statement must be answered because it has been asked by grown men.
Answer One.-Ought the operative, bound as he is willing to be by the Terms of
Agreement which has been in existence for thirty years, to interfere with the Management?
Answer Two. Can the Union itself agree on what is Shoddy, and impart that know-
ledge to its members ?
Answer Three. - Ought that to be the perogative of the Union ?
Answer Four. - Is not the simplest, safest, and best way to stamp the shoes as they
do in the City of Leicester for the Australian market- "Warranted Solid Leather Outsole
and Insole, Wood Heel"? We should then be able to eliminate the practice now made
by those one would describe as "Shoddy Dealers," who are known to the trade, although
not to the public, with enticing people with a genuine line of misfits and samples and surplus
stock, and then sandwiching in a line of rubbish of the pick-pocket kind. Until each
industry takes up the purification of their own industry, they may be held responsible
for the crimes committed in their name. Rumour has it that one factor who advertises
largely, is said to be buying stuff from a non-union centre where hours and wages don't
matter so long as men get work, and the employers persuade the "natives" that if they
join the Union they will lose their work, so give a ls. rise for a few months, then take it
off again, and by this means keep the operatives in constant fear. We hope to be able to
give the opinion of the Medical Profession on the danger to health of the Shoddy goods
we wish to see marked down, or rightly named, as this form of espionage must cease.
LEICESTER WOMEN'S BRANCH.- This Branch had cause to carry a resolution of protest
against a federated firm who prosecuted a young woman for leaving without notice. The
facts are, as this young woman was on short time, she wished to leave; she asked per-
mission, and was refused. She was then advised to leave, as such an attitude on the part
of the firm was unreasonable. In Northants the law of the land is carried out, a full week's
work or a full week's money on either side. Leicester Branches only claim for the same
time as the factory is making when a member is discharged, and they expect no obstacle.
If, when working short time, an operative asks permission to leave, they should be per-
mitted. I have a case in mind where an employer put out a paper -" Wanted: an
Operative." One applied. "Are you out of work?" "No!" says the operative, "I want
to better myself and intend leaving." He was promised the situation. After he left, his old
firm objected to another employer setting one of his workmen on unless the man was
thrown out of work first, or allowed his late employer to give him a rise to keep him. I
know an employer who has a workman who was bought in three times by one firm;
apparently his worth was only recognised each time he got a better berth offered him.
What a pity commercialism only moves when pushed. Leicester Branches ought to have
a better understanding on this subject, as the Women's Branch have expressed their
determination to contest all such cases, and had the operative informed the Branch they
would have sought legal assistance. The Leicester No. 1 Branch also passed a strong
resolution on the subject, and do not permit the employers to enforce on their members
the right to refuse a reasonable request to leave a firm when working short time, and my
indictment against this firm, or any firm, is that had the Employment Exchange funds
been used to pay this young woman to stand by for the convenience of the firm, they dare


---
13
not have prosecuted, but as the Union funds were at stake only, no respect for the Union's
funds were regarded as of any importance. This matter cannot be left where it is.
SPITALFIELDS DISPUTE -This strike still continues, and additional attempts have
been made to bring about a settlement. We are in the following position: Some twenty-
three agreements are already in existence prohibiting the holders from calling in either
the Trade Union representatives, or the Employers' Federation representatives, in case
of dispute between the firm and the signatories, and we want the reinstatement of the
strikers who have been reduced to nineteen. To leave the accommodators in, is a big
s'ice of over-generosity on our part, and we want an opportunity to organise the rest of
the firm before we agree to settle. All this must, even if modified, be reduced to writing
by the Ministry of Labour and a real settlement made that will not jar on the nerves of
anyone interested. There are others in London whom the settlement will affect, if well
settled.
ADVISORY COMMITTEE OF TRADE BOARDS.We have held a further meeting of this
Committee and have appointed deputations to the War Office and Admiralty with a view
of asking them to extend the training time from six months to at least twelve, to those
men who are leaving the service at the end of their period, and to where possible allow
them to remain as Hand-Sewn Makers, on similar lines to the men engaged at Eastney
Barracks, where they employ some fifty men in the Hand-Sewn shop. It would at least
find more employment by paying out more wages and keep many of these men from being
thrust into an already overstocked human market. We also find a big difference on policy
and scope with the legal department of the Ministry, who have taken so narrow an attitude
that may have such far-reaching results as to jeopardise any benefit we, or the Trade,
may have received from Trade Boards, and the enemy is already being helped by those
unions who have experienced the apparent weakening of the Boards which appears to be
very obvious since the advent of the Tory Government. Prepare yourselves, fellow
members. In railway trains and other places you hear the rumbling of "what are they
going to do with the Trade Unions"?
TRADE BOARDS' EXECUTIVE. -A meeting of this body has been held at Eccleston
Square, in the General Council Room, and the report of the work of the Executive Council
carefully examined, because one Board in the Distributive Trade had deliberately broken
the 48-hour week by extending the hours. One Union has been compelled to withdraw
their representatives from that Board rather than be responsible for extending hours of
labour. Had these employers shown any wisdom they would be well advised to shorten
the hours and give employment to those now receiving payment without working.
BARWELL.-I attended a meeting there to try and remove the impression that when
we ask our members for names, ages, and wages, that we have specially sought some
individual firm for treatment. I think they ultimately agreed that it was the wisest course
when some imputation has been levelled at a district, that a couple of representative firms
should be taken until we are able to take others. Our five organisers will be a long time
taking this evidence from the 800 factories connected with the Federation, as a week is
required to take one firm if each department has to be summoned to a meeting, and the
evidence then obtained, but the Leicester method of filling up cards by the operatives
from the worker to the Central Office is most reliable.
MESSRS. JOHN CLEMSON LTD., DERBY.-Owing to the operatives on this firm falling
in membership, we called a special meeting, specially warned, to be held not five minutes,
walk from the firm; so few turned up that I drafted a circular to each operative informing
them that there were more out of the Union than in, and as the governor belonged to the
Federation, I felt sure he would be disappointed to know the true state of affairs on the
firm. I simply hoped we should be able to be content with the progress made by the
end of the month without going any further.
C.W.S., DERBY -We have had to call the attention of the Management of this firm
to the small earnings of the Turn-Shoe Department, and the fact that although the Manage-
ment had signed statements as far back as August, 1923, there were girls working contrary
to the National Terms, in wages, hours, overtime, and conditions, with the result that
a 10 per cent. increase has been given and the shortcomings in the Management minimised.
This is very unfortunate when a firm with a reputation admit nearly all the complaints
made on behalf of the operatives, and then would look upon you as the culprit. If they
will attempt this on a National Officer, what chance has a local one with them ?
MANSFIELD.-Two visits have been paid to the firm of Messrs. Faire Bros. who have
somewhere about 130 employees at wages far below the scale, many of them being on
piecework. They cut Slipper Soles, Insoles, and make Stiffenings. We have organised
about 100 of them, and we have appointed four Shops' Presidents. Now the test comes;
will the Management do as they did before, call the girls into the office one by one and
induce them to leave the Union; the firm won. I have promised them help before Easter
if they prove their loyalty to the Union.
BURTON-ON-TRENT has been visited four times. Having no local Secretary, a hall
had to be obtained, bills printed and distributed. Not many came to the meeting, although
Mrs. Bell-Richards was advertised as an inducement to the girls to attend. We are

informed that the Rossendale Slipper Union has many members, and although two of our
Organisers have been over and were permitted to stay, we appear to have had little effect

LEATHER EXHIBITION AT LEICESTER.—I visited the Leicester Leather Exhibition,
which was held from 12th to 17th January, and the exhibits were very fine indeed, showing
the wonderful progress being made by the County in attempting to imitate an improve
ment of the industry as represented by the City's products, and being so successful. It was
a really good Exhibition and worthy of a visit from all within fifty miles.
"DAILY HERALD."—On Sunday, the 18th inst., Mr. Frank Hodges attended at the
De Montfort Hall, to press upon the labour movement the need for all adherents to buy
and continue to use all reasonable endeavours to increase the circulation of our valuable
little paper. My own criticism of the Herald is that we get too much Communism, and
too much of one or two individual's and their families, and many have held, or told me,
that these were their impressions, but as those at the head of affairs have been also informed,
we must do all we can, even though the non-Unionist element shines most in the world
for whom the Trades Unionists have provided an organ and kept it going, and many of our
members do not belong to our Socialist movement. I hope, therefore, that we shall get
enough trade union supporters and readers to make the paper a paying proposition, and
thereby cease to be held up by the Trade Unionists of the country, who are the only real
power. The absence from Mr. Frank Hodges' platform on the 18th of the local trade
union Aldermen, Councillors, Guardians and Executive, looked middling. I hear they
had not received an invitation. This is poor organisation. Let us hope such will not
occur again.
TRADE UNION STAMP.—In the meantime wear only those goods made under Trade
Union Conditions, and only patronise honest firms.

BRANCH REPORTS.
ARBROATH.—Our members have had an extended holiday for the p
pose of enjoying the start to a " Happy New Year," and by the time th
written each and all will be wishing for the feel of some " filthy lucre." T
only good point affecting a considerable number is the fact that no benefit
lost at the Labour Exchange over this holiday, because it is long enough
have it paid in full. We wish our friends in the Bristol and Kingswood Distric
the best of luck in their protest against this iniquitous deduction. It sho
never have been authorised in its present form, and it is up to the Unions
object to the rule affecting their members too harshly. A great many of
members, however, lose the benefit for the customary holiday because the
period is less than the time stipulated for it to be paid. When the customar
holiday does not even serve as waiting days, the position created produces
hardship to an extreme degree. A point made in our reports some time agr,
deserves attention. The present practice is based upon the assumption that
industrial conditions are normal, whereas they demand the same emergency
provisions which were applied during 1921. The assumption of normality
and the payment of benefit to be hedged in by limitations which are justified
only by normal conditions of employment, may be good for preserving the
Unemployment Fund, but it simply throws on to the Poor Law large numbers
who cannot live otherwise. We should demand still the treatment of idleness
as an abnormal condition, and the payments of benefit to be governed b
emergency regulations. No doubt it sounds plausible to be asked to consent
to the application of general principles which will restore the true purpose ci
Insurance, but in the continued absence of stable conditions in industry, our
first thought should be for the misery and unhappiness produced prolifically
by unemployment. And the cost is not being reduced by the present method.
even although it falls on two different departments-Insurance Fund and
Poor Law and the only justification for such a course is the trouble and
harassment the recipient is put to in the matter. We referred to two matters
of importance last month, the Divisional Office decision affecting claimants
at Labour Exchanges with less than 12 stamps to their credit, and a Central
Office of the Ministry decision re returned emigrants from abroad. The first
is still being maintained, although it seems likely to be withdrawn, but the
second failed in its intention. It is not cancelled yet, but payments have been
authorised until Central Office of the Ministry lays down a ruling after full
consideration. The change of front in each case is due to workers' repre-
sentatives on Labour Exchange Committees convincing those bodies to protest
to the Ministry, and the opposition has been taken up by some Unions also.
Departments can be influenced, and officers and branches should be ready
always to join in with attempts to correct injustices, the more so with Un-
employment Insurance because this Department bases its defence of regulations
on the way in which the country has received and accepted them. We have
won an important point in this area on the question of potato-lifting as a
" test " form of work to offer claimants. Through the Labour Exchange
Committee, and the Court of Referees, we have arrived at a position that no
man will be asked to take this work in future unless the remuneration is doubled.
Further efforts are being put forward to establish fair and acceptable conditions
for country work, which will put a stop to farmers claiming underpaid labour,
and using as a lever the threat of reporting men who refuse. Although progress
is slow, it is comforting to get there sometimes

BELFAST.--Trade remains very bad. The firm of Williamson Bros. when
stopping for the Christmas holidays informed the workers that they would
be sent for when required. We sincerely hope that trade will soon pick up
again. The Boot and Shoe Repairing Trade Board (Northern Ireland) has
been reconstituted, five seats out of the twelve having been allocated to members
of our Union.
CHESHAM. -Trade here remains fair.
CHESTERFIELD.--Trade is again falling off and all our members making
new work are again on short time.
DERBY.--Trade in Derby continues fair, all firms being practically on
full time, but we have a good number of shoe-hands who are unemployed or
on temporary work.
EDINBURGH.--Trade during the month has been very quiet. Factories
have had an extended holiday. Some of our members have been compelled
to claim at Labour Exchange to help them over their bad period. Repairers
have also experienced rather a dull time during December, but when sending
report trade has improved greatly. We are now working to new prices for
Rounding and Channelling. Our experience is that even with the additions,
the deductions for this work are too much. Our members in Repairing Section
are of the opinion that the twenty points in cost of living between 70 and go
are too great, and some alteration should be made. Something on the same
lines as are at present when prices fall below the 70 mark. Others again want
the present 7 per cent. to operate when a workman who is on piece rates has
earned the minimum wage and over.
HIGHAM AND RUSHDEN.--Trade has been affected by the holidays,
some firms closing for 14 days, and a few for three weeks, but generally the
usual week was kept as holiday. Trade seems to be reviving slightly all
round, except at Finedon, where two firms dismissed most, if not all their
employees, viz., Messrs. Bailey & Son, and Knight's. Those not dismissed
have been asked to stand off.
We regret to report the death of Mr. Tom Wilson, of Finedon, for
fifteen years Secretary of the Finedon Branch (before it was included
in the Higham and Rushden District Branch). The Finedon Branch was
taken over by us on 30th November, 1905.
KILMARNOCK.--Trade is still fairly good at Kilmarnock, but we are
sorry that we cannot say the same of our Section at Kilmaurs, where the
members have been suspended from work for the past five weeks. We are,
however, hoping that after the New Year holidays are over that the trade in
Kilmaurs will pick up. Will Branch Secretaries please note the change of the
address of the Kilmarnock Office: Mr. William Henderson, 11 Fowlds Street.
KINGSWOOD AND DISTRICT.--At the time of writing this report
98 per cent. of the firms have not reopened after the Christmas holidays.
At a recent meeting of the Kingswood Arbitration Board the "Industrial
Councils Bill "--as introduced last year by Mr. F. Murrell, ex-M.P. for Weston-
super-Mare, was under discussion. It was resolved that the Secretary should
write Miss Tomlinson and Mr. E. L. Poulton, J.P., requesting them to issue a
joint letter to all Members of Parliament, asking them that, when balloting
Private Members' Bills, precedence should be given to an Industrial Councils
Bill. The National Union and the Employers' Federation (September, 1924)
have again expressed their strong opinion of the need for legislation which will
give statutory power to the National Agreement. Having reached agreement,


---
that power of legal enforcement, similar to that provided by the Trade Board
Act for Boot Repairing Section of the trade, should be applicable to the cor
ditions governing the making of boots and shoes. The question arises as to
whether the Joint Executive who signed the National Agreement, have an
definite proposals as to the exact form this proposed legislative power to
proceed against an employer who evades the National Conditions-shoul
be expressed. In October, 1924, a conference was held-under the auspice.
of the Bristol Association for Industrial Research at Penscott, Somerset,
consider the Bill introduced by Mr. F. Murrell, M.P., and was read a second
time. A close study of the details of the Bill proved conclusively that if the
Bill became law in its present form, it would be ineffective, and even dangerou
It may be argued that the Bill would have been amended in its Committe
stage, but we wish to suggest that our industry, which has been commended fo
its ability to legislate its own Agreements, should note that the Bill under
discussion proposed to establish a "Central Industrial Council."-Clause
par. I. Also sub-section of Clause 4 reads: (c) the avoidance of conflicting
decisions by Industrial Councils in different industries, and the harmonising
of the effects of such decisions in the interests of industry throughout Great
Britain. What is intended here? (Clause 4). The implications have not
been thought out, and surely we could not tolerate interference from such a
body as this Clause proposed to constitute. It will be noticed that Sub-Section
D. of Clause 3, states that it shall be the duty of the J.I.C. concerned to take
such proceedings against such persons with a view to his conviction and punish-
ment. This Clause was originally drafted to read: The Minister of Labour
shall take proceedings, &c. It will be noted that in its present form, no power
of enforcement is provided. We understand that 19 J.I.C.'s are definitely
pledged to support the Industrial Councils Bill, and 25 are sympathetic, but
are embarrassed by the hostile attitude of the Trades Union Congress to the
Bill. The Conference formulated its conclusions to the effect that Industrial
Councils should be empowered to obtain legal sanction to their determinations;
that they adhered to the principle of the Bill, that the power of the Minister
to make an order should be permissive and not obligatory; that the penalty
clause is too drastic; that Clause 4 is not essential; that questions such as
Clause 4 provides for, cannot be properly decided by an assembly composed
of probably 100 persons. That a Central Board might be formed to (a) advise
the Government on industrial and economic questions, and (b) to give general
assistance and advise in the work of Industrial Councils. That in the opinion
of the Conference the expenses of the Central Board should be provided out of
money provided by Parliament. In conclusion we may state that Mr. A. G.
Randall attended as a delegate from the Branch, and was impressed with the
value of the decision formulated above, and trust that the interest of the
members will be stimulated thereby, particularly as it is probable that a similar
Bill will be introduced into this present Parliament.
LEICESTER. -Trade is slightly better than last month, but there is not
the improvement anticipated.
LEICESTER WOMEN'S. We have to report trade improving, our un-
employed having gone down to eleven this week. Our Branch Officers are
being kept busy. There is an attempt to cut down labour costs to the minimum,
9th inst., one of our members was taken to the Police Court and sued for a
week's notice. The member, who is only 18 years of age, did not acquaint
us of the summons. The first we knew was the report in the Evening Paper.
The Branch immediately sent the following resolution to the Press: " The
Leicester Women's Branch of Boot and Shoe Operatives deplores the fact that
a firm should take a member to the Court to force a week's notice or a week's
money, on one-sided evidence, that member having asked permission to leave.

LIVERPOOL. At the time this report was written the year 1924 has
become a thing of the past—another milestone on life's journey towards the
great beyond. With regard to the boot repairing trade it has finished up
better than it began. We have not paid out any unemployment Union benefit
for the past six months. As a nation we have muddled through without
disaster, and from time to time mirages of better trade have gladdened our
hearts, but looking back over the twelve months we now know we have done
little beyond marking time. We still have a great army of unemployed, and
our house builders have not made that progress that we expected. Except
in the early part of the year we have been fairly free from industrial strife.
We have certainly made some progress towards the re-settlement of Europe,
and according to the Press the sovereign is to-day worth 19s. 6d. in New York.
If we have had no summer our winter's have been mild, and that is something
to be thankful for. The New Year came in with a brisker step and a brighter
face than did the old. In welcoming it, let us all resolve to do everything
we can in the spirit of real brotherhood to make it the best we have known
since the outbreak of the war.
LONDON SOUTH.-At our monthly meeting the chair was occupied by
the President, Mr. W. Owen. After the usual business of reading and passing
of minutes, the President informed the members that the Organisers, Mr. Len.
Smith and Mr. J. H. Baum, had organised the firm of Lynn & Co., and the
Secretary was pleased to state that he had the names of thirteen members.
A proposition was put and carried, wishing the Council and all of the members,
old and new, a Prosperous New Year, and success to the Union.
NORWICH.-The new year has commenced very badly for many of
the Norwich operatives, the number unemployed being greater than at any
time since the recovery from the slump. Turnshoe makers are feeling the
depression most acutely, there being no great amount of that trade in any
factory in the City.
PLYMOUTH.-Looking back over the past year we must say trade has
been bad, with short time from January to December. This has meant small
wages and short rations. We sometimes doubt if the necessity for an eight-
hour day will ever arise again, especially when all the unemployed are set to
work and the modern machinery coming into our trade is set in motion. This,
with the many devices for saving labour all have a tendency to displace man-
power, unless the organisation of the workers keeps pace with the many changes
of our age and demand a shorter working day. This custom of working short
time with low wages is beginning to be accepted as inevitable, but is really no
more inevitable than bobbed or shingled hair, but is just a custom sprung up
since the war, because the workers have allowed the privileged classes to take
more than their fair share from modern progress and invention, and have been
too modest in their demands. We commend to our comrades the words
written by Dickens, and taken from "Little Dorrit," “Be as rich as you honestly
It's your duty, if not for yourself, for others."

GREAT YARMOUTH.--Sorry to report Water Boot trade slow in Great

SHODDY FOOTWEAR.
Bill to Prevent ts Sale. Women's Shoes that Injure Health.
LEICESTER, Saturday.
Recent investigations have satisfied the Leicester Boot Manufacturers' Association
that the time has arrived when a determined attempt must be made to prohibit the sale
of shoddy footwear which, in the words of one of the members, " is a disgrace to British
manufacture and a grave menace to the health of the nation."
To-day I have discussed with Messrs. Arthur Wilkes, Harry Roberts, and William
Heath, three prominent manufacturers, the causes which have led them to demand immedi
ate action. These causes, they declare, are to be found in every town and village in Great
Britain, being boots and shoes, but especially women's shoes, exhibited in the window,
of those boot-sellers who particularly cater for the middle and working classes.
They are shoes made in the latest styles from inferior leather, wood pulp and material
which is frankly cardboard and even paper. Mr. Wilkes declared :
Even an expert can be deceived at a cursory glance, so perfect is the imitation
finished, so it can be understood how an ordinary purchaser is imposed upon.
These shoes are real "gullers," and the public should remember that more often
than not the thing they see in the window is not the same thing as they are sold in
the shop. In many instances the shoe in the window has been specially prepared
for window dressing.
Mr. Harry Roberts said:
It does not always follow that shoes warranted all-leather are the most reliable
or are above the category of shoddy footwear, because in some cases shoes made of
good quality substitutes are in wear better than those made of bad or inferior leather.
Sweated Labour.
Mr. T. W. Smith, secretary of the Leicester Boot Manufacturers' Association, produced
two women's shoes that on dissection had revealed their shoddy components. One appeared
to be a smart glacé kid walking shoe with a patent leather toe-cap. It was sold retail
at 5s. to 7s. 6d. per pair and wholesale at 3s. 9d. per pair. Mr. Wilkes said:
That shoe which is a real "guller" would practically fall to pieces in wet weather.
At the best it would always be sodden, and not only represents so much waste of
money on the purchasers' part, but also strikes at the health of the wearer, for she
would always have damp feet.
In a factory which conforms to the national agreements between employers
and employees that shoe could not be made for the money at which it is sold. The
labour alone would cost 3s. 3d. per pair.
To make the sale of such footwear impossible reputable manufacturers through their
associations are promoting a Bill in Parliament to make the adoption of the national
agreements as to hours, conditions of labour, and rates of pay compulsory.
This alone is not thought to be a sufficient safeguard for the public, nor is the com
pulsory stamping of boots as "all-leather" regarded as entirely satisfactory for the reasons
given by Mr. Harry Roberts, who urges that the sure guarantee of quality, so far as the
public is concerned, is the manufacturers' branded article. Because, he says, "it would
not pay manufacturers to advertise their goods unless they had made them up to standard
quality and maintained that standard." - Daily Mail, 5th January, 1925.
NO SHODDY SHOES IN NEW ZEALAND.
Interesting Debate on Amending Legislation.
As already reported in the Record, an amendment to the Footwear Regulation Act
1913, has been introduced into the New Zealand Parliament. The principal clause of the
amending Bill is the provision THAT WHERE FOOTWEAR IS NOT ALL LEATHER IT MUST BE
PLAINLY STAMPED WITH A STATEMENT OF THE NATURE OF THE MATERIAL USED.
of the introduction of the Bill.
An illuminating debate took place in the New Zealand Parliament on the occasion


---
Mr. Sullivan (a Christchurch Labour member) said he did not agree with the recom-
mendations of the Bill as it stood. It ignored the wishes of all branches of the boot trade,
and was contrary to the interests of public health. All branches of the boot trade, speaking
with a united voice, desired that no boots be sold in the Dominion anless made entirely
of leather, but the Bill permitted boots to be imported, manufactured and sold even if
they were composed of a composition of cardboard, brown paper, &c. There was a pro-
vision that this footwear must be branded in such a way as to indicate the material of which
it was made, but this was not a sufficient safeguard to the public, who would seldom see
the brand. He hoped the Bill would be amended in the direction of insisting that all
footwear sold in the Dominion be composed of leather.
Mr. J. A. Lee (an Auckland Labour Member) urged the prohibition of imported shoddy,
adding that New Zealand manufacturers used sound material.
Mr. J. M'Combs (Lyttelton, Labour) thought the question was a difficult one, and
that certain composition stiffeners used in footwear were better for certain purposes than
leather stiffeners. One could easily brand a boot "leather," which would be composed
of leather scrapings, and would be the worst type of shoddy.
Mr. W. Parry (Auckland Central, Labour) said Labour would endeavour to have
inserted in the Bill provision to protect the long-suffering public against the importation
of rubbish.
Mr. H. E. Holland (Leader of the Labour Party) said he thought shoddy should be
prohibited, and Mr. W. J. Girling (Awarua--a Blenheim draper) said he was glad an effort
was being made to prevent the importation of shoddy footwear, and he thought the Minister
might look into the question more than he had done. Mr. A. L. Monteith (Wellington
East, Labour) said he hoped legislation would be passed which would do away for ever
with shoddy.
Mr. Harris (Government Member) said that the demand for the all-leather boot had
come as the result of keen competition from overseas, which local factories had felt. Foot-
wear was much cheaper in Britain than in New Zealand. He was not sure that undue
profits were not being made by boot retailers in New Zealand on imported boots. The
agitation was not so much for the continuation of branding, but for the absolute restriction
of boots not entirely made of leather, and in that he saw danger.
Mr. T. W. Rhodes (Thames, Liberal) said he was convinced that under the present
system of branding the public were deceived, but on the other hand, the public had to be
protected from deceiving themselves. While it might increase the initial cost to buy
all-leather shoes, it would be cheaper in the long run. The greatest obstruction was
local prejudice, and local manufacturers had had to use names for their goods which gave
the impression that they had come from overseas.
Mr. J. S. Dickson (Parnel-a draper), chairman of the Labour Bills Committee, said
that few members seemed to understand the position. Shoddy footwear must be stamped.
To-day some of the worst shoddy wer all-leather articles. It had been practically ad-
mitted to the committee that New Zealand manufacturers were far behind Australian
manufacturers, and ought to specialise in certain classes of boots.
" There is leather and leather," remarked the Hon. G. J. Anderson, Minister of Labour
in reply. He explained that some chrome leather would absorb water like a sponge
It was principally used for children's boots, and on a wet day wearers could not possibly
keep their feet dry. On the other hand, some substitutes, even of paper, had been sub-
jected to tremendous pressure, and would resist water more effectively than some kinds
of leather. There was not sufficient evidence to warrant the extreme step of prohibiting
the importation of footwear other than leather. It was an extraordinary thing that
such a step was not favoured by any of the Department's inspectors of footwear, who were
all experienced bootmakers, thoroughly conversant with the trade.
When he first called a conference of parties interested in the subject, added the Mini-
ster, the opinions expressed were so diverse that no conclusion could be obtained. He
was surprised at the sudden unanimity of the boot trade on the question of prohibiting
the import of shoddy in ladies' footwear. Wooden heels were more efficient and lighter
than leather heels.
The Australian Leather Journal states that the committee has added a new clause
dealing with boots and shoes in stock when the Act commences. If the holder of stock
which does not comply with the Footwear Regulation Bill delivers a full statement thereof
to the Inspector of Footwear, he will be permitted to sell it without complying with the
requirements of the Bill that the use of material other than leather shall be plainly
indicated on the goods by a legible stamp showing the nature of the substitute The.
Show and I eather Record, oth January, 1925.


---

SHORT TIME AND NOTICE.
That the custom of a week's notice on either side in the boot
industry is not affected by the necessity of working short time was the
ruling of the Leicester Magistrates when they ordered a girl operative
to return to her former employers and serve her notice, or, in default,
pay the equivalent of a week's wages.

SHOE OPERATIVE FINED.
(To the Editor of the "Leicester Mail.")
SIR,---May I on behalf of the Members of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Opera
tives, express my indignant disapproval of the conduct of the Magistrates, who on Wednes
day last decided against a boot and shoe operative, and ordered the girl either to return
to work and work out a week's notice, or pay a week's wages.
The girl had asked to leave, and as she was on short time thought the firm would
allow her to do so, but instead they have proceeded against her in Court for leaving witho
notice.
Had the girl been on the National Funds of the Labour Exchange, no such actio
could have been taken. Will my working class Tory friends notice the difference in thi
class legislation? There is evidently one law for the Labour Exchange and a different
one for the trade union. Yours, &c.,
T. F. RICHARDS
(General President of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives).
In his letter Mr. Richards makes an attack on the Chairman of the Magistrates, who adjudicated
in this case. As the Magistrates were merely carrying out the law as it stands, we ha
deleted this attack from Mr. Richards' letter.
This is not a matter of personalities, but of the law, and it is only fair that there should be one
law for the operatives and the employers. If the employers had wanted to discharge the
girl, they must either have given her notice or have paid her wages in lieu of notice, and
the same procedure must apply in the opposite direction. Does Mr. Richards claim that
operatives can leave when they please, but that employers must always observe the law
with regard to notice or wages?-Editor, "Leicester Mail."
The General President replied as follows to the Leicester Mail, but the newspaper
was not courteous enough to publish the letter :--

MEETING OF THE C.W.S. HELD IN LONDON ON 3rd JANUARY, 1925.
The following matters were discussed :-
Direct Supplies of Grain.
Mr. Charter. in reply to a delegate, stated that the Board had no grain elevators.
The question was being seriously considered by the Board. He had no doubt that the
policy the Board were carrying out in regard to flour would have a leveling effect on the
Hour and wheat markets of the world.
As one of the deputation who had recently returned from Canada and America, he
might say tha, they had spent a good deal of time in discussing the question, with a view
to getting behind the influences governing and controlling the wheat market, and in getting
into direct touch with the co-operative farmers in Canada. They hoped by the mutual
ownership of the necessary machinery in Canada they would be able to attract their pro-
portion of Canadian wheat straight from the co-operative farmers to the Wholesale Society's
flour mills in this country. Action like that carried to fruition could only have a very
great effect on the wheat and flour markets.
He stood in the Chicago Wheat Market, and had heard a thousand
brokers calling out at each other in buying and selling wheat which
they had never seen. He also stood in the Winnipeg Market and had
seen the entire field crop of Canada bought and sold twice over
in a week.
This would give them some idea of the whole horde of people standing between the
Canadian and other producers and the consumers in this country. It was their business
to get through these people, and to draw their supplies as economically and direct as
possible to use in their own mills in the interests of the consumers of this country. This
was the board's policy. (Applause).
The Boot Trade Booming.
Mrs. E. Palmer (Southampton) said they were all pleased at the increased trade in
the boot and shoe department. She thought it would be right in saying that this was
largely due to the great improvements effected in connection with the production, which
compared very favourably with the best houses. As far as quality, finish, and price were
concerned, she suggested there was a demand for a cheaper shoe.
Mr. Oliver replied that the board were determined to keep up the quality of the boots
and shoes. The board believed that they were catering for all requirements. They had
opened at Northampton the best equipped factory in the kingdom.
The report was approved, as were also the Committee's recommendations with regard
to the purchase of land and properties and the charitable grants.

GENEROUS FIRM
Crockett & Jones give over £20,000 to Workers. A Provident Fund.
With generous solicitude for the welfare of their employees, Messrs. Crockett & Jone,
shoe manufacturers, of Perry Street and Artizan Road, Northampton, have set aside
large sum of money, variously stated as being between £20,000 and £25,000, to establish
a provident fund in which the staff and the workpeople in all departments participate.
The money has been invested in the names of trustees, and is to be administered in
accordance with a trust deed prepared for the purpose.
On Friday evening each employee received a book in which was entered the amount
which has been placed to his or her credit. This amount is arrived at on a calculation
of an employee's earnings spread over a period of years, and is on a percentage basis,
according to status and length of service. The sums vary considerably, therefore, and
we understand that some of the workpeople who have been employed by the firm for many
years have had over £100 placed to their credit.
The firm's action is very deeply appreciated throughout the factory. and the scheme
is considered to be an extremely good one.
The amount standing to the credit of each member of the fund becomes payable a
follows:-
(1) At the age of 60 years in the case of men, and 50 years in the case of women.
(2) At the death of a member, to the next of kin or such other person as the member
may have appointed.
(3) Twelve months after a member ceases to be in the employment of the firm.
(4) In the case of a woman, six months after her marriage.
(5) At the discretion of the trustees, in special circumstances such as the prolonged
illness of a member.
Interest on the amount standing to the credit of each member may either be left
in the fund or be paid out each year. The money in the fund is the property of the members
in trust, and the firm may from time to time make additions to it, but are under no obliga-
tion to do so.
An Echo reporter, who sought information about the scheme this morning, found
Sir James Crockett, J.P., and other members of the firm, too modest to discuss it, and the
foregoing particulars have been obtained as the result of inquiries in other directions
They are, nevertheless, perfectly accurate.—Daily Echo, Northampton, 7th January, 1925.

CO-OP. TRADE UP £6,400,000.
Sales for 1924 Nearly 73 Million Pounds. C.W.S. and Unions.
Retail Societies to Vote Shortly.
Last year's trade of the Co-operative Wholesale Society showed an increase of no less
than £6,400,000 on that of the previous year.
This announcement was made at the general quarterly meeting of the C.W.S. held
in Manchester on Saturday by the chairman, Mr. H. J. A. Wilkins, of Plymouth.
The total sales for the year amounted to £72,900,000, and the
supplies from C.W.S. productive works were valued at £24,210,000,
representing an increase in Co-operative workshop productions of
£3,500,000.
This, said Mr. Wilkins, may be regarded as a big forward step in the trade of the
movement.
They were doing well in flour, and the sales of tea were going up week by week. They
were now hoping for an improvement in the textile trades.
The boot and shoe trade had been considerably improved, and all the works of the
C.W.S. were now on full time.
All round there was a brighter outlook for 1925.
C.W.S. and the Unions.
The question of compulsory membership of a trade union among employees of the
C.W.S. was further discussed.
It was raised (as at the divisional meetings the previous Saturday) on a resolution
from Wallsend Society, which was to the effect that the decision of the previous quarterly
meeting on compulsory Trade Unionism be rescinded.
Mr. Rigg (president of the Wallsend Society) said he thought the position of com-
pulsory membership of a trade union had been forced upon them by the apathy of the
Conservative element of the movement, on the one hand, and, on the other hand, by the
persistency of "professionals," who hoped to make Co-operation a happy hunting ground
for trade unionists.
He thought this attitude on the part of trade unionists was going to interfere with
the progress of the movement, which existed to remedy the anomalies of the present
industrial system.
No decision was arrived at, as the directors of the C.W.S. had decided to submit the
resolution to a referendum of shareholding societies. Voting papers will be distributed
within the next few days.—Daily Herald, 10th January, 1925.

MESSRS. J. SEARS & CO. LTD.
Another Successful Year.
The Directors of Messrs. J. Sears & Co. (True-Form Boot Co.), Ltd., in submitting
their thirteenth annual report, state that the profits for the year 1924, after charging all
working expenses, including Managing Directors' salaries, and after providing for reserves
and for taxation on the profits of the year, amount to £172,948 16s. 7d. (against £169,695
last year).
After provision for dividend accrued on the 7 per cent. Cumulative Preference Shares,
and on the 12 per cent. Cumulative Preference Shares to 31st December, 1924, and pay-
ment of a final dividend of 3s. per share upon the Ordinary and "A" Shares, making a
total for the year of 4s. 6d. per share free of Income Tax, together with the transfer to
general reserve of £25,000 (same last year), a balance is carried forward to next year of
£104,312 13s. 7d. (against £87,900 last year).
8/- WEEK FOR BRAKE AS HOME.
"What a Delightful Place?" Plight of a Sileby Family.
Man Now in Hospital.
Strong comments were made at a meeting of the Barrow-on-Soar Rural District
Council meeting to-day, when the Sanitary Inspector reported that a man, his wife, and
two children, aged 14 months and two months, were living in a brake in a field on the
Barrow-Sileby road, for which he was paying 8s. a week rent, and also 3s. per month
ground rent.
The officer said that the man was now in hospital. The brake had been partitioned
off for a bedroom. There were no sanitary arrangements, and the vehicle let in water
and was mildewed.
A Member: Eight shillings a week for a dog kennel!
Ald. C. Goodacre moved that the owner be served with a statutory order asking him
to put in sanitary arrangements and water.
Mr. V. R. Pochin said it was an outrageous state of affairs. They ought to consult
the Ministry on the matter.
It was decided that Mr. W. L. Everard, M.P., consult the Ministry.
Mr. Bunney said there was a somewhat similar case at Cropstone, where a man was
paying 10s. and 2s. 6d. ground rent for a hut.-The Leicester Mercury, 20th January, 1925.

A League of Nations Union delegation is being organised to visit the 7th Session of

NEW PREMISES FOR THE INTERNAΤΙΟΝΑL
LABOUR OFFICE.

Mr. E. L. Poulton, J.P., the British Workers' delegate to the International
Office, and member of the Governing Body, made the following statement on 24th
1925, in reference to the hatred displayed by the Rothermere Press towards the
tions concerned with the improvement of the conditions of labour. It attac-
unions; the co-operative movement; the salaries of teachers because they e
children of the workers " above their station "; the Ministry of Labour bec
ministers Unemployment Insurance and Employment Exchanges; in fact mot for
activity which seek to raise the standard of life of the working people.

One of the chief objects of its rancour at present, is the International Labor
at Geneva, against which it carries on an intermittent campaign of abuse and misre
tion. In its latest effort to discredit the Office it has surpassed even itself in fals
On the 16th inst., there appeared in its columns an article headed "Labour's Pala
Geneva," with a sub-title "British Taxpayers foot the Bill." It stated that the new b
of the International Labour Office, which is nearing completion, was like a royal pa
that it was built to contain bureaucrats who did nothing, and declared that the
affair was a sheer waste of British money.

It will surprise no intelligent person to learn that this effusion is full of inaccu-
and is deliberately calculated to mislead the public.

The new building is one of simple character; it is built mainly of artificial st
without any architectural embellishment. Visitors from England who have seen it
described it as being a barracks or a workhouse. It is, indeed, designed to be a ho
work, and not an adornment of the landscape. Its total cost will not exceed ₤125.000
of which the share of Great Britain will be ₤11,000. It will be noted that the he
of the article implies that the whole cost will fall on the British taxpayer. As a mar
of fact, the British proportion is 9.4 per cent. of the total.

The new building was ordered to be erected by the League Assembly, because
present temporary building in which the International Labour Office carries on its acti
is inconvenient and relatively costly. The cost of the new building will mean a saving
rent and other expenses of over £5,000 per annum, so that the erection of the buil-
means in reality no additional cost to Great Britain, or to the other countries which be...
to the League of Nations.

As to the statement that the Office does nothing, this is too foolish to need reíntar
Indeed, it was refuted by the Daily Mail itself the other day when it quoted with appro
certain publications which the Office had issued.

One other point should be mentioned; the Rothermere Press is always prote-
against the idea that there is a class war.
everything that Mr. Wheatley has recently said on this subject. The International Lab
Yet its whole attitude towards Labour justif
Office is governed by representatives of Governments, employers and workers, who m
together for the purpose of coming to a common understanding with regard to lab.:
problems. The results of these endeavours are well known. Yet the Rothermere Pres
is constantly seeking, by its attacks upon the Office, to demonstrate that all constitution

to be that the class war advocates are right. Does the Rothermere Press really wish:

various countries cannot but be advantageous, not merely to one country, but to all the
countries who are suffering at the present time from industrial and economic troubles.

SHORT TIME AND NOTICE.
Protest by Boot and Shoe Operatives' Union.
The Leicester No. 1 Branch of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives has
passed a resolution strongly protesting against any employer refusing to give permission
to any operative to leave their employ without serving a week's notice when on short time,
after the operative has asked permission to leave.

This, apparently, is the sequel to the decision of the Leicester magistrates that
workman is not entitled to leave without notice even though his employer cannot keep
him fully employed.---The Leicester Mercury, 10th January, 1925.

BOOT TRADE PROSPERITY.
In spite of unemployment and other adverse influences British boot manufacturers
continue to enjoy considerable prosperity. Their foreign trade is expanding, and the home
demand, especially for the fancy varieties of women's footwear now in vogue, is very heavy.
Foreign competition long ago ceased to be formidable, and though imports increased last
year they were again substantially exceeded by the exports, the not imports being valued
at £1,750,000 and the exports of British manufactured boots and shoes at somewhat over
£5,000,000. The increase in the exports exceeded £700,000, and was, it is true, largely
due to abnormal shipments to the Irish Free State in anticipation of the imposition of an
import duty by that country. But even if that exceptional circumstance is allowed for
the record of the industry is extremely satisfactory. All the Dominions, except Canada,
are large consumers of British boots, and business with other countries is progressing.
Even in the improbable event of the Irish Free State's experiment in protection proving
a success, British manufacturers will still be able to find elsewhere a good market for the'r
wares.
Results just announced by that representative Leicester undertaking, Freeman,
Hardy & Willis, reveal further progress in the development of that company's extensive
business now carried on through upwards of 500 retail branches scattered all over the
country. The directors refer to largely increased competition, but that has not prevented
a further improvement in profits to a figure equivalent to over 26¼ per cent. on the issued
share capital. For the tenth consecutive year Ordinary shareholders receive a dividend
at the handsome rate of 17½ per cent., of which 5 per cent. is payable free of tax, while,
including a provision of £50,000 for income-tax, £149,000 is set aside for other purposes.
In addition to paying a handsome dividend the directors propose to capitalise reserves to
an extent sufficient to provide a bonus to Ordinary shareholders of one Six per cent. Pre-
ference share for every two Ordinary shares now held. Even when that operation is
carried out the company will have reserves to the amount of £113,500 in hand. Its
financial position remains extremely strong, for while liabilities to creditors fall short of
£400,000, stocks, British Government securities and cash balances together exceed £1,000,000.
The directors, therefore, are fully justified in assuming that the position disclosed will be
a source of much pleasure to the shareholders. ---Financial Times, 14th January, 1925.

The Board of Trade Returns, published this week, for December last, show that our

pairs a month during 1924. To be exact, the total for the whole year was 11,986,296

As will be seen, the largest quantity exported in any one month was during July, when

pairs recorded in each of the five preceding months may be attributed to the long holiday
period which it included, and does not necessarily indicate that overseas trade is decreasing.
Generally, the last six months of 1924 were the most satisfactory in any recent year,
and, if the same rate of progress be maintained, firms interested in export business will
have little cause for complaint when they reach the end of 1925.
There was a fairly substantial increase of imports last year of footwear made wholly
or mainly of leather. The total importation for 1923 was 2,282,604 pairs, valued at
£1,147.951; and that for 1924 totalled 2,744,640 pairs, valued at £1,413,166. Compared
with the aggregate sales of boots and shoes in this country, the business done in imported
goods represents a very small percentage, and is probably no larger in proportion than that
of any recent year. It should also be remembered that overseas visitors to this country
were more numerous than usual last year, and those who purchased footwear during their
stay would, in many cases, favour imported shoes. A certain amount of trade in foreign-
made footwear will always be transacted, no matter how good the shoes produced in this
country may be. While, however, the total imports are no larger than at present, British
manufacturers have no cause for anxiety. The Shoe and Leather Record, 16th January,
1925.
