ORGANISERS' REPORTS.
During December we have again had some difficulty with the operative, working
at Hertz's. So serious was the position that the Branch placed the whole matter in the
hands of the Council. We have been dealing with this firm for the past three weeks
and with a certain amount of success in so far that they had adopted the 48-hour week.
The present difficulty was in the Lasting Department, which unfortunately was aggravated
and intensified by the attitude of the men.
We have held two meetings with the clickers working at Levine's. There appears
to be some misunderstanding with regard to the Terms of Settlement, and further, and
with the result that matters were adjusted, and that in order to deal with the rapid
changes in designs were a little confusing to them. We interviewed Mr. Izelman, and
prices, he decided to put the men on piecework, working to the London Clicking Statement.
We have also met the operatives at the following firms:- Solomon's, Meltzer,
Cohen's, Wackman's, Lipman's, Franks', Cunnington's, Hyam's, Mindle's, Franklin's.
Pursuing our investigations, we are far from satisfied with the conditions existing at
of these firms. So serious is the position that the London Federation will be compelled
to take the matter in hand, and demand that all their members carry out the Terms of the
National Agreement. The clickers are fairly well organised, but the system of working
is a gross violation of the London Clicking Statement, while in the other departments
the tendency on minor operations is to get as near the minimum as possible, and so far as
the youths are concerned, no due regard is paid to the Graduated Scales. The girls are
not well organised, consequently the wages are considerably less than in other organised
centres. At some of the meetings we have held we have gone very fully into the method
of working, and from our inquiries the system of working is antiquated. It is just the
old way, that the only method to conduct a business is to pay as low a wage as possible
because they have not got sufficient technical skill to manage a business unless they take
it out of labour. It is very encouraging to find, therefore, especially where the clickers
are concerned, that continued pressure is being applied, which inevitably must mean the
adoption of more up-to-date methods. The difficulty of organisation in London is very
largely the result of the cosmopolitan nature of the population, together with the fact
that many of the operatives reside considerable distances from their employment. This
mainly accounts for the insular mentality which is such a pronounced feature of the average
London operative, that produces a mind which, if he belongs to a Trade Union, will willingly
work by the side of another operative without inquiring if he is a member of a Trade Union.
We are confident only by persistent work that we shall eventually raise the standard of
the London operative. Mr. Mason is untiring in his efforts, as local president, and his ready
advice and assistance is invaluable in all the work that we endeavour to carry out.
The strike at Jackson & Joseph's is still continuing, and we have now entered on the
26th week. The men are remaining firm, and negotiations are proceeding, which we hope
will bring about an honourable settlement. We wish to thank all those branches who
have responded most generously to our funds.
During the past month we have been engaged in the London area, steadily pursuing
our policy of trying to consolidate the district. We have been devoting our attention
chiefly to those firms who are not complying to the whole of the terms of the National
Agreement. We have also rendered some assistance to the local branch, in order to
enforce the London Clicking Statement. Meetings of clickers from a number of firms have
been held, and interviews arranged with the firms. As a result prices have been adjusted
on new designs, and a general improvement has taken place in the working conditions in
the clicking departments. We have endeavoured to negotiate with the following firms
Kay's, Solomon's, Steinhart's, Wackman's, Mindle's, N. Bloom's, Lipman's, in order
that they should adopt the Holiday Scheme. None of these firms definitely refused to
adopt the Scheme, and promised to give the matter their consideration. From our
observation there appears to be a number of firms in this district who produce a similar
class of work, and each claim that owing to the competition of the other, they find it
impossible to include the scheme in their costs of production. This position presents a
deplorable condition of affairs, and demonstrates as to what methods many of the buyers
will adopt, in order to enrich themselves at the manufacturers' expense. But while they
can find employers willing to crush labour, and prevent them from adopting the National
Agreement, there will always be a number of buyers of atavistic minds, ever ready to
exploit any conditions without any consideration for fair dealing, and with no considera-
tion for the operative; and less for the consumer, who never receives any benefit whatever
prices the shoes are produced at. This position is at present receiving the consideration
of the local Board of Arbitration, and so far as we are concerned we are determined to deal
with these firms. The whole of the operatives have been met working at a number of the
firms, and we are gradually building up a position, which though slow will eventually
lead to a gradual levelling up of conditions in this industry.

W. R. SMITH.
Bozeat Operatives and the Minimum. Action Decided at Mass Meeting.
Manufacturers Complain of Unfair Competition.
Trouble that has been threatening for some time has arisen at Bozeat, relative to the
wages paid by the Bozeat boot and shoe manufacturers to their employees. We are
informed that the rate of wages paid in Bozeat is five per cent. less than the minimum,
and this state of affairs has brought complaints from Leicestershire, and, in the immediate
district, Raunds, Wollaston, and Irthlingborough.
Mass Meeting Called.
The National Union of Boot Operatives took steps in the matter, and arranged a
mass meeting at the Council Schools, Bozeat, on Wednesday evening, presided over by
Councillor C. Bates, J.P., of Rushden (branch president). The speakers were Mr. T. F.
Richards (general president), Mr. W. A. Wyman (secretary of the Wellingborough branch),
and Mr. W. Langley, J.P. (secretary of the Rushden and Higham Ferrers branch).
Minimum Not Paid.
In the course of the meeting it was explained that complaints had been received
from workers and manufacturers from many parts of the country, as Bozeat was the only
district in the country where the minimum rate was not paid.
Mr. Bates gave a resume of the history of trade unionism in Bozeat, and stated that,
as the whole of the employees were federated, they would be bound to pay what the work-
men demanded.
First Trouble for Thirty Years.
Mr. Richards stated that the employers were aware of the demands, and it was so
unanimous that they would have to comply with it. This was the largest meeting of
operatives ever held in Bozeat, and, he added, it was the first instance of national trouble
for 30 years. Discussions had taken place between the speaker and Mr. A. E. Marlow
(the late president of the Manufacturers' Federation) as to why Bozeat was permitted
to pay is. less prior to the war. He was also informed that a Northampton manufacturer
had raised the question at National Federation meetings, and there the officials had pre-
mised to deal with the matter.
Other Manufacturers Anxious.
A manufacturer a few miles from Leicester had made the demand that he, too, should
pay the same rate of wages as the Bozeat manufacturers. They were, he said, his com-
petitors. The Wollaston manufacturers had requested the speaker to bring pressure on
the Bozeat manufacturers, and the secretary of the Employers' Federation had also asked
him when the Union were going to bring Bozeat manufacturers to pay the minimum
rate of wages. He had replied, "As soon as the time is opportune." The present, he
thought, was an opportune time.
Peaceful Means before Striking.
In the course of his address, Mr. Richards dealt with the methods to be used in the
situation. Arbitration was preferable to striking; peaceful means should be used before
anything drastic was resorted to.
Peaceful Persuasion.
Mr. Langley, the branch secretary, briefly referred to the fact that they had in Bozeat
about 300 members. Six members had joined the previous week, and 20 had joined the
---

---
Wellingborough Branch. There remained, however, about 20 people w
members, and in this matter he advised the members to use peaceful persua
to join. At any rate, strict measures should be taken with non-membe...
outside the Union after 31st January.
A resolution, carried unanimously, was to the effect that the demand for
in wages should be made to the manufacturers at once by the General So
E. L. Poulton.---The Evening Telegraph, 23rd January, 1925.

UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACTS, 1920-24.
Decision Given by the Umpire.
CASE NO. 8561, SECTION 8 (2).-EMPLOYMENT LEFT VOLUNTARILY-SHORT-TIME WORKER
GAVE UP SPARE-TIME OCCUPATION IN ORDER TO QUALIFY FOR BENEFIT ON DAYS
OF UNEMPLOYMENT-NOT JUST CAUSE.
The applicant, a spinner, was employed on Wednesday, Thursday and Friday in each
week under a system of short-time working. On Saturdays he was employed during the
evening as a pianist at a local hotel, and for this additional employment he received ten
shillings. He had carried on the spare-time employment as a pianist for 25 years, but
on the 8th March, 1924, he gave up this employment in order to become eligible for unem-
ployment benefit on the three days in each week, viz., Saturday, Monday and Tuesday,
on which he was not employed in his usual trade as a cotton spinner. Under the regulations
governing the payment of benefit the applicant was not entitled to benefit in respect of
Monday and Tuesday in each week, as he was "not unemployed" on Saturday.
He gave as his reason for leaving the spare-time employment that he would have
received more by way of unemployment benefit for the three days in question than he did
by playing the piano, and that he wanted to qualify for benefit which would be set off
against an overpayment of benefit recorded against him at the Employment Exchange.
Recommended by the Court of Referees that the claim for benefit should be allowed
on the ground that the applicant was justified in leaving his spare-time employment,
but the Insurance Officer declined to accept the recommendation of the Court of Referees
and referred the matter to the Umpire.
Decision.-" On the facts before me my decision is that the claim for benefit should
be disallowed.
"The applicant had two employments. Three days a week he was employed in his
usual occupation of a cotton spinner, and on Saturdays he had a spare-time employment
which he had followed for 25 years, in respect of which he received 10s. a day.
The Insurance Officer claims that he voluntarily left this spare-time employment
without just cause and therefore is disqualified for benefit for 6 weeks. His only reason
for leaving it was that, so long as he followed it, he was employed on four days in each week
and therefore was not entitled to benefit in respect of the two days on which he was un-
employed.
"It sometimes happens, no doubt, that a person would be better off when unemployed
and in receipt of benefit than he is whilst employed, but in my opinion this is not in itself
just cause for leaving employment, and in several cases it has been so held (see Cases
Nos. 637, 1257, 1770).
"The Court of Referees appear to have been of the opinion that there should be no
disqualification on the ground that Section 8 (2) of the Act of 1920 has no application to
spare-time employment. I am not prepared to say that that Section is applicable to all
kinds of occupations the following of which would disqualify for benefit under Section 7
(2) (a), but I see no reason for thinking that the spare-time employment followed by this
applicant was not 'employment' within the meaning of that expression as used in Section
8 (2)." The Ministry of Labour Gazette, January, 1925.

HOUSING.
MR. E. L. POULTON, J.P. (Boot and Shoe Operatives): I beg to move :-
This Congress instructs the General Council to make urgent representations
immediately to His Majesty's Government to adopt still further measures providing
for the erection of houses for the working classes.
The Congress would notice, said Mr. Poulton, that the terms of the resolution were
general terms. That had been deliberately done. They wanted to support to the utter-
most the present Government in the work they had undertaken in getting houses for the
people. They certainly had an interesting discussion, which should make them ashamed
of what had been happening in many instances up and down the country in consequence
of the shortage of houses. This was not merely a question of dwellings. It was also a
great moral question. It was also a great health question. But he had not time to go into
the matter in consequence of the time limit imposed on the debate. He would, however,
call attention to the fact that at the Housing Conference on the previous Saturday, at which
were present representatives from all parts of the country, delegate after delegate got up
and implored them to do something to accelerate the pace at which houses were being
provided for the people. Moreover, there was one other point, and this, he was bound to
add, he considered most important. He referred to the overcrowding which was taking
place. By that alone they were unwittingly themselves at present reducing the standard
of life amongst the people. It was alarming how in a short while they willingly agreed to
that reduced standard because there was nothing else to take its place. "I trust, there-
fore," said Mr. Poulton, "we shall not only carry the resolution, but support the Labour
Government and our party to the utmost of our power in insisting upon, in the shortest
possible time, an adequate supply of houses for the people."
MR. W. PITTS (Boot and Shoe Operatives) seconded the resolution. He had, he said,
very great sympathy with the workers in other parts of the world. He could tell them
that in Northampton there were at least a thousand people waiting to get decent dwelling
houses. Mr. Pitts invited Congress to endeavour to force the pace with a view to helping
unemployment. Mr. Poulton had pointed out the serious effect upon health and morals
in the case where grown-up families were congested in two rooms, and he trembled to think
of what the conditions would be in another twenty years unless there was great improve-
ment. In the course of further observations Mr. Pitts was understood to refer to the
desirability of getting more labour into the building industry for the purpose of putting
up houses, and that the payment might be made on a piecework basis, a suggestion that
provoked some dissent.
The resolution was carried. Extract from Trades Union Congress Report, 1924.

Steady progress has been made in 1924 by the International Labour Orga
of the League of Nations in its various fields of activity. The following brief
surveys the more important events connected with its work during the year.
The Annual Conference.

at the sixth annual Session of the International Labour Conference, which ou
Geneva on 16th June. Complete delegations--two representatives of the
and one each of the employers and workers-attended from 29 countries,
Rumania, Cuba, and Argentina.
The Conference adopted a Recommendation dealing with the provision of
for the use of workers' spare time. There were also adopted provisionally, for final
at the seventh Session next May, three Draft Conventions and one Recommen
One Draft Convention and the Recommendation dealt with the equality of treain
national and foreign workers as regards accident compensation, while the ch
Draft Conventions dealt respectively with the weekly suspension of work in glas
facturing processes where tank furnaces are used and the prohibition of night
bakeries.
A resolution was also adopted approving the placing on the agenda of a future S
a Draft Convention and a Recommendation dealing with compulsory disinfecti
horse hair and the like against anthrax.

to give effect to its decisions and 83 others have been proposed.

Improved Persian Conditions.
Information received this year by the British Foreign Office shows that wide sweeping
reforms have been made in the conditions under which children work in the carpet weaving
factories in the province of Kerman in Persia as a result of a friendly communication
made to the Persian Government by the International Labour Office after hearing the facts
of the unsatisfactory conditions which had hitherto prevailed.

The 1925 Budget.
The Fifth Assembly of the League unanimously adopted 7,087,595 Swiss francs
(about $280,000 at par as the figure of the budget for the International Labour Organisa-
tion in 1925.

Industrial Health.
The Advisory Committee on Industrial Hygiene, composed of exports from a large
number of countries, held its second meeting at Geneva in July and formulated suggestions
regarding the disinfection of hair, horns and hoofs, and measures for the protection of
workers in certain occupations against anthrax; the assimilation of certain industrial
diseases to industrial accidents for the purposes of compensation; the functions of medical
men in factory inspection; and the lines to be followed in the periodical medical examina-
tion of workers in unhealthy occupations.

Insurance Funds in Ceded Territories.
In accordance with the provisions of the Treaty of Versailles, a commission was set
up by the International Labour Office to consider the terms of transfer of social insurance
funds in the districts of Upper Silesia ceded by Germany to Poland and held three meetings.
It consisted of five members-one from each of the parties and three experts appointed
by the Governing Body of the Office from countries having no interest in the transfer.
Among its recommendations it fixed at 26 million gold marks, payable in six annual
instalments, the lump sum which Germany is to transfer to Poland for the various classes
of insurance.

Deck Cargoes.
The Deck Cargoes Sub-Committee of the Joint Maritime Commission of the Inter-
national Labour Office met in London in December and agreed unanimously on a reply
to the British Board of Trade's criticism of the proposed regulations relating to wood
deck-cargoes, drawn up by the International Shipping Conference. They reaffirmed
their view that the proposed new regulations would adequately safeguard ships and their
crews and constituted a distinct advance from the point of view of safety.

Life in Soviet Russia.
The International Labour Office has added greatly to the available information
regarding conditions in Russia by its publication during the year of "Industrial Life in
Soviet Russia, 1917-1923," the information in which is taken entirely from Soviet sources.
Soviet legislation and its effects, as far as they can be judged, are given on wages, social
insurance, collective agreements, the settlement of disputes, labour inspection, trade
unions and the regulation of the labour market. This is supplemented by various inter-
esting statistics.

The Housing Problem.
Another important publication has been "European Housing Problems since the
War," wherein is included information regarding the housing crisis and the efforts made
to remedy it in the various countries of Europe. The International Labour Office has
also published a volume showing the various experiments made in different countries
along the lines of paying special allowances to workers with families.

Facts of World Labour.
These publications and others, dealing with the world causes of unemployment and
the position regarding hours of work in different countries, are in addition to its regular
publications, Industrial and Labour Information (weekly) and the International Labour
Review (monthly), wherein are brought together the latest facts concerning world labour
movements, special attention being paid to such subjects as cost of living movements,
wholesale prices, and emigration and unemployment figures.

THE PRODUCTIVITY OF LABOUR IN SOVIET RUSSIA
The question of the productivity of labour has latterly become of supreme in
for Russian national economy and the Soviet Press is now devoting considerable
the discussion of this subject. If hitherto no remedial measures have been taken
authorities in this connection, and if little attention has been given to this prob
reason may be said to lie in the general economic depression of the Soviet Union.
During the period of Communism (1917-1920), the complete disorganisation of
mic life, the great fall in wages, the state of famine in the industrial centres and the
political outlook, alı contributed to diminish the productivity of labour which,
fell to 29 per cent. of the figure for 1913, and to 25 per cent. of that for 1916 (th
preceding the revolution).
As a result of a recent enquiry published in September, 1924, a Commission app
by the Soviet Supreme Economic Council, came to the conclusion that the prod
of labour in industry as a whole was only about 50 per cent of the average pre-war
The Soviet Press explains this situation by: (a) a low individual output of the worl
(b) the absence of discipline in the industrial undertakings; (c) the bad condition ci
machinery and other equipment of the undertakings.
As the necessary repairs cannot be executed at present by the State nationa
industry, because of financial difficulties, the whole attention of the competent authent
is directed towards an increase of the individual output of the worker.
THE CO-OPERATIVE MOVEMENT IN SOVIET RUSSIA.
A reduction in the number of co-operative organisations; a decrease in the num
of members; a considerable weakening of the finances of the co-operative movem
an abnormal development of the administrative system: such are, in the opinion cf!".
Prokopowitch, ex-President of the Central Committee of the Congress of Russian
operative Unions, Professor of the Russian Universities of Berlin and Prague, expre
in an article in the International Labour Review, the features of the present position of 1
co-operative movement in Soviet Russia.
The history of the Russian co-operative movement under the Soviet régime mar
divided into three periods. During the first of these from the end of 1917 to the t
ginning of 1919-the co-operative system continued to exist as an independent organis
tion. It was, nevertheless, hampered by the general policy of the Government, wh
changed the economic system of the country from top to bottom. During the sec
period the movement was deprived of its independence and became a State instituti
All the forms of co-operation are comprised within the communities of consumers
which are State organs for the food supply of the population. In the third period, beginni..
in the Spring of 1921, with the introduction of the new economic policy, co-opera
autonomy was gradually restored, although its economic revival proceeded but slowi
owing to the fact that the heritage of the previous policy weighed too heavily upon it.

TRADE UNIONISM IN CHINA.
Before western influence penetrated China, the great social questions which nowadays
distract the industrial countries of Europe and America were unknown. It was only
when large ports began to be opened to foreign trade that the modern economic system
was introduced into China. Then spinning mills, corn mills, steel works, match factories,
and railway workshops began to be built and the aspect of social life changed.
Concurrently with this change, a whole series of complicated problems unknown
before began to arise and to become urgent. Questions such as the cost of living, wage
rates, hours of work and hygienic conditions began to be discussed. Naturally, also, the
idea of the association of the workers and of trade unionism grew up, and strikes began to
take place, at first at long intervals, but later more and more frequent.
The trade unions found a form of organisation already to hand in the old corporations
and clubs. It may be noted that the tendency to associate is a very distinctive trait of
the Chinese character.
The first trade unions appeared on the southern coast. Thence the movement spread
to the interior along the great trunk lines.
China may, from the point of view of trade union organisation as it exists at present,
be divided into three zones-the North, the Yang-tze-kiang Valley, and the Kwang-tung
province.
At Shanghai 47 trade unions were created in 1922, and out of a total of about 120,000
Chinese workers engaged in industry in the district, about 80,00o are members of trade
unions.
But the greatest progress has been made in the South, in the province of Kwang-tung.
There are 200 trade unions at Hong-Kong, and 300 at Canton, and some of them are
very powerful.
At the present moment the trade union movement is tending to overstep the bounds
of districts and to constitute itself as a national organisation for the whole of China.
THE FORTY-EIGHT HOUR WEEK AND INDUSTRIAL EFFICIENCY.
The relation between the 48-hour week and maximum industrial efficiency is examined
in an article in the International Labour Review, by Dr. P. Sargant Florence, of the Depart-
ment of Economics in the University of Cambridge.
In the view of Dr. Florence, the results of a scientific study of the effects of changes
in the hours of work, or of introducing rest pauses into working hours, and of variations
in output during the working day, all tend to one conclusion. This conclusion is that on
the whole the 48-hour week is probably the optimum length of hours, giving for the majority
of industrial operations maximum output with minimum accidents, lost time and overhead
charges, and permitting an efficient distribution of working hours throughout the week
and day.
The inquiries on which this conclusion is based were made by the author in factories
both in the United States and in Great Britain. The author's own inquiries are compared
with others made by the Industrial Fatigue Research Board and other institutions.
FAMILY IN A CELLAR.
Hottentot Life in Lambeth.
"There is as much decency among the Hottentots as there is in some of the houses
in Lambeth," said Mr. Collins, a member of the Board, in protesting, at a meeting of
Lambeth Guardians yesterday, against the delay in the conversion of Prince's Road
Workhouse into flats, proposed some months ago.
The Clerk explained that the consent of the Ministry of Health had not yet been
received.
Mr. Collins declared that the housing conditions in Lambeth were deplorable. He
knew of the case of a man, his wife, and four children, living in a cellar beneath a rag-shop.
Children were not innocent, he said, from the moment they left the cradle; they
possessed an unhealthy knowledge.

CHANGES IN COST OF LIVING: STATISTICS FOR 1st JANUARY, 1925.
Summary: Average Increases since July, 1914.
All Items included .. .. .. .. .. 80 per cent.
Food only .. .. .. .. .. 78 "
FOOD.
At 1st January the average level of retail prices of food was slightly lower than at
1st December, owing to reductions in the prices of eggs and sugar. There was relatively
little change in the prices of the remaining articles of food included in the statistics, except
fish, which was dearer at 1st January than a month earlier.
As a net result of all the changes recorded, the average increase over the level of
July, 1914, in the retail prices (in Great Britain and Northern Ireland) of the articles of
food included in these statistics fell to about 78 per cent. at 1st January, as compared
with approximately 80 per cent. at 1st December.
-The Ministry of Labour Gazette, January, 1925.

MONTHLY REPORT.
23RD FEBRUARY, 1925.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
TRADE
is about the same as last month, the number of unemployed being almost the
sa ne number as in January. The figures issued by the Ministry of Labour

BOOT AND SHOE INDUSTRY.
Employment during January remained moderate, on the whole, and there was no
material change compared with the previous month. Short time was worked in most
centres.
The percentage of workpeople unemployed, as indicated by the unemployment books
lodged at Employment Exchanges, was 11.0 on 26th January, 1925, as compared with
11.8 on 22nd December, 1924, and 9.5 on 28th January, 1924.
Returns from firms employing nearly 37,000 operatives during the week ended 24th
January, 1925, showed that about 30 per cent. of these operatives worked short time in
that week, to the extent of about 12 hours each, on an average.
Employment continued slack in London. At Leicester short time working was
fairly general, and employment was moderate on the whole; but there was again a slight

HEAVY GRADE STATEMENT COMMITTEE.
The Committee which deals with the Heavy Grade Statement met on the
12th inst., in London, under the chairmanship of Mr. T. F. Richards, to review
the position in those districts where Heavy Work is manufactured. After a
very full discussion extending over three hours upon the general situation,
the following resolution was adopted :-
"THAT HAVING REVIEWED THE VARIOUS PROPOSED AMENDMENTS
TO THE GREEN BOOK STATEMENT, IT IS HEREBY AGREED THAT IN THE
OPINION OF THE COMMITTEE, THE TIME IS INOPPORTUNE TO REVISE ANY
PRICES, AND THE MEETING BE ADJOURNED UNTIL JANUARY, 1926."
SHODDY FOOTWEAR.
Our members will be fully aware of the fact that the General President
in his report from month to month has dealt with the question of Shoddy
Boots, the object being to keep alive the subject and bring about such
public opinion as will insist upon the refusal of "shoddy," more especially in
relation to children's footwear, having regard to the bad effect such shoes have
upon the health of the children. In this connection it is interesting to find
that the Leather World for the 5th inst., states as follows :-
"Mr. T. F. Richards again returns to the attack on shoddy shoes
in the January report of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives.
But will Mr. Richards tell us all how to set about it? As we have
repeatedly pointed out, the avarice of retailers is one of the main causes
of industrial unrest, but until we get a Napoleon with powers to shoot a
few pour encourager les autres, they will still ride in their motor-cars
whilst their patrons use shank's pony!"
B

94
Without resorting to the summary method of "shooting," we
if all parties connected with the Trade will deal with those matter
the standpoint of the health of the community and honest trading,
can speedily be brought about such an attitude of mind amongst the
public as will insist upon the abolition of what is known as "s
footwear.

HOUSE OF COMMONS REASSEMBLES.
Parliament has reassembled, and judging by the opening proceedings
matters are likely to be lively, as the Labour Party is determined althoug
a big minority-to constantly keep in the forefront the position of the pat
of Great Britain, whether it refers to food, general conditions, housing
unemployment. We trust the members will not feel weary at our cons
repetition regarding these important questions. We know, however,
experience, that in order to bring about reforms we must be constant
reiterating our demands, and evidence is ever accumulating as to the ba
effect upon the general health of the people, and also upon the social relati
of many through the shortage of so many hundreds of thousands of housest
Expressions of sympathy-whilst quite good in their place will not of them
selves bring about improvement. We trust the members will not only watch
the proceedings in Parliament and their own Members' actions and votes
but will do all they can in their districts to so rouse public opinion
determine the present Government to do something to relieve the situation
In this connection we would call especial attention to the
ROYAL COMMISSION
as wil
which is now sitting in connection with Food Prices. If it was not for the
tragic side, it would indeed almost amount to comedy to hear the statement
witnesses have made representing, as they do, the Milling and Meat industries


---
Here is the extracted text from the image:
95
because despite the high prices the public have to pay for flour, bread and
meat, it would seem that these great businesses are really making no profit
whatever; in fact, judging from their statements it would appear that the
reason they are in business is because they are philanthropists. No one is
making profit; prices are high; where then is the money going to? There
can only be one conclusion if these great business houses are being run prac-
tically without profit whilst the public have to pay excessive prices for the
necessities of life, i.e., there ought to be a drastic alteration in the methods

to the witnesses, to find out where the money goes, and who has the profit,
or who has the difference between the first business transaction and the food
being bought by the public, only to find the answers to such to be merely a
repetition as stated above, that it is done for the "love of the country." The
proceedings of such Commission ought to act as an additional spur to all those
who desire to ease the tremendous burdens which the bulk of the people are
carrying.

DEATH OF MR. FRED H. SEGON.
We regret to report that MR. F. H. SEGON, President of the Norwich
No. 2 Branch, died on the 14th inst., with lamentable suddenness. For
some years he had suffered indifferent health, and eventually decided
to have an operation. Although the operation appeared to have been
successful, he died a few days later.
Although reserved and reticent in manner, Mr. Segon has spent his
life in the labour movement, helping to secure improved conditions for
the workers. He has acted as full-time President of the Norwich No. 2
Branch nearly five years.
To his Widow and Son we tender our sympathies, and trust that the
work done by Mr. F. H. Segon and the esteem shown will enable them to
bear up under the loss they have sustained.

"THE NEW CITIZEN."
The General Council of the Trades Union Congress, and the Executive
Committee of the Labour Party, have had under consideration the question
of extending the present weekly Labour News Service into a weekly newspaper
to be known as The New Citizen, believing that the movement as a whole
would benefit by such a paper being circulated.
The proposals for such a newspaper, however, cannot go forward unless
there is a possibility of the same paying its way. The size of the paper will be
about the same as the Labour Leader, and will consist of eight pages of four
columns each.
The Committee desire to launch this paper as soon as possible. It is
asked, therefore, that branches consider the matter at once and send their
orders to
The Secretary,

GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT
FELLOW MEMBERS,
THE INDUSTRY. - It is indeed refreshing to find that the President of the ployers' Federation has been speaking out with no uncertain voice as to the Industry, and among other things says in regard to output, that in 1907 the week consisted of 54 hours (this was not so in Co-operatives, they only worked 1901). In 1913, 52½ hours. In 1923, he says, they collected statistics from operatives out of a total number of firms in the industry, between 950 and 1,050 employing approximately 120,000 which means that 420 non-federated firms employ about 40,000 operatives.
In 1907 the output of Boots, Shoes, Slippers, Rubber and Canvas, was pairs, or nearly 98 million pairs, and the number of persons employed 131,301. average number of pairs per annum of 746 pairs each. In 1923 the approximate was 100,000,000 or (one hundred million) pairs, and the total number of employees
The working week had been reduced to 48 hours, with a mean rate of amounting to 9.4 per cent., and yet the output per employee was 833 pairs. One to machinery, and better organisation. The present capacity of the personnel employ advanced in 1923 to about 90 per cent. Materials accounted for from 50 per cent 60 per cent., labour from 18½ per cent. to 30 per cent. of the total costs, and that lai costs were at least 100 per cent. higher in 1923 than in 1913, and in 1919 working o were reduced by 8 per cent. The percentages, he says, of the total cost for other char including manufacturers' charges, travelling expenses, discount and profit, accounted said also that so far as the Home trade was concerned the industry was quite able to hole 18 per cent. to 21 per cent. of the total cost, and showed little change with pre-war competition. He then deals with the Home and Overseas trade, and points out the benes of the Magna Charta of the Industry, viz., our National Agreement, and its stead its own in best and ordinary grades of Men's and Women's Footwear against Overse out the things needed to improve, in his judgment, the industry, the first five points bein effect, and also instances the agreement for better organisation by both sides and poirs. and No. 7 asks for the protection of the public against the unwitting purchase of shoddy requests to the Government; No. 6 asks for the passing of the Industrial Councils P footwear, i.e., footwear in which leather substitutes have been introduced into the com ponent parts. Both the Federation and the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operati are unanimously agreed on the importance of this. Australia, New Zealand, and Swede have footwear regulations Acts which have for their object the checking of importatio of boots and shoes of inferior quality. He then deals with the Bankruptcy Acts, and asks for amendments, and everything considered is for our trade a very important stat
ment.

Concerning the above, my own view is that we can rely upon Mr. Bostock and Miss Tomlinson doing their best to give the industry the most reliable information they can and we thank them for the trouble taken. A few things stand out clearly we hav and only about 85,000 organised. We want that other 35,000. We have the good wishes, 11,000 less people in the industry than we had in 1907. We have 120,000 in our industry, help and advice of the Federation towards eliminating the studied deception practise faithful public, and in the tightening of the Bankruptcy and other laws which, while by some in the industry to play the "Spider and the Fly" on an innocent and often they will always fail to make dishonest men honest, will at least give the exploiter as much trouble as possible.

TRADE BOARD.-We have again spent two days on this work which is certainly not making the genuine headway we expected, owing to the convenient way in which the Department is administering the Act. If they persist in their present attitude, then ne Government Contractor will be troubled by the Administration, nor will any Fair Wage Clause be of any use. To my mind this is due absolutely to the Tory idea of their old plan of crippling the Trade Union as the Ministry have also refused to interfere with the breakaway from the 48-hour week owing to the appointed members on the Governing Board giving their vote against this very measure of reform. It is the intention of some of the Unions affected by this to withdraw from the Board thereby crippling the workers activities.

Most notable were the young men and young women assembled which augurs well for the two Branches, whose officers are indeed very alert as to the organisation of the Branch and its Sections, although they even have their

BRANCH REPORTS.
ARBROATH.—Trade is very bad in our district still, and our main
thoughts centre round questions of unemployment. We have been interested
for some time too by the obvious anxiety of Council in maintaining the agree
ment inviolate. We gather that attempts are being made to break in upon
the National Terms, and the Council are fully warranted in protesting against
any weakness amongst the members on such issues. In our own district
we are being introduced to a subtle attempt to undermine existing conditions
in the factories. It has often been pointed out in our reports that a certain
amount of piecework prevails here, and that is the point at which the clouds
are gathering. It was found impracticable with us to put some departments
on piecework, and since its inception it has only operated in the Clicking and
Finishing Rooms. During the long depression the pieceworkers in those
departments have been better off than their fellows in regards to pay; although
of course they had to work jolly hard to be so. For some time back this fact
has worried the management in one of our factories, but instead of taking the
matter up with the Branch in the only competent way, we learn of unfair
pressure being applied to the individuals in order to secure revision of price-
rates. When we think back and recall the unscrupulous eagerness on the part
of employers in 1919 to force the workers up here to go in for piecework, we
are somewhat staggered to know of as determined an attempt to force them
out of it. The only and somewhat obvious reason is to get unlimited output
without paying for it, and to be in the position of badgering the worker in-
cessantly. Without a doubt piecework keeps the whips off, while set wages
allow of constant nagging about amount of work done. Even the rather subtle
excuse that it is being done to save the industry up here is too thin to find
believers, and one wonders why economies should always start at the wrong
end. When you witness a numerous and expensive staff maintained from
month to month and year by year without pecuniary loss, and then find economy
only affect workers who have two and three days' work per week, it makes
for serious trouble. Drones are not worth favour, and it is a pity they get the
honey. Workers keep the hive going and alone deserve preference. Alleged
directive ability is often a mere pretence, and an ounce of real productive skill
is of more commercial value even to-day. When employers learn this elementary
truth they will be in a much better position to compete in the open market.
Don't economise unnecessarily on the bottom dog, but try a little judicious
cutting at the top for a change, and a truer sense of value will be reached.
In good times a little display on ornaments may be excusable, but in testing
times they should be dropped. The skilled producer is the salt of the earth,
and alone can make the harvest worthy of garnering.
[The fact of a firm working either Daywork or Piecework from the point
of view of wages—if our agreements are carried out—is not detrimental to the
workers, it being distinctly understood that Dayworkers must measure the
amount of work they do for the wage they receive by the Piecework Statement.
Any deviation from the same should be reported to the local officers to enable
them to deal with the matter.-E. L. POULTON, General Secretary.]

month. Trade has improved slightly, but not to the extent of engaging fresh
hands yet. We are sorry to report the death of two of our old members,
Messrs. G. Wilkins and A. Vincent. To their relatives we extend our sympathy.
Mr. G. Wilkins was a very quiet unassuming member, but nevertheless a very
sound trade unionist. Mr. A. Vincent in the old days before the National

LIVERPOOL. The month of January is when the shopkeepers make
the "big push" to clear off their surplus stocks at slaughtering prices, real
and imaginary. Consequently, boot repairers get a lean time at this par-
ticular season of the year. We note with regret that there is a movement on
foot to undermine the Trade Union Movement, not from the capitalist but
from the ranks of the workers. Rule by minority is their slogan, yet at the
same time they ask all minorities to combine and make one strong fighting
force. This would appear rather comical if it was not fraught with such
serious consequences. Moral :- "Beware of the wolf in sheep's clothing."

SOUTH LONDON.-It is the desire of the Executive of the Branch that
members should attend the meetings and try and do their best as shop-
mates to get their fellow shopmates to join up, for it is the everyday case of
the members getting in touch with those that the officials are not able to get
in touch with.

MANSFIELD.-Trade here is very quiet in light work, good in strong
work. We have had Mr. T. F. Richards down several times during the last
month. Pleased to say we have now got 102 new members from the Stiffening
factory, who are working far below the minimum rate of wages.

MAYBOLE.-Trade is in a deplorable state, between 30 and 40 members
signing for Out-of-Work Benefit, and this will be increased by over 100
shortly through the firm of Messrs. John Lees & Co. giving every employee a
week's notice. This firm has only been working three days a week. This will
be another drain on the Union funds, but will go to show the members what
boon the Union is in times of need.

WHAT TARIFFS DO?
21,126 Fines in Irish Smuggling Case.
Fines totalling £1,126, or in default 15 months' imprisonment, were imposed last week
at Swanlinbar (Co. Cavan) District Court on Felix M'Govern, a boot merchant, for Customs
offences. One of the charges related to illegal possession of four boxes of boots-18
women's pairs and 164 men's pairs-when his house was raided by Customs officials in
November last. Superintendent Murphy, Longford, described the discovery of the goods
in an outhouse.
The Superintendent said the boxes seemed to have been scarcely opened, and Mr..
M'Govern produced invoices for the boots for April, 1923. When, however, the boxes
were unpacked, copies of a newspaper dated September, 1924. were discovered.
Mr. Keenan, solicitor for the defence, pleaded guilty, and a fine of £213 3s. was inflicted,
or in default six months' imprisonment. The justice also ordered the boots to be forfeited
as well as froo to release his lorry. There were other charges of smuggling, and the total
fines came to £1,126.
The defendant accepted the alternative, 15 months' imprisonment, without hard
labour.- Shoe and Leather News, 29th January, 1925.

NORTHAMPTONSHIRE JOINT DISTRICT COUNCIL.
SECRETARY'S REPORT AND BALANCE SHEET, 1924.
Trade Unionism is the star around which revolve the universe of Utopian indu
It flickers or radiates according to the intere st displayed by it member
tralism.
brightness can be the guiding light toward, social and industrial happiness; it dimme
but reflects the fitckering of expiring hope.
Conscious of its warmth, of the true beauty and purpose of the pulsating life within, if
Leings nearer the day when joy will replace despair; when life, full and free, will knoss
not the slavedom of modern industrialism.
'Tis a lone star, hanging pensively in the heavens; we can reach out and embrace it
it only the workers will.
The record of the work of the above Council for the past year clearly indicates the
usefulness and happy influence which the Council is wielding. Since its inauguration
the Council has, under many difficulties, laboured to be of real service to the Union, and
1024 marks a distinct advance in this direction. Not only has the Council done much
in bringing to the fore the real problems and conditions of employment in the industry.
it has also won the approbation of more than one National Official who previously viewed
with suspicion the objects underlying the formation of the Council. This is exceedingly
Let me here repeat, for the benefit of
satisfactory, as obviously the full value of our efforts cannot be appraised so long as
suspicion from any source is directed towards us.
whom it may concern, what has been stated at our meetings on many occasions, the
Council exists, not for the purpose of exercising power rightly placed in the hands of the
National Executive, but for the purpose of drawing together the members of the Branches
within our area of jointly discussing the problems with which we are confronted-of
stimulating the desire for education, and of arousing a political and trade union con-
sciousness sufficiently strong to achieve the objects for which the Union exists.
The direct work of the Council may best be summarised under the following headings:
Meetings.
Four quarterly meetings have been held. These have taken place successively at
Rushden, Northampton, Kettering and Wellingborough. The first constituted the
Annual meeting of the Council, at which Mr. S. J. B. Barnes, who had so successfully
carried on the work of the Council since its formation, retired; his place being taken by
the signatory to this report. Discussion chiefly centred round the Secretary's report,
out of which an attempt was made to establish a quarterly industrial report from each
associated Branch. The principle here involved is admirable in its conception, having
as its basis a further interchange of local difficulties and problems. Before it can be
successfully applied, experience has proved that some form of standardisation will have
to be established. Restricted as has been the success of the motion it has been of con-
siderable advantage. The second and third meetings were devoted to a discussion on
"The problem of youths and their proper absorption by the trade."
The problem was first introduced by Mr. W. Townley, Northampton No. 1, who gave
a comprehensive survey of the internal growth of the industry, and the way in which,
of recent years, machine labour has denied craft and opportunity to a large section of the
operatives. The grave concern with which the problem is viewed, was well illustrated
by the long and reasoned discussion which followed, so much so, that it was decided to
reintroduce the subject at the subsequent meeting of the Council.
At this meeting the subject was sectionalised under the following headings :-
a. Relationship of Boys to Men. Introducer, Mr. W. Langley, Rushden.
b. Reduction of the age for the application of the full minimum wage. Mr. W.
Birt, Northampton.
c. Reduction of working hours. Mr. J. E. Chapman, Kettering.
d. Provision of special operations as stepping-off points, and Pensions at 60.
Mr. L. Poole, Wellingborough.
The application of each section to the problem was well thought out, and provoked
a further prolonged discussion.
It early became apparent that the Council could not lay down, within the confines of
the present organisation of the industry, any hard and fast proposal for the solution of
the problem. It was felt, however, that much could be done-provided the Employers'
Association could be persuaded to discuss the matter with the National Council of the
Union-to alleviate an increasingly serious evil. With this object in view the Secretary
was empowered to draw up a report based on the discussions which had taken place.
This was done, and at the following meeting the report was approved and authorised to be
forwarded to the National Officers and Members of the National Executive Council.
Whether or no the report was discussed by the National Council, or any consideration

Conferences.
Two Conferences have been held. One at Irthlingborough on 9th February, and the

ferences were well attended, delegates being present from a large number of associated
organisations. This feature of our work cannot be too highly commended. The Con
ferences set in motion a large cycle of wheels within wheels, and the subsequent discussions
and reports must be of considerable value in the creation of conscious and thoughtful
public opinion.
Special.
The Council adopted at its second meeting a proposal of the Executive, which had
behind it a new aspect of educational activity and influence, namely, that of visiting
works in connection with industries allied and contributory to our own. The British
United Shoe Machinery Company, of Leicester, was suggested as the most attractive
works for initiating the proposal, and, by the goodwill and courtesy of the Manager, Mr.
A. C. Benson, the visit took place on 18th September, 192.4. It is not for me to enlarge
on the success of the visit, except in so far as to say that educationally every delegate
of the to who attended, received impressions and enjoyed experiences which will be per
manently valuable to him. The Officials of the Leicester Nos. 1, 2, and 3 Branches also
attended and assisted in making the visit successful.

Political.
No direct political work has been undertaken during the year, largely because of the
importance of the other activities of the Council. Branches, however, have not been idle
and considerable influence has been wielded amongst the members. In view of the con
siderable losses to Labour in the County, referred to later, it is obvious that much pro
paganda must be undertaken, and no doubt the Council will give thought to the matter
at an early meeting.
Finances.
Owing to the necessity for a recent call for affiliation fees, the finances of the Council
are very satisfactory, and will probably prove sufficient to meet the expenses of the ensuing
year, without further contribution from branches. The sum of £23 4s. rod. is being
carried forward for 1925.
Recognition.
At the conclusion of our second meeting, and in conjunction with the Union side of
the County District Board of Arbitration, a presentation was made to Mr. S. J. B. Barnes,
for his services to the Union in the capacity of Secretary to the Union's side of the Board,
and as Secretary to this Council. The presentation, which consisted of an inscribed Gold
Watch and Chain, was made by Mr. T. F. Richards, who, in a few well-chosen words voiced
the unanimous feeling in respect to our late Secretary's services. Mrs. T. F. Richards
also honoured the Council by attending, and, on behalf of the Council, presented a Gold
Wristlet Watch to Mrs. Barnes. We can only repeat the expression of Mrs. Richards
as a permanent record of our appreciation, "That they may both live long and continue
to enjoy the respect of their fellows and that happiness which comes from well-doing."
Thanks.
I should like to place on record our appreciation of the services rendered to the Council
by Mr. E. Law, as President, and to Mr. T. F. Richards for his help and attendance at our
meetings during 1924.
This concludes my report on the direct work of the Council during 1924. May I now,
very briefly, comment on one or two factors of general interest, which have some signifi
cance and indirect connection with the Council.
Membership.
Perusal of the figures relating to membership of the branches represented on the
Council, indicates a remarkable growth of membership during 1924. No less than 1,486,
net increase in membership is reported. The figures must be approached from the stand
point that we were previously strongly organised, and the result therefore indicates that
a very considerable effort has been made to attain maximum membership. It would
serve no useful purpose to individualise in this respect, but it is quite safe to assume that
all branches have very nearly, if not quite, reached this desirable end. Unless, therefore,
trade and employment considerably increase, the present year is not likely to witness a
corresponding increase. It must be some little satisfaction to the National Council,
and a very clear exemplification of the policy of the Union, that the membership relative
to the numbers employed, stands so high. It must also be a source of satisfaction to
ourselves that out of a total Union membership of 78,745, the Northamptonshire Branches
and this Council can claim 31,728, or approximately 40 per cent. of the total number.
Labour Representation.
Out of three seats held by Labour in Northants, only one has been retained. I need
not recount the reasons or the methods our opponents used to achieve this end, but it
does seem desirable to state that very considerable educational and political propaganda
is needed amongst trade unionists in particular. We must create a consciousness and a
conviction which is going to stand the tests of "bogeys" at Election times. However,
despite the unprecedented nature of the attack, it is pleasing to observe that the votes for
Labour candidates in four constituencies in Northants has increased by 2,710 in one year.
But for the " Red Herrings " the increase might have been thousands more.
It is not within my province to anticipate events likely to arise in consequence of the
accession to complete power of a Tory Government. There seems every reason to believe,
however, that ere long the scope of trade unionism will be subject to considerable debate
in the House of Commons. The Council will do well to watch forthcoming legislation,
and prepare itself to do battle in the interests and protection of the present legislation
in regards to Trade Unions.

Application of the New National Agreement.
The Council has on more than one occasion expressed its satisfaction with the application of the 1921 Terms of the National Agreement. The application of the matter has come more prominently to the fore the problem to which this Council has devoted more attention during the past year. The reduction of the application of the full agreement to youths from 23 to 22 years of age, exceedingly good in itself, has accentuated the problem. This is illustrated by the work of the ... whose youths engaged on minor operations. This is illustrated by the work of the ... with the terms in this respect. We courteously suggest to the National Official that inquiry should at once be made as to how the new terms are being complied with, and also of the difficulties which Branch Officials are experiencing in respect to the application of the terms.

General.
STATE OF TRADE - Employment during the year has not been generally good, and districts have maintained a uniform mediocre level, others have been good at times, but poorer during other periods. Altogether, however, 1924 seems to have been slightly better than the preceding year. The slump curve seems to be now set in an upward direction, but it is improbable that the inevitable boom will take place at all rapidly.

INDUSTRY. - There are many changes taking place in the industry which it is well to note and analyse. Two illustrations only need be used in this respect. The method of lasting Welted work by the aid of the Consol Lasting machine, is rapidly giving place to lasting by Bed machines. It is claimed for the latter that they are quicker, the operation is simpler and that better results are obtained. Opinions may differ in this respect, but what does seem certain, though maybe only temporary, is the elimination of the Consol machine in connection with Welted work. In the same department, Welted lasting, we are rapidly witnessing the elimination of pure hand work. Machines have been introduced to do this and that operation which were thought to be immune from any mechanical device. Man's ingenuity has, however, evolved a machine, less perfect surely than hand craft, but acceptable to the employer, who is ever and perhaps necessarily ready to mechanise the industry ad extremum.

Conclusions.
Although there are many other problems and matters of interest affecting the Union and the work of this Council, I trust I have said sufficient to quietly, yet truly, justify the oft repeated expression as to the justification of the Council. We have our limitations - no one is more conscious of them than ourselves- but within the compass of our opportunity we have done useful and necessary work. To bring co-ordination and trust, the past so laboriously laid must the future rest. This Council may well feel proud of the stones it has laid in the interests of the Union and of the boot and shoe industry.
31st January, 1925.
On behalf of the Executive Committee,
Yours fraternally,
GEO. CHESTER, Secretary.

NOTE.-It should always be borne in mind that Mr. J. Gribble, J.P., was the first Secretary to the Northamptonshire Joint District Council, and held office for 1915-1916.
T. F. RICHARDS, General President.

A MENACING POSITION.

"The Times," from articles upon "The Dominions and Foreign
Policy," February end, 1925.

War, because it threatens security, trade, and life, is and must always be the primary
concern both of Great Britain and the Dominions alike. Every nation will do almost
anything to avoid war. The unity of the Empire ultimately depends on whether it
six nations are satisfied that British policy is that best calculated to defend their security
and legitimate rights and to solve international problems as they arise, justly and without
war.

The Risk of War.

Under present conditions war, or the risk of war, whenever it appears above the
international horizon, subjects the unity of the Empire to a terrific strain. There is no
principle in Imperial affairs which has become more clearly established than that the
decision as to whether any nation in the Empire should go to war or not rests solely with
its own Parliament. If the Parliaments of the Empire are united in backing a policy
for dealing with a dangerous international situation, well and good. But if they are not,
what is to happen? Directly Great Britain or any Dominion becomes involved in a
conflict with any important Power, then the only way in which the other nations can
escape belligerency is by seceding from the Empire. There is no other way.

Yet war, or the risk of war, is much nearer to all of us than we generally realise. It
may arise, as it did in 1914, because of a condition of international tension between con-
flicting ideals and peoples which has become intolerable. Or it may arise because of the
mishandling of any one of the international problems which are continuously coming up
for settlement. It is well to remember sometimes that the end of our much vaunted modern
civilisation has been, since 1895, the greatest series of wars the world has seen—the Chino-
Japanese War, the Spanish-American War, the Boer War, the Russo-Japanese War,
the Turko-Italian War, the Balkan War, and the World War. And even since the Armistice
there have been some ugly incidents—over the Straits, about Corfu, in Egypt, in the
Ruhr, in the Amercian Senate's handling of the problem of Japanese immigration, in the
collapse of parliamentary government in China and the emergence of a triumphant mili-
tarism. Any of these incidents, badly handled, might have resulted in a local conflict;
and in the modern world any war, anywhere, immediately affects the trade and commerce
of all nations, and is liable, like a prairie fire, to spread far beyond its original zone.
War, indeed, is an ever-present possibility in international affairs. It is a risk
inseparable from national sovereignty. The risk of war can never be abolished so long
as the world is divided into separate sovereign States. Nothing short of the immensely
distant World State comprising all nations will end war. The League of Nations has
improved our procedure for dealing with international disputes. But it has done, and can
do, nothing to abolish war itself, for no League can discharge the functions of a State.
Moreover, fundamentally even the League of Nations itself is a covenant to go to war to
compel obedience to certain canons of international right.

It is essential that we should face these facts, for only so can we escape being beguiled
by the illusions of unthinking enthusiasts, and realise that the only sure preventive of war
is the wisdom, courage, and resolution with which the leading Powers, through the League
of Nations or otherwise, deal with threatening international situations as and when they
arise.

LEICESTER BOOT OPERATIVE AS LABOUR LEADER IN AUSTRALIA.

Mr. J. W. Billson, who was at one time closely identified with the Leicester No. I
Branch of the Union, died in Australia recently. He originally worked at the C.W.S.
Works, Knighton Fields, Leicester, and later had a leather and grindery business.

Thirty-eight years ago he emigrated to Australia, securing employment in a boot
factory at Melbourne, and to him with others, the Australian Boot and Shoe Union owes
its existence.

Later he became president of that Union, and thirty years ago stood for Parliament.
Seven years later he was returned as member for Fitzroy. From that time right up to his
death he retained the seat.

As Deputy-Leader of the Victorian Parliamentary Labour Party, he was recognised
as a leader, because of his power to win respect and confidence of his colleagues.

Mr. Billson leaves a widow and two daughters.

"AS SEEN BY OTHERS."

Multum in Parvo. The Jackson & Joseph Strike.
We are pleased to report the conclusion of the dispute between the National Union
of Shoe Operatives and Messrs. Jackson & Joseph, an East London firm of boot man-
ufacturers, which, in the ordinary way, would be printed without special comment.
It is never our practice to seek to inflame the wounds which invariably remain after
industrial hostilities of this nature.
In this instance, however, we propose to depart from our usual rule and offer
our congratulations to the Union on its victory.
In doing this we are in no way actuated by bad feeling toward Messrs. Jackson &
Joseph.
No doubt the firm was honestly convinced its policy was justified. We do not think
it was, and we rejoice accordingly in the failure of its attempt to beat the Union.
There was much more involved in this dispute than a casual observer would note,
and much more in the Union victory than would appear in the unobtrusive paragraph in
which the conclusion of the strike is announced.
The National Union, in fighting the firm, was carrying out an obligation it entered
into with the Manufacturers' Federation, which was to secure National conditions both in
Federated and Non-Federated firms.
Messrs. Jackson & Joseph are not a Federated firm, although at one time they were
members of the London Manufacturers' Association. They did not dispute the fact that
their workers, numbering nearly 400, were perfectly satisfied with their rate of pay, and
they were not conforming to the National Trade Terms, and adduced as justification that
could not obtain a better situation in any London factory, and that they were not in favour
of the Holiday Provision Scheme.
All this may have been perfectly true, and as we have already said, the firm wa
probably honestly convinced it was justified in ignoring the Union and evading the con-
ditions imposed upon the trade by the National Terms; but this admitted, does not alter
the fact that in some respects they were not complying with certain conditions which are
obligatory to all other shoe manufacturing concerns.
In questions of this kind it is not unusual to meet opposition, and frequently from
most unexpected quarters. There is a latent kick in some mentalities for anything which
savours of compulsion. It is the mentality of those who are "agin the law," irrespective
of whether the law is right or wrong.
So far as the boot trade is concerned a vast majority of employers and employees
have agreed to the National Terms. Those who are not working to them, or who are
trying to evade them, are, for the most part, negligible in number, and importance, but
their default cannot be condoned or permitted to continue. Hence the National Union,
after failing by patient negotiation to get Messrs. Jackson & Joseph to recognise the
conditions, had no alternative but to call its men out and picket the factory.
Additional to the pressure of the Union have been influences brought to bear upon the
firm's customers to withhold orders until such time as the National Agreement was recog-
nised.
The fight has been a long one (it began in June last) and has ended as always seemed
inevitable, for the Union could not call off a contest of this sort whilst it had a copper
left in its coffers. A victory for Jackson & Joseph would have been a bad body blow to
collective agreement and good government.
As is usual in disputes of this nature there have been personal encounters and some
ill-feeling has been rife. Now the fight is finished may we express the hope that in burying
the mythical hatchet that the accumulated rancour may also accompany it, never to be
exhumed, and finally, that the result may have such influence upon those who happen
to disagree with the National Terms and try to avoid working to them, as to cause them
to reflect upon the unwisdom of continued resistance. -Shoe and Leather News, 29th
January, 1925.
Trade union balance sheets do not, as a rule, afford very encouraging reading, but
there is food for reflection in the figures presented in the annual financial statement of the
National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives, to which we refer in our news columns.
They show, for instance, that the union funds now amount to the substantial sum of
£436,928, or over five guineas per head for each of the 78,745 members of the union. This
is a very creditable fact in itself. Such a record is an index of the health of an industry.
and a much happier state of things would be revealed if the funds of every union in the
land were in a similarly robust condition. We say this because the large balance to the
credit of the Boot and Shoe Operatives is obviously due to the circumstance that the
industry has not been distracted, nor the union's finances dissipated, by a national dispute

A BOOT TRADE CUSTOM.
Week's Notice Held to Apply to Shoe Stiffeners.
A case of interest to Leicester shoe stiffener manufacturers arose at the City Police
Court to-day, before Councillor J. Mantle Hubbard, and others, when the magistrates
held that the custom of the week's notice on either side, which applies in the boot and
shoe trade, should also, except where specifically stated otherwise, apply to the shoe stiffener
industry.
The question was raised when Walter Thompson, a pressman, 22 Berkley Street,
and William Bousher, a pressman, of 46 Larch Street, were summoned by Messrs. W.
and E. Butterworth, stiffeners manufacturers, of Vauxhall Street, for £2 and £I Ios.
respectively in lieu of notice.
Mr. Headley appeared for the plaintiff company and Mr. Rees Jones for the defendants.
It was stated that the two defendants left on a minute's notice one Tuesday midday,
not having worked the full week. They said that they had agreed, when taken on, to a
minute's notice on either side. No notice had been exhibited in the factory to countermand
this.
For the plaintiffs it was held that the custom which applied to the boot and shoe
trade generally also applied to the stiffening trade. A notice had been put up to the
effect that a week's notice was both given and required.
The Bench found for the plaintiffs, and awarded £1 3s. 4d. in the case of Thompson,
and 17s. 6d. in the case of Bousher.-Leicester Mail, 18th February, 1925.
UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACTS: REQUIREMENT AS TO CONTRIBUTIONS.
The Minister of Labour, on the 11th February, gave the following reply in the House
of Commons to a Member of Parliament who had asked whether he was enforcing the
requirement laid down in the Unemployment Insurance (No. 2) Act of last year that
applicants for unemployment benefit must have paid at least 30 contributions since the
beginning of the last insurance year but one:—
"Under the Unemployment Insurance (No. 2) Act, 1924, this requirement is to come
fully into force on 1st October next. Up to that date the Minister is given power to waive
the requirement in particular cases. At present the requirement is waived in the case
of applicants who, although they have not paid 30 contributions within the time prescribed,
which is from two to three or even four years, have paid 12 contributions since entry into
insurance, and also for others in whose favour the Local Employment Committee so
recommends. I have not thought it right to make any change in this rule up to now,
but I think the time has now arrived when some preliminary steps can properly be taken
in anticipation of the general application of the statutory requirement which comes into
full force on 1st October. I propose, therefore, that as from Thursday, 19th February,
the requirement shall only be waived if the applicant for benefit can show either that eight
contributions have been paid during the prescribed period or, alternatively, that a total
of 30 contributions have been paid at any time since entry into insurance. In the case
of disabled ex-service men not satisfying either of these conditions, the requirement will
be waived if it appears on the recommendation of the Local Employment Committee
that the failure to pay the requisite number of contributions is due to the man's disability."
The Ministry of Labour Gazette, February, 1925.

MANOR HOUSE LABOUR HOSPITAL.
At the Hull Trades Union Congress held in September, 1924, a resolution was passed
to the following effect:
"That this Conference calls upon the Trade Unions affiliated to this Congress
to bring before their respective branches the work that is being done for members
of Trade Unions by the Industrial Orthopædic Society at the Manor House Labour
Hospital, Golders Green. It is a Trade Union Hospital, and has treated 900 in-patients
and 3,600 out-patients during the two years, 1922 and 1923."
Consideration has been given to this resolution by the General Council, and they
decided to ask the affiliated Unions to use every available means for bringing the work
done at the Manor House Labour Hospital to the notice of their members.
The orthopædic treatment afforded at this Hospital is of a kind which victims of
industrial accidents find it extremely difficult to get at the ordinary institutions. The
Hospital possesses the latest and most improved electrical massage appliances, a large fully
competent massage staff, X-ray installation, &c. No charge is made for treatment beyond
their delegates to the Executive Committee. It will be possible to open a Women's
the entrance fee of Is. and a contribution of Id. per week; and the subscribers appoint
Section as soon as sufficient financial support is forthcoming.
Arrangements can be made with the Secretary to the Hospital for a speaker to attend
your branch meetings, or appointments can be made to visit the hospital.
We attach leaflets describing the work of the Hospital, and further particulars
n be had from the Secretary, Manor House Labour Hospital, Golders Green, London,
W. 11.
The General Council cordially invite the attention of affiliated unions for the purpose
of encouraging and supporting the Hospital.
THE TRADES UNION CONGRESS GENERAL COUNCIL,
32 Eccleston Square, London, S.W 1.
6th February, 1925.
Yours sincerely,
FRED BRAMLEY, Secretary.

SOME REFLECTIONS ON BEING IN OFFICE.
By MARGARET G. BONDFIELD.
Nineteen twenty-four the amazing year which saw the Labour Government in,
and out of, office- has provided a hard, but enriching experience for those who were called
to Ministerial positions. I shall always be glad that my experience was gained in the
Ministry of Labour. In no other Department of State is the work so closely allied with
that of the Trade Union Movement. Although largely partaking of the same nature,
the subjects are seen from such a new angle as to permanently widen the vision and under-
line the essential points in those problems which wait for solution.
The work of the Ministry is divided up into four main sections :---
(1) Unemployment Insurance;
(2) Conciliation Department, dealing with trade disputes;
(3) Trade Boards Department ;
(4) The Department which controls and co-ordinates the British section of the
work of the International Labour Office.
Labour Department.
The Ministry of Labour is one of the new Departments of State. In the past it has
been treated far too much like the Cinderella of the Department. The machinery has
been cramped, some of its sections have had to struggle along under the threat of extinction,
because Governments were in power which did not want it to exist, or if it existed did not
want it to function. I am confident it will have to be raised to the position of a first-class
Department, because its work is of vital consequence to the trade and industry of this
country. It is a Department which depends tremendously for its development and its
efficiency upon a progressive and intelligent understanding by its political chiefs of the
important part it plays in the task of good Government.
It is indicative of the rightness of changing ideas and of the growth of social respon-
sibility; its routine administration affects the lives of millions of our fellow-countrymen-
nothing sensational or catastrophic-but in other respects its work is
really revolutionary in the right sense of that much overworked word,
and it deserves the whole-hearted and intelligently critical support of
the Trade Union Movement.
-Extracts from General and Municipal Workers' Journal, January-February, 1925.
