CO-PARTNERSHIP BOOT RESULTS.

Kettering Union Boot.
The half-yearly meeting of the Union Co operative Boot and Shoe Productive Society,
Ltd., Kettering, was held on Thursday evening in the Kettering Co operative Hall, Mr. E
Barratt (president) being in the chair, supported by Mr. H. J. Potter (secretary and
manager).
The General Committee's report stated that the net sales for the half-year were £12,299.
The trading results for the half-year, after depreciating land, buildings, plant and machinery,
and making provision for interest on share and loan capital of £270, showed a loss on
trading account of £80.
Mr. Barratt, moving the adoption of the balance-sheet, said that he was sorry to see
a loss, but Mr. Potter and the committee were looking forward to brighter times, which
they hoped were ahead.-Kettering Telegraph, 30th January, 1925.

Higham Ferrers Boot.
Higham Ferrers Co-operative Boot and Shoe Productive Society had sales of £14,782
for the half-year ended December 31st last. After providing for interest on shares, loans
and depreciation to the amount of £312 and depreciating the fixed stock and building
by £122, there was a disposable balance of £71. For the whole of 1924 the sales were
£30,577. The society has £9,292 share capital, £3,093 as loan capital; its stock was
£8,380; the plant stands at £2,000 in the accounts and the land and buildings have been
written down to £700. Among the expenses for the last half-year were £5.977 for wages
and travelling, £858 for new plant, and £212 for repairs and renewals. The purchases of
materials totalled £7,763. After paying 5 per cent. on share and loan capital, the balance
is being added to the interest guarantee fund, which now stands at £1,114.

Crompton Boot.
This Desborough Society has had sales for the last part of 1924 amounting to £20,466,
an increase of nearly £4,000 over those for the corresponding period of 1923. The total
for the year is £42,212.
The surplus for the last half-year is £1,374, of which £298 goes to the shareholders.
Customers get £430 and the workers receive £316 as dividend on wages at Is. in the f.

Equity Boot Society.
The sales for the last half-year were £24,747, an increase of £900 over the same period
of 1923. The similar increase in the first half of the year was £2,000. The total profit
for the year was £2,999, of which the workers received £595 as a dividend on wages at 6d.
in the f. Customers received £850, while £127 was placed to the Provident Fund, and
£42 to the Education Fund.

Midland Boot.
The sales for the year are £28,730, and the surplus is £327. Interest was paid on
shares.

MR. A. V. ALEXANDER, M.P., ON "WHAT CO-OPERATION STANDS FOR."

Mr. A. V. Alexander, M.P. for Hillsborough (Sheffield), speaking on the policy of the
Co-operative Party, said that to hear some of their leaders even co-operation was nothing
more than a great commercial business. "We are that, but we must be something far
greater. We are first and foremost a challenge to, and secondly, a definite substitute for,
the existing system of society." The definite co-operative gospel had to be maintained,
and here he felt they could not lean all their weight on the fiscal purity of the Labour
Party in the matter of upholding free trade. "We as consumers claim the right of free
trade, first and foremost, not merely because there once were Cobdens and Brights, but
because we believe as a great consumers' organisation in the right to maintain free exchange
of the products of labour between the workers of every land. We have there a special
definite point of view as co-operators which has to be maintained." He also alluded to
the dangerous leanings of some people in the Labour Party towards a State monopoly
of the importation of food and other supplies. But more than all that, there was the
campaign against co-operators. He believed that within the next six months, co-operation
would have to face the greatest economic struggle in its history, a struggle that would be
fought not only in the counting-house and shop, but in the Government departments,
and at Westminster, against an attack engineered by the Federation of British Industries.
Lastly there was co-operative policy in international affairs. Here they had means at
their disposal, through the International Co-operative Alliance, to develop the influence
of co-operative principles in international affairs to an enormous extent.---Statement at
Co-operative Conference on the Political side of the Movement, Manchester, 31st January,
1925.

LITTLE SLAVES IN CHINA.
Pressure Needed to Enforce Them.
Attempt to Get Better Factory Conditions. New Regulations, but
The torible condidions existing in Chirotese factories were described in the " Daily Herald "
Cast Monday by Dame Adelaide Inderson, late principal Wontan Inspector of Factories in
Great Britain.
Mr. E. L. Poulton, General Secretary of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives,
in the following interview, describes attempts to get reform, but urges the need of public opinion
as a driving force to ensure success.
Mr. Poulton is British Labour representative on the Governing Body of the International
Labour Office.
"In my judgment," said Mr. Poulton, commenting on Dame Anderson's article,
"we may be doing more than improve the conditions of the Chinese workers when we deal
with that matter."
It was an advantage that there existed, in the International Labour Organisation of
the League of Nations, a focus for world opinion on this international question, and a
machine which, in time, could put things right; but if reform was to be assured there must
be an educated public opinion behind the effort.
Proposals for Reform.
Mr. Poulton recalled that at the I.L.O. first conference, held at Washington, in 1919,
special proposals with regard to China were put forward.
It was suggested that there should be a 10-hour day or 60-hour week for adult
workers, and an 8-hour day or 48-hour week for persons under 15; that there should
be a weekly rest-day; and that this legislation should cover all factories employing
over 100 workpeople.
The Chinese Government, however, in 1920 decided to do nothing, and there for the
time the matter rested.
After further pressure from the International Labour Office to supply information
for the annual conference, the Chinese Government in 1923 reported that a special depart-
ment had been set up to deal with labour, and communicated certain provisional factory
regulations.
Mr. Poulton indicated some of these regulations as follows :-
Start Work at Ten.
Employers (it is provided) shall not engage boys under 10 or girls under 12 years of age.
Young persons, i.e., boys under 17 and girls under 18 years of age, shall be employed
only on light work.
The hours of work of young persons shall not exceed eight hours a day, and those of
adults 10 hours a day exclusive of breaks.
Employers shall not employ young persons at night (between 8 p.m. and 4 a.m.).
Adult workers shall be ensured at least two days' rest a month.
The employer shall see that young persons and adults who have not yet completed
their education are provided with facilities for further education in his factories, and shall
bear the cost of such education.
The employer shall reduce or suspend the employment of sick or injured workers,
according to circumstances, and shall bear the expenses of medical treatment for injured
workers, and shall not reduce the wages of persons who fall sick or are injured in the
course of their employment.
A rest period of five weeks and a suitable allowance shall be granted to every woman
worker before and after childbirth.
Not Carried Out.
" These regulation. are important," said Mr. Poulton, "because (among other reasons)
they mean that the Chinese Government has accepted the principle of factory legislation,
and that it is sensible of the weight of public opinion in other countries.
" But regulations are of no use unless they are enforced. I myself raised this point
in the Governing Body of the I.L.O., and again at the conference last June.
" I said that we in England were constantly hearing reports, true or false, which did
not suggest that the provisions had been given any real force. Dame Adelaide Anderson's
report seems fully to confirm this.
"The International Labour Office is doing what it can, not only to collect full informa-
tion from the Chinese Government, but also to tell the public what the position of affairs is.
" But if we want the situation in China to be improved rapidly, we must make it clear
that the I.L.O. has the weight of public opinion behind it."---Daily Herald, 2nd Feb., 1925.

WORLD STUDY OF WORKERS' INSURANCE.
The Next International Labour Conference.
Preparatory work is well advanced for the Seventh Annual Session of the International
Labour Conference of the League of Nations.
One of the most important items on the agenda is the discussion of a general report
on social insurance which is being prepared by the International Labour Office and which
will contain, not only the existing law and practice throughout the world, but also some
indications of the general social insurance problems which arise at the present day. Such
discussion by representatives of Governments, employers and workers, should, it is felt,
› of the greatest value as an introduction to the work on social insurance to be subse
ently undertaken by the International Labour Organisation. It is possible that the
nference may place particular questions of social insurance on the agenda of a sub-
quent Session or adopt a resolution indicating the lines on which the subject should be
studied by the Office.
The Conference will also discuss the question of world rules for workers' compensation
with the view to the adoption of an international agreement.
A final vote has also to be taken on three Draft Conventions and one Recommendation
which were provisionally adopted by the Sixth Annual Session last June. The subjects
of these are :-
Equality of treatment for national and foreign workers as regards workers'
accident compensation (Draft Convention and Recommendation) ;
Night work in bakeries (Draft Convention) ;
Weekly suspension of work for twenty-four hours in glass-manufacturing processes
where tank furnaces are used (Draft Convention).

ALCOHOL AND ACCIDENTS.
Effects on the Workers' Safety.
It would be a conservative estimate to say that the industrial accident risk is about
three times as high among drinkers as among men in general, including ordinary alcohol
States an article by M. T. Vojonmaa in the February issue of the International
Labous Revrea, the monthly publication of the International Labour Office of the League
consumer
of Natio
Keterning to studies that have been made on the relation of alcohol to accidents,
"it is noteworthy that the particular accident risk of drinkers exceeds
M. Voronmaa says:
Moreover the excess of the drinkers' accident risk over the
the general accident risk, especially in the younger age group, z.c., among men between
15 and 34 years of age.
general risk is proportionately higher in the group of severe accidents than in that of
slighter ones. To judge from the figures chronic alcoholism imposes a heavy additional
charge upon industrial accident insurance."
After a detailed study of the information at present available, M. Voionmaa reaches
the following conclusions :-
(1) Chronic alcoholism, which can be diagnosed with a high degree of certainty.
appears to be a very potent cause of industrial accidents. Persons medically certified
as excessive drinkers have been found to be about three times more liable to accidents
and to injure themselves much more seriously than other persons, including ordinary
drinkers.
(2) Acute alcoholism or drunkenness does not at present appear to be an important
direct cause of industrial accidents owing to the reduction of industrial drinking (i.e.,
during working hours). The effect of drunkenness can be determined only in respect of
accidents outside working hours, and in this respect it has been found that drunkenness
is directly and solely responsible for a number of particularly severe accidents and possibly
contributes indirectly to about one-fourth of the accidents to workers in their spare time.
(3) Industrial drinking has been found to increase the accident risk; by merely con
trolling the sale of liquor in the factory or by stopping the supply of free beer, accident
rates have been decreased by 30 to 60 per cent. Managements and official inspectors
have thus been increasingly led to forbid workers to enter the factory when intoxicated,
and to prohibit drinking during working hours.
(4) Convivial drinking (i.e., during leisure hours) seems to be the most usual source
of the harmful effects of alcohol consumption. It is, however, extremely difficult to deter-
mine its precise influence on accident incidence. Taking first the effect of Sunday drinking,
a well-known practice, it can hardly be disentangled from other causes rendering Monday
work less efficient and more hazardous than other. A British experiment comparing
the accident rates on Mondays during the periods of free and restricted sale of alcoholic
liquors does, however, furnish proof in support of the theory that the use of alcohol is one
of the factors in the Monday accident risk. Secondly, the effect of regular evening drinking
has been shown in the particularly high accident rates in the first spell of the night shift,
a result only to be explained by the mental condition of the workers, which is certainly
influenced by the use of alcohol.
THE DREAMER.
For his dream they gave him neglect and scorn,
The man with the seeking eyes:
He talked of the things they could not see,
Of the things they said could never be, -
And they were accounted wise.
Neglected he starved, and dreaming died ;
And, "See what has come of his dreams," they cried.
The dreamer died, but the dream lived on
In the souls of a seeing few.
Then, more and more, men caught the gleam,
And the world grew glad in the brightening beam,
And the dream one day came true.
God gives the dream for the world's uplift,
And the dreamer too is His gracious gift.
-CUTHBERT ELLISON.

being men on whom we can rely; should, however, any errors creep into them, upon the

correction as to the original matter. As these Reports are exclusively for the use of Members,
the information contained therein must not be divulged.

MONTHLY REPORT.

23RD MARCH, 1925.

FELLOW MEMBERS,
TRADE
remains about the same as the previous month. There are still a very con-
siderable number of members on the unemployed fund, as well as many on
short time. The figures recorded in the Gazette issued by the Ministry of
Labour are as follows:-

BOOT AND SHOE INDUSTRY.
Employment during February was generally moderate, but slightly better than in
the previous month.
The percentage of workpeople unemployed, as indicated by the unemployment books
lodged at Employment Exchanges, was 9.5 on the 23rd February, 1925, as compared
with 11.0 on the 26th January, and 9.1 on the 25th February, 1924.
Returns from firms employing over 38,600 operatives during the week ended 21st
February, 1925, showed that about 27 per cent. of these operatives worked short time in
that week, to the extent of about II hours each, on an average.
Employment in London was moderate, and slightly better than in January. At
Leicester some improvement was shown, and employment on the whole was fair. It
was also fair, and showed an improvement, at Hinckley. At Northampton a large number
of firms was reported to be working less than full time; employment, however, was
generally fair. Depressed conditions again prevailed at Wellingborough, and the majority
of factories were working only three-quarter time; at Finedon and Raunds, on the other
hand, there was a slight improvement. There was also a slight improvement at Kettering
and a fair number of factories were running full time during the month. Employment
was fair at Higham and Rushden, and, as in January, full time was largely worked; and
at Irthlingborough there was even a little overtime.
At Leeds the heavy boot industry continued depressed, but slightly less short time
was worked during the latter part of the month: the light boot and shoe trade continued
good. Employment at Stafford was very slack, and showed a further slight decline,
the majority of operatives losing one or two days a week. At Norwich employment was
fairly good; in the machine-sewn section, in which employment was somewhat better than
in January, little short time was worked; in the turnshoe section, 25 per cent. of the
operatives were reported to be working only half time. At Bristol and Kingswood employ-
ment was still very quiet. At Street it was fair, and slightly improved. In the slipper
trade of the Rossendale Valley there was some improvement, and employment in general
was good.

NON-COMPLIANCE WITH CONDITIONS.
From time to time complaints are received, and National Officers have
brought to their notice, the fact that conditions nationally and the local
agreements based upon national agreements are not being fully complied
with. This also applies to conditions of employment under the Boot and
Shoe Repairing Trade Board, a report of which appears on page 184. We
would impress upon the members that it is their duty to report any devia-
tion at once to their local officers, rather than allow the matter to drift,
and have to be found out by the officials. It is much easier to deal with
the matter if reported at once, than to allow it to go along and have to be
dealt with after some days or weeks. The obligation upon the members to
do this is fully stated in Rules 156 and 157, and the procedure is equally
clearly laid down on pages 35 and 36 of the rule book. Compliance there-
with will not only assist officials generally, but will tend to help the efficient
working of the machinery set up to deal with any required adjustments
from time to time.
POLITICAL.
The political situation from the standpoint of the workers is very un-
satisfactory. Despite statements that may be made from time to time as to
the necessity for there being a good understanding between all sections of the
country, it is a lamentable fact that the volume of words as against the real
facts, stand out in glaring contrast. Take for instance the attempt that has
been made during the month to alter the whole position in regard to what
has become generally known as the
TRADE UNION LEVY
for political work. It should be made plain to our members that the one
shilling contribution per week for the full member, includes the small amount
for political purposes-3d. per full member per quarter; Id. for females and
half members, or less than 1d. per week per full member. We at once took
the matter up and sent out 194 letters to Members of Parliament where the
shoe industry is carried on, calling their attention to this matter. A copy of
the letter is appended :--

GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
TRADE UNION POLITICAL BILL.-The great Conservative Government has
become alarmed at being persuaded by their Die-Hards to harass the Trade Unions, and
to my mind, this is the first time that the great Conservative Party have funked at the
Trade Unions. As explained in my previous reports, they-and when I say they, mean
the Prime Minister and the majority of his Cabinet-have still recollections of 1905 and
the result. Mr. Baldwin has crucified his party once over Protection, and to do the same
with the Trade Unions of the country is more than he is prepared to be answerable for.
In this connection our Union approached all M.P.'s representing Shoemaking constituencies.
How many have replied is not at the moment at my disposal, suffice it to say that the
Conservative Member for South Leicester replied claiming his respect for Trade Unions,
but expecting more liberty for the individual, or words to that effect, reminding us of the
large number of exemptions-7,500 or thereabouts. As he, in his lack of knowledge
about Trade Unions had come to the conclusion that an exempted person was neither
conscripted, or was he a Conscientious Objector, to use terms this soldierly gentleman
might comprehend, therefore could not decline because no request for payment had been
made to them, and even the appeal of this gentleman's agent to supply forms and give
advice and perhaps create a real live revolution by appealing against the tyranny of the
Trade Unions who for all the Labour work that is done for our members should cost them
each less than one farthing per week, a sum so large that members express their disgust
with those who raise any real protest against so small a payment for a national, or local
service. Of this I am firmly convinced, that all our members irrespective of their political
traditions, fully believe that ninety per cent. of our political work is based on the sincere
desire to eliminate the problem of poverty from our midst, and also solve the Unemployed
problem, which can only be accomplished permanently by pooling the work, the services,
and the results for humanity's sake. Neither the Tranquility advocated at a previous
election or the new problem of Peace of the Prime Minister last week can solve the problem
of either the hungry man or the Unemployed. Let us hope that the Prime Minister will
soon pick another quarrel with the Trade Union movement, of which he is so fond. Rumour
has it that the Government are going to raid the Insurance Funds to provide Mothers
with Pensions. Don't ask the rich to provide them, ask the poor. Let us see, when this
becomes known, the kind of reception it will get if this is attempted. Some of us may
take the Prime Minister's statement that he is an honest man, at its face value.
TRADE BOARD.-This work has occupied two more days, and we do not feel that we
are making much headway since the present Government has come into office. In the
first place employers appear to have had some such advice, as the Legal Department
give to the Committee, which makes one think that the Inspectors, the imputed repre-
sentatives, are not by any means diverse in their views to the statement of the Minister of
Labour himself in hesitating to declare for the forty-eight hour week, ratified by the
Washington Convention, and who have up to the present been very loath to declare right
away for a reform likely to remain for many years to come. The Board would be of little
use to our Union if they complete the reactionary methods they appear to favour. Of one
thing we can, and would be sure of, that would be no responsibility for its work in future.
One would think that any Government would see at once that with 40 Trade Boards that
we have at least 40 trades immune from strikes, which in itself ought to get Mr. Baldwin's
support.
MANSFIELD.-A meeting of the operatives of Messrs. Faire Bros., and the attempt
by the Management to influence the loyalty of the girls of the Union, needed a hurried visit
and as hurried a meeting when the conditions of employment were at once obtained.
The conditions were found to be very unsatisfactory. In big businesses Managers can risk
the reputation of a firm in a few months or weeks-sometimes in a few hours. We have
been forced to move quicker than we expected, but our claim is quite complete, and as
one knows the firm, we expect no antagonism, and it is only a question of time as to
putting the firm in order somehow to meet our requirements. Being only an auxiliary
Branch to the manufacturing, our demands are only in conformity with our treatment
of other similar businesses.
LONDON.-We have during the end of last month held a large meeting at the Shore-
ditch Town Hall, London, on behalf of the Metro., Sew-Round and South London Branches,
and to say the least, the meeting was creditable to our old loyal and true members and
many young ones too. As meetings go it was indeed a good meeting. We hope it will
have some influence on all concerned.
MOUNTSORREL has again been visited, and here we had several members who had
claims upon the firm for a reconsideration of their position respecting the operations upon
which they are engaged, but we find that the state of trade being so very slack at the
firm visited, that we have a promise to take those not yet dealt with in their order when
trade revives.
---

---
EARL SHILTON AND BARWELL. We have held meetings at both places and discussed
the domestic affairs of these Sections which have in them some seventeen hundred members,
and in accord with the advice given by the Organisers, that such sections would be able
to better organise if they became a branch, this has caused the Council of the Union to
review the situation, and to declare as is our experience, that any body of men of a dozen
members to decide without any pressure, but without withholding any of the facts such
or more we think do better as a branch than as a section. In any case it is always for the
as they alone would be held responsible for the organisation, and status in factories. As
at present constituted, they don't seem to be able to keep a record of the large numbers
who are outside the Union because so many live in the surrounding villages. I am asking
the employers, some 47 in number, if they could oblige me with the number of employees
working for them for census purposes. We shall then be able to speak of the actual
position. Two of these meetings have been poorly attended, showing the members don't
feel strong, but some of those present were not aware that all benefits came direct from
the Union, and for this reason we think that more open-air organising meetings must be
held during the coming summer.

LEICESTER No. 2 BRANCH. We have again visited the two firms mentioned in our
last report concerning the Holiday Pay, and we obtained a promise from them in the light
of our attending to some of their competitors to whom it was to our credit to attend with
interest, and we hope that before this report is in print that the claims will have been
fully met.

BOZEAT. We have again met the employers in this district and produced evidence
to make owing to their isolation, there are others who look upon the cost of carriage of
their goods as being an indirect restraint of the amount of trade they would be able to do
from other areas and were able to show that although they may have some allowances
if they were not so handicapped. Our case was such as to get them to make an amended
offer which we shall place before the Council at their next meeting. We held a meeting
of the operatives two days afterwards and they have, as before, left the matter with us
to do as we think best for them.

SILEBY. We held an open-air meeting at this place outside a particular firm to better
organise the shop as a whole. We were listened to with a certain amount of confidence
if expressions are any guide. We also saw the Principals of the firm afterwards, who have
always been friendly, although the only friendliness I know in Trade Union circles is when
an Employer, Manager or Foreman makes it plain that the resolution of 27th January,
1920, should be carried out without any equivocation.

Will all our Officers in every Branch give this point attention and ask every employer
in their district where there are any non-unionists to please oblige us by putting the
otion in their factory as a proof of their friendliness to the Union.
That thirty-two thousand non-members outside our ranks ought to be searched for,
I hope we shall find them; to do so will find our Organisers and myself plenty to do
some time to come.

C.W.S. We are still pursuing the C.W.S. to give us a list of the firms with whom
they place orders, before completing that order, in the same manner as do the Government.
They even now refuse to receive a deputation I asked them to receive. Let us hope this
is not due to a change of personnel, because if we cannot get on with the Committee we
must adopt other methods. They now ask me to supply them with a list of fair houses,
which is a tall order, seeing that there are about eight hundred of them, and the others
we are making fair by degrees. This supposed friendly movement of ours are more difficult
to deal with than, as I said before, the Tory Government. This gives us an insight of the
official mind when it has not troubled to help the Trade Union movement. I am still
of the opinion that for our C.W.S. factories to be linked up with the Employers' Federation
is not to our credit, unless the employers show the same spirit of Trade Union membership
for all their employees.
The Daily Herald is the best little paper on earth; with all its faults you do get your
money's worth, if you are interested in Labour matters.
Beware of Shoddy Boots; warn your neighbours against them, and deal only with
the houses of repute who sell Stamped Goods.
Yours fraternally,

60 LADY SOMERSET ROAD,
KENTISH TOWN, LONDON, N.W. 5.
17th March, 1925.
General President.

**ATTACK ON UNIONS FAILS.**

With a flourish of trumpets the recent Conservative gathering, embracing delegates from all parts of the country, carried a resolution supporting the attack on the trade unions of this country. They have received most valuable support from the Home Secretary, who has published figures concerning the Union I have had the honour to represent for 33 years.

These figures show that the Union has 7,544 members who are exempted from its political fund, and they have been quoted by the member for the South. We have had to inform him that of this 7,544 only 145 belong to the conscientious objector class. The other 7,399 are not asked or expected to contribute, owing to their not being full financial members. These few objectors belong to six branches only of the 67 branches of the Union.

The Member for the Southern Division of the City had already accepted the Home Secretary's figures as accurate, and intended to convey to the public at large that our Union had 7,544 conscientious objectors.

Let us hope that the crushing reply of Mr. Locker-Lampson, on behalf of the Home Secretary the other day, will have a salutary effect on the detractors. This was to the effect that they had had only 33 cases of complaint in 12 years against all the unions.

The Government, with the above information, and the resolution from their supporters, are leaving the trade union detractors to their fate, because they have not forgotten 1905. Further, eight million organised men and women in the trade unions of this country will not permit their funds to be tampered with or their liberties curtailed. And, although the Tory agent in the City so freely offered his gratuitous services no one appears to have accepted the offer only at its full value, which means that if Tory working men and women had to pay for their Toryism there would be none.

T. F. RICHARDS,
General President, National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives.
-Leicester Mercury, 5th March, 1925.

**SHOE OPERATIVES AND TRADE UNION ACTS.**

A circular issued by the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives states :-Mr. E. L. Poulton, J.P., general secretary of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives, calls attention to the fact that the figures which recently appeared giving the number of exemptions from the Trade Union Political Act, 1913, are somewhat misleading. In the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives it was stated there were 7,544; as a matter of fact not more than 150 members of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives have asked for exemptions, the difference between the 7,544 and the 150 arises from the fact that 7,394 are in a different category, and pay a different rate of contribution, and, as a consequence, have never been asked to contribute to the political fund.

In the annual return to the registrar, it states :-" Members at end of year exempted from contributing to the political fund," which is an entirely different matter from contracting out.-Leicester Mail, 28th February, 1925.

**APPRECIATION OF UNION MEMBERS.**

Mr. W. R. Smith, of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives, has been appointed as a member of the Forestry Commission in the room of Sir John Stirling-Maxwell, Bart., resigned. Mr. Smith, who was Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries in the Labour Government, represented the Wellingborough Division from 1918-22, and was elected for Norwich in the December election, 1923. - Shoe and Leather Record, 6th March, 1925.

**VALUE OF GOOD BOOTS.**

Dr. W. Scatterby, reporting on the medical inspection of Keighley school children, states that "unsound footwear is not infrequently the cause of many colds and bronchial attacks which lessen the average attendance during the winter months."- Shoe and Leather Record, 13th March, 1925.

FELLOW MEMBERS,
D. MCCARTHY.
In submitting this, my first report since resuming work as Organiser, the previous
ones have been joint with my colleagues in connection with our work in London, I am
bound to say I find it a great contrast to the work of the previous year, when I was privileged
to occupy a humble position in the first Labour Government of this country.
change gives the opportunity of realising that much work has to be done outside before
From the Ministry of Agriculture to the East End of London is a wide step, but the
our work is likely to be as effective as we would wish inside the House of Commons. The
position in the East of London is not what it should be, this being in my judgment largely
It must be our endeavour to change this condition, and make the name of the National
due to what has long been a hindrance to our movement, viz., the apathy of the workers.
the larger shoe centres. The growth of the industry in these areas proves conclusively
in this part of the country as

---
that our Union and the conditions it seeks to enforce is no real detriment to prosperity
within the industry of boot and shoe manufacture.

It may be that we are as a Union somewhat to blame for the position in London,
bearing in mind what a centre of activity this was years ago, and the further fact that the
Union has made such headway on behalf of its members, raising the industry from the
awful conditions that followed the general application of machinery, to the conditions that
arise out of our National Terms of Settlement, and which prove conclusively that the
policy adopted by the Union has been right and sound, we ought to take more frequent
opportunities to instruct our members in the work of the organisation, and emphasise the
need for whole-hearted co-operation of all its members in maintaining the conditions
obtained and making them the stepping stone to greater things. I would like to suggest
that in all our large centres, and in those that are relatively backward more particularly,
mass meetings of our members should be held fairly regularly, and always after the
fixing up of a new agreement.

I think those of us on the platform at the meeting referred to were convinced that the
result justified the effort made. True the attendance might and should have been larger,
but the weather was not favourable, and with so much sickness about there is a tendency
not to take risks. I am certain the audience appreciated what was said, and one can only
hope that the result will be stimulating all round. Before leaving this subject of meetings,
I think it would be advantageous to have a series of meetings for propaganda and
educational work.

During the month I have visited Colchester, and shall have to do so again, as the
conditions of some of our members there need attention. I have also been busy in Norwich,
where the sad and unfortunate death of Mr. F. Segon, of the No. 2 Branch, and the health
of the Secretary made it necessary for me to take up the work of compiling a Quantity
Statement for the Press Room of one of our largest factories. This seems to be necessary
if the wages of the operatives in that department are to stand comparison with the other
parts of the factory.

I have further given some amount of time to the Food Commission that has been
appointed to find out whether there is profiteering in food. I expect our members will
need little to convince them that prices are too high for the wages earned, and that having
regard to the state of trade generally in the country the position of a large number of
people is thus rendered difficult indeed. It is doubtful whether the limited powers of
a Royal Commission are adequate for the task given to us, but we must do our best to
make its work fruitful to the mass of our people.
WALTER R. SMITH.

Continuing our work in the London District we have visited the following firms, espe-
cially for the purpose of organising the women at Levine's, Polikoff's, De Larnge, Turner's
and Goodman's. We are not satisfied with the women operatives at these firms, who are
enjoying all the privileges of the Union, and are not prepared to recognise their obligations.
We have also visited the firms of Lipman's, Franklin's, Chissick & Kirshenstein's, Wach-
man's, Mintz's, Meltzer's, Hyam's, Lazarus', H. & S. Solomon's, Solomon's, Morning Lane,
Jackson & Joseph's. The operatives have been met and meetings arranged at a number
of the firms. In one instance we called a joint meeting of three firms which was well
attended. We have endeavoured to concentrate on those firms where our membership
is weak and where they are not conforming to the National Agreement. Our efforts in
organising is now meeting with success, though we are not satisfied that the rate of progress
is as rapid as we desire. At one of these firms frequent attempts had been made in the
making departments to organise the men, but on every occasion we were doomed to
disappointment. By persistent efforts we have now very happily made a beginning,
with the result that within a very short time the men will all be members. At other
firms we are very pleased to report progress, though the difficulties are great, and in one
case clear indications were shown that the firm were trying to prevent the operatives
from coming to the meeting. Despite this pressure our conversations with the men
reveal a great deal of dissatisfaction with the general conditions under which they work,
and at every firm that we visit where the Holiday Fund is not in operation the operatives
are continually urging upon us the need for its adoption. This we are continually pressing
upon the employers, and is one of the questions that we are endeavouring to, negotiate
upon with a number of employers.

We have had a further meeting with these employers, but we were not able to come
to a satisfactory agreement, and the meeting was again adjourned. We are confident
that nothing short of a complete adoption of the National Agreement will bring any
satisfaction to the operatives or the employers. When this class of employer makes up
his mind that the labour charges must be included into his costs of production, and those
charges are in conformity with the National Agreement, then be no longer the willing tool
of that class of unscrupulous buyer who has no honour in business, but who is only con-
cerned with enriching himself, and caring nothing about the effects on the operatives,
or even the conditions under which the goods are produced. It is in this direction that we

Wages and Hours "Census" by Ministry. Conditions in 1924.
For the first time it is proposed to tabulate the earnings and hours of labour of the
workers of the United Kingdom.
The Ministry of Labour is about to undertake a general inquiry relating to 1924.
The first " census of production" was taken in 1906, but earnings were not then included in
the scope of the inquiry, the report on which was published in eight volumes.

BRANCH REPORTS.
ARBROATH. -We are pledged this month not to refer to bad trade,
and consequently would not venture near temptation. But while that topic
is ruled out we can still exhibit a much greater experience of the bad than of
the good. We thank the General Secretary for his footnote to our report last
month. What a pity members will not show sufficient courage when the system
is altered from piecework to set wages. It is a fatal policy to go on still pro-
ducing work valued at far more than you are paid for in the shape of wages.
If you are working to fair rates under payment by results, then it is equally
fair to work still to those prices when you are paid a fixed wage. We cannot
be surprised of course that workers allow fear to master them at such times.
Apparently all the odds are against them in resisting the pressure of employers,
and there is such an upheaval when you are "sacked" without a chance of a
start at the trade in your own town. But after all Unions exist to remove
the grounds of fear, and loyalty on the part of members could establish an
insuperable bulwark against it. Only when you fail to trust your fellow
members do you allow this corroding fear to weaken your own resistance to
unfair compulsion. Our advice to our members is always to stand firm. On
every condition and conception included in the National Terms there should
be no compromise and no surrender." If an employer orders or condones
a relaxation of or departure from, any jot or tittle of the Agreement, the worker
should show his mettle at once. Never argue such matters. Never even dis-
cuss such points with representatives of a firm. Refer them always to your
Union Official. The official is the one to take up questions of that kind, no
matter in which department the attempt is made. Therefore, fellow members,
in future if foremen, manager or boss, puts before you any proposal altering the
conditions or terms of your job, never take the matter up as though you were a
law unto yourself; never give your personal consent to anything; firmly and
and courteously tell them to take up the matter with the Union Official. Fear
magnifies dangers, and there can be little danger if the feelings are kept in check,
while if the official is brought in at the beginning of every trouble instead of at
the end, as is too often the case, then a great deal of unfortunate friction is
avoided. We are very glad Central Office has issued that circular letter dealing
with the need of attendance of our representatives at all meetings of Local
Employment Committees. Without a doubt claimants for benefit suffer if
workers' representatives are not present, and we could give scores of instances
where the point of view of the workers' representatives has been the means of
keeping claimants in benefit. Our officials or members should also make a
strong effort to be represented on Courts of Referees, because here again justice
is at the discretion of those in session. We hope our Union is taking note of
the fact that at present the Government intends putting into operation on the
Ist of October, 1925, the revised first statutory condition for the receipt of
benefit, which is that each claimant must have an account of 30 contributions.
The "waiver" condition of 8 stamps since July, 1922, will be taken away,
and unless a great change occurs, thousands now drawing benefit will be struck
off. This is a serious matter, and our Union should get the Trades Union Con-
gress and Labour Party to prepare an effective protest while there is time.
Our attitude should be a demand for unemployment to be dealt with on emer-
gency lines until the number unemployed reaches a figure which can be treated
properly on definite Insurance principles. That point has not been reached
yet, and we should object to the Poor Law being used as handmaiden to the
work of the State.

leaving all too many of our men without either work or pay, although it is
pleasing to note that more men were in employment at the close of the month.
We report with sorrow and regret the death of the President of the No. 2 Branch,

NORWICH No. 2.—During the month our Branch sustained a serious
loss by the death of our late President, Mr. F. H. Segon. He had been in
indifferent health for a considerable time. He underwent an operation on
Monday, February 9th, and to all appearances had recovered from that, but
the following Saturday afternoon, while Mrs. Segon and one of her sons was
visiting him, he died with tragic suddenness. During the six years he has
been full-time President he has carried out his duties, more especially in fixing
up prices for the many and varied patterns that have come into existence since
the war, in such a manner as to gain not only the confidence of our members
but most of the manufacturers and managers as well. The interment took
place at the Norwich Cemetery on Thursday afternoon, February 19th. The

Compensation for Refund Regulations, 1924.
THE UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE (COMPENSATION FOR REFUND) REGULATIONS, 1924,
DATED 10TH SEPTEMBER, 1924, MADE BY THE MINISTER OF LABOUR UNDER THE
UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE (NO. 2) ACT, 1924 (14 & 15 GEO. 5. C. 30).
The Minister of Labour, by virtue of the powers conferred on him by Section 9 of the
Unemployment Insurance (No. 2) Act, 1924, and of all other powers enabling him in that
behalf, hereby makes the following regulations:
1. Application for a payment under section nine of the Unemployment Insurance
(No. 2) Act, 1924 (hereinafter referred to as the said section nine) shall be made in the
appropriate form prescribed in the First Schedule hereto or in such other form as the
Minister may in any particular case accept.
2.-(1) In making the calculation referred to in paragraph (c) of subsection (3) of
the said section nine regard shall be had to the following matters, that is to say :-
(a) the minimum number of insurance years which in the case of any insured
contributor must have elapsed before a repayment under section twenty-five of the
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1920 (hereinafter referred to as the principal Act),
could have been claimed in respect of him;
(b) the fact that an insured contributor may not live to attain the age at which
a repayment under section twenty-five of the principal Act could have been claimed
in respect of him;
(c) the fact that contributions in respect of the number of weeks required by
section twenty-five of the principal Act might never have been paid by an insured
contributor;
(d) the fact that contributions may cease for a period comprising five insurance
years to be paid in respect of an insured contributor;
(e) the fact that payment is to be made to an insured contributor as at the
seventh day of July, 1924, instead of at the date at which he would have been entitled
to receive a repayment under section twenty-five of the principal Act.
(2) For the purposes of this regulation-
(a) the minimum number of insurance years referred to in paragraph (1) (a)
thereof shall in the case of any insured contributor be taken to be either the number
ascertained by dividing by fifty the number of contributions necessary in his case
to complete the number required by section twenty-five of the principal Act or the
number of insurance years which must elapse before he could attain the age of sixty,
whichever is the greater (any fraction of an insurance year being reckoned as an
insurance year); and
(b) the rate of compound interest to be taken into account for the purposes of
paragraph (1) (e) thereof shall be five per cent. per annum.
3.-(1) Whereas the figures shown in the column of the table contained in the second
schedule hereto (hereinafter referred to as "index figures") have been calculated in
accordance with the provisions of the said section nine and of the last foregoing regulation
so as to show in respect of each £I of the credit balance of an insured contributor the
present worth as on the seventh day of July, 1924, of the amount of the excess value of
the contributions paid by him as increased (in the case of an insured contributor who has
not attained the age of sixty years) by the compound interest mentioned in subsection
(1) of the said section: now therefore, as respects any insured contributor the present
worth of the amount of the excess value of his contributions as increased by any compound
interest as aforesaid, if any, shall be calculated by multiplying his credit balance by the
index figure appropriate in his case.
(2) For the purposes of this regulation-
(a) the expression "credit balance" means the sum by which the total amount
of the contributions of which account is to be taken paid by an insured contributor
exceeds the aggregate of the sums received by him by way of benefit; and
(b) the index figure appropriate in the case of any insured contributor shall be
the index figure shown in the column of the said table representing the number of
insurance years in the period during which contributions of which account is to be
taken have been paid in respect of him upon the line representing the minimum
number of insurance years which must have elapsed before a repayment under section
twenty-five of the principal Act could have been claimed in respect of him.
4. These regulations may be cited as the Unemployment Insurance (Compensation
for Refund) Regulations, 1924.
Signed by order of the Minister of Labour this nineteenth day of September, 1924.
II. J. WILSON,
Secretary of the Ministry of Labour.

In submitting the 64th Half-Yearly Report and Balance Sheet, the Sales for the
half-year amount to £27,218 155. 7d., an increase of £2,931 25. IId. compared with the
corresponding period of last year. The total Sales for the year amount to £55,215 65. 2d.,
an increase of £6,323 155. Iod. compared with the previous year. After providing for
Interest, on Share and Loan Capital to the amount of £1,037 45. 4d., and depreciating
Fixed Stock, Buildings, &c., £1,314 2s. 3d., there is a balance profit of £1,010 185. 3d..
which, with the balance of £261 175. 4d. brought forward from last half-year, gives a total
of £1,272 158. 7d. for disposal. This should be apportioned as shown in the Disposal of
Profit Account.
Eighty-eight new members have been added during the half-year, 50 of these being
Co-operative Societies, 6 have withdrawn, the present number of Shareholders being 605.
The Committee consider that the result of the half-year's work as shown by the above
figures is exceedingly good, especially in view of the still prevailing depression in trade.
The increase in trade compared with the corresponding period of last year is very gratifying.
and following the success of last half-year is a good indication of the Society's progressive
development, which we hope to maintain. The Balance Sheet generally also shows the
for Depreciation, Reserves, Investments and Bank Balance. The Branches are making
strong financial position to which the Society has attained, and in particular by the items
good progress, particularly London, where a very good connection for high-class colour
work is being established, and a substantial increase in trade is shown.

CHEAP EDUCATION.
Penny Wise and Pound Foolish.
More money on warships more money on the Army but less money on children
and then preparation for life.
Such seems to be the Government's deliberate policy. It has no compunction in
adding nearly five millions to the unproductive expenditure on the Navy, but it cuts
down productive expenditure on education by a million and a quarter. Lord Eustace
Percy, President of the Board of Education, has been at pains to let us know that this
cut is made of his own free will. It is not forced upon him by "a ferocious and niggardly
Chancellor of the Exchequer." Mr. Fisher and Mr. Trevelyan, to give them both their
due, know that they were not spending as much as was needed for the welfare of the schools
and the children. But Lord Eustace Percy is positively proud of it. The cut is his own.
A State which neglects to educate its children is neglecting the future of the whole
body of its citizens-it is failing to equip them for the work of life, to make them sound
competitors in the world's industrial race, to make them happy.
Every year we condemn thousands of children to uselessness, thriftlessness, unemploy-
ment, and-at the worst crime. We refuse to spend money on continuation schools,
and prefer to spend it in doles. We prefer to create charges on the State for habitual
paupers rather than to invest the same money in creating useful citizens.
We have got the wrong idea of education. Wise expenditure on it is productive
and remunerative. Niggardliness in it is like letting the plant of a factory run to rack
and ruin. If we go on as we are doing now we shall see our army of unemployables grow,
and our race-relatively to the rest of the civilised world-deteriorate.-The Daily Chronicle,
21st March, 1025.

ORGANISING LONDON OPERATIVES.
Mr. T. F. Richards and Mr. E. L. Poulton at Shoreditch Town Hall.
A largely attended meeting of London shoe operatives was held at the Shoreditch
Town Hall on Tuesday evening. Mr. T. F. Richards, General President of the National
Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives, occupied the chair, and was supported by Mr. E. L.
Poulton, J.P. (General Secretary), Messrs. W. R. Smith, J. H. Baum, and Len. Smith
(National Organisers), A. Mason (President, London Metro. Branch), J. Woodward, W.
Brown (President, Sew-Round Makers' Branch), W. Mulligan, and members of the London
committee.
Mr. Richards said that the meeting had been called to see whether it was possible to
put a little more vim into the London membership. The position in the metropolis was
not the same as that in the provinces. In most provincial shoe trade centres the operatives
lived and worked close together, and it was not difficult to approach them ; in fact, all the
men talked boots and shoes. The London operatives in most instances lived a long way
from the factories, and after their work was done they did not get together. This created
a problem for the Union organisers which it should not be impossible to get over.
Foresight.
The position in London was unsatisfactory because some shops were well organised
and others were not. It was the duty of the Union to prevent unfair competition caused
by certain manufacturers making their own terms as regards hours and wages. The men
who accepted a lower standard of pay were not only doing badly for themselves, but were
injuring others who would be affected by the poor conditions thus established. They were
fortunate in having one big Union in the trade, which was formed, largely owing to the
foresight of their predecessors, out of six distinct departments and was in a position to
negotiate with the employers as representing the majority of the workers. The member-
ship, however, was only 78,000, and statistics showed that about 120,000 workers were
employed in the trade.
He hoped the members present had studied the National Agreement. In connection
with it he pointed out that there were not, so far as he was aware, more than two industries
in which a scheme was in force for the payment of wages during holidays, and the boot
manufacturing industry was one of them. If the members would weigh up that one
tions and left them with a profit on the year of 4s. He asked them to take that matter
into consideration and point it out to all non-members.
A Farthing a Week!
Mr. E. L. Poulton spoke briefly on the political aspect of trade unionism, and pointed
out that the Union levy for political purposes amounted to 3d. per quarter, or 1d. per
week. Members who had been urged to stop paying the levy were in many cases not certain
of the amount they were contributing, but on discovering the facts had no objections to
make. Continuing, Mr. Poulton dealt with the conditions under which female operatives
were working in London, and said that his colleagues were sorry to find that the minimum
was paid in so few instances. It should be remembered that their minimum was not the
maximum; in fact, 85 per cent. of the members throughout the country, were earning
more than the minimum. Yet in London, where expenses were higher, wages were lower.
He urged the members to talk to women workers and explain to them the benefits offered
by the Union.
Their organisation could claim to be in the first flight among trade unions, but the
officials were not satisfied with the general situation. When they saw a chance to do some
thing to benefit the workers they were ready to spend money, as they had done recently
in London. One dispute had lasted seven or eight months, but they had kept it going in
spite of the expense, and eventually reached a satisfactory settlement. At the same

Mr. Len. Smith said London operatives might be able to show other centres something
about craftsmanship in certain classes of goods, but when it came to organisation the
provinces could give London about 360 yards start in a mile. Organisation was ineffective
when one shop was all right and the next all wrong, and that was the position in London.
A certain group of manufacturers were being tackled because they were doing a great
injury to the industry as a whole. In one shop they found girls, nineteen years of age,
working for IIS. to 13s. per week, which was not half the minimum, and these operatives
were surprised when they were asked to join the Union. It was astounding to find in
factory after factory in the year 1925 that even the men did not know that there was a
Union. (A Voice: "They don't want to.") Mr. Smith agreed that the ignorance might,
in many cases, be assumed, but he appealed to the members to see that nobody in their
shops was unaware of the work the Union was doing.

SAVING THE LIVES OF THE CHILDREN.
How Infant Mortality has been Reduced at Northampton.
Opening of Dychurch Lane Welfare Centre.
Striking figures concerning the reduction in the death rate among Northampton
children were given at the opening, on Wednesday, of the Maternity and Infant Welfare
Centre which the Town Council has recently established in Dychurch Lane.
Councillor J. Gribble, J.P., chairman of the Maternity Infant Welfare Committee
of the Town Council, handed the key of the premises-gaily decorated with red, white,
and blue ribbon-to the Mayoress (Mrs. H. W. Dover), who unlocked the door and gave
admission to the building.
Inside, Councillor Gribble took the chair.
The Mayoress, in declaring the centre open, said it would be a very great acquisition
to the town, not only to the mothers, but to the workers of the Infant Welfare Association,
who were doing such a splendid work.
Councillor Gribble emphasised the town's good fortune in having such an able Medical
Officer as Dr. Shaw in charge of the work.
There had been a great improvement in the vital statistics in relation to their work.
For the five years ending 1900, the number of deaths of infants in Northampton under
one year was 162.5 per 1,000. To-day it stood at 52.1 per 1,000. It was a magnificent
work, and the figures had been materially reduced since the welfare work had started.
What was more, however, Northampton was 22.9 per 1,000 lower than the average
for the country, which was further justification of the money spent on the work.
After Twenty Years.
Mrs. Green, the hon. secretary of the Voluntary Association, gave a brief report of
the year's work, and expressed pleasure that the hopes of twenty years had at last been
realised by the opening of that, their first, centre.
In was in 1902 that Infant Welfare work was first started in Northampton.
-Northampton Echo, 14th March, 1925.

REPAIRING TRADE BOARD.

Report on Inspections.
The statistical department of the Ministry of Labour has issued its report on inspection
and enforcement of Trade Board orders during the year ended 31st December, 1924.
The number of firms on the lists of the Boot Repairing Trade Board on 1st January,
1925, was 29,106. Of this number 501 were inspected for the first time during 1924,
and 81 firms, where irregularities had previously been discovered, were reinspected, a
total of 582 inspections during the year.
Of the firms inspected, 32 employed no workers, 309 not more than 2 workers, 207,
from 2 to 5 workers, 22 employed from 6 to 10 workers, nine employed 11 to 20 workers
in three cases 21 to 100 workers were employed, and in one case over 100 workers. Tr

inspected on routine, and 449 employed by firms inspected as a result of complaint
During the year 305 complaints were received, and 268 complaints (including 38

gation of the 70 complaints outstanding at the end of 1924.

TRADE BOARD ACT PROSECUTION.
Shoe Repairers Heavily Fined.

INTERNATIONAL LABOUR OFFICE NEWS
WORKERS' COMPENSATION.
International Labour Conference and World Agreement.
Important suggestions regarding the lines which world rules for workers' compensa-
tion should follow are contained in a report, just issued by the International Labour
Office of the League of Nations, in preparation for the Seventh Annual Session of the
International Labour Conference which will open at Geneva on 19th May, 1925.
Following its usual custom with regard to items placed on the agenda of the annual
Conference, the Office sent a series of questions regarding the possibilities and scope of an
international agreement on the subject of workmen's compensation to the 57 States which
are members of the International Labour Organisation, and has already received 26 replies
including many from the more important countries. The Australian and Canadian
replies include individual answers from the various States and Provinces. The report
embodies these replies and the conclusions to be adduced from them.
"The Governing Body of the International Labour Office took the view that the
question of workmen's compensation for accidents might be dealt with by Draft Con-
vention (by which States undertake a treaty obligation strictly to observe certain regula-
tions). Nearly all the Governments are agreed on this point," states the report.
The
British Government, however, considers that the great differences which exist between
systems in force in the various countries would make it difficult to adopt a satisfactory
Convention, and that the Conference would therefore be better advised to content itself
with a Recommendation (which is to be taken as a guide in passing national legislation
or issuing administrative orders). In spite of the differences of practical application,
there are certain fundamental principles and questions of general scope; and it may be
said, with the reservation that the British Government does not take this view, that the
Governments are agreed on these points and that they can readily be dealt with in a
Draft Convention."
The report contains proposals for two Draft Conventions and two Recommendations
for the consideration of the Conference. The first Draft Convention on workmen's com-
pensation for accidents includes provisions for applying accident compensation to every
worker except the "home worker"; additional compensation if the injured person needs
the constant help of another person; the inclusion of medical aid in compensation; the
furnishing and renewal of artificial limbs. The second deals with workers' compensation
for occupational diseases and contains a minimum list of diseases to be included. The
first Recommendation deals with the minimum scale of compensation and the second
with jurisdiction in disputes on workmen's compensation.

ASFORDBY'S AWFUL HOVELS.
Home Sweet Home Thing of the Past. Homes for Heroes.
Life in a Lorry.
Mr and Mrs. John Thornton are bringing up a family and seven children in a con-
demned cottage in Pump Lane. Six of the children are under 12 years of age. The
cottage consists of three rooms, one large ground floor room and two bedrooms.
Diabolical Damp.
The latter are rendered almost untenable by the dilapidated state of the roof.
The damp has stripped all the paper from the walls and the plaster of the roof no
longer adheres to the lathcs. It sags and cracks in an alarming manner and may at any
moment collapse bodily into the room. The owner of the cottage says that he dare not
touch it in case it should fall in.
When It Rains.
When I examined the room this morning the ceiling was waterlogged. The mattress
of the bed was soaked with water, and Mrs. Thornton explained that during the night the
rain had poured through while her daughter Olive, aged five, was in bed.
Dare Not Make a Fire.
For six weeks the house was without a fire. Débris had choked the only chimney,
and no one had dared to clear it in case worse collapse followed.
Under these conditions it is small wonder that Mr. Thornton contracted pneumonia
last November, from which he has only just recovered.
He served in the 8th Leicesters and in the R.A.M.C. from 1914-1919. He pays 3s.
a week rent for this shack.
Mr. Stephen Robert Sutton, also an ex-service man, serving in the R.E.'s from 1915-
1919, and his wife, have lived for the last four months in a converted lorry.
They have two chairs and a stove, and sleep on two seats. For this accommodation
he pays 5s. a week.
One room is the lot of Mr. Charles Tuck, his wife, four young children, and their
grandmother, aged 75. It is a converted outhouse, in the yard of the Crown Inn. But
they are regarded as lucky, for although they possess only one room it is large and airy.-
Leicester Mercury, 4th March, 1925.
GOLDEN HOUSES.
An Example of Profiteering in Sub-Letting.
Allegations that owners in the suburbs of London are exploiting the present house
shortage by making profits out of sub-letting are persistent, and a preliminary investigation
revealed that both owners and tenants have complaints to make.
A big and gloomy house in the Brixton Hill district is typical of others. The various
apartments have been let off without conversion and this is the division:-
Basement: Two rooms and small kitchen. Rent £1 12s. per week.
Ground Floor: Two rooms and small kitchen. Rent £2 5s. per week.
First Floor: Two rooms, kitchen, and bath. Rent £2 12s. 6d. per week.
Top Floor: Two small rooms and kitchen. Rent £2 12s. 6d. per week.
Same Floor: Room partitioned off and let at 15s. per week, tenants to share the
kitchen.
The rent and rates of this house amounted to about £2 per week, but some time ago
it was bought by the owner for £300, and now it brings in an income of £7 5s. 6d. per week.
The furniture in the rooms is shabby. - Daily Mail, 10th March, 1925.
BIG INCREASE IN C.W.S. SALES.
Half-Yearly Report.
The Co-operative Wholesale Society's total sales for the half-year ended December
27th last were £37,946,733, an increase of £3,441,872, or 97 per cent. on the corresponding
period of previous year. For the year the sales were £72,888,064, an increase of £6,131,636,
or 94 per cent. on the previous year.
The total supplies from the various productive works for the half-year were £12,918,188,
an increase of £2,234,880, or 20% per cent. For the year the supplies were £24,252,481,
an increase of £3,241,382, or 15% per cent., on the previous year. Co-operative News,
14th March, 1925.

THE SECRETARY,
INTERNATIONAL FEDERATION OF TRADE UNIONS,
TESSELSCHADESTRAAT, AMSTERDAM.
DEAR COMRADES,
29th January, 1925.
Your letter of date of 5th of December was examined by the Presidium of the
U.S.S.R. Central Council of Trade Unions at its Session held on January the 29th,
1925. The latter cannot hide its surprise with regard to the letter in question, which
in our opinion, could only have been the result of either a misunderstanding or ten-
dentious interpretation of our perfectly clear letter.
Paragraph 2 of your letter is so worded as to make it appear that we were pro-
posing as a first step towards the realisation of unity, the convening of an International
Congress of all trade union organisations, whereas, we, considering for our part that
this measure is the most correct, most just and most expedient step towards the
realisation of unity in the International Labour Movement, had all the time been
urging on you as the first practical step for the attaining of unity among the trade
unions, a joint conference of representatives of the International Federation of Trade
Unions and the U.S.S.R. Central Council of Trade Unions.
This, and this only, is our practical proposal to you at the present moment. We
consider that such conference of representatives of the I.F.T.U. and the U.S.S.R.
C.C.T.U., made up of an agreed upon number of representatives of both parties (say,
six comrades from each side) must make it its task to work out ways and means on
the basis of which full unanimity could be arrived at which would secure the creation
of a united international organisation of trade unions to be joined by all trade unions
at present affiliated to the I.F.T.U. and the R.I.L.U.
Neither the one side nor the other must be bound to this initial step by anything
other than a sincere desire towards the establishment of the Movement's unity which
must be done first of all. Any preliminary conditions whatsoever would only hamper
the cause of International Unification.
It seems to us that if a common base could be found at this joint conference, all
the other matters would present no difficulties.
It therefore appears to us that the initial step must take the form of just such a
convening of a conference as already spoken of by us and laid before your Council
for consideration.
The idea of an international unification of the trade unions is making ever greater
headway in many countries among the workers irrespective of their political camp.
This makes us feel sure that at last we will be successful in moving the cause of Inter-
national Unity forward to a practical conclusion.
President of the U.S.S.R. Central Council of Trade Unions,
(Signed) M. TOMSKY.
Secretary to the U.S.S.R. C.C.T.U.,
(Signed) A. DOGADOV.
This was the position when the General Council of the I.F.T.U. met in Amsterdam
on the 5th February, 1925.

FELLOW MEMBERS,
MONTHLY REPORT.
27TH APRIL, 1925.
TRADE.
Although there has been no spurt in trade, at the same time from the
evidence we have, it would appear to be quite up to the normal compared
with the past year or two.
BOOT AND SHOE INDUSTRY.
Employment in March showed little general change, an improvement in some districts
being counterbalanced by a decline in others.
The percentage of workpeople unemployed, as indicated by the unemployment books
lodged at Employment Exchanges, was 9.2 on the 23rd March, 1925, as compared with
9.5 both on the 23rd February, 1925, and on the 24th March, 1924.
Returns from firms employing about 38,250 operatives during the week ended 21st
March, 1925, showed that over 31 per cent. of these operatives were on short time in that
week, to the extent of over 10 hours each, on an average.
Employment in London was moderate, and showed little change. At Leicester
and at Northampton employment was again fair on the whole, though there was a good
deal of short-time working at both centres. At Hinckley there was a decline, and many
firms were working short time. At Wellingborough employment was very quiet; prac-
tically all the firms were on short time. Employment was poor at Higham and Rushden,
and worse than in February; at Irthlingborough, on the other hand, employment was
fairly good. There was little change at Kettering, where about three-quarter time was
worked on the average.
At Leeds employment showed a further slight improvement; it remained bad in the
heavy boot section but good in the light shoe section. Less short time was worked at
Stafford, and there was an improvement both on the previous month and on March, 1924;
employment was, however, still described as slack. At Norwich employment was again
good in the machine-sewn section; in the turnshoe section it was relatively quiet. At
Bristol and Kingswood there was an improvement in the light boot trade but a decline
in the heavy trade; nearly all the firms were working irregular short time; at Street
employment remained fair. Employment at Bacup was good, but in the slipper trade
in the Rossendale Valley a large amount of short time was worked.

SICKNESS.
We regret to have to state there has been for many weeks past an increased
number of members declaring on the sick fund, and at the time of going to
press there does not appear to be any appreciable decrease in the same. On
the contrary, the number is rather on the increase, rather than the decrease.
We hope that with the prospect of better weather and more sunshine, that we
shall be able to report sickness has fallen to what may be considered to be
the normal number of members on the fund.
DISPUTES BETWEEN UNIONS.
As the members are doubtless aware, there are from time to time, disputes
arising between Unions, not only upon demarcation of work, but also upon
the appropriate Union to which a worker should belong. This matter is
usually one of the items dealt with at the Trades Union Congress, and resolu-
tions regretting misunderstandings and calling for agreement have been
passed at the various Congresses. It will be remembered that in our January
issue, we reported an agreement between ourselves and the N.U.D.A.W.
regarding the question of members joining either one or the other Union, and
agreeing to consult with one another before so doing.
The General Council of the Trades Union Congress is constantly having to
deal with this particular question, and have issued the following circular in
connection therewith :-
The General Council have had under consideration from time to time
during the current Congress year, reports from the Disputes Committee
in relation to complaints as to the alleged poaching of members, and
matters which have given rise to friction between certain of the affiliated
Unions.
The General Council are of the opinion that much of the cause for
the complaint would be obviated if affiliated Unions would conform to
the principles laid down in the Report of the Disputes Committee which
were submitted to the Hull Trades Union Congress, 1924. These principles
were as follows :-
(1) The application for membership form of the Unions should contain
an inquiry to be answered by the candidate as to whether he is or
has been a member of any other Union, and, if so, what his financial
relationship to that Union is.
(2) As a general principle, no member of any Trade Union should be
accepted into membership in another without inquiry from the
Union concerned.
(3) No member should be allowed to escape his financial obligations
by leaving one Union while in arrears and by joining another.
(4) Under no circumstances should a Union accept members from
any other Union which is engaged in a trades' dispute. It should


---
Here is the extracted text:
210
be a general understanding that both national and local officials
of Trades Unions should refrain from speaking or acting adversely
to the interests of any other Union during any period in which
the members of the latter Union are participating in a trades'
dispute. Much trouble could be avoided if Unions about to
participate in a trades' dispute would take care to inform other
Unions whose members would be likely to be affected thereby.
Paragraph 87 of the General Council's Report wherein these observa-
tions were set out, was approved by the Hull Congress, but the General
Council feel that the matter has not been brought so prominently to the
notice of the affiliated Unions as is desirable. The General Council are
convinced that the application of these principles by affiliated Unions
would be in accordance with the best interests of the Trade Union Move-
ment, and I am to request that your Union will take all appropriate steps
to bring the principles set out above, prominently to the notice of your
members.
The General Council also desire me to ask you to be good enough
to supply this Office with a copy of your present Application for Membership
Form in order that the Council may consider as to whether it is possible
to compile a model application form which could later be submitted for
the approval and adoption of the affiliated Unions.
The Council feel that they can confidently expect the co-operation
of your Union on this matter.
Yors sincerely,
FRED BRAMLEY,
Secretary.

POLITICAL.
At the time of going to press Parliament is not in Session. The result of
the labours of Parliament for the past few months has not, we venture to say,
brought about any considerable improvement in the position of the workers
or in relation to its influence of the nation amongst the continental nations.
In fact the Rt. Hon. Austen Chamberlain (Foreign Secretary) speaking in the

House of Commons recently, when talking of the Geneva Protocol and the

"Fear, haunting, restless, brooding fear, haunts the councils of
every nation and the homes of every continental people; fear that warps
the judgment and affects the policy, which leads to irritating acts, to fresh
provocation; which renews day by day the offences of the war, the
bitterness of the war, the rancours of the war. If this continues, sooner
or later, Europe will march to a new Armageddon. The statesmen
of this country have some responsibility. Our policy, not wholly through
our own fault, has been wavering and inconsistent. Our influence-nobody
can move, as I have done, among the statesmen of Europe and of more
