HOW OPPOSITION TO REFORM IS BEING WORKED UP.
Do They Want to Ruin Us?
The new Bill will multiply the huge army of men and women now out of work, because
it quite arbitrarily increases the amount of air space which must be provided for each
worker from 250 to 400 cubic feet. It will be entirely out of the question for every industry
simultaneously to expand its accommodation. There is neither the building labour nor
the plant, and there is not the money in this country to do it. This new restriction will
therefore mean that in numerous establishments 37 per cent. of the workers in actual employ-
meni will have to be discharged. Of all the crimes which have been committed in the name
of philanthropy this will be one of the cruellest.
When the British electors by a veritable landslide of votes last year turned out Mr.
MacDonald and put the present Government into power they wanted to be rid of Socialism
and its incessant meddling and waste. What they are getting from the present Government,
where they are getting anything at all, is a blend of sloppy Socialism and half-baked senti-
mentalism which threatens to be deadly to industry. A wise Government, realising that the
difficulties which confront our manufacturers are not to be conjured away with words,
would months ago have set to work to review and revise existing Acts which have a harassing
and crippling effect on trade. Instead of passing a new Factories Act it would now be
examining the working of those already in existence.
The above statement is taken from the leading article of the Daily Mail, of 18th April,
1925. Such statement refers to the proposed new Factory Bill. The Council of the
Union, through its Monthly Address, has repeatedly pointed out how necessary it is for
our machinery to be kept in good order to be able to repel the attacks that might come at
any time from those who desire to hold back necessary reforms in our industrial system.
To be forewarned ought to result in counter propaganda, and thereby nullify the reactionary
forces that exist in the country.-E. L. POULTON, General Secretary.]

GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
May Day. By the time this Report is in your hands we shall have passed another
May Day, or Labour Day, which many years ago we decided should be made at least a
National Holiday. I am of the opinion that we ought to, as a Union, set an example in
this respect by recognising whatever day the first of May falls upon, to be to all employers
and ourselves a general Labour Day of the year. In this respect I hope to approach my
colleagues on the matter, both the Council of the Union and Branch Executives, and trust
we may set an example to employers and their people that this is not a passing phase but
is a serious factor in the industrial lives of our members.

by the Northants District Council to address them on the subject of the legalising of
Agreements, and whether the proposition was likely to be beneficial to our Union in

in this particular question, as they do in all subjects, and appreciated the fact that there

LONDON. We are meeting some sixteen members of the East End of London, to see
whether we can persuade them to adopt in its entirety our National Agreement. In this
respect we are anxious that these firms shall bring themselves up to the status of our
ordinary or average firms. We are well aware of the inducement that is offered them to
make cheaper lines, so much so, that there are instances when some of them are driven
harder than is justly reasonable, and as a consequence, they are compelled, owing to
economic conditions, to be fretful as to whether they can meet the demands of the industry.
We are hoping to be able to persuade the Joint Industrial Council at its next meeting
to give us more support than in the past, in endeavouring to organise the operatives in
various firms throughout the kingdom, and also to endeavour to arrange a conference with
the big buyers, multiple shopkeepers, and factors, with the intention of trying to purify
the industry from the "shoddy" goods that are sometimes placed upon the market.
If we can get the assistance of the organisations above-named, we shall then certainly be
able to record an improvement in the boot and shoe industry.
LEICESTER. We have been compelled to hand in notices to two auxiliary factories
in this city, owing to their non-compliance, after some sixteen weeks' notice, with the
Holiday Payment Scheme generally respected in our trade. We have the authority of
the employees, who believe that they should have not less than the conditions of employ-
ment that prevail in the boot and shoe manufacturing firms, and we would welcome the
formation among the auxiliary branches of the industry of an organisation similar to the
one which prevails with the Heel Building firms of Leicester, where we present our biennial
demands or requests, as we do with the boot and shoe manufacturers. We hope in future
to so organise these gentlemen if they will permit us so to do that they will have an
Association of their own, and we can meet them and treat them with that respect which
is due to them and their businesses. It is unfortunate that we should have to ultimately
give notice to any firm, as we prefer the arbitration method for settlement of disputes.
MANSFIELD. I have had to visit this town owing to the fact that the rates of pay
agreed upon in the Statement were not being carried out. The explanation given was to
the effect that as the class of shoe in discussion was made on the tennis shoe principle,
the firm doubted the wisdom as to whether the Statement called for a price which we claim
ought to have been paid. In fact we are informed that as it is our desire to insist upon
that rate of payment to control the department in future, the firm will withdraw the shoe
and cease to make it, as the quality and price paid for such an article would not justify
their paying men's price for a shoe that is used mainly on tennis courts.
BOZEAT AND RUSHDEN. - We have been considering the position at Bozeat, where, by

GOAT SKINS AND GLACE KIDS.
British Tanners Improving their Processes.
[From a Correspondent.]
To the ordinary man in the street goat skins are seldom heard of, but as a matter of
fact they are a most important commodity in the world's commerce. It is estimated
that the total number available annually throughout the world is about one hundred
million, of an approximate value of twenty-five to thirty million pounds sterling.
America imports the largest quantity, and during the year 1920 the total value of
her imports of goat skins was over seventeen millions sterling, while Great Britain was
responsible during the same period for about only three million. France, Germany and
other countries absorbed the remainder.
The greater proportion of these skins are manufactured into glacé kid for the uppers
of boots and shoes, and are produced in all shades. But the bulk is used for blacks only,
and the process of manufacture has reached such perfection that it is sometimes difficult
to distinguish it from patent leather when made up into boots.
British tanners of goat skins have vastly improved their processes during recent years,
and their productions are considered superior to those of any other country.
Goat skins are used for numerous other purposes; for the production of morocco for
upholstery, fancy bags, purses, pocket books, cigar cases, &c.
India is the chief source of supply of raw and tanned goat skins, producing a total
annually of about 25,000,000. Arabia produces about 7,000,000; South Africa, 5,000,000;
North Africa, 3,000,000; West Africa, 8,000,000; East Africa, 3,000,000; China,
6,000,000; South America, 10,000,000; Europe, 5,000,000; Russia, 5,000,000.
These figures are approximate, as statistics are not available. There are many other
sources of origin which are too numerous to mention in this short description of the generally
despised goat.-Shoe and Leather Record, 17th April, 1925.

**BRANCH REPORTS.**

ARBROATH.—All our members have been drawing Unemployment Benefit for a few weeks back, although as we write comes word that one factory in Carnoustie is again to go on full time. It relieves the situation greatly to have even one factory making good time, and we are forced to the conclusion that sensible methods of dealing with the difficulties of markets can accomplish much at the present time. We wrote in a former report of the folly of competing against the Midlands on wrong lines, and here we have proof of our view that a good trade can be built up on distinctly Scottish productions. Our Carnoustie factory has had full time during three of the last four years, and it has been possible because of attention to detail not only in production, but in distribution as well. Great care has been exercised in dealing intelligently with customers, and a valuable discretion in quoting has been the means of securing many orders. Taking the road with samples may often be a disheartening experience, but so far as the trade in Scotland is concerned, it pays far better for the firm to do this rather than depend on factors of any kind. The factor after all is human, and yields to self-interest, while he has no authority to meet a strong competition with an equally bold counter-stroke. In the above instance it is this kind of policy that has scored, and it is the opposite policy which has proved barren elsewhere. Orders never come through the post, unless there is persistent and clever efforts being made to capture the wayward fancy of the buyer, and this can best be done by each firm keeping in close personal touch with potential customers so as to respond to every need as it arises. It looks alright to select a factor with wide connections, and then rely on his efforts to put you in touch with "good houses," but it is too often the case that you get double-crossed with such an arrangement. There is or get, fair and square dealings, and it is not surprising to find trickery practised simply because it pays. We are very glad the British Trade Union Congress has taken up the question of administration of Unemployment Insurance, and although we haven’t seen the result of the inquiries they have made up and down the country, we can guess their eyes should be opened to serious abuses. It is time that the full force of organised labour was directed towards an improvement in the administration of this important legislation. As we have often pointed out the claimant loses benefit often through ignorance of Rota Committees or Courts of Referees. In our area for instance the Court of Referees invariably reject "domestic circumstances" as a ground of appeal, and lately have also formed the opinion that "medical certificates" are to be likewise ignored. This limits the grounds of appeal in such a way that very few appeals are allowed. We had a case under Section 9 (1923) Act where the Court unanimously, after a close inquiry, agreed to a "good faith" decision, and yet the C.I.O. sent the case to the Umpire, who decided there was not a reason for "good faith." A Court on the spot, after interviewing the claimant, could accept the "good faith," but an Umpire in London, who never saw the claimant or heard any evidence, could decide there was none. But present administration is full of anomalies, and unless a determined opposition comes from the British Trade Union Congress, all the supposed rights of contributors will be stultified by the very machinery which was supposed to safeguard those rights.

BELFAST.—Trade continues to remain very bad. We very much regret to record the death of Shopmate P. Rice, who had been ailing for a considerable period, from Pulmonary Tuberculosis. To his sorrowing wife and family we tender our deepest sympathy.

BRISTOL AND KINGSWOOD No. 2. Trade is bad, and sickness
claims very heavy. The latter should become lighter with the present welcome
improvement in the weather. The Umpire's decision confirming the Court of
Referees recommendation that three days is the normal Christmas holiday in
this district, bas been received with satisfaction. This decision affects some
hundreds, and had the result been different, it would have inflicted a distinct
hardship on those engaged in our industry. It is a further proof, if that were
needed, of the valuable work our Union does for those engaged in the industry.
It should stimulate members to greater interest in the work of the Union,
and encourage those who are not members to no longer hesitate, but to join up
and de their part in making the Union stronger than ever.
CHESHAM-Trade here still remains very slack and long rests from
work during Easter were general.
CHESTERFIELD.-Trade is bad with members making New Work.
Fourteen days holiday was given at Dronfield & Co's. Some of our members
there have received a week's notice to finish at the Easter holiday break-up.
DERBY. All the firms in Derby are on full time, although we have a
good number of shoe operatives out of work, several of whom have been mem-
bers of the Union some time back, but have ceased paying when they got in a
shop where it was not compulsory. We hope it will be a lesson to them when
they commence work to pay into the Union so that they can obtain the benefits
which it provides. We are also sorry to have a heavy sick list.
DUNDEE.-Boot manufacturing in this area is in such a shrinking and
decadent condition as to suggest a state of temporary collapse, if not finality.
Let us hope it is but temporary. To write in a pessimistic vein is not to our
liking. Nevertheless, it must be admitted our trade is passing through a very
disquieting period, which is causing considerable anxiety to all identified with it.
Indeed, we seem not to have reached the bottom yet of the stagnant industrial
pool. Spring has come, bringing no glad tidings of a trade revival, which
stifles the happy anticipations of a good season's trade. Therefore, the hope
that this year would excel in prosperity that of its predecessor, has entirely
evaporated. As the moving hand of time writes, many changes are brought
about. Those of us who are old enough to remember the advent of the Blake
machine, can well remember the progress Dundee was making in shoe produc-
tion. At that time tanning and currying was carried out on an extensive
scale. The tide, taken at the flood, flowed on progressively for years. Then
came the ebb, the progressive industrial channels are well-nigh dried up, and
where many hundreds were employed, it has dwindled down to a mere fraction.
'Tis all very sad, but perhaps, some day, it may again rise, Phœnix-like.
HIGHAM AND RUSHDEN.-Trade during the month has fallen off
considerably at time of sending in this report. The whole of the male opera-
tives at the largest firm in Bozeat are under notice. At Finedon trade is very
bad; Irthlingborough and Higham Ferrers fair. We have had to take police
court proceedings against one employer for discharging eight pieceworkers in
Heel-making Factory at Ringstead. The Thrapston Bench awarded average
weekly wage for previous month as week's wages in lieu of notice.
KILMARNOCK.-Trade in Kilmarnock is improving, but there is still
no signs of work in our section at Kilmaurs. We are sorry to say that our
late Secretary, Mr. A. Flanagan, has met with an accident at Shieldhall, and
is at present lying in the Western Infirmary, having had a piece of skin grafted
from his hip to his arm.

scarce, and the serious position reported from the coalfields will add still

BOOKS TO READ.

Labour Year Book.

Every worker should get a copy of the Labour Year Book for 1925; it is the
most comprehensive, reliable and up-to-date reference book for trade union officials and
branch secretaries, and all others who wish to keep themselves fully informed regarding
national and international affairs. Copies can be secured for 3s. 6d. post free, from Labour
Publications Department, 33 Eccleston Square, London, S.W.1.
Life of Sir Charles Dilke.

Conspicuous among those of high social standing who have given the working-class
movement the benefit of their splendid talents and unstinted service is Sir Charles Dilke.
Many who knew him will read with absorbed interest the two large volumes of his biog-
raphy written by Miss Gertrude Tuckwell and Mr. Stephen Gwynn; for trade unionists,
however, the price of those volumes is prohibitive. A cheap abridged edition has therefore
been issued by Miss Tuckwell at 5s. per copy, with foreword by Mr. Arthur Greenwood,
M.P. Dilke's greatest effort was perhaps in connection with the agitation to protect the
sweated worker, and in the passing of the Trades Disputes Act. Miss Tuckwell's book,
written out of the ample knowledge acquired as his secretary for trade union work for
many years, tells the story in great detail, but also conveys a vivid and consistent picture
of his personality. Copies of the book will be supplied from the Joint Publications Depart-
ment, 33 Eccleston Square, London, S.W.1.
LEICESTER COUNTY BOOT AND SHOE TRADE.

A meeting of the County Arbitration Board was held at the City Hall, Leicester,
on Wednesday last.
Mr. G. A. Denman presided. The Manufacturers' Side were represented by Messrs.
W. Harvey, T. J. Bellamy, J. H. Bott, W. H. Keywood, J. W. Hunt and F. Wain: and
the Operatives' Side by Mrs. M. J. Bell-Richards, Messrs. D. Astley, T. F. Richards, W.
Warner, J. H. Osborne, A. Needham, W. Woodward, M. A. Parker, G. Smith, F. Leader
and F. W. Burchnall; H. A. Flavill, Secretary.
The piecework statement prepared by the Joint Committee for the Press Department
was received and confirmed, and it was decided that it should come into operation from
the commencement of the first working week after Easter.
A question which has arisen concerning the application of the Nurseries' and Children's
Statement prices for Lasting to 7-8 work was referred by the Board to the Statement
Committee for settlement.
In pursuance with a requisition which had been lodged it was decided to convene
a meeting of the Finishing Statement Committee to fix the price to be paid for cleaning
heels with aluminium plate insertions.
The name of Mrs. M. J. Bell-Richards was added to the Enquiry Committee for the
South Leicestershire District when questions affecting female operatives were under
consideration.

24th April, 1925.
D. MCCARTHY.
During the past month the work in the East End of London has been continued.
Like most districts (which fortunately now are strictly limited) where the operatives are
not fully organised, and therefore to some extent outside our influence, the progress made
is not so rapid as we would wish. But that we are making headway is I think certain,
and we must hope that the gains already made may act as an inspiration and encourage-
ment towards a stronger trade union attitude being adopted.
It is generally understood that isolation of workers, as in such industries as agriculture,
is a factor in preventing organisation becoming really effective, but there is certainly no
isolation here, unless it is that the individual gets lost in the mass of population around
him, and therefore the general result is the same; anyway, a lack of confidence in each
other is to be found which could not be beaten were the operatives miles apart. It is our
task to remove this, and endeavour to get that recognition of identity of interest that has
been of such value to us in other centres.
There is undoubtedly reasons to be given that are not easy to overcome. The cosmo-
politan nature of the population in the East End is one of them, creating as it does occa-
sionally, race suspicion, which the difference of language has a tendency to develop.
Another reason is that the modern methods of boot and shoe manufacture does not develop
as in other centres, and the higher costs incurred in this manner are in a way compensated
for in other directions.
It is not, however, that wages are low all round in London; one comes across cases of
earnings that will compare with any in the country, while in other cases they are low.
It is the absence of correct balance between departments that is the trouble, and as gener-
ally happens in such circumstances it is the weakest that suffer, and in this case I think
it is the women who are the victims.
There is only one way out, the problems of London at bottom are no different to any
other centre, and organisation among the operatives must be the first step. The work
has proceeded along this line together with interviews with firms for adjustment in con-
ditions. Success has followed with the Holiday Scheme, a number of firms agreeing to
same following a meeting with some of them at which the General President was present.
This we hope will be the beginning of the end so far as this matter is concerned.


---
Meetings have been held of the operatives at Jackson & Joseph's, following the settle-
ment of the dispute. The firm raise no objection to the operatives joining, and one is
pleased to say a good number have done so. If the matter is handled with discretion
locally, further success will, I am sure, follow.

The Statement for Pressmen that had engaged attention at Norwich has not, I regret,
been forwarded during the month. This is due to the unfortunate illness of the employer
concerned, and one hopes that a speedy recovery will enable him shortly to go further
into the question by negotiation, with beneficial results to our members.

The visit to Colchester last month has been followed up, but with a result that can
hardly be termed satisfactory. For reasons which perhaps the Co-operative Society are
not entirely to blame, the wages of the benchmen in the repairing department were, and
are, exceedingly low, and justified an appeal for consideration. A request was made for
a to per cent. increase on Trade Board rates, a condition that is by no means unusual
in other districts in the Co-operative Movement, and by which they seek to justify their
claim to being if not ideal employers, at least to rank among the best.

Though the request in this instance, as I have said, had every justification, I have
been informed that the matter had been fully considered by the main Committee who have
declined to concede the modest increase asked for. One cannot help thinking that this
cold communication is not to the credit of a movement that held out such high ideals in
working-class life.

25th April, 1925.

During the past month we have been engaged in London, and the following firms
have been visited H. & S. Solomon's, N. Bloom's, Kreitman & Son's, Lazarus's, Meltzer's,
Jackson & Joseph's, Lipman's, Franklin's, Chissick's & Kirchenstein's, Wachman's,
Casper's, Mintz's, Melrose's, I Webber's, Muller & Joseph's, Kay's, Phillips', Franks',
J. Branch's, McAfee's, Bloom & Phillips', M. Solomon's. At all these firms we have made
attempts both by meetings, and personally canvassing the operatives, in order to increase
our membership. We are still endeavouring to negotiate with a number of firms who are
not fully complying with the Agreement. The employers have been met, and there is
every prospect that before another month has elapsed a good number will adopt the
Scheme. It is fairly evident that the operative has changed his point of view, and every
time we meet them continued representations are made to keep up the pressure. This
is very largely accounted for, by the constant and persistent efforts that have been made
in this area during the past two years, and demonstrates the need of keeping in touch
with those firms who have not adopted the National Agreement. The recent decision of
the London Federation in expelling a number of firms for not complying to that Agreement,
is conclusive evidence that united pressure is being brought to bear in order to deal with
a position which cannot be regarded as satisfactory. In interviewing a number of these
firms, a great deal of hesitancy exists in their minds, of boldly facing the position. We
have endeavoured to get them to include into their costs of production the full terms of
the National Agreement, but they all seem afraid of one another, and frequently quote
another firm and say that it is impossible for one to pay unless his competitor pays. All
these firms produce a similar class of work, and the conditions of the operatives are about
the same in every firm.

It is utterly impossible to make any comparison with other districts, so far as the
methods of production are concerned. The only thing that seems to matter is, what
price the shoes can be produced at, and somehow or other the employer thinks that what-
ever price the buyer offers, he is bound to accept the order, which inevitably means that
it is impossible for him to pay the National agreed terms. Though some classes of the
goods produced are of a "shoddy" character, there is a gradual improvement taking
place in the quality of the goods produced, which makes it absolutely essential that special
attention should be paid to this class of firm. Judging by the information that we have
been able to obtain, of the actual price paid for the class of shoes produced at these firms,
and the price paid by the consumer, the impudence of the buyers is astounding. It would
be amusing if it did not have such serious consequences upon the industry, for one to hear
these buyers loudly boast of their initiative and enterprise, which they claim to have
put into their business, which has enabled them to be such successful business men. A
great deal of imagination is required for anyone to discern what initiative is used, for a
buyer to deliberately and wilfully ask an employer to produce shoes, for the purpose of
exploiting the consumer, well knowing that where such goods are produced it means that
the operative is forced to accept lower standards of wages than those which are accepted
as a basis in our National Agreement. We have made progress in our membership in this
class of firm, but unfortunately we have not the whole of the operatives members, with a
distinct weakness with reference to the women; which is very largely the outcome of bad

WOMEN'S TRADE UNION CONFERENCE.
DELEGATES' REPORTS.
I have to report that on Friday, the 20th March, 1925, I attended a Conference at
the Boot and Shoe Trade Hall. Leicester, on the Organisation of Women Workers, called
under the auspices of the Trades Union Congress General Council. The Conference was
presided over by Miss Julia Varley, supported on the platform by Miss M. Quaile, Mr.
L. Poulton, Mr. Conley, Mr. Ben Turner, Mr. Ogden, and Mr. F. Bramley, Secretary
to the Council.
There were 39 delegates representing 26 Unions, three of the delegates being men.
Four resolutions were submitted to the Women's Conference, all proposed from the
platform; three by men, and Miss Quaile the first, the three men being members of the
Women's Group of the National Council of the Trade Union Congress.
Early in the Conference it could be felt there was an atmosphere of impatience at the
"cut and dried" procedure adopted, some delegates protesting at being treated like
school children.
In answer to inquiries from the floor of the Conference as to what we were called for
or whether amendments could be submitted to the resolution, the Chairman informed
Miss Margaret Bondfield that she could not add any addendum or amendment, but all
we were there for was to make suggestions that could be taken back by the Women's
Group to the General Council for consideration.
The addendum Miss Bondfield wished to add to Resolution 1, put forward as a sugges
tion, was that Trades Councils should form Women's Groups, and that there should be a
chief woman officer on similar lines to the Labour Party.
Miss House also suggested, as she could not move an amendment nor add to the
resolutions, that five women be elected to work in conjunction with the two women on
the Council.
The women delegates began to realise that their time was being wasted, and moved
that the resolutions - after the first one-be not discussed, the Chairman objecting to this
course. It was then proposed, and carried, that resolutions 2, 3, and 4, be taken as a
composite resolution.
The proposers of the Congress resolutions - of which the Women's Conference was the
outcome, protested that the Conference as called was not what was intended by their
resolution, there being no freedom to move in any way from the "cut and dried" pro-
gramme submitted.
The ultimate outcome of the gathering will be watched for by all delegates who
attended.
M. J. BELL-RICHARDS,
Leicester Women's Branch.
An important Conference of Women Workers held under the auspices of the Trade
Union Congress General Council, was held at the Trade Hall, Leicester, on Friday, 20th
March, 1925. It was the first occasion upon which such a Conference had been held in
this country. The object of the Conference was to consider the Organising of Women
Workers. Miss Varley presided, and was supported by Miss Quaile, Mr. Ben Turner, J.P.,
Mr. E. L. Poulton, J.P., Mr. J. W. Ogden, Mr. A. Cinlay, Councillor Smith (Leicester), and
Mr. Fred Bramley, Secretary, Trade Union Congress General Council.
Councillor Smith, Vice-President of the Leicester Trades Council, extended an official
welcome to the delegates. He said it was important that they should go the whole hog in
the organisation of Women Workers. He thought Leicester warehouses and shops com-
pared favourably with other cities in this country. From his own personal observation
he could say that some were an absolute disgrace to the industrial movement. Some
of their telephone girls laboured at times under disgraceful conditions.
Miss Varley, the Chairman, said they felt that Leicester was rather better organised
than perhaps a large number of towns were. She was not going to throw too many
bouquets to Leicester on that point for there was room for a larger organisation than at
the present time. At the present time it was estimated that there were four million
women engaged in domestic service. It was one of the worst professions to organise on
account of the isolation of the workers. Between 700,000 and 800,000 women were mem
bers of trade unions. The employers, she added, were able to get at the men by using the
women who were not organised. Women were sufficiently organised, however, to alter
the course of industry.
Mr. Fred Bramley (Secretary, Trade Union Congress General Council), said the menace
of cheap labour had not been sufficiently recognised by the unions, and women could exert


---
a wonderful influence on the industrial world if they organised themselves. They ought
not to have close upon 2,000,000 women outside the Trade Union movement. They had
to get rid of their narrow sectional view.
Miss Quaile moved that this Conference, in view of the fact that a considerable number
of women employed in industrial and other occupations are not organised in Trade Unions,
calls upon Trade Union Officials, Executive Councils and Members, to make special efforts
to secure the adherence of Women Workers to Trade Union organisations.
Miss Margaret Bondfield referred to the uneasiness with regard to the instability of
women membership. They must increase the educational opportunities for the new
members. They needed a complete elementary Trade Union education for young girls
who had no experience of the struggles in the past, of the present senior trade unionists.
She was greatly in favour of the formation of mixed trade unions. She urged the need of
area conferences for all kinds of women organisations. A great help would be a woman
congress week. As a sort of coping stone they needed a woman official to act as secretary
pointed out. Ald. Jabez Chaplin, of Leicester, said that women do not understand trade
unions. Scores of meetings had been held in Leicester for women, and none had turned
up. No city in England had given women more opportunities and they had not been taken.
It was not the fault of the men who did not know how to help the woman. The latter left
the union as soon as they had found work. Other members supported the resolution,
which was passed unanimously.
Mr. Conley moved that trade union members be called upon to do all in their power
to influence their wives and daughters to become members of the trade unions.
Varied opinions were given regarding the responsibility of men in connection with
the support of women's organisations. It was said that out of 800 delegates to the Trades
Union Congress only about 30 were women. There should be a separate conference
annually of at least 500 women delegates. Three resolutions were moved and discussed
together, calling on trade unionists to use their influence to increase union membership
amongst the members of their families, calling on the need for the organised trade union
movement to give help to unions engaged in organising women workers, and requesting
the General Council to procure the further discussion and adoption of the resolutions.
Mr. Saunders said that only by organised entertainments in connection with the
meetings would the young girls between 16 and 25 be brought to trade union meetings.
Mr. Ben Turner said there were too many trade union men who had not the trade union
conscience. It was a great misfortune.
Mr. Andrews said his trade union (Postal Workers) had, for a cost of about £400 filmed
their members at work and had shown the film throughout the country. There was not
a union which could not show on the screen a forcible story.
The Shop Assistants' delegate said that a girl had been working for four years in a
shop and had never been a trade unionist, although her father was a trade union secretary.
Delegates said that men who would strike if they had to work with a "blackleg" allowed
their daughters to go to work without joining a union. The idea among men that women
did not need trade unions was the root of the trouble.
The Conference closed urging trade union officials and members to do all in their
power to increase trade union membership among women.
31st March, 1925.
N. DUNNETT,
Northampton No. 2.

Miss Varley presided, and I was surprised at the very few representatives of women

Following the President's address and Secretary's report, four resolutions were put

Quaile, Mr. Conley, Mr. Ben Turner and Mr. E. L. Poulton, respectively, calling upon all
Trade Unions, Trade Union Officials, Executive Councils and members to use their influence
and make special efforts to secure all women workers of this country into the Trade Unions.
At the present only one third of the women workers were organised.
and debate the resolutions were ultimately carried.
The business was of a more lively character in the afternoon, and after good discussion
V. HOWARD,
Norwich Branch.

INADEQUATE HOUSING IN SCOTLAND AND SOME OF ITS CONSEQUENCES.
There are 1,000,037 houses in Scotland. Of that number 548,000 are one and two-
room houses. That is to say that 52 per cent. of the houses in Scotland to-day are either
of a one or two-room type, and 48 per cent. of the population live under those conditions.
The result, as the Parliamentary Under-Secretary has very well pointed out, is that we
have the highest death rate in the British Isles : of infantile mortality of the general
death-rate, and everything in that direction. The highest sickness rate of any part of
the British Isles obtains in that great country of Scotland. We do not escape the expendi-
ture.
We have got to spend the money in sanatoria, in hospitals, and in the economic
loss occasioned by men who are lying sick, so that we gain no advantage whatever in that
direction. You have reduced the standard of the houses. Let me give an illustration
of what is taking place, as I have done before on the few occasions on which I have addressed
the House, by using my own city. It is not by any means the worst, though it is the
largest. In other parts of Lanarkshire, Linlithgowshire, and Stirlingshire you get these
conditions: here they are actually worse than what they are in Glasgow.
Quite recently the Medical Officer of Health for Glasgow published a report dealing
with this very subject. In that report he condemns root-and-branch the building of any
more two-room houses. He points out that there are 40,000 houses in Glasgow slightly
under, but I give it in round figures-in which there are living more than three persons
This represents
to a room. The standard anywhere is two per room in Scotland. It is not apparently
considered injurious that there should be more than three in each room. that are
inimical to their health. - Extract from speech of MR. J. STEWART, in House of Commons,
April 6th, 1925.
TO CURB HOUSE PROFITEERS.
Re-Sale of Subsidised Dwellings. A Five-Years' Ban.
In the House of Commons on Thursday, 2nd April, 1925, Mr. Trevelyan Thomson
(L., West Middlesbrough) asked the Minister of Health if he was aware that considerable
profiteering was taking place in the re-sale of subsidy houses, and would he make it a
condition of the grant of any subsidy that no house should be sold within five years of
receipt of subsidy at a higher price than that on which the subsidy was granted.
Mr. Neville Chamberlain said he was not aware that considerable profiteering was
taking place in the re-sale of subsidy houses. It was open to any local authority to make
a condition on the lines suggested by Mr. Trevelyan Thomson.
Mr. Trevelyan Thomson: Will the right hon. gentleman make a recommendation
to the various authorities and circularise them on this point, so that they can protect the
public against profiteering?
Mr. Neville Chamberlain: I do not think it is necessary to issue a circular. I should
not hesitate to give advice to any particular local authority if I thought it necessary to
introduce a provision of this kind.

7 Overcrowded in Black Hole. Blind Twins,
The parents and their five children (ranging in age from 13 months to five years)
lived in one room 8ft. 6in. square. All slept in one bed. A piece of sacking over the
window kept it in perpetual darkness.
These facts were related by an inspector of the N.S.P.C.C. yesterday at Enfield Police
Court, when William John Goy, of Jasper Road, Enfield Highway, and his wife, Lottie
Goy, were charged with neglecting their children.
Remarking that it was one of the worst cases that had come before them, the Bench
sentenced the man to six month's hard labour and his wife to one month's imprisonment.
The inspector said that when he removed the sacking he found the three elder children
huddled together, while the 13-months-old twins were crying piteously.
Regarding the twins, the assistant medical officer of the North Middlesex Hospital
stated that they were in such a terrible state of neglect that one had lost the sight of one
eye, and the other, if it lived, would be totally blind.
The father told the Bench that he had made several applications for a Council house,
but being out of work, had been unsuccessful. -Daily Herald, 31st March, 1925.

NOTICE OF PROPOSAL D. (27) - MODIFICATION OF THE TRADE BOARD'S APPRENTICES
SCHEME.
At their previous meeting, as has already been reported, the Trade Board decide
male apprentices in accordance with the Proposals contained in the Notice D. (2
subject to certain modifications, to vary Minimum Rates of Wages and conditions
Notification of the variations made by the Trade Board was sent to the Minister of Late
immediately after the last meeting of the Trade Board with the request that the Minister
would confirm the variations and make them effective.
At the present meeting the Board considered a letter which had been received fr
the Minister of Labour requesting the Board to reconsider certain of the provisions decided
on and suggesting some amendment in the form of the new provisions.
After careful consideration of the Minister's letter and consultation with an Officer
of the Department certain of the provisions relating to apprentices were redrafted an
these provisions will be again submitted to the Minister of Labour for confirmation.
Due notice of such new rates and provisions with regard to apprentices as may be
confirmed by the Minister of Labour and made effective will be sent to all employers in
the trade.
OVERTIME RATES.
For some time the Board has considered the question of varying the provisions o
their Notices with regard to Overtime Rates, with a view to allowing employers and
workers some elasticity in arranging the number of hours of work on any particular da
and especially with a view to allowing nine hours to be worked on a Monday before Over-
time Rates become payable instead of eight hours as at present.
Provisions to carry into effect this object of the Trade Board had been drafted by the
Administrative Committee and were adopted by the Trade Board, who decided to insert a
Proposal to make the changes agreed upon in the next statutory Notice of Proposal issued.
Before the new arrangement becomes operative the Proposals of the Trade Board, after
publication, will require to be considered by the District Trade Committees and the Boar
will consider any objections which may be lodged against the proposed change.
VOCATIONAL TRAINING IN THE SERVICES.
It was reported that a deputation from the Administrative Committee of the Trade
Board had been received by the "Navy Personnel" Committee of the Admiralty, and
had discussed with them the position of men in the services who had received vocation
training in Boot and Shoe Repairing. The "Navy Personnel " Committee propose to
place before the Admiralty the views of the Trade Board, and it is understood that the
Admiralty will thereafter communicate with the Trade Board.
Arrangements have also been made for the visit of a deputation on the same subject
to the War Office.

GENERAL MINIMUM PIECE RATES FOR REPAIRING.
The Trade Board have finally adopted a table recommended by the Administrative
Committee consolidating the tables set out in paragraphs 2, 3, 4 and 5 of the Notice D. (26),
and have also adopted a large number of recommendations made by the Administrative
Committee with a view to removing anomalies in the existing lists of piece rates.
Notice of Proposal to make the above-mentioned changes in the existing lists of piece
rates will be given by the Trade Board on the occasion of the next issue of a statutory
Notice of Proposal to Fix and Vary Minimum Rates of Wages. All employers in the
trade will thereafter have an opportunity of considering the Proposals in detail and the
Proposals will come before the District Trade Committees.
WORK PREPARATORY TO ROUNDING AND CHANNELLING MACHINES-LONG SOLES UNDER
HEEL.
The Trade Board approved of a recommendation from the Administrative Committee
that General Minimum Piece Rates be fixed for soles under heel where such work is pre-
paratory to rounding and channelling machines. Piece rates for this work have been
agreed upon and Notice of Proposal to fix such piece rates will be given on the occasion
of the next issue of a statutory Notice of Proposal by the Trade Board.
PIECE RATES FOR MACHINE FINISHING.
The question of fixing piece rates for machine finishing is still under consideration by
the Trade Board.
ADMINISTRATION.
The Board had a long discussion with regard to the administration of the existing
Trade Board Orders and they are in consultation with the Ministry of Labour on the
subject. Further consideration of the matter is postponed pending the result of this
consultation.
WORKERS' LOYALTY.
BY ROBERT WILLIAMS (General Manager of the "Daily Herald ").
There are upwards of four and a half million men and women organised in the Trade
Union Movement of Great Britain.
At the last General Election, five and a half million men and women voted steadfastly
for the Labour Party and its candidates.
In the Co-operative Movement there ar organised five million members of various
retail societies.
As Trade Unionists, we have organised ourselves into our respective societies because
we have no confidence in our particular employers and in the employing classes in general.
If an employer or his manager were to ask for leave to attend a Trade Union branch in
order to justify low wages or bad conditions, this would be instantly and properly refused.
When the various Liberal and Conservative candidates made their specious claims
for the suffrage of the workers, they failed to secure it for the simple reason that five and
a half million voters have lost confidence in them and their parties.
Millions make their purchases from the Co-operative Stores because they believe in
organising their spending power upon a co-operative basis. They refuse to be exploited
by the great multiple firms, and prefer instead that any profits made in the co-operative
undertakings shall be disposable as dividends to members.
One wonders, therefore, why Labour voters, Trade Unionists and Co-operators, con-
tinue to have their minds warped and their better judgment over-ridden by the millionaire
Press. It has, of course, taken many years to bring our Trade Union Movement up to
its present strength; it has taken an equal length of time to establish our Co-operative
Movement upon the sound financial basis it stands on to-day.
Labour's one daily-The Daily Herald-has fought nobly and strenuously for some
twelve or thirteen years, and in the face of overwhelming and sometimes almost insuper-
able odds, we have raised our circulation to about one-tenth of the number of those who
voted Labour at the last General Election.
Workers by hand and brain, therefore, should give the Daily Herald that measure
of support which they recently gave to the Labour Party. Do not allow carping critics
to make unfair comparisons of the Daily Herald with the ordinary Capitalist newspaper.
The Daily Herald sets out to give the news from the workers' point of view.

MR. DAN ASTLEY, J.P.
New Chairman of Hinckley Rural Council.

At the first meeting of the newly-constituted Rural District Council at Hinckley
to-day, Mr. Daniel Astley, of Earl Shilton, was unanimously appointed chairman for
the ensuing year.

Mr. Astley, who is the Earl Shilton official of the National Union of Boot and Shoe

THE UNITED FRONT.
By Clifford Allen.

There is at present no end to vague demands for unity amongst the workers, but
few tell us what shall be done with that unity, and they are blind to the fact that a con-
structive objective is the only means whereby that unity itself can be secured.

Political Labour constantly asserts that we need a united industrial and political
policy. What avails such a belief if it fails to tell us how to arise or even to maintain the
present wage standard? Meantime industrial Labour is spurred on by small groups of
sincere enthusiasts. I know of nothing more dangerous than the way in which a few men,
whose incomes are secure, and who know little of the risks and privations of a prolonged
and unsuccessful strike, often incite Trade Unionists to desperate encounters without a
well-considered object. We should give vigorous support to every effort by the General
Council of the Trades Union Congress to secure united mass action by a Trade Union
Movement, skilfully led by a central authority. But even if we possessed-as we must-
this highly-equipped Trade Union machine, we must have a common object for which
to fight.- The New Leader, 17th April, 1925.

YEAR'S SURPLUS OF £3,658,884.
Mr. Snowden's Good Budgeting.
Some Contrasts.
Congratulations to the Ex-Chancellor.
Mr. Snowden received many congratulations from financial experts last night on his
remarkably accurate estimate of this year's surplus, writes our Lobby Correspondent.
He anticipated a surplus of £4,024,000; the actual amount is £3,658,884.
Mr. Snowden is the first Chancellor since the era of Big Budgets whose estimate of
the balance of revenue over expenditure has been within less than £400,000 of the actual
amount
deficit of £100,000,000!
Some of the Conservative critics of the first Labour Budget prophesied last year a
The result has not only proved them bad prophets, but demonstrated beyond cavil
that a Labour Chancellor of the Exchequer, in his first year of office, was better able to
fiance the financial resources of the country than any of his predecessors.
The actual figures for the year, compared with 1924, are given in the final returns
issued last night as under :-

An examination of the detailed accounts shows that the Customs revenue for 1925
showed a decrease of no less than £20,614,000.
Excise revenue showed a decrease of £12,842,000, and under the heading Miscellaneous
Special Receipts, a decrease of £9,838,285 is recorded.
Income Tax Up.
The largest increase over the preceding year was revenue from property and income
tax, the respective figures being £273,836,000 and £269,331,000, showing an increase of
£4,505,000. There was an increase from postal service revenue of £2,010,000, and from
super-tax of £2,040,000.
Motor vehicle duties (£1,473,000 increase); estate duties (£1,650,000), stamps
(£1,280,000), excess profits (£700,000), and telephone service (£610,000), also yielded
more than in 1924.
The total floating debt outstanding on 31st March, 1925, was £742,195,000, compared
with £774,475,500 on 31st March, 1924, showing a decrease of £32,280,500.—Daily Herald,
1st April, 1925.
SURPRISES IN MR. CHURCHILL'S BUDGET SPEECH
Pensions for Widows and Old Age Pensions at 65; Workers to
Contribute 4d. a Week. McKenna Duties again on July 1st.
Reduced super-tax and income-tax, the reimposition of the McKenna Duties as from
1st July, increases in Death Duties, new duties on imported hops, silk, and beer, return
to the gold standard, and a contributory scheme of Widows' Pensions to start next January
-these were the chief features of Mr. Churchill's Budget in the Commons yesterday.
Mr. Snowden, the ex-Chancellor, expressed the Labour Party's opposition to the
reduction of the standard rate of income-tax, the concession to super-tax payers, and to
the proposed Protective duties on Imperial produce. As to the reimposition of the
McKenna Duties, he declared that at the first opportunity these would be repealed by the
Labour Party.
BUDGET AT A GLANCE.
New Taxes, Remissions, and Contributory Pensions.
Outstanding points in the Budget were :-
GOLD standard to be restored, but not gold coinage.
INCOME-TAX reduced from 4s. 6d. to 4s.
DEATH DUTIES increased to yield additional £10,000,000.
SILK.—New duty of 4s. per lb.
Hops.—Duty of £4 a cwt. for four years.
BEER.—Small duty on imported beer.
MCKENNA DUTIES. -Reimposed on 1st July.
IMPERIAL PREFERENCE. - Increased for tobacco, dried fruits, wine, and sugar.
New scheme of contributory widows' pensions and old age pensions at 65. Con-
tributions to start at 4d. per man and 2d. per woman, and rise by 1d. per man and 1/2d. per
woman in 10-yearly periods to 7d. per man and 31d. a woman in 1956. Employers to
contribute at similar rates.
Benefits to include pensions for widows at 10s. a week, with extra for children till
youngest son reaches age of 141. Daily Herald, 29th April, 1925.

EXTRACTS FROM MR. J. R. MACDONALD'S WEEKLY
REVIEWS IN "THE DAILY HERALD,"
"One thing is certain the wages paid to the workers are not responsible for the
handicaps from which British industry suffers. Despite all the vigorous attacks which
have been made upon organised Labour, that seems to be established as a result of the
discussions which are taking place."

Impossible Burden.
"What," asked our representative, "is really at the bottom of the present disaster,
state of industry?"
"There are many reasons," answered Mr. MacDonald, "but two are worth special
consideration.
"First, it is quite clear that a large number of concerns are heavily over-capitalised.
Managers are asked to perform the impossible task of returning dividends upon capital
which has never been used in production and which only represents an increase in the
price of shares.
"For instance, during the so-called cotton boom the capital of 238 firms was increased
from £10 millions to £33 millions, and profits had thus to be paid on three times as much
capital as before. How can industry flourish if it has to carry such an impossible burden?
"Secondly, it is becoming increasingly evident that British capitalists have not been
so alert in the organisation and management of their businesses as some of their com-
petitors. This is a very serious aspect.
Fact to be Noted.
"Do take note of this fact," he continued, "that since the adoption of the Dawes
Report there has been a DECREASE IN THE HOURS OF MANY GERMAN WORKING PEOPLE.
According to official figures the general average of those working more than 48 hours a
week in seven great industrial groups fell from 54.7 in May, 1924, to 45.4 in November
of the same year.

Why Bother?
"And now the House of Lords?" I asked.
"Why bother? Liberals apparently want to tinker with the Constitution again.
I can understand Lord Selbourne and his friends wanting to strengthen the House of
Lords, but why Liberals should be anxious to do so I cannot understand. I hope Labour
is not going to waste a breath on these things.
"What with Referendums, Proportional Representation, Elected Cabinets, House of
Lords, and all the other 'cure-alls, one would think there were no economic problems.
The 'solution' of these is not delayed a week, and would not be hastened a day, if all
the proposed changes in constitutional machinery were made to-morrow." Saturday,
28th March, 1925.

GERMANY AS THE DANGER SPOT OF EUROPE.
"What is your Easter message to Labour?" asked our representative when he saw
Mr. MacDonald on the eve of a strenuous week-end speaking campaign.
"To be of good heart," he replied. "We are rising. This has been a wonderful
week of electoral victories all along the line. Never in the history of the Movement have
we had such indisputable proof-concentrated as it has been in the space of a few weeks-
not only of our numerical strength, but of our fine fighting spirit, If the late Government
did nothing else, it has certainly given Labour a magnificent political position, has taught
it how to fight, and has established it firmly throughout the length and breadth of the
land. That was something worth doing.
"The task of destructive criticism is accomplished; that of Socialist construction
must be carried forward. All skilled hands to that job.
Danger Spot of Europe.
"One thing," said Mr. MacDonald, after a pause, "I am much interested in at present
is the contact or lack of contact-between our trade unions and the German trade unions.
Germany is the industrial danger spot of Europe. I get weary beyond words of the parrot
phrases about the Dawes Report. It has no more to do with the present unsatisfactory
condition of German Labour than my shoe. I wish people would take the trouble first
of all to get facts and then consider them.


---
235
We ought in every way to encourage the German trade unions to fight for higher
wages, shorter hours, and better conditions. If we fail in this, and the German worker
is abandoned to a direct conflict with his own capitalists, he will find it quite impossible
to keep his end up.
A mere policy of the prohibition of the import of sweated goods into this country
is of little use, as it leaves the foreign market open to them. German conditions must be
levellerd up.
This is the problem which the trade union and political Labour Movement has to
face and in doing so it is wasting time and strength to talk about a separation between
the two wings. They must work out together the solution of these difficulties and give
the necessary support.
Take Counsel With Germany.
"Why should not," he asked, "the united movement send a deputation to Germany
to take counsel with the trade unions there not only to find out facts, but to come to
agreements about policy?
Vigorous action on the part of combined Labour on this side, working directly
with Germany's combined Labour Movement, and through the machinery of the Amsterdam
dissipate some of the grave
workshops are now confronted.
Now is the time for the trade union and Socialist policy of mutual aid and self-
defence to be worked out and put into operation." Saturday, 11th April, 1925.
MR. MACDONALD REPLIES TO HIS CRITICS.
WHAT LABOUR HAD TO FACE.
"Pressed by Maze of Interests and Prejudices."
A direct and trenchant reply to his critics was made by Mr. Ramsay MacDonald
at the I.L.P. Conference at Gloucester yesterday.
"It is important," he said, "for our critics to remember that there is a big difference
between carrying on a Government and passing resolutions at an I.L.P. Conference.
"The conception you have here," added Mr. MacDonald, "is of a Labour Govern-
ment composed of a body of men and women who have a steady, clear path along which
they can tread if they like, and, if they do not move, theirs is the responsibility for neglect
of duty.
"This is an absurd conception altogether. What is the position in which we find
ourselves in the House of Commons ?
"We are surrounded right and left by a seething, surging crowd, and what we have
to do is to keep ourselves together.
"We have got to keep our minds centred on Socialism, and we have to take steps
sometimes on one side and sometimes on the other side-sometimes even we have to make
a slight retreat in order that in a tremendously complex and pressing maze of interests
and prejudice we may make some progress.
"That is the problem of the Labour Opposition, and what the Labour Government
had to face.
Drama in Commons.
"Until you get that position into your minds and that is the dramatic situation
in the House of Commons-you will never be able to help us by your criticism or do us
justice by your praise.
"My answer to the criticisms that have been levelled against me and my colleagues
at this conference is in the language of the slave who was captured and was told by his
judge that he had got a good master to go to, that he would get good employment and
have a fine time.
"The slave's answer was, 'Very well, you take it yourself." (Hear, hear.)
"My observation to you and to many of my critics is: 'I wish yours was the job.'
"It is not enough to express sound ideals. You have got to help us to provide a
sound method of applying those principles. A Bill introduced in the House of Commons
on the lines of the resolution passed at this Conference (i.e., that calling on the Government
to appoint a National Commission to determine a living wage for all workers) would not
live for half an hour.

PARLIAMENTARY DEBATES.
CONDITION OF THE WORKING CLASSES.

gressive advances towards the social ownership and democratic control of staple industries
House declares that no permanent solution of the problem is possible apart from pre
and the banking system."
A few weeks ago the Prime Minister made a very eloquent plea for peace. He wa
attempting to defend the Party of which he is leader and to proclaim the difficulties

men fought in the War, and they produced nothing; but when they produced nothing
they had good suits of clothes, good boots, good food. To-day, they are producing and
working, and living on a starvation ration. We want peace. I hate strife; I hate con-
flict between people who ought to co-operate; but you cannot get peace on those terms.
Improve our conditions, and we will join hands with you to make the lot of our people
better than it is.

RUSSIA AND INTERNATIONAL UNITY.
Report to Affiliated Societies Trades Union Congress.
Meeting of General Council of International Federation of Trade Unions,
held at Amsterdam, 5th to 7th February, 1925. Discussions and corre-
spondence submitted.
(Continued from page 189 in the March Report.)
BRITISH GENERAL COUNCIL AND RUSSIA.
It is necessary to report what had also taken place between the British General Council
and the All-Russian Trade Union Congress.
The Russian delegates who attended the Hull Congress had extended an invitation
to the British General Council to attend their annual meeting which was to be held later
in Moscow. The General Council accepted the invitation, at the same time instructing
their delegates to take advantage of their visit by making an enquiry, for the benefit of
the organised workers in Great Britain, into the social, political, and economic conditions
of the people in Russia.
The result of their enquiries has been published separately, but during the time the
British delegates were in Moscow the Russian Trade Unionists requested the British
delegates to meet them in order to have informal conversations. At these gatherings,
suggestions were made by the Russian Trade Unionists with respect to International
unity, the nature of which will be indicated by the following reply, which the British
Delegation instructed the Secretary to send to the All-Russian Trade Union Council:
M. TOMSKY,
President, All-Russian Trade Union Congress.
DEAR COMRADE TOMSKY,
17th November, 1924.
In reply to your letter, dated 16th November, which you handed to me, I have
to inform you that the British Delegation met this morning and directed me to reply
to you as follows :-
I. The British Delegation desire to place on record their appreciation of
the action taken by the Presidium of the Russian Trades Congress for the purpose
of promoting international unity in trade union organisation and action, and
welcome the opportunity for consultation.
2. In recognition of our representative capacity, and being responsible to
the Trades Union Congress General Council as representing the All-British Trade
Union Movement, we will convey the proposals submitted to us for the con-
sideration and decision of our Council.
3. We declare our intention to move quickly with regard to the project,
and trust that the joint action of the Russian and British trade union organisa-
tions will stimulate the progress towards international trade union unity.
We are prepared to take the responsibility of agreement with the Russian Trade
Union Movement, such agreement to make provision for the promotion of the
following:-
1. To request the Amsterdam International to agree to a free and un-
conditional immediate conference with representatives of the Russian Trade
Union Movement.
2. To secure for the Presidium of the Russian Movement and the General
Council of the British Trades Union Congress full power to act jointly for the
purpose of promoting international unity.
With fraternal greetings and goodwill to yourself and your colleagues, on behalf
of the British Delegation.
Yours sincerely,
(Signed) FRED BRAMLEY.
Upon their return to England, the British delegates duly reported to the General
Council the result of this special meeting with the representatives of the All-Russian

MEETING OF THE I.F.T.U. GENERAL COUNCIL, AMSTERDAM.
Federation of Trade Unions met in Amsterdam, the major portion of the time being taken
From the 5th to the 7th February, 1925, the General Council of the International
up by a consideration of the relations between the I.F.T.U. and the All-Russian Trade
Union Council.
The following were present at the meeting:- Messrs. A. A. Purcell, President; the
three Vice-Presidents, L. Jouhaux, C. Mertens and Th. Leipart; the three Secretaries,
J. W. Brown, J. Oudegeest and Johann Sassenbach; the following representatives of the
various countries and groups of countries:- Messrs. Fred Bramley (Great Britain), Grass-
mann (Germany), D'Aragona (Italy), Caballero (Spain), Tayerle (Czecho-Slovakia)
Buisson (France), Dürr (Switzerland), Stenhuis (Holland), Zulawsky (Poland), Jaszai
(Hungary), Madsen (Denmark), and the three representatives of the International Trade
Secretariats, A. J. Cook (International Miners' Federation), E. Fimmen (Internationa
Transport Workers' Federation), and G. J. A. Smit (International Federation of Com-
mercial, Clerical and Technical Employees).
Before the debate opened, Mr. Purcell referred to the correspondence which had been
received by the I.F.T.U. from various affiliated national centres, containing statements
which he said misrepresented him, so far as they gave the impression that he was acting
in the capacity of President of the I.F.T.U. To infer in the slightest degree that he ever
spoke when in Russia as President of the I.F.T.U. was contrary to truth and to facts.
As regards the question of a World Congress he stated he was opposed to such a congress
as a preliminary step to unity. He also pointed out that each side was complaining
bitterly that the other side misrepresented it, and this fact alone could be used as an
argument for having a meeting to endeavour to come to some understanding.
In the debates reference was made to the tactics of the Communists in various countries,
to the unwarranted attacks upon the character and honesty of certain Trade Union Officials,
and, further, special reference was made to the suggestion the Russian Trade Unionists
had made of a World Labour Conference, overlooking the fact that this suggestion was
only made tentatively and as a point for discussion when the two parties met together.
The fact seemed to be quite ignored that the International Federation as it now exists,
is not even a European Federation, let alone a Universal Federation of Workers, and that
therefore the possibility of obtaining the accession of millions of new members should
induce a less rigorous and exclusive attitude on the part of the I.F.T.U.
It was proposed by the first speaker on the subject that the Secretariat should be
structed to communicate with the Russian Trade Unions to the effect that it was con-
sidered that the question was finished and that all correspondence must end. Another
speaker asserted that unity in the Labour Movement was the least of the cares of the
Russians, and that what they aimed at was to transform the Unions into instruments
to carry out the policy of the Russians. Another representative declared that to agree
to the proposal emanating from Great Britain would be to sign the death warrant of the
I.F.T.U.


---
241
The British point of view was put by Mr. Bramley, who moved that the proposal
contained in the letter quoted above, asking for an unconditional conference, should be
adopted by the meeting.
Mr. Bramley, in supporting the request of the British General Council, first of all
pointed out that the question of a World Conference had never been before the General
Council of the British Trades Union Congress, and he could not commit the British Section
to the proposal. Passing then to an analysis of the correspondence which had passed
between Moscow and Amsterdam. Mr. Bramley contended it showed that too much effort
had been made to emphasise points of disagreement and too little effort to discover points
of agreement. Further, it was foolish to attempt to settle such differences as existed by
means of correspondence, which was an obsolete method of discussing such important
and complicated questions. "We knew at Vienna," he said, "that before any inclusion
of Moscow Trade Union conference discussion would be necessary to prepare the way.
We never
conceived the possibility of settling the differences by means of correspondence, and we
never assumed for one moment that the conditions of affiliation would be the conditions
laid down as a preliminary to a Conference discussion."
Emphasis was also laid on the loss to the International Federation itself by the ex-
clusion of so important a country as Russia, the effects of whose industrial and economic
developments upon other nations were likely to be many and extensive.
That the British had spoken with the Russians in Moscow on the question of Inter-
national unity, was he claimed, no breach of the constitution of the I.F.T.U. " The
policy we are pursuing," he asserted, "is the purest international policy we can think of.
We are as much concerned regarding the welfare of the workers in all other countries in
this matter as we are concerned regarding the welfare of our own people whom we represent.
We believe that the inclusion of Russia would enlarge the influence of our International
Trade Union movement. We believe that the inclusion of Russia into our international
movement would strengthen the economic and political position of the working-class
throughout the world. We believe that the inclusion of Russia into the international
movement would also assist towards the establishment of world peace. We believe it
necessary for the Trade Union movement to be in the closest possible alliance with the
Russian Trade Union Section, especially for the complications we shall be called upon
to deal with probably in a short time arising out of the position in the East."
Continuing, Mr. Bramley declared that the policy of the Executive Committee of the
I.F.T.U. was a policy to which the British were entirely opposed. The policy seemed to
be this: "We have differences with Moscow, therefore no conference. If we were in agree-
ment with Moscow, then we would have a conference." That seemed to him to be turning
the process of logic upside down, and they could not understand it.
Mr. Bramley concluded his speech thus: "I appeal to you to set aside prejudice,
to try to develop before you settle this question a spirit of toleration with the weaknesses,
with the methods, with the tactics of those to whom you are opposed. In Great Britain
we take the view that the development of an all-inclusive International is desirable.
Unity of purpose is a very important question. A united Trade Union movement will
make a wonderful difference regarding our relationships between one country and another,
and for those reasons I submit the proposal of the British section in direct and uncom-
promising opposition to the resolution suggested this morning."
After other representatives had spoken, a resolution was moved by Mr. Stenhuis,
of Holland, and Mr. Smit (Secretariats) which declared that the I.F.T.U. should convene
a conference when the All-Russian Council of Trade Unions intimated its desire to be
admitted to the I.F.T.U.
A member of the I.F.T.U. General Council suggested that a Committee of Enquiry
should be sent by the I.F.T.U. to Russia, whilst a further suggestion was made that, as
there were so many differences of opinion, a small Committee should be appointed to
endeavour to arrive at a compromise.
VOTING ON RESOLUTIONS.
The Resolution moved by Mr. Bramley was then put to the vote. It reads as follows:
"The British Section propose the convening of an unconditional conference for
informal discussion purposes, at which both sides would be free to express their
representative opinion without being tied to any formulæ or constitution, it being
understood, of course, that the findings of such a conference should be considered
as a preliminary to a mandatory conference to follow after reports of the preliminary
discussions had been given to the bodies responsible for the final conclusions."
The result of the voting was :
6 for the resolution,
13 against,
I abstention.

NOTHING ATTEMPTED-NOTHING DONE.
First Instalment of Tory Rule Ended. Mr. Baldwin's Barren Record.
With the first round of the Parliamentary battle at an end, it is possible to look back
over the past four months and make a few comparisons.
Two facts emerge from such a review: firstly, that the Tories have made no attempt
to fulfil their election promises, and, secondly, that the accomplishments standing to their
credit are infinitesimal when compared with those of the Labour Government during the
corresponding period of 1924.
Last year, in the period preceding the Easter recess, Labour had only 47 Parliamentary
days, as compared with the 57 Parliamentary days which Mr. Baldwin's Government has
enjoyed this year.
Self-Confessed Failure.
In his manifesto at the last election he proclaimed that the "Unionist Party would be
unfaithful to its principles and to its duty if it did not treat the task of grappling with
the unemployment of our people and with the serious condition of industry as a primary
obligation."
The figures show, by his own criterion, that the Tory Party has been unfaithful to its
principles, for whereas the number of unemployed when Labour went out of office was
1.247.000. it had risen by 84,000 to 1,331,205 when the official statistics were compiled
for the March issue of the Labour Gazette.
Hope Deferred.
Another of Mr. Baldwin's election pronouncements was that "the problem of the
cost of foodstuffs is one which demands careful investigation by a Royal Commission."
Careful "whitewashing" would have been a much better expression to use, in the light
of what has transpired at the Commission, but even the whitewash has not yet been pro-
duced, despite the oft-repeated promises of the President of the Board of Trade. Time
after time the report was promised, and as regularly its publication has been deferred.
The penultimate promise was for Easter, but a question asked two days before the adjourn-
ment revealed that another three weeks will still have to pass. In the meantime the cost
of living is still 79 per cent. above pre-war level.
Disregard of pledges, too, has been the keynote of the Government's policy in regard
is essential," said the
to national expenditure. "The most rigid economy
Prime Minister in his manifesto. And yet he has produced Military, Naval, and Air Force
Estimates which show an increase of more than £6 million over those of the Labour Govern-
ment last year. Moreover, the ₤11 million saving which Labour effected by abandoning
the Singapore Naval Base has been despised, and the taxpayer is to be burdened with
that unnecessary sum.
One of the most appealing of Mr. Baldwin's promises was that in which he foreshadowed
increased old age pensions, and pensions for widows and fatherless children. These have
not materialised, and after being questioned four times in four successive weeks the Premier
has had to confess that his scheme is not ready.
Farmers Forgotten.
Similarly, nothing has been done to redeem the pledge that "the great basic industry
of agriculture should be not merely preserved, but restored to a more prosperous condition."
Neither farmers nor farm workers have yet received anything for which they can thank
the Government.
A few things, of course, the Government has done, but these are mostly in the nature
of class legislation. The Bill to extend the Rent Acts is frankly a landlord's measure.
Not only does it provide that control can come to an end in two years' time, but it declines
to sanction any reduction in the 40 per cent. excess rent which may now be charged, nor
does it bring back under control the thousands of houses that have escaped from the
meshes of the Act by becoming vacant for a period.
In international affairs Mr. Chamberlain has thrown over the Geneva Protocol, which
paved the way for universal peace by arbitration, disarmament and security, and proposes
in its stead to enter into the same type of restricted alliance that led to the great war in
1914, despite the Tory professions of faith in the League of Nations which were embodied
in Mr. Baldwin's manifesto at the last election.
Viewed on the performances of its first session, the Government has failed lamentably
to fulfil its promises. And unfortunately there is no reason for supposing that as it gets
older it will improve.
C. E. L.
-Labour Press Service, 16th April, 1925.
