SINISTER ATTACK ON WORKERS.
Meaning of Campaign against International Labour Office.
The 8-Hour Day. Mr. Poulton's Acid Test for Premier.
“The Conservative victory in the British General Election has undoubtedly produced
a reactionary atmosphere in employers’ circles, and this is having its effects in international
quarters," said Mr. E. L. Poulton, General Secretary of the National Union of Boot and
Shoe Operatives, yesterday.
Mr. Poulton had just returned from attending the meeting at Geneva of the governing
body of the International Labour Office, on which body he is the British workers' repre-
sentative.
He stated that at that meeting it was made clear that a powerful section is determined
to take advantage of the existing situation to hamper and weaken the activities of the
Office.
“They do not attack the Office openly," he said, "but by insidious newspaper
campaign they are seeking to create the impression that the Office is useless to the workers
of Great Britain.
“At the same time attempts are made to curtail the work of the Office, and to reduce
it to the position of a mere registering machine.”
Child Labour in the East.
The ostensible reason for this endeavour was that if the Office did more than this
it was going outside its powers.
“This,” said Mr. Poulton, “is an entirely false interpretation of the functions of the
Office as set out in the Peace Treaty.
“It is one of the duties of the Office to collect and distribute information with regard
to conditions of labour throughout the world. To do this, it must get into touch with all
kinds of bodies.
“For instance, in regard to the conditions of labour in the East, especially child
labour, it is necessary to use the information collected by the Y.M.C.A. and other 'pro-
pagandist' bodies, and to correspond with them.
“As a matter of fact, the Governing Body itself, at its meeting last week, passed a
resolution welcoming the report on child labour, and expressed the hope that the Shanghai
municipal authorities would secure the enforcement of adequate limitations on the employ-
ment of child labour. It also expressed the desire that similar action would be taken in
other concessions and settlements, in which factories exist.
“The real reason, I believe, for the hostile attitude towards the International Labour
Office is that the critics look upon the Office as the institution which keeps alive the possi-
bility of an international eight-hour day.
“They hope that, if they can hamper and weaken the Office, they may be able to
prevent an Eight-hour Day Act passing.
“They know very well that the chief reason why Germany, France and Belgium and
other States have not ratified the Convention is that Great Britain has not done so, and
that British employers intend that, so far as they are concerned, it shall not be ratified.
“If they can, as they hope, prevent the Office from carrying out efficiently the duties
imposed upon it by the Peace Treaty, they believe that the demand for ratification will
gradually die out, and they may then be free to institute a longer working day or week.
Workers Warned.
“I utter this warning, not only to the British workers, but also to our Continental
comrades.
“If the International Labour Office is turned into a mere lifeless concern for registering
Government decisions, then good-bye to any speedy improvement in the lot of the workers.”
The workers’ organisations, therefore, should use every effort to ensure that the Office
and its work on behalf of labour all over the world was maintained, and that the employers’
campaign against it was fought to the utmost.
Mr. Poulton proceeded to ask what had Mr. Baldwin to say with regard to the attitude
of the employers ?
He had preached peace, and appealed to the workers and employers to discuss their
problems amicably together.
Was he prepared to make good his words and to work for industrial peace and progress
through existing machinery of which the Office was an important example ?
If he was sincere, then the Eight-hour Convention and the Whi e Lead decisions should
be at once dealt with by Parliament.—The Daily Herald, 8th April, 1925.

CHANGES IN COST OF LIVING: STATISTICS FOR 1st APRIL, 1925.
Summary: Average Increases since July, 1914.
All Items included .. .. .. 75 per cent.
Food only .. .. .. .. 70 "
FOOD.
The average level of retail prices of food was appreciably lower at 1st April than a
month earlier. This was mainly due to seasonal reductions in the prices of eggs and of
milk, but fish, potatoes and tea were also cheaper, on the average, at the later date, and
the price of bread was reduced (by d. or Id. per 4 lbs.) in about a quarter of the places
from which returns were received. On the other hand, there were small increases in the
average prices of British mutton and of bacon.
As a net result of all the changes recorded, the average increase over the level of
July, 1914, in the retail prices (in Great Britain and Northern Ireland) of the articles of
food included in these statistics was about 70 per cent. at 1st April, as compared with
about 76 per cent. at 28th February.
-The Ministry of Labour Gazette, April, 1925.

AGED WOMAN BURNED TO DEATH.
Smoke issuing from the letter-box of 57 Beaconsfield Terrace, Northampton, yesterday
morning caused Mr. W. Pitts, Secretary of the local branch of the National Union of Boot
and Shoe Operatives, who lives next door, to force an entry at the back. He found the
house full of smoke, and upstairs in a back bedroom the body of Miss Elizabeth Austin,
88, who lived alone, She had apparently been dead some hours, and appearances suggested
that she had risen during the night and lighted a taper, which had ignited the bedclothes.
Morning Advertiser, 30th March, 1925.

I.L.P. BUSINESS.
Sale of Boot Factory that is no longer Paying.
As the business is no longer a financial success, the National Administrative Council
of the Independent Labour Party has decided to discontinue its boot business at North-
ampton.
This business was founded seventeen years ago to furnish funds for the local and
National I.L.P.
Until 1919 the undertaking was a distinct financial success, and several thousands
of pounds were sent to the national movement.
After 1919 the company suffered from the slump common to the shoe manufacturers
of the country, and during the last five years it has only just kept its head above water.
One of the officials told the Daily Sketch that the position was largely due to a mistaken
policy, but he was of opinion that matters would have improved had the council held on.
When the Northampton committee had the business in their own hands, he continued,
it was under the complete supervision of men who had spent their whole lives in the indus-
try, but the National Committee had not sought local assistance outside that of the manager.
-Daily Sketch, 28th March, 1925.

INDUSTRIAL COUNCIL AND ORGANISATION.

"One ship drives east and one drives west
By the very same wind that blows:
'Tis the set of the sails, and not the gales,
That tells which way she goes.
Like the waves of the sea are the gales that blow
As we journey together through life:
'Tis the set of the soul that determines the goal
And not the storm or the strife."
I gave a beggar from my little store
Of well-earned gold. He spent the shining ore;
He came again, and yet again, still cold
And hungry as before.
I gave a thought, and through that thought of mine,
He found himself a man, supreme, divine,
Bold, clothed, and crowned with blessings manifold,
And now he begs no more.

INTERNATIONAL LABOUR OFFICE NEWS.
ACCIDENT COMPENSATION.
Equal Treatment for Alien Workers.
An international agreement placing the alien worker on the same footing as the national
worker in the matter of accident compensation will be voted upon at the Seventh Annual
Session of the International Labour Conference, which opens at Geneva, on 19th May.
A provisional Draft Convention was adopted on this question at the Sixth Session
in its desire to make its work still more effective. In preparation for the final vote at the
opening, any amendments they considered necessary to facilitate ratification of the pi
coming meeting, Governments were asked to send, not later than four months before it
posed Draft Convention, and a report has now been issued by the International Lat
Office containing the amendments received.
Great Britain suggests an amendment which is merely a question of improving the
drafting and bringing the English text into closer correspondence with the French text.
The German Government thinks that it should be definitely settled that the Con
vention in no way applies to anything which happened before it was adopted and proposes
an amendment to that effect.
Norway is of opinion that residence in a country should be an essential condition of
receipt of accident compensation by a foreign worker, and that other cases should be left
to reciprocity agreements among individual States. India agrees to the principle tha
there shall be no qualification as to residence, but does not wish to bind herself to a genera
conclusion of agreements with other countries regarding the special arrangements to be
made for non-residing workers.
A certain number of Governments have informed the International Labour Office
that they have no amendments to propose and will be glad to consider those suggested
by other States.
The Conference will also finally vote on a proposed Recommendation on the settle-
ment of disputed points in connection with the payment of compensation for accidents
to workers not residing in the particular State.
SAFETY IN THE FACTORY.
Industrial Safety Survey is the name of a new publication which is being issued
once every two months by the International Labour Office of the League of Nations.
The first number, which is now ready, contains, besides many articles, reproductions of
"safety first" posters from the United States, Japan, Great Britain, China, Belgium,
Chile, and the Netherlands.
"to serve as a medium for the
The aims of the new publication are given in a foreword which, after recalling the
attitude of "almost fatalistic pessimism" which used to prevail regarding accidents in
the factory-" industrial accidents being regarded as a more or less inevitable incident
in the process of production "-states that its desire is
direct exchange of ideas and experiences both between the different countries and between
employers, workers, and factory inspectors. It will publish articles on technical develop-
ments in the sphere of accident prevention, articles discussing accidents of special interest
and the lessons to be learned from them, and statistical studies on the progress of accident
prevention in the different countries or in separate industries or processes.
"At the same time it is not proposed to limit its contents to articles such as these,
which presuppose certain definite results; it is also intended to record the efforts and
activities in the field of accident prevention which are going on from day to day." The
Industrial Safety Survey will therefore report on new regulations in the various countries,
subject. The Survey will also contain regular reports from the industrial safety organisa
factory inspectors' reports and the like, and will review fully books dealing with the
tions in a large number of countries.

INTERNATIONAL FEDERATION OF TRADE UNIONS.
CHILD LABOUR IN THE UNITED STATES.
After five hours’ discussion, the Republican Party of the United States Parliam
has decided to take no action on the Child Labour Amendment (enabling, not compell
the various Federal States to pass legislation restricting Child Labour). By this de
the Republican Party has definitely ranged itself on the side of the organised manuf
turers, although it had earlier declared in favour of ratification of the Amendment.
The storm centre of the Child Labour agitation is North Carolina, one of the
important textile manufacturing districts of the U.S.A. It was in North Carolina.
the suits originated which led to legal decisions denouncing two federal child labour
as contrary to the American Constitution. But the textile manufacturers were not ca
to bear the odium of figuring in the public eyes as the champions of child labour. So
literature against the Amendment which flooded the country was sent out by the Par
States Rights League; and it is only recent investigations of the United Textile Wor
Union which have brought to light the fact that the League is the creation of the edit
a textile bulletin, and that its chairman is a millowner!

MONTHLY REPORT.
25TH MAY, 1925.
TRADE
for the month is about the same as the previous month, the figures in the
Ministry of Labour Gazette being as follows:-
BOOT AND SHOE INDUSTRY.
Employment showed a decline in most districts compared with the previous month.
Much short time was worked throughout the industry, and in most districts the factories
were closed for extended holidays at Easter.
The percentage of workpeople unemployed, as indicated by the unemployment books
lodged at Employment Exchanges, was 10.2 on the 27th April, 1925, as compared with
9.2 on the 23rd March, 1925, and 10.2 on the 28th April, 1924.
Returns from firms employing over 37,500 operatives in the week ended 25th April,
1925, showed that about 31 per cent. of these operatives worked short time in that week,
to the extent of about 1 hours each, on an average.
Employment remained generally moderate in London. It was quiet, and not so good
as in March, at Leicester; a good deal of short time was worked, and the Easter holiday
was extended by most firms. At Northampton there was much short time, and most
firms closed for periods varying from five to ten days at Easter; but employment, taken
as a whole, remained fair. It was poor, and worse than in the previous month, at Hinckley,
and the great majority of workpeople were reported to be on short time. Employment
varied from poor to fair in the Higham and Rushden district; it was generally not quite
so good as in March. At Wellingborough employment showed a decline, and was very
slack; short time was worked in practically all the factories. A decline was also reported
at Kettering, where employment was generally slack; not more than three-quarter time
was worked on the average.
At Leeds employment again declined and was bad in the heavy boot section, and most
factories closed for ten days at Easter. Factories in Leeds producing light footwear
continued busy. At Stafford most of the factories were reported to be working full time
but employment in general was still slack. There was a decline at Norwich, largely in the
turnshoe section of the trade, and employment was only fair on the average; much short
time was worked. In the Bristol and Kingswood district employment was again slack,
and slightly worse than in March; extended holidays at Easter were general, and, when
the factories reopened, irregular short-time working was common.

HOLIDAY (PROVISION) SCHEME AND OUTWORKERS.
Decision of the National Joint Standing Committee.
A Meeting of the National Joint Standing Committee was held on Tuesday,
28th ult.. to consider a case remitted to the Standing Committee dealing with
the Statement for Louis XV. Heel Work (London Wholesale Trade), as
follows:--
In January, 1925, the Standing Committee for the Statement for Louis
XV. Heel Work (London Wholesale Trade) considered a claim, which had
been made by the operatives concerned, in the following terms:--
"That the Holiday (Provision) Scheme under paragraph 9 of the
National Conference (September, 1924) Agreement, shall apply to out-
workers employed under the Statement for Louis XV. Heel Work (London
Wholesale Trade)."
The contention of the employers concerned was that the Holiday (Pro-
vision) Scheme is only applicable to indoor workers.
The question in issue involves the interpretation of paragraph 9 of the
National Agreement, September, 1924, and of the Holiday (Provision) Scheme
therein referred to, and the Board of Arbitration, being unable to reach agree-
ment, referred the whole matter to the National Joint Standing Committee
under paragraph 23 of the said National Agreement.
The said Joint Standing Committee met on 28th April, 1925, and heard
the representatives of the operatives and employers concerned.
The decision of the Committee is that, upon the proper interpretation of
paragraph 9 of the said National Agreement, the Holiday (Provision) Scheme
therein mentioned is applicable to operatives who are outworkers as well as
to those who are indoor workers.
It is not within the province of the National Joint Standing Committee to
give directions as to the manner in which employers should apply the Holiday
(Provision) Scheme to their particular operatives who are outworkers, but the
Committee would point out that the contribution of Is. 2d. provided in the
Scheme was originally based upon a weekly wage of 56s., which is equivalent
to one farthing in the Is. paid, and that this method of contribution, which
has already been adopted by some firms in respect of their outworkers, seems
to be a proper compliance with the requirements of the Scheme; subject
always to the proviso that there is no obligation upon either employer or
operative to contribute beyond the sum of Is. 2d. per week.
Neither is it within the powers of the National Joint Standing Committee
to determine the date from which their decision shall operate, but the Committee
suggest that in this case a convenient and equitable date would be on the
expiration of the forthcoming Whitsuntide holidays.
Dated this 30th day of April, 1925.
W. ADDINGTON WILLIS,
Chairman.

SUDDEN DEATH OF OUR COLLEAGUE, MR. C. BLEAKLEY.
It is indeed with sorrow and very extreme regret we have to record
the passing away of our colleague, Mr. BLEAKLEY, in a very sudden
manner. Mr. Bleakley was in his usual health, when on the 17th
inst. he had a sudden attack of heart failure, resulting in his death within
one hour of the attack. This is indeed a blow to us, the more so on
account of its suddenness. Our colleague died "in harness," he being
engaged, right up to his passing away, in work on behalf of and for the
Union. Mr. Bleakley for many years gave of his best to the workers.
whether for our members or the wider sphere of the workers generally.
His death will leave a gap in the ranks of those who day in and day out
spend themselves in the movement for the benefit of mankind.
Mr. C. Bleakley was for 14 years a member of the Council, and we
always found him a staunch upholder of the workers' cause and deter-
mined to do all possible to help forward the work of the Union. We
tender to Mrs. Bleakley and the family our sincere and heartfelt sympathy
in this tragic loss which has befallen them. We know the pain and sorrow
must be increased by the suddenness of the loss. We trust that such
sorrow and pain may to some extent be lessened by the fact of the high
regard with which Mr. Bleakley was held by those who knew him for
his sterling value and worth.
POLITICAL.
Parliament is now in session ; one of the first things to be introduced
after reassembling was the Budget for the year 1925-6. All sorts of rumours
were about as to what the Budget would contain, and the relief it would give.
We venture to say from the standpoint of the workers, who form the over-
whelming majority of the inhabitants of the country, that it is a very consider-
able disappointment. Here and there may be found remissions of taxation,
but there is no radical change whereby real relief is given on the one hand,
and there is an absence of that feeling of securing of income for the workers
on the other. Those who pay
SUPER-TAX,
which obviously only refers to those who have most of the material wealth, will
have reductions ranging from 9d. in the £ on incomes £2,000 to £2,500; to 6d.
on incomes £10,000 to £15,000, but no change above that total; whilst on the
other hand, although named in the Budget that an Insurance and Old Age


---
Pension Scheme is to be introduced, the workers will be called upon to pay
then quota weekly. Numbers of publications have unhesitatingly called this
the "Rich Man's Budget."
The Labour Party in the House are doing what is possible day by day to
not the reactionary clauses of the Budget, and to make it if at all possible
tredoveptable to them, which means also to the great majority of the people
of this country. Their task is a very formidable one, because of the big majority
by which the present Government is backed up. It certainly seems to us a
powiat war of insuring that

"PEACE IN OUR TIME,"
which the Prime Minister pleaded for in a recent speech in the House of Com-
mons
For "peace to obtain in our time," which the Premier asked for,
clearly implies justice and equity being predominant, and such plans adopted
as will ensure help and assistance to those least able to help themselves. Take
for instance the vast army of unemployed in this country, and add to that
army the number of dependants upon them for their daily bread. We venture
say that these people will wonder where their relief comes in, and ask what
the Budget is to them in their task of striving day by day to find employment.
in this connection we would make special reference to the attitude of the
Government in regard to the
48-HOURS WEEK.
A Bill was brought in for its Second Reading on the 1st inst. by the Labour
Party upon the lines agreed at the Washington Convention in 1919, at any rate
so far as Great Britain is concerned. Everything was done by the Labour
Party to put the points before the House, and to call attention to the obliga-
tions entered into by this country; all were of no avail, because when the
vote was taken for the second reading there was a majority of 95 against.
We hope the members will not only take note of these things, but that
they will have the effect of acting as a spur and inspiration to continually
keep our point of view before the public, so that sooner, much sooner than
some anticipate, there may be a Government in power who will really deal
in a drastic manner with the conditions of the people of these islands.

What the "Shoe and Leather News" of 30th April, 1925, says upon
Banks. Extract from an Article:
"WHAT'S WRONG WITH TRADE?"
We are afraid that it is not too much to say that the banking interests of Britain are
using their now tremendous power for their own profit regardless of immediate trade
considerations.
It is a false policy and hard to understand even from the point of view of the bankers
themselves.
The power of the banks has become immense, and assumes something like a peril
to the whole commercial fabric.
They appear to have the Government-or, at any rate, the Exchequer, in their
pockets, and regardless of all intentions and efforts to nurse commerce back into health,
vitalise enterprise, and solve or allay unemployment, the banking interests are now
throttling trade.
Is there no way in which their selfish ramifications can be successfully thwarted ?
We imagine the Government-aware as they must be of the circumstances-have
this question seriously under consideration.
With more elastic credits and renewed confidence trade will, we believe, quickly again
get into its stride!
Commercial fate is at the moment in the laps of the gods (the banks and the
Exchequer). We hope they will be kind.

LEAGUE OF NATIONS UNION.
Forms of Application for Corporate Membership may be obtained from 15 Grosvenor
Crescent, London, S.W. I. Individuals of branches are admitted as Corporate Members
of the League of Nations Union at an annual subscription of £1.
The objects of the Union are :-
1. To secure the whole-hearted acceptance by the British people of the League of
Nations as the guardian of international right, the organ of international co-operation,
the final arbiter in international differences, and the supreme instrument for removing
injustices which may threaten the peace of the world.
2. To foster mutual understanding, goodwill, and habits of co-operation and fair
dealing between the peoples of different countries.
3. To advocate the full development of the League of Nations so as to bring about
such a world organisation as will guarantee the freedom of nations, act as trustee and
guardian of backward races and undeveloped territories, maintain international order,
and finally liberate mankind from the curse of war.

BRANCH REPORTS.
ARBROATH. Our trade still remains bad, and there seems little chance
of its recovering any this year. All over our little township things are bad, and
the lack of purchasing power has its reflex in this fashion. The Employment
Exchange figures at the end of the month show 1,030 claimants drawing benefit
for total unemployment, with 199 working short time. The number affected
altogether must be very large, and such a shrinkage of the power to buy has a
very bad effect on the market. That, of course, is not the only factor which is
keeping our factories in a stagnant condition. People still require footwear,
and it is a curious revelation after inquiry to find local people buying outside
makes instead of patronising factories nearer home. Not that people will
ever allow their choice to be interfered with to any great extent, but it would
seem only a matter of drawing their attention to the matter, to get a fairly
and in spite of general sympathy with the poor shoe-working fraternity, the
large measure of support for a local industry. This does not work out, however,
public in this quarter make little or no attempt to help the trade by concen-
trating their demand on local products. Of course manufacturers would need
to play the game in return, and give full value in return, even if that varies
not fixed too high. Many of the sample lines seen up here are cheap enough,
but have a style and finish equal to the best, so when manufacturers attempt
to imitate they should aim at what compares equally and not waste time and
money on a copy of a style vitiated by a wrong choice of materials for the
purpose. Coarse-grained inferior leathers never lose their appearance or
cheapness, and however well made will repel a customer, whereas the same
customer may, as like as not, be tempted by something just as cheap but which
has been chosen with this elementary understanding of psychology uppermost.
We are always hoping for this kind of insight and acumen on the part of local
employers, to come to the rescue of our members, and so provide them periods of
employment. Last month we wrote of some methods of getting orders, and we
sometimes wonder how it would do for a manufacturer to produce several
thousands of a cheap line with an attractive appearance, and then let them be
disposed of by means of "bargain sales" in populous country districts. Every
now and again shops are opened by strangers who have large consignments
of cheap boots and shoes to sell, and it is an object lesson to see the stocks
dwindle. We have seen this happen even when the stocks were of the trashiest
description, and we could imagine an honest, all-leather line meeting with
similar success. As an auxiliary form of trading we recommend this to our
manufacturers, and even although little profit was realised, it might keep the
machinery running fuller time, and keep men from rusting in idleness. It may
not seem so dignified a business as the present production for the ordinary
market, but what it lost in dignity it might compensate for in sales. At present
all those skilled workers are walking the streets for two-thirds of a working week,
and any effort would be justified which absorbed their labour power to the full,
even in the way of producing and hawking alternately.
BELFAST.—Trade is in a very bad state at present, without the least
sign of improvement.
CHESHAM.—Trade here is still very slack, and at present very little
sign of improvement.
CHESTERFIELD.—Some of our members unemployed, and some of our
shopmates are only making 21 hours per week.
CORK.—Trade continues to remain good.
DERBY.—Trade in Derby continues fair, but we still have many shoe
operatives out of work, and we continue to have a very heavy sick list.

DESBOROUGH.Trade with us is very bad, most of our members being
on very short time. On Saturday, 18th April, the Northants District Council
held their quarterly meeting at Desborough, when the General President.
Mr. T. F. Richards, gave an address on "Should National Agreements be
Legalised?" Mr. Richards gave a very good and thoughtful address, advancing
many arguments in his usual able manner. A good discussion followed, with a
majority of the delegates in favour of legislation.

We regret to report the death of Mr. R. M. Sanders, the first secretary
of the Desborough Branch. It was largely due to his untiring efforts
that a branch of the Union was formed here in 1893. Mr. Sanders was a
man of great ability, and served the town well in many ways. His wife
pre-deceased him by only two days, and both were buried at the same
time, on Thursday, 14th May. We extend our sincere sympathy to the
family who have so suddenly been doubly bereaved.

EDINBURGH. - Trade in the Repairing Section has been farly good
during the past month. New workers, however, are still doing short time.
We have now concluded negotiations with the Yuot Manufacturing Co. They
have agreed to put our Minimum Rate of Wages into operation on an agreed
date. This may seem very little progress, but when it is considered that until
recently the firm did not allow their operatives the right to join up into the
Union, some progress has at least been made, again showing how needful it
is for all workers to be organised. Another successful meeting of the Scottish
Advisory Committee has been held. If for no other purpose than the exchange
of views which take place this Committee is justified. Now about organising.
There is certainly in some of the Scottish districts a good field whereby our
organisers could work. Of course, we notice by the Monthly Report that our
organisers are nearly all employed in the London area, which, we believe,
needs them, but some might be spared for other districts which also need
wakening up. We had one of the best May Day Demonstrations held on
3rd May under the auspices of the Local Committee. It takes some time to
get the worker to understand that May Day is his day; but when once it has
dawned there is no going back. One is pleased to see how the younger members
of the movement are adhering to this annual festival. Congratulations to our
colleague, Mr. W. R. Smith, J.P., on his report of the Food Commission.
GLASGOW. Trade with us is fair, but some of the factories are having
a very lean time, scarcely working alternative weeks. Although the month
has been very wet the shoe trade shows little activity. Our sick expenditure
is a little high for the month.
HIGHAM AND RUSHDEN.-Trade during the month has fallen off
considerably. At Bozeat Messrs. Drage & Sons have discharged the whole of
their staff, about 170, most of them residing in Bozeat, but a large number at
Olney (in the Wellingborough Branch); also in surrounding villages. Hopes
are entertained that the firm will be able to come to a satisfactory arrangement
with their creditors, whereby the firm may recommence early in May and
re-engage at least two-thirds of their old employees. At Finedon trade remains
very slack, a large number still being unemployed, with no immediate hope of
work. Higham Ferrers and Irthlingborough are about normal. In Rushden
a slight increase in the unemployed lists. Wollaston trade is very poor. We
are informed at the local Labour Exchange that two to three hundred are
drawing Government Unemployment Pay owing to (1) working part time,
and (2) standing off. Raunds is fairly well off, except for the usual unemploy-
ment common to this section: in other words, it is usual for certain unemploy-
ment between Easter and Whitsuntide in respect to Government work, but
it is much better than last year. We wonder why these Departments do not

KINGSWOOD AND DISTRICT. - Trade very quiet, unemployment

LEICESTER WOMEN'S. - We have to report that unemployment is

Mr. C. Bleakley's sudden death, and send our condolences to his family, and

LIVERPOOL. - The boot repairing trade is steadily improving. Those of
our members who are fortunate enough to get annual holidays with pay are
taking them in relays, as we are not like manufacturing districts in the matter
of closing down; repairing shops are always open except on statutory holidays.
Since writing up our last report we have had the Budget presented to us with
the usual rhetoric eloquence, and whilst we admit there are some good points
in the scheme which will ultimately benefit the workers, yet at the same time
we have to confess to an antipathy against swallowing the Protectionist medi-
cine that is given with it, notwithstanding the thick sugar coating of the remedy.
MAYBOLE. - Trade is very slack but sickness light. It is generally
rumoured that there is better times in store in the course of a few weeks. We
hope this is true as the people in this district have had a very bad time. We
look forward to a spell of good work, when we hope to try and organise the
Branch to what it should be.

NORWICH. No improvement in trade during month.
PLYMOUTH. We regret to report sickness and unemployment unusually
heavy while short time still continues. This leads us to view the new Pensions
Bill of the Government from a different angle to many of our fellow workers
throughout the country, for while we feel that insurance against old age,
sickness and unemployment are most admirable schemes for those with a living
wage and fixed or secured incomes, we must say that the future cannot be
faced without a good deal of anxiety and perturbation by our members, whose
wages from week to week are an unknown and unreliable quantity. Many of
our members are asking this simple, yet difficult question:
How shall I live"?
Fivepence health insurance, sevenpence unemployment, now another fourpence
halfpenny for old age insurance; total one shilling and sixpence halfpenny.
This must be paid how short the time worked or how small the wage earned;
then the landlord must be paid, the grocer, the tailor, the butcher, and a host
where does the strong arm of the law come in to enforce a living wage for the
of others, or the strong arm of the law is brought in to enforce payment; but
worker on short time unable to swim against the tide? Are all the powers
that be going to be brought in, to draw money from a working-man's pocket
that has never been placed therein? No wonder the workers are scratching
their heads and swearing in unknown tongues. Is it not time we were assured
of a living for the present? Will someone get an amendment into this new
Pensions Bill, exempting from payment any worker not receiving a living wage?
Certainly this is not impossible, seeing that for many years it has been found
practicable to exempt persons from paying income tax with an income of £250
per annum.
STREET. There is no improvement in the state of trade and very
irregular time is being worked in consequence. We are pleased to be able to
say that a dispute which had arisen over closing prices is now satisfactorily
settled. It was submitted to Arbitration with Mr. Addington Willis as Umpire.
An agreement, however, was finally arrived at by the employers consenting
to give the price which we originally asked for the particular shoe in dispute.
We had the assistance of our General President and Mrs. M. J. Bell-Richards,
and we are grateful to them for the help given. A meeting of members, which
was addressed by Mr. and Mrs. Richards, was not so well attended as we would
have liked, but it was none the less a most useful meeting, and the information
given, together with a strong appeal for loyalty among members, is bound to
bring a closer adherence to Union policy.
WATERFORD.-Trade continues fair.
WELLINGBOROUGH.-Trade seems to have taken wings, unemploy-
ment in the town and district covered by the branch being simply awful.
GREAT YARMOUTH.-Trade in Great Yarmouth is very slow.

FELLOW MEMBERS,
The first week of the past month was spent in the London area, where further efforts
were made to strengthen our position. Following upon the agreement reached with some
employers in regard to the Holiday Scheme, a number of other firms were visited with the
view of extending the understanding so far as this part of the Terms of Settlement are
concerned. It can truthfully be said that it is not lack of pressure from the Union that
is the cause of any failure to establish these conditions, but where obstinacy on the part
of employers is linked up with indifference of the operatives, the task is not an easy one.
It is up to us to find out some other method of compelling observance. I am persuaded
this can be done, and I trust a rude awakening may be the lot of those manufacturers who
fail in their obligation to the industry.

A meeting of the operatives at Wachman's was held to see how far it was possible to
to use our organised strength to the advantage of our members there. But there appears
to be great difficulty in obtaining that real trade union spirit among many of the operatives.
At all these meetings much of our time is taken up by attempts to stiffen up the workpeople
to an attitude of manliness and self-respect regarding factory conditions. We keep on
in this work in the hope that some day our efforts will bear fruit.

From London I proceeded to the Leicester district for work in the county area.
The Leicester branches had taken steps to make the efforts of Mr. McCarthy and myself
as successful as possible. The No. 1 Branch being more affected in these places, had
arranged for us to get to work without delay, and a number of meetings have been held
at Syston, Rothley, Whetstone and Cosby.

The state of trade has not made our work easy, as on one or two occasions the standing
off of the operatives prevented the meetings being held, and at others fewer were present
than otherwise would have been the case. But on the whole the work has been productive
of good, and I am persuaded that increased membership will follow.

The position in these areas is very interesting. There is so far as we can judge not any
great evasion of our conditions, nor is there any opposition to the operatives becoming
members of the Union, as one found in some instances direct encouragement rather than
otherwise to the operatives becoming members of our organisation.

There has been a readiness on the part of the workpeople to come back earlier, whereby
a reasonable chance is available for a meeting. On one occasion we had a full 15 minutes


---
287
talk, which gave an opportunity to state our case with greater fullness than is usual at
dinner-hour meetings. There is a little stubbornness on the part of some which it is our
task to break down, and by return visits to these particular places we hope to succeed in
time.
Our claim on these operatives is a strong one. It is obvious that in these small places
had our Union not exercised its influence, the conditions would have been far below what
they are to-day. The whole standard of comfort has been raised, a new outlook on life
has been made possible, and the original idea of some of the firms that went into the
country from the town to escape our conditions has been frustrated. The notion that
these firms now compete unfairly with the larger centres is somewhat dispersed by the
state of trade at many of them.
In conjunction with the Executive Council 1 attended a meeting of the Joint Industrial
Council. The various items on the agenda were dealt with, and the one that in my judg-
ment is of the utmost importance to ourselves, and indeed also to the employers, was dealt
with on lines that one hopes, if pressed on firm and wise lines, should be productive of
observance of our National Agreements. It is an obligation that should be accepted
much good. It is obviously the duty of both sides to use all their powers to secure the
fully and completely, and if the best minds are brought to bear upon the matter, I am
convinced a way will be found that will strengthen our position as an industry, and our
methods of procedure will be further justified.
Another attempt has been made with the Pressroom Statement at Norwich, the
employer concerned having recovered from his recent illness, and we hope that the next
few weeks may see something fixed that will be of help and advantage to our members
in that area.
I trust I may be pardoned a reference to my report as a member of the Royal Commis-
sion on Food Prices. I greatly appreciate the decision of the Executive Council to print
same in the Monthly Report. It has meant a somewhat strenuous effort, and one can
only hope that it may open up a line of thought which will be productive of good in the
not too distant future. I am fully persuaded that in this question, like many others, we
have reached a stage when drastic steps are essential for our national purpose. Conditions
are changing daily; almost at any time this country may find itself dependent for 50 per
cent. of its fresh meat supplies upon a foreign monopoly. If that monopoly uses its power
to enrich its shareholders, what would be the result here?
Again, in all the large food-producing countries, the producer is organising to protect
himself; this specially applies to the Dominions. This can only be met by an organisation
of consumers, not on lines of antagonism, but on lines of co-operation, and how can the
consumers organise here unless it is through the State, not on bureaucratic lines, but on
sound business principles, in the interests of the whole people. I hope this question will
be well thought out. I should be pleased to help in any way to further explain the
policy I have submitted in my report.
WALTER R. SMITH.
23rd May, 1925.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
During the past month we have been engaged in the London District. We made
a special attempt to hold a conference with a number of employers, who have recently
been expelled from the London Federation; unfortunately there was not so good a response
as we anticipated. The General President presided over the conference, and explained
the National Agreement, with special reference to the adoption of the Holiday Fund.
After a lengthy discussion the firms represented agreed to give the matter their considera-
tion, and a definite promise was made that those present would agree to adopt the Holiday
Fund. As a result, the following firms agreed to adopt the fund from 4th May, 1925:
Wachman's, Chissick & Kirschenstein's, Krietman's, Mindle's, and Mintz's. There are
still a number of firms who refuse to adopt the Scheme, and appear to adopt an hostile
attitude. In this respect the two most prominent firms that are causing us a great deal of
trouble are H. & S. Solomon's, and Lipman's, and who are no doubt using their influence,
that is determining the action of others. Very serious intimidation is taking place in the
firm of H. & S. Solomon, with reference to the men and women joining the Union, which
very seriously intensifies our position. But despite the attitude of the firm, we make

PARLIAMENTARY DEBATES.
HOURS OF INDUSTRIAL EMPLOYMENT BILL (OTHERWISE
THE 48 HOURS WEEK BILL).
MR. BUCHANAN, on 1st May, 1925, on behalf of the Labour Party, moved "that the
Bill be now read a second time."
Mr. Buchanan recited the many reasons why such a Bill should become law and
pointed out amongst other arguments the following:-
"It is somewhat appropriate that I, being the Member for Gorbals, should move
this Bill, because it was my predecessor, Mr. George N. Barnes, who was largely the designer
and the pioneer of this particular Measure. It was he who was selected by the Coalition
Government of 1918-22 as their delegate to the Washington Conference, and it is important
that the House should remember that not only did he go there prepared himself to support
and vote for the 48 Hours Bill, but that, in a speech which he made in this House in 1921,
he laid it down, further, that not only did he do that as the supporter of the Bill himself,
but that he was instructed by the then Government to vote for this convention. After
the War, there was a great feeling in this country, as, indeed in most countries, that, seeing
that the War had come on, seeing that there had been a fellowship of the trenches and of
employer and employed, there ought to be in every country some universal recognition
of the working-class effort during the period of that War. Therefore, we had, immediately
after the War, all kinds of schemes, Whitley Councils and others, designed to improve to
some extent the conditions of the people. One of the outcomes was the Washington
Conference itself, and at that Conference one of the pledges and promises made to the
people by the Coalition Government at that time to the men who had been in the Army,
to the men who were returning to industrial occupations in particular-was that the
convention regarding a 48 hour week would be carried into effect.
MR. KIRKWOOD seconded. He pointed out amongst other points the deplorable
state of the Engineering Industry, and reminded the House of the statement of Mr. Lloyd
George during the War :-
"If you give us your ability as an engineer to finish the War, never will the conditions
that prevailed before the War exist after the War, because we are going to make this a
land fit for heroes to live in."
A number of other speakers followed both for and against the Bill.
SIR A. STEEL-MAITLAND (Minister for Labour), on behalf of the Government, opposed
the Bill, basing his main arguments upon difficulties of enforcement and other countries
interpreting Conventions differently from ourselves, and therefore, they, the Govern-
ment, could not agree to support the proposal.
MR. T. SHAW (ex-Minister for Labour), strongly supported the Bill, and stated among
many points in favour of the Bill the following :-
We were told at the outset of the discussion that this was a political Bill; that it was
introduced for political purposes. The Bill is a reprint of the Bill which I introduced
when I was sitting on the Benches opposite, and it is now introduced by the same party
that introduced it from the Benches opposite, and is the Washington Convention as
arranged by Government draughtsmen. The Washington Convention was promised to
us by a Government which was not a Labour Government, and which had in its Cabinet a
number of Members belonging to the party to which the hon. Member belongs. We
were told we ought to use our influence with other workers on the Continent before coming
here and asking for this Measure. I have said without hesitation, and with knowledge
of what I am saying, that the relative position of the Continental worker as compared with
ours now, is infinitely better from our point of view and from theirs than it was in 1913-14,
that the difference in extra hours worked on the Continent is infinitely less now than it
was before the War broke out.
It is a question of honour. When we talk about an Englishman's word being his bond,
what do we mean? Is this declaration in the Treaty of Peace an Englishman's word or
is it not? I use the word "English" because it is often used on the Continent when the
term ought to be "British." When the Conference took place at Washington, the Govern-
ment representatives actually accepted this Convention.
Nobody expected in Washington, certainly not the Labour representatives, that
there would be any question about this word being kept, that there would ever be a question
of men's words being regarded merely as scraps of paper. Then there were the employers'
representatives. They consented to the Convention, and when they came home the
employers raised no objection to their having done so. Now the employers turn round,
and, apparently, they want to break their word to the workers and to scrap the Con-
vention.

In Government circles, it is reported, very little is expected to result from the report

For the plain fact is that the Commission was set up in order to avoid doing anything,

function of Royal Commissions.

and futile. If what these contain were all that could be suggested, any Government
would be justified in deciding that it was not worth while to do anything.

culture) was on the Commission. And, like the minority on the Poor Law Commission
16 years ago, he has produced a report which is not evasive, but constructive, offering

report which holds the field, which alone deserves serious consideration, and which the
Government must not be allowed to ignore without showing adequate and convincing

NOTE ON THE PRINCIPAL CHANGES EMBODIED IN THE TRADE BOARD'S NOTICE D.
RELATING TO MALE INDENTURED APPRENTICES.
The Trade Board's Notice D. (29) which supersedes the Notice D. (25) contains a
number of important alterations which should be carefully noted. The principal altera.
tions are indicated below.
The following must not be regarded as a complete or authoritative summary of the
Trade Board's Notice. The Notice itself must be consulted in regard to the obligat.
imposed by the Trade Boards Acts.
The references below are to the numbered paragraphs of the Notice D. (29).
Apprentices Indentured on or after 11th May, 1925.
1. The special rates for Male Indentured Apprentices indentured on or after
May, 1925, apply only to Apprentices who :-
(a) are registered by the Trade Board (paragraph 5 (c)).
(b) are under 21 years of age (paragraphs 1 and 4).
(c) commence their apprenticeship under 18 years of age (paragraph 1,
in the case of apprentices who are provided by the employer with boa
lodging and certain other specified necessaries, on or before the worker'
17th birthday (paragraph 3 (b)).
(d) are apprenticed for a period terminating not earlier than the worker's 21st
birthday (paragraphs 1 and 3 (b)).
(e) are apprenticed to either :-
(i) Boot and Shoe Repairing in all its branches, including reweitin
hand-sewn repairs, benching, finishing by hand or machine
and patching; or
(ii) Hand-sewn making, or Hand-sewn making and Repairing; cr
(iii) Repairing and Rivet and Combination making; or
(iv) Closing of Uppers for Bespoke Work (paragraphs 1 and 3).
(f) are employed under an Indenture which contains certain conditions which
the Trade Board consider necessary for securing the effective instruction
of the apprentice in the trade (paragraph 5 (a)).
(g) are employed under conditions where the proportion of apprentices to Journe-
men is limited in the manner specified by the Trade Board (paragraphs
5 (d) and 6).
(h) in whose case the covenants specified in the indenture for securing the effective
instruction of the apprentice in the trade, including the conditions with
regard to the proportion of apprentices to Journeymen specified by the

2. The special rates for Male Indentured Apprentices indentured on or after 11th
May, 1925 (other than those provided with board and lodging), vary with each variation
of 10 points in the Cost-of-Living Figure from 70 down to 30 (paragraph 1). The special
rates for apprentices provided with board and lodging are not subject to variation with

WHO SERVES HIS COUNTRY BEST?
Who serves his country best ?
Not he who, for a brief and stormy space,
Leads forth her armies to the fierce affray,
Where men are killed by thousands in a day.
He serves his country best
Who joins the tide that lifts her nobly on;
Who lives pure life, and doeth righteous deed,
And walks straight paths, however others stray,
And leaves his sons, as uttermost bequest,
A stainless record which all men may read:
This is the better way.
No drop but serves the slowly lifting tide,
No dew but has an errand to some flower,
No smallest star but sheds some helpful ray,
And man by man, each giving to the rest,
Makes the firm bulwark of the country's power;
There is no better way.

EIGHT-HOUR DAY IN BRITAIN.
Government Statement at Geneva. Workers' Protest.
The principle of the 48-hour week was generally recognised in Britain, but movements
for the five-day week and such agreements as those of the railwaymen made ratification
of the Washington eight-hour day Convention difficult.
This was the statement of Mr. Betterton, British Government Representative, at the
International Labour Office Conference at Geneva yesterday.
The Government, he said, was in full accord with the principles of Part 13 of the
Peace Treaty. It intended to explore every means of preventing retrogression in the
hours movement in the chief industrial countries.
He reported, as indications of the British Government's good intentions, the fact
that all the Conventions and recommendations adopted by previous conferences had been
submitted to Parliament.
Workers' Disappointment.
Mr. Betterton's statement drew from Mr. E. L. Poulton, British Workers' Repre-
sentative, an expression of disappointment. He appealed to the Governments and
employers to allay this disappointment, and referred to rumours that there was to be
another Berne conference of Ministers of Labour of the important industrial countries of
Europe to study the question of difficulties of ratification.
He maintained that Mr. Betterton's objections were met by the articles of the Con-
vention itself.—Daily Herald, 26th May, 1925.
"THE LEGAL MINIMUM."
Mr. J. Hallsworth, of the N.U.D.A.W., has published a book under this heading.
In this book, the writer traces the history and explains the chief features and results of
the several methods by which minimum wages are fixed and enforced by legal authority
in Great Britain, and also deals with the question of legal regulation in relationship to
Trade-Unionism.
It is felt that the book will be of considerable assistance, not only to all Trade Union
officials-national, district, and local-but also to rank-and-file members, in the considera-
tion of wages questions and their settlement.

INTERNATIONAL LABOUR OFFICE NEWS.
"LABOUR ATTACHÉS" AT GENEVA.
How States Keep in Touch with the I.L.O.
The growth of a system of accredited representatives in Geneva to maintain permanent
contact with the International Labour Office of the League of Nations is shown in the
annual report of the Director of the Office, M. Albert Thomas, to the Seventh Session of
the International Labour Conference which opened at Geneva on Tuesday, 19th May.
The Japanese Government was the first to adopt this plan by appointing a hig
Government official as its representative and also head of a mission of a number of officia
which was responsible for keeping in permanent touch with the Office. Japan has bee
followed by Poland and Sweden in appointing such special representatives. The Brazilia-
Government recently set up an organisation in Geneva which practically amounts to
embassy to the League of Nations, and contains a special department for liaison with th
International Labour Office. Finland, Hungary, the Irish Free State and Canada
permanent representatives in Geneva who are accredited both to the International Lato
to maintain liaison with the International Labour Office and the League of Nations
Greece, Italy and Venezuela have instructed their diplomatic or consular representatives
Office and the League of Nations. Albania, Bulgaria, Chile, China, Czecho-Slovakia
with the International Labour Office only.
"It is desired to lay special emphasis on the services which these permanent repre-
sentatives have rendered both to the Office and to their countries," states the reer
"The Office frequently applies to them for information or documents which are urge.
required. The Director also invites them to attend periodical meetings at which questions
of common interest are discussed."

WORLD LABOUR PARLIAMENT.
Delegates Appointed.
A large number of Governments have notified the International Labour Office of the
League of Nations of the delegates who will represent them at the Seventh Annual Session
Each State is entitled to send four delegates, two representing the Government and
each the employers and workers of the country.
Among the first lists to be received were such widely separated countries as Cuba,
Denmark, Esthonia, Great Britain, India, Japan, South Africa and Switzerland, all o
which have appointed their full complement of delegates.
It is interesting to note that a number of the delegates appointed have had pas
experience of the Conference, such experience adding greatly to the smooth running
and speed of work of a new Session; among the British delegates, for example, are Mr
H. B. Betterton, M.P., Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of Labour (Government
Mr. James Lithgow (Employers), and Mr. E. L. Poulton (Workers), all of whom have
attended the Conference before.
Among other familiar names of those who have been present at the Conference are
Dr. Aguero y Bethancourt (Cuban Government), Sir A. C. Chatterjee and Sir L. J. Kersha
(Indian Government), Mr. N. M. Joshi (Indian Worker), Mr. H. Pfistor (Swiss Government
Mr. C. Schurch (Swiss Worker), Sir Joseph Cook (Australian Government), Mr. P. M.
Draper (Canadian Worker), and Mr. A. Mannio (Finnish Government).

YOUNG WORKERS IN JAPAN.
Demand Larger than Supply.
Though unemployment among adult workers in Japan has assumed serious proper
tions, there is reported to be a considerable unsatisfied demand for young workers, states
Industrial and Labour Information, the weekly publication of the International Labour
Office of the League of Nations.
It is stated that, in spite of great efforts made by public employment offices for young
workers in Tokyo and Osaka, the demand in the course of a year is several times larger
than the supply.
Employers, it is explained, generally ask for workers between the ages of 14 and 19
who have just completed their course in the primary school. The number of children due
to leave the primary schools this spring is about 1,600,000, of whom 700,000 are girls.
Of this total, it is estimated by the Bureau of Social Affairs, about 1,440,000, or go per cent.,
will not continue their education in the secondary schools, but will seek employment.
The remainder, however, will not be available for employment, and, though the number
of these is relatively small, it is steadily increasing; hence, the shrinkage in the supply of
young workers.

**THE GREAT STRUGGLE IN DENMARK.**

As already announced in the I.F.T.U. Press Reports, the Danish Trade Union Congress held at Copenhagen from the 5th to the 8th May adopted, after lengthy discussion, a resolution in which the following proposals were made to the employers: (1) Cessation of the lockout for those trades in which the employers' and workers' organisations had settled their differences and concluded new agreements; (2) The inauguration of negotiations in all trades where complete agreement has not yet been reached on all the points at issue; (3) Direct negotiations between the two parties in the metal industry, and workers in other industries. The resolution also calls for a system of direct negotiations between the various employers' and workers' organisations in any one trade, such negotiations to take place before the expiry of the wage agreement. In future, it must only be possible to refer unsettled points to the national organisations or the Conciliation Institute after direct negotiations between the organisations concerned have failed.

The employers declared their willingness to negotiate on these points, but refused to lift any part of the lockout; the employers' association having passed a resolution that agreement must have been reached for all trades before the lockout can be terminated. The workers, however, maintained their declaration that they were willing to reopen negotiations, which were therefore reopened for all trades, many points hitherto unsettled being now agreed upon. But on 16th May the negotiations between the Union of General Workers and the employers were finally broken off, as it was found impossible to agree upon the wage question. For the present, therefore, there are no prospects of settlement. Moreover, the struggle will be greatly intensified, for the transport workers' strike which was notified by the Union of General Workers, has come into effect.

This strike, which will affect all members of the Employers' Association who are engaged in shipping, will paralyse the whole of the ship transport industry, including the export of agricultural products, which is so important for Denmark. The transport workers' strike may thus have very far-reaching effects, and greatly extend the conflict. The Union of Seamen and Stokers are already contemplating the proclamation of a sympathetic strike, and the transport workers' unions in Norway and Sweden have taken steps to prevent all work on Danish ships in Norwegian and Swedish ports. The transport workers' strike has diminished the chances of a speedy settlement of the great fight, and everything considered, it is to be feared that a long and weary struggle is before the Danish workers.

**MEMBERSHIP OF THE SCOTTISH TRADE UNIONS.**

As stated at the recent Trades Union Congress the Scottish trade unions now have a membership of 536,432, the total number of workers being estimated at about 1,655,000, and 36 of the larger unions contain about four-fifths of the total membership, while 81 unions have less than 100 members.

**FROM THE WOMEN WORKERS' MOVEMENT.**

GREAT BRITAIN.—The British Labour Women's Conference will be held at Birmingham on the 27th and 28th May. Among the questions which will be discussed are social politics, the school, emigration, and the anti-war campaign.

UNITED STATES.—The International Ladies’ Garment-Workers’ Union has been waging a lively campaign for new members; as a result, they have recruited over 1,000 members in the industrial district of Chicago.

Increase in percentage unemployed as compared with a month ago, 0.6. Decrease in percentage as compared with a year ago, 1.0.—The Ministry of Labour Gazette, May, 1925.

Minutes of the Ninth Meeting of the Joint Industrial Council held on Tuesday, 28th
April, 1925, at 2.30 p.m., at 7 Tavistock Square, London, W.C. 1, Mr. T. F. Richards
presiding.

MINUTES. The Minutes of the previous meeting having been circulated were endorsed,
and the Chairman signed the same as a correct record of the business transacted.
APOLOGIES.-Apologies for absence were read from Messrs. B. J. Hanly, W. H.
Tomlinson, F. T. Riley and G. Winterbottom, of the Employers' side, and Messrs. J.
Buckle, J.P., and C. Bleakley, of the Operatives' side.
ELECTION OF OFFICERS.-On the motion of Mr. Owen Parker, Mr. T. F. Richards
was unanimously re-elected Chairman for the ensuing year; Mr. H. J. Bostock, J.P.,
Vice-Chairman ; Miss Ruth Tomlinson and Mr. E. L. Poulton, J.P., Joint Secretaries.
Before proceeding with the business of the day the Chairman desired to acknowledge
on behalf of the Union Executive, the moral support and financial assistance given by the
Federation in connection with the recent London dispute, and expressed the hope that
co-operation between the two organisations would be still closer in the future.
INDUSTRIAL COUNCILS BILL.-The discussion was opened by the Chairman, and replied
to on behalf of the manufacturers by Mr. H. J. Bostock, J.P., and after a general exchange
of views regarding the Industrial Councils Bill and the importance of organisation of both
sides, it was unanimously resolved that-
"This Joint Industrial Council reaffirms its request for the passing of the Indus-
trial Councils Bill as being essential for the proper observance of the National Con-
ference Agreements made between the Federation and the Union, and for the
preservation of Industrial peace and the efficient working of the Whitley Council.
It is further of opinion that in order to make voluntary action more effective, pending
the passing of this Bill, both sides of the Boot and Shoe Industry should consult as
to what other means can be taken to secure conformity to the various agreements."
A sub-committee of three representatives from each side was appointed. Each side
undertook to submit names of representatives in due course.
It was further agreed that the resolution submitted by Mr. T. F. Richards regarding
the importance of organisation in industry, which was recommended by resolution of
the Joint Industrial Council, January, 1920, and for which Mr. Richards asked greater
prominence in factories; and the question of the desirability or otherwise of holding a
Joint Conference with representatives of distributors and other buyers, should also be
referred to the above-named sub-committee.
SOUTH AFRICAN TARIFFS.-This question was introduced by Mr. H. J. Bostock, J.P.,
who stated that recent information in the Press would seem to indicate that the South
African Government in their new tariff proposals do not intend to give Great Britain the
advantage of "most favoured nation" treatment. The following resolution was unani-
mously agreed :-
"That this Joint Industrial Council for the Boot and Shoe Manufacturing Industry
is gravely concerned at the reports in the Press regarding South African tariffs, and
attaches the greatest importance to the maintenance of the 'most favoured nation'
clause."
SHODDY FOOTWEAR. It was agreed that the Chairman should circulate a memorandum
upon the subject for consideration by the sub-committee firstly, and secondly, for report
to the next meeting of the Council
RESIGNATIONS. Upon the suggestion of Mr. Owen Parker, it was unanimously
resolved that the resignations that had caused three vacancies both on the Employers'
and Operatives' side, should be filled. Each side undertook to submit nominations at
the next meeting of the Council.

STRIKE IN SHANGHAI.
Chinese Workers and Japanese Employers.
The Japanese Press during February reported a strike of Chinese workers employed
in Japanese silk mills in Shanghai. The strike which involved, according to some reports,
as many as 30,000 workers and lasted nearly three weeks, began in the Nagai-Men spinning
factory on the 10th February, when 6,000 Chinese stopped work. The dispute soon
spread throughout the factory, in which 13,000 Chinese men and women are employed.
A declaration to the following effect was issued by the strikers.
Though we work more than 12 hours a day, our wages are extremely low. We demand
the following conditions :-
1. Henceforth, no beating of workers shall be tolerated.
2. Our wages shall be raised by 10 per cent.
3. The workers who have been discharged shall be reinstated, and the workers
who have been detained shall be released.
4. Wages shall henceforth be paid fortnightly.
5. Wages shall be paid for the period of the strike.
6. Henceforth, no worker shall be discharged without proper cause.
On the 12th February about half the strikers in this factory returned to work; but
the strike quickly spread to other factories, where is assumed the character of a riot rather
than orderly strike. A number of men, armed with revolvers, rifles and other weapons,
attacked some work premises and smashed the machinery.
Within a week, eight out of 11 silk works owned by Japanese were involved; in
terms of spindles, only 86,000 out of 913,000 remained unaffected. In view of the grave
outlook the Spinners' Federation of Japan held a meeting in Osaka on 18th February,
and, in the name of 16 spinning companies, adopted a resolution calling on the Govern-
ment to open negotiations with the Chinese Government with regard to the dispute. A
telegram from Shanghai dated 27th February, reported that the strike came to an end
on the previous day, and that all the workers had returned to work. According to the
Jijn, of the 27th February, a compromise was reached on the following terms :-
1. The workers will be treated kindly, as heretofore. If any case of maltreatment
is found, the workers may appeal to the factory owner and redress will be
given forthwith.
2. Workers who are content with their present conditions will be invited to remain
in their present employment.
3. The detained workers will be released.
4. Grants for the encouragement of workers' savings will be given to workers
who have been employed for more than five years. In the case of workers
with a specially good record, the grants may be given even if they have not
been employed for that period.
5. Wages will henceforth be paid fortnightly. -Industrial and Labour Information..
27th April, 1925.

MONTHLY REPORT.

22ND JUNE, 1925.

FELLOW MEMBERS,

TRADE.

There is no improvement in trade compared with last month. As a
matter of fact there is an increase in the amount of Union benefit of over 15 per
cent. as compared with the previous month, although it is lower than the
corresponding month of 1924. The figures given by the Ministry of Labour
Gazette are as follows :-

BOOT AND SHOE INDUSTRY.

Employment remained depressed, and there was no marked general change as com-
pared with April, slight improvements in some districts being counter-balanced by declines
in others. There was a slight improvement in the last week of the month, some firms being
busy getting out orders; but, speaking generally, the increased activity that usually
occurs before the Whitsuntide holiday, was almost entirely absent, and much short time
was still being worked throughout the industry.

The percentage of workpeople unemployed, as indicated by the unemployment
books lodged at Employment Exchanges, was 10.1 on the 25th May, 1925, as compared
with 10.2 on the 27th April, 1925, and with 8.3 on the 26th May, 1924.

Returns from firms employing 37,000 operatives in the week ended 23rd May, 1925,
showed that 37½ per cent. of these operatives worked short time in that week, to the extent
of about 11½ hours each, on an average.

Employment continued moderate in London. It was quiet at Leicester and North-
ampton, with much short time being worked; a decline was reported at Leicester. Employ-
ment remained only moderate, on the whole, in the Higham and Rushden area; while
at Hinckley it was quiet, and worse than in April. Practically all the operatives were on
short time at Wellingborough, and employment was generally slack and worse than in
the previous month. At Kettering also it continued slack, and very few firms were on
full time.

Much short time was worked during the month at Leeds. Employment improved at
Stafford, and was fair; although there was still some unemployment, full time was worked
at most factories. Employment continued fair, on the whole, at Norwich, and showed
a slight improvement; but many operatives were working less than full hours. General
slackness again prevailed in the Bristol and Kingswood area, with most factories working
short hours.


---
THE FORTY-EIGHT HOURS WEEK.
Considerable attention is still being given to the question of the forty-eight
hours week and the possibility or otherwise of it becoming law. At the Seventh
Session of the League of Nations International Labour Office the question was
discussed at length, and we regret to report that the attitude of the Government,
through its representatives, is one of disappointment. Many members of
the League have already ratified the Convention of 1919, but will not put it
into operation until the British Government has done so. We trust that our
members will do what is possible to keep this matter before their local repre-
sentatives, and thus create such an opinion as to show the Government that
the Convention must be ratified, and that at an early date.
The Seventh Session of the I.L.O. also passed conventions in favour of
the abolition of Night Baking, Equality of Treatment of Workmen and
Foreigners' Accidents, and Compensation for accidents and industrial
diseases.
It is, however, very regrettable to have to record the fact that the attitude
of the British Government, instead of leading in industrial matters, as we
contend they should do, they either remain neutral or are reactionary. This
has very considerable effect upon other nations, and undoubtedly reduces
the influence of Great Britain upon other nations' representatives.
This is additional evidence of the necessity to as far as possible, and as
early as possible, change the representation of the country so as to ensure the
Labour Party not only being in office, but in real power, and thus give an
incentive to progress and peace amongst and between the nations of the
earth.
We wish to congratulate the General Secretary upon his re-election as the
British Workers' Representative upon the Governing Body of the International
Labour Office. Mr. Poulton was elected at the top of the poll, and was also
one of the acting chairmen of the Conference, which is indeed an honour for
the Union.

GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.
