CO-PARTNERSHIP WORKSHOP.

Report of the Leicester Co-operative Printing Society Limited for the
Half-Year ended 1st August, 1925.

We have pleasure in submitting the 65th Half-Yearly Report and Balance Sheet.
The Sales for the half-year amount to £27,170 15s. 6d., a decrease of £825 15s. 1d. compared
with the corresponding period of last year. After providing for Interest on Share and Loan
Capital amounting to £1,034 11s. 11d., and depreciating Fixed Stock, Buildings, &c,
1,336 6s. 3d., there is a balance profit of £705 9s. 2¼d., which, with the balance of £237 19s.
brought forward from last half-year, gives a total of £943 8s. 2½d. for disposal.
We have added 13 new members during the half-year, I have lapsed, the present
number of Shareholders being 607.

The decrease in Sales and Profits is somewhat disappointing, but the corresponding
half-year with which the comparison is made was an exceptional one with regard to large
orders of a special character which could not be repeated. At the same time the half-year
just completed has been one of the busiest we have experienced, and in view of the general
condition of trade which is reflected in the printing industry the Committee consider
that the result is satisfactory. The London Branch is doing remarkably well and shows
a substantial increase in trade. Another valuable machine for rapid printing has been
installed there during the half-year and has already justified the rather heavy outlay.
The Kettering Branch has maintained its position fairly well and continues to render
good service.
Detailed figures for the half-year's trade are as follows -

£ s. d.
Leicester Printing Works 16,790 11 11
Box Department 5,891 8 7
London Branch 3,365 15 0
Kettering Branch 1,123 0 0

We are glad to be able to report that a definite scheme for the rehousing of the Box
Department is now in hand. The Society has purchased a freehold building site in Gravel
Street, separated only by a narrow passage from the Printing Works in Short Street.
Plans are being prepared for consideration for the erection of a three storey, well-lighted
and up-to-date factory, with provision for an additional two storeys when future needs
warrant an extension. The advantages of having this department in closer proximity to
the general offices and works, with the extra accommodation and facilities generally that
this scheme provides are obvious, and we feel sure will lead to considerable expansion
and development of this important branch of our business.
The present half-year has opened well with a considerable number of orders.

WAGE BOARD IN SOUTH AFRICA: NEW ACT.
The Under Secretary of State for Dominion Affairs has transmitted to the Ministry
of Labour a copy of an Act recently passed by the South African Parliament which provides
for "the determination of conditions of labour and of wages and other payments for labour,
the appointment of a wage board and investigations as to wages and conditions of labour.
Persons exempted from the application of the Act are those engaged in agriculture and
forestry, domestic servants in private households, officers of Parliament, those whose
wages are governed or regulated by any Act relative to the public service or the railways
and harbours service; workers covered by an award or agreement which has been made
binding under the Industrial Conciliation Act of 1924 and which provides for wages not
lower than those in force under the new Act; and apprentices under the Apprenticeship
Act of 1922.

MONTHLY REPORT.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
26TH OCTOBER, 1925.
TRADE
is, from the point of view of employment, very slow indeed. there being a
considerable number of members in receipt of unemployment benefit. In
fact, from the Union funds we have paid during the past month the sum of
£7,784 18s. 9d., whilst £10,857 0s. 9d. was paid on behalf of the Govern-
ment scheme, a total of £18,371 19s. 6d. for one month. This sum of
money we know helps the members to meet their obligations, but we would
remind the members that the scale of payment from the Union funds would
be quite impossible, on the present contributions, were it not for the fact of
the method by which the Industry is governed, i.e., by National Agreements,
and the local arrangements based upon the same, all of them being dealt with
and adjusted from time to time by the system of arbitration; thereby
avoiding-without giving up any principle-the spending of money upon
constant strikes. As a consequence the funds can be used from time to time
to assist members who are unfortunately unemployed, needing as they do at
such times, something to fall back upon. Moreover, the payments of these
sums is a real contribution towards reduction of local rates, saving thereby
calls upon the ratepayers.
There are, in addition to the number entirely unemployed, a very large
number working short time; it will, therefore, be seen that the outlook is not
at all promising. We would urge upon all the members, nevertheless, to pay

THE LABOUR PARTY CONFERENCE.
During the past month the Labour Party Conference has been held at
Liverpool. The Conference was not only very largely attended, but the
spirit of the delegates was one of optimism and determination. The over-
whelming majority of votes recorded upon policy and support of the Executive
was very significant, making it quite clear that there must be on the part of
those who from time to time are nominated for positions that they must adhere
to the Party and its declared policy. Two votes especially we would call
attention to-the one dealing with the claim of the
COMMUNISTS,
and the one dealing with the question of another prospective Labour Govern-
ment. In the first case the vote against the Communists was for referring

THE PASSING OF MR. FRED BRAMLEY.
It is with sincere regret we have to record the fact that Mr. FRED
BRAMLEY, Secretary to the General Council of the Trades Union Congress,
passed away very suddenly whilst attending a meeting of the Inter-
national Federation of Trade Unions in Amsterdam on the 10th inst.
It is well known that Mr. Bramley had been ill for some time he felt,
however, after a recent sea voyage, somewhat improved, and determined
to take up the work in which he had spent most of his life.
It was seen both at the Congress at Scarborough and the Labour
Party at Liverpool, that he was not at all well. His desire, however,
to help the movement was so great that he felt compelled to carry on the
work, and it may be truthfully said he died in harness. As a matter of
fact he died after attending a meeting, and passed peacefully away in
his sleep.
Mr. Bramley did yeoman service for the cause of trades unionism
generally, and it was hoped he had some years of service in front of him ;
this was not to be.
We can only hope that the loss of Mr. Bramley will be a spur and
incentive to others to continue to carry on the work of humanity in
which he spent most of his life.
To Mrs. Bramley and the family we beg to tender our sincere con-
dolences and trust the appreciation and high regard in which Mr. Bramley
was held by his colleagues will be some consolation to them in their
irreparable loss.

Please Note. CHEQUES NOT "PRINTED PAPERS."
The Postmaster-General draws attention to the fact that considerable numbers of
cheques are posted in open envelopes prepaid 1/2 d. only. Cheques, whether crossed or not,
and paper money generally, are inadmissible at a lower rate of postage than that applicable
to letters, and if packets containing them are posted insufficiently prepaid they are liable
to be surcharged double the deficiency.

THE GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.
60 LINDSEY STREET ROAD.
KENELON TOWN,
LONDON, N.W.5.
19th October, 1924.

FELLOW MEMBERS,

Buy no boots unstamped or unbranded; the makers are usually ashamed
of them.

The work for the month calls for great comment, inasmuch as the LABOUR
CONFERENCE by overwhelming majorities decided to prevent any new organization in
disrupting the Party by personal attacks on the leading and Executive members,
has been the policy of a section calling themselves Communists and based upon the Ru
régime, most of them openly advocating the change made in that country as a legitima
although all of us, proud of the term Socialist, know full well that the communal iss
means for a similar movement to take place here; but history counts in the matter
mankind is worth striving for; also that dictatorship by any section or class is the dress
opposite to the policy advocated by the genuine Communists such as the late Willia-
Morris. When these new organizations come forward with old ideas, rehashed, and po
force put forth as a remedy, one would think that only by such means can a natio
change be brought about. Our opponents were never tired during the past twenty
in telling the public. My own experience in West Wolverhampton was mainly take-
up during the seven years of my close attachment to that constituency. We were con
stantly assailed with the statements that the advent to power of the Labour Governme
or Socialists would see a violent revolution, but Labour has been in office, although co
in power, for nine months, and left the state of the country better than they found
Communists has left a lasting impression on the movement since their attack on the
and not a single institution suffered nor been afraid. The attitude of these so-called
and their belated friendship is looked upon with suspicion. If they think they have
Chairman of the Labour Party and Leader in the House at the Woolwich By-Election
and everywhere that they have the chance. Those of us who admire their enthusias
find it difficult to distinguish between their policy and that of the Anarchists of old, an
claim on the workers for support, then let them proceed with their propaganda anywhere
the Syndicalism of a few years ago, but we only have to look at their ideal country, Russia
and we shall not be happy until the Soviets, instead of electing themselves, go to the
polling stations and take their power from the elected of the people. We are informer
ment of the Russian Social Revolutionaries is being continued, and this is because they wil
by deputation from the General Council of the Trades Union Congress that the imprison-
towards the revolutions when Kerensky was in power. Without the ballot box this
not give an undertaking from doing the very self-same thing that the present régime dii
served power when having no one to fight, they fight each other, and if war is bad, it is no
method appears in all countries where violent revolutions have taken place, that having
better having vanquished the enemy to then turn your attention to your friends. In
Italy (Mussolini), in Ireland (the deaths of Mr. Griffiths and Michael Collins remind us),
in China several would-be dictators, and in this country the Communists only believe in
Parliamentary action for a purpose, and it is for these reasons that my colleagues and myseli
voted against these attempts to be party of a party whose constitution and policy ther
were opposed to. Their motto should be " Do as we say, not as we do."

In spite of all this, I consider it a most disgraceful thing if a Minister of the Crown has
publicly gloated over any of this country's citizens being placed under arrest. There
will be time enough after the trial to express his joy, but at present one can safely say
that the Home Secretary will be greatly disappointed if he cannot bring about a conviction
in the light of his alleged hilarity. It is only those of us who have been condemned behind
our backs that can vividly feel for others so placed.

NORTHANTS BOARD OF ARBITRATION had referred the price of a Blucher to be dealt
with by the Army Board, and upon inquiry it was found that a special price allowed some
years ago, and then withdrawn, had been maintained. This was a very unusual thing,
and if permitted, once the facts were known, would have resulted in a firm being permitted
to make something in leather at a rate less than the statements provide for under the
heading of "all other leathers." That in itself provides for this particular article, and
ultimately the Army Board came to the conclusion that the statement already
provided for this boot, and the same was referred back on that understanding.
---

---
STREET.—A visit was paid to Street to confer with the Branch on a proposition
whereby bulk orders could be dealt with at rates less than the existing statements which
have been compiled on a system of small orders and sizeable lots. The details were placed
before me and after working them out, the matter will be placed before the Executive of
the Union, as there appears to be an advantage when a firm makes for the wholesaler,
compared with firms who deal only with the retailers.

MARKET HARBOROUGH has been again visited and we have had a very pleasant inter-
view bordering on our activities with the firm’s customers who had helped us to bring
about the change, and we are hopeful that as we have removed our embargo, that the
firm will do the same, because we cannot vouch for the future unless this is done in a
friendly spirit.

FAIRE BROS., MANSFIELD AND LEICESTER. Mr. A. W. Faire, Shoe Manufacturer,
of Messrs. Smith, Faire & Co., has taken this matter in hand, and we have had two inter-
views with the firm. It is well for us that a gentleman so much respected, and with whom
we have always been able to deal without friction, should have undertaken the unwelcome
task of straightening out a tangle that would never had occurred if the Management of
the Mansfield firm had made themselves acquainted with the customs of the trade. We
hope to be able to report more favourably later.

SUPERANNUATION.—The Council of the Union has been considering this matter and
have had special meetings and sub-Committees appointed for the purpose, and when they
have formulated their proposals, will place the matter before the members.

LEATHER FAIR.—Our visit to the Fair did not enlighten us much, as officers, owing
to the small amount of machinery of the newer kind being shewn. The tendency seems
to point in the direction of the coming together of buyers and manufacturers, machinery
having appeared to have made itself master of the industry. There will always be minor
improvements, but few convulsions.

TRADE BOARD. —Three more days have been spent in this work and several important
things done. The removal of anomalies has taken much time in trying to make the rates
and operations more uniform and understandable. A fall back rate for juveniles has been
recommended to the District Committees, which means that if any employer exceeds
the number of boys allowed, then he must pay from 7s. to 10s. per week more to that boy,
than any other boy, as a penalty or deterrent, as the Ministry are advised that to claim
the adult rate would fail to get any bench of magistrates to commit. The extension of
hours from 48 as govern factories to longer hours by one employer to the Shop Hours Act
limit, on the pretence that no repairing is to be done over forty-eight hours, has been
referred by the Minister of Labour to the Law Officers of the Crown.

INSPECTION. — The number of firms inspected for the first time—over nine hundred.
Number of firms inspected during the six months—over one thousand, and the claims for
back pay amount to nearly two thousand pounds. This alone is sufficient for the justifica-
tion for the existence of Trade Boards, and although some grumble at the Inspectors,
I am going to pay them this tribute that with all their shortcomings, THEY ARE DOING
SPLENDID WORK, and deserve much more praise and encouragement than they get. In
fact they are more thorough than many Trade Union Officials (whom I know), some of
their inspections taking over four days time. Take the case of the London firm who were
fined £10 each, man and wife, and £5 5s. od. costs, because their Manager caused false
records to be made and over £20 in arrears of wages ordered to be paid.

I wonder there is any man in the repairing trade mean enough not to pay his weekly
contribution to Trades Unionism, who benefits and receives the advantages obtained by
his more generous shopmates. I make this appeal to all repairers to join up, and also to
the Trade Union element: Don’t take your repairs to any shop where non-unionists are
employed.

FROME. With Mr. J. Manners we met the Executive Committee of this Parliamentary
Division respecting the appointment of an Agent, and we gave reasons the Council had
for not appointing an Agent at once, and as they were going to review the matter in six
months’ time from August, there is little doubt of the matter being favourably considered
then, should nothing occur to hurry matters in that division.

JOINT INDUSTRIAL COUNCIL.—The sub-Committee appointed by this body has met
and considered how best to help on the principle of the legalising of National Agreements.
Negotiations are proceeding with the General Council for a Deputation from our Union
to the Ministry. The resolution re joining the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives
is proposed to be strengthened, and I hope, get put up in every factory.

BRANCH REPORTS.
BELFAST. - Trade continues to remain very dull in Belfast and district,
while the Derry Section sends the encouraging report that trade is good with
them. A meeting of the Trades Board (Northern Ireland) was held on the
and September. This was the first meeting of the reconstituted Board,
which is composed of thirteen members on each side. Our Union has five
seats allocated to them on the Board, all of whom we are pleased to state were
present at the meeting. The most important items on the agenda for the
sonded by Mr. Kerr, "That the Time and Piece Rates be reduced by 25 per
sidering was the motion from the employers' side, moved by Mr. Smyth and
There were two motions from the workers' side sent forward by the
Branch Secretary: one was for a 10 per cent. increase on the present Time and
Dive Rates, and the other motion was one complaining of the unsatisfactory
system of inspection, and urging upon the Government Department responsible
to increase the staff of Inspectors so that the regulations made by the Board
would be better complied with. After considerable discussion, which occupied
the whole day, it was agreed to defer further consideration pending reports
from District Committees which have been set up till the next meeting of the
Board.
CHESHAM. - We are pleased to report a further improvement in trade
for the month, and that some of our members who have been unemployed for
a long period have obtained work again.
CHESTERFIELD.-Trade is still improving; we have, however, several
members still out of work.
DERBY.-Trade in Derby has slightly improved, but it is still very bad.
We have had two of our National Organisers with us, Messrs. J. H. Baum and
Len. Smith, who are doing good work, their only difficulty in making a good
number of new members is the short time that is being worked. Mr. Baum
addressed a Special Meeting of the Branch, when we had a fair number of
non-members present. He gave us a very good address, and answered a
number of questions satisfactorily. We, in Derby, are of the opinion that if
we could have the services of our organisers more often in the district we should
not be one of the backward centres.
DUNDALK.-Trade remains very uncertain, with future prospects
nothing more than hopeful, notwithstanding the fact that this, the boot indus-
try, happens to be one of the numerous tariff protected industries which exist
in the Irish Free State. Basing one's remarks on, if not authoritative, at least
pretty authentic information, we regret to say more pairs of boots and
shoes, particularly in the better class have, and are being imported into the
Irish Free State than before Protection. Something is wrong. We wonder if
the ministerial advocates of Protection fail to see the opening Protection
affords (profiteering!) Or are there only going to be two elements which
shall derive benefit from Protection-first, the Government; second, the
capitalist. The Government, by way of revenue raised from imported con-
signments; second, the capitalist by availing himself of the opportunity of
putting an additional three shillings on every pair. Boots or shoes usually
sold for £1 may now be sold for £1 3s. od. This may suit the classes, but what
about the masses? Are they beneath consideration? Painful rumours are
afloat in regards to solely appointed agencies extracting or rather endeavouring
to extract a 90 per cent. profit. Further, it is rumoured interesting aspirants
must do likewise or go without the goods. This state of affairs, if true, is
desperate, without even waiting to get hold of the market as business concerns
do. We are heading for the precipice of catastrophe, present omens prog-
nosticate industrial and commercial stagnation. The consumer, who pays the

D. MCCARTHY.
During the past month I have chiefly been engaged in the Derby district, visiting the
following firms: C.W.S., Clemson's, Maden & Ireland's, and the Derby Boot Company
Unfortunately trade is not very good, and has therefore interfered with any marked
improvement in organisation. I have frequently met the operatives working at Maden
Ireland's, where our organisation is very weak, many of the operatives having ceased
membership some time ago. They have been working very short time for some months
now, but by coming in personal contact with them and explaining the work of the Union,
further interest has been added, which I think over a period of time will eventually have
beneficial results. No Holiday Fund is in operation, and the operatives consider that as
two other firms in the town are paying, the position is not fair. This appears to be an
excellent reason why they should all belong to the Union, but as I have pointed out to them,
that until they show a better appreciation of the power of organisation, the matters that
they complain about can never be adjusted. With trade improving, I think that by
consistent work the operatives' confidence can be regained, whereby negotiations could
proceed which will gradually improve their conditions. Clemson's have also been working
very short time, and a fairly good number have lapsed, but definite promises are being
made that as trade improves they will eventually commence paying. Conditions are
decidedly bad at the Derby Boot Company, the operatives are not very responsive, only a
few of the girls seem to have any spirit, the rest accept the conditions and just grumble.
Fear appears to be the usual driving force at this firm, and no doubt the employer would
be at a loss if he depended upon anything else to conduct his business, and the only way to
end this condition of affairs is for the men and women to assert their position as human
beings, and demand humane conditions of employment.
I called a meeting of the whole firms in the town, which was fairly well attended.
A good discussion took place on the work of the Union. As a result of this meeting several
matters were raised with reference to the C.W.S., which no doubt will be adjusted.
I have again visited Mansfield, and met the operatives working at the Mansfield
working at Faire Bros., but no improvement is possible until negotiations are completed
Shre Company. Our organisation is steadily improving at this firming also met the girls

MONTHLY REPORT.
25TH JANUARY, 1926.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
TRADE.
The New Year was ushered in with a slight improvement in trade, the
amount of unemployment benefit paid to members being lower than of late.
We can only hope we shall speedily see a further improvement. The figures
in the Ministry of Labour Gazette are as follows :-
BOOT AND SHOE INDUSTRY.
Employment remained moderate during December, but there was a further slight
improvement in the Midland districts, and fuller time was worked; in some centres,
however, the factories closed for extended holidays at Christmas. The recent improve-
ment in this industry is largely a result of the demand for Russian boots.
The percentage of workpeople unemployed, as indicated by the unemployment books
lodged at Employment Exchanges, was 8.5 on 21st December, 1925, as compared with
9.4 on 23rd November, 1925, and with 11.8 on 22nd December, 1924.

The exports of boots and shoes in December, 1925, amounted to 97,719 dozen pairs,
or 9,774 dozen pairs less than in November, 1925, but 5,286 dozen pairs more than in
December, 1924.
THE NATIONAL JOINT STANDING COMMITTEE.
The National Joint Standing Committee met on the 8th inst. under the
presidency of Mr. W. Addington Willis, C.B.E., when two cases were down
for decision.
The first case was sent by the Leicester Arbitration Board regarding the
employment of female labour on heel building. After hearing evidence from
both sides the Committee decided :-
"That the Committee regret it should have been found necessary to bring this
matter before them as it seems one which should have been capable of amicable
adjustment between the parties concerned. After considering the matter, the decision
of the Committee is that the National (Conference) Agreement, 1924, like its two
predecessors, expressly recognises, in Clause 8c, the employment of women upon heel
building without any exception in so far as districts are concerned."
The second case was remitted from London to the effect that "the advance
of 130 per cent. on the first class statement of wages which has been operative
since 1919 be revised, so as to make the same conform with the present
percentage on the cost of living above pre-war rates." Here, again, the
Committee arrived at an unanimous decision as follows :-
"This case involves the same principle as that decided by the Committee on
24th November, 1925, when the Joint Committee then decided that the proposals to
alter existing statements, en bloc, by a flat rate percentage reduction or increase
would not be in accordance with the principles of existing agreements, or with the
practice hitherto recognised in the industry, but neither that decision nor this debars
either side from taking before a local Board items in any existing statements which they
contend are anomalous and require revision."


---
7
It was further agreed that a deputation from the National Union should seek
an interview as early as possible with the Minister of Labour regarding the Industrial
Councils Bill.
It was also agreed to place on record the fact that the revised resolution of the
Joint Industrial Councils of 24th November, 1925, dealing with "Organisation of
Industry," had been sent by the Federation to all known boot manufacturers, and
that the National Union has issued leaflets containing the resolution to all boot and
shoe operatives.
Mr. Horrell and Miss Tomlinson undertook to see the Chesham manufacturers
with a view to inviting them to resume membership of the Federation.
SHODDY FOOTWEAR. - On the question of Shoddy Footwear, it was agreed that
Mr. Owen Parker and Mr. T. F. Richards should jointly wait upon the Ministry of
Health in accordance with the terms of the resolution of the Joint Industrial Council
relative thereto.
THE LONDON POSITION. - The London position, arising out of a letter sent by
Mr. Poulton on 5th November, 1925, from the Executive of the Union to the Federa-
tion was next discussed. After careful consideration of the matter, Mr. Horrell
suggested that representatives of the firms named in Mr. Poulton's letter should be asked
to meet the Sub-Committee, such meeting to be held prior to the Conference with
the Factors, &c. It was further decided to try and arrange the meeting with the firms
named in the National Union's letter on 5th November, 1925, including Messrs. Jackson
& Joseph, on 27th January, 1926, at 2.15 p.m. It was suggested that Mr. G. Pocock
be asked to attend the meeting as President of the London Association.
THE HALF-YEARLY STATEMENT OF ACCOUNTS.
The Half-yearly Statement of Accounts is presented herewith. It may
be taken as one more reminder of the very valuable work the Union is doing
on behalf of its members. Apart altogether from the work carried on daily by
the Union's officers regarding statements, wages and conditions of employ-
ment, a great volume of other work is constantly being undertaken in the way
of dealing with unemployment and sickness. The amount expended under
these two headings for the past half-year total £48,150 16s. 1d.
The Trade Fund shows a loss of £1,983 2s. 7d.; this is entirely
accounted for by the large increase paid under the heading of Unemploy-
ment Benefit which reached a total of £31,175 4s. 3d. from the Union
Funds.
The Sickness and Funeral Fund shows a gain of £11,578 15s. 1d.
The aggregate amount of money in these two Funds, i.e., Trade and Sick
Fund, despite these heavy payments, is £340,749 17s. 8d.
This, no doubt, seems a large sum of money; indeed it is. What has to be
taken into account is the fact that it belongs to a large number of members,
and thrown over the whole of the membership it is not a large sum.
Having regard to the very heavy calls upon the funds during the past
few years, they are in a healthy condition.
We can only hope there will be an early improvement in trade with a
consequent reduction of members claiming upon the funds of the Union for
both sick and unemployment benefit.

DEATH OF MR. HARRY MORETON.
We regret the passing away of one of the stalwarts of the Union in
the person of MR. HARRY MORETON, who had reached the ripe old age
of 88 years. For many years he was secretary to our Wolverhampton
Branch, and for some time a member of the Executive Council. Mr.
Moreton rendered yeoman service in the earlier days of the Union when
it was struggling for existence, and although latterly he had been unable
to take an active part in the work, he maintained an interest in the
work of the Union to the last. We were represented at the funeral by
the General President (Mr. T. F. Richards), and Mr. Alex. Smith
(Council Member for the district).
We tender our sympathies to the relatives.

THE GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.

60 LADY SOMERSET ROAD,
KENTISH TOWN, N.W. 5.
19th January, 1926.

FELLOW MEMBERS,
CZECHO-SLOVAKIA. You will, I am sure, remember that I have from time to
time mentioned Czecho-Slovakia. I have been supplied with a report entitled "Evolution
of Socialism," from the Secretary of the Social Democratic Workers' Party, issued from
Prague in 1924, and I recall this statement: The first Workers' Council has been introduced
in the Mines with success, at the same time as the law of Workers' Councils, a law was
passed that Miners should have a 10 per cent. share in the profits of the Mines, and at
present every concern employing continuously more than 30 workmen has its Workers'
Council, which keeps a watch on the carrying out of the collective agreements and arbitra-
tion decisions regarding wages and factory discipline. The Workers' Council also has the
right to be consulted in regard to the dismissal of workmen and participates in the adminis-
tration of Benevolent Institutions for workmen besides having the right to propose to
the employers regarding the administration of the concern's working methods in the
production of the works and so on.

THE WORKERS' COUNCIL HAS ITS REPRESENTATIVE ON THE ADMINISTRATION COM-
MITTEE OF THE CONCERN. THE EMPLOYER IS BOUND TO ASK THE OPINION OF THE WORKERS'
COUNCIL ON THE POINTS ABOVE MENTIONED, AND IN ADDITION, HE HAS TO PRESENT EVERY
SIX MONTHS A REPORT ON THE CONCERN.
OF BUSINESS CONCERNS EVERY EMPLOYER EMPLOYING MORE THAN 300 WORKERS.

WE HAVE NOT GONE SO FAR AS THIS YET !

ORGANISATION OF INDUSTRY. -The new resolution " Organisation of Industry," has
been circulated, and is probably in your hands by this time. If not, I hope you will make
enquiries from your various branch offices, and the officials will supply you with sufficient
for yourself and for any interested. To my mind this is a wonderful step forward in so
much as this combined resolution is the work of both organisations. In my humble
judgment it will allay the feeling that some of our members possess, and also the opposition
of some of the manufacturers who do not belong to the Federation. It will behove all
our members to distribute this resolution on every available occasion, especially among
the non-Unionists in organised shops, and among non-Unionists in non-federated shops.
It has been my duty to draw the attention of the membership on several occasions to the
fact that whilst we can in round figures estimate that there are not less than 120,000
people engaged in the industry, we have only 80,000 within our ranks. If we make allow-
ance for other organisations such as the Amalgamated Union and the Slipper Workers'
Union, and various small Hand-Sewn bodies throughout the country, we can only account
for 90,000 organised people, even if we are generous, and for this reason we feel that with
the help of our members on every occasion that presents itself, we ought before the end
of this year to get that other 30,000. With the resolution like the one referred to, I feel
certain that the lukewarmness of one or two employers with whom I am associated, will
find a little more warmth in supporting this policy of organisation of both sides, which I
hope will lead to a better understanding between the two bodies and thereby create a
feeling of confidence between the employer and the employee, such as we cannot expect
whilst we are living under the present industrial conditions. I am unaware that any other
industry has a resolution of a similar character, and although I have already been in
correspondence with a kindred organisation, I was surprised to receive from the Secretary
of that Union a letter stating that it was a well known fact that their organisation was
just as much opposed to the employers as the employers' organisation was opposed to
their Union. I do not share this view, although economically it is perfectly true, but
anything, always providing, as is my experience, the officials are determined to see all
that the National Agreement gives them. We have not won our present position by sheer
antagonism towards our employers, and it is very creditable to find, and for me to say,
that I cannot recall the name of a single manufacturer who has suggested to me that
there should be a diminution or a reduction in either our minima or our scales. This,
at least, is creditable to the members of the Federation, and it is this confidence that causes
us to work so much in harmony with them in many other directions.

JOINT INDUSTRIAL COUNCIL. We have just held a meeting of the Joint Industrial
Council Sub-Committee at which the meeting discussed as to what action we are likely
to take in regard to the resolution carried at the Trades Union Congress in asking for the
legislation of action to be applied to our National Agreement, as we had already promised,
---

---
13

as a Union, that we were about to approach the Board of Trade and the Minister of Health
upon this matter, and as regards the Shoddy parts of a boot, we were about to solicit the
backing of the Minister of Health by deputation. This will be done in the very near
future. This meeting appointed the President of the Union, and an ex-President of the
Federation, to also wait upon these Ministers with the object in view, pointing out, that
although we as a Union were willing separately to approach these Departments, it was
decided, as being necessary, that both organisations should be represented in making a
joint appeal. This Committee also had under consideration the East London position,
and it was decided to send out a circular inviting those gentlemen who were once members
of the London Association (which showed that they at least had some sympathy with
organised labour), with the object of pointing out to them how necessary it is that all
associates should rejoin their respective organisations, and they should assist us in making
the National Agreement the important factor for peace in the industry. We are also
asking for the help in this matter of the Chairman of the London Association, who will,
I am sure, give that assistance, seeing that he is the Vice-President of the Federation.
We also propose to meet the Factors and large Buyers regarding this subject at an early
date.

In addition to the above we have had a meeting of the JOINT STANDING COMMITTEE
presided over by Mr. W. Addington Willis, in which the Committee were invited by the
London Association of Employers to allow a reduction from the 130 per cent. which was
added to the first class statement in 1919. After some amount of consideration, it was
decided that according to the National Agreement a wholesale reduction was not per-
missible. We pointed out to the representatives of the London Employers that anomalous
items can be dealt with, but general reductions are not permissible. A similar opinion
was given on a case sent to the Committee some time ago by the Northants County Board.
We, who have spent so much time, and have so much experience with statements, would
rather deal with any anomalous operation than permit a wholesale reduction, because
if that were permitted, minimas would be reduced. Ability and power, quickness or
slowness, only permits them to, with effort, earn the minimum rate, and it would be
outraging our own agreements if we encouraged this to be done. I am convinced the
statements we have in various Departments at the present time only want alteration
and amendment as conditions require.

We also had under discussion a question respecting two of the Leicester Branches,
in which there was a difference of opinion. The Committee's resolution unanimously
agreed to was as follows:-

"That the Joint Standing Committee regret it should have been found necessary
to bring this matter before them, as it seems one which should have been capable of
amicable adjustment between the parties concerned. After considering the matter,
the decision of the Joint Standing Committee is that the National (Conference)
Agreement, 1924, like its two predecessors, expressly recognises in Clause 8, C. the
employment of women upon Heel Building without any exception, in so far as districts
are concerned."

MANSFIELD. Several visits have been paid to this town by myself respecting the
conditions of employment at the Mansfield Shoe Co.'s works. I have for a long time
been trying to get this firm to see their way to adopt the statement of prices regarding
girls on Clicking Presses, and although this firm has, some two or three years ago, promised
to bring about a change in this direction (seeing that there is not a volume of male labour
available), boys and men in most cases prefer to work in the Pits, rather than in the Shoe
Factory. We have only one alternative, which to my mind must be pressed to its logical
conclusion, i.e., that the rate for men must be paid unless piecework prices are agreed
upon, which must be the same, irrespective of sex. Upon that particular point we have
already been threatened by the firm to the extent that they should remove the girls and
bring our Union into disrepute. That I told them would be decidedly unfair; the girls
have a right to the statement price equally with men.

We have a difference with the firm in regard to the Rodeo or Top Boot prices that
can only be settled by reference to the Secretary of the Leicester Association, and I have
invited the firm to send their patterns to that gentleman who is willing to give them help.
We have also a difference with them regarding the Seat Sinking; they claim Consol
operators should sink their own seats without extra pay. Boy labour is rampant in this
particular firm, in spite of the fact that they say they cannot get boys, yet they appear
to be able to get more than the National Agreement promises. The Canvas work price is
very unsatisfactory regarding their method of cutting, which is four at a time, as compared
with two at a time in other places. Here our Organisers have been doing their very best
to organise the operatives, and I am pleased to say that at the present moment, the major
portion of the more important operatives are members of our Union, and I am hoping
when these complaints have been considered by the Mansfield, Nottingham and Derby
Board of Arbitration, they will have met with such support that our relationships will be
better in the future than they have been in the past.


---
FAIRE BROS., MANSFIELD. An effort has been made by the firm to meet in part the
claims made against them. Already I have received from the Chairman of the Directors
copies of notices to be put up showing them the scale of wages applicable to our girls
and women, to be paid as from 14th January, 1926. Two sets of prices for Skivers
and Moulders have been accepted. The one for Pasters, I am not sure of, and therefore
am making further enquiries. I have thanked them for what they have done, and I have
requested them, through a brother of the firm, to please comply with time-and-a-quarter
for overtime (if any is worked), Holiday Pay, Men's rates for the Girls on Presses, or the
Men's piecework prices for each particular operation, according to the Leicestershire
statement, I have further made a request that the firm should at least place the organisa-
tion where they disturbed it six months ago when they discharged 25 girls, causing our
110 members to cease paying. The least they can do is to put up the " Organisation of
Industry " document in a prominent place on the firm. This is all we ask, which is similar
to what is being done elsewhere, and I am hoping that the matter will soon be settled.
I am not likely to give up until it is.

LOOMS, MARKET HARBOROUGH. Mr. Looms, of Market Harborough, has not yet
replied to my recent letters. I have asked him to place in a prominent place in his factory,
the resolution " Organisation of Industry." If this is done, I think that within a very
short period we could congratulate ourselves of good feeling between Mr. Looms and us.
firm is enabled to beat other people in the same industry, which, whilst being no concern
of ours, only lends colour if Mr. Looms prevents his operatives from belonging to our
Union and from getting advice which they would be entitled to have, if they were members
of our Union.

I am still hopeful that he will yet see the wisdom of this recommendation as the above
resolution will be, I hope rigidly applied to everybody working in the industry.

KETTERING. I have had occasion to visit Kettering regarding a case at Messrs. W.
Timpson Ltd., and I should like to say that this is one of the very best firms in our industry,
and although my visit there was of minor importance, still the opportunity of meeting
the Managing Director, Mr. Timpson, and his Manager, Mr. Hawthorne, will I think
remove any doubt if they ever entertained any, but that we as a Union hold them in
the highest esteem and regard, and therefore if at times there is a difference between
ourselves and our friends the employers, such as this firm are, we get rather askance from
looking at one thing from different angles. I hope a short interview, such as we had with
the firm, will allay any probable friction that might arise.

HEEL BUILDING MANUFACTURERS (NORTHANTS.). - As reported in my last month's
report we endeavoured to hold another meeting of the gentlemen in this industry, some
thirteen in number, on the 16th December, but on that occasion only four firms put in an
appearance. I rather came to the conclusion that being so close to Xmas these gentlemen
did not feel with the festive season upon them, likely to make a new move in the direction
we had indicated on organisation. Whilst it may be strange for Trade Union Officials
to try and get together employers of labour, still, we don't hesitate, because we feel that as
a Union we are likely to benefit by getting them all to work to either day or piece, which
will ultimately allay competition between themselves, the butt being labour conditions.
At present we have no complaint to make, although there is headway still to be made.
I am pleased to say that since that last meeting, the suggestion was made that we should
call another meeting some time in February. We have been enabled to elicit the services
of a very prominent member of the Federation, who is willing to give us assistance on any
future occasion. With this object in view, we have circularised the whole of the firms,
asking them to choose one of three dates which we trust they will not hesitate to do, and
we are rather inclined to think that we may make some headway on the next occasion.
Be that as it may, the third time " might pay for all," and we hope to be successful.

TRADE BOARD. The Midland District Trade Board was held at Birmingham early
this month, and the recommendations of the Committee were considered pro and con,
the anomalies gone over, and the fall back rates for boys not registered either as learners
or apprentices were accepted unanimously, which means that a firm which starts a boy at
15 years of age without having him registered or indentured as an apprentice, will have to
pay 23s. 6d. per week to him. The Ministry of Labour argued that the magistrates of this
country without this amended clause would never have given a judgment, seeing that an
unregistered learner or apprentice was entitled to 60s. at the age of 15, and although we
only issued that according to what we understood at the time to be the law (and as we
have legal minds on our Central Committee), they rather held the view that it was not
until the Ministry of Labour on the advice of the law officers of the Crown, suggested to us
that we should give a fall back rate of probably 10s. more than the usual learners' rate
was fixed. The other rates for persons who have served twelve months or less at the
industry, only apply to ex-Soldiers, ex-Sailors, and ex-Airmen, who are leaving the service.
manship. This also we unanimously accepted.

From the workers' side of the Board, we proposed that in the repairing of the Rodeo
or Top Boot, 2d. per pair should be paid the benchman. This was agreed to, the Central
Board to discriminate as to its distribution or whether it was to apply to top-piecing a
pair of ladies' top boots, as well as soleing and heeling them.

A meeting of the LONDON DISTRICT BOARD has also been held, at which I was present,
and on this occasion an attempt was made to increase the rates for juveniles mentioned
above as a fall back rate, but this was not pressed after the chairman, Mr. Addington
Willis had informed the meeting of the many hours the Central Board had spent upon this
important part of their work, and ultimately the recommendations made were unanimously
accepted.

We again brought forward the repairing of Top Boots or Rodeo, and on this occasion
the Board unanimously supported the Birmingham recommendation, and also asked the
Board to consider what extra should be given for fastening a new heel on a ladies' top
boot from the inside. Further, a new lining for the heel. This lining, owing to the boot
having no lace or strap across the instep wear out rather quickly through chafing. This
matter we unanimously accepted and referred to the Central Board adjudication.

C.W.S., LEICESTER. - I have also visited the C.W.S., Duns Lane, regarding the rates
paid to the Consol Operators and Sole Attachers employed at the Abbey Mills, Derby.
It was pointed out that the men had an idea that they would get an increase in wage over
what he makes, and the Maanger, Mr. Clifton, assured me that this was so, but at the same
time he preferred, what we know in the trade as a set wage, and it was evident from his
figures that the men get a better condition than they would get from the statement, but
at the same time whilst he is willing to give them this advantage, he thinks by a set wage
arrangement there is a better type of work done by the operatives rather than by spas-
modical rise and fall, according to the man's ability. I am pleased to say that I am
reporting to the operatives upon this point, and hope to be able to promote a better feeling
than has hitherto prevailed.

NORTHANTS DISTRICT ADVISORY COUNCIL arranged a conference at the Rockingham
Road Schools to be addressed by Mr. J. W. Muir, Organiser of the Workers' Educational
Association, who took for his subject "The Educational Proposals of the Trades Union
Congress," &c. Mr. L. House, B.Sc., Headmaster of one of the local Schools, occupied
the chair, and said if anyone asked him what was education he would find it very difficult
to answer. Mr. Muir dealt triumphantly with Education proposals, and sought to make
it quite clear that education to him meant by hard work and study to bring out all that
was best, according to their own fitness of every human being. Personal gain was not to
be the aim, or education for oneself, although study and training make the mind more alert
and prepared to measure, weigh and sift arguments, statements and the passing phases
of life. He dealt with our great unpreparedness, if at any time the working section of the
community were called upon to act by carrying on industry altogether. The best educa-
tional address I have ever listened to for practical common sense.

FOREIGN COMPETITION. -- Respecting foreign competition and other matters in general
I have had correspondence with the Spaulding Fibre Co., of North Rochester, N.Y.,
America, in which I have asked some very important questions, and informed them that
we are anxious to be fair and just even to people in America, and that we expect the
conditions prevailing there to be no worse than the conditions prevailing in our own
country among the Stiffening Makers. Before giving publicity to their answer, I shall
have to ask them further questions, the present not meeting all we require. As an illus-
tration, there is no payemnt for holidays, night work, and Sunday work is only paid time-
and-a-half, and so on, but I am asking for further information before expressing a definite
opinion. I am also in correspondence with the Bennett Stiffening Co., Chanbley, Canton,
Quebec, Canada, and I am asking similar questions. Also I am in correspondence with
Mr. Chamberlain, Nailsworth, Glos., who believes he is a fair house, and have put a point
of interest to the operatives where they benefit under our National Agreement. If by
this means we can bring all these people to at least give conditions equal to our own, then
we shall have made some headway.

Beware of Unstamped Boots and buy the *Daily Herald.*

Yours fraternally,

M. F. Richards
General President.

BRANCH REPORTS.
BELFAST.- We regret to report that trade continues to remain in a
very bad state; the firm of Williamson Bros. has closed down the Bottoming
and Finishing end for an indefinite period. We would remind our branch
members that only by conforming to the rules can they be paid Union benefits.
We would also remind our members that the branch meetings are held on the
first Monday in each month at 8 o'clock, in the Typographical Hall, Frederick
Street. We feel that we are not making an unreasonable demand upon any
member's time when we ask them to give two hours in the month in considering
and discussing matters pertaining to their interests and welfare.
CHESHAM. - Trade here still remains very good. At the time of writing
this report our old friend, W. R. Smith, has just concluded a visit to Chesham.
He has visited some of our manufacturers and renewed old acquaintances.
An effort was made to create some enthusiasm by arranging a special meeting
for members, but the effort was most disappointing to us, only a mere handful
of members attending the meeting. We had an inspiring address from our
friend, and hope to be able to again have his services in the near future.
CHESTERFIELD. - Trade is only fair and has fell off during the month
both for repairers and men on new work.
DERBY. - Trade in Derby is a little better this month, and shows signs
of improving. We still have Mr. Baum and Mr. McCarthy coming to Derby
to consolidate the position at Maden & Ireland's, where we have over 100
members now. Since they have joined the Union this firm has formed what
they call a Thrift Fund, which is practically the same as the Holiday Fund of
our Union. Of course that is only a sop to deter them from joining the Union.
DUNDALK.- It is with pleasure we find ourselves in a position to be able
to forward for registration the names of our members who have completed
their probationary period. Furthermore we wish to congratulate the members
on their steadfast fidelity to so glorious and inspiring a cause, a cause promoted
on unselfish motives. Even more its one primary object is the emancipation of
the toiling multitudes, regardless of their racial or religious aspirations. On
reading in prehistoric annals the mighty conquests of Spartan Greece, or the
empire-building powers of Alexander the Great, few of us there are who can
restrain the throbbing heart or resist the instant impulse of wishing we were
in train. Again, in the late mediæval ages, we should like to have participated
in the almost supernatural conquests of Napoleon Bonaparte. Still, in prac-
tically all these engagements, those who were to wear the crown of laurels
were well in the background, and even on the rare occasions when leaders
formed the vanguard, what did humanity gain? Nothing save the demoralisa-
tion of its own fundamental construction, the working slave, slain by a brother
slave, in an endeavour to retain the militant ambitions of a despotic ruler.
On the other hand how few there are of us who ever commemorate the memory
of those unarmed leaders, who by constitutional means nobly fought and
bravely won for us humble working men an eight-hour day and a living wage.
Fellow workers, those of you who have fallen away, we invite you to begin the
year 1926 well by returning to the fondling and caressing embrace of the National
Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives-a Union of democratic principles, a Union
of the workers, for the workers, and by the workers.
HIGHAM AND RUSHDEN.- We wish the General Officers and Staff
the Compliments of the Season. The holiday has been a lengthened one in
most factories. Most have now resumed work and trade is slightly better.
The monthly meetings approved of doubling the Affiliation Fees to Labour
Party for one year only.


---
KILMARNOCK. Trade in the Kilmarnock Branch is fairly good. There
is also an improvement in the repairing trade, but our Kilmaurs Section is
still very bad. We are also pleased to report one of our oldest members,
Mr. J. Campbell, celebrated his silver wedding on Hogmanay, in the Riccartion
Institute, representatives of the Branch being present. We spent a most
enjoyable evening and wished Mr. and Mrs. J. Campbell long life and happiness,
which we know will be heartily accorded amongst our members and friends
in the trade.
KINGSWOOD AND DISTRICT. 1926, with all its hopes and aspirations,
opens its vista before us, and as the years pass behind us we realise the nature
of change more vividly. Our retrospect of the year that has passed is one of
many changes friends that comforted have passed away. The year before
us is one that must have possibilities. Much work of an educational character
requires to be done. Changes in methods of manufacture will require constant
encouragement. The employers who study the desires of the public in lighter
recent Board Meeting the need for joint discussions of matters affecting the
welfare of the industry was under discussion, and it is hoped to extend the
opportunities for employers and workmen to face the facts, and by a combined
effort pull the Kingswood boot industry out of the conventional rut. The
members at Branch Meeting approved of the Educational Scheme published
in the October Report, and signed by Geo. Chester, on behalf of the Northants
Joint District Council.
LEEDS No. 1. There is little improvement (if any) in the heavy footwear,
but in reference to the medium and light class there is a slight improvement.
The result of the second ballot for Branch Secretary is as follows :-A. F. Peat,
304 votes; H. Caywood, 88 votes.
LIVERPOOL. During the past month the boot repairing trade has been
much the same as in previous years a general slump towards the end, but the
New Year has opened out with brighter prospects and increased business in
so far as our particular industry is concerned. The District Committee of the
Boot and Shoe Repairing Trade Board (Lancashire and Cheshire) were sum-
moned to a meeting in Manchester on 11th December, to consider the new
proposals that have been sent out recently, the principal item being the new
scale for youths or men as learners or apprentices.
LONDON SOUTH. Arbitration Board met on the 30th November, 1925.
Proposed Piece Statement for Machine Sewn Turnshoe. After a long dis-
cussion with regard to the ground work, the employers wanted the One-Bar
Shoe to be the above, but on the workmen's side we claimed the Court Shoe to
be the proper ground work to start from as on the Louis Heel Statement, as
the One-Bar Shoe is much harder to turn than the Court Shoe. After a long
discussion the workmen's side gained their point. It was then adjourned for
the employers to reconsider the prices which they offered, no workman would
make them at the price agreed. Adjourned discussion then took place upon
the reduction of the First Statement. Of course the workmen's side could
not entertain any alteration until the cost of living went down below 70 points.
The first class employers present thought it was coming off, but after a long
discussion the matter was adjourned for the employers to ask the Standing
Orders Committee if the Board has power to alter the agreement until below
70 points. Agreed.
MAYBOLE. We are sorry to report that trade has fallen off a bit and in
consequence long holidays and suspensions are very general here. We hope
this will not be for very long. We are pleased to report sickness very light,
which is something new at this season of the year.


---
PLYMOUTH.-Our members had before them at their Branch Meeting
the Council's letter concerning Education, and although this opens up a very
wide field of thought and discussion, we must admit that the subject left our
members cold. This is not because we do not believe in the best of education
being obtained for all, but the Slough of Despond in which we find ourselves,
owing to bad trade, has left us in despair of ever being able to reach the Celestial
City; that is, if we regard it as a place of comfort and plenty. It appears to
us that the general progress of education, owing to its national character,
has been far more rapid than the economic advancement of the workers.
Possibly there is little to regret in this, seeing that one is bound to follow the
other sooner or later, but the immediate necessity seems to us to be a general
advancement in the material well-being of all workers, not because we regard
the material things of this world as the end of all intellectual and moral effort.
but because the education already received at school, in the factory and our
branch meetings, makes our hearts vearn for a larger and fuller life. We know
that without the common necessities of life this is impossible. Thus, we get
back to the same old problem, "How to live." We doubt sincerely, if all the
learning of Oxford and Cambridge were made accessible to every worker,
that there must be many whose education would lag behind in the race, and the
cunning and greed of a few would endeavour to enslave their fellows, as we see
at the present moment. The conclusion is forced upon us that just a few are
greedily devouring the family cake, while the many pick up the crumbs. Could
not something be done to stop this rapacity, and all incomes over a certain
figure be utilised for replenishing the family larder? The common morality
of a well-regulated family should be made applicable to the national family,
and the familiar gospel of "Bear ye one another's burdens" given a chance.
SILEBY.-Trade is fairly well in the Sileby District. We have had the
pleasure of our Organisers, Mr. Baum and Mr. McCarthy with us. They have
been to several of the factories and addressed the operatives, who have listened
to them with interest in the splendid way they have pointed out the objects
of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives. Good results are bound
to follow.
WATERFORD.-Trade still continues good.
GREAT YARMOUTH.-Sorry to report Water Boot trade very slow
again in Great Yarmouth.

13 GRANGE STREET,
EDUCATIONAL SCHEME.
KILMARNOCK,
5th January, 1926.
FELLOW MEMBERS.
At the Conference of the Union to be held this year at Blackpool it is expected
that more consideration than usual will be given to the question of an Educational Scheme
for the members, and bearing this in mind I think we ought to devote a little space and
time to the consideration of this question.
At the present moment we have two bodies claiming to supply educational schemes
for trade unions, the Workers' Educational Trade Union Committee and the National
Council of Labour Colleges, both of which bodies operate under a joint scheme with the
British Trades Union Congress.
Up till the present moment the majority of unions adopting educational schemes
have placed them with the N.C.L.C., because it provides Independent Working Class
Education, and unlike the W.E.A. (of which the W.E.T.U.C. is part) the N.C.L.C. is
entirely financed and controlled by the Trade Union and Labour movement.
According to Rule 20 one of the objects of the Union is "the socialisation of the
means of production, to be controlled by a democratic state in the interests of the entire
community, and the complete emancipation of Labour from the domination of Capitalism
and Landlordism, with the establishment of a social and economic equality between the
sexes." The W.E.A. does not stand for this object, otherwise it would not receive State
support. On the other hand the N.C.L.C. does stand for this object, and it would only
be consistent with the policy of our Union as laid out in the rules, to arrange an Educational
Scheme with a body subscribing to principles similar to our own.
The following table taken from Plebs (July, 1925) shows that the great majority of
British Trade Union Educational Schemes have been placed with the National Council of
Labour Colleges and its constituent Colleges :-
Unions with N.C.L.C. Schemes
Unions with W.E.A., W.E.T.U.C., and Ruskin
College Schemes
No.
25
9
Membership.
1,689,215
621,630
Bearing these facts in mind, fellow members, I think it is clearly our duty to support
the educational body which is out along with us for "the complete emancipation of Labour
from the domination of Capitalism and Landlordism," namely, the National Council of
Labour Colleges."
Yours fraternally,
THOMAS CAMPBELL, No. 96068.
TARIFF RESULTS.
It was announced a few days ago that the Irish Free State Government, in its forthcoming Budget, would not increase the existing duty on imported boots. It was also
stated that it was not intended to add to the present list of taxed imports. The view of
the Government is that no further duties should be imposed until sufficient time has elapsed
in which to form a definite conclusion as to the effects of the present tariff. A correspondent suggests that this policy may have been adopted on account OF THE FAILURE
OF THE 15 PER CENT. DUTY ON BOOTS TO PRODUCE THE NUMEROUS ADVANTAGES PROMISED
BY ITS SUPPORTERS. The extent of the failure of the tariff has been emphasised by Major
Bryan Cooper, who is a member of the Dail. Speaking at Rathmines last week he said
that, since the duty was imposed, the number of workers in the Free State boot manufacturing INDUSTRY HAD INCREASED BY ONLY 488, WHILE THE REVENUE PRODUCED HAD
TOTALLED £225,206. ON THE OTHER HAND, THE COST OF BOOTS HAD INCREASED BY 16
PER CENT. In the circumstances it is not surprising that the Government is disinclined
to indulge in further " tariff experiments "-as they were originally described by the
Minister of Finance.

The results bear out the generally held opinion that 1925 was an unusually successful
year for the retail section. They may also be regarded by some members of the traul
veestablishing the contention that present-day conditions provide greater rewards ade
distributors than they do for manufacturers. Producers, including tanners and leather
distributors, will certainly emphasise the fact that whereas Freeman's, Sears, and
Stead's each show progress, the accounts of Weber and Phillips disclose a falling off. and
the strength of this it will doubtless be alleged that retail distributors are obtaining an
undue proportion of the profits made by the industry. It is by no means certain that
und wiew is accurate. In our Shoe Distributor Section will be found an analysis of Free-
man's figures from which it will be seen that the net profit per branch represents a sum
which, given sufficient capital and modern equipment, a single shop retailer would rightly
regard as inadequate. The profit earned by the multiples is not due to the exaction of
high prices, but to keen buying, shrewd judgment in gauging the trend of public taste
and to efficient organisation. Similar ability is being displayed by private shoesellers,
and the results of their trading are, in many instances, probably, better in proportion
than those shown by their great rivals.--The Shoe and Leather Record, 22nd January, 1920.
IMPORTS AND EXPORTS IN 1925.
The Board of Trade Returns for December last, issued this week, complete the
accounts for 1925, and are, therefore, of more than usual interest. Regarded as a whole,
the results shown, in relation to the export trade of the country, are not satisfactory, but
so far as the shoe and leather industries are concerned, there is no serious cause for com-
plaint. Indeed, it can be said that in a year which was not a prosperous one for export
business generally, the shoe and leather industries have done well to hold their own in
overseas markets. In value, our exports of leather boots and shoes last year reached
£4,638,597, as compared with £5,023,875 in 1924. There was, however, a comparatively
small difference in the quantities exported which were as follows:-1924, pairs 11,973,336:
1925, pairs 11,837,196. An interesting feature of the past year's exports is that the
number of countries which increased their purchases of British-made shoes was larger
than the number which imported less freely than in 1924. The markets which showed
an improvement were-Egypt, the United States, British East Indies, Australia, New
Zealand and the British West India Islands. Those who showed decreases included the
Netherlands, France, Irish Free State, South Africa and Canada. The fluctuations were,
however, comparatively small, except in the case of the markets grouped as
Countries." Collectively, they increased their imports from 1,026,404 pairs in 1924 to
1,380,396 pairs last year. In view of the recovery of trade with the countries included in
this group it will probably be decided to show some of them separately in future. The
two most important markets are Norway and Denmark.
Other

The figures for 1924-2,746,944 pairs, valued at £1,414,778-show that there was a small
increase in purchases of foreign-made shoes, but in view of the large excess of exports
over imports there is little cause for uneasiness on the part of shoe manufacturers. There
was a decrease in imports of footwear made of other materials than leather-chiefly
slippers-which, in value, represented £17,880, and in quantity 126,228 pairs.

year's total, against 120,405 cwts., value £1,095,416 in 1924. Imports of dressed leather

and 1925, 174,801 cwts., value £7.319,117. The United States supplied a larger share of

TRADE UNION CONGRESS GENERAL COUNCIL.
Land Workers and Town Workers.
We preach solidarity, but we only creep towards its practice by slow degrees. A big
move will be made when we can get land-workers and workers in towns to pull together.
There is nothing which cannot be done if such unity can be achieved.
The Trades Union Congress showed true awareness of these facts at Scarborough in
September last, and the Report on the Organisation Campaign for Agricultural Workers
was received with such strong approval that the Campaign is now being extended to fresh
areas,
Last year, it was conducted in Lincolnshire, Northampton, Notts, Norfolk, Dorset,
Anglesey, Cheshire, Hereford, Surrey, Cornwall, and in a few months' intensive work,
Over 10,000 agricultural trade unionists were enrolled, and many new branches opened.
This work cannot be carried on without funds, and though Congress voted £500
towards its continuance, an appeal is now being issued to all organisations affiliated to
the Trades Union Congress, for additional support. Every trade unionist who can offer
any help-however little-will be helping not only the agricultural worker, but the whole
movement.

**64**
**CAPITALIST ECONOMY ??**

United States.

Articles of food consumption have recently become exceedingly dear in the United States. Whereas in June, 1925, prices stood on an average at 55 per cent. above the pre war rates, by November they had reached 67 per cent. (and in Chicago even 76 per cent.).

Perhaps the most outstanding case in point is the price of bread, which the recently formed Bread Trust aims at keeping at the present high level, while at the same time it is attempting to cut costs, and so get the business and resultant profits into its own hands.

A POUND-LOAF OF BREAD IN FARGO, N.D., in the heart of the great Red River wheat country, COSTS 10 CENTS, AND YET A FOUR-POUND LOAF IN LONDON COSTS 9 PENCE, NOT QUITE 18 CENTS, OR 44 CENTS PER POUND. It will be realised just how significant this is when it is remembered that more than half the bread of London is made from wheat shipped from North America, largely from the region centring in Fargo. To get to London, this wheat must be carried to the coast by rail or lake and rail transferred to steamers and then taken across the ocean. And yet, after all these expenses, the finished product costs half as much in London as in Fargo-though we may be sure that the London bakeries don't lose in the sale of their bread, but see to it that they make their bit.

**CHANGES IN COST OF LIVING: STATISTICS FOR 1st JANUARY, 1926.**

**FOOD.**

At 1st January the average level of the retail prices of the principal articles of food showed a decline as compared with 1st December. Decreases of over 2d. per lb. in the average price of butter and of about d. each in the average price of eggs more than counter-balanced increases in the prices of flour and bread, and other less important increases.

As a net result of all the changes recorded, the average increase over the level of July, 1914, in the retail prices (in Great Britain and Northern Ireland) of the articles of food included in these statistics was about 71 per cent. at 1st January, as compared with about 74 per cent. at 1st December, and 78 per cent. at the corresponding date in 1925. - The Ministry of Labour Gazette, January, 1926.

Every precaution is taken by us to ensure accuracy in these Reports, our correspondents
being men on whom we can rely; should, however, any errors creep into them, upon the
same being pointed out to us, we shall be most happy to give the same prominence to the
correction as to the original matter. As these Reports are exclusively for the use of Members,
the information contained therein must not be divulged.

22ND FEBRUARY, 1926.

**FELLOW MEMBERS,**

**CIRCULARS**

REGARDING SEVERAL IMPORTANT MATTERS have been issued during the month;

**TRADE.**

With few exceptions there is a slight improvement in trade, and we can
only hope it will speedily still further improve, not only in our industry, but
in the general trades of the country, thereby finding employment for that large
army of men and women who have been vainly looking for work for a long
time past. The figures issued by the Ministry of Labour Gazette are :-

**BOOT AND SHOE INDUSTRY.**

Employment was moderate on the whole during January, and there was no marked
general change compared with December or with January, 1925. As has been the case
for a very considerable time, a large proportion of the operatives were on short time during
the month.

The percentage of workpeople unemployed, as indicated by the unemployment
books lodged at Employment Exchanges, was 8.7 on 25th January, 1926, compared with
8.5 on 21st December, 1925, and 11.0 on 26th January, 1925.

POLITICAL.
The House of Commons reassembled on the 2nd inst., and once more
the Government have presented the King's Speech to the House, which in
our judgment is very disappointing indeed looked at from the standpoint of
the nation as a whole, especially bearing in mind the fact that there is still over
one million unemployed. There is one paragraph in the Speech to which
we would call attention; after a reference to the Coal Industry the Speech
goes on to say, "but the interests of the nation are paramount." We can only
hope the "interests of the nation" will be dealt with as being paramount
above all sectional interests, and to this end, however far-reaching it may be
B


---
26
found necessary for bringing about alterations, we trust the force of public
opinion will be such as to ensure drastic treatment of not only the Coal Industry,
but other vital matters which are long overdue if the "paramount interests"
are to receive not only proper attention but an effective policy laid down.

The Labour Party has been active day by day in endeavouring to force
the pace in regard to the many matters for which the Labour Party stands.
The vote, however, from time to time is cast against them. Nevertheless,
the work continues and will continue, but it will become the more effective
if the people in the country show they are taking a live interest in the pro-
ceedings in the House of Commons from day to day. We therefore appeal
to the membership to do their part in this work so that the Labour Party,
although they may be in a minority, may see their work become increasingly
effective because of the backing of public opinion outside the House.

There are two other matters to which we wish to call special attention.

THE WASHINGTON CONVENTION-HOURS OF LABOUR.

This Convention the British Government supported, but despite all efforts
made since 1919 by the Trades Union Congress, the Labour Party and other
organisations, the Government still refuses to ratify the Convention. Amongst
the excuses made it is stated our system of jurisprudence is different from that
on the Continent. We are told there are Voluntary Agreements, and the
Railwaymen's Agreement, although it is pointed out that there are clauses in
the Convention to deal with special cases. Quite recently the Railwaymen
ed to a formula to meet the position. The utmost that has been done is
he Minister of Labour to enter into negotiation with some of the represen-
ives of the principal Continental countries. The fact of Great Britain
refusing to ratify the Convention is constantly used by other nations as a
reason why they cannot do so, they stating that Great Britain being the chief
industrial country of Europe it is essential that Great Britain should ratify,
when they will do so. Thus it is not only the non-fulfilment of an Agreement
entered into affecting Great Britain, but has a much wider effect in retarding
this beneficial reform being put into force in other countries.

THE FACTORIES BILL.

This Bill has been promised from time to time and is constantly being
shelved on the plea that there is no time to deal with it having regard to the
many matters before the House of Commons. We venture to suggest that
if the House of Commons procedure was replaced by an up-to-date system,
time could easily be found for dealing with many reforms which are long
overdue. If the proposals of the Trades Union Congress and the Labour
Party were put into practice a better state of health would be brought about.
We hope the members will keep these matters alive, because it is only by
constant pressure that reforms are brought into being. The Prime Minister
