THE GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.

60 LADY SOMERSET ROAD,
KENTISH TOWN, N.W. 5.
16th February, 1926.

FELLOW MEMBERS,
BRITISH GOODS. - You often meet the cry "Buy only British Goods." I have
had occasion to make inquiries, and in support of the above find that no country pays
its operatives (with the exception of America) as well as ours in the Boot and Shoe Industry,
and therefore those people who would like to help their own countrymen first-I say
first-can find no Boots or Shoes produced under more humane conditions than the British
article, unless it may be in America. In this continent I have my doubts, and wish it to
be known that the American Fibre Stiffenings cannot be recommended by us for use in
British Boots. Our evidence from one particular firm itself shows that the labour engaged
is non-Union, that the rates (considering the cost of living) are economically lower than
ours, that the National Agreement's conditions of this country are much higher than that
in the American factory. They pay no Holiday Pay, they pay no overtime rates; they
only pay time and a half for Sundays, when we demand and get (if we work), double time.
They pay time and a half for night work, for which we claim double time. I am also
informed by our friends in the American Boot and Shoe Operatives' Union that the con-
ditions in Canada are no better than the conditions in America in the Stiffening making
trade.
Further, I have obtained information respecting Gloucestershire, in this country,
which leads me to say that we cannot recommend the Stiffenings coming from that district,
and it really behoves every Manufacturer, who deals with these people, to ask himself
this question: "Having had the intimation made to me that a part of the goods I sell
have been produced under conditions worse than used to prevail when we produced our
own Stiffenings, ought I to encourage a lower standard of life for workers in the Auxiliary
Branches of the trade, when I can get these articles from British makers who produce
them, and if I don't, WHERE DOES MY PATRIOTISM COME IN?" All I ask is, every Manufac-
turer in the trade, be he Tory, Liberal, Socialist, or non-partisan, should the above continue,
with the information obtained from the source of supply (not from me) but direct. No
one would agree that our Union's Executive in these early stages should advise our members
what action they should take. We prefer to give publicity first, then allow a short respite;
then see the Federation and the various Associations, then to advise our members to
deputise their respective employers (with an officer of the Union) with the object of getting
all Auxiliary Firms to respect the National Agreement in its entirety, or to take up the
attitude that we do not patronise. The above will cause some qualms of conscience
respecting the law on libel, the most elastic word and the most uncertain in the English
Dictionary, which has caused more frights than the word "Death," but we have neither
fears nor qualms, because we wish no harm, no misrepresentation, no malice. All we
ask is, as in the spirit of the Fair Wages Contract Clause of the British House of Commons:
THAT YOUR CONDITIONS OF LABOUR ARE NOT WORSE THAN THE BEST HOUSES IN THE TRADE.

Our National Agreement is more than that, much more. It is backed by 80 per cent.
of the trade, whereas the above would prevail if only 30 per cent. of good firms practised
better conditions than the other 70 per cent. I so well remember the debate upon the
Amended Fair Wages Resolution, viz.: that the better firms, though few in number,
should really be the influence and guide.

MANSFIELD. This town is of real importance to us, if only we could so arrange affairs
in complete harmony with our National Agreement at the firm of Messrs. Faire Bros.
We have been attending to the organisation of this firm during the past twelve months.
This firm, after we had organised more than 95 per cent. of its employees, and who had
refused an appeal of the Management, had remained loyal to the Union, but upon the
discharge of 25 of the employees on the plea of shortness of work, the whole of the members
ceased paying, and for months refused the appeal of our organisers and myself. Thereby
we had to resort to other means and that was to appeal to the trade. For this purpose
we drew up a manifesto and placed the contents before the friends of the firm, who gave
such advice that has caused us to withhold our action, and we are requested to again see
the firm who have given us a promise that they will conform. Upon this we are acting,
and hope there will be no further trouble.

The SHERWOOD SHOE COMPANY, of the same town, has for some time been acting in
such a manner that has caused us to make several appeals to them to refer the several
differences between us to any of the tribunals for which the trade has provided for the

deal with the points in dispute, but owing to a prior engagement in one case, and a mis.

CO-PARTNERSHIP IN COAL.
Sir R. Redmayne's Suggestions.
Sir Richard Redmayne was the principal guest at the monthly lunch of the Labour
Co-partnership Association, held at the Holborn Restaurant, on 10th February, 1926,
and made suggestions for improving the present state of the coal industry. Mr. J. H.
Stobart Greenhalgh presided.
Sir Richard Redmayne said that coal and agriculture were the two greatest industries
of the kingdom, and coal-mining, as the greatest exporting industry, helped more than
any other to supply the nation with its food. The depression in the coal trade was not
confined to Great Britain, and the fact that British coals were the best and the coalfields
near the ports had combined to maintain our pre-eminence in the export trade in face of
increasing competition. We were still by far the biggest exporters of coal in the world,
and, he thought, always would be. Still, the fact remained that while there was an average
profit, taking all the mines, in 1913, of nearly 2s. 5d. a ton, there was now a loss of Is. 6d.,
or, if the subvention was allowed, a loss of about 2 d. That was a desperate position.
He would take a leaf from the German book and concentrate upon improved selling
arrangements and selling direct. He knew the middleman would shout, but if they took
a good Sheffield coal costing 23s. a ton, and added 14s., which made 37s., that should be
the price of household coal delivered in London. He wanted to know where the extra
135. a ton to-day was going to before that coal was put into their cellars. He did not
believe that the coal merchant was making exorbitant profits-he thought he was making
profits-but, either he was making exorbitant profits or something else was wrong some-
where with the distribution system. In the next 10 to 20 years, he thought, the biggest
question this country would be concerned with, after the housing question was settled,
was a simplification of distribution, on which far too much was spent, and especially
now they had motor haulage at their diaposal.
Further, he would endeavour to bring about a system of co-partnership. He was
not concerned at the moment to state how it should be done, but surely some system
was capable of being established, though before that system could be evolved the soil
on which it could grow must be different from that existing to-day. There would have
to be an end to these wild, blatant speeches made by some so-called leaders of the miners
and others. He could not believe that the coal trade, difficult as it was, was incapable
of the application of a co-partnership system, of which the South Metropolitan Gas Com-
pany was such an outstanding successful example. (Cheers.)
A vote of thanks to the speaker was moved by Sir William Chance and seconded by
Mr. Basil Peto, and Sir Richard Redmayne, in reply, reiterated that he thought in co-
partnership lay a solution of the present difficulties.

for the wage-earners, and those lacking courage and consciousness on this point will play

are often placed at a disadvantage, and often give us information which reveal a condition
of affairs that are far from satisfactory. Consequently our efforts should be in the direction
of complete organisation on this class of firm. It is very necessary to keep on increasing
our membership, and at the same time keep our members well informed of the prices that
should be paid for the operations performed. This is the problem in the Sileby District,
though it is exceedingly slow. Our members are growing more conscious of the power of
organisation, which is being reflected in their earnest desire, that the conditions they are
employed in should be up to the standard of other districts. I am fairly confident that
three firms need our attention, and can be dealt with only in so far that our membership
is strong enough to enforce the legitimate demands of the operatives.

J. H. BAUM.

FELLOW MEMBERS,

The past month has been spent between London and Kingswood, mostly in the
former place, where there is apparently always something to be done to keep the position
of the Union before both operatives and employers, as each section has a tendency so far
as certain firms are concerned to forget or overlook the merit of the condition that has
been established.

There is, however, a tendency towards the fixing of prices for the lasting and finishing
departments in conjunction with machinery, and one cannot but think that if this could
be done there would result an improvement of conditions for the operative and a stability
in regard to labour costs that would be of some advantage to the employer.

I am fully persuaded that an uncontrolled condition of things inside the factory so
far as costs are concerned is in the long run no good to employer or employed. It produces
bad organisation in the factories, causes loose methods in the departments, develops
an attitude of mind in regard to supervision that is in the long run very bad, because it
concentrates upon methods that are penny wise and pound foolish.

This is amply borne out by what is taking place in the different centres. The growth
and development of firms is greater where the Union policy is most firmly established.
Our conditions are no bar to progress in business, while the workers gain therefrom in a
manner that permit of no doubt whatsoever. This is, I believe, the experience of all our
branches and few could be found that would wish to go back to the old state of things.
This also applies to the employers who have always been ready to accept in the right spirit
the principles upon which the machinery and policy rest.

One would like to urge that our London members should make a big effort to get into
line in this respect. There are several large factories in which quantity statements could
be established with advantage all round, and in an area, where perhaps close supervision
is not so easy as in most provincial centres. This policy is essential if labour conditions
are to be what we aim at as Trade Unionists. By this means abuses can be better checked,
and in the end lead to a recognition of our organisation by employers who are in need of
improvement in that respect. It may be of course that all this will not be accomplished
without some trouble here and there. That only proves we are right in our methods.
C

BRANCH REPORTS.
CHESHAM. Trade here has fallen off. We are pleased to report that
during the month a claim for compensation on behalf of one of our members
has been settled for a lump sum of £75 and legal expenses; this, in addition to
part wages for three-and-a-half years, is considered satisfactory by the member
concerned.
CHESTERFIELD. Trade here has fallen off again and members are
working from 8 a.m. till 4 p.m., for men and women making new work. Repairers
are fairly well employed.
DERBY. - Trade in Derby has slightly improved which has resulted in
members bringing down their arrears and others rejoining. There is still
great dissatisfaction at the C.W.S. at Derby, where the Management seem to
think the minimum wage should be the maximum. For instance, two efficient
Consol operatives only get £3 each a week. We have had our General Presi-
dent down on their behalf, hoping things will be satisfactory speedily.
DESBOROUGH. Trade with us is moderate, but a great improvement
on the previous month, most of those in employment making fairly good time
but there seems no chance for those who are unemployed to get into work again
at present. Our sick pay during the last month has been very heavy, and we
regret there are no signs of a decrease at present.
DUNDALK. Trade continues good. During the present session of
Parliament the question of extending the tariff so as to include numerous
commodities at present exempt, and at the same time increase the tax on
articles already taxed. When the existing tariffs were proposed and sanctioned,
the Minister of Finance definitely stated that the duties were tentative and
experimental, and there was no intention of embarking on a large measure of
Protection. But, in the interval that has elapsed, various interests, in which
a selfish element is plainly discernable, have been at work, and pressure is
being systematically applied to the Government with the object of inducing
them to include many commodities which now enter free of duty. While
it is conceivable that a particular industry or a certain locality may be benefited
by the adoption of a tariff, it is, however, also demonstrable that such a policy,
if generally applied, must tend to increase the cost of living. In the column
reserved for correspondents of the January Monthly Report, Major Bryan
Cooper, Member of the Dail, is reported in part as saying, at Rathmines,
Dublin, "that the number of workers in the Free State boot manufacturing
had only increased by 488, on the other hand the cost of boots had increased
by 16 per cent. In the circumstance it is not surprising that the Government
is disinclined to indulge in further protection experiments." While readily
admitting our incapacity to experiment with his brobdignagian views, we
might, nevertheless, remind the honourable Major, that while we admire the
worthy motives which inspired his remarks, that Pittsburg, U.S.A., one of the
most flourishing cities in the world, largely owes its greatness to protection and
moderation. Of course moderate profits are essential to industrial and com-
mercial prosperity. Furthermore, we are of the opinion that at least some of
the boot manufacturers feel satisfied with a moderate profit. As regards the
workers, to the honourable Major we can definitely say, they in no way have
contributed to the increased cost of boots, in factories where employers and
workers consider their joint interest, rather than personal ones, and we are
proud as a humble branch of a broad-minded Union, to say, that we meet
broad-minded men at the helm here, and personal interests do not prevail,
only joint interests exist, solely because we examine together the divergencies


---
between us. It would be a pity if the middleman, whether an agent or not,
should endeavour to destroy by exorbitant prices the generous facilities placed
at our disposal by an infant Native Government.
HIGHAM AND RUSHDEN. Trade still remains poor. Rushden and
Higham, no change. Irthlingborough, worse than last month. Irchester
Wollaston, Bozeat and Finedon, fair. Raunds (Army and Navy Work).
improving, and if Government and Crown Agents' contracts materialise, it
will be much better.
KILMARNOCK. Trade in the Kilmarnock Branch is fairly good, but
there is no sign of any improvement in Kilmaurs. Many of our members are
going about idle, who have been unemployed for a considerable time. I may
also say the Repairing trade is also very dull, throughout this district.
KINGSWOOD AND DISTRICT. There is no improvement to report,
the condition of trade being very depressed. Several organising meetings have
been held during the month, and a vigorous programme will be carried out
during the coming months. The services of W. R. Smith during the previous
months have been much appreciated, and his vigorous manner of address has
been commended. This tireless propaganda should bring good results to the
Union membership when trade improves, and inspire the rank and file to be
resentful of all attempts by employers to encroach on the conditions embodied
in the National Agreement.
LEICESTER No. 1. Sickness is rather heavy. We are pleased to report
a further improvement in trade.
LIVERPOOL. The boot repairing trade has been fairly busy during the
past month, we hope it will continue. With regard to the Union Conference
(Blackpool), we suggest that the rules ought to be altered or amended in the
case of a member failing to obtain work in his (or her) own district, travelling
to another town where there is a branch and finding employment which is
likely to last for a considerable time. We are of the opinion that transfers
ht to be compulsory, that is, they ought to report to the branch secretary
e town or district where they obtain employment and pay their contribu-
to that branch, and not wait till trouble comes along in the form of un-
ployment or sickness, and then claim benefits from an official they have
never met, although perhaps working in the town for years, otherwise how are
we to know whether they are getting the proper rate of wages or working
under Union conditions. The same ought to apply to Approved members.
We get arrears cards to send out to members we know nothing about. As an
illustration we quote the case of the Liverpool Rubber Co., Walton. In 1923
they closed down for reconstruction, and two members from the Northants
district claimed unemployment benefit, which after correspondence with their
respective branches, we agreed to pay on condition that they paid us con-
tributions. One member found constant work with another firm here, but he
has never paid us any further contributions. The question is, did he drop out
or revert back to his old branch. The same sort of thing is going on now the
above-named firm have practically discharged their hands, and the members
are now looking for unemployment benefit from us although they belong to
the Northampton branches. We like a fair crack of the whip.
MAYBOLE.-Trade is still very bad, the worst we have experienced for
a long time. All the works are working about half time, some less. We hope
it will not be long before we have to report an improvement.
NORWICH. Sickness in Norwich has been heavy during the month,
but I am pleased to report trade has improved considerably during the same
period, with the promise of a continuation of better trade.


---
PLYMOUTH. - Our members discussed with interest the Draft Proposals
dealing with the Rules and Regulations of Superannuation Fund, and a generous
spirit of appreciation and loyalty to all the permanent officials of our Union
was evinced. It was generally recognised that many of the Union Officers
spend their lives in the service of their fellows, with very scant appreciation
and too often, inadequate reward. Therefore satisfaction was expressed with
the endeavour to provide each and all of the full-time servants of the organisa-
tion with some little security in old age, and their dependents assistance in
time of trouble, but while expressing their approval of the scheme, our members
voiced the opinion that they hope the time is not far distant when similar
proposals will be submitted for the inclusion of every member of the National
Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives, believing this would greatly help to keep
the membership stable, our policy sane, and encourage a pride of membership
much to be desired. Now Council, and Conference (Blackpool), can this be
done on 3 per cent. of our wages? If so, Plymouth is all in. We are afraid
not, but come what may the scheme is a generous one.

SHEPSHED. - The following Officers were elected at our Annual Meeting:
President, Mr. J. W. Smith; Secretary, Mr. E. Peberdy; Auditors, Messrs.
Lakin and Knight; Trustees, Messrs. A. J. Bennett and W. Wright, with a
strong Committee. We are hoping to increase our membership very soon.

SILEBY. - Trade is fairly well at present. Pleased to say that the valu-
able help our Organisers, Mr. J. H. Baum and Mr. D. McCarthy, are rendering
to our Branch is bearing fruit. We have increased our membership by forty,
although there is need for a large increase taking into consideration the numbers
that are working in the trade in and around the district.

STREET. - We are glad to report an improvement in trade and the
number of our unemployed members considerably reduced. There is still,
however, much room for further improvement as quite a number are working
short time. We have been successful in adding to the number of our repre-
sentatives on the Urban District Council of Street, as owing to the recent
death of a former member a by-election was necessary, when Mr. T. Baskerville,
a member of our Branch Committee, was put forward and was well supported
by our members, with the result that he headed the poll by 194 votes above
the next candidate. There were four aspirants for the honour and we are
naturally very proud of Mr. Baskerville's success as he is a most ardent and
active worker in the cause of Labour.

WATERFORD. - Trade still continues good.

Terms of Settlement.

NORWICH. - Delete Items A, B, C, and D of Resolution 5, as follows: -

a. No board shall require an employer to employ any particular workman,
or a workman to work for any particular employer, or shall entertain
any questions relating to such matters except for the purpose of
enabling a workman to clear his character.

b. No board shall claim jurisdiction over the conditions and terms of
employment of workpeople outside its district, provided that no actual
work shall be sent out of a district which has been the subject of an
award in that district.

c. No board shall interfere with the right of an employer to make reason-
able regulations for timekeeping, and the preservation of order in his
factory or workshop.

d. No board shall put restrictions on the introduction of machinery, or
the output therefrom, or on the adoption of day or piecework wages by
an employer in cases in which both systems have been sanctioned,
subject to the conditions prescribed in resolutions 2 and 3. No
question referred to in sub-sections a, b, c, and d shall be made a matter
of dispute by the Union.

GENERAL SUGGESTIONS.

BRISTOL NO. 1. - "This Conference instructs the Council to consider and
prepare a Voluntary Scheme for the Superannuation of all members, and
report to the next Conference."

BRISTOL NO. 2. - New Rule. - "That a Superannuation Scheme be established
for all members. The scheme be incorporated with the Sick and Funeral
Fund as this Fund is rapidly increasing. The Council to make a report
as early as possible on the extra contributions required to give members
a superannuation of 15s. per week at the age of 65. Conference to decide
what amount is to be drawn from the Sick and Funeral Fund and set aside
for this purpose. To approach the Manufacturers' Federation to see if
anything of a joint effort can be made to cover the industry."

LEICESTER NO. 1. - "That the Council prepare a Superannuation Scheme for
the members, such scheme to be submitted to the members and a ballot
be taken for their approval or otherwise."

LEICESTER NO. 1. - "That all members who are paying 1s. per week con-
tribution shall be entitled to full sick pay."

LEICESTER WOMEN'S. - "That the Executive Council of the Union, when
considering the next National Agreement, press for ONE minimum wage
for all operatives in the industry."

NORTHAMPTON. - "That instructions be given to the Council to draw up a
scheme of Pensions for members and report to a special conference."

NORWICH NO. 2. - "That the Norwich No. 2 Branch is of the opinion that
Clause 17 of the National Conference (September, 1924) Agreement should
be amended so as to include the Boy Labour restrictions in the Fitting-up
and Preparing Departments, and it be an instruction to the Executive
Council to press for same in future negotiations with the Manufacturers'
Federation. And that it be placed on the Agenda for discussion at the
next Conference.

THE 1919 SESSION (WASHINGTON) ADOPTED SIX DRAFT CONVENTIONS:-
1. Application of the principle of an eight-hour day and a forty-eight hour week.
2. Preventing or providing against unemployment.
3. Employment of women before and after childbirth.
4. Employment of women during the night.
5. Minimum age of employment of children in industry.
6. Night work of young persons employed in industry.

SIX RECOMMENDATIONS WERE ALSO ADOPTED CONCERNING:-
1. Establishment of public employment exchanges.
2. Reciprocity of treatment of foreign workers in regard to social legislation.
3. Prevention of anthrax.
4. Protection of women and children against lead poisoning.
5. Establishment of Government Health Services.
6. Application of the Berne Convention of 1906, on the prohibition of the use of white
phosphorus in the manufacture of matches.

THE 1920 SESSION (GENOA) ADOPTED THREE DRAFT CONVENTIONS:-
1. Age for admission of children to employment at sea.
2. Unemployment indemnity in case of shipwreck.
3. Facilities for finding employment for seamen.

FOUR RECOMMENDATIONS WERE ADOPTED CONCERNING --
1. Limitation of hours of work in the fishing industry.
2. Limitation of hours of work in inland navigation.
3. Establishment of national seamen's codes.
4. Unemployment insurance for seamen.

THE 1921 SESSION (GENEVA) ADOPTED SEVEN DRAFT CONVENTIONS:-
1. Right of association of agricultural workers.
2. Workmen's compensation in agriculture.
3. Minimum age of employment of children in agriculture.
4. Use of white lead in painting.
5. Minimum age of employment as trimmers and stokers at sea.
6. Medical examination of children and young persons employed at sea.
7. Weekly rest in industry.

EIGHT RECOMMENDATIONS WERE ADOPTED CONCERNING:-
1. Development of techical agricultural education.
2. Prevention of unemployment in agriculture.
3. Social insurance in agriculture.
4. Night work of children and young persons in agriculture.
5. Night work of women in agriculture.
6. Protection of women in agriculture before and after childbirth.
7. Living-in conditions of agricultural workers.
8. Weekly rest in commercial establishments.

THE 1922 SESSION (GENEVA), in addition to formulating a number of amendments
shown by experience to be necessary in the constitution of the International Labour
Organisation, ADOPTED ONE RECOMMENDATION CONCERNING:-
1. Statistical and other information regarding emigration and immigration; (each of
the States Members to communicate this to the International Labour Office every
three months, and, yearly, to inform the Office of the number of emigrants and
immigrants).

THE 1923 SESSION (GENEVA) ADOPTED ONE RECOMMENDATION CONCERNING:-
1. General principles for the organisation of systems of inspection: (a) to make
provision for an agreed standard of factory inspection in each country; (b) to secure
the enforcement of the laws and regulations for the protection of the workers.

THE 1924 SESSION (GENEVA) ADOPTED ONE RECOMMENDATION CONCERNING:-
1. Development of facilities for the utilisation of workers' spare time (i.e., provision
or improvement of educational and recreational opportunities offered to workers).

THE 1925 SESSION (GENEVA) ADOPTED FOUR DRAFT CONVENTIONS :-
1. Equality of treatment of national and foreign workers as regards workmen's
compensation for accidents.
2. Night-work in bakeries:
3. Workmen's compensation for occupational diseases.
4. Workmen's compensation for accidents.

1. Minimum scale of workmen's compensation.
2. Jurisdiction in disputes on workmen's compensation.
3. Workmen's compensation for occupational diseases.
4. Equality of treatment for national and foreign workers as regards workmen's
compensation for accidents.

THE FIRST 1926 SESSION (GENEVA) WILL CONSIDER:-
1. Simplification of the inspection of emigrants on board ship.

THE SECOND 1926 SESSION (GENEVA) WILL CONSIDER:-
1. International codification of rules relating to seamen's articles of agreement.
2. General principles for the inspection of the conditions of work of seamen.
(These two Sessions immediately follow one another, and for practical purposes form
one Conference.)

INDUSTRIAL PROGRESS IN NEW ZEALAND.
At the opening of the New Zealand and South Seas Exhibition at Dunedin, on 17th
November, 1925, the Prime Minister, the Hon. J. G. Coates, gave statistics showing the
Dominion's progress since the International Exhibition at Christchurch in 1906. The
figures for that year and 1924 are as follows:-
1906.         1924.
Manufacturing establishments          3,517         4,461
Employees          50,205         77,461
Wages and Salaries          £4,111,521         £14,573,441
Materials used          £12,772,720         £47,027,033
Total products          £22,425,000         £76,996,397

In the same period the value of production in the following industries increased as
follows:-
Industry.     Increase.
Engineering and agricultural implements          £1,613,000
Clothing          £2,091,000
Printing          £1,555,000
Biscuit-making and confectionery          £1,020,000
Furnishing          £800,000
Woollen          £1,025,000
Tanning, woolscouring and fellmongering          £1,000,000

These figures, the Prime Minister stated, were impressive, especially when it was
remembered that New Zealand was still to a large extent in the development stage. They
showed that the manufacturing industries were increasing in importance; and it was
necessary to remember the value of the industrial activities of the Dominion, because
it was erroneously considered purely as a producer of agricultural and pastoral products.
—Extract from Industrial and Labour Information, I.L.O., 1st February, 1926.

Summary : Average Increases since July, 1914.
All Items included          73 per cent.

FOOD.
At 1st February the average level of retail prices of the principal articles of food showed
a decline as compared with 1st January. This downward movement was mainly due to a
further seasonal fall of about 1d. each in the average price of eggs. Butter, cheese, bacon,
fish and butchers’ meat were also slightly cheaper than a month earlier. On the other
hand, flour, bread and tea were slightly dearer.
As a net result of all the changes recorded, the average increase over the level of July,
1914, in the retail prices (in Great Britain and Northern Ireland) of the articles of food
included in these statistics was about 68 per cent. at 1st February, as compared with
about 71 per cent. at 1st January, and 76 per cent. at the corresponding date in 1925.—
The Ministry of Labour Gazette, February, 1926.

HONOUR TO UNION STALWART.
The name of MR. JAMES GRIBBLE is well known to many members of the Union and
the work he has done on behalf of trades unionism generally. Owing to ill-health, and
failure to secure employment after the winding up of the Pioneer Boot Works, Northamp-
ton, Mr. Gribble now resides at Hastings. It was felt that he could not be allowed to
leave Northampton without some recognition of his very valuable work, and on the 26th
January, 1926, he was presented with an illuminated address and a cheque for £32 by the
members of the Northampton Labour Party.
For Mrs. Gribble there were a flower bowl and a pair of flower vases in beaten English
pewter but, unfortunately, she was unable to be present to receive them.
The address, framed in oak, and bearing Mr. Gribble's monogram and the Labour
Party's badge, was worded as follows: -
Northampton Labour Party
to
Mr. James Gribble, J.P.
On your departure from Northampton we desire to express our great appreciation of
the splendid services you have given to the Labour Party and the Trades Union movement
over a long series of years.
We gratefully recognise that it is largely due to your courageous efforts as a pioneer
and your self-sacrificing zeal in many directions that our cause occupies its present high
position.
To the merits of your work on the Town Council testimony has been borne by a
parties, whilst the immense value of the Gribble scheme of hospital contributions has
already been the subject of public recognition.
We trust that you and Mrs. Gribble will have a happy and prosperous future, and that
it will be long before your powers for usefulness know any diminution.
Signed, W. F. BELSON, President.
G. D. SIMPSON, Vice-President.
B. T. SPENCER, Secretary.
The ceremony took place in the Council Chamber, and the chair was occupied by
Mr. W. F. Belson (president of the Party).
The Chairman said the Party naturally regretted they would be losing the services
of Mr. Gribble, but they felt they could not persuade him to stay in the town in view of
the circumstances, which made his departure inevitable, and also that they could not let
him go without some expression of appreciation and goodwill from the comrades amongst
whom he had worked for so many years. The desire to make that expression was a spon-
taneous one within the Party.
Mr. Gribble was the builder of the Party. They knew he had to adopt methods ar
which some people looked askance, but there were often times when drastic measures
were necessary to call public attention to matters which were of vital importance to the
people.
No reference to Mr. Gribble's work would be complete without mention of the famous
march from Raunds to London, and his subsequent unauthorised speech in the House
of Commons. He undertook much hardship in working on behalf of those men, in marching
with them, and suffering exactly as they did, and it was because he felt their need was
great that he was prepared to suffer with them.
Mr. W. Pitts (secretary of the Northampton No. 1 Branch of the Boot and Shoe
Operatives' Union) referred to Mr. Gribble's early work in the movement.
Mr. E. Law (president of the No. 2 Branch of the Boot and Shoe Operatives' Union)
referred to the services which Mr. Gribble had rendered to that Union. "His advice to
me once," said Mr. Law, "was 'Keep a straight line, never turn, be fair, be firm, be solid,
and I am sure in the end you will make success.' "
The Chairman then handed the address and cheque and Mrs. Gribble's gifts to Mr.
Gribble, who, when he rose to speak, was greeted with loud and prolonged applause.
Mr. Gribble returned thanks and was much affected by the warmth of his reception.
said that everything he had been able to do had been a pleasure to him.
"I have certainly had a rather remarkable career," he continued, "as a Trade Unionist
and a Socialist. You all know I was a soldier at one time, and served my Queen and
country for seven and a half years with the Colours and some time with the Reserve.
I ceased to be a soldier on 10th January, 1893, and on 4th March of the same year joined
the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives, and have been a member ever since.
On 4th November of the same year I joined the S.D.F., and have been connected with that
ever since. As a Trade Unionist I have done all I possibly could to help on the great


---
121
ideals of the movement, and I have in my possession letters of thanks from most of the
local branches of the various unions and from some of the national organisations for the
work I have been able to do for them."
Mr. Gribble mentioned that he was the first National Organiser of the Boot Operatives'
Union, and started in adverse circumstances.
Speaking of the historic dispute at Raunds, which was concerned with the recognition
of a statement which had been formally agreed to, and which culminated in the march to
London, Mr. Gribble said the outcome of it was that the basis of the present fair wages
clause in all Government contracts was established. He had written to Government
officials in connection with the trouble and they kept asking for more information, and at
last the march was decided upon.
Continuing to speak of his trade union work, Mr. Gribble said he wanted the Union to
establish an educational college for training officials.
Mr. Gribble informed the company that he was forced to leave Northampton because,
although he did everything he possibly could, he could not get a job, "If I could have
got one," he said, " I should have stayed in Northampton, but fate was against me.
I love
Northampton. (Hear, hear.) Hastings is a beautiful place, but so is Northampton.
I can never understand, however, why my old town has been so long holding back from
its proper place in the councils of the country. It should have sent a Social Democratic
representative to Parliament years and years ago, but I believe you have a great future
before you.
I regret very much having to leave you, I shall always watch North-
ampton, and anything I can do to help the movement I shall be only too ready and pleased
to do." (Loud applause.)

CONDITIONS IN CHINA.
Changsha Shoemakers.
Shoemakers in Changsha, Hunan province, are divided into three classes: (1) makers
of foreign-style footwear, (2) makers of Chinese shoes, and (3) cobblers. The last-named
do not make shoes, but mend old ones. By custom they are also considered as members
of the shoemakers' fraternity.
These three classes of artisans recognise the same patron saint, Sun Chu, but maintain
separate guild headquarters and separate places of worship. The foreign-style footwear
makers have a temple dedicated to Sun Chu at Lu Hsin Hang, which also serves as the
office of their guild. Each shoemaker's shop is required to pay a membership fee of 12
dollars on admission to the guild, this contribution being used chiefly for the maintenance
of the guild.
Some of the shoemakers are also tailors or dealers in ready-made clothing. On
admission to the guild, the master shoemakers must pay a membership fee of 20 dollars
if their establishment is engaged exclusively in making shoes, and 10 dollars if it also
deals in clothing. The worker in a shoemaker's shop is also required to pay an admission
fee of 4 dollars, and an apprentice, 2 dollars.
The cobblers keep no establishment, but ply their trade in the streets with portable stands.
They also worship Sun Chu, but have a guild of their own. Owing to the large number
of workers, the cobblers' guild always finds it difficult to enforce the guild regulations
on its members, whose ranks are constantly swollen by immigrants from the country
districts or by the unemployed from the shoemakers' shops.
According to the regulations of the cobblers' guild, any fresh immigrant from the
country districts or non-member of the guild must pay four strings of cash before being
allowed to do business in the city. Formerly, an effort was made to extract fees from
shoemakers turned itinerant cobblers; but they objected, arguing that as shoemakers
they had already been initiated into the shoemakers' guild. The dispute was carried
on for several years in the Changsha local courts, and was finally settled by a compromise
whereby the unsuccessful shoemaker undertaking cobbling work was required to pay
only one-half of the sum required of an ordinary newcomer. Cobblers of this class now
distinguish themselves from the rest by a red stick on their portable stands. - Extract
from Industrial and Labour Information, I.L.O., 1st February, 1926.

DERMATITIS IN THE BOOT AND SHOE TRADE
(STOCK ROOMS).
A recent inquiry into the occurrence of dermatitis (inflammation of the skin, eczema)
among the workers in the stock rooms of the Boot and Shoe Trade has been made by the
Factory Department.
This inquiry has disclosed the fact that there is a small incidence of dermatitis among
those workers applying "cleaning" solutions in stock rooms. The usual ingredients for
in these solutions varies, and evidence is strong that the higher the percentage of ammonia,
these solutions are ammonia, methylated spirit, and benzine. The strength of ammonia
the greater is the incidence of dermatitis. A cleaning solution containing the lowest
proportion of ammonia compatible with the requirements of the work, therefore,
desirable.
Methylated spirit is responsible for some cases of dermatitis.
Dermatitis- the prevention of which is so much easier than the permanent cure
may be avoided by adopting the following precautions for those workers applying " cleaning"
solutions" to boots and shoes in stock rooms :-
(1) by providing the workers with gloves, for which the only satisfactory materia
(2) by the provision and use of good washing accommodation; and
(3) by the recognition and treatment at first aid boxes of all minor injuries whic
would be leather;
destroy the natural protection afforded by the unbroken skin.

MEETINGS. 126
Four quarterly meetings have been held. These have taken place
successively at Rushden, Desborough, Daventry and Northampton. The first constituted
the Annual Meeting of the Council at which the Officers for the year were appointed, and
the ordinary annual general business transacted. The discussion, somewhat protracted,
centred round the Secretary's report, and admirably displayed the very real keenness
with which the affairs of the Council are viewed. The second meeting, devoted to a
discussion on " The Legalisation of National Agreements," was very admirably introduced
by the General President, Mr. T. F. Richards. Many new viewpoints were introduced,
and a number of misconceptions cleared up, with the result that, with one or two notable
exceptions, the proposals were unanimously approved. The third meeting gave members
the opportunity of knowing more of the work of the International Labour Bureau of the
League of Nations. Mr. E. L. Poulton was the speaker, who, by virtue of his honourable
position in the bureau and the responsibilities he bears in connection therewith, was able
to authoritatively comment on the value of the work performed.
Three important aspects of the meeting are worthy of record :—(a) a resolution
appreciation to Mr. Poulton for his unique work in connection with the Bureau was passed;
(b) a verbatim report of his speech was circulated; (c) the meeting was held in the historic
borough of Daventry. The fourth meeting enabled the Northamptonshire delegate
who attended the Trade Union Congress to report on the principal resolutions and matters
which were brought before the Congress. Mr. W. Townley dealt with the Industrial
side of the Congress resolutions; Mr. L. Poole summarised the purely Political, and Mr
G. Chester dealt with the Educational proposals. The chief factors arising from these
reports were (a) the fundamental changes proposed in respect to trade union structure
and function, and (b) the comprehensive scheme of education adopted for the Trade Union
movement. Altogether, the meetings were of a relatively high standard, and most of the
discussions were of a keen and analytical character. It should, however, be borne in mind
that, whilst those attending gain most from the meetings of the Council, the resultant
delegate reports to branch meetings constitute a basis of educational propaganda of
extreme value to the members in general.
Our appreciation to the General President and General Secretary are very cordially
expressed for their valuable assistance and interest during the year.
COMMITTEE MEETINGS.—The Executive have met on four occasions. They have
been faced with many difficulties, but loyalty to the Union and to the Council, and the
desire for efficient service, have enabled them to materially assist in the success of the
Council's work.
EDUCATIONAL.—Branch work in this respect has not been quite as definite as in former
years. Northampton continue to send members to a Tutorial Class; Rushden completed
a third year study-group in the early part of the year, but were unsuccessful in reforming
the Class in the autumn owing to the retirement of the Tutor; Kettering has been unable
to reform previously successful Classes, but has done good educational work at frequent
meetings of Shop Presidents; Wellingborough successfully continued in the early part
of the year the experiment of a special speaker at Branch meetings. Altogether the
direct educational work of Branches, though limited in character, has been decidedly
valuable and of practical advantage to the Union.
The Executive Committee, consequent on the Educational proposals of the Trade
Union Congress, formulated a number of suggestions which had for their basis an Educa-
tional scheme for the Union. These were submitted to the National Council, and were
also published in the Monthly journal. An inquiry has been addressed to branches by the
National Council, the result of which will, it is hoped, be the submission of a scheme by
the National Council to the next Conference of the Union.
Consequence on the Trade Union Congress proposals a Conference was organised
and held at Kettering on 5th December. Over 80 delegates attended to hear Mr. J. W.
Muir, of the Workers' Educational Association, lecture on “ The T.U.C. proposals in relation
to the Trade Union Movement." In a brilliant and racy speech Mr. Muir showed the
absolute necessity for Education in the Trade Union Movement, and described how schemes
of education could be arranged between Unions and the Workers' Educational Trade
Union Committee. This was the only Conference of its kind held during the year, but
another to be addressed by the Secretary of the National Council of Labour Colleges will
take place in February at Wellingborough.
SPECIAL.—Following the precedent established by Resolution the previous year,
the Council, in conformity with the desire to obtain first-hand knowledge of industries
contributory to our own, visited, by the courtesy of the Directors, the Nene Valley Chrome
Tanning Company, Irthlingborough. About 50 delegates attended, and under the super-
vision of representatives of the firm an intensely informative visit ensued. Many of the
processes of tannage were quite new to most of the delegates, and the experience clearly
proved how desirable it was to know more of the industries assisting in but outside the
actual production of boots and shoes. The visit also proved our very close kinship with the
employees in the leather trades and how valuable would be the amalgamation of the two
Unions concerned.

FINDING WORK FOR SEAΜΕΝ.
End of Private Agencies in Japan.
Following a conference between the Government, shipowners and seamen, states
Industrial and Labour Information, the weekly publication of the International Labour
Office of the League of Nations, held last November, the Japanese Government announced
that it proposed to abolish private employment agencies by the end of 1925. It was also
proposed that the employment exchange work should be transferred from the Japanese
Association for the relief of Seamen (representatives of which were present at the con-
ference) to the joint control of shipowners and seamen.
These arrangements carry out the obligations which were undertaken by Japan by
her ratification of a Convention on the subject of finding employment for seamen adopted
by the second Session of the International Labour Conference, held at Genoa in 1920.
Progress is also reported regarding the measures taken by Japan to put into operation
the Convention on unemployment (which includes the establishment of free public employ-
ment exchanges for industrial workers) adopted by the first Session of the Conference at
Washington in 1919. Under the Employment Exchanges Act of 1921, over 170 employ-
ment exchanges were set up throughout Japan. Many fee-charging agencies, however,
it was not easy to abolish them. In the meantime, in accordance with the principle laid
continued to exist. So long as the public employment exchanges system was not perfected,
down by the Unemployment Convention and by the Employment Exchanges Act, the
authorities have endeavoured to place the fee-charging agencies under a strict and uniform
national control. They were already subject to control by the prefectual authorities, but
this control was not provided for in any legislation. In order to regularise this position,
the Department of provided for in reported to have drafted an Order containing the
following provisions -
(1) The establishment of a fee-charging employment agency is subject to the
strict control of the Prefectural Governor. No agency-charging fees may be started

SHELVED FACTORIES BILL.

Boot Operatives' Union Dissatisfied: Health of the Workers.
Deep regret at the decision of the Home Secretary not to proceed for at least twelve
months with the Factories Bill, is expressed by Mr. E. L. Poulton, General Secretary of the
National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives, who for a long time has been in communica-
tion with different Government departments on the question of conditions in factories and
workshops.
In a message to the Mercury he says:
In relation to the Factories Bill not being presented for at least another year,
feels in considerable difficulty at the refusal of the Home Office to take steps to bring
the Factories Act up-to-date, especially when one remembers the appeal of the Prime
Minister for ' Peace in our Time."

"There can be no peace when such an outstanding example obtains of refusal to
and that, on the ground that it will add to the burden of industry."

Ensuring Good Health.
"We are reminded by the Minister of Health of the necessity to do everything pos-
to ensure the good health of the people, and are told of the millions of days lost each year
by sickness. A good deal of this could be avoided if healthy, light workshops and better
conditions for the carrying out of industry are enforced, yet the Home Office is constantly
putting off the very thing that would bring about better health, so necessary in the interests
of the nation.

"That any Minister should make the question of unity of hours an additional excuse
for delay in bringing about reform is surprising, and it is to be hoped that public opinion,
without regard to party, will bring pressure to bear upon the Government to ensure its
reconsideration of the matter as will result in a bona-fide determination to bring the
up-to-date Factories Bill.

Washington Obligation.
"So far as the meeting of the nations is concerned in relation to the hours of labour,
although I feel very strongly that the Government should have honoured the obligation
entered into at Washington in 1919, I believe a step has been taken towards the ratifica-
of the Convention.
"One can only hope that the result of such an enquiry will be the bringing about
speedily of an understanding as will ensure a rapid passing of an Act of Parliament em-
bodying the Washington Convention proposals for a 48-hours week." -The Leicester
Mercury, 4th February, 1926.

48-HOUR WEEK IN DANGER.

During its period of office, and again last year, the Labour Party introduced a 48-
Hours Bill for the purpose of ratifying the Washington Convention of the League of
Nations.

So far the Tories have done nothing in this direction, nor does the King's Speech
state that they intend to introduce such a Bill during the coming year.
They are, however, arranging a Conference with the Governments of Belgium, France,
Germany, and Italy in order to consider the possibility of securing an international agree-
ment.

Judged by the statement of the Prime Minister, however, there is a grave danger that
the Washington 48-Hours Convention may be sabotaged, and that some other agreement
less favourable to the workers may be arrived at in substitution.
The qualification in Mr. Baldwin's speech which gives rise to suspicion is as follows -
"Even if we do not come to a definite agreement, or an agreement so definite,
yet I have every hope that we may usefully come to SOME agreement.

MONTHLY REPORT.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
22ND MARCH, 1926.
TRADE.
Trade has slightly improved during the month, although a large
number of our members are still unemployed or working short time. The
figures in the Gazette of the Ministry of Labour are as follows :-
BOOT AND SHOE INDUSTRY.
Employment showed a slight improvement in almost all centres of the boot and shoe
industry during February, but was still only moderate on the whole; short time was
still prevalent in many centres. There was also a slight improvement as compared with
February of last year; though a few districts showed no improvement, or even in some
cases a decline.
The percentage of workpeople unemployed, as indicated by the unemployment books
lodged at Employment Exchanges, was 7.7 on 22nd February, as compared with 8.7 on
25th January and with 9.5 on 23rd February, 1925.
There was a further slight improvement in London, and employment in general was
fairly good. A seasonal improvement was reported in the Leicester and Northampton
districts; at Leicester employment was good, and better than a year ago; most operatives
were working full time, some being on overtime. Employment was still only moderately
good at Northampton. At Hinckley employment remained quiet, with short time general.
In the Higham and Rushden area less short time was worked and employment improved
to fair. At Wellingborough there was a slight improvement, but employment was still
quiet, and short time rather prevalent. At Kettering there was an improvement, and
employment was fair; but there was still a good deal of under-employment and (among
men workers) unemployment.
Employment remained moderate at Leeds, with much short time; it was better,
however, than in January, and than in February, 1925. At Stafford it was good with
most firms, and better than in January or than a year earlier; some hundreds of work-
people, however, were suspended for varying periods during the month. Employment in
the turn-shoe department at Norwich was still slack; but in other departments there
was an improvement, and employment was fair; overtime was occasionally worked.
There was a slight improvement at Bristol and Kingswood; but employment, especially
at Kingswood, was still poor, and decidedly worse than a year ago. At Street employ-
ment continued fair. It remained only moderate in the Rossendale Valley.
Employment was moderately good at Glasgow, and showed an improvement at Ayr;
elsewhere in Scotland employment remained poor, with a good deal of short time.

UNEMPLOYMENT AND UNPAID CONTRIBUTIONS.
It will be seen from the following question and answer given in the House
that it is very important to see that the cards are stamped weekly, unless a
special arrangement is in force in any particular factory.
Wednesday, 3rd March, 1926, relating to "Unstamped Cards,"
of Commons on
UNEMPLOYMENT.
Employers' Contributions (Bankruptcy).
MR. T. THOMSON asked the Minister of Labour whether, in the case
of the bankruptcy of an employer who has previously deducted from
wages an employee's contributions towards the Unemployment Insurance
Fund but omitted to stamp the card, the insured workman is treated as
having lost the benefit towards which deductions have been made from
his wages owing to the subsequent bankruptcy of the employer?
"SIR A. STEEL-MAITLAND: In the circumstances described in the
question contributions have not been paid and cannot be credited. The
Department would, wherever practicable, make a claim in the bank-
ruptcy proceedings, and under the Unemployment Insurance Acts such a
claim would have priority in respect of contributions for four months. I
should add that the employer making deductions without first stamping
the unemployment books infringes the law, unless he has made a special
arrangement with the Department for postponed stamping and has paid a
deposit to cover the period of postponement."
BENEFITS AND PROBATIONARY PERIODS.
We beg once again to call the special attention of officers to the circular
letter of 13th November, 1925, relating to the payment of benefits before the
probationary periods have been served. It is NOT enough, and does not
comply with the rule, because a person has been in the Union 52 weeks to say
they are entitled to benefit for sick pay, unemployment pay, and out-of-work
contributions. Rule 38 makes the matter very clear that from the date of
registration with the Council, members must serve a further 26 weeks' pro-
bation, and also pay a further 26 weeks' contributions from the date of regis-
tration.
Unless the rule is complied with it MUST BE CLEARLY UNDERSTOOD
that payment of benefit to members CANNOT be allowed. If any such
claims are paid there is NO alternative but for the General Secretary to strike
out the claims as not being in accordance with the rules.

EDUCATION.
Increasing importance is being given by the Labour Movement to Educa-
tion, both of children and adults. For many years the Trades Union Congress
have passed resolutions upon the subject and in many ways increased facilities
have been placed at the disposal of the workers whereby knowledge can be
placed at the disposal of the movement by the splendid gift of Lady Warwick
acquired. Another, and in many ways a unique opportunity, has now been
in handing over to the General Council of the Trades Union Congress, Easton
Lodge and 900 acres of ground for the purpose. In Lady Warwick's own
words :-
"To-day I am handing over to the Trades Union Congress my old
house as a gift in perpetuity for the purpose of a college for the use and
benefit of the organised workers.
"Easton Lodge has been my home from childhood, and it is very
dear to me as the home of my family for 300 years. But I feel no sadness
in making the gift, because I sympathise so deeply with the purpose to
which it is to be put, and because I believe that those who come here from
working-class homes will learn to love it for its beauty and will carry away
from here an inspiration for their work."
The Trade Union Movement is indeed fortunate in having such a building
placed at its disposal.
The General Council in accepting the property for and on behalf of the
movement, through its Chairman, Mr. A. Pugh, expressed the thanks of the
workers. The General Council will proceed to develop its schemes for Education
upon a broader basis than was formerly contemplated. There may have to
be a call for some money to start the College. We feel confident, however,
that the movement will rise to the occasion and thereby give the General
Council full power to go ahead with the scheme which means so much to the
workers.
Further references to the matter will be found on pages 188 and 189.
POLITICAL.
The struggle in the House of Commons is indeed an interesting one at the
present time. It is true, as we have repeatedly pointed out, and shall continue
to point out, that the Labour Party is in a big minority. Nevertheless the
members of the Labour Party are continually putting up the case for Labour
and putting the Government on its defence. The opposition is not merely
to oppose, but to show how, on the one hand the Government is remiss in its
duty to the Nation, and on the other what a vast amount of leeway is to be
made up before legislation which will really help the people and give them
greater security so far as an income is concerned. We cannot go into details
of the work day by day, but would impress upon the members to read day by


---

159
day the Herald. They will see within its pages the record of the Party, a
record which we feel sure is building up such a position as to place in authority
the Labour Party in this country when the next appeal is made to the country.
The outlook industrially is not a bright one; the position of the country
in relation to one big subject, viz.:- the Coal situation-is indeed a serious one
and calling for Statesmanship of a high order to deal with the same. We cannot
say what the outcome will be. We would, however, warn the members that
as one of the Unions affiliated to the Trades Union Congress, it will be our duty
to fall into line with decisions that may be arrived at. We hope that reason
will prevail and that not only will there be a settlement, but one that will
inflict no injustice upon the Miners whose position is one which must call for
full consideration, especially when one remembers the dangerous and unpleasant
occupation that Mining is.
THE "DAILY HERALD."
We hope that all our members will take every available opportunity to
push the Herald, the only daily paper owned and controlled by the movement.
By purchasing the Herald daily a full report of the political world as seen by

REMEMBER THE FIFTEENTH!
Once again we feel bound to call the serious attention of Branch Secretaries
to the fact that the FIFTEENTH day of each month is the latest day for
returns reaching the General Secretary. If Branches fail to send off their
returns to reach the Central Office before the 15th of the month it tends to
upset the organisation of the work in the General Secretary's Office. We beg
to intimate that unless returns are in before the 15th of the month, the Secretary
has been instructed to put into force the Rules governing the same. Returns
Sheets MUST also bear the signature of both the Branch President and Branch
Secretary, or they will reluctantly have to be returned for completion.
TRADE UNION STAMP.
This is a matter which we have stated before rests with the members to
make a success. It is in the interests of members themselves that "Stamped
Footwear" should be increasingly purchased; therefore, push the Trade Union
Stamp. Members and their families should wear only "Union Stamped
Footwear."

THE GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.

60 LADY SOMERSET ROAD,
KENTISH TOWN, N.W. 5.
17th March, 1926.

FELLOW MEMBERS,
SHODDY. We are again faced with the subject of Shoddy and have had occasion
to deputise the Board of Trade, but although we are not in a position to say what trans-
pired, they were certainly very sympathetic and appeared to us to have the object in
view that articles sold should be properly described, but as we have other spheres of
influence to endeavour to organise, we should leave the matter where it is for the moment
and other organisations in such a way as to present a united front. Then we feel sure
until we have the whole of the industry, including Manufacturers, Retail Dealers, Factors
that the Government of the day, whoever they may be, will give us that help we deserve.
I am still of the opinion that the best way is to describe the component parts of boots, and
to also ask the public to please be aware in future when talking of leather that they mean
solid leather. An all-leather boot is not sufficient. " All Leather " does not describe
and leather, but when we say solid leather we all know what we mean by that, that the
and need not include good leather at all, as most men and boys know there is leather
the trade sufficiently to form a strong deputation and to place some tangible proof and
evidence before the Minister concerned.
MANSFIELD. During the past month I have on several occasions had to see the firm
of Messrs. Faire Bros., regarding the organisation there, the Directors having alread
signified their intention (as reported on previous occasions) of meeting our wants and
requirements and putting themselves on a level with the industry. The item respecting
the women who are working on presses is of vital importance, because as these women
were in these situations before we organised the factory, we cannot very well ask for their
removal, but on the other hand we must insist upon one of the two courses that the
must either be paid the same piecework rates as men, or they must receive the men
graduated scale or minimum according to age. From those two points we cannot depart.
The holiday payment is being put into operation, and I have a definite promise from the
firm that our "Organisation of Industry" resolution will be exposed in the building.

Respecting the other firm in the same town, The Mansfield Shoe Company, we held a
Committee of Inquiry there, and the firm agreed that in all future "cut-outs," and in all
future Rodeos, the statement prices paid in Leicestershire shall be rigidly observed. The
one difference that is yet unsolved between us is what is a Ward Shoe? In this respect
may I ask our members in all centres to please bear in mind the evidence given to us is
that in such unorganised districts as the East End of London they are sending out boots
called Ward Shoes with a two-inch heel. This we refuse to accept, and ask our members
to make it clear, and to the employers generally, that if they are making one-bar shoes on
a last that will carry a two-inch heel, it is very evident that is outside the category of a
Ward Shoe. There are several other matters in connection with this firm which are not
yet straightened out, but with the constant and continued attention of my colleagues
(the organisers in this particular town), I think we shall get the firm at last working within
the ambit of our Union.
NOTTINGHAM.—I am very sorry to have to report that the firm of Messrs. Seymour &
Harding, of Nottingham, gave our men and women notice last week to close down, as they
had come to the conclusion that owing to one of the principals retiring from business, the
other one could not see his way clear to continue. This means that 30 or 40 people will be
thrown out of employment, although I believe that the major portion of them will be
found employment at Mansfield, who have already taken a goodly number. This will be
to our advantage I hope.

WELLINGBOROUGH. We have again had to visit the firm of Messrs. Craddock Bros.,
who have made up their minds on this occasion to put in machinery. This firm has had
our attention during the last eighteen months or two years, and as they are now working
day labour, and paying the minimum, we have given them until the first week after Easter
to meet all our conditions. We think there is no doubt that this will be done, although
one has to be very sympathetic towards businesses of this character who are struggling,
and it would not give us ar.y pleasure to have the responsibility thrown on our shoulders
are over that the firm are likely to bring themselves into compliance with our desire.

We have had one firm in Leicestershire who has refused to post our
Industry resolution, giving as an excuse that they have never had anything of the kind
and are not likely to in the future. This is a matter we are bringing before the County

I think it is very unfortunate that the good relations that exist between our Union and the
trade generally should be marred by one or two firms, whilst in this connection I am bound
to report that the Mountsorrel School Boot Co., who have had quite a run of luck for this
last two or three years, and where my colleagues have been able to organise a goodly
number of their operatives, have taken the bull by the horns, discharged our Shops Presi-

tion of Industry" resolution, if others are doing the same, although this Managing Director
promised me three years ago that he would put up such a resolution, and which I believe
has been put up already, but being typewritten is hardly discernable. Since we have
organised the men the firm and the Manager do not appear to have as much regard for my
colleagues as they used to do, and it is a bit irritating when we find that a federated firm
should discharge twelve operatives at one time, or in other words, suspended them; but
I am not content with the suspension which was indefinite, but asked for something more
tangible, and they have got out of the difficulty at present by sending two weeks' wages
to each of the operatives at their homes. We are taking this matter before the Committee
of Inquiry and I presume, the full Board. I well remember Lord Buckmaster's recent
remark in which he said he felt that employers ought to bring themselves more into contact
with their operatives, and by so doing avoid any of these unnecessary frictions. This
firm could have done what other firms are doing in the City of Leicester and the County
too; it could have given these men a share of the work, be it much or little, but I am
convinced in my own mind that this is a deliberate hostile act and the firm may take it
for granted that we shall do our best to defend our membership.

It is pleasing to report the Federation President for North Leicestershire, Mr. Burton,
of Messrs. Newbold & Burton, very willingly put up our Agreement in the only Department
that was unorganised, viz., the Girls, as soon as we made the request.

THE BOOT AND SHOE TRADE.
Extracts from Speech by Mr. J. H. Marlow at Annual Meeting of
Northampton Boot Manufacturers' Association, 5th March, 1926.
A Greater Output.
Concerning the state of trade generally, he thought there had been a greater output
in 1925 than in the previous year. It was a big strain on the manufacturers to keep
up with the demand for fashion shoes, for they meant new patterns, lasts, and leathers,
and a considerable amount of capital and brain work. He was inclined to think that
fashion shoes had helped and created increased trade, but like most good things it got
overdone.
The industry gave employment to over 120,000 workers, it produced an estimated
output of 130,000,000 pairs of footwear yearly, and had a value of over 40 million sterling.
Mr. Marlow pointed to the machinery existing in the boot trade for dealing with
disputes, and asked why that system could not be adopted by the other industries. The
boot trade had a record to be proud of in that there had been no serious trouble for over
thirty years, and in the threatened crisis he called the attention of the coal and engineering
industries to that record. They all knew that terms eventually must be agreed upon in
conference, why not now rather than later?
Last year, Mr. Marlow recalled, he suggested a five years' truce, and he would now
go further and suggest that national agreements should be legalised.
Collective Bargaining.
"My final message," he continued, " is a plea for peace and unity, and I urge every
member to do his utmost towards this end. Personally I am a strong individualist, and
nation it is to-day, but as things are to-day, I think it is imperative that we accept the
complete organisation in industry. With manufacturers and operatives belonging to
principle of collective bargaining. I would, therefore, emphasise the importance of more
their respective organisations, there is some hope that unified conditions of employment
will obtain and unfair competition be reduced to a minimum."

ORGANISERS' REPORTS.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
Since my last report I attended the Council Meeting on the 21st, 22nd and 23rd
of February. The Council agreed that Mr. Baum and myself should continue our efforts
to strengthen the Sileby Branch at Mountsorrel, Rothley and Sileby, as well as paying
attention to Derby and Mansfield. Also that I was to visit Liverpool and Manchester.
When the Labour Party Conference was held at Liverpool last October, Mr. Walter Smith,
Mr. Len. Smith and I took advantage of the opportunity and went to the Works of the
New Liverpool Rubber Co., at Walton, and joined a good number of young women in the
Rubber Shoe Department in the Union. Since then trade has fallen off and the earnings
have been small-at best they are small, it is a sweated industry-and the people who
wear this class of goods are unconsciously patrons of the sweater. The Dunlop Company
have taken over the Works at Walton. I visited the place on 3rd March and learned that
the girls had ceased paying solely through poverty of income. They are getting busy now,
and about 400 fresh girls have been started. Dunlops have given an increase on one bad
line to the pieceworkers. Some of the shareholders in those rubber shoe works are big
men if we take money as the test of their standing. The Irwell Rubber Co., Green Gate,
Salford, make plimsolls and canvas shoes with crepe soles. The management claim that
they pay better weekly wages and piecework prices than the firm at Liverpool, or the four
companies in Scotland. Mr. Mason (Secretary, Manchester Branch) and I waited on the
manager of this firm over the piecework prices for lasting canvas shoes. The prices were
per 10 pairs, children's 1½d., maids' 2d., women's 2½d. The girls doing this work would
be from 16 to 18. The uppers are ready solutioned at the edges. The upper is pulled
to the last, the insole slipped in and the upper is then worked in with the fingers at the toe,
and smoothed over at the sides to the seat, where the full pressure of the fingers are needed
as at the toe. A small hand roller is then run over the toes and seat. Fourteen of the
girls were called in to prove that we were wrong in regards to the time taken to do 10 pairs.
One said she could do them in 15 minutes, another said 20 and another 30 minutes. This
was contradictory evidence for our case, but I am convinced from the time it took a fore-
woman to do one shoe that it would take an exceptionally smart girl to last 15 pairs in
one hour. In the Lawn Tennis Department of this firm we have no cause to complain.
All belonging to the Union and we negotiate matters without friction. The weakness on the
other side is that the piecework prices were fixed by the management without the workers
of a Union having a voice in them. If the girls at this firm would only stick to the Union,
their conditions, by persistent appeals and action, would be soon improved. Some of
them got impatient because we could not get everyone in the shop to join at the same time,
and get immediate improvements, unmindful of the fact that they were unorganised before
and allowed the management a free hand in regulating their conditions.
Mr. W. Warner and I had to visit a closing factory at Nuneaton on two occasions over
a little friction there. Mr. T. Vallance and I went to Barwell, when an outstanding grievance
of the clickers was satisfactorily settled.
At Derby Mr. Baum and I took note of the conditions of the lasting and finishing
departments of one factory and of the clicking in another. Twenty new and lapsed
members have recently joined from one of these shops. At Mansfield we got particulars
from the pressmen which will be beneficial in negotiating improvements. One firm at
Mountsorrel evidently got alarmed over the number of young men who lately joined the
Union, and were talking of demanding piecework instead of weekly wages.
them were suspended, presumably because of slackness, but as they were told to take
their Health Insurance cards with them, we interpreted the so-called suspension to be the
"sack" in order to create confusion and disorder in our ranks. The General President
(Mr. Richards) took the matter up at once, and the twelve were sent two weeks' wages in
lieu of notice in registered letters. The firm is federated and Mr. Richards has called the
Enquiry Committee of the Leicestershire Board to deal with the matter. Personally,
I wish that the other fifty odd members in the shop had taken action on their own at the
time. We have done our best since to prevent a stampede at the shop. The Sileby
Secretary is doing good work by his constant visits to Mountsorrel.
20th March, 1926. D. MCCARTHY.

WALTER R. SMITH.
AN ENLIGHTENED BRITISH TRADE UNION.
There is one trade in Great Britain, however, which stands out as a notable exception
to the general attitude. The boot and shoe operatives, guided by far-seeing trade union
leaders, have for many years past pursued an enlightened policy of co-operation with the
employers, who, in turn, have admitted certain obligations and responsibilities which
some other groups of employers are loath to recognise. The initiation of the policy dates
back to the beginning of last century, when the British boot trade was threatened with
ruin by the swift development of the use of new labour-saving machinery in America.
The manufacturers decided to scrap the old plant and to operate American machines
under license. The workers, under the stress of necessity, acquiesced in the new policy
and made the best of the difficulties of the transition period. Trade was recaptured,
and since that time the leaders of the industry have quickly adapted it to each mechanical
change that offered advantages. One outstanding result is the maintenance of fairly good
conditions in the industry during the trying period of general trade depression since 1920.
Along with short hours and relatively good wages there has been high productivity, and
boot prices in England to-day are more favourable than those of most of the necessaries
of life. The wages agreement provides for a base rate and a cost of living bonus, and the
base rate, if it is ever reached, will insure the workers a substantially higher real wage
than the pre-war earnings.
A policy of "settlement of all disputes without stoppages if possible," has been
adopted by the Union, and through the Joint Industrial Council both sides strive to make
this policy successful.
More recent developments of this co-operation have an economic and social importance
extending beyond the sphere of the industry itself. The Joint Industrial Council has just
declared for a policy of the most complete organisation possible on each side in industry,
as the best means of eliminating strife, improving the general conditions of the industry,
and promoting the highest degree of efficiency. Following this it has drafted a Parlia-
mentary Bill which would make it obligatory on every firm and all workers in an industry
to carry out the provisions of agreements entered into by a joint industrial council. After
much opposition the Boot and Shoe Trade Operatives' Union has now gained the acceptance
of this basic idea by the Trades Union Congress.
Another highly interesting development is the decision of leading boot and shoe
manufacturers to co-operate with the Union in a campaign to eliminate from the industry
the production of shoddy boots, made with soles of substitute materials which afford no
protection against wet and cold. It is suggested that by legal enactment it should be
made obligatory on all manufacturers to stamp the soles with the name of the firm and a
description of the material used. The success of this form of co-operation is so great
that it is bound to be developed in other ways for the mutual advantage of the workers,
the general public, and the employers. The Christian Science Monitor, 25th February,
1926.
