LEGAL CASES AFFECTING LABOUR.
Trade Boards Acts, 1909-1918.
MINIMUM RATES OF WAGES - UNDERPAYMENTS - CLAIM FOR PAYMENT OF ARREARS -
FALSE RECEIPTS.
The Trade Boards Acts of 1909 and 1918 were passed to secure minimum rates of wages
to workers in certain trades, the rates being fixed by a body known as a Trade Board and
consisting of an equal number of representatives of employers and workers in the trade,
with a certain number of independent members of whom one is the chairman. The Act
of 1909 applied at the outset to four trades only, set out in the Schedule to that Act, being
trades in which the wages then being paid were exceptionally low. Power was given to
the Board of Trade, and later to the Minister of Labour, to apply the Acts to other trades,
and in 1919 the Acts were applied by the Minister of Labour to the paper bag trade. The
Acts require every employer in a trade to which the Acts have been applied to pay wages
to his workers at not less than the minimum rate that has been fixed by the Trade Board
and any agreement for the payment of wages in contravention of this provision is declared
by the Acts to be void.

A case was heard before Mr. Justice Talbot and a jury at the Devon Assizes recently:
when S. C. F. Clarke, paper bag manufacturer, and J. W. Hunkin, clerk, both of Plymouth,
pleaded "not guilty" to 17 counts charging them with conspiring to utter forged receipts
for arrears of wages amounting in all to £65 due to certain workers in the paper bag trade,
and with forging and uttering the same receipts. In common expression, the defendants
were charged with attempting to conceal the non-payment by them of arrears of wages
that had been found to be due to their workers, and which they sought to prove they had
paid by producing to the Ministry documents purporting to be receipts from these workers,
but which documents were, in fact, forgeries.

In June, 1924, a Trade Board Inspector of the Ministry visited the defendants and
inspected their books and wages sheets, and found that the defendants had in their employ-
ment many young girls who had not been paid the proper minimum wage. Correspondence
ensued, and a claim was made by the Ministry for payment of the arrears. The defendants
at first admitted they had not paid these workers the proper amounts, but later suggested
that the workers were not enaaged in the paper bag trade at all. This they did by getting
the girls to swear affidavits which were intended to prove that no arrears were due. After
making further enquiries the Ministry said that the affidavits could not be accepted, that
the arrears must be paid, and that proceedings would be taken if they were not paid.
The Ministry asked that the arrears should be sent to them for distribution amongst the
workers, or that the defendants should pay the workers and forward the receipts to the
Ministry for inspection and record. The defendants replied that they would prefer to
make payment direct to the workers and would send receipts. The defendants were
pressed to settle the matter, and ultimately on 4th June, 1925, "receipts" were forwarded
to the Ministry, which the prosecution alleged were forgeries, and which it was said the
two defendants had conspired to produce. The signatures on the receipts were authentic,
but it was shown that when the girls signed the "receipts" the papers which they signed
were blank, or else something was held over the top, so that they did not know what
they were signing. Later, after the facts had been discovered by the Ministry, each of
the girls received a cheque for the amount of her back wages. The cheques were each
dated 4th June, 1925, which was the date that the "receipts" had been forwarded to the
Ministry. For the defendants it was stated that the cheques were actually drawn on 4th
June, but were put into a drawer and forgotten, whereas the case for the prosecution
was that they were hastily written on 23rd July, when the facts had been discovered,
and were antedated to 4th June. The jury found both men guilty. Clarke was sentenced
to 12 months in the Second Division and Hunkin to 3 months in the Second Division.
Rex v. Hunkin and Clarke. - Devon Assizes. - 10th and 11th February, 1926. - The Ministry
of Labour Gazette, March, 1926.

EASTON LODGE AND ITS OPPORTUNITIES.
A New Chapter in the History of Working-class Education.
Mr. Arthur Pugh, Chairman of the Trades Union Congress, broadcast the following
message on Wednesday, 24th February, from Easton Lodge, on the occasion of the formal
handing over of the building by Lady Warwick to the Trades Union Congress as a Trade
Union College.
I feel this is a moment of historic importance in the annals of adult working-class
education.
Throughout its history the Trades Union Congress has strongly urged the need for
greater educational opportunities for the people it represents, and the Trade Unions have
for many years taken an active interest in the development of education for adult workers.
More than seventy years ago, when the leaders of the Christian Socialist Movement
turned their thoughts to educational work, the Trade Union leaders joined with the late
Rev. Frederick Denison Maurice and Thomas Hughes to establish the first Working-men's
College in London in 1854.
For more than a quarter of a century the Trade Unions have been actively associated
with the work of Ruskin College, established at Oxford by three Americans- Mr. and
Mrs. Walter Vrooman and Charles Beard. Later important Trade Unions associated
themselves with the establishment of the Labour College, London, and in the course of
years hundreds of young Trade Unionists have benefited by residence at those institutions,
and thousands more have taken advantage of the facilities offered by correspondence
courses and teaching in history, economics, political science and other subjects.
Specialisation.
Trade Unionists joined with representatives of the Co-operative Movement and a
group of University men to establish over twenty years ago the Workers' Educational
Association, and as a development of the Labour College, London, the National Council
of Labour Colleges finds its support from Trade Unions.
These bodies last year enrolled over 48,000 students in classes, resident week-end
and Summer Schools, study circles and so on, and including the Education Department
of the Co-operative Movement-year by year means are provided to bring educational
facilities within the reach of many thousands of working people which otherwise would
not be available.
The fundamental aim of all these educational activities is to enable the workers to
develop their capacity for effective service, and the means whereby those taking up respons-
ible leadership in Trade Union, Co-operative, and other similar organisations, or as repre-
sentatives on public bodies, can be better equipped for the duties thus undertaken.
Trade Unionism to-day calls for a mature and highly specialised form of ability and
experience in the administration of Union affairs, in negotiations on questions of wages
and working conditions which often involve prolonged and exhaustive discussion of
intricate industrial and economic facts.
Many people who read in the newspapers of industrial disputes, negotiations and
inquiries in which the Trade Unions are involved, can form only a vague conception of the
immense amount of detailed work they entail, of the complexity of the interests which
have to be considered, and of the care and patience that have to be exercised in dealing
with industrial affairs.
By far the larger proportion of questions affecting working people that are made the
subject of negotiation, never come to the knowledge of the public: they are settled after
full consideration by representatives of the Trade Unions and the Employers concerned
in joint meetings without the public hearing anything about them. Still less can the
average person realise the vast administrative work connected with the control of the great
modern Trade Union organisations.
Realising the need for adult educational work in the Trade Unions, the General Council
of the T.U.C. has given much thought to the best methods of developing the work of the
various educational bodies, such as those I have named, and to frame a co-ordinated
policy for carrying on all these educational activities, and the creation of a central educa-
tional fund, to which the General Council itself contributes an annual sum of £2,000.
The munificent gift of Easton Lodge to the Trades Union Congress gives our General
Council an opportunity to realise the project of centralising the residential educational
work of the Trade Unions. Through the generosity of Lady Warwick we can now see
our way to establish and equip a real Trade Union College under almost ideal conditions,
with every prospect of success.

TRADE FACILITIES BILL.
Discussion in the House of Commons on 11th March, 1926,
MR. PURCELL Said I want to approach this question in a rather different way from
that in which so far most members have approached it. I think it is important that we
should face the position. It is not a question, to my mind, of political considerations at
all. You have a new country in which a terrific change has taken place.
I think that even if you recognised, for example, the Czarist debt and what is known
as the War debt for materials and munitions supplied during the War, it does not seem to
me that you would find work for the people unemployed at present in this country. So
that brings us to the third and most important bar in the way, that is, the payment for
things supplied. It has been put to me in this way that if you purchase a pair of boots
and you do not pay for them it is very difficult to get your boot supplier to let you have
another pair of boots until you have paid for the first pair. I want to face the case of hon.
Members opposite. If material for railways and material for factories and for the equip-
ment of factories had been supplied and so many traders had been at the present time
nationalised by you, the very least you ought to do is to settle the account due for former
supplies. That is what is said. There is another point almost as important as that one.
I understand it to be that there are no Courts in Russia comparable to the Courts that
exist in this country in which a Russian or a Britisher can recover a debt. Apart altogether
from political considerations, we have to see if these difficulties can be met. To ask us
to get over these two hurdles by merely seeing that education is developed, that industry
is developed, that the organisation of the country is developed, and all this kind of thing,
does not appear to me to be sufficient to enable us to get over these great difficulties.
If those two difficulties could be surmounted the path could be very easy. We have
to keep in mind that as Russia develops, as it will certainly develop, and as it will rebuild
and reorganise, it is a totally different Russia from the pre-War thing.
We ought to see whether something could not be done to show them from the industrial
point of view a kinder feeling, whether by way of treaty, agreement or any other sort of
negotiation so long as you get there. That seems to me the thing to do. We want this
mass of work. I want to see Russia develop. We ought never to talk about other people's
mistakes. We have a few to our record and what I desire to urge is this. So important
is this question that I believe it is the duty of both Liberals and Conservaties together
with the Labour Party-if they could do that-to sit down and find out just how this
question of supplying the requirements of Russia and upon what basis and conditions
and how the difficulties can be surmounted, can be met. It would be helpful to us. I am
an Internationalist, but I am also a Nationalist. Many of our highly skilled men in this
country are already unemployed, and some of us fear that unless they get work soon
much of their skill will be lost; those fine shipbuilders on the great rivers of this country,
my opinion, for want of a better word, are rotting away.
It seems to me that that calls for us to get ahead if we want to restore and get back
to the old position of something approaching the workshop of the world. Trust Russia,
not because they are Russians or Bolsheviks. but because they have trade to give, and our
business is to get business for this country.

INTERNATIONAL INFORMATION.

WHITE LEAD PROHIBITION IN FRANCE.

International Convention Ratified.
According to information received from Geneva, France has formally ratified the
Convention concerning the use of white lead in painting, adopted by the third annual
Session of the International Labour Conference of the League of Nations, held at Geneva
in 1921. This ratification follows the unanimous adoption of the French Senate, earlier
in the year, of two Bills, one providing for ratification and the other for the modification
of the Labour Code in accordance with the terms of the Convention.
The Convention provides that the use of white lead shall be prohibited in the interior
painting of buildings and shall be strictly regulated in all other classes of painting. It
also provides that no woman or youths under eighteen shall be employed in any painting
work of an industrial character involving the use of white lead.
The Convention has already been ratified by Austria, Bulgaria, Chile, Czecho-Slovakia,
Esthonia, Latvia, Poland, Spain and Sweden.

WORLD LAWS FOR SEAMEN.

International Code Discussions at I.L. Conference.
The question of an international code for seamen will be discussed at the annual
meeting of the International Labour Conference of the League of Nations this year, the
second Session of which, opening on 7th June, will be devoted to maritime questions.
The particular problem to be studied will be the codification of the rules relating to
seamen's articles of agreement, a subject which has been continually studied by the Inter-
national Labour Office and by the Joint Maritime Commission, a body of shipowners
and seamen's representatives set up to advise the Office on such questions, since a previous
Session devoted exclusively to maritime problems in 1920.
The study of the possibility of a seamen's international code goes back to the dis-
cussions of the work in front of the International Labour Organisation at the Peace Con-
ference in Paris in 1919, and took definite shape when a committee was set up by the
1920 Session of the International Labour Conference, mentioned above, to survey the
question in all its aspects.
Drawing attention to the advantages of such a code, this Committee said :-
"Unlike most other workers, seamen must often follow their calling in various
countries, in each of which it may be necessary for them to know something of the
law as to their relations with their employers and their fellows. Even when not in
foreign countries, much of the seamen's work must be done on the high seas, outside
the usual reach of public authorities. Moreover, on board ships of most countries
the crew frequently comprise many nationalities. It is not unusual for seamen on
a ship neither to speak the language of the country to which the ship belongs nor to
understand its laws. Seamen form what is indeed an international community, and
as such there are many circumstances in which it would be advantageous to have
applied to them a uniform law, whatever flag be flown by the vessel on which they
serve. Such a law can only be secured through common international action."

CARE OF THE EMIGRANT.

Success of Examination at Departure Port.
The plan of inspecting emigrants from Great Britain and the Irish Free State to the
United States before departure is believed to be a complete success, according to an announce-
ment of the United States State Department, quoted in the Monthly Record of Migration
published by the International Labour Office of the League of Nations. The Department
is prepared to extend the plan to other countries whose Governments request similar
facilities as rapidly as funds and staff are available.
Definite requests for the installation of a similar system have been received from the
Governments of the Netherlands and Belgium, and these requests will be complied with.
Public health surgeons and immigration officers will be sent to Rotterdam and Antwerp
to act as technical advisers to the United States consuls there. No other European
Governments have yet made similar requests, but enquiries indicating keen interest in
the plan have been received from several quarters.
The present policy has developed from a Conference which was held in April, 1925,
between high officials of the Departments of State, the Treasury, and Labour, and aims at
remedying a state of affairs in which many immigrants sold their possessions abroad and

if those countries, with the result that the number of rejections of British and Irish
immigrants in the United States ports has been reduced to a minimum and the number
place in Great Britain and the Irish Free State, in co-operation with the Governments
ot refusals, on legal grounds, to issue consular immigration visas has greatly increased.

HOLIDAYS WITH PAY IN BRAZIL.

A Decree of 24th December, 1925, sanctioned by the President of the United States
of Brazil, on 26th December, brought into force an Act instituting paid holidays for
employees in commerce, bank clerks, workers in industrial undertakings, and salaried
employees in all kinds of journalistic undertakings.

The Act guarantees to such workers an annual holiday of fifteen days, either in a single
period or in separate days, without prejudice to any salary, wage or remuneration to which
may be entitled.

UNION CONFERENCE, WHITSUNTIDE, 1926.
RULES AND REGULATIONS OF SUPERANNUATION FUND.
THE COUNCIL.
1. The Fund shall be held in Trust by the Management Committee (Execu-
tive Council of the Union) for Superannuation purposes, and shall be adminis-
tered in accordance with the following rules:
The objects of this Fund are to provide a Superannuation allowance to
permanent (full time) officials and clerks of the Union or branches, and a
payment to the dependents or representatives of a deceased official or clerk,
according to the scale set forth in these rules.
The Fund shall be used for no other purpose.
Those eligible to participate in its benefits shall be permanent officials and
clerks of the Union and branches of 21 years of age and upwards.
Contributions to the Fund shall be compulsory by all permanent officials
and clerks over 21 years of age.
Retirement Conditions.
2. Where an official or clerk over 21 years of age with over ten years'
service has retired from service on account of inability to efficiently perform
his duties owing to infirmity or ill-health, and under 60 years of age, he shall
receive pay on the scale of Superannuation named in these Rules subject to
the discretion of the Management Committee, who shall have power to review
such cases from time to time. An official or clerk shall not be entitled to
claim Superannuation on the grounds of age alone until he has attained the age
of 60 years, but he must compulsorily retire at 65 years of age.
No superannuated official or clerk shall accept office with a rival organisa-
tion.
Scale and Basis of Payment.
3. Superannuation benefit shall be paid to a permanent official or clerk
on the undermentioned salary basis :-
Years of Service. Fixed Benefits.
10 years 35 per cent.
plus I per cent. for each additional year's completed service, the salary at the
time of retirement being the determining factor for the amount of pension.
Contributions and Refund of Same.
4. The rate of contribution shall be 3 per cent. of wages received from
National officers and Central office clerks, and 3 per cent. from Central Funds;
3 per cent. from Branch officials and Branch clerks, and 3 per cent. from Branch
funds. When an official or clerk has been superannuated he shall cease to
contribute to the Fund.
5. An official or clerk upon resigning, or his services being dispensed with,
or failing to secure re-election, shall (in cases where there is no title to a pension)
have refunded to him all contributions paid by him to the Fund plus 4 per cent.
on the total amount due to him when leaving the service of the Union. A
similar refund shall be made to the dependents or legal representatives of any
official or clerk who dies before completing ten years' service.

SUPERANNUATION FUND.

National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives' Scheme.

At an ordinary meeting of the Kingswood Branch of the National Union of Boot and
Shoe Operatives, held at the Moravian Schools last evening, a proposed scheme to form
a fund to provide a superannuation allowance for permanent (full time) officials and
clerks of the Union or branches, and a payment to the dependants or representatives of
a deceased official or clerk, came up for discussion.

Councillor S. Iles presided, and was supported by Mr. W. E. A. Payne (Branch Vice-
President), Mr. A. G. Randall (Local Secretary), and Mr. J. Manners (National Executive).

Mr. W. R. Smith (National Organiser), ex-M.P. and former Parliamentary Secretary
to the Board of Agriculture under the Labour Government, made an appeal for more
support and interest in the Union and its affairs, which was merited by the achievements
of the past. During the past five years they had paid out, in out-of-work benefit, £300,000,
ample testimony to what the organisation had done for its members in the difficult times
that had been experienced. He wanted members to realise the importance of the task
of maintaining the obligations and responsibilities of keeping intact this force which had
been so helpful in the past. The new step in regard to the proposed establishment of a
superannuation scheme was an important one and a step forward. Criticisms had been
levelled against the scheme, but it was for the members to take an interest in it and to make
their desires known, so that the organisation might consider them.

In view of the poor attendance it was decided that the meeting should be adjourned
for a week.

Unemployed Deputation.

Before an adjournment was made, the Chairman moved the following resolution :-
"That this meeting urges the Warmley Board of Guardians to allow the deputa-
tion, as appointed by the Kingswood Unemployed Association, to make representations
to the Board on behalf of the destitute unemployed."

This was carried. - Western Press, 5th March, 1926.

THE ECONOMY BILL.
Protest by National Union Approved Society.
At a meeting of the Executive Council of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Oрега-
tives Approved Society, held in London, under the presidency of Mr. T. F. Richards,
a resolution was passed emphatically protesting against the proposal embodied in the
Chancellor of the Exchequer's Economy (Miscellaneous Provisions) Bill, under which it
is proposed to reduce the State grant towards benefits paid to insured persons, thus relieving
the taxpayer at the expense of the wage-earner.
Whilst believing that the insured population was willing to make every reasonable
effort to assist the nation in its financial difficulties, it was submitted:-
(1) That the Royal Commission unanimously recommended that money within the
scheme should be devoted to extending services, and
(2) That the proposed reduction of the State grant was not real economy, inasmuch
as it prevented the provision of allowances for the dependents of insured persons, and
restricted other developments in the services for the prevention and cure of sickness.
The resolution passed demanded, in the interest of the nation as a whole, and of insured
persons and their dependents in particular, the withdrawal of that section of the Bill
respecting health insurance.
The manager, Mr. R. D. Mayes, was instructed to send copies of the resolution to the
Prime Minister, the Minister of Health, and the leaders of all parties in the House of
Commons.
NATIONAL HEALTH INSURANCE ACT.
Approved Societies' Surpluses.
SIR F. HALL asked the Minister of Health whether, seeing that approved societies
under the National Health Insurance Act are required, after disbursing fixed benefits,
to devote any surplus in the grant of additional benefits, he will state what is now the
amount of the undistributed surpluses of approved societies?
SIR K. WOOD: On the closest estimate of which the conditions permit, the aggregate
amount of the surpluses at 31st December, 1925, is computed to be about £65,000,000.
I may point out that a society is only allowed to apply to the provision of additional
benefits such part of its surplus as is certified by the valuer to be disposable.-Extract
from Parliamentary Debates, House of Commons, Monday, 22nd March, 1926.
PAPER INSOLES BLAMED FOR FAILURE.
Boot Dealer "Couldn't Fight Millionaire Firm."
Percy Fowler, boot dealer, Loughborough, whose deficiency was £777 9s. 3d., stated
at Leicester Bankruptcy Court, that his failure was due to a wholesale firm supplying
him with inferior shoes containing paper insoles, instead of leather. HE GAVE 15s. 3d.
PER PAIR FOR THE SHOES, WHICH HE COULD HAVE BOUGHT ELSEWHERE FOR 8s. 6d. A
PAIR. His customers complained, and his trade went down so badly that he might as
well have shut up shop.
The Registrar: Why didn't you sue the firm for damages?
Debtor: I couldn't fight a millionaire firm in a court of justice.
The Registrar: Why not?
Debtor: Well, I hadn't got the money.
The examination was adjourned for a statement of certain receipts and payments
to be furnished.-Nottingham Guardian.

HOLIDAY PROVISION SCHEME.
East End Manufacturers Successfully Sued by Member of
National Union.
At the Old Street Police Court on Tuesday, Jackson & Joseph, Shoe Manufacturers,
22 Princelet Street, E., were summoned by E. Rowe, operative, who claimed 7s. under
a contract of service in respect to a period between 16th November and 26th December,
1925.
Mr. W. II. Thompson appeared for the complainant, and Mr. R. T. Sharpe for the
defence.
Rowe said he was a member of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives,
and had been employed by the defendants at different times. He knew there was a dispute
between the Union and the firm in May, 1924. After the dispute he started work at the
firm's factory on 2nd March, 1925. Apart from insurance, there was a deduction from
wages for a holiday scheme. The men were paid on Fridays, and they paid IS. 2d. on
Saturdays towards the scheme. After 2nd March that sum was deducted each week.
and on the Saturday after Easter, 1924, he received 14S.; and at Whitsuntide he drew
14s. on the Saturday after the holiday. About two weeks afterwards he went in the
ordinary way to pay his 1s. 2d., when the foreman said, " I am not taking it." He asked
why, and the foreman said, "The guv'nor has promised to pay the 1s. 2d., and you should
not pay yours on account of the clerical work."
He (witness) reported the matter to the Union. From that date he received his full
wages, and on the Saturday after the Bank Holiday he was paid gs. 4d. He worked on
10th August, and was stopped on 11th August. He worked again on 16th November,
and continued from then until 26th December. He asked Mr. Jackson about his holiday
pay on 2nd January. He and a good many more men went together. Mr. Jackson
said, "Hullo, what are you round here for?" and they said, "Our holiday fund." Mr.
Jackson said, "Let it stand over." He (witness) again went to the Union. Mr. Jackson
did not say they were not entitled to it, but "Let it stand over."
Later he (witness) heard that a number of men had been paid out, and he saw Mr.
Jackson again. Mr. Jackson said, "You were not here in August." He replied, "I was
here in August, but I was discharged in August." Mr. Jackson said, "You will have to
start in the New Year." Witness went on working until 17th February. He had not had
the Is. 2d. per week in respect to Christmas, nor had he had anything for the time since
Christmas.
Cross-examined by Mr. Sharpe, the witness said he knew a number of men started
work between holidays, but he did not know that many did not get the holiday pay.
Mr. Sharpe: An announcement was made by the foreman to all of you that there
was a change? Witness: Only when we went up on the Saturday.
Mr. Thompson (re-examining): Did they tell you that if a workman started in the
middle of a holiday period he would not get any holiday pay? Witness: No.
Mr. Albert Mason, president of the Metropolitan Branch of the Union, said there
was a dispute with Jackson & Joseph, which was settled in 1925. Immediately a man
started work he came within the holiday scheme, and would be entitled to Is. 2d. for each
week of his service. Several men reported that they had not received the money, and the
defendants said something about other firms who had not carried out the agreement.
It had never been suggested until that day that the complainant was not entitled to the
Is. 2d. because he started after a holiday.
Cross-examined, the witness said he had not heard of Jackson & Joseph having said
that the Union having failed to get in all firms, they had altered the scheme to suit their
case. Owing to clerical work a number of manufacturers preferred to pay their holiday
fund quota and not stop the men.
Mr. Sharpe said that following negotiations between the defendants and the Union,
they accepted a scheme if the Union would do their best to get all the employers who were
in the Manufacturers' Federation to fall into line. Following that arrangement the
defendants, from February to Whitsun, carried out the letter of the scheme. Then they
said the Union had not got the other employers in and they thought a change ought to be
made. They then inaugurated a new scheme of their own.
Mr. Clarke Hall (magistrate): The contract was to do their best to get the others in.
Mr. Sharpe (continuing) said that after Whitsun the defendants instituted their
variation of the scheme. The position was that Rowe drew out all his money in June,
and carried on until August. At the August holiday he was paid his money under the
new scheme, so that he had accepted the alteration. All the men were paid on that basis
and not under the National Agreement scheme. Rowe then left their service, and came
back in November, and must have come back on the terms that were ruling at the time
he left.


---
201
Mr. Arthur Isadore Jackson (partner in the firm) said a variation of the scheme was
decided upon in June last, and he gave instructions to his foreman.
William Bailey (foreman) said he told the men they would not pay their Is. 2d.,
but that Mr. Jackson would pay his Is. 2d. if they worked full time.
Mr. Clarke Hall said the case turned mainly on a question of fact. Bailey gave his
evidence very well indeed, but he (Mr. Clarke Hall) could not refrain from thinking that
his recollection of what happened in June was very vague. He thought Rowe's recollection
the trouble in the bookkeeping involved in paying the Is. 2d. per week.
was clearly right, and that he understood that the alteration had been made by reason of
He believed
Rowe when he said that he did not hear Bailey say anything about any further alteration.
He found for the complainant for 7s. and 10s. costs. -The Shoe and Leather Record, 26th
March, 1926.

WHOLESALE BALANCE SHEET.
1925 Sales show increase of £5,000,000. Review of Productive Activities.
Details of the half-year's trading are contained in the balance sheet now published.
These show that the society's sales for the half-year were £39.425,445, an increase of
1478712 or 35 per cent. on the corresponding period of the previous year. For the
whole year the sales were £76,585,704, an increase of £5,022,264, or 7 per cent. on the
previous year.
The supplies from the society's productive works for the half-year were £13,337,197,
an increase of £191,597, or 1½ per cent., but the return for the year works out at a remark-
le total of £20,900,865, an increase of £2,554,590, or no less than 103 per cent. on the
previous year.
The net surplus in the trading department, after providing for all expenses, interest,
depreciation, &c., amounts to £566,059 19S. 3d., which, with the addition of £132,548
13s. 11d. brought forward from the previous half-year, gives a total disposable surplus of
£468,008 13s. 2d.
The banking department forges ahead. Its deposits and withdrawals for the half-
year amounted to £297,885,465, which is £18,318,302- or 6½ per cent. more than for
the corresponding half-year of 1924; but the transactions for the whole year amounted
to £45,713,273- or an increase of 8½ per cent. which amounted to £45,209,840. That
is an enormous business arising out of the accounts of co-operative societies, trade unions,
friendly societies, clubs, other mutual organisations, and individuals, which give a total
20,184 current accounts and 26,249 deposit accounts. It is worthy of note that only
thirty-one co-operative societies do not bank with the C.W.S.
The tea, coffee, and cocoa departments show increases of ½ per cent. in tea, 26% per
cent. in coffee, 1½ per cent. of cocoa, and 6½ per cent. on chocolate. These rates are based
on the weights sold, not upon the money value; and it is noteworthy that the tea sales
represented 28,500,754 lbs. for the half-year. -The Co-operative News, 20th March, 1926.

SECURITY.
The total assets of the Co-operative Wholesale Society Limited are £56,000,000.
The Share Capital is £6,000,000, while Reserve, Depreciation, and Insurance funds amount
to over £7,000,000.
If the Banking Department is taken separately, of the total liabilities to our depositors,
viz., £31,000,000, the sum of £10,500,000 is invested in Treasury Bills and Municipal
Loans at short notice, £15,000,000 in British, Colonial, and Guaranteed Railway Stock,
&c., Cash in hand and at banks represents £1,900,000, and advances to customers £3,780,000.
All the Share Capital and Reserves of the Society stand behind the Banking Department,
and from the standpoint of security, therefore, the Bank is undoubted.

Education, in his report for 1924-25, said: "Official reports include with
almost wearisome repetition a record of the sanitary defects of school pre-
mises."
MANY CHILDREN GO TO SCHOOL HUNGRY. Local Authorities have power to
provide meals for school children, where they are so underfed that they cannot
obtain full benefit from the instruction afforded.
Only 10 million meals were provided last year, however, as compared
with 14 million in 1913-14. This looks as though Local Authorities
may not be fully availing themselves of the facilities.
MORE SECONDARY EDUCATION NEEDED. Experts compute that 1,000,000,
children are intellectually capable of profiting by secondary education,
but only 360,000 secondary school places are available for scholarship and
paying pupils combined.
-Speakers' Notes, 25th February, 1926.

SCOTTISH CO-OPERATIVE BOOT PRODUCTION.
The sales of the boot and shoe department of the Scottish Co-operative Wholesale
Society for the half-year ending 26th December were £425,551, making a total of £872,927
for the whole year. These figures compare with £415,670 in the last half of 1924 and
£850,060 for the whole of that year. In the boot and shoe factory of the society the pro-
duction was £206,766 for the last six months of 1925 as compared with £201,099 in the
corresponding half of 1924. For the whole year the boot and shoe production was £430,827.
an increase of £3,546.--Shoe and Leather News, 4th March, 1926.

WHERE THE MONEY GOES.
How manifestly unfair it is for the Government to continue economising at the expense
of the social services whilst increasing expenditure on fighting services, is shown by an
analysis of the various categories of our national expenditure, which the Chancellor of the
Exchequer was unwillingly compelled to give to the House the other day.
This showed that for every £1 spent on peaceable social services, nearly £5 went towards
paving past, present, and future wars.

Education grants-£1 IS. 4d.

TRADE BOARD EVASION.
Underpaid Employees.
At Rhyl on 11th March, Arthur Langley, bootmaker, Caradock Terrace, Prestatyn,
was summoned by the Ministry of Labour under the Trade Boards Act for paying lesser
wages than fixed by the Board to two of his employees. Mr. St. Vincent Coules, who
appeared for the Ministry of Labour, said that defendant had been warned for months
and months, and he would neither keep a wages book nor pay the proper rate of wages
to his pieceworkers. He had underpaid one man as much as 35. 5d. in one week, and in
another case to the extent of 6s. 22d. Evan Evans, one of the employees, admitted that
he learnt all he knew about the bootmaking trade whilst he had been with defendant,
and added that other men had been paid proper wages, and that he, himself, was satisfied
with what he was paid. An inspector of the Ministry of Labour said that if defendant
paid another employee named Parry, whom he said was an apprentice, time wages, he
would have to pay him 1s. 3d. per hour, and that would mean that Parry would have had
£os. per week instead of £I IIS. rod., the sum paid. Witness added that he understood
that Langley did not do boot repairing, but was a commission agent. Langley: I am a
boot repairer, and I taught these men all they knew. The Bench imposed a fine of £2 in
each case, and ordered defendant to pay arrears of wages amounting to £4 11s. 9d. and
£2 15s. 2d., together with £4 5s. 6d. costs. - The Shoe and Leather News, 18th March, 1926.
MEETING OF THE TRADE BOARD
(Northern Ireland).
At a meeting of the Boot and Shoe Repairing Trade Board (Northern Ireland), held
in Belfast on the 11th inst., it was decided to vary the general minimum piece rates and
general overtime rates for male indentured apprentices, and certain general minimum
piscerates and overtime rates for male and female workers in certain districts.
rates, as varied, if confirmed by the Ministry of Labour, will become effective as from the
12th April, 1926, and due notice will be sent to all employers in the trade who are known
to the Board.
It was also decided to issue a notice of proposal to fix piecework basis time rates of
Is. 3d. per hour for male workers and 10d. per hour for female workers in the trade.
These rates will not come into operation unless and until fixed by the Trade Board and
duly confirmed by the Ministry of Labour. - Belfast News Letter, 13th March, 1926.

A LONG, HAPPY LIFE.
Sir George Newman, K.C.B., on How to Attain it.
I believe it is absolutely true to say that the principal asset of the nation is its
health, and the principal liability of the nation is disease.
Sir George Newman, K.C.B., M.D., F.R.C.P., Chief Medical Officer to the Ministry
of Health, thus opened a forceful address at a special meeting of the Leicester Personal
Health Association, in the Art Gallery, Museum Buildings, last night.
"If," he continued, "that is true, we ought to be engaged in doing the utmost we
can to establish and maintain the health of this country. Unless you have health you do
not have a surviving race. Unless you fully meet the liability to disease you cannot
have health. Of all the problems the nation has to face the greatest is its health."
Turning to National Health Insurance, Sir George said we had in this country a
method by which 14,000,000 people were insured and received the medical service of
between 13,000 and 14,000 doctors. Under that scheme the doctor made a note of the
causes which brought an insured person to him as a patient. A little more than half of
the 14,000,000 became patients every year. So they had returns of 7,000,000 people in
1924 with regard to the causes which took them to their doctor. They also had 500,000
death certificates and 750,000 births.
Twenty per cent. went to the doctor because they had bronchial catarrh, or a common
cold; 10 per cent. because they had something in the nature of influenza; 12 per cent.
because they had dyspepsia; 10 per cent, because they were injured 14 per cent. with
various complaints described as rheumatism, neuralgia or lumbago; and 7 per cent. with
local septic conditions. That accounted for 73 per cent. But missing from the
list were all the great mortality diseases of the human family.

Healthiest Age.
Those trifling, mild diseases, though they did not kill the people, wasted 23,000,000
weeks of time in 1924; and £13,000,000 had been paid in benefit by the State. Those
diseases laid the foundation of the other diseases which ended life. Yet they were nearly
all personal in origin. Why should there be 12 per cent. of dyspepsia? Because people
did not know how to live. This was the healthiest age ever recorded in England. But
40 per cent. of the population that died were under the age of 50. Robert Browning had
said: "Ignorance is the great human curse."-Leicester Mail, 27th February, 1926.

FARMERS ADVISED TO SABOTAGE CROPS.
WASHINGTON, 13TH FEBRUARY.-In a statement issued by the department of agri-
culture, farmers are advised to reduce production.
"Any general expansion in production this year would tend to place farmers in a less
favourable economic position than at present," the statement says.
The department discusses wheat, corn, live stock and other production, and makes
this direct appeal to sabotage the potato crop:
"There is danger that potato growing in the late producing states may plant too
heavily. Increased acreage of more than 10 per cent. is inadvisable."
Anti-unionists who continually lecture labour on "failing to produce" have ignored
this statement by the department. Labour has never adopted a "go-slow" policy,
but the anti-unionists refuse to be convinced. -American Federation of Labour, Weekly
News Service, 13th February, 1926.
[One more instance of the need for alteration of laws, whereby the needs of the whole
will be considered rather than the profits of the few.-E.L.P., G.S.1.

MONTHLY REPORT.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
TRADE.
26TH APRIL, 1926.
There is some improvement in trade but not such as to absorb any very
considerable number of our unemployed members. The figures in the Gazette
are as follows:-
BOOT AND SHOE INDUSTRY.
There was a further slight improvement in March in some of the principal centres ;
and towards the end of the month many firms were busy getting out orders before the
Easter holiday. Employment was also better than a year ago in most districts.
The percentage of workpeople unemployed, as indicated by the unemployment books
lodged at Employment Exchanges, was 7.4 on the 22nd March, as compared with 7.7
on the 22nd February, and with 9.2 on the 23rd March, 1925.
Employment remained fairly good in London. At Leicester it was good, better than
in February or than in March of last year; most factories were on full time, and some
overtime was worked to complete deliveries before the holiday; a little difficulty was
found in filling vacancies for skilled workers. At Northampton there was a further
improvement, and employment was fairly good, though some short time was still worked ;
the Employment Exchange register was lower than it has been for five years past. In the
Higham and Rushden district employment showed a further improvement, and was fair.
At Wellingborough there was a further increase in short-time working, and employment
was generally very poor. At Finedon employment was slack; at Earl's Barton it remained
fair. At Kettering employment showed a further improvement.
Employment at Leeds remained slack at factories producing heavy boots, but at
those producing sports goods and other light footwear it remained fair. At Stafford
employment was fair, and better than for some months past. At Norwich employment
in the turn-shoe trade was still slack, but in other sections there was a decided improve-
ment, and employment was good, with a little overtime in some factories. Employment
improved at factories in Bristol producing light footwear; but in the heavy boot factories
at Bristol and at Kingswood employment remained very poor, and was worse than a year
ago. At Street employment continued fair. There was a slight improvement in the
Rossendale Valley.
Employment was fairly good at Glasgow and at Kilmarnock; at Arbroath an im-
provement was reported; at most of the other Scottish centres employment was quiet,
with much short time.

INTERNATIONAL FEDERATION OF TRADE UNIONS.
Rights and Duties of a Member of the League of Nations.
Brazil.
During the negotiations at Geneva concerning Germany's admission to the League
of Nations, Brazil showed that she insisted upon its full rights as a member of the League.
If this country had a true conception of what may reasonably be expected of a member
of the League, little would remain to be said on the matter. This is, however, far from
being the case. Brazil emphatically stated at Geneva that she was determined to assert
her rights and not to be placed at any disadvantage. Before adopting such an attitude
abroad however, the Brazilian Government would do well to examine how the rights of
the citizens are respected at home.
Notwithstanding her membership of the League of Nations and the International
Labour Office, the Constitution has been tampered with in the last few years by the passing
of certain new acts which practically make it a dead letter. The measures adopted by
the authorities in respect of foreigners, political refugees or otherwise, are extremely
rigorous. Ambiguous clauses in the regulations enable the Government to deport anyone
whose presence they consider for some reason to be undesirable. Participation in a
strike by an immigrant renders him liable to instant deportation. Any Socialistic pro-
paganda is made virtually impossible. The Act passed in 1923 to restrict the freedom of
the Press, empowers the authorities to arrest anyone openly criticising the actions of the
Government. For three years Central Brazil has constantly been under martial law.
Although, according to the Brazilian Constitution, the right to hold meetings or to form
trade unions is guaranteed, employers may have any meeting of workers which "might
possibly" declare a strike, broken up by the police.
The authorities show exceptional activity in regard to censorship. All overseas
correspondence is opened and the right to privacy is violated in the most outrageous
manner. Attention has been previously drawn to this unendurable state of affairs, though
with little effect. For that reason the secretariat of the I.F.T.U. recently sent in a letter
to the Brazilian Home Office, in which it stated, inter alia, "On several occasions it has
come to our notice that letters addressed to befriended organisations in Brazil have not
been delivered.
Needless to say that this fact has occasioned the greatest surprise, as this attitude
does not in any way correspond with the spirit of Chapter XIII. of the Treaty of Peace.
We feel confident that your Government will take steps to see that our correspondence is
not subjected to further delays or detention." It is to be hoped that in this direction the
Brazilian Government will in the future also give more evidence of " its great interest in
the League of Nations and its aims."
C

THE GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.
60 LADY SOMERSET ROAD,
KENTISH TOWN, N.W.5.
20th April, 1926,
FELLOW MEMBERS,
MINING SITUATION. - The outstanding feature during the past month is the
very grave situation created by the Mine Owners and the Government who appear to find
the rates, both requests being unreasonable and devoid of humane treatment of one's
as yet no reasonable way out of the Owners' desire to either lengthen the hours or decrease
fellows. As has been said many times, the Miners have as much right to a living wage
know that the Miners will have the backing of the whole Labour Movement, which they
deserve, and its moral and financial support to stem the attacks on all other workers.
The figures given by the Miners themselves show 170,000,000 tons of coal were produced
at a profit; 84,000,000 tons were produced at a loss, although an aggregate profit for the
year over the whole 3,000 pits, is no less than 14 MILLIONS for 1924. The pre-war
period of 1913 shows £13 millions only, so that whilst we have the Owners improving
their position to the tune of one and a half millions, they ask the Miners to either work
longer hours or accept a reduction, an impossible position, and one that in my judgment
the Government appear to consent by the stoppage of the subsidy without making any
arrangement for the natural co-operation of the industry that is bound to come if we
have to be controlled by the Nation in a National sense irrespective of the trembling at
the knees of Liberal and Tory Statesmen when the word “Nationalisation” is mentioned.
the War when £440 millions was saved the country on Shipping. In the light of
this experience my contention is let us have more and more Nationalisation. The failure
of the Mine Owners, who, like Lord Tredegar gets £30,000 per year for the use of a five
chain mile of road through Tredegar Park subscribes not a copper to the upkeep of the
railway line; this, and many other taxes upon the Mining Industry, make the same a
reason why the Miners cannot possibly act as the Owners wish. My own view is that
the Owners and their class, ever anxious to live at the expense of the Nation, want a
continuation of the subsidy. I think the subsidy should be transferred into Government
control; under a Labour Government that would have been the case. Why have the
Government subsidised their pals in the spending of the many millions without any voice
of protest from the manufacturing or business community? We are all proud of the
statesmanlike answers of the Miners to all the points raised by the Commission, but one
cannot expect experts to think in terms of equality among men, irrespective of birth,
consequently they have not been humane and commercially-minded enough to support
whole-heartedly the findings of the Sankey Commission. Therefore, come weal, come woe,
we must and will stand by the Miners, who with the rest of us, suffered a reduction in
1922 of twelve million pounds per week in wages.
NATIONAL BURGLARY BY THE TORY GOVERNMENT. - The next item of public interest,
and which affects all our members, is the mean and contemptible robbery of the Insurance
Funds. What are the facts? Short of the Nationalisation of Industry, the Government
of the day introduced a scheme of Insurance during sickness and this fund has been
described contemptuously by its opponents and other ne’er-do-wells as the DOLE, and so
successful has the enemy been with this word that even some Labour people (save the
mark !) repeat it. What are the facts ? The latest published figures are for the last
four years :-
Workers' Contributions £62,015,000
Employers' 71,527,000
State 46,080,000
So that in round figures the State contribution is less than 4d. in the shilling. In other
words the workers and the industry find the overwhelming portion of the money, and the
Government have the impudence to control the methods by which it is spent. To cap
it all they have now decided (this Minority Government who represent the smaller portion
of the Nation), to use their marionette majority in the House of Commons to steal from
the Insurance Fund no less than eleven hundred thousand pounds, whilst at the same
paying super taxes as before. Is there any wonder that a portion of the public become
eruptive ?

MARKET HARBOROUGH.-Here again the firm has not played the game, they having
informed a prominent member of the Federation that they would put up the "Organisation
of Industry" resolution, and we can get no evidence to the effect that they have done so.
MOUNTSORREL SCHOOL BOOT Со.-This firm has been summoned by me before the
Committee of Inquiry for discharging twelve of our members whom we had instructed
to work to Statement in accordance with Clause 2 of the Terms of Settlement, and the
Committee were in a quandary as to the action of the firm in dispensing with the services
of twelve operatives at a time. The employers said the seriousness of the position was
that the firm worked Day Labour and refused to allow the men to work to Statement.
The meeting has done much good, but oh for the lack of stomach amongst the operatives!
NOTTINGHAM. On two occasions I have had to visit Nottingham owing to their
asking for one of our Parliamentary Candidates, Mr. J. H. Baum, to allow himself to be
nominated for the Eastern Division of Nottingham, that portion of the town in which
Mr. A. Hayday, M.P., resides, and the district upon which he hesitated to fight.
Having toured the Constituency with Mr. Baum, at the kindly request and assistance of
the Chairman of the Party, Mr. Ashworth, we witnessed the worst conditions of houses
and homes it has ever been my lot to witness, and recalls Bobbie Burns' couplet:
inhumanity to man makes countless thousands mourn." Our money will be well spent
in the effort to rescue our fellow creatures from these horrid and sordid surroundings.

BRANCH REPORTS.

CHESHAM. - Trade here remains quiet. In order to try and create some
enthusiasm in our members a Tea and Social Evening was held on the 8th
March. Seventy-three members sat down to the tea, after which a very
inspiring address was given by our friend, W. R. Smith, and we are hopeful
of good results. We are pleased to report the success of one of our members
at the local U.D.C. election. Three Labour candidates were nominated, two
returned, one being a Labour gain.

DESBOROUGH. - Trade with us is rather slack at present, and whilst
the majority of our members are on full time, others are very short indeed.
We have had Mr. L. Smith, Organiser, here for a week. Meetings have been
held each day outside the factories and a few members have been gained,
but owing to the Easter holiday intervening we have not been so successful
as we hoped to be. We intend, however, to follow up Mr. Smith's good work
by house to house visits, and expect to increase our membership considerably.

DUNDALK. - Trade continues good. Through the kindness of the
management we have obtained an athletic ground convenient to the factory.
Needless to say this should be looked upon as of vital importance to the workers,
as it is intended to provide them with suitable accommodation for indulging
in healthy outdoor exercises. In this, as in all enterprises, some outstanding
figures manifest themselves. We find the controlling valve-the firm's
mainspring-assisting physically, mentally and financially-financially, only
rivalled by his honourable contemporaries, without even exclusion.

HIGHAM AND RUSHDEN. - Trade is fairly good in the District in
comparison with rest of the country. The Army district is fortunate in securing
several big Government contracts.

LEICESTER WOMEN'S. - We have no women out of work in this
Branch. New patterns are still coming in to be priced. There seems no
ending to the fantastic designs which at times we find great difficulty in dealing
with. We wonder how fancy shoes in our other branches are being dealt
with if as much time is given to the valuing of operations as is necessary in
this Branch. The officials are finding plenty of work to do apart from their
many other duties. A Conference is being held on Saturday, 17th April,
for the purpose of discussing the better organisation of women in trade unions.
We are sending four delegates, although we do not agree that a women's
conference should (as we believe will be the case in this instance) have a larger
proportion of men delegates than women. However, we shall await events.
The Leicester Labour Party are sending six men and four women to this
Conference.

LIVERPOOL. - Trade is much the same as the previous month. The
burning question of the hour is Coal, and what is going to happen at the end
of the month. Will it be war or peace?

NORWICH. - Trade good, unemployment less.

PLYMOUTH. - During the month we have protested against the attempt
of the Government to economise at the expense of the insured workers, who
were promised a definite contribution towards their Health Insurance when
the Act was passed in 1911. Indeed, many of us remember the much advertised

leading jockeys of the day, but whether the horse threw the rider or the rider

I.F.T.U SUMMER SCHOOL AT BRUSSELS.
I have been requested by the Secretary of the International Federation of Trade
Unions to inform you that a Summer School will be held at the Uccle Labour College
near Brussels, Belgium, from 18th-31st July, 1926.
The fees for the school will be three pounds fifteen shillings (£3 155. od.) for the fort-
night, inclusive of board, lodging and tuition and excursions. Lectures will be given in
French, English, and German, and translations will be provided in each case.
I should be glad if you would place this notice before your Executive Committee
and the members of your Union. If any members desire to attend this school, or wish
for further information, application may be made direct to the Secretary, International
Federation of Trade Unions, 31 Tesselschadestraat, Amsterdam, from whom printed
application forms and programmes of the Summer School can be obtained, or
W. M. CITRINE,

COMMITTEE ON INDUSTRY AND TRADE.
The volume entitled "Survey of Industrial Relations" which is being published for
the Committee on 26th March, by His Majesty's Stationery Office, price 5s., deals with
such matters as the growth and distribution of the industrial population, rates of wages
and systems of wage payment, hours and other conditions of labour, unemployment,
and machinery for dealing with industrial disputes. Not only are the present position
and tendencies under these headings dealt with, but information is given as to the main
changes which have taken place since the years immediately preceding the war.
siderable amount of information is also given about the position in other countries as regards
some of the subjects mentioned, e.g., hours of labour and negotiating machinery. The
contents of the volume are mainly derived from official sources and the Committee have
prefixed an introduction calling attention to certain important considerations arising
from the Survey.

ORGANISERS' REPORTS.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
My last report to you was on 20th March. After the Council meeting on the 22nd
I went to Leicester on Arbitration work. The Leicester No. 1 Branch made a claim
for extras on the finishing of Rodeo Boots. The Leicester Arbitration Board has a sub-
committee of employers and branch officers for dealing with matters like this before send-
ing them to the Arbitrators. I am sorry, for the sake of the principle of arbitration, that
the employers' side on the Finishing Sub-Committee treated lightly, almost jokingly, the
bulk of this work at once, and pressed the manufacturers accordingly. The men responded
to the limit of their speed and skill. Figures got out by the employers' side showed where
the finishers were mainly engaged on this work for a number of weeks that their earnings
went down by nearly 7 per cent. In the several houses that I discussed this case with the
employers, there was not the slightest admission on the employers' side that the men had
worked out of the rate to oblige them and their customers. There isn't much gratitude in
business any more than in politics. This claim has gone to the Umpire now.
From 22nd to 27th March, Mr. Baum and I went to a number of shops in Sileby and
Ireland's workers. On the 30th we went to Atherstone to see if we could stir the non-
district. On the 29th we went to Derby and had a satisfactory meeting of Maden &
unionists at the one factory there. From time to time different lovers of cheap labour
among the manufacturers have tried to make money here, but failed. The present owners
do not seem to be making it a merry-go-round, as we found the place nearly at a standstill.
From then up to the Easter Holidays we worked round Leicestershire. With the
exception of three days spent at Liverpool and Manchester, I have spent the remainder of
the time with Mr. Baum trying to strengthen the position of the Sileby Branch. The
New Liverpool Rubber Co., at Walton, Liverpool, where Plimsolls and similar goods are
made, has changed hands to Dunlops. Some of the directors of this great concern are men
who have held high positions in the State. We had a meeting of the young women at
these works on 22nd April, and the particulars of earnings and conditions given by them
would shame the owners of hell. Fancy making a dozen pairs of Plimsolls for Is., and a
dozen pairs of canvas uppers with crepe soles complete for Is. 6d. The Wellington Rubber
boots, which fetch a good price in the shops, only yield a wage to the women who make
them, which limits them to a "bun and tea" dinner.
26th April, 1926.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
D. MCCARTHY.
During the past month I have been engaged in Northampton and Northamptonshire,
visiting Earls Barton, Wellingborough, Kettering, Burton Latimer, Desborough, Olney, and
Kempston. In the majority of these places the organisation, so far as numbers are concerned,
is good; and it is difficult to understand the apparent disinterestedness that exists. Opera-
tives, both male and female, must realise that the question of organisation and a lively interest
in the Union's activities are very essential: it is a bread-and-butter question to them, and
should engage their most serious attention. It is not good enough that any official should
have to follow up "Dame Rumour" and dig out complaints; it is the duty of all members
to report to their local officials any diversion from the National Terms that is taking place,
and get the matters dealt with at once. To grumble in an hostelry over the cup that
cheers doesn't get the complaints put right. I have held a number of meetings at Des-
borough and find the organisation good, but there are still an obstinate minority who are
prepared to receive the benefits derived from and obtained by the Union without con-
tributing to the Society. These people are being dealt with by the Local Executive, and
pressure will be brought to bear, if necessary, to make them see the folly of their ways.
Meetings have been held at Kettering, where the organisation is very good. There are
still a few factories where the daywork system is being worked, and although the local
officials have done all in their power to keep the operatives to quantities, which would
earn their day wage, according to statement prices, the tendency is that by continual
pressure from the management such quantities are exceeded. All the meetings were well
attended and a great interest taken, whilst the exact position has been explained both by
speech and handbill. The position at Burton Latimer is somewhat similar. On the
whole a good organisation is in existence, the local section Secretary collecting the mem-
bers' contributions at their homes. This system creates a difficulty, owing to the large
number of operatives who come in from outlying villages. The solution lies in adopting
an efficient Shops President System. My work in the Wellingborough, Earls Barton
and Olney district was hampered by slackness of trade, short time being almost general.
I held meetings of operatives in Northampton with a view to tightening up organisation,
which were very successful. Attendance at the meetings was satisfactory, lapsed members

During the Easter week, however, I was able to pay a visit to Chesham, where the
Branch had arranged a tea and social. This procedure was adopted as a method of getting
into touch with those who rarely come to the ordinary meeting, whether for Branch business.
or if called for organising purposes. The venture in this case can be voted a success, as
the majority of those present were not the ones usually met at purely organising meetings.
The branch officers took no risks, as I was called upon to speak before those present left the
great interest, and the various points made in relation to the value of the work done by the
tables following tea. An address lasting threequarters of an hour was listened to with
Union were much appreciated. This is not surprising, as a comparison of conditions to-day
with those that existed when I formed the Branch in 1913, gives a contrast that I am
certain no one would have thought possible, and is practical evidence that only by sound
organisation and loyalty can the workers obtain that which is best in their industrial life.
Chesham is a case where evidence exists to show that the earlier fears have not been
justified by results. It used to be a stock argument that Union conditions would make
trade impossible, and many operatives viewing the situation perhaps too much from a
selfish point of view, have been influenced by that specious cry, and kept outside our
organisation. Having regard to all this, it is indeed pleasing to know that last year Chesham
had more than their share of the trade that was going, some firms even working overtime.
pelling greater efficiency our agreements lead to improvement of the industry, better wages
This is, in my judgment, conclusive evidence that instead of hampering firms by com-
consuming public, or even increasing the price they are called upon to pay.
and conditions for the workers, without extracting anything unfair or unreasonable from the
This should er courage us in our work and justify our claims for further improvement,
a reduction in working hours not being the least important among the changes that one hopes
aread. Before leaving Chesham I would like to add that the one grievance that existed
has been put right following my visit to the factory; this means that so far as present
information goes everything is satisfactory in regard to our National Agreements in that
town. This is, I am sure, gratifying to both the employers and ourselves after the stoppage
of 1922. It means that all concerned can feel the effort and the expenditure was not in
vain.
Part of my time has been spent in Norwich, where I have resumed the effort made last
year to get a statement fixed for the Press department. Up to the present such does not
exist in any factory, but I have always felt that it was inevitable sooner or later, and as one
of the largest firms is pressing the matter, and the situation not being so free from diffi-
culties as might be, my services have been sought to help in getting what we hope will be
a satisfactory set of prices when completed. I am glad to report that greater progress has
been made than was possible a year ago.
Some time has been spent in London where the work that has been in hand so long
has been followed up, but here the great difference between operatives in the Union and
the operatives outside is shown by the way firms are willing to listen or otherwise to what
we have to say. In areas where so much is urged on behalf of so-called extreme ideas and
opinions the absence of Trade Union organisation is remarkable, or perhaps would be
if we did understand the hopelessness of much that is put forward purporting to be what
labour stands for. All this shows what has been so often urged, viz., that the basic test
of real effort leading to improvement in working-class life is membership of a Trade Union,
with that as a basis, and the power accruing therefrom, properly and intelligently applied,
other things will follow, but there must first be organisation, carrying with it individual
responsibility. To the boot operative in the East of London we say: Come into your
Union and give us the opportunity of dealing with the many grievances that now exist.
Further meetings have been held in connection with the Parliamentary position at
Norwich. Our people are asking for another chance of testing the electorate. The record
of the present Government up to date is surely a guarantee of our success if intelligence
exists in the minds of the average elector. The description given in the House of Commons
by Labour members when dealing with the so-called " Economy Bill" are fully justified.
No Labour Government could hope to excel the present one in class legislation, and no
government could possibly sink so low in punishing the poor in an effort to help the rich as
is contained in this so-called economy stunt. The more helpless the people, the greater
the punishment. The down-and-out unemployed, the helpless sick, and the innocent
child are those picked out to carry the burden of the nation's so-called economy, and all
that the wealthy may have less taxes to pay. No wonder our people feel and declare for
an election as soon as possible.
At the time of writing the Coal Crisis seems to overshadow everything. The outlook is
black. None can blame the miners. There is not a section of the great working-class
movement in this country, who, if placed in the position the miners are at this moment,
could do other than refuse to accept the cuts the mineowners are seeking to impose upon
them. I am sure we all desire to see peace reigning in this great industry, but it must be
peace resting upon justice. In their efforts to obtain this we must be wholeheartedly
behind the miners.
24th April, 1926.
WALTER R. SMITH.

Weekly Rest Day.—It is agreed that any hours over and above the weekly limit of
48 which are required by the nature of the services rendered to be worked on the weekly
rest day other than hours covered by Articles II. (c), III., IV. and V., shall be treated
either as hours to be dealt with under the provisions of national legislation relating to the
weekly rest day or as hours to be dealt with under the provisions of Article VI.
Railways. It is agreed that railways are covered by the Convention. In so far as
Article V. and Article VI. (a) are not sufficient for the needs of the railways, the necessary
overtime is permissible under Article VI. (b).

Time lost by Holidays.—It is agreed that in cases where a State allows hours to be
worked in excess of 48 per week in order to make up time lost by reason of holidays (other
than national holidays or holidays with pay), such hours must be included in the maximum
number of hours' overtime fixed in virtue of Article VI., and must be paid for at the over-
time rates laid down in the said Article.

Article XIV.—(1) It is agreed that each Government will insert Article XIV. in their
legislation to carry out the Convention.

(2) It is agreed* that use can only be made of Article XIV. in case of a crisis which
affects the national economy to such an extent that it threatens the existence of the life
of the people. An economic or commercial crisis, however, which concerns only special
branches of industry cannot be regarded as endangering the national safety within the
meaning of Article XIV., so that in this case the suspension of the Convention would not
be justified.

It is agreed that the English, French, German and Italian texts shall be equally
authoritative.
It is further agreed by the representatives of the Governments participating in the
Conference that they will report to their respective Governments the conclusions, as set
out above, which the Conference has been able to reach, so that those Governments who
have not ratified the Convention may, taking account of the agreements reached, be in a
position to proceed with their consideration of the question of the ratification of the
Washington Convention.
The conclusions of the Conference will also be reported formally to the International
Labour Office by the British Government, which took the initiative in summoning the
Conference.—The Ministry of Labour Gazette, April, 1926.
* Provisionally on the part of Great Britain.

WHY THE WORKERS NEED PROTECTING.
New Factory Act Long Overdue.
There are countless reasons why improved protection should be given to the workers
without delay.
THE CASUALTIES OF INDUSTRY.
For the year 1924, according to the report of the Chief Factory Inspector :-
169,723 WORKERS WERE INJURED SUFFICIENTLY SERIOUSLY TO
NECESSITATE ABSENCE FROM WORK.
956 WORKERS WERE KILLED.
These figures are exclusive of the
1,294 killed and 203,522 injured in the Mines, and
263 killed and 21,198 injured on the Railways.

IT LOST OWING TO STRIKES AND LABOUR DISPUTES."

Act.

The proposals for the protection of women are important-AND NECESSARY.
WORKING DAY AND NIGHT.
Cases from 1924 report of Chief Factory Inspector :-
Mantle and Dressmaking-women worked 9 a.m. till midnight for six consecutive
days, and then given work to do on Sunday. After a fortnight stocks had accu-
mulated, and they were dismissed.
Women and young persons of 14 years of age employed 6 a.m. till 11.30 p.m.
during week, and then had to work on Sunday.
Women employed in pork pie factory 8 a.m. till after midnight, starting again
at 8 a.m. next day.
Four women and girls employed continuously in bleach-works for 36 hours.

Women in woollen mill lifting pieces of cloth 200 lb.

MANAGERS AND FOREMEN SUPPORT JOINT
INDUSTRIAL COUNCIL RESOLUTION.
At the twelfth Annual Conference of the Federation of Managers and Foremen's
(Shoe Trade) Registered Associations held at Easter at the Bell Hotel, Leicester, when
matters of importance to the administrative and managerial side of the industry were
considered, Mr. Geary (Bristol) moved: "That this conference considers the advisability
of sending to the Manufacturers' Federation and also to the National Union of Boot and
Shoe Operatives, the following resolution: "That in the best interest of the trade,
all findings of Arbitration Boards which have been agreed to be made
binding by law." He said that two years ago, owing possibly to their feeling the
effects of the evasion by local manufacturers of Arbitration Board findings, Bristol
thought something must be done.
No reasonable arguments had been used against the proposal. It was not a contentious
matter and they were only ranging themselves alongside the best members in the trade
operatives also who evaded them. For the latter they felt nothing but pity. If the
Federation was to be of any benfit to the trade it was time they made their opinions felt on
such matters and established themselves on the side of all that was best in the industry
Mr. Britton, who seconded, remarked that the question had been threshed out in the
past.
Mr. Billington suggested that they ought to add to the resolution the words: "Upon
the whole industry." Evasion of the findings of Arbitration Boards prevented the lifting
up of the trade. His Association felt that they wanted no competition in the matter of
wages. They could have as much competition as they liked in styles and materials, but
not in wages. Competition in wages did not mean any increase in the production or the
consumption of footwear.
Mr. Gook said he felt that they should not interefere with what he called the politics
of the trade. His instructions from the Norwich Association were to remain neutral.
Mr. Wilson said it was not a question of taking sides. Those who visited Bristol a
few weeks ago saw something of the conditions prevailing there and they were astonished.
It was time something was done to wipe out the bad conditions prevailing in the Kingswood
district.
Mr. Merricks said that a year ago he was opposed to the idea, but since then he had
been to Bristol, and he was astounded at the conditions prevailing there.
Mr. Billington urged that the words he suggested should be added, as they would
have the effect of making findings of Arbitration Boards legally binding on the whole
trade whether a manufacturer seceded from the Federation or not. The resolution was
carried with the addition referred to.
SOME BOOTS.
Mr. Blackwell (Gloucester) regretted to see a deficit on the boots department. He
knew some makers made boots to sleep in, but the C.W.S. manufactured boots to walk in.
"I had a pair of boots forty-five years ago
(Laughter.)
The Chairman: Were they made in Leicester ?
Mr. Blackwell: You may catch me there because I don't know the date Leicester
was established. They were made under the auspices of the C.W.S., and were spring-side
elastic sides. I wore them for twenty years, and could not wear them out, and then I cut
them down and made them into a pair of Oxfords. Can't we get some of those kind of
boots now?
The Chairman: It would be very nice to have that pair photographed.
Mr. Oliver said it would be no use for the boot factories if boots wore for forty-five
years. Explaining why there was a deficit, he said they were experiencing difficulties
with the continual change of fashions, and it was well-nigh impossible to keep up with
the changes.

WHAT IS A WARD SHOE?
A ward shoe is generally regarded as a simple one-bar with a low square heel-less
than an inch high, including the rubber top-piece, if any. So far as we know, the question
has never been raised before, but if a detailed specification is required there should be no
difficulty in drafting one. The Shoe and Leather Record, 9th April, 1926.

**FOOD.**
At 1st April the average level of retail prices of the principal articles of food was
appreciably lower than at 1st March. This was mainly due to seasonal reductions of
nearly d. each in the average price of eggs, and d. a quart in that of milk, but there
were also slight reductions in the average prices of most of the other articles of food included
in the statistics.

As a net result of all the changes recorded, the average increase over the level of
July, 1914, in the retail prices (in Great Britain and Northern Ireland) of the articles of
food included in these statistics was about 59 per cent. at 1st April, as compared with
about 65 per cent. at 1st March, and 70 per cent. at 1st April, 1925. The fall in the per-
centage as compared with a year ago is accounted for chiefly by reductions in the prices
of flour and bread, potatoes, sugar, meat and butter. - The Ministry of Labour Gazette,
April, 1926.
