LABOUR PARTY CONFERENCE
(SCOTTISH COUNCIL).

Owing to the regrettable death of Mr. C. Bleakley, I was able to attend the above
Conference in Glasgow on the 13th March. Mr. T. E. M'Donald, Chairman of the Execu
tive, presided over a large attendance of delegates. The platform was a strong one, too
strong for a one-day Conference, as the time taken up with speeches from fraternal delegates
encroaches seriously on the time for ordinary business. The opening address lost much
of its effectiveness through the Chairman having a weak voice, although of course, good
matter should be valued at its true worth, apart from sound or length. Mr. C. T. Cramp
(National Executive), Mr. A. Walsh (Co-operative Delegate), Mr. Elger (Scottish Trades
Union Congress), Mr. Neil McLean (Parliamentary Labour Party), and others, spoke very
well, but the one address which was outstanding in its matter and spirit came from Mr.
Arthur Henderson, Secretary of the National Party. While paying a tribute to Scotland
for its excellent response to the political appeal of Labour, he thought still that points of
organisation required emphasis, and therefore detailed forms of development which he
was of opinion should engage the attention of the movement in this country. He urged
the desirability of securing individual members as one of the first steps, and gave many
practical reasons for that belief. Next was the matter of collecting small contributions
from sympathisers in every constituency. He maintained this method was the most
important and the most successful when carried out properly. By means of such system-
co-operation with the Party, the work of fighting an election was made ever so much
atic contact with an ever extending body of electors, and by bringing them into financial
easier, and more effective. The great secret, he believed, was to seek small weekly sums,
which were easily paid, and yet gave the giver a sense of attachment to the Party, which
last of all, was the question of
Figures were submitted to show that this important work was most highly developer
where success was greatest or vice-versa. In this, Scotland was far behind England,
and Mr. Henderson argued that much as Scotland had done, greater and more enduring
success would follow upon a more extensive campaign amongst the women electors. Point
after point was closely followed, and when Mr. Henderson concluded with a fighting appeal
to supporters, it was felt that the best speech of the day had been made. And so it proved
to be.

The business part of the Conference was disappointing. The Chairman was nearly
inaudible, and this had a disturbing effect on delegates. Only seven items appeared on
the Agenda, but other resolutions had been sent in — two or three by Glasgow Trades
Council—which were not included. This led to a wordy duel, the defence being that the
excluded resolutions were not competent, as they infringed the rights of the National
Party. As the Scottish Council acts as an advisory body it should not be competent to
submit or discuss matters which the National Party has the authority to settle. The
Secretary, Mr. B. Shaw, had sent the offending resolutions to headquarters for a ruling,
and the decision was to keep them off the Agenda.

After the Secretary had explained, Mr. Egerton Wake (National Executive), put up
the case for headquarters, but still a substantial doubt existed in the minds of delegates
as to rightness of the procedure. I must confess that I do not accept the defence as
adequate, and many others agree with me on the point. More will be heard of it, as the
Glasgow men can be trusted to see the whole thing tested fully before giving in to this
decision.

The first resolution, "Improvement of Labour Party Organisation," suffered un-
intentionally by Mr. Henderson's speech, although the supporters attempted to say again
what had been so well said before. It was agreed finally to leave it to the Council to act
upon. The resolution on "The 48-Hours Bill" met a similar fate, and was referred to the
Executive. The "previous question" was successful against two proposals relating to
"Alternative Methods of Housing" and "Employment of Civil and Corporation Servants-
Pensioners in Ordinary Avocations," while "Education Authority Elections" was turned
down, and "Date of Local Government Elections" and "Payment of Local Government
Representatives" were accepted.

That, in brief, is the practical result of the Conference. The Executive Report was
an admirable document, carefully written in Mr. Ben Shaw's best style. Here you get
an orderly presentation of the year's work, and if anyone thinks such executives to be of
doubtful advantage, they should get a copy to read. By-elections in the area; Com-
munist difficulties; Education Authorities Election; Co-operative Joint Committee;
Housing and Rents question; Local Government Elections; Finance of Parliamentary
Elections; Women's Conferences; and reports of Deputations are some of the interesting
maintain an intelligent interest in the needs of the hour. If the Conference itself was tame,
yet the work of
the work with the best wishes of all friends of the Labour Movement.

JAMES P. REID, Delegate.

INTERNATIONAL INFORMATION.
YOUNG PERSONS AT SEA.
Great Britain Ratifies Two World Conventions.
It is announced from Geneva that Great Britain has formally notified its ratification
of two Conventions, dealing with the welfare of young persons at sea, which were adopted
at the third annual Session of the International Labour Conference of the League of
Nations, held in Geneva in 1921.
The first Convention provides that no young person under the age of eighteen years
shall be employed or work in vessels as trimmers or stokers. This has already been
ratified by Bulgaria, Denmark, Esthonia, Finland, India, Italy, Latvia, Poland, Roumania,
Spain and Sweden.
The second Convention provides that any child or young person under the age of
eighteen shall only be employed in a vessel on production of a medical certificate of fitness
for the work and shall be medically examined each year until reaching that age. This
has already been ratified by Bulgaria, Esthonia, Finland, India, Italy, Japan, Latvia,
Poland, Roumania, Spain and Sweden.
Great Britain has now ratified nine out of the sixteen Conventions adopted at the
various Sessions of the International Labour Conference between 1919 and 1924.
WORLD LABOUR INFORMATION.
Growing Work of the I.L.O.
The steady growth of the International Labour Office of the League of Nations in
answering requests from all parts of the world for information on industrial and labour
matters is shown in the report of the Director of the Office, M. Albert Thomas, for the last
year, which will be presented to the eighth Session of the International Labour Conference,
opening in Geneva on 26th May.
The report states that 687 requests for information were received in 1925, as against
505 in 1924 and 402 in 1923. The list is headed by Great Britain with 120 requests,
followed by Germany with 94, France with 78 and Switzerland with 68.
It is interesting to note the subjects which particularly appealed to Governments,
employers' and workers' organisations (each of whom sends representatives to the annual
Conference). The Governments asked mainly about workers' insurance against accidents
and disease, health questions and safety, and unemployment; the employers about
comparative wages in different countries; health questions and safety, and weekly rest
day and holidays with pay; the workers about general working conditions; weekly rest
and holidays with pay, and workers' insurance.
It is also stated that the value of the library of the "I.L.O." is being increasingly
appreciated, many visitors come to Geneva specially to consult it. As the different States
are acquiring the habit of sending all their publications to it, the Library is becoming the
official world depository of all publications connected with labour legislation. Last year
10,485 additions were made to it as against 8,691 in 1924.
BOOT AND SHOE TRADE: LONDON.
The two sides of the Standing Committee for the London Wholesale Hand-Sew
Louis XV. Heel Trade, also the two sides of the Board of Conciliation for the Boot and
Shoe Trade of London. Difference. --Motions by the Workers' Side of the Committee and
the Board and amendments by the Employers' Sides in connection with the provision of
Factory Workshops for the Operatives. Being unable to agree, the respective parties
made application in accordance with their Rules for the appointment of an Umpire under
the Industrial Courts Act, 1919. The Minister appointed Mr. W. Addington Willis,
C.B.E., to act in this capacity. Award. The Umpire was of opinion that the Workers
had established a case for at least an effort to be made towards effecting the change and
laid down conditions to be satisfied before such change should become effective. Dated
13th March, 1926. The Ministry of Labour Gazette, April, 1926.

THE MINING SITUATION

PROPOSALS FOR CO-ORDINATED ACTION OF TRADE UNIONS.
[It should be understood that memoranda giving detailed
instructions will be issued as required.]

1. SCOPE.

The Trades Union Congress General Council and the Miners' Federation of Grea-
Britain having been unable to obtain a satisfactory settlement of the matters in dispute in
the coalmining industry, and the Government and the mineowners having forced a lock-on
the General Council, in view of the need for co-ordinated action on the part of affiliated
unions in defence of the policy laid down by the General Council of the Trades Unice
Congress, directs as follows:-

TRADES AND UNDERTAKINGS TO CEASE WORK.

Except as hereinafter provided, the following trades and undertakings shall cease wor-
as and when required by the General Council:-

Transport, including all affiliated unions connected with transport, i.e., railways, sea
transport, docks, wharves, harbours, canals, road transport, railway repair shops and
contractors for railways, and all unions connected with the maintenance of, or equipment,
manufacturing, repairs, and groundsmen employed in connection with air transport.
Printing Trades, including the Press.

Productive Industries.
(a) Iron and Steel.

(b) Metal and Heavy Chemicals Group. Including all metal workers and other
workers who are engaged, or may be engaged, in installing alternative plant to take the
place of coal.

Building Trade.-All workers engaged on building, except such as are employed
definitely on housing and hospital work, together with all workers engaged in the supply of
equipment to the building industry, shall cease work.

Electricity and Gas. The General Council recommend that the Trade Unions
connected with the supply of electricity and Gas shall co-operate with the object of ceasing
to supply power. The Council request that the Executives of the Trades Unions concerned
shall meet at once with a view to formulating common policy.

Sanitary Services. -The General Council direct that sanitary services be continued.

270
statement issued by Mr. A. Pugh, Chairman of the General Council, on behalf
of the Congress, it was stated that :--

"The Initial cause of the deadlock was the mine owners' arbitrary attitude
in refusing to conduct national negotiations as recommended in the Commis-
sion's report, and their action in giving notices to enforce a general reduction
in wages. From the moment the mineowners issued lock-out notices to their
workpeople, the question at issue, so far as the General Council was concerned,
was the withdrawal of those notices as a condition preliminary to the conduct
of negotiations. From that we have never receded. The Government rep-
resentatives insisted that the miners must first declare themselves definitely
as willing to accept a reduction in wages. In these circumstances, and in view
of the inevitability that there would be a stoppage throughout the coalfields on
May 1st if the notices and demands of the mineowners were pressed, the General
Council decided to call a conference of the responsible Executives of the unions
affiliated to Congress to take their decision upon the course to be adopted in
supporting the miners to resist the demands made upon them. The decision
of the conference held on Thursday, April 29th, was one of supporting the
miners and instructing the General Council to proceed with negotiations with a
view to an amicable settlement, but subject to the condition that the threat of a
lock-out must be removed so that negotiations could be carried on under proper
conditions. It was under these instructions that the Negotiating Committee of
the Council proceeded with its efforts on the Thursday evening, and continued
during the following day. It is significant that the General Council Committee
persisted in its efforts until nearly midnight on Friday, April 30th despite the
fact that while this was proceeding, scores of thousands of men throughout the
coalfields had already been locked out. The Committee failed to induce the
Government to get the notices withdrawn, or to depart from their attitude of
demanding, as a preliminary condition to negotiations, that the miners must
definitely agree to a wages reduction.

Despite the request that had been made by the miners in their earliest
discussions with the Mineowners' Association that they should be informed of
what was proposed in the form of reductions, it was not until the afternoon of
Friday, April 30th when the lock-out was actually operating, that proposals
were received through the Prime Minister, which involved a substantial all-round
reduction of wages and an increase of hours to eight per shift.

REFUSAL TO WITHDRAW NOTICES.
Our Conference of Trade Union Executives was kept waiting hour after
hour during the whole of Friday. At midnight we had to report that, notwith-
standing all our efforts, it had been found impossible to give effect to their
resolution to get the lock-out notices withdrawn. Negotiations had completely
broken down, and as the majority of the men had already been locked out,
nothing remained but to give the fullest support to the miners in resisting the


---
Here is the extracted text:
271
atrocious demands which had been made upon them under the pressure of the
lock-out. The conference on the following day decided on a course of definite
action in support of the miners. At the same time the General Council intimated
to the Prime minister that, even at that stage, they were ready to make a further
effort at negotiations. The result was a meeting of our Committee with repre-
sentatives of the Government on Saturday night, and in the early hours of
Sunday morning the Government representatives submitted the following
formular for our consideration:-
"The Prime Minister has satisfied himself as a result of the conversations he had
had with the representatives of the Trades Union Congress that, if negotiations are
continued (it being understood that the notices cease to be operative) the representatives
of the Trades Union Congress are confident that a settlement can be reached on the
lines of the report within a fortnight."
The Trade Union representatives agreed to arrange to discuss the situation
with their full body as well as with the Miners Executive. Owing to the latter
having left London to be present in their districts to advise their members in
consequence of the lock-out having come into operation, not expecting anything
to transpire that would require their presence during the Sunday, our Committee
found that the Miners Executive were not available, but immediately tele-
graphed to them to return to London.
SUNDAY NIGHT'S ULTIMATUM.
Meanwhile, the discussions with the Government representatives were
reported to the General Council, and consideration given to the formula referred
to. This having been done, an intimation was sent to the Government that our
Committee desired a further meeting to discuss the situation. The meeting
took place on Sunday evening, and we intimated that while we could accept the
formula in principle, there were certain of its terms which our General Council
required should be further considered. Arising from this, many exchanges of
opinion took place as to a suitable formula. As the miners' representatives
were now present in the building we left the Government representatives so
that we could consult the miners, and were actually making an arrangement
when, without warning, we received the ultimatum of the Government that in
consequence of what had transpired with the "Daily Mail" newspaper, and
that, as certain of the Unions had advised their members with regard to a strike,
negotiations were broken off.
I desire to make special reference to the statement by Sir Douglas Hogg,
which reads as follows :-
"In the course of a two hours' discussion, the Trade Union Leaders dictated what
they stated to be the utmost they were prepared to submit to the miners. It was in
these words:-
" "We will urge the miners to authorise us to enter on a discussion with the
understanding that they and we accept the Report as a basis of settlement, and we
approach it with the knowledge that it may involve some reduction of wages. With
this resolution in their pockets the Congress representatives went off to consult with
the miners, who by this time had got back to town, and the Ministers on their side
returned to report to the Cabinet." "

272
The foregoing statement, we have no hesitation in saying, is a gross mis-
representation of the facts. While, as we have indicated, the matter was
explored by the meeting, no such formula was ever dictated by the Trade Union
representatives, nor assented to by them or in their possession. The only
formula was that written by the Government representatives, quoted above
and handed to us in the early hours of Sunday morning. It was this which
we proceeded to discuss with the miners, and upon which we were making
progress towards an arrangement when the Government's ultimatum put a stop
to the proceedings.
We repeat, and defy cantradiction, (1) that the breakdown of the negotia-
tions was, in the first instance, due to the failure of the Government to obtain
a withdrawal of the lock-out notices, and its insistance upon a prior agreement
by the miners to accept a reduction in wages as a preliminary to giving effect
to the terms of the Commission's Report by negotiations; (2) that the second
attempt on the part of the General Council to get negotiations on foot was
defeated by the action of the Government in closing the door to negotiations
while we were actually discussing arrangements with the Miners' Executive-
and this because of the action taken by the Printers in regard to the "Dail
Mail," an action which was quite unknown to our representatives while we were
in the Government Building, and which was promptly repudiated as soon as the
facts were brought to our notice."
However, every effort was made to keep the door open, and on Tuesday
evening the 11th inst. a hurried meeting of the Trades Union Congress Genera
Council was again called, the meeeting lasting until nearly 3 a.m. on the 12th.
The Congress was again in session at an early hour that day, and later issued
the following report to all Unions :-
The General Council, through the magnificent support and solidarity of
the Trade Union Movement, has obtained assurances that a settlement of the
Mining problem can be secured which justifies them in bringing the general
stoppage to an end.
Conversations have been proceeding between the General Council repre-
sentatives and Sir Herbert Samuel, Chairman of the Coal Commission, who
returned from Italy for the express purpose of offering his services to try to
effect a settlement of the differences in the Coal Mining Industry.
The Government had declared that under no circumstances could
negotiations take place until the general strike had been terminated, but the
General Council feel, as a result of the conversations with Sir Herbert Samuel
and the proposals which are embodied in the correspondence and documents,
that sufficient assurances had been obtained as to the lines upon which a
settlement could be reached to justify them in terminating the General Strike.


---
The General Council accordingly decided at their meeting to-day to
terminate the general stoppage, in order that negotiations could be resumed to
secure a settlement in the coal mining industry, free and unfettered from
either strike or lock-out.

The General Council considered the practicability of securing a resump-
tion of work by the members in dispute at a uniform time and date, but it was
felt, having regard to the varied circumstances and practices in each industry,
that it would be better for each Executive Council itself to make arrangements
for the resumption of work of its own members. The following telegram was
despatched to you to-day :-

"General Council, T.U.C., have to-day declared General Strike terminated.
Please instruct your members as to resuming work as soon as
arrangements can be made. Letter follows.

PUGH, CITRINE."

Throughout the negotiations and during the whole of the stoppage, the
General Council have declared that they have been fighting to protect the
Miners against ar intolerable degradation of their standard of life and working
conditions. It was with this object, and this object alone, that the General
Council assumed the grave responsibility of calling upon its affiliated organisa-
tions to unite in strike action to enforce the cancellation of the lock-out notices
and the withdrawal of the new wages scale posted in the mining districts. No
attack was at any time contemplated upon the established political institutions
of the country, and it is a testimony to the loyalty and discipline of the Move-
ment that disorders have been practically unknown.

The Unions that have maintained so resolutely and unitedly their generous
and ungrudging support of the Miners can be satisfied that an honourable
understanding has been reached.

The General Council accept the consequences of their decision with a full
sense of their responsibility not only to their own membership but to the Nation
at large. They have endeavoured throughout the crisis to conduct their case
as industrial disputes have always been conducted by the British Trades
Unions, without violence or aggression. The General Council feel in taking
the last steps in bringing the crisis to an end that the Trade Union Movement
has given a demonstration to the World of discipline, unity and loyalty without
parallel in the history of industrial disputes.

Yours fraternally,
ARTHUR PUGH, Chairman :
WALTER M. CITRINE, Acting Secretary.

MANUFACTURERS' FEDERATION.
The unofficial understanding which is existing between the Manufacturers'
Federation and ourselves was again brought into being during this dispute, and
at a meeting of the Federation held at Leicester on the 5th inst., under the
chairmanship of Mr. C. W. Horrell, the following important resolution was
passed :---
THE EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE of the FEDERATION, fully realising the
disastrous effect the General Strike will have upon industry throughout the country,
recommends its members in the best interests of the industry, to adopt forthwith
universal half-time before the entire closing down of their factories becomes inevitable.
and so prolong employment as long as possible. This recommendation is based upon
the Emergency Orders of the Government, relative to the reduction of power and light
to 50% of their usual period.
The COMMITTEE would point out that the grave dispute is not one between boot
and shoe manufacturers and their operatives, who will equally suffer therefrom, and
trusts the goodwill so long existing in our industry will not be disturbed by the serious
industrial conditions now prevailing.
FINANCE.
At the Memorial Hall Conference held on the 1st May, referred to on
page 269, paragraph 6 (b), Unions that were not called out were asked to
render financial assistance, and has always been our custom, we pledged the
members of the Union to subscribe our quota to the General Fund. Although
the stoppage has ended it will be some time before we are in a position before
all the workers resume full work, and naturally great expense has been incurred
on account of Dispatch Riders and the Organisation which had to be put into
being, and also in assisting those who answered the call. In this connection
we feel we are carrying out your wishes by making a subscription of £20,000
to the General Fund, and feel confident we have your full support in so doing.
To meet the position created by the stoppage of our members owing to lack of
transport, we also decided that
"Members thrown out of employment owing to the Coal Dispute, who may
be out of work entirely, i.e., either dismissed or suspended for the time being,
week by week, and not merely on short time, shall be treated under the special
powers of the Council conferred by Rule, and
Payment may be made at the rate of Out-of-Work Pay and under the
same conditions as to probationary periods for Unemployment Benefit. Under
this special method payment shall count for the purposes of payment to the
member as Out-of-Work Benefit; if, therefore, a member has already drawn
the ten weeks' benefit he will NOT be entitled to any pay under the circum-
stances. Odd days must NOT be paid for when operatives work one day and
stand off another.

THE STRUGGLE
has been the greatest in the history of the industrial movement, and one
which will have very far reaching effects in the years to come, the result of
which no one can foresee. The question may be asked as to the wisdom o
efficacy of a general strike. It should be borne in mind that the position was
that the trade union movement promised their help to the miners in resisting a
method of attack by the mine-owners to accept a considerable reduction in
wages without the opportunity of discussing the same. Having decided, there-
fore, upon this vital point, loyalty called for that support being given which had
been promised. It is true one cannot always see the results which will follow
one's pledged word. The movement could do no other than having once given
its word to honour it. Hence the tremendous upheaval through which we have
passed, an upheaval which must leave to all sections of the community who had
the well-being of the country at heart to determine-if we are to be worthy of
humane civilisation-and see that better methods are adopted to secure the
primary rights of the people being assured.

THE GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.

60 LADY SOMERSET ROAD,
KENTISH TOWN, N.W. 5.
18th May, 1920,

FELLOW MEMBERS,
THE GREATEST STRIKE in the history of the world has ended by saving the
situation of imposing a reduction in wages and a lengthening of hours. The paralysis
of industry for a few days only has had the desired effect, which is to show that the wage
earners are big enough to stand by the Miners, who already receive too little for the
strenuous work in which they are engaged. Their average earnings for full weeks worked
comes out at 48s., and if we compare this amount with the latest statement adequate
to keep himself, wife, and the average family of three, the amount required would be
61s., or 13s. per week more than the average Miner receives at present. The position
of the Miner is such as to make him very desperate, and if as Cardinal Manning once said,
" A starving man has a natural right to his neighbour's bread," then read in its full sense
we have no right to refuse to share with the man who is a creature of circumstances
which he has no control, and as the art of government is the welfare of the people, then
is no party other than the Labour Party who would begin at the bottom first, and attend
to those in most natural need, and then raise up by steps to as high as the economic force
of the people can give.

All the above trouble could have been avoided had the Government told Northumber-
land and Londonderry that there must be no wage cuts, no increase in hours until
terms set out by the British Ministers of the Churches had been carried out. Instead
that the business was allowed to stop until such time as the Government realised th
their threats availed nothing. That lesson will, I feel very hopeful, prove at the ner
land. This stoppage was similar to the one-day stoppage we advocated in 1921, at the
election that the feasting of the rich by the robbery of the poor has killed Toryism in ou
self-same unanimity, the powers that be would not have risked the effort. The Miner
Kingsway Hall, for the benefit of the Unemployed. Had that taken place with this
are said to be dissatisfied, so were some of us in 1895, but we have made good, and the
Miners can do the same on the conditions offered by the Trades Union Congress
they give it a trial. At the the same time attend on Boards trying to improve the
ditions would produce more and better results than attacking the enemy first and when
you want a divergence attack colleagues and friends. When this kind of propaganda is
muzzled the better for the mine-worker.

SILEBY.- As mentioned on previous occasions, the firm had refused to post our notice
on the Organisation of Industry, and I complained to the County Association and sent the
case to the Committee of Inquiry as an hostile act, complaining too of the firm deliberatel
starting women to work in the Finishing room, as defined in the National Agreement
and also to object to interference with a girl who had left them after working several years
in the Lasting room to go to another firm owing to statements made distasteful to the gir
We were pleased to learn the firm had posted the notice, and they had every reason t
believe that poaching had been done by the firm mentioned, to some extent at least. As
we could not prove or interfere with the acts of employers towards each other we could
express no opinion. Let us hope that Unionism will again be triumphant at this firm.

During the Great Strike we visited this town again and held a very good meeting :
those not working, which was the day after the settlement, and had arranged for a meeting
later in the day at Mountsorrel, where we would have held an open-air meeting had the
weather been fine, but we had no opportunity as it rained unceasingly until nine o'cloc
at night.

RUSHDEN. A small firm here with a number of Hand Lasters have refused to pay our
rates according to Statement, with the result we shall have to press our full claims after
Whitsuntide, and hope the firm will not try to build up a business on a 20 per cent. less
wage than that which prevails elsewhere. In fact, had we got all robust men in our midst
whose unionism and manliness was bound up in their price, we should not have to forgive
these few aged and weak ones from taking work at any price so long as they got some work.

SUPERANNUATION. A further special meeting of the Council has been held to consider
the lines of a scheme of superannuation for our members. This can only be done by an
additional contribution, and the present position is threepence or sixpence extra. The same
will be submitted to the Conference and ultimately to the members, who I think, after
hearing the matter explained, will in meeting assembled vote by ballot "Yes," or "No."

LEICESTER BRANCHES AND THE STOPPAGE.
A Mass Meeting of the Leicester No. 1, Leicester No. 2, and Leicester Women's
Branches of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Operatives, held in the De Montfort
Hall, on Thursday evening, 13th May, 1926, in support of the Miners; over 4,000 attended.
The Meeting was preceded by a procession with Band and Banner of the Leicester
No. 1 Branch, starting from Humberstone Gate, proceeding through the centre of the
City; 2,000 in the procession.
The meeting commenced by the singing of the "Red Flag."
Ald. Hill, J.P., Chairman, supported by Mr. T. F. Richards (General President of the
Union), Messrs. D. McCarthy and J. H. Baum (Union Organisers), Mr. J. Wheeler and
Mrs. M. J. Bell-Richards (Council Members), Messrs. M. A. Parker, J. Greaves, G. Parbury,
A. Worth, G. Smith, C. Wade, Miss Muir and Miss Sherwin, and Local Executive members.
Ald. Hill said we had met in consequence of one of the greatest fights in the history
of Trade Unionism in this country. The response and loyalty of the workers had exceeded
all expectations, and has proved the solidarity of the working-class movement. (Cheers.)
Mr. T. F. Richards outlined how the negotiations broke down, and recalled the year
1895, when a Lockout occurred in the Boot and Shoe Industry, after which Arbitration
Boards were adopted. We have asked our members for a levy and I hope this will be
unanimously responded to. (Cheers.) He appealed to the meeting to try to visualise
the deplorable conditions under which the miner had to work, and the utterly inefficient
wages he received.
Messrs. D. McCarthy and J. H. Baum also addressed the meeting.
The Chairman then moved that £10,000 be granted to the Miners. This was carried
without opposition.

BRANCH REPORTS.

CHESHAM. —Trade here at the time of writing this report is very disturbed
owing to the Coal dispute. Five factories are working part time, others have
closed down until the dispute is ended. We were glad to know the Council
had decided to help the Miners in their struggle against a reduction in wages,
and hope the whole Trade Union movement will stand firm until at least this
condition is assured.

DAVENTRY. —Trade with us has been very slack for the past two
months and much short time has been worked. It has been decided here to
run the factories half time only during the present crisis. This will make it
very difficult for many members to pay the proposed levy in addition to their
contributions. A Mass Meeting of the Branch was held on the 5th inst., when
there was a crowded attendance, who listened attentively to the Council
Member for the District, W. R. Townley, J.P., and Mr. Len. Smith (National
Organiser), who dealt with the events leading up to the Mining lockout, and the
steps taken on behalf of the Union by our Executive Council in regard to it.
The meeting was a most successful one, and the number present was easily a
record for our Branch.

DERBY. —Trade in Derby is very bad at the C.W.S. and Clemson's,
some of the operatives having been suspended now for about a month with no
prospects of better times.

DESBOROUGH. —Trade with us is still very quiet, and part of our
members are on short time. Our sick payments continue to be very heavy.
We have had Mr. L. Smith, Organiser, with us during the month. A public
meeting was held, Mr. Smith's subject being "The Coal Crisis and its effect on
the Boot Trade." An excellent address was given and our only regret was the
attendance, still we hope the good work he has done will help us in the future.
A few have joined and no doubt others will soon follow. We regret that during
the last few months so many members have left us, but nearly all of these have
either left the town or gone into some other occupation.

HIGHAM AND RUSHDEN.—Trade remains fair. Our new Heel-making
Works (Messrs. J. White, Boot Manufacturers) are about to open in a factory
formerly used by the late Advance Boot Co. Raunds is busy; Bozeat, Wollaston
and Finedon, poor; Higham, Rushden and Irthlingborough, fair to good.

KINGSWOOD AND DISTRICT. —The condition of trade in this centre
maintains the same character as last reported, with the prospect arising from
the industrial crisis of a still larger number standing off. Great sacrifices will
be demanded in this great protest from the workers, and we sincerely trust
that the reward will justify the hopes of the workers in this supreme effort
to defend the standard of life which twentieth century ideals demand.

LEEDS.—At a large gathering of our members on 4th May, at the Leeds
Trades Hall, a presentation was made to our ex-Secretary, Mr. J. Wescoe, by
Shopmate Abbott, who deputised for the General Secretary, who was unable
to be present owing to the National Dispute. Our President, Councillor A. J.
Dobbs, took the opportunity of explaining the dispute at some length. Mr.
Wright, the Solicitor for the Branch, in a few well-chosen words, supported
Shopmate Abbott in the presentation.

NORWICH. The month of April saw a decided improvement in trade in
Norwich. More pleasing was the fact that the fillip in trade was general in
the city, being spread over large and small manufacturers alike. It is, of
course, needless to say the Turnshoe section was exempt from the improvement
shown, in fact our turnshoe trade appeared further depressed, many additional
becoming unemployed during the month. The Branch has reached a
membership higher than at any previous period of the Branch's history, due
mainly to the organising efforts of the officials and the loyal co-operation of
the members. In the midst of this success we see the coming of the crash
between the Miners supported by the British Trade Union Movement, and the
mineowners supported by the Government of private capitalists. Come what
may, the Miners must win, and when next we write from Norwich we hope to
record the greatest victory by organised labour since the commencement of
the industrial era.
PLYMOUTH. Our Branch has decided with a unanimous vote to support
the Council in acting in conjunction with other organisations affiliated to
Trades Union Congress, in their endeavour to secure fair wages and conditions
for those employed in the Mining industry, and to the proposal to impose a
levy upon all members of the Union in order to provide necessaries of life for
the dependants of those actually engaged in the struggle. Our special meeting
was one of the best we remember. All who attended were determined to resist
any attempt to lower the present standard of life, and secure fair terms for the
Miners. While we write there appears a basis for negotiations and agreement
in the latest message broadcast by the Prime Minister, Mr. Baldwin, as follows:
No honest person can doubt that my whole desire is to maintain the standard
of living of every worker." What a tragedy it is that the Prime Minister
should have broken off negotiations when a settlement was in sight, and what a
mystery it is that he did not give the Trade Union leaders a guarantee that the
present standard of living of every worker should be maintained. We hope
that in this latest message of the Prime Minister the spirit of peace may be

PREMIER'S COAL PROPOSALS.
Scheme Subject to Both Parties Accepting.
£3,000,000 SUBSIDY.
Suggested Temporary Wage Reductions.
The Prime Minister last night sent to the miners and to the owners proposals which
in his opinion form a reasonable and fair basis for a settlement of the mining dispute.
The proposals are as follow:
(1) In accordance with the recommendations of the Royal Commission, all practical
means for improving the organisation of the industry and increasing its efficiency shall in
adopted.
(2) The Government shall take the following immediate action :-
posals of the Commission regarding amalgamations, to provide for a welfare levy a
(a) Introduce and endeavour to pass this session Bills to give effect to the pr
royalty owners and to further the establishment of pit-head baths, to restrict recruitiva
in mines, to set up for the coal-mining industry a National Wages Board on the lines
the Railway Wages Board.
(b) Set up the proposed National Fuel and Power Council, which will cortar
representatives of Labour.
(c) Set up the proposed Wagon Committee.
(d) Appoint a committee to investigate the question of selling syndicate,
(e) Appoint a committee to examine the profit-sharing proposal of the Com
mission and family allowances.
(f) Prepare a scheme for the establishment of pit committees.
(g) Prepare plans for the assistance of men displaced from pits.
(h) Set up a committee on housing in colliery districts.

recommendations of the Commission, a full statement of the step proposed shall be all
(3) Coal Advisory Committee. Before any legislation is introduced, or committee
before the Coal Advisory Committee of the Secretary for Mines.
It shall also be the duty of the Advisory Committee to review from time to time the
progress made in giving effect to the recommendations of the Commission, and to make
recommendations on the subject.
In the event of any recommendations made by the committee not being adopted by
the Secretary for Mines, he shall lay them before Parliament, together with a statement
his reasons for not adopting them.
(4) Apart from any expenditure that may be necessary under 2 (g), the Government

yield 45s. per week or less for a full customary week.

(v) The Board shall issue its decision within three weeks.

MR. BALDWIN ON THE SITUATION.
Buses, Trams, and Tube Agreements.

RAILWAY TERMS.
In the House of Commons yesterday afternoon, Mr. Baldwin made a brief statement
on the situation.
With regard to the docks and certain forms of transport, he said negotiations were
still going on and pursuing their normal course.
Work was to be resumed on buses, trams and the underground railway system.
Agreement had been reached, but the terms were not yet available.
With regard to the railways, he had received a telephone message from Mr. J. H. Thomas,
who hoped that by the time he (the Premier) was making this statement a settlement
would be signed between the parties, which Mr. Thomas believed would be satisfactory
to all.
He then made his statement on the mines situation given elsewhere.
Mr. Ramsay MacDonald said that so long as they had the assurance that negotiations
were going on relating to the three important points, the best service that could be rendered
was to say as little as possible.
They were very glad to hear the Prime Minister's statement, and he wished to offer
one observation with reference. This was on the mines, and is reported elsewhere with
Baldwin's statement.

RAILWAY TERMS FOR RESTART.
Signed by Representatives of the Three Unions.
Terms for the resumption of work on the railways were reached yesterday afternoon
after a conference lasting several hours between representatives of the three unions and
the railway managers.
Pending further instructions railwaymen had been ordered to remain on strike, and
this order was obeyed.
The terms agreed upon were set out in the following agreement:--
(1) Those employees of the railway companies who have gone out on strike to be
taken back to work as soon as traffic officers and work can be found for them. The principle
to be followed in reinstating to be seniority in each grade at each station, depot, or office.
(2) The trades unions admit that in calling a strike they committed a wrongful act
against the companies, and agree that the companies do not by reinstatement surrender
their legal rights to claim damages arising out of the strike from strikers and others respon-
sible.
(3) The unions undertake (a) not again to instruct their members to strike without
to take any unauthorised action: (c) not to encourage supervisory employees in the special
class to take part in any strike.
(4) The companies intimate that, arising out of the strike it may be necessary to
remove certain persons to other positions, but no such persons' salaries or wages will be
reduced. Each company will notify the union within one week the names of men whom
they propose to transfer, and will afford each man an opportunity of having an advocate
to present his case to the General Manager.
(5) The settlement shall not extend to persons who have been guilty of violence or
intimidation.
Signed on behalf of the General Managers' Conference: Felix J. C. Pole, H. G. Burgess,
H. A. Walker, R. L. Wedgwood, R. H. Selbie.
On behalf of the Railway Unions: J. H. Thomas and C. T. Cramp (National Union of
Railwaymen), J. Bromley (Associated Society of Locomotive Engineers and Firemen),
A. G. Walkden (Railway Clerks' Association).
Mr. J. H. Thomas, in a statement to the Press at the conclusion of the Conference
after signing the agreement, said :-
"Having regard to all the circumstances I consider it an eminently satisfactory
settlement.
"When one considers the bitterness, the disorganisation and the difficulties surround-
ing the whole situation, I hope that the men will accept it in the spirit in which the com-
panies and the leaders signed the agreement, namely, a genuine desire to do all that is
humanly possible immediately to restart the wheels of industry."
Mr. Bromley, secretary of the Associated Society of Locomotive Engineers and Fire-
men, said :-
"Those who, like myself, know all the difficulties with which we were at first con-
fronted in negotiating for a settlement, will, I am sure, feel as I do, that finally a very
satisfactory arrangement has been arrived at.
"Naturally, when the first position of the railway companies following the end of the
General Strike was known, my members solidly refused to return to duty, and a similar
action was taken by the other unions.
"I feel now that my members generally will accept the position and work will be
resumed and carried on smoothly."
Mr. Walkden, secretary of the Railway Clerks' Association, said that although it had
taken many hours of very strenuous argument and persuasion before they could arrive at
the conclusions they had reached, he felt convinced that the settlement would prove
satisfactory.
He was grateful to the railway managers for the magnanimous spirit in which they
had concluded the discussion, and was equally grateful to the leaders and members of the
other two unions for the spirit in which they had co-operated in helping to bring about
this settlement.—British Worker, 15th May, 1926.

SCOTTISH TRADES UNION CONGRESS.
Delegate's Report.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
On behalf of the Scottish Section of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Opera
tives, 1, along with our brother member, Mr. J. P. Reid, of Arbroath, attended the 20th
Annual Conference of the Scottish Trades Union Congress, held in the Wesleyan Central
Halls, Inverness, on 21st, 22nd, 23rd and 24th April, 1920.
In the report of the Scottish Trades Union Congress General Council, a scheme was
outlined, arising out of a remit by the 1925 Congress, for co-ordinating and increasing the
Trade Union movement. The General Council's scheme, submitted after consideration,
was to form Local and County Trade Union Committees in addition to those Trade and
Labour Councils already existing. Notwithstanding that existing Trade and Labour
Councils have already Industrial Committees as well as Political Committees, a lengthy
discussion took place on this question, in the course of which the Secretary stated that
most of the existing Industrial Committees were so only, on paper, as the Council never
received any replies, even to their letters of enquiry. Ultimately a vote was taken on this
question, and it was decided by 144 votes for Council's scheme to 30 against, to adopt
Council's scheme and set up Trade Union Committees.
As our members would read in the Press, there was a resolution from the Glasgow
Trades and Labour Council which was of a somewhat important nature, namely, that a
workers' defence corps should be formed. Some of the Press gave more publicity to this
resolution than perhaps was to the best interests of the Trade Union movement. The
resolution was defeated by a large majority.
A resolution was passed that the Congress demand the immediate ratification of the
Washington Convention by the British Government stabilising the eight-hour day and
making adequate provision however for those workers now enjoying conditions better
than the minimum conditions which the Convention prescribes. The Congress consider
that if this measure is adopted by Great Britain it will have the effect of stimulation to
other Governments.
An emergency resolution was passed unanimously that the Congress co-operate and
utterly endorse the fight of the Miner at this time, and calls upon all Trade Unions to give
their support in the Miners' cause.
The General Council was instructed by Congress to co-operate with Trades Councils
and affiliated Unions to keep the question of unemployment prominently before the
country, and call upon the Government to carry out National schemes of work such as
roads, bridges, &c., to relieve unemployment and to insist upon Trades and Labour Councils
having representation upon local employment committees, as they are in the position to
represent many small unions not now represented thereon.
I would like to emphasise the last paragraph, personally, and draw the attention of
our own branches to the importance of having representation on Local Employment
Committees and also co-option on Rota Committees. I have taken a special interest in
this question of Labour Exchange Committees, and would advise all our branches to apply
for representation on same, which would be to their own interests and also in the interest
of their fellow workers and the unemployed generally, as we as trade unionists must fight
and fight hard for justice (at least) in these Committees, and I would suggest when branches
are sending representatives to above Committees they take care to send men who can get
away from work when required for Rota work without endangering their positions.
A resolution was passed referring to the General Council the question of Sick, Un-
employment, Compensation, Death Insurance, Pensions for Widows and Orphans, and
Old Age Pensions, to formulate a scheme of State Insurance which will adequately insure
the workers against Sickness, Unemployment, Accident and Death, and to press upon the
Government and the Labour Party the necessity of Pensions for Widows and Orphans and
Old Age Pensions being granted on a non-contributory basis. Many other important
measures were discussed and the Conference was most successful, and most magnificently
conducted, and I am sure will be the means of further advancing the Trade Union cause.
Yours in Unity,
GEORGE HANDLEY, 16084.

Once more Bata, in Czecho Slovakia.

International Boot
PRAGUE,
11th February, 1926.
In reply to your letter from 29th October, 1925, we have to inform you that
conditions of employment existing at the firm Bata were thoroughly examined by the
competent authorities. Several times the workers' organisations lodged complaints
about the infringement of the 48-hour week and the weekly rest on Sundays. The
complaints were partly well founded and the inconveniences stated, were caused in the
main by the rapid development of the factory for which the existing buildings did not
suffice any more. For these reasons several complaints had to be rejected, especially
when concerning works being of urgent need, and moreover of temporary character were
exempted from the legal prescriptions relating to working hours and weekly rest.
Where, indeed, infringements were stated, the competent authorities rigorously
intervened, and Bata was considerably fined.
workers' organisations exercised at the same time, brought it about that the condition
This action of the competent authorities and also the influence of the respective
at that factory became altered, especially the observance of the legal working hours
secured, owing to the insistence of the trade inspector, who urged upon the factory to stop
the electric machines after eight hours. Night-work was stopped too, so far as it did not
concern exemptions. As to Sunday work, the trade inspector pays strict attention to
that; in case that there are concerned exemptions, the workers employed get their weekly
rest during the week.
In regard to these statements one can expect that the complaints about inconveniences
at the factory cease and that the legal prescriptions are observed in the future.
MINISTER:
SIGNATURE.
In connection with this question, COMRADE SRB, Secretary of the Czech Boot and Sho
Operatives' Union, wrote the following :-
As to Bata, it is true that the Ministry rigorously intervened. Bata has been con-
siderably fined several times, and the legal working time is not surpassed for the time being.
Whether that be the consequence of the ministerial intervention, is difficult to state,
because Bata has few orders. It is true, too, that the trade inspector has strict command
to pay attention to the severe observation of the legal working hours. Bata has built
a good deal during the past two years. In autumn, when he had many orders he tried
to make work two shifts. He pointed out he was unable to employ more workers before
the new buildings were finished. Owing to our intervention the Ministry did not give
its permission and Bata was forced to give orders to other factories. There are a good
many small firms willing to carry out orders that Bata is unable to do.
In our Journal we have published already 13 articles about Bata that caused much
sensation and called the attention of the authorities to that firm. Probably more attention
will be paid to it now.

FROM THE NATIONAL UNIONS.
DENMARK, BOOT AND SHOE OPERATIVES.-Conditions continue to be slack. Despite
the beginning of the season we have 1,075 members unemployed, being a percentage of 23.
GERMANY. REVISION OF THE AGREEMENT FOR THE BOOT AND SHOE INDUSTRY.-
The Joint Conference between the Employers' and Workers' Federations set to revise the
Agreement, having failed, the Ministry of Labour intervened to establish the Economic
Peace in the Boot and Shoe Industry.
As far as our Industry is concerned it is the first time that any State Arbitration
Board tried to establish an understanding; not only in wage matters but to bring about
the revision of an Agreement as a whole. That the struggle against the employers' demands
was hard, is clearly shown from the fact, that the proceedings at the Arbitration Board
took six days. The Umpire seemed to be deeply impressed by the stereotyped phrases
of the employers. Conditions in our industry are very bad, though our representatives
could prove by decisive documents that the wages and charges of social insurance influence
the least the level of prices. From these circumstances it resulted that the workers'
demands could not thoroughly be realised. Nevertheless we were able to modify several
employers' demands in favour of the workers.
The advantages we secured concern piecework prices—the agreement interdicts to
apply the premium system in connection with this matter—apprenticeship and time wage
rates for particularly skilled workers. Other favourable terms refer to the passing from
piecework to time work, to the interdiction to reduce the piecework prices and time wage
rates, to the regulation of wages at the reopening of factories closed down.
As to disadvantages, contained by the award, we have to register the permission for
the manufacturers to have overtime worked on Saturdays, whenever it depends upon the
agreement of the factory council.
Sick indemnity is limited to cases of sickness lasting more than 12 days. The minimum
wage rates for girls are settled at 70 per cent. of the rates for males. This must soon be
repaired. The paid holidays have been reduced to 6 days instead of 7.
The agreement will remain in operation until 31st March, 1927.
The General Council of the Union immediately assembled to discuss the award.
They were of the unanimous opinion that the disadvantages contained were of a serious
character. On the other hand they had to put the question—“ What will happen if the
agreement is rejected "? This question was thoroughly considered too. It is no secret
that the employers occupy the more favourable position at present. If the agreement be
rejected, continual conflicts would occur. Another important point of view was the fact
that we are not bound to the wage rates settled, on the contrary we are able to put wage
demands at opportune times.
With the exception of three colleagues the General Council finally decided to adopt
the award.
The attitude of the Manufacturers—The big and leading Federations of Manufacturers
of the boot and shoe industry also adopted the Award.

NORWAY.

Conditions in the Boot and Shoe Industry, from Skotoiarbeideren,
February, 1926.
Unemployment is still widespread and many factories have closed down, at the others
much short time is worked (3 or 4 days), a few are working full time.
About 35 per cent. of our members are wholly unemployed and little hope of improvement.
Nobody can buy, neither people nor merchants. Everybody is waiting for the enormous
decline of prices in consequence of the revision of agreements.

293

But we fear that this is a false calculation. Whenever a reduction of wage rates may
be passed, this will not influence the prices of footwear. The wages play a small part as
to the settling of prices. If the prices of footwear become lower, the prices of raw materials
and the profit of commerces have to be reduced first. That is the chief point.

The Employers Prepare the Attack, from Skotoiarbeideren, March, 1926.
The manufacturers have given notice to terminate the agreement for the boot and
shoe industry at 1st April. Even the non-federated manufacturers and the masters of
hand-sewing shops have done so.
The employers' federation invited us to hold a joint Conference on Friday, 5th March.
We immediately stated that there was no hope for a good result. The employers' demands
were too arrogant. The joint Conference was broken off at the first meeting.

On 10th March the State Umpire interdicted to withdraw from work and at the same
time began his activity to settle the matter. The first meeting took place on the 11th
March. The Award has not yet been made.
The North Secretariat for the boot and shoe industry has the intention to call a
Conference during the month to consider this conflict.
In connection with this matter Comrade Gundersen states:-
OSLO,
9th March, 1926.

Conditions show a slight improvement. At the time being the percentage
unemployed is approximately 30.
However, it seems that there will be coming a serious conflict in Norway. The
manufacturers have given notice to terminate the agreements among those for the boot
and shoe industry. We must expect every day that the manufacturers announce the
lockout for the 31st March. Though the index figure of cost of living declined by 15
per cent. only, the employers demand a reduction of wages by 25 per cent., moreover to
exclude the two youngest groups of boys and girls from the agreement and to reduce the
holidays to 8 working days instead of 12. We held a joint Conference, but the employers
insisted upon their demands, and it was broken off. Now the State Arbitration Board
has intervened. If any lockout occurs, it will concern about 2,000 of the 2,541 membes
of the Union.
While I am writing this, I received the news that 2,000 of our members have been
given notice to be discharged. But I still hope that we will succeed in settling an agree-
ment to avoid the conflict. Failing in so doing we must expect a serious conflict and shall
be compelled to ask for help at the International.
The Unemployment strongly engaged our unemployment fund. In January and
February we paid altogether 150,000 kr.
CZECHO-SLOVAKIA.
Conditions in the Leather Industry
Continue to be very slack. There are a few orders at the tanners and the boot and
shoe operatives. Short time is widespread. Only the factories producing coloured shoes
are better employed. Of the tawers, too, a good deal are unemployed, so that we may
have to pay large sums in benefits.
This period of unemployment caused to the Union a loss of 600 members. But the
Communist Unions, too, lost a good many of their members.
In the Saddlers' trade conditions are terrible. The saddlers are disappearing more
and more. It is difficult for them to pass over to other departments of the leather industry,
because in several of them conditions are slack too. The bagmakers only enjoy rather
good conditions and have very few unemployed.
As to the belt-gearing industry, many difficulties are to be surmounted. The
employers have given notice to terminate the agreement, intend to suppress the paid
holidays and to reduce the wages. Certainly a strike will occur. Similar attempts have
been made in the auto industry, up till now in vain, but we have to expect others. In
Spring, conditions will probably improve somewhat, because the military authorities will
place orders. But in general small shops will receive same, situated in country districts,.
so that the workers in the cities do not profit much.

GERMANY.
Unemployment in February, 1926.
After an inquiry made by the Allgemainen Deutschen Gewerkshaftsbund, comprising
3,296,714 organised workers, there were 728,008 members unemployed, or 21.1 per cent.,
and 704,085, or 21.4 per cent. working short time.
Unemployment in the boot and shoe and leather industry largely surpassed the
average.
Leather Workers 23.2 per cent. unemployed.
46.7 working short time.
Saddlers 36.4 unemployed.
31.0 working short time.
Boot and Shoe 40.3 unemployed.
43.1 working short time.
From these figures it follows that the boot and shoe industry is most heavily involved
by this crisis. In March, no improvement could be registered either, so that we must
expect a further duration.
Slight Decline of Unemployment.
The number of workpeople unemployed did not change much towards the end of
February. The number of male workers unemployed decreased by 22,000 as compared
with the 15th February, 1926, and that of females increased by 20,000 approximately.
The total number of workpeople unemployed was 2,056,807 on 1st March, as compared
with 2,058,392 on the 15th February, being a decrease of 1 per cent.
Act on Workers' Holidays.
FRANCE.
The Minister of Labour submitted to the Chambre des Deputes a Bill relating to paid
holidays for workers. In the statement of reasons that heads the Bill it is indicated that
holidstate and Municipal functionnaries are entitled to have yearly holidays. As well,
the employees in private undertakings have secured yearly holidays by special agreement,
As to the workers it is absolutely necessary to grant to them a certain period of holidays
in addition to the daily free time and the weekly rest, to maintain and to strengthen
their productiveness. For these reasons the workers must be granted yearly holidays
like the State functionnaries and the private employees.
The Bill provides for at the least 8 holidays after one year's service, a fortnight at
least after two years. The period of holidays is to be increased at factories of a dangerous
and insalubrious character, as well as for boys and girls under 18 years of age. The holidays.
are not redeemable.
Increase of Cost of Living.
The following figures show the increase of the index figure of cost of living in 1925
till January, 1926. These figures base on the retail prices of 13 different articles, available
in Paris—(Bread, Meat, Bacon, Butter, Eggs, Milk, Cheese, Potatoes, Beans, Sugar,
Petroleum, Oil and Brandy).

ITALY.
The Reorganisation of the Italian Trade Union Movement.
(I.F.T.U.) -In view of the difficult position of the Italian Unions brought about by
Mussolini's tyrannical restrictions, our Italian comrades are pursuing a policy of saving
what they can. They have not attempted to pit themselves against the inevitable, but
are doing everything to stick to their principles.
One outcome of this policy has been the formation of a mixed Trade Union Federation
for all those trades the membership of which is small. The object of this new Federation
is to facilitate the recruitment of all the supporters of the Italian Trade Union Centre.
It is directing its attention to isolated workers workers who are organised locally again
in mixed organisations and National Trades or industrial unions which have lost their
independency. The organisation is to give moral and financial support to the members,
who have to pay a total subscription of 20 lire.
WAGES IN POOR DISTRICTS.
Writing to the Editor of the Shoe and Leather News, on the 24th April, 1926, a Mr. H.
Williams, 47 South Street, Liverpool, says-
"The article, 'Wages in Poor Districts,' by Mr. H. Crabb, contains the same amount
of eyewash as usual. He says I am responsible for a proposal for a reduction of wages of
10 per cent. all round. He omits the vital part of my proposition, i.e., the reduction of the
minimum rate by 10 per cent.
. . I ask Mr. Crabb seriously, would it not be better for those men to be employed
at 455. per week, than to live on the 'dole' or the guardians ? I commend his statement to
the consideration of the Minister of Labour, as he practically admits these men could be
working, only that the minimum is too high.
... One thing Mr. Crabb has done by his article. He has made many of us believe
that those who are supposed to represent the employers on the Trade Board, are represent-
ing the men, and should be moved at once. Mr. Crabb should study the miners' position,
their minimum is 7s. 6d. per day, and I think that should be the minimum for the boot
repairer."
IT IS EVIDENT FROM THE ABOVE, THAT THE WRITER OF THE
LETTER DESIRES TO BRING DOWN THE MINIMUM RATES OF PAY FOR A
BOOT REPAIRER TO A POINT WHICH WOULD MAKE WAGES BELOW THE
STANDARD OF 1914. IT IS THEREFORE AS WELL THAT MEMBERS SHOULD
KNOW THERE ARE SOME REPRESENTATIVES BELONGING TO THE BOOT
AND SHOE INDUSTRY WHO WISH TO DEPRESS WAGES TO A POINT AT WHICH
IT WOULD MEAN A MERE EXISTENCE.-E.L.P., G.S.].
APPRECIATION FOR WORK DONE.
A successful smoking concert organised by the members of the local branches of the
Operatives' Union was held on the 4th inst. at the Trades Hall, Upper Fountaine Street,
Leeds. Councillor A. J. Dobbs occupied the chair. Mr. George Abbott, one of the oldest
members of the branch committee, handed a cheque for £142 to Mr. Joseph Wescoe, who,
until his recent retirement, had been a branch secretary for 39 years. The sum was
collected by the various branches of the Union, and was supplemented by a contribution
from the National Council of the Union.-Shoe and Leather Record, 7, 14, 21 May, 1926.

STANDING ORDERS.
BIENNIAL MEETINGS.
RULE 80.- Biennial Meetings of the Conference shall be held on Whit
Monday and subsequent days.
TIME OF CONFERENCE MEETING.
RULE 81.-On the first day of Conference the Delegates shall assemble at a
place provided for the purpose, at Eleven o'clock a.m. prompt,
and shall proceed to the election of Two Tellers, and shall also
consider the President's Address and Council's Report; after which
the Conference shall adjourn at 12.30 p.m. and re-assemble at 2 p.m.
and proceed with the business of the Conference and adjourn at
5 p.m. On Tuesday and each succeeding day, the time of meeting
shall be 9.30 a.m., adjourn at 12.30 p.m., re-assemble at 2 p.m., and
adjourn for the day at 5 p.m.
DELEGATES' QUALIFICATION.
RULE 82.-The Conference shall consist of Delegates who have been elected
in accordance with General Rules 71 and 77, which read as follows:
"Delegates shall be elected in accordance with the number of Financial
Members returned in the December Report previous to the date on which the
Conference is to be held. All Permanent Officials shall attend the Conferences
by virtue of their office, over and above the maximum of representation. The
basis of representation for delegates shall be one delegate for every 1,000
financial members, with a minimum representation of not less than fifty
delegates (one-third to form a quorum.)"
"The latest date for sending in amendment and additions to Rules, or
Standing Orders of Conference, shall be February 15th, in the year in which
the Conference is due to be held, and they shall be published in the February
Monthly Report. Nominations for delegates shall be taken on the February
Monthly Meeting Night, and voting for same on the March Monthly Meeting
Night."
The Council to attend by virtue of their office.
PRESIDENT OF CONFERENCE.
RULE 83.- The President of the Union, by virtue of his office, takes the chair
at all Conferences.
STANDING ORDERS COMMITTEE.
RULE 84.-A committee of five persons shall be elected from the Delegates of
the Conference, whose duty it shall be to examine the Delegates'
Credentials, and report thereon. They shall also be at the service of
the Conference to consider any questions or matter that may be
relegated to it with a view to reporting thereon during the sitting of
Conference. For such extra services they shall receive additional
pay, to the amount of 10s. each.

PROPOSED NEW RULES, ALTERATIONS, OR
AMENDMENTS TO RULES.
THE COUNCIL.
SUPERANNUATION FUND.
1. The Fund shall be held in Trust by the Management Committee (Execu-
tive Council of the Union) for Superannuation purposes, and shall be adminis-
tered in accordance with the following rules:
The objects of this Fund are to provide a Superannuation allowance to
permanent (full time) officials and clerks of the Union or branches, and a
payment to the dependents or representatives of a deceased official or clerk,
according to the scale set forth in these rules.
The Fund shall be used for no other purpose.
Those eligible to participate in its benefits shall be permanent officials and
clerks of the Union and branches of 21 years of age and upwards.
Contributions to the Fund shall be compulsory by all permanent officials
and clerks over 21 years of age.
Retirement Conditions.
2. Where an official or clerk over 21 years of age with over ten years'
service has retired from service on account of inability to efficiently perform
his duties owing to infirmity or ill-health, and under 60 years of age, he shall
receive pay on the scale of Stuperannuation named in these Rules subject to
the discretion of the Management Committee, who shall have power to review
such cases from time to time. An official or clerk shall not be entitled to
claim Superannuation on the grounds of age alone until he has attained the age
of 60 years, but he must compulsorily retire at 65 years of age.
tion.
No superannuated official or clerk shall accept office with a rival organisa-
Scale and Basis of Payment.
3. Superannuation benefit shall be paid to a permanent official or clerk
on the undermentioned salary basis :-
Years of Service.
10 years
Fixed Benefits.
35 per cent.
plus I per cent. for each additional year's completed service, the salary at the
time of retirement being the determining factor for the amount of pension.
Contributions and Refund of Same.
4. The rate of contribution shall be 3 per cent. of wages received from
National officers and Central office clerks, and 3 per cent. from Central Funds;
3 per cent. from Branch officials and Branch clerks, and 3 per cent. from Branch
funds. When an official or clerk has been superannuated he shall cease to
contribute to the Fund.
5. An official or clerk upon resigning, or his services being dispensed with,
or failing to secure re-election, shall (in cases where there is no title to a pension)
have refunded to him all contributions paid by him to the Fund plus 4 per cent.
on the total amount due to him when leaving the service of the Union. A
similar refund shall be made to the dependents or legal representatives of any
official or clerk who dies before completing ten years' service.

TO RULES.
PROPOSED NEW RULES, ALTERATIONS, OR AMENDMENTS
Inasmuch as under Regulation 8 of the Rules made by the Commissioners
of Inland Revenue pursuant to their powers under Section 32 (4) of the Finance
Act, 1921, the Trustees of the Superannuation Fund are liable to account to
the Commissioners for Income Tax at one-third the standard rate in force at
the time of refund on all contributions (with any interest additions thereto)
returned to members of the Fund during the life-time of the members, a
deduction shall be made from contributions returned to a member during his
life-time, and such deduction shall be at the rate of one-third the standard
rate of Income Tax in force for the year in which the repayment is made.
Any official or clerk dismissed for dishonesty shall have no claim on the
Fund whatever.
Payment on Death.
6. In the case of death of an official or clerk before participating in the
Superannuation Fund, provided that he has from 10 to 15 years' service, the
dependents or family of such an official shall be entitled to ONE YEAR'S super-
annuation allowance; where his services exceed 15 years and under 20 years,
18 months' allowance shall be paid, and where the service exceeds 20 years,
the dependents shall be paid TWO YEARS' allowance in accordance with the
scale, or a refund may be made as named in clause 5, whichever sum is the
greater.
Where an official or clerk has been superannuated and dies before receiving
two years' allowance, the Management Committee shall grant the dependents
or family the balance of two years' superannuation allowance according to
scale.
This shall be considered a final payment in such cases.
An official or clerk entitled to benefit from the Fund can nominate any
person to receive such sum as may be granted in the case of death. In the
event of there being no dependents, the Management Committee shall grant
such sum as will cover all necessary funeral expenses.
General.
7. The Union shall guarantee the benefits of the scheme.
Retirement for the purposes of claiming superannuation benefit shall be
suspended until 1st January, 1930, but in the case of those 65 years of age
and over at the commencement of the scheme, it shall be optional for them to
retire on 1st January, 1927. In such cases they shall be deemed to have
completed not less than ten years' service with the Union.
Payment of contributions to the scheme shall be payable from 4th Septem-
ber, 1926.
8. In the event of a permanent officer being returned to Parliament he
shall continue to pay contributions at the same rate as were paid before being
returned to Parliament.
9. The Fund shall be controlled by a Management Committee consisting
of the Executive Council of the Union.
10. If the Union shall be dissolved or amalgamated with any other Union,
the Trusts constituted by these presents may, subject as hereinafter provided,
thereupon determine. Otherwise the said Trusts shall continue during the
life of the survivor of the issue now living of her late Majesty Queen Victoria,
and 21 years after the death of such survivor and such further period, if any,

**42**

**EXISTING RULES.**

**Duties and Powers of Branches and Branch Executives.**
*RULE 153.* Economic and Industrial History Classes may be formed by any branch whose members express the desire for the same.

**4. CONDITIONS OF MEMBERSHIP.**
*RULE 32.* No person shall be admitted into the Union who is physically unable to follow his employment.
*RULE 38.* Any member who has paid 26 weeks' continuous contributions, and has served a probation of 26 weeks from the date of his joining a branch of this Union, shall be returned to the Council as a financial member, and be entitled to trade benefits. Should he, however, not be clear upon the books at the time he has paid 26 weeks' contributions but does not owe more than 8 weeks' contributions, fines and levies combined, he shall also be returned to the Council, and be entitled to trade benefits. Such members shall serve a further 26 weeks' probation, and pay a further 26 weeks' contributions from the date of their registration with the Union, TO ENTITLE THEM TO OUT-OF-WORK BENEFIT, sick pay and funeral benefit, the payment of their out-of-work contributions if Rule 228 is complied with. All members must have paid 52 weeks' contributions before becoming entitled to out of work, sick, and funeral benefits. If the debt, including fines and levies during the latter probationary period should exceed 8 weeks, the member shall serve four weeks' probation from the date of reducing his debt down to 8 weeks, before becoming entitled to benefit. If, however, the arrears during such probationary period exceed thirteen weeks including fines and levies, the period before which benefit can be obtained shall be in accordance with Rules 42 and 169. Youths and females after they commence to pay full contributions serve half probation only before receiving full benefits (that is, 13 weeks for trade, and 26 weeks for out of work, sick, and funeral benefit); always providing that to be entitled to this preferential treatment youths and females must have been paying members to the Union for at least two years previous to claiming such preference.
*RULE 39.*-A branch must belong to the Union twenty-six weeks to be entitled to trade benefits, and fifty-two weeks before it can become entitled to out of work, sick, and funeral benefits, or make application for an advance of wages to be voted upon by the Union.

**Branch Secretaries.**
*RULE 302.*-Failing to send a quarterly balance sheet to the General Secretary to be fined 2s 6d.

EXISTING RULES.
RULE 137. Branches shall have power to invest their branch funds in the
shares of Co-operative Productive Societies, always providing that
not less than 5s. per member shall be left in hand. They shall also
have power to levy their members one penny per week for such
purposes.
Bond Notes.
RULE 206.-Any member who has belonged to the Union thirteen weeks
and is clear on the books, shall be entitled to a Bond Note of
and any branch wishing to give Bond Notes of greater amount or
additional Bonds, or Bonds to members who have not belonged to
the Union thirteen weeks, can do so, but on their own responsibility
RULE 207.-If a member has made away with work, and the Union has made
it good, all expenses so incurred shall be placed as a book debt against
such member, who must repay it, serve twenty-six weeks' probation
and be clear on the books before becoming entitled to trade or sick
benefits, the probation to date from the time he makes his first pay-
ment towards the book debt. The Council shall have power (on the
application of the branch) to mitigate the amount as they may deem
fit.
RULE 208.-The Union to be at the cost of prosecution under this law, and
no Bond Notes to be issued but those supplied by the Council.
RULE 209. In all cases where the parties so entrusted should abscond with
the work, or any portion thereof, the employer must make application
for them at their addresses, and should the employer fail to recover
the property he must be prepared to prosecute or the Union will
not indemnify him.
RULE 210.-All Bond Notes to be returned by the members to the Secretary
who issued them, or a note from the employer to show that all the
work has been finished up properly.
RULE 211.-The Union will not be answerable to employers for any work
kept out above fourteen days, unless the said employer notifies the
same within fourteen days of that date.
