Here is the extracted text from the image:
their interests.
117
collecting Agencies so far as contributions are concerned. Many
opportunities occur, however, in which Approved Society officials
can be of service in pointing out to applicants the provisions made in
Under the provisions of the Act Insured persons
cease to pay contributions both for Health Insurance and Pensions, on
reaching the age of 65, but the Employer continues payment of the
WHOLE of the Pensions Contribution. This has necessitated an
amendment of the Health Insurance Act. In accordance with this
provision an adjustment of one penny per week has been made in the
Health Insurance contribution, seeing that Health Insurance liability
ceases at the age of 65 instead of 70, as hitherto. Medical benefit,
however, continues under the same conditions as previously. The
Council desires to emphasise the importance of members keeping in
touch with their Agents, and the Central Office, either when unemployed
or sick. and receiving no benefit. The records of the Society are the
only means of reference when pensions are claimed, and vexatious
delay in receiving Pensions may be caused by members failing to
acquaint the Society of their whereabouts. A member having 104
contributions to his credit, and having been in Insurance for the
prescribed periods under the Act, remains entitled to benefits under
the Pensions Act, even though unemployed, or incapacitated, provided
the Society is notified of his position and is thus able to credit the
necessary contributions.
(9) Schedule V. shows an analysis of members ages. Men 40 years
and under number 13,786; Women 7,638. Men 41 and over number
11,149; Women 720. The average age of men is 38.39-that of women
being 26.45. An increase of three years is shown in the average age of
men, since the census taken eleven years ago. This, notwithstanding the
fact that upwards of 13,000 new members have joined the Society
at 16 years of age during the interval. This factor has to be borne in
mind in considering the question of excessive benefit payment, seeing
that the higher average of age carries greater sickness risks.
(10) In conclusion, the Council desires to thank all Agents and
Members for their loyalty to the Society in the past, and expresses the
hope of increased membership and greater usefulness in the future.
General President.

ALD. A. HILL (Leicester No. 2) proposed Item 10:-
Leicester No. 2.-Rule 2, Section 1.—Delete "But he must compulsorily retire
at 65 years of age."
Some men at 65 years of age are worth their money and their place in the world. Another
reason why I think the position should be considered is because some people think it does
not matter how much income you have, you will get an old age pension at 65. If I under-
stand the Act properly no pension will be paid to non-contributors until the age of 70 is
reached, that is so far as the means clause is concerned. I know in municipal offices,
government departments and teaching profession, people are growing up, and they are
looking out for preferment. There is no analogy between our position and those I have
named, because those people have a job for life, whereas our officers have to retire every
so often. I am not complaining, because generally speaking our officers are re-elected.
A man may be smart and clever in some directions which would take him to the top of the
teaching profession, but unless you have some personality you cannot get a trade union
official position. I think 70 years of age is sufficiently early enough to compulsorily retire
any officer. There will be a number of our present officials who will be put in a tight
position if they have to go before, and I ask you to support this resolution.
Mr. T. W. LEWIS (Northampton) seconded the resolution. To compel a man to

provision should be made. There are few officers that have been with us ten years who
could not have bettered their position. (Cries of "Question.") I have had many offers
and so have others, but we prefer to stay with those for whom we have spent our lives.
A little while ago a man was retired in the trade union world on £300 a year. His successor
killed himself with work: the present holder of the position is not over strong. We have
Charlie Harper, of Wolverhampton, and it will be a long time before he desired to retire.
A compulsory retirement of men because you have not courage enough to tell them they
are incompetent is not straight. Will Thorne could have had a pension years ago, but he
goes on with his work. I shall support Mr. Hill.
Mr. F. C. JEX (Norwich): I rise to speak against the amendment. You cannot

HERR J. SIMON said: I take this opportunity of saying how I appreciate the
good organisation of trade unions due to better improvement. The English workers
have strong phases in their constitution. There have been frightful conditions in Textile
Industries, where many children have been employed. The British workers have succeeded
in getting their places; they have been recognised by the employers and can arrange
their agreements by arbitration. The German constitution is one of the most free in the
world on paper only. You have the democratic idea; the German democratic idea
is not put into practice, but Germany is ruled by capitalists. Mr. Richards stated there
must be all sorts of reforms secured, which can be done through Parliament. The Com-
munists tried to establish Governments in several countries which will make all sorts of
trouble. It is impossible for German people to live without raw materials and food from
abroad, and the Communists tried to prevent it. If the Socialist Party had tried in 1918
to socialise Germany, we should not have succeeded, because the Government would not
allow it. The Russians hate the Germans because Germany will have nothing to do
with them. I am persuaded that the Germans will continue to repulse all attacks
by the Communists. I stayed in Norwich in 1912 and have been several times,
and I admire the discipline shown by English workers, which is due to the fact that they
live in a much more salubrious atmosphere. We are very sorry to have to go away; we are
satisfied you are prepared to stand with the German workers. I trust the good feelings
will grow and that the International will grow also, and liberty for all be realised. The
next International Congress will be held in England in 1927. (Applause.)

NATIONAL CONFERENCE (SEPTEMBER, 1924) AGREEMENT.
CLAUSE 8.
The General Purposes Committee of the Federation met on Thursday, 27th May,
and after careful consideration of the invited views of local associations, it was agreed
that Clause 8 of the National Conference (September, 1924) Agreement should become
operative on the first full pay day in June, viz., 9th, 10th or 11th, in accordance with
the joint circular letter issued to manufacturers bearing your signature and mine,
copy of which I enclose for your reference.

Item 48 was proposed by Mr. W. WYMAN (Wellingborough):
Wellingborough. The Council shall have power to lend money upon mortgage
to local branches, who desire to purchase their own offices.

Mr. T. RABBITT (Wellingborough) seconded.
Mr. A. MASON (London Metro.): I hope this will be passed to enable the London
office to borrow money to build offices; at present we are in a private house and have
cramped quarters.
Mr. T. VALLANCE (Leicester No. 2): If this resolution is adopted what would

THE CHAIRMAN: We invest our money in Corporation Loans. We invest the
money for the benefit of other people, but not for our own. We know the position of
Wellingborough. Metro. is awkwardly placed. Just as the Council loan money, and before
doing so make enquiries, they would make enquiries before lending money to branches.
We are not prepared to build palaces. I only know of one branch likely to make early
application, and that is the London Metro. Wellingborough got out of their difficulty
by the kindness of the Higham and Rushden Branch. For the welfare of the Union
I think this should be carried, as our branches are not likely to peter out. You could
leave the matter in the hands of the Council.

attention to the bad conditions in Kingswood, due to outdoor labour.
not been idle in endeavouring to get manufacturers to provide workshops, a large propor-
tion still work outdoors. There are about ten per cent. outdoor workers in our area.
I thought if this Conference expressed their approval of our request we feel the Council
will be enabled to bring their influence to bear upon the Manufacturers' Federation, which
is also a powerful influence. There is a tendency for manufacturers to leave the Federa-
tion in our district and we want to try and stop it.
Mr. J. MANNERS (Council Member) seconded.
THE GENERAL SECRETARY: Mr. Randall occupies a responsible public position
I should like to ask him whether he gets any assistance from the Medical Officer. We have
been able to get much assistance from medical men generally.
THE CHAIRMAN: The Trade Board sent a deputation to the Home Secretary.
What we want is every place used as a workshop to come under the Factory Act. One
member of the deputation who went with us admitted he had never been asked to fill up
the proper schedule for three years giving the number of outworkers he employed.
Mr. A. G. RANDALL (Kingswood): Every assistance is rendered by our Medical

THE CHAIRMAN: Yes.
Mr. D. MCCARTHY (Organiser): The organisers have called attention to this
matter from time to time, because of the state of some factories, and we have been able

Mr. J. MANNERS (Council Member): The great difficulty in Kingswood is to
get the full conditions established. No one who knows anything of our district will forget
that we produced heavy grade footwear which was made outdoors. Whilst we have a
few manufacturers who have built factories, many have the old domestic system. Whilst
this system prevails, there is always suspicions that conditions are not carried out. This
adds to our difficulties. We have instances where employers have offered work at a certain
price; when refused, the employer says Mr. So-and-so is doing it. Upon investigation
we find no truth in the statement. We have had a slump for four years. The astonishing
thing is that we have been able to hold on as well as we have done. We hope to abolish
the outdoor system, and sweep away half the so-called factories in the district and have
up-to-date factories erected in their places.
The resolution was unanimously adopted.

and carry out the decisions of the Trades Union Congress and National
Labour Party."

I should like you to know we have many Labour M.P.'s drawn from trade unions. If our
members select national officers, and they get elected to Parliament, it should be the duty
of the Executive Council to provide them with clerical assistance to allow them to go to
Parliament.

Mr. W. LANGLEY (Higham and Rushden) seconded.
Mr. W. R. SMITH (Organiser): I feel this Conference should know what they are
doing before passing this resolution. Parliament is a full time job if a man does his job
properly. So far as our Union is concerned they look after their officials all right, and I
do not see any necessity for a change of rule. More and more time-if Parliament is going
to serve the people-must be given to the work, and more calls will be made upon men in
Parliament. If during the recess the Union wanted the services of one of its M.P.'s,
they can address either political or industrial meetings. I am fully persuaded that it is
not practical for one officer to hold too many positions. I do not think any Parliamentary
representative should hold two positions.

Mr. A. CROUCH: Why not?

Mr. W. R. SMITH (Organiser): If so, then one of your representatives would be
having £800 a year and I ask, do you consider it is fair?

THE CHAIRMAN: When I was in the House of Commons I was amongst the first
seventeen members for four years' attendance. One could run for the L.C.C., accept a
J.P.-ship, go on the London Board of Guardians, and you would not object. I am a
London resident, and a London voter, so could stand for any of those positions. You allow
members to hold several positions, even if you are M.P. This objection only applies to
permanent officials. I know the Labour Whip said you should attend to your duties.
We have members of Parliament anxious to take part in our work, simply because it is
convenient. There has never been a General President or General Secretary who has been
removed from his position, because the big thing is the lack of security of employment,
and I am glad we have now got over that.

Our local officers go on to the councils and we should let the general officers have this chance

Item 94.
Norwich. - Delete Items A, B, C, and D of Resolution 5, as follows:-
a. No board shall require an employer to employ any particular workman,
or a workman to work for any particular employer, or shall entertain
any questions relating to such matters except for the purpose of enabling
a workman to clear his character.
b. No board shall claim jurisdiction over the conditions and terms of em-
ployment of workpeople outside its district, provided that no actual
work shall be sent out of a district which has been the subject of an award
in that district.
c. No board shall interfere with the right of an employer to make reasonable
regulations for timekeeping, and the preservation of order in his factory
or workshop.
d. No board shall put restrictions on the introduction of machinery, or the
output therefrom, or on the adoption of day or piecework wages by an
employer in cases in which both systems have been sanctioned, subject
to the conditions prescribed in resolutions 2 and 3. No question referred
to in sub-sections a, b, c, and d shall be made a matter of dispute by
the Union.

Mr. F. C. JEX (Norwich): The Terms of Settlement provide for arbitration by
which the Agreement is governed. We find in working these terms of arbitration shall be
the basis of discussing certain questions, but there are exceptions also. The Union should
use either the strike weapon or arbitration. but our Union has not been able to say we shall
have arbitration upon every occasion. You cannot negotiate with an employer under a
certain set of circumstances. We feel that we ought to be able to do this because if there
is discontent in a factory, and the employer refuses to see the men, or the union officials,
as was the case in Norwich recently, what is there left to do but strike. We claim we should
have the right to deal with such cases in a constitutional manner, and I hope you will
adopt this suggestion.
The resolution having been seconded,
THE CHAIRMAN said: There are some clauses we should like softening a little.
We have already softened some of them, and we shall certainly try with others the next
time we meet the employers in Conference. Lord Buckmaster asked in the enquiry over
the Norwich case why the employer refused to see the men? If the employer had seen the
men the stoppage would have been prevented, and it saves a lot of internal trouble. The
operatives have more confidence in the head of the firm than a manager or foreman.
(Hear, hear.) I think you should support this resolution.
Agreed.

Item 98. 48-Hour Week.
Street. - "That a local adjustment of working hours per week be allowed even
in excess of 48 hours during certain weeks provided the 48 hours as con-
tained in the National Agreement are not exceeded on the average over the
period of one month, in order to provide for a holiday or half holiday when
desired."
Mr. E. HANSFORD (Street): Some delegates may feel this proposition will lead
us into difficulty, but we are on safe ground as it has been tried for about two years. When
our national officers fixed up an agreement they tried to get the best conditions for the
members. When that is done, it should be left for local branch officers to make any
adjustments to fit local circumstances. I do not think there will be any objection to this.
It should only apply by local arrangement between the employers and the local officers.
Our employers have asked the workpeople to go in on a Saturday morning after working
45 hours, and the operatives have had time-and-a-quarter.
Mr. W. PAINE (Kingswood): I hope the Conference will oppose this. Only this
morning a resolution was adopted asking for the abolition of overtime. That should be
sufficient for the delegates to oppose it.
THE CHAIRMAN: For three weeks these people work overtime without pay.
I went to the firm because a man was given notice because he refused to work overtime.
I found those who believe in football wanted half a day off, and those who wanted to go to
work could not as a consequence. Then the firm wanted this time making up.
If we are
going to do that kind of thing it breaks our agreement whether it is 48 or 44 hours week.
As soon as orders drop off and orders are slack, why not close the factory on Saturday
morning? I find those factories who adopt this method when trade is poor get no grumble
from the operatives.
Mr. F. C. JEX (Norwich): If you turn this down it seems to me within the Terms
of Settlement that there are provisions for it to be done as time to be worked for holidays
requested by the workmen. This three hours in one week could be claimed to come under
that clause.
THE CHAIRMAN: I have consulted other manufacturers. We do not think
the narrow interpretation as given by Mr. Jex could apply. The reason that clause was
put in was because during the war people lost time to see their friends off. Tavistock
Square think they are breaking the Agreement when this thing was done at Street.
Mr. J. MANNERS (Council Member): You are dealing with a branch in an
isolated part of the country, all on its own. It does not break the spirit of the Agreement.
The operatives there feel it is a great advantage to have Saturday morning off. It may be
argued, as the President put it, that firms should give Saturday off when they are on short
time. With that we shall all agree. It is a different thing to meet a firm to get them
to give up the right of working on Saturday and this suggestion from Street. I venture
to say members in that area are as strong as ever they were. The esteem by which our
Union is held has never been so high.
Mr. A. BUTCHER (Norwich) opposed the recommendation. The hours may be
extended to 49 or 50. They could easily work 48 hours in five days.
The recommendation was eventually withdrawn.

create something permanent and lasting for the men and women of our industry, not for-
getting those who built up our organisation. It is pleasurable to think that we have
spent this week in such important work, in lovely surroundings. I hope you will not
forget the words of Herr Simon. As a Continental he feels, as secretary of the International,
and as President of the Boot and Shoe Workers of Germany, that the workers themselves
will have to work out their own salvation. It is only the regard we have for each other
that we shall benefit as a result of this week's work.

submit a resolution on War, and let all boot and shoe operatives in the world know what
we think of war. We could give our membership a lead on the subject.
I shall ask the Council to bring a resolution before you on that occasion, so that we
might all agree upon the subject and broadcast it to the world.
I hope you all feel the benefit of spending the week at the sea. When our work was
done, we have been able to get some hours in the fresh air. If the Council can get a more
salubrious place than Blackpool for the Conference in 1928 I am sure they will get it.
I want you to work with heart and soul, night and day, to bring our membership up to
120,000. I declare this Conference closed. (Applause.)
This concluded the business of the Conference, but before the delegates retired, they
lustily sang "Auld Lang Syne," followed by three hearty cheers for the National Union
of Boot and Shoe Operatives.
The Conference closed at 4.49 p.m.

FELLOW MEMBERS,
REPORT.
22ND JUNE, 1926.
TRADE
is, owing largely to the Mining situation, in a somewhat unstable condition,
a very considerable number of members being on short time, apart altogether
from those out of employment. We have paid out from the Union funds
for Out-of-Work Benefit during the month the sum of £14,368 5s. od., and from
the State side the sum of £10,561 5s. 3d.
The figures of the Ministry of Labour Gazette are as follows :-
BOOT AND SHOE INDUSTRY.
Employment, which is usually at its busiest just before Whitsuntide, was seriously
affected in May, 1926, by difficulties of transport consequent on the general strike, and by
shortage of fuel and power owing to the coal dispute. Many orders were cancelled during
the general strike. Some firms were fairly busy in the third week of the month, endeavour-
ing to overtake arrears before the holiday; some firms on the other hand who closed
during the general strike did not re-open until after Whitsuntide. Many firms stopped
for a whole week at Whitsuntide. The heavy boot trade remained very depressed.
The percentage of workpeople unemployed, as indicated by the unemployment books
lodged at Employment Exchanges, was 19.5 on the 24th May, 1926, as compared with
7.2 on the 26th April, and with 10.1 on the 25th May, 1925.
Employment was reported as fairly good in London, except during the actual strike
period. At Leicester and Northampton there was a great increase in unemployment
and short time. During the general strike, manufacturers found much difficulty in getting
supplies and in delivering goods owing to lack of transport. After the strike was over
some firms worked full time, and even a little overtime, to expedite deliveries before the
holiday; but the Whitsuntide holiday was extended to a week by many firms. In the
Northamptonshire country district (except at Raunds, where employment was good)
there was a great increase in unemployment and short time; many firms closed entirely
during the general strike, and some were still closed at the end of the month. At Kettering
many firms worked half time or less before the holiday, and closed for a whole week at
Whitsuntide. At Stafford employment was poor. At Norwich it was reported that at
least three-quarters of those who were working were on short time, some working only half
time. In the Bristol and Kingswood district employment in the heavy boot industry
remained very depressed; the light shoe trade, which had been steady before the general
strike, also showed some decline, and much short time was worked. Employment at
Leeds, especially in the light shoe trade, was less affected than in some other districts;
on the whole, however, it was poor. Much short time was worked in the Rossendale
Valley; there was little or no increase in total unemployment, however, and some firms
at Bacup were working at the end of the month to the fullest extent that their coal supplies
permitted to complete orders for seaside and holiday footwear.

The exports of boots and shoes in May, 1926, amounted to 80,514 dozen pairs, or

AT THE BLACKPOOL CONFERENCE
a good deal of business was transacted which will have important results so
far as the members are concerned. Questions relating to education, finance,
and unemployment were dealt with, they being treated from both the National
and International aspect.
The Mining situation and the General Stoppage in support of the miners
was also fully discussed, and the policy pursued by us, whether in relation to
the grant of £20,000 from the Union funds to the General Council Relief Fund,
or our method of dealing with payment to our own members, was generally
upheld.
The Conference is now a thing of the past. It may fairly be said that
it was one of the most successful conferences the Union has ever held. Amongst
the more important decisions arrived at by the delegates were :-
A Superannuation Fund has been created for permanent (full time) officials
and clerks of the Union and Branches.
A Superannuation Fund was adopted in principle for members. It was
decided that this scheme, which will be published at the earliest possible moment,
should be brought before the members at their branch meetings and amend-
ments thereto submitted to the Council, after which a Special Delegate
Meeting will be held for one day, preferably in Leicester.
We wish to emphasize the importance of this matter and trust it will
receive earnest consideration of members at their branch meetings.

In connection with this part of our work the membership is not growing as rapidly as we should like, the present membership being 33,295. We appeal to the members to do their share in looking after the young people who come into the industry, and induce them to join the Insurance Department as well as the Trade Union side, thereby still further increasing the usefulness and influence of the Union.

**OFFICIALS AND STAFF SUPERANNUATION SCHEME.**

There appears to be some misunderstanding regarding this Fund, it being mixed up with the proposed members' scheme, and comparisons are being made between the payments of benefits of the two schemes. In our judgment they cannot be so compared; one scheme is for those in our employ, and the other for the membership of the Union.

Moreover, in the proposals for the members the amount suggested as a contribution from the members is threepence per week, whilst those who will contribute to the scheme for Officials and Staff will be anything from two shillings to six shillings per week; thus, if the matter is looked at impartially, it will be seen that for the benefit proposed to be given, the members' scheme for the threepence weekly gives a greater ratio of benefit.

We feel confident the members will endorse our doing what many firms and trade unions are already carrying out, and thereby prove that our words as to assisting one another are really meant to be applied as and when the opportunity occurs.

**THE MINERS' POSITION.**

The Mining situation is still in a deplorable state. Despite the Prime Minister's statements from time to time as to peace and goodwill it does appear to us that he woefully falls short in action to ensure peace and goodwill. Here is a dispute which not only affects mine owners and mine workers, but has a vital effect upon the industry of the country, seeing how dependent the nation is upon an adequate coal supply. Despite this fact the Prime Minister allows week by week to go by and matters to drift along, producing a paralysing effect upon the trade of the country, and causing suffering, privation and pain, beyond calculation.


---
On 15th June in the House of Commons, the question was once more
debated, and the Prime Minister made a long statement about the position
as he conceived it to be, and said among other things, the following: "We have
come quite definitely to the conclusion for a return to a longer working day."
He regarded this form of sacrifice as one which, in his opinion, was a
preferable alternative to the greater sacrifice of wages.
"We intend to leave the Seven Hours Act on the statute book,
but to introduce legislation to enable an extra hour to be worked during
a period of time.
"This does not prescribe longer hours of work, but it does permit
serious negotiations to be entered into upon the basis on which it is obvious
that a far better scale of wages could be paid than upon the existing
basis.
"We have in preparation a Bill which we hope to introduce in a
few days to give effect to the Commissioners' recommendations re-
quiring legislation which we think it may be possible to pass into law
this Session, and which are likely to have an immediate effect on the
industry. The responsibility for settlement rests, as it always has rested,
on the two interested parties."
The report of the proceedings in the House of Commons shows some amount
of interruption, and no wonder, when there was shown as in the above state-
ments such a lack of what is required at the present time.
Mr. Hartshorn, as a Miners' representative, who followed the Prime
Minister, after making a very effective speech outlining the miners' position,
finished up by stating he had intended to ask the Prime Minister some questions
and to make some suggestions as to the line on which he thought they might
have proceeded. But after listening to the Prime Minister's speech he thought
the situation was pretty hopeless. Legislation on the question of unification
or amalgamation was not to come into effect for three years. A settlement
which was not possible without that step being taken was deferred indefinitely.
If the Prime Minister had represented the policy which the Government
intended to pursue, he regretted to say that he did not see the end of the
stoppage. (Cheers.) It would be prolonged for goodness knew how long;
he did not. If anybody imagined that the leaders were going to call off this
strike on the speech to which they had just listened, whether at the end of three
months or six months, he was very much mistaken. There would be no
settlement within the industry. The House had to settle the matter, and the
sooner they got down to beating out a solution the better it would be for all
parties.
Other Labour members followed upon the same lines. Their appeals
were, however, not complied with. Thus the nation is forced to this unnecessary
suffering because of an attitude being taken up which means that once more


---
317
the workers must endure this agony because of failure of those in authority
to rise to their proper responsibility. Yet once again we must emphasise the
need for putting into authority those who will make an honest effort to put
into practice the programme of the Labour Party, and thereby usher in that
better era which is so badly needed.
POLITICAL.
The political work in the House of Commons by the Labour Party brings
out clearer and clearer the absolute necessity for a strong opposition against
the present Government. Time after time, apart from what may be termed
the routine work, proposals call for action against the policy being carried
out by the party in power. The following are amongst some of the outstanding
questions dealt with during the month :-
LEAD PAINT BILL. Friday, 4th June, for regulation instead of
prohibition of white lead. For the Bill 131; against, 56.
THE MINING POSITION.
BUDGET. Tea Duty; 7th June. Mr. Alexander moved to reduce
the duty from 4d. per lb. to Id. There voted for 105; against, 241.
SAFEGUARDING OF INDUSTRIES. 8th June.
In connection with the Lead Paint Bill, this was introduced by the Home
Secretary for regulations in connection with the matter, as against the Con-
vention passed in 1921 at the International Labour Conference, for the prohibi-
tion of white lead. Despite the fight put up at the second reading, the Bill
was carried by 131 votes to 56. Lord Henry Cavendish-Bentinck, a Conserva-
tive member, described the Bill as a "dud" Bill, and went on to say-
"I am really more annoyed than I can say that the Home
Secretary, in a Conservative Government, should have brought in such
a useless and rotten Bill as this. All that I can say is, that I feel
very strongly that it is in the vested interests which have advised
him to bring in this rotten and absolutely piffling Bill."
The duty on tea was again taken in hand by the Labour Party, and attempts
made to secure a reduction of the same, more especially having regard to the
fact that this duty falls the heaviest upon the poorest class of the community.
The voting for the reduction was 105; against, 241.
A strenuous fight was also put up against what is termed "The Safe-
guarding of Industries Bill." In connection with this Bill it becomes clearer and
clearer that it is
PROTECTION
as generally understood that is emerging from the policy which is being pur-
sued, and one, moreover, which will ultimately develop into reprisals from
other countries.
The need is, therefore, to keep in being in all parts of the country the
political machinery and propaganda to inform the public that when the next
appeal is made to the electorate, it may result in a majority being returned
to the House of Commons of those who support the Labour Party and its policy.

**THE GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.**

60 LADY SOMERSET ROAD,
KENTISH TOWN, N.W.5.
18th June, 1926.

**FELLOW MEMBERS,**

**MINING DISPUTE.** In addressing you this month, one is bound to deplore the continued struggle in the coal industry. As a human being, I can do no other than sympathize and support the miners to the best of my ability. It is unfortunate that the Government permitted a stoppage to take place. The Trades Union Congress, and Ministers of the Gospel of all denominations, asked for the old conditions to prevail as were in working during the month of April last. Had this position been created and the men allowed to go on as they had been going on, the subsidy could have continued for a short period, at least until such time as the trade had rehabituated itself. There are those who say that the subsidy ought not to be given to any industry; to that I entirely agree the alternative being that the Government, if the product of that industry is essential for the life and well-being of the nation to be continued, should be taken over and controlled in the name of His Majesty's Government. When we speak of subsidies we want to realize whether it is not more just to pay the subsidy to an industry from the Taxes of the country rather than from the Rates and through the Poor Law Guardians, which in itself is often demoralizing to the recipients, as 90 per cent. of the people in this country much prefer to earn their income rather than to receive it from such a source and under such conditions. One cannot help but hold the Government responsible for championing the claim of the mineowners and against the humane demands of the miners themselves, although the miners have to make a declaration that they cannot extend the hours or receive a reduction in wages. I have yet to meet the individual person who considers, and will vouch for the fact that mine workers are getting sufficient to live a life of comparative decency. Regarding the earnings of the miners, according to the statement made in the House of Commons, for several years the average rate of the miners has varied from 48s. 1d. to 53s. 2d.; a definite statement which stands unchallenged, made on the floor of the House of Commons by Mr. Vernon Hartshorn, a Miners' Agent. We have had occasion to take no small part in this matter by the fact that the conditions of employment governing our industry were likely to be broadcast by the Chairman of our Con- ferences, but owing (says the Postmaster-General) to "the matter being controversial," other people might ask for similar privileges. Without claiming too much, I venture to Miners' Executive have already agreed to the suggestion that they would meet the mine- owners and endeavor to work out a settlement with an "Independent" Chairman, provided the independent chairman only acted or gave a decision when both sides asked him to do so. This has ever been the policy that has governed our own Union during the past 31 years, and to all who have had this matter explained, whatever industry they have been connected with, compliment the Boot and Shoe Operatives Union on what they describe as a common-sense policy in dealing with trade matters. I am still of the opinion that this is the most binding method that can be adopted. Both sides, after weighing up each other's strength, wit, wisdom and desires, mutually agree to govern the trade for a further period of time, and as nothing succeeds like success, we have been enabled for the period above-mentioned to work in comparative harmony with our employers—may such a policy continue.

It will be of interest to the members to know that approximately ten thousand and thirty-six members were stopped as a consequence of the General Stoppage and the Mining Dispute, and for this the Union paid £10,163 7s. 9d. as Suspension Benefit. Since writing the above I have induced the Right Hon. T. Shaw, M.P. to take up our case, as follows:—

THE RT. HON. T. SHAW, M.P.,
House of Commons,
London, S.W.1.

15th May, 1926.

DEAR MR. SHAW,

Enclosed please find the case of the National Union of Boot and Shoe Opera- tives as mentioned to you a few days ago. The Manufacturers' Federation and ourselves drafted a memoranda for Broadcasting. The Government refused to allow it to be broadcast, because they say it is controversial. I say they refused because we do not allow our Chairman, appointed by the Minister of Labour, to decide in any case until we ask him, which we have never done yet, and as the Government want the Miners to accept a Chairman with compulsory powers, our conditions if broadcast, would show the Government as trying to impose compulsory arbitration.

We would not accept the offer of the Government.

EXTRACT FROM Hansard, DATED 17TH JUNE, 1926.
BOOT AND SHOE TRADE (CONCILIATION SCHEME).
MR. T. SHAW (by Private Notice) asked the Postmaster-General if it is a fact
that the employers and the workers in the National Boot and Shoe Trade had agreed
to broadcast a description of their conciliation scheme, which had prevented any
general upheaval for upwards of 31 years; whether the Independent Chairman of
the Conciliation Board in the industry had agreed to broadcast; and for what reason
the Postmaster-General refused to allow the broadcasting to take place ?
THE POSTMASTER-GENERAL (Sir William Mitchell-Thomson): The facts are as
stated. The only point of such a broadcast at this moment was that it should imply
the advocacy that a similar scheme could and should be forthwith applied to the
Mining Industry. A suggestion of this nature may or may not be desirable, but it is
undoubtedly controversial, and consequently was not permitted as a broadcast.
MR. SHAW: May I ask if there was a single word in the message which it was
proposed to broadcast, which in any way even gave the impression that the scheme
might be applied to the mining dispute ?
SIR W. MITCHELL-THOMSON: If that be the fact, then I do not think the broad-
casting will suffer by being delayed a little.
MR. RAMSAY MACDONALD: Will not the Postmaster-General reconsider his
decision in view of the fact that this is interesting information which the country
ought to have; and if it is prevented from being broadcast, does not that show that
the broadcasting company is being controlled for political purposes.
SIR W. MITCHELL-THOMSON: There is not a shadow of foundation for that
suggestion. I have to do the best I can to try to keep matters of political controversy
out of broadcasting. May I remind the right hon. Gentleman that this matter is
very closely allied to a Debate which took place a couple of years ago upon the
Industrial Councils Bill, which was very largely supported by those who sit on this
side of the House, and opposition to which, if I remember aright, came entirely from
the right hon. Gentleman's side of the House. There is no doubt whatever—and I
do not think the right hon. Gentleman will dispute this—that arbitration which is
compulsory to the extent that it depends upon the forfeiture of a guarantee is a subject
of political controversy, and in my judgment so long as the rule about subjects of
political controversy stands I must enforce it.
MR. SHAW: In view of the unsatisfactory nature of the Postmaster-General's
answer, I give notice that I shall raise this matter on the Adjournment at the earliest
possible date.
My very best thanks to Mr. Shaw for his kindness.
For further information see pages 340-343.
BLACKPOOL CONFERENCE.—Our Conference was as usual, a decided success; the
attendance of delegates as is their custom being all that could be desired. The only bone
of contention which is very controversial throughout the Union with all whom I have
come in contact, is the question of Superannuation. The Conference decided to adopt
the recommendation concerning superannuation for officers and clerks. The voting on this
particular subject was entirely satisfactory, and the Council recommended a referendum
vote to be taken on the question of members' superannuation.
Our visitor to Blackpool was Herr J. Simon, who brought friendly greetings from the
German Trade Unionists and the Boot and Shoe and Leather Workers' International.
He and Dr. Schenk, who acted as interpreter, gave us some valuable advice, but the great
theme was, and is, co-ordination of the workers of the world, more confidence, more sym-
pathy, more unity. It was well that Herr Simon was with us because we have interested
him in the discussion that we are having to take up on behalf of our membership regarding
Czecho-Slovakia and other nations. For the moment we can only say that the conditions
as we see them look as though conditions are best in our own country, but at the same
time we are broad-minded enough not to come to a definite decision until we have sufficient
evidence. In this respect the President of the Federation and myself have challenged

ORGANISERS' REPORTS.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
My report was minus in the May Monthly Report. There was little for me to
report owing to the bulk of the factories running only a few hours a day. I spoke at
several big meetings in Leicester and County during the memorable strike. Those who
say the great strike was a failure may be put down as lukewarm friends of trade unionism
or actual enemies of it.
The Leicester No. 1 Branch made a claim last season for extras on the finishing of
the Russian or Rodeo Boot. The Leicester Board, so far as the employers' side went,
turned it down, and the matter was referred to Mr. C. H. Roberts, as representing the
employers and myself as the nominee of the Leicester branches. We had several meetings
on the matter, but failed to come to any conclusion satisfactory to me. We asked Mr.
W. A. North to act as Umpire. He consented, and heard both sides of the case. I am
pleased to report that Mr. North has awarded an extra of ten per cent. on all operations.
Since the Conference Mr. Baum and I have been working round Sileby, Derby and
Mansfield. It was gratifying to us when we went to the latter town on 2nd June to hear
that sixty-six non-members had joined as a result of our previous visit.
On 10th June we had a big open-air meeting at Sileby representing the Leicester
Hosiery Union and our own. Mr. T. F. Richards presided. Alderman Chaplin and a pro-
mising young hosiery worker spoke for their Union. There was no croaking here about
the General Strike being a failure. It gives one an opportunity to put the political side
of our cause as well as the trade union side at meetings like this.
On Sunday, 13th June, the General President, Mr. Baum and I went to Mountsorrel
and held a fine meeting on the Green. It was a delightful morning, and we were well
repaid for our labour by the good attendance and sympathy shown. The recent reduc-
tions in our minimum wages and piecework prices need not have taken place if the employers
were more farseeing men when making the terms with us a few years ago. We pressed
again and again that the £3 minimum and the £1 16s. should not be lowered till the cost
of living dropped to point 60. We even tried point 65 when we failed at the 60. The
manufacturers as a body say that they gain little or nothing by the change. The public
gain nothing by it, but our people on the minimum suffer more than the position warrants.
Had point 65 been accepted there would be no disturbance in costing or debating with
factors, and no fair employer would be any the poorer for it. The organisers have many
questions put to them on the cost of living, and the why and the wherefore of proof for the
need of a reduction. I know the branch officers get similar posers. The worst of it is
that the get-rich-at-all-cost type of employers who give the blind eye to increases when
officially announced, are the first to spot the winner on the slide down.
I am pleased to say that the Sileby Branch is gaining in membership and strength.
The Conference in remitting portion of its debt, and thereby enfranchising the branch,
will have evidence at the next Conference, I believe, that the new Secretary, Mr. Waring,
was worthy of the sympathy shown to him.
D. MCCARTHY.
21st June, 1926.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
My work during the past month has been in various Branches and Sections of North-
amptonshire. Following the Conference there were many questions, varying in their
importance, which members required more information upon, and by attending the Branch
meetings I was able to take the questions asked, which were mainly superficial, and give
the background upon which such matters had been decided. The Six-day Suspension
Period was the question at issue, particularly where our members had been hit the hardest
during, and since, the General Stoppage. No doubt there were many cases of personal
hardship, but when the history of the application of Suspension Benefit was explained,
the reason and the cost in 1921-22, without exception, those who complained agreed that
the Council had dealt with the matter generously. The question of the Levy also came
under discussion, and here again the seriousness of the position had not been realised.
Although the E.C., on behalf of the members, had made a large grant towards the T.U.C.
Relief Fund, it is still essential that all individual members should subscribe to the common
fund. How many are there that remember the Miners' dispute of 1921 ? How few realise
the accumulative results of that dispute? All Settlements of Terms in all trades, including
our own, felt the effects. Without very substantial financial support is forthcoming,
as it was in 1921, so it may be in 1926. "Verb Sap" (a word to the wise is sufficient).
The question of Superannuation has been discussed at all meetings, and many suggestions
have been made, which have been taken note of and, no doubt, will prove useful to those
who have the task of building up the general scheme. No opposition to the principle of
Superannuation is apparent, and questions of detail will be for future discussion.

Our visits to Mansfield at once brought us in touch with the realities of the mining
dispute. We met the operatives at the Mansfield Shoe Company, and the Secretary

FELLOW MEMBERS,

Since reporting last several things of importance have taken place. We have
passed through the first General Strike that has been attempted in this country.
This
is a weapon that has frequently in the past been advocated as the one that would bring
the opposition to their knees. We can now judge as to the accuracy or otherwise of that
forecast. It would be impossible to say that it was a success for the object it presumably
That
had in view, viz., the saving of the miner from reduced wages or increased hours.
is an issue which has still to be decided. The miners are still locked out, as determined
as ever in their resistance to these proposals, while the mine owners are apparently equally
determined to impose their will on those whom they may employ. No, the General Strike
did not achieve what was its immediate object, but it would be sheer nonsense to say on
the other hand that it was a failure.

As a demonstration of working-class solidarity it was wonderful, it was splendid.
The greatest optimist never expected such a response to the call as was given by all sections
who had to take their place in the fighting line. There was no difficulty in getting men
out; it was, on the other hand, not easy to keep them in where the orders were in that
direction. But mass action of this kind is difficult to maintain; there are so many factors
entering into the situation that are not easy to overcome. The sheer weight of the thing
was too much to carry, as in all kinds of war we must punish ourselves in the endeavour
to punish others, and in a way our very success brings with it difficulties almost as great.
It was so in this case, and concessions must be made in the interest of the general com-
munity. That weakens the whole position, and it is practically impossible to maintain a
situation that implies almost a complete stoppage, when it becomes necessary to decide
whether this or that section shall remain at work or come out.

Still, notwithstanding all that may be said to the contrary, it will in the long run
be the means of helping our movement. Such a manifestation of whole-hearted deter-
mination to sacrifice everything to defend a standard of comfort in life, which has been
won in the past, cannot but bring in its train greater strength and power for our work.
We shall better understand what our real power is, we shall obtain a clearer idea as to what
is the best method to concentrate upon, we shall better understand what the obstacles
are that have to be overcome, we must in the end shape ourselves in a way that will lead
to greater and yet greater success. It has been an experience that was perhaps worth
while, if we can only learn the real lessons that evolve therefrom. In the meantime we
must concentrate upon helping the miners, and those who are the victims of the strike
itself. We claimed they were fighting for us all, it is our responsibility to sustain them now.

The Blackpool Conference of the Union is also now a thing of the past. It was on
the whole a useful and pleasant gathering. If one were to raise a discordant note it would
be in the direction of regretting that in certain respects a broader view was not taken in
the discussion of some questions; but even in that respect nothing of real serious import
took place. One can only hope that the decisions reached will add to the power and useful-
ness of the Union for the purpose and object that lies in front of us. It is pleasing to meet
as Conferences come round the old familiar faces from the different areas where our
branches exist, we are all better for the contact it gives. We miss some who have been
with us at past gatherings, we wonder who we shall miss at the next. This should bring
home to us all that the opportunities given to any of us are none too great, and should
be used to the full to render what service we can to help in the work necessary to bring
about the changes that are essential for those whom we would serve. Much that has to
be done is purely ambulance work; it must be done, but let us not in the doing of it fail
to realise that basic and drastic changes must also be made, new foundations must be laid
upon which shall be built the new order: let us try to give to the full that individual effort
necessary for its earliest realisation.

So far as organising work goes this has been rendered somewhat difficult by the lock-
out, creating as it has an uncertainty that is not good for regular running of the factories,
but useful work has been accomplished in the helping of Mr. Mason, of the London Metro.
Branch, in the establishing of statements in some of the factories in the London area.
It is, I believe, the opinion of all who helped in this district that this is a most desirable
and essential step to take. After all, it is the best basis to rest the wage-earning position
upon: it is a guarantee that cannot be well attained in any other way. By this means
we value the amount of work done so that wages shall accrue in proportion to the effort
made. We hope during the next few days to complete some of this work, which should
be extended to other firms at the earliest moment.

A visit has been made to a firm who cut soles, &c., for the trade. This is a develop-
ment that must be watched. Where firms start in a shoe centre they can easily be dealt
with, and the same control and influence can be obtained as in the boot factories, but the
danger lies where they start in more or less isolated places, and have a tendency to establish
It is possible for a boot manufacturer
labour conditions on a lower standard than our own.
to buy in a great deal of his requirements so far as bottom stuff is concerned, but none

One regrets that an amount of time has had to be given to a Federated firm in London during the past two months that should not be necessary in face of the clearness of the conditions laid down in the Terms of Settlement. BRANCH REPORTS.

CHESHAM.--Trade here is still very bad.
DERBY. Trade in Derby is very poor, the C.W.S. have nearly been
closed down for about six weeks, Clemson's only making half time with a
number standing off.

EDINBURGH. One of our factories was made to stand off owing to
the want of material during the General Strike, but are now at work again.
The Branch has started to help a local fund in place of the national levy, which
we expect will receive a hearty response. Certainly there is need for financial
assistance to help the miners to fight their case. As usual there are some who
don't see eye to eye with the Miners' Federation, but they are fighting a working-
class battle at this time. We think we are correct in saying that the last time
the miners had a reduction in their wages the general case was most other
workers had also to suffer reductions. However, if this fight continues long
there will be somewhat more people thrown out of work. However, let us
hope that both sides will get round the table and show by good reasoning that
they can overcome any difficulties which are in the way of a settlement. At
the same time we don't think the miners can afford to have any reduction of
their wages. This is the general feeling of all workers who have taken any
interest in the dispute. Good luck to the miners in their splendid fight.

HIGHAM AND RUSHDEN.--The Branch has been seriously affected
by the General Strike, about 2,500 being unemployed on benefit as a result:
Rushden, 1,300; Higham, 80; Irthlingborough, 300; Finedon, 300; Raunds,
69; Stanwick, 13; Ringstead, 12; Wollaston, 200; Bozeat, 75; Irchester,
93. Reckoning probationary members and members who had previously
drawn 10 weeks during the year, there must have been 2,600 members out of
work. At the moment, however (except at Finedon), trade is as good as can be
expected under the present conditions, and manufacturers are trying to keep
factories running. Len. Smith (Organiser) is at present in the district and
rendering good service. He attended two of the four monthly meetings held.
There is a certain amount of criticism by the members who never attend
meetings of the £20,000 grant to the Trades Union Congress Relief Fund, but
the Rushden meeting approved the grant, and also granted £5 as first instalment
to the local miners' relief funds.

LONDON SOUTH. A joint meeting of the Arbitration Board met on
the 17th May, in connection with Sewround Statement and the Indoor Work-
shop question. The employers' side agreed with the findings of the arbitrator
in favour of the workers' side. The employers want such a great reduction
for the use of the place provided, also for the finding of light and grindery.
The workers' side wanted the men inside first, to see if they could get a living
wage before any reductions could be entertained, for we believe on our side
of the Board the men will want an increase of wages, because they would be
working under factory conditions. Of course we could not agree so the question
was referred back to the employers, together with Committee appointed by
both sides, to see what terms can be arrived at to be brought before the next
meeting. Other items on the agenda were adjourned until next meeting.
The London South Branch during the strike have been holding meetings every
Tuesday at the Club House. The meetings have been well packed. We have
had great help from several speakers, including Dr. Dick Connolly Beech, of
the Strike Committee. Everyone enjoyed themselves because he drove home
to some of the weak ones the true principles of trade unionism. We shall try
to get the Branch to have these meetings once a month for educational purposes
for the members.
C

LONDON SEW-ROUND. Trade is very quiet in the Sew-Round work,
but fair in the Louis XV. heel work. The Umpire's award in reference to factory
workshops for Louis XV. heel makers is now before the Board
and is to be dealt with by joint meetings of the Board of Arbitration and
for both branches of the trade at the same time. We have not made much pro-
gress as yet, only that present statements are to remain for out-workers.
The employers are asking for a revision of Statements to compensate them for
cost of grindery and accommodation they will have to provide, but have not
come forward with any suggestion in reference to same. We stated we are
prepared for revision of Statements if earnings call for same three months after
makers have been in the factory.
LIVERPOOL.-During the past month the General Council of the Trades
Union Congress thought fit in their wisdom or otherwise to declare a
General Strike, with the avowed intention of helping the miners. The question
now is, was it a success? Did it help the miners in any shape or form? We
leave it to our members to judge for themselves, and refrain from expressing
an opinion as we can all be wise after the event. We hope our members will
read their Monthly Report, especially pages 275, 276, and then refer to Union
Rules-page 54, Rules 253, 254, 255. Referring to Half-yearly Report issued
in January last, we find that the aggregate of money in the Trade and Sick
Funds was no less a sum than £340,749 17s. 8d. Our reason for quoting these
items is because as soon as a General Strike was declared a few of our members
"got the wind up," and threw up the sponge, refusing to pay any more con-
tributions. Evidently they were like the rats, thought the ship was sinking,
and did not intend to be sucked down in the vortex. We have a few copies
of Union Rules which can be obtained on application to local secretary, also
Union Buttons, 6d. each.
NORWICH. Trade in Norwich has been seriously affected by the Coal
Dispute, many firms being unable to overcome the difficulties of the present
industrial situation. Toward the last days of April the numbers of unemployed
fell to the lowest point for many months past, but by the end of May the
numbers had increased in an alarming way. The firm of Phillips & Son (late
of Leeds, 1919) were declared bankrupt very suddenly, throwing out some
three hundred operatives, and with restricted work at neighbouring factories,
very little opportunity is offered for fresh engagements. The Norwich members
responded splendidly to the levy, even when very slow time was being worked.
Three hundred and fifty pounds have already been sent with expectations of
a similar amount to complete the month's collections. We are continuing a
voluntary weekly collection for the miners' wives and children, and our members
are giving from small earnings wholeheartedly, eighty pounds being realised
the first week. The miners are fighting splendidly with almost a unanimously
united country behind them. We hope most sincerely sufficient financial
help will be given to enable the men (however long the dispute may last) to
succeed in spite of the combined forces of private owners and Government
interests.
NORTHAMPTON No. 1.-Trade continues slack which it is bound to
with the continuous lack of earnings of the workers, amounting to several
million pounds per week. In spite of the serious drop in earnings our members
have contributed £750 to the Relief Fund, which in very many cases has been
a real sacrifice. Let us hope the end will be in favour of the miners, and the
solution of future difficulties by the nation coming into their rights by the
ownership of mines.
PLYMOUTH.-The General Strike is now off, but the miners continue
their heroic struggle against a miserable wage and extended hours of labour.

We are asked the question, "What has been gained"? How this question is
answered largely depends upon our political and industrial make up. An
editorial of the Daily Mail would answer one way and the Daily Herald another,
but are there no facts apparent to the intelligent mind, which would lead to a
correct conception of an event unparalleled in industrial history? We think
there are. First of all we must set it down that the General Strike was not for
gain. It was purely defensive a great effort to maintain the established
rates and conditions for the miners. Whether or not this was successful
must of necessity remain unanswered until the miners return to work. The
General Strike was thought to be a very powerful way of helping, but there
are many more, if silver bullets were found for the defence of England,
surely they may be found for the defence of miners, their wives and children,
fighting against a miserable existence. Three million men ceased work in a
most dramatic and astonishing manner, and the attention of the country was
focussed on one of the first principles of a Christian State a fair living for all,
no sweating and no slavery. Certainly if the constitution of our land stands
for anything it stands for this. When over a hundred years ago we abolished
slavery, and nearly twenty years ago we placed an Act (Trades Board Act 1909)
upon the Statute book, declaring it to be a crime to pay working men less than
the established rates. Further, we have such things as "The Fair Wages
Clause," and we have sang for many many years, "Britons never shall be
slaves." When our great lawyers talk so eloquently about an attack upon
the constitution we suggest they try their legal skill in making out a case
against the mine-owners who sought to establish a miserable wage by a lockout,
and thus lower and degrade the standard of life dear to an Englishman.
SILEBY.-Trade here is fair considering the mining dispute. What we
want is more solidarity amongst the workers to fight the problems of the day
that are constantly coming along. Our General President (Mr. T. F. Richards),
with Mr. J. H. Baum and Mr. D. McCarthy, have made their presence felt at a
meeting here. Mr. Baum and Mr. McCarthy also addressed another open-air
meeting in connection with the miners' lockout, which was considered the best
every held in our district.
WATERFORD.-Trade shows a falling off during the past month.

Trade Union leaders to obtain a settlement of the mining problem on the basis of the
Commission Report should end in failure. What more could they do than they had done?
They had striven, up to the very hour when the lock-out notices were due to take effect,
to obtain from the Government some positive and material contribution to a settle-
ment.
They had pleaded with the Government to secure a withdrawal of the lock out notices in
order that negotiations might continue. Their plea
would first agree to accept a reduction of wages. At midnight
when the Trade Union leaders faced the executives of the unions at the Memorial Hall
conference, they had absolutely nothing to show for all those hours of pleading, of argument,
and appeal addressed to the Prime Minister and his colleagues the Govern-
nothing to say but that the miners must agree to a reduction of wages.
was met by a refusal, unless the miners
on Friday, 30th April,
That was the position on Saturday morning, 1st May, when the responsible executives
of the Trade Unions decided upon the grave step of calling a general stoppage in the railway
and transport services, the printing trades, and the metal industries. But even then the
Trade Union leaders continued their efforts, although they knew that the Government
had already prepared for war, and a proclamation had been issued declaring that a state
of emergency existed. They declared that even at that critical hour they believed an
honourable settlement could be reached. They again approached Ministers and pressed
for a withdrawal of the notices, and were again faced with a refusal unless they were ready
to give an assurance that the miners would accept wage reductions. On Saturday night,
Ist May, after renewed discussions with the representatives of the Industrial Committee,
the Prime Minister felt himself able to say that if negotiations were allowed to continue--it
being understood that the lock-out notices were withdrawn-" the representatives of the
Trades Union Congress were confident a settlement could be reached on the lines of the
Report within a fortnight." The Trade Union leaders were considering in a joint meeting
with the miners' representatives the meaning of this declaration, preparatory to further
discussion with the Government, when, at midnight on Sunday, 2nd May, the blow fell.
Summoned from the meeting by the Prime Minister's secretary, the leaders returned with
the announcement that the Government would not continue negotiations until the General
Council had unconditionally withdrawn the instructions for a general stoppage and had
repudiated "overt acts," of which they had then heard for the first time. No oppor-
tunity was given to the General Council to ascertain the facts about the "overt acts."
Before any reply at all could be returned, in fact, when the ultimatum was delivered, the
Prime Minister and his colleagues turned out the lights and went off to bed. So the strike
came-because the Government made no genuine effort to pursue the path to an honourable
settlement that the Trade Union leaders had opened out. - Labour Magazine, 19th June,
1926.
DENMARK AND SHODDY SHOES.
New Regulations for Marking Imports.
It is announced by the Board of Trade that the Commercial Secretary to H.M. Legation
at Copenhagen has forwarded copy and translation of a law regarding the use of paste-
board, artificial leather, artificial leather board or chemically prepared fibre board in
footwear made in, or imported into, Denmark.
The provisions of the law as regards imported footwear are in the main the same as
those formerly in force, but it is provided that the marks "A" or "B," the word "Unden-
landsk," with the name and the address of the importer, and the identification mark allotted
to him, must be effected in the following manner:-In the case of footwear with leather
soles the mark "A" or "B" and the identification mark must be placed on the hollow
of the sole close to the heel, and the other marks are to be placed where they are visible
in the uppers, or on the outside of the sole or by means of a steel stamp in the hollow of
the insole.
"
Rubber footwear may be marked by means of engraving or vulcanising on the inside
or outside of the hollow of the sole, or by means of a coloured stamp on the inside of the
hollow of the sole or on the lining.
The following have been exempted from the provisions of the law by a Ministerial
Notice, effective as from 1st May:--
Children's footwear, 16 cms. or less in length; felt, silk straw and wooden footwear;
leather and textile footwear, with soles of other material than rubber and without heel,
even having a layer not exceeding 1 cms. in thickness including the sole; turned foot-
wear with leather soles, footwear entirely of rubber lined or not; goloshes and rubber
overboots (snow boots).
Textile footwear with a heel piece (Bagkappe) of artificial leather, artificial leather board
or chemically prepared fibre board, may be imported into Denmark until further notice,
when it fulfils in other respects the requirements of the law. -The Shoe and Leather Record,
18th June, 1926.

The Insurance Officer did not agree with the Court's recommendation. He considered

Decision. On the facts before me my decision is that, if the above-named employed
person had made a claim for unemployment benefit, the claim would have been disallowed.
"The hours and holiday agreement under which the applicant received two days'
pay follows closely, but not exactly, the agreements which were considered in Decision
No. 8820, and in some later cases which have not been printed.
The agreement in this case provides that every employce should be granted one
week's holiday per annum, to be paid for at the ordinary rate and to be taken (unless
otherwise agreed) between 31st March and 30th September, and that in the event of any
employee leaving his employment such employee shall be entitled to a pro rata allowance
in respect of the week's holiday, on the basis of one day for each completed two months'
service. When the applicant left his employment he received, in accordance with this
agreement, the equivalent to two days' wages. I am satisfied that that sum was 'wages,'
but it is not clear in respect of what days it was paid. It was contended before me that
it was paid in respect of some unascertained two days between March 31st and 30th Septem-
ber, when the applicant may be taking a holiday. If there were anything to show that
the payment was expressly appropriated at the time of payment to any particular period
of two days I should have held that it was paid in respect of those days, but in the absence
of such appropriation I must hold, as in previous cases, that the two days' wages were
paid in respect of the two days immediately following the loss of employment, at about
which time the payment was made, and that the applicant continued to receive wages in
respect of those two days."

Case No. 1069/26. (11/5/26.) Section 8 (2) of the Principal Act-Employ-
ment left voluntarily.
APPLICANT LEFT REGULAR EMPLOYMENT TO JOIN HUSBAND WHO HAD OBTAINED CASUAL
WORK IN ANOTHER TOWN.
The applicant stated that she had left her employment as a box maker in Bradford
on the 9th March, 1926, in order to join her husband, who had obtained work in Liverpool.
Her claim for unemployment benefit made on the 16th March was accordingly disallowed,
on the ground that she had voluntarily left her employment without just cause.
It was elicited that the husband, whose employment was of a casual nature, had
secured rooms in Liverpool and had sent for his wife a week after he found work.
Recommended by the Court of Referees that the claim should be allowed. The Court
were of the opinion that the applicant was justified in leaving her employment.
The Insurance Officer did not agree with the Court's recommendation. In his opinion
the applicant had not shown just cause for leaving.
Decision." On the facts before me my decision is that the claim for benefit should
be disallowed.
The applicant, who had regular work in Bradford, left her employment because
her husband obtained casual work as a builder's labourer at Liverpool. It would have
been otherwise if he had obtained regular work and was taking a house in Liverpool."
-The Ministry of Labour Gazette, June, 1926.

SCOTTISH TRADES UNION CONGRESS.
The Congress met this year during April in Inverness, and the undersigned attended
on behalf of the Union. The difficulty of getting to such a place seems to suggest that
undue inconvenience. So far as the Capital of the Highlands is concerned, it is a splendid
to the early season. A large number of delegates were in attendance, and when reported
on, it seems that Trade Union interest is increasing North of the Tweed.
After the customary welcomes, and certain routine machinery elected, the Chairman
delivered his presidential address, Mr. Joseph Duncan can be relied upon to put down
sane and intelligent handling of the vexed matters he had to refer to in his opening state-
ment. No doubt since then, he and others have had occasion to think back, and it would
be interesting to get his views now in the light of recent experience. It was eviden
from the start that the Council of Congress was to steer a sane course through the troubled
waters of the Agenda, and that early impression was confirmed as the days went on
Glasgow Trades and Labour Council served up the "hot stuff" in a number of resolutions
but never at any time did they seem likely to carry the delegates with them. Their
Congress, and resolution after resolution failed. It is true the Glasgow Trades Council
resolutions were well enough argued, but the Council managed to put a better case befor
men were not the only ones to favour out and out methods, but still the substantial majority
were not that way inclined.
The Council's Report was a splendid document, stating clearly and concisely the
attitude adopted on the issues which had confronted Council throughout the year, and
also explaining the important new scheme for trade union organisation which was sub-
mitted to Congress for approval.
This produced the best discussion of the week. The task of submitting the scheme
fell to the Congress Secretary, Mr. Wm. Elger, and as everyone expected, his statement
was masterly in its temper, in its form, and in its ideas. Without referring to a single
note, he dealt with the complex question of existing organisation in Scotland, what had
been accomplished; what had still to be accomplished; what were the difficulties; how
they could be overcome; what new organising principle should be introduced on the lines
of the Council recommendation, and throughout giving facts and figures to drive home
splitting his infinitives was noticeable from first to last.

TARIFFS DO NOT HELP.
British boot manufacturers catering for the Irish Free State will be interested to learn
that the Government has appointed a Tariff Commission. The new body is to be com
posed of three civil servants, whose duty it will be to investigate claims for protection
and present recommendations to the Cabinet. This procedure is not approved by those
who are anxious to secure "safeguarding" without a preliminary public inquiry, but it is
consistent with the policy of the Free State Government. The latter has all along regarded
existing tariffs as experimental, and until it has been proved that they are beneficial to
the industries concerned it is not intended to impose any additional protective duties.
So far, according to an Irish correspondent, the duties already in existence have proved a
greater boon to the Minister of Finance than they have to consumers. For instance,
despite the tariff of 15 per cent. on boots and shoes, the imports of footwear
are said to be as large as ever, while the prices charged to wearers have
increased by 25 per cent. The Irish Free State Government is keenly alive to the
fact that the agricultural section of the community is hostile to the safeguarding of industries.
And in Ireland it is, in the last resort, the farmer's vote that will dominate the fiscal policy
of the country. - The Shoe and Leather Record, 4th June, 1926.

AGRICULTURE.
Conditions of Agricultural Labour in Russia.
Congress of Agricultural Workers.
During the Congress of the Russian Union of Agricultural and Forestry Workers,
which was recently held in Moscow, considerable discussion took place on conditions of
labour in agriculture.
Agricultural workers employed by the peasant proprietors are in general paid according
to the minimum rates fixed by the State, and not only do the peasant proprietors rarely
exceed these rates but often, especially when they feel themselves free of supervision,
they reduce them. Workers on Soviet farms also complain of being greatly underpaid.
Conditions of labour in general leave much to be desired. The non-observance of the
terms of collective agreements by the employers, who are subject to little or no control,
is a source of great hardship to the workers.
Woodcutters and other workers employed in the forests have in many cases never
even heard of the eight-hour day, and there is no legislation in force to cover them in this
respect. Agricultural labourers, for whom a prolongation of the working day beyond
eight hours is allowed by law, complain that the employers abuse this right and compel
them to work from 12 to 14 hours a day, and in some cases longer.
Nor is the position of workers on Soviet farms much better; numbers of skilled
agricultural workers are leaving these farms on account of the low wages paid.
HOUSING.
Complaints are rife on all sides concerning housing conditions. The workers are
forced to accept the accommodation offered them by the employers even when that
accommodation, in spite of the law, is practically uninhabitable.
GENERAL CONDITIONS.
Large numbers of agricultural workers, and the majority of the workers employed in
the forests, have no weekly rest-day, while the indemnity for annual holidays not taken
(as is generally the case) is never paid, although provided for by law.
One of the assessors' delegates stated that the assessors could not continue to work
under present conditions, a remark that was repeated by one of the forestry inspectors,
who added that each inspector, besides being required to do a thousand and one things
outside his competence, was entrusted with the supervision of about 200,000 hectares.
It was further stated that each of the agricultural experts and land assessors had
between 100 and 200 villages under his supervision, and could not possibly hope to carry
out the work assigned him. -Extract from Industrial and Labour Information, International
Labour Office, Monday, 24th May, 1926.

In this connection I would explain that we have very few strikes owing to our method
of Arbitration. This does not mean, however, that the workers case is in any way injured
on the contrary, by Conciliation and Arbitration, adjustments and settlements take place
day by day by National and Local Officials without the members being called upon to lose
any time, the following being an extract from the Rules controlling Arbitration Boards:-
Extracts from Standard Rules of Arbitration in connection
with the Trade.
The procedure in cases of disputes between an employer and his workmen should be
as nearly as possible the following :---
(a) The workmen shall first bring the matter before the employer or foremar.
(b) Should they not be able to agree, the representatives of the Employers ard
the Employers' Association and the representatives of the Workmen's
Union shall endeavour to settle the matter in dispute.
(c) If the representatives referred to in sub-section (b) are unable to arrange
terms, the Secretary of the Board shall forthwith advise the Committee of
Enquiry of the dispute.
(d) In the event of the Committee of Enquiry being unable to settle the dispute,
it shall be referred to the Board, and failing a decision, then to the Umpire
or Arbitrators, who shall be asked to give their decision within seven days
from the date of hearing.
When a dispute cannot be settled between an employer and his workmen, or the repre-
sentatives of both, the same rate of wages, or hours of labour, or conditions of employment
that obtained prior to the dispute, shall continue until a decision is given by the Committee
of enquiry, or Board, or Arbitrators, as the case may be. If there be no precedent as to
wages, hours, or conditions, a provisional resolution on these questions may be given by
the Committee of Enquiry, or Board, or Arbitrators, and must be observed, but without
prejudice to either party to the dispute.
