There must be no suspension of work, either at the instigation of the employers or
workmen, the main object of the Board being to prevent this. If any suspension of work

paid out from the Union Funds since our 1923 Conference in London, on the 21st 26th
May, to the Conference in Blackpool recently, for unemployment, no less a sum than
£133,107 19s. 6d. In addition, to keep members in benefit, the sum of £4,822 18s. 5d.
has been paid to the members in the form of paying their contributions over the same
period of time.

In addition, as showing the further help given to the members for the same period,
there has been paid to them from the Union Funds for Sickness, £96,594 16s. 4d. and for
Funeral Benefits £9,807. Thus in these four benefits the big sum of £244,332 14s. 3d.
has been paid to the members in the short period stated to help them in their time of need.
This is one of the very real and practical ways in which day by day the Union shows how
valuable an organisation it is to those belonging thereto.

In connection with the Repairing of Boots and Shoes we have what is known as a
Trade Board-that is a Board set up by the Ministry of Labour. This Board is composed
of representatives from the Unions, from the Employers, and by "Independent" members,
appointed by the Ministry. This Board has also done very good work in raising the
standard of wages, shortening hours of labour, regulating apprentices and generally
dealing with the business of the Repairing side of the industry. This Board's decision
have the force of law behind them, and if an employer refuses to comply with the con-
ditions laid down, an Inspector goes into the complaint, and if there is still refusal to
comply, the matter is reported to the Board and prosecutions may be ordered. During
last year 1,836 inspections were made and many cases of infringements of the law were
found out, with the result that many hundreds of pounds were ordered to be paid to workers
who had been improperly paid. Thus in this way also, the use of the organisation is proven
to the workers.

The Conference of the Union recently held at Blackpool was a very successful one
and marked another stage in development, apart from the general survey and instructions
to its officers, it decided upon a scheme of Superannuation for its full time officers and
staff, thereby helping to make the latter days of one free from those cares and worries
financially, which usually beset one. The Scheme is one wherein the Union intends to
put aside a sum for starting the Fund, and those who join up under the scheme will pay
into the same 3 per cent. of their salary, the Union contributing a like 3 per cent. from its
Fund; the age of retirement being 65. It is hoped by this method to meet a situation
which will enable one, when past their best, to have some leisure time in the evening of
life, with an assured income.

The International situation is one causing continual worry, nevertheless, we must not
only continue this work, but make it increasingly effective. In this connection we were
very pleased to see at our recent Conference, J. Simon, along with Dr. Schenk; his presence
was much appreciated, as also were his statements dealing with the International outlook
and the need for courage and steadiness in the face of the present situation. I would
like, therefore, to emphasise that it is imperative for a real understanding to be not only
arrived at internationally, but also that the spirit of real comradeship should be cultivated
along with the full determination to so act, one towards the other, that a policy shall be
pursued which, allowing for differences in method in the various countries, shall be such
a policy as will ensure that the lives of the workers be amply safeguarded and their em-
ployment be of such a character as to assure to them such a wage as will enable a reasonable
standard of life to be maintained. The need for this spirit of real comradeship is greater
than ever, having regard to the general outlook, whether in the political, social or economic
sphere. The world has greater need than ever for its resources to be so conserved and
thereby enable the clamant needs of the workers to be met. We cannot afford to have
division in our ranks, the cry for Unity must be real, and one which is shown by acts to
be sincere. The word "Unity" is a good word; it must not, however, be allowed to be
used as to really hinder unity and progress. Let us determine that for ourselves we will
act in a real spirit of unity and goodwill, making the world a fit place for all mankind to
dwell in, a place where Right and Justice will prevail, where the only wars to be waged
will be against sickness, against unjust treatment, against ignorance, vice and militarism,
and more and more the hand of fellowship shall be grasped in friendship and goodwill,
nevermore to be relaxed between all the peoples.

THE POSTMASTER-GENERAL (SIR WILLIAM MITCHELL-THOMSON): I make no com-

have secured peace in this trade for over a generation is the best testimony to their efficacy,

FINISHING STATEMENT.
UMPIRE'S AWARD.
IN THE MATTER OF THE ARBITRATION upon the Claim of the No. 1 Branch of the
Operatives' Union for extras in the Finishing Department in connection with Women's
Rodeo or Cossack High Leg Boots.
I, THE UNDERSIGNED, THE UMPIRE to whom the Arbitrators to the Board referred
the above claim for settlement or determination under Rule 7 of the Board,
having heard the representatives of both sides and duly considered the evidence
placed before me in relation to the claim, DECIDE AND AWARD:-
That an extra of Ten per cent. (10%) shall be added to the Statement Prices
for all operations done in the Finishing Department in connection with
Women's Rodeo or Cossack High Leg Boots.
AND I further determine that the extra fixed by this Award shall come into operation
and be paid from and including the working week commencing on the 20th, 21st or 22nd
May, 1926.
DATED this 26th day of May, 1926.
(Signed) W. A. NORTH,

LEATHER WORKERS. CONDITIONS IN THE LEATHER AND LEATHER GLOVE INDUSTRY.
No earlier period of unemployment had ever so fatal an influence on the trades grouped
by our Union than the existing one. Until October, 1925, unemployment and short time
were moderate, since that time they increased immensely.
WORKERS UNEMPLOYED AND ON SHORT TIME, 31ST MARCH, 1926. In Tanneries:
On Short Time, 16,089; Unemployed, 8,179. In the Tawing and Dyeing Trade: On
Short Time, 515; Unemployed, 807. In the Leather Glove Industry: On Short Time,
2,093; Unemployed, 1,792.
Two-thirds of workers unemployed or on short time in the Glove Industry were females.
This widespread unemployment and short time was of great disadvantage for the
financial position of the Union. Our income decreased, in addition we had to pay large
sums as out-of-work benefit.
This industrial depression also stopped the development of the Union as to member
ship, as the following figures show:-
ANALYSIS OF MEMBERSHIP, 31ST DECEMBER, 1925. -Males, 30,907; Females, 8,046;

HAMBURG.
On 12th to 15th April the Union Conference was held at Hamburg. Blum reported
on Union work during the last three years. He pointed out that the Union had to surmount
enormous difficulties. Since the exchange rate has become stable the exportation of
leather goods has decreased to a minimum. Consequently unemployment is as widespread
as ever, especially in the first quarter of 1926. The percentages of members unemployed
and on short time were:-

GENERAL NEWS.
THE BALKAN TRADE UNION CONFERENCE.
The Balkans have been for centuries the battlefield where the imperialistic interests
collided and innumerable conflicts and wars occurred, involving their peoples in continual
revolutions. This is an essential cause for the backward state of industry and civilisation
there.
compared with pre-war times. In addition the Trade Unions still existing are split into
The number of organised workers has considerably decreased in the Balkan countries,
to push forward "the World Revolution" there from the east to the west, tried to win
The Communists being of opinion they would be able to forward their purposes and
the masses of workers who joined the Trade Unions after the Great War. They easily
succeeded, indeed, for these workers were without any industrial and political education.
The Communist tactics lead to all sorts of disturbances and conflicts with the authorities
the Unions were suppressed, the leaders imprisoned. Consequently, most of the workers
became indifferent again and the organisations were unable to accomplish their tasks.
How fatal the Communist tactics were, results from the fact that in 1920 there was in
Yugo-Slavia one united organisation and about 200,000 organised workers. In 1924
there were only 28,000 in two split organisations. Conditions are similar in Bulgaria,
Greece and Roumania.
From these thoughts the Balkan Conference sprung, called by the I.F.T.U. and held
in Sofia. It was preceded by a meeting in Belgrad, where the directive rules for the
Sofia Conference should be discussed. It was agreed that only delegates representing
the Amsterdam platform should be admitted. On the other hand the representatives
of the Moscow orientation should not only be entitled to attend the Conference as fraternal
delegates, but the several Commissions too.
There were represented:-Bulgaria, by 10 delegates; Yugo-Slavia, by 10 delegates;
Roumania, 3 delegates; Greece, 3 delegates.

347
The Hungarian Federation of Trade Unions was represented by two, the Czech
Federation by one delegate. Vice-President Mertens and Secretary Sassenbach repre-
sented the I.F.T.U. In addition the following International Secretaries attended the
Conference: Smit, Employees' International; Fimmen, Transport Workers' Inter-
national; Wilhelm, Food and Drink Trades; and Simon, Shoe and Leather International.
The Trade Union Centres of the four Balkan countries had presented reports which
described the trade conditions there and the position of the organisations. From these
reports the delegates were able to become acquainted with the Balkan conditions.
After the opening of the Conference three Commissions were set: One to settle the
demands regarding the right of coalition; the second to work out the directive rules for the
Trade Unions; the third to lay down the industrial demands.
The International Secretaries were principally interested in the work of the Com
mission II., which presented the following two resolutions:
PRINCIPLES OF TRADE UNION ACTIVITIES.
Trade Union organisation is a necessity for the manual and non-manual workers in all
countries where capitalism rules.
The task of the trade union movement is to protect and promote the economical
social interests of the workers, to strengthen the national and international solidarity
of the working class, and to support any action, both nationally and internationally, in
the struggle against their exploitation.
The most immediate task of the Trade Unions in the Balkans is to improve the material
and cultural position of the workers by:----
a. Shortening the working hours.
b. Raising the wage rates.
c. Creating social institutions such as insurance against illness, old age, un-
employment benefit, &c.
d. Raising the intellectual level of the workers.
Strikes should in general be undertaken only for economic reasons and only after
most careful consideration.
Efforts to establish a more equitable social order are primarily the task of the political
parties. It is desirable that the class-conscious worker belong both to the political and
the trade union movement. Political strife, however, should not be introduced into the
trade unions.
ON UNITY.
This Balkan Trade Unions Conference urges all trade unions of the Balkans where
unity has not yet been established, but which accept the policy of the I.F.T.U., to enter
into negotiations at the earliest possible moment under the auspices of the I.F.T.U. with
the object of achieving unity. The negotiations shall be conducted separately in each
country, and shall have as their object the formation of a single National Trade Union
Centre.
The other two Commissions also worked out respec tive resolutions which were adopted
by the Conference after thorough discussion.
In connection with my visit to the Balkan Conference, I took care to have conversa-
tions with several officers of Leather Workers' Unions. I am very sorry to have to state
that in all these countries the Leather Workers' Unions are very much weakened by
splitting, sometimes they are mere names. On the other hand I am glad to be able to state
that both orientations understood the urgent necessity to create united organisations.
It is understood that I tried to support this opinion.
In Sofia I addressed a Conference of tanners, attended by about 120 persons, reporting
on the position of the movement and the International.
At Belgrad I made a rather disagreeable discovery. You all know that the Paris
Conference was attended by a representative of Yugo-Slavia. I now was told that this
J. Manojlovich, who was registered as a tanner, was no leather worker at all; but an
employee of the COMMUNIST METAL WORKERS' UNION in Yugo-Slavia. This shows anew
how the Communists work. How can mutual confidence grow when such deceiving
methods are continually applied.
Let us hope that the relations I established with our colleagues in the Balkans will
bring about good results.
Yours,
J. SIMON.

STATE TREATMENT OF TUBERCULOSIS.
A Memorandum prepared by the Advisory Committee on Public Health.
Thirty-five years ago one person in seven died of tuberculosis in England and Wales,
to-day only one in fourteen so dies. In 1800, 183 deaths from tuberculosis of all forms
occurred per 100,000 persons living; to-day only about 100 per 100,000. Fifty years ago
240 per 100,000 died every year from consumption; to day only 80. The age at death in
pulmonary tuberculosis has gradually advanced, especially in the towns, so that now the
commonest age at which death occurs from consumption is between forty and fifty. This
possibly means that more efficient treatment applied earlier has an effect to carry on to the
later ages a considerable proportion of the persons affected. The total number of deaths
in England and Wales from tuberculosis of all forms in 1000 was 61,302; in 1924, 41, 103.
Notifications of all forms of tuberculosis in 1913 in England and Wales were 117,139, and
in 1924 81,158.
The anti-tuberculosis measures undertaken by the State, which began about twenty
vears ago, are probably acting better, or as well as anything else, in bringing modern
medical science and a large understanding of hygiene to the people as a whole. Hence such
schemes can be credited in large measure with the improved death rates. Health pro-
paganda and the educational value of the sanatorium have done much to broaden the
appreciation of the open window and of adequate bodily amd mental rest. In other lands
where the State has intervened to provide treatment, the decline in the death rate from
tuberculosis is marked; whereas in such places as Japan, where little State action has
taken place, the reverse holds good. Labour Bulletin, June, 1926.
[The above statement is confirmation of statements made in earlier years that with
proper treatment consumption can be prevented. Therefore, insist upon the municipal
authorities putting into operation their full powers, and thereby still further lower the
sickness and death rate. - E.L.P., G.S.]
WAGES IN SOUTH AFRICA.
Government Board to Hold Investigation.
It is notified in the "Union of South Africa Government Gazette" of 21st May that
the Government Wage Board appointed under the Act passed last year is about to in-
vestigate and report to the Minister of Labour upon the wages, hours and conditions of
labour of persons employed in the leather industries and persons employed in the packing,
despatch and delivery of the products of such industries in the Union of South Africa,
who are not subject to the provisions of the Industrial Conciliation Act, 1924.
Employers and employees, or registered trade unions or employers' organisations
affected, or likely to be affected, by such investigation, are notified that they will be afforded
the opportunity of making representations, either orally or in writing, on any matter
covered by the enquiry. Any written representations or notifications of oral representa-
tions are to be in the hands of the Registrar of the Wage Board by 21st June.
The final paragraph of the Government Notice is of a premonitory nature. It reads :-
"The attention of employees and employers is drawn to section 13 of the Wage Act,
which makes it a criminal offence, subject to substantial penalties, for an employer to
dismiss or otherwise injure an employee for giving evidence or information on matters
dealt with under the Act. In addition to such penalties as the Court may impose upon an
employer under this section, it may award to the employee such damage as he can prove
that he has suffered through the action of the employer." -Shoe and Leather News, 17th
June, 1926.
TARIFFS.
Textile Mill Owners Deceive Congress.
Washington, 12th June.-The owners of the textile industry of the United States
begged Congress to give them a high protective tariff on imported textiles so that they
could pay high wages and then deliberately pocketed outrageous profits themselves and
pauperised the workers, according to Edward F. McGrady, legislative representative of the
American Federation of Labour, in a statement made before the Senate Committee on
Labour in support of the resolution for an investigation of the wages paid in tariff-pro-
tected industries.
"The textile workers of New England are being pauperised," McGrady said. "These
mills broke their word to Congress, yes, to the Republican Party.
"They were given a high protective tariff so that they could take care of their
workers as American workers should be employed, but they did nothing."-American
Federation of Labour News, 12th June, 1926.

SELLING BOOTS UNDER COST.
of the firm of Messrs. Phillips (Norwich) Ltd., the Shoe and Leather News
We have no desire to anticipate the work of the liquidators or of their committee.
The creditors at the statutory meeting were unanimous in expressing the view that the
company's transactions required the strictest investigation.

We agree, and if in the process it be found possible to make the various members of
the Phillips' group, who are liable to the company, repay to the utmost of their capacity
the last penny they owe it, we believe it is only a measure of elementary justice to the
company's creditors that the full power of the law should be called into operation for
that purpose."

Referring to the same subject in the Shoe and Leather Record for the 11th inst., the
Editor says :-
"The Company which has now gone into liquidation was registered in 1919, and it
had a nominal capital of 40,000 shares of £1 each, all of which were issued. How much
real money was paid into the business is not clear. It was a family company, and most
of its tangible assets seem to have been mortgaged for a considerable time. Meanwhile,
the directors were drawing substantial sums from the business, which they should have
known were not being earned out of profits. To account for the loss which was made
creditors are asked to believe that goods were SOLD AT A LOSS OF 4S. A PAIR, SPREAD OVER
A LARGE TURNOVER. An analysis of the costings showed wages at 42 per cent. on selling
prices, which is very far above the average of any shoe factory I know. If the directors
could be examined in bankruptcy, as they might be if they were not protected by the
Companies Acts, a few searching questions might be directed to them regarding their
payments on wages account."

The Leather World, 10th June, 1926, says:-
"The disclosures made at the recent meeting of the creditors of Phillips (Norwich)
Ltd., support the view that we have long held, that the multiple shoe concerns often
profit at the expense of the manufacturer. In this case, it was revealed that a loss of four
shillings per pair was made on no less than 228,946 pairs of shoes-and from a perusal
of the list of creditors, and the remote prospect they have of getting any sort of substantial
dividend, it seems certain the cheap shoes produced by the firm means that the leather
trade has helped the buyers to a biggish gift. It was, in fact, stated at the meeting that
prices of goods supplied to multiple houses had been cut in order to obtain their support.'
Such support, however, is a costly business for the suppliers of the material to make shoes,
and the admission throws rather a lurid light on the way in which struggling firms are
handicapped by the methods of the big shoe buyers."

INTERNATIONAL LABOUR CONFERENCE.
Opening of Ninth Session.
The ninth Session of the International Labour Conference of the League of Nations
opens in Geneva to-day.
The International Labour Conference meets annually and each of the 56 states (includ-
ing Germany) which are members of the International Labour Organisation is entitled
to send four delegates, two representing the Government, and one each the employers
and workers.
This year two consecutive Sessions of the Conference are being held, the eighth which
has just closed being of a general character and the ninth being devoted exclusively to
maritime questions. Among the subjects to be particularly discussed are the codification
of rules relating to seamen's articles of agreement and the inspection of the working con-
ditions of seamen.
The British delegates to the ninth Session are:-
Government. Viscount Burnham, who has already been President of the Inter-
national Labour Conference in 1921 and 1922. Mr. Humbert Wolfe, Principal Assist-
ant Secretary, Ministry of Labour.
Employers. Mr. Cuthbert Laws, General Manager of the Shipping Federation
and Member of the Joint Maritime Commission of the International Labour Organisa-
tion.
Workers. Mr. Arthur Pugh, President of the General Council of Trades Union
Congress.
GENERAL COUNCIL OF THE TRADES UNION CONGRESS AND THE
MINERS' FEDERATION OF GREAT BRITAIN.
JOINT STATEMENT.
The General Council of the Trades Union Congress had called a Conference for 25th
June, 1926, for the purpose of reporting to its affiliated bodies on its policy in the recent
national stoppage. In consequence, however, of the attacks which the Government and
the employers are making to reduce the standard of life of the workpeople, and in particular
the decision of the Government to pass legislation for increasing the hours of labour in
the mining industry, in direct opposition to the Report of the Coal Commission, the General
Council and the representatives of the Miners' Federation of Great Britain have fully
discussed the situation created by the Government action, and have mutually decided
that it is in the interests of the Miners and the movement as a whole that the Conference
called for 25th June, 1926, should be postponed until after the mining dispute is settled.
The General Council and the Miners' Federation consider this imperative so that a united
policy may be adopted to resist to the fullest possible extent the Government's action.
It must be clearly understood that neither the General Council nor the Miners' Federation
desire to postpone unduly the Conference, but they regard the design of the Government
and the coal-owners to increase hours of labour as being of such fundamental importance
to the working-class movement both nationally and internationally as to make it essential
to concentrate upon the present position rather than to devote attention to past events.
The General Council and the Miners' Federation regard it as of the greatest importance
at this juncture that all sections and parties should avoid statements, either in speech
or writing, which create friction, misunderstanding and divert attention from the purpose
in view.
The General Council and the Miners' Federation feel assured that the affiliated
organisations and rank and file of the movement generally will appreciate the importance
of this declaration, and in the circumstances with which the movement is now faced will
accord this agreed policy their fullest approval and support.
The foregoing statement was signed on behalf of the General Council of the Trades
Union Congress :-
ARTHUR PUGH, Chairman,
A. B. SWALES, Vice-Chairman.
W. M. CITRINE, Acting Secretary.
And on behalf of the Miners' Federation of Great Britain :-
HERBERT SMITH, President.
THOMAS RICHARDS, Vice-President.
W. P. RICHARDSON, Treasurer.
A. J. Cook, Secretary.

BOOT AND SHOE REPAIRING TRADE BOARD (GREAT BRITAIN).
Report of Proceedings against a Boot Repairer.
At the Prestatyn Petty Sessions, on 11th March, 1926, Arthur Langley, Boot Repairer,
Caradoc Road, Prestatyn, was summoned for paying less than the General Minimum
Piece Rates fixed by the Trades Board.
Mr. Langley was inspected in February and June, 1925, and on each of these occasions
it was discovered that workers employed by him had been paid at less than the General
Minimum Piece Rates fixed by the Board. There were difficulties in the way of a pro-
secution on these occasions on account of the imperfect character of the piecework records,
but he was warned as to the consequences that would attend any further infraction. In
October, 1925, a further inspection was made and it was found that two workers were under-
paid, and that arrears amounting to £7 7s. od. had accrued since the date of the inspection
in June, 1925.
Proceedings were instituted against Mr. Langley in respect of two charges of under-
payment. He pleaded not guilty, and stated that the workers were inexperienced and
not worth the Trade Board minimum piece rates. He was convicted and ordered to pay,
within 14 days, the following amounts:-Fine of £2 on each charge, £4; Arrears, £7 7s. od.;
Costs totalling £4 5s. 6d. Total, £15 12s. 6d.
BOOT TRADES' ASSOCIATION CONFERENCE.
At the Annual Conference of the National Federation of Boot Trades' Association,
held in Blackpool during the week commencing 14th June, the following resolution was
passed by the delegates.
Mr. W. C. Alderton moved:
THE SHODDY EVIL
"That in view of the great volume of evidence in the possession of the Federation,
received from Medical Officers of Health, school medical officers and other public authorities
in all parts of the country of the dangers to health-especially to children-arising from
the manufacture and sale of shoddy footwear, this conference registers a strong protest
against the continuance of this trade and directs the executive council to ask the President
of the Board of Trade to receive a deputation from the Federation, and to hear repre-
sentations on the urgent need for Government action in some form or another to restrict,
in the interests of public health, the manufacture and sale of shoddy footwear."
He went on to say they intended to follow the resolution up very vigorously, and it
was hoped that in the near future the Government would take this matter up in a serious
manner. Mr. Bellsham seconded. He suggested that a petition would be better than
lobbying or approaching a department.
Mr. Mundy supported the motion. He had taken the matter up in 1904. Things
were better now, but they still had too much shoddy.
Mr. Talent (Leeds) thought it would be better to act in conjunction with the other
sections of the trade. Mr. Alderton, in reply, said the manufacturers and the operatives
had approached the Minister, and had been told he wanted to hear what the distributors
thought about it.

Nearly three-quarters (423) of all the final settlements were effected by direct arrange-
ments or negotiations between the parties or their representatives without the intervention
of third parties. Only ten disputes were settled by arbitration. Nevertheless, as the
chief dispute of the year (that in the wool textile industry) was settled through the medium
of a Court of Investigation (the parties having agreed to be bound by the recommendations
of the Court), the number of workpeople directly involved in disputes settled by direct
negotiations and by arbitration respectively was approximately the same, or 44 per cent.
of all workpeople directly involved in settled disputes. Seven per cent. of all settlements,
involving seven per cent. of all workpeople, were effected by means of conciliation, in most
instances through the instrumentality of an officer of the Ministry of Labour. The largest
dispute in this group (involving over 15,000 employees of London bookbinding and printing
firms) was, however, settled through the agency of the Joint Industrial Council. Return
to work on the employers' terms without negotiations was recorded in the case of 12 per
cent. of the disputes, involving three per cent. of the workpeople. Of the 44 disputes
settled by methods other than those mentioned above, strikers were replaced by other
workpeople in the case of 29 disputes, the strike of seamen, of whom 5,000 are estimated
to have been involved in British ports, being the only case of any magnitude which was
so concluded; in the case of three small disputes the establishments or departments
concerned were closed down. The Ministry of Labour Gazette, June, 1926.

HOUSING??

Eight Living in One Room.

Appalling Conditions at Village Near Ashby.

Appalling overcrowding conditions in the village of Blackfordby, near Ashby-de-la-
Zouch, have been reported to the Ashby Rural Council by the Sanitary Inspector, who
states that a small bedroom, eight feet long, seven feet wide, and six feet nine inches high,
was occupied by a man, his wife, and a girl aged six.

The larger bedroom, 13 feet long and II feet six inches wide, was occupied by a man
and wife, two girls 14 and seven, and four boys, aged nine, six, four and three years, making
a total of eight persons in one room.

Both rooms were badly lighted and ventilated, and one daughter had
already been sent to a sanatorium suffering from tuberculosis.

It was stated that the man with the larger family had been turned out of an Ashby
Council house, and the problem was what would happen if the family were disturbed
from their present abode, suffering as they were from consumption.
It was decided to serve the owner of the house with a notice to abate the overcrowding.
- Leicester Mercury, 9th June, 1926.

HOSIERY INQUIRY.
The Demand for British Goods.
The Board of Trade Committee, which is inquiring into the application for a duty on
imported hosiery and knitwear, met again at 5 Old Palace Yard, yesterday, when further
evidence was called Sir James Calder presided. Mr. Barnard Faraday appeared for
the applicants, and Mr. Entwistle for the appellants.
Mr. Arthur Burns, departmental manager of F. W. Millington (1920) Limited, Dale
Street, Manchester, said that English manufacturers NEED FEAR GERMAN COMPETITION
LESS THAN THAT OF ANY OTHER COUNTRY TO-DAY. Since the war he himself had paid
visits to various Continental countries, including Holland, Belgium, France, Germany,
Czecho-slovakia, and Austria, and had just returned from a visit to those districts in
Germany where most of the German hosiery and knitwear were made. It was no exaggera-
tion to say that the German manufacturers were in a very bad way indeed. In Germany
at the present time there were upwards of 500 bankruptcies each week, and the mills and
factories which had to close down in the underwear and hosiery-making districts could be
numbered in hundreds.
The lost trade in woollen underwear, particularly for women, he held, was due not to
foreign competition, but to the popularity of silk and artificial silk. ANOTHER FACTOR
CONTRIBUTING TO BAD TRADE WAS THE HIGH PRICES CHARGED BY RETAIL ESTABLISHMENTS
FOR HOSIERY AND KNITWEAR. A GREAT STIMULUS WOULD BE GIVEN TO TRADE IF SHOP-
KEEPERS WOULD BE SATISFIED WITH REASONABLE PROFITS. The public would be able
to buy more. Complaints on this score were heard on all sides among manufacturers,
the witness said, and he suggested that publicity would do good.
Mr. G. R. Timmis, hosiery buyer for Messrs. J. and N. Phillips & Co. Limited, Manches-
ter, said his firm did a much bigger trade in British goods than in foreign before the duty
was put on. His purchases in 1925 were approximately 70 per cent. British and 30 per
cent. foreign. The ratio of British purchases was increasing every month. The British
manufacturers were simply concentrating on the most profitable trade and leaving the
foreigner to supply low grade goods.
Mr. H. R. Burns, buyer for Messrs. J. & N. Phillips, gave the names of four British
manufacturing firms which, he said, had concentrated on cotton and art silk goods, and
could now beat the German and the Swiss manufacturers except in the very lowest qualities,
for which there was only a small demand. In 1913 his purchases of underwear were 45,
per cent. British and 55 per cent. foreign ; in 1925 they were 80 per cent. British and 20.
per cent. foreign. The Times, 4th June, 1926.
SHOE MANUFACTURER'S BEQUEST.
£12,000 Legacy for Stafford Infirmary.
Under the will of the late Mr. David Hollin, a former boot and shoe manufacturer im
the town, a legacy of £12,000 has been left to Stafford Infirmary for the purpose of erecting
and, as far as possible equipping and endowing, a "Nurses' Home," to be called the "David
Hollin Nurses' Home." The bequest is conditional upon the erection of the Home being
completed in two years after the death of testator's widow, Mrs. Emma Hollin, who passed
away on Thursday last at her residence, "Highfield Manor," Newport Road, Stafford, at
the age of 84.-Shoe and Leather News, 6th, 13th, 20th May, 1926.
FREE STATE IMPORTS MORE.
Two years ago the Free State Government imposed a 15 per cent. tariff on imported
boots and shoes, but the imports, instead of showing a decrease as a result are increasing.
substantially. For the whole of the year 1925 the imports of boots and shoes into the
Free State exceeded those for 1924 by 48,540 dozen pairs. For the first quarter of this
year there was an increase of 934 dozen pairs, and in the month of March there was an
increase, as compared with the corresponding month in 1925, of 9,626 dozen pairs.
The value of the imports in March was £247,723 against £236,307 for the corresponding
month last year. The value of the hides and skins exported from the Free State in March
last was £34,414 against £56,526 in March, 1925.-Shoe and leather News, 6th, 13th, 20th
May, 1926.

THE EIGHTH INTERNATIONAL LABOUR CONFERENCE.
The Eighth International Labour Conference opened at Geneva on May 25th, 1926,
thirty-seven States being represented. His Excellency Mgr. Nolens-Chief Government
Delegate of the Netherlands was elected Chairman.

BRITISH DELEGATION.
Government Delegates. Mr. Humbert Wolfe, Principal Assistant Secretary, Ministry
of Labour.
Employers' Delegate. Mr. G. E. Baker, Assistant Secretary Mercantile Marine
Department, Board of Trade.
Workers' Delegate. Mr. R. Snedden, National Confederation of Employers'
Organisations.
Mr. Arthur Pugh, J.P., Chairman of the General Council
of the Trades Union Congress.

Decisions of the Conference.

(1) SIMPLIFICATION OF EMIGRATION REGULATIONS.

The Conference adopted
(a) A Draft Convention providing that the inspection of emigrants on board
ship should be undertaken by not more than one Government which should
be, as a general rule, the Government whose flag the ship flies. The in
spector should be in no way dependent on or connected with the shipowner
or company, and should concern himself solely with regulations for the
protection and welfare of emigrants on board. He should report to the
Government whose flag the ship flies on the termination of each voyage,
copies of this report being sent to other Governments concerned, if desired.
Voting 73 to 35.
(The British Government and workers' delegate voting in favour;
the British employer against.)
(b) A Recommendation providing that, where 15 or more women or girl emigrants
are travelling unaccompanied by a responsible person, a woman inspector
should be placed in charge of their welfare.
Voting 89 to 19.
(The British Government and workers' delegate voting in favour;
the British employer against.)
(c) A Resolution recommending that, where 50 or more emigrants speaking a
language other than of the country whose flag the ship flies are on board
an emigrant vessel, an interpreter shall be provided.
Voting 48 to 37.
(2) ENFORCEMENT OF CONVENTIONS. - Article 408.
The Conference adopted a Resolution providing machinery for a more adequate
examination of the Annual Reports submitted by Governments on the enforcement of
ratified conventions. (Article 408 of the Peace Treaty.)
The Governing Body is requested to appoint for a period of two or three years a
small committee of six or eight experts in international law and international labour
conditions which shall examine these reports in detail; and after requesting such additional
information as is required from the Governments concerned, shall forward an explanatory
statement as to the methods of enforcement in each country to the Director of the Office.
This report shall be submitted each year to a special committee appointed by the Annual
Conference from among its delegates.
Voting 66 to 36.

(3) DOUBLE DISCUSSION PROCEDURE.
The Conference adopted a Resolution proposing an amendment of the Standing Orders
to allow of a double discussion of the terms of each Convention adopted to avoid unnecessary
delay in ratification due to small faults of drafting of the Conventions. It recommends
that each question placed on the Agenda shall be discussed in general principle at one
Conference on the basis of a comparative survey on the existing law and practice on the
subject prepared. A questionnaire on the subject shall then be drawn up in the light of
---

---
Here is the extracted text:
361
this discussion and circulated to the Governments in the intervening year. In conformity
with their replies the office shall draw up a Draft Convention for submission to the succeed-
ing Conference.
Adopted unanimously.

(4) HOURS OF WORK.
The Conference adopted a Resolution declaring the agreement reached at "the Con-
ference of Governments held in London with a view to the ratification of the Eight Hours
Convention" to be " a progressive step," and whilst expressing no opinion as to the inter-
pretations of the Washington Convention reached on that occasion, urging the Director
of the I.L. Office to continue his endeavours to obtain speedy ratification of the Convention
by the States' Signatories to the agreement, as it appeared that as far as these Powers
were concerned objections to ratification no longer existed.
Voting 64 to 21.

(5) UNEMPLOYMENT.
The Conference adopted a Resolution expressing the hope that the forthcoming Inter-
national Economic Conference would discover effective methods of mitigating unemploy-
ment.
It requested the I.L.O. to increase its efforts to secure adoption of the measures
against unemployment adopted at previous sessions of the Conference (communication by
Governments of information concerning unemployment; creation and extension of un-
employment insurance systems and admission of foreigners to these systems on conditions
of reciprocity; creation and extension of public employment exchange systems, placing
the recruiting of foreign workers solely under their care; and the organisation of public
works so as to counteract fluctuations of private business).
It decided to place unemployment insurance on the agenda of the 1928 Conference.
It recommended that the work of the Joint Committee on Economic Crises should
be actively continued with a view to the development of the series of statistics known as
"Economic Barometers" with a view to studying the best methods of preventing trade
fluctuations leading to periodic crises of unemployment.
Voting 78 to 0.

(6) SCIENTIFIC MANAGEMENT.
The Conference adopted a Resolution requesting the I.L. Office to devote special
attention to questions of the scientific organisation of industry and to carry on its studies
actively in this sphere.
Voting 84 to 1.

(7) NATIVE LABOUR.
The Conference adopted a Resolution welcoming the decision of the Governing Body
to undertake an enquiry into conditions of native labour, and hoping that, as a result of
the labours of the Committee of Experts which it was proposed to establish it would be
possible to present a preliminary report on the matter to the Conference of 1927.
Voting 78 to 3.

(8) NATIONAL CORRESPONDENT IN INDIA.
The Conference adopted a Resolution requesting the Governing Body to come to a
decision as to the appointment of a national correspondent in India as soon as possible.
Voting 79 to 0.

(9) DIRECTOR'S REPORT.
During the debate on the Director's Report it was announced
(a) that Belgium had ratified unconditionally the Washington Hours of Work
Convention.
(b) that Japan intended to enforce the terms of her Factory Amendment Act
of 1921 as from July, 1926.

(10) DELEGATIONS.
One hundred and thirty-one delegates were present including 71 Government dele-
gates, 29 employers and 31 workers, with 8 substitute delegates and 106 advisers. The
number of incomplete delegations was 6, a smaller number than at any preceding Con-
ference.

EMIGRATION AND IMMIGRATION PROBLEMS.
Important Findings of World Congress.
Migration Offices. How Every State Could Help in Solution.
As a result of four days' deliberations, the World Congress on Migration came to
important decisions at the Holborn Restaurant, London, yesterday-decisions which will
demonstrate to the world that Labour is solid in its determination to see that the people
who make wealth shall enjoy the fruits of the earth.
It was emphasised that emigration is a phenomenon which is inevitable as a result of
Capitalism, and that all Governments should provide for the solution of migration problems
in the manner best conducive to international peace and goodwill.

Freedom of Migration.
In the earlier days of the proceedings, considerable divergence of views had been
expressed as to the right of people of all nationalities to go where they willed, and the
fundamental principle of Labour in this respect had been emphasised ; but at the con-
cluding session yesterday Mr. F. Adler, secretary of the Second International, pointed out
that a proposed resolution demanding complete freedom of migration had been dropped in
order to secure unanimity.
Dr. Evat (Australia), who had previously made a strong speech against absolute
freedom of migration, said Australia and Canada and the other new countries would help
in the effort to improve the conditions of the workers throughout the world.

Steps Forward.
The resolutions adopted by the Congress proposed that every country should establish
a State Migration Office, on which the trade union organisations should have adequate
representation.
In addition, it was determined that an International Migration Office, also with
adequate trade union representation, should be created within the framework of the Inter-
national Labour Office, to draw up international conventions and recommendations con-
cerning migration and to provide reliable information on the subject.

The habit of Governments and private agencies of persuading people
to migrate was discussed and it was resolved that all propaganda in this
direction should be abolished.
Another resolution demanded that all Labour bodies should co-operate to secure for
immigrant workers complete equality of treatment in all forms of social insurance
established by law.
This resolution had particular reference to the fact that in New Zealand, natives are
barred from the enjoyment of old age pensions.—Herald, 26th June, 1926.

FOOD.
At Ist June the average level of retail prices of the principal articles of food was about
the same as at Ist May. Bacon, fish, flour, bread, sugar and potatoes were all slightly
dearer than a month earlier, but these upward movements were counterbalanced by
decreases in the average prices of milk, butter and cheese.
As a net result of all the changes recorded, the average increase over the level of
July, 1914, in the retail prices (in Great Britain and Northern Ireland) of the articles of
food included in these statistics was about 58 per cent. at 1st June, the same as at Ist May,
as compared with 66 per cent. at the corresponding date in 1925.—The Ministry of Labour
Gazette, June, 1926.

INTERNATIONAL FEDERATION OF TRADE UNIONS,

Important Statement by the Belgian Minister of Labour
on the Eight-Hour Day.

THURSDAY, 17TH JUNE, 1926.

Wanters, the Belgian Minister of Labour and Industry, who has long consci-
ously aimed at the unconditional ratification of the Washington Convention for the eight-ho
ur day, made a remarkable speech on the working of the eight-hour day and the consequence
of ratification generally on the occasion of the general debate which took place in the
Belgian Chamber before the ratification was agreed to. In the course of his speech he
made the following remarks :-

It has frequently been maintained that the eight-hour day is injurious to production.
If we ask ourselves whether there is a single industry in which conditions have been worsened
as a result of the existing eight-hour day in this country, the answer is that production in
Belgium is generally on the upgrade. Our industrial activities were never so extensive
as at the present moment, and our agricultural production is also growing. We have the
smallest unemployment of any country (4.5 per cent.). In short, the application of the
eight-hour day has not had the results feared in one quarter or another. It is therefore
not necessary to wait for the conclusions of another enquiry. We know in advance that
there are arguments both for and against. It must, however, be pointed out particularly
that there are elements among the industrialists still in a state of mind of complete apath-
who do not take steps to introduce improvements into their concerns. These are the people
introduced the eight-hour day immediately after the war and adapted themselves to the
new conditions.

When industrialists grasp the fact that the eight-hour day, like compulsory education
is here to stay, they will have to turn their attention increasingly to the improvement of
their works. The eight-hour day therefore is not a danger, it is a factor in social
progress.

Further, we must not neglect to take into account the moral and intellectual position
of the workers. They can only produce to the extent that they are enlightened and
educated. From the social standpoint we are concerned in their fitness for and under-
standing of their trade. They cannot improve in this respect if the length of the working
day leaves them no time for study.

It is a matter of importance that the number of those attending trade and technical
schools is increasingly notably, while the number of public-houses has decreased by 110,000.
This marks a long step forward.

It is noticeable what efforts the workers are prepared to make to get better houses,
and to have them better furnished ; how libraries are being built, and how the circulations
of our newspapers increase in proportion as the workers become better educated. All of
this is largely the result of the eight-hour day law. Never before has a legal enactment
worked out in so gratifying a manner as this law, whether from the economic, the social
or the moral standpoint.

The ratification of the Washington Convention runs for ten years from 1st June,
1921. Countries such as Czecho-Slovakia, in a more difficult situation than ourselves,
have preceded us in setting a good example. The Convention does not impose upon us
greater obligations than those already enforced under our eight-hour law. This alone is
a sufficient reason why we should proceed. The Ministers of Labour at the London Con-
ference undertook to submit to their parliaments Bills in accordance with the Washington
Convention, and we know that in Germany the matter is already under way.

Special conditions were duly taken account of at the London meeting. Nobody
supposes that a single human being in time of great need, as, for instance, floods or drought,
&c., would fail to do everything possible to come to the aid of his fellow creatures. The
Act includes certain exceptions it is true, and one member has already charged me with
frequently forgetting the interests of the workers. One must, however, not leave certain
needs out of account. If the workers are going to oppose exceptions required in the interests
of industry, then I must tell them plainly and openly that they are wrong.

It is our duty to ratify the Convention. It will be a significant step forward in this
era of social progress if all people of goodwill will do their best to promote good relations
between employers and workers, and to raise the level of our economic life.

BOOT AND SHOE INDUSTRY.
Employment in this industry was poor, especially in the heavy boot trade, and worse
than a year ago; and in nearly all localities a great deal of short time was worked. Diffi-
culties of transport in some centres, together with a fairly widespread curtailment of power
supplies, restricted employment. As has been the case for many months, employment
was worse in the heavy boot factories than in those producing medium and light footwear.
The percentage of workpeople unemployed, as indicated by the unemployment books
lodged at Employment Exchanges, was 13.6 on 21st June, as compared with 19.5 on 24th
May, and with 10.2 on 22nd June, 1925.

with the corresponding week of the previous month and a decrease of 1.5 per cent. as
compared with June, 1925. The total wages paid by these firms showed a decrease of
2.7 per cent. in June, 1926, as compared with the previous month and a decrease of 8.6
per cent, as compared with June, 1925.

HALF-YEARLY STATEMENT OF ACCOUNTS.
The Half-yearly Statement of Accounts is presented herewith. It will
be seen that the Union expenditure has exceeded the Income by £22,744 5s. 4d.
This is due to four causes :-
1. The Grants to the Trade Union Congress Relief Fund in connection
with the Coal Mining Industry and the General Stoppage, and the
developments arising therefrom.
2. The abnormal amount of Unemployed Pay.
3. The expenses of the Biennial Conference, and
4. The double contributions to the Labour Party from the Political
Fund.
We, nevertheless, feel that under the circumstances our financial position
is one that is fairly satisfactory. The Sick Fund shows a small gain; this
however, is brought about by the interest all being allocated to this Fund.
This method which has been adopted to put the fund into its present position,
is one which from now will be altered, and the interest will be divided up as
between the funds in their fair proportions.
The note appended to the Auditor's Report is being dealt with by Circular
No. 375, and branches will act according to the instructions named in such
circular.

INDUSTRIAL AND POLITICAL.
The Industrial and Political situation continues to be overshadowed by
the Mining situation; despite efforts made during the month to bring the same
to a conclusion, such efforts have not been successful; in fact, the Government
have passed into law an Eight Hours Bill in connection with Mining. This
has really aggravated and intensified the opposition of the Miners to proposals
for settlement, once more pointing out the absolute necessity for seeing that
on the Political as well as on the Industrial side, we are adequately represented
in the place where laws are made, viz., the House of Commons, and thereby
prevent on the one hand reactionary legislation being passed; on the other
hand promulgating progressive laws which will enable the people to more fully
develop their lives and to enjoy more of the real amenities of life. The business
in the House of Commons during the month has been of such a character as
to call not only for constant attendance by the Labour Party, but for vigilant
watch and constant fight, which though carried on under adverse circumstances,
nevertheless has kept ever to the front Labour's aspirations and demands.
The need is for more members, therefore, keep the machinery in order so that
when the appeal to the country does take place, we shall be ready.
WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION CASES.
We are pleased to report that the following cases have been settled by our
Solicitor, Mr. Evan Barlow :-

are not obtainable by law, and only by agreement, and members should report
any accident to their local officers immediately, as a solicitor cannot be engaged
until consent has been obtained from the Central Office.

our smaller branches, Mr. Nicholson did all he could to improve the lot
of the workers in that area. We beg to tender our expressions of sym-
pathy to his wife and family, and hope that the work of the Branch will
not suffer as a consequence of this loss.

OVERSEAS TRADE IN JUNE.
The Board of Trade Returns for June, issued this week, allow a survey to be made
of our imports and exports during the first half of the present year. Although the general
strike in May affected export business, the shoe and leather industries have not, apparently,
suffered a serious setback. Indeed, but for the loss of business experienced in that month,
the figures for the past half-year would compare favourably with those of the corresponding
period of 1925. If our exports of leather footwear can be maintained at the total reached
in June, this year will end showing an improvement on its predecessor. The probability
is, however, that the increase recorded last month was due partly to the despatch of ship-
ments held up by lack of transport in May. The table below shows the quantities and
values of leather footwear exported in June and in the corresponding months of 1924
and 1925-

£110,526. This brought the total exports for the six months nearly up to the quantity
shown at the end of June last year. The figures for these two periods are:-To June 30th,
1925, 5,603,592 pairs, valued at £2,160,750; to 30th June, 1926, 5,432,004 pairs, valued at

It will be noted that the value of the goods imported this year is higher than was the case
in the previous year. This probably accounts for the slight decrease in the number of
pairs purchased abroad. Imports of footwear made of materials other than leather
(excepting rubber) were smaller in June than in the corresponding month of either of the
two preceding years, but on the six months' trading there was an increase of 477,228
pairs in quantity and £61,593 in value as compared with 1925. The total value of the
imports of this class of footwear is, however, no more than £234,177 this year. The Shoe
and Leather Record, 16th July, 1926.

THE GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.
60 LADY SOMERSET ROAD,
KENTISH TOWN, N. W. 5.
23rd July, 1926,
FELLOW MEMBERS,
CONTINENTAL CONDITIONS.
Probably the most important event during the
month has been a deputation by the President of the Union and Mr. W. R. Smith, at
the request of the Council, to visit the boot and shoe factories in several continental countries
for the purpose of comparing rates of wages, methods of working and conditions of employ.
ment. It was our purport to visit Prague, Czecho-Slovakia, and to call upon a certain
large firm in that particular district, situated about an hour's train ride from Prague,
in a small town known as Pard-u-Beatz, where we met a gentleman who had spent a number
of years in Leicester, at Messrs, T. Brown & Co. He is managing the firm of Propphets,
Crudin. From there we went to Messrs. Bata & Co., of Zlin, Czecho-Slovakia, and from
there we travelled all night to Vienna, where we visited the firm of Beka, Boot and Shoe
Manufacturers, at Moddling, about an hour's run from Vienna itself. We were shown all
over the factory with the greatest courtesy from both these firms. We were also shown
over the factory of Bally, of Vienna; here again the greatest courtesy was shown to us
and we left Vienna, better known as Wein, at 7.30 p.m., and arrived at Zurich, in Switzer.
land, the next day. We then approached the firm of Bally's, whose offices are situated
in Zurich, and here the Manager kindly made arrangements for us to visit the great factory
of Bally's at Shoenwernd (pronounced Shooenwent) the next day (Saturday). We left
early in the morning and were met by a motor car at the Station at Aarau (pronounced
Arrow). We were met at the station by Mr. Cumbar, the General Manager of Bally & Co.,
and were conveyed to the factory, where we were introduced to Mr. Euvan Bally himself
which is situated in the most pleasant surroundings it has ever been my lot to find a
Here, again, every consideration was shown us, and we went over the whole of the factory
factory in. The firm left off at 12 o'clock, and we saw as much as it was possible at this
particular firm. After visiting the firm we returned to Zurich, and we left on the Sunday
afternoon for Stuttgart, in Germany, where we arrived in the evening. The next morning
we journeyed to the firm of Salamander, one of the largest shoe firms in Germany. Here,
again, both the Chairman of the Company, his Nephew and Staff, made us very welcome.
with whom we spent the whole of the day looking round the firm. We left Stuttgart
at midnight, and arrived in London at midnight next day, after a very strenuous period.
At the time of writing, our report is not yet available for presentation to the members,
which will be the case very shortly. If there are any of our members interested in Boot
and Shoe production, it would be well worth their while to read the statement made by
Bata in the Shoe and Leather Record, of 16th July, 1926. The firm there makes an interest-
ing statement, which it is the intention of myself and colleagues to reply to at a very early
date.
There are many things in the Boot and Shoe Industry on the Continent of which we
do not approve, and also in some instances at home. We congratulate no man or men
who interferes with the personal freedom and independence of the working man and
woman. We do not appreciate men investing money in the factory in which they work.
I am speaking for myself in this matter, and do not appreciate men who are compelled
to invest money in businesses before they can get employment. A man is at a disadvantage
who lives in an employer's house; he is at a disadvantage if he does not belong to a Trade
Union, but is at a greater disadvantage if he has not a voice in what remuneration he shall
receive for his labour by being represented by some person who is not subject to the will
and pleasure of his employer. He is at a disadvantage if he lives on the employer's pre-
mises; he is at a disadvantage if he has a share of the profit, but has not a share or a voice
to the amount of profit that has been made and its distribution; he is at a disadvantage
when work is given out to him, he has to finish that day's work before he can go home.
✔ese are some of the disadvantages which we see among men who do not belong to a
ade Union and who cannot very well remove from a particular area owing to the fact
hat their eggs are all in one basket.
MANSFIELD. We are still in communication with Messrs. Faire Bros.' Mansfield
factory, and hope with the assistance of at least one gentleman who is interested in our
welfare that we might bring some pressure to bear upon this particular firm to meet the
wants and requirements of the trade.
LEICESTER. I have had occasion to call upon two of the largest buyers in Leicester
who have signified their intention to attend, all being well, the next meeting that the
Federation and ourselves are calling, to discuss ways and means to press upon the workers
of this country the suitability of Boots and Shoes made in our own particular country.
We hope this will meet with some approval from the general public, if adopted, as I believe
it ultimately will be.

NORWAY BANS SHODDY.
Adulteration of Shoes and Leather Prohibited.
The text of the regulations dealing with the Norwegian Government's campaign
against shoddy shoes and leather are now available. H.M. Minister at Oslo has forwarded
to the Board of Trade the following translation of the new law:-
The importation, manufacture or sale of footwear of the following kinds is prohibited:
I. Footwear in which ordinary cardboard is used. II. Footwear in which artificial leather,
artificial leather board or chemically prepared fibre board is used for purposes other than-
(1) for filling of bottoms, for arches, toe stiffening and strengthening and strengthening
of the upper leather under the heel; (2) in the heel, but at least 12 mm. from the top piece
in men's footwear and 15 mm. in women's footwear; (3) in turned footwear for inlaid
soles and in the heel, without the restriction mentioned in (2).
Imported goods must be marked with the word
"Utenlandsk," and also with the
name of the importer. They must also be marked with the letter "A" or "B" at least
6 mm. high. The letter "A" is to be used if no artificial leather, artificial leather board
or chemically prepared fibre board has been used in their manufacture or if they have
only been used to the extent indicated above in II. (1). The letter "B" is to be used if,
in the manufacture of the goods, artificial leather, artificial leather board or chemically
prepared fibre board has been used to the extent indicated above in II. (2) and (3).
In the case of footwear with leather soles the marking must be imprinted with a steel
punch on the inside of the uppers, on the arch and also on the outer sole, and in the case of
rubber soled footwear the marking is to be effected by cutting or vulcanising inside or
outside on the arch or by coloured stamping inside on the arch or on the lining.
The following classes of footwear are exempt from the regulations, viz. :-1, Children's
footwear up to 16 cm. long (No. 24); 2, footwear of silk, felt or other cloth; 3, footwear
of straw; 4, footwear with wooden soles; 5, footwear wholly of rubber, with or without
lining, goloshes, and golosh overboots; 6, leather and stuff footwear without heels or with
lists the height of which, including the sole, does not exceed 17 mm.
The weight of sole leather, upper leather, cow leather or belting leather must not be
increased by the aid of materials which are not necessary for the tanning or for the further
preparation of the leather. Tanning materials must not be added to such leather with the
sole object of increasing its weight.
Barium salts, magnesium salts, lead salts, tin salts, and other mineral salts, as well as
glucose, dextrine, molasses and similar organic stuffs may be used in small quantities
for bleaching and sizing. These regulations apply also to leather of the above-mentioned
kinds used in footwear.
Each piece of leather of the kinds mentioned above imported into Norway must be
marked with the word "Utenlandsk" and with the name of the importer.
Leather and footwear which do not comply with the regulations regarding weighting
of leather are prohibited to be imported or sold.
The regulations referred to above were to come into force on 7th June, but it is under-
stood that certain exemptions and exceptions will be temporarily allowed. The Shoe
and Leather Record, 2nd July, 1926.

4. The Fund we propose should be for FULL MALE MEMBERS only, and that

In order to finance the scheme, a capital sum of not less than £150,000 will be required

5. We suggest when Superannuation Benefit is payable to members at 65 years of

legal assistance (in case of accidents in a factory) and funeral benefits.
6. Any member ceasing work at 65 years of age and being in receipt of Superannuation
Benefit shall not be entitled to receive any other benefit except funeral pay.
7. All members in receipt of Superannuation Benefit and continuing at work will
pay a contribution of SIXPENCE per week only, 3d. of which shall be placed to the credit
of the Superannuation Fund and 3d. to the Funeral Fund.
8. Funeral Benefit. We suggest that in the event of a member contributing to the
Superannuation Fund, and death supervening before receiving such Superannuation
Benefit, his dependants shall receive an extra £2 Funeral Benefit, in addition to the sum
named in the Rules, making a total of £8 for men and £5 for women.
9. Women Members shall be allowed to Voluntarily join the Superannuation Scheme
if they desire.
Amendments to this proposal must be sent to the Central Office before 30th September
1926, to enable the Special Conference to deal with the matter on 21st October, 1926.

ORGANISERS' REPORTS.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
Following up the work of previous months, in conjunction with Mr. McCarthy,
Sileby District, Anstey, Derby and Mansfield have been visited. It is fairly apparent
in visiting the firms in these areas, that the continuance of the Mining Dispute is having
a very serious effect on trade. Despite this fact very good meetings have been held, and
a continued interest added to the work of the Union. All the firms in the Sileby District
have been visited, and I am convinced that with a return to anything like normal con
ditions, a further progressive increase will be recorded. There is undoubtedly a better
spirit existing in this district, due in a large measure to continuous work, and the new
Secretary attending to detail work, which is an essential feature of all administrative
work. There are two firms in this district that need attention, but unfortunately they
are not so well organised as one would desire, and in both cases pressure is brought to bear
on the operatives, by all the well-known methods, to convince them of the paternal welfare
of the management, and the awful disaster that will result if they join the Union. One
of these firms are federated, and have fairly impressed it upon the operatives, that if the
minimum wage is paid, they have the right to demand considerably larger quantities
from them, than the wage calls for. We have continually pointed out to them their folly,
but with that blind obstinacy, and with a willingness of putting complete confidence in
the management, they still continue. This represents an aspect of our work which
inevitably results, where the operatives are not well organised. In other firms, one finds
a department where they are all members, and they, having asserted their will, statement
prices are fully complied with, while in other departments on the same firm, when the men
are not fully organised, so long as they are near the minimum, very little notice is taken
of statement prices. These men are fully conscious of this fact, but nursing up some
imaginary grievance in their own mind, still go on, disgruntled, waiting for something
to turn up which will not call for any sacrifice on the part of themselves.
A few visits to Anstey at once revealed quite a different spirit so far as our membership
is concerned. Though it is in the same county, the difference in mentality is most marked.
The girls in this district are not so well organised as we would desire, and a number of
youths were rounded up as a result of our visit. Acting on the advice of the local Secretary,
who informed us that a number had joined, we followed up our work by holding a meeting
in the centre of the Village, Mr. J. Wheeler and Mr. G. Parbury (Leicester No. 1), attending.
It was a splendid meeting, and for upwards of two hours we kept the meeting going, and
judging by the questions asked at the close of the meeting, it was fairly evident that a
good number of our members are fairly well informed in the Union's activities, and were
desirous of extending the progressive influence of the Union.
Though trade has been very bad at Derby, we were pleased to learn that there was
some slight improvement at the firms that we visited. We attended the Branch Meeting,
and despite the bad trade, the Secretary reported that the increased membership was
keeping up well. The policy of keeping their members well informed by a wise distribution
of the Monthly Reports, is having a good effect on the members.
In visiting Mansfield, one at once realises the awful effects of the Mining Dispute.
The poverty and distress in this area is fairly apparent, yet in the midst of it all, the
courageous stand of the miners, which the passing of the Eight Hours’ Act has not dimin-
ished, is a magnificent display of human solidarity. Our firms in this district are working
short time, and our position is fairly satisfactory. One of the firms which employs nearly
all girls, and who have been induced to pay a majority of them our scales, don't seem to
appreciate the effective power that the girls might have if they belong to the Union. The
Managing Director, who by his actions, don't quite convince one of his capacity to fill
such a position, because of his earnest desire to interfere with the efforts of those who
belong to the Union, makes our position very difficult. But I suppose that some people
would not think that they were performing their duty, unless they asserted their authority.
It seems to be a special virtue for some men to play the part of a tyrant, but they can only
last so long as they can find persons who they can tyrannise over. Such is the power
which an individual can wield under the present commercial system, and where our organisa-
tion is strong, we can effectively curb an individual's power, and so make the conditions
of our operatives more tolerable. J. H. BAUM.
The work of the past month has been of an exceptional character in the sense
that three weeks of same has been taken by a visit to factories abroad.
The first week of the month was spent in London, where as a result of further negotia-
tions, certain quantity statements have been completed. This should be a great help
to both operative and official, and Mr. Mason, who as President of the Branch, has been
largely responsible for the compilation of these prices, will be able to better assist the mem-
bers concerned if there is close co-operation between the factory and the office of the branch.
The merit of our various statements lies largely in the correct application of same,
and this cannot take place unless the official responsible is placed in a position to advise
on points that generally arise, more especially in the early stages of the operating of the

During the past month I have again been engaged in the County of Northampton,
ally slowing down and members are feeling the loss of wages as a result, very good interest
has been taken in the meetings held. I have endeavoured to bring home the facts relating
to the present industrial crisis, always pointing out how necessary it is, especially at the
present time, to maintain, and still further develop industrial organisation, economic
circumstances operating against most of the heavy industries in the country, are bound to
have their effect upon all other industries which are in a somewhat subsidiary position,
and it is essential that we, being in the latter position (taken as an industry) that we should
be completely organised, and all members should take a greater interest in the work of
the Union, by the very fact that our labour power has to be expended in conjunction with
each other, necessitated by the division and sub-division of the processes which go to
make up the finished product. It is all the more necessary that there should be a com-
plete understanding between the whole of the operatives working at the industry. Many,
and varied, are the ways in which unscrupulous employers attempt to nullify our Terms
of Settlement. Therefore, it is up to our members to be ever vigilant in seeing that all
engaged in the industry should get the full benefit of the Terms.
interest taken, although not everything that could be desired, is growing, and progress
Our organisation and membership in the town and county is very good, and the
is being made. I am looking forward to the time when our Branches will have to engage
the largest halls obtainable to hold our monthly meetings. The Union has been built up
by the interest and enthusiasm of men and women whose names may never appear in the
limelight, and it is up to our younger members to-day to follow in the footsteps of these
old pioneers. There is still work to do, still building to be done, with the ever-changing
economic circumstances. Our old slogan is still applicable, "Agitate, Educate, Organise."
LEN. SMITH.

BRANCH REPORTS.
ARBROATH. Trade remains very poor in this quarter, and so far as
shoemaking is concerned, our members have come to regard it as a
accessory in their lives. The big stoppage, combined with the plucky fight
of the miners, has helped to make a great impression here as elsewhere. The
National Stoppage was a gesture on the part of Labour which cannot be ignored,
and while it was not persisted in, still the demonstration was needed. It is
evident, however, that something more is required, and all the strength of
industrial action be effective until a much greater political power is wielded
organised labour must be concentrated on the political weapon.
It is pitiful to read all the tosh about a "threat to
the nation," "threat to the constitution," and "threat to everything," except
what it really was, a threat to the greed and selfishness of the governing class.
How long will a fourth of the nation be able to impress its will on the other
three-fourths? Certainly that wretched fourth holds the reins of government, the Press and all other forms of publicity, but in enlightened days like
the present, it hardly seems credible that the thing is done. And yet since
the "victory" of wealth, one finds supporters of things as they are, showing
an ill-concealed hostility and impatience towards representatives of labour
who are engaged in administrative work. Some day the great "submerged,"
three-fourths of the population will waken, and then woe betide the praters
who mouth smooth phrases about "illegal action," "menace to the nation,"
"attack on constitution," and such like, when the downright justice and
sense of labour's demands will brush aside such irrelevancies. Our members
have been going through a purgatory of another kind in connection with idle
benefit. Headquarters of the Ministry took exception to the way in which
short time extended benefit was being paid to our members, and for about two
months that benefit was in jeopardy. However, we have got a fairly good
arrangement again, although it seems temporary. Our members have been
unable, through long continued idleness, to pay a levy to the miners, but those
who can are paying on local sheets, and the Branch has voted a first payment
of £10 to the relief funds.

BELFAST. There is very little of an encouraging nature to report.
Trade still remains in a deplorable condition, many of our members finding it
impossible to obtain work and most of those who are employed are working
short time, and have been for a considerable time past. We are pleased to
report that the Managing Committee of the Belfast Co-operative Society
has granted to those employed in the Society's Boot Repairing factory an
additional ten working days' holiday with pay. This with the six statutory
holidays and the Co-operative general holiday, makes seventeen days' holiday
in the year. We regret that when the additional holidays were granted the
Manager of the Boot Factory suggested giving them in such a way as to be of
little benefit or advantage to our members, with the result that the Secretary
had to write the Managing Secretary of the Co-operative Society on the matter,
who has sent a satisfactory reply.

CHESHAM. Trade here remains quiet.
DERBY. Trade in Derby is very bad, the C.W.S. having had about a
third of their employees suspended for over two months, which has been a
very heavy claim on the Out-of-Work Fund.

DESBOROUGH. Trade with us is bad and is gradually getting worse.
Many of our members have not restarted work since the General Strike. About
eighty members are on the books drawing unemployed benefit (suspension).
This has been a great help to our members, and shows the wisdom of joining
the Union to prepare for any bad times that may come.

PLYMOUTH. Trade with us is still very quiet, and although our members
are all on short time, the 5 per cent, reduction in the Trade Board Rates has
been made effective throughout the district. We must call attention to this
matter as on previous occasions, and point out that this further wage reduction
has not been accompanied by any reduction of the charges for repairs. We
remind them that there is generally acknowledged to be two partners in the
business one the emplover, the other the worker, and if one is going to pocket
all the overplus obtained from the purse of the customer, the other fellow will

from his own pocket several shillings each week. We are reminded of the

SILEBY - Trade here is being affected by the Coal Dispute, which is

factories during dinner hour. We wish to thank the Conference for remitting

more interest when it is solely for their own benefit.
