NORTHAMPTONSHIRE JOINT DISTRICT COUNCIL.

Minutes of Quarterly Meeting held in the Assembly Room at the Trades Club, Church
Street, Wellingborough, on Saturday, April 17th, 1926, commencing at 2.30 p.m.

PRESENT. In the absence of the President, Mr. J. E. Chapman presided, and was
supported by Mr. Langley and a full representation of delegates from Branches. The
Chairman, in opening, apologised for the absence of the Secretary through illness.

MINUTES. - The Minutes of the previous meeting having been circulated, it was resolved
that same be accepted as read.

The Minutes of the last meeting of the Executive Committee were then submitted
These were approved. Mr. T. F. Richards complained that the Central Office had not
received any notification of the meeting, and it was only by accident that he got to know
that the meeting was to be held. Mr. Campbell explained the difficult circumstances
arising from the illness of the Secretary, and also stated that he had informed Mr. Richards
of the meeting when he met him the previous week. Mr. Richards then moved that a
vote of sympathy be sent to the Secretary in his illness, and said that it would be a good
thing for their own sakes if some officials could be compelled to rest occasionally, so that
their health should not suffer. Mr. E. Law seconded the resolution, which was carried
unanimously.

* [NOTE. Notice of the meeting, also the minutes of the previous meeting, was
sent to the Head Office, directed to the General President at the same time as the other
minutes were sent out. -G.C.]

BUSINESS. - The Chairman having again called attention to the Agenda, asked for
an opening to the discussion.

MR. PENDERED (Northampton No. 2) was the first delegate to speak, and he said
he wished to discuss the Resolution submitted by the Norwich No. 2 Branch with regard
to Mass Production (page 116, February Report). He stated that the Northampton Branch
had had the matter under discussion for a long time and they had tried their best to get
the matter brought forward. He thought that mass production was bound to come in
and they should welcome it because they welcomed progress, but we must take care to
organise it as it comes along, because it is a part of our trade and should be organised in
our Union. It was immaterial where the soles were cut if trade union conditions were not
being observed we must try and get our terms of settlement introduced. It is the duty of the
Council to investigate these factories, and I should like to send a resolution asking one or
two organisers to be told off to look after this question of mass production.

MR. T. F. RICHARDS said that he and the Council were quite in the dark as to the
complaint of the Norwich Branch. They knew nothing about it until they saw it on the
Conference Agenda. He said that many months had been spent in trying to organise
these people in mass-production factories. He gave numerous examples of what was being
done in this respect, remarking that he had been in communication with firms in America
and Canada. He said that we must insist that our members should not work for non-
union employers, and it was the duty of all members to give the Council full information.
We could not, however, concentrate solely on this particular work, but if the information
was given they would do their best. One method would be to report to the General
Purposes Committee of the Federation and tell them that they must not buy stuff produced
under improper conditions, and we had the right to see the firms and tell them of the
conditions under which the stuff was produced, but if they still used it the members of the
Union must refuse to work it up.

MR. E. LAW (Northampton No. 2) said that everything possible was being done
with the position. Most of these mass-production factories were outside the usual boot
and shoe centres, and those members who worked in the cutting-up departments were in
danger of losing their jobs. He said it was the fault of the people who worked in these
factories; our officials and organisers could not be blamed. Let us as a District Council
vote for the resolution of the Norwich Branch, asking for greater power to be exerted in
the organisation of these people.

AGRICULTURE.
We have in this country considerable contrasts in the size of our farms in com-
parison with our neighbours. In England, we have 66 per
acres-these figures are from the Report of the Agricultural Tribunal-in France and
Holland, 90 per cent.; in Germany, 92 per cent.; and in Denmark and Belgium, 95
per cent., and some of those countries esteem so highly the advantage of small holdings
that they have been at special pains by their legislation to encourage their provision."
Statement of Minister of Agriculture, Mr. Guinness, on Friday, 16th July, 1926, during
discussion upon "Small Holdings " Bill.-Column 785, Parliamentary Debates.
AN AGRICULTURAL POLICY FOR LABOUR.
Labour's draft policy for dealing with Agriculture has been approved by the General
Council of the Trades Union Congress, the Executive of the Labour Party, and the Execu-
tive of the Parliamentary Labour Party. It will be submitted to the Trades Union
Congress in September and to the Labour Party Conference in October, and when adopted
by them will become the official Agricultural Policy of the Labour Movement. The draft
Report is an interesting and important document and covers a wide range of problems.
It declares for the public ownership of land on a basis of compensation to present holders,
sets out the procedure for the transfer of the land to the community, and outlines the
financing of the Compensation scheme. The proposed system of tenure, the public control
of the land, and methods of local and central administration are explained in detail. The
agricultural worker, and his right to a living wage, to increased responsibility in the farming
industry, and to easier access to land are all provided for, while in another chapter the
provision of new cottages with adjacent land and gardens, the improvement of existing
cottages, the abolition of the "tied" cottage, and the need for social amenities in the
rural districts are dealt with. Another principal Section is concerned with the importance
of marketing and contains a number of constructive proposals and practical suggestions
for improving the chaotic system. Transport, Credit, Currency, Insurance, Research
and Education are all covered as well as Rural Industries, Afforestation, Electric Power
for the countryside, the Game laws, and the future use of Deer Forests.
It will be seen from the foregoing that the draft Report is very wide in its scope,
and that care has been taken to produce a policy that seeks "to establish agriculture as
a prosperous industry and the countryside as a rural society enjoying the opportunities
and amenities which are the moral right of a nation's citizens."
The draft Report will be issued in a few days as a joint pamphlet by the Labour
Publications' Department, 33 Eccleston Square, London, SW.


---
TRADE UNIONS AND FREEDOM.
It is easy to find fault with the Trade Unions, but it is difficult to find remedies for those
faults, and the last person on earth we should expect to find remedies would be Lord Banbury,
whose Bill to repeal the Trades Dispute Act was discussed in the House of Lords yesterday.
Lord Banbury would practically make Trade Unions illegal or confine their activities
to those of mere Friendly Societies, for that would, in effect, be the result of depriving
Trade Unions of power over any member to sell his labour in any way he thought fit,
As a matter of fact, no wage-earner can, under any circumstances, be free to sell his
labour as he thinks fit unless he is in a position to decline to labour at all. A shoe operative
is not free in Northampton to work for any wages; the Boot and Shoe Operatives' Union
sees to it that if he is an ordinary able man he shall not work for less than 50s. or thereabouts
a week, and, of course, the Liberty of that shoe operative is, it is true, restricted by the
Trades Union. But if there were no Trade Union and no minimum for which he should
work, would he be any freer?- would he be free to demand the wage and the conditions
which he desired? Of course not. His freedom in reality would be even less than it is
when he seeks employment as a Trade Unionist. He would be compelled either to starve
or to work for a wage which would be certainly very much less than the wage which he
now obtains. The only man who is able to sell his labour in the way he thinks fit is the
man who has sufficient income to refuse to labour at all if he thinks fit, and Trade Unions
do, to a limited extent, provide a man with a measure of liberty. The law itself does not
allow a man to sell his labour as he thinks fit. Conditions were so shocking fifteen years
ago in industries where this "freedom" existed that the Government was compelled to
interfere and establish Trade Boards. - Northampton Echo, 21st July, 1926.

TARIFFS.
Taxed Footwear.
Despite energetic campaigning by the opposition the Irish Free State Government
is adhering to its decision not to add to the list of imported goods on which a tariff is to be
imposed. The Government has adopted a "wait and see" policy. Last week in the
Senate it carried the second reading of the Tariff Commission Bill under which manu-
facturers who desire a tariff will have to show good cause. In the meantime the Govern-
ment is being pressed to increase the present tariff of 15 per cent. on footwear. Some of
the arguments put forward in support of this plea are curious. According to Senator
O'Hanlon, there will be no increase in the production of boots in the Free State until the
tariff is fixed at 65 per cent.! On the other hand, Senator Fanning pointed out that owing
to the 15 per cent. duty English importers had been compelled to reduce the quality of
the goods they shipped to Ireland. The result was that wearers were having to buy three
pairs where formerly two pairs sufficed. This, he said, accounted for the 50 per cent.
increase in the quantity of shoes imported from England. When the Irish farmer and his
labourers grip the fact that they are being compelled to pay higher prices for lower quality
boots they will, we believe, insist on a drastic revision of the existing tariff. -The Shoe
and Leather Record, 16th July, 1926.

CIVIC TRADING KEEPS RATES DOWN.
Municipal socialism in Birmingham continues to pay, and at the same time is helping
to keep down the rates.
Annual reports of Birmingham Corporation trading departments, presented to the
City Council show that the gas department had a surplus of £86,397 on last year's working,
£41,200 OF WHICH IS TO BE CONTRIBUTED TO THE RELIEF OF THE RATES.
The electric supply department has also had a most successful year. After providing
for all capital charges (including £202,455 for redemption of debt) there remains a surplus
of £184,011 on the year's working, as compared with last year's surplus of £89,370. £153,011
of the surplus is being put to the renewals account, AND £31,000 TO THE RELIEF OF RATES.

Increase in Business.
The revenue of this department last year was £1,323,831, an increase of £141,209
over the previous year. The increased revenue represents 16 per cent. more business,
but, in spite of this increase, the working expenses show a decrease of £9,318. It has
also been possible to reduce the average price for all classes of supply 3 per cent.
The tramways department will report a net revenue of £259,057, after paying working
expenses and sinking fund charges. This is an increase of £975 over the previous year.
£219,057 is being put to renewals and special expenditure account, AND £40,000 TO THE
RELIEF OF RATES.
Birmingham also claims to have the largest Corporation allotment site in England.
The area under the control of the Allotments Committee comprises 1,200 acres, bringing
in a rental of £7,000 a year from 14,000 holders. -The Daily Herald, 6th July, 1926.

TRADE BOARD PROSECUTION.
Bristol Repairer Fined.
On Monday, Arthur Elijah Chivers, of A. E. and A. J. Chivers, boot repairer, 3A
Berkley Place, Clifton, was summoned at the Bristol Police Court for paying wages less
than the minimum rates laid down by the Boot Repairing Trade Board; with having
produced a false record of work; and with having failed to keep a record of wages.
Mr. Coules, who prosecuted on behalf of the Board of Trade, said an inspector inter-
viewed the defendant in November, 1924, and discovered that no records of work done
were being kept. The defendant undertook to comply with the regulations, and did so
for a time, but when an inspector called in February last no records were again available.
In regard to paying wages which were less than the minimum, there were arrears
amounting to £38, for which sum the defendant had now signed a cheque. He had em-
ployed a man as a learner at 35s. per week, but there being too many learners in proportion
to the number of journeymen he was told that the man could not be considered a learner.
Dealing with the charge of having produced a false record of work, Mr. Coules said
that when the inspector interviewed the defendant in February last it was found that the
man concerned was being paid for a 28 hours' week. The defendant maintained that the
man worked that number of hours. The inspector, however, made further inquiries,
and saw the defendant again. The man, in defendant's presence, said that Chivers had
told him it would be well, when the inspector came, to tell a few lies. The man, whose
name was White, informed the inspector that he worked from 8.30 a.m. to 6.30 p.m. on
a full day, and from 8.30 a.m. to 1.30 p.m. on a short day, while his working week was
45 hours.
The solicitor for the defendant said White was simply a finisher and not an all-round
man. When he was engaged he was told that he would be employed as a finisher at 35s.
per week, with which he was content. White, while on the premises, was for periods
waiting for work, and his actual hours during the week were only 28. It was for that
reason that his time card stated that he did only 28 hours' work.
Chivers was fined £4 on the first and second counts, £2 on the third, and £1 1s. costs.
The Shoe and Leather Record, 9th July, 1926.

Man's First Problem in Statesmanship. World's Endeavour.
not for
The first problem in statesmanship is not international, nor national, it is personal.
The man who is a great statesman begins by being a great statesman in his own life," said
Christian Endeavour World's Convention at the Crystal Palace.
Turning to the problems of the immediate future, the ex-Premier said :
"Our youth,
to-day perhaps more than ever-on account of the misery that has been wrought upon the
world, very largely by the failure of the Churches themselves, the misery that we have
been reaping now for the sowing of a few years ago-requires a discipline more severe,
more drastic, more hardening in spiritual things than has been called for by any generation
in the last century or so.
Acts, not Words.
We want acts, not words. Every act strengthens. Every word unsupported by
act weakens. Words, mere pious words with a scent and a savour in them, but no sub-
stance, are like tuberculosis on our moral being. They soften it, they deteriorate it, they
make men lazy.
"Anybody can imitate and quote, but action is difficult because you yourself have
to act. Nobody can act for you and you feel the benefit of the act. Do not be misled
by beautiful language. Rugged, honest, strong, powerful, faithful yet humble acts-
that is what we have to try to achieve in order to make our lives worthy."-Daily Herald,
22nd July, 1926.
FACTORY FIRE.
£5,000 Damage at Earl Shilton. Two Leicester Firemen Injured.
Damage roughly estimated at £5,000 was caused by fire at the factory of Messrs.
Marvin, Garrett and Marvin, wholesale boot manufacturers, Earl Shilton, on Tuesday.
The factory was completely gutted, and the whole of the machinery and stock was
damaged, despite the fine work of the local body of fire fighters and Leicester Fire Brigade.
The effort of the local volunteers was largely instrumental in saving a portion of the building
threatened with total destruction.
The office furniture and books were saved.
Two Leicester firemen were slightly injured, and a villager was severely cut about the
eye by falling glass.
The damage, it is understood, is covered by insurance. Leicester Advertiser, 26th
June, 1926.

GERMAN BOOT WORKERS' CONFERENCE.
The Conference of the Boot and Shoe Operatives of Germany was held during the
week commencing 21st June - 26th June, at Frankfort-on-Maine, Josef Simon in the chair.
With eleven other fraternal delegates I attended the same, having been previously
at the meeting of the Executive Council of the International Boot and Leather Workers.
There were, apart from the officers and fraternal delegates, about 70 delegates, making
in all about 100 present. There were three women delegates.
I gathered that the Executive and Officers were appointed every two years.
The
country is cut up into nine districts and a permanent Organiser is delegated to each district.
These officers are not subject to re-election, neither do they attend the Executive Meetings,
their reports being sent to the Executive.
pursued.
The Council's report was not printed, but read by Mr. Lex. I gathered from the
discussion, up to the time of my leaving (Tuesday), that a good deal of trouble had been
created by the Communists, and it was evident some plain talk took place about the policy
A proposal was also made that Messrs. Simon and Lex, with Dr. Schenk, should
pay a visit to America and ascertain at first-hand what were the real conditions of employ-
made by employers that America was knocking them (the Germans) out of the market.
Some opposition was shown to this proposal by the Communist delegates, who wanted the
visit to be to Russia instead of America. The answer of the Executive was it is not
and they must ascertain what obtained in America. After a long discussion the proposal
necessary to go to Russia, they were not in competition with them, but America was,
This proposal was brought forward by the Executive because of many statements
ment.
was agreed to.
In addition to the address printed on pages 338 and 339 of the Monthly Report for
June, owing to the fact that there were a number of fraternal delegates present, I was
asked to convey the joint fraternal greetings of all the delegates, and in doing so, said:-
I do so with the greatest possible pleasure, and beg to assure you that my colleagues
hope your Conference may be the most successful one of your number. The outlook is
one of great difficulty for us all and one, moreover, which is beset with all kinds of obstacles.
Nevertheless, my colleagues wish to assure you that they much appreciate the good work
you have done in the past days.
The world is greatly in need of some power to lift it out of the present terrible mess
in which we find it at the present time. We are convinced that amongst the organisations
which will make for the solving of the troubles are the Trade Unions of the world, which
have not yet been properly valued as to the work they have done, and are doing, to put
humanity upon the right road.
We have, in the course of our work, encountered opposition from a certain type of
employer, and alas, from some workpeople also, who are always prepared to take what
the Unions secure in the way of advantage, and refuse to pay anything towards the cost
of the upkeep of the Unions which have done so much to help the workers in the struggle
for a better condition of life.
The work we are engaged in is a great humanitarian work and a work which is bringing
together the workers in all parts of the world.
The world is full of unrest, largely because of the World War, bringing, as it did, in
its train, such suffering, privation and pain. In the midst of the same we remain deter-
mined to do all that is possible to bring peace and goodwill amongst all the peoples.
We have a great task before us and one which, great as it is, we shall not shrink from,
nor shall we ever forget that we must aim more and more at securing good relations one
with another, no matter what part of the world we may happen to live in.
To attain this object we must have REAL UNITY IN OUR RANKS. Unity which in acts
and not words will prove beyond a doubt that the spirit is really intended of loyalty and
comradeship one to another.
The days are full of perplexity, clouds befog the issue, obstacles are around the path-
way; nevertheless, so sure as the sun which is now shining so brilliantly, having emerged
from clouds and having overcome the obstacles to its present glorious outburst, tells us
of brighter days in the physical world; so let it act as a spur to us in the economic and
industrial world, to put forth more and yet more effort in the determination to ensure
success.
We must not lose heart because of the apparently slow progress being made, because
we are making headway. I assure you my friends that my colleagues feel very strongly
about this important question, and I would remind you that in the International Labour
Office at Geneva, where 38 nations have recently been in Conference, and to which office
56 nations are affiliated, headway is being made in, and upon many questions affecting
workers in an International capacity. It is my pleasure and honour to sit on the Governing
Body of such Office, and my Italian, Canadian, Norwegian, Dutch, German, French,

THE ATTACK ON TRADE UNIONISM.
Clear evidence is accumulating of a systematic campaign against the Trade Union
The adversaries of Labour are not waiting for the legal and Parliamentary attack
develop as foreshadowed by Lord Birkenhead and Viscount Cave.
They are preparing the ground beforehand.
SOWING THE TARES.
Articles and letters from correspondents are appearing in the newspapers with
picious frequency, all harping upon the same note.
This propaganda appears to emanate from a common source, and is distinguisha),
wherever it appears by a sly and malicious perversion and misrepresentation of the fas
about Trade Unionism.
PLAYING THE EMPLOYERS' GAME.

sections of members of Unions to break away from their organisation and to form v
Unions.
Non-unionism also is insisted upon by some employers as a condition of employme
as in the case of Scottish newspapers.

Employment varied as between different parts of London, but was fair on the average
At Leicester it declined, and was slack, and worse than a year ago; many operatives
were working only half time, or even less, this being in part due to the curtailment of
power supply. It was very quiet, and worse than in June, at Hinckley. At Northampton
the power supply was being maintained, and a few firms were able to continue full time
working, though others were on short time; employment, on the whole, remained fair
It was poor, with short time working fairly general, in the Higham and Rushden area
though there was no curtailment of power in this area. At Wellingborough employ-
ment was generally very poor, with nearly all factories working short time, with
reduced staffs. At Kettering most firms were on short time and made extended holiday
stoppages.

Employment at Stafford remained fairly good, with little total unemployment,
although some operatives were working reduced hours. At Norwich employment showed
a decline, but was not so severely affected as at some centres; there was, however, some
short time as a result of restricted supplies of fuel and power. There was a further marked
improvement in the Bristol and Kingswood area, especially with firms at Bristol making
the lighter class of goods; but employment in the heavy boot trade was generally poor,
and worse than a year ago, owing to cancellations of orders and to the curtailment of
power and fuel. Factories at Leeds producing sports footwear were fairly busy: at
other factories employment was again slack, and much below the level of July, 1925
staffs had been reduced, and a great deal of short time was worked. Employment in
the Rossendale Valley was irregular, and below the level of a year ago.

Short-time working in Scotland was still very prevalent, although slightly less general
than in the previous month. Employment was fairly good at Kilmarnock and fair at
Edinburgh; a great improvement was reported at Maybole : at Glasgow employment
showed a decline.

POLITICAL.

Parliament, despite the terrible mining position, has prorogued
November; this to us, and we feel sure to the membership generally, will
looked upon as clear evidence of the lack of appreciation of the country
need. Surely the supreme authority ought to have devoted its energy an
influence to bring about a settlement of the dispute before breaking off for such
extended holiday. This fact by itself ought to bring home clearly to
The Labour Party has during the Session done what is possible to pre
people the need for other representatives being sent to the House of Comme
anti-progressive legislation being passed. The Party, however, is in a hopeless
minority when the voting takes place-hence the Government are assur
beforehand of the vote being and going in their favour. Nevertheless, we
must keep on plodding away and bring before the country the real position
affairs. This will assuredly tell, as in fact in the recent By-Elections it has
done, and that in no uncertain way. Nevertheless, from present indications
and statements by supporters of the Government, it is pretty clear that attempts
in the not distant future may be made to curtail the sphere of activity of Trade
Unions, and to make more difficult the work of the Trade Unions. It is there-
fore of greater importance than ever for members to so use their influence
as to make it clear to the supporters of the Government that if attempts are
made to reduce the power and authority of the Unions, it will be met with
sustained hostility and increasing effort to thwart any such procedure from
becoming effective.

POVERTY AND THE DEATH RATE.
In the Report by the Medical Research Council on Studies of Child Life in Cities and
Rural Districts of Scotland (Special Report Series, No. 101, H.M. Stationery Office, Ios.
net), we are told on page 117 that:-
The general Death Rate per 1,000 persons is 9 per cent. more in single room
houses than in four roomed houses.
The length of life in a four room house is on the average 20 years longer than it
is in a single room house.
The average Death Rate per 100,000 from diarrhœa, acute bronchitis, broncho-
pneumonia and meningitis, is in the case of a four room house 19.6, and in the case
of a single room house 59.8.

ORGANISERS' REPORTS.

FELLOW MEMBERS,
After the Council meeting of 26th July until the factories closed for the August
holidays, I worked with Mr. Baum in the Sileby district and paid a visit to Burton-on-Trent
with the General President, Mr. T. F. Richards. Many of the factories closed for fourteen
It was an opportune time for me to have my holidays and I had them. Our
members get a consideration for holidays that we used not to get in the past, but not
enough to meet the responsibilities of keeping home for nearly three weeks without any
I used to tell the foremen at the Wheatsheaf years ago that holidays we
pay meant a lockout for us. Holidays are necessary for all workers, but neither mind
or body can have the full advantage of them when wages are cut off. Some of us co
Association, take pride in the way we settle disputes and try to avoid them. But what
a revelation it would be if every case of wilful non-observance of agreements by Federate
manufacturers were published."
To-day, 24th August, Mr. J. Waring, Secretary of Sileby Branch, and I visited a
manufacturer over two of his operatives not being paid the minimum wage. The manager
said they offered themselves for what he was giving them. The men were to blame from
our point of view for engaging themselves for less than the minimum. Poverty, unless
men are strong in trade union ways, make men do things that they otherwise would not do
There was no excuse for this Federated employer for breaking a contract that he is a party
at a price. The old hireling economists of the employing class called this freedom of
contract. The miners are getting now some of this freedom of contract, and their leaders
are called impossible men for not paying homage to it. What an all-round earthly paradise
we would have if employers had a free hand in fixing wages and hours of labour. There
is to be said though for most employers, even mineowners, they believe in the workers
having a grand time in heaven when they die. I have heard them say so on Sundays.
D. McCARTHY.

FELLOW MEMBERS,
My work during this month has been in Northampton and Wellingborough.
During the week preceding the holiday I was able to address dinner-hour meetings outside
of several of the large factories in Northampton, and a considerable amount of interest
was taken, owing to the fact that the proposals for members' superannuation was published
in the local Press, and also the proposed modification of the present Terms of Agreement.
By these proposals being made public, it gave me an opportunity of drawing the attention
of our members to the objects of the Union, printed in the Rule Book, and to point out the
necessity of bringing those objects forward on every possible occasion, in order to realise
their attainment. Stabilisation of wages, shortening of hours, and abolition of overtime
are the most discussed items, and the pleasing feature in these discussions is the number
of the younger men who are eager to be informed on the various questions affecting the
industry. This is as it should be, as it is only by question and answer and ensuing dis
cussion that the facts can be brought out.
Trade in the Wellingborough area is still very slow, largely owing to the coal dispute.
Many of the manufacturers rely almost entirely upon districts where coal miners form the
major portion of the population for their orders. This shows clearly the interdependency
of one industry upon another, and that the state of poverty that exists in one large industrial
area, from whatever cause, must have its reflex in other areas. Therefore it is up to all
of us who are able to assist the miners in every way possible in their fight for a decent
standard of life and comfort. Realising all the time that in helping our fellow workers
in tines of distress, we are helping ourselves.

FELLOW MEMBERS,
LEN. SMITH.
Holidays, and the continuance of the Mining Dispute, has interfered with my
work during the past month. Many of the firms in the Sileby District have had extended
holidays, due, no doubt, to the Mining Dispute. With Mr. McCarthy I have met the
operatives at a number of firms in this area, and very good meetings have been held.
In one case we have met with a little difficulty on prices, and though it may appear a mere
detail, there is undoubtedly a principle involved, which cannot be accepted, and if accepted
it would soon be copied by other firms in the district. We are endeavouring to deal with
this matter, and I am fairly confident that matters will be adjusted satisfactorily.
We have experienced some difficulty in obtaining information from the operatives
in a non-federated firm, though the employer has promised consideration of the wages
paid. The manager exercises his power in terrifying the men of the awful consequences

JOINT MANIFESTO ON THE MINING SITUATION.
For sixteen weeks the miners have been locked out. They have endured hunger
and privation in a determined struggle to maintain their standards of life and working
conditions. Every day the lockout lasts adds to the distress and misery in the mining areas.
Actual starvation has invaded the miners' homes. Women and children are suffering
through the action of Poor Law authorities, with the connivance of the Government, in
cutting down scales of relief, and through the curtailment of school meals. In trying to
bring the miners to subjection the Government has not scrupled to endeavour to check
the generous impulses of the public in subscribing to the voluntary relief funds by which
the worst consequences of the tragedy in the coalfields have been hitherto partially alle-
viated.
The necessities
To-day the needs of the miners and their dependents are much more acute than in
the earlier stages of the lockout. With the breakdown of negotiations for a settlement
of the dispute contributions to the relief funds are more urgent than ever.
of the miners' position call for a redoubling of the effort to provide relief. If help is not
given now in greater measure than before, the sarcifices of the miners and of their wives
and children in resisting for so long the degradation of their standards will have been made
in vain. It will mean that the miners, just at the time when they need to be fortified in
resisting an enforced settlement on the mineowners' terms, will be weakened in the struggle.
It is already evident that the owners are determined to make no contribution towards an
equitable settlement. They refuse to make a national agreement and are adamant in
their demand to enforce brutal wages reductions and an eight-hours working day. Their
insistence can only be explained by their assumption that a continuance of the lockout
with the penury and hardships entailed, will weaken the resistance of the miners and compel
them to capitulate. If the miners are forced to settle now on the only terms the owners
are prepared to offer, all the sufferings and sacrifices of the past sixteen weeks will have
gone for nothing, and encouragement will be given to attacks on the standards of the
workers generally.
We earnestly appeal, therefore, to the organised workers in all trades and to the public
at large not to diminish their support but to give increased help to the miners at this
critical stage. The statement of the Prince of Wales in which he declared that it was wrong
that a struggle of this character should be decided by the starvation of women and children,
found an echo in the hearts of all right-thinking people. Help must be forthcoming
quickly to ensure that the workers shall emerge successfully from this struggle. STARVATION
MUST NOT BE ALLOWED TO DECIDE THE ISSUE. Through the generosity of the workers and
fair-minded supporters and sympathisers at home and abroad a strenuous fight has been
maintained against starvation. The struggle has now reached the stage where it is neces-
sary in the words of the American Federation of Labour " to give until it hurts" to save
the miners from defeat by starvation.
20th August, 1926.
Signed, on behalf of the
Trades Union Congress General Council :----

ARBROATH. Trade is still very poor in Arbroath, although it has improved in Carnoustic. This is, by the way, to lead to a difficulty, as the increased business in that town is creating a demand for machinists, and which can be met only in Arbroath. All the latter machinists are signing at Em- ployment Exchange for part-time benefit, and so are available to be offered this work elsewhere. While no one would complain about them getting the offer of better employment, the question really is, what will Arbroath do if the trained machinists are taken away? Although the factory in Arbroath is working only two days per week, still the machinists are required, and if lost it is difficult to imagine how the factory would carry on. The matter will be found. Our members have voted on the question of the £50,000 loan to the Yorkshire Miners' Association, and the £20,000 grant made to the Council of the T.U. Congress. A large majority favoured the action of assisting the miners in these practical ways. The suggested Superannuation Scheme has been carefully considered by most of our male members, and while it will come up again later, the bulk of our members are of opinion that the scheme is im- practicable altogether. In view of the fact that superannuation requires such a long probationary period, with an addition to the contribution of 25 per cent., it is felt that the whole scheme should be dropped rather than be made compulsory. At present it would seem that a compulsory clause regarding it would lead to the loss of a great many members. Since Colin Grant's factory closed down in 1923 several shoe workers have failed to secure re-employment in the trade, and they are now being refused idle benefit at the Exchange, Even although they pass the local Rota Committees, who are satisfied they are genuinely seeking work, the D.O. in Edinburgh is rejecting the claims. All over Scotland this abominable practice is at work. Rota Committees pass cases and, in spite of local knowledge and experience, the officials in Edinburgh are refusing benefit on the ground of " not a reasonable period of employment during the past two years. This is leading to a dangerous situation.
CHESHAM.-Trade here is still quiet, and the prospect of working full time seems very remote unless the coal dispute is settled, which we all hope will soon take place and the miners obtain a just settlement.
CHESTERFIELD. -Trade is very bad here and most of our members are still unemployed, and those who are in work, except a few members, are not making much above two or three days a week.
DERBY. -Trade in Derby has not improved during the last month ; two firms are not making half time. Great dissatisfaction now operates at the C.W.S. at Derby. Every year up to 1926 they have paid a full week's wages to all employees with twelve months' service regardless of time lost by short- ness of work at the break up for the August holiday, but this year they have not paid for the weeks the operatives have been off, and in one case the deduc- tion was £I IS.
GLASGOW.-Trade with us is exceedingly bad, the effect of the coal crisis being that a large number of the members are suspended for a week or more alternatively. About 25 men in the heavy team at Shieldhall have now done 12 consecutive weeks. Other factories are working 10 to 4 p.m.
HIGHAM AND RUSHDEN. -There is little to report in regard to trade. A slight improvement in some factories and less trade in others. Generally, trade is poor, except in Army District, which is fairly busy.
KINGSWOOD AND DISTRICT. -Trade in this centre is moderate, and in view of the industrial situation we are thankful for small mercies. Several

during the month, one from our little Bideford section, North Devon, and the
other from Plymouth. Our Bideford member was one of the gallant band who
has helped to keep the flag flying, without any assistance from our Union
Generals or even Branch N.C.O.'s, in the far North Country made famous by
the writings of Kingsley and the fascinating story of Westward Ho ! There
were men good and true in those days in the north country who knew how to
stand alone; men good and true are still there, and we have no doubt Bideford
Section has laid to rest one of the best. Our Plymouth member was a younger
man, and very popular with the Freemasons with whom he held important
positions. He leaves a wife and three children. We much regret the loss of
these members from our ranks, for members are difficult to get in the repairing
trade, and it would appear from our experience even more difficult to keep now that
the trade is under the Trade Board. Possibly the many years of bad trade and
short time has more to do with this aspect of the question than we imagine.
Certainly, during the long period of depression the Trade Board has only been
able to secure a bare existence for the workers, and many of our members are
of the opinion that Trade Unions have found it beyond their power to do more,
but were there ever a time in the history of Trade Unionism when advances of
wages were secured, or the workers' standard of life even maintained, while
trade floundered and sunk in the Slough of Despond ?
SILEBY.-Trade is very quiet with us, most of the factories closing very
early for the August holidays. We are hoping that when trade is more normal
and the Coal Dispute is settled we shall, with the great help of our Organisers
(Mr. J. H. Baum and Mr. D. McCarthy), make a decided improvement in the
membership of our Branch. When one sees the numbers working in the boot
and shoe trade having to wait at Labour Exchanges two hours to sign who,
by becoming members of our Union, can get all the benefits from us is deplor-
able from a common sense view.

Fictitious Wages.
The next item was the striking, fictitious wages over the ten years totalling £24,000.
The method adopted in passing this through the books was a very ingenious one.
ants kept two books—for wages and staff wages. At the end of each week they added
wages and staff wages, and entered them up as wages. The real amount was then entered
up as staff wages. The effect was that the staff wages were entered twice and the defend-
ants kept the extra amount of staff wages and for 10 years the total was £24,000. At the end of
these books was written by one or other defendant, at varying times, “No mistake,” and
initialled by one of the Neys.

SOUTH AFRICAN SHOE TRADE.
How Phillips (Norwich) Ltd., Undercut the Market.
[By Our Own Correspondent.]
Port Elizabeth, the shoe manufacturing centre of South Africa, is in a very flourishing
condition. And the footwear manufacturing concerns have in no slight degree assisted
in creating this favourable state of things, seeing that the wage bill of these factories
represents a very substantial amount-thousands of pounds per week.
Duty Free Materials.
The manufacturer here is certainly on a first-class wicket, for he has every encourage-
ment to make good-duty free materials and grindery, plus a 30 per cent. tariff. He is
not selling his products any cheaper than the prices at which overseas footwear can be
landed. The consumer is certainly not receiving any advantage from lower prices, as
the oversea products can be sold as cheaply as the local.
The winding up of the business of Phillips (Norwich) Ltd., has cleared the air so far
as this side of the water is concerned, with the result that those semi-wholesalers who
were buying shoes at 3s. or 4s. per pair less than producers' cost will now have to pay
reasonable prices for their requirements. Then, too, the agent who is carrying a 20s. in
the£ proposition in the way of samples will come into his own again. It puzzled him to
know how goods could be offered at Phillips' prices, because retailers were able to produce
invoices to prove that competing Norwich lines were quite out of the market. There
can be no excuse for such deliberate price-cutting by men of experience-by men who
could not claim to be ignorant in regard to costing methods. I hope the matter will be
sifted to the bottom and drastic measures taken to prevent such happenings in the shoe
trade. Or as far as this country is concerned, action will be taken to see that goods are
not dumped into the Union below cost of production.-The Shoe and Leather Record,
20th August, 1926.

INTERNATIONAL INFORMATION
WORLD HOURS OF WORK REGULATION.

Belgian Move Forward.
A further step in the international regulation of hours of work has been taken by the
decision of the Belgian Senate this week in favour of the unconditional ratification of the
Eight-hour Day Convention, adopted by the first Session of the International Labour
Conference of the League of Nations, held in Washington in 1919.
This decision is the first important result of the London Hours Conference which
attended last March by representatives from Great Britain, France, Germany, Italy,
and Belgium, and which reached a comprehensive series of conclusions regarding a mutual
interpretation of the clauses of the Washington Convention.
At the eighth Session of the International Labour Conference, held at Geneva at the
end of May, the German Government representative stated that a Bill which had already
been introduced regarding ratification of the Hours Convention had been altered as a result
of the London Conference. He hoped it would be presented to Parliament this summer.
Germany's ratification would be dependent on ratification by other principal industrial
countries, but he hoped that this would take place at a very early date.
The British Government representative at the same International Labour Conference
said that, owing to conditions in Great Britain since the London Conference, his Govern-
ment had not had the opportunity of considering the result of the London Conference in
leisure and in calm, and for that reason they had not been able to arrive at a decision.
The Commercial Committee of the French Senate has recently approved a Bill for
ratification, dependent on ratification by Germany, which has already passed the French
Chamber of Deputies.

CHINESE WORKERS' CONGRESS.
A "Charter" of Working Conditions.
Interesting information regarding the aims of organised workers in China is contained
in the current issue of Industrial and Labour Information, the weekly publication of the
International Labour Office of the League of Nations, in an account of the recent holding
of the third Congress of Chinese workers in Canton.
Four hundred delegates, representing 1,240,000 organised workers belonging to 400
unions in 19 provinces, were present, as compared with 540,000 workers represented at
the second congress, in May, 1925, and 200,000 at the first congress, in May, 1922.
Reports were presented and resolutions passed on the following subjects: Organisation
of the labour movement: reorganisation and working of trade unions; objects and pro-
gramme of the economic struggle; strikes; the relations between workers and peasants;
workers' education; young workers and the trade union movement; unemployment;
co-operation; labour legislation.
The following resolution on the right of association and conditions of work was
adopted :-
(1) Workers should enjoy freedom of association and combination and of the Press;
(2) Workers should have the right to strike, but, under the Republican Govern-
ment, disputes may be submitted to conciliation procedure under the direction of
the public authorities or the interested parties;
(3) Workers' organisations should have the right to conclude collective agree-
ments with employers;
(4) Workers should be free to join a trade union;

FORWARD MOVES IN INDIA.
The membership of the Indian Trade Unions has improved notably during the first
six months of 1020. The membership of Trade Unions in the Bombay Presidency has
gone up since the end of 1925 from 40.318 to 64,572, an increase of over 30 per cent. There
are now to trade unions in Bombay City, eight in Ahmedabad (the second cotton centre)
and 20 in the rest of the Presidency.
The figures are conservative estimates based on returns made by the more efficiently
organised trade unions. -Industrial News, Trades Union Congress, 3rd August, 1926.

IRISH FREE STATE TRADE.
98% Export Trade is with Great Britain and Northern Ireland.
An Adverse Balance of £6,750,000,
The Free State trade returns for the first three months of the present year disclose an
adverse balance of £6,750,000, a slight increase on the figures for the corresponding perio
of last year. Ninety-eight per cent, of the Free State's export trade is with Great Britain
and Northern Ireland, and while its foreign imports are increasing there is no compensating
improvement in Free State sales.
For instance, Algiers sends the Free State goods to the value of £32,000 and buys
nothing. Poland's imports from the Free State amount to the value of £5 note, but she
sells goods to the amount of £82,000 to Irish customers, Other countries reap even
richer harvest. Rumania's exports to the Free State for the first quarter of this year
came to £85,000. Her imports from this country were worth exactly £1. With countries
like Germany, France, Belgium, and the United States trade is slightly better, but in all
these cases the Free State's purchases exceed its sales by enormous sums.
To all intents and purposes the Free State's only customers are Great
Britain and Northern Ireland, and Irish business men recognise the fact
that the country's adverse balance never will be adjusted until the Govern-
ment's efforts are concentrated on the encouragement of trade with its
neighbours.
For that reason there is a growing belief that the executive council's policy of pro-
tective tariffs (on boots and clothing, &c.) is doing more harm than good to the national
economy. The demand for free trade within the British Isles is (says the Dublin corres-
pondent of The Times) likely to play an important part at the general election, which will
be held next year, for the economic situation is beginning to cause considerable anxiety
throughout the country. — Shoe and Leather Record, 6th August, 1296.

AUSTRIAN CUSTOMS.
Increased Duty Imposed on Footwear.
VIENNA, 28th July.
The Austrian Parliament finally approved to-day the new Customs Tariff increasing
duties chiefly on iron goods, textiles, boots, butter and frozen meat. Commercial interests
strongly opposed the higher tariff contending that it would raise the general cost of living.
Iron and textile industries, however, declared that higher duties were necessary for their
very existence.
Only a few of the new duties can be introduced immediately as the greater part are
fixed by various commercial treaties.
The new tariff is regarded as indicating that Austria is forced to pursue a policy of
high protection so long as neighbouring countries continue to maintain their present trade
barriers. Reuter. — Shoe and Leather Record, 6th August, 1926.

TAXED FOOTWEAR.
Unbearable Increase in the Cost of Living.
At last week's meeting of the Westmeath County Council, Mr. Thomas Glynn moved
a resolution expressing the opinion that the duty on boots imported into the Irish Free
State had caused an unbearable increase in the cost of living (particularly
on account of the present depression and scarcity of money and the large
amount of unemployment) and calling on the Government to defer placing
any tariffs on imported goods until the people were in a better position to
bear them.
Mr. P. Brett said he was not in favour of Mr. Glynn's motion, but, at the same time,
a lot of tariffs had been put on purely for the purpose of getting in revenue.
On a division the motion was defeated by seven votes to five. — Shoe and Leather
Record, 30th July, 1926.

4. The Fund we propose should be for FULL MALE MEMBERS only, and that

approached at special meetings, with a view to securing £50,000 from Branch Funds;

5. We suggest when Superannuation Benefit is payable to members at 65 years of
age, it can be claimed whether members are continuing at work or not, it being understood
that members having once drawn Superannuation Benefit, they shall only be entitled to
legal assistance (in case of accidents in a factory) and funeral benefits.
6. Any member ceasing work at 65 years of age and being in receipt of Superannuation
Benefit shall not be entitled to receive any other benefit except funeral pay.
7. All members in receipt of Superannuation Benefit and continuing at work will
pay a contribution of SIXPENCE per week only, 3d. of which shall be placed to the credit
of the Superannuation Fund and 3d. to the Funeral Fund.
8. Funeral Benefit. We suggest that in the event of a member contributing to the
Superannuation Fund, and death supervening before receiving such Superannuation
Benefit, his dependants shall receive an extra £2 Funeral Benefit, in addition to the sum
named in the Rules, making a total of £8 for men and £5 for women.
9. Women Members shall be allowed to Voluntarily join the Superannuation Scheme
if they desire.
Amendments to this proposal must be sent to the Central Office before 30th September,
1926, to enable the Special Conference to deal with the matter on 21st October, 1920.

AN INTERNATIONAL ANNIVERSARY.
I.F.T.U. will Celebrate its 25th Birthday.
Next month the International Federation of Trade Unions celebrates its twenty-fifth anniversary.
On 10th September, therefore, in all the countries affiliated to the I.F.T.U., meetings and demonstrations will be held to mark the importance of this event in the development of international working-class unity. Nearly half of the total number of organised workers in the world are linked up through their national Trade Union centres in the International Federation. The I.F.T.U. represents close upon 17,000,000 organised workers in twenty-three different countries. The affiliated membership has more than trebled in the course of the history of the I.F.T.U.
A remarkable feature of its work in recent years has been the organisation of international campaigns, such as the one promoted in 1920 in support of the Eight-hour Day, and the campaign against war and militarism in 1924. It has been active also in raising funds, by international appeals, to assist the workers of various countries. No less than £150,000 was raised in this way to provide supplies for the Russian people in the famine, and over £100,000 to help the destitute Austrian workers. It also assisted the German Trade Unions to the extent of over £42,000 when their incomes were reduced practically to vanishing point by the depreciation of the mark. Large sums have been raised too for the Indian workers.
But the chief function of the I.F.T.U. is to focus international working-class opinion upon the great questions of policy affecting the peoples of all countries. It has done this with extraordinary success at various international congresses, and in the vigorous campaigns it promoted against Fascism and other forms of international reaction. It has also displayed great activity in organising international summer schools and in fostering the working-class educational movement.
Twenty-five years of effort and sacrifice have placed the international working-class organisation on a firm foundation. It is well that the British workers should give thought to the achievements that have been won, and to the work that has yet to be accomplished in the international field.—Industrial News, 10th August, 1926.

J. R. MACDONALD ON VALUE OF PARLIAMENT.
Sometimes I wonder if some of my friends quite appreciate what is involved in a loss of the moral authority of Parliament. It is nothing less than a Fascist or some other form of Dictatorship. In view of the work that is in front of us and of the nature of the opposition we shall have to face, we must hold fast to Parliament as our sole bulwark of defence. An essential condition of our success is a Parliament which holds its place high in the respect and confidence of the country. That gone, everything has gone. - Forward, 31st July, 1926.

BELGIUM AND THE HOURS CONVENTION.
Minister for Labour upon Beneficial Effects of an Eight-hour Day.
The Belgian Chamber of Representatives by 119 votes to 3 against on 4th June, 1926,
passed the Bill for Ratification of the Hours Convention.
The Minister of Industry and
Labour, MR. WAUTERS, said: He denied that the Eight-hour Act of 1921 (which was
wider than the Hours Convention) had impeded production
as in other countries, the reduction of hours of labour had been a stimulant to production.
for it had led employers to improve their plant and their processes and land in production.
He quoted figures relating to various industries in support of this contention. The intro
duction of the eight-hour day had given the workers increased leisure, much of which was
being devoted to technical training. There had been a marked diminution in alcoholism;
110.000 public houses had disappeared. More and more workmen were acquiring their
own houses, and the number of public libraries was increasing year by year.
Referring to the situation in the chief industrial countries as regards the eight-hour
day, MR. WAUTERS said the position was such that Belgium could ratify the Hours Con-
vention in complete confidence and with complete safety. As regards the London inter-
pretations, he pointed out that the conclusion of the conference as to the meaning of
Article 14 of the Convention was couched in very wide terms and met, to a large extent,
the Belgian point of view.
In his opinion, the Eight-hour Act would create better relations between employers
and workers and thus contribute to the promotion of industrial prosperity. By ratification
of the Convention, the workers would obtain an assurance that the ground they had
already won would not be lost, while the employers, seeing the Act of 1921 finally con-
firmed, would turn their attention energetically to the adoption of more modern methods,
the improvement of their workshops, and the tightening-up of the organisation for pro-
duction, sale and exportation. He therefore urged that Belgium should ratify, uncon-
ditionally and immediately, the Washington Convention.
Some discussion took place on the question whether the amendment proposed by
MR. JACQUEMOTTE was in order. It was eventually ruled that the amendment could not
be discussed; a Convention having been submitted for the decision of the Chamber,
the Chamber must adopt it or reject it as it stood and without amendment.
The Bill was then adopted by 119 votes to 3, with 5 abstentions.-Extract from
Industrial and Labour Information, Monday, 19th July, 1926.

WE PAY MORE THAN THE CZECHS.
Leicester Firm's £100 Challenge.
Wages Comparison.
A claim of Bata's, a boot and shoe manufacturing firm in Czecho-Slovakia, that they
are paying wages in their Zlin factories equal to the wages agreed upon by the Boot and Shoe Manu-
facturers Federation,
has led to a controversy in the trade journals.
In a joint letter, Mr. J. E. Richards, General President of the Union, and Mr. C. W.
Horrell, President of the Federation, challenge the accuracy of Bata's statement,
intimate that if the minimum wage rate for shoe operatives in England is represented by
100, in Czecho-Slovakia it is represented by 74.
The Shoe and Leather News has published an article which says that in an advertisement
Bata stated that " their wages would compare favourably with those paid in any shoe factory
in the United Kingdom, and they set out the wages they paid and compared them with
what they said were the wages paid as a minimum in Great Britain.
In reply to this advertisement it is urged that Bata's figures of the wages paid in Great
Britain are incorrect, and the wages of Eatough's Ltd., Earl Shilton, are put forward in
proof of the misstatement.
67 Per Cent More.
Bata's wage list works out by striking an average for all workers from 15 years of age
and upwards, at 27s. 0 d. for each worker per week ; whereas Eatough's, on the same basis,
for the week ended 10th July, shows 45s. 9 d. for each worker.
"So," it is added, " our labour costs, for similar goods, 67 per cent. more than Bata's
(exclusive of staff wages).
This fact gives the foreign manufacturer a good help to enable him to send his surplus
stock into this country at a profit, assisted also by the low rate of exchange, which makes
his task much easier, to the detriment of the British worker, who is taxed up to the hilt so
that his country may balance the yearly budget.
"We have no means of ascertaining if, in addition to the payment of lower wages and
the low rate of exchange ruling, we are further handicapped by increased daily output per
operative (at Bata's) as compared with Great Britain.'
Eatough's, in order to establish the accuracy of their wages statement, intimate their
willingness to give an opportunity for any certified accountant to examine their wages
book, the auditor to be selected by the Mayor of Leicester. "If," they add, " the figures
we have given are found to be exaggerated we will forward to the Royal Infirmary a cheque
for £100." -Leicester Mail, 11th August, 1926.

70,000 HOUSES SHORT.
Big Task Facing London.
There is a shortage of over 70,000 houses in London, according to Col. Levita, Chairman
of the Housing Committee of the London County Council.
At yesterday's meeting of the Council he stated that in 1919 the shortage in Greater
London was 50,000. There had also to be added the normal requirements for the increas-
ing population, which were 17,000 houses a year.
In 1925, for the first time since the war, the normal annual requirements had
been exceeded, for in that year 23,547 houses were built and 694 were demolished,
leaving a net increase of 22,853, or nearly 6,000 in excess of current requirements.
In the previous five years the provision fell short of the current requirements by
28,000 houses, so that the excess of 6,000 in 1925 left a deficiency of 22,000. Therefore
in 1926 and onwards a deficiency of over 20,000 houses on current account had to be dealt
with before they would begin to touch the shortage which existed in 1919.
On that basis the shortage began with 50,000 in 1919, rose to 78,000 in 1923, and fell

INTERNATIONAL FEDERATION OF TRADE UNIONS.
The Fight for Trade Union Unity in Yugo-Slavia.
By Bogdan Krecik, Secretary of the United Trade Union Federation of Yugo-Slavia.
The political gains of the first three years, as shown in the number of
seats in Parliament, have little by little been completely lost. It is also due to the
movement is not only to be ascribed to the political reaction that a large part of the
workers have been won over to the views of the various non labour
parties and are giving them political support.
We advocated trade union unity on the basis of the chief demands of the
workers, and the independence of the trade unions from political parties.
Although this aim was sympathetically received by the masses of the workers, it was
resisted violently by certain groups. In the first place it met with the hostility
of the Communists, all the more because the Communist Party must exercise influence on the
trade unions, and use them as an attacking force. The unity efforts resulted in the
formation of two distinct tendencies inside the Communist trade unions:
one section
favoured unity, while the other wanted to retain their existence as a separate national
centre, acting in this matter under direct instructions from Moscow. It goes without
saying that those trade unions which were under the influence of anti-labour parties,
such as the Croat Labour Union, in Zagreb, and the Christian and national-socialist organi-
sations in Slovenia, opposed unity.
At the end of 1925 in spite of all hostility, unity was reached between the socialists,
a part of the Communists and a part of the neutral unions.
The Communists understood only too well the danger which unity threatened to
them, and collected all their forces to wreck the unity movement.
There is no room whatever for doubt that the unity congress of the two national
centres was a great victory for Amsterdam and a corresponding disappointment
for the Communists.
It can be said that on the whole the trade union movement of Yugo-Slavia is at the
present moment in favour of the efforts to attain unity.
-Press Reports of the International Federation of Trade Unions, 5th August, 1926.

BE ON YOUR GUARD!
Functions of Trade Unionism.
"The experiences we have gone through this year and the loss and suffering inflicted
upon the whole country, and particularly upon the trade unionists in the great basic
industries, have undoubtedly raised questions about the functions of Trade Unionism and
their bearing on the general welfare which must go forward to an issue.
"The question which the nation will now have to consider is whether these privileges
have not been grossly abused; whether the trade unions, instead of being,
as they should be, the social bulwarks and guarantees for the well-being of their members,
are not being used as a tool of faction against society, inflicting great injury
upon the country, and in particular, upon those very trade union members which it is the
duty of trade unionism primarily to protect.
"The question is raised whether, for instance, a handful of wirepullers, in virtue of
some resolution passed on a card-vote without any guarantees that the opinion of their
constituents has been properly obtained, should have the power to lay an interdict on
all the industries of the country and to challenge the sovereign right of Parliament and
the State itself."-Extract from speech of Chancellor of the Exchequer, Mr. Winston
Churchill, M.P. (delivered at Swansea), 18th August, 1926.

RUINED BY RICHES.
The extraordinary wrongness of our present industrial system is shown once more
by the outcry at the bumper crop of American raw cotton. One would think that a recor
crop of this kind would be greeted with delight by the user as well as by the ultimate
consumer as a guarantee of abundant raw material, low prices, and correspondingly brisa
expanding trade. But it appears that in the world constituted as it now is abundance
raw cotton is a positive calamity. Stated coldly like that, the only possible inferer
from the assertion is that the world is quite mad. The facts are, we believe, that in value
the export of British cotton to India, for instance, is now greater than in 1913, but the
volume is from various causes very greatly less than the volume exported in 1913. This
state of things is all very well for the banker and the financier; it is ruin to the unfortunate
operative who is on permanent short time; because to him the volume manufactured is
everything. But there must be something wrong with a system in which a trade can
flourish financially while the people who are engaged in it are in desperate straits, and in
which the prospect of ample raw material takes on the air of a positive calamity.-Da
News, 11th August, 1926.

OIL FROM COAL.
BY HERBERT TRACEY.
After months of delay, the Government has set up a standing committee to consi
and advise upon questions concerning the economic use of fuels.
It is, as Government appointments go, a good committee. It includes two Lab
men, Mr. John Baker, M.P., of the Iron and Steel Trades Confederation, and Mr. Frans
Hodges, Secretary of the Miners' International. Other members are experts in scienti
and industrial research; there are directors of colliery and iron and steel concerns,
distilleries, and of gas and coke companies; specialists in electrical power problems and
the carbonisation of coal. And Sir Alfred Mond, M.P., is a member.
At last, it would seem, something is to be done to develop a national coal and power
policy by which the mining industry will be transformed from one concerned only with
the production of raw coal into a new industry for the conversion of the raw product into
electrical power, gas, coke, oil and smokeless fuel.
The Coal Commission emphasise the fact that every million tons of coal carbonised
by suitable processes will produce 15 million gallons or more of liquid fuel. We imported
in 1924 no less than 1,270 million gallons of crude petroleum oil or derivatives. If it
were possible (says the Commission) to subject to pre-treatment the 147 million tons c
coal now burned in its raw state, the greater part at least of our present requirements
of oil could be supplied from home resources instead of being imported from abroad.
From the national point of view the burning of raw coal is a wasteful and unhygienic
proceeding. The labour of a million men for three days every year is devoted to producing
the soot which pollutes our atmosphere-three million tons of potential fuel escapes into
the air from domestic fire-places and industrial chimneys.-Industrial News, 24th August,
1926.

THE MUNICIPALITY AS COAL MERCHANT.
Cut out middlemen's profits and leave more for the miner.
By OUR POLITICAL CORRESPONDENT.

It is typical of the antagonism of the Tory Government towards the miners that in
implementing the report of the Samuel Commission they have devoted their attention
mainly to those recommendations which operate to the disadvantage of the miners, whilst
neglecting almost completely those which might have been calculated to confer some
benefit upon them.
For instance, they have unceasingly advocated lower wages, and even though longer
hours were not favoured by the Commission, they have argued that these were necessary
too. On the other hand, they have taken no serious steps to give effect to the Com-
mission's definite recommendations for the State Acquisition of Royalties, the systematic
Reorganisation of the Industry and the Distribution of Coal by Municipal Authorities.
All of these measures, by eliminating either unnecessary profits or uneconomic expenditure,
would tend to increase the resources available for distribution in miners' wages, and thus
to diminish the force of the mineowners' constant demands for lower pay and longer hours.

Where does the difference go?
That there is an unjustifiably wide margin between the price of coal at the pithead
and the price charged to the consumer is shown by the figures that were placed before
the Samuel Commission. At a time when the average price of coal at the pithead was
145. 2d. a ton, the prices that were being charged in London varied from 40s. to 56s. a ton.
Surely the discrepancy there is sufficient to condemn the present system of distribution
after coal leaves the pithead !
The Labour Government thought so, and through their Minister of Mines, they had
a scheme prepared which would have empowered local authorities to enter into com-
petition with the profiteering merchants. But the General Election arrived before the
scheme could be put into operation, and when the Tory Government came into office
the plans were pigeonholed, as were many others that had as their object the protection of
the workers from exploitation.
The Samuel Commission also thought that the municipalities should be empowered
to trade in coal, and recommended that at least a two years' trial of the system should be
given. The Government, however, has abstained from giving effect to the recommendation.

Municipal Trading Pays.
The Municipalities are well equipped for entering the coal trade, and many of them,
like Birmingham, Manchester, Liverpool and Glasgow, already buy over a million tons a
year for their gas and other undertakings. Moreover, municipal trading generally has
proved itself to be a sound proposition, and just as it has cheapened the price of gas,
electricity and water to the consumers whilst at the same time making a profit for the
community, so could the same be done in the case of coal.
In refusing to act on the recommendation of the Commission, the Government has
shown once again that it is more concerned with the protection of vested interests than
with the standard of living of the workers and the welfare of the community at large.
-The Labour Press Service, 25th August, 1926.

WORSE THAN FIVE YEARS AGO.
One-Room Houses in Glasgow.

"To say that we have turned the corner with regard to housing is utter nonsense
so far as Scotland is concerned; the fact is that in Glasgow we are worse off to-day than
we were when we started our schemes five years ago."
This was the comment of a Glasgow housing expert when approached regarding the
Minister of Health's statement as to the position of housing in the country. "We have
not touched the fringe of the question," he said.
At a Parliamentary inquiry at the end of last year, Glasgow's need was given as
100,000 houses. Under the local authority schemes 7,500 houses have been built and
occupied in Glasgow, 6,500 are at present under construction, while ground has been
bought to permit of the erection of a further 9,000 houses. Practically all these are
subsidised houses.
According to the Medical Officer of Health for Glasgow there were at the 1921 census
40,689 houses of only one apartment, populated by 132,146 persons, and 78,781 persons
were living more than three in one room, while in 108,968 two-apartment houses there were
514,537 residents and 181,625 living more than three in a room. -Daily News, 28th July, 1926.

REGISTERED SOCIETIES.
Management Expenses.
COMMANDER FANSHAWE asked the Minister of Labour what proportion of the total
annual income is used for management expenses, including salaries, by societies registered
under the Friendly Societies Act?
THE FINANCIAL SECRETARY TO THE TREASURY (Mr. Ronald McNeill): I have been
asked to reply. No statistics are available which give the precise information desired.
Societies registered under the Friendly Societies Act include not only Friendly Societies,
but also working men's clubs, cattle insurance societies, benevolent societies, and especially
authorised societies. The management expenses ratio on these four classes has never
been calculated. In 1924 friendly societies (other than societies with branches, which
include 50 per cent. of friendly society membership, and collecting societies) received
total contributions of £6,430,000 and spent on management £690,000, or about 7 per
cent. of contributions. In the same year collecting societies SPENT 34 PER CENT. OF THEIR
TOTAL INCOME ON MANAGEMENT. - Extract from Parliamentary Debates, House of Commons,

MONTHLY REPORT

24TH SEPTEMBER, 1926.

FELLOW MEMBERS,
TRADE.
Trade still continues stagnant; largely, as stated last month, due to the
Mining situation, a situation which can only be described not only as tragic,
but as one to call for the utmost condemnation of owners and the Government
in the attitude taken up in the past days. One might imagine that such
Lock-out was a comparatively small affair, instead of one which is affecting
the nation adversely, both morally, physically and materially.
We continue to pay out considerable sums of money due to lack of employ-
mont, the amount paid from our own Out-of-Work Fund during the month
being as follows: £7,120 13s. gd. and from the State side £11,196 1s. 7d.
The Ministry of Labour figures relating to the industry are as follows :-
BOOT AND SHOE INDUSTRY.
Employment remained poor, on the whole, especially with makers of workmen's
boots. In most centres the factories closed for extended periods at the holidays. After
the resumption of work, employment was generally on a short time basis, but slightly
better than in the previous month.
The percentage of workpeople unemployed, as indicated by the unemployment books
lodged at employment exchanges, was 13.6 on 23rd August, 1926, as compared with 14.3
on 26th July, 1926, and with 12.3 on 24th August, 1925.

Returns from firms employing 41,500 operatives in the week ended 28th August, 1926,
showed that practically 50 per cent. of these operatives worked short time in that week,
losing, on an average, about 12 hours each.

Employment in London declined and was only moderate on the whole, more short
time being worked than in July. Many firms at Leicester extended the bank holiday
stoppage, and when work was resumed employment was very slack, with short time working
prevalent. At Hinckley employment was bad, and worse than in July. At Northampton,
after extended holidays, few factories were able to work more than half time; but during
the latter part of the month there was a slight improvement. Short time working continued
with some firms in the Higham and Rushden area, but employment on the whole was fair.
There was an improvement at Wellingborough, but employment was still poor and short
time working prevalent; at Irthlingborough employment remained moderately good.
At Kettering there was a slight reduction in short time working when the factories re-
opened after the holidays, but the average hours worked were still only from one-half
to three-quarters of normal.

Employment at Stafford was fairly good, and slightly better than in July, but many
operatives were working reduced hours. At Norwich more short time was worked than in
July, and employment, with most firms, was only moderate. A further slight improve-
ment was reported in the Bristol and Kingswood area; employment was, however, much
below normal for the time of year, especially in the case of factories producing heavy boots.
In the Leeds area less short time was worked than in July, but employment was still poor,
and worse than a year ago. In the Rossendale Valley employment was about the same
as a month earlier and there was a considerable amount of under-employment in the Bacup
and Rawtenstall districts.

In Scotland, taken as a whole, there was a decline as compared both with July and
with a year ago. Employment was good at Maybole and fairly good at Kilmarnock,
and an improvement as compared with the previous month was reported in each of these
