BOOTS AND SHOES MADE ABROAD.
On pages 533-546 will be found an interesting and informative report
dealing with the manufacture of Boots and Shoes on the Continent. The
report is one from our own colleagues, Messrs. T. F. Richards and W. R.
Smith, who have, at first hand, investigated the methods of production.
The report proves to us how necessary it is for yet more interworking and
understanding with our comrades in other countries, and thereby make it
possible for general standards to be set up and prevent unjust conditions of
employment to obtain either in this country or elsewhere.
NEW NATIONAL AGREEMENT.
On Tuesday the 21st inst. we met the Executive of the Manufacturers
Federation at 7 Tavistock Square, W.C. 1, to deal with the proposals sub-
mitted in connection with National Agreement. Mr. W. Addington Willis,
C.B.E., presided.
After considerable discussion upon the whole question it was decided
that the existing Agreement (with the deletion in Clause 8 of the words "June
or" and the words "April or," which means that a yearly, if any revision
of the wage rates, instead of half-yearly, take place, and which will only operat
if the Cost-of-Living Figure falls to 70 or lower. Also the important deletion
will take place of the "B" rates of pay for Males; thus in both these cases
advantage accrues to the workers, and should be re-signed for another two
years.
A Committee is also to be set up to deal with certain obscure points of
reading in the Agreement and the Terms of Settlement, more especially the
question of Regulation of Wages by the Statement when daywork is the method
of payment, and to report to the full body later on.
We feel sure the members will, if they take account of the existing con-
ditions in the industrial world, fully support this procedure. We have preserved
and really improved the position, which is not a small thing at the present
time, and we confidently appeal for a big vote in support of the policy we
have pursued. The actual resolutions passed were as follows:
MR. C. W. HORRELL proposed and MR. T. F. RICHARDS seconded:
"That the National Agreement as at present existing be re-signed,
and made operative for a further period of two years, with the exception
of the elimination of the words 'June or,' line 4, and 'April or' line 5.
Paragraph 1, Clause 8; and the necessary amendment of the heading of
Schedule A, in view of the elimination of Schedule B."
"That a Joint Sub-Committee be formed under the Chairmanship
of Mr. W. Addington Willis, with instructions to consider the phraseology
of the various clauses of the National Agreement, and to make recom-
mendations of drafting alterations to the next National Conference;
but the alterations shall not be such as to vary the principles embodied
in the National Agreement."

THE MINING SITUATION.
We had hoped that it would have been possible this month to have reported
a settlement in connection with the above-named question. Such however
cannot be done, the position being one wherein it appears that the owners of
the mines have made up their minds to insist upon breaking down the method
of National Agreements, relying upon hunger and suffering to bring about such
breakaways from the Miners' Federation as will mean the end of such body.
We hope that their strategy will be defeated and public opinion become so
vocal as to compel reason and justice to triumph. In this connection the Trades
Union Congress passed a resolution calling upon all to support as far as possible.
the Miners, financially. We know it is not an easy matter for many so to do,
having regard to their small income. We, however, appeal to the whole
membership to give as much as possible to help our comrades, their wives and
children in the tremendous fight that they are engaged in, and make it possible
for them to emerge therefrom with honour.

The Trade Congress which was held at Bournemouth, 6th to 11th Septem-
ber, under the Presidency of Mr. A. Pugh, the Chairman of the General Council
of the Trades Union Congress, was, despite the "prophets," very successful.
The expected "hot" times did not take place, and except for one short period
on Thursday afternoon, the business was conducted in an orderly and expedi-
Mr. Pugh made an excellent Chairman. Many questions of
tious manner.
vital interest to the people were dealt with, it being clear to those who were
present that despite its detractors the Congress is a powerful organisation
and one that helps to focus public opinion and to secure attention to matters
concerning the well-being of, not only the people of Great Britain, but also

This paper is our own paper and gives information upon labour questions not

the country. Do your part in helping to still further extend its circulation.
The General President and the General Secretary were re-elected members
of the General Purposes and the General Council respectively. Mr. W. R.
Smith, although not elected as delegate to the Canadian Congress, polled
exceedingly well, and was second on the list.

THE GENERAL PRESIDENT'S REPORT.

60 LADY SOMERSET ROAD,
KENTUSH Town, N.W.
22nd September, 1926.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
THE NATIONAL AGREEMENT. The best thing we have done this month was
when we signed the new National Agreement yesterday, which will remain in operation
until the end of 1928. Our members should carefully consider the Agreement and see
what has been gained. Owing to the cost-of-living figure being 72 points above 1914.
We shall now return to the 60s. minimum for all males on the first pay-day in November
All pressmen and men in the shoe rooms will receive 3s. rise on their previous minimum,
making 60s. in all. In addition the employers were generous enough to concede to us a
change in the date as to when the adjustment should be made, which means that in future
the figure will only be taken annually, and that on the September figures issued in the
Labour Gazette, which figure has always been favourable to the operative. The suggested
change in the Holiday Benefit Clause, submitted by the Federation, was withdrawn and
will remain in the new agreement. Further, it is interesting to learn that we have em-
ployers in our midst who at the Conference did not hesitate to say progress in industry
would not be made at the expense of a reduction in wages. That is the spirit. It has
caused me to give some thought and consideration upon the subject, and I have made a
careful study of Mr. Henry Ford's book "To-day and To-morrow," by the multi-millionaire
motor-car maker. He has been the pioneer and is to-day, in the question of big wages
and low costs. The pivot upon which he works is that of organisation, a subject which
will never be thoroughly understood whilst human beings are on this earth. It is inter-
esting to know Mr. Ford has only been in business 18 years, and this year has made his
13,000,000 car or tractor. In 1908 he had turned out 10,000 at a cost of £950 each. By
4th June, 1924, he had turned out 10,000,000 at £290 each. It will be seen he lowered
the cost of production by more than 200 per cent. He employs at the present time in his
works 200,000; then he has 200,000 men distributing, and another 200,000 engaged in
the raw material, and claims responsibility for the welfare of 3,000,000 men, women and
children. The wages of his operatives in 1922 was 8s. 4d. per day; he conceived the
idea of giving them a rise and increased wages to 25s.; there are men receiving more than
this amount. Mr. Ford claims there is not a man receiving less than 25s. per day. Two
Cambridge graduates have visited Ford's works in Detroit, and they report in a book of
their own that when Mr. Ford gave increased wages, the local shopkeepers put up their
prices in order to have a share of the increased wages. In order to check the rapacity
of these people he started a commissariat department, where most of the operatives can
get a real good American meal for 7½d. per head. This department is so vast that 900,000
dollars was spent in it last year. Mr. Ford has several maxims, and I think some of them
are worth reprinting here :-

All workers need a sufficiency of food; clothing; housing and pleasure.
Workers should learn not to fear big business.
Politicians who think politics can do what business ought to do are wrong.
Work is the salvation of the race.
Every man should have an occupation providing he is healthy enough to do it.
True prosperity means a reduction in prices.
Men must be taught generalship of industry.
All business must be of service to the community.
Professional finance ruined Germany.
Professional Reformers ruined Russia. (It is too early to say yet-T.F.R.).
Finance runs the League of Nations.
Power is not Gold.
Money Brokers are not business men.
Gold is now taking its proper place as a help.
Business without profit will die.
All profits should be used for extensions.

He evidently does not think much of trade union officials, he says they "want to
hold office and make speeches."
Twenty-five years ago Mr. Ford would have considered £500 per annum a fortune
for life. To-day his wealth is estimated at £17,000,000, which of course includes his plant
and not dollars in the bank. Every day another 80,000 dollars are added to the pile.
A short time ago he wrote out a cheque for £953,000 income tax.
Compare this firm with Bata, of Czecho-Slovakia. The system of Bata is rather
abhorrent to those who are accustomed to individual freedom. If our members will
carefully peruse the report appearing in this issue, they will find the impression we gained

BOOT AND SHOE CONDITIONS ON THE
CONTINENT.
FELLOW MEMBERS,
The following is our report of the first attempt made by our Union to obtain
first-hand information as to the conditions and methods of working obtaining in our
industry outside this country. It may be that visits have already been made to boot
factories abroad, but they have been largely incidental to visits for other purposes rather
than for the obtaining of definite and specific information appertaining to the manufacture
of boots and shoes. Our experiences in this connection convinced us that such
ventures are of great value, giving, as they do, useful first-hand information which is
available at all times in the interest of our members.
No time was lost following the decision of the Executive Council in putting in hand
the arrangements necessary for our visit, and at the end of a week we had started on our
journey. We arrived at Prague on Wednesday, 7th July, and were met at the station
by Comrade Novak, whom we had written to act as interpreter for us, also Comrade Srb,
the Secretary, and another official of the Shoe and Leather Workers’ Union. We cannot
speak too highly of the help given us during our stay in Czecho-Slovakia. Comrade Srb
did everything possible to make our visit both profitable and pleasant, while the services
of Comrade Novak as interpreter were invaluable. He was with us early and late, nothing
was too much trouble for him to do, and we place on record our appreciation of the great
help and the many kindnesses we received at their hands.
A great sports-gathering, called "Sokol," which is an annual affair, and is arranged
by workers’ sports organisations, had just concluded when we arrived. It has
grown in numbers until this year no less than 17,000 men and 15,000 women took
part. We regret we were too late to witness any of the performances, and it was
unfortunate for us in another way, as it constituted the holiday period; the factories
being closed, we were prevented thereby from visiting any of them until the Monday.
However, we used the time at our disposal to ascertain as far as possible the general
conditions of the country, the relative position occupied by the workers, and their
standard of living compared with our own. We attach a table showing the cost of
different commodities in our money. (See page 546.)
There appears to be no doubt that their standard of living is lower than our own,
but great efforts are being made to raise it and bring about improvement in the condition
of working-class life; they have already accomplished a great deal. Mr. Srb thought
that after making all allowances, they were about one-third below us.
The State of Czecho-Slovakia is less than eight years old, being one of the number
that were created an independent State under the Treaty of Versailles, upon the break-up
of the old Austrian Empire. But like other countries they had their revolution towards
the close of the War, and without the loss of a single life, declared their independence
and set up a Provisional Government. In their early days they laid the foundation of a
real democratic State. The Government came into being on 28th October, 1918; they
established the eight-hour day by law on the 18th of December of the same year, a rather
smart performance. It is still in operation. In many respects the legislation affecting the
workers is unique. Every business which has more than thirty workpeople has its Works
Council, which keeps a watch on the carrying out of the collective agreements and arbitra-
tion decisions regarding wages, and on factory discipline. The Works Council has the
right to be consulted in regard to the dismissing of workmen, and participates in the
administration of benevolent institutions for workmen. It has a right to propose to the
employer improvements in the administration of the concern, in working methods, in the
protection of the workers and so on. The Works Council has its representative in the
administrative committee of the business, the employer is bound to ask the opinion of the
Works Council on the points above-mentioned, and also to present every six months a
report on the business. This supervision of the administration of business is stricter in
the enterprises employing more than 300 workers. The guarantee, however, in the
application of this lies in the workers being organised, as we shall show in the case of Bata.
At the beginning of national independence there was a difficulty regarding offices
for Government purposes. These having all been in Vienna previously, found them
without a single building. There was neither time nor means to erect what was wanted.
It was therefore decided to take possession of the big houses and mansions of the aristo-
cracy. A careful inventory was taken of the contents of the building required and these
were preserved for the owners, but the mansions were taken and are still being used as
Government Offices by the State. This action was described as bolshevism in kid gloves.
They also took possession of the land and let it out at moderate prices to those who
cultivate it. They destroyed all the privileges enjoyed by the aristocracy as such, including
those appertaining to the franchise, and established adult suffrage, all men and women
being equal in this respect.

The Shoe and Leather Workers' Union, like the Constitution, is only seven years old,
though it has members of long standing as trade unionists, it being an offshoot from the
pre-war Austrian Union, and it is fighting manfully and well on behalf of its members.
and many agreements with different employers have been made, and we saw evidence of
It adopts a policy similar to our own, negotiation and conciliation whenever possible,
the respect in which it is held by the firms. They do not, however, surink from strikes
when all else has failed, and the success that has followed their efforts shows conclusively
that the Union was right and their policy sound, as they invariably win something for
their members when they take action.
The Union has no easy task, as the movement unfortunately is divided into many
sections. There are six Central Trade Union Organisations in the leather trades. They
have no common policy, rather are they conflicting elements to the advantage of the
employer. The trade unions follow or associate with political parties, and there is also
the question of nationality which is a basis of organisation, and therefore the differences
which separate them are not so easy of adjustment. There are signs, however, of better


---
understanding, many of the Communists are returning to the old Union. There is also
hope in the fact that the employers are combining regardless of nationality or politics,
and the workmen are beginning to see they must do the same. May they soon see the
light and consolidate themselves into one body. The officials we met would, we are
certain, welcome it and do all possible to make it a success.
A word may be inserted here of the general activity of the Social Democratic Unions
which is shown in a very fine building they have built in Prague for the offices of The Trade
Union Federation, and a number of the Unions. A picture of the front of it appeared
in the Daily Herald of 31st July. It is well equipped for its purpose, containing five floors
with commodious rooms for the different Unions. It also possesses a very nice hall for
conference purposes or meetings, and a restaurant of an up-to-date character. Not the
least interesting feature of it is that it was built with Government help in the shape of a
substantial money grant.

The co-operative movement is also active and successful, the Social Democrats
having officially decided in 1901 that it was their duty to support it. We visited several
shops and were impressed by their apparent efficiency, those in charge readily showing
us over the different departments. There is one shop that sells the various costumes
and dresses issued by the sports organisation; this is for the whole of Czecho-Slovakia
and ensures uniformity and low selling prices. We also, on the Saturday morning, visited
a co-operative bakery. Established in 1907, it then employed seven people; its staff
to-day is 329 and they produce 150,000 loaves of bread a week, besides fancy roll and
pastries. It is a fine building, not so good and well equipped perhaps as some in this country,
but a splendid manifestation of working-class effort.

There are many other matters of interest that we were informed of and witnessed
during our stay, but we have confined ourselves to explaining in brief form those that
are associated mainly with working-class effort, or that are related to working-class con-
ditions; the general public endeavour, however, is of a high order as reflected in their
parks, public halls and art galleries, showing an evident determination to put civic adminis-
tration on as high a level as possible. We may perhaps add that we visited on the Sunday
a co-operative farm. This was originally the property of a nobleman, but was taken
over with the land in the early days of the revolution. The old steward is still retained
as manager, and the farm is well equipped with machinery and stock. Our visit was
too short to enable us to obtain as much information as we would wish, but we saw sufficient
to convince us of the practical way in which they have dealt with their land problem
since the war.

On the Monday we commenced our visits to the boot factories, the first being Messrs.
T. L. Popper, of Chrudim. We reached this place at midday, and had a meal at a Labour
Temple or Workers' Home. This is a fine building which contained a good restaurant,
a large meeting hall, a small hall, a room used as a library, and a children's theatre. It
was built by the shoemakers of the town at a cost of 2,000,000k., or £12,500; evidently
the shoemakers in Czecho-Slovakia are in the forefront of progressive forces. We were
received at the factory by the manager, Mr. Zaba, who could speak English, having some
years ago lived in England and worked at T. Brown's, Leicester. The principals, Mr.
Popper and his son, also spoke English, but were engaged with customers; we saw them,
however, before we left and their greeting to us was very cordial. The factory is new,
having been built last year. It is perhaps one of the best we have seen, the different
floors (it was a five-storey building) were well lighted and equipped, the operatives having
ample space in which to work. On every floor a woman was continually engaged in
sweeping up; not a particle of dust or anything was left about; she had a small iron trolley
on wheels, and with dustpan and brush she moved round gathering up anything that lay
about; you cannot imagine a cleaner factory.

The relationship with the Union was very good, an agreement having been made
under which not only are wages fixed, but the firm pay 30 per cent. of wages during sickness
on top of the 60 per cent. paid by the State. The State compels a week's holiday with
pay after one year's service; the firm gives this if the operative has been there only one
week. Excellent provisions are made for the operatives in the erection of seventeen
shower-baths, well arranged, while round the very ample room that is used for hanging
their clothes, wash-basins are also provided. We were informed here that if a firm wants
clean work they must provide the means for clean operatives. Workmen are not dis-
charged when old, but small pensions are granted. The firm evidently believe that good
shoes can only be produced from good material, as they purchase in the best markets and
obtain their supplies from Germany, Austria and England-we saw some from Leicester-
also using home productions. The firm was very short of work, a reduced number of
operatives working 36 hours a week. The capacity of the factory would easily be 12,000
a week. We saw little juvenile labour, and evidently the women continue on in the factory
longer than they do in most places at home. The class of goods manufactured range from
small children's to men's, with all varieties in between, including children's 7 to 1 welted
boots. All the goods were of the best material and workmanship, their production being
of a high order. The machines used and methods adopted being similar to our own.

The firm claims to be good employers of labour, pointing to many features of the business
as evidence in that direction. Bata evidently believes in prohibition, as all over the

believes in the value of advertisement, as the name of Bata appears everywhere
have shops in many countries, and from what Mr. Bata told us, he is still looking for fresh
fields to conquer in the Far East, India's teeming millions being much in his mind. We
were informed by a lady over from Chicago that the firm opened a shop there, but had to
close it, the grade of goods not being equal to American requirements.
Whilst in Prague we passed a shoe repairing shop Novak suggested we should go in.
The old shoemaker, who was repairing on the knee, was very indignant at having to repair
Bata's work, describing them as rubbish. He showed a pair he had repaired where the
good half sole had pulled the upper to pieces. Perhaps Bata has heard of this kind of thing
as he cut short soles at his factory, and his repair shops scattered about the country
repair the foreparts at one shilling a pair.
The firm employ in all 7,000 people, about 6,000 in the making of boots and shoes.
Zlin being little more than a village, the question of accommodation is an important one.
Bata is meeting this by a building programme, erecting 200 blocks with four tenements
in each, thus providing for 800 families. We were informed that these cost 1375 a block
to build he makes his own bricks. We did not go inside them so cannot express any
opinion on the actual accommodation provided, but they appeared from an outside view
to be fairly good, though somewhat limited in space. The rent charged, we were told,
is 2s. a week, which is very low. This, if correct, must represent a loss to the firm as they
pay 10 per cent. on money invested with them, and the bank rate is 12 per cent. The rent
of 25. would only give a return of a little over 5 per cent. without any allowance for repairs,
upkeep, insurance, &c., and as the firm claim they never do anything out of charity, but
always with a view to commercial results, this wants a little explanation, or it may be we
have not got the figures correctly. There is also a large hostel to accommodate 800 to
1,000 single men, who lodge there at a low rate, about 1s. 6d. a week, buying their own
meals, which are also provided by the firm. The firm serve a midday meal to 3,000 people
in 25 minutes every day of the week, and charge 3d. for it. The break is two hours at
midday. We had one of these meals ourselves, and were informed that Bata himself
and the staff also partake of it. The superintendent and others did so on the day we were
there. The meal consisted of soup, a kind of beef stew and cherry tart. We were informed
there are about 100 boys who, as they start with the firm, are housed and fed on the place,
and who have to attend evening classes where their education is improved, languages are
taught, English being a compulsory subject.
A free news sheet is issued every week and is printed at the works. This department
employs 40 people; they also print their own posters and a paper for the customers,
which are distributed in his 300 retail shops. He also publishes a comic paper for workers,
in which he describes his opponents in ways most suitable to his own taste. His operatives
in many cases are fetched and taken home by motors and lorries, and he seeks to show the
workers, who are mostly drawn from the peasant class, that he is a one and only benefactor.
The method of working is by piecework with a bonus, but how prices are fixed it is
difficult to say, as no Trade Union is permitted a voice in dealing with same. Presumably
they are fixed by Bata, and it is impossible therefore to speak as to their fairness or other-
wise, but there is a great deal of suspicion in the minds of the Trade Union Officials on the
matter. At the entrance to the factory there is a large-scale diagram illustrating the
variation in prices and wages. The average price of shoes has fallen from 229k. in 1922
to 69k. in 1926, but it should be mentioned that the krone or crown has changed in
currency value during that time; it now stands at 164 to the f. The firm are not content
with giving the average price for completed years, but it will be noted include 1926. They
also have a forecast for 1927, which is 53k., as compared with 69k. for 1926. While
prices have fallen as shown above, wages are stated to have risen, the figures given in the
diagram for the average of men's wages being :--
Year 1922 1923 1924 1925 1926 1927
Wages 146k. 180k. 205k. 230k. 240k. 350k.
Bonus 50k. 60k. 80k. 100k.
It will be seen again that a return is given for 1926 and a forecast is made for 1927, and that
on a basis of substantial increase in both wage and bonus. This may be a kind of bait
or it may be realised by a special selection of operative. There was one thing that struck
us in going round the factory, the absence of operatives that were even approaching
moderate old age. The wages are paid weekly, but half the bonus has to remain in the
business, 10 per cent. interest being paid upon it. This, we were informed, can be drawn
out at any time, but certainly when the worker leaves the firm. The amount of bonus
is decided each week and is related to profit, while in every room is shown weekly the
amount of wage and bonus taken by each operative.

We have already mentioned that the eight-hour day is established by law, but Bata
longer, and has been prosecuted and fined on several occasions. We were informed that
evidently thinks he is above the law because he has continually worked his operatives
notwithstanding
evidence of Bata's intention to do as he chooses with his workpeople, a most dangerous
attitude. Evidently the firm has no difficulty in obtaining labour, as when we arrived
at the factory at 8.45 a.m., there were about 100 men round the office seeking work; when
we left at 3.30 in the afternoon there were still as many waiting; the depressed state of
trade in other places may account for this, as would the fact that the volume of trade in
the country has decreased since the war, while the restriction placed by America upon
immigrants also has a bearing upon it.
There are many stories told of Bata, one which we were assured to be true being that
every employee as a condition of starting with the firm has to invest so much money in
the business, this applying from the boys upward. Some time ago it was noticed that the
operatives who came from a distance looked fagged out when they reached the factory;
Bata at once had cycles built on the premises and supplied same; he also had the roads
improved so that they might start work as fresh as possible. On another occasion a
foreman noticed that what appeared to be a very smart operative was not giving satis-
factory quantities. He watched him to ascertain the reason. He noticed he had long
hair which he continually brushed back with his hand; the man was told he must either
have his hair cut or leave. He indignantly refused to part with his locks and was dis-
charged. Rumour has it that after being out of employment for some time he returned
and agreed to be shorn of his hair.
The town of Zlin some while ago required the laying of a new sewage scheme, the

Paragraph 2. Submitted and approved.
The top part of Page 11. Paragraph 3, Page 11.
THE GENERAL PRESIDENT: Under the heading of Paragraph 3. Matters
Arising from the Conference Agreement. I want to draw the attention of Conference
to the third portion: The most important of these, in our opinion, is the absence of the
aggressive principle of Trade Unionism in our movement. Much of this is due to two
causes for which our past policy has been responsible. Firstly, the burden which Branch
Officers have to bear, of taking from the shoulders of members every shred of negotiating
responsibility. It is on that particular part of this paragraph that I want to call the
attention of Conference to, and I hope at least that we will be able to visualise the difficulty,
not only the Executive Council but of the Branch Officers up and down the country.
As I see it, there is a lack of interest on the part of the members of our organisation in
showing some spirit of Trade Unionism such as is necessary to keep our Union alive in the
full sense of its responsibility. Some of it may be due to this fact, that during the past
ten years we have had a new generation of shoe makers coming into the industry, who
see in the National Agreement something expressed for them that calls for no consideration
on their part, that calls for no looking at the ideals and the principles of Trade Unionism.
In consequence there has been a kind of severance between the branches and the member-
ship, more especially with the younger members, and it has also had the effect that in some
districts the younger people have not felt a sense of responsibility to make application
for the wages which the Conference Agreement calls for. That has been proved in some
districts, where an examination of the wages has shown that it is not just a few isolated
cases, but a number have not been getting those wages which the graduated scales in the
National Agreement provide for. We feel that it shows a need for the linking up of
members with the activities of the Union, and not only with the activities of the Union,
but also in the activities of the greater Trade Union movement of this country. I believe
consideration and deliberation, and if we are going to get the best out of the difficulties
in the next few years we may face difficulties that may call for careful judgment, careful
aims of our organisation and to the spirit of Trade Unionism and the understanding which
attended in sufficient numbers for our members to keep in touch with the movement and
we expect from our members. One deplores the fact that our monthly meetings are not
its activities. One does deplore the lack of interest which members show, and I believe
in the future it may be necessary for all branch officers to examine this problem and see
contact with a wider group of members than in the past. It is necessary that we should
how far it is possible to extend the activities of Trade-Union propaganda and bring closer
get that. It is necessary that we should maintain a strong membership.
There are
instances where there is room for improvement in the numerical strength of particular
branches and in the activities of local officers, in spite of the difficulties which I under-
stand and appreciate and which this particular paragraph emphasises. The work of the
administrative side, which our local officers are undertaking in ever-increasing variety and
scope, has made it difficult for the local officers to pay that attention to the wider work
of the Trade Union in the sense that we desire to express it. We hope that with the

THE KING'S SPEECH.
The King's Speech read in Parliament yesterday covered a wide range of subjects-
Plea for Peace in Industry. Increasing Need for Economy.
Electricity, the Land, Housing, Rating problems, Control of Road Vehicles, and London
Iraq, Disarmament, the Italian Debt, Hours of Labour, Economy, the Industrial Position.
Poor Law Finance.
The full text of the Speech is as follows:-
Vy Lords and Members of the House of Commons,
Mr relations with foreign Powers continue to be friendly.
Since Parliament rose my Ambassador at Constantinople has proceeded to Angora
with a view to arrive at a definite settlement of questions in connection with the Turco-
ment for the promotion of the friendliest relations between Turkey and Great Britain.
Iraq frontier. My Government cordially reciprocate the desire of the Turkish Govern
A Treaty between myself and his Majesty the King of Iraq, carrying out the stipulation
laid down in the decision of the Council of the League of Nations, has been signed by our

Hours of Labour.
Invitations are being issued to the Governments of Belgium, France, Germany, and
Italy to attend a Conference in London to consider the possibility of securing an effective
international agreement for regulating hours of labour.
Members of the House of Commons,
The Estimates for the Public Services will be laid before you in due course. My
Ministers have given earnest consideration to the increasing need for national economy.
Proposals for effecting reductions of public expenditure are now being formulated
and you will be asked to pass measures required to give effect to them without delay.
Proposals will be laid before you for authorising My Government to guarantee loans
for the development of the British dependencies in East Africa and of mandated terri-
tories.
My Lords and Members of the House of Commons,
The improvement in trade and industry at the end of 1924, which it was then thought
would result in an appreciable decrease in the volume of unemployment was unfortunately
checked early last year by the widespread depression which occurred in coal mining.
Since the autumn of last year signs of a revival of industry have again begun
to appear, but the growth of confidence on which revival depends is being arrested
by the fear of industrial strife.
Coal Position.
is now
The result of the inquiry into the economic condition of the coal industry, which
being conducted by my Commission, will shortly be laid before you.
I am well aware of the difficulties that are inherent in the whole situation.
But the interests of the nation are paramount, and I appeal to all parties to face
the future in a spirit of conciliation and fellowship and to avoid action which would
again postpone the return of good trade and prosperity for which we have so long
hoped.
With the object of securing greater economy and efficiency in the generation and
transmission of electrical energy in the future, my Government have devised a scheme
of reorganisation. A Bill to give effect to these proposals has been prepared and will
shortly be introduced.

Health and Food Services. - The General Council recommend that there should be
in their power to organise the distribution of milk and food to the whole of the population.
no interference in regard to these, and that the Trade Unions concerned should do everything
With regard to the hospitals, clinics, convalescent homes, sanatoria, infant welfare
centres, maternity homes, nursing homes, schools, the General Council direct that affiliated
unions take every opportunity to ensure that food, milk, medical and surgical supplies shall
be efficiently provided.
2. TRADE UNION DISCIPLINE.
(a) The General Council direct that, in the event of Trade Unionists being called
upon to cease work, the Trade Unions concerned shall take steps to keep a daily register
to account for every one of their members. It should be made known that any workers called
upon to cease work should not leave their own district, and by following another occupation,
or the same occupation in another district, blackleg their fellow workers.
(b) The General Council recommend that the actual calling out of the workers should
be left to the unions, and instructions should only be issued by the accredited representatives
of the unions participating in the dispute.
3. TRADES COUNCILS.
The work of the Trades Councils, in conjunction with the local officers of the Trade
Unions actually participating in the dispute, shall be to assist in carrying out the foregoing
provisions, and they shall be charged with the responsibility of organising the Trade Unionists
in dispute in the most effective manner for the preservation of peace and order.
4. INCITEMENT TO DISORDER AND SPIES.
A strong warning must be issued to all localities that any person found inciting the
workers to attack property, or inciting the workers to riot, must be dealt with immediately.
It should be pointed out that the opponents will in all probability employ persons to act as
spies and others to use violent language in order to incite the workers to disorder.
5. TRADE UNION AGREEMENTS.
The General Council further direct that the Executives of the Unions concerned shall
definitely declare that in the event of any action being taken and Trade Union agreements
being placed in jeopardy, it be definitely agreed that there will be no general resumption of
work until those agreements are fully recognised.
6. PROCEDURE..
(a) These proposals shall be immediately considered by the Executives of the Trade
Unions concerned in the stoppage, who will at once report as to whether they will place their
powers in the hands of the General Council and carry out the instructions which the General
Council may issue from time to time concerning the necessary action and conduct of the
dispute.
(b) And, further, that the Executives of all other affiliated unions are asked to report
at once as to whether they will place their powers in the hands of the General Council and
carry out the instructions of the General Council from time to time, both regarding the
conduct of the dispute and financial assistance.
A. PUGH, Chairman.
WALTER M. CITRINE, Acting Secretary.

THE WORK OF THE I.L.P.
Its Relation to the Labour Party.
By J. Ramsay MacDonald, M.P.
Socialism is not going to come by the legal declaration of a minimum nominal wage and
If there is one thing that I can prophesy with some certainty of being right, it is that
untold industrial difficulties, and is to foredoom our first great Socialist offensive to disas-
consequential nationalisation of bankrupt industries. Such a method is to swamp us in
frous defeat. It will be our Verdun.
Our movement works for a general transformation of economic and industrial organi-
rather than to its dead parts as the places from which the transformation is to come.
sation. It has always taken society as a going concern, and has looked to its living parts
The real distinction between the evolutionist and the revolutionist is that the former
believes that Socialist growth is to come from the vigorous activities of society forcing
new forms of life, whilst the latter uses the unhealthy and dead parts like sweating-
for his purpose.

One of the dangers we are now running is that, having adopted a form for stating

ins that the increasing sensitiveness to human distress, also insensibly, is pushing der

their own merits. They are not Socialism. High wages wrung from a Capitalist are not
Socialism. Socialism and its movement must never be diverted from its essential purpose
of putting an end to an "acquisitive society" and establishing in its place one of co-opera-

Everywhere I hear complaints that Socialist speeches are too old. They show little
signs of advance in experience. The audience has been thinking, the speakers too often
have not. On the other hand, good I.L.Peers come and tell me they are getting "fed up"
with some recent developments and want to know if it is worth while going on with the
I.L.P. I have not changed my mind as yet. There is abundant work for the I.L.P.,
and the work is essential. It is to keep Socialism alive as an invigorating and guiding
idea. That requires constant hard intellectual work of a concentrated kind.-Foraari,

COST OF LIVING.
At 1st April the average level of retail prices of all the commodities taken into account
in the statistics compiled by the Ministry of Labour (including food, rent, clothing, fuel,
light, and miscellaneous items) was approximately 68 per cent. above that of July, 1914.
as compared with 72 per cent. a month ago and 75 per cent. a year ago. The corresponding
figures for food alone were 59, 65 and 70 respectively. The decline in the figures since
Ist March was mainly due to seasonal reductions in the prices of eggs and milk, but there
were also slight reductions in the prices of various other articles of food.
These statistics are designed to indicate the average increase in the cost of maintaining
unchanged the pre-war standard of living of working-class families. Accordingly, in
making the calculations, the changes in the prices of the various items included are com-
bined in proportions corresponding with the relative importance of those items in pre-war
working-class family expenditure. - Ministry of Labour Gazette, April, 1926.

SCHEME FOR MINES SETTLEMENT.
Letter from Sir Herbert Samuel to the General Council of the Trades
Union Congress. 12th May, 1926.
DEAR MR. PUGH,
As the outcome of the conversations which I have had with your Committee, I attach
a memorandum embodying the conclusions that have been reached.
I have made it clear to your Committee from the outset that I have been acting entirely
on my own initiative, have received no authority from the Government and can give no
assurances on their behalf.
I am of opinion that the proposals embodied in the Memorandum are suitable for
adoption and are likely to promote a settlement of the differences in the Coal Industry.
I shall strongly recommend their acceptance by the Government when the negotiations
are renewed.
Yours sincerely,
(Signed) HERBERT SAMUEL.
A. PUGH, Esq.,
President, General Council,
Trades Union Congress.
SIR HERBERT SAMUEL, 12th May, 1926.

Returns from firms employing over 46,000 operatives in the week ended 19th Decem-
ber, 1925, showed that nearly 34 per cent. of these operatives worked short time in that
week to the extent of 9¾ hours each, on an average.

In London employment was fairly good for the time of year. In Leicester there was
a further improvement, and employment was fairly good, and better than in December,
1924; the greatest activity was at factories producing Russian boots, and some were
reported to be working overtime. At Northampton employment showed a further
improvement but still remained quiet, with much short time. At Hinckley employment
remained fair, with most of the firms working full hours. In the Higham and Rushden
area there was a slight decline, except for some urgent holiday orders immediately before
Christmas; employment on the whole was poor. At Wellingborough, where employment
was reported as fair, there was a slight upward movement, but 50 per cent. of the firms
were working short time. At Kettering there was again a large amount of unemployment,
but the bigger factories were working fairly full time, and there was a reduction in the
amount of short time worked by the smaller factories.

At Leeds some firms closed for a week or 10 days at Christmas; before the holiday
employment continued moderate, with much short time, except with firms making Russian
boots, who were busy. At Stafford there was a marked improvement, and very little
short time was worked. At Norwich employment was only moderate on the whole;
the turn-shoe section was still very slack, with many operatives totally unemployed,
but employment in other sections was fairly good, and showed an improvement. In the
Bristol and Kingswood district employment was, on the whole, poor, worse than in Novem-
ber and worse than in December, 1924, especially in heavy boot factories. At Street
there was a slight improvement, but employment was only moderate and there was a good
deal of short time. Employment remained good in the slipper trade at Bury, but short
time was general at Bacup and Preston.

There was an improvement during the month at Glasgow, and employment was fairly
good on the whole. It remained fairly good at Kilmarnock and Maybole, but at Edinburgh
it declined and was very quiet, with nearly all the operatives on short time.

INTERNATIONAL INFORMATION.
RUSSIAN LABOUR LAW REVISION.

Difficulties of Application.
The Russian Commissariat of Labour is now engaged in a revision of the Labour
Code, states Industrial and Labour Information, the weekly publication of the International
Labour Office of the League of Nations.

It would appear that the Code will be amended in such a way as to contain only the
fundamental labour laws and there will be special Acts to adjust those laws to the various
branches of industry which cannot be ruled by a rigid and uniform legislation.

The existing Labour Code was published in 1922, at a time when the "new economic
policy," which put an end to the regime of Communism pure and simple, had just been
introduced. The Code nevertheless retains a number of clauses which are inspired by the
previous policy, and which the Soviet press has described as "explanatory passages,"
intended to satisfy the aspirations of the working masses, without any regard to reality.

"Our Code," the Commissary of Labour has said, "was drawn up for the use of
heavy industry and is not adapted for home work or for artisans, and still less for temporary
or seasonal workers. This defect in the Code is the result of the fact that the possibility
of its enforcement in practice was never seriously considered. When an attempt was
made to introduce the eight-hour day rigidly on the railways, certain of the railwaymen
were unable to finish their work within the time-limits fixed by the Act, and were con-
tinually obliged to work overtime, while others worked from three to four hours only
per day. Special legislation had to be introduced on the subject of hours of work in
transport undertakings. Similarly, in the State peat industry, it was from the first clear
that an enforcement of the eight-hour day would ruin the industry, and, a fortnight after
the publication of the Labour Code, it became necessary to extend hours of work in the
industry to ten per day. Finally, special Acts had to be passed for all seasonal work in
view of the fact that the eight-hour day was inapplicable in such cases.

Inadequate Factory Inspection.
Further, even in those industries to which the Labour Code is more especially adapted,
enforcement has met with considerable difficulties.

The Commissary has pointed out that, although the factory inspectors carry out their
work better than at first, they are still not equal to their task. "The factory inspector,"
he says, "is insufficiently educated and very often is unable to find his way about the
various labour Acts. Thus he often passes over infringements of labour legislation."
Up to the present, factory inspectors have only devoted their attention to private under-
takings, in dealing with which they have been extremely rigorous; but they have avoided
visiting the State undertakings (the whole of large scale industry and a considerable
proportion of medium scale industry has been nationalised), in order to avoid unpleasant-
ness. It is only recently that they have begun to exercise their control over the national-
ised undertakings, but even so they are not sufficiently severe.

As a result, despite the acute unemployment crisis, the ten-hour day is still wide-
spread, and particularly in the State metal industry. It is true that this is mainly due to
economic causes, e.g., the necessity of increasing production while there are not enough
skilled workers, or when the lack of housing accommodation is a barrier to the engagement
of the necessary workers; but these conditions are mainly attributable to the absence
of any proper control over conditions of labour. Care should therefore be taken that the
new Labour Code is strictly observed, and for this it will be necessary to increase the
efficiency of factory inspection, and it will further be necessary to modify certain pro-
visions of the Code which are no longer enforceable in practice.

Excessive Number of Decrees.
Since the provisions of the Code, as has been indicated above, are often in the nature
of general statements, it has been necessary to issue Decrees to explain and comment on the
various clauses of the Code and to define their application to the various branches of
industry.

The number of these Decrees is excessive. They take up 2,000 pages of print, whereas
the Code contains only 24 pages. These various successive, and often contradictory,
Decrees have created such a state of confusion that even the Commissariat of Labour is
not always able fairly and accurately to define the meaning of a given paragraph of the
Code.

In this connection, a characteristic Decree is that concerning unemployment insurance.
It was followed, three months after its coming into force, by four supplementary Decrees
published in the space of four weeks. The same thing may be observed in many other

10 (a) The day-rate wages of the operatives who, when this Agreement comes into
operation, are employed at or above the minimum wage or graduated scale rates applicable
to them by this Agreement shall not be reduced in consequence of this Agreement, beyond
the amounts of reductions made in the corresponding minimum wage rates provided for
in this Agreement.

(b) Where Piecework or Quantity Statements do not at present exist, Local
Arbitration Boards will forthwith prepare new Piecework or Quantity Statements on a basis
to ensure the average worker earning not less than 25 per cent. over the minimum wage
and where necessary will revise the existing Statements on the same basis.

(c) Local Arbitration Boards are recommended to exercise their power of review-
ing on the request of either side, existing Piecework or Quantity Statements, other than the
Government Green Book Statement Handsewn List, for the purpose of adjusting any
specific anomalous item or items, whether unfavourable to employers or operatives, brought
before the Boards in accordance with the customary procedure; provided always that
any adjustments of existing Statements or any new Piecework Statements shall ensure the
average worker earning not less than 25 per cent. over the minimum wage in operation for
the time being.

11. Local Arbitration Boards operating in outlying district accustomed to manu-
facture goods of lower grades shall, in the compilation of Piecework or Quantity Statements,
have regard to the grade when estimating the productive capacity of the average worker.

12. In the event of differences arising on a Local Arbitration Board as to the pro-
cedure to be adopted in giving effect to Clauses 10 and 11 either side of the Board may
require the Standing Committee of the Conference to advise upon such procedure, provided
always that the Piecework rates to be finally fixed shall be determined in accordance with
the rules of such Board.

13. The employers shall retain freedom of contract with all operatives under 15
years of age.

14. The minimum wage or graduated scale rates shall not apply to clerks, engineers,
mechanics, electricians, stokers, porters, sweepers-up, lift or hoist men, caretakers and
timekeepers, or to labourers and odd job men not engaged in actual manufacturing.

LUMINOUS WATCH DISEASE.
Cases in American Factories.
A disease called "radium necrosis," regarded in some quarters as a new occupational
disease, is held responsible for the death of five persons and for numerous cases of sickness
among the workers employed in a New Jersey factory in the application of luminous
paint to watch and clock dials according to Industrial and Labour Information, the weekly
publication of the International Labour Office of the League of Nations. It is stated
that the disease resulted from the practice of the dial painters of pointing their brushes
in their mouths.
The U.S. Department of Labour, it is reported, has given instructions that observa-
tion should be kept over all establishments in the country which use radium, in order
that data may be collected with regard to any occupational diseases which might be
attributable to the handling of radio-active substances. Should it be found that the
disease in question is occupational in its origin, efforts will be made to obtain its inclusion
in the schedule of the workmen's compensation laws.
The American Association for the reduction of the frequency of this disease. In particular,
the Association is endeavouring to secure the adoption by the New Jersey Legislature
in favour of measures for the reduction of the frequency of this disease. In particular,
a Bill requiring employers to take more effective steps to counteract the risk, and also
providing for a scientific investigation in regard to any toxic or injurious substance pro-
posed to be used in industry.
It is interesting to note that the seventh annual Session of the International Labour
Conference of the League of Nations, held at Geneva in June, adopted a Draft Convention
establishing the principle of compensation for occupation diseases and setting out a short
list of diseases which should be recognised by all nations as fitting for such compensation.
INTERNATIONAL LABOUR ORGANISATION.
The Year's Work.
Steady progress has been made in 1925 by the International Labour Organisation of
the League of Nations in its various fields of activity. The following brief summary
surveys the more important events connected with its work during the year.
The Annual Conference.
Forty-six States, represented by 144 delegates, were present at the seventh Annual
Session of the International Labour Conference, which opened at Geneva on 19th May.
These included the important industrial countries of the world with the exception of the
United States and Russia. Among the distant countries were Japan, China, Australia,
India, South Africa, Canada and the South American States. Complete delegations
consisting of two representatives of the Government and one each of the employers and
workers were sent by thirty-two States, the other fourteen being mainly of lesser industrial
importance. Dr. Benes, the Czecho-Slovakian statesman, was unanimously elected
President of the Conference.
Four Draft Conventions and four Recommendations were adopted by the Conference.
The Draft Conventions dealt with the prohibition of night-work in bakeries, equality
of treatment of national and foreign workers as regards accident compensation, workers'
compensation for accidents and workers' compensation for occupational diseases. The
Recommendations dealt with the minimum scale of workers' compensation, jurisdiction
in disputes on workers' compensation, workers' compensation, workers' compensation as regards accident compensation.
A Draft Convention to establish a weekly suspension of work in the glass-making industry
was rejected by the Conference.
The Conference also held a preliminary discussion of the general problems arising out
of workers' insurance. A resolution was adopted requesting the Governing Body of the
International Labour Office to place the questions of general sickness insurance and of
invalidity, old age, and widows' and orphans' insurance on the agenda of future sessions,
and also calling upon the Office to prepare information on these questions along certain
stated lines.

*Disputes in which no final settlement has yet been reported (June, 1926).

In 1925, as in most years, the disputes resulting in compromises or partial successes outnumbered either the complete successes or the complete failures. 154 settled in favour of the workpeople and 183 in favour of the employers (15 disputes were still not finally settled at the time of going to press). So far as numbers involved are concerned, compromises usually outweigh all other results; the only exceptions occurring when some dispute of outstanding importance results in a definite success for either party.  In the dispute of outstanding magnitude in 1925 (that in the wool textile industry, the workpeople were successful in their opposition to a reduction in wages; hence the preponderance of settlements in favour of the workpeople in that year, so far as judged by the numbers involved, both in the textile group and in the total for all industries. In the mining and quarrying group of industries the high proportion of workpeople involved in disputes ending in favour of the employers is largely accounted for by the result of the dispute in the Anthracite District of South Wales referred to above. Of the other principal disputes in 1925 in which a final settlement has been effected, the majority terminated in compromises.


In the case of eight disputes, directly involving 15,100 workpeople, work had been resumed pending further negotiation and a final settlement had not yet been reported, and in the case of seven disputes, directly involving 12,300 workpeople, work had not been resumed at the time of going to press.

MONTHLY REPORT.
23RD AUGUST, 1926.

FELLOW MEMBERS,

TRADE.
Trade is in a very unsatisfactory state largely due to the situation obtaining in the Mining Industry. We have paid out during the past month from our own Out-of-Work Fund the sum of £9,292 17s. od., and from the State side the sum of £13,675 18s. 7d.

The Ministry of Labour figures are as follows :-

BOOT AND SHOE INDUSTRY.
Employment in this industry continued to be affected by the shortage of fuel resulting from the coal stoppage, and was poor, and slightly worse than in June; a great deal of short time was worked. As has been the case for many months, there was less slackness in factories producing light footwear than in those making artisans' boots.
The percentage of workpeople unemployed, as indicated by the unemployment books lodged at Employment Exchanges, was 14.3 on 26th July, as compared with 13.6 on 21st June, and 11.8 on 27th July, 1925.
Returns from firms employing 37,200 workpeople in the week ended 24th July, 1926, showed that about 53 per cent. of these workpeople were on short time in that week, losing on an average 14 hours each.

MONTHLY REPORT.
17TH MAY, 1926.
TRADE.
Owing to the general stoppage in the country reported upon later, a number
of our members all over the country have had to cease work owing to the lack
of transport.
NATIONAL CONFERENCE AGREEMENT.
Now that the cost of living figure is down to 68 points the alterations
shown in Clause 8 of the Agreement comes in operation on the first pay-day in
June. This means that only one minimum will apply to all male operatives.
THE GREAT STOPPAGE.
It is well known to everyone that for several months past a National
Commission has been sitting to enquire into and report upon schemes for
dealing with the coal mining industry. This report was presented to Parliament
in February of this year and although a number of weeks were left before the
subsidy which the Government have been making to the miners was to autimati-
cally cease, the Government were very apathetic and only a real move was
made a few days before the 30th April. Owing to the serious position, the
General Council of the Trades Union Congress, with the approval of the miners,
appointed a Negotiating Committee to carry on negotiations between the
Cabinet and the General Council as representing the whole Trade Union

Industrial Health and Safety.
،،
The Office has issued the first parts of Occupation and Health," an encyclopædia
of industrial hygiene which is intended to bring together all the information available
in the various countries concerning industries and processes which may be considered
unhealthy and is being compiled with the assistance of eminent authorities in all parts
of the world. The Office has also begun the publication of a new two-monthly periodical,
the "Industrial Safety Survey," the aim of which is to serve as a medium of exchange
of ideas and experiences in the field of safety measures both between different countries
and between employers, workers and factory inspectors. Laws and regulations in all
parts of the world are recorded and notes are given of new publications on the subject.
Facts of World Labour.
These publications and others issued during the year are in addition to the regular
publications of the Office, Industrial and Labour Information (weekly) and International
Labour Review (monthly) wherein are brought together the latest facts concerning world
labour movements, special attention being paid to such subjects as cost of living move-
ments, wholesale prices, and emigration and unemployment figures.
Denmark.
APPALLING UNEMPLOYMENT IN DENMARK.
The unemployment figures for the first week of the new year show another tremendous
increase. The number of workers in receipt of benefit from the trade unions has leapt
up from 73,000 to 84,000; that means that one out of every three organised workers is
out of a job. These figures only apply to organised workers; the total number of unem
statistics are not available, but the total number might probably be estimated at something
ployed in the whole country is of course considerably higher than that. The official
like 100,000 or more.
It is just possible that this very serious state of affairs will improve somewhat during
the next few weeks, as a great number of the works extended the Christmas holidays
until the middle of January on account of business being so slack.

TO LABOUR.
Shall you complain who feed the world ?
Who clothe the world ?
Who house the world ?
Shall you complain who are the world,
Of what the world may do?
As from this hour
You use your power,
The world must follow you.
The world's life hangs on your right hand,
Your strong right hand,
Your skilled right hand;
You hold the whole world in your hand-
See to it what you do!
Or dark or light,
Or wrong or right,
The World is made by you!
Then rise as you ne'er rose before,
Nor hoped before,
Nor dared before,
And show as ne'er was shown before
The power that lies in you!
Stand all as one.
Till right is done!
Believe, and dare, and do!-- CHARLOTTE PERKINS GILMAN.

HOURS OF LABOUR.
LORD HENRY CAVENDISH-BENTINCK asked the Minister of Labour if he is now in a
position to state the number of workers in this country who are working 48 hours a week
the industries, apart from the continuous processes, where the normal working week
or less and the numbers working more than 48 hours:
exceeds 48 hours?
; and if he will give the names of
THE PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (Mr. Betterton) :
I am not yet able to give the figures asked for by my Noble Friend, but from a sample
tabulation of returns recently received from employers in most of the important industries
(including agriculture, the retail distributive trades, the railway service and dock labour)
it would appear that about 90 per cent. of the workpeople work a normal week of 48 hours
of workpeople not engaged on continuous processes is returned as working a normal week
or less. In each of the main industrial groups a varying, but usually small, proportion
of over 48 hours.
VISCOUNTESS ASTOR: Does that include the catering trade ?
MR. BETTERTON: I think not. That, I think, is included in the retail distributive
trades.-Extract from Parliamentary Debates, House of Commons, Wednesday, 10th
March, 1926.
[The answer given above as to the large number of workpeople whose working hours
are 48 per week or less, is a great tribute to trade union activity and its effectiveness
during the past twenty years, which activity is very often overlooked because of the
smoothness with which these advantages are secured. There is, however, another step
which should be taken to make these hours secure; i.e., the Ratification of the Washington
Convention (Hours of Labour) so as to place it beyond the power of any employer, or
federation of employers to force a strike or lockout upon the question of the working
week, which has been done in some cases; thus showing the need for constant vigilance
in this respect.-E.L.P., Gen. Sec.].
CONTRIBUTORY PENSIONS ACT.
MR. TAYLOR asked the Minister of Health whether a man or woman of 61 years of
age or over who has been insured under the National Health Insurance Acts for a period
of not less than 10 years, but who has left an insurable occupation, is accepted as a voluntary
contributor for an old age pension at 65 years of age after the 2nd January, 1928, or on the
fifth anniversary of his re-entry into insurance ?
MR. N. CHAMBERLAIN: The second alternative is the correct one. No person can
acquire a title to an old age pension before the expiration of five years from the date of
his last entry into insurance.
MR. TAYLOR asked the Minister of Health whether a person re-entering insurance as
a voluntary contributor in order to qualify for an old age pension at 65 is, notwithstanding
the provisions of Section 13 (5), also required by his Department to fulfil the statutory
conditions in Section 8 (a) of the Widows', Orphans' and Old Age Contributory Pensions
Act, 1925?
MR. CHAMBERLAIN: The answer is in the affirmative. - Extract from Parliamentary
Debates, House of Commons, 25th February, 1926.
